_childDocuments_.review: (Note: I played this with the Committee of Zero community overhaul patch and I recommend others do as well. The original translations seem to be very poorly done and there is a surprising amount of censored content in the game. Both of these problems are fixed with the patch. It also comes with other bug fixes, translated CGs, and generally just makes the experience better.)This game is a very strange beast. It very much puts you into the mindset of the main character, that being the mindset of a schizo who is constantly doubting the world around him and is extremely paranoid of the smallest things. For the majority of the game, I had a hard time understanding where the game was gonna go. I say this as a compliment mind you. Now having fully completed the game, I can say that it was quite the emotional experience and I enjoyed it greatly. One thing I can say for sure is that the characters in this game are very well-developed. This isn't always obvious at first and for some characters it takes a while, but by the time the game wants you to care about the characters, you do. Truthfully this game is very difficult to describe, and whilst I'd love to describe it in greater detail, it's sort of something that you have to see for yourself to understand.One of the main criticisms I have with this game is that if you want to get an actual proper ending, you need to go through all of the different character endings. This itself is not a problem and in fact I think it just gives you a better appreciation for the characters and their storylines, however it is slightly tedious to have to start at the beginning, make whatever choices are needed to be made, and then skip through over half of the game just to reach the route. The skip function is really fast so this is more of a minor nuisance than anything but it can still be a little annoying. Additionally the game has a tendency to over-do it's descriptions of violent events, not in a way that is too gorey but more just being overly-verbose.Overall, a very weird but good visual novel that takes you on quite the wild emotional ride, 9/10.Whose eyes are those eyes?

_childDocuments_.review: I could write a whole essay titled , but I'll try to keep this brief. That said, I think the impact C;HN's story had would not be the same if the protagonist wasn't as pathetic as Taku is. The plot is engaging on its own, of course, but beyond the fantastic science fiction mystery, this is a character driven narrative about debilitating social anxiety, its effects on the psyche, and how we can come to accept ourselves and embrace a world we perceive to be hostile toward us.  I really love Takumi so much. I would go as far as saying he is probably my favorite protagonist in a VN ever. He's not the most moral person, and he's certainly not noble, but that's what makes him so very human. He rejects the world because in his mind, he's a disgusting otaku who would never be accepted by it. I could empathize with his spiteful thoughts towards others around him and their juxtaposition to his timid demeanor. It's hard to love a world that you feel you have no place in. Anyway, if you like character driven stories, appreciate a well-written antihero, and are ready for a psychological horror that truly emphasizes the psychological aspect, I'm sure you'll find C;HN worth your time. Bishi!

_childDocuments_.review: "A person's mind can only take so much before they reach their limit and can take no more. And when they do, a single act of cruelty or compassion can mean the difference between tears of joy or utter despair."CHAOS;HEAD Noah is the remastered (remade?) version of the visual novel originally released all the way back in 2010, with lots of changes and additions that weren't present in the first edition. Prior knowledge of it is not required, although it helps following the storyline. A storyline which is -as you might have guessed- full of depressing, painful to watch or just downright horrifying scenes that are guaranteed to make you feel awful unless you're someone who's already dead inside. And you have to see it all, because the true ending won't unlock until every route's been explored, the persona and motivations of each character and how their lives are intertwined through the joys and tragedies they experience.As far as graphics is concerned, it's gotten a great upgrade over the original's 800*600 resolution with a quality bump all over, although capping it at 1080p is a bit of a pity for everyone playing at 2K or above given that the difference can sometimes be fairly noticable either with the background or character sprites. That said, it doesn't happen very often, so it shouldn't bother people as much as one might expect at first.Music is still the same OST we have grown to love, with one notable difference - while the OG featured Itou Kanako's Find the Blue song at the intro, it was replaced with a different one this time which doesn't carry the same impact sadly. On the other hand, it still returns for the final confrontations and there weren't other changes, so thankfully nothing's stopping us from enjoying the OST fully. Well, except for not being able to buy the OST as a DLC maybe. That would have been nice.So what do we get in this novel in the end? Existential crisis, personal tragedies and incredible character development forming a rollercoaster of emotions the likes of which very few visual novels can pull off in a way that nails you to your chair. And Nitroplus did it. Seriously, if you like any one of these themes, you *have* to see this game. Just prepare enough tissues. You'll need them.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating first so you can stop reading here if you want - 8/10. If you like VNs with good stories, especially those in the Science Adventure series (Steins;Gate and co), then it's definitely worth a play.~~~~~First off, the content of the game - for anyone that's into visual novels with good stories, the SciAdv series in particular, I don't think anyone would be complaining about the content. Most negative reviews would be about the sloppy translation.I'm one of those people that was dying for the western release of CHN, and couldn't wait the extra time for the unofficial patch to come out. I'm reviewing from that perspective.Ultimately, the translation is fine. There are a few select points where it can be a bit rough - I remember one point where a line seems incorrectly repeated, and there's another point where some characters don't get given proper capitalisation or grammar (this is because of the kinds of characters they are, but even so, as a reader it looked awful and I think it hindered more than it helped). But, if you're really keen to play it and can't wait for the unofficial patch, you'll be fine with the official translation.Storywise, it's all around pretty solid. You can tell this is the first game in the series and that they really hit their stride with Steins;Gate, but for a first entry (well, second version of the first entry) it's quite good. The main drawback from the story is that Takumi (the main character) is intensely unlikable. Fortunately, in some of the endings his actions redeem bits of his character, and the fact that he's flawed works when you consider the other characters in the story, but my goodness you wish you could just punch him sometimes.Finally, the biggest drawback to how enjoyable this game was is that Chaos;Head Love Chu Chu - the *canon* sequel - hasn't had an English release or fan translation, and as far as I can see there's no talk of any in the works. I myself had to read a synopsis of it just so I'd know of the canon story beats if they came up down the track.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head Noah is one of those once in a lifetime experiences that only come by every once in a blue moon. As someone who's played a lot of story games throughout my years, it's rare that one truly sticks out to me as something special. There aren't many I can think of off the top of my head - Red Dead Redemption 2 stands above all else as what I believe to be the best written game of all time as well as the most technically impressive, Death Stranding is a game that I hold high as a very misunderstood experience that truly separated itself from all others that came before, and Chaos;Head Noah captivated me instantly with its ethereal atmosphere and mystery that kept just enough details from me to keep me hungering for more.I went into this game a fan of Steins;Gate, not the visual novel, but the anime. I assume like many other SciADV fans, our interest in the series began there. Steins;Gate is an anime that I hold very near and dear to my heart as one of the most tightly written stories out there. I loved the main cast, I loved the story, and there are just so many moving parts that it would take me hours to truly sort out all of the thoughts I have surrounding it. I firmly hold the belief that there is truly nothing else out there like it. I knew that it came from a larger series of visual novels, but I never had much interest in them. Fast forward about a year later and I finally decided to give the larger Science Adventure series a try, starting with where it all began, Chaos;Head Noah.With it being a visual novel and all, I wasn't sure what to expect out of this game. The only other VN that I'd played was Doki Doki Literature Club in 2018 because it was popular at the time. Looking back, I don't even remember if I ever beat it. I think I did, but I truly just don't remember. Regardless, DDLC was a short game, and Chaos;Head is a visual novel you can expect to read for a good 50 hours if you're going for the true ending. With some reluctance, I pressed the play button, truly wondering to myself if it could ever hold a candle to it's sequel anime that I hold in such high regard.The prologue immediately caught my attention. The scene was quiet, except for the words of the protagonist and the quiet piano playing in the background. Depicted was the ruins of a city. Not a soul was there. Not a soul was moving. Not a soul was left alive. Not a soul other than the protagonist and a mysterious pink haired girl. The words of the protagonist captivated me, in a speech that I frequently look back to just because I find it so interesting."If she and I were the only ones left in the world...If we stared into each other's eyes like this for all eternity...Would my world be reduced to the reflection in her eyes?Would her world be reduced to the reflection in my eyes?The only thing reflected in her eyes... is me.The only thing reflected in my eyes... is her.When I think of it that way, the world immediately seems so much smaller."The prologue continued, and eventually came to a close. Next thing I was introduced to the protagonist, Nishijou Takumi, a high school student living inside a storage container atop a building. He was a glorified shut-in, only attending school according to a minimum attendance chart telling him what specific days he needed to attend in order to just barely meet graduation requirements. I was introduced to him, as well as the hum of his computer, located opposite of the door to his dimly-lit one room apartment. Ever since he was young, Takumi had experienced a strange feeling. The feeling of being watched. Every so often, he feels a sharp gaze piercing the nape of his neck. "Whose eyes are those eyes?" he would ask. He wrote a poem about the feeling in the fourth grade. Alone in his storage container, he gets that feeling quite often. He tries not to look back, but he always gives in eventually. Behind him lies the entrance to his one room. If someone, or something came inside, he would have nowhere to run. Throughout the game, you'll be in Takumi's room when he feels the gaze, and his paranoia will rub off on you, as you wonder to yourself, when he turns around this time, will something be there?That feeling of paranoia and dread is what I would consider the staple of Chaos;Head. The game builds the perfect atmosphere for making you question Takumi and the world around him. Your only insight into this world is through the eyes of a delusional young man who isn't even sure what's going on himself. The soundtrack is simple, so is the artwork and backgrounds, successfully building an atmosphere unlike any other I've ever seen throughout any video game, movie, television show, etc. The whole game is permeated with an ethereal feeling of uncertainty and dread, and it had me captured from beginning to end.Combine the creepy atmosphere with the story, which lands Takumi directly in the middle of a strange series of incidents called the "New Generation Madness" by the general public, and you have the recipe for a perfect psychological horror experience. You'll find yourself wanting to know more about New Gen, or who Shogun, the mysterious boy in a wheelchair is that's haunting Takumi. As these questions are ever so slowly answered, you'll find yourself engrossed in a story just as tightly written as Steins;Gate, and you'll be glued to this visual novel the whole way until you've seen the true ending through.I can't go into much more detail without spoiling the experience, so if any of what I've said sounds interesting, I urge you to give Chaos;Head Noah a try. This is one of the most original and interesting experiences I've had in years, and it's shown me just how capable of a storytelling genre visual novels really are. Chaos;Head Noah is one of my favorite games that I've played not only this year, but also of all time. I've learned that the deeper Science Adventure series past Steins;Gate is truly worth your time, and I have this game to thank for pushing me to continue past the Steins Gate into a series ever more interesting than I once knew it to be. And as a side note, this game should be played with the Committee of Zero fan patch, which restores a good amount of censored content as well as completely re-translates the game making for a much better experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head Noah is an enhanced version of the sci-fi visual novel Chaos;Head which was originally released in 2008, but never got a Western localization until now. This is actually the first game in the Science Adventure series, predating Steins;Gate and Robotics;Notes and also serves as the prequel to Chaos;Child which was already localized several years ago. Plot: You are Takumi Nishijou, a reclusive, anti-social, insecure otaku who lives alone in a shipping container on top of a building. Everyday you live out an existence playing online games, hentai games and talking to your anime figurine Seira and generally dislike talking to ‘real’ people. One day you find yourself in the middle of a series of gruesome murders, dubbed the ‘NewGen’ killings, and you become the prime suspect of one of the murders. Then girls with gigantic swords start showing up in your life, mysterious voices talk to you, throwing your life into chaos.. Whose eyes are those?Gameplay: The main gameplay element is reading text like in other visual novels, except that Takumi suffers from ‘delusions’ which means he is able to alter reality depending on whether you want him to suffer from a ‘positive’ delusion or a ‘negative’ delusion. These delusions generally do not impact the story, but its interesting to see alternate scenes play out. -Takumi Nishijou, a reclusive, anti-social otaku who can barely even form coherent sentences to other people. He usually stutters a lot when he talks to ‘real’ people.-Shogun, a mysterious figure who seems to be out to get you-Rimi Sakihata, a cheerful girl who appeared to you one day during a murder scene, and later tries to befriend you-Yua Kusunoki, a girl who stalks you and seems to want something from you-Ayase Kishimoto, a singer from a popular indie band, who also seems to have her own sword-Sena Aoi, a hot headed girl who carries around a big sword all the time and isn’t afraid to use it-Kozue Orihara, a mute who speaks instead telepathically, who also has her own sword-Nanami Nishijou, your cheerful ‘bratty’ little sisterGraphics: Chaos;Head Noah uses beautiful anime graphics and sometimes the characters blink on the screen making it appear more like an anime, I think this is definitely a great looking anime type visual novelMusic: The music is just fine, it’s not super memorable but it fits the mood of the scene and the story and that’s all right by me.Conclusion: 10/10. This is one of the most interesting visual novels I’ve ever played, it’s up there with YU-NO, Muv Luv Alternative, Steins;Gate, etc it’s a S tier sci-fi visual novel. What makes it so interesting is a few things, the fact that the protagonist is one of the most helpless pathetic protagonists I’ve ever played. He’s hopelessly insecure about himself, depressed, depraved and of course delusional. It’s very rare that that you play a game with such a flawed main character. The other girls are all flawed in their own way too, the delusion mechanic is interesting and unique, and the story is genuinely gripping. Be aware that there is a lot of graphic violence in this novel and there will be scenes that will make most people uncomfortable. This game can get downright disturbing, but if you bear through it you will be in for a real treat because the story definitely has some interesting twists and turns. The main issue I have with the localization though, is that it doesn’t distinguish between when the characters are talking and when they are thinking. This is a real problem, because the story often times shifts between perspectives of different characters, and some characters are telepathic as well, so if you don’t know what is being thought and what is being said well… that can get confusing. Other than that, the actual translation jobs are superb.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head is hated by many for mainly one reason: Its otaku freak protagonist, Nishijou Takumi. I would never be one of these haters, however. I love Nishijou Takumi. Chaos;Head Noah was a thrilling ride from beginning to end, and what I initially thought was just a murder mystery turned out to be so much more. The game receives my praise for having an interesting, unorthodox choice system, which is positive or negative delusions that make the game much more entertaining. Our man of the hour boasts an impressive life of locking himself in his shipping container with his endless waifu figures, playing ESO all day, and hoarding mountains of eroge (literally me) and even talking with his 2D wife Seira-tan, he undoubtedly makes one of the most interesting main characters I have seen in fiction. There are numerous things that make Chaos;Head great, but Takumi is the best one. Sadly, I found myself relating scarily well to his inner thoughts and delusions to where I realized that he is a more realistic and grounded character than previously thought, albeit a little extreme.80% of Chaos;Head is just his inner monologues, overly paranoid reasoning, and crazy delusions, which I really appreciate from this game. Trying to figure out what is real, and what is not was a great challenge that I enjoyed solving. The delusions genuinely add so much character to Takumi, and it was all so interesting. The game raises an incredible amount of questions on the first playthrough, and you slowly figure them out one by one... It's a satisfying experience; they did it really well.As for art, of course it could be better, though I think the artstyle fit the game really well. The music and sound design is of particular note to me, as the atmosphere and ambience of the game were great. I was surprised to see that the music doesn't play all that often, but when it does, man is it a good soundtrack. As for characters, the only stand-outs were Takumi and Rimi, with the rest not being incredibly relevant. The best part of the game was easily the Common/True End, while the character routes were interesting, they didn't interest me as much. Chaos;Head was an amazing experience that I will never forget.Whose eyes are those eyes?

_childDocuments_.review: This game harbors very, very complicated feelings for me.The writing is incredible, and as per usual the Science Adventure series incorporates online culture, science, and conspiracy beautifully.However, I must say that this game is a master's test run.While this game is undoubtably high quality writing wise, the themes, execution and characters themselves are flawed.The overtly edgy tone isn't what I would call *unnecessary* but rather "tryhard" for a lack of a better word. As if the game is trying to be seen. I feel as though every character has an almost comically horrific story, not to say that it isn't necessary, but it feels overdone.Also, the main character, Takumi is insufferable, heartless, and degenerate. That is not a flaw, but it is a discussion to be had. I don't think there was any real reason why the writers had to make Takumi so terrible. He is rarely triumphant over his degeneracy, and when it is, it's so late in the story. There is no joy or charm in his disgusting behavior to make up for it.I do however feel that it's beautiful, in a twisted way, his mangled personality. Especially because of the main endings of the game, A, B, and AA.The character endings are hit or miss.However, in some endings there isn't enough information given to us, However, cynicism is a trademark aspect of this game.Is the game's stance tasteful? In my opinion, no, but it's still *well done.*The mechanics of the game are quite innovative, but the delusions themselves are either edgy or horny, rarely any fun to go and do.Plus the torture of having to see the characters around Takumi have to endure his ridiculous behavior is a chore.Finding endings is also exhaustingIn the end, I give this game a solid 8/10.Incredibly written, however emotionally challenging, and at times for no real rhyme or reason. It's a masochistic experience at times.The team wields an excellent sword, however they slash their weapon at anything that looks their way.However, they learn to control this weapon.Their strong suits coalesce into Steins;Gate, a true masterpiece.Chaos;Head Noah had potential. If it had a little more maturity and experience, it would go from something partially remarkable to something every VN enjoyer should play.My play time ends at a whopping 52 hours and 24 minutes. I've got every ending. The album rate is only 95% as I didn't feel like going through every delusion, and I've found every single ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head Noah is an unpleasant experience that could have worked, but doesn't.  The raw story components - an examination of social isolation, ostracization, paranoia, and the power of delusionary thinking - are fine, and actually a solid framework.  The presentation values are good for a VN.  The game legitimately has creepy and horrifying moments; the content warning on launch is not there without reason.  The way the game presents the murders at the core of the plot and the way they impact society around them is actually interesting.The main problem is that the point of view character is awful.  Chaos;Head Noah puts you into a scenario where you're spending 20ish hours listening to the internal monologue and voice of a character that is utterly repulsive from the jump and never really gets better.  Prepare yourself for hours of whining about other people, the merits of 2D women over 3D women, talk about how he just wants to go home and wank to his favorite anime waifu, blaming everyone else for his problems, and so forth.  This doesn't even get into the delusion system, which lets you trigger either positive or negative delusionary scenes at certain points; the positive ones tend to either be fantasy "and I lived happily ever after" ones or those that practically adopt a script from a hentai game; the negative ones usually turn violent quickly.   The character specific routes you go through to reach endgame vary but are often similarly unpleasant, and we won't even go into some of the delusions the MC has about his biologically related sister.  By endgame, when the protagonist demonstrates some actual degree of initiative and agency, it's built off so much garbage that there's no catharsis or excitement from it, just vague surprise that he's actually doing *something*.  It's not that stories inherently need to be based around fully functional human beings, but if you're going to center your narrative on a broken individual, then the character growth they experience needs to be commensurate to the struggles they have, and CH;N whiffs badly in this.If you want to try to play through CH;N just to see what it's like or to take a completionist approach to the Science Adventures titles, grab the Committee of Zero fan translation patch, and just buckle up; you're in for a bumpy ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Still playing through the base route, but I've played the original release with Committee of Zero patch, so here goes. No spoilerinos.Firstly I'd like to say that I'm not really too sure about the translation issues as it were. I've heard plenty of people talking about them in negative reviews and off-handedly in a youtube review I had listened to. From what I can gather so far the translation isn't awful. I've never been too much of a language buff to care, though. I have been able to comprehend everything I've read so far. As far as the content goes, Chaos;Head NoAH is a wonderful story. It's jam-packed with intrigue, and often has frequent breaks in perspective and will swap points of view on a dime at points. The author beautifully uses this with just enough restraint to keep your on your toes and not COMPLETELY disorient you. It's also hard to overstate just how atmospheric this game is. At points in the story, it's oppressively intense. You're kind of at the whims of the author with all the twists, turns, and well-deserved payoffs that occur throughout the story. That being said, this game is unique (at least for me) in the sense that you're playing an unreliable narrator. The main character is prone to having delusional breaks and they occur frequently in the story. It's a central mechanic. It's really hard to distinguish fictional events in the story with what's actually going on because of just how well the player can be immersed in the protagonist (Taku's) thoughts.So where does that leave things? Well, I can safely recommend this game just by source content alone. The original Chaos;Head is still there. You only have things to gain from this release. There's significantly more content in this release as well as story routes for each of the main heroines. If this is your entry into Science;Adventure proper, there's no better place to start than Chaos;Head. It's the first chronologically and paves the groundwork for the additional entries. If you're coming from another Sci;Adv release (like Steins;Gate/0 or Robotics;Notes) you'll probably enjoy this one. Even if these visual novels have a habit of having really obscuro mechanics when it comes to progressing through the game. You're gonna want a spoiler-free guide once you get to the different routes.Will update this post when I'm finished.

First off,  I don't think this game is as good as Steins;Gate or maybe the other games in the series since I haven't played them yet(except right now I'm playing Robotics;Notes Elite), but it definitely is pretty good as a first game. Comparing to Steins;Gate this is  more violent, sexual, darker and depressing than it. Also, Takumi as a protagonist is definitely more fitting to those terms than Okabe. Takumi is basically hikikimori, has terrible communication skills, quite perverted, is paranoid of everybody, is cowardly and can be a pretty messed up protagonist in general. It was fun having him as a protagonist, but Okabe is definitely more appealing. The characters are also not as memorable as they are in Steins;Gate. I think one of the best things this game does is to create tension and atmosphere. There are many parts of the game that give you good anticipation of what will happen next. Also, the delusion triggers are an interesting systerm. Tho I personally mostly chose the negative delusions as they seemed more memorable. Whereas the positive ones were mostly just Takumi thinking up a horny scenario in his head. This game is  Overall I recommend getting it if you liked Steins;Gate and want to play more from the SciADV series or maybe you just want to play good horror visual novel.Whose eyes are those eyes?

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the fact that I loved the Steins Gate games as well as Chaos Child, I would end up liking this game too but there's just too many bad points that I kept having with this game that has now forced me to stop playing this because I cannot be bothered to sit and play this game anymore. I did have high hopes for this but no longer.TL;DR: The game has got an interesting plot that can be intriguing to watch and see how it unravels based on your decision but the characters are boring, the protagonist sucks ass and the story takes too long for it to get anywhere that bingeing a show would be more entertaining than this.  ------------(SPOILERS)-----------Pros:PLOT: The plot is, basically, a young teenager is having delusions and paranoia after seeing a murder. After that, it unravels after meeting several girls who may or may not be out for his life and several murders take place. You see that the world becomes more unnatural as the chapters go on with people acting weird and supernatural things occur. This is a unique story that I haven't seen much in novel games so at the start, I was all for it but as you will see, that didn't save this game for me.GREAT CG'S: The CG's in this game are so well done that you can the developers took real good care in making it as detailed as possible, ensuring you see every bit of detail that they are allowed to provide. Also, the little reference to other anime's was real nice to see.Cons:YOU!!: You are actually the WORST thing about this game and by you, I mean the Protagonist. Like I get it, he's a shy and timid otaku who cannot talk to an actually person but HOLY HELL DOES THIS GUY DO EVERYTHING TO MAKE HIM A SCUMBAG!!  You'd think the main baddies of the game would be the people you'd hate but I literally was rooting for them to make the MC have a horrible life. His VA (no hate for the man doing it) gave him this voice where he constantly couldn't say a single word without making it sound like hes scratching his nails on chalkboard. He constantly thinks of women as people from H**tai games, he bad-mouths his little sister who is always nice to him, he thinks he has the worst life, he cannot do anything by himself and blames others for his misfortune and his girlfriend, or wife as he puts it, is a literal 2-D figurine women who speaks to him in his head. I honestly hate this guy more than most game antagonist.CHARACTERS: The characters are a real bore in this game where it made me feel like they weren't even part of the actual story and were instead put into the game just to make up the numbers. It took up until chapter 7 where the characters are actually relevant to the main story and even then, I wasn't interested in them up to that point because of the next big problem.STORY IS TOO LONG: 10 chapters...10 chapters with MC constantly having a grating voice, making scum-ish remarks and decisions, uninteresting dialogue that leads to nowhere and a drawn out detective viewpoint makes this game, for me, a chore rather than an enjoyment.Like I said before, I love visual novel games like Steins Gate, Zero Escape and Chaos Child but this game just thoroughly made me roll my eyes towards most of the characters, the dialogue and MC's decisions. Maybe I'll go through this game to the end and get every ending but honestly, I'd rather replay both Steins Gate games than do that.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin, let me preface that despite the small playtime I actually got the true ending. That is getting all endings possible. This is a 40 hour game on normal pace, but it's so excruciatingly drawn out and boring, that I developed superhuman speedreading, something I genuinely didn't know I was capable of.CHAOS;HEAD has an interesting storyline that gets squandered fast by it's length and drawn out writing.I genuinely believe this is among the best "written" VNs out there, in the sense the sentences flow really well and perfectly describes the scenes and characters. But man is it a drag.The common route for this bad boy is a whopping 20 hours. And is absolutely abysmal. The most unsatisfying ending with the most unlikeable SciAdv character still being unlikeable.Now I really liked Takumi in the beginning. As a matter of fact he's among the most interesting protags in VNs because the writers  took a bold stab at creating a generally under-represented person. He's not strong, he's weak. Socially inept and abysmal at communicating. Something I could relate to especially since it was like looking into a mirror for me at times. That is until halfway through the game where instead of a rising above challenges and becoming a new person arc, he stays the exact same making infuriating decisions and being a sore loser. The writer does NOT want you to be the hero. He specifically writes some moments to really reel you into Takumi and insert yourself a bit, before doing some really stupid ♥♥♥♥ to insult the both the reader themselves and the time they spent.Takumi redeems himself in the last 2 hours of the true ending. Ah, after almost 15 whole hours of my gameplay (I speedran it, naturally it should take an average reader around 40 hours). And still it ends up being a half-hearted sappy cringe ass pull fest that doesn't feel worth the trouble of reading this abomination.The entire gameplay loop is Takumi leaves his man cave, interacts with really fun characters, cool story revelations...goes back and yaps for 2 hours. And then we're back out, cool stuff happens...and we back to the man cave to talk about more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.The character designs, good. The soundtrack, not bad. The story, fantastic concept but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ execution. If the concept of Chaos;Head was given to any other reputed VN creator it would've been a masterpiece, but it had to be MAGES, the masters of YAPPING non-stop and wasting your time.Give this a wide-berth. You can read plenty of phenomenal VNs for the size of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely one of the most convoluted and longest visual novels I’ve ever played, but I mostly enjoyed it. I remember when I finished the original version that my main complaint was the lack of interactivity, there was hardly anything to do but read (yes, yes, I know that this is to be expected from this genre, but still, you know what I mean, there are VNs out there with much more stuff to do in them). Not surprisingly, this is still the case here, however, we get many more endings, and reaching all of them requires a bit more work and thinking, which was a nice surprise for me, something I found a welcome addition – not to mention the graphical enhancements and all the new songs.As for the story, the main part of every VN, well… it’s not light reading material, that’s for sure. As I already mentioned, it’s quite lengthy and crazy complex, full of many scientific and technical terms – I have to admit, I still don’t understand it completely. Nevertheless, the characters are interesting (except for the extremely irritating protagonist, I know I was supposed to sympathize with him, but I simply couldn’t…), the soundtrack is solid, there’s a little bit of humour, mystery, romance, thriller, horror… and quite a lot of gore and physical/mental torture, so keep that in mind. Recommended only for mature audiences!I really enjoyed , and I’m interested in the whole  series in general, so I don’t regret buying this one, either – especially after all that chaos (pun not intended…) surrounding the Steam release. The publisher deserves every support for standing their ground, if you ask me. Anyway, give this one a try, even if you played the original version, you’ll find more than enough new content in it.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game as a whole. I played the game with the patch, so I don't know what is the exact state of the game without it, but the issues I have with it are on fundamental level. First reading of the game is neat. It starts pretty slow, but by chapter 4 or so I was pretty interested. I also liked the original ending, characters, and even the pacing. The only character I didn't like was MC, but well, even MC didn't like himself. It's interesting exploration of shut-in otaku, delusions, and dividing anime from reality.The problems starts once you finish the game. During your first run all the choices are locked - you have only one way to finish it. From the second run you can find choices. Maybe. The game hides choices in different delusions or in reality. You never know if current place will have a choice to be made - if you're unlucky you can miss them all. Unless you're using a guide. But that's bad design.Furthermore there's one ending that has so obscure way to find it that you won't manage to do it without a guide. You won't even have a hind what's the proper solution. And then all the decisions are made in chapters 1-3, out of 10. Afterwards you have to skip trough most of the game. You can set it so it doesn't stop on delusions, but you have to be around while autoskip is wasting energy, because the game will stop once or twice for each route, to show you additional 3-4 sentences... that don't really bring much to the story.What's worse, the additional endings also don't bring much to the story. Those mostly explore the characters you meet around... but the things you learn around them are things you already learned in the main run. There's just a little more detail. Those are nowhere as interesting or good as different endings in Steins;Gate, for example.Furthermore there are some places where autoskipper of read sections doesn't work well. There are some moments where each version of delusion shows the same effect... but it's not recognised as the same text. Even though it is. When you get to the different route final chapters they often have a lot of text in common with the regular route, but that text is not skipped. It's treated as new one.Furthermore, even if you find a choice for different character route... You might answer the prompts incorrectly. Each choice is made of 5 yes/no questions. Get even one of them wrong and you will not get the character route. But in most cases you don't know instantly if it was wrong or right. Only Yua's route got some new text instantly. Otherwise you have to just... hope you were right. And while most of those answers are straightforward, sometimes they are quite tricky and you might end up answering wrongly. To that, a guide is also a solution - but if I'll be using a guide to have "good" experience then the game is badly designed. But who cares about all the optional endings! Just go to the true ending! Is that what you'll say? Alas, you can't. The prerequisite to get the true ending is to get all the other endings. I figured very quickly that , but even then I had to suffer trough all of them. But once I figured it out I cared less.Somehow the developers probably knew their solution was a pain, because the true route starts in the final chapter from the decision point. But it's 95% identical to the base ending, with only tiny differences here and there. Most of those texts by that time you've seen multiple times, so you'll be uninterested and skipping stuff that you saw, then accidentally you'll also skip the dialogue you haven't seen, and you'll read it in the chat log.Oh, and for some endings the final movie starts from writing some text of lines, which looks like regular ingame text. By trying to make them appear faster you'll skip the whole ending move. Bad solution. I had to watch half of them in gallery...And in one route there's a section that automatically moves the text forward without your input. I read pretty fast - if I'm using auto in this game I have text appearance speed at max and wait time at minimum, and I have no problems reading it. But that section ignored auto settings, and was too fast for me. I usually only read half of the sentence before they went to the next one. I had to constantly stop it and read the chat log. It was an interesting scene that revealed a lot of info about the crimes and they made it really bad experience.I also wasn't fan of all the delusions, they were interesting on first go, but when I realised what effect they have on the story  I found them waste of time in my future plays. I still read them all, and I tell you, it was not worth it.So, I will recommend reading the game once then watching the true ending on Youtube. I can't recommend the game as a whole, as half of the playtime is wasted on bad game design decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: I've already fully completed this game before it came out on steam in English, hence the low playtime.I think this game is great, but it's not a game for everybody. This game's main character (Takumi) as well as the ambience and themes are its main strengths. Takumi will probably make or break the story for most people. He's very well written and it can be really interesting to explore the psychology of someone who is so fundamentally broken, seeing how he changes over time. However, he is written to be unlikable, creepy, constantly scared and trying to run away, etc, which is something that will probably put a lot of people off the game. You're not supposed to like Takumi, but if you can't appreciate how he's written, then I think the story mostly breaks down. Plus, I don't think the story would even work with a more, "normal" main character. I also feel the story is badly paced as well, which would make it frustrating if you're not interested in seeing how the main character thinks and what he's like as a person.The themes and ambience presented in this game are also a highlight. The isolation and paranoia felt through the murders always manages to keep things feeling dark, making moments of hope all the more powerful.Most side characters (with a few notable exceptions) are bland and uninteresting. They feel more like props to support the story. The focus of this game is really on Takumi and his experience, rather than anybody else.The art definitely shows its age as well. Some CGs look really good, whereas others look quite amateurish. The developers also decided to make Takumi's home 3D which looks really out of place when a 2d character sprite is portrayed in it. The music is okay, but nothing special. There are a few stand out tracks, but I don't think it's up to the same quality as other tracks in the series (especially Steins;Gate's and Chaos;Child's).I have mixed feelings on the character routes, I found half of them to be uninteresting or a waste of potential (Nanami, Yui, Kozue), whereas the others I really like and add a lot of depth to the characters, the story, or the world (Sena, Ayase, Rimi).I heard bad things about the English translation quality of the game so I played through the intro scene to check for myself and I have to agree. About 70% of it is fine, but the rest ranges from questionable to flat out wrong. I believe there's supposed to be a fan translation patch in the works, so if you're reading this review when it's out, I would definitely recommend that, or, if you can, read it in Japanese.This game has a lot of things wrong with it, but I find the main character really interesting and I think the ambience and themes are very powerful at times, which, in my opinion, offsets the game's flaws, but I'm also well aware that this will not be the case for everybody, and its weaknesses could bring this game down significantly.Overall 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this to the average person out there? No.There's a lot to dislike here in an already niche genre. You are looking at the world through the eyes of one of the most unlikable protagonist out there, which was hard to bear at the beginning but became milder as he develops throughout the chapters. I liked the general concept and theory of delusions which forms the basis of the story, and loved the psychological attacks dealt to the reader in the first 6 chapters and trying to wrap my head around them, but the delusion choice system was not intuitive at all. I tried going through three playthroughs to find the other endings of my own, which all lead to nowhere. You will most likely not get anywhere without a guide, so save time and don't do what I've done.And in the promise of these alternate endings, is where am I disappointed the most. I understand why the true ending is structured the way it is. However to me, there's isn't enough emotional payoff in return for completing all the character routes. The true ending would have made sense if you just went through one character route. Extending that further, I feel that the whole story could have been done by omitting everything else but the true ending. There isn't enough substance, depth, and additional characterization for me in the alternate and character endings to justify the need for them. I want to see more people mentally break down, more swords swinging around, more eyes plastered around everywhere, more aftermath in that ruined world. To illustrate how short the true end is, I'd liken the amount of new content in the true ending to be slightly a bit more than Aokana's epilogue after completing its four character routes, bearing in mind that Chaos;Head Noah and Aokana are roughly of the same length. I was also not impressed by how brief some of the character routes are and their endings, which had much more potential to showcase more of the other characters. There is bias in the character route writing, that much is generally acceptable in this medium, but we can't have a whole route wrapped up within an hour of reading in a 40 hour read, can we? Also why tease us with that tidbit at the end of Sena's route when you don't even bother to mention it anywhere else, not even at the true end. Minus points for being a self-contained story, which one could only hope will be further explored in the other titles.And I genuinely hope it will be better in the other ones.  This is my first exposure to the SciAdv universe in any form of media, and I've heard many praises sung for the SciAdv heavyweights of Steins;Gate and Chaos;Child. I want to believe that that isn't a delusion after sinking in many hours into the universe.

_childDocuments_.review: CHAOS;HEAD NOAH is nothing short of a masterpiece in the realm of visual novels. Its intricate storytelling and immersive narrative had me glued to my screen, sacrificing sleep just to unravel the next twist. The game's ability to weave complex themes with engaging character development is a testament to the creators' prowess in crafting a compelling story that resonates with its audience. However, no masterpiece is without its flaws. CHAOS;HEAD NOAH offers a plethora of endings and routes, which, while ambitious, ultimately feels like a double-edged sword. The narrative sometimes feels dragged, diluting the impact of its core story. Personally, I only wanted the routes/endings of my waifus Nanami and Rimi, I couldn't care less about the other girls. Voice acting in CHAOS;HEAD NOAH is a mixed bag. On one hand, the voice actress for Nanami delivers a performance that is nothing short of perfection. Her portrayal of a cute, sometimes fiery little sister is spot-on, complete with adorable high-pitched noises that add a layer of authenticity to her character. It's exactly how I'd imagine a lovable yet spirited little sister would sound. On the other hand, Takumi's voice actor sometimes misses the mark. His over-the-top delivery can be grating, detracting from the immersion and occasionally making it hard to sympathize with the protagonist.For those considering diving back into the chaotic world of CHAOS;HEAD NOAH, or for newcomers ready to embark on this emotional rollercoaster, I highly recommend checking out the Custom DLC. It's a game-changer that significantly enhances the overall experience ;)In conclusion, CHAOS;HEAD NOAH is a visual novel that will take you on an unforgettable journey through its gripping narrative and complex character dynamics. While it may stumble in its ambition with an overabundance of routes, the heart of its story and the strength of its key characters make it a journey worth taking.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head is a really interesting game for me. I originally played it as an angsty teenager who just wanted to play it due to the fact that "it looked cool and the story seemed scary". What I was left with was an experience that had deeply influenced me, and honestly I don't know if it was for the better or for the worse. The thing you have to realize going into this story is that the protagonist isn't a good guy, nor is he a role model who you should strive to be like. He's a loser, and what makes the story so interesting is observing him and seeing how he reacts and eventually finds resolve in the situation he's been placed in. As a 16 year old when I originally read this, I didn't understand this and thought "woahhhh this guy sure is cool...". Don't do that. Really stupid idea. Looking past my personal conflict with that though, I think the story is solid, and it really does give an interesting look at the toxic otaku culture from Japan during the mid 2000's. Would I suggest you read it? I'm not sure. It's clearly very intentive with what it's trying to portray, but you'll need a decent literary understanding to fully appreciate what the themes are trying to tell you. It isn't the tale of a hero or some great guy, it's a story about a disturbed individual trying to save his life. If you're cool with all that, then it's worth a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the game (first route) and will share my thoughts.WARNING, VAGUE SPOILERS AHEAD! Nothing that would spoil the story though.While it has an interesting start, it starts dragging on. The main character (MC) is absolutely insufferable, going on and on about who might be out to get him or not, and it only gets worse as the game continues. The pacing is horrible. If you are familiar with the 7 Point Story Structure: What feels like the Midpoint happens in chapter 3 or so, but it actually is a red herring, somewhat soon followed by Pinch 2. Absolutely nothing that advances the plot except for another "pinch-esque" event and lots, and I mean LOTS of whining and lamenting.The story is somewhat fine, bit the game is probably four times as long as it should be, and the ending is a somewhat explained but still too sudden deus ex machina, and the ending too outstays its welcome by a lot.I enjoyed "Devil on G-String" a lot more than this. The MC in C;HN is NOT proactive except for the fake Midpoint that results in nothing and the ending where he suddenly grows a pair.I wouldn't say that the game is a waste of time, but it does use up far too much of it. _childDocuments_.review: This review is written after finishing the first chapter. Noah is an average VN overall. The writers managed to create a compelling mythology and an innovative mix between sci-fi and fantasy elements, not unlike the persona series. The presentation is above average too, namely with its artwork a slight cut above most other VNs. However, that's where the praise ends. A lot of the soundtrack lacks punch, making the thriller aspect suffer. The story lacks tempo, further weakening the thrill with long segments dominated by uninteresting inner monologue and events. Much to my surprise, the characters are vapid and difficult to emphasize with, a poor fit for a character driven story like this. For example, the voice acting sounds fit for a comedy with its old 2000's exaggerated flair, and the characters lack emotional dynamism and are too predictable with their line delivery. To great annoyance, the main character is quite stupid and lacks any redeeming skills or strengths. Instead, he relies mostly on luck and his relationships with other characters seem completely undeserved. He also suffer from what I call the "camera man effect", where he observes the events around him too much instead of being proactive. Finally, the unique delusion trigger system. It's an amusing quirk, but that's it. There are better VN's out there, so I don't recommend to bet on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one. I will be reviewing this game from a  perspective.First of all, you should know that this is the first game in the SciAdv series, so it kind of lessens the blow a little bit, especially when the direct sequel to this game is literally Steins;Gate , which I consider to be one of the best media pieces to ever come out of Japan.    Simply put, this game is a mess. I wholeheartedly believe they put "Chaos" in the title because the story was so convoluted they had to point it out in the title, in a move to maybe acknowledge the total trainwreck that happened in this story.    I won't go in much detail here to not spoil the game entirely , but this game really  . It is sometimes a horror mystery, sometimes a slice of life, sometimes a sci-fi adventure, sometimes a drama, sometimes meta, sometimes extremely cheap, sometimes stupid and very often, . If there is a word to define this game, inconsistent is it.     The first chapters capture the life of a troubled, isolated and confused protagonist, which understandably does not translate into a cohesive pace of events. That I can respect, but the issue is that this kind of pacing is TERRIBLE for who is reading the story. I don't think this is a good enough excuse for the pacing of the script being so bad during literally  the chapters though. It is telling that in Chapter 5 (halfway through the game) the muder mystery is simply dropped to be replaced by a fantasy shonen-like storyline. The writers really dropped the ball while writing this. The ending I didn't have much of a problem with, it was the logical conclusion to what they built through chapter 5+, but the asspull to try to tie the murder mystery to anything was just baffling. Not to mention of course the obvious  "inspired" plotline that is way too ambitious for it's own good.    To be honest it almost feels like a  for what Steins;Gate would come to be in the future. It's like the writers just threw everything that sounded cool for them at the time and just didn't care if all these elements together made any sense.    This game has a element that would appear in S;G later on, for example: the overly descriptive text of a scene that just doesn't need that much thought put into it. However, in this game it is MUCH worse, since a lot of the scenes are incredibly mundane, a lenghty description of them just serves to drag the story longer than it is necessary and to bore the reader. I kind of liked it in the beginning, but oh my god did it make me want to skip the text and just jump to the important moments.    But it had it's moments. I really liked the concept of the  for example. It's a shame that they just halfassed/dropped it like almost everything in this game.The delusion trigger is also interesting, but in my opinion poorly implemented. It is fun in the beginning, but after some chapters it is just a nuissance to deal with, since it acts like a extra scene for that situation. It is almost like you are watching a show and in the middle of a scene it cuts to a blooper, I mean, okay, that might be funny the first or third time, but damn it gets annoying. Of course you have the option to view none at all, but that gets old FAST.    To be honest the emotional drama is strong in this one and you will like it if you like that sort of stuff, but myself personally just couldn't stand it at the end, everything was so poorly constructed that it was kind of hard to feel anything for the characters on screen, which unfortunately were very hollow and weren't really expanded upon like, at all. I liked the struggle of the protagonist for example, even though he was despicable most of the time (that was the point after all!), which means his character succeeded somehow in grabbing my attention.    Hollow characters, interesting tory and presentation, controversial yet intriguing protagonist, terrible pacing, good ideas, a bunch of holes and asspulls, and etc. I could go on forever, but I think this is enough to show that in general the aspects of the game are very mixed in my opinion.    Would I recommend this game? Maybe. If you like VNs and already played the best that there is and wants to try something different and a bit experimental. So because I'm a bit over the fence on this one since it is very  in my opinion, I will have to give it a thumbs down.OBS: I used the Commitee of Zero Patch for this playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe Chaos; Head Noah in a single sentence, I would say that it is an interesting amalgamation of ideas. But unfortunately, it's hard for me to say that a majority of these ideas ever carried any weight beyond their initial premise. A good example of this would be the delusion system that is present throughout the game. At the start, when the game has more of an unsettling tone, it does a decent job of striking some sense of fear into the player. But the more the game progresses, the more it feels like this entire system only exists to pad out the already padded-out runtime of this game, when each delusion typically goes the same way over and over. The "green" delusions almost always just end up being the main character having a perverted fantasy about any woman he talks to, and when this happens every single time, it eventually doesn't add much.But I wouldn't even say this is the game's biggest problem. Its biggest problem is that it's boring. It's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring. I don't think I've ever completed a more boring game in my entire life. It is a game so dull, that completing it took me over two months and a lot of unhappy play sessions. Almost all of the characters are two-dimensional and bland until the final two chapters of the game, and when the writers realized they needed development they crammed it all into the last few hours. The game constantly has moments where it begins to pick up steam as some concept is finally explained and things start to connect, only for the game to lose focus on that concept and introduce an entirely different one. It's like I was being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ edged for 20 hours but wasn't allowed to climax for the entire game.  The "story" is just exposition for things that have an underwhelming payoff in the end. These aren't necessarily bad concepts either, a majority of them are quite interesting, but the game is always trying its best to describe them in the most uninteresting way. To be fair to the game, there are times when an excellent job is done in both premise and execution, but these times are rare and only occur towards the end of the game after you have already suffered through a bulk of its monotony. My biggest problem with this game, however, was how it ended. You would think that after all the suffering the game puts you through to see the credits roll, there would be something of value at the end right? There is not. The ending has to be one of the most disappointing things I have ever seen, especially after the game did a good job in the last 2 hours setting up its conclusion. But instead, it is this abrupt and meaningless conclusion that made me feel like I wasted my time.And in short, that's how I would describe this game. A waste of my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time. I'll concede that I did not see all the endings and routes that this game has to offer, and I'll concede that maybe those other routes make the game better. But I cannot force myself to play another second of this boring, dragged-out, piece of ♥♥♥♥ game.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Within the first 15 minutes of this game you will learn a few things about the character through which you will experience this story. Without exaggeration or hyperbole. The MC, in whose head you reside as the 'player/reader' of this game is: - A bona fide incel (expect constant and unprompted hatred and objectification of women)- A pedophile who fantasizes about sleeping with his own sister (immediately after his sister is introduced, he talks about how he would masturbate to her)This is what the game leads with. That's the main character we are talking about. For what kind of audience was this intended? It's really disgustingThen again, Japanese games are rife with sexual abuse that is played for laughs. So who knows, maybe whoever wrote this thought these things are funny. What disturbs me the most is that teenagers have played this, and they are too immature to understand how wrong this is. The fact that these awful things are just kinda thrown in makes it worse in that respect. It's not as though these are topics which are broached in some kind of integral or progressive way to the story. These are thrown in as literal afterthoughts. While NOTHING is happening, except that we are inside the main character's head. And this is what his thoughts are about. That's literally it.-----Other than that, the delusion mechanic feels arbitrary. The MC is already delusional and constantly unironically questioning the most basic observations. It lacks any kind of meaning. The story gives you no reason to care about what MC thinks is or isn't real. There's no incentive to choose between any delusion, if there's no reality as a reference point. If you want to dazzle your readers with a chaotic and convoluted plotline, you need to have a solid core to incentivize their investment. 13 Sentinels is a good example that comes to mind. But while you are grasping for some kind of reason to give a damn about this story, what the author gives you is incest and pedophilia. Enjoy

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure if my younger self had read this VN 15 years ago, he would have found it a masterpiece. Reading it now... kinda stinks.The plot itself is good, and the writing is decent. Structured as it is, its a bit cumbersome to trace back every ending, but overall it is the less tedious part of the ordeal. Visuals are passable, sound design acceptable, the premise is pretty funny and the initial chapters while slow, keep the player entertained and willing to see how far this mega autist will go. I'd say the main drive for me was the mystery aspect, which coming from the sciADV sequels, felt pretty lackluster halfway through. Chaos;Head has none of the finesse of Steins;Gate nor the charm of its characters, let alone the satisfaction of its conclusion, nor the solid interactions of Robotics;Notes. It's very rough around the edges, and the content is spread far too thin, while leaving a lot of needless prose in between. Relating with the protagonist is very hard, let alone impossible at times, and the excuse brought up to justify why he is what he is rings hollow. The "heroines" routes might as well be just other bad endings, why would anyone want to re-read the thing a second time is beyond me, just give the player free choices in the first playthrough, the added knowledge has no place being scattered around like that. _childDocuments_.review: So I did experience Steins;Gate and Robotics;Notes prior to reading through Chaos;Head NOAH, and prefer both of them over this one. That being said, I still think this is a fairly entertaining read that is worth giving a try if you enjoy visual novels in any capacity.This visual novel is tremendous at it's ability to create suspense and paranoia. I felt on edge a majority of the time, but kept wanting to press on to see what happens next. The delusion mechanic adds to the paranoia effectively. Huge credit to the writing, background art, and soundtrack for nailing this atmosphere. There's definitely a 2000s trope-y TV anime vibe going on here though, which may not be everyone's cup of tea.The main character we spend most of our time with is, to put it bluntly,  pathetic. However, the writing is fully aware of this and pulls no punches, and I found myself fascinated by the struggles of this human disaster and how he navigates the problems and people thrown at him. He just feels . So yeah- You will likely feel disgusted and appalled by his thoughts and actions, but how you interpret it is up to you. If you prefer your narration to be stable and well-adjusted, then you may want to skip this one.The format is a mixed bag for me here. Like other visuals novels in this genre, we are mean to experience multiple routes to get the full experience. However, the setup to get to each route requires fast forwarding through 85% of the content over and over again, which feels like a waste of time. In addition, and this might be partially due to the delusion mechanic, the routes don't seem all that connected to each other. When I have to re-experience the same plot points continuously, I expect to at least gain new perspectives as I do so. But because of the whole delusion/paranoia angle (which I do think adds to the tone effectively), I end up unsure if what I'm reading is actually contributing to the bigger picture. It certainly feels like the game is trying to tie threads together, but just can't quite pull it off because of the very themes it has committed to.Overall, I enjoyed reading through this. It's not a world beater, and is overshadowed by the other entries in the SciAdv series (at least the ones I have already read), but I don't think it's bad by any means. I would not recommend this to someone blind, but I'm fairly confident those who are familiar with Steins;Gate or anime culture would find some level of enjoyment here.I'd give it a solid 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: ...And I don't mean that in the sense that its mediocre; Rather, CHAOS;HEAD is perplexingly both an extremely interesting and enjoyable visual novel and possibly the worst thing I have ever read/played.Let me get this out of the way right now. If you, who is likely coming from Steins;Gate, found that game to be difficult to stomach, then this is not the novel for you. While that game had areas of contention and problematic moments from time to time (*cough* *cough* ), Chaos;Head dials it up to 11 in its bold decision to be both exceedingly violent and exceedingly horny at all times (to which, may I add, most of the characters are HIGH-SCHOOLERS). Even in this steam release, which apparently censored and removed a lot of content, there's a good deal of gore and  of fanservice. If you have a weak tolerance for either, then I recommend you skip this one.As you've probably seen from many of the other reviews, Takumi Nichijou (the protagonist [First, Last]) is a much maligned character. He's a Katamari of horrible personality traits, but the most prominent is that he is perhaps the biggest incel coomer ever found in a video game that's primary purpose isn't arousal. He is pretty inexcusably terrible almost the whole way through, and yet, Chaos;Head would be a significantly worse game if he were tolerable. As he is, Nichijou serves as the perfect protagonist for a game that tackles such grand themes of isolation and reality. Seeing the world through his eyes is what give this story any kind of weight. Additionally, Nichijou provides an interesting window of self-analysis; it is amusingly horrific, discovering some of your own negative qualities through him. tl;dr: the protagonist sucks really badly and is probably the main reason you'll want to drop it, but is a really great fit for the game overallChaos;head has 9 endings total. After beating the game once, you gain access to choices you can make throughout the game to get new endings, several of which being, for lack of a better term, "heroine" routes for those in the loop (for those who aren't, they're character specific ending that likely end in some kind of deeper relationship forming between Nichijou and that character. Eventually, they all culminate a true ending. I have only experienced the first ending as of writing this and I am debating going back for the rest. Though I still have lots of questions, Ending A to me seems like an alright ending; it feels it should end that way. I'd put the length of your first play-through at around 25 hours, which is more than enough bang for your buck, but if you want more than go for the rest, be prepared to re-read a lot if you don't use a guide to put saves in the right spots.At best, Chaos;head is a mind-bending, horrifyingly woven narrative about the nature of reality and your own existence, but at worst, feels like a cheap eroge seen through the eyes of a teenager that has had unregulated internet access since birth. It's a game I thoroughly enjoyed and enjoyed hating, but I wouldn't fault for killing yourself in the first few hours.I touched upon it earlier, but CHAOS;HEAD NOAH censored several aspects of the original game, of which I am unaware of. Most of the SCI;AD games have a community retranslation called the Committee of Zero patch. which is supposedly the definitive way to play them. The research I did on the patch yielded some mixed reception towards it. As such, I'll use my own testimony: I first bought this game in April right on the heels of STEINS;GATE, and decided to download the Cof0 patch for it. This was because it was generally recommended on both the subreddit for SCI;AD as well as Chaos;Head Noah's steam reviews. I got about halfway through but ended up dropping it for a while due to a busy schedule. By the time I got back to it,  it was October and I had a new computer. It was then I found the mixed results on the patch, and opted to reset my game data and play through it without the patch. Here's what I noticed:1.) The patch retranslated some terms to be more sensational (i.e Pregnant man ---> Manchild or the most notable change "Whose Eyes Are Those" ---> "Whose Eyes Are Those Eyes")2.) Nichijou in the original version spoke using far more "Otaku" terms as well as using more l33t-speakThose were the only 2 things I personally noticed, but then again, the time between my playthroughs was  decently long, and I'm not the most vitriolic towards that of censorship; I'm not really the guy the patch was made for I think. Anyways. use the patch if you want, but I found both translations to be very readable.

_childDocuments_.review: 7.0/10. Interesting story with strong atmosphere and thought-provoking themes fails to say anything of note, while suffering from a character portrayal that is unconventional in occasionally contrived ways. There's something here, but not enough.Technical details/PresentationC;H is a visual novel. It's pretty middle of the road on this front - nothing bad, but nothing standout either.GameplayAs a VN most of one's time is spent reading. You don't pick dialogue options--instead, there are "delusion triggers" where you can choose between positive and negative delusions. At very specific points you may choose between yes and no options but by and large there's not much interaction here. Additionally, these delusion triggers don't really change the plot very much outside of the small character routes.StoryChaos;Head is the first game released in the "Science Adventure" series by the company Mages. The series is primarily known for the VN Steins;Gate, which I read before encountering this game.Chaos;Head tells the story of a character named Takumi Nishijou, a creepy, loser otaku who internally monologues about how much he can't stand him, but who outwardly can't look people in the eye and can barely speak without stuttering. Like Steins;Gate the MC is a person who is off-putting for a significant portion of the story; here however it seems far more extreme, with Takumi having clearly crippling mental issues for most of the story. In the abstract this distinctly unflattering portrayal is great for a genre that usually suffers from the opposite, but at points it seemed a bit too far - times where the main character would see a news story online and work himself into a frenzy leading to him screaming at the top of his lungs in fear. Contrived at times. That said, the development the character goes through is significant and commendable.Like many visual novels the MC is surrounded by a passel of girls who he can develop relationships with and spin off into individual routes, but these are not mere fanservice scenarios. Each expounds on the nature of the individual in question, in some cases turning on its head their original portrayals. A few of them also give hints to the broader lore of the series in interesting ways. Their general portrayals seem well done.The story has a big focus on delusions: occasionally you'll be presented with a choice to select a positive or negative delusion, and Takumi will experience a short snippet of a fantasy, often violent and gory, before snapping back to reality. This also happens a bit outside of the player's control, and various other characters have similar issues. There's an interesting focus on perspective seen throughout all of this.I've avoiding discussing the main scenario because it's worth experiencing mostly blind. Just a broad statement - in the Science Adventure series, seemingly supernatural elements are given "scientific" explanations. Some of these are more obviously dumb BS than others, and that's the case here.Despite that, and despite - or perhaps because of - the nearly insufferable protagonist, this VN has an oppressive weirdness that you don't see much in the medium, and it's worth experiencing.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I've since looked into the CoZ patch/localization issues more, and while I think a lot of my points would still stand even if i played with it, the patch very likely offers a much improved experience, so be sure to get that.This is a really frustrating game. In its best moments, it's a 7 or even 8 out of 10. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but but it has enough interesting or good about it that it's an enjoyable experience which pulls you along. But at its worst, it creeps as low as 4 I'd say, just a boring, redundant slog that squanders its good aspects. As it is, I'd mostly only recommend this to mega weebs, or people familiar with and forgiving of the worst tendencies of visual novel writers, which this game has a lot of (excessive dialogue, repeating itself, overlong, etc). I had a whole screed written out, but I'm mostly just gonna bullet point a few bugbears I have, since nobody wants to hear me whine, but I still wanna vent my spleen. Also, a year passed between when I got endings 1/2 around launch, and the rest just this year, so I may make some mistakes due to forgetting.Takumi is a pretty controversial protag, which I get, but I think it's a really compelling concept. The problem is, they don't really do anything with it. He has a bit of an arc, but it's all backloaded, and for most of the game, he never really stops being a gross coward, with occasional moments of trying to be good. And for all his gross perversions and misguided anger at the world, the game never really challenges his viewpoints, and he never really learns why all he was wrong. The delusions are an interesting mechanic, but ultimately, I felt like they weren't all that meaningful, or used effectively. They illustrate Takumi's tenuous grip on reality, but ultimately have little to no relevance or effect on the plot, aside from minor changes, or as a totally arbitrary method to unlock alternate routes. Also, the few yes/no segments in the game are also pretty much pointless, and again, merely an arbitrary way to unlock alternate routes, or shunt you into annoying game overs.I especially have a bone to pick with all the routes and endings. I really see no point in having any of them, aside from "this is a visual novel, of course we have to have them!" The first two routes are fairly identical, with the second offering some alternate character viewpoints, and getting these back-to-back burned me out for a year. All the character routes have some additional context for the highlighted character, but they're mostly what-if scenarios with no bearing on the main plot, and the characters/scenarios aren't compelling enough to keep these from being slogs. I don't know why they couldn't just fit in more scenes with these characters into the main plot, make the true route/ending the only one, and scrap the what-ifs. This isn't a dating sim, so it seems pointless.That's all the whining I'll do. I played this because fans of SciAdv insisted it would improve the experience of Steins;Gate and the rest of the series, so I'm hoping that proves true. But improved context and whatnot for later entries can't really be used as a positive for the game when viewed as a standalone story. I don't regret playing Chaos;Head, but it had just too many moments holding it back to be really great.

_childDocuments_.review: Whose eyes are those? What a masterpiece.I’m truly impressed with how the story unfolds, things get more and more interesting the more I play it. I was confused and amused at the times as to why everyone was after Takumi, or was it all in his head? And how crazy this guy sounds to normal people.The MC may put off people, however, I found him relatable, interesting and funny. I liked his comparisons between video game experiences and the reality of day-to-day life.Chaos;Head Noah has a creepy atmosphere throughout the game and had me hesitating before continuing to certain scenes, as it was quite frightening. We sometimes find ourselves experiencing the same internal conflict of not wanting to face certain situations or circumstances, yet knowing the importance of overcoming them even if they’re scary. The concept of delusional thinking and hallucinations was presented in an unsettling manner. I found the exploration of mental illness in Chaos;Head Noah highly thought-provoking and effectively-handled.His perspective as an inconsistent narrator makes for an intriguing storytelling style as he struggles with delusions and reality. Takumi’s perception is clouded by delusions, creating a sense of uncertainty as to what is true and what is not. This is further enhanced by the inclusion of the Delusion Trigger system, an interactive element that allows players to choose positive, negative delusion or able to choose none.I highly recommend this VN to those wanting to get into the SciADV games (it’s the first game to the series) and if you’re into Denpa horror VNs.
