_childDocuments_.review: Press any key for schizophrenia.CHAOS;HEAD is a really interesting story. On the surface it appears to be a murder mystery story but it's not really that. There are murders and mysteries, but they don't meet in the same way that they would in a whodunit. I guess I'd rather call it a psychological horror, even if it's not really outright horror. And much like STEINS;GATE, the entry in the series that people are probably the most familiar with, it is rife with conspiracies and larger implications. Really enjoyed myself as I read through it for the first ending.The meat of the story is really in the common route, which then unlocks the other routes and endings after having completed it once. The character-specific routes aren't that special even if they do flesh out some of the characters a bit more and have some good elements. The most outstanding one of them is the Rimi route, which gives the most exposition for the common route, although I did also enjoy the Sena one too as a Sena fan. The endings also felt a bit lacking compared to the emotions I felt from the common route. Even the true ending didn't really change things up that much or be more detailed than the base ending. Thankfully the common route was interesting so I don't feel soured by these issues.The protagonist Takumi is a flawed but interesting character. An anti-social, delusional otaku hiding from the world in his shipping container home. And because of those delusions, he becomes an unreliable narrator for the story, making the reader unsure what parts of the story are real and what are delusions. He enters a delusion, then something unexpected happens and you can't know if it's still a delusion or not. Or he encounters a stranger that supposedly knows him and you can't know which is true. The unreliability of his delusions really fits the whole mysterious and disturbing theme of the story very well.The delusion triggers are pretty interesting system that allow having a positive delusion, a negative delusion, or no delusion. The delusions will then trigger either a small scene with no relevance to the plot, or change the actual routing (at least if you answer a quiz correctly). While the game does have an explanation as to why this would happen, it's still pretty hard to figure out why having a negative delusion in a given scenario would result in a different ending. Not quite as opaque of a routing system as the text message system in STEINS;GATE was, but still mixed up a bit. You'll probably want to look up a route guide for this one.Art in CHAOS;HEAD is just about alright. Some of the character sprites and CG images have a derpy feeling to them, with the characters looking like their facial features are trying to escape their faces. I didn't find the art fundamentally flawed but it did definitely stick out, even in some quite pivotal parts of the story. The characters also have animated mouths but there's not much animation beyond that and some camera pans. And while the CG did have some quality issues, the amount of it was just fine. I guess this isn't really the most visual of packages.But what was actually superb was the sound design. The sound design in this game is fantastic. Takumi is fully voiced and Yoshino does a superb job at voicing his uncertainties, fears, delusions, paranoia and other ailments. Maybe his performance was actually too good, since it overshadowed some of the side characters, even though there were also good performances there. Like for example Takahashi Chiaki's performance as Yua. The music and sound effects are also to the point when it comes to producing a creepy, supernatural and mysterious atmosphere. There's very few times when I'm impressed to this point by just the sound design in a visual novel. You'll definitely want to have audio on for this experience. Bonus points for an excellent insert song.You’ll also want to have audio on because it’s very hard to figure out who’s talking without it. The user interface has no indication on who the speaker at the moment is, or if the text is just narration. If you’re deaf, you can go get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as far as CHAOS;HEAD is concerned. The interface is also kinda ugly in general and the text display is kinda rough. This is probably a function of the game’s age, as it’s already 15 years old. Not a dealbreaker but something I did definitely note during it.For what it's worth, installing the Committee of Zero patch does clean up the text display so maybe consider doing that.Whilst it's largely overshadowed by its excellent younger sibling STEINS;GATE, CHAOS;HEAD is still an interesting story and recommended reading despite some of its flaws.Maybe I should now check why everyone hates the anime adaptation…

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I enjoyed any of my time with this game. Future games in this franchise have stronger characters and are logical to follow. Chaos;Head Noah has a main character who does almost nothing to further the story, so most of the time is spent watching him piss all of his time away. While characters like this can be subversive if done well (Okabe from Steins;Gate, Subaru from Re:Zero), Takumi just doesn't want to be involved with anything. Most of the story is spent reminding you of this fact. By the time Takumi wants to change, it's the last chapter of the 15-hour story, and the catalyst for this change doesn't feel earned.The supporting characters are surface-level intriguing. There are a few truly unsettling moments that trick you into thinking the story is about to get good, but the story doesn't have a very interesting mystery or reason to keep reading. Above all, you just feel drained reading it, and by the time you finish, the few interesting questions that have been posed are not meaningfully answered or setup to motivate you to complete the optional chapters.Finally, I can't quite put my finger on it, but the UI is cumbersome to navigate, on either controller or keyboard. _childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head Noah is an expansion of the original visual novel Chaos;Head that added new routes, scenes, and dialogue. That being said, when this was originally released on Steam it was butchered requiring a fan translation to add in lost content and proper terminology and acceptable prose. If you're playing this to get more Steins;gate style story or humor you'll not find it here. You should go into this game with fresh eyes as the first in the series that is experimenting with themes and personalities. Let me be clear, the protagonist is not likable and that's on purpose. The game maintains a serious, frightening, and depressing tone that only breaks if you take the time to find the humor in the mental insecurities and failures of the protagonist.To me, this novel is better than Steins;gate because it has its own unique approach to storytelling. Characters are highly flawed and others call it out. There is tragedy and a critique on Japanese politics as well as society in general. It tackles serious subject matters. Overall it comes highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head Noah, an expanded edition of the original visual novel developed by 5pb., offers a riveting journey into the intricate realm of psychological suspense and supernatural intrigue. This adaptation introduces additional content and perspectives to the captivating narrative, creating a more immersive experience for fans of the genre.Visually, Chaos;Head Noah retains its distinctive anime-inspired art style. The character designs are both expressive and detailed, capturing the psychological nuances of the narrative. The visual novel format allows for a dynamic presentation of the story, incorporating both static images and subtle animations to convey the unfolding events effectively.The soundtrack of Chaos;Head Noah contributes significantly to the atmospheric tension. The haunting melodies and ambient sounds enhance the psychological elements of the story, immersing players in the eerie and suspenseful world. The audio design, including voice acting and sound effects, adds depth to the characters and the overall mood of the narrative.Gameplay revolves around making choices at key points in the story, influencing the protagonist's path and the unfolding mysteries. The non-linear narrative structure allows for multiple branching paths and endings, encouraging players to explore different choices and unravel various facets of the complex storyline.Where Chaos;Head Noah excels is in its narrative depth and psychological complexity. The story weaves a web of conspiracy, delusion, and supernatural occurrences that keep players on the edge of their seats. The exploration of the protagonist's mental state and the blurred lines between reality and delusion contribute to the overall sense of unease.The addition of new routes and perspectives in Noah enhances the original Chaos;Head experience. It allows players to delve deeper into the backgrounds of certain characters, uncovering additional layers of the overarching mystery. The expansion adds value for both those revisiting the narrative and newcomers eager to explore the intricate plot.The community reception to Chaos;Head Noah has been positive, with fans appreciating the expanded content and the opportunity to revisit the gripping narrative with fresh insights. Discussions around the psychological themes, character development, and the game's impact on the larger Science Adventure series are common within the visual novel community.In conclusion, Chaos;Head Noah is a compelling addition to the visual novel genre, offering an enriched and more immersive experience for fans of psychological thrillers. Its striking visuals, atmospheric soundtrack, and intricately woven narrative create a captivating journey into the realms of delusion and suspense. If you're a fan of immersive storytelling and psychological mysteries, Chaos;Head Noah is a thought-provoking adventure that will leave you questioning the boundaries of reality and imagination.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit of a rougher start to the Science Adventure series but an important first step since it has at least some impact on every entry thereafter. It's not terribly flawed from an intrinsic standpoint but the material can be a bit cumbersome to get through or offputting at times. I read the original release some years before we got Noah in the west, so I knew what to expect going in and found myself satisfied with the upgrades that this new edition delivered (mostly new routes, higher quality CGs and cleaner UI). Chaos;Head has a fundamentally unique story with wild twists, lots of interesting ideas and concepts, some cool characters & great attention to detail but it meanders a lot on the protagonist's overbearingly psychotic internal monologue, with almost every line peppered in cringy internet lingo. The first-person perspective of a mentally disturbed individual works to the narrative's strength sometimes and can do a great job instilling a sense of paranoia in the reader by finding ways to justify the logic of someone who's completely delusional with seemingly tangible and real incidents, but you also have to hear him ramble on about his crippling addiction to MMOs and porn and other vices for a significant chunk of the story. He does eventually mature and learn to carry his weight, and him being a gross nutcase is at least intentional since the story is obviously trying to highlight negative aspects of hikkikomori lifestyle and internet addiction, plus there are plenty of intermissions focused on other more interesting characters that keep him from getting too frustrating to read about, but it can nevertheless be a difficult part of the experience. It can also get a bit over the top to the point of being edgy with its gore, but the manner of each death in the serial killings that the story focuses on are still rationalized in a way that makes sense once you've got the full picture.The new routes added by the NOAH release are mixed quality with some being really good and expanding on the setting across the whole series to come (like Sena's) with a couple of others feeling like filler rushed out solely to shoehorn each one of the heroines into the spotlight. (Nanami's and Yua's)Overall I want to say it's pretty good, but my appreciation of it was found mostly in hindsight once I connected all the pieces of story together in my head and I think it will be the same for most people. It demands you to commit to it way before you will know it's worth sticking through to the end and for this reason I think not many will, unless they started the series on another entry like Steins;Gate and already know how good things can get.Please note above all else though that the localization is terrible, often straight up refusing to translate many terms with seemingly no attempt made to equate them with anything in English (this is admitted outright by whoever did the translation job in many of the TIPS), and that this should be read with Committee of Zero's patch to fix the translation quality, something which is par for the course with this series at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos;Head was one of the first visual novels I ever played a few years ago. I really enjoyed it at the time, even with it's sometimes wonky translation. It was unfortunate that it was not really available in the west at the time, but it set me on a path to play all the other SciAdv games in order as well. C;H NoAH had a fan patch that was in the works for years, and there was always a promise around the corner that it would come out any time. I've been looking forward to NoAH since I first played C;H, and boy did it deliver. I purchased as soon as it came out on steam, but I still waited for the CoZ fan patch. This group of dedicated individuals rebuilt the game from the ground up, making sure it looks as pretty as it can, has the highest quality sound, images, etc. While I very appreciate Spike Chunsoft for going through the effort to do their translation and localization, I must include in my review the experience I obtained with the fan patch.In any case, this game is EASILY a 10/10. I knew this from the earliest moments in this playthrough. It is everything that's great about the original, plus tons of extra content. Not only is it higher quality, but so much extra backstory is provided, much fan service is included. The extra routes are great (most of them), and the music is rocking. This is a very disturbing game, but a masterpiece in it's own right. I love the CGs and whatnot that are added in NoAH. It truly is the complete package. I didn't know what I was missing with the Chaos;Head PC of old. All that said, check out Chaos;Child! It is just as good and better in many ways than even Chaos;Head is! I look forward to future releases, Anonymous;Code, Hopefully the Love Chu Chus are coming (I know CoZ are working on fan ports), maybe we can even look forward to an English steam release for Occultic;Nine. I understand the company is going through some changes with Chiyo moving places, but I appreciate the effort that went into bringing this title to steam and in English, and all the work the fans have done to bring it to its full potential. Steam tried to cancel NoAH, congratulations and a massive thank you to the visual novel community for sticking up for this title and getting it on this platform.

name: Monochrome Mobius: Rights and Wrongs Forgotten
detailed_description: A new JRPG from AQUAPLUS, announced in commemoration of 20 years of their hit Utawarerumono franchise. Produced by legendary composer Naoya Shimokawa and penned by Utawarerumono writer Munemitsu Suga, with support from the studio's superb art direction spearheaded by character designer Mi, Monochrome Mobius: Rights and Wrongs Forgotten focuses on the heart of every great RPG: the story. Story In the small province of Ennakamuy, on the frontiers of the great empire of Yamato, there lived a young man with his mother and sister. One day, at the local lord's behest, the young man was investigating a small irregularity when he encountered a girl he’d never met. The words the girl spoke were what shocked him: She told the man that his father was still alive. Seeing a trace of his father in her and resolving to learn the truth, the young man and the girl set out together towards the land of Arva Shulan—a country that doesn’t appear on the map. Faced with trials and perils, the boy chases his father. He meets new friends and comrades who join him on his mission. There will be struggles and victories and failures and partings. The fickle vagaries of fate will place an epoch in the young man’s hands— And one day, this man will be sung of in legends. Characters A young man living in the frontier province of Ennakamuy. Oshtor lives together with his mother Torikori and his younger sister Nekone, and though still young, he possesses discipline and a strong sense of right and wrong. His meeting with the mysterious Shunya gives him questions about his father’s death, and he sets out for an unknown country to find answers. A girl whose path has crossed Oshtor’s by chance or by destiny. Guileless and still with something of a babyface, Shunya's words and actions create more questions than they answer. She informs Oshtor that his father, whom he thought a martyr, still lives, and the pair embark on a journey together. The daughter of Murasame, the ruler of Izumo. As demure and polite as she appears, Munechika shows hints of a warrior spirit. She assists Oshtor and joins him on his mission. A young man who barged in on Oshtor when he was training. Mikazuchi is strong and somewhat brash, but he never bends for anything, and a current of integrity runs through everything he does. A good friend to Oshtor and a good rival too, the two spur each other on through thick and thin.

_childDocuments_.review: Not quite as much as Mask of Deception or Mask of Truth, but it's a fantastic JRPG -- especially for Aquaplus' first real turn-based JRPG! -- and if you made me pick, I'd say it's the best game I've played this year. I'd strongly recommend it to anybody who is either already an Utaware fan or just likes story-heavy, turn-based JRPGs.It's got nuanced character development, great writing, great music, and I think it's accessible as its own story but also contributes a lot to the series' overarching lore. Combat feels fast and snappy, and the difficulty feels just right. Aquaplus obviously took a lot of inspiration from Dragon Quest here, down to having their own equivalent to slimes: ambulatory daikon radishes whose most notable feature is their butts. They understand the roots of the genre and why they work. I could say that this game "feels like a PS2" game, and that would be a strong compliment; it would feel right at home next to games like Dragon Quest VIII, Final Fantasy X, or Suikoden III.The graphics are, for the most part, very good! The artwork is gorgeous, and the PC models and scenery look great. I'm honestly really impressed at the density of the foliage in outdoor areas; you can really get overwhelmed navigating through areas like packed jungles. The choreography in cut scenes is also good and the fight scenes are fun to watch. The elephant in the room is the background NPCs; there have been a lot of complaints about them due to having very low-quality models, and... I can kinda get that, because they don't look great, but most of the time they also just blend into the background. Occasionally you have to talk to one for ten seconds to turn in a side quest or something. I do think Aquaplus could make them look better and still be stylistically distinct, but it doesn't really bother me.The worst part of the game  its technical issues; I hate to say it, but the PC version was kind of a mess on release. The good news is that most of the issues has been fixed and the game is in pretty good shape now.  Just make sure you do  set "Vsync" to "Fast" in your Nvidia control panel, otherwise it will cause certain cut scenes to lock up.I don't have a lot of other complaints, but I will say that while the first four chapters of the game move at a fast pace and are constantly pushing the story forward, it eventually hits a point where the plot drastically slows down.  This isn't inherently a bad thing; the game proceeds to take a lot of time to flesh out the characters and setting while the overarching plot takes a back seat.  If you've played any of the other Utawarerumono games, you'll know what that feels like, but if you're not an Utaware fan, you might end up feeling like the game is just meandering aimlessly in the middle.  Enjoy the opportunity to relax while you can, because I promise that eventually the plot will kick back in and tie everything together when it races toward the ending.And, as Aquaplus themselves said, the heart of an RPG is its story.  That's what really matters here, and this game delivers.

_childDocuments_.review: Any fan of the Utawarerumono series will enjoy this game. I can't say I'd recommend it to anyone who hasn't experienced the series, however.Story: 7/10 - The pacing of the first few chapters is executed well and actively keeps the audience engaged, but eventually begins to feel condensed and rushed in the middle. Fortunately, the pacing returns in the last few chapters to round it all out. My main complaint is that there are some details that take away from the world-building and immersion set by the preceding Utawarerumono titles. Characters: 8/10 - Solid cast and development pertaining to each main character. Although subtle, the story also develops other familiar supporting characters in nuance. Many new characters are introduced in this title, some more well-written than others. Music: 9/10 - As always, the music is beautiful and plays a pivotal role in the world-building of the series. My only complaint is that some scenes that are meant to be emotionally heavy fail to reach their intended heights due to choice of music. Gameplay: 7/10 - Classic JRPG with its own flair. Difficulty: 3/10 - Unfortunately, this game is among the easiest of any that I have completed. Not sure if it is due to the balance changes that were made because of so many players complaining due to their inability to play anything moderately difficult, but there was not a single moment in the game where I struggled. I cleared Hard mode in approximately 44 hours of gameplay and was unable to explore all aspects of gameplay since it was too easy; for example, I used items approximately five times throughout the entire series. Please create an additional level of difficulty so that stronger players have the chance to enjoy the game in its entirety and call it "Denebokshiri." I would love to replay this game again and feel challenged by a higher difficulty setting.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't bring myself to recommend Monochrome Mobius - not because it's a very mediocre JRPG, which it is, but because it lacks many things that made the previous three Uta games compelling. It's as if Uta got rid of everything that made it unique and decided to be a poor man's Dragon Quest. Remember charming character interactions, the political intrigue and the larger-than-life plotlines of the previous 3 Uta games? Let's deemphasize that, the game said. Let's be more of a "true JRPG," it proclaimed. What does that entail, you ask? Trekking in complete silence through miles upon miles of empty open maps filled with copy and pasted recolored monsters for you to grind so you are actually strong enough to defeat the token boss monster at the end of each map. The JRPG gameplay sections were absolutely soul-crushing and are the exact opposite of what I look for when I play these games. The first 10 hours were just relentless JRPG gameplay with a paper-thin, microscopic story. They were the most miserable first 10 hours I've spent with a videogame in a while. Now, I don't hate JRPGs. Some of my favorite games of all time are JRPGs, and that is exactly why I have very high standards for them. Monochrome Mobius is not so much a JRPG as it is a skeleton of one. The gameplay is shallow, boring, and only serves to pad out game time in between story beats. And even when the characters do open their mouths to talk to each other, their interactions don't hold a single candle to what the casts of Uta 1, 2 and 3 brought to the table. Strap in folks, I have a lot to say about this one. Firstly, let's talk about the characters. Monochrome Mobius just has nowhere near the same level of character-writing as Uta 2 and 3. At the beginning, the journey is mind-numbingly boring because Oshtor and Shunya, the only two characters in the party, have zero chemistry with one another. They have no real meaningful interactions beyond just being nice to one another. I know that is supposed to be the point since they just met, but if you'd just take a look at Mask of Deception, you'll know that there are many ways to make interactions between two newly-acquainted characters very interesting and entertaining. Hell, even later into the game when these two start to warm up to each other, they were still extremely boring to watch. I think the problem is that both of them as individual characters pale in comparison to Haku and Kuon. The latter two are just objectively more compelling characters to follow on their own. Slap these two together and you get the dynamic duo that we see in Uta 2 and 3. The same cannot be said for Oshtor and Shunya. Slap two middling characters together and you get a middling combo. But then, I tried to remember what Oshtor was like in Uta 2 and 3, and I remember him being a lot more interesting there than he is here. Well, that's because this game shows him when he was still a pretty boring guy. It is through this game that he gets his Akuruka, develops his Ukon persona, and made the friendships and connections that he has in Uta 2 and 3. Same with Mikazuchi - the game explores his life and his long-standing friendship with Oshtor. Learning how far back these two go together really recontextualizes how Mikazuchi must have felt in Uta 3. All this was quite interesting, but it was still not enough to bring them to the level of Haku and his posse of peeps for me. Haku walked around with 5 dudes, 8 girls, a big bird and a squid. They hemmed and hawed and yelled and bantered. They were practically tripping over one another to make some kind of funny joke or interesting observation whenever they encountered something new or unexpected. Compared to that, Oshtor and crew feel like they're half a vicodin away from cardiac arrest. He and his mumblecore support group can barely keep their eyes open when they're entering mythical ruins and countries that literally no one even knows exist. I'm exaggerating a bit here but that's because if I didn't, I'd fall asleep too. This leads me into my next complaint:Monochrome Mobius felt very low-energy and emotionally subdued compared to previous games. When I played Mask of Deception and Truth, I laughed my ass off during the funny parts, and genuinely felt sad during the sad parts. Those games had this infectious energy and genuine human quality to them, and there was a never a dull moment where I didn't feel at least some kind of emotion. However, when playing Monochrome Mobius, there were points when I felt like I was staring into a dark void. Everything just feels a lot more... serious and straight-faced? Uta 2 never took itself too seriously, and Uta 3 took itself seriously in all the right ways, but Monochrome Mobius is just serious for the sake of being serious. The country is not at war yet, guys, you can chill the ♥♥♥♥ out. Well, the one bright spot this game had in the upbeat department was when the cast made it to Yamato and spent some time there. This was when the game felt less like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dragon Quest and more like the Utawarerumono we know and love. However, it was both short lived and too little, too late. The game had already spent the last 10 hours souring itself for me, and this was just not enough to keep my interest at all. It doesn't help that I already know what happens to these characters in the end - I've played Uta 2 and 3. The character developments, deaths, and all that stuff are already spoiled for me, so I really struggled to find any reason to subject myself to another 30 hours of JRPG gameplay for some story that won't even matter by the time the events of Uta 2 happens. TLDR: The series simply did not make a graceful transition to being a true JRPG at all. The gameplay does not meld well with the story. All it did was introduce way too much downtime in between character moments and plot developments, courtesy of token JRPG things like grinding for exp and running through big, empty maps, etc.. Contrast this to the previous Uta games, where we constantly got gut-bustingly hillarious and compelling character interactions and worldbuilding every minute. The combat sections in those games were also always relevant to whatever the story was doing at the time, and when it was over you went straight back to the story, no BS. Beyond the gameplay issues, however, the cast of Monochrome Mobius is simply not as interesting as the previous ones. It breaks my heart that I could not enjoy this game as much as I wanted to. I love the Uta series. I love the world and characters and stories, and I know Aquaplus released this game as a sort of celebration for their 25 years of making games. However, what I ended up getting was a very subpar prequel to an infinitely more interesting set of games with infinitely more interesting stories and characters. A heavy "been there, done that" vibe permeates every inch of this game, and there was never a single moment where I did not wish we'd gotten a sequel to Mask of Truth or at least something fresh instead of what we got here.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are already a fan of Utawarerumono then you will be interested in the fiction and world building of this game at the very least, that said this game is pretty mediocre with some major flaws. I will recommend it only for those who already are invested in this world. If not then I would not waste your time.Starting with the good, the world building and setting are great as usual. Also the established characters are pretty much true to form, though younger versions of themselves.The bad mainly has to do with three items: the character models, two of the main protagonists, and the jarring comedy. To start the character models are borderline uncanny valley. It's very clear that Aquaplus for all its VN chops and tactics game chops does not have what it takes to do full 3-D models. The faces are poorly done and expressionless. The NPC's are super lazy. The posture of the models is weird, with all the characters standing with their chest thrust out at weird angles constantly.Second, Shunya is just not a good character. The relationship with Oshtor is a fairly creepy. Her character design is probably the worst out of them all in terms of uncanny valley. I just don't find her a sympathetic character or as cute as they try to portray her. The voice acting isn't too good for her either. Overall I find her obnoxious.The second is Halu is supposed to the cute mascot character but fails due to a bad character model. Again it just looks creepy and annoying. Third the comedy is super jarring and inappropriately timed. There are some just flat out out of character moments for Munechika that really destroy her character, which is a shame. The bro down between Oshtor and Mikazuchi could have been funny at times but becomes tedious and stupid.Overall the plot is okay, it could have been better with more exploration of the enemy group and their history. The music is also okay and harkens back to the other games in the series. The RPG elements are okay but the crafting and upgrade system is introduced too late in the game and in the end game it basically doesn't appear again till the very end. There are balance issues also with the last boss which is typical for these games sadly.For those wanting another good tactics game you won't find it here this is a bog standard JRPG. That's not a bad thing perse given the story they want to tell, its just that the execution is lacking. That said if you want to see how Oshtor, Mikazuchi, and Munechika meet and come to prominence this game tells that story. I just would be prepared for some uncanny valley issues with the models and annoyances in terms of characters.

_childDocuments_.review: [Early Review]Expectations matter. Do you expect a good innovative JRPG? If so, then this is the wrong place.Do you expect a good narrative which Aquaplus is known for with decent gameplay? If so, then this is the right place.Aquaplus isn't known for good JRPGs, but for really good and interesting stories. (as in Valve isn't known for good burgers)That's why this game won't go beyond the typical JRPG gameplay. It does try to freshen up the combat system with a ring timeline system, which does add something different to it. However, besides that, it's your typical JRPG. It never goes out of the comfort zone. Is that a bad thing? No. but for some it might be.Is it worth the price? Only, if you like the world/characters from Utawarerumono. (which I do)or if you like Aquaplus as a studioor if you want a good story with decent gameplay. ---Some technical problems/design flaws I should mention:1. The graphics options are lacking in every way. You only have 3 options: -windowed/fullscreen -resolution -graphics quality (low to high)(I honestly can't comment further on the pc port, my pc specs are rather high, so I can't check if performance is optimized well or not. It runs perfectly fine without stutter or other problems, using an RTX 3080)[FIXED]3. The not important NPCs look like ps1 low poly characters. Is it a big problem? Not really, it's actually funny how bad they are. (but to each their own)4. The character models for important characters can look "lifeless". The pupils don't help here. The eyes itself aren't really moving a lot either. The characters only blink when the story wants them to. You could stop in dialogue and the characters would never blink for eternity, while steady breathing animation is playing.--Edited:After playing for 20 hours (not completed), this is my current opinion. The story itself isn't groundbreaking by any means. However, the characters and the world are brilliant. From my perspective, this game seems like a big portion of more Utawarerumono for Fans. "OHHHH!, So that's how this happened in the series!" happens a lot. Sadly, there is a problem. This will be a problem for some. The story sometimes forces the player to go through slice of life story parts that will be become annoying for some. I already played the other Utawarerumono games and already expected this. It builds character and makes the world building more impactful, but this can and most likely will annoy some.Gameplay does change a lot after finishing a certain story part. Additional effects can be activated later on like a treasure map that automatically marks treasures on the mini map. As with every other JRPG, the amount of party members is important for enjoyment and it takes roughly 10 hours to have a full party of 4. With that, the gameplay loop changes. Instead of being on an adventure, you have a base now and you operate from there (roughly, want to avoid spoilers in review)

_childDocuments_.review: Read a couple of negative reviews on here that made me go on the fence but I am glad I caved in and didn't let them affect my decision.First things first, the game looks brilliant on my Steam Deck with no tinkering, basically plays very well right out of the box, this is a verified game after all.Mobius plays like an old-school turn-based JRPG; think Final Fantasy X or any JRPGs that utilizes "turn-based" battle mechanic in general. Enemies are visible as you travese the vast world map, interacting with the enemy will pull you into battle, hitting the A button (action button) will allow you to strike your adversary giving you a headstart if the strikes connect, however, the reverse will happen if the enemy pounces on you.Animation sequence are decent just don't expect Final Fantasy/Square-Enix calibre, I still enjoy the look of Fire Spells (Fiery Net), ice spells (Hellfreeze), etc. Another aspect I appreciate about this game is that once you are overleveled, enemies will start to run away from you, feel free to chase after them; strike them down to gain instantaneous cash, experience points and possibly items (saves a lot of time), though, if you still want to duke it out cause you wanna try out some new skills you just earned or to blast them away with Shunya's spells cause you just felt like it, then just run up against the enemy and you will be pulled into battle, I like it when games give me choices.Speaking of choices, leveling up will net each party member BP (Brave Points) to pump into specific stats, nice, new skills are earned via leveling up, I wish there was a Skill Tree though.Graphics are typical Utawarerumono (this IS an Uta game in case you didn't know), kinda ethereal, bright, basically it looks good to my eyes, I'm not all that fussy and as I mentioned earlier if you are playing on the Deck this one looks good.Story has been okay so far, intriguing with a balanced ratio between visual novel style (with voice-acting only in Japanese) and gameplay but seeing as I am only around 9 hours in, I am not sure if this will change?I also noticed a couple of things that annoys me but they are minor. You can set shortcuts on the d-pad (for deck) and one of the option is to set "Tools" (items) to a shortcut but I think this feature is broken; only specifically the Tools option as selecting Tool assigned to a d-pad shortcut will bring up the main menu still in the Stat page but then the option just go haywire when you start selecting. Meh, I don't really know how to put it into words but it's no biggie.Another "issue" (if I can call it that) is jumping, you cannot jump over rocks, fence or whatsoever, I believe this feature is solely to progress the story. Not a bug or an issue but so annoying thinking I could jump over obstacle.All in all, I am glad I did bought this game and it's well worth every penny as I keep coming back to the game. If you have the spare cash to spend, sure, if you are strapped then wait for the game to go on sale, whether you pay this in full or half you are bound to enjoy Mobius if you are a JRPG and an Uta fan.

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono is my favorite series of all time, and I wish this game didn't have such a weird and confusing name for newcomers who aren't familiar with the series, the marketing wasn't ideal imo... That said, I think this game is a fantastic addition to the series, and a pretty decent attempt for their first time making a JRPG.It is a prequel this time around, set in-between Prelude to the Fallen and Mask of Deception, with the story focusing on Oshtor, with a new heroine in the form of Shunya. It has some pretty intriguing elements from the get-go for a fan of the series but REALLY hits its stride past chapter 3, which is when it completely hooked me in and proved itself worthy of being part of Utawarerumono.The JRPG mechanics here are pretty solid, while I really miss the Chain Attack system from the previous games and don't understand why they didn't keep that aspect as it would work just as well here as it did for the SRPG battles, I really really dig what they did with the Action Ring mechanics. Maps are pretty big and fun to explore. There are some QoL issues, but those get resolved over time, such as the lack of map markers for treasure chests and gathering spots being an upgrade you can get later on in the game, and you also get fast travel and a mount.It has some jank and some technical issues, there is a pretty annoying bug with text not showing up sometimes when you boot the game and you gotta restart it, notably the NPCs here are incredibly low-poly and very out of place compared to the detailed main character models, it can be quite jarring at times, but I got used to it over time and ultimately it's not something that hurts the game much overall. The visuals are otherwise fairly good and I'm even somewhat impressed by the animations in some of the cutscenes, it's not as static as you'd think and makes some pretty good use of camera work and framing.I haven't finished it yet, and might update this review once I do, but so far, it is an excellent game that comes highly recommended for fans of the series, and while it COULD work on its own, I urge you to play Prelude to the Fallen, Mask of Deception and Mask of Truth beforehand, they're absolutely fantastic games and it will make this one hit so much harder.EDIT: I have since finished the game, and written a thread review on twitter you can read here

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of issues with this game that made me pretty much hate it by the end. The base characters and story are fine, can technically go through it without knowing much the of Uta story and be ok but some stuff makes more sense if you do know the Uta story stuff. Though in a not knowing the story situation the ending really sucks.The base combat is pretty by the books for 3d rpgs with the only semi-unique addition being an action wheel that is hit or misss (big miss with it not having some stagger lock resistance. If your characters do get staggered by a group of enemies there is a non-zero chance they can stagger lock you making it so you never get to go again until you lose the fight. It's rare but I did have it happen once.)Graphically it's fine, not amazing and kinda similar to 3d rpgs made in the ps3 era. One exception is town npcs which end up looking straight out of some ps1 or ps2 era game.Ran into major and minor bugs and glitches, stuff from cutscenes visually freezing and audibly stuttering to a ladder animation not ending, me getting back on the ladder to try and fix it only for the game to hardlock and require a force close. Also game seems pretty unoptimized, without a semi-fix from the forums just being in some zones stutter so bad it can induce headaches.This is a bit of a nitpick but enemy variety is actually really bad, except story bosses and like 1 lone exception in the last zone most enemies are seen pretty early into the game with everything afterwards being recolors, resizes or both. Even the optional super bosses are just recolor/resizes of enemies you've been killing the whole game.And my biggest gripes and honestly the reason I'm not recommending this is a couple things compounded. 1. So many things in this game have required small animations that need to play to do stuff, like jumping down a 1-way ledge requires an animation of walking to the right spot and hoping down. A ladder requires a walk up and fade to black animation to get on it followed by a climbing animation. and you do these things a lot, even more when farming materials in certain areas (also areas like the mine the game has you go through multiple times that has multiple ladders you need to climb which really adds up over the course of the game.) Also the pacing of some cutscenes, in an early part of the game you go to a desert, get a cutscene walking in, the walk to a building and get a cutscene of the building. After getting a sandstorm cutscene (that also has a shorter cutscene that'll play every time you trigger the sandstorm after the first time) and finding 3 statues that have mini-cutscenes for each one you go back to the building and do 3 more mini-cutscenes doing 3 actions (one of which is the only use of the jump in the game) afterwards you get a cutscene of a door opening, walk into it for a load screen into a cutscene which leads to a boss that goes into a cutscene, then you walk a little bit to a plaque which then has a cutscene, then you walk a couple more steps and then get another cutscene. This is probably one of the worst offenders of this but it made me pretty off put at the time.2. This has aspects of the previous section but the final zone you go through called the Mausoleum, while cool in concept as a big space of interconnecting bio-spheres you go between with different tilesets and enemies the zone itself almost made me quit the game outright. Basically every door to another sphere has a cutscene that always plays usually then into a load screen (not a long one but still) and some spheres can be rotated to connect doors to other spheres but the first time you rotate a sphere (like every sphere that can rotate has this the first time you do it) you get a long cutscene of the sphere disconnecting form other spheres then zoom in to see it rotate from inside and then doors lighting up if they connected with a final zoom on the "switch" that just moves back to a default position. Every other time you rotate it you just get the spin and then the zoom in on the interface thing.Alone these wouldn't be that big of a deal but unfortunately you got through these zones multiple times, with some paths being multi-sphere length dead ends and have to fully back track, along with rotating the rooms multiple times. Also one of the lowest achieves for the game is filling out the ABLs and the reason for it is a couple require materials from enemies in the Mausoleum and these materials have super low odds of dropping. I took multiple hours trying to get singular drops from enemies and it involved going through a 3 sphere path, then back tracking all the way out and going back in again which involved seeing door cutscenes and load screens 10 times per route and you only get to fight 1 of each of the mobs with rare drops per this cycle. To add to that the game has insta-kill for enemies lower level than you, specifically enemies 5 levels lower that your parties average level and you need to get a field preemptive strike on them to trigger it. This of course has the exception of "big" enemies which are just scaled up enemies that no matter if you're 10-50+ levels over them you are forced to go in and manually kill them which added to the time because every one of the rare drop enemies were "large" types. You should really be able to auto-kill large enemies at 10 levels over, it's dumb not being able to.Much to what the game is it's very obviously the teams first attempt at a normal 3d rpg and it shows. And despite buying it on sale (~40$) and spending like 40 hours almost 100%ing it (I way over grinded and wasted time, some of it was also just leaving the game open) it didn't really feel worth the money spent, the good aspects were overshadowed by the bad for me and by the end I just wanted all the cutscenes to end so I could close the game and not look at it again. Hopefully if the team does make some form of a sequel they got enough feedback from this to fix everything but there's no telling.I just can't recommend the game with how it felt for me while playing it and after finishing it. There's much better 3d rpgs out there either through visuals, or functionality and many that are either cheaper or go on sale for cheaper than this one does. It really feels like a 3d rpg from the ps3 era and not something that came out within the last couple years.

_childDocuments_.review: Just to preface: I really enjoy Utawarerumono. I like the zany characters, the unique setting, and the way that the stakes go from low to extreme at a moments notice. I also, however, like the detailed gameplay, the stories that keep me guessing and, often, surprise me completely, and the heart that the games are made with.MM has some of the things in the first category, and none of the things in the second. It's painfully clear that this game is basically 2 games that were halfway completed and stitched together into a Frankenstinian mess. Everything, save perhaps the voice acting, is halfway right. You'll run around a beautifully detailed character model, while some of the villagers look like un-textured blobs of color in UHD. A cut scene will have an incredibly rendered attack, whereas the next one will have a character falling to their knees with all the nuanced motion of a 5 year old's puppet show. The JRPG elements are the same; like most games they tried to introduce a mechanic to spice things up a little bit with the "turn wheel", but it's clunky, half-baked, and doesn't really add much to the gameplay. Add to that the fact that the fights are ridiculously easy, that character customization is non-existent, and that after a couple levels no HP or MP management are even required. I would forgive all that if the story had me, but the fact is that it was half-baked as well. First, the stakes are pretty low, which is a weakness of all prequels. At no point do I wonder if any of the characters will have a sudden turn of fortune, since with only a couple exceptions I know what their futures hold. Second, there was no point in the game that completely floored me; unlike the game's predecessors. Everything plodded along in a predictable and forgettable manner.  To sum up: If you're not an Utawarerumono fan: don't play this game. It's not a good game. If you are an Utawarerumono fan and really need an Oshtor, Munechika, or Mikazuki fix, then have at it. But be prepared to be bitterly disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: "The heart of a true RPG is the story"Thats the tagline at the end of the trailer for this game, and its certainly aware of where this game shines. From a gameplay perspective, its a fairly run of the mill jrpg similar to dragon quest. Some of the corners of this game lack the same quality that a higher budget game would have, so things such as sidequests, npc dialogue, item chest rewards, enemy variety, etc. are pretty forgettable. Where this game truly excels is in its writing, music, voice acting, character designs, and world building. If you're coming in as an Utawarerumono fan you'll be pleased to know that these aspects are at a similar quality to the visual novel series. The downside is that there is less of it, proportionally. Still, I think existing fans will have a good time with this game.For fans unfamiliar with the Utawarerumono triology, this game takes place between the first and second games of the trilogy, but prior knowledge is not required. That being said I think it'll enhance the experience of this game and I recommend the trilogy pretty highly anyway. You can often find it on sale on steam for 70-80% so I'd say give that a try first if you're interested. If the idea of going through a text based VN sounds unappealing, I think you probably won't end up enjoying the parts of this game that shine and will be left with a fairly average jrpg experience

_childDocuments_.review: Kept me mildly entertained, until the ending.It leaves huge gaping plotholes, ending on a cliffhanger just so you'll feel enticed to buy the sequel in hopes that they'll fill in said gaping plotholes.  Story was pretty much a wreck, felt like a 13-year old wrote it.  Characters were extremely bland.  Combat was mediocre at best.  If you buy hoping for a full story, you'll be sorry.  If you buy hoping for an epic adventure, you'll be entertained for a while.I guess they were trying to model it after the cliffhanger Masks of Deception ended on, but they honestly failed miserably.  With the ending of MoD, we knew what was going on, we knew the goals and backgrounds of our heroes and antagonists, and Masks of Truth expanded on and completed that story.  This game has none of that.  The goals of the antagonists are only very vaguely explained, and they're not fleshed out as individuals at all.If you want to get this storyline just because you liked Utawarerumono, I highly suggest you wait until they decide to come out with a sequel.  Playing this game right now will only leave you with regret.

_childDocuments_.review: The fourth Utawarerumono game you can find on Steam, even though it's not labelled as such   Unlike the visual novel/strategy RPG hybrids of before, this one is a traditional JRPG    However, it comes with certain quirks    First of all, the game looks pretty bad. This is not what one would normally expect from a 2022 3D JRPG that released on PS4/PS5/PC  Now this wouldn't be much of a problem except for that it looks like a downgrade from the beautiful 2D art of the previous games. This game still retains some of that 2D art and introduces a few of its own, but the majority of the game takes place in typical 3D JRPG style maps, and they're just not good in comparison     The game is rough and feels like a new developer's first attempt at making a JRPG (which is close to the truth since while they have assisted with some big JRPGs before, this seems to be their first time making one all by themselves). It seems the game had performance issues at launch, but with patches over the next couple of years, the game now runs pretty well in that regard. I came across one dungeon with some odd frame rate drops, but other than that, it's been smooth sailing    The gameplay itself is what feels clunky, with even the way characters move on screen when you move the left stick feeling a bit weird  This game uses a rather unique "action ring" system for its combat, and while I can respect their attempts at trying to innovate, this system just ends up being a pain, especially when it comes to using buffs and debuffs (Fortunately, at least on Normal, you don't have to worry about buffs and debuffs for the most part)    But then I don't really approach Utawarerumono looking for amazing graphics and riveting gameplay anyway   The story is very entertaining, focusing on three characters existing fans will already know well, and another newcomer who grew on me very fast. It has its issues, and falls into some typical prequel traps sometimes, and goes a bit off the rails at a few points, but it managed to hold my interest throughout its runtime (Though the pacing meanders a bit in the middle). It does a good job of handling certain things that become very important in the Mask games, though some of this might be divisive    However the biggest thing about this story is that it's incomplete  It ends with a very blatant sequel hook, and no, neither Prelude to the Fallen nor Mask of Deception works as that sequel. There's a big gap between the ending of this game  and the start of Mask of Deception which leaves a lot of things unexplained    Now Aquaplus has announced a new Utawarerumono game for 2025, but it's yet to be seen if it's related to this or something new altogether   So I can recommend this game under certain conditions   1) You're already into Utawarerumono (if not, look into Prelude to the Fallen or Mask of Deception)  2) You can put up with some rough gameplay and graphics    3) You don't mind that the story is incomplete and that it may never be completed

_childDocuments_.review: Go play Utawarerumono Mask games first. Could be a starter entry into the Utawarerumono series, but I wouldn't recommend it. Enjoyable JRPG that may yet pioneer a new legend in Utawarerumono history. In case you haven't already noticed from the dozens of other reviews,  And yes, I think you definitely should play the other Uta games first. I rue to say that Monomebi uses the Mask games as a crutch, but it kind of does (at least that's how it feels to me). The mask games enhance the experience of Monomebi by a lot and Monomebi does spoil the Mask games in a sense. Anyways, I quite enjoyed Monomebi (), but I also understand that it's flawed in a lot of ways. You can see a fair amount of reused assets as well as some battle segments that felt more like story prolongment (). I only had this problem with one area, but the PC port isn't exactly optimized, so there can be some extreme lag making the game unplayable. If your PC should be good enough, but is lagging anyways, try to relaunch the game.Personally, I'm pretty okay with the 3d npc models, but I do think they could've polished our main cast models a wee bit more in cutscenes.The story isn't quite up to par with the Mask games, understandably so. Monomebi felt stretched thin by trying to focus more on the JRPG elements of the game while still keeping a decent story. Enjoyable nonetheless, but since this isn't primarily a visual novel, I'll give it a pass since it's understandably hard to balance gameplay and story transitioning into a JRPG style. I really do wish they took their time more for the storytelling. Particularly for The JRPG combat itself is mediocre, but I do appreciate that they let you kind of  combat by instakilling field enemies once you're strong enough. That aspect helps with farming materials, and at some point I ended up way more overleveled than I intended to be, but I play this game more for story than combat, so it is what it is.The English translation was mostly good, but there were definitely a few times where translations felt out of place/character within a conversation accuracy wise. At the same time, there were also places that the translators implied character's lines adding their own flavor text. For me, these implied feelings were a hit and miss with most of them being hits. In the translators' defense, I do think that at least a few of the implied dialogues originally spoken in Japanese could have some more elaboration. Overall, I think the translation was good enough thoughDekopompo clown shoe noisesWe finally have an origin story for Oshtor and co. It's not exactly perfect, but its still very nice to see how these characters came to be where they are in the Mask games even if its an incomplete history... for now.Experiencing the land of Yamato first hand made for a fun experience I couldn't have in the Mask games. This is probably the strongest point of the JRPG transition in my opinion since the world is fleshed out as an experience as opposed to textually. Lots of expansion into the Uta universe's culture and world. We come to understand that there are (Endgame spoilers)Overall, as an Utawarerumono fan, I think this game is great and has a lot of future potential. While this game is unpolished in a lot of ways, I see promise there. Monomebi is Aquaplus' experimental transition into JRPG Uta, and I look forward to seeing how they expand on it both mechanics wise and of course story wise.  This game brings so many new factors and loose ends that make me think of theories and new possibilities for the franchise to expand on, and I'm just craving Utawarerumono again...

_childDocuments_.review: I would not recommend playing the game on hard like I did. There were 4 or 5 boss battles I got walled on for hours, retrying over and over, because there was nothing else I could do. The vast majority of EXP comes from boss fights, and if a character is dead when a battle ends (as was often the case), they don't get any EXP. Level grinding is very tedious and only gives you a marginal increase in performance. Some of the battles come down to just getting lucky with the boss not spamming one shot attacks repeatedly. My clear save says 57 hours, but Steam says I have 67 hours. That was 10 hours spent walled on boss fights. If for some crazy reason, you do play on hard, invest all of your points into HP, defense, and spirit.Game is fine. It's the most traditional turn based JRPG ever. Aside from the action ring, there is nothing to write home about it gameplay wise. Could use a few QoL improvements, like being able to skip battle animations or being able to give up during battle, but it was remarkably bug free for a VN's studio's first time releasing a JRPG.The story is fine, but it isn't quite what I wanted out of a prequel. It doesn't show how Vurai's beef with Oshtor got started, or how Ougi came into Oshtor's service. The story was interesting at first with Oshtor visiting a hidden country to the West, but then the story goes back to Yamato, a place we've already spent 100 hours and 2 visual novels in. Big stuff happens in Yamato, creating continuity problems that can't be reconciled with the VN duology in which Yamato has been an uneventful period. The story is unresolved, which might be resolved in a sequel, but again this depends on there being a sequel, which we might not see for a few years.

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of the utawarerumono series. The game has alot of the same pros as the visual novels, like a good art style, incredible music, and excellent voice acting. Its really cool to be able to walk through the fantastic areas from the visual novels and see old characters from a third person perspective. But the gameplay has taken a steep decline from their previous titles, to the point where continuing the game is a real struggle for me.Going to get a bit ranty from here.Its a bog standard jrpg so far besides their strange turn order mechanic, which could be interesting. Being able to take your turns faster or going up a priority is a cool idea, but the wheel your characters and the enemy move around is based on your speed stat. So its very hard to tell who is actually going to go next in turn order with 3 different sized circles overlaping. Also no real character building choices besides the BP mechanic carried over from the previous game, which is just boring stat attribute increases. Increase attack on your physical characters, and increase intelligence on casters. Not much going on there.Big issue I ran into was buffs and debuffs affect the turn order wheel instead of any targets. So if you use a buff to increase your parties defense it will place a blue area on the circle that covers about 1/3 of it. And your characters will only get this buff when their icon is in that blue area. Cool idea but how are you going to make sure your whole team is affected when a boss uses a big damage attack when everyone is going around the wheel at random times. Also nothing in the tutorials or hints tells you about this.DO NOT make the same mistake as me and pick hard difficulty. Unless you want to just grind out of your mind, encounters give very little exp and even basic enemies can just one shot a key party member because they can attack anyone in the party since there is no system of taunting or defense. Getting pulled into a battle with 4-5 basic enemies and they all decide to hit your healer before you have a chance to act  and downing them is not fun. Boss fighting so far have also devolved into spamming healing items and revives until you can slog through to the end. I finally hit a boss that I cant just use the item tactic so now I need to grind my levels, which is just spamming high damage moves, hope the enemy doesn't just focus down one character, return to camp when MP is low and repeat. There is no real tactics or strategy involved. Encounters also give an abysmal amount of exp, giving about 100-200 xp when I need over 3000 to reach the next level. Also said enemies are level 18-21 when I am at level 15.Not even close to being worth the $60 price tag. Only pick it up if your a huge fan of the previous Utawa games and can slog through a generic jrpg. I can tell theres a great story here and I will probably finish it but I would honestly suggest to watch a youtube playthrough or something to experience it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are not a fan of the Utawarerumono series or haven't played MoD/MoT this game will probably seem lackluster. In this game Aquaplus decided not to go with a grid-based tactical combat system, instead it plays like a traditional JRPG with turn-based combat, 3D characters, free camera movement and field exploration. It seems basic and lacking in depth compared to other JRPG's... BUT for any utawarerumono enjoyers I can strongly recommend! The abundant references, seeing young but familiar faces (& new faces/art for the character names we've only heard of from the the past games), recognizing towns/battlefields from past games mapped out to be able to explore freely, the way they still incorporate visual novel aspects, the outstanding music, great voice acting (they have Char Aznable's voice actor!), and many other smaller details on top of the main story knowing that it occurs before MoD, all these things kept me excited throughout the game enough to forgive the cons of it. A great addition to the Utawarerumono series!

Mobius offer you a lot of skills for characters but you can use 2-3 skills and you will won battle in 80% without any troubles.8. No Vsync. It's really hurts my eyes when image just distorted after camera rotation, ouch. Tolerable, but it's most important setting in any modern game, even indie.Alright, now I can move to PROS.1. Awesome opening. Suara still nailed it. Music overall also is good and sending to you pleasure feelings, something nostalgic-like in some way.2. Story is interesting and this is main reason why I still didn't drop game at all. Plus it's big possibility to look on familiar characters before Utawarerumono 2-3. Oshtor, Munechika and Mikazuchi. Controls is comfortable from controller - playing on xbox series gamepad. _childDocuments_.review: The first thing about Monochrome Mobius to be answered is who should play it. Do you have to be a fan of the previous Utawarerumono games? What if you're just a fan of classic open world fantasy JRPG's? I'd say you'd need to be at least one of those things, because Monochrome Mobius is unapologetically appealing to both. For the fan of classic turn-based fantasy JRPG's from the era's where they had a massive scope to their stories (think 3D Dragon Quest, Xenosaga, Trails In The Sky) you owe it to yourself to give this game a shot. There are very few developers out here still trying to capture that style and this is a great freshman attempt from the studio AquaPlus. It's not totally archaic, it's clearly been paying attention to the past 10 years of JRPG's and makes some smart choices to keep the game feeling brisk (and some dumb choices too). It has a very quick pace to its combat animations that is kind of jarring at first but I started appreciating it pretty quickly. Nowadays pretty much every turn based JRPG ships with a Fast Forward button to help speed things along for people who find that combat slow (I find myself, admittedly, reaching for Fast Fwd quite often in the modern 100+ hours Trails games and when replaying classic Final Fantasy). But MonoMobi avoids the need altogether, with combat animations that keep the flashy stuff flashy, and zips through the menial animations in a scant few frames. The map design is also a standout feature of this game; while the towns you start out in feel like they've been cursed by the god of invisible walls, once you hit the massive overworld it feels like you're breaking rules in the way you can slip through overgrowth into semi-secret paths and out of the way groves with treasure. Sound design is another area of strength in this game, in a way that is just uncommonly great for a JRPG. Sure the music is great (as usual for the franchise), but actually exploring the world feels so convincing with the diegetic sounds of wind as you cross treacherous heights, the cooing of birds and ooh-ing of monkeys as you walk through the jungle, and the chittering of angry insects behind the walls of the caves. It really pulls you back into the environment in a way that other JRPG's may just feel like they lose as you rush to get your sidequests done. And the environments themselves are gorgeous, and feel both creative and grounded in the lore of the game. You aren't going to bounce around a dozen unique settings, you're travelling through a large persistent country but it has a lot to offer. The textures on the rocks aren't going to impress you if you zoom in on them, but the environments are very pretty to take in when you step back and look at them as a whole. As for the bulk of the JRPG gameplay, it's all pretty familiar stuff. The action ring system takes some learning just with how it interacts with buffs and debuffs, and the stagger system seems more like chance than anything, but playing on Hard mode felt just right to me. Big story bosses would usually take me 3-4 attempts, and I'd eventually overcome them usually by refining my strategies more often than feeling the need to go back and grind levels. But Hard mode was pretty stiff for me as a veteran, so I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who wasn't planning on doing 100% of side quests or isn't looking for a challenge. You shouldn't have to go out of your way to grind on Hard, but you should be engaging with all the game's content to get through it relatively unscathed. The game performs adequately, I hit the usually stable 60 fps cap on my Lenovo Legion laptop through most of the game outside of the densely detailed shrine dungeons, but I have heard your mileage may vary.Are there negative aspects to how the RPG mechanics are? It plays it safe in a lot of areas to not have any MAJOR hangups, it's just going to appeal to any traditional JRPG fan but doesn't  have some killer mechanic to hook non-fans. In the exploration, I do feel like the towns are poorly laid out. Beyond the aforementioned invisible barriers everywhere, the game's main city almost feels like every useful part of it is put on the opposite ends adding a good extra minute of running around to any trip back to gear up or turn in side quests. This is also where you'll find the dreaded low-poly NPC's, though once you see the density of the crowds you'll kinda feel why the non-detailed NPC's were necessary similar to the random citizens of Tokyo in Persona 5. One design decision in this game I can't wrap my head around is the stamina meter in the overworld. It seems to just add an extra element of risk when it comes to trying to skip all the enemy encounters in dungeons, but in some of those narrow dungeon halls it seemed risky enough already to try and run past so I can't say I feel it was necessary. There were also technical issues I dealt with at launch, including a couple of crashes, but I was able to get past them and by time of writing the major ones have been patched. Similarly some awkward translations seem to be getting worked on as well, and I hope the developer and publisher can continue cleaning up this release, because the game is well worth it.That's all I can really sum up unique to this game for any JRPG fan interested. But any JRPG fan unfamiliar with the series they should know it takes its time and tries to immerse you with its world and characters and lore before it really starts to kick off the plot. This should also be familiar to any JRPG veteran as "It gets really good 20 hours in!" is basically the genre's battlecry, but Monochrome Mobius is really good from the start once you settle into the rudimentary 3D visuals and start enjoying the characters and environment around you.For any Utawarerumono fan interested, I'd say of course you'll enjoy it as another chapter of this series. Take heed of what I was saying before and don't try Hard mode unless you're in for a challenge, but if you just want to enjoy the story there's a lot to enjoy here. I wasn't too excited hearing about a game led by Oshtor, Mikazuchi, and Munechika but it does seem like getting fleshed out in their own game was just what they needed. The story leans into Utawarerumono's habits both good and bad, but by the end it feels like it's aware of the bad and starts to look at these characters critically. The new heroine Shunya, is immediately pretty likeable, if a bit goofy. But her attitude and role in the story are very well played, subtle but clear that there's more to her than meets the eye as her story develops. Now, in the event you happen to be a fan of 00's era JRPG's and the Utawarerumono series, well I guess it's a no-brainer, buy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd read that AQUAPLUS had made Monochrome Mobius as a gateway game for the series... in that regard I'd say they've failed without question. If you're a returning fan, though, I'd definitely recommend this. While, in itself, there is a lot left to be desired, I greatly enjoyed this game. As Utawarerumono was traditionally a visual novel format, it's slow in the first couple chapters (maybe three/four hours?). Still, after that, there was always something to pay attention to. Many times, having played the other games, I went "Hey, I know that reference!" or "I remember you!" (it's a prequel after all). Point is, while there are gaps in the story itself, there is plenty of new explanations on many things that were treated as mundane in the main games.Overall... relative 8/10. I had a lot of time to play, and thus put up with the games' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so I still had a lot of fun. If you go in with lower expectations (imagine you're playing one of the first games from a new studio), you'll have lots of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It might seem a bit hypocritical of me to give this game a thumbs down, considering that I played it to 100% completion, but I honestly cannot say that this game would be worthwhile for most people.The mainline Utawarerumono visual novels are chock full of vibrant characters who inhabit a world that truly feels lived in. The stories the games tell are funny, serious, dramatic, and always chock full of intrigue. When I first played through them, I skipped sleep to advance the story - something that usually only happens to me when reading books. Monochrome Moebius has bits of that wonder in it, sprinkled very thinly over a vast expanse of nothing. The emptiness makes the vivid and detailed world of the visual novels feel small and underwhelming. So, who is this game for? I'd say for people who love Utawarerumono enough to overlook the bad points in order to spend some time with Oshtor, Mikazuchi, Munechika, and Shuunya (OC, do not steal!). We get some background lore - like how Ukon and Sakon came to be, and the fact that Uluuru and Saraana might be a lot older than they look, but much of the story carries the burden of a prequel - it all must lead to the events of the main story. For example, we can assume that the OCs are going to die, or otherwise go away forever, because they are no longer hanging around Oshtor later. Probably in the teased sequel, if the game ever gets one. It does have a few good points - Mikazuchi gets a lot of character growth,as does Munechika, (Oshtor is, unfortunately, very shonen protagonist coded in this game, so no growth for him) we get a few nods at jokes from the main series, and slashing through underlevelled enemies while backtracking is cathartic. If you know Japanese, go play the mobile game Utawarerumono: Lost Flag instead. It manages to capture the feel of the mainline series much better than this one.Spoiler:

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so this is coming from someone who never played the previous games but got interested to try this one after seeing the trailer and being a fan of anime-style JRPG.The game starts pretty fun and until Munechika joins the party and you visit Arva Shulan it's really compelling. But after Mikazuchi joins at the Imperial Capital the game goes downhill. The story stalls a lot from that point onwards, with a lot of useless extremely long dialogues and like 90% of the time spent in the Imperial Capital, which has a good OST but you stay on it for so long that it gets repetitive lolThe nice 3D from the trailer is also a big lie. More than 80% of the dialogue, including VERY important ones (like the one with Murasame and the Raven's crest), are told through boring 2010-era 2D panels. This is a brand new PS4 game, they could've done better than that.They made the gameplay simple, there are way less stats for you to care compared to many JRPGs. The combat they tried to inovate with that circle thing but at the end of the day it just made it worst and confusing. There are no HP info or any detailed data about the enemies so you never know what attacks are the best/what the enemy resistances are/how much HP the enemy has left, and so on.Also, you can jump. For no reason whatsoever. It's compeltely useless, you can't jump even over rocks lmao. There are no puzzles or anything where you are required to jump either. Really weird lolThe OST in general has its moments but nothing really stands out. The scenery is okay but lacks variety. Enemy variety is good, way better than the likes of Hyperdimension Neptunia for instance lmaoRegarding the cast, Shunya is my favorite despite still having her annoying moments. Oshtor is almost irritating with its politeness, Munechika is just eh (her 3D model is weird) and Mikazuchi can also be really annoying with its "I'm stronger than u all" way of acting. Halu has some great fun lines overall.Difficult wise the game is definitively at the easier side, which I don't mind. You don't even need to grind much and you already reach the point of one shoting enemies at the field way before Munechika joins. Halu makes things even easier for the tougher opponents coming from side quests. You will rarely use items or any of the Buff/Debuff spells (well the action ring already makes them confusing enough to begin with). You will also easily have hundreds of thousands of Sen saved, and that is always buying the more expensive gear. Upgrading stuff is an option but you'll never need it. The only really useful thing added on Chapter 5 is the Halu ABL thing, that is REALLY useful.Anyway, TL;DR, it's an extremely Meh JRPG.

_childDocuments_.review: First let me start out by saying I'm a big fan of Utawarerumono as a whole so keep that in mind. I honestly really loved this game. It was turn-based in a way that didn't feel stale, the music was on par for the series (really good), the story was amazing and fit in nicely with the series and opens up some more possibilities with where they can go next. Graphics were also a massive improvement (No chibi nonsense). If your a fan of the series this is a must buy. If you're not the answer is a bit tougher. Gameplay, story, music, and everything is still very good but this definitely isn't the best game to get into the series with. Most of the characters and general world your expected to know and have developed an attachment to. This gives some more neglected characters time to shine and it does it very well but there's so much "oh so this is how this happened" or "oh they did the thing!" that you'd be missing out if you didn't get the context. Still a great game and if your a JRPG buff who hates strategy games and visual novels you could still pick this up over Utawarerumono mainline games and have a good time.TLDR: If your already a fan of the series you will love this game. If not, not the best starting point, it'll be fun but you'll miss a lot of Easter eggs.
