_childDocuments_.review: The original Valkyrie Profile captured my heart with the tragic stories of fallen souls that eventually lead the Valkyrie in that game to find her own humanity and gain a higher purpose to her fight. Elysium captures that in a great way, the cast interacts with each other and the Valkyrie a lot more, combined with their well voiced audio backstories that you unlock via side quests. Towards the end I felt ready to fight with this team of flawed folks who tried their best - even in death. To be able to lead them on a mission that feels just as powerful as the original; it manages to convey the core theme: No matter how regretful and tragic the einherjars's lives, their still deserve to be understood and valued for their spirit and will. Seeing the cast support and interact with each other (i.e. one character who fought against strict gender roles to be herself and do what she values gets to finally be supported, and vice verse be supported by two other badass women) brought a smile to my face. Especially considering that the society they grew up in were not kind to them, the einherjars still have that desire to do something for humanity. Honestly don't know why they don't just go 'sod it'. but heyho that's why they've been chosen!I quite enjoyed this more small scale tale and cast. Moreover the technical combat system based on elements is a joy to play for as long as the game lasted. When you start mastering the system it feels incredibly satisfying. The subpar visual design and lack of environmental storytelling (collecting flowers are alright but the world lacks any props that lead to historical/narrative intrigue). Still it didn't have to be, to be a meaningful and fun experience, for me at least. No regrets in buying it that's for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, at this point, I would recommend this game.  The graphics are nice, the gameplay is solid, and the story is serviceable, mostly a vehicle for gameplay.  It helps that I have no connection with the original Profile games, because from what I've heard about those games, I would be upset at this "sequel", but in a vacuum, its solid, and with every hack and slash game trying to be Dark souls with its combat, its nice not to have a game that punishes every mistake you make, and is just mindless fun.  Performance has been pretty good, no crashes, no stutter.  Doesnt seem to wanna go past 60hz, but that is more than tolerable.  On the other hand, the camera is horrendous in the heat of battle and you get hit from offscreen an awful lot with no indicator of it happening  If you like non complicated hack and slashes, and can look past the fact that its not Valkyrie Profile, you should pick it up.  The Naruto run she does seems kinda silly for seriousness its supposed to convey

_childDocuments_.review: Having never played a Valkyrie game before this, I'll say it's not bad, just not full price good. Wait for a sale to pick it up.The story is mid and takes a while for anything to happen. Like last three chapters are when things start to pick up. The characters are decent. Honestly, the einherjar are more interesting than the protagonist herself. Probably due to the lore you can get by doing their respective quests that builds their past. Eygon is best bro btw.The English voice acting in this ain't bad. Henry McEntire (Noah from Xenoblade 3) does a great job as Armand, even if it was barely 10 lines. Odin, Eygon, and Kristoffer stand out to me.The world is a bit empty. It's mostly just large areas that you fight enemies and move on to the next large area. There's really no reason to explore or back track save for a couple of quests. Weird design of having a locked door with a chest with a key a few steps away from said door. Why even put a locked door there to begin with? That happens multiple times. Same concept with paths that can only be opened using a specific einherjar. You'll only run into these after getting the required einherjar. The combat is all right. Weapons are similar to Nier Replicant where each weapon has its own unique combos and enhancing them unlocks more skills. Still not sure what raising proficiency does besides locking skills. The einherjar summon system feels good and it's a fun time when you're able to summon all your einherjar at once and mess things up. While the monsters out in the fields are mostly reskins and boring to fight, the boss fights are actually fun. None that I remember had any dumb mechanics or cheesy attacks.Overall: 6.7/10It ain't that bad. Probably not up to par to previous entries but I like the direction this one takes. Seems like things were rushed during development and a lot was left out, like the story. Wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: First, disclaimer: Valkyrie Profile is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. Valkyrie Profile 2, not so much? And the PSP game is pretty solid, cursed by the fact it's on the PSP.I wasn't sure what to expect with Elysium. I haven't beaten the game yet, I'm playing on the hardest difficulty ("Valkyrie") and I'm currently on Chapter 6 in the main story, but I think I played enough to understand what the game is about.It's an action RPG with a heavy influence on elemental damage. Think Genshin Impact but instead of waifus you get a bunch of boring characters. First and foremost let me preface this review with this: DO NOT PLAY ON VALKYRIE DIFFICULTY. Everything is so damage spongy that 999+ hit combos are commonplace. And this factors into various other problems the game has.First, the game looks and  Really not a huge fan of how many locations are 'desolated old castle' which fits the first three areas to a tee. The new Valkyrie look is eh? Seems generic in my opinion but that's just me. None of the music really stands out or anything. It's just...okay.Controls are fine, I never experienced any issues barring it being clear when you can resummon your Einherjar. Which turns out to be a bit important.Gameplay itself, you directly control Valkyrie (As of my time playing she has no actual name) and in a Nioh-style setting you perform missions. While the zones are quite large in these missions areas are locked off to you. As a Valkyrie you have access to various weapons and spells, and of course your Einherjar....Which you have next to no access to early game, and let me tell you, early game is MISERABLE. Very limited amounts of elemental damage to stagger enemies, no Einherjar which not only help with combat but help to soak damage, and no skills to aid in your own defenses, the hardest part of the game thus far is the very first chapter. You have a block (which is nigh useless as you're guard broken after one or two hits) and a dodge (which only has iframes after a skill is learned), with light and heavy attacks.Combine this with a horrible autosave checkpoint system and you're in for a rough time. In the first chapter there's a castle segment involving about ten fights. If you die in ANY of them, you're restarting from the start of the castle segment. Which means 30+ minutes. There are checkpoints similar to Bonfires in that they'll heal you and allow you to save, but they won't actually count as checkpoints, and if you retry upon dying will act like you didn't even save at all. This includes character and weapon upgrades. You will have to quit to the main menu and manually load the save if you want anything to stick.It's like they borrowed a page from Platinum, but didn't catch what made it work. Complete with a rating system after every mission, where you're judged for using items and dying heavily.Speaking of items, hope you didn't expect a shop or any other reliable source for items. Healing items are in very limited supply, as are just about any other item. There's no shop or crafting to resupply: The few treasure chests that don't contain a mountain of upgrade gems are what you get.It gets better as you get along: You get important upgrades like Iframes to your dodges and parrying (And you better learn to parry: Some bosses are next to impossible unless you master that particular art), you get new spells, and you get your Einherjar. And this brings me to elemental damage.The elemental weakness system is the biggest pain. You have four spell slots and four Einherjar that also count as elemental damage. Einherjar are temporary summons that take a portion of your Soul Gauge, depending on how long you set them to summon.  If you max out an enemy's elemental weakness bar, they get staggered and you can just wail on them.Only problem, four spell slots, way more than four weaknesses, and you can't change your Einherjar's element. You are constantly going to have to pause your game to adjust your spells to fit whatever encounter comes to mind. And one of those spell slots is guaranteed to have Heal which both heals you (the only renewable source of healing) and gives you immunity to damage during the heal. It's easily the best spell in the gameThe Einherjar are AI and do their own thing, they perform two specific special attacks upon being summoned (No Finishing Strikes here, sadly...) And after a duration they vanish and need to be resummoned.  It's not horrible, but it's hard to keep track on when you can resummon them, leaving you in a eternal balancing act of making sure the Einherjar are being kept up, and you selecting the right one to bless your weapon with the right element.Combine this with the fact your Einherjar get upgraded depending on how much they're summoned, and it's a bit of a hassle making sure you're on top of it. I'd prefer them just...being there.Overall the game is fun to actually play, once you get used to it, but there's so much to juggle. Balancing is also all over the place: The only decent weapons I've found are the starting sword, and a light twinblade spear. Magic is all over the place as well, with Heal, again, being a must have as you have no other source of renewable healing. Skill wise, playing without Parry (which successful parries gives you healing and other resources) and iframes on your dodge is a death sentence.Which leaves me to the story and characters. I can't judge it fully on this front as I'm not done with the game. I am interested enough to finish the game to see how it ends at the least? It seems Lenneth and the others are completely wiped out, and only Odin remains wounded after the events of Ragnarok. Not even Freya is making an appearance as of yet.It kinda stinks because all the characters are boring? You have Valkyrie, who as a goddess is pretty stoic. You have Knight Man, who is knightly. You have Merchant Man, who I like the style of but is likewise one dimensional, and as of typing this you have Knight Woman, who is also knightly. I do like her design, though.There's also Hilde, who may be Hrist? She has the same exact look, and I do like her design but she does the usual antagonistic thing of 'Oh you don't know what's really happening well now I'll teleport away bye.' And my current objective is getting four McGuffins.Overall I'm liking the game more than I initially did upon starting? I think it's fun, but it's a very lukewarm recommendation for now. If you like Valkyrie Profile I'm not sure if you'll have much to like here. If you like action RPGs there's certainly better offerings, but it's not bad?Just, again, don't play on Valkyrie mode. Trust me.

_childDocuments_.review: This does not follow the same Valkyrie Profile formula as done before~ this is an entirely new concept of play which in of itself is a fun time but understandably, many aspects done before are missed.COMBAT:- The combat is more action combo based solely focused on Valkyrie herself rather than linking the entire team together. While it is still possible to link moves from your Einherjar it isn't always possible to summon on a flash without having to Soul Chain cancel or dash cancel the attack animation.- It is quite difficult to isolate some enemies down. You're gonna need to constantly move your camera to have visual on where attacks are coming from. Some enemies of which have a bit of an unfair advantage if you can't execute your current target fast enough. There is some level of frustration in that aspect.EXPLORATION:- unlike its predecessors, exploration is more linear and when you return to previous areas, you will need to replay the story chapter included.STORY:- You can anticipate what's going on if you read listen into it enough. It's not all that complex but clarity occurs when you also read into the Hollow Blossoms you find as well as reading up on the descriptions of things in "Collections". There were also moments that felt like the character development was too fast or was confusing how it made sense.- Regardless it had a straightforward story to tell and it was interesting to see how things linked to one another if you look hard enough.While I'd recommend it to be played, best WAIT FOR A SALE (DISCOUNTS), because I definitely had a fun time despite the CONS it had, however I wouldn't take that on full price for that same reason.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a lot of potential, but only if it was made by Tri-Ace. Unfortunately Square-Enix thought they can do it better and BOY did they not deliver. The biggest issue is the graphics. If your eyes will not hurt you on console then you are better than me, but on PC the modding community came to the rescue and removed the annoying cellshading outline. They also added PS Controller button icons instead of xbox, I mean, if you are using xbox controller then fine, but not everyone does.I wonder if Capcom is aware that Square Enix stole their DMC game and turned it into Valhalla themed DMC? Valkyrie Elysium is literally that, a Odin slapfaced DMC where Dante turns into a pretty girl (not beautiful but still quite attractive) and all his moves are now unlocked by upgrading weapons instead of stances. Which is kinda weird if you ask me because we still have more souls I mean gems to collect and we get punished at the end of the level for using items that you can’t hold too many anyway, or dying because the boss or monsters were of an element you were completely not expecting to encounter and you have no magic against them.Still reading ?Don’t let me discourage you from buying this game until I explain the biggest issues this game has in this beautiful and rich franchise, beautiful in visuals and rich in narrative, which this game only has ONE of those things, Visuals, and that’s only on PC and only if you grab a mod that removes cellshading outline from the game, you’re welcome, you experience now improved by 80%And that’s still low on the scale if I’m being honest.The game has so many problems with itself it hurts watching. So lets dig into those problems without spoiling the (?)fun.First on the agenda is weapons, there are 2 types, swords and spears, that’s it, need more?Well, hold your horses, which you won’t find any of in this game, because the story is so convenient there are no horses in this game, they died out. I think.So, we have Swords, and Spears, There’s like 5 swords and 3 spears, the amount of weapons is kinda like in DMC 4.All weapons have a distinct Nordic name to them, except the rapier, nords didn’t do rapiers, I have no idea why this game has a Rapier and why it has a Nordic name to it, but know what ? it’s super OP and it’s the only sword you should care about really, you need to level all weapons to at least proficiency F to be able to unlock Einherjar support slots, but this Rapier ? you need to use it ALLLLLLLL the time, that’s the only weapon you should care about really, proficiency SSSSSSSSS if you can. The Rapier is a stupid weapon, it makes no sense to have it in this game, it’s the weakest weapon, and it’s your BEST Weapon in the game, unless they release some DLC in the future that will change this, but honestly even then, this weapon is stupid OP.Valkyrie has access to magic as well, I have no idea why, it’s against the rules, but apparently no one cares. Unlike Einherjar, Valkyrie has more than 4 spells to collect, and all of the spells come in numbered versions. Kinda like Final Fantasy spells in English versions, you know, Fire I, Fire II, Fire III etc. You get it. So while you only get 4 Einherjars, which can only use 1 element each, Valkyrie can cast 4 spells at a time, from all Elements in the game, except water. For some reason.The list of Magic Elements available to Valkyrie are:Fire,Ice,Dark,Holy,Earth,Lightning,Non-elemental.No Water, despite some enemies clearly using it 😉Einherjars, well, Valkyrie Elysium has 4. WHOLE 4 of them.Valkyrie Profile games had like 20! EACH !We get 1 Biribiri boiWe get 1 Cool boiWe get 1 honestly better looking character fitting the Valkyrie trope than Valkyrie herself, and she uses HOLY!We get Jeanne d’Ark, kinda literally. Kinda not, Kinda kinky. Not gonna spoil more than her being a FIRE LORD, or lady. She is actually the most useful one aside from the Holy one.Yeah, cool huh? we get 4 Einherjars and you can actually summon all 4 of them into battle at once, and that’s it. They will buff you with element they wield making your elemental spells stronger, which is cool, but you only need the electric guy for Lightning Bolt cuz it’s the most damaging spell in the game I think. Meteor Swarm is for when you have a TON of enemies surrounding you, but if you let that happen you are masochistic, I’m not judging.Visually as I already explained the game looks great, on PC, with the mod.Without the mod your eyes will turn on you and probably attempt to kill you.I speak from personal experience.But enough about that, is the STORY good?Ehhhh.Not really, especially if you played Valkyrie Profile games, which I honestly more than recommend doing instead of playing this game.The story is extremely short, which explains why they stonewalled it behind a GRIND FEST of levels.I think the entire story is an hour long, I could just play the game again and record it and check after editing how long the story takes, it would probably be an hour.That’s how long the story is, and the game is like 20 casual hours long. I’m playing this game casually and I’m at the end already and I’m 16.4 hours in. Yeah. 15 hours of levels, combat, gathering items I never use and finding magics I rarely use because Einherjar. As for weapons, really, RAPIER Stick to it.I don’t mind doing side quests, Valkyrie Profile Lenneth and Silmeria had them too, no biggie, but in THIS game ?You get to unlock those quests by finding a spirit or talking to 2 humans that are not scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to stand outside when Valkyrie fights monsters. Freaking gigachads if you ask me.But every single subquest needs to be completed separately, which means revisiting the same area up to 6 times, yes, this game actually has more side content than main story, which is weird, all things considered that I did ALL of them and still haven’t hit 20 hours mark. If this was Steven He you would hear WHAT THE HAIL!?! But it’s really how shallow the game is.There are 2 main antagonists, Hilde, and Fenrir, and for whatever reason Fenrir is a SHE.No idea why, can you guess? 😉Of course if you played the previous games you know where the real villain is, and you are correct, however, it’s so downplayed. Just like in previous games you know it from the start, but unlike in previous games, the Valkyrie is stupid. Yes she is made to obey, but she was created the very same way any other Valkyrie was in this franchise. That is the point. Lenneth quickly started to question her mission in Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth, and Silmeria had a completely different experience as well, she was quickly disillusioned. She was incredibly intelligent, so why is this Valkyrie here so stupid the rocks are smarter. Because Valkyrie was so hard brainwashed she doesn’t know better. And obviously by the time she starts connecting the dots, things get hairy.Honestly at the start of the game I kind of hoped this would be a prequel to Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth but NO! This Valkyrie is a new one, created for one task and one only. And she is good at it until Odin tells her to 2 tasks now, and she fails because she is not made for multi-tasking.Creature designs are awesome btw, some of the truly corrupted enemies are magnificent, the detail is insane and some bosses feel right out of lovecraftian mythos. Excellent. Too bad the game is so repetitive you will hate those designs because the only thing separating one undead from another of the same rank is the color representing their element. Yeah kind of a bummer. But if you love DMC style games know that this game has ITEMS, SOUL GEMS, and punishes you for using items and dying, you get lower score, which has NOTHING to do with anything of note. So feel free to use items and carelessly die. BTW you can counter the dying part if you saved recently at a Save Crystal.if you die, go back to main menu, load game, enjoy(?) the battles, and don’t get counted for dying I guess.DO NOT BUY UNLESS 40%-50% disc

_childDocuments_.review: Great combat system, but not much to do when there's barely like 6 enemy types(bosses notwithstanding). The environments are bland. I'm very forgiving of this sort of stuff, but when you got me yawning for going through similar looking areas, you know that this stuff was made lazily.The animations in cutscenes are horrible. The character interact very jankily. I really think they made this game with little time to spare because of it. They seemed to have focused on the core:  a good combat system and a a story that makes sense. Yeah the story isn't going to win any awards, but it's consistent and well paced enough, though the endings could have been handled better.I recommend this game if you know what to expect. I'm a huge VP fan and this game was cool to play. I want to see more of the series. Maybe not worth 80 CAD + taxes, but 50% off would be a good point of entry. _childDocuments_.review: It's alright, nothing too fancy. My playtime consisted of all endings and side quests.Story itself felt to me like a band of adventurers travelling to fulfill an objective, watching them closely get along and that's what I liked the most.The overarching plot though isn't the greatest, there's only so much you can tell with 20~ hours of playtime. Do this, find that, meet this person, until you reach the end, that's pretty much it. There's some hints to uncover later on which are interesting, but it's not the best thing ever. Personally love the combat but it has its flaws, definitely would love to see it improve if the Valkyrie series keeps going.One thing I wished is that the story had some of the very dark elements that you only get to see via text like a story told to the player. If the overall story was as dark as that texts go, it would be more to my personal taste.Overall, it's an alright game for 20~ hours. Sorry if my review kinda seemed vague, tried to describe stuff without giving too much away in terms of story. It's a game I'd recommend, but I'd personally wait for a sale because I'm more of a story lover myself, so to me, I would've preferred a longer fleshed out story as that would give it more worth especially with how they did some of the story telling via Collections.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: Haven't played any other Valkyrie game before. Also minor spoilers ahead.TLDR: Not great, not terrible. Recommended only if it goes on sale. Good enough to spend some time on until a bigger title releases.Basic hackNslash gameplay. Story is as straightforward as it is predictable, there are multiple endings but they just depend on a handful of requirements and the order you play the last chapter in. The elemental and summoning systems are as basic as can be. Elements don't have an affinity towards each other, it's literally just "this enemy is weak against only this". I would expect a system where multiple elements impact each other to varying degrees at least. Maybe even combinations through combo's?Auto-summoning is also problematic in combination with the elemental system:Summoning makes you deal elemental damage based on the element of whoever you summonedObviously you summon someone based on the enemies you are fighting and the element they are weak against.Auto-summoning allows party members to temporarily perform an attack when you, the player, do a special move like parrying or perfect dodging. The auto-summon will then change your damage attribute to something that you do not need or want. This auto-summon can probably be turned off, but you need to unlock them in your skill trees and grind weapon proficiency to use them in the first place. All this makes the auto-summon a little stupid...Lack of NPC interaction, even interactions between your own party are few and far between. One reoccurring NPC leads into a choice for multiple endings, but the connection and story between them and the player is halfbaked and not in-depth enough. The world feels too empty, I understand it's supposed to be Ragnarok but surely we could have a bit more life sprinkled around the areas?

_childDocuments_.review: Thsi is a Decent A-JRPG, that was a fun game to play and complete. But it is not perfect, and while it was fun to play, it was too short. It would have been much better if there were several additional levels, and more expansion on the story - some points of the story seemed rushed, like there was cut content in between sections.Technically, there were several issues too. Most notable was the draw distance being offf, tho that mostly only affected scenes in fields of flowers (and this was only 2 zones). Additionally, The game had issues with stutter in any close-up in cutscenes, probably due to the detail of the hair on characters - it did not need that level of detail for the art style, and was not worth the performance hit. Additionally, several spells and skills would cause some stutter in battle. Overall fps was stable apart from those exceptions.Essentially, a decent game that could have been better.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say that this game is lacking in a lot of ways and it is definitely not what Valkyrie fans were hoping for. That being said, i really enjoyed the game and the combat is a lot of fun albeit being very simple. I should mention that the game is quite short and if you are just following the main quest line that might leave you a tad weak towards the end, so i at least recommend doing some side quests. The game isn't terribly difficult but can be a challenge on a higher difficulty. In closing, i would say that its a shame that more budget did not go into this game, it needed a bit more fleshing out and more complexity when it came to monster variety, skills, and world-building. It is for this reason that while i recommend it, i would only do so while its half off. Here's hoping that Square gives us an actual Valkyrie game next time, but i enjoyed this for what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like challenging hack and slash kind of games like Kingdom Hearts, Devil May Cry, ,etc., then you might want to try this one. The game is enjoyable enough as far as the battle system is concerned. However, the story and the world map design is very lacking. I've played both the Valkyrie Profile PSP and PSX Lenneths, and Covenant of the Plume. In my opinion Covenant of the Plume is by far the best Valkyrie Profile game yet with the wide roster of Einherjar, decent plot, good non-monotonous map design, and enough endgame content to keep you busy after you complete all the endings. I really want to like this game for everything it offers but aside from the hack and slash battles, I honestly feel like the game could have been better. The game's world design may have been intentional as it takes place in Ragnarok, or literally when the world "should have ended", so just about everyone and everything should have been destroyed and/or in ruins. This is at least worth a try if you're loyal to the series, want to improve further in the hack and slash action RPGs because this game is challenging enough, or both.

_childDocuments_.review: Kind of janky game that i wouldn't recommend until you can get at least 50% off. If you liked the combat is Scarlet Nexus you will probably love the combat here. The music is also fantastic and helps bring the bland but cool setting to life. The game kind of gives me Nier vibes sometimes which is a welcome feeling.The best part of this game is that it supports Ultrawide which is a rarity in low budget games from Japanese publishers. I highly recommend you download 'Universal Unreal Engine 4 Unlocker' to unlock the framerate. Simply select the game process, inject 'UniversalUE4Unlocker.dll' into it and then press ~ in game and type t.maxFPS # (It is annoying but you need to do this every time you boot the game if you want fps past 60). Running the game on max settings @3440x1440 with a 5900x and 3090 I get 140-165 fps depending on what is going on.

name: Cuisineer
detailed_description: Welcome to the world of Cuisineer, a wholesome food-focused game where you play as Pom, a young adventurer turned restaurateur. One day, you return to your hometown of Paell to manage your parents’ restaurant only to find it closed for business and deep in debt. The only way to pay your debt is to re-open the restaurant and make it thrive. And to do THAT you've got to go dungeon-delving! Pursue adventure in the world outside Paell, wielding your cooking utensils against giant chickens, artillery shrimps, fire-breathing peppers, and other pesky perils, sipping boba tea along the way. Collect ingredients from the land, then take them home to cook up a frenzy and grow your derelict eatery into a sensational restaurant that will make your parents proud. Just watch out for that lunch rush! Craft Your Own Delicious Culinary Experience Cook over 100 different recipes from around the world, from crunchy Popiah rolls to rich Kaya jam, from double-fried crispy chicken with zesty lemon, to sweet treats piled high with berries. Get the right dishes to the right customers, and customize your kitchen and dining hall with the help of local artisans. A Smorgasbord of Dungeons Explore the Green Ruins, Frozen Fjord, Konpeito Swamps and other procedurally generated biomes that change their size, shape, and resources every time you visit. Master the Flavors of Fighting Knock out monsters and rivals with Salty, Sour, Sweet, Bitter, Umami, Frosty and Toasty powers that unleash flame, poison, chain lightning and other fantastic effects. You can also fight with unique utensils and gourmet gear, like Spatula, Smackerel, Swordfish and Tenderiser! Take Quests to Go From Naicha the Bubble Tea seller to Alder the big friendly carpenter, Paell is full of sweet and spicy townsfolk to befriend. While you’re dungeon diving, be on the lookout for items the townsfolk need. You’ll be rewarded with gold, new items, and even more recipes to take your cooking and adventuring to new heights.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I seriously want to like, but balancing issues prevent me from doing so.First, let's talk about the things that make this game great, which is the art and the music. The art is adorable, the colors are vibrant, the villagers are full of life, the food looks absolutely delicious even in drawn form, and I'm willing to bet that the boba sisters are going to get a lot of fanart if this game takes off. If there's a reason to buy the game, it's for the art alone. The music is upbeat, fun, and hasn't gotten old for me during my 8-9 hours of game time.Now, let's talk about the things that are holding this game back. The balancing. It's not just numbers for combat, it's numbers of progression, side quests, etc.Let's talk combat. Combat feels absolutely great. However, the problem lies with the numbers. Enemies are HP sponges and are able to tank lots and lots of damage. Normally, this isn't a problem if the enemy quantity is done right, but enemies are ultra-plentiful and this means that unless you're wielding huge AoE weapons, you're going be spending a lot of time just smacking enemies to death. Weapon upgrades are pitiful. They only boost damage by a few points at best and take a day per piece of gear to upgrade. This hardly makes upgrades worth it. The traits you can place onto the weapons are interesting, but are locked away behind the "Brew" system which has no in-game tutorials on how to utilize and teach you. You're forced to experiment. Normally, experimentation isn't bad... except that each brew attempt takes a full in-game day, too. What needs to be changed is to ditch the day-requirement for equipment upgrades and brewing.Now, let's go onto the dungeons. Floors in the dungeons are way too long and large. You can enter a dungeon empty handed and fill up 40 slots worth of stuff within 2 floors. Every item in that dungeon can be acquired from each floor, which means there's really no reason to travel too deep. Sure, you can fight bosses on floors 3 and floors 6 of each dungeon, but all they do is drop a treasure chest full of the same loot items you get from fighting regular enemies anyway. But because bosses drop a chest full of the loot you can already acquire, this makes fighting bosses ultra risky as they're a lot harder than normal enemies. If you die in the dungeon, you lose a ton of your items so the risks of fighting bosses aren't worth it. There's a chance boss chests drop equipment, but all of the equipment is 1-star, and can be acquired through the town shop. There's some quests that require you to beat some of these bosses, but these bosses are largely optional as there is no benefit in clearing the dungeons outside of the first time for the sake of it or for quests. What needs to happen is shrink the floor sizes, make bosses more incentivizing to fight (ie. drop higher tier weapons and armors), and give bonuses for clearing the dungeons.Crafting and upgrades simply cost way too many materials. I'm talking like Korean MMORPG-tier requirements. For example, early upgrades and stuff for a cooking station require 10+ of an item (and a stack of an item is usually 20). You churn through stacks of these items like no other for a single upgrade. At mid-tier, upgrades can cost 60 to 100 of an item (once again, the usual item stack is 20). This means multiple back to back trips to a dungeon just to get all the materials needed to upgrade a cooking station once. And there's four different cooking stations. And this are just mid-tier upgrades. What needs to be changed is that the required numbers need to be dialed back to maybe a full stack of items at most for a single upgrade. Not multiple stacks of items.Quests are also pretty badly balanced though not nearly as offensive. However, I still question why a character who's looking to eat some pizza needs to eat 10 full pizzas in order to have the quest fulfilled. Or why do they need an entire stack and half of a material (like adamantine). The reward that you get for fulfilling these quests are food recipes for the restaurant. I get that these food recipes are what the game is all about, but the quest requirements are just nuts. And speaking of requirements, talking to the quest NPC's don't even tell you how many of an item is needed the first time. You gotta either go into the quest menu or revisit their quest option AFTERWARDS in order to know how much of an item is needed. What needs to change is that required quest item numbers need to be reduced as well as letting us players know what is actually needed without us needing to go to the quest menu or talking to the NPC again.Now, let's talk about the restaurant. I would say that for the most, the restaurant mechanics are fine. However, what feels like the game is missing is the ability to hire more staff. Being able to hire some chefs, waiters, and a cashier would be great. Even moreso if they can run the restaurant while you head off to the dungeons to refill the ingredients supply. When the restaurant gets big, it just becomes a giant mess of trying to juggle everything at once. The cooking stations also suggest that they can cook multiple dishes at once, but nope, it's actually just a queue. While this isn't unmanageable, it is very misleading. When you place this on top of customers with different behaviors, from slow moving customers, to customers in a hurry, some customers demanding you bring their dishes to them, and other customers that are trying to dash out without paying, yeah, let us hire some help to manage the restaurant.Ultimately, the game art is cute. That's its strongest selling point. However, past that, everything is hugely unbalanced and until those things are addressed, players are very likely to find this game to be ultra grindy.

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a beautifully crafted, cute, and fun roguelite game. Two hours in and I can see the appeal of the game. It's easy to pick up and play, and does not require massive time expenditures to get "into" the game. The artwork is gorgeously crafted, and the characters are all wonderfully rendered. Pros: + Intuitive gameplay, obviously Hades inspired with the dashing, weapon selections, dungeon generation, and boss fights. + Clear gameplay loop: slaughter helpless monsters for their meat, turn your plundered goods into food, feed town for money, buy better gear so you may slaughter more monsters in the dungeon. + Amazing artwork, clean and well rendered anime style. + Well polished combat gameplay with many ways to clear dungeon. Well balanced progression of enemies and weapons.+ Many hours of potential gameplay loop justifies the price tag. Potential Oversights:Polish:- Day/Night cycle timer runs when viewing inventory. This was incredibly frustrating when I was thinking about how much wood/stone I needed to bring to the carpenter, and it turned out that I missed a third of the daytime time counting wood. - Talking with NPCs triggers a half second fade-in/fade-out animation. It's OK the first dozen times, but it becomes jarring after a while- Controller icon when selecting items creates a large icon that hides the item icon in the inventory. I had to switch back to M+K several times to correctly get inventory items and to see what's needed for recipes. - Several times in conversations, portraits are mirrored in the incorrect direction. Early on, Praline is on the left side of the dialog window, but looks left instead of right. Gameplay: - The naming of days as "sweet, salty, umami, etc." was not immediately clear that these were the Paell version of days of the week. Sticking these icons and a number under the world map threw me for a confusing loop until I deduced they were the icons for the season, day of the week, and the icon for the day of the week. - Having weapons and non weapons in the inventory was annoying. With inventory slots being so valuable in the ingredient gathering part of the core game loop, it over emphasizes how fast you need to get inventory slots from the llama tailor because you will need to carry 2-3 weapons for dungeons to defeat bosses. You can upgrade them from the dragon brewer, but it still removes 2-3 slots from your inventory at all times. - Spatula special weapon uses icon from NextFest, but uses a cast iron pan model. Was confusing until I remembered it was the same special weapon from the Demo. - Why can't we change the location of the cash register? Obviously players will put it right next to the stove so they have minimal movement during restaurant opening hours, but if we don't have to carry food to the customers after it's done, it seems to exist only to force the player away from the stove/oven.Overall, the game is already well polished and delivers an entertaining experience. Future patches will likely (hopefully) iron out the oversights that I saw in the game. Regardless of what complaints I found, the hours I played were certainly entertaining and I can't wait to see how this game's supported in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE now with 30.6hrs of playtime. I want to change this game to recommended because i did get some good play time out of it, but it just needs so many improvements that I can't bring myself to do it. I think I have gotten as much content as I can out of this game. I am pretty much at the end, and its just a tedious gameplay loop of getting ingredients and running the restaurant, really no big payoff or incentive to finish the game. Even the dungeons get repetitive. Honestly, not much else has changed. The only item of note is that i received 3 additional slayer requests, but again the rewards remain the same. An additional improvement i would suggest is better rewards for clearing a dungeon. there is literally no reason to go all the way through a dungeon ever except for the one recipe relate quest and maybe achievements (not sure why your hunting those on a casual game but you do you). Still, thank you Dev team for the effort you put into making this, I hope it is improved and not left to gather steam library dust. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Initial review with 13hrs of gameplayI hope the Devs read my review and take notes of possible improvements, I would love to see this game succeed. If you want a cute little rogue-lite to relax for bit, its great for that but I find it hard to recommend because that novelty wears off really quick. I paid $21.64 for this game, and I think that was too much. I really wanted to like it but it has some glaring issues that I want to share. I will say, i plan to keep playing as I am curious to see if it improves. but at  13hrs i am doubtful.Pros:- Very cute, love the character design and monsters- works on Steam Deck (first load-up is long and some text is small but runs great)- its fun to build and manage your store- good art, day mechanics, rotating shops, interesting cuisine, and lots to cook, and cool furniture.- no penalty for not making it to bed on time, and you can't fall asleep in the dungeon. -most upgrade materials are pulled directly from your box, you don't have to carry them around with you- your health decreasing depending how late in the day you go to the dungeons is a very cool idea. - most customers grab their own food. you don't have to wait on them. - the day ends when your dungeon run ends. no matter how long or short you are there for so plan accordingly. Cons (Very long unfortunately)- there is not much guidance. I was halfway into the second season before the brewery was explain in a mail letter. very little is explained about running the restaurant and the different cooking appliances needed. - there is no way to know what shops are coming what day unless you memorize it. - Combat is clunky. enemies mob you and move much faster than your weapon can swing. (flour everywhere)- quests are mainly boring fetch quests with maybe 4 slayer quests sprinkled in. - tons of cooking items but very few healing or run variance items in dungeons. There are health fountains occasionally but you won't ever get a healing item drop or an interesting weapon mod unless you get lucky/replace what you have. - the weapon variety is lacking. the knife and hammer function the same, the only difference is the special. same with the fish and spatula, and kebab and sword fish. - NPC dialogue is very repetitive and not at all special, even though some of the characters are very unique - its difficult to raise funds because the only way to make money is through your restaurant which really only makes money during the lunch and dinner rush, if NPCs buy your expensive items. You cannot alter your menu. every recipe you have is orderable, even if you want customers to get the omelette and not the boiled egg. So you end up serving 5 boiled eggs and make like 40 coins instead of 5 omelettes for 200. there is no way to change this, and it gets really annoying late game when you really want to rack up cash but keep selling fried rice and noodles instead of chashu ramen. If you could alter the menu that would be a much better system to ensure you are making the cash needed to buy restaurant upgrades and progress the story. - Upgrades for weapons appliances and purchasing furniture can be expensive coin wise (not material wise) which can be annoying considering how much coin is needed for everything and the only way to get it is through running your shop which takes all day and can end up barely making 2K. Weapon upgrades are the worst as they only improve the attack by one point. the abilities and elemental associated do not go up. Same with health, very difficult to raise from the starting amount. - why pay 800 for a royal chair when there is no benefit other than it looks nice. but if you get a window that'll up the elderly visitors. I think that should be reversed or at least give the chairs and tables a bigger effect on the restaurant. - Pom clips through the wall if you turn her bed (more of a bug)Improvements I would love to see- hiring restaurant staff- altering menu- gifting/relationship building with the town (why know their birthday if I can't give them a gift?)- selling dishes on the side for extra cash- buffs from eating your own meals- healing drops in the dungeon/Better drops (I had a chest that gave me stone and wood with one cheese??)- more weapon variance (elements are cool though) maybe more character improvements via outfits or something, not just armor. you'd think the metal boots gave more health than leather but nope. -Better weapon upgrade system (adding slots for mods, upgrading mod vs attack, bigger atk buffs than 1 for 1K coins. - improved character dialogue ( based on progression, reputation, character type, quests completed, season etc.)- Menu alterations in the restaurant- maybe a cooking mini game?- better quest rewards (weapons, cash, reputation gained) - onscreen quest tracker instead of it tucked in your journal. - improved tutorial explanation (maybe increased explanations by chatting with vendors like "what did you want to ask?")- rewards from improved reputation (such as more expensive meals, decreased prices in town, etc.)- ability to purchase materials based on reputation and progression ( i don't want to need one stone and have to make a dungeon run thus ending the day and essentially wasting it cuz I have no fridge room and needed one stone)Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of Cuisineer sounded interesting and I liked the graphical style so I have given it a go.I enjoyed most of my time with the game, though some things feel tedious.After 17 hours, there are few things I wish for or have complaints/suggestions about (I havent finished the game yet so they may be available):1. Being able to employ staff to the restaurant. It becomes really tedious the more you grow the restaurant and even simply having a waitress would be amazing but maybe being able to employ people with different skill-sets to run restaurant during the dungeon runs would be useful and more rewarding.2. Meaningful weapon upgrades. 1 dmg on a fast hitting weapon makes a difference but it is nothing on a hard hitting weapon. It feels like weapon/armor upgrades were just an afterthought and only the perks the weapon can have are important.3. Difficulty of the maps. I have beat first two maps with basically nothing upgraded on my character and I am having a very easy time on the 3rd map. It made me feel even more strongly about 2nd point but the fire map feels over-tuned a bit in comparison to the frozen map.4. Glitches. Not frequent but run ending glitches are still present with the most common one stopping me from being able to continue the dungeon run as no matter how I try to move, I always fall into the water. Sometimes, I am able to use various skills to try to move through the stage but most of the time I have to end the entire run if it occurs. It feels like due to combination of movement and skill, I am getting under the textures or something but it simply shows as falling into the water.5. Time that it takes to upgrade/modify weapons/armor. At the beginning, it feels like it is made this way to enjoy the game more but the more I play, the more it feels like it would take forever to test different builds making me focus on the one I found working instead of diversifying. I must say that this roguelike/restaurant management game is fairly comfortable to play in comparison to plenty of others on the market and I highly recommend giving it a go (even with points I mentioned earlier, it is still worth playing). I will definitely try to progress to 4 stars everything (to my knowledge its the highest level) and complete a "story".Update 1: Added points 4 and 5.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought pretty long and hard about what I wanted to say about this game. I wanted to say positive things because I (mostly) had fun and enjoyed the cutesy visuals and the individual parts of the game like most of the dungeon crawling and the restauranting. I was also deeply charmed by the appearance of so many South East Asian foods in the menu that were given such appetising descriptions. But the more I thought about it, the more criticisms came to light. When you die in the dungeon, and you will with varying frequency, you'll lose most of your gathered inventory including any spare equipment you might've been carrying around. Ostensibly an update was made to let you keep a portion of it. Unfortunately the items you do keep invariably wind up being ingredients of which you already have excess stock and none of the important things that you were down there trying to gather in the first place. You have no way of selecting or swapping out what you get to keep as death loot. Like, I would rather be able to keep 10 pieces of cheese than another 40 bags of flour that I don't really need. The game also punishes you for trying to play efficiently. Opening your shop for a shift to earn some quick gold (perhaps to purchase curatives or pay for a shop upgrade) will earn you a health malus if you try to go dungeon crawling on the same day. You're basically forced to divide your playtime uncreatively by strict days, on top of working around the schedules of your fellow shopkeepers for upgrades.- The various menu assets/items. This is a pretty innocuous issue. While the assets are very pleasant to look at, you realise that some of the first tier items are oddly basic, like sliced tomatoes or a bottle of spice mix. They have no business being in a menu and yet customers will come in and order a bottle of that powdered spice and huff it like that's normal. You get the feeling that the cooking tier system was meant to be more in-depth and build upon the simplier tier one dishes. The sheer quantity and ease at which you accumulate certain ingredients like flour and rice also lends itself to that suggestion, as if you were meant to pre-bake loads of bread or prepare a lot of noodles/pre-cooked rice in advance. At some point, those plans were probably abandoned, but since they had all the artwork done already, it just got left in as part of the menu. - The inordinate amount of time-gating each feature has, from upgrading your equipment to your shop has all the makings of a mobile game. - The same goes for the shallow character relationships and rewards systems which are also mostly characteristic also of mobile games. I did think that it was pretty interesting to see so many randomly generated NPCs coming and going through town, but after a few hours, I stopped talking to most NPCs unless they had an active quest icon hovering over them because... my relationship with them didn't really matter. They don't show up to your house to chew the fat or make requests, they just stand around mostly static waiting to be spoken to. And when you do speak to them, they just ask for things and in return they would give you a recipe. This kinda loops around to my weird feelings about the menu assets. Pom never really comes up with her own menu, she's wholly dependent on other people giving her recipes instead of building upon what she already knows. - The fact that you can't even sell your excess equipment, ingredients, and pre-cooked food, and are wholly reliant on the randomly generated ingredient trading with an NPC  is again another example of the game not respecting your time. You'll spend hours picking up more bags of flour than you know what to do with and then you can't get rid of them in any meaningful way short of trashing them. - You can't curate your menu, which is why your customers still order plain boiled potatoes and bowls of unseasoned rice. The closest you can get to controlling the menu is the private fridge that's given to you after you progress a bit into the game. Ingredients stashed in the private fridge are inaccessible from the kitchen and thus, considered out of stock so the NPCs don't try to order dishes using those ingredients. - Inability to curate your menu makes 'craving days' more worthless than intended. I think some players complained on release that the order rate of 'craved' items were unsatisfactory and the developers increased the request rate. But this still doesn't change the fact that there's no point in hoarding a particular ingredient for a craving day, when all your customers are just going to order mostly the cheapest option on the menu. Imagine hoarding all that cheese, and everyone orders a cheap plate of melted cheese instead of pizza. - The max 30 item per stack limit also feels arbitary and seems to exist only to artificially create a superficial sense of resource management. Again, the fact that you can't meaningfully dispose of anything just makes this a point of frustration rather than any purposeful challenge.I feel like some of these things should've been caught in QC and play testing, or maybe it's because the game was optimised for keyboard & mouse instead of a controller. When your inventory is full, it's extremely frustrating to open it to see what you have, only to have a pop-up window (explaining the item) blocking your view. If there is a way to close it, it's not immediately apparent. All you can do is move your cursor to a corner where the window doesn't block anything.When you've upgraded your fridge enough to get a second page/tab, there's again, no apparent easy way to change pages using an x-box controller. And again, the pop-ups just get in your way. There is *so much* noise pollution during the restaurant-running phase of the game. I'm not even talking about the eating noises, but the game has a chime for everything from NPCs coming in, to placing an order, to getting their order received, to the order being prepared and later being served. Not all the sounds are meaningful and only serve to confuse the player. I eventually gave up and just looked out for !s at the stove. The tabs on the upper left hand corner are also not particularly meaningful and the game doesn't even take any time to explain if there is any significance to them. There really isn't outside of story/quest beats. There are bosses on the third and sixth floor of each dungeon, and the chest loot you get for beating them isn't unique. Even making the effort to try and fight the boss monsters feel more like a 'if you feel like it' challenge (again except for quest purposes) because the rewards are so paltry. Not to mention the fact that because you have to make the dungeon crawl from the first floor each time you challenge it, you just get annoyed after a while because there's literally no reward to make up for the effort and you just get punished for trying since if you die, you also lose all your interesting loot. Despite all of my criticisms though, I did and do genuinely have fun playing Cuisineer. I just think there's so much more room for improvement. Maybe later patches will address these issues, fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: Aesthetically, the game is delightful. Everything looks and feels cozy and friendly and delicious. Mechanically, the game has all the elements it needs to succeed. A hack'n'slash roguelike dungeon crawler where you farm ingredients, then a restaurant management sim where you sell them. The ideas and foundations are well in place.The problem is that neither half of the game seems to know what to  with its content.The restaurant sim appears to have enough depth that it could be engaging. Numerous upgrades, customers, dishes, and cooking stations. But they all play exactly the same, and you never really  anything. Just wait for a timer, then click a thing. There's no skill involved, no decision making, no challenge, no variety. You can unlock more stations to add more timers to click on, but the gameplay doesn't change; if anything, it gets more boring after you purchase some basic upgrades. Again, it really feels like it has all the content and gameplay systems it needs to be interesting - it just needs to rearrange how some of those systems interact. Steadily increase the difficulty and complexity; steadily provide new gameplay elements to look forward to and engage with; make the different dishes you can cook have meaning instead of just being slightly different icons; maybe let players recommend dishes or have specials... There's a huge amount of things the game could try, and I honestly think it doesn't need to do much more to go from mediocre to great.The combat is similarly unsure of what to do with itself. There's clearly lots of content, a variety of enemies and mechanics to engage with, and lots to upgrade and unlock. But it all feels a bit directionless. You just sort of wander through random dungeons and pick up random loot, and that's it. No decision making, very little sense of progress. There's extensive lists of equipment and mechanics available right from the start, but given how expensive everything is, it really seems to discourage experimentation, making the game feel even more monotonous. Again, a waste of great content that could probably be solved with relatively minor changes. Make it easier for players to experiment with equipment; make it so players can deliberately search for types of enemies/ingredients; let players permanently progress through dungeons; make enemies more noticeably stronger or weaker to different types of items, encouraging the player to diversify; and clearly  players how to engage with the mechanics.Teaching is another weak point of the game. For how many different systems there are, you're given almost no tutorials. After 5 hours of play there's still plenty of things that seem like they should be really basic interactions, but which I can't figure out how to do, or if it's even possible. Which brings us to another issue: while the game is very polished and has some good quality of life features, they're applied very inconsistently. There's a 50/50 chance of any interaction triggering either an "Oh, that's a nice touch" or a "Wait, there's no convenient shortcut for this? Seriously?". Once again, simple things that should be easy to include, like indicating where to go to turn in your quest, or letting you click on UI elements instead of requiring keyboard presses.Finally, the game just doesn't give me a lot of reason to care. The main character is basically a blank slate, with no real goal other than "I guess I'll become a cook now." Compare to something like Recettear, where Recette's personality is clearly shown through every single conversation. And while Recette is given a strong narrative justification to go on risky dungeon explorations and push herself to become a better shopkeeper, Cuisineer doesn't. The game does eventually introduce a tax man who provides the main quest of "pay off your debt". But since there's no time limit, and he never comes to hound you for money, it never feels like a serious motivation. You might as well buy all the upgrades and play around decorating your shop before paying him back.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is BEAUTIFUL.  Like the sprites and environments are really great. But at the price I can't recommend it for the amount of content you get out of it. Here's what I need from the game for it to feel "fixed" and worth a positive rating: - Make all weapons distinct enough between types where choosing between them feels meaningful.  Both heavy weapons feel samey. Two of the light weapons are almost identical as well. - Make the Q effects for weapons wind up and send a lot faster so they feel worth using, right now they're totally wasted IMO. - Fix upgrade paths so that upgrades feel meaningful the upgrades as-is are kinda a joke- Balance out the gear enchants better there's effects that are super strong but most of them feel basically worthless. DoT effects need to be much stronger cause what's the point of them if I would have to stop womping the enemies to see any meaningful damage totals out of them? - Ranged weapons and their reload mechanics feel really bad, especially the lack of auto-reload and the delay between an empty clip and it reloading by itself eventually- I need a sustain mechanic for the dungeon. Make sweetness or something heal a tiny bit when you kill enemies with it, since the premise is "take less damage from enemies" it pairs well with a sustain concept. - Figure out a way to make umami actually make sense and feel good to use and explain it properly to the player, I'd love to play around with this umami bomb concept but I've yet to see a bomb even while shielded and it's just like, why bother when it's this annoying and convoluted to leverage? - Spice up the enemies a bit in their variety and behaviors - Figure out a way to procgen maps so they're not so samey and repetitive- Give me ways to get recipes that don't involve the townspeople extorting me for resources every 5 seconds- Dungeons should be more floors, floors should be shorter, there should be minibosses and more boss encounters, and things should get more difficult as you go deeper- Traps and Hazards are boring, including falling off the ledge, I'd remove like 90% of both- Stack sizes and inventory limits are boring, I'd recommend doubling both at a minimum- Heavy weapons in all aspects are just too slow to feel properly viable, and they don't scale with their attack speed, so a push effect and push related damage on a heavy weapon does the same damage a fast weapon does, totally negating the benefit of the heavy weapon doing more damage - heavy weapons need to be significantly stronger and/or scale with their attack speed and other item effects so that they're not useless compared to light fast weapons

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game and I do genuinely enjoy the majority of it. However there are some glaring oddities about the experience that make me scratch my head wondering what the Devs were thinking. I'm not going to deep dive the experience and give meaningless platitudes about the parts of the game that I adored; rather, I'm going to cover the most confusing choices that I've seen and hope for some kind of feedback about them.There is no social system whatsoever. No friendships, no romance options, no gift giving and no rewards to earn. I'm not saying that every wholesome game like this requires one, but it would have really helped Cuisineer in my honest opinion. The character design is really good and the art is super satisfying. Being able to get to know the other villagers to a meaningful degree would have been really nice. Instead you'll just receive requests to complete a task periodically and get a recipe each time. It works as a good way to get new recipes, but I would have loved to have seen this fleshed out a bit more.Hired Help. Much like Moonlighter, from which the game clearly draws much of its inspiration, it would be nice to be able to hire help or put premade dishes into a kiosk or stall outside the restaurant to make money while the character is out and about. Instead, the Devs appear to have made a conscious choice to force the player to only make money running the restaruant. Eating the food seems like a novel idea in a game all about making delicious looking recipes and selling them to customers. You heard me right, you can't eat the food you make. Cooked food is dead weight in your inventory. It can't be consumed or sold after its made. To add another layer to the irritation, the NPCs will periodically gift you food items with which you can literally do nothing. It would be great if you get a food item that you don't have the recipe for and you could deconstruct it and learn the recipe, but nope. The NPCs gift you food on ***Their*** birthday and the only thing you can do is throw it in the trash. Such an odd choice. I would have loved to see a system where each dish that you prepare has different buffs and by experimenting with the food items you could come up with new recipes and then prioritize ingredients for the recipes that provide your preferred effects, but nope. There is no such system.Progression is super lackluster. When you're running the restaurant, you're always looking for ways to improve your bottom line or better the experience for your customers, however the game doesn't provide any meaningful way for you to do this. The recipes that you get are automatically added to your theoretical menu and any customer can select any recipe with no rhyme or reason for their choice. The only caveat here is that, (Typically), lower income customers order lower tiered food items and higher income customers order higher tiered items. While we're on the topic of the Nobles and Peasants, the only way I've been able to determine that you get more wealthy clientele is by raising the reputation of your business, but the progression for your Reputation takes so long, that after 79 days in game, I'm only at level 16. I've never seen a noble person and the most common tier of customer I get are peasants by a vast majority. I've upgraded my restaurant to level 7 and have all the nicest looking (to me) furniture. I even went so far as to buy and install the items that have arrows pointing up with a picture of a noble next to them, but there's no perceivable difference in my clientele. There is no way to customize your menu so I can't force the customers to buy items that I have ingredients for either. Instead they come in with a predetermined preference that you often can't facilitate. Then they just stand by the door and get angry before leaving in a huff.Progression Cont'd: Weapon progression. Weapon progression is super irrelevant with the player needing to grind for an immense amount of time and expend an immense amount of resources only to receive a minor increase in weapon or gear effectiveness. Upgrading an item takes a whole day and requires exponentially increasing amounts of materials in addition to the vast amount of money to get a meager +1 to dmg per level for weapons and 5 HP per level for gloves/boots. The added effects or bonus traits on the items do not upgrade with the weapons either. The only way to get better bonus traits is to find them in the wild or purchase them in the shops for a huge markup in value. Additionally you can use the "Brew" system where the NPC in charge apparently dunks the item in their cookpot before blindfolding themselves and then grabbing ingredients for their stew and throwing them in the general direction of the cauldron, hoping they'll produce an effect. There's a very odd and confusing UI for the Brews that on one tab shows you all the various effects that are possible and then lets to gamble for a random upgrade. You cannot choose the bonus trait you want or select from an option, instead you roll for it and get charged 500+ money the first time, 605 the second time, 675 the third time, 750 the fourth and so on to hope you get the desired effect. To put that into perspective, if I open my restaurant for a full day, from the moment I wake up, to the moment the game forces me to sleep, I can make between 3500 and 6000 money. So each try for a bonus trait eats up the equivalent of 10-100% of my daily earnings. That's asinine. Even after you've upgraded your gear and weapons all the way to max, the fights don't go quicker to any meaningful degree anyway. Enemies from the first area onward are just damage sponges that take 4-10 combos worth of damage to kill; all while dishing out run ending amounts of damage with unblock-able attacks and debilitating effects. There is no option to increase the game speed during the portions of play where your restaurant is open. Much of your open time is going to be spent standing in one place waiting for customers to pick their items or walk up to pay. I would love the option to kick up the game speed during these times to x2 or x3. The tutorial or journal desperately needs to be further developed. Many of the functions or features of the game are not discussed at all anywhere that I've seen. Apparently there's a way to reflect enemy attacks based on some of the bonus traits on weapons and gear, but I've never been able to figure out how. One of the traits mentions an Umami Bomb, but I've never seen or figured a way to do that either. A more diverse and useful journal or guide in your menu would be super helpful. You can't name the business. I may have mentioned this above, but you don't get to name the restaurant. It would be such a small thing, but you're forced to keep the generic name of your parents' business: Potato Palace.There should be an icon or emblem on each of the food items in your recipe book that indicates what cooking implement is used to make it. Another idea for the progression system would be to allow the player to upgrade the quality of the recipes they know. That way you could avoid having to give us a menu with customization options in lieu of keeping the same system with upgraded recipe quality. Food items would ideally increase in payout based on their current quality tier. Keep the star system as well. Honestly the game feels very superficial. Its aesthetically pleasing, but everything below the surface is lacking. It looks great and the initial feel of the game is really satisfying, but the longer you play, the more you see the gaps. If you're looking for a casual gameplay loop and pretty art I still can't recommend the game because the combat is too intense and challenging for players that like that type of game. Its like the creators of the game came up with a great concept, then outsourced the development to three different companies, none of whom talked to each other during the development.

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer presents a visually charming world accompanied by enjoyable gameplay. The art, animations, and character designs are delightful. However, gathering materials for upgrades can often feel like a tedious grind.━━━━━━━⊱⋆⊰━━━━━━━⊱⋆⊰━━━━━━━The diverse range of furniture available adds an extra layer of customization, allowing players to personalize their restaurant. Yet, this variety comes at a higher cost than coins—it requires substantial grinding. Acquiring materials for upgrades and furniture can feel like a lengthy process, particularly for someone like myself who enjoy that type of customization.The gameplay loop itself is engaging, and the combat flows quite smoothly. However, enemies tend to be spongy, absorbing a big amount of damage. Fighting hordes of enemies bombarding you with projecticles from all angles and charging at you relentlessly can quickly become frustrating.While boss battles are fun, they lack any real rewards. Their defeat offers little beyond what has easily been gathered during your dungeon run, making the risk of fighting them and potentially losing your inventory not worth it. Moreover, the upgrades for weapons are underwhelming, hardly feeling like an upgrade at all.On the narrative front, Cuisineer falls a bit short. The story lacks depth, and the absence of a friendship or relationship system makes NPC interactions feel underwhelming. Though doing the side quests unveils snippets of character stories, I believe more could have been done to flesh out the characters. The main character also lacks a compelling backstory or motivation.Despite these shortcomings, I've had a fun time with the game, and so far the developers have been actively adressing community feedback and plan to make some changes in upcoming updates. ˶ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶

_childDocuments_.review: My take on Cuisineer is the same as when I played it during the beta there are essentially a lot of charm to this but in terms of overall enjoyment, do I enjoy it? It's borderline between love and hate. Here's why:There is very little hand holding in this game and if it requires someone to guide you through via a reply in a steam thread; then there's an essential component missing to ease your players into a first time user flow. When there is a town loaded with NPC, in comparison to all farming sim/town there is always a form of mini-map or map that players can refer to. Quest indicators do not appear as edge of screen indication which means there will definitely be missed opportunities for users who do not perform a routine run around town to check. The date/time opening for stores is never apparent even with the signage as they do not POP for players.The initial intro segment seem to have been cut short as there seem to be some semblance of a tutorial but it's like it was left in the dust so that someone who is very verse with the game can play it straight. Horrible if you're new to this genre of game.The dungeon crawler aspect is the only part of the game that feels somewhat intuitive. For a game heavily reliant on the clock, it baffles me why did the clock continue to run as I'm sorting through my inventory and storage. Especially when this is a single player game, opening the inventory/checking the journal entries or any instance when you as a player need to have another UI on-screen should not incur time lost. There's no clear instructions/indicator regarding seat and table placements. There is a specific side that NPCs use to enter seats. The remainder of the game makes it extremely confusing in terms of the button mapping considerations. And it's extremely confusing for NPCs to arrive with orders that the player can't deliver on. (e.g. requesting for a food that is not unlocked for the player on Day 2 is extremely frustrating) If you so wish to get more ways to prep dishes in your store, these are actually tabled in a later quest but without that quest it's very confusing that there is a kitchen/cookware limit when there is still space in restaurant. It's extremely taxing to try to find any NPCs or understand their behaviour routes.There are NPCs traders who swap in and out has no clear sign of when they change or how often they change. The NPC that upgrades your backpack and belt should be a staple NPC present and not one that appears on random.The green ruin combat varies randomly. At times it feels like it's a walk in the park and at other times it feels blatantly broken and you have to resort to kite and fight. This makes it extremely boring as the combat depth that a player have access to at the initial start of the games is very limited and as a player you're subject to having a mass of enemies with different attack patterns hitting you. There is no clear indicator/sign of enemies winding up a move especially for the smaller enemies that may be hidden behind a map doodad or large enemy. The punishment for dying in combat equates to losing an entire day's progress and all the items looted on said day. Whenever this happens I opted to just straight quit due to the saving of the game is at the beginning of each day. This becomes a serious problem for me as I'm at the beck and whim of RNGesus that if I was to venture into a space with too many mobs and there's no safe spot to exit the dungeon fast, I basically lose all time spend playing that 1 Day of hoarding materials for 0 gain. To me this is a dealbreaker and why I would prefer to play other games that cater for player even if they lose (e.g. Hades) or if as a single player game I can resort to saving prior to engaging further in dungeon If i so choose.I really really want to enjoy this game. But fluff over good UX flow and game design considerations have really made me feel otherwise. I hope these do get address in a later date but for now I'll leave this on the backlog till more improvements have been made.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my few hours of play time but cannot in good conscience recommend this game. This game is bad Hades mixed with bad Mystia's Izakaya. The art is cute, the dialog is kinda amusing at times, but everything else is mediocre at best. I thought my few hours of play time was an okay experience, kinda fun, though not something i'm likely to pick up again. But realizing at the end of my session that this game costs as much as Hades does (and over four times the cost of Mystia's) gave me a bad taste in my mouth.You would not want to play this game for the action RPG roguelite part alone, and you wouldn't want to play it for the cooking management alone, so combining both of those into a gameplay loop makes it only very slightly better. The art and characters is by far the best part. But I instantly forgot the music after playing it for 3+ hours straight, which is a pretty bad sign.
