_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: I'm friends with the game devs.Cuisineer's blend of roguelite and restaurant management will appeal to a certain type of audience. People who like the idea of fighting through dungeons to get rewards but hate the reality of losing constantly before finally achieving victory; people who like the idea of managing a restaurant but hate the reality of getting quickly overwhelmed by juggling the various demands of serving customers. Cuisineer's core game loop is finely tuned to give you an experience that feels engaging without being too frustrating. I usually managed to get enough items in a single dungeon run that I could serve customers all day the next day. A day operating the restaurant usually gives you enough money to buy or upgrade something, so the two halves of the game bounce off each other well.Unfortunately my recommendation comes with a few caveats: firstly, if you're after a game with more depth and challenge; this game simple isn't for you. Secondly: the game while functional needs a lot of quality of life improvements. UX is a little on the clunky side; you can't upgrade equipment unless you unequip it first, menu layout could use improvement, it would be nice if you could hand in quest items straight from your stash. The tutorial is almost none existent and the early game is a bit too slow. I'd say the game starts to become engaging once you can seat around 3 customers and serve them tier 2 dishes so the first few in game days are a bit of a slog.The game also has this life sim thing going one where certain vendors are only available on certain days and upgrades take in game days to complete. I get this is part of the cozy aesthetic and designed to get you to slow down and/or plan your errands, it's a valid design choice, but if you just want to get stuff done ASAP then you'll find it annoying.While I said earlier Cuisineer isn't grindy there is one exception to this: weapons and gear upgrades. These upgrades are pricey, need lots of crafting materials and barely increase the base stats of the gear. This issue is somewhat mitigated by the fact that upgrading weapons doesn't seem to be a hard requirement to progress in the dungeons. (I can survive in the second dungeon long enough to fill up my bag with just a set of 1 star gear). The backpack inventory upgrades (arguably the most important in a game like this) are much cheaper and cost only money so it seems like a set of high level gear is an optional luxury.Overall Cusineer has a solid foundation with potential.As friend of the devs: I recommend it.As a consumer... I say wait until it gets a few updates. <.<

_childDocuments_.review: In Cuisineer, you play as Pom who returns to her hometown of Paell to visit her parent's restaurant only to find out that her parents have left on a journey and entrusted the restaurant to her (along with a bunch of debt too). This sets you off on your adventure to manage the restaurant and explore the dungeons to bring the restaurant back to it's former glory and repay all the debts.Cuisineer is a pretty comfy chill game that is kind of a blend of a bit of Recettear, Overcooked and Hades. You pretty much shuffle between dungeon exploring, ingredients gathering and restaurant management. The artstyle is very cute and has a wonderful soundtrack which adds to the atmosphere of the game. If you enjoy games like what I listed above, you will probably enjoy playing this game as well.A couple tips that I would like to mention is that dish tiers are locked behind workstation upgrades, so you should try to gradually upgrade them to be able to sell higher tier dishes to customers. Another tip is to try to find armour/weapons with mods that synergize with your playstyle. Weapon upgrading is quite negligible so if you find a weapon that you vibe with, you are fine with staying with it.I do have a couple gripes about the game though. - First is the weapon upgrading. I feel that it needs some balancing because currently each upgrade only adds 1 attack per star and upgrades get fairly expensive later on.- Second is the arena chests. I feel the rewards feel a bit lackluster (just random materials/ingredients and occasionally weapons/armour). It especially feels underwhelming after beating arena with the mini boss.- Third is the lack of depth with the townspeople. It would be nice if there was more bonding with the different NPCs. The townspeople themselves are quite likable, with Zhenzhu, Naicha and Alder being some of my faves. But unfortunately, aside from their designated roles in the town, you don't really learn much more about them.- Fourth is the brewing system. I am aware that they have adjusted the brew costs to be more cheaper between attempts (previously it used to be much more expensive per attempt) so I am glad they have made that adjustment. Although I feel that the 'feature' that locks the 2nd modifier slot after using brewing on that specific weapon/armour is unnecessary.Regardless, I did enjoy playing the game overall. I've sunken pretty much 100 hours into the game and 100%ed all the achievements. I enjoy customizing my restaurant, although it would be nice if we could also be able to adjust the placement of the cash register and the dish counters. Aside from the gripes that I have noted, it is still a decent game to check out. If this game seems like something that catches your attention, then I recommend trying it out for yourself and explore the world of Cuisineer!

_childDocuments_.review: I can't tell if I like this game or not. I love the art and the characters of this game, but a lot of the issues I have are from the game play. As of right now, I feel like this game could use quite a few updates to flesh it out more and hopefully they'll be able to.The combat and restaurant management feels not great. The combat itself isn't too bad since you can combo two different weapons with each other but it feels awful when enemies are damage sponges. I can't really get to the final boss of the dungeon because by the time I get a full inventory or I'm empty on pots cause it takes so long to kill anything. The enemies that drop rice and flour should probably only be limited to 1 stage. Since they spawn in groups and most customers don't order their ingredients a lot, it feels like you kinda want to skip these enemies after a while. Something I really hoped for was vendor characters coming to the restaurant and eating as well but most of the time you only see like the same 4-5 customer npcs. It would be nice to see a unique character come in and order something or to have a more interesting interaction with customers. Right now it's just move slighting, cook, move slightly to get paid and that's really it. There's some special interactions like someone not paying but it's very rare to see it. Later on in the game after you built up your restaurant to level 8, it starts to get more interesting. The restaurant game-play starts to feel a lot faster. I know the devs stated they wanted to add help with this feature and issues people have so hopefully with more updates the game will be flesh out a lot better.

_childDocuments_.review: The simplest way of describing Cuisineer would be restaurant management meets rouguelite dungeon crawler. Second, most obviously, is that the game is cute. The characters and animations are so soft and smooth; it feels like something you've seen before yet its still entirely unique. The general gameplay loop consists of opening the shop for funds and running to the dungeon for more ingredients to feed your customers and complete various side quests. I'm very happy to say that the music and sounds are still pleasing to listen to despite hearing them so many times over each day.Now for some things I appreciate:The world and characters are super vibrant, and the characters in particular have tons of variety in their outfits and body shapes. As a result, there'll be at least one that appeals to you.The food! A major focus of the game is all the recipes you'll collect to cook in your restaurant, and of course each one looks incredibly tasty, but my favorite part about the recipes is when the character gifting it to you describes it. In only 2 lines they paint this incredible picture of all the qualities, flavor, and texture contained within each dish. I'm always amazed at how they can get my mouth watering every time.The combat, though simple in its nature, has added depth with the brewery system and weapon variety, meaning you can tailor your combat experience to a specific playstyle you enjoy.Additional notes:Here is where I would discuss the negatives and problems I've had while playing the game, that is to say if the devs weren't so responsive to feedback. On release I certainly had issues with the game, which aren't even worth discussing in this review because the devs were surprisingly quick and receptive to criticism that they fixed basically any issue I had on release. One issue I thought I had with the game, and a sentiment I saw shared by other players in reviews and discussions, was that some enemies were health sponges. Though semi-true in the early hours of the game, the more I played and earned modifiers and upgrades for my gear, the less of a problem I saw it as. As a result, you end up having a way of tangibly feeling your character growth, as you slowly grow in power, making you feel stronger than when you started. Because of that, what people initially saw as a negative, ends up being a positive. (At least in my eyes) Seeing the good changes they've made so far, I look forward to seeing what they add next.In conclusion, if what I've described is appealing to you, a cute game with a simple restaurant/roguelite gameplay loop, then I can certainly recommend Cuisineer.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel a little bad about this since I don't really hate *playing* Cuisineer I am more than content to brainlessly while my hours on this but also at the end of the day Cuisineer is kind of largely incoherent as a management/simulation type game? It's fine that it doesn't want to be challenging or pressure the player with a time limit but it does illustrate why this genre usually uhhhh does?Like it has various mechanics from this genre like time management, a day/calendar system, a penalty for going to the dungeon in the same day as opening the restaurant but it doesn't seem to understand why? Since there's no actual time limit to manage there isn't really a need to consider how to efficiently use your time? Just pursue your current upgrade interest wholeheartedly, who cares, pick up a foot ball.Sidequest design is very basic, almost MMO-esque of the "bring me twenty tomatoes" variety. that sounds like a joke but there is literally one like that and they're not really backed up by solid writing or interesting characters either which would be the last bastion of the game given that its wonderful portrait art and cozy style would allow it to lean on a charming narrative even if the other factors don't really check out, but your interactions with the townsfolk are thin, none of them really have a story to tell.Also bears mentioning, it's a very slow paced game? You will grind out cash and materials for hours to get you whatever upgrade you're pursuing at that moment. Cuisineer seems to have compensated for its lack of time pressure by making things just take a very long time and while I do actually find gradual number go up kind of relaxing I'm not sure I should really be awarding any points for that.you know how in this genre of time limit management game there's usually a post-game or NG+ where after you've cleared the main objective you can just keep playing free of any limits? Cuisineer feels like a game that starts there, for better or worse, you start after any real need to understand or engage with managing or time nor is there any real plot that is going to compel you forward at this point. The devs seem committed to making QoL fixes and that's respectable, I will probably plink away at this regardless but I'm not sure any amount of patching can resolve what I perceive as fundamental structural problems in the core gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer? A Delightful Culinary Adventure! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)In the whimsical world of Cuisineer, players embark on a charming journey as Pom, a young adventurer turned restaurateur. The game seamlessly blends the thrill of dungeon-crawling with the joy of managing a bustling restaurant, creating a unique and enticing experience. The premise of reviving a struggling family restaurant by delving into dungeons and concocting mouthwatering dishes is both endearing and original.One of the standout features of Cuisineer is its delightful art style, characterized by vibrant colors, adorable characters, and enticing food illustrations. The game successfully creates a visually appealing and immersive environment that captures the essence of its culinary theme. The diverse range of characters, from the boba sisters to the townsfolk, adds depth to the game's narrative.However, Cuisineer, while undoubtedly charming, is not without its flaws. Some users have raised concerns about balancing issues, particularly in combat. The game's combat mechanics are praised for their fluidity and enjoyment, yet some players find the enemies to be excessively resilient, leading to a grind-heavy experience. Balancing issues extend to the dungeon design, with overly lengthy and repetitive floors, making the exploration less engaging.The upgrade and crafting system, a fundamental aspect of the game, faces criticism for being resource-intensive. Users point out that the high material requirements for even basic upgrades can make progression feel excessively grindy. The lack of clear in-game tutorials for certain mechanics, like the Brew system, leaves players in the dark, requiring unnecessary experimentation.On the positive side, Cuisineer offers a diverse selection of over 100 recipes from around the world, allowing players to craft their own culinary experience. The game's intuitive gameplay, inspired by titles like Hades, provides a clear and enjoyable loop of defeating monsters, gathering ingredients, and serving customers. The roguelite elements, coupled with the charming aesthetic, make Cuisineer easy to pick up and play.In summary, Cuisineer is a game that excels in visual charm, engaging gameplay loop, and the potential for a delightful culinary experience. However, it faces criticism for its balancing issues, intricate upgrading systems, and some design choices that hinder player immersion. As the developers plan to address certain concerns in future updates, it remains to be seen how Cuisineer will evolve and whether it can satisfy the appetite of both casual and more dedicated players.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: A cute and heartwarming action game where you play as Pom. You'll be tasked with collecting your resources to create furniture, upgrade workstations, and cook a hearty meal for your customers. Talk to some townsfolk and see what they have to say. Then the ending kicks in...The game plays well with both the keyboard and controller. I played the game using a controller. Very simple and well-labelled controls that can be seen on the screen and in the control menu. The game doesn't pause when you are viewing your inventory, but there is a dedicated pause button when needed. There are also several options and settings worth looking into to cater to your needs.Pom gets a letter from her parents to visit her parent's restaurant. You'll be required to run a restaurant with a variety of workstations to create various dishes for your customers. Dungeons will provide your ingredients and materials for cooking and crafting. These dungeons are randomly generated but use pre-set layouts per tile. You have 4 equipment slots allowing the player to wear 2 weapons, 1 pair of gloves, and 1 pair of boots. There Each piece of equipment can hold several traits that help tailor to your play style. These traits can occur naturally in equipment or added using the brewing system.Once you set foot in a dungeon you'll be tasked with exploring the area. Defeating enemies and destroying the environment drops resources that you'll bring back to town. You'll be able to hold 30 items in a single stack, giving the players plenty of backpack space to carry what they need. If you run out of health you'll drop your inventory items leaving you with only 5 stacks of items to return. Fortunately, the dungeon occasionally spawns healing fountains, and if you're in a bind, you can drink a healing potion from your belt.It's a cute action RPG. You manage, decorate, and expand a restaurant. A balance between adventuring for goods and turning a profit. As the story unfolds you gain access to new areas and resources to collect. There's a nice balance between serving customers in the restaurant and dishing out pain in a dungeon. On top of all that, it's satisfying to find new gear, and work towards a better restaurant. Tables don't match the walls? Carpets clashing with the decorations? Who cares, your style your way.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a tough decision but, ultimately, I cannot recommend this game.  Several other reviewers have highlighted some of the problems with this game in much more eloquent words than I could probably find (lack of automation, autonomy, no character/relationship depth and time management are some big issues), but my personal dealbreaker (and the reason I've hung it up) mostly comes down to the combat.I really tried hard to understand, appreciate, and respect the dungeon crawler/combat aspect of this game and simply couldn't make it happen.  I find the dungeons stressful and unfun. The combination of annoying enemy mechanics (and absurdly huge aggro radius), huge amounts of the terrain being taken up by 'lava' and traps, the difficult to understand (and even more difficult to implement) gear upgrade system, and the extremely high punishment for death just make it so tedious that I don't enjoy it at all... and since you spend so much of your time in dungeons, it doesn't make sense to continue to play a game where I don't enjoy half of the content.It's a very cute game that sounds, looks, and (mostly) feels good - also worth noting that it's a remarkably better experience on a controller and I recommend it even less on a keyboard/mouse setup - but it just falls a bit flat.  I love the suggestions some of the others have made, like letting you hire help for your restaurant (or acquiring materials).  I'd be so happy to see them add difficulty levels... and/or perhaps level up and skill trees, so you can make tangible progress in the dungeons without having to min/max the perfect gear? With some future updates and quality of life increases, I think it could be great, but it's just *not* in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game.  Even if catgirls and cute things aren't your thing, if you like cooking, food porn, and basic management sims this will definitely scratch an itch.  Some of the mechanics that need explaining aren't, and some mechanics don't mean a whole lot.  That being said, the gameplay is so straight forward its almost a reward to find the little mechanics and combos.  I do recommend the devs keep at it with updates and communication, because this is a special game that is a little rough.  A few things that would make this game great (potential spoilers)- Have a card/food/etc mini-game or something to do during the night, you're forced into nighttime from a dungeon and if there's no new quests to pick up, it's just a pretty nighttime scene.- Resources need to be obtainable by small breakables around town or some other fashion than only being from dungeon runs.  Obviously the bulk would be from dungeons but more options for trade or small collectibles would prevent having to go for a dungeon just because you're missing 1 mushroom.- Nobles need to be introduced much earlier.  They are mentioned in a tutorial at the beginning and then not seen for tens of thousands of gold.  They would be a great boon at early levels.- Selling food and items needs to be a thing.  If not for straight up gold, some other currency.  Maybe some trader that offers cosmetics or furniture for certain recipes or you can sell food to.- Cooked food in your bag has to be able to go onto your bar during restaurant mode.  Accidentally cooking something during non restaurant hours is painful.  Just let us do something with it other than brewing.- Cut the size of dungeons, enemy quantity, and potentially enemy HP by 10% at least.  Dungeons are a slog to even get through, just because you have to run so far.  Its clearly meant to be for opportunities of farming materials, but if you reduced the map size and made the exit room have massive amounts of farming (more than it already does) it would offer incentive for finding the exit. I'm not a game dev, and know that this game has a lot of time and love put into it.  I can't even imagine how much work would go into implementing even one of these suggestions.  There is very clearly a vision to this game and I can't praise the devs enough. The restaurant aspect is really well designed, no game breaking glitches and everything works in a very easy to understand way.  The charm is oozing everywhere.  It is a very bright game, but damn if it isn't pretty.  Thanks for reading this nerd ♥♥♥♥.  Roll with the Tenderizer and dash attack everywhere, praise the Crab ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ risus and their one star orders.  peace im out

_childDocuments_.review: -Link to a video below-TLDRCuisineer has some fun mechanics and an interesting concept, but there are a number of design issues that are getting in the way of making this a spectacular game. Inventory management issues, unnecessarily punishing combat, and lack of incentive to progress in dungeons raises a few causes for concern. While the game was fun for a time, it ultimately felt a bit shallow and surface-level compared to others in the genre. 6.5/10 In Cuisineer, you play as Pom, a woman who dives into dungeons to gather ingredients for her parent's restaurant. The overall concept of the game is quite fun! You get to choose when you go to the dungeons, and they are procedurally generated, too. You can choose to open your restaurant for breakfast, tea-time, and/or dinner, and you can accept a variety of quests from the townspeople. If you look at it as a casual game, you can do what you want, when you want to do it.  However, the game raised my eyebrows on multiple occasions for design choices (and not in a good way). You have such little inventory space to start, and maximum stacks of 30, that lead to frustration more often than excitement. Killing bosses in dungeons is difficult and often not-rewarding as they don't provide unique ingredients, nor are you assured weapons or upgrades from them. Ironically, my inventory was often maxed out before getting to a boss-fight anyways. Additionally, I wasn't impressed by the fact that the second dungeon had almost entirely the same mobs as the first dungeon.  The restaurant portion is largely fun! I found myself grateful to be in charge of cooking and working the register, with guests stepping up to the counter to grab their own food. I was grateful that ingredients were automatically pulled from the refrigerator, and I applauded additional mechanics, such as helping royal guests by going above and beyond or catching people who tried to dine-and-dash. The two major downfalls I found in the restaurant were decoration and menu management. There are certain tiles you are unable to utilize, and certain items (such as the register) that you aren't allowed to move. Additionally, you cannot control what people order. As such, this led to frustration when people were using up some of the rarer ingredients on basic, cheap dishes as opposed to ordering a more complex and expensive item.  Overall, I appreciate this game and I would give it a mid recommendation if I could. It's definitely a + or - type of game, but I am grateful I played it.  6.5/10, get it on sale

_childDocuments_.review: Update: So with the latest patch put out, I would say this game has been raised to the point where I would recommend it. Decreasing brewing costs from 500 to 100 and only increasing future brewing costs by increments of 10 is a very welcomed change. Also increasing item carry capacity from 20 to 30 is a nice plus as well. I will also say there is still room for improvement however. The developers have stated they're looking into the stuttering and memory leak issue as well as adding V-Sync. While the brewing has been significantly improved, I think what would make it ideal is being able to see what mods you will get based on what dish you're using before committing money to it. The developers have demonstrated that they are looking to improve the game and take player feedback into consideration so I think this game will only get better as time goes on. The upgrade and modification system using brewing needs better communication or a serious rework. If you want to change or add a mod to your weapon or armor you need to pick a dish in a certain category (pick spicy soup to have a CHANCE of adding a fire related mod to your piece of equipment), then pay money to see what kind of mod you get. But it's not guaranteed you'll get a mod in the category of your dish and if you don't like the mod you get, you don't get your money back. Personal example: I had boots that had the same mod as one of the mods that was on my gloves and since effects don't stack, I wanted to replace it with something else. I tried adding spicy soup to keep with the fire theme but the mod it gave me was an increase to my starting health. You COULD reload your save for the day and try again but that's not a good solution to this problem. Also there was constant stuttering with character and camera movement. It was alleviated when I switched from G-Sync to fixed refresh rate, but the stuttering comes back and gets worse with time the longer you play it until you restart the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Omg i love this game. It looked like it was going to be a stupid over easy cozy game with not much difficulty and i was WRONG. Its so indepth and there is so much to do. The dungeon crawling is NOT easy but is super rewarding and fun. Everyday something is different, between the NPC's quests, dialogue, music, gameplay... its always different. The running the restaurant part totally scratches the diner dash itch but mixed with stardew?! Plus super cute names, graphics, the food looks so good too. And its so fun to decorate! Really good game - and ABSOLUTELY worth the $25.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: **Update** the new patch is out and it truly does address a lot of the issues many players were concerned about. I would say at this point the most glaring issue us that gear upgrades still feel a bit lacking for the investment but the Devs are looking into that currently———I'm 10 hours into this game and absolutely loving it. I'm truly enjoying the fun little blend of cooking game and rogue-like. Both the game playloops (combat/dungeon exploration and running the restaurant) are a lot of fun.I find running the dungeons to be engaging, though I do have some slight concerns with the beefiness of the enemies but my assumption is that will tune down as I begin to upgrade weapons and equipment. I also find that the game is oddly kind yet cruel upon death. You only loose some of what is in your backpack and wake up the next day at home but be warned that can include weapons and gear, not just ingredients. I learned the hard way after equipping a new weapon to try out and then promptly dying and loosing an absolutely boss Smackeral I had. Speaking of upgrading, that brings me to my biggest complaint about the game: I feel that the upgrade/brewing for weapons and gear (not cooking equipment) cost to much for their returns. It's 1k a pop to upgrade a piece of gear and you either get 1 damage (weapon) or 5 hp (defensive equipment) and that feels like a huge investment for such a small return. Now granted I don't know how much 1 damage or 5 hp will skew things in favor of the player instead of monster because I'm only 10 hours in but I do know that the as of the most recent patch [Dev update #1] they are planning to review, discuss and revisit the balance for the combat system so that may assuage my concerns there.My other concern with Brewing (adding special modifications to your gear) as been addressed as of Dev Update #1 and I find the cost is now much more fair for the returns. I also quite enjoy running the restaurant verse going in the dungeon. Both are very fun, but I appreciate the kind of chill vibe of opening up and serving the townsfolk, it's very relaxing after farming in the dungeons for ingredients and materials. This is also one of the places the game is very kind to you. You can control your pace via how many tables and chairs you put out, meaning you can tune the restaurant portion to your specific desires.Speaking of the restaurant, you can also upgrade your building and all your cooking tools! I actually find the pricing for upgrades on these items to be quite fair as the returns you get for upgrading is significant for the investment. For example, you upgrade your cooking tools twice (about 2,000 gold to do so) and access tier 2 recipes. This brings in such a significant amount of money that you end up seeing a return on these upgrades almost immediately. I was extremely pleased with that.But that also brings me to my next, smaller, complaint: The game isn't clear about how to upgrade your fridge/cooking stations. While it does show in the UI when you are inside the item it's not easy to notice and when you get the piece of mail discussing upgrading cooking stations it doesn't mention what button to use to do so.There are a few other minor complaints I have, such as being unable to move the register in the restaurant or time not pausing when in your inventory while in town but to be honest a lot of those concerns are things that can easily be fixed with polish and feedback. Plus, I'm pleased to say that it does seem like to Devs are taking the feedback to heart as the Dev Update #1 addressed most of the major concerns I've seen coming from the community thus far.All in all while not perfect this game provides, in my opinion, exactly what they set out to do: a fun little romp that combines a cooking game with a rogue-like.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: A culinary adventure with a dash of disappointment.Praising Cuisineer proved to be a challenging choice, particularly given my initial optimism after experiencing the demo. I had hoped that the developers would leverage feedback to enhance the game, anticipating a more refined and polished gameplay experience, especially in the realm of restaurant management. Regrettably, my encounter with the full version left me with a blend of satisfaction and disappointment.Rather than a failure to respond to player feedback, the issue lies in a missed opportunity to refine the game after the demo phase. Cuisineer's restaurant management aspect falls short, as the cooking process lacks depth, reduced to a simple click-to-cook mechanic that strips away the potential for an engaging culinary experience. The irregular restaurant layout adds unnecessary frustration when setting up cooking stations and tables. Additionally, the need to serve food, coupled with an excess of ingredients from dungeon runs, turns what should be an enjoyable aspect into a burdensome and forced gameplay mechanic.Furthermore, the game's progression is hindered by a notable grind, and there's a lack of incentive to swap weapons or invest in upgrades due to the time-consuming upgrade process. The time investment required for these activities detracts from the overall enjoyment and fails to provide a compelling reason for players to engage in these aspects of the game.While the dungeon combat remains a redeeming feature, delivering an exhilarating experience of running through monsters, and the art style injects charm into the game, the lack of UI polish hampers the overall gaming experience, casting a shadow on the potential of what could be a fully-fledged PC title.In summary, my decision to give Cuisineer a positive review is primarily influenced by the acknowledgment that it comes from a smaller indie team. While the game has its drawbacks, including a lack of meaningful progress and a need for rethinking the restaurant management aspect, I appreciate the efforts of a smaller team in attempting to create a unique gaming experience. The potential is evident, and with continued dedication and refinement, Cuisineer could evolve into a standout title. My positive review is a recognition of the challenges faced by indie developers and an encouragement for them to continue refining their vision.P.S. ---- It's worth noting that the idle pose in the restaurant management section makes the main player appear as if it's in a T-pose, which can be visually distracting and takes away from the immersive experience. Puhlease consider addressing this in future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly fun and addictive, if you enjoy Roguelites and food you'll definitely enjoy this game.The storyline and main character's motivations are straightforward, the NPCs and merchant characters are all diverse and attractive in their own way, and each and every one of them will speak varying bits of dialogue at different points of the game that help immerse the player fully into the world; you will find it so easy to fall in love with Paell and its residents. Speaking of illustrations, don't play this game on an empty stomach because you will definitely feel hungry looking at all the delectably drawn cuisines.Gameplay is simple, open-ended, and highly customizable, though lacking a certain finesse. The player is, for the most part, thrown into the game right from the beginning without much of a tutorial, left to figure out the mechanics on their own. Gameplay tips come in scarce, and often show up a little too late into the game by which point the player would have already figured things out on their own, and there is certainly plenty of room for quality-of-life improvements such as a notifier when your backpack is at full capacity, a reload timer, more detailed weapon info like attack speed etc., more graphics options (a windowed mode might be nice), though I'm quite confident that future patches will address these concerns.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable gameplay loop, and the art is just absolutely gorgeous - every single one of the dishes will make you hungry in real life to look at There's a handful of issues with the dungeons feeling a bit in need of optimisation, and the progression system for combat could probably use a bit of changing (I imagine that will come in future patches), but I have really, really been enjoying what I have played of it after 15 hours in-game time!I also have not yet figured out how to kiss the friendly wolfman carpenter, but am certain that I will learn how to do so in the future
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very relaxing and comfy game! Theres not a lot to do in all honesty, you run a restaurant, to get ingredients you explore a progressively more challenging dungeon, there are a couple of different weapons, and each weapon can have up to two different effects (which there is quite a pool to pick from), the max difficulty is what feels like the easy mode on a lot of games, which seems perfect for this game, since it ends up being a very nice and casual experience.Overall its a very good game, definetly recomend it to anyone who likes dungeon crawlers and/or is looking for a comfy game to pass the time!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This is a sad review from me, I would love to recommend this game to people but after 32 hours I just can't.I love the art, the actual feel of gameplay from combat to running the restaurant, but Cuisineer is a 1 foot wide puddle that is 1 inch deep.The gameplay loop itself is so repetitive and grindy it sucks the fun out of what should be a great game.I have upgraded my restaurant far enough to get better paying customers and I still only need 10 chairs to keep up during rushes. I buy items to attract more customers but it doesn't seem to do anything. My restaurant is mostly empty floor because you just don't need to use all of the space.I am decent at the combat but have found the best method to dealing with enemies is kiting one at a time, otherwise you are just dodging ranged enemies attacks, it makes dungeon runs take so much time as if you die you lose most of what you've collected. This game does not incentivize diving deeper into the dungeons as the rewards deeper in are not worth the risk of losing most of your items.Upgrading ANYTHING is a slow chore capped at waiting a day to upgrade ONE weapon/armor at a time and two days upgrading your restaurant.There are other issues I have with the game but I feel I have gone on long enough. In short, this game is worth 10 bucks tops, there just isn't enough content and what content there is, is bloated with artificial time waste to keep you playing longer.4/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Love this!!! dungeon-crawling mixed with restaurant management in the most delightful way. You go to dungeons to fight cute monsters and collect ingredients, then head back to your restaurant to cook up delicious dishes. It's quite addictive. The art is so goooood~ all the dishes are mouthwatering, especially the crab meals. I LOVE CRABS!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of the ‘dungeon crawling in order to maintain resources and taking care of your main hub’ appeal that Cult Of The Lamb does, and it scratches an itch in my brain that loves that game but has played it to near exhaustion and was looking for something similar. That plus a very cute artstyle and delicious food portraits makes it a nice aesthetic experience. That said, this game is lacking in areas. The in game goals of repaying your debt have no deadline despite being stated otherwise, which on the one hand lets you take the game at your own pace but also makes it feel incredibly sluggish when there’s no sense of urgency. The restaurant tending portion can begin to feel repetitive at points if you just want to make money and your customers keep ordering the cheapest dishes. And the resource management doesn’t feel as tight compared to again, Cult Of The Lamb.I’d say to get this game only if it goes on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: To say that Cuisineer is an enjoyable cozy game is like saying the sun is hot. I'm not sure if its inner wannabe chef or something else, but this game speaks to me. It's easy to understand and grasp gameplay cycle is a balm to my busy work/life disaster zone. You collect ingredients, you run your diner, you upgrade your place and gear, and then repeat. While not ground breaking, the combat is a joy even when it starts to feel a tad tedious. You'll face laser beam blasting shrimp, flame breathing peppers, sword wielding crabs, exploding coconuts, angry leafy greens and so much more. You'll also have a unique arsenal to fight with; such as, spatulas, meat tenderizers, exploding egg timers, and a "Smack"-rel. I would have loved to customize my own character, but Cuisineer sates my appetite for such things by letting me customize the interior of my diner with different furnishings. The weakest part of the game is its story. It's fairly simple and there's not much to grip onto. That said, the writing itself is lovely and shines through in your interactions with other towns folk. I love Cuisineer and I think you'll love it also. It's at least worth a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review I have most of the achievements and have made it to the end of the game. Meaning that I've seen all the content the game has to offer.My review of Cuisineer is a bittersweet one. While I'm happy with my experience and can appreciate the hard work put in - I'm constantly reminded of where the game falls short as I played it.For those who are considering playing, enjoy it. I had 50 hours of casual fun where I didn't have to think so much and that is my preferred game. However, keep these healthy expectations in mind so you're not wishing for more than what Cuisineer can provide.I love all of these characters. None of them really listen to you and there are no dialogue options. Yet most of them are charming, while others don't have much to them at all. I really wanted to see more of what they had to say. But most of their dialogues repeat and there's not much, if any, character development at all. The biggest downside of the game for me.At first it's a little odd to get used to. It can be challenging if you play on the normal difficulty. But most of the time when you're scouring a dungeon it's not too bad. That's until you get to some of the bosses. To be brief, 90% of the time it's casual yet engaging enough to enjoy. The other 10% is dedicated to random moments where there's a lot of annoying enemies and the bosses at the end where there is a large difficulty spike. I managed to stay on normal difficulty (the highest one) but man did I not like those moments.With any rogue-like you can upgrade many things. Also you can cook. I'm being vague on purpose but for good reason. It's not that complicated and figuring everything on your own was one of the most rewarding parts of the game for me. Just don't get anxious about it, take your time, you're not on a time limit.It's beautiful you will recognize a few color pallet swaps, though all mobs are unique.You cannot change the appearance of your character, but you can customize some parts of your home. It's nothing too in-depth and there's not much if any benefit besides self satisfaction. I do wish I could've done more.After completing the game - I do not have the same urge with similar titles to play it over again. Not today, tomorrow, or even a year from now. It's a one run experience for me. That would change instantly if the Steam Workshop was available for this game - which it's not.Final thoughts: I wanted more out of this game - it feels half-baked. Yet I would still recommend it to those who are interested as I really enjoyed the game. I would love to see what another year of development could've done to make it one of my favorite games in this unique genre. Though I don't really see the developers putting that work in. The last update was in April that made some quality of life changes but they didn't signal that this was a work-in-progress title.For those who played:
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Hades meets Overcooked with a little bit of Animal Crossing sprinkled on top of it. Cuisineer is a refreshing roguelite that quite literally reinvigorated my love for gaming. For the past couple of months, I've been struggling to find a game that could keep me hooked for hours on end. Often, I would find myself dropping a game after 2-3 hours. Not with Cuisineer.Managing the restaurant and crawling through the dungeons is a lot of fun. Enemy variety is good enough and some designs are even kind of clever. The dishes look absolutely mouth-watering and the overall artstyle in this game is beautiful. The music sounds very Genshin-esque, which to me personally makes it feel nostalgic. Now for the negatives that this game unfortunately suffers from. As many have already stated, the enemies in this game are absolute sponges in terms of how much damage they take before dying. It just takes way too long to kill even a tiny, lowly creature and it unfortunately makes the combat feel less smooth and more frustrating at times. For me, that's really the biggest downside of Cuisineer. I honestly don't understand the complaints about the game not having a friendship or romance system because I think this game is - at its core - still more an action roguelike than a cozy game. It would be interesting if they eventually added such a thing as DLC, but I don't personally feel like it's necessary. All in all, Cuisineer is on the more fun side of games I've played this year - and that is coming from someone who doesn't really play wholesome games. I'd give it a solid 7.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: It's like moonlighter. However, instead of owning a item shop, you own a restaurant. The general idea is you can either open your shop all day or open your shop from morning til lunch rush is over and then go spelunking. You collect ingredients from randomly generated instances and use them to make dishes for the customers. So yes it is a dungeon crawler and just like any dungeon crawler games, it does not tell you what to do. So it can be a bit confusing. One thing that surprised me is that I thought I would be making dishes, but it's just one of those queue crafting mechanic. So basically for the restaurant it's just queue customers recipe, let the dish make itself, customers serve themselves once its ready and lastly I ring them up.The game is cute, but don't expect there to be rapporting (can't build relationship). There are a lot of decorations to work with for your restaurant. And yes going into the dungeon is a must to get your ingredients. You can set the difficulty to "BLAND" once in game to make the fighting easier.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: The artwork is great and very cute. But unfortunately I think there's some pacing issues in this game. We spent about 20 mins for each of the "restaurant" session and honestly my GF almost fell asleep and I'm already asleep. Perhaps the devs can draw some inspiration from Dave the Diver. I'm pretty sure the devs can work it out through some balance patches!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Very relaxing and smooth gameplay. Currently loving the game and I really recommend the game if you like games like Rune Factory and Stardew Valley. I got it mainly because the game was from xseed and they always make really good games when it comes to farming progression and management games like story of seasons. I'm liking the combat style a lot and the restaurant management feels great. I either go out to collect materials for my house/restaurant or I'm staying in the village and serving people.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Whatever I paid for this, it was too much. I'm very picky about the games I keep, so it speaks volumes that I went from being charmed enough to keep this game to deeply regretting it within so few total hours of game play.I have the same complaints as the other negative reviews - gorgeous design is the only positive aspect; all other aspects are severely lacking or deeply annoying. Only a few hours in and I'm already bored of the quest-dungeon-restaurant loop. Nothing gives you any sense of achievement or progression, everything is so tedious. And after dying three times in a row in the second floor of the dungeon and losing all my relevant inventory, I'm rage-quitting forever. This sort of game should be chill, or at least be super rewarding. This is neither. It is punishing and exhausting in all aspects. As another reviewer perfectly put it: "too hard for a casual game."
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really wanted to like this game. It has everything I love: dungeoneering, cooking, crafting, I was so excited to get to play it. But the actual game is really disappointing. It feels unpolished. The tutorials are scant, and it's very hard to figure out how to do stuff like set up your restaurant. I finally got it through trial and error, but there's no feedback to tell you what you're doing wrong. (There's a limit to the number of cooking stations you can have, but if you try to put more down, the game doesn't tell you why you can't, it just prevents you.) A bunch of little things feel wrong. When you close the restaurant, it doesn't let your last customers finish up, so you have to time things very carefully not to waste a plate or miss out on a payment. Which is a little thing, but it's Quality of Life and it's frustrating. The dungeons are bland, the enemies feel very repetitive. I desperately want to increase my storage capacity to make dungeoneering more efficient, but nothing in the game has told me how to do that. There's no obvious way to reserve ingredients, so if you stash stuff that you need for a quest, people will order it and use it up.Compared to a game like Dave the Diver, that has really similar systems, the difference is very obvious. In DtD, you get the sense that every system was endlessly fussed over. Everything feels polished and smooth. Clear and easy to interact with. Even something dumb like having the characters talk about why the ocean reconfigures itself every time you go in makes the game feel more real. Here it's just like "Oh, go check out the dungeon." and that's it. The game doesn't feel alive.I'm bummed, because the art is cute and the basic gameplay is ok. But right now, this doesn't feel finished and the experience isn't great.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun for the first few hours but then it falls off quickly.Everyday you have to decide if you want to stock up and gather ingredients or make money with your restaurant, because it's not possible to get both. Was expecting the BFF to help out in the restaurant so you earn some money while you are gone but that is not the case. She helps you out by standing around the town like any other NPC.You can't sell equipment or ingredients you have found while adventuring which would bring a huge change for me.That way I can atleast gather some stuff and earn a bit of gold.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this a lot more than expected. Starts off with your parents literally ditching the country and leave you with their failing, debt-ridden restaurant. That dialogue alone gave me a lot of hope on how the game was going to go. Tax man shows up and then you go murder the forest creatures to pay off your debt while serving restaurant patrons bottles of spice that they asked for AND will eat right in front of you. What a wild ride it was watching people come in to order a $98 glass of water.The game itself has a good blend and it's something I didn't know I needed. It gave me a lite version of Plate Up along with a casual Hades. Multiple difficultly levels to adjust to anyone's play style. The scaling was pretty consistent overall but I did find the restaurant pre-level 8 was painfully boring. An adjustment could be made there to make that less mind numbing. Overall I really liked the dungeon crawling aspect too. A decent variety of creatures to spatula to death and a lot of available resources to help you with your other upgrades. Artwork was adorable and the character designs themselves were good.Honestly if they made another one of these, I'd be pretty happy. If I had to describe it, it was a more involved casual game. Enough to keep you engaged, but not enough that you felt like one wrong choice was going to end up with the whole village burning down.Around a 7/10 for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I really do want like this game but there is to many things that just add up to be annoying. 1. the restaurant part of the game feels more like a mobile game with how little you have to do. I had a hard time not falling asleep2. So many of the enemies are just damage sponges and swarm you. If they wanted to make a musou game the mobs need to be easy to kill3. I wouldn't mind the enemy sponges or even the swarming if the weapon upgrades meant anything. it costs an absurd amount of money to add 1 damage and then you have to wait a day. Imagine someone takes your money in promise of an upgrade and all they do is look at and say done
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: You get introduced to all weapons within the first few dungeon runs (even if you don't make it that far in) and the only combat element that offers some variety are modifiers which are difficult to obtain early game as they are RNG-based and, even when you find something you think you'll like, it will take you another day of waiting for it to complete so you can test it. Depending on the weapons of your choosing the gameplay will feel more or less clunky overall but I didn't mind it. Additionally, while the diverse themes of the levels are enjoyable, the enemies within them sometimes feel mismatched to their respective levels.The cozy atmosphere of running the restaurant quickly became tedious with limited options upgrades related to anything other than how many dishes you can queue at once or the rarity of the dishes you can offer, and no options for staff hiring even late game. So the gameplay loop has no real variation over time, making it fairly similar 1 hour in or 50 hours in. Also, while decorating the restaurant offers potential for creativity as there are many options and themes, which I really appreciate, it's something I didn't explore that much as everything is so expensive and it would require a lot of further grinding for simply redecorating your restaurant (note that pricier or costly decorations don't impact the gameplay in any significant fashion).You are only able to store non-food related items in select store boxes that are given to you (1 or 2 at a time) as you achieve certain upgrades/milestones, which means that you can't really store a lot of materials in advance for later upgrades as storage is very limited (note that each dungeon level has a different wood and stone resource equivalent so there are a lot of different types of materials required at all times). Once I finished the game I still had only 5 total storage boxes (which cannot be upgraded for higher capacity) and 5 personal fridges, which ended up empty as there is very little incentive to store anything in them once you are done with the NPC quests (as their may use for me was to hold ingredients for the quests so as to not spend them during restaurant opening times).
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: very cute and entertaining dungeon crawler.The art style is definitely one of their strong points, alongside a varied and engaging dungeon system. Cooking and raising the reputation of the restaurant is also quite entertaining although there are some operational flaws. Overall, I really like this game as it's a great way to unwind after a hard day.Pros:-Dungeon system with dungeons-exclusive drops and ingredients-Decorate and organise your restaurant... and your bedroom-Quests do not have a time limit and can be completed independently from each otherCons:-There are certain items in the restaurant that are placed and locked, therefore making it slightly less fun to decorate-NPCs are only around certain days and times, so make sure to keep checking if they don't appear-The only way to make money is to open the restaurant, you can't sell equipment or ingredients
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I love the game, it has cute art, satisfying sounds and very calming music. the game play is fairly easy and fun for casual players. I would like them to expand on the game more i think it has a lot of potential for more development and maybe improve weapon system especially the brew system. I got the DLC art PDF too and i think a lot of the weapons could be added in for future expansion and visit the dragon folks country too. I find the restaurant part of the game a bit lacking, though its fun having to deal with dine and dashers the serving part is bit annoying especially when its pack and you can accidentally click on the wrong bubble. I wish we could hire some help.As fun as furnishing the shop is some areas i do wish we could customise more, like the counter tops, cash register, doors and exterior of the shop. it felt like they wanted a NPC system with the birthday and calendar but it feels like they didnt have enough time on it maybe in the future they will come back and give and NPC system so it feels more immersive.  I love this game very much and i hope it gets expanded on in the near future!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of farming or food games have a lot of intricate moving parts. I like Cuisineer because it simplifies the genre so I can sit back and relax. No need to min max each day or feature of the game. I would suggest this game to anyone who wants to fight cute creatures and run a restaurant without worrying about complex numbers.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a middling review, because its not bad, it's just got some very rough edges to it.Gameplay loop is mostly solid, but the grind of it isn't fun, and it stops being fun after the first upgrade rather quickly. I liked the aspect of the side-quests being you helping people in exchange for recipes to further your restaurant, but the tedium of then needing to go out and grind for materials on top of grinding for cooking materials quickly made it feel like a chore rather than something enjoyable. And unfortunately if you want to get a good restaurant, you need to expand space, buy more tables/furniture to entice certain customers in to give you more money, and then you need materials for upgrading all your cooking equipment.There's also side upgrades like your belt, for carrying more boba, your bag to gather more materials (which is necessary when the stacks of item you can carry cap out at 30, which is...a choice in a grind-heavy game) and then upgrades to the boba themselves, which you do by cooking a certain number of certain dishes to either upgrade the boba, or research another one. Any time you come back from a dungeon the game automatically puts it to 11pm at night, which means you can't go to a dungeon and come back to run the restaurant in the same day.The music and art are both beautiful, and I enjoyed the cooking, straightforward and simple as it was. I also appreciated that for the "debt" portion of the storyline, you didn't have an exact timer, and could offer chunks of payment, versus needing to have the whole thing in three days or something. The story was also very cute. But this game could def have used a bit more polish, or at least a discussion about how much grind is too much. I recommend getting this game on discount, and maybe playing it in brief spurts - or mod it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This game is SO punishing for failure that it is no longer fun to play I just wanted a relaxing cooking game and this is one of the most stressful games I've ever played if you die you lose the whole day's progress AND all the resources you have gathered. There is no way to recover things you can lose hours of progress and it is easy to get overwhelmed and killed in the dungeons.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible restaurant management game with a cool adventurer theme to it.I really enjoy exploring the dungeons in this game, the combat seems simple but it gets challenging the further the player progresses, and really fun too.I absolutely love the diversity the player eventually has in decorating the dining area for the restaurant as well, I enjoy designing a restaurant that both looks good and attracts and appeals to my customer base.The game is very enjoyable, and relatively relaxing. It doesn't go into extreme difficulty, and while it might seem slightly grindy at first, it gets much better with time, and the recent updates improved things an awful lot. It is so much better after the updates that came out for this game.I highly recommend this game if you like a cozy relaxing cute game that has plenty of challenge in the adventuring side of the game. Stay for the calm and relaxation, but enjoy some fun and excitement to boot when not on down time. So very good.The characters in this game are delightful too. Such friendly faces.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This review was made in the first 3 hours of gameplay. This review may be updated later.A restaurant themed Rogue-lite... who knew this could work so well?This seems to have heavy inspiration from Cult of the Lamb, another stellar rouge-lite, with the promotion of dungeon crawling as a means to providing for your customers. I enjoy the cute art style, and animal theming, as this caught my eye from the beginning.Unfortunately, not every character feels truly unique. There's your best friend/assistant, the shop keepers, the tax collecter, and then just about everyone else. They all have different animal designs, but many of the characters are just referred to as "Noble" or "Elderly". Though with the cast that was given, it's pretty solid.That being said, the main goal (as of early game) pulls an Animal Crossing. Paying off your debt. It's not even your own debt at that. It feels sudden, although not exactly unexpected or random, but there doesn't seem to be any feeling of incentive to it. The collector explains that they'll sell to the highest bidder if you don't pay up, but as of now, there seems to be no deadline, leaving the incentive pointless.Despite its flaws, it's still a great game with good graphics and a fun Restaurant Sim X Rouge Dungeon Crawler, and I highly recommend trying it. My most important note: The "requirement" on RAM is 16GB. My computer runs at only 8GB. So, I would like to clear this up for you, dear reader. As long as you have a decent GPU and Memory of about 8GB, this game should run perfectly fine. If stuck at the Loading screen (black and white art, not transitioning to color, and no music playing), restart the game, lower the resolution, and then reset it back once you enter the game. From this point on, it should work fine with just 8GB of RAM.Here's to a long and delicious adventure. Itadakimasu~!

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, y'all...I liked this game..... until I tried to Actually Play it and get a little optimized, as one does with shopkeep games. At this point I realized that there's /nothing/ going on in this game.First, the sum up is:  The game is not engaging.---The town is empty. Talking to people is pointless. There is nothing beyond the town square. There are no relationship scores. Birthdays do not matter. You cannot give anyone items as gifts. It's not that kind of game. This is disappointing, because the impression that you get is that it might have been or that the foundation for anyone to mean anything is or was there. ---The restaurant is boring. It is impossible for this to get difficult because of how the restaurant mini-game operates. You always cook full dishes and the dish a customer needs automatically populates on the specific preparation area it comes from. Clicking on the prep area you can simply mash confirm then close and you're good. Unless it's a noble, the customer automatically picks up their food (so that you don't need to worry about server staff I suppose.) What this creates, however is a poor system:  You **NEVER** need to know or care what you are cooking or what your customers ask for. You can legitimately space out and click on exclamation points, slide your finger from confirm to cancel and you've taken care of that order, whatever it was, whoever it was for -- it doesn't matter, thanks for the coins. You don't need to cook one dish to get another (i.e. Noodles > Pasta Carbonara) and once you get the higher tier dishes, the lower tier ones cease to matter at all.---The Dungeon is mashy.  Gaining more damage or performing better in the damage ends up being stacking more and more effects on yourself such as elements on your dash, proccing extra attacks instead of upgrading your weapons. Upgrading weapons is generally pointless since 1 more damage, up to a maximum of 5, does not really do anything for the number of times you have to hit the monster. Thus, fighting things, for me, devolved into hithithit>dash>dash attack, hithithit>dash ad infinitum. This never changed and never needed to change. In fact, once you get shielded or icy dash I was incentivised to do nothing else.  Shield completely nullifies a few bosses, too. Plenty of times in a dungeon I thought "gee there sure is a lot of trash on the screen" due to all of the effects that I needed for damage.  And also the engine does not really appreciate this. If you send a dash attack of Durians through like 5 waves of rice sprites or flour fluff, the game noticeably stutters.  Anyway, it's not challenging, it's just absent-minded mashing.---The quests don't matter.  The reward of nearly ever quest is a recipe. Others are blank equipment you probably already have and have brewed effects to perfection on. Quests are always presented the exact same way and your reward is pointless.... because once again cooking in the kitchen doesn't matter. The recipes you learn could be replaced with a silhouette and ???? for the name and nothing would change.  Additionally, it's annoying to have to find out what amount you have to do to complete the quest. It's never told to you by the townsperson. You always have to click on them again, click into the quest, and then see.Game's cute, sure.  But that is all it has when you're beyond the "I'm Playing A New Game!!!" phase.  The rest is just sleepy, unengaging, brainless mashing and that's not what i'm down for and it's not what I would recommend to my pals.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly fun and well-balance; The art style is pleasing to the eye, the action in the dungeon is exciting and fun, and the fast-paced nature of running the restaurant is extremely fulfilling.I have 2 grips.> This first is that some quests require ingredients that you can accidentally use when your restaurant is open. This makes it a lot more difficult to manage any quests that require ingredients. Any of the following changes would solve this issue:1. Toggle recipes that are available when the restaurant is open2. Deny a order (so the customer doesn't hog a seat)3. Have a lock-box freezer where ingredients stored in it can't be used when the restaurant is open or "lock" ingredients so that they won't be used.> The second grip is that the restaurant auto closes at 23:00. If a patron is in the restaurant, made their order, and the food is still being cooked while the restaurant auto closes at 23:00... then the patron leaves and the food is left to rot on the counter. OR if a customer who makes 2 orders and only eats 1 order then the restaurant closes, they don't pay for their first meal that they ate! It would be nice if this was fixed to patrons already seated w/ orders already placed are able to quickly complete eating their order + pay.Also, it'd be cool if:+ we could romance NPCs + alternative ways to make cash (for example, selling extra equipment that's not needed instead of throwing it away)+ customize the appearance of the kitchen appliances (ie. oven, cutting board, fridge, etc) so they can better match the appearance of our restaurant. + customize Pom's appearance (like different clothes, hair color, etc)+ add stats and/or upgrades to equipment effects. Currently, it feels like upgrading equipment doesn't make any difference when in the dungeon/fighting monsters/bosses. It'd be nice if we could upgrade stats (strength, speed, dexterity, etc) and/or equipment status effects (ie. flame, frozen, poison, sweenten, etc) so that it does have an effect when in the dungeon.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun game that has some minor but annoying flaws. The game basically consists of two different things: running a restaurant, and crawling through dungeons. The restaurant part is really fun. I really like how detailed the artwork for the food is and there is plenty of stuff to upgrade. I also really like how much you can customize your restaurant with furniture and wallpaper, kind of like the Sims. I wouldn't mind seeing more customization options like that. It really adds a lot more playability to the game besides the goal of "upgrade everything to max level". The dudgeon crawling part is where the problems are. Fighting the enemies is initially fun and combat is satisfying. The first problem is that the layout of the dungeons change each time you visit them, and it's randomly generated. That means that you can't ever learn where to go in order to quickly get through an area. The second problem is that there are no checkpoints. You have to go through all the levels of a dungeon on a single attempt, get to the bottom and fight the boss. And running past enemies isn't really an option because again, new layout each time. To add to the problem, you can only carry a few health items and enemies don't drop health items. This leads to the really frustrating experience of trying to run past 10 million enemies, all of which are slowly trying to chip away at your health, while trying to solve a maze at the same time. Even Dark Souls usually gives players a checkpoint before the boss, or at least gives them the option to run past most enemies once you know where to go. When people are trying to beat a boss they don't want to have to re-fight the same small-fry enemies and use up all their health items before they ever get there. Another unintended consequence of randomly created level layouts is that the levels feel kind of sloppily designed. Instead of being a well-crafted experience that someone spent a lot of time planning, it's just really random. Another problem is ingredients. You get ingredients from the dungeons. Certain enemies drop certain ingredients. The game will also give you tips like "Cheese is going to be popular tomorrow so stock up!". But what am I supposed to do with that information? The only way to get ingredients is from enemies in the dungeons, but they spawn randomly. Basically I have no control over what ingredients I get. And when you come back from the dungeon it's always the end of the day no matter how much time you spent there. So if the game tells you "cheese is popular tomorrow" and you go into the dungeon and don't find enough cheese, you can't just go back the next day because the day that cheese is popular on will pass. There is a guy you can trade some ingredients for other ingredients with but he's only there on certain days and options are extremely limited. My advice to the devs is this: Make the dungeons a fixed layout that is well-designed. If you want some randomness to keep things interesting then make the enemies you encounter random. Maybe add a checkpoint before the final dungeon boss so players can fast travel to it after they die. Add a way to buy specific ingredients without going to the dungeons. If you want to give the players incentive to keep going to the dungeons, then have some quests require gear or items or something that can only be found there. Also a way to make at least a little money on the super common items that you end up with too much of would be nice. That way I don't have to just throw it away. Also some more options for furniture, art, and wall design might not be bad since it gives players a reason to keep playing the game after they start making tons of money and have already upgraded all their stuff. Overall it's a really good game and worth playing. I hope if there's ever a sequel or anything they will make some changes.

_childDocuments_.review: Just wretched.  Combat is awful. Dungeons take place in cramped, narrow corridors cluttered with traps and natural obstacles like bushes and rocks for you to get hung up on when trying to avoid a dozen foes coming to gang bang you. Enemy projectiles fire at you from offscreen and require no line of sight, passing through everything on their way to your face. Most enemies are tiny and your attack range is extremely short. There are so many particle effects, you can't tell where the hell you are or if you're taking damage.You can tell it's trying to be like Hades, but your attacks are just terrible, with heavy blows having slow wind ups and lengthy cool downs.  Your various weapons all suck with random pathetically weak effects, but don't worry, you can pay a fortune to have them upgraded so that they're slightly less useless, oh but you'll have to leave your weapon with the blacksmith for a few in-game days for the privilege.The UI does not automatically compare gear drops with currently equipped items so good luck manually comparing that ♥♥♥♥. If your bag slots are full, you have to chuck something to make room just to compare!Lastly, the story is so paper thin, you wonder why they bothered. Pom has no discernible reason to be doing what she's doing.  Returning home after years away, her worthless parents stick her with their debts. The townsfolk act like she never left and only see her as a gopher.  Why would she care and not immediately leave again?  Doesn't matter; get your ass in the kitchen and make food, woman.

At the end of the day I would definitely recommend it to people because the art is cute, collecting recipes is fun, the story is good, decorating your restaurant has ALOT of variety, and there are a good amount of places to explore. 7/10
