_childDocuments_.review: After fully engaging with this game to the point of all achievements, I cannot say I liked it. While I did feel the game was enjoyable, that enjoyment ran dry fairly quickly. The confusion of whether it wanted to be a rogue-lite or cozy cooking game didn't help with that. As it stands I cannot recommend Cuisineer. Let's start with the positives:The art direction of the 2D art great, the food looks delicious, and the unique character art is wonderful. Even the generic NPCs are great for a while until you realize that they are all palette swaps. The Characters have wonderful personalities, but there isn't much to do with them. The premice is fun and the 3D isometric world looks charming. The storytelling is good for what of it there is. I enjoyed the main quest, and a handful of the side quests had me smiling. I also am glad for everyone who may not want a challenging experience that there are damage reduction options in the menu. While I did not take advantage of this the game was designed as both a combat-driven game as well as a cozy experience and I think that this addition allows cozy gamers to enjoy the game more fully.This however is where the positives end. The game isn't offensively bad, but there are a large number of sticking points for me as someone who enjoys this genre of game.Town/Restaurant:I felt that my restaurant ran itself and the only reason I opened it was to get money to feed a loop. I didn't worry about the craved item or even what ingredients I had because there wasn't a need to. I would open the restaurant, I would seat and serve a hundred customers in a day, and I wouldn't even think twice about what I was cooking. There wasn't ever a time that I didn't have the dish a customer wanted even on a craving day. I wasn't even cooking, I would open a menu at one of 4 different cooking stations, it selected the dishes automatically that I needed in a tab specifically there to make it streamlined without a thought, and on occasion, I would take a plate to a customer. This game may as well have been servineer as all I did was take orders to the kitchen and bring food to some guests. Cooking stations in the restaurant are a whole different issue though. Upgrading them was fine, requiring materials from across all the dungeons was also fine, but adding more queue spaces felt like it bordered on futility. I've never filled all the queue slots in my stations since 3 slots were available, because by that time I was able to have at least 2 of every cooking station in my kitchen. Upgrading the stations to reduce cook time (Since there is no food prep) or perhaps allowing multiple dishes to be cooked simultaneously so as to reduce the need to upgrade multiple stations to quite the same heights would be ultimately a more impactful and rewarding feeling. Guest variety was another thing I found lacking. Perhaps I never stumbled upon it, but I never once had any guests outside of the tourists attempt a dine and dash. So outside of tourists, and the two different varieties of nobles, I never even found myself thinking about the other guests. On the topic of Townsfolk and guests, what is the point in having named characters with birthdays if they never enter the restaurant? You can't give them things, why isn't there some form of friendship-building system in the game? The special characters should have likes and come in on their days off or something.Reputation eventually flowed in so quickly that I always had quests available to me. One time I opened a quest from upgrading my restaurant (Which I didn't realize was even a requirement) and suddenly I was able to complete 3 quests in one day from the same person. Side quests feel more important in the game than the main quests as all the recipes you receive are through completing side quests, and the main quest has no urgency to it.Upgrading Boba feels more tied to the restaurant than the dungeon because you require recipes to do that which you unlock through restaurant activities. Upgrading weapons is again about the shop using the money you earn with only a small amount of materials that you can gather on the first floor of any given dungeon. The Pot felt poorly explained and overcomplicated, using only the icons of the given effect types and leaving it to you to experiment and hope you got something meaningful or useful. I didn't even realize that brewer buffs had different tiers until I stumbled upon a 2-star buffed item in the dungeon as it is not explained anywhere that I can see.Dungeon:Dungeoning feels lacking in systems, leaving any meaningful increase in power for the dungeon to be gained in the town. This leaves adventuring feeling only like a means to an end rather than a meaningful part of the game. Trudge through a dungeon to get ingredients to cook meals to make money to upgrade your shop or pay your debts to go to a new dungeon, but never feel a meaningful increase in power. Even equipment upgrades felt lacking, being that they're only as much as 1 extra hit worth of health or 1% of an enemy's health increase in damage. Mob density is absurd, I feel like combat is balanced around being able to freeze everything constantly. If you're unable to then you take massive damage from enemies that you may even be actively comboing. Guarding isn't a thing, you either get hit or you dash, and even then you'll sometimes still get hit. If you're not being spammed with 40 enemies in a room all of which have limitless health then you're in a room with 30 Spike plates or other various traps, some of which blend in with the environment far too well or are placed behind walls at the bottom of a map. Sometimes you may even be besieged by enemies at the spawn of a new floor. Dungeons aren't unlocked through dungeoning, which feels odd to me, they're not unlocked through anything other than running your restaurant. You could get to the final encounter of the game and never have fought a single boss. The only indication that there are any bosses in the game is the Lancet quest. Bosses don't have unique drops or even drops related to what they are for some reason. You would think that killing a boss for a large quantity of meat or other relevant ingredients would make sense, but instead, you get a chest of eclectic items and a kick out the door.I would love to see more changes to the game in the future to better expand upon the townsfolk, restaurant interactions and perhaps unique recipes from special boss ingredients.

_childDocuments_.review: The last update (Patch 1.03) has broken the game's capacity to be played via a Steam Deck or via controller. It is now impossible to open the correct storage unit or access the correct kitchen device because the game now selects multiple items at once. Even when standing directly in front of one object, the game will choose to open another adjacent device off to one side making it impossible to access certain objects.Examples: -When standing directly in front of my fridges the game will select 6 different devices in the general area. Upon trying to open a fridge the game selects the cutting board.-When standing in front of the cooking pot and trying to select it, the game selects the frying pan instead.-When attempting to open a private fridge in the bedroom, the game selects a storage chest.Additionally, When the restaurant is open, it is now impossible to pick up a cooked dish for patrons who want their food delivered to them. Now, upon trying to pick up a dish, the dish hops to the next open space on the counter every time I try to pick it up, making it literally impossible to complete said food orders. Tested the game on PC and because of the mouse's versatility this is not an issue as you can click directly on the device you wish to use. However you can still see that the game selects multiple devices at once upon approaching a group of devices. Happy to change my review once the game is made playable again on Steam Deck & via controller. Otherwise have enjoyed the game. :)

_childDocuments_.review: The game received several major updates since my previous Not Recommended review. I clearly see the work that the developers put into this game.To begin with, the game is now super optimized and runs smooth at steady framerate. The adorable art style blends well with the game concept, and now the loading screen is animated!Players can now opt-in to a lower game difficulty, which I personally appreciate as a farming sim lover. It has a really amazing feedback loop right now, where you can chill out at the restaurant, and fight to the nerves in the dungeon at the same time. _childDocuments_.review: I liked this game at first, but after playing it for 30 hours. I can not recommend it. In theme and dialogue, this game is quite wholesome, charming, and cute. The basic combat can be fun. But, later on when rooms are just full of mobs. You will often aggro mobs off screen and it turns into bullet hell. Most mobs are HP sponges and take a while to deal with. Your upgrades don’t feel impactful. You spend a lot of resources, cash, and wait a day. Then all you get is +1 damage. I upgraded all my gear to 4 stars and got them enchanted. It still felt like it didn’t matter. Clearing mobs felt like it took the same time, and I was still getting shot up from across the map. With that said, this game is not an action roguelike. It is more like an old school hack & slash dungeon crawling. You don’t get runs where you randomly pickup some upgrades that can make or brake the run. You upgrade your equipment, load up on potions, and delve into a dungeon until your index finger gets tired from all the clicking.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game so far despite some of the big issues.  Reminds me of all the fun I had playing Restaurant City (refered to as RC) by Playfish back in the day on Facebook (circa 2009-2012).+-Great art/music/overall theme-Restaurant customization-Good story plot-Variety of weapons and skills/builds--Game performance in dungeons needs to be optimized... many situations where I am fighting multiple mobs and game starts to lag/lose frames (biggest issue imo)-No social system... should be a way to visit friends/others restaurants, One thing I loved in RC was you could see all the top restaurants including your friends, as well as could interact with their restaurants and characters (to hire).-Some enemy types (i.e icebergs, spinach)  blend in very well and are barely visible; should make those specific enemies slightly different hues for better visibility-No red indicator when low health... hard to pay attention to health bar while dashing and smashing enemies.-Lackluster Boss rewards; should reward more rare ingredients and better weapon drops-Tanky enemies, not tough to kill but takes too long to kill all those damn rice spiritsFeatures I would like to see added the future:-Ability to hire staff; i.e. waiters to give food to nobles, cleaners to keep restaurant clean and chefs to start the food.  -Ability to hire staff to either Adventure while you work or work at restaurant while adventuring-Market open everyday to exchange ingredients-Market to purchase ingredients for coin-More opportunities to purchase storage space-Ability to unlock all slots for weapon rolls-Dungeon/restaurant perks (or skill tree to further optimize)Despite these issues the game is still very entertaining, it has a solid foundation and has plenty of potential to grow into a highly successful game!

_childDocuments_.review: Its a fun little game, and quite frankly I don't mind the pretty shallow gameplay loop of "fill inventory, deal with that in various ways and do it again" as to my mind its not different from No Mans Sky, albeit with less flying and so-forth.Combat is kinda a pain though. Stuff takes forever to die and it might be worthwhile to take a look at minor enemies HP pools. I shouldn't have to be smacking around a chili pepper forever.I was waiting for a game of this sort that combined the concepts of a Moonlighter (which I did not like as much), and Battle Chef Brigade Deluxe (a game nothing I've seen has attempted to sorta replicate until now -- a lightning in a bottle concept that you could really tie a Monster Hunter-esque sort of gameplay loop to. Perhaps someday...) Managing the restaurant my favorite aspect by far. _childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer was just the top down dungeon crawler mix with simple restaurant management and town interactions that I was looking for. Both the dungeoning and managing are simple but engaging enough to make me think "just one more run, just one more lunch time rush, just one more in game day."In it's current state the game doesn't have a thorough in game user guide. However I've found that reading the tool tips, and some player intuition and exploration will answer most questions you have. If not you can always wait for the tip to arrive in your in-game mailbox, or ask the steam community. Otherwise I've had great fun exploring town, finding new recipes, and mastering the movement and attack mechanics in the dungeons (not perfectly, I just picked up the "WHY!?!?!?!?" achievement). There are difficulty options to reduce the amount of damage taken, but so far I've found it challenging but fun.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's cute, cheap, and simple. At the 30 hour point I really don't see myself picking it back up, but for a 25 dollar game, that's a great value. Literally a dollar an hour to be entertained lol. High notes: Golly is it cute. There's something mind-numbing and addicting about it that lets you go into peak smoothbrain soothing glazed-over mode and that's all I can ask for from this kind of game. You get your money's worth.Critical notes: My biggest complaint about this game is how slow and sluggish the restaurant aspect is, considering it's necessary. You can buy as many chairs as you like, but they won't be filled most of the time, and I bounce my leg impatiently wishing I could put it at 2x speed or something. This picks up after certain more demanding customers show up but it's still pretty slow. The enemies are meatbags if you're using anything but the slow heavy weapons, but with the amount of mobs on the field at any given time, you're a lot more likely to take damage using those. Upgrading equipment should never take a full day where they physically remove it from your inventory, that's goofy, especially because upgrades barely affect the stats, or they do it unreliably. Xseed has some banger titles so I chalk this up to being a lower budget release and still enjoyed my time playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: After essentially completing the game, here is my review.Pros:- Cute art style.- Amusing character personalities.Cons:- Essentially everything else.The progression is very lackluster over the course of the game. You get a few bare bones upgrades to your equipment. Fully upgrading your weapon only adds +5 damage, when the "great sword" style weapons start at 35, it's not a super noticeable change. The modification system for equipment is interesting, but over the course of the game I didn't really ever bother to use it, as the game hands you complete "sets" of equipment as you progress the story, and you have little reason to branch out from a complimentary set. I got my ice-set and pretty much used that for the rest of the game.The game also does VERY little to explain to you about different weapons as options, I didn't even realize there WERE different thrown weapons until I'd almost finished the game.You unlock recipes almost entirely by completing side-quests, very few of which take more than 5 minutes to complete, and the few that do often you end up having the NPC disappear and you have to wait multiple days for them to show back up so you can complete it.You cannot sell any items. Even though you can pick up a GLUT of items each dungeon run, you can't do anything with your collected items other than a) use it for cooking, b) use it for quest turn-ins, c) use it for upgrades, or d) throw it out. No gifting, no selling. And with very limited storage space both in-run and at home, I found myself throwing things away during every dungeon run and almost always throwing stuff away when I got back because I realized I didn't have enough space.You can't eat the food you cook. You can cook food, you can even put it in your bags, and some NPCs even give you food. But then... nothing. You can't do anything with it other than serve it. I guess if you wanted to go super meta with this you could cook up a bunch of food in advance, store it in your bags, and then try and serve it? Honestly don't even know if that would work. But it's kind of baffling that the game GIVES you food you can't use.The dungeons are tedious. You will need to go into the dungeons CONSTANTLY to keep stocked up on supplies, especially as you progress to bigger restaurant sizes and get tons of customers. The dungeons themselves are procedurally generated, but from a fairly small set of tiles. You'll rapidly become accustomed to the composition of each tile, and after a certain point the patterns seem to either repeat or come in a very limited set, as you can eventually figure out your exact path after a room or two.Game performance: most noticeable if you're trying to rush to lower floors of a dungeon, but the game can be surprisingly laggy. If you try and rush through a dungeon and end up with a lot of beasties trailing you, the game can stutter HARD. This also seems to happen if you get too many customers in your restaurant at the same time.Restaurant management: early on this isn't really an issue, but especially once you get to rank 10+ of the restaurant, it can become a massive pain, especially if you decorate to attract nobles. Nobles demand you personally run them their food, but once the restaurant is big enough you literally can't see the whole thing on your screen, so you have no idea if a noble came in and sat down by the door. You can either run around constantly scanning for nobles, or try and notice if food is lingering on the counter too long and realize there's a noble waiting. You can't hire anyone to help (even your best friend who constantly talks about helping), it's literally just one person managing a massive restaurant. You also can never move the checkout counter, so every time you want to check someone out, you have to run across the entirety of your restaurant, collect their money, then run back to the kitchen. This feels more like a forced-time-sink than anything else. So much of the plot is about the MC being a great restaurateur, but what restaurateur runs it entirely on their own with no staff? Even the MC's parents ran it TOGETHER.Boss Fights: With the exception of the final boss, very few of the bosses are all that compelling. By and large it's just dash-hit-dash-hit-dash-hit repeat ad infinitum until they die. Then the final arc of the game dials this up DRASTICALLY, and you end up having to fight multiple bosses at the same time while on a time clock, which sent my blood pressure through the roof. Not a great difficulty curve there.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been enjoying this game so much over the past day! (10 hours in! wheehee)Lovable characters, beautiful sound design and mouth-watering graphics! The routine-like dungeoning, fetch quests, and earning money is a comforting sequence of steps for anyone who enjoys a rinse-and-repeat type gameplay with steady progression.The dungeoning aspect reminds me of Hades and Cult of the Lamb with its procedurally-generated maps and monsters. Its sure to engage your reflexes as you delve deeper in the dungeon and keep you on your toes. Yoou can adjust the difficulty from Normal > Mild > Bland according to the difficulty you'd want to experience in-game.The restauranting phase is simple and chill, not like a Diner Dash type situation, so it's manageable and not so overwhelming, which is a nice change of pace after the tough dungeons!There are some early game inconveniences like getting your items consumed during the restauranting phase, and not knowing where or when the NPCs come out, There are many features that are not given to you directly! This is not the kind of game that handholds you, but one that gets the viewer to keep playing to discover various features on their own.Story is simple and focuses on the gameplay! But the characters are charming enough to keep me invested XDTl:dr Smooth gameplay and controls (I have a pretty beefy PC tho), lovely graphics and music, relatively easy to get into but more features gets discovered as you keep playing, obvious steps for progression (paying off your debt and finishing quests).

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR ; This is a fun game with inspired ideas that fail to reach their full potential and a mod was required to fix stuttering issues for me.It has a game-play loop that consists of your character going into dungeons to collect ingredients from slaying monsters and breaking objects in the environment, and then returning home to use then run your parents' small, humble restaurant. It is a satisfying if not repetitive loop that unfortunately grow dull quickly as neither of these tasks have enough meat to them to be fully fun. In dungeons, you can equip two weapons and two pieces of equipment that can be bought in-town or dropped from monsters with randomized abilities giving it a bit of a Diablo flair. The randomized abilities can be re-rolled through a vendor in-town and you can aim for certain properties by offering him food dishes you make. Each weapon type also has unique special abilities that are always tied to them like the Frying Pan will pancake enemies then set the area on fire, and the Plates which are a ranged throwing weapon can be thrown in a fan pattern. Sounds fun and promising on paper but the combat itself is dull and doesn't feel satisfying mainly because enemies have SO MUCH HEALTH. Most encounters your just mashing the attack button while waiting for your ability to come off cool-down. Returning to town, you can opt to run your restaurant for a time and go dungeon diving later or spend an entire day serving the hungry locals and tourists that come through town. Your gathered resources will manly be used for this as it is your only source of income. This feature also gets halfway there to being fun. It sort of scratches a Diner Dash itch with customers seating themselves then displaying their order in a thought bubble over their head. You simply find the appliance that makes the dish and click the dish to queue it up to be made. Then that's it. You could deliver it but all customers except for stuffy nobles will shuffle their way to counter and grab their dish. I'm not saying I don't like the idea that people have to go grab their own food rather I think if this is included there should be more required of me behind the counter.**Also smaller note but the performance is known to be oddly chopping and there is a wonderful , easy to install mod on Nexus to fix this and tweak some aspects of the game but its a bummer that I needed this to play the game for more than 10 minutes without getting a headache...I don't think this is a bad game by any means but there could be more fleshed out to fully realize its potential in this genre. Even if the combat remains as it is, I think just adding co-op could make a lot of my gripes melt away a little more. I understand if the game was meant to be dialed down a bit in favor of the cozy trend going on but I don't think the button mashing dungeon diving really backs that up. I really love the ideas presented here, just wish they were a bit more polished. So because I felt like I was forcing myself to play to find enjoyment and needed a mod to not vomiting from the stuttering, I cannot recommend this game in its state at the time of this review. I wish the devs nothing but the best and hope they feel inspired to polish this game or continue on to make something even better.

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoy the time I've spent with it so far, I feel like Cuisineer needs a little more time in the oven before I can feel comfortable reccommending it to others. While I'm only at the 3rd big tax number to grind towards there are many things that have been sapping at my interest. For one thing, the adventuring is less rogue-like and more inventory management. I understand that with the controls and layout there are only so many room designs one can make, but the variety does feel underwhelming. At the same time, I find myself unmotivated to venture deeper than floor 3 or 4 of any region as even with a nearly maxed backpack for the point in story the pack still fills really fast. While I can only imagine how bad it was before things stacked to 30, I find myself less and less interested in challenge and boss rooms. This is mainly because of chest rewards. By the time I find and complete a challenge my back pack is already close to full, so when it releases a bunch of gear it can feel more a nuissance than anything. As I can't look at the enchantments unless their in my inventory, I have to continue to throw stuff out and pray that it actually picks up the gear instead of a random egg over and over, and even then I've yet to feel motivated to really dig in and mess around with the enchantments because even if I've collected some gear with 3 star enchantments, I have to upgrade them now twice and possibly deal with enchanting before they're usable, taking three days and lots of resources. Maybe a way this can be improved is by allowing us to view the stats of an item even if it's not in an inventory, and possibly give a percent chance for an item to be upgraded on pickup. While that could come with the direct issue of collecting gear that is higher quality than what one has, it would balance out with the fun of your means of play changing as you venture deeper. without that the only reason I hold onto any gear is if my inventory happens to be able to handle it, and even then it's just to sacrifice the gear to quests anyways. Said quests are another point of tension. I can't help but suspect that the order fo which quests are given are random. That's not inheretly a bad thing, but it's frustrating when given a quest to produce a certain dish when it takes weeks to actually be given the quest which rewards the neccessary recipe. It's also frustrating to be given quests wanting dishes and cuisine from regions you've yet to unlock, so you'll have side quests sitting their with their thought bubbles unachievable for a while. i also find it frustrating that while buying and upgrading will cleanly take from your private chests and fridge, quests do not. It means I have to go back, grab all my quest completion materials, run around to see if the specfic person is even out, then put them back every single time. Even if you still want to require speaking with the person to complete quests this one difference is a nuissance. I also am a bit underwhelmed with the restaurant section. Once the house is upgraded enough to have one of each cooking utensil the only real challenge is making the restaurant navigatable for yourself. While I suspect that serving a dish directly probably increases the tip slightly, it never feels worth it as you have to wait for the customer to return to their seat to even serve them, which for certain customer tyoes makes it feel like serving takes more time than just letting them pick it up. There's also the issue of while house upgrades allow for more cooking stations, I have no interest in buy any more until I can have two of each type as I can't find the worth in having another thing that needs a bunch of upgrades before it's at a satisfactory state with everything else, especially when the amount of customers wanting recipes from a specific cooking utensil never seems to exceed its capacity. And with the dishes being auto selected on order and the only spike in difficulty per say is people trying to not pay, the diner being the only way to make gold becomes a frustration more than anything. maybe this could be spiced up not just with the craving days, but days where customers only buy from a certain dish element or utensil, or otherwise. At least give the ability to hire someone to do serving so that you can get some of that theoretical bonus without needing to wait for the customer to sit back down, and it could take a percent of the day's earnings so it's a give and take. Heck, even just let the shopkeepers come into the restaurant so you can build a relationship beyond customer and rnadomly getting materials you won't have any use for until you get further in the plot or just for a chance of an enchantment. I know that was a lot but I say this all with the hope that this game will be better fleshed out.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review, I'm currently on Year 2, Spring 3 (over 100 days), and have 24 hours logged in game. I thought this was about the perfect time to write a review of how I feel about the game.I think this is a very enjoyable game! It's very cute, and I really enjoy the restaurant management and upgrades to grind for. The dungeons I think are somewhat incomplete with how they function, though. I still haven't managed to fully complete a dungeon despite my best efforts, and I am not entirely sure if it will be any time soon before I do. I think this would be fine if it wasn't for the fact that it doesn't feel very rewarding going through them after a while. After my first 7 hours of the game, I couldn't only be focused on playing it, and would have a stream or cartoon to watch on the side while I was grinding. I don't fully consider that a bad thing though, since I really enjoy having something like this to unwind with after a long day. I wish that after dying in a dungeon, all my stuff wouldn't go to waste...I feel like games like this are kinda based on the fact that you die and try again, and I just don't really enjoy such a heavy punishment. It really feels like I just wasted a good 20-30 mins for absolutely nothing.I think another thing it does really well is focusing primarily on side quests. This just isn't a game that really needs a plot, so it just being a debt you have to pay is nice. I also enjoy getting new recipes as my rewards for doing them! _childDocuments_.review: It's an adorable dungeon crawling, restaurant management game, with a one time charm cycle~ And what I mean by the one time charm cycle, is because the end-game doesn't have much replayability other than just making your restaurant looks more efficient and nicer looking~ The restaurant management part of the game is the gem of the game. It's very cozy, simple, adorable, and very mouth-watering illustration of cuisine from all around the world. The East-Asian cuisine itself is what personally pulls me to play the game, cause it felt like a small representation of the local dishes I had growing up~ The dungeon crawling aspect tho,...it could've been better~ The combat is a bit wonky I feel, and unless you had prior experience to roguelike game, or top down combat, you might wanna play as safe as you can, as dungeon in this game is the main sole source of ingredient to open your restaurant, and dying in a dungeon results in 90% of your item being drop, which is very brutal for an adorable game~Once you reached further points of the game, combat gets harder, but you may not necessarily be stronger tho~ (You can always change the difficulty at any time, for the ultimate easy ingredient hunts experience)It's fairly manageable, and you have access to modifiers that can effect your combat difficulty, aka combat builds like Freeze, Burn, Poison, Shock, etc~And that would've been the one redeeming quality of the dungeon crawling, if it weren't for the fact that your equipment can hold 2 mods, but if you decide to change one of the mods in a brewery, it'll lock the unmodified mod, permanently~Meaning, if it's a mod that can get a higher tier, you're now stuck with a low tier one, so getting an ideal builds is almost nigh impossible without a lot of patience and day skips~Pair it up with the fact that equipment shops won't always sell the equipment you need, and even when it does, it may not be the right mod you're looking for. So you're lowkey forced to fight with whatever weapon they have in stock, or dropped in the dungeon with a messy mix of mods that won't synergies that well~I've barely scrapped the tip of the iceberg really~Low item capacity, max at stacks of 30, so collecting stuff is really hard as you're forced to give up certain ingredient to make room for other more needed resource~No selling options, So you really just trash without gaining any returns~ Limited item rotation makes hunting for equipment a bore. That, and upgrading an equipment only gives 1 digit of  improvement, which is such a miniscule amount, lots of people don't even bother upgrading their armor/weapon~ Over excess of certain ingredient and scarcity of others. Makes it hard to hunt for certain ingredient, when the spawn rate is being hogged by , for example~High aggro radius, and even higher enemy artillery range. Really doesn't make sense when you don't even see the enemy yet, and they already chasing after you. And the range enemy type just start aiming at you, so you had to dodge whilst looking for the enemy. Even worse when you spawn in a room that has multiple of those range type, but in different parts of the dungeon~And etc etc~I actually think if the brewery lock is just removed altogether, that would make combat more fun and acceptable,...to a degree~ I feel they have a talent when it comes to restaurant games, and food related games, but combat related game is a whole 'nother textbook, and they should really just focus on one, or take more time furnishing the dungeon mechanic~Other than that, if you dun mind it all, it's a really great game to play, very lovely, and the NPC is just iconic~

_childDocuments_.review: Delve into dungeons, stock up on ingredients, serve customers and earn money. A simple gameplay loop I was looking forward to grinding out for a while, so the rather sparse variety of dungeon layouts didn't bother me much.But there are so many scuffed aspects to this game that make it feel unfinished.You can upgrade your restaurant size over time, but the cash register and the 200m carpet leading up to it have a fixed position. You have to design the seating area around it.Decoration takes up floorspace which you want to fill with tables, so you are left with decorating the one wall that is visible. Surplus ingredients and equipment can't be sold, so if they clog up your inventory the only choice is to trash them.Putting new modifiers on equipment is rng-heavy and takes a day.Game only saves at the end of the day. Dishes that were picked up can not be put down anymore or served out of your inventory. Decoration costs way too much gold. Visually the game looks great, and combat is nice, but everything surrounding the town and your restaurant is janky af. Serving customers isn't engaging either, as all you do is queue dishes and it auto-cooks and plops onto the counter for guests to pick up. It is mostly waiting for guests to walk around or decide what they want, and jumping between cash register and kitchen to press one button to queue or complete the next step.If this was early access, I'd be excited to wait for qol changes, but for a full release this game is lacking an astonishing amount of thought in how things were implemented.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Having made it to the final boss, I need to change my opinion. Cuisineer is NOT a cute cooking game where you dungeon-crawl for ingredients. It's an isometric hack-and-slash with a pretty vestigial cooking minigame attached.The second-last challenge is a frustrating but also easily exploitable mix of cooking and harvesting, but the FINAL challenge is just a boss rush and I cannot be bothered rerolling and grinding mats to re-level a set of boss killing gear to replace my dungeon farming gear.The last fight is pretty nakedly aping Hades which is a shame because the designers have included none of the story impact or a satisfying power curve.Reluctant thumbs down---Original Review---I like this game. I do like it. But there are a lot of rough edges and weird design decisions that prevent me from loving it. Let's get the parts I like out of the way: The art is gorgeous and the character designs are wonderful. The visuals are what made this an instant-wishlist item when I saw it at PAX AUS. The general premise and world are also adorable and make for a very approachable, comfortable setting. The music easygoing and even the boss themes have a kind of ball-pit playroom quality to them.The game is broken into roughly three parts: Dungeon crawling for ingredients, running the restaurant and downtime.Dungeon crawling feels good at first, and the scenery is easy on the eyes. Every dungeon is a semi-randomly assembled series of square cell templates that always have the same enemies and layouts, which is good for gaining a sense of mastery of your environment but can get old quickly if there's not a whole lot of variety.The real pain is that there's very little scope to power up, so enemies that are spongy and frustrating at the start of the game are just as spongy and frustrating in the late game. I'll cover the upgrade system below, but the bottom line is that having to fight a conga-line of enemies that take 2 complete combos from the game's slowest weapon is excruciatingly dull.It's unfair to compare Cuisineer to Hades, but at the same time, the lessons Hades has to offer aren't exactly a secret, so it's frustrating to see a game make this mistake. You can pour millions of coins into upgrading your gear, but the improvements are capped and so incremental that even at five stars you may as well not have bothered.The purpose of the dungeon-crawling is to gather ingredients and building materials, and as you progress you gain access to areas with different combinations of enemies, however the frequency that you encounter enemies is not balanced against the rate you consume ingredients for dishes: As of writing I am perpetually throwing chillis, rice, flour, chicken, eggs, leafy greens and sweet sap (dropped by multiple frequently appearing enemies) in the garbage while I'm starved for beef and fish because the enemies that drop them are so uncommon, or don't drop them reliably.This means it takes several runs to supply myself for a single day of service because so many of the endgame recipes have such a high ingredient cost.Running the restaurant was the real selling point for me, because I love retail/hospitality sims (Diner Dash, Recettear, Dave the Diver, Potionomics) exactly as much as I hated working retail/hospitality in real life. Again, the music and visuals do a lot of the heavy lifting because the frustrating fact is that there's really not a lot to the sales aspect of Cuisineer.People walk in, seat themselves down, think for a bit and choose a dish. No menu needed, no drinks, no input from the player. They only ever choose from the list of dishes available (except in the very early game when they demand dishes you don't have stations for for some reason) and there are no custom orders, and preparing the dishes is never more complex than clicking on the relevant cooking station and clicking on the recipe: The game will even hide any items not currently requested to prevent you from cooking an item by mistake.The food cooks automatically, appears at the window automatically and the vast majority of customers will go to the window to collect it themselves. They'll eat the food and then see themselves to the register to pay - another one-click interaction - unless they're trying to eat and run in which case you need to catch them - yet another one-click interaction. Ultimately, what you're left with is just a series of one-click prompts, which I found very disappointing.The implication with certain recipes like Kaya and Caramel is that you would need to prep raw ingredients into processed ingredients for complex dishes, but no - customers will literally order a jar of caramel and dishes like "Kaya Toast" only require the raw ingredients needed to make kaya and toast separately.I'm probably being too harsh here: Food service is a high volume, low margin industry, so you can't have haggling mechanics like you do in Recettear and Potionomics and trying to balance price and quality on some kind of skill-based minigame for every dish would create an APM nightmare, but there's very little cooking in this game about cooking.I'm running out of steam, but there's not much to be said about the town: Again, it's beautiful and the music is lovely, but the vast majority of the townsfolk are typical stationary NPCs offering side-quests whose rewards are only ever recipes, so once you've filled out your book, there's nothing more to do for them.The exceptions are the service providers- Brewing is not explained at all and is basically a way to randomly generate buffs to fill one of two slots for your items. These buffs are broadly useless and supposedly influenced by using dishes to alter the odds, but I've seen just as many 1-star buffs burning 4-star dishes as I have 3-star buffs using no dishes at all. The escalating expense of attempts and overwhelming number of buffs with no value make save-scumming compulsory.- The equipment shops usually has at least one of each item type (6-ish weapons, gloves and boots) with randomised buffs, but as mentioned above, most buffs are useless and store-bought items never have buffs higher than a single star. You can upgrade the fastest weapons to do 1 more damage per hit, or the slowest weapon to do... also 1 more damage per hit. Neither of which is actually true - 2 rounds of upgrades on my ranged weapons and I was still doing exactly the same damage, so there's some opaque math involved that I can't be bothered diving into.- The Boba Tea shop functionally sells potions, but only 1-star healing potions are available. You can upgrade them or research new potions, but the buffs from the non-healing potions are so situational that you may as well not bother.- The carpenter sells furniture and also upgrades the size of your building. Different furniture is supposed to increase the appeal of your store to certain types of customer, but I've bankrupted myself several times with no discernible effect. The resource costs of each piece of furniture are so high that even a full endgame run's worth of materials is only enough for a few pieces. I understand that the devs have recently increased stack sizes to compensate for this, but it's a grind no matter how you look at it.- There's a pair of carts with rotating retailers that broadly aren't worth mentioning, except the panda who has been my favourite way to offload the massive stacks of useless ingredients for a tiny amount of what i need.I know all of this reads like a 1-star review, and I really want to emphasise that I don't consider the 40 hours I've played it to be a waste, but the repetitive dungeon grind, the imbalanced resource consumption, the flat power curve and the oversimplistic sales gameplay really make me itch to play similar games doing similar things but better.

_childDocuments_.review: I would really like to be able to enjoy and recommend this game, but there is a notable lack of meaningful progression, gameplay or strategy during the restauranting sections. There is little to optimize in the restaurant setup, and the multitasking-oriented gameplay you'd expect from the restaurant mode seems to be non-existent.I get to unlock lots of recipes, but I never look at them past the initial unlock, as all you do is click on the recipes as they pop up, and everything else happens automatically. If you could choose which recipes you want to serve within the day (e.g. having up to 5 recipes equipped at max simultaneously), and involve the player in some of the preparation work (e.g. getting the required ingredients together and serving the meals to the correct customers), it could make the restauranting more engaging.The combat is enjoyable. I like the enemy design and variety, and the combat is relatively challenging. It does get slightly stale when you get to floors 4 or 5, as the same rooms, enemies and arenas are repeated throughout.I hope that future patches will bring the required depth to make this game feel more rewarding to play. I love the aesthetic of the game, and aside from a few other minor nitpicks (e.g. limited settings), it feels pretty well polished. My review is a recommend only because I want this game to succeed. Maybe things will change and I can update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so sad that I cannot recommend this game because the art if beautiful, the characters are enjoyable, and the core gameplay is solid enough. But it all just falls flat due to one flaw.The amount of brainless, boring grind in this game is just too damn high.You need money to progress the story, but the flow of money is insanely slow until you upgrade your restaurant and your cooking supplies so you spend money to increase that flow, but every single individual upgrade is too insignificant to make any difference so you spend even more money to do that but in order to have that money in the first place you gotta delve into the dungeons for materials, but first you need money to upgrade your dungoneering supplies so you can deal more damage, survive longer and carry more loot, but again - you don't have that money in the first place and even if you had, just like with upgrading your restaurant, each individual upgrade to your gear is barely noticeable so YOU NEED MORE MONEY.So how do you make your money? By opening up your restaurant of course! And here lies the problem: the activity that you are REQUIRED to do in this game and the one you will spend THE MOST TIME on is also THE MOST BORING and LEAST ENGAGING activity in the whole game.There is just... nothing there. You just press the button to automatically cook whatever somebody ordered then once it's done the client will grab it himself, eat it, and the only other thing you have to do is to press another button to grab the pay. Occasionally you have to make sure somebody doesn't run away without paying but that's like once every blue moon.You cannot even chose your menu for the night, the customers will just order whatever is available based on your stashed ingredients, it's just too automated like a brainless mobile game.It gets a little better near the end game when you start serving high nobles that gives you better income and you have to serve food them yourselves, but it happens a little too late and by then the boredom has already set in.And it's like - Touhou Mystia's Izakaya is right there on Steam, with superior cooking mechanics, with almost no grind, with every single cooking night lasting just enough time for you to never get bored or overwhelmed. Devs could have lifted a single mechanic form it - be it singing, or personal menu, or serving requirements that has risk of messing up, or special guests or ability to cook manually with additional spices, and it would make the cooking so much better.But okay, that game has no dungeons so it could concentrate on the cooking part, this one is more action oriented so its unfair to compare them. So let's compare it to the classic Recettear - the shop opening part of the gameplay had actual skill requirement because you had to arrange your shop and its supply to make most amount of money and you also had to haggle smartly to get good experience bonus. There is nothing like this here, it's way too brainless.Aside from that there are other smaller issues such as memory leaking so game has to be restarted occasionally, story feels rushed at times especially beginning and the ending and the general lack of "push" to make the player feel motivated to continue.So at the end the game is just a grind and a slog. It could have been a good game if it was balanced and paced better. Maybe future patches can rebalance money and material requirements so you don't have to constantly grind for both to do anything, but as the game stands right now at the time of writing I cannot recommend it with a clear conscience, which is a crying shame as it has potential to be good and maybe it will reach it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: (I had this game in my wishlist and I got it the very second it came out! And it was on sale I call that perfect timing!)Okay, personally I think the game has had a few harsh reviews considering this game just came out less then a week ago.I wanted to get a fair amount of playtime in before I could give a fair review, and here are my honest opinions.I think this was an amazing idea for a game as it gives me flash backs dating back to Diner Dash, while also including having to really work to have a nice space. Taking a place from the ground and having to build up to make it your own really gives a satisfying feeling being able to see your progress in achieving a goal.Also I think its funny that in my opinion the game is more controller friendly then keyboard and mouse. Not a big deal to me though! :bI kinda wish there was a hiring option for some characters for like waitresses and I still cant figure out if theres a way to counter those dine and dash customers -~- If there is a way I think I missed that part of the tutorial lol.however I will say that in my opinion the dungeons are a little bit.. unbalanced? sometimes its almost unbearable to continue when you have like 10-20-30 enemies not only shooting you from all directions but then being rammed and slashed by others all at the same time at only floor 2-3 q-qAlthough, once mastering dodging and timing your weapon hits it gets a lot easier and if you dont get better at mastering that then its honestly just a skill issue lol.more to it I kinda wish there were more illustrations while it would be a little less boring sometimes seeing the same slide over and over can get kinda old after a bit.A few other things I would like to include is the small glitches, I dont know about anyone else but the game tends to frees or sometimes (rarely) you can get stuck in corners or small spaces and sometimes the amount of rocks and trees, while super easy to collect having those plus the obstacles can almost make being in dungeons completely unbearable ;-;Again still probably a skill issue)All being said this is still a brand new game and I think it is worth the cuteness and relaxing yet (sometimes really stressful) vibe you get off of it! _childDocuments_.review: Sadly its a negative, It's super fun but its just a worse version of a bunch of other games in the genre, (think hades and moonlighter as some examples) game feels like worse hades in the combat and has moonlighter aspects with the restaurant. _childDocuments_.review: I love the art, and it's better executed than harvestella but there's a lot left to be desired by this game. The primary gameplay loop is collect ingredients in the dungeon, return to town, run your restaurant to make money, use money to get upgrades, repeat. In classic format you can either open new dungeons, or go deeper in existing dungeons to unlock new ingredients, required for various upgrades, dishes, and quests. The problem is you will spend all your time and health running through the same low level of the dungeon, without being able to meaningfully progress and having to constantly dump low-level items from your inventory. It makes the whole thing feel like a giant waste of time rather than a fun game. Add to this that levels are randomly populated so you can't consistently grind for specific ingredients and it's really annoying. There needs to be something like stardew valley's elevator system so you can go to specific floors. The restaurant part of it feels a little lack-luster too, there's no way to dump the copius amounts of low-level ingredients you'll pick up, so they feel like a waste. Also, you can't sell items at all so there's no way to vendor weapon and armor pick-ups, you just have to trash them.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer has adorable artwork and an interesting gameplay loop that's like Hades meets Plate Up. You explore dungeons with Pom who has food themed takes on swords, spears, and large swords to hunt mobs for ingredients instead of loot. When you come back to town you use these ingredients cook food to earn money to get better gear to clear out dungeons, get better ingredients and build a bigger restaurant. I'm just getting started, but it's a lot of fun running a restaurant and trying to optimize the space to fit the most customers in.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm on day 9 and so far I only have a single complaint! I have no idea what I'm doing. There was virtually zero tutorial. I don't know what the symbols on the clock means, and I don't know what the symbols below it mean (the ones that highlight certain days). I also didn't know about birthdays, or where to get certain upgrades, or if I could upgrade. I have never played a game like this before; I really only bought it for the art style and the restaurant management part. The game is a couple months old already and there isn't a discord server or anything for it. If I knew a single thing about the game I would make one myself, but I think someone who knows everything about it is more suited.With that being said, with each bit of info I learn, I enjoy it more and more! I love the mechanics SO much. The fighting is perfectly balanced between not too easy but not painfully hard. That goes for the damage as well, not too little or too much. The art style is just absolutely stunning, thought some npcs are repeated and not as detailed as main characters. Overall this is the PERFECT game if you want something fairly mindless, a bit grindy, doesn't use many brain cells (this sounds negative but after a day of work as well as college, I do not want to think), BEAUTIFUL, cute dialogue, diverse characters (diverse in too many ways to list), FOOD, management, etc. But also don't play this game if you want your hand to be held. But when theres no possible way of learning it (the symbols and day times) then it's a bit annoying. No it doesn't say anything when you hover either haha.

_childDocuments_.review: Full playthrough here: First off it's a good game, but I think a lot of quality of life changes would make it significantly better I don't believe there's a way to take certain items off the menu or to stop the devil rampant amount of homeless children who come in and CONSTANTLY order dishes worth virtually nothing while using some of your most difficult to gather ingredients you need for your bigger dishes which is severely annoying. It also took me forever to figure out you need your restaurant about size 8 to attract nobles I honestly thought it was more a matter of decorating and being able to cook fancy dishes but no the one thing I was missing was a certain size restaurant I wish the game was a bit more explicit on telling you the size restaurant required since I could make 4 star dishes sit everyone easily but nobles were boycotting because I hadn't made the restaurant larger than it needed to be to seat everyone. Potatoes are broken strong they attack faster than your heavy weapons swing and do 30 damage if they hit you with the full spud which is more than most boss mobs hit they're ranged and when you get to the end of the game where the creators just said F it and chucked in a billion monsters it gets freaking annoying. Tomatoes are tanky for some unknown reason I'd wager like most mobs in the game they have more health than you. Music is great character design is dope but man does it drag towards the end it's very repetitive and I feel like since there are no mini games for the cooking the game is just a simple crafting game rather than a cooking game luckily it's simple enough a crafting game noob like myself could enjoy it a good bit, but I was hoping for more cooking aspects in the game play. You barely gain in strength for adventuring which is annoying you get more and more difficult monsters, but even a fully upgraded weapon doesn't feel necessarily powerful which makes it even more of a slog to finish the game towards the end and Cuisine Challenge 3 was one of the hardest things in the game the final boss fight is fair, but cuisine challenge 3 is toxic.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. But after 16 hours of grinding through the surprisingly unforgiving dungeons and lackluster restaurant management sim portion of the game, I just can't recommend this game. The art is beautiful, the soundtrack decent, and the mechanics of the game are solid. This game has the potential to be fun, but that's all it is: potential. You can tell the developers really put effort into making this game look and play well, yet they failed to actually make the game's gameplay loop fun enough to want to keep going. I kept expanding my restaurant, doing some upgrades with my weapons (which only give you a +1 damage bonus each upgrade so and you can only only upgrade them 4 times, each time becoming aggressively more expensive in coin and resources that doesn't make it overall worth it), and throwing myself into the dungeon in hopes that maybe I'd finally get to the part where it becomes intriguing to keep going and fun.It never happened. The arts is lovely, but the substance is lacking. All combat ends up being is just whack things enough times by spamming the button/mouse until it dies, and most enemies just end up being sponges and track your movement until the *very* split second before they attack, so you'll still get hit even if you see their telegraph and dodge behind them, meaning you can't effectively dodge until the very last moment before the attack comes out. The NPCs in the village look okay enough, with many just being palette swaps of the typical Old Man/Woman or Child Boy/Girl NPCs wandering the town or visiting your restaurant. The ones that do stands out as unique have very little to offer in terms of character and show they are just meant to be side-quest hawkers or vendors and nothing more.Ultimately, the game has so much potential to be something fun and interesting, but it's all shine and little substance. The developers clearly tried to make it fun to play, but I can't say they succeeded.

The game is fun at most points and is worth the $25 price tag for what's probably at least 30+ hours to finish the game. Not a game for everyone though and there's definitely room for improvement.

Even if you feel like you have to manage your expectations a tad, you'll do fine in Battlebrew Productions' latest, especially with the isometric attack-savvy bits where you let a cat girl go hog wild with a flame-powered spatula and grenade egg timers against fire elemental yaks and sentient potatoes tossing projectiles.Full review:

_childDocuments_.review: You know, I just played that, and this is crazy…But Cuisineer is an action roguelite. And not a bad one at that, either.Cutesy design and silly weapons aside (the Smackerel is a perennial favorite of mine here), the game consists of 2 elements. The restaurant part is where you earn money for upgrades and unlock new dungeon and gameplay elements, while the dungeon part is where you get ingredients to turn into money and raw materials required for upgrades.Upgrades also are locked behind time progression. Nothing too bad - not all vendors are available on all weekdays, and the wandering merchants rotate in and out depending on the weekday as well. And upgrading gear takes a day, during which the item in question is unavailable.The same goes for quest NPCs, which may not be around at all due to the date.There’s plenty of stuff to fiddle with, though. You have 4 item slots (primary and secondary weapon, and gloves and boots which act as armor. Each has two perk slots and 5 upgrade levels, with one of the vendors offering perk rerolls for money (and food items to influence the results…).Perks range from stuff like infusing elemental status conditions (which keep the theme…they’re sweet, toasty, bitter, salty etc.), exploits like extra damage to afflicted enemies, to stuff like temporary shields or spawning projectiles.This ties into the combat which can be described as hades light (though the calories are probably a lot higher), with dashes, knockbacks, projectiles and weapon-based special moves to help declutter the screen and fill the fridge. Difficulty is still challenging, though the game doesn’t exactly go out of its way to murder you.On death, you are teleported back to town, but lose most of the gathered loot. Your inventory is limited (but can be expanded), so it’s a bit of a balance game on knowing when to hold’em and knowing when to fold’em to get the most out of your run.Healing and special effects are available via your potion slots, and take the form of boba tea. I’m sure the Rule 34 folks will have a field day with the fact that the two girls that sell them are udderly well endowed cows.The tea strength and selection can be upgraded, but the investments required for unlocking and upgrading them are pretty daunting at first.So, unleash your inner catgirl, grab a large fish or kitchen implement, and try to save your parent’s restaurant. Hilariousness awaits!Culinary arts, ho!PSA: Playing the game can induce pretty fierce hunger pangs. The food artwork is pretty nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: A marvelous management game that makes you crave for more.Your parents have gone off for a long trip and left you with their family business to take care of. However, you soon discover that they have amassed a great debt(s) that you need to pay.It starts very simply, with a single table to serve and a tiny little stove. As you progress you start expanding the space, your tools and start attracting different clients. Your list of recipes also starts small, but as you run errands around the town you learn more. You can fully customize your restaurant, and the different styles you choose will attract different types of customers.For your ingredients, you will need to travel to a series of dungeons in order to collect them. The combat is very simple but it has a degree of complexity. The equipment you get has various stats and abilities on it, and some stats and abilities are more rare than others. To get them you will either need to hunt tougher enemies inside the dungeons or try your luck with the brewer and mix a cooked dish with your equipment in order to get the stat/ability you need. Each dish has a specific element which affects the chances of receiving certain stats.If you are looking for a cute, simple yet complex with a lot of choices management game, this is the perfect game.  You will get a lot of content for its price.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Cons:- Gameplay is as shallow as a puddle- Poorly optimized, frequent and almost random framedrops- Zero combat variety- Nonexistent story- Resources are poorly spread out, lots of useless garbage, samey equipment and ingredients outside of its respective area- No furniture drops, which is the only thing that actually matters aside from cooking ingredients- Furnishing is too damn gaudy or strictly themed, mixing and matching is minimal- Large catalogue of items without a formal search bar, finding things is tedious- "Procedural generation" only consists of like 8 different layouts- There's technically only 3 major areas, one is pretending to be a 4th- The worst upgrade system in any game, demanding an excessive amount of time and resources for marginal gains, one of which is compounded with unnecessary RNG.Upgrading anything important is a multi-step process of:1) Writing down what you need2) Going into journal to figure out what items are needed to cook that item3) Going into the shop and sifting through an awful sliding menu to find the necessary item (You have a fully functioning, perfectly organised tab system in the journal, but not the in the cooking equipment? What the hell?)4) Spending half an in-game day to cook these items (this is with multiple cooking equipment)5) Click the items so it's in your inventory6) Go to the NPC and give them the item7) Then wait an in-game day to use it8) Repeat this process 10 more times so it's actually useful- Basically a mobile game but only prefers to waste your time without asking for moneyPros:- The food looks really really good- All recipes are described with fetishistic detail- It's cute10/10, it's okay. Feels like an early access game, but sold as a complete game under the additional hours of tedium.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have to play a lot to see it's an Asian take on the Moonlighter formula but with Furries and cooking. The formula works well, so you have here an enjoyable casual game that is less harder than Moonlighter but you still get do a lot of fighting against a wide cast of enemies. You have a part where you gather ingredients and a part where you cook and serve in your restaurant to make money. Then buy a various range of upgrades for your character and your restaurant in order to make more money and to kill things faster. Rinse and repeat. If you liked Moonlighter for it's loop, you will enjoy this game. If you are looking for a casual cute game that is not a farming sim game, then you'll enjoy this game as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I gave this a good ol' college try, but I can't really recommend it as is. Between balance issues, questionable progression (I'm 6 hours in and I have no idea how to get "stronger"), high restaurant upgrade costs, and some clunky UI choices, it all adds up to a negative experience. The female tourist customers are what finally tipped me over the edge for this review because they show up, taking "customer" slots, and then ask for dishes you don't have ingredients for. If you try to keep every ingredient for every dish in stock across all the dungeons, you won't have any room and it'll take 2-3 days of dungeon grind (because different dungeon = different ingredients, with some only showing up a few levels in) and all that time you're not making any money because you get a debuff if you try to hit the dungeon and run the restaurant at the same time.That said, I do want to call out the genuinely lovely art style, including the mouth-watering dishes, and that I love the concept of the game overall as a cute cozy moonlighter wannabe. I loved moonlighter, and I wanted to love this just as much.

_childDocuments_.review: I typically like cute games with food, and stockpiling resources, and definitely enjoyed this game. I almost quit the game before truly getting started because it was glitching so badly that I couldn't move from one spot for several minutes because my avatar kept falling through the ground when I tried to move. After finally getting past the first area, it was not very often throughout the playthrough that I encountered this glitch again. Buuut when I started a second playthrough, the exact same thing happened, so be aware that the very beginning of the game may just be glitched.One thing that I found to be a minor flaw is that some of upgrades take quite a bit of resources, and in the case of weapons, it's for very small increases. It can start to feel a little too grindy when you're trying to max something out.Also be forewarned that this game is insanely difficult with high item-loss penalties for dying. It crosses the line between being challenging and being a pain in the behind at some points, leading me to set aside my gamer pride and turn down the difficulty settings.So, I spent a lot of time on the negatives because I feel that they could be deal-breakers for some people, but despite its flaws, I did enjoy this game enough to complete it and start a second playthrough. If you like cute food games and resource-collecting as much as I do, then this game definitely fulfills both of those things, and I found it highly satisfying to build up from next to nothing to a big, fancy, customized restaurant.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been hooked on this game recently! While it has a bunch of balancing problems I really don't care and I keep coming back to it. When I first played this game it didn't have difficulty options (or at least not an easy option) and I really struggled to get through the dungeons and very quickly gave up (I'm terrible at combat in games) but I came back to it like six months later and was able to select a difficulty mode where you only take 20% damage and now I can't stop playing. In the dungeons you find random equipment (weapons and armor) that all have either one or two special effects and I find it really fun to experiment with different combinations of them. I also enjoy that instead of just selling stuff you find in the dungeons you make money with a restaurant management mini game where you use all the ingredients you find in the dungeon runs (though it's a very basic one I still find it enjoyable) and it does get a little more involved the more you upgrade your restaurant. The dungeons themselves have a nice atmosphere and a variety of different enemies to fight. The runs can take a bit of time to get through and can get a little repetitive but I still find them satisfying. The issues come in with things like equipment upgrades that are way overpriced and basically useless so I don't really bother with them. There's also a brewery where you can gamble by paying a fee and using random dishes you make to get different equipment enchantments at different strengths but it is not explained what dishes do what (but you can find that info online easily) so I haven't experimented with that yet I prefer to just find equipment in the dungeons. There's also a boba shop where you can buy boba (basically one time use potions) and upgrade them using a combinations of different required dishes  and they can be helpful but I've only managed to unlock one of I think eight different bobas and upgrade it one time after over 20 hours. This is mostly because to unlock all the required recipes you have to wait until you receive and complete quests from the towns people and then make sure you have the right cooking station at the right upgrade level and have unlocked the region where you can find the right ingredients to make the recipes required to upgrade the bobas. I also haven't figured out what unlocks the different types of bobas yet even though I've upgraded my restaurant quite a bit and unlocked the first three regions and done all the quests I've been given but I'm sure I'll figure it out soon and for now the health boba I do have unlocked has been quite useful. But overall I am having a blast with this game and I will probably continue to play it for a while. It's definitely not gonna be for everyone but if you're like me and appreciate a good cozy/casual game with just a little bit of challenge and don't mind some things not being super optimized/balanced then you might also really enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Recettear, Moonlighter. Game is split into 2 halves; a dungeon looter and a restaurant management game. Depends on your playstyle. There are no time limits, so you can take your time to fulfil quests. And the dungeon exploration doesn't count time so you can stay as long as you want. However, the NPCs only appear on certain days, you cannot open the restaurant after 6pm and time passes quickly in the town and in your restaurant. So if you are the type to cram as much into a day as possible, you will be rushing everywhere. Isometric auto-generated maps. Mobs are damage sponges, recommend you start at the easiest  difficulty. Gameplay and mechanics are generally quite fun. Some maps (*cough* Konpeito Swamp) are visually cluttered, with odd bits of foliage which looks passable blocking passage. This sometimes makes combat frustrating as some game skills require a level of precision to execute... and you are blocked. Also, encountered a fatal bug several times where the system thinks the ground you stand on is deep water, forcing you to quit the dungeon. Starts off easy- basically click on orders to cook them. When nobles appear, it gets hectic as you need to serve the cooked food to the nobles. This adds a dimension where you need to rearrange your furniture for efficiency and access. Kind of meh. Essentially you repeatedly grind the same 4 areas  for material to stock your restaurant, and to upgrade your equipment. And the dungeons can take a while to clear if you're not well geared. Worth it for the price, will scratch your Recettear itch. The basic gameplay is fun, it deserves more love, polish and content to make it shine. Kind of let down by the annoying UI - e.g. it spams you with a "are you sure" popup needing you to click every time you try to discard a equipment from your bag.

_childDocuments_.review: A simple and cute dungeon crawler and restaurant simulator. The main idea of the game is to do dungeon runs to gather materials and ingredients to work on the restaurant.The dungeons are randomly generated. You have 4 equipment slots: 2 weapons and 2 armor piece. The weapons fall under 4 category: swords (fast light swings), spears (fast with more straight range), great swords (slow swings that do big damage), and projectiles. Weapons have a normal attack and a special attack that goes on cooldown. Each equipment can have 2 different modifiers. These modifiers can inflict status effects, enable critical damage, grant you more health, shield, and even fire projectiles.As for the restaurant, customer comes in and orders a dish. You run up to the facilities and select the dish they order. The cooking is automatic and the customer comes up and grabs the dish to eat. Afterwards you collect their payment at the counter. Relatively simple. Most of the time you will be running back and forth between the cashier and the cooking stations. Some customers may dine and dash so you can to catch them for the money. Later nobles comes in and you're require to bring the dish to them, an instance where you can accidentally serve the wrong dish if you're not careful. Outside of the restaurant you can do quest for new recipes, upgrade equipments, buy new furniture, and even upgrade your restaurant.This game has a really huge flaw: the pacing and progression is really bad. I believe the reason is that the numbers they used for everything is out of proportion. For instance, at max inventory upgrade you have 40 slots. A material stack caps at 30 per slot. This by default makes gathering very slow. You can barely get make it half way through the dungeon before you maxed out on inventory. This slows down the pacing tremendously because the requirements for upgrading also requires an absurd amount of materials. You gameplay loop ends up like this: dungeon for materials, upgrade 1 thing, dungeon for materials, upgrade 1 thing, restaurant for money, repeat. This makes the game incredibly grindy from start to finish. You basically need to do dungeon runs to hunt very specific materials for upgrades. The amount of work you need to do for how little of a payload is insane.Dungeon runs becomes a pain after the honeymoon phase. Even with good upgrades and modifiers, fighting enemies is such a chore. The enemies seem to have way too much hp where even the basic enemies require at least 2 combo strings to defeat. You never feel strong is this game. They swarm you with large group of enemies and very often there is one or two that just starts sniping from outside your vision. Boss fights aren't that bad because it is a bit more controlled environment but you never need to do a boss fight after beating them once since they don't have unique drops.Some positives:-this game has a very cute art style and character designs-you use boba as healing potions in dungeons.-music is fine-decorating the restaurant is fun if you're into that but upgrading the restaurant kind of screws with the layoutOther nitpicks:-the endgame section fully highlights how much of a pain in the ass the combat becomes-dying in a dungeon is very punishing in a game where you need as much resources you can get-you can only save when you end the day, no midday saving-the inventory menuing can be a pain to use-upgrading gear is very minimal stat gain-it takes a day to upgrade/modify gear, if that is your main gear you're stuck being unable to do a dungeon run that dayI enjoyed the game enough but it is very hard to recommend to people. I really like the concept but I think this game needs more time in the oven.If you're interested, there is a mod that can help alleviate some of the problems.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I really like playing this game.  It's a cute restaurant simulator plus dungeon crawler and is fun on both fronts. The atmosphere created by the music and art style is very chill, and I really like managing the restaurant.  I also really like the characters.  If you like operating a successful restaurant on your own and you're okay with some fairly straightforward combat, you should give this game a go.
