_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game pretty much for the Art Style alone, which is a 10/10. Everyone and Everything is cute.On the topic of art I adore the art done for the food, makes me want it IRL, not a game to be played while hungry :PThe restaurant gameplay: Starts off as pretty slow at the start, but as you build up your reputation it starts to get busier. When they introduce Nobles into the mix which require you serve them personally it can become somewhat chaotic, but not overwhelming. 8/10. Hopefully they don't add in any sort of automation to this, would simply kill the fun of it.The dungeon gameplay - Enemies: Plenty of different critters with their own attacks. Big fan of the crab enemies and the punchy octopuses in the Fjord. Not so big a fan of the wild rice enemies, especially the shamans. Bosses have bigger, flashier attacks that may catch you off guard on your first go, but on subsequent runs can be easy to read and react to accordingly, especially if you can come up with a strategy to take them on (like killing the BBC with its own ranged feather attack with some cheeky shields).  8/10The dungeon gameplay - Combat: While simple, the combat in this game has a solid amount of variety with weapons and gear, as well as the mods that can be attached to them. With fast-hitting light-damage and slower-hitting heavy-damage weapons, as well as a few different ranged weapons for when you need to keep your distance. I try to have one of each for different scenarios. With modifications you can focus on offence, defence, or a combination of the two, though having a shield mod is pretty much necessary to avoid damage from the ranged monsters in higher density fights. Arenas are fun. 8/10The dungeon gameplay - Resource Collection: Probably the weakest part of the game comes from collecting resources, which you'll need to do a lot in the later stages of the game. Bashing trees and rocks for construction materials, and defeating enemies for ingredients. At the beginning you start with very little bag space, meaning your bag will probably be full before you even finish the first floor of a dungeon. Inventory expansions are pretty cheap, going up to a total of 40 slots in the bag. The main issue, and why the start of the game and later stages are pretty rough, is the stack limit, which is a max of 30 per stack. You'll find yourself managing your inventory a lot, especially after Arena chests which drop a lot of armoury items, which will have you backing in and out of your inventory pretty often. Some adjustments to stack sizes and perhaps an increase to inventory space, perhaps separate compartments for ingredients, construction materials, and armoury, could potentially solve these issues. 6/10 Overall it is very cute and fun game which can eat your time away if not careful. I definitely recommend the game in it's current state, and hopefully will see some positive changes in the future, as it is still a pretty new game. I give it an overall score of 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game for about $10 which made the gameplay more justifiable for the price.It's a really pretty and cute game and the characters are so nicely designed. Sadly they are pretty surface level in interaction and they aren't super involved outside of being merchants.The rougelite parts are fine and the weapons are cute but somehow it doesn't feel very exciting and there aren't a lot of "builds" or random events to keep it interesting in the long term.The restaurant portion has potential but it is so long and boring and desperately needs a speed up option. I usually have to play a video in the background so I don't nod off. Hopefully it gets better as I progress. So far I would recommend it for $10 but anything more, probably not.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun game. This is divided into two halves. Dungeon progression, which you don't need to complete. The second half is running a restaurant and doing quests. The short of it, is that the goal is to pay off debt. While a simple, system it has a bit of work to it. The better your restaurant such as how you design it and the rep affects your profits.In the dungeons you gather materials, recipes are unlocked through side quests. The story itself isn't much, a character that is an adventurer returns home, and ends up running a restaurant while her parents are on vacation. She ends up having to tackle her parents debt, or lose the restaurant.The characters are nice, and it is really a calm and entertaining experience. If anything, I'd say the dungeons needs less monsters. This can cause performance issues, the aggro range should be smaller, and it needs a better way to get stronger.This is a slight issue, but not game breaking. Overall, I can recommend it. Though, with one more issue to be aware of. The game is extremely unbalanced.

_childDocuments_.review: I watched people play this and it is in line with other games I play that I really enjoy. But I just can't enjoy this game. Even with the difficulty turned down, it's just too punishing which makes it really unfun to me. I'm not a 'hardcore' gamer, I just like to play games sometimes to have 'me time' and relax.The restaurant part isn't all that enjoyable since the main components to it are automated - you queue up their order and the cooking items make the food for you, most of the customers get up and get their own order, then you cash them out when they leave. Overall the whole game is just pretty basic. Nothing in it has much depth. You can't carry very many health items, which just makes the dungeons even less fun because you do a floor or two and then have to quit since you can't heal and you'll loose basically everything if you continue. The item to take you out of the dungeon is so slow and if you get hit while activating it you have to start all over again so it's not the "emergency leave" that they initially tell you it is. My friend also tried to play it and the screen lag bothered him to the point he couldn't play. We both work in IT and tried adjusting the settings and monitor to fix it, but the issue seems to be within the game itself that it stutters at times. I wish I had quit playing earlier so I could get a refund. I was just trying to force myself to like it since I waited so long to buy it, and I wanted to make sure I actually put some time into it so I wasn't quitting before the "game" even began. But it just never really felt fun to play.

_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop just kills me after about 20 hours of the same. The constant gating to go to new areas, gating to get the better patrons, gating to get furniture, gating for new recipes.. The game didn't tell me at all how to make more money, I eventually figured it out after like 10 hours of grinding what feels like pennies. Restaurant to 8 > focus debts for 3rd/4th area. If I had a change I'd 100% make it would be the nobles showing up around rank 4, which is weirdly around the same time you're told about nobles only for them to be nowhere to be seen..The game needs to explain these things, or the content needs to be more than that loop that I don't care that it took that long. The restaurant flow and minigame in general need work, I think. It's basically a bunch of menuing until you unlock nobles.Upgrades shouldn't take a day to make, it's just a waste of time turning in the weapon and then going to sleep. It make me decide not to upgrade anything. The stat changes are basically nothing anyway. All of this points out another issue, that the day/month cycle and sleeping does essentially nothing as there's no punishment or change in finishing the game in 10 years or in the first one. I can open the restaurant for breakfast and immediately close and sleep after the rush, nothing changes.I really want to recommend this game, it's cute, the NPCs are all great and I enjoyed all of them. The roguelite aspects are ok, but I think the formula, particularly the restaurant, the unlocks and the way sleeping and time in general functions, all need work.Also, the game runs TERRIBLY if you want to just run through an area and kill a boss. I have a very good PC and I saw as low as 5 FPS when a ton of chickens and little wheat guys were on screen at once. It was like a slideshow.  I also t-posed in all 3 of the final challenges while delivering the food to judges.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I recommend this game! It's adorable, fun and the character and food design is lovely! There are a few issues I've experienced that I think people should be aware of before buying it though:- The game has horrible frame rate issues. There's a chance it's my own computer at fault here, but sometimes in the dungeons my frames can drop to like 10 if there are too many smaller enemies on the screen. It's caused me to die because I couldn't dash in time to dodge things.- The game does have some bugs, though the worst of them is sometimes...you'll just fall through the floor of the dungeons? It's rare, at least in my case, but I've had it happen twice so far in 12 hours of gameplay, one of which wouldn't let me walk away from the spot and I kept falling until I ran out of HP. Another annoying bug is I had an arena that just...wouldn't let me out? I waited for about 5 minutes, AFK'ed, still couldn't leave. Thankfully the game /does/ let you leave the dungeon whenever you'd like, but it basically halted my progress for the day. Annoying more than anything.- The game has some UI/gameplay issues, namely with how some things are not explained well. I think it's fine for a game like this to just throw you in! It's pretty easy to learn the basics. But I went through the two debts at the beginning without selling a single tier 2 dish because I thought a tier 2 appliance would...cook tier 2 food, but it doesn't. Tier 3 does. Maybe this was explained and I just missed it! But it did confuse me.- The game is pretty easy. I feel like I'm just blasting through it! Which is okay, but it depends on how you view price to game time. I bought it while it was 50% off, which I find worthwhile, so it's up to you to decide if the full price is worth it.But overall it's a fun game that is nice to play and is quite relaxing!! I recommend it above all if you can get passed a few bugs and some lag.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DRGame is good, if you like recettear: an item shops tale you will love this. Do not give up during the early/mid game, it gets way better.Rewriting this whole review in light of some more gameplay.Buy on sale, I still don't know if I would feel good about my purchase if I paid $30, but it definitely feels worthwhile at $20The following are some tips that will help you get through the early game to the good bit.The early game is... bad, The game leads you in one direction and then when you transition to the lategame it abruptly turns around and has you do the opposite. I had like 15 paragraphs written about this previously so I will keep it brief this time, there is a tutorial but it is woefully inadiquate, you need to go and figure out things like upgrading your healing boba and how to modify your weapons at the brewery yourself, any upgrades you do on gear early is useless because you will need to buy completely new gear if one of your spice slots is locked with a 1 star modifier.the early/mid game is significantly better if you learn to throw away cheap ingredients so that your customers wont order noodles and boiled eggs and pay you $12 every time, customers only order what is available meaning in the midgame you will want to trash all your eggs and flower. you will then immediately regret doing this as the higher level recepies commonly require lower level stuff that gets combined into a part of the recipe (eggs+exotic fruit =kaya, which is used in high level recipes) this is a game where you need to hit every rock and tree for wood and stone, if you hate farming for that kind of thing you should avoid this game honestly, farming for ingredients and materials is probably %75 of this gamePrioritize quests, the recipes from them are very useful, also the characters go hard describing the recipes they are going to trade youboba sisters are IMPORTANT, upgrade whichever of the first two boba you like ASAP, the tutorial does not teach you this and because it requires so many random things (in small amounts) it can overwhelm you and make you skip it, dont skip it, upgrade your "estus flask"Get frost + damage to frosted enemies on melee weapons and pierce + shock on your range for AOE, you will thank me.I would like to see improvements to the tutorial and the brewery system to make the early game not feel so bad, but most of my negative thoughts on the game have gone away with time.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a super adorable game that is worth your time if you like managing a restaurant. You do delve into dungeons to get ingredients, but the simple combat isn't going to be a barrier of entry for most players. Losing a lot of items on death might, however, be discouraging. Be sure to leave if you're out of potions and low on health!The game does expect you to grind a bit to pay off your debt or just unlock things. You are going to be in the dungeons a lot. There is gear to help you conquer them more easily, but certain upgrade systems for gear are kind of unintuitive. I recommend the game because of its art style and charm, but if you're looking for a game with exceptional systems, you might be disappointed. If you like shop/management games you'll likely enjoy it; especially at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: It's a laid back dungeon crawler & restaurant game (similar to Moonlighter / Recettear / World End Diner)I *really* enjoy the fact that I don't feel rushed or pressured at all time/schedule wise. You run dungeons to gather goods, do quests for townsfolk & run your restaurant; whenever & however you feel like it.  Lots of recipes, decorations, upgrades for your shop & gear.There are seasons, special dates & times; but you don't feel rushed and there's no fomo events, nothing has a time limit.The day/night cycle is really laid back, much slower than most games with the mechanic. There are no relationship building mechanics. (no gifting / no relationship levels, etc)Quests sort of get bulk dumped on you as you progress certain things.. You can turn in any amount of quest items at any time (when the npc is available). Dungeons are not timed. You can go for as long as you'd like (inventory and HP are the limiting factors)The only 'punishments' I've come across is if you die in dungeon you lose 80% of your inventory and go back to town. Cons : - Time doesn't stop when you open your inventory/chests in town- Combat is a bit clunky/unrefined feeling- Upgrading weapons & gear feels... almost pointless - Enemies have a bit too much health / take too long to kill.- Gear stats and effects are poorly described- Gear is a useless pain to level up and getting good stats relies on RNG that takes forever.- Can be pretty grind-y with how many items are required / how expensive some things are to upgrade or buy + how repetitive quest tasks are.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: First review ever on Steam, because why not.Honestly I really enjoy this game. I usually am not a fan of those real time "Get your material in the field" type of games, like the Atelier Series, because it's usually coming with missable events, but not this one. It's intuitive, it's fun, lots of side quests, weapons and all that, the artwork is cute and well done. For the cons, it remains just an opinion, and I'm being picky here, but I would have like to move some of the unmovable items. Since there is a specific area that are for potential customers waiting for a table and another for your cooking appliances, the cash register makes you lose a bit of the space available where it's at. Also, I would have preferred for the crafting characters to have a specific written schedule. It's a bit of a bummer to have your cash in hand, ready to buy some tables, but the carpenter is chilling next to the Smith,Not necessarily a negative, but it would be great if in the first side quest where it is asking you to meet all the important townspeople, to have added the belt and bag upgrade guy. Took me about 7 game days before I notice that one of the two in the town center is giving you the opportunity for more spaces, since you quickly realize that you can fill two rows in one floorLet's grade it, hum... 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: While this is a thumbs up recommendation, please take this with a grain of salt.If you're looking for a casual and fun little restaurant sim with a bit of a grind when it comes to resource gathering then this game might be for you. Just ignore the last bit of the game after you unlock the last biome as it feels as if it were tacked on just for difficulty sake. It honestly clashes with the cozy / casual vibe the rest of the game had going for it up until this point.Aside from that there are some performance issues like frame drops / stuttering / input lag that I've noticed (either when my play session exceed an hour or maybe it had to do with how many in-game days had passed) and a game breaking bug in the third biome that I've encountered more than once where an arena will spawn enemies outside of it which you cannot kill to end said arena, essentially making you have to go back to town to keep playing (save and exit). Now you might be thinking "Oh, just avoid arenas in the third biome" which is excatly what I thought and tried, except sometimes with the way that the procedural engine creates a dungeon you HAVE to go through an arena to proceed to the next floor or to fight the boss. Having said all this, I would recommend getting this game on a discount as I feel $30 is a bit steep if I'm suggesting to ignore the "end game" / story conclusion. You can get a feel for the game well within the 2 hour gameplay limit of Steams return policy as not much changes from that going forward if you want to try it without a sale. The cozy vibes of the art, music and the restaurant management might be worth it for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I'm gonna rewrite my review since I've wanted to go back on my words.I love the style and character designs of this game! I want to play through the game entirely, but as another review said, this game doesn't really respect your time at all... A lot of the game is sulking around in what feels like a very empty town, where everyone requests you to be their errand girl for a recipe while you just skip through their dialog and not have any reason to use the chat button for them.For the Dungeons, they get repetitive fast, with similar layout pieces with not a lot of variations, swarms of common enemies to make some ingredients more rare and more expensive to sell, but leads to the problem of having a limited inventory, needing to constantly take out the things you don't need, and relying on running past most mobs to get specifically what you need, etc. Bossfights are fine, but most dungeon crawls you don't even get near a boss to fight, you just stay on the first floors to grind.  There isn't enough variety to the dungeons which makes me not want to  explore and just rush to the end and get what I need. Attacking in this game feels like so much is off, attack sfx's feel incredibly mute, alongside barely any ambiance to these maps/dungeons, and fights just feel like m1 battles where you'd rather just get the heavy swingers to stun on first hit so you can combo off of the first swing so they can't fight back.For your Restaurant, it gets even more boring! I'm sorry, but the only interactivity for it is clicking to cook what they want, no asking for orders or anything else, you don't even have to bring their food to them.       Lets compare this to Mystia's Izakaya, where you get a waitress and also have to get orders from the customers, drinks, and can experiment on what they like with ingredients with different traits! In Cusineer, you don't really have any interaction with anyone, and no special characters show up to keep your interests up with them. Most characters you find in this game look amazing, but feel incredibly one sided and would rather just skip through dialog to get what you want. Another Comparison to Mystia's is that you get recipes for serving and talking to them to increase relationships with recipes being earned feeling like something that character would eat!        In this game, you get: No Waiters, no assistance, no creativity, no spice, no nothing. You just click to get what they want, and the game plays out the rest itself. Why should I feel like I should customize my Restaurant when it feels a lot better to focus on upgrades so you can spend as little time in dungeons as possible? The only part about serving is seeing the great art for the foods, but at a point you just stop caring to even look at them too.For the Town, it feels so empty and unlively, I don't know why, but you feel like everyone isn't even a character, just quests to get new recipies. The Baristas are cool, but I never had a reason to upgrade their drinks and it felt like a chore to even try to spend my resources to upgrade. The armor perk guy also felt like this, why should I bother trying to change things when its easier to just get armor pieces in dungeons! I remember getting a very strong mackrel melee and just ignoring any other weapons I found just because it was a set up weapon that had its perks matching together great already! Decor stands? Not much of interest. The weaponry area? Lackluster! Upgrading felt pointless, as you spend money to BARELY change your damage! For buying weapons/armor, you'd only really do it if you found a good combo at random, but that never happens so I just never ended up buying anything. The rest of the town? Completely pointless to explore and bland with no interesting qualitys to it. The game also tries to make you feel like the other characters in the town are people with things like Birthdays, but all it does is reward you with something little, then completely forgets about it. They don't visit your restaurant and just sit in town waiting for you to complete tasks for them.For the Story, it even starts off being lackluster and no interesting points, sadly! There's no intro story/cutscene to the game, you just get started in a dungeon with no controls being shown off, you just dash to the end and go to the town. You're supposed to feel like you're caring for your family's restaurant after your family decides to explore the world just to be shoved taxes in the daughters face. I would've loved having an intro seeing the main character talk about herself and her returning to town, but you then realise that this game doesn't have any interesting cutscenes or any interests in learning more about characters and story when its all very barebones or just fall off flat to me. It feels like there's so much this game is missing out on, and I'd like there to be more... It just feels like "Oh hey Ma and Pa- oh, thats taxes...", you don't even interact with what I believe is your Sister much after the start of the game.To sum up The Restaurant segments, its just click to serve with no interesting features or gameplay requiring your attention.To sum up The Dungeon segments, its just lack luster and not really interesting, resulting in you wanting to avoid most of it since it feels so off and bland.To sum up the Town/story, you don't really get enticed enough to really care, and most of it is just dialog with nothing else to go alongside it, no voice acting, no cutscenes, yada. You feel as though you are in a empty one sided town where everyone just leeches off of you to do their chores/requests...I WANT to spend time playing this game, I WANT to Recommend this and show this game off to people, but I just don't feel like the game respects my time nor anything of interests to keep me going or to show to others. Sorry, Cusineer, I like your art, but everything else is just empty and lacking of game itself...

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. Originally I was going to hold off on writing a review on it until I got all of the achievements and many more hours into it but an event took place that I feel needs to be addressed. I hope the Devs take some time and read this because I'm in-love with your project!I want to talk about the restaurateur part of the game first. My restaurant is level 8 at the time of this review. Organizing and customizing the restaurant is very satisfying. Gaining new recipes is easy and rewarding. Managing the restaurant when its open is satisfying and requires little mental overhead save for noble guests (The customers you must bring the food to) and even then its just a small thing you have to pay attention too. Customers can try to leave without paying though I've only had this happen to me once in my 15 hours of play at the time of writing. In my opinion the restaurant management is this games strength and while simple at its core I find myself having the most fun in this part. Now for the dungeon part. I'd like to start by saying I've played through Hades multiple times. Its one of the only games I have 100% all achievements for on steam. That being said, Cuisineer is surprisingly challenging. there's plenty of enemy diversity to keep you on your toes and the two regions I've been too are pretty to look at. However, I think Cuisineer's dungeoneering is hard for the wrong reasons. my character feels WEAK. Weapon combos aren't enough to Finnish off any enemies besides the basic chickens, forcing you to stand still and do a combo again, and again while avoiding potential projectiles. Weapon upgrades early on are expensive, and take an entire day (sometimes two if the shopkeeper takes the next day off) to Finnish and, without being crass, I CANNOT feel the difference of the first two upgrades. combos maybe clear enemies in one-less hit than previously. Bosses take incredibly long in the early game because of this. When I get to a boss i usually just go back home to save my stuff because: -and this is arguably the worse problem Cuisineer has- You lose 90% of your acquired goods when you die. This is a horrendous setback if you die to the last boss after clearing every floor 100% for materials. This is the event that caused me to write this review. Is it a skill issue? maybe. I've beaten that boss before with less health. But losing 90% of my goods (And you cant even pick what you take back of the 10% remaining) after grinding the entire region for materials is egregious. I'm aware the brewing system exists, Its very in-depth and the various flavors you can use all seem to be unique (except poison and burn which are objectively the same) but brewing, just like upgrading takes an entire day (sometimes two) and is only really worth it once you can make 3* dishes. Which you cannot do until you get to the 3nd region I believe. I really like this game, I don't want it to get easier, just less punishing. Quality of life changes for the upgrade system would be appreciated. Choice in what you take back if you do die would be meaningful. The 90% loss causes a really risk-averse play style that's stressful and overall unrewarding.Other very small nitpicks that are overall irrelevant: -Regardless of what time you leave to explore it will always be night time when you return.-The inventory screen seems to pause the game but NOT the enemies.-Customers will sometimes enter your restaurant and complain a dish isn't available, This is completely irrelevant. they wont order anything else and leave shortly after. This has no effect on reputation. There's no way to know how to acquire the recipe they wanted either. I'm very excited for the continued development of this game and look forward to its bright future!

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a mix between a dungeon grinding and cooking game. You enter dungeons to receive gear as well as ingredients to cook with in your restaurant that you have taken over from your parents. Overall it does this decently well.It shines with its cute graphics, decent music and a fast paced combat system with various weapons and combinations. Overall at my pace it's probably around 30 hours gametime to see most of the main story parts of the game, with another 30 grind heavy hours to clean up everything, collect everything and max everything out.Cuisineer does extremely well with several aspects of a game and feels a little lacking in others. First of all, the mix between time management and cooking as well as the action combat is extremely well integrated. It's a very relaxed title, that never puts any time pressure on you during your "off time" in town, which I really like, while still giving you action combat time in limited time bursts that make for fun activity to shake things up. You never feel like you run after the main story and can take as long as you like.The graphics are really cute and well done, all the way from the characters, world down to every interface button the style fits very well together. Music score, while limited in variety, is also really nice and matches well together with everything else.The game features an awesome storage system. You can access your ingredients from your chests both for cooking and for upgrades. If you hover over ingredients you even see the amount of items you have in your storage and inventory, which is awesome for tracking amounts you already collected while out exploring. The only time you grab items directly for handing them over is for quests.The downsides are there as well, though for me it was mostly about the "I wish there was more" kind. The game lacks a bit in depth and variety. it offers no ways of automation, both in collecting ingredients as well as well as running your restaurant. No waitress job positions to hire, no cashier to collect the money, you run back and forth for everything on your own, which is fun the first few times you are doing it and part of the action, but I wished for more improvement mechanics late game as it definitely gets dull after ou've done this countless times.I really hope to see some DLC at some point to add more layers and depth to the already nice basis and offer more end game focus. More automation, more variety in both weapons and their synergies and maybe a sprinkle more customization for the parts of the restaurant like the counters and entrance carpet, that currently is fixed and unchangeable.To sum it up, for me Cuisineer is definitely worth the money if you enjoy a grind intensive collection and cooking game mix and I really hope to see more of this title/series.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Cuisineer for a couple days and despite having a lot of playtime, it feels like I'm just scratching the surface. Cuisineer has the look and feel of Bastion and Transistor with combat and dash-dodging like Hades paired with restaurant management where you can customize/upgrade your restaurant layout, cook meals, serve guests and collect their payments. Cooking is one-dimensional and uninvolved but it doesn't prevent me from having fun and enjoying watching my profits rise in real time. Ingredients are gathered through combat in rogue-like dungeons you can visit endlessly. Dying means losing most of the ingredients you had in your bag during a run, so don't get greedy. You unlock new recipes by completing side quests for villagers, this almost always involves giving them materials, ingredients or cooked dishes but also some rare instances of "kill x of specific monster type or boss". Main story progression involves paying off a tax debt your lackadaisical parents have accrued and neglected, this unlocks new dungeon biomes for you to explore. The game does a good job of explaining all the mechanics and upgrade routes through gameplay, no lengthy tutorials here, this is always refreshing. Lastly there are some cool modifiers and a variety of weapon types that allow you to customize your combat style, I like to use slow swinging tenderizer hammer. It didn't take long for me to fall in love with this game.I would easily recommend this game once some issues are fixed. First, this game should not be hitching/stuttering AT ALL on a high end computer. I followed instructions online, gave the game high priority in task manager and disabled Steam overlay but hitching/stuttering still occurs. Vsync does help with the screen tearing on 60 Hz TV but I leave it off on my 144 Hz monitor because the game ends up looking fuzzy when moving. Menus have an issue where sometimes 2 selections are highlighted and you have to guess what your selection is and hope you don't enable/disable something on accident.As far as gameplay feedback; none of the modifiers stack and it would be helpful to have UI elements/text letting you know that you have 2 of the same modifier in your loadout. Also you're not told that you can reload your ranged weapon, found out by accident, the whole time I was just waiting for my ranged attacks to reload on their own so I stopped using them altogether until I found out you can reload.TLDR: gud gaem but pls optimize it

_childDocuments_.review: I saw Cuisineer at PAX East in 2022 and I fell in love with the game back then. Clearly it is a dungeon crawler mixed with Diner Dash (Yes I'm that old). Speaking with the Devs, Recettear was another clear inspiration. Moonlighter is the other game in a similar space, but that is about it. Not many time management shop keeping games combined with dungeon crawlers. Personally, I love the formula, so for me even if this game was mediocre, I would have liked it. But this game is fairly well polished! I LOVE THE ART. The mechanics overall feel solid. And the music is enjoyable. I think it has a good balance of the 2 mechanics and the bosses provided a fun challenge. It feels really rewarding to beat enemies up and gather your ingredients. The money going up while running your store is a huge dopamine hit. Small nitpicks include: I was occasionally dashing out of bounds, sometimes it is hard to choose the specific cooking table with a controller, and maybe the inventory could be a bit bigger. One bigger gripe is that I think the upgraded weapons should do a bit more damage. The upgrades don't really feel worth it. They are also kind of expensive, so I never really felt like upgrading one until late game.Overall, this game is great. Give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gameplay loop. The dungeon crawling surprisingly doesn't hold your hand. Your ability to dive deeper into the dungeons depends on you avoiding damage and saving your healing items. But the worst that will happen to you if you die is losing half your collected items. I don't think there's a game over state. Even the debt you have to pay off doesn't seem to have a due date so you can just play the game at your own pace. There is a time and date system but it's more to indicate what npcs are available on different days and when you can make the most money from the restaurant during the lunch and dinner rush.I feel like the shop that lets you upgrade your bag should be a permanent shop instead of only showing on certain days. It wasn't very clear how to upgrade the bag at the beginning and you really need to upgrade it early or you'll end up wasting a lot of loot. A QoL feature I wish it had would be if you could provide quest items from your storage instead of needing to have it in your bag.Cute and fun game that controls well. It's also very affordable. I highly recommend it if you think you might like this type of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game on my ROG Ally handheld device and it runs very well.Cuisineer is incredibly cute and lighthearted, even when you're beating up chickens and other animals for food. The art style, sound effects and setting is very cosy - I didn't feel that combat was that difficult (though it can be visually confusing at times), but it could be difficult enough for a very casual player. It's one of the most perfect games I've used my handheld for: casual and cosy, easy to pick up for 20m - 30m, simple enough mechanics...The core loop is clean and very good, you battle through dungeons to gather ingredients that you use to run your restaurant. It can get quite grindy, especially when you continuously need ingredients from the first dungeon (it gets quite boring once you've completed it a few times), however I think that's a balancing issue that is very fixable. Still, I had a good 10+ hours of fun before I started feeling too much grind. I would say the main feedback I have for the game, apart from general balancing, is the tutorial - it wasn't obvious to me to level up cooking equipment or experiment with weapon effects and I wasted time upgrading the restaurant without upgrading the equipment at first. I didn't realize the link between upgrading equipment and serving higher tier dishes until quite late, and I wasted a lot of resources upgrading the restaurant (which upgrades capacity) thinking that was linked to higher tier dishes. Apart from that, I really enjoyed my time playing Cuisineer! I'm sure the game will continue to get even better. Congrats to the devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Too many flaws and bugs but still a fun game...It is a simple hack and slash with progression... It does require too much grinding as well as I wish you can hold more items. Even maxing out your backpack isn't enough later in the game...I still enjoy its simple story as well as gameplay and graphics. My main complaint is time continues to tick even when you are in the menu trying to organize, determine what to drop, and do some freaking item management. Especially with collecting new gear and determining whether to keep it or not...That is the most aggravating thing next to a bug where after playing the game for 30 minutes you can see stuttering... It only gets worst the longer you play the game and the only fix is to just go to sleep to save and close and get back in...I am running a 3080... This kind of thing should not be happening...My last complaint, for now, is the roguelike aspects... It seems that they created sections and all they do is just mix around its location... I have seen the same designed structure. You will notice it too after a few play through of the same map...Overall the game is nice I would give it a 6/10. Fix a few things and it can easily be an 8... I can recommend the game only because it is the kind of game I enjoy. It is a little grind heavy as well as being a pretty linear roguelike but I still felt I got my money's worth.Update: Well now I can't progress to the 2 part of the cuisineer final challenge... _childDocuments_.review: In the second phase of the boss fight it becomes almost impossible unless you have a ranged build.1) Tracking shots take a full minute to dissipate, so you cant go after the boss when he gets exhausted, at most you get 1-2 sword hits in before you have to continue dodging the shots.2) Shield "deflects" the tracking shots and makes umami bombs but the shots still freeze and damage you so it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ useless then. Either a bug or developer just trolling.3) Actual laser attack range is further than the visual, so you can still take damage and die when you are 3/4 of the arena away from the boss.At the start of the game, needs a trigger to keep out customers who only want specific dishes when I don't even have the specific cooker unlocked yet. I don't need 5-10 customers in a row coming in and getting pissy because I don't serve bread like wtf do you want me to do.. It just wastes your restaurant's operating hours and slot for other customers. I.E 4 in-game hrs just to serve 2 paying customers...Restaurant game is pretty lackluster, just stand in one spot to cook dishes and collect payment. Not much engagement here like serving and cooking the food yourself like in standard restaurant games, until the later half when you have to serve the Nobles. No ability to hire additional staff to work in the restaurant as waiter/cook/cashier. Tutorials for mechanics like brewing etc need better explanations. E.g. it's just too vague on what brewing does, what different dishes do to the weapons. If I have to google or look in the community hub for guides on basic mechanics, then something is wrong.Reduce the RNG from brewing, because that ♥♥♥♥ just makes everything even grindier when you can't even select a specific flavour mod to put on your gear, let alone the specific modifier effect from the list of flavour mods. It basically forces you to grind for more ingredients to craft the specific food to roll, and ingredients to open the restaurant since every brew on the same gear just raises the cost of the next brew. Even when it repeatedly gives you the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ shield dash modifier every time when you just want a salty effect.Dungeon levels are too similar. You have different bosses after descending a certain amount of times, but the monsters and dungeon layout on each level are procedurally the same no matter how far you go down.Can't use keyboard to advance dialogue, only mouse left-click does anything.Also needs a guide to tell you where to get certain recipes.Make it clearer on the off-days for shop opening hours so we know when NPCs go off and do whatever... People generally use mon-fri instead of flavours to indicate working/off days.No place to sell excess ingredients/weapons/dishes, so you just dump it on the ground like a degenerate.Town is too bright in the day, not enough contrast for streets and buildings, everything just blends in so it's hard to focus.Can't see the main character behind objects in-town, should be doable since you can already see through objects in the dungeon.Annoying that the character actively blocks item placement during restaurant customisation, can't just remove the character and then shift them away if they are blocking a space. At least allow the character to move during customisation.Losing all your items without being able to choose which items you want to keep is stupid harsh, even Dave the Diver lets you select the 1 item you want to keep. If the counter-argument is that the items in the top 5 slots are saved, that ♥♥♥♥ is decided by the auto-sorter in the game, I don't have the luxury to swap out the items right before I get curbstomped by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a shrimp boss.Game is pretty and fun, but gets really tedious and samey during the respective restaurant/dungeon sections.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I downloaded it when it was first released, so adjust your expectations accordingly. I know the developers are improving it as we speak. So, I like relaxing games, and boy golly gee this wasn't relaxing. However, it has the right amount of stress for me to enjoy the game but to not get anxious over it (assuming I don't get sent back in the past with my PTxD as a server at a restaurant). I like figuring stuff out, and this kinda made me more cognizant to how I spend my time each day. It's similar to games like stardew or moonstone island in that you have until 23:00 before it automatically moves onto the next day.Prioritizing what to upgrade is a big thing especially when upgrading things like the health potions, buffs, and equipment, facilitate the dungeon runs. It is highly satisfying getting achievements when I beat big bosses because I spent so much time upgrading my stuff. I think it is a bit grindy because sometimes the monsters seem to be very tanky at first. However, it seems there's more to it than just combat with the aforementioned upgrades. There's a restaurant you run and you upgrade it too and buy furniture for it. You meet different types of customers with different needs (ex. kids are impatient. elderly take their time), and having to run that restaurant for a portion of the day does affect how you spend the rest of your time.So if you're into a combination of time management strategy, dungeoneering, and grindy stuff, I think this game is good for you. It's cute, developer coming up with new patches, and overall (imo) relaxing and satisfying when you achieve certain things.

_childDocuments_.review: It is good for the short time I have played so far! This is a 2 part game where you run a restaurant trying to earn money fulfilling your customers demands with whatever resources you have and you decide when to venture into the dungeon to fight for said resources with fast-paced combat. With the money and resources you earn you can progress your gear or customize your shop.Can see that the game is inspired by games like Recettear for the shop sim aspect and Hades for the combat aspect.The art style is great, cute and vibrant. Item variety is good. Combat is pretty challenging with a decent amount of gear properties and effects for you to choose how you want to fight while keeping to the food theme.My only concern is that they release in this state where I feel that the game would need somemore QOL changes and improvements/polish to some basic game mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a delightfully cute dungeon crawler in the same vein as Recettear or Moonlighter, albeit with simpler mechanics all around. If you're in the market for deep, rogue-lite dungeon crawling with hundreds of build options or carefully-tuned economic management, you might be a tad bit disappointed. However, if you're in the mood for a relaxing game where a catgirl slaps little pepper monsters with a spatula then serves up lovingly rendered fantasy soups, this is the game for you.There have been a lot of criticisms of the current state of combat, many of which the devs have acknowledged and are currently working on tuning. If you want the smoothest combat experience, it might be worth waiting a month or two to pick up this game. If you don't mind a little sponginess in your enemies, my only other recommendation is to find a piece of equipment with 'Shield Dash' on it as soon as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a fun game that mixes elements from a few different other games. In this game, you're a cook that goes hunting for food to serve it to your customers. The restaurant management reminds me a lot of moonlighter, whereas the exploration part is similar to a roguelite version of Rune Factory.The game is pretty fun but it's honestly flawed all over the place and there's a lot that could be improved. The balance of the game especially doesn't make any sense at all. I just can't understand some things, like why the most basic tutorial messages only appear at Day TWENTY (and that’s only first the very first one) to tell you useful info that should have been explained right away and which you probably figured out on your own in the meantime. It's the same for everything in the game, from some systems like weapon upgrading being seemingly useless to the amount of resources required being too much or too little, to the difficulty of the restaurant management... The game is still fun though but it would be a top contender of the genre for me if it was more focused.The start is extremely slow with a lot of things left unexplained until way too late and systems that sort of discourage experimentation. For example, brewing costs 500 coins and there's no explanation for how it works until you try it out a few times to understand it. It's actually a pretty cool system but it's too expensive (the devs lowered the cost to 100 now thankfully), it takes your weapon away for one day and you don't have any idea what the weapon mods do either, nor are you informed that brewing will lock one slot forever. It also takes quite a fortune to acquire your first weapons.The game made me actually believe I'd quickly be given one equipment of each type, because every new area gives you a new weapon and paying the debt gives you one piece of armour. But guess what? It took me over ten hours to pay the second debt and get... basic boots, something I already bought and dropped in dungeons for a good ten hours as well. Eventually you get a lot of weapons just from running the dungeon but they're mostly useless and the way the equipment mods work, I find that nearly every piece of equipment I obtain is unneeded. You can't even sell them so it really feels like cumbersome junk, especially considering that they take inventory slots.This creates a displeasing gameplay loop where you don't even want to go any further than needed in dungeons. Why go beat a boss when my inventory is full? I only get the same materials as normal monsters and random equipment which is no better than checking the daily sales of the smith. I don't even get money and can't sell them, thus there's never any incentive to beat a boss. All you get is an achievement for beating them once and one quest requires you to beat floor 6 of the first dungeon, that's it! This part of the game could really be improved.As for dungeoning itself, it's the best part of the game. The combat is solid and the maps, albeit a bit repetitive in patterns you can start to recognise (the dungeons are essentially a random arrangement of pre-made rooms) are beautiful and fun. Still, there are once again many flaws. My biggest gripe is probably how the cooldown of special attacks is so long, thus making the combat pretty monotonous as you can only spam the same basic attacks for most of the time. It would have also been a great addition to be able to switch between the two weapons you can equip, instead of only having one main weapon and the second slot being used for the special attack. A few more special attacks would have really made this game into a very awesome dungeon crawler.That aside, the combat is tight there's no denying it. A lot of the bosses are fun and special mention to the second boss of the snow area which is straight up awesome. It's too bad the game doesn't really reward you for beating them. On another hand, the mobs can get annoying sometimes: the rice sprites are just about everywhere which really gets tedious at some point, especially considering how 1) they're so small you can hardly track them 2) they get hyper armour from their buffs and thus can easily destroy your crowd control. Hell, they can literally become immortal if two rice priests are buffing them and it's hard to notice. Oftentimes the combat can get really messy with many enemies and the screen being unreadable and this is where a few more special attacks would have shined.As for the restaurant, it is also very unbalanced. First of all, running the restaurant an entire day (which is pretty much required) is twenty minutes!!! This is insane compared to a game like Dave the diver where this part of the game is very short (and also, unlike here, very involved with the player being actively tasked to do things). It's long and mostly very boring, especially at the beginning. For most of my ten hours of play, I never had enough customers to fill the restaurant and be busy and now that I have upgraded it to the maximum level and almost gotten max reputation, only now do I get to actively play the restaurant. This took me about 15 hours!!! And this is only during three times of the day (lunch, afternoon tea and dinner) during which customers are increased, the rest of the day is still very calm with perhaps two to three customers at once. This part is very obviously flawed.The restaurant gameplay is very simple and could be improved too, but overall it's pretty good for what it is, if only you had enough customers. It doesn't require much thinking and doesn't offer much in the way of management but it's still fun to run and watch. Still, a game like Dave the diver really shows a lot of things that Cuisineer could have taken inspiration from. There's also a tight balance between dungeoning to get resources and running the restaurant which... also is pretty messy. Throughout the whole game I had way too much flour and rice (they're everywhere...) and I was mostly fine with most ingredients, but some of them like the pork and beef meat as well as cheese are extremely difficult to obtain because the enemies dropping them only appear in specific areas and are rare. Yet they end up being the most prized ingredients for your recipes and endgame recipes can even use five pieces of meat at once! One dungeon run would give me about twenty pieces of the ingredient I needed!!!Finally, while the game introduces itself like a farming sim with a clock, a town with villagers to talk to… All of that aspect is extremely superficial. The dialogue is extremely uninteresting be it optional dialogues or the main quest which resumes itself to “pay your debt”. The villagers don’t react to anything you do, not even beating bosses for example and every side quest is structured the same way where they give you a random situation requiring you to find them an item and then explain what’s great about the recipes they’re giving you, but it doesn’t feel very convincing to read that part either and the repeated structure just gets previsible and boring, very fast. There’s very little to do in town other than buying things and completing your quests. There are birthdays, but it seems only two people a month (so eight in total) get to have a birthday out of all villagers and having them give you gifts instead of you doing it seems like a convenient way that the developers scrapped a planned social aspect. As for the clock, it really doesn’t matter : there’s little point to only running the restaurant for half a day and it doesn’t matter any more when you go dungeoning, because you get an unlimited amount of time and come back at 11pm. The clock could have been more useful if for example your dungeoning time was limited or you could come back and forth, for example dungeoning during the calm morning and coming back for the lunch rush. Once again, I think Dave the diver figured out a great way to handle this with days being separated into multiple parts and getting to do one

_childDocuments_.review: This definitely has some serious potential, and atmospherically is very enjoyable. The reputation system to build up your bond with the town and open new upgrades and recipes is a nice mechanic that keeps you checking for new opportunities, though most critiques of the game seem to forget that the game is played through the filter of a child rather than an adult character, so expecting romantic content is kind of off the table, and a lot of deeper thought mechanics are perhaps outside the purview of a tween catgirl trying to keep a roof over her head through a gift at cooking. You have to contextualise expectations.But there's two major aspects that really hold back the gameplay to me.1. No material sink for individual ingredients save for disposal. Yes, there is the Trader, but some items just insistently stay out of rotation or another brutally overstocked item is offered as return. A more permanent grocer strand with a trade system would be better, with the Trader present to offer rarer drops (spices, cheese, ice, etc)2. Defensive mechanics in combat need enhancement. Yes, there is a dash, which is situationally safe to use to get out of the way, but there are scenarios where the density of traps, terrain and instantly charging mobs just don't offer the opportunity to make much use of it. There is the possibility to use emergency boba (AoE freeze, etc), but with how limited belt space is and the fact that its shared with health restoration items makes their carry expensive, not to mention a one-shot. Being able to parry, block or have a shield ability associated to the thrown dishes would really be a game changer and allow better control and longevity in dungeons.3. The bullet hell aspect of this game is honestly tiring. Especially in the honestly contrived endgame, just getting locked in a box with dozens of enemies able to fire overwhelming salvos of projectiles that inevitable cause gratuitous health and time attrition is really a massive annoyance. Considering the length of the animation locks in this and the complete lack of combat fluidity, there are long periods of nothing but dodging until you can get a crack at returning fire with weapons that deeply lack visual accuracy.4. Gear progression is completely unrewarding. Honestly, it feels rather pointless and there's no power reward whatsoever. Considering the wall of opposition which you have to hack through to get to bosses or achieve timed clears later on, this is an absolutely unforgivable omission if any type of 'forging' system is to be provided.Not sure what the complaints about grind and daily CDs are about, since this is clearly not a speedrun game, but rather a quiet day to day life sim. A few major furniture pieces and a gear upgrade a day seems pretty normal pace. Combat balance and gear progression is such a lacking aspect that it overshadows everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this a thumbs down, because I was looking forward to this game for months, even following the game's progress towards release on Twitter, based on the demo and what I'd seen of the game otherwise. However, in its current state, I cannot recommend it. The art and music are wonderful, and the restaurant management part is basic but serviceable... the trouble is, there's the everything else.So, the combat. Nearly every enemy (and particularly the bosses) are huge damage sponges, and your weapon upgrades range from pitiful and limited (wait a day and spend money and increasingly ludicrous numbers of other resources to get +1 damage on a weapon a maximum of 4 times, in a game where 30 damage isn't that much) to impactful but confusing and extremely limited (cook equipment with dishes to get elemental effects in two slots). Basically, the combat would be fine to okay IF the HP values for every enemy were slashed by a good 25 to 50 percent since you as the player have little to no ability to increase your damage to compensate for the increasing levels of sponge. Also, I sure hope you like ranged and outright homing ranged enemies hitting you from multiple screens away in later dungeons.There's also a lot of padding of the "twenty bear butts" variety that sees a side quest ask for a given food, only for you to check the quest log and see that by "a food" they meant 10-25 of that food. Better go interact with the combat some more to get more ingredients!The "story" also decides to take a smoke break after showing up for about five minutes at the start of the game and never really comes back. The focus here was clearly on a gameplay loop carrying this thing, which I respect, but I mention this just in case others thought we'd get a bit more in terms of story as the game went on.Just play Recettear, or maybe give this a look once it's had a few patches to fix things up. The first patch alone improved the experience a fair bit, so if this review is old enough, most of these gripes will probably be patched out.

_childDocuments_.review: Very adorable and easy to pick-up. Everything in the game is very charming. However, there are more than a few spots of tension that might have you bounce off.1. Turning in quest/upgrade materials is too tedious. If you don't have a perfect memory of what NPCs are available + what their quest items are, you'll have to make many round trips. While the quest log can help, tracking what the boba tea upgrades need is also very annoying because of this.2. Way too many loading screens between moving through your personal room, restaurant, and town. If you're not taking notes (quickly because time moves fast!), you'll have to do this dance with many loading screens to get the correct materials for quests/upgrades.3. Progression feels very ephemeral. I can't really tell how my character is improving very much at all. While upgrading storage + potion belts are easy to grasp... It seems like the main upgrade progression for equipment are the randomly generated effects? It's not particularly satisfying with the current pool of effects that I've seen so far.4. Upgrading (anything, but mostly the equipment) feels like too high a cost for too little an effect. A majority of my gold + materials gets me +1 attack on a weapon. On a 10 attack sword, this feels like it adds 10% damage which is good... But it realistically doesn't actually help me kill anything that much quicker.5. Feels risky to upgrade any equipment. I'm not sure if there's a way to transfer equipment upgrades to a new piece of gear. Since it's so costly, there's a lot of anxiety on committing to something. This pretty much leads me to not using it at all.6. Comparing equipment on the spot is very tedious for four reasons: Hovering over items shows a tooltip that covers everything. Time continues moving while checking equipment in town which leads to rushed observations. Found equipment takes up space while in dungeons. And, of course, you actually can't see things side-by-side.I want to stress that these critiques come from a place of love and well-meaning. The overall experience has been very enjoyable and the fundamental dungeon-crawling-> restaurant management loop is very solid.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so freakin cute but IT'S SO MUCH MORE THAN THAT!!! The combat is fairly mundane, mostly just attack dodge repeat, but the upgrade system makes it so that has enough nuance and change over time to be fun and repeatable. The dungeons are made of rooms that are pre-made, randomly fitted together in new patterns, so you get both familiarity over time and never-the-same-map-twice. Running the restaurant is so much fun, getting the rhythm of it really triggered the "you have succeeded" part of my brain. Death isn't punishing, or at least in my opinion, not overly so. The only feature I can even think of to ask for would be a zoom in (and back out to normal) function for dungeons or in town, and even then, that's because I'm using an atypical video output setup, not because the game needs it.TL;DR: This game is a mishmash of different rpgs and Flo's Diner, of all things. Buy it for a friend if you're on the fence. They will love it and so will you.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game.I recommend buying and playing it as something I will likely put another 30+ hours into however I have to recognize where it falls short.The adventuring part of the game is rather same-y, I love the bosses and some of the challenge rooms however moving through the map and filtering through mobs is an grinding patience. Weapons don't feel more effective even with upgrades for anything other than chickens, and i spend most of my time counting down how many more combos before this stun-locked mob dies and i can move onto the next room.The restaurant-ing part of the game has arguably bigger issues. I have no incentive to upgrade my restaurant past having room for 4 cooking units. The cooking units, tables/customers, food counter, and the checkout counter can be positioned and reached without having to move Pom at all, turning the open restaurant into an idle clicker. At that point, upgrading my cooking units is giving me consistent income where I have no benefit other than aesthetics to change the layout of the restaurant. I think reducing Poms interaction area may be necessary to break this cycle and if that is too unbalanced, allowing them to carry 2 food items. I also feel that the furniture/decorative system should have more meaning to the customers and their food preference. We already have a calendar for days with preferred food but honestly I haven't actually noticed its effects. Anecdotally, the distribution of chosen foods doesn't seem to differ much on preferential food days. I feel like there is some depth missing between preferential foods, customer types, and furniture. Hypothetically, if I want to be lazy, just fill my store with rugs and paintings for the young customers who move fast to pick their cooked items - maybe they are weighted for cheaper meals to discourage me from that as I won't turn a profit.Also customers getting up to get their food should have a small delay, maybe a half second from when the food item is complete. God it really chafes me waiting for an old couple to sit back down when both their items are ready at the same time.I genuinely like this game and its potential to bridge genres. I will keep playing it. I am not sure if my critiques/suggestions above are necessarily correct however I feel I would enjoy the game more if these perceived issues were acknowledged and addressed.

_childDocuments_.review: 20-ish hour into the game and going to write something about this game. Might update this review afterwards.Edited: Added another 10 hours run, and i found some problems AFTER longer time invested into the game.TLDR: Playable but need some balancing adjustment and QoL updates. Pros:1) Game objective is straight forward, familiar systems so shouldn't be hard to understand the game.2) As a Malaysian, the cuisine is just fascinating!! All the cuisines are very close to real life food!3) Dungeon difficulty wise, its not hard, but it won't go easy on you. All you need is to be patient.4) Unlike Stardew, the dungeon doesn't follow in-game time. instead, it will automatically become 23:00 when you exit the dungeon so no need to rush the dungeons.5) Restaurant layout placement is kinda fun. Almost fully customizable so you can spend like hours just to make your restaurant looks nice.Cons:1) Personally think in-game time pass too fast. If you want to rearrange your fridge/storage, most probably you are going to burn the whole in-game day. Running in town to talk to NPC is also like wasting too much in-game time in running.2) Some normal monsters are dealing way too much damage than the others. I am not sure if this is intentional or by accident. You can solve it by simply lowering the difficulty level though.3) Difficulties doesn't gives better rewards, making it kinda meaningless. Boss chest also worthless. Its just some random gears, and some resource (yes, SOME. not even a stack).4）The amount of projectiles (and their HP) from monster is ridiculous. Monster invulnerability is also doesn't make sense at all.5) Homing projectiles are also too annoying. Even if you are like 1 area away, they still can lockon on you and keep shooting at you.5) Weapon damage balancing also is a problem. fast weapons need to hit 3 to 4 hits to match 1 hit of heavy weapon. If you count by Frames, definitely heavy weapon is the weapon to go. Besides each hit of heavy weapon guaranteed to stunlock normal monsters, while fast weapon need to hit the last hit of the combo to stunlock. Fast weapons are good to get rid of projectiles though, which is the most painful part of the game.6) There is no way to move your cursor from left page to right page immediately. You need to keep pressing RIGHT(or vise versa) to move to the right side panel so i think this is very clunky.7) Some ingredients are using up too fast, so you ended up need to open 1 day restaurant, run 1 day of dungeon (just to get 1 or 2 specific ingredients) and loop. running 2 days of dungeon will cause your storage overflow, so maybe considering adjusting the drop amount for those regular use but using up too fast (meats, coconuts and cheese especially), and some ingredients are way toooooo much (chili and rice yes, i am talking about you).Overall, the game experience is still fun to me, but it annoys me when i need to keep running dungeons just for 1 or 2 ingredients.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this review by saying I was drawn to the game due to its art style, gameplay of material gathering and shop management, and introductory discount. While I am enjoying the game so far, I don’t typically play roguelike games so most of my gripes may stem from its grindy, gameplay loop nature.CURRENT STATS:<Bland> difficulty mode120+ in-game daysRestaurant level 999% of recipes unlocked (missing 1 Tier 4 recipe)All Boba Teas maxedPROS:+ Pleasing art style+ Easy combat style+ Notification of which station to cook dishes for customers+ No time limit inside dungeonsCONS:- Small stack size: I saw that the devs will be addressing this issue by increasing the stack to 30 in a future patch but I feel like the stack limit for regular ore/wood should be at least 50 given how pretty much everything is bought/upgraded with these. - Limited storage space for restaurant and personal: Your restaurant level affects how many fridges you can place inside your restaurant and when Alder gives you chests (for equips/ores/woods)/personal fridges (for ingredients you don’t want used in the restaurant) for your room.- Rigid restaurant layout: You can’t move the register, the rug associated with the register, the serving tables, and trash can.- Lack of restaurant efficiency improvements: As your restaurant expands, the space between cooking dishes and ringing up customers grows, making you run back and forth more all while having to keep an eye on serving nobles and watching out for dine-and-dashers, especially during rush hours.While upgrading your restaurant gives you access to the wealthier clientele (nobles, greater nobles) and upgrading your stations allows for higher tier recipes to be made, there’s nothing to help increase your efficiency. Rather than allowing for upgraded stations to speed up cooking or having the option of hired help to assist, the game’s solution is to simply buy and upgrade more stations to counterbalance running out a customer’s timer. Because you need to be in range to use the stations, you basically have to clump them in an unsightly mess to improve efficiency.- Lack of progression between areas and gear: Maybe it’s because I don’t play a lot of roguelike games, but when I upgrade my gear, I expected to progress easier in earlier game areas but there is little incentive to swap weapons in terms of attack power as the high cost of money and resources nets you a measly +1 attack.Day 100+ in the first dungeon feels just as grindy as day 1 with enemies seemingly taking the same amount of time to die despite upgraded gear. While others may enjoy this kind of gameplay loop, it’s not for me.CONS ADDRESSED IN DEV UPDATE:- Time doesn’t pause while looking at inventory/storage- Lack of information regarding how brewing works (This is something I completely avoided using because I didn’t understand how it worked and I didn’t want to waste my resources; perhaps I would have an easier time in the dungeon if I used this? Unsure.)Overall I plan to continue playing but the limitation of inventory space has me ending my dungeon runs early (I think I've only cleared a dungeon twice) and the lack of efficiency options for the restaurant makes me wonder if I should bother leveling my restaurant any further.

_childDocuments_.review: Eating while playing this game is such a satisfying experience.This game is like a soufflé - cute, fluffy, moreish and leaves you feeling pleasantly sated. It is a relaxing venture into building up a small-town restaurant, complete with exploration and dungeon-crawling to obtain tasty resources from adorable enemies. The characters are charming, the dialogue is witty, and the recipe art and descriptions are . You will definitely get hungry playing this.I recommend visiting the market regularly, especially if you want to trade excess ingredients for ones you're hankering for. There's a lot of opportunity for restaurant customisation, and different decor will attract different types of customers. I found you need to have a lot of one decor type to draw in certain customer bases. I tried a row of regal tables and chairs for nobles on one end of the store, and wooden tables and chairs on the other end for the common rabble, but it didn't work the way I wanted.As an aside, I like that the chickens will square up with you and then run away in terror when you defend yourself. I enjoy chasing them down and slapping them into the afterlife with a salmon.Mild critiques:- There were times when I accidentally cooked the wrong thing, or I closed the restaurant before a dish was completed (resulting in the customer leaving and not taking the food), but the meal couldn't be repurposed for quests or upgrades. This meant a sad disposal of tasty food.- There isn't a way to isolate store quest ingredients so they won't be consumed during restaurant opening hours, even if I have them in my backpack. This makes it hard to accumulate elusive ingredients while operating the restaurant, as it doesn't seem like you can edit the menu. Overall, if you liked Stardew Valley and enjoy some dungeon hack 'n slash, you'll have fun with Cuisineer.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute game. In Cuisineer, you play as Pom, a young restaurateur, seeking to re-establish Potato Palace after her parents... bequeath it to her.The core gameplay loop in Cuisineer is go dungeoneering for crafting materials and ingredients, complete sidequests for more recipes, run the restaurant and make money, upgrade the restaurant and pay off your parents' debts. Not unique by any stretch, but it's enjoyable enough.The game is quite flexible as far as day-to-day activities go. You could open the restaurant for lunch hour and set off for a dungeon after, head to a dungeon as the sole activity for the day, or skip the dungeon altogether and just manage the restaurant. You can even close the restaurant midday, buy new furniture from the local carpenter, and reopen the restaurant after setting them up.The dungeoning aspects of this game might be a dealbreaker for some people. Baseline combat is serviceable and has great hit feedback. However, a lot of the enemies feel like they have a little too much HP, and bosses feel significantly more difficult than mobs, almost to the point of being a different game.There also isn't a huge amount of variety in dungeon rooms, and you'll see similar room layouts between floors and even dungeons.Weapon and gear upgrades are a little expensive (and additionally use the same materials as restaurant furniture), which makes the game a little grindy. They're not necessary to progress the game but are quite helpful for the later bosses, despite the fact that +1 attack doesn't look particularly impactful.Restaurant management, on the other hand, is quite solid. Open the restaurant, fill customers' orders with one click at the appropriate cooking station, serve them if they're nobles (commoners are fine with counter-serve, go figure), collect their money. Can optimize your restaurant layout for better pathing but it's not necessary.Ultimately, I did finish the game on "normal" difficulty and fully enjoyed it. The music and art are simply superb; the food art even gives me food cravings IRL. The story is a little trope-y but fine, definitely carried by the character art. The combat aspects were good enough for me and never felt too unreasonable or unfair. I would happily pick up content DLC or a sequel if they were to exist one day. Would like to see a food-to-brew guide somewhere in the journal though.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a hard time deciding, but in the end I chose to recommend this game. However, I do have some pretty major reservations. For one thing, there is no social system, which for me is the biggest problem. The characters in this world are really interesting and adorable, and I think choosing not to implement a friendship or romance mechanic with gift tastes and heart events is a huge missed opportunity. Additionally, operating the restaurant is extremely simplistic, to the point where it feels a lot like a free mobile game minus the ads. The 'debt' system, where you owe debts to the tax office, is very lax in that you owe debt in the way you owe Tom Nook a mortgage-that is to say, there is no strict repayment schedule, which for some people may be a pro, but for me personally, it's a con. And on top of all of this, combat is fairly simplistic, which is a little frustrating for me.That said, there are many good points to this game. The character art is gorgeous, as is the general art style. The gameplay may be incredibly simplistic, but it's still fun. And while the combat is a bit simplistic, it does get the job done. While I find this game to be a bit shallow and rife with missed opportunities, in the end I personally think the pros slightly outweigh the cons. That said, if you're looking for a shop sim with more interesting characters, a more complex shop management system, and a strict repayment schedule that isn't Recettear, I would recommend Potionomics-though word of warning, there is no post-game mode, so you need to get everything done in the set 50 days. And if you want a fun dungeon-crawling roguelite you may not have heard of, may I recommend Going Under? It's massively underrated, mostly because it came out the same week as Hades. Granted, the art style is very corporate, BUT that's because the game is a satire of Silicon Valley culture. Anyway, have fun playing!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like if Diner Dash were an RPG. Although it's more relaxed than a lot of games in the genre, I wasn't prepared for just how much stuff there is to do in this game; oh, I need more ingredients for a proper restaurant service, I need more wood to upgrade the restaurant itself, THIS WOMAN NEEDS SPARKLING WATER, STAT!!! It's honestly a little overwhelming at first, but once you fall into the gameplay loop of adventuring and running restaurant services, it's easier to play at your own pace and decide which course of action you wish to pursue at any given time.  From what I can tell so far, there are no real time limits for doing anything in the game either.  There are so many recipes I can't even make half of the ones I've collected so far since I can still only buy level 1 cooking stations.  Running the restaurant is simple at first but can become pretty hectic once you start expanding and putting in more tables, but it's manageable if you pay enough attention and find a good balance between putting in orders and cashing out customers ready to pay.  The fact most of the early game customers pick up their own orders definitely helps as well.  Overall, it's a very robust and addictive experience that ensures you'll always have a goal to aim for while playing.
