_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. It's really cute and a lot of the characters are very enjoyable. While I can give this game a positive, recommending review, there are quite a few issues that need to be addressed.For starters, the game is really cute, the characters are enjoyable, and the gameplay loop is casual and easy to learn. For $25, I'd say that it's worth it, especially since I could get home from work, hop on, and just enjoy a few easy hours of grinding in dungeons and restaurants with cute characters doing cute things. Then there are the flaws. There are a few pretty massive ones, and quite a lot more minor ones, possibly nitpicky or just personal opinions. (THEY HAVE LOWERED THE HP FOR A FEW PARTICULARLY ANNOYING RANGED ENEMIES) First and foremost, they are planning to fix the monster HP, but as of my entire playthrough, monsters have INSANE hp pools. Some in the first area can be super dangerous, heavy hitters with 250-300 HP. And they stay this way in the first zone ALL THE WAY THROUGH TO THE END OF THE GAME. A simple solution would be having enemies scale to be easier in the first area, and a bit tankier/harder in the end, but as it stands, that boar is gonna be as much of a tank in zone 1 as it is at the end. Related, the scaling on enemies doesn't exist, so the only fundamental differences between zones in terms of difficulty is due to traps, not really the monsters (their stats remain the same between zones). Second, the mod and weapon systems and early game economy go hand in hand to make the early game miserable. The first debt is $2000. Which is sizable for that point in the game. Weapons are about half of that, and their price stays the same throughout the game... What ends up happening is a choice the player has to make. Do they use an entire day of sales to buy a new weapon (and possibly be disappointed in said choice, especially with no reselling?) Or do they just upgrade the restaurant or simply do literally anything else with the money? It then becomes a pretty obvious choice. They did make mods less expensive, but you still need to sacrifice a food item for what I believe is a 50% chance to lower the list of possible mods on the weapon/gear you're enhancing, then if the mod is good, you have to wait a day to get the item back... two if the upgrader has a day off the next day... It gets tedious and anti-experimental really, really quickly with this waiting and RNG going hand in hand. The "easiest" way to get gear/mods is to explore dungeons, which is much easier said than done because enemies are HARD in the early game (see first paragraph). And even then, the weapons and mods are RNG and there are a LOT of pretty bad/underwhelming mods. Like, way way too many. (THEY HAVE FIXED THE LAG AND ADDED FPS OPTIONS) Third, lag. The lag in some dungeons is borderline unplayable. I can play so many games like Elden Ring at 60+ fps with zero issues whatsoever. There is no reason I should be experiencing 10 fps in some dungeon floors for the ENTIRE FLOOR. Fourth, there's very, very little dialogue, no romance, no gifting to characters, etc. There's very little reason to interact with characters via Chat because they have like 4-5 lines it seems and then nothing else. Slight change on character birthdays and that's it. Minor issue, but it really is a detriment to this game because this is exactly the kind of game where you would expect character interaction to be a more major component and yet, they're just there to sell you stuff.Fifth, some enemy drops are incredibly rare. By the endgame, I was swimming in things like rice while I would be permanently out of beef. Yes, you can farm in dungeons, but when you need 4 different wood types and 4 different stone types, you have to use time in dungeons that don't have a monster with a loot that you really need for higher-yield dishes and it just feels really, really bad.And last for now, the playstyle for this game really encourages safe and slow play a lot more. Which is very personal opinion, but it really makes it so ranged weapons are just so much better than melee. Melee procs statuses on last combo hits while ranged procs on every projectile, so freeze is less reliable and easy to take damage trying to proc via melee while proccing it with ranged is a joke and trivializes most fights. If they made melee weapons stagger better, and made the heavy hitters faster than basic chicken attacks, maybe they'd be better? As it stands, I played the whole game with just timer egg bombs and cannot imagine trying to play with any melee weapon because oh my god the damage taken in the game is punishing.Now, after reading all these criticisms, you might wonder why I would give this game a positive review. While I can't give it incredible praise for its current state, I would recommend it because it is on the cheaper side of things, it's cute, and I truly believe it can be a really good game. At the moment though, unless you're just REALLY sold on the designs like I am, it can be a bit of a slog or a painful experience at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Cuisineer is a great game with superb art and a fun gameplay loop. It is what I would call a time-sinker due to its relative grindy-ness- I like the customization you can do to the shopCons : - Weapon damage upgrades feel somewhat unsatisfying- The performance of the game has been hit or miss of a very high-end setup- A lot of the explanations to the game seem to be coming too late, I kept on wondering how to do certain things just to be told 13 hours in how (when it should've been maybe 2 or 3 hours in) IMO Those should have been set as "quest tutorials" instead of the morning mail thing, specially since you tend to forget it a few hours after.Overall, something of a 7/10; I think this can be improved on if the developers keep updating the game a bit. _childDocuments_.review: It's not particularly deep and the dungeon-crawling aspect takes some getting used to, but I find this to be an extremely enjoyable experience overall. There's very little hand-holding but the game also doesn't punish you harshly for making mistakes and taking your time. Inventory management is hard early on so make sure to go check the travelling merchants early on, one of them sells bag upgrades on the days they're there.I see people complaining about weapon upgrades only adding +1 damage to the weapon, but the combo system makes it so that +1 scales to more damage on subsequent hits. It takes a lot of resources to upgrade your weapon, but you also don't have to rush it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Put up my folks wanted posters right by the restaurant door while I work on their damn debt.Cuisineer is a delightful little game that breaks up a pretty damn tough dungeon crawler with light restaurant management, where you serve up the pieces of dungeon monsters on a platter to your customers. The dungeon crawling is reminiscent of Hades dressed up in an absolutely adorable, pastel colored art style. You have to be quick on your feet, avoid traps, dash carefully, and pay attention to not draw too many enemies toward you at once. Their pathing can very much lead to little rice soldiers outflanking you. Too many ranged enemies at once can be a real headache, requiring some careful positioning. The procedurally generated, individual levels of the dungeons do not come in the shape of separate rooms, but all at once, and some backtracking might be required if you find yourself at the end of a branch.The restaurant management side is nothing complex, and for me personally serves as a way to wind down and vary up the gameplay. Customers will come in, seat themselves, and tell you their orders. You need to go to the correct crafting station, which will automatically show a list filtered by active customer orders. The food cooks on a small timer, after which (most) customers will proceed to pick up their meals themselves. Just pay attention for the occasional dine and dash-er.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Tiny enemies just too tiny to be seen, especially effects will cover EVERYTHING, including hazard region, tiny enemies and their projectiles. Already found GREEN vegetable enemies are small enough to hide everywhere in the GREEN forest's background? There's mushrooms! MORE TINY.1 stone/tree/any breakable obj that block your move = about 6 hits = 6 btn pressing. Just found this may be more harmful for my fingers than playing Armored Core 6 with all achievements got. Weapon upgrade? ATK 10 to 11. Big thanks for 10%.Shop management is a little shallow designed (rank 8 currently so maybe too early to say, but it's already a over 5 hr experience), almost fall asleep when opening the restaurant. You can decide when to open and close so maybe just open in rushing hour(launch and/or dinner) is a good choice.Inventory menus didn't stops time, so you'll found time lost when you're just putting things in or out. Also time runs at real time and 24:00 will interrupt everything you're doing, so don't cook at night or you can easily waste things.And can somebody tells me is there's any way to put cuisine BACK to table? If you take them when restaurant is closing, they will be put into inventory and can not be use for sell.The user experience may change a lot between controller/joystick and mouse+keyboard. Art is great but that's all. The boring combat system with visibility issue mentioned above is the reason I don't recommend currently.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much fun. Think of this game as a mix between cozy gaming and dungeon raiding. The controls are easy to understand, even without a tutorial (I'm playing on a PC). Artwork and graphics are top-notch, as well as the beautiful soundtrack. I'm enjoying the mix of raiding dungeons for recipe ingredients, plus getting to work the restaurant like some of my favorite sims. I haven't gotten to the actual dungeon bosses yet, but the dungeons are really fun so far - even without attacking the bosses (but I'm sure I'll love those too). The game and its graphics also caught the attention of my husband (a big Final Fantasy player, as well as FPS games), who came over to watch me play for a little bit. Highly recommend. I hope the developers continue to expand this game and provide us new dungeons, quests, recipes, etc. as this game continues to grow!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Still relatively early into the game, but I'm loving it so far! Absolutely gorgeous artwork and character design, fun gameplay, all the food looks so good I get hungry just looking at it. Incredible game.My only Minor complaint is that, at least for my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, it's difficult to run at times. The poor thing heats up so fast that I can only really play in short bursts.If it's possible, I'd love if this game could add graphical or performance settings in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: If you combine dungeon crawlers like Hades, Binding of Issac, or Enter the Gungeon, mix it with cooking management and a very adorable artstyle, you will get this game! I learned of this game through Twitter, and looked very excitedly for its release, and I am very happy with its appeal. I love you can change the difficulty level to reduce how much your character takes, and I love the cooking curve of how to unlock recipes and cooking equipment. Anyone reading this, please give this a game a try; it's worth the money, I promise!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game at PAX West 2023 and immediately knew it had the makings of something great; now that it's available for everyone. I can't say I am disappointed. Plus if you love food, puns or both this game is also a delight in those areas as well.This game has a nice mix of themes from the farm/life sim games coupled with hack and slash, loot hoarding, dungeon crawling goodness. The game is just fin and mostly relaxing to play. The game is well polished and consistent in both the art styles and mechanics that the game just honestly feels good, and nothing feels really forced or mcguffin'd into the game for some random reason.  Given that this game is not being released under early access; it's a nice change of pace to see such a good game right out of the gate. I think the only downside to this game is that progression is a little slower than what some might find enjoyable. However, once a flow is set it's pretty easy to forget about progression and more about the fun being had, and also why those fire breathing pepper monsters are so damn dangerous!
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute game, adorable and delicious looking artworks.Gameplay loop is fun, and game runs "well" on the steam deck.I'll only put the negative stuff in this review:- Game optimisation is very bad. My first boss fight was running at ~20 fps on the Steam Deck. Despite the good looking arts and models, the game should not run that bad. Other than that, I get a 38-40 fps experience most of the time (I locked the refresh rate to 40 fps).- Too many loading screens, each one needs from 3 to 8~10 seconds to complete between each screen, including going in and out the bedroom from the restaurant.- Gamepad inputs are somewhat weird, mainly during inventory management. Be careful not to accidentaly delete a stack of items by pressing RT.- Steam Deck related, probably related to the first point: launching the game asks for a very long time (with the steam logo spinning) before getting to the main menu. Heavier games do not ask that much time and loading screens.Despite that, I have a very good time playing Cuisineer, and recommend it to anyone looking for a chill-but-not-so-much game mixing simple dungeon crawling, simple cooking and a very cute setup.
_childDocuments_.name: Cuisineer

_childDocuments_.review: Had this on my wishlist since I got to play the demo from Steam's nextfest. Have to say it's one of the most charming games I've played in years, and I'm glad to now own it. ♥ The entire game just oozes cute charm, and it really feels unique and refreshing for it. There are some things I almost wish were a part of the game, such as maybe more interactions with the villagers or have that be more central as a mechanic, but for what the game is, I'm very happy and would recommend it. Combat is fun, gameworld is charming, characters are adorable, art style is amazingly done, and I'll continue to play this for awhile when I have the time to. :)

_childDocuments_.review: *edit, changing to a negative review upon playing for 24 hours.this game is beyond grindy, and the fact that i had to take a break ever so often to rest my right hand because clicking so many times just to finish filling up my maxed out inventory (yes, filling my inventory, NOT finishing a dungeon. i have never finished a dungeon because the risk of losing an entire inventory just to kill the final boss for MORE normal drops that i have no space to fit them is not worth it.) is actually killing my right hand from the amount of clicking i have to do. and yes, i could rebind the attack key, but all targeting is based on where the mouse is pointing, so its more intuitive to use left and right click if i have to use the mouse to point attacks, which also makes it quite infuriating to use when i cant see where my mouse is during super hectic dungeon moments with a lot of mobs, and makes using the dash attack for the kebab skewer difficult since i cant see where i'm going. an option for a separate targeting system, such as using character direction or specific mob targeting, would be appreciated. also if we could just hold down the button to perform combos, or make mobs less plentiful but drop more items, would also be great. the dungeon art, though cute, gets pretty stale after having to go in there so many times with the same few floors. also, i don't understand why trees and stones get a sparkly effect to denote that they are breakable to get items, when jars are also breakable to get ingredients sometimes, are not sparkly. dungeon crawling itself gets boring because most of the difference in play is your main weapon, which only has a basic combo, dash strike and the special. equipment mods adjust the playstyle somewhat, but not much. having power-ups you can pick up throughout the dungeon might help with the 'randomness' of the dungeon, and also make gathering ingredients less monotonous.if restaurant dishes can take items directly from the fridge, and upgrading the restaurant/buying from alder in general can take items directly from my storage chest, i don't see why i have to manually submit quest items to npcs instead of directly taking from my storage/fridge. also, having to check the journal for how many of the item i need, then rummaging through my fridge and storage just to see if i have the item, is frustrating especially when you have several side quests, have multiple storage/fridges, and have a bad memory, especially since you have to do this quickly and take all the items in one trip because you're wasting time on the clock and then i get fatigued for no reason. Make the journal a bit more useful, and instead of indicating like 0/20 rice to show how many items i need to submit, to show that i have 200/20 rice and reflect what i have in my inventory/fridge so that i don't have to check whether i have the item or not. the markers above the quest npcs could also change to a green tick at that point if i can finish the quest, instead of having to check whether the npc with triple dots above their head is the correct quest npc to finish the quest.the time really needs to be stopped when you're not running a restaurant. when you're just trying to cook up quest items or looking through your side quests in the journal, time ticks away and suddenly its the lunch rush or you have 10% fatigue. it's very frustrating when you honestly just don't have a good memory or if you're just trying to run around and brew your items.speaking of brewing, it shouldn't take 1 day to brew, pretty much forcing you to run the restaurant or use other suboptimal equipment. having brewing consume a dish to increase chances of certain mods is also another pain point. i make 1 sparkling water in my restaurant, run to the brewery, then it spits out a sweetness mod, which of course i don't want if i'm aiming for an ice mod. then i have to run all the way to the restaurant and repeat. i can't make multiple sparkling waters because on the chance that i do get the mods that i want, all the extra sparkling waters i've made have literally gone to waste because i cant use them in the restaurant, i can't sell them, the only way to get rid of them is use them in brewing or for quests. and while i'm running around trying to brew a useful mod, time is running down fast. an alternative might be just requiring particular dishes if you want a specific mod, of course using higher tier dishes for better mods.the ingredient drops need to have better balance, especially since we aren't able to choose the menu offerings. i'm literally overflowing with rice and flour while my meats and other things are always running out because 1: the customers tend to order certain dishes when it's in stock and never others for some reason e.g the moment i have any amount of coconuts, the curry prata sells out like hotcakes, and in early game my pork kept running out all the time because everyone orders boiled pork instead of noodles, and 2: the amount of mobs in the dungeon for any ingredient that's not like the staple mob (e.g flour and chickens for 1st dungeon, chili spice for 2nd dungeon) isn't consistent, and even if i'm so desperate for more pork, i can only pray that they spawn. 3rd dungeon has better spawns for the new ingredients you'll find at that point e.g tentacles, crabs, fish. i find that especially the 1st dungeon has way too many varieties of ingredients to get, e.g i could get half of all available ingredients in the game just from the 1st dungeon, and that made farming the non-staples mobs like pork, cheese, sap and others very difficult especially in early game since we might not even encounter enough of these non-staple mobs. a more linear progression when it comes to ingredients would make it more feasible to gather what you need, instead of just throwing half the mobs in the game in 1 dungeon. Or, you could implement a lure system where players can buy lures and use it before dungeons to increase spawn rates of certain mobshonestly i have a lot more to say but i literally don't have enough space :') i was waiting for this game to be out but i'm really disappointed in the game design and qol in general._i need romance options to date ankhiluun please :3cits a fun and cozy little game, going very much at your own pace. there isnt a push to open your restaurant daily and instead go hunting for ingredients for the whole day, though experienced players can have a bit more challenge with leaving the gathering part for the later part of the day with some handicaps.other than that, basic tutorials/qol could be improved in general e.g: - this is generally quite universal, but putting wasd in the top left hand corner for movement would prevent people totally new to the game from trying to click the floor or using arrow keys to move- personally i would prefer an option for a targeting system because i suck at aiming and i constantly forget my mouse is where my attacks will be aimed at instead of where my character is facing-- brewery isn't very intuitive to use at the start, and the list of mods are a little convoluted (e.g for sweetness small increase or big increase, it can be condensed down to one box and mention more arrows means better)- since there are schedules for every other shop, maybe having schedules for caravans could be an option as well?- had a quest for fried egg since the beginning and i only realised how to actually make the fried egg on day 7 after staring at the recipe book and finding out i needed a separate equipment for frying things- for the people who might want to be a little more involved in the cooking process, it might be cool to add in an option to do a little cooking mama style of mini game, of course still having the option to just let things auto cook, but you also get more money if you do the mini game- i would prefer if we had the option to choose what the restaurant can serve on that day, sometimes all i have r chicken n noods :')

_childDocuments_.review: I have been anticipating the release of this game since playing the beta, and I'm quite pleased overall! Changes in opinions and further updates will come later.Cuisineer is an ideal game for those who are looking to play a cozy, adorable roguelite. In addition, the game runs fairly well on the Steam Deck and it's my preferred way of playing this game. The dungeon crawling aspect of this game is excellent. The monsters are all cute. _childDocuments_.review: My review is based on the state of the game when I played it during the Steam Next Fest in June, which I played for around 10 hours. Probably the best demo I've tried this year. The demo had 1 dungeon available, but still huge amounts of content. I might edit the review later based on the state of the full release. TL;DR: I had a blast with the demo and just wanted to come back for more. There are some (minor) issues but it never took away from the experience from me as a whole. Positives: - Fun and engaging gameplay loop: You adventure through dungeons and defeat enemies to gather materials that can then be used to upgrade your restaurant or for cooking. Then you serve customers at your restaurant and cook meals from the materials you gathered. This will get you money to pay back the debt you have to pay and also to upgrade things that can again be useful for dungeon sessions or your restaurant. It feels like simple items have more utility than in other games that only consist of the dungeon crawling aspect. - Charming graphics and character artworks- A lot of options to upgrade your restaurant and your equipment/health when going to the dungeons- Mini(bosses), of which 2 were in the demo, had an excellent difficulty level in my opinion. They were challenging, but not too difficult so it was still possible for me to beat them during the first encounter. - Music is quite pleasant to listen to (even if there could be more variety in some areas, I never felt like this was an issue though)Negatives (felt like minor issues to me though): - Having the game installed on the HDD can cause quite a bit of loading times. And the game will enter loading screens a lot, even for areas that have been loaded before (I assume they just unload everything except the current area you're in to have more optimized ram usage, but not sure). So that time adds up. - I like the game loop and balancing a lot, but serving customers in the restaurant can get a little repetitive after a while - and you'll do this a lot. While there are still some micro decisions you can make, it mostly boils don't to just going through the same steps without much thought. The system still works well but I think the problem is just spending too much time with it. - You might find some (side) missions a bit grindy. It mostly comes down to either gathering materials from a specific dungeon for someone or cooking meals from those materials for someone. A lot of missions can be done quite quickly, but sometimes it can be hard to gather enough of the required materials, so you enter the same dungeon multiple times for the same mission. It was fine for me still, and that's the whole game loop after all, but it might not be worth for everyone to try to complete every mission. Someone mentioned there there are virtually no quality settings for the graphics. I understand this is a pain point, but from the games and demos I played recently, this game ran relatively smoothly on my notebook. My notebook has a great base hardware (i7-9750h, rtx 2060 mobile), but has big issues with heat and usually thermal throttling sets in during playing. Even with that, this game remained relatively playable in that situation where other's didn't. Your mileage might vary.

The game play is smooth and you wont really get bored if you like Diner Dash with some Roguelite dungeon crawling.I'm almost 3 hrs in and overall i would rate it the following:Gameplay: 5/5Cuteness: 5/5Good Vibes: 5/5Hunger Meter: 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to the world of Cuisineer, a cute food-focused game where you play as Pom, an adventurer who has returned back to her hometown of Paell only to find out that you've inherited the family restaurant but it is in debt and on the brink of collapse. The only way to pay back the debt is to reopen the restaurant! And to do THAT you've got to go dungeon-delving!

name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie
detailed_description: Key features: Meet a vibrant cast of fully-voiced characters Enjoy a magical soundtrack by Lena Raine Make your choices by seeing their future outcomes Unravel a mysterious and emotional story, and discover multiple endings Play as Polly/Harmony, an Oracle of two colorful and rich worlds In the very near future... When Polly returns home after a few years abroad, to look for her missing mother, she quickly realizes that her hometown has drastically changed. A megacorporation named MK is using its power to control the population, and her community is in danger.    She soon discovers that she has a gift of clairvoyance that connects her to Reverie, the realm of the Aspirations of Humanity: Glory, Bliss, Power, Chaos, Bond, and Truth. In this world, Polly becomes Harmony, a goddess who has the power to choose the Aspiration that will ultimately rule over Reverie and restore the delicate balance between the deities’ world and ours.     The fate of humanity is at stake. To which destiny do you aspire? As Polly, or Harmony, each action you take will affect both worlds and send you down sprawling narrative paths. See into the future and explore the consequences of possible choices in the Augural, a game board and visual representation of Polly's gift of foresight. In pursuing whichever destiny you desire, you’ll also bond with and obtain crystals from the Aspirations. These will unlock different paths at important crossroads that will change how the thread of the story unravels, and ultimately the fate of humanity. Whichever Aspiration comes to lead Reverie, with Harmony’s help, will also become the heart of humanity. Their personality and style of rule will change Reverie while also giving the people of our world a new direction too: when the link between worlds is stronger, Reverie has a bigger influence on the state of our world. Glory, Bliss, Power, Chaos, Bond, and Truth are all wildly different entities with their own distinct personalities, goals, and opinions on how to make things better. You’ll get to know each of them as visit Reverie in your dreams as Harmony, but only you know best – as Polly – what your world needs.     As you play, revel in artistic direction that is bright, vibrant, and futuristic. Immerse yourself in the daily life of a Mediterranean city and get to know its people, with a cast of characters who are fully voiced and animated. Enjoy an enchanting soundtrack by award-winning composer, Lena Raine.

_childDocuments_.review: First, the positive: The art and animation are top-notch. Gorgeous use of color throughout. Character designs are dynamic, expressive, and memorable. The backgrounds are beautiful and just subtly animated enough to feel alive. The voice acting is really well-done. Even ambient sounds and sound effects are well selected. The user interface is really well-designed, with smooth animations and pleasant graphic design.Now, the reason I wouldn't recommend this game: The weakness of the writing. The opening act suffers from a lot of telling without showing; the exposition is clumsy and heavy-handed in general until the story finds its feet. Transitions between scenes can be jarring and abrupt. This is partially due to the Augural mechanic of the game where you choose the flow of the scene, which requires you to shift between the Augural view and the dialogue. This could have been better mitigated if the player didn't need to shift back to the Augural when there is only one possible node/choice to visit next; I as the player shouldn't need to be taken out of the scene just to double-click a circle. These abrupt transitions aren't exclusively due to Augural choices, though. In several spots, a transition mid-node or between chapters is jarring or disorienting. Places where the writer(s) chose to abridge the dialogue with a text description of what's being said lessens the impact of several sequences. Small writing flaws/inconsistencies are peppered in just enough that it's irritating. Characters reference details casually that contradict previously established facts or that they should not know (from routes you did not choose). Several emotional choices are railroaded in favor of making less interesting and less consequential choices elsewhere. The final chapter is especially guilty of telling instead of showing. The premise is interesting and unique, but this execution takes all of the air out of it.Edit:Went back and played a second route because I thought my review might have been a bit harsh. I'm more sure now that my initial review was warranted. Here are some additional observations from the second playthrough. - All animated sequences appear to be unskippable- both the cutscenes and the transitions into new locations. There doesn't seem to be an option to start over from any place besides the beginning once you've finished the game, which is a problem when the first act is so dense with exposition. When you're playing through a node you've already seen, you have to hit the dialogue advance button over and over; it would have been simple enough to allow holding it down to skip through dialogue quickly. All of this poses a barrier to replayability. Given that this game's emphasis on choices and branching paths relies on replayability, it makes replaying a slog.- The music is mostly ambient, but it's really good. - Certain nodes are reused between paths where your allegiances differ, but the way the characters react to one another does not change. So you'll have two characters act antagonistically about a plan when 2 nodes before they agreed to work together on it. It's tonal whiplash.- The section after act 3 is almost entirely on rails no matter which choices you make. The note I made about not wanting to be taken out of the story/scene just to double-click a circle is especially relevant here. I considered it might be an intentional choice, to contrast with the act before and after which are full of branching paths, but my faith in the writing is so tested at this point that it just comes across to me as lazy. It would have been more powerful storytelling and less frustrating gameplay to completely deny access to the Augural view full-stop and serve up the scenes one after another, or to provide the very few choices (none consequential) that this section offers in a different format, outside of the Augural view.

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony is a very good game, let's get this out of the way. It has a VERY strong focus on choices. Choices are used as the main gameplay element and I think it's fair to say that this makes Harmony a visual novel first and foremost.Harmony convinces with breathtaking visuals, bright colors and an interesting plot. It's a smart mix of mystery and science fiction, some metaphysical questions are raised early on but over time the plot becomes much more relationship-focused. You could say your job is to manage relationships, not only your own relationship towards NPCs but also on many occasions their relationships they have towards each other. The voice acting is one of Harmony's strengths for sure and carries the plot. That goes both for the main cast and supporting characters. Would I have completed this as an audiobook? Quite possibly.What made me a bit sad is that some important scenes are extremely well animated, with cartoony sequences and beautiful art while others are merely explained with words. Can't really give an example without spoiling the plot so I'll just leave it like that. Missed opportunity though.Also, due to the overwhelming number of choices it's sometimes difficult to tell whether you did good or not. But there is no game over screen, every decision carries you forward. So even if you mess up, the game will find a way to make it work in a different way. Sometimes that makes scenes feel a bit arbitrary, as if your choice is more of an illusion but only another playthrough could prove if that suspicion is warranted.For me that's not a big deal anyway. Harmony offers a thrilling plot with high stakes and relationships you have to manage as you walk a path of chaos or collaboration, of authority or love. Ultimately it's not about game overs, relentless antagonists or the classical hero journey. The main character is already a strong woman, her personality never really changes during the plot. What you get here is mainly a fascinating, colorful adventure where you meet beautiful people and solve mysteries with them. The mystery surrounding your family, but also that of the fate of the world and the meaning and purpose of Reverie and the Aspirations that live there.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is  latest release. It follows in the footsteps of their previous games with a narrative emphasis and diverse choices but changes up the formula to resemble that of a static visual novel. The story is rather mature about mega corporations and tyrannical schemes, whilst mixing in extensive in-game lore.  Set in a futuristic and vibrant world, the protagonist Polly heads back to her hometown to visit her mother after hearing of her disappearance. The streets look vastly different to what she remembers, and a large corporation called Mono Konzern (MK) has taken hold of the place she once called home. During the search for her mother, she is pulled into a world she can barely fathom, The Reverie. The Reverie is the realm of Aspirations, Glory, Chaos, Bliss, Truth, Power, and Bond. Polly becomes Harmony and can switch between the two realms at ease. There is a vital balance between Polly’s world, and that of Reverie’s. It must be restored to bring back peace and stability, but which Aspiration will you choose to follow? Or is it best that they are all kept equal? Each decision made is typically linked to one of these Aspirations, but it is not as clear as you may think. There is no enemy character, only the corporation MK, which is faceless. It touches on real world issues and concepts, hence describing it earlier as a mature narrative. However, it also brilliantly encompasses grief, the struggle to continue, and the reality of a rebellion and search for justice. The emotions felt raw, but righteous, and the writing was simply fantastic. This comes as no surprise given  extensive background in games such as  and  It also seamlessly includes LGBTQI characters within the story without bringing their sexuality or gender identity to the forefront of the games focus, but merely just forms part of the characters backgrounds, which I found brilliant. Despite the many intricacies of such an extensive plot, I enjoyed witnessing the battle the characters were fighting as I was there deciding their next move. Fighting for freedom was symbolic, but pertinent. The actions they were taking and choices available were harsh but felt pragmatic. That is, until the final chapter where it all becomes a tad jumbled and the focus is placed back on greater powers (the Aspirations). Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is a visual novel with capacious choice elements. Unlike  there are no third-person exploration segments, it is all written text and choices. Choices are made through the Augural, which is a visual representation of the choices and their future consequences. It is a sprawling branch tree, split into chapters and can be quite overwhelming at first. Some nodes will directly impact other nodes in the future, meaning if you make a certain decision, you will be locked out of corresponding decisions in the future. Specific nodes also have “crystals” for each of the Aspirations and may only be unlocked if you have obtained a predetermined number of these crystals by making decisions that correlate to particular Aspirations. Some nodes will also have a barrier around them, which is only attainable after reaching a specific node below it and so forth. I found this Augural to be overly complicated and at times I did not find it clear which node was actually accessible to me, nor was it feasible to look into the very distant future to see exactly how the choice will impact the game later (also, many future node descriptions are blocked to avoid this). Furthermore, during later parts of the game, there was only one choice node available, and it would only last for a few sentences, and then it would take me back to the choice selection again. This was repeated numerous times and felt incongruous. The constant jumping back and forth between the real world and the Augural was taxing and disruptive to the overall story. Especially considering as there was only one option to pick, I do not see the purpose of bouncing back and forth just to click on a node and repeat this over a dozen times. I would have preferred if the game automatically continued where there were no choices to be made as it would create a more immersive and sequential experience.Choices matter, and there are clear consequences for them, which ultimately makes players want to make different choices. However, text and scenes are unskippable, as well as there being a lack of a chapter select. Understandably, the number of decisions made in one playthrough is astronomical, and everything is intertwined, but I would have appreciated being able to go back to specific sections and continue playing from there, as opposed to having to play the entire game again.Despite being a very different style to  previous games, it was a welcome change. The vibrant, futuristic setting was emanating colour and prosperity, juxtaposing the selfish stone-cold nature of the corporation slowly taking hold. Whilst there are limited backdrops and animated character poses, it was a great addition to the game, and I enjoyed the developers trying out something new. The soundtrack is aptly described on the store page as “enchanting” and that it is. The cast of characters are fully voiced and each does an impeccable job conveying emotions. Bliss was extremely uppity yet naïve, Power being authoritative but not dictatorial and more. My only complaint would be that I wish there were more animated cut scenes, especially those that had voice-acting in them to better showcase the talents of the cast. 6 hours, but I am a very quick reader. I suspect this could take up to 8-9 hours. Player choice. Yes, with a plethora of different endings and choices, the game is designed for this, but there is no chapter select.Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is an excellent and unique addition to  growing catalogue. As always, they are unafraid of discussing mature, raw themes and feature inclusivity throughout their cast of characters. Although the sprawling choice design seems overly convoluted and can even become disruptive at times, the well-written and engaging narrative has a lot to offer fellow story enthusiasts.

_childDocuments_.review: Game desperately needs a skip button. It's meant to be replayed and it has a lot of text and cut-scenes you will beg to skip the second time around. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to give this game a positive review. It does a lot of things well, and it's overall an enjoyable experience, but I cannot in good conscience recommend it, much less at full price. As other reviewers have said, the game's weakness is its writing, which is catastrophic when the game is, in essence, a visual novel and reliant on its narrative. The story is compelling; I personally had no issue with its political tone or motivations. However, the entire time I was playing the game--and I replayed it just to make sure--I felt like I was missing important information. It was akin to reading a novel while skipping every three sentences or even every other page. You get the general idea, but a lot is lost along the way. Unfortunately, a lot of the story suffers as a result. The characters feel flat--I know next to nothing about most of them--or change off-screen without me witnessing the character development. So much is untold. There is a lot of telling and not showing, and sometimes not even telling OR showing. It's deeply frustrating when the story has so much potential to be great.Therefore, the story, ultimately, feels unfinished. Unpolished. Amateur. It's bones are there, but there is very little meat. Part of the problem is the gameplay itself. While the Augural is neat as a visualization of the story paths, I don't think they could quite figure out how to marry the concept of it to the actual narrative. Constantly switching back to the Augural view between story beats broke the immersion and disrupted the flow. This becomes especially annoying in Act 4 and abysmal in Act 5 when the writers seem to give up on actually letting us play the game and give us the conclusion in bullet points. Even worse, there were times when I would pick an option in the Augural based on what it seemed to mean, and then whatever was said after picking it made no sense to me whatsoever or was in opposition to what I thought I was choosing. I love the idea of being able to visualize the impact my choices have and, thus, strategize based on what outcome I want, but the logic of it fell apart in some sections. Furthermore, so much information was just dumped into the Codex instead of explained in the game. I really thought the Codex would just be to help you remember the terminology as the game progressed, but, no, it really functions as an infodump for things the writers were too lazy to put into the narrative.For a game that is obviously meant to be replayed, they have no options for skipping seen dialogue or skipping animation. You can't even replay the story from certain points unless you want to restart an entire act, which saves over/deletes your previous progress, meaning you have no way to go back in and look at the Augural to make different choices. It's so frustrating.Now, the positives:The art style is absolutely gorgeous. It was what first caught my eye when I learned about the game in a Nintendo Direct. There are fully animated cutscenes in the game, as well as detailed animations when the characters are speaking. The backgrounds are 3D-rendered and have some motion elements (e.g., public transit passing by, drones flying, waves moving, etc.). The very first words out of my mouth when the game started was, "Oh my God, I love this art style!" The bright, saturated colors on Mediterranean architecture and the fun street art of Atina; the whimsy of the clashing decor and novelty of the pool-turned-living space at the Naiads; and the surreal fantasy of Reverie and its realms, all make the world of Harmony: The Fall of Reverie feel so realized. Even better, however, is the character design. Both the humans and the Aspirations have such lovely designs, though some characters' designs feel less polished than others (like Laszlo). We have a wide berth of races and body types represented, which is refreshing. For the humans, I am particularly fond of Jade's and Nora's designs and outfits. I love how Ursula has teal lipstick and fingernails, similar to Chaos' own lip color. The Aspirations' designs are what really take the cake for me though. Bliss' wild colors and streetwear, hearkening a Western-bent decora harajuku style, perfectly suit her child-like nature as the embodiment of happiness and fun. Chaos wears a princely outfit, topped with an onyx crown, with a strange sort of clown makeup that I absolutely love and suits his playful personality. Glory, who spends much of the game off-screen, has one of the most striking designs, her towering height accentuated by a floor-length waist cape over wide-leg pants. She has a gold septum ring and glasses with opaque red lenses, which make her seem so ominous and badass. Power is giving an imposing Sean Connery vibe, Truth leans into Tilda Swinton and Annie Lennox's androgyny, and Bond's design is clearly inspired by South Asian and Hindu iconography. All of the Aspirations prominently feature grays, blacks, golds, and reds in their design, except for Bliss and Truth, who is all white with gold accents and a black third-eye. Harmony, Polly's Reverie counterpart, is dressed in an a-line blue gown with gold arm bands. It's so feminine and striking.The voice acting is quite excellent. I felt much more engaged--and more relaxed--because I wasn't having to keep my eyes on the dialogue box the whole time while on autoskip. The music is also very nice, though I don't have much to say beyond that I found it really atmospheric and enjoyable. All in all, I wouldn't say I necessarily regret playing it, but I do regret that it failed to live up to the potential that was clearly there. I cannot recommend this game, unless purchased at a large discount and with these caveats in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is a real visual novel, with a nicely developed story and fascinating characters to follow.In Harmony we meet Polly. After a time of absence, she returns to her hometown of Atina to look for her missing mother.Watch a snippet of gameplay here: Soon you discover that Polly is a psychic, a gift that connects her to Reverie, the realm of human desires: glory, happiness, power, chaos, connection and truth.In this world, Polly grows into Harmony, a goddess with the power to choose the desire that will ultimately rule Reverie and restore the fragile balance between the world of the gods and our world.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot that this game does correctly. The interesting character designs, the moving soundtrack, and the emphatic voice acting are all phenomenal. But the story falls short.In the first three acts, you've got a clear goal and your actions seem to have very real consequences. You have to choose who you side with, potentially hurting others in the process, so you have to decide where your morals lie. But, during act 4-5, the game changes drastically.No longer are you following the original plot, since that's already been resolved, and now you are faced with something much more unoriginal and boring. Some plot points were even thrown out completely,  and all the characters feel empty near the end of the story. I no longer cared about any of my choices since every felt so... lifeless. Honestly, I wish I stopped playing after act 3.Act 5 was definitely the most difficult to play. There is barely any dialogue, and the story just rambles on and on. Something that could be explained in five minutes goes on for twenty. It's frustrating because the game was going places, until it wasn't.That's why I cannot recommend the game, at least, not for the price it's currently at. It's a somewhat short and not well thought out game I see being worth maybe $10. The animation and art style may be beautiful, but it doesn't excuse the price tag. My recommendation would be to buy it on sale, if at all.

_childDocuments_.review: It seems my number one problem ended up being that I cared about the story.The only mechanic to the game is this overlay web looking thing that sort of shows you what choices will lead to other choices and outcomes and what kind of "crystals" you will gain or loose.I would try planning for a certain path and outcome. Only to get there and find it was locked. Sometimes it was unclear as to why that option was locked other times it was because of some small choice I had made chapters before. I spent the whole game trying to work in a particular direction but got forced down paths that I didn't want to go down. Ultimately, the last hour of the game was being stuck on rails pushing the same button to "play" through to an end I didn't even want. This game gave me the illusion of choosing and controlling the direction of the narrative but there were too many restrictions. With a game that is ONLY pushing the button to select what path you take, I didn't appreciate those restrictions. I wanted to explore the story and the possibilities, and it wasn't interesting enough to invest another 10 hours to play again in an attempt to figure out the magic equation to get to the end I was hoping for.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a shame because I don't like leaving negative reviews. And there is a lot I love about this game, but it ultimately left me unsatisfied. I generally didn't vibe with it at the start. The way you make choices takes you out of the narrative to a sort of butterfly effect menu. I found this jarring at first but eventually got over that and appreciated what it was trying to do. The middle of the game I genuinely got invested in and started to enjoy my time with it. The story, characters, plot, it was all starting to hit. Sadly it completely trips all over itself at the end. The games starts taking on a more macro view and moves at a breakneck pace. You are no longer interacting with characters and major events happen one after another being told in what feels like some epilogue wrap up. All my investment vanished. And when I finished the game I just felt nothing, empty, wondering why it couldn't have kept it's footing.It truly bums me out because I loved so much of what the middle of the game was doing. I was, for a time invested, but it ultimately lost me again. I guess the lesson is: don't zoom out on a narrative game. people play these for the character interactions, once those are gone you aren't really left with much.

_childDocuments_.review: After getting word that her mother has mysteriously disappeared, Polly returns to her home town of Atina to help with the search. The place has changed immensely from the one she knew, and is now run by a mega corporation called MK.A strange attraction draws Polly to a necklace which transports her to another dimension called Reverie. Here she meets the aspirations who reside over Reverie and see Polly as their savior from a collapsing world. Polly becomes Harmony, and is now able to travel between dimensions and see into the future using the Augural, a choice-based map of things to pass. Choices she makes in one world can have an instant effect in the other, and future choices are determined by events that have happened in the past. Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is a visual novel with full voice acting with character and scenery animations, which should last around eight hours, but subsequent play throughs will offer different outcomes if choices are different. The story develops through character interaction, where all characters are fully voiced and animated; Polly’s own thoughts, which act as an aside to the story; and the Augural, where choices are made which mold the story as you progress. Polly moves between Reverie and Atina when the story dictates. In Reverie, she becomes Harmony, a priestess who must pick the right aspiration to rule over the kingdom. Each aspiration represents a characteristic and has their own personality and ideas on how to solve certain issues that arise. For example, Power wants to use force or intimidation to resolve issues, whereas Truth is more diplomatic and believes in being honest and forthright. Other aspirations include Bliss, Chaos, Glory and Bond.When using the Augural, often choices made will be linked to an aspiration, and picking that choice will earn you crystals and favor with that aspiration. It may also lose you crystals and favor with others. Having enough crystals can affect whether a choice is revealed or not. For example, a choice might only be possible if you possess two truth crystals and one bliss crystal, otherwise you will have to pick another choice.There is no way of getting stopped in your tracks. There will always be a choice to be made, but it isn’t always the one you want to make because of the way the system works. Some of the scenes in Atina are animated and they always look bright and vibrant with nice artwork. Expect the odd cutscene here and there. Characters look good and their personalities are heightened through use of basic animations. I particularly liked the way they appeared and disappeared of the screen effortlessly. A really nice soundtrack, with some superb voice acting which is full of emotion. You can tell they had a big budget for sound and it makes all the difference.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Weak as both a visual novel and a choice-centric game. I played through twice to see if there was a more coherent story I was missing, but no, the disjointed and arbitrary story seems to be intended. This feels like a huge step backward for Don't Nod.As a visual novel: There's no skip function. Anything billing itself as a VN that should be replayed several times but that doesn't have a skip function (not even for the cutscenes!) was pretty clearly made by people who don't play or understand the genre. You can't save or replay from checkpoints either, since as soon as you finish a chapter its choices are locked in and can't be changed except by restarting the whole game. As a choice-centric game: Outcomes feel arbitrary. I usually felt more at the mercy of the augural than in control of it, but the most frustrating part was that the scenes I unlocked often had little or no impact on the storyline. This is especially egregious in the final act.The overall result is that the game makes it very clear that nothing you did in that section actually mattered and the outcome had nothing to do with you. It just happened, and so you get to react. The Aspirations later praise Harmony for bending reality to her will, but... you mostly just play out the nodes you're required to in that section of the game, and the optional ones have . You actually have less ability to affect the story in that chapter than you do in earlier ones. It's just bizarre design and writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie is a big disappointment to me, not least because I bought it at full price right after it was released only to find it didn't even run on my PC. It's a VN, but unlike every other VN under sun which runs on a potato, this VN has (admittedly gorgeous) 3D rendered graphics that cause a hard crash on Intel chips prior to Iris Xe. Still, my Surface was due for an upgrade, so I bought a whole new damn computer to play this game and... it sucks.The protagonist seems a likeable enough person, but from the very first scenes she is surrounded by selfish figures from her past who keep trying to pull her into their own personal drama. The worst part is that none of these people are even interesting. The singular motivation behind all the characters is... they don't like the evil megacorp that apparently controls every industry on the island. Quelle surprise. Meanwhile the motivation of the gods is to hold you hostage as their oracle because apparently they are incapable of resolving their own disputes without someone to make decisions for them.Nobody has a compelling back story. You can't even hate them for constantly guilt-tripping you because all other aspects of their personalities are thoroughly milquetoast and inoffensive. It's so frustrating, because Dontnod used to be really good at writing characters with passion and nuance and complexity, something to make you want to care. But in this game, I didn't care about anyone. I'm not surprised the main character left the island 10 years ago, because it's boring as hell. So I just clicked through 5 hours of tedious dialog where nothing of consequence happened, and then I headed back home. It all felt so pointless.At least it is pretty to look at. The graphics are fantastic. And the overall concept of exposing the skeleton of a VN is an interesting one, although it has some rough edges in that the choice overview screen interrupts the flow of the dialog and ends up being a bit of a distraction from what little story is actually there. This game had so much potential. But lacking characters with realistic emotions and personalities, it misses the heart of the genre. Someone on the Steam forums compared it to Dreamfall: The Longest Journey. Superficially the settings are similar, but unfortunately this game is far, far behind the emotional impact of that series. Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge Don't Nod fan and my expectations were quite high.Having that in mind here is a quick spoiler-free summary of my opinion:::My spoiler-free opinion on the story:The first few chapters met and even exceeded my expectations. But about a third into the game I already knew where this was going. And it's a story that's already been told, only this time with a new facade. I was expecting more of a twist. The good thing: as far as I know, there are  endings and each of them has its own chapter dedicated to it.I think it's worth the full price only if you're planning to play it multiple times. Otherwise, wait for a discount!

_childDocuments_.review: There's so much I could share on why I recommend this game, but I don't want to give away too much.My advice on this - for your first play through, go with the choices that interest you, and take note of which proverbial doors open/close based on those decisions. That way,  you can do another play through and choose differently to see what you missed.I like how this game handles LGBTQ+ inclusion - characters with those identities exist, but it isn't a significant plot point. The most I've seen show up in two play throughs are references to name/pronoun changes, how one character has a flag in their room as a sign of allyship, or how one of the characters (I'm assuming AFAB) doesn't want to wear their hair long or wear dresses. Another thing that I like - the messaging around mental health. Your character experiences an emotionally significant event and that affects their ability to use the Augeral (the "choose your own adventure" mechanics). It's good to see a game where processing trauma is part of the storytelling process.

_childDocuments_.review: I think its hard to say if I recommend this game or not.  The animation and voice on the characters is amazing but the story itself didn't really manage to catch my attention, and besides the choices there is no gameplay at all, so maybe it is a good choice for visual novel fans.   There is also a weird glitch in wich the animated scenes will have their audio play much quicker then the video itself, so I hear all the audio at once and spend the rest of the scene with no sound while the video is catching up to what I already heard.  Unfortunately none of the characters really stood up to me, wich is pretty upsetting since usually dontnod's characters are very interesting and captivating, but this is just a personal opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess I should've known not to trust Don't Nod to give me a satisfying final chapter.
