_childDocuments_.review: First off, be aware that this game is more or less a traditional visual novel. If you're reading this because you have enjoyed Life is Strange or other similar Don't Nod games, this is different and may not be your taste. The game is gorgeous, well acted, and has a well told story, but interaction is limited to multiple choice selections while that story is read to you.This is  game about enacting change in a society that no longer values you. It tells that story through interactions with supernatural beings, but also through humans who are isolated, hurting, and who suffer real, permanent losses. There are some great characters here, and you will likely find yourself both allied with opposed to each of them at different points in the story. The ultimate ending that I got was hopeful, perhaps even bordering on naive. I don't know if that's true of all of the endings. I enjoyed my time with the game, but am disinclined to replay it to try other options.My major criticism of this game is mechanical. Story choices are presented as a flowchart. The player is both able, and expected, to plan their way through the conversation tree to reach a desired outcome. Occasionally some options are hidden temporarily, and sometimes it's difficult to untangle all the complexity of a path in advance, but most of the time you will pick a path at the start and then click your way through. In game, this represents the ability of the protagonist to see the future, which is central to the story being told here. But, meta game, it all feels a bit detached from the immediacy of what is happening. Also, both this mechanic and the large number of variations with the ending really encourage the player to restart chapters and to play through the game multiple times. Which makes the lack of a fast-forward feature particularly painful.Criticism aside, if you're looking for a smart, beautifully made visual novel, don't miss this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game.The voice acting is great. The music and the art are beautiful. If you haven't yet, watch the trailer, you'll see what i mean.The story is amazing. Often stories about resistance against oppressive structures don't feel very genuine. Or at the very least they often feel like they don't quite understand how those structures or  the resistance against them can function. This one does.Thank you to everyone involved in making this game, it is truly something special.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: It´s a really boring game plagued by bad design choices, tedious, unnecessary navigation, through an uninspired Story that never delivers. The presentation is as boring as the rest of the game, the music lame etc. This is far away from the quality of Pentiment or the emotional games Don´t Nod produced in the past. Save you money and buy a decent book instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Fun visual novel with a fairly heavy choice & consequence element.The last act did seem a bit restrictive in its direction, but that's probably just consequence coming to fruition.Also, a very quick playthrough - not generally complimented in gaming circles, but a great palate cleanser after, say, two full runs of an extremely long CRPG, and the "more hours of filler padding = better" take needs to die. Short games have their place, too, and I loved this one.Give it a whirl, it's a great story that actually almost entertains an anarchist perspective, which is almost unheard of.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: Truly don't know how to feel about this one. While I loved the concept of the story, the navigating of the many trees of possibility wasn't executed as well as I had hoped. As a visual novel? It's incredibly beautiful, well voice-acted, and the dialogue is well written. Worth a look for fans of that genre, hence my thumbs up review. I love DONTNOD.This kind of game where choices matter is so hard to develop when there are so many variants; players can get frustrated easily when they don't have a satisfying outcome. With Harmony, I felt like many of the choices I made did have meaningful effects, but in ways that didn't always feel satisfying, and the feedback and design on the UI/UX for the augary was frustrating. Some of the pathways presented also felt disingenuous to the game's premise . Overall, I felt really locked into pathways, and would often get annoyed with how little wiggle room there was.I feel like I immediately want to go through and see what other situations could have played out, which is definitely part of the fun of a game like this. However, I feel like I want to go look it up rather than actually play through the game again, which is disappointing. Also... I genuinely would love to get data shown to me on what other players have experienced! I want to know how rare my ending choice was, and see if I have a similar experience to others, or if I had a more unique take on the choices. That feedback to players in this kind of game feels quite important to me, and it's just missing as far as I can see. as a visual novel, the art is gorgeous and the premise and setting was great, but marred with confusion overall. This mashup of novel and choice-trees was just overwhelming.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: People slept a bit too hard on this game which is a shame, because while it doesn't completely stick the landing, Harmony: The Fall of Reverie boasts some really cool ideas and some genuinely thought-provoking questions that you can never walk out of with a straight answer. The art direction, voice performances, and Lena Raine's score really impress too, and it's hard not to find its designs inspired, its story entrancing, and its adventure one to remember. The recent patch fixed some QOL issues I had too, so if you haven't played it now, give it a chance before the year ends.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a bad way to ruin a story! On the surface it looks like this VN has a lot of choice driven story moments, but in reality they are connected in such a way that you hardly have any wiggle-room. The story tree seems like an awesome idea, at first, but it constantly takes you out of the story to focus on your next "choice". I find the lack of agency in this VN frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: As I wrote this review, I realized the extent of my dislike of the last act of the game, so here's that paragraph at the startPlot spoilers, obviously: Honestly I'm not sure the extent to which the last act ruins the first 4 for me. I was deeply engrossed before the last act and I was really enjoying my time with the game despite the cons below, but the plot really really REALLY did not stick the landing in the last act.Does that ruin the game for me? Not as much as you might think. I think I would still recommend the game for the first four acts because they are well written and I really enjoyed the augural mechanics of having detailed hints of the future, but having to  correctly navigate my way there while avoiding undesired inevitable outcomes and still making choices I wanted to make.The rest of the review:Pros:- excellent music and voice acting, specifically the aspirations all have fun and unique voice acting- i really enjoyed the aspiration's characterizations, i found them all interesting - a unique storytelling format that is interesting and a story that is short enough that it doesn't get boring by the end- a story which reflects current events and current realities. it was interesting to see how the events of the last few years are directly reflected in the game Cons:- as many have mentioned, the story post act 3 is well, really unrealistic. It kinda ruins the great realistic narrative that was carried through the earlier acts, only to completely vanish by the last act. Even the characters acknowledge - the augural mechanic inherently cuts up scenes and forces the writers to write them to flow well no matter what order they're played in, which is obviously an impossible task- choices mean a lot less when you can see in the augural that it doesn't matter, which in a way is a strength (interesting storytelling arises from polly having the augural) and a con (a bunch of choices really are just meaningless)- as mentioned in other reviews, there are plot points that feel like they get dropped, though this may be because they end up being locked behind other outcomes that you miss. Since there's no easy way to replay the game, the end result is that some plot points are left unresolved, || why was bond involved with truth's destruction? what happened with all that? || Patchable cons:- there not being a skip button, cmon...My recommendation: play through the game once, get very immersed in the augural at the beginnings of each chapter, attempt to navigate to your desired outcomes, but don't restart if you don't get what you want.Do I recommend it? On sale and if you like interesting storytelling mechanics? Go for it, the first four acts are great. Full price, definitely not since the game is short and the ending is weak, it's hard to justify the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Presentation focused VN. Not doing too much new with the story beats but the engaging characters, art, and music make up for it. Biggest complaint is there was no option to speed past or skip text you've read before. I can understand that the first time through, as a penalty for choosing to restart a chapter but it got very old on replay.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: The game's "inaugural system", a logic map that displays all possible branching paths and how to get there, is one of the worst designed mechanics I've seen in a narrative focused game. The story literally plays out like this: You see Node A, B, and C, each with an ambiguous description on what they are. You click through node A, and a 1-2 minute sequence plays, crafted of coursed with top-notch art/music. By the end of it, you're pushed back to this logic map, needing to pick which of the nodes you'd like to go next. You then choose node B, only to find that it occurs at a completely different time/place/with different characters than the prior sequence. This is so immersion breaking that you almost feel like watching a puppet show, with each canned scenes represented by one of these nodes. Imagine playing a visual novel, and instead of the story progressing naturally, you have to exit out to the menu every 2 minutes to choose which scene plays next. By displaying the exact "outcome" of each route at the very START of chapters & number of points needed to get there, the game 1. Spoils any surprise completely; 2. At each step of the way, encourage the player to not pick according to their heart, but how many points an option gets, and whether it has any short-term bad endings to it (yes, you can infer that through this map, where some paths are comically shorter than others). Instead of being the main character and saving two realms, I ended up feeling like I'm just min-maxing some janky puzzle game. I'm a big fan of the developer and adored many of their past work. But this new venture, as novel as it might look, I absolutely cannot recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony is a weird game for me. It one of those rare games that manages to let you experience its theme rather than spectate it. A a prescient character, you'll be going through the story using a partially revealed flowchart of actions and consequences. This does disconnect you with the plot and the characters, which is maybe one of the worst part of the game. However, it's how you get to "feel" what prescience would be: you can be callous in a scene,  because you know it will work out in the next one; you "game" your interactions to reach specific points in the timeline to reach a distant future you can only glimpse, short term consequences be damned. If you saw or read Dune, .It's not the best narrative game I played, but it's an interesting one !
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is a prime example of misplaced priorities — the animated cutscenes, voice acting, and the game's overall presentation are all well done, but the actual story is unengaging and boring. The characters, aside from the Aspirations, are also bland and superfluous. The Aspirations are an interesting concept and are fun to interact with, but for most of the game you will be talking to the boring human characters instead. I feel like the intricate mythology and the esoteric concepts that the game introduces are wasted on the subpar story. Perhaps it gets better in acts 3 and 4, but I simply don't have the patience to keep on drudging through this dull tale.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a huge fan of DONTNOD. Sadly this game doesn't belong in their catalog. You can actually just keep clicking at random and get through the entire game. And the choices don't lead you anywhere different. Each chapter ends all the same no matter what. And its really just a lot of reading. The "game play" is very much nonexistent. If you're expecting anything like their other games, you will be sadly disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a big fan of Don’t Nod games, they give me both an escapism to different realities as well as allow me to experience social situations and relationships that I am unable to in reality.With Harmony: Fall of Reverie there is another layer on top of all this: the ability to partially oversee the consequences and choices leading from my actions. As someone on the spectrum, guessing, envisioning and ever trying to dial into the intent and intricate social nuances of people is something I normally spend a lot of time and energy on. Being able to have this super power of insight feel fantastic.Yet it is by no means an omniscient and absolute precognitive gift. You might be able to see parts of the possible futures, but there will always be unforeseen events, action by others and consequences of your own previous actions that force you into situations. It’s this balance between control and being subjected to the consequences actions of both yourself and others that makes for interesting mechanics.This balancing game is also found in choices between Reverie and Brittle (our reality). Choices you make that affect the one might not line up with what you want in the other, and vise versa. A person or aspiration you like might have views or designs that you don’t want to follow and those that you like less might come up with tempting or reasonably sounding options. In this way you are constantly juggling between the outcomes you’d like, the people/aspirations your want to endorse and the collection of the egregor resource which will ultimately determine your stories flow and end results.For me, those end results came kind of unexpected and did not align with what I was aiming for. Perhaps I divided my attention across too many aspirations, maybe I should have made more strategic than moral choices. Either way, I ended up with only óne of the aspirations being able to help me which in turn meant that all the problems had only a single solution which detracted greatly from my final choices. Never the less, it is another testament of how impactful the consequences of your actions are.The flow of the story feels very dynamic, as this is by far the most core visual novel/choose your own adventure style game they have done. Some choices directly shape the narrative, others come back far later. It is also quite decently balanced in action. There are many moments of distress, fear and action but these are countered by slower moments to talk or think things through. It is however, quite heavy and front loaded with concepts, mechanics and metaphysical ideas to wrap your head around.The game, as is with standard with Don’t Nod, touches on many difficult subjects. Repression, consumerism, mega corporation corruption and moral consequences are core to the story. But many personal problems that could be triggering are presented as well. Depression, running away from problems, abandonment, loss of loved ones and parental issues are among these.Overall, I greatly enjoyed the story and game. The mechanics are engaging, fun and feel impactful, the story is once again brilliantly written. The aspirations are a joy to interact with, the people in Brittle feel maybe a bit less vibrant than usual, but this makes up with them feeling more real. The cast is diverse with many natural representations (the non-binary neutrality of the aspiration of truth is fantastic<3), as you can expect from Don’t Nod. The voice acting was wonderful and suffused the characters with life. And, of course, the bright and vivid art style makes the worlds come to life.Thank you for another wonderful experience that I will no doubt try again to try out the many other ways to resolve the story!
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a CS nerd so I loved the unique choice making aspect of being able to look across the tree of choices. I would say that this game has intense themes around grief, but I think it is done rather tastefully as someone who's lost a close friend. I will say the game Pre and Post act 3 is very different. This game relies heavily on the knowledge of how aspirations egregore works to get the desired end you want, but it can also be interesting to see how your natural choices effect the aspirations since they reflect humanity's choices in game. I liked the artistic take on the story overall. Thought it was a beautiful visual novel and I somewhat hope for a another game to expand the lore that wasn't really touched on by the end, but I doubt that will happen.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: At first, I wasn't convinced by Harmony, mainly due to the art style that I don't really like, but the demo sold me on the game! Don't Nod definitely delivered a great, engaging, and compelling story with multiple branches that I can't wait to see what outcomes will they bring. A must-play for fans of interactive storytelling and previous works of the studio!
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a Don't Nod game distilled down to the fundamentals:- a story- your choices- your consequencesThere are no point and click elements. And no 3rd person gameplay elements.So what is it: A visual novel. But one that is well done and full of colorful and memorable characters.You play as Polly, the new oracle. And as an oracle, you can see into the future. You see all the paths of a chapter, all the choices you can make. Some will have clear impacts, some don't.Navigate the future are your own risk, as loss is part of the story being told.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I love choices matter games, but the time I spent on this one was more stressful than it was intriguing. I found myself excited to get to a certain point, only to realize I chose a node chapters ago that locked the progression I wanted. The concept of the augural is great, execution not so much.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting premise both in plot and in gameplay. It's mostly a visual novel but you do get branching trees to decide what to do next and can even see vague details about what those branching paths might lead to, so sometimes it's wise to stop and calculate what you might need to do to reach a final goal you want rather than only thinking about what the next step is. The voice acting is excellent, the art is very nice as well. The actual plot is very metaphysical and I was turned off by it initially but it grew on me over time. I think there may have wanted to be a bit more time warming the player up, and at the mid point there's a crisis that happens that also went on for too long without much gameplay input besides clicking "next scene". Otherwise, if you don't mind a visual novel experience it's very good.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: the dialogue is amazing, and so believable.the characters really feel so alive and you find yourself getting attached and growing wary of them so naturally. you have to put aside your own personal gripes against figures like Chaos and Ursula and do what's ultimately right to see the most -ous side of the game.I don't understand why the reviews are so mixed, nor why the game's so... underrated. it deserves so much more and so much better. Polly and Yana's relationship is so mature and well handled. so is Polly and Nora's. there's this air of grace surrounding DontNod's handling of such complicated and messy topics, especially for an exclusively male writing team.Part of me will always wonder how the writing would end up more balanced in DontNod games if women were lead writers, but until that day, this is still a massive, colossal step up from Life Is Strange's characterisations and writing.This game has attracted a lot of trolls and bad actors due to its representation of women, queer women, transgender and non-binary people, plural systems (such as Bond), and concepts that transcend gender stereotypes (Chaos, Truth). If you want a wonderfully queer story that makes you , then give this game a chance. The Augural is also an amazing puzzle to think through to get the outcomes "you want" per chapter, but they're not always what you .
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting but ultimately disappointing one.The production values are mostly great, the voice acting is all brilliant and I love a bit of diversity. However, ambition meets reality and the game kind of falls apart after Act 3. But it wasn't great getting there, either.As a visual novel, the game is only visual in certain ways. It does a lot of telling you what happens instead of showing. For example, the major climax point in Act 3 happens offscreen while you're playing silly games with the godlike characters in another world. But this kind of thing happens all the time, and the game does an absolutely abysmal job of describing anything to you.It's just constantly telling me stuff.Oh hey we went into some old ruins. Why can't I see them (other than some vague cave background mocked up by an artist in a couple of hours)? An underground illicit newspaper printing facility? Yeah, game, I wanted to see that place too.And. This. Keeps. Happening.I was already lukewarm on the game up to Act 3, and then it just becomes a torrent of self-pitying and incoherent nonsense in Act 4. Characters become one-dimensional, the plot grinds to a halt, the egregore mcguffin mechanic kind of just takes on a mind of its own and paths seem to lock themselves arbitrarily.I gave up playing. The post-Act 3 portion of this game turned out to be a disaster.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: It is very good! You'll enjoy the branching story and VA! And its unique spin on the Visual Novel genre makes it even more interesting to play and actually plan a route even in your first play through.Also the only Visual Novel that I am aware of that has such pretty 3D backgrounds!What got me hooked are the themes, stories and problems of these characters. From the anarchist culture that is dealing with a seemingly huge mega corporation, queer characters, the loss of loved ones, these characters feel human and genuine to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately its overall not a fun game.I was intrigued by the Demo and decided to give it a shot. I love games where you can make choices and those choices matter. However i think the choices have to make sense too. Sometimes choices you make in the game in really small details come back and really limit a path that you would have wanted to take and in a real world shouldnt be that limiting. There's still the big chance that im just legit not playing the game 'right' and not fully using all the mechanics but meh. The story still seems intriguing and the mystery is still something that im interested in but for the meantime i'm gonna return this and wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: It's the first game I bought on day one and my first visual novel. I loved it. Definitely will have couple more playthroughs to understand the narrative more fully. Felt like the story's too complex to be flashed out properly in the scale of the game, but it was amazing journey nonetheless. Especially thanks to artstyle, music and voice acting. ε>

_childDocuments_.review: Great story with plenty of replayability options, but could have a better intro as the first few minutes are abit confusing. I've done 2 playthroughs at the time of writing this review. Each playthrough takes about 10 hours or so.Don't expect any gameplay as their Life is Strange series. In this game you watch a story and make choices that affects it, and you can "plan ahead" as you'll get hints to what your choices could do later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Simple and amazing game, I love this style of game where you read the story and interact with events. The story is good, related to human feelings and social interactions, and makes you think about how we think about our attitudes and how we interact with others. It's a good game for your social maturity, both to develop and to exercise.---------------------------------------------In "about this game" it says that Harmony has the power of clairvoyance, but it's actually premonition. In clairvoyance the events have already occurred, in premonition not yet.For example, in a test where the person asks you to guess a single card that you have hidden in your hand, the card is already chosen, you just need to know what it is, that's clairvoyance. If in the test the person asks you to say which card will be that hasn't even been chosen yet, that's premonition.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: GOOD: I absolutely adore the Augural mechanic of the game! Not only does it allow you to make your choices, but it also makes it easy to predict outcomes of your choices and plan routes, even if its your first run through the game. One issue I have with a lot of visual novels is that its hard to remember previous choices and where they led, so when you replay the game you make mistakes or have to look up specific pathways to the story routes you want, but the Augural almost completely removes this issue. The voice acting in this game is absolutely amazing and I highly recommend taking the time to listen to it rather than just speed reading. It will definitely take more time than just going through it (took me 10 hours for my first run through), but i think it helps immerse yourself in the story.The graphics, especially the few animated scenes, are gorgeous! You can tell they put a lot of time into making the game look visually stunning, sound amazing (both VA and music-wise), and had interesting mechanics.BAD: There are a few timeline inconsistencies though that's probably due to the huge amount of choices you can make, but overall doesn't affect the plot at large. Also there is no ability to go back to previous save files since the game automatically saves after you finish a node. The auto save feature is nice, except it means that if you want to try a different path you have to completely replay the game up to that point on a different save file. Which i see why they did it (to encourage full replays rather than partial ones), but still could be annoying to some players.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I would highly recommend this game. Beautiful graphics and art are interwoven with a complex plot shaped through a variety of decision options. The element of clairvoyance introduced allows countless replays of situations impacting divergent consequences later in the game, with seemingly endless possibilities to explore in the moment (definitely replayable). Each scene is sensory rich, filled with vibrant colours and continuous audio allowing you to get truly lost in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are nice especially the characters.  There is some beautiful animated sequences but unfortunately not enough. The backgrounds mostly felt a bit static.  The story was interesting but seems a bit derivative of the longest journey/dream-fall (or maybe both games are getting inspiration from a common source.) I felt sometimes there wasn't really enough information behind particular story choices though; like what does it mean to pick this plan over this plan since you haven't really explained what either plan is. So a lot of the time it felt a bit 50/50 rather than making a conscious decision. Maybe this is by design. The descriptions on the story nodes don't help either, they are always pretty vague.My biggest issue with the game is the UIOne minor gripe is that you have to play the whole game with a drop down at the top labeled "controls" Not sure why this had to be on screen at all times.However by far the main issue with the UI relates to the story navigation mechanic which is basically the only game-play. Maybe it was just me but several times I would plan my path through the nodes of the story only to find out to my surprise that I couldn't proceed in the direction I wanted, by playing some particular node it locked my out of another or by playing some node it forced me to play another which then locked me out of another. I just found it confusing at times.Overall I found it a bit more frustrating then relaxing.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Choose Your Own Path in the way that the Star Wars hotel did it...One of the few games I regret buying. Harmony is a visual novel that let's you 'see into the future' to shape the story and the outcomes that you like. However, the abundance of choices and diverting paths are more often than not a lie. This game will HARDLOCK you at EVERY TURN. For my first playthrough, I decided I was going to work towards a specific outcome, but no matter how much I sided with one person or followed their advice, I still got locked out of the scenes and outcomes that I wanted just because I did something three chapters ago. Also, this game does NOT come with a SKIP BUTTON, which is a crime against visual novels that are specifically designed to make you replay them over and over to get different outcomes. I restarted certain chapters so many times, because I unexpectedly got locked out of the path I wanted only to spend 15 minutes manually clicking through dialogue. It's a disservice to the voice acting.There are some beautiful aspects to the game like the voice acting and the cut scenes (the regular sprites are hit or miss), and the world is interesting and well thought out, but it's too much of a slog to really enjoy and I can't see myself every replaying it without a mod or something that allows skipping.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: Continuing their long-lasting tradition since , Don’t Nod is back again with another gripping narrative title based on player’s choices and consequences. In this visual novel you play as Polly, a girl returning home to the island of Atina after being away for a very long time. Here she finds out that her mother has mysteriously gone missing. Polly tries to find clues about what happened by getting in touch with her old friends, and discovers that her hometown has changed over the years because of an evil corporation called MK who aims to control everything.Thanks to her mother’s necklace, Polly becomes Harmony and is teleported into the world of Reverie; a dreamlike world populated by spiritual beings called Aspirations, who represent different human emotions such as Bliss, Truth, Power, Bond etc. and tell Polly that she is the only one who can save the world. This is of course a typical premise you have probably seen many times, but the interesting thing is that these Aspirations will give you access to the Augural, a branched tree from which you can see the future and view potential consequences based on the different choices you make. Sadly, this is also the only “interactive” game mechanic present. The game is essentially a visual novel in which you take multiple choices, but thanks to the Augural, you can now see the possible outcomes before making any decision. Each Aspiration will approve their preferred choice, which also helps to define Polly’s characterization. Making a choice approved by one of the Aspirations will grant you a token, which you can use later on to unlock a new specific choice that otherwise would have been blocked. This means that you must see in advance the other choices you can make, how many tokens they cost and from which Aspiration you should get them. This also means that you are not really free to make any choice you want, but you must try to plan your path in advance.While the Augural mechanic is certainly fascinating, nobody loves to have the consequences of their actions spoiled by knowing about them in advance. I mean, part of the beauty of a game based on the player’s choices is precisely not knowing what is going to happen. I understand that this mechanic is linked via the narrative to Harmony’s fate, but on the other side it takes away a few of the story’s surprises. It also removes the freedom of making whatever choice you feel at the moment, only because you haven’t collected enough tokens from a specific Aspiration. Unfortunately, the only interesting gameplay mechanic is also the weakest point of the game for how it’s been wrongly designed, in my opinion.The writing is great for the most part, with uniquely designed characters and mature dialogues, though sometimes it can be very inconsistent, as it often gets lost in very long explanations and even gets unnecessarily political, as in  before. The story is a great allegory of modern times and you understand it soon enough, but the writing keeps pushing the same political themes over and over again like they aren’t already clear, which partially ruins the story. Animations look good enough and I love the vibrant and colorful art style. There are some pretty cutscenes too, but they are often reserved for the more important moments. Characters are fully voiced and they sound really great. The music is also good and changes according to the different characters’ emotions and situations. Unfortunately, visual assets are often re-used through the entire game. You will see all the characters with the same clothes and even the same poses, which is not good for a visual novel that already feels too static and passive due to the lack of interactivity (other than the Augural system).I love Don’t Nod for what it has achieved in the past with games like ,  or  and Harmony certainly shows a lot of passion despite being more like a niche project. While its colorful universe is populated by well-voiced characters with distinct personalities, the story never grows in complexity and it’s more like a tale about relationships and an allegory of modern times. The Augural mechanic is interesting on paper, but the execution clearly shows some design problems. Still worth a try if you enjoy visual novels that lack interactivity but somehow compensate with beautiful art style and lot of choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I was disappointed with this game. First of all, parts of it are not fully voiced, which makes it feel more like a straight up visual novel. It's more clicking through dialogue than I expected, and there's no walking around. _childDocuments_.review: This might be one of the worst games I have ever played as far as story is concerned.  Like yea, I don’t doubt there are overall worse games…but the writing in both dialogue and overall narrative is so monumentally bad in this game I was at times speechless as I went through this travesty of a narrative.  It feels like the writing team literally never read a novel in their lives or if they did they only read Virginia Woolf’s “The Waves.”  I want to be clear “The Waves” is a masterpiece, this game is like that without the writing skill of Virginia Woolf .  Maybe I wouldn’t care so much, but as far as visual novels go the production values here are mindblowing.  The soundtrack is outstanding, although it is only like a 10 hour game, but still the soundtrack through those 10 hours borders on perfect.  It attempts to convey the themes and the emotions these characters are feeling, which the writing doesn’t even come close to even hinting at.  It’s also a fully voice acted game and the actors are exceedingly skilled, but when you work with trash there is only so much the voice actors can do, despite the dialogue bordering on nonsensical characters like Nora are still able to convey the tragedy of their life, while Poly’s conveys how constantly regretful she is.  The game is also gorgeous.  From environment backgrounds to character designs.  Everything pops and conveys the beauty of this world, kind of reminds me of the art direction in Hades.  The character designs especially for the Gods perfectly exemplifies each God’s specific emotion.   For a visual novel it is also striking because characters and backgrounds also have movement to them in these scenes which few visual novels have.The actual gameplay is handled rather poorly, but with a better narrative and writing would probably have been ok.  The problem is this is a visual novel, the only gameplay is picking choices.  This game attempted to do a bit more and your character gets to see the entire board of choices and where decisions can lead.  However, in practice this is a disaster.  Choices become meaningless because in game you don’t have enough narrative idea of why you should select a lot of these choices because not enough information is given to understand them.  Meanwhile, looking at the decision tree board isn’t helpful either because it is exceedingly easy to accidently lock yourself out of decisions without even meaning to, because you will be making choices that have an affect later on in the board…but the board won’t tell you want choices are necessary to get to that point on the board.   This game design simply does not work.  This game should have taken a hint from all those Zero Escape games where you are able to jump around to any point on the board at anytime to go down a different path if you want to.  This game foolishly doesn’t allow you to do that without replaying an entire chapter which you are not realistically going to do. The main issue though is the horrifically bad writing.  I got to say I’m literally baffled at what the story these people were trying to tell is.  So I guess these developers hate Capitalism…like a lot…weird you charge $25 for your game when you hate Capitalism so much, by this games logic it 100% should be free.  Your corporation has oppressed me by charging me money for this game!  Which is actual dialogue the characters in this game would say if they lived in our world.  It’s looney tunes level of crazy.  The entire plot of this game revolves around a corporation called MK and the main character and her friends/family that wish to abolish it.  There are a million ways you could tell a narrative about the oppressive nature of capitalistic systems…and sure this is I guess one of them…but it’s like the worst and most incompetent way.  For instance why not make a straw man argument where your communist characters are all great people that go out of their way to help people and the corporation is literally oppressing these people and making things worse in this island nation.  It’s a fictional story you could do that…the writing of this game leads me to think that’s what you thought you were doing.  I would instead say you made like a Tin man argument.  Instead of building up a faulty premise for you to knock over, you created a faulty premise which is literally stronger than your arguments against that system.There is almost nothing about this MK company that comes across as problematic.  The game starts and you tell the player that prior to MK’s rise this island nation was pretty much a garbage place where the water was literally polluted and people had to rely on Ursula’s commune for food and shelter because there were like no public services.  Then when MK comes to power they go about closing the beaches to clean up the polluted water (which they didn’t cause) and your characters scream that they are oppressing them?  You then talk about how MK went around buying up slums…but paying people for those slums so they could fix up the architectural integrity of the old city…and creating parks and other public work projects.  When it’s revealed they are trying to dig up the ancient civilizations artifacts to commune with the gods…the characters flip out because MK won’t allow people access to archeological dig sites?  What a shock that an archeological dig wouldn’t want random people who are untrained going into these dig sites…and sure they are doing this to find these artefacts but you then say their plans are to put a lot of this stuff in a museum for the public?  Seriously whatttttttttt are you doing.  Eventually, you say they kidnapped people and were using them…but honestly I don’t trust the characters telling me these things because those same characters are describing all the above acts as horrific oppression.  All these main characters seem detached from reality.Nothing is shown in this game.  You could have had like characters find MK holding people against their will.  You could have had interactions between your character and some high ups at MK that shows their motives are evil or their cruelty.  You could have shown them shooting people or taking some horrific action…but you didn’t.  Instead for the majority of the game you have delusional characters talking about how MK giving people jobs and employing 50% of this island nation as “oppression.”  Then instead of having your characters have clear conversations with each other you are constantly forcing the player to go to the “choice board” and picking lines of dialogue and choices there instead of just having a constant conversation with characters with dialogue choices.  The end result is I honestly barely know any of these characters as instead of talking to them I’m picking choices that I have no idea how they relate to what is going on in the story.   The entire first half of the game you are searching for your mother and I didn’t even realize this for quite a while because you spend more time talking to Gods about their problems then what is even happening in the world.   This needed to be like a 30hr game with a ludicrous amount of more dialogue and character interaction and an actual villain instead of the villain being the overall oppression of capitalistic systems on society.  Why didn’t you just make a God called “Capitalism” and have them embody that entire societal system which your character could actually talk to and interact with?!?  You literally made a game where Gods represent different aspects of Humanity and you couldn’t just have done that?  This game isn’t even half baked, it’s completely uncooked.  Go play something like Disco Elysium or Teenage Excolonist instead, both games which make pretty clear what the problems of capitalistic systems are but in compelling narratives  where characters actually can talk to each other instead of just shouting “CAPITALISM IS OPPRESSING US.”  This game comes across as a parody of an anticapitalism game.

_childDocuments_.review: 3/5It's not ... bad. I just feel it could've been better.The Pros:- everyone is hot and everyone is queer- I really love the art- decent story- kept me hooked so that I played it for 5 hours straight to finish- I like personifications of abstract concepts, and these are well doneThe Cons:- The loading screens/scene transitions. Oh my god. I feel like half my playtime was just waiting to do the next click.- The game interface. I understand what the developers were aiming for with seeing "all" paths, but it's not well made. I still don't really know where I went wrong for a few decisions where I wanted a very specific outcome, and it ended up being blocked. Being able to see the one you want to click but not having the option is incredibly frustrating.- Did I mention the loading screens- On one hand, it feels like there were so so many options that I missed and would like to explore, but on the other, I get the feeling that the story would be so linear that replaying it would be a pain. Also because of the loading screens.- I didn't really feel like my choices made that much of a difference. But maybe they did and I do need to replay? I will probably go and read about different endings to form an opinion on that and, if necessary, update this review.Overall, it's an okay game. I enjoyed playing. I will likely not replay.

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is imo really subpar despite being so important for a VN like game like this. I didn't expect such a failure from DONTNOD tbh.I lasted exactly 30min and then deinstalled the game. The characters are super flat and I couldn't relate even with the main character. Reverie and Harmony's mother couldn't be more irrelevant to me.Why didn't they let us play some time in the past first to build a bond with the main char, the mother and world etc. To get to know these people and stuff, y'know? And THEN the mother dissapears and you find the amulet etc. Instead, everything is introduced in like 3 slides and 5 textboxes and instead of discovering the people, world and lore yourself, it just gets shoved in your face.This is the case even with the underlying mechanics. Why didn't they let the player make choices through dialogue or interacting with the game world instead of directly making them in a bland decision tree.Yes, her mother is gone and there is this strange world and you are the only one who can save her, bla bla. And what do I care? I have no connection to the characters at all, know literally nothing about them and thus haven't exactly zero motivation to help or talk to them.Also, you have the constant feeling that you are missing some information. Right at the first decision concerning Nora and MK, for example, the dialogue implies that this company is somehow "evil". But it is neither said why nor does the codex entry give any clues. When I then selected "be supportive" others characters and harmony herself saying things like "you're just avoiding a confrontation, that will be nora's downfall, this is not right" etc., although there is no evidence of this and I can't see why this company should be an issue at all.Additionally I find the menus and navigation pretty clunky and unintuitive, too.Visuals are nice. Voice acting and music is OK I guess but that's it.Definitely a refund for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Harmony is a game where a They/Them PoC polycule does BLM against Google or something.You will face the moral concerns of Twitter users in 2016 such as "can revolution against capitalism be peaceful"There is a unique system of visualizing the "choices matter" story tree in great detail such that you will spend a 10:1 ratio of your time in the menu plotting out your course so that you can make a decision that provides 1 line of dialogue and then you go straight back to the menu. The game bombards you with tutorial screens to explain every tiny and very obvious concept, making the already sluggish experience a complete slog in the opening segments. Despite the painstaking lengths they go to explain everything and how obvious it all seems - I still found myself messing up. Did they really need "inevitable" AND locking/unlocking? I feel like they could have made use of just unlocking and made everything more clear. There were times I had made big decisions to go down one path and despite doing everything in my power to keep on it I seem to have messed something up that I didn't really understand and schizophrenically switched paths resulting in my being dissatisfied with everything that happened.There are several times I felt that I would like to go back and make some changes, but the game doesn't really accommodate this. You can entirely start a chapter over if you like... so perhaps that is the accommodation. Otherwise it seems to expect you to simply push forward and accept the consequences of whatever choice you made. I'm torn on how I feel about this as I am the type to overthink and try to perfect things as I go vs. simply experiencing organically. Perhaps I should play through one time organically and then plot the perfect path the second playthrough. I am just not really seeing myself playing this a second time.I think it's interesting that they made it a plot point that you can "see the future" which reflects your gameplay ability to observe and interact with the story tree... however, it never really FEELS like that is true in the story. They simply SAY that it's true... it never really manifests in any other way. The character is consistently surprised by events and at no point do they behave as if they had some sense of what was coming up. It would be like if in Undertale a character simply said "Saving is like the ability to control time" and just left it at that without ever addressing the assertion in any meaningful way. Having an advisory counsel of "Gods" that represent concepts in our relationships with one another is a cool like "Pillars of Eternity" feeling thing - but every character and interaction is sort of lame. It feels very hard to care about these characters, this world, this story.Cool animations and art style, great execution thereCharacter design and writing not so greatNovel gameplay mechanic, totally understand the thinking behind it - but not actually fun in execution.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is all right. Has quite a slow start but I'd say I got hooked around two hours into the game. _childDocuments_.review: Beautiful. I almost left a review too early and that would have been a mistake. It takes a minute for the story to develop but it becomes quite the ride and the characters develop well with time. I would recommend that people not leave a review until after Ursula has been in the picture for a few chapters. This game is pretty, it's deep, its relevant, its existential and expansive. _childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely amazing visual novel. The story is very interesting, I love how the mechanics are built into the the world is very cool and it's fun to see medium term results of the choices I make. There are 3 results of this game, with one of them having 6 different flavours, making total of 8 endings. Even when I say the flavours I might be understating the difference, as the story steps to get to them are quite different.My only real gripe with the game is the music. It is good overall, but if you go afk and can still hear it, it can be a bit overbearing.However the rest of the audio is spectacular, the ambience is great and voice acting as well as character design and animation are amazing making you fall in love with characters (Omar and Chaos were stands out for me, but all the characters are at least very good). I have completed the game four times in the last month and I haven't skipped any of the dialogue and VO, even the fixed scenes you see every time.In all fairness I do have to admit that after playing the game the four times, you do find a couple of places where dialog flows a bit oddly with some choices, where they used just one node rather than having two, but it doesn't happen often. That said I definitely plan to play st least 4 more times to get the rest of the endings and then probably some more to see how some of the bigger choices interact with each other.If you like visual novels, this game is a no brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: What an  game. Despite its queerness and choiceyness, not really what I would have expected from DON'T NOD. _childDocuments_.review: is an absolutely beautiful and extremely imaginative visual novel adventure game from DON'T NOD, the studio behind instant story-driven classics such as Life is Strange.✅ Loads of potential choices & branching paths✅ A mesmerizing & unique art style✅ Superb voice acting and incredible sound design✅ An emotional, sophisticated narrative⛔️ Very Minor stutters when transitioning between scenes⛔️ Loading screens sometimes pop up every few lines, taking away the immersionThe game takes place in the near future and has you playing as Polly who visits her hometown to find out it has changed drastically and that her mother is missing. Soon after she gets transported into a different realm called Reverie, where she is called Harmony. The game's story where you'll be controlling Polly/Harmony is exceptionally written and feels real and very mature. The narrative succeeds in connecting the player with the characters for a truly rich experience.The first thing in this game that will most likely catch your eye first is the incredible art style. With an opening cutscene that looks like a moving painting and is accompanied by some beautiful music, the game let's you know you are in for a ride. It's all very colorful and during every scene transition you'll just be itching to see what the next screen or character you meet is going to look like. Every screen has it's own matching sound design so it is highly recommended to play with good headphones to get the full experience. The game has a very talented voice cast and every character you meet has a defining voice to match.Mostly built as a visual novel, the game's branching path system is where it truly excels. Also called the Augural, the choices screen is where you'll be doing the majority of the actual gameplay, thinking and deciding which choice is the best for the given characters, or the situations they are in. Many of the choices will obviously lead to different outcomes, so the replay value is very high, which is very much helped by a "restart chapter" button on the main menu. The game also has the codex, which is a journal of sorts where you'll be able to keep track of the places you visited, the characters you met, and all their defining qualities. You can also visit the Augural to check previous story entries and read previous chapters and conversations.🔹 This review was completed on a Desktop PC. The specs for this unit are as followed.🔹 CPU: Intel I5-12600KF🔹 RAM: 32GB DDR4🔹 Graphics Card: GigaByte GeForce RTX 3070tiA few minor stutters when environments and scenes are loading up don't harm the game's visual spectacle in the slightest. is an incredible narrative adventure with meaningful choices that I heartily recommend for any fans of previous works of DON'T NOD, or to anyone who just wants a rich, unique experience that is harder to find in today's triple-A video game market.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review: I hardly ever play VNs, but I was intrigued to see Dontnod made one. I love all of their work, and with the set-up they gave, I seriously had to try this. There's only a few good VN type games I can recall that emphasize the aspects of branching choices or themes of time. Time travel, seeing into the future, etc, this kind of stuff is practically made for the visual novel genre. Dontnod has once again thoroughly surprised me. Seeking a new genre yet seeing its familiar groundwork was very natural for them. Their experience with storytelling (especially involving time and human connection) has created another intriguing adventure. This game features a lot of branches and choices. It may seem overwhelming at first, and the game can get pretty slow at points. Despite that, seeing things to the end was satisfying. This VN really gives a lot of control to the player and shows reasons for outcomes that actually make sense. Everything really does feel reflected based on the player and their own beliefs. Definitely play this blind and find the path that speaks to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

_childDocuments_.review:
In the very near future... When Polly returns home after a few years abroad to look for her missing mother, she quickly realizes that her hometown has drastically changed. A megacorporation named MK is using its power to control the population, and her community is in danger. 

She soon discovers that she has a gift of clairvoyance that connects her to Reverie, the realm of the Aspirations of Humanity: Glory, Bliss, Power, Chaos, Bond, and Truth. In this world, Polly becomes Harmony, a goddess who has the power to choose the Aspiration that will ultimately rule over Reverie and restore the delicate balance between the deities' world and ours. 
 
The fate of humanity is at stake. To which destiny do you aspire?
_childDocuments_.name: Harmony: The Fall of Reverie

name: Double Dragon Gaiden: Rise Of The Dragons
detailed_description: DISCORD
about_the_game: Prepare to throw down the Double Dragon way in this fresh addition to the iconic beat ‘em up franchise. It’s the year 199X, and nuclear war has devastated New York City leaving its citizens to fight for survival as riots and crime engulf the streets. The city has been overtaken by criminal gangs who terrorize its ruins as they fight for total dominance. Unwilling to endure these conditions any longer, young Billy and Jimmy Lee take it upon themselves to drive the gangs out of their city. Explore the early beginnings of the young Double Dragon brothers as they take on both new and familiar enemies in this alternate story. In this fresh roguelite take, every playthrough is a brand new chance at new action. Featuring a unique and dynamic level structure, the difficulty of the missions you take on will change depending on the order you have selected them. Tag in and out as the classic duo Billy and Jimmy, switch it up with Marian and Uncle Matin, or experiment with 12 additional unlockable characters, each with their own special moves and unique playstyles. With 2-player online and local co-op, the action quadruples as you and a friend clean up the mean streets. TAG TEAM ACTION – Choose two fighters and seamlessly switch between them, giving you a multitude of strategies for devastating combos, defensive and offensive moves. BEAT ‘EM UP WITH ROGUELITE ELEMENTS– Experience endless playthrough possibilities with a dynamic mission select function; the order in which you choose your mission will affect mission length, number of enemies, and overall difficulty. Choose where you improve with randomized purchasable upgrades for your characters at the end of each mission, or save your cash to revive your players in-mission. 16 UNIQUE PLAYABLE CHARACTERS – Start the fight with Billy, Jimmy, Marian, and Uncle Matin. Earn tokens along the way to unlock a diverse roster of 12 more characters, each with their own playstyle and strengths. Strategically choose your fighting duo by taking into account each characters’ strengths and weaknesses. ONLINE & LOCAL CO-OP – Grab a friend and clean up the city streets together with online and local co-op that supports up to two players. SHAPE YOUR EXPERIENCE AND REWARDS – Adjust game difficulty to affect the amount of tokens earned per session and use those tokens to unlock content from the Token Shop including characters, tips, and more. Modifier can be used to enter permadeath or even infinite mode. SURVIVAL MODE – Test your might against a barrage of enemies in this wave mode that increases in difficulty the further you progress. Use tokens to unlock this mode, as well as special backgrounds during runs. VERSUS MODE – Select two characters and upgrades to battle against your friends to prove who is the ultimate Dragon Warrior. This mode and special backgrounds are unlocked via the token shop.

Tag in with 2 of 4 starter characters or unlock 12 additional characters, each with their own special moves and playstyles. Online & Local Co-op.

_childDocuments_.review: The Best Double Dragon Ever; Period.  This is the Double Dragon game that I've been waiting for forever.  After Double Dragon II, the franchise fell into quite a long slump. The vast majority of the games following The Revenge were either outright trash (DD III Arcade version; DD V Shadow Falls; DD II WOTD), mediocre or flawed in some regard (DD III NES version: Super Double Dragon; DD Neo Geo), or obscure/semi-obscure regurgitations of the first game (DD Advance; DD Zeebo; the various mobile phone versions etc.)       Double Dragon Neon was the first legitimately great entry in the franchise in a ridiculously long time.  However, gameplay wise it did not quite feel like a Double Dragon game in terms of the feel of the combat, lack of grappling, etc.  Nevertheless it was a step in the right direction and a shot in the arm of fresh ideas and production values that the franchise desperately needed.  Which made the utterly baffling decision of making the follow-up game, Double Dragon IV, into a glorified ROM hack all the more infuriating.  But now, they've finally nailed it.  Firstly, the combat just feels so right.  The hits have just the right amount of weight to them, and the unique timings and wind ups for the various characters make for a unique experience with each one.  Grappling being back (i.e. grabbing, and kneeing and throwing, etc.) was critical for me, and does not disappoint!  What I especially love the most is the ability to chain multiple Special Moves together consecutively and within normal combos, depending on how much super stock and super stock enhancing inventory power ups you have.  And I can't forget to mention the innovative tag system.  I've never seen this done before, to my knowledge, in another beat 'em up, and it adds all the more freshness and uniqueness to this Double Dragon entry.  Being able to play and switch between two characters creates so many interesting possibilities.  Whether it is as simple as tagging out to allow your primary character to recover their health after taking a beating.  Tagging out to interrupt an enemy combo, or tagging in to extend a combo that you are already in the middle of.  Not to mention the novelty of being able to alternate between two completely different playstyles, depending on what the situation calls for  Speaking of inventory power ups, the end of stage power ups are varied and have concrete effects on how you play and approach the game from a strategic manner.  Do you want to fit out your team to be brute force bruisers?  Do you want to have safety nets installed in the event that things go sour for your play through?  Do you just want to disregard any power ups whatsoever and just focus on getting more money for continues or tokens for buying unlockables like the numerous additional characters, artwork, tips and music?  You can do it all and more!Finally, the game's stage progression design is absolutely genius in terms of drawing you back in to play again and again and again.  The game, on normal standard difficulty, should take you about 2ish hours, give or take, to complete.  A perfectly fine length for a modern beat 'em up.  But what really gets you to play repeatedly long after, other than the voluminous unlockables is how the game changes depending on what order you play stages in.  Whatever gang boss you start at, you will have one stage to complete.  But the following boss will then have two stages for you to complete.  The 3rd and Final gang bosses afterwards will have three stages each to complete.  Since you won't see all three stages of each boss, depending on what order you play them in, on the first go, you absolutely have to play through multiple times in multiple different ways in order to see the entire game!  And the difficulty changes depending on what order you go in.  In other words, play Lady Okada's stage first, and she will be an absolute push over.  Play her stage last, and she becomes borderline final boss material. In terms of constructive criticism and room for improvement, I have only a couple of observations.  First, I think they should implement more i-frames when one executes their Special Moves with a character.  Sometimes I found myself executing Special Moves, only to get knocked out of said moves by enemies performing attacks that just came off as unfair.Second, I hope that in a future patch/DLC/etc. that they implement a training mode, that allows you to practice and experiment with moves and combos for the various characters.  A survival mode would be nice as well.  Also looking forward to online co-op play.   On a final note, to those who are put off by the game's art direction, I ask that you would give it a fair shot.  I too had some misgivings about the aesthetics of the game sprites, but once I watched, and then got deeply into the excellent top tier gameplay, all of those concerns melted away and are non-existent now.After so many years of so many franchise missteps, I feel like how I imagine Cubs or Red Sox fans felt after the end of the many decades of going without a World Series championship win.  Yes, it's that good. The Best Double Dragon Ever; Period.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a long time Double Dragon fan ever since the Arcade and  and of course the home console versions.  I want to like this game but can't.Pros: The music is nice with some familiar tunes. I like the idea of a prequel... but this later becomes a con4 playable characters from the start and a bunch to unlock. (not as much DD IV though) Having a level select is a nice change of pace.Spending money for upgrades/tokens is kinda nice and they seem randomized which is nice.I like the idea of the tag system as its nice to not have to be locked to one character the entire play-through.  Adjustable difficulty. Cons:The combat doesn't feel great or impactful.  The game heavily just encourages bunching enemies up and unleashing a super move to disrupt the game play and  put food on the ground for some reason.   This food if you are at full health awards you money instead.  So there is always the incentive to do this over and over. The game is very short.  While most Double Dragon games were never very long to begin with this one feels way too short for a $25 asking price.While the idea of a prequel is neat it is executed poorly.  Double Dragon has never been very story heavy this one  could have offered more.  The nuclear war has happened and the gangs have risen.  But it doesn't go beyond much further than that.  This game oddly decided to go the Super Double Dragon route and make Marian a cop.  So... I guess this is the prequel to Super Double Dragon...  what an odd choice.  No online coop.No gameplay modes beyond story.  At-least IV has the endless tower climb.Very low replay value.  Sure the character unlocks help this a bit but once you get familiar with their moves there isn't really much motivation to continue to play.Unlocks are really lame.  Characters are fine, but the rest is "hints"  which give the most obvious advice and makes no sense for them to be unlocks to begin with.  "Music" which how often are you going to boot up this game just to hear a certain song from the soundtrack?  You might as well just go to YouTube.  Then there is the concept art, which is meh, small and nothing exciting.Controls are a bit annoying.  Characters feel a bit stiff and slow.  Once in a blue moon my character just won't make a jump that clearly should have made it when jumping to a higher area.I can't recommend this game unless it was heavily on sale.  Maybe $5 would be more reasonable.  Instead check out  Double Dragon Neon,  River City Girls 1/2,  heck even Double Dragon IV if you want a more classic feeling Double Dragon like experience.   There are a lot of good modern beat'em ups and this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:After having played the game now after it's patches and new content update, the game has improved significantly. Throws and command throw moves are now significantly more useful, double tap dash is an option and crowd control popups can be removed. These things improve the quality of the game a lot. But not really enough for me to be able to really recommend purchasing the game. Movement still feels INCREDIBLY slow and clunky and I still feel that to improve game feel enemies should be able to be juggled still after they have been Special KO'ed. I would also like to add some extra complaints I notice playing now that I didn't really consider in my original review. The reason for a lot of the insane recovery on moves is because of the game's tag mechanic, cool in concept but flawed in execution. You can skip recovery on many things using specials and/or tagging in your other character. The problem here is the tagged in character will appear in the air and also their jump attack out of that will always be their running jump attack instead of the normal one. As a result of this, due to large variance in how actually useful running jump attacks are and which special moves some characters are able to use while airborne, certain characters simply do NOT play well with the tag mechanics at all which makes a large portion of the character roster just feel awful to play. I think having the ability to use special moves tied to a meter that can ONLY be used when it's full is also just awful. There is now an ability you can unlock in runs that allows you to expend health for specials when the meter is not full functionally making the mechanic similar to how special moves worked in Streets of Rage 3 or Fight n Rage which improves the game a lot (I believe this ability was not in the game at launch though I may be misremembering) however I think a function like this should just be part of the standard moveset and not an RNG unlockable. Which brings me back to one of the biggest fundamental flaws of the game and one that really cannot be fixed, it's roguelite nature. The run-based roguelite nature of this game harms every single aspect of it's gameplay and just results in a tedious mess with a heavy lack of replay value and the ability to make the game feel good to play is entirely reliant on getting the right combinations of upgrades in a run.I applaud the developers for continuing to support the game, and the changes they've made have absolutely been for the better, unfortunately DD Gaiden is just so fundamentally bad in so many ways that I'm not certain it ever can be turned into a worthwhile beat em up without completely reworking the game from the ground up.ORIGINAL REVIEW:There is a potentially solid game here, but with some major flaws that drastically damage the flow of the game and make it a chore to play at times.- Every time you kill 3 or more enemies using a special move (something that happens very frequently) the game freezes to pop an image on your screen for far too long. This happens extremely frequently and it should never happen at all. There is no way to disable it. This alone is enough reason to recommend avoiding this game for now, this feature alone completely breaks the flow of the game.- Complete lack of invincible options. These are incredibly important to any beat em up, and yet are mostly nonexistent here in DD Gaiden. Throws and neutral specials SHOULD be invincible, as is standard for beat em ups but here they are not.- Movement is incredibly slow and clunky, which isn't helped by the fact that the only way to dash is by holding a button. Implementing the ability to double-tap dash would help alleviate this but either way the game's movement is something that would need to be entirely redesigned to fix fully.- Probably the most minor issue here, but one that greatly affects game feel to me is the inability to juggle enemies after they have been special KO'd. The game has some potential for combo depth, but you can't really enjoy it because all of the enemies will be dead before you even get started with it. Having the ability to juggle corpses would improve the feel of the game a lot.There is a lot of potential here with it's characters and interesting tag mechanics but all of these issues combined add up to make the game very difficult to enjoy.
