_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- Very relaxing experience in terms of art style, music, level themes, decorations, simplicity, etc.- The train theme provides puzzle mechanics which are very easy to understand and combine. Everything is about train carts avoiding each other in a limited space and arriving in the correct order, so it's only those conditions which get progressively harder to reach when new mechanics are introduced.- Interactive cutscene art ... very cute :3- It's good that there is a straightforward main path without much frustration, and more difficult bonus puzzles which you can play in any order.Neutral:- Hints are well implemented. They give you a few of the tracks as a starting point and add more of the solution if necessary. The problem for me was that for later (more difficult) levels, the first hint was pretty much necessary, otherwise the puzzle would be one big guessing game of where to start.- If you play the main path first and then the bonus puzzles of that chapter afterwards (which you will most likely do), then the order and difficulty of the bonus puzzles seems pretty random.Negatives:- The completely timing based puzzle system wasn't as fun and satisfying as I expected. You can make use of certain track setups and behaviors, but there is almost no way you can see (or piece together) the solution of a puzzle just by looking at the tracks, especially when you also have switches and other elements. Instead, it takes a lot of trial and error.

_childDocuments_.review: A relaxing rail-based puzzle game! Railbound is a puzzle game using the universally praised concept of steam locomotives and their respectful tracks. It's fairly similar of this kind of game but makes up for it with it's style and relaxing atmosphere and difficulty! Gameplay of Railbound consists of a handful of worlds with a bunch of main and bonus puzzles. Your basic main task is to connect the passenger car to the back of a train. The game elaborates on this basis by including more elements such as more cars being added, special track parts, and much more. With each of these elements introduced and/or featured in each world. From there it's as simple as figuring out the right solution via trial n' error and gaining that satisfaction from completing a puzzle on your own. Thankfully however the game does come with a few accommodations for some assistance.As there isn't too much to talk about I will say the the style of this game, having this 3D Cel-Shading artstyle for the main game is very visually appealing and also ties into the extremely well done artwork for the world interlude images. Overall, Railbound is just a all around good puzzle game involving trains. it's a familiar formula that's made unique by it's artstyle and relaxing atmosphere. Though I think the price is a bit steep considering the content, as there's not much replay value once you do everything. Maybe down the line a level editor and online sharing of levels could really extend the life of this game. But hey what's here is great and I'm glad the game impressed me during that Steam Next Fest!

_childDocuments_.review: It's very satisfying to see trains go round in circles. The puzzles are a bit hit or miss. This is one of the first instances I've seen where some of the puzzles give the player too much information. Difficulty is also pretty inconsistent from level to level. You would assume the bonus levels are meant to challenge you, but I've done some of them in seconds, even at the later worlds, while some main levels stumped me for a long time. All that being said, it was fun to discover the ways the mechanics enable certain track structures, it positively made my brain swirl (sometimes I didn't even understand why something I did worked and had to go back and see it multiple times to wrap my head around it). There are some real head-scratchers in there. I think this has enough content for its price.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful little puzzle game! I easily get stuck when trying to figure out puzzles :0) But there's a great hint system that slowly reveals the solution (click "hint" once, you get a few clues. click "hint" again, you get more clues). I would recommend Railbound to anyone who enjoys a nice puzzle game and/or someone who enjoys trains (the trains are crazy cute!)
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: A hard, but mostly fair puzzle game. There's a very kind hint system if you get completely stuck on a puzzle too.Difficulty is not quite perfect, the first 7 worlds (not counting bonus levels) are probably half the play time and then the final world ramps it up an insane amount.A lot of fun if you enjoy puzzles. Also, I like trains. So 8/10. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful little puzzle game.The mechanics are simple and build on each other as you progress, making it easy to keep track of how things work and how to interact with them to progress. There were stages where I felt like I needed to work out some gimmick or tight timing cheese, but the eventual solution was always a clear application of spatial reasoning and resource management that felt gratifying to solve.The game also includes a progressive hint system and the ability to unlock all levels if you want to simply find the answer to a puzzle you can't solve or skip ahead to work on something else.If you like puzzle games where you work out complexity to find satisfying answers, I feel pretty confident that you'll have a good time with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Railbound is a cute little puzzle game about placing tracks down so the train cars get to the locomotive in the proper order. As you progress, the game will throw more mechanics at you. The base puzzles aren't too difficult but the bonus puzzles can be real head scratches. It's actually very relaxing with the cute aesthetic and calming music while it can be frustrating while you're racking your head on how to solve some of the more complicated puzzles at the same time.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Get your Trainconductorhat and make sure you are on time!I got this game in a tripple bundle for <10€ so I definatly got my moneys worth with as of now 10 hours of playtime!Railbound is a fun puzzlegame with cute graphics.The games different mechanics are tought to you in the beginning of each chapter , which are 8.This is a game where you can come back later after having been stuck on a level and suddenly you find the solution first try! I am almost done. 4 of 8 chapters complete with bonus levels. Stuck on the main path of 8 and some bonus levels here and there to complete. All in all I love this game! My only two problems: I wished it was longer AND more mechanics would interact in later levels (but maybe I am just not there yet?) I hope it will get more content in the future!  EDIT: New content announced for late 2022! WHOO WHOOO! CHUGGA CHUGGA CHU CHU
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Would you like to break your brains, while playing with trains?Look no further, Railbound is an adorable, cozy puzzle game. Puzzles start easy, but will get increasingly difficult.I had much fun figuring out the solutions, but it is not always easy.The music and the art are like a warm blanket that hugs you while you break your brain.Loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: If you like puzzle games, I definitely recommend. Filled with puzzles of varying difficulty and a variety of fun mechanics that spice up the challenge. The pace that mechanics are added and taken away is also really well done. You're not bombarded with new changes and I never felt a mechanic was overdone before the next world came along. The aesthetics are also nice. From the postcards to the music to general visual style.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: I like railway games and I like puzzle games, so I should really like this game.But for some reason I don't. I think the reason is because the puzzles are stripped down, presumably to keep the interface simple. I've played games like this before where each level gives you a certain number and type of each tile. Here, you are just limited by the number of tiles. As I result of this, I spend quite a bit of time clicking through the tile options. I really don't completely understand why this is less interesting for me, but it is.I think for what it is, it is well designed and programmed, but unfortunately I didn't enjoy it and refunded it. However, I'll recommend it, at least to give it a try, you might like it more than I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and lovely game for puzzle lovers. Starts really simple as you would expect, but gets really hard and challenging quite soon.As an addition, I'd suggest the devs to add a preview of how things switch when triggered, specially with the addition of button controlled lane-switching trails, which are quite hard to imagine without playing the level for every little thing you change and figuring out on a try and failure basis.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Starts out nice and easy and gets quite tricky, but in the good way. You'll need to exit and come back often for inspiration on a solution to a puzzle but that's ok to keep things fresh. The art is great and who doesn't like trains anyways? Buy it, celebrate the successes and curse the moments you get stuck but then celebrate once you've figured it out :)
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Toot toot puzzle game.The fun graphics and train noises elevate what would otherwise be a fairly straightforward puzzle game. Gameplay: Eight worlds about ten levels per world plus extra levels per world which are more difficult. So there is a fairly decent amount of content, of course that depends on how hard you find the puzzles. Each world has its own gimmick which keeps things interesting. The final 'extra' levels are basically sandboxes which was neat to not be under a build limit and just go crazy. :)I've 100% the game and only had to look up a few levels that were a bit tedious. Fun little time waster overall...
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is my #2 favourite puzzle-game of all time. I played it at launch and found it pretty frustrating as the regular speed of the train cards made readability difficult on some levels. The game has since updated with great accessibility features, including that mentioned ability to slow-down the speed when running the track as well as a robust hint system that gives you a starting point if you hit a brick wall (or are simply overwhelmed), I've tried it a few times and it's really good, it gives you a place to start/continue without giving the puzzle away making you still feel like you solved the puzzle instead of having to exit out of the game and go for a guide that will spoil too much if you can't progress on your own. Game has great mechanics, good puzzles and just fantastic game. I've loved all of Afterburn's games was saddened that I didn't with this one on launch, but can now say I do. Looking forward to their next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: Pure, unadulterated puzzling fun with an attractive art style and calm, chill music. Enough challenge to make you think, but rarely enough to make you frustrated. What a great distillation of art and puzzling! For what it's worth, I could see a map building/sharing feature being a GREAT addition here to allow for endless replay-ability. Priced just right, as well. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: Railbound

_childDocuments_.review: A relaxing puzzle game about fixing train connections and travelling the world!

name: Sunday Gold
detailed_description: Finalist in the 2022 Gamescom Awards for both ‘Best Role-Playing Game’ and ‘Best Indie Game’, Sunday Gold is a point-and-click, turn-based adventure game set in grim, dystopian future. Play as a ragtag trio of criminals to hunt down and expose the dark secrets of an evil mega-corporation and the malevolent billionaire behind it. Experience a unique hybrid of escape room style puzzles, turn-based combat, and RPG mechanics tied together with a dark and cinematic storyline. Delve into the dark underbelly of near-future London Once bustling and full of life, the city of London is in a dark and dismal state. Unemployment and homelessness are at an all-time high. Ethical boundaries are being stretched to their limit and corrupt billionaire, Kenny Hogan, is up to no good. It’s up to ragtag band of criminals Frank, Sally, and Gavin, to put a wrench in Kenny Hogan’s plans and bring him to his knees. But this is no simple job and there’ll be a smattering of obstacles they’ll have to face along the way… Lose yourself in a dark and dystopian story Immerse yourself in a gritty and graphic world with a storyline narrated by fully voice-acted characters. Experience stunningly hand-drawn environments, 2D cinematics and comic book inspired sequences as well as cliff hangers that will keep you on your toes. Puzzles that will get you scratching your noggin Explore each room and solve a combination of observation, deduction, and inventory puzzles to progress on your mission. Hunt for clues, hack terminals, bust down a door (or two) and test your wits in mini game challenges unique to each “hero”. Stylish turn-based combat inspired by comic books Face off against your opponents in stylish and cinematic RPG style battles. Each team member possesses their own unique set of skills as well as their own strengths and weaknesses. Plan your moves strategically, master winning combos and kick your enemies to the curb. Keep your composure and try not to sweat Battle your own stress levels as well as enemies! Disturbing and pressured situations will wear down your characters’ composure causing them to act impulsively. Maintain your composure with consumables and leadership abilities. Lose your mind, lose the mission! A modern twist on point-and-click games Sunday Gold takes the traditional elements of a point-and-click game and mixes them with fierce RPG combat and a gritty storyline.

_childDocuments_.review: In a dystopic future UK where cyber-surveillance peaks and corporations reign supreme, grizzled lowlife Frank, always broke, is desperately looking for the next heist to cash in (and pay his outrageous pub tab while he’s at it). His friend Sally, animal caretaker by day and underground boxer at night, proposes to him a job involving corporate espionage - of course, he accepts. Alongside the latest entry, the disgruntled and easily-shaken IT worker Gavin, the trio of anti-heroes sets off to get rich or die trying in a big corporate shakedown.This is a world where animal cyber-engineering is commonplace, and the next step up the chain is not too far off either. Climate change flooded most of London, the UK brought to its knees by degenerating geopolitics, economic crashes and crime. Sounds familiar? The portrayal of such a setting is well-depicted and plausible, as SG doesn’t spare high amounts of gore, blood and general brutality on a regular basis. The trio isn’t depicted as heroes nor should they; rather, they’re lowlifes trying to get by and that don’t shy from murdering and conning for that end. The writing of each protagonist is excellent, as they react coherently with their character and stay consistent for the whole adventure. Each map is divided in a series of rooms, most of which inaccessible at first, depicted as a static 2D background with your 3D characters being able to explore them in a point-n-click fashion. Many objects can be examined, used, opened, picked up and so forth - but beware, in most cases such actions will cost Action Points (AP), that will eventually run out and need a Turn to pass to be recovered, or the usage of consumables such as drugs if you have any. At each passing turn the global Alert Level may increase or decrease, and also enemies may spawn to hinder your advance (on top of the regular, predetermined ones). All characters have unique skills to solve problems; for instance, only Frank can lockpick closed containers. In more than a few instances your team may get separated, so you’ll also may have to find a way to reunite them in order to progress. Other than ‘mandatory’ exploration, there is a plethora of optional puzzles and secrets that often hold useful gear and consumables, but also require more time to deal with - and you’re always on the clock. Some elements of the environment or events may increase or decrease the characters’ composure, which is basically their mental stability, that gives debuffs and hallucinogenic effects if it gets too low, but can be restored with items and certain skills.Plays out in a turn-based fashion, with each character having their own turn with unlimited time - unless their Composure gets too low, in that case you’ll be on a short timer to decide what actions to take. Attacking enemies costs just 1AP, while using the numerous offensive, defensive and support skills of each will cost usually more. There’s a variety of status effects both you and enemies may inflict like Stunned, Bleeding and so on, each ability has different buffs and/or debuffs it may grant to one or more characters; some consumables also have a chance of inflicting debuffs. Enemies may be resistant or weak to one of the four damage types (Slash, Pierce, Blunt, Tech) so equipping your team with a flexible loadout to take advantage of such weaknesses is very important - special ammo and some gear pieces may also alter the damage type of weapons.Most puzzles have an investigative or logical tone, and involve collecting files to extrapolate the correct sequence in machinery, deduct the correct item to pick based on the info at hand, or using a series of items in the correct order in order to obtain a key allowing you to progress. They are varied, fun and never frustrating - some could be better-explained, but overall pretty good. Minigames are logic or reflex-based segments: Sally’s power checks will involve balancing a needle in a given area, Frank’s lockpicking is about clicking with the right timing, and Gavin’s hacking is about deducting a numerical sequence by trial-and-error.Equipped gear and levels are the two means of progression. Each character can hold two weapons depending on their specialties, several gear pieces that grant passive improvements, and also unlimited consumables that are free-to-use out of combat but cost a turn in a fight. With a level cap of 10 and two skill points per level, with a respec options in-between chapters as well, you’ll be able to experiment with the various abilities and build the three to your liking - possibly breaking the balance in the process, since come combinations are too strong for their own good.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold has fantastic art, fantastic music, and industry-best voice acting. The combat has a strongly cinematic feel to it, with comic book cut out frames and dramatic camera moves that really help sell the tone. The story is alright, having a setting players have seen before and a predictable narrative, but it has enough unique design and memorable villains to meet along the way that it still makes for a fun ride, even if you already know where it's going.Unfortunately, since this is a game, the biggest thing holding this title back is the gameplay- and it's not just one element.     •  Run out of points in the field? You have to 'end your turn' to replenish them, which initially when you enter an area has a 50% chance of initiating combat, that escalates up to a 100% chance, the longer you're in a given location. So say you end the combat with low action points- suddenly you're back to the map, without the ability to do anything, so you have to end your turn, which has a 50% chance of immediately spawning another fight... Your only option to be efficient, is to draw out every combat with extra turns towards the end specifically to have each character block so that you can finish combat with the ability to do anything back on the map. It makes reasonably forgettable fights take even longer for the duration of the game.     •  I believe the basic painkilers heal something like 15-20% of your health... which enemies will knock out in one attack, so it's much better to use Sally's substantially better healing skill than a consumable item. Most items are like this- they don't have enough impact to ever justify using them instead of just attacking on that turn.     •  It feels a lot someone sat down and created a list of 'it'd be cool if you could...' but then never playtested them to find out if they were actually useful. Each character has about 10 skills (with a decent amount of overlap) of which, 1-2 are useful in combat. By the end of the game you get to a point where you're doing 300 damage on a basic attack on enemies, and if you apply bleed to them... Bleed will do 5 damage at the start of their turn. It really feels like there was no effort to test or balance the status effects.     •  It's a nice idea, each character having a unique skill they bring to the table, but the amount of times you have to do them, without them ever changing gets real boring about halfway through the game. Additionally (and this may be because I played the game on an older system), Sally's strength game can either be extremely buggy, or just downright undoable. The arrow you're meant to control skipped around wildly for me, even on easy challenges, which eventually led to me switch the accessibility options for making the mini games easier on. Similarly, Frank's minigame would occasionally read a miss incorrectly when the icon was squarely inside the 'sweet spot.'     •  where you drag your mouse around looking for the interactable thing that you need to get that hidden security log. There is an ability to highlight interactive items on the screen but by default it costs 5(!) action points, of your 7 on that character. You can level the skill up in the tree, but why would you when you can level up skills that help you in combat instead?    •  which requires a lot of remembering who picked up a specific item, navigating through the poorly designed menus, selecting the item, selecting the trade option, selecting the recipient, exiting the inventory, selecting the correct character to use the item and then doing the action that costs action points... And you have to do this for every kind of item. Wrong person picked up a weapon they can't use? Got a gear item you want to use on a different character? Got a key item you need to give to a different person? Here or there, this may not have been terrible, but by the end of the game you're doing it constantly. Sure, it adds to the realism, but someone along the road should have asked "Is this adding to the game? Is it making it more fun? Or just tedious?" There are some fun puzzles, There's a lot of weapon variety with different parameters, and equipment with different options that can even effect your weapon types, giving you some freedom in customization of your characters builds. The exploration can be rewarding when it nets you some new variety of weapon/gear. There's a fun balancing system of damage type weaknesses and resistances in enemies that keeps you thinking about and promoting having a diverse team. but could have been substantially better if more time had been taken to test and balance the gameplay elements, with anywhere near as much as love as went into every other aspect of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the first chapter, liked the second, despised the third (and last).The world and characters are interesting, but the gameplay and design range from fun to godawful. Gameplay is kinda a mix of RPG combat and point&click adventure. the point&click part is awesome, liked that. The RPG combat was fun during the first and most of the second chapter but took a complete nosedive in the last chapter.The bossfights are atrocious, think the worst final fantasy bossfights, meaning you play for 30 mins and boom, enemy suddenly gets completely healed for some reason and 30 mins of annoying combat were made totally pointless. The enemies also get multiple actions per turn (at least 3) while each of your characters gets 1 (so if you fight 2 bosses you get hit by 6 attacks while  you can only do 1 action per character, at least 1 (usually 2 or all 3) are spent on constant healing and rezzing so you barely do damage while your enemy is happily pummeling away at you.It's just no fun, killed the whole game for me. Even tried cheat engine but they seem to have protected the stat values, I am not good enough to find stuff like health and there are no working tables available. As it currently stands I am  at the final fight and have no interest in trying that again.It's just so badly designed, what a shame, like I said the world and characters are fun and interesting. If they at least had put in a difficulty selector (I'd set that to lowest available in a heartbeat) but nope, badly designed rpg combat which you can't escape. At least final fantasy fights give you more options to use (multiple spells, potions) so you can try different tactics, here it's just not complex enough and just becomes irritating and frustrating.As it is, I can't recommend it, the boss fights and combat in the third chapter really kills it. I also encountered a bunch of little bugs (from background graphics not appearing, the HUD occasionally deciding to be in the foreground so you can't click on stuff in the world behind it to crashes, there is sure to be something for everyone).What I find a bit weird, the bugs and the badly designed fights started at the end of chapter 2, it was fine and decently balanced before and I had no bugs. I hope that is just coincidence and they didn't just push this out without polishing the latter half of the game since by that point you can't refund anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Don't know, but it is something special, though. Not so easy to explain, it fuses different gameplay styles together, and as always, you can only enjoy the result if you enjoy all the different gameplay mechanics. You play three petty crooks (a healer, an IT guy and a brawler) trying to expose the evil doings of a self-made billionaire and his company. You arrive at a scene and play like an adventure (searching, examining stuff, hacking gadgets), but every move costs action points and the longer you take the higher the alert level of your enemies. Some of the actions play out in different mini games, like hacking things, picking locks or when trying to move heavy objects. The puzzles are not easy, often requiring quite a bit of detective work to solve correctly, either by parsing computer logs or picking up on other environmental clues, such as post-it notes, phone messages, paintings or calendar entries. When you encounter enemies, you fight them in classic JRPG-style turn based combat, where you can use skills and items. Some of the fights can take quite some time. All this is presented in stylish visuals and atmospheric music and fully voiced. You might enjoy it - if you like the adventuring part AND the often quite long turn-based fights.Play three low-lifes fighting an evil billionaire in this quite an interesting mix of point and click adventure, jrpg-style turn based combat and little minigames.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially found  on some sale page, a nice 50% discount and a flashy store tile luring my cursor over to check it out. Once on the page, the description of “…a point-and-click, turn-based adventure game…” enticed me further, and seeing the slick animated images in the description and the half-off price easily pushed me over the edge into seeing what it was about.What it’s about is a very unique, somewhat messy, but ultimately gorgeous game.On the surface, you take control of a team of criminals out to do some heists for hire, their contact in the first chapter accidentally getting them in well over their heads. It’s set in a dystopian future England and follows the team’s exploits around a corporation’s dark and sinister secrets after they get sucked into the middle of them.To go back to the description of “a point-and-click, turn-based adventure game,” the game is exactly as advertised. It takes old static background adventure games and adds a limited amount of action points with which to do certain interactions. Moving around and examining things are free, as are some basic actions, but doing anything like searching or activating something in the environment will cost some of those limited AP. They’re replenished by ending the turn and raising the alert level, which also rolls the dice on a random event at the end of the turn.The other half of the gameplay is combat, either when that random event comes up with a patrol or you happen to do something in the adventure game portion that causes an encounter. The combat is a very simple turn-based RPG system with basic attacks, defenses, abilities, and items. Positioning doesn’t matter and the only real tactics that do are sometimes enemies will use attacks that take a turn to charge up, meaning you have to react to them.And that’s the high-level overview of the game. You wander around environments solving puzzles akin to classic adventure games and constantly go through combat with the various guards and such that get in your way.One of the primary issues, however, is the shared pool of action points between the two modes. If you run low or out of points in the adventure mode and end the turn only to get into combat as a random encounter, you will begin the encounter with little to no action points. Similarly, if you end the encounter with little to no points, you start back into the adventure mode essentially needing to end the turn immediately with nothing to show for it. Each character also has their own special minigame for the adventure segments that are guaranteed to cost AP, don’t refund them if you fail, and aren’t difficult beyond the occasional hiccup of the game not registering them correctly. Even still, they aren’t fun in the least.More issues surround the game’s items and combat. Items are found constantly all over the place and even dropped in combat, however, the vast majority of them are next to useless. Characters earn experience and level up, unlocking, and leveling skills. Unfortunately, as with the items, most of these are either useless or simply no better than brute forcing your way through combat.These issues are worsened in the last chapter of the game, where combat is constant, each screen has several objects requiring the use of AP to interact with, and items are even more ineffective against the high-level enemies you’ll encounter during this segment.Another thing that’s less of an issue if you’ve previously played old Lucasarts or Sierra adventure games or even some of the newer Wadjet Eye games is that true to form a lot of the adventure game sections boil down to pixel hunting and running your cursor over every inch of the screen. Thankfully items are limited to only what they can actually be used with or who by and even tell you who can use what item on them. Another welcome relief is that most of the puzzles in the game avoid “adventure game logic” and are fairly intuitive, barring a couple that are more problematic in interface than design. Almost as an ineffective compromise, one character has the ability to highlight every useable object in a scene at a massive cost of AP, making the ability a poor choice to use in all but the worst situations.Despite the issues, the gameplay has in both modes and the frustration that may arise from it, that frustration is thankfully mild, barring the last couple of hours of the game. It’s helped infinitely by the production value that is far and above what a smaller indie game usually offers. The visuals are absolutely beautiful, both in the character art and the backgrounds. The setting and scenery are interesting despite being a relatively common trope, and the voice acting is absolutely stellar. It’s actually in large part due to the game being such a visual and auditory treat on top of not-that-bad gameplay that makes this an easy recommendation., despite suffering from a myriad of minor issues and annoyances, is overall a highly enjoyable adventure game with some turn-based RPG combat and mechanics shoved in there. It shouldn’t work half as well as it does and hopefully, if they ever make another game along these lines they can refine it and turn it into an even easier recommendation. As is, 50% off is a no-doubt recommendation while full-price (at the time of this writing $21.99) is a little bit of a stretch but still an easy sell.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: I want to be able to recommend this game. I really do. I picked up Sunday Gold because the artwork makes it look like it would ooze style and I'm a sucker for stylish point & click games. (The fact that it was on sale for the price of a cup of coffee didn't hurt, either.) I'm pretty tolerant of weird gameplay design choices and janky mechanics provided that the story is enough to suck me in. I'm a few hours into the game and my verdict on the story is: "Eh... it's okay, I guess?" That's not exactly the reaction you want when it comes to a heist game. When it comes to gameplay mechanics, I feel like Sunday Gold is suffering from some kind of identity crisis. It's a weird mashup of point and click and tactical RPG mechanics. You click around to interact with the world, but there's also turn-based combat with leveling and skill trees. The mechanics kind of conflict with each other in a way that I find frustrating. I enjoy point and click games because they encourage exploration by allowing you to *click on everything* so you can try the weirdest possible item combinations. Sunday Gold's turn-based, action point system actively discourages you from doing that kind of exploration as most interactions eat up action points. Once you've used up your action points, you're forced to end your turn. Each turn raises a general awareness/alert level. When that exceeds a certain threshold, guards come dashing into the room your characters are in, and you're forced into combat.The combat is also quite trying on your patience. Your combat actions are tied into the *same* action points as the ones you use to interact with the world. This means you can start a round of combat with a huge disadvantage since all of your characters could potentially be AP starved. There's also no indication of when a battle is going to happen, so there's no way for you to know when you should end your turn to re-up your AP before going into battle.I think the devs made this deliberate design choice to build a sense of urgency and tension. I guess they succeeded in their goal, because I was certainly tense from frustration.I feel like all of the elements were there to make a really good game. The mechanics just didn't really come together in a way that made sense.

_childDocuments_.review: The style, writing, and voiced-acted characters carry this to what could have been a true hidden 9/10In the sense that it is basic and boring, and there is too much for how simple and brain-dead it is.It's not even "Babies First X-com", it's more that it's not really needed, they could cut it out and it would be better for it.There is a reason it's Mostly Positive, but I do disagree with most saying the final act separating your crew makes it impossibly hard. Your crew is a tech dude looking like Asmongold, a melee-smoking chad, and a badass healing tomboy. In the first half of the final act, the healer is alone, so your two dudes can't heal. This is a real spike in difficulty, but I was actually digging it because other than the final boss, I had to think about my turns and managing my action resources. Also, they reuse a boss fight, in a game whose combat is already lacking variety.I have no real complaints about the rest of the game, it's got great banter with a cast that feels genuinely like real people. The exploration is creatively turned-based, where each turn has a chance to summon more combat; real tension after knowing how boring the combat is. The cool thing with your action points is they are shared between exploring and combat, so you can't just spam during exploring or you'll start combat with low action points and will need to waste a turn to rest.I cannot overstate how the style of this game will see, they have a darkest dungeon sanity meter that is interesting and can spice up combat from ice cold to lukewarm.The puzzles, character minigames, and inventory aspects are tactile and interesting and varied so much, just wish the combat got the same attention.I hope their next game keeps this style because I seriously dig it.I enjoyed it enough to waste wayyyyyy too much time to make these and didn't even end up releasing these:

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so conflicted. I was a bit skeptical of the mixed ratings, I tend to stick to "overwhelmingly positive" myself, but the trailer really intrigued me so I figured I'd give a try and refund it if it didn't click. It very very much did click. I want to say I love it so badly. But there are a few problems.If you comb through every review of this game under the sun, you won't find a single bad word said about the voice acting. Every single dialogue line has absolutely stellar voice acting, and honestly, it's the best part about this game by far. Every single person did a perfect job, I cannot overstate how fun the voices are. The music, a bit less so. It's pretty good, don't get me wrong, but there's so little variety that you're much better off listening to your own music and then putting the earbuds back in when there's dialogue.The gameplay is a mix of point and click and party based rpg. There are consumables, skills that you level up, weapons and gear you can find, i's very "video gamey" for a story that takes itself pretty seriously, but it's not a bad combo. The combat isn't the best, but that really only encourages you to be more strategic and meticulous about what you do in the point and click section. Each character has action points that you spend on puzzle stuff and once they're out , you "end your turn" upping the security level and pretty often spawning a fight (although you can save scum ending turns to get the outcome you want). It's fun! Multiple times I've had a character do a bump of coke to avoid a fight, which is super funny, but also a fantastic way of making the gameplay (fights being hard and costing a lot of health) intertwine with the story (you're breaking into places, of course you can't spend a ton of time there). It's a great mechanic that unfortunately is ruined once you get too good at the fights. Towards the end I used fights like refueling stations, I would kill everyone except 1 enemy, heal to full, recharge all my action points, and then knock their head off.Which comes to the reason this game is good and not great. The end. Like most point and clicks, it all falls apart the deeper in you go. It gets more glitchy towards the end, but the puzzles get absolutely f*cking ridiculous at some points, you get lost super easy, it just starts getting tedious. And unfortunately, although I loved pretty much every second of the story until the end, this game might have the worst ending of all time. 5 things happen in quick succession, each one making less sense then the last, and then the game is over. No closure, no tying up loose ends, not even the team celebrating their victory. Just a very confusing string of events and then the credits.About 70% of this game is impeccable. I had so much fun. However, it falls off hard and doesn't give you the closure you're looking for with the end6/10. I'm real glad I played it though

_childDocuments_.review: I've had my eye on this game for a while. I loved the art style and the fact that it was about a rag-tag bunch of heisters in a dystopian future akin to Disco Elysium. Upon finishing the game, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Sunday Gold, even with its small slew of problems.In Sunday Gold, you follow a thief named Frank. He's gotten into some money troubles and needs to pay off some loans quickly. One of his friends, Sally, hooks him up with a job to help make a ton of money. She has found a man named Gavin who wants to sneak into a facility to find some dirt on Kenny Hogan, the head of a huge mega-conglomerate company that has been doing some shifty things. Upon taking on the job, this rag-tag group starts to learn a lot more than they bargained for.Sunday Gold is a blend of Point-and-Click adventure mixed with turned-based RPG. During the Point-and-Click sections, you will have the group examine and interact with objects on the screen, find items, and solve puzzles. Each one of them excels at different things and sometimes you'll have to use their skills in a mini-game to progress the plot. Frank has the lockpicking mini-game, Sally has to focus her strength on a meter to move heavy things, and Gavin has to do hacking mini-games. What makes this fun is on certain parts of the game, the gang will split up and you'll want to backtrack to certain areas just to make sure you check everything.The game uses an Action Point (AP) system so doing certain actions will drain their points. You can use items to replenish these points or end your turn in which time will move forward and there is a chance you will get into a random battle. There are even some moves/abilities you can learn to make your skills cost less AP which I found pretty nifty. Let's look into combat.The Turn-Based RPG combat is very simple and I found it fun. Different weapons and abilities you use have different properties and can greatly damage types of enemies. For example, robot enemies are weak to moves that have "TECH" or blunt damage. (So Gavin usually knocks them out pretty well). BUT, you can find weapons and accessories that change the property of your attacks. So while Frank by default has Slashing damage, you can find a bullet upgrade that turns his shots into Blunt damage. The mix and matching of combat makes it fun. You also have to be mindful of your AP usage in combat as well as different moves that cost more or less AP. Spending too much will make your character lose a turn to get AP back. Luckily, defending refunds a lot of AP and makes you take less damage. I love it when RPGs give you a good reason to actually defend aside from just taking less damage.Another system I liked was the Composure system. Throughout the game, you'll have to be mindful of the main cast's composure. Story events or enemy abilities will make them lose composure and it affects them in and out of battle. In battle, if their composure gets low, they will start to panic and your turn is suddenly timed. The lower the composure, the less time you have to take your turn before they freak out and just do a random move. Out of combat, the composure affects their mini-games. Frank will be more shaky on lockpicking, it'll be harder for Sally to keep her meter centered for focus, and Gavin will start to forget numbers and symbols in the hacking game. Luckily, there are items and moves you can use to raise their composure again, but I really liked this mechanic from a narrative and gameplay point of view. Another touch I liked is that as their composure gets lower, their character portraits start to look frightened and weird, great artistic touch there.Now for gripes. For as much as I loved this game, it did have issues. For one, Frank's lockpicking mini-game gave me a ton of issues where I was sure I had the marker centered in the sweet spot but the game said I didn't. Luckily, you can change this in the options to make it easier, but then it makes Sally's mini-game too easy. The turned-based combat is fun, but it's very slow and after a while, you may find yourself getting annoyed by how long some battles take, especially the boss battles where the boss takes multiple turns. A fast forward or 2X speed would have been great to fix that. I've had some music glitches in the game sometimes but nothing game-breaking that a quick restart didn't help. The majority of the puzzles were fun to figure out, but there was a small handful where I just looked up the solution because it wasn't fun trying to figure out how to solve them. And lastly, what most of the other reviews are saying, the ending. It is very rushed and it makes me sad. You can tell that had big plans but either ran out of time or money. There are still lots of unanswered questions and it's sad it ends so abruptly.Final verdict? Despite the long list of gripes, I absolutely LOVED this game. I loved playing as Frank, Sally, and Gavin. Loved the voice acting and the overall theme of the game. I loved solving the puzzles and hitting the "AH HA!" moment when the answers just clicked. I loved having a good synergy with my characters when I leveled them up. I would love a Sunday Gold 2 with the crew returning and trying to take down another company. I say grab this game when it's on sale if you are on the fence. There are hard bits and it is clunky on some points. But overall, I enjoyed my time with this game and would recommend it to those who want a fun Point-and-Click game with some RPG elements thrown in. Thanks for reading! Cheers Guvna!

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold shines in terms of its characters, which are charming, unique and nicely voice acted. However, this is one of those eye-catching games that looks like pure gold at first, but the more you play it, the more you realize it's all work and no play. The point and click adventure is ok and presents an interesting innovation in terms of time management, but it devolves into tedium a bit too often. Indeed, every room feels samey and requires you to brainlessly spend your action points on all interactive objects, rather than feeling you are solving a narrative puzzle. Similarly, combat is grindy, has minimal enemy diversity and feels unsatisfying. Bosses are a chore, being damage sponges that can heal and summon allies. I witnessed a single bug in my playthrough, but what a bug: the game froze on me after about 30 minutes of slowly chipping away at the end boss' health bar. So frustrating. All in all, not a terrible game, and some good narrative moments, but quite lacking in the fun department.

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a point-and-click adventure game that features a rag tag trio of criminals, an evil mega-corporation, and a malevolent billionaire all wrapped into one incredibly stylish package. Taking place in a dystopian London, your group will work to expose and stop Kenny Hogan from his corrupt ways. Using turn-based combat to deal with your foes, you will have to manage your composure to keep your allies sane while upgrading their skills and leveling them up. Will you be able to bring justice while keeping yourself sane?Personally, the gameplay of Sunday Gold is right up my alley and generally the type I really enjoy, but the artstyle steals the show. The game is so visually interesting and appealing with wonderful animations and, paired with the solid voice acting, is a joy to experience. As a game, I believe Sunday Gold is a fantastic one that I will be enjoying for quite some time, but we are here to discuss how it plays on the Steam Deck, and I definitely have a couple things to say.Because of Sunday Gold's artistic direction, the intensity of the game on hardware is on the lower side. This shows most since playing without any setting changes works perfectly fine with a FPS cap! After testing with the settings, I felt out of the box performance was the best coupled with the visual fidelity. The biggest question for me in terms of performance was framerate. Due to the way the game is animated, a higher framerate isn't necessary, but I felt 40 FPS was better than 30. Even though the battery drained a little more, I felt selecting items was more responsive and animations were slightly more fluid. Both of these together made it a much more enjoyable experience for around 3 hours of battery.A framerate of 30 was quite nice to have to conserve battery when needed though. Other than the item selecting, the game still felt great at this framerate and would add around half an hour to an hour of battery life. This was great for when I forgot my charger and was able to maximize my game time with a simple framerate switch.Sunday Gold is a near perfect experience on the Deck, but two big things hold it back from being a Best on Deck game. First, there is no native controller support. For some games on Deck, using Steam Input and the gamepad works great, but unfortunately, it can't account for everything. In this case, navigating menus is a little bit of a chore which, if implemented, native controller support would fix. It would be awesome to have better navigation selecting items and some better support for the minigames, except the hacking one, but using the right touchpad or touchscreen of the Deck to control isn't as bad.The other issue I believe would need to be addressed is small text. Now this isn't apparent in the entire game, but in some dialogues, menus, and the overworld, the text can be very small. You can use the magnifier tool (Steam button + L1) but it comes out blurry without actually making the text readable. Having an option like in Pentiment or Disco Elysium would be very useful here.I believe those are the only two issues I have with the game on the Deck. I have emailed the publisher, Team17, regarding these and asking if they will be added to Sunday Gold in the future. I will update this review when I hear back.Sunday Gold is such a damn good game with an intriguing story, interesting characters, great gameplay loops, and a unique artstyle. On the Steam Deck, the game runs very well without needing any tweaking except for a framerate cap with optional TDP limits to keep the game from pushing the battery too hard. If there was native controller support and text resizing, this would easily be a Best on Deck game. Hopefully, it is something that will come in the future and I can happily upgrade this!

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a satire of real world London, clad in an aesthetic colour pallet with an exaggerated plot that involves cybernetic animal blood-sports, secret cyborg labs and billionaires gutting an over-industrialised city. Visually it's such a stylish wash of comic book colours and action panels resulting in gorgeous, detailed artworks to tell the story. This coupled with onomatopoeia and synth music makes you feel as if you’re actually reading a neo-noir comic. It's a turn-based combat game with mild RPG elements like assigning weapons and armour to your party of three (think Persona 5). However, unlike P5, all exploration and interaction you do in a level, it will all be turn-based. Meaning each action in the game performed by any of your three character will reduce your AP and to replenish it you've to end your turn. And this is where Sunday Gold's downsides come as ending your turn will risk a chance enemy encounter; you might end up in a loop where you use up all your AP in fight, end a turn and face enemies again instead preserving your AP for exploration. Besides that, the game still lacks in-depth combat system and you'll end up using the same few attaks throughout the campaign.However, despite all it's flaws, I would totally play a sequel to Sunday Gold because of the charming trio of characters and impressive world building. Their constant sarcastic banter is definitely a plus point. This coupled with a detailed world building via newspapers, emails, magazine covers, posters etc will cure that itch you got after playing Disco ElysiumYou can read my full in-depth review here:

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting mix of a point n' click adventure and a turn based RPG. Limiting the puzzle solving with action points makes it so you can't just brute force your way out by trying every possible combination. The characters are well developed (except for the fake British accent) and the story well told. And I really liked the puzzle solving aspect of the game.But what ultimately ruins the game are the random surprise enemy encounters. At the end of every turn, the game can just throw enemies at you in order to deplete your action points, health and healing items, leaving you running on fumes until you finally arrive at a fight that's actually in the script that you can't now get past. Not that you would have a chance even when fully rested, as bosses have attacks that can drain half of your health bar with single strike, and can have multiple attacks per turn, which means you're already lost.Your characters also have sanity meters. Practically this means, when character gets low on sanity, you get a timer on your turns in combat encounters, like a cherry on top.Also the skill mini games vary in quality. Sally's strength challenge is very simple and easy, while Gavin's codebreaker is trivial once you got the strategy (start with 1111, replace the amount of wrong numbers with the next number until you got all right, maybe in wrong places, and then mix until you got them right), and Frank's lockpicking minigame is buggy and is purely by chance if the game decides if you got it right or not.The boss characters, aside from being nigh impossible to beat, have a hard time staying dead, which is super annoying. "Oh, you've shot me in the face, punched me in the groin and broken every bone in my body. I'll just hop in this elevator. See you soon"Many have compared this game to Disco Elysium, but the similarities start and end with the artstyle, and maybe a little bit with the point n' clicky nature of both.Mielenkiintoinen yhdistelmä osoita ja klikkaa -seikkailuja sekä vuororoolipelejä. Ongelmanratkonnan rajaaminen toimintapistein tuo haastetta, kun ettei voi vain väkisin kokeilla kaikkia yhdistelmiä. Hahmot ovat hyvin kirjoitettuja (poislukien tekobrittimurre) ja tarina hyvin kerrottu. Ja erityisesti pidin pelin ongelmanratkontaosuudestaMutta pelin pilaavat satunnaiset yllätyshyökkäykset. Jokaisen vuoron päätteeksi pelillä on mahdollisuus vain heittää vihollisia kehään, ihan vain viedäkseen toimintapisteitä, elämää ja parannusvälineitä, joten kun viimein pääsee henkihieverissä sellaiseen taisteluun, joka on käsikirjoituksesta, on siitä mahdoton päästä eteenpäin. Ei sillä, että edes täysin levänneenäkään olisi mitään mahdollisuuksia, sillä pomoilla on hyökkäyksiä, jotka kevyesti vievät puolet elämästä, ja ne voivat hyökätä useasti samalla vuorolla, mikä tarkoittaa että peli on jo hävitty.Hahmoilla on myös mielenterveysmittari. Käytännössä se tarkoittaa, kun mielenterveys on lopussa, taisteluihin ilmestyy lisäksi vielä aikaraja, kuin kirsikkana kakun päälle.Monet ovat verranneet peliä Disco Elysiumiin, mutta yhtäläisyydet alkavat ja päättyvät taidetyyliin, ja ehkä kummankin osoita ja klikkaa -luonteeseen.

_childDocuments_.review: to be honest, i don't get how the reviews for this game are this positive..it starts out really strong but gets really annoying after a while.personally i'd rate this game 3.5/10the artstyle and the voice acting are really really awesome imobut the negatives are just too much for me to recommend this gameto name a few: - the complete inventory system is meaningless and annoying, doesn't add anything more than unnecessary clicks- the background music bugged out in act 3 and was just a mess.. my ears need vacation now- save system is bugged, doesn't show the savetime (just 01-01-0001 for every save) and you cannot rename the saves that causes other problems like: not beeing able to hit "continue" on the main menu because it will load the first save on the list, which is not the correct one 90% of the time (you have to load manually and guess the right save) this problem exists since launch and even though the dev's know about it - it's still not fixed- the combat is REALLY slow and some bosses take forever to defeat, but you have to sit there and watch everything, since when it's your turn and your sanity is low.. the game forces you to react quickly (forced time-limit)i'm sure all those problems could have been adressed and fixed by now, but for me it seems the dev's abandoned the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam had a 'Maybe' score.I was first charmed by the characters, the music and the vibe of everything and I still enjoy that after 11 hours, but all that is held back by the nitty-gritty of mechanics and an abrupt, barely fulfilling ending that just stops after a literally twenty second cutscene after the final boss is killedThe adventure game and puzzle element itself is fine, but each character has a limited of action points they can spend in a 'turn' before events progress and things, most often bad things happen. At first the idea is neat, but the problem lies in the fact that there is no way other way to increase that limit in any way, or those points other than a very rare consumable that comes with some negative effects. Because of this, you'll be fighting alot of battles which I'll explain below but in battle you use the same points you get back to use on actions that you would on actions in battle. This means you can end your turn, get a random battle which feels like an 80% chance that only gets higher, spent all your points in battle winning it only to end it with none left and having to end turn again.. which leads to another battle. So on and so forth, you'll be fighting alot for very little gain.Unfortunately the battles like the rest also look fine but quickly turn into tedium with their health being nothing short of stupidly spongy, your own damage being very minimal until you learn to invest in certain skills, and remember, each point you use in battle is one you don't have for the adventure game part, which yes, includes healing and you'll need to heal ALOT.I don't regret my purchase, but I feel like I only tolerated this game when I should have loved it. Really needs some good and thorough QoL update or something

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game dripping with style and coherent artistic vision, good performances and a story that's easy to follow.Combining what is essentially a straightforward point-and-click adventure game with a tactical element is quite inspired, and while that gameplay aspect might be a little simple, it functions marvelously in the context of being an intruder and thief, as It helps nail the tone of being under pressure, while not forcing you into an uncomfortable stressful situation. I was pleasantly surprised by the mixing of genres, and genuinely impressed how well it worked to get me in the proper mindset.The turned based classic RPG combat, while functional and stylish, does have a tendency to drag out a little too long at times. The ability to skip combat animations I had seen dozens of times would have been appreciated.While you're given options to play around with, and are encouraged to experiment to a degree that I would welcome in any game of the RPG genre, I never really found a reason to deviate or really adapt to any given situation. It's the classic  problem with games of this type. Sure, I could have been more strategic, or I could just pound on foes and constantly heal until I win.It's composure system -a system that represents your characters stress level which can negatively impact the combat by first and foremost giving you a timer to select actions- while at least a little interesting, feels like the biggest misstep in an otherwise solid design. I either didn't need to worry about it at all, or it was forced onto me without really having that much of an impact as I'm used to navigate menus. I'm just imagining it ultimately being more of an accessibility hindrance rather than a feature. One could have replaced it with a randomized roll of the dice, or being denied a random ability and having to improvise (or both) and it would have been more interesting, urgent and engaging to deal with.Still, minor gripes. Ultimately, it's a game well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold definitely stands out for its unique visual style. It's dark but fun, with a team of lovable idiots as main characters. The comic-book-like style and great voice acting really nail a great tone for the game.You spend most of the game breaking into buildings, where the gameplay is a mix of point-and-click-ish exploration and turn-based battles.When exploring environments, the game is one of the best point-and-click games I've played. I usually dislike the way a lot of point-and-click games encourage an approach to just try everything. In Sunday Gold, actions take time, which increases the alert level of enemies. It's not so impactful as to discourage curiosity altogether, but enough to make you carefully consider whether an action makes sense, and what you hope to accomplish with it.To allow you to play like this, the game usually gives pretty clear hints as to what you need to do, or where you could look, so there is not much "guesswork" involved. I liked it.The turn-based battle system works for some casual fun: it's straightforward enough that you don't have to spend hours reading about the intricate mechanics and considering the best strategy, but also not trivial. That said, the harder battles often felt like they "dragged on" for a long time. I think in my ideal version of this game, the battles would be over quickly, when you either die or you win. Still, you'll probably have a decent time with the battles even if you are not normally into turn-based strategy games.I was a bit hesitant to try the game because I liked the visual style but I'm not normally much into point-and-click games and only occasionally play turn-based strategy games, but had a lot of fun with the game regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: Bloody hell, Sunday Gold is quite the cracker, isn’t it? 🎮 It drags you into its gritty world with a narrative that twists more than a politician's promises. The art style is smashing, and the soundtrack keeps you on tenterhooks. The characters are a right bunch of misfits, but you can’t help but get attached to the lot of them.Gameplay? Well, it's a cunning mix of strategy and skill. The combat system is like trying to drink tea without spilling a drop—tricky but satisfying. ☕ And the puzzles? Just enough to make you feel clever without needing a degree in rocket science.All in all, Sunday Gold is a proper gem. If you're after a game with some bite and a bit of wit, give it a go. It’s a bloody good time, I say! 🎯

_childDocuments_.review: I liked my time with Sunday Gold, it's slick and compelling with a fun gameplay loop. The game however categorically fails to communicate the way it saves your progress, or in other words, the game autosaves at only certain sparse points throughout a mission. This is at odds with the difficulty and challenging design of the combat. I liked being challenged by the combat and the ways it made me think of effective ways to solve the combat challenges. I did not like running up against a bossfight which was much harder than the goons before them and losing only to discover I had lost a literal hour of gameplay in the process. I thought it was a mistake to be throwing me that far back only to discover it was indeed the most recent existing savefile. If you're not going to autosave generously it needs to be made abundantly clear nowadays. Games that are upfront about how saving is on the player don't draw this ire. Games that are not upfront with this fact cause people to get burned and stop playing. I don't think I'll be picking up Sunday Gold to play to the end which is a shame. Buyer beware, I hope you have a better time than I did.

I don't regret my time with the game, it was a pretty good ride until the last bit. Your mileage will vary. And though i would like to, i cannot in good conscience recommend a game that fought me every step of the way and ultimately left me feeling so disappointed at the end.

_childDocuments_.review: If "I ain't readin all that," go to the bottom From what I can say starting chapter 2, this game is a very mixed bag. I really like the ideas happening in this game, but there quite a few issues that bring it to like a B- maybe C. The art direction is absolutely phenomenal, going almost for a Disco Elysium but more exaggerated and gritty, and the voice acting is most great apart from some minor roles.The general gameplay ties the Point and Click segments to the Combat segments with Action points, where quite a bit of actions take AP, and if you get into a fight, they don't top up, so you'll have to use a turn to get them back up, or wait a turn in the PaC mode. but what is a weird design is when you end a turn in PaC, the alert meter goes up, which raises your chances of getting ambushed by guards, which creates a weird dynamic with exploration, feeling like you're getting punished with fights for exploring the environment. I would this kind of style for maybe a procedurally generated game but with finely crafted maps, you want to explore everything, even more so with achievements. Another big segment is the skill minigames to do certain things like hack terminals, pick locks, or brute force objects, which brings the game down quite a bit because they aren't very fun or feel that good to do, like the strength minigame is where you have to move an arrow on a slider to the glowing area to pass a check, but instead of the needle like having some force on it, it's jittering wildly, so it feels like luck passing a check. the lockpick minigame is very precise and not very forgiving. I personally like the hacking minigame because it's like number wordle, but I can see it taking some time and it definitely ruined the tension for one part in act 3. The combat is a little funky, like YIIK without the minigames. they have a like levelheaded meter that gives you debuffs if it gets low which is a cool mechanic that also ties PaC and Turn Based Combat, like when it gets low, you have to do your turns within a time limit or you're skipped. ***This will be updated when i finish the game, but from 4 hours in i can say:9/10 visuals - very stunning10/10 voice acting - very natural line reads6/10 story - fun characters and good dialogue writing but general plot is not great5/10 gameplay - cool ideas but not done very well, trying too much at onceoverall 7/10 - hope the rest of the chapters get better but that won't change core game issues

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the tabletop RPG Blades in the Dark in the way that it flows.  The jobs are followed by a trip back to the hideout to tie up the jobs details and discuss the next job.  It leverages stress heavily, and there are negative health conditions that impact your efficiency.  Each character also has class specific special abilities.  It leverages timers.  If you like those mechanisms in Blades, you will find this game familiar and likely fun.  I think it's really well done.  The art is unique and looks great.  The action point system is leveraged in and out of combat, and felt fluid.  It always feels like each move that you make counts, and there is always some form of pressure.  I liked the characters and the story.  I'd buy it again.

_childDocuments_.review: A thief, a bouncer and a hacker walk into a bar.....Sunday Gold offers an engaging blend of casual RPG, storytelling, and puzzle elements, all seamlessly integrated into an intuitive point-and-click system. While the experience is generally enjoyable, there are occasional moments of frustration, like when the battle menu inexplicably vanishes during a crucial decision.Players embark on a wild journey alongside two unruly hooligans and a disgruntled employee, all with a shared goal: to strike it big and exact revenge on the formidable corporation. The journey unfolds in three distinct chapters, each with breaks in-between to enable players to reevaluate and redistribute their character's skill points. Throughout each chapter, players grapple with a series of puzzles in their pursuit of revealing concealed truths, all while maintaining a low profile. The battle system operates with clarity and simplicity, affording players the option to choose from a variety of skills, items, and more as they face off against their adversaries.As they journey forward, the heroes uncover disturbing secrets hidden below the surface. These unveil a dark side of sinister activities kept from the public eye. With each step, they unknowingly delve deeper into a dangerous path. Secrets unravel to reveal a nightmarish world, full of danger and sinister schemes. Each revelation puts them in a riskier situation, challenging their determination and bravery. What started as a simple journey now becomes a frightening adventure, where the heroes must navigate through a maze of terrors, burdened by their newfound knowledge.Overall I would recommend Sunday Gold. The game play was fun, the characters were decent, and the story was well....play it for yourself and see. PROS:+ Art Style+ BGM fits theme+ Story+ Gameplay LengthCONS:- Low variety of enemies- Menu click detection sometimes glitches- Weapon variety- Abrupted ending

_childDocuments_.review: Wow...Disco Elysium meets Guy Ritchie meets a classic JRPG with elements of an adventure game!I fully endorse this game for the style, the excellent characters and voice acting, beautiful stylish art, and compelling original story. It's a fun and challenging action roleplaying tactics game with lots of interesting unlockable skills and the puzzles do require a fair bit of investigation of the environment. The plot is fairly standard cyberpunk tropes of evil corporations and shady anti-heroes, but there's enough deviations to make it feel fresh like the uniquely cockney attitude.THAT SAIDThis game can be very frustrating. I found some of the 'puzzles' a bit finicky as they required you to know what to click in the environment with little feedback. Case in point one puzzle needed a key item to be combined with another item, but you can't do that from the inventory! I needed to find a special location to do what the characters insisted they could do by themselves. Secondly you're constantly losing Composure and action points and advancing enemy awareness while you look around, gather items, upgrade or use items, complete challenges...etc. This does not reset by itself so there's a number of times I accidentally activated a item or location that drained my composure constantly until every member of my team was a nervous wreck during random encounters. Loss of composure effects EVERYTHING. Your screen gets shaky and full of random words. Mini-games will shift graphics to disorient you. During combat you need to speed through your attacks or skills if you're panicking to avoid a character freaking out and attacking his own team. It's VERY unforgiving. You can limp away from one fight only to get thrown into another one with fresh enemies moments later before you even have time to heal from the last one. There's also some story situations where characters leave your party, and the group does NOT have a joint inventory. It is incredibly annoying when a character decides they'll sit out a combat...while taking all your EMP grenades and healing items with them. Characters can upgade items from any inventory, but only use them from their own special inventories: a little irritating. But regardless, I'm enjoying this game a lot. The near-future dystopia is intriguing, the characters are all shades of crazy or damaged but it fits the sci-fi noir feel to everything and they're never dull to hang around with. Combat is speedy and dynamic, although it does start out a BIT spongy. You tend to do very little damage and enemies can soak it up if their resistance to a specific type is high. Sometimes it's just trading misses, but there's always a ticking clock because your composure will take a hit when enemies breech allied defenses or you're so crazy you see a robot and freak out so you can't infinitely whale away at mobs. It's all balanced to feel tough but fair clearly and I'm interested enough in the events to follow them through. I did eventually relent to a walkthrough for the puzzles though (I was clicking in the wrong place)I'm happy I picked up this game, although I primarily did so to support the company so they'll make Dredge.Now THAT is a game I'm looking forward to!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, as it has a great mix of point and click adventure games, turn based combat, and rpg weapon and skill trees.  The puzzles are engaging enough to hold the users interest without being too easy or too difficult, and exploration is rewarded in the items you can find and the side quests that pop up.  I think with a few tweaks this game could be amazing, but as it stands I cannot recommend it, as some of the mechanics make it a real slog to get through.Here's where it falls short:- Towards the end, the exploration is stifled by the fights that pop up.  Each character has a limited number of actions they can take within a certain round, and these get eaten up quickly (2 action points to unlock a safe, and an additional 3 to then search it, really?!) and then the round resets, and often this means a pointless 10 min battle.  The issue is the Action economy used in the fight is the same action economy used in the exploration, so if you use up a character's AP to win the battle, that character can't do anything until you reset the round again, often leading to another battle.- The boss fights, especially in the final chapter are horribly imbalanced.  Bosses get multiple actions on their turn, and you have to watch a time consuming cinematic every time they go.  You also fight the same boss over and over again and in multiple chapters you won't know when the final battle is, as there is a final series of battles.  Battles are long and feel more like wars of attrition than engaging gameplay.  - Load out of weapons and equipment cannot be changed mid battleThere's a mechanic of what type of weapons each enemy is weak against and what they are strong against, but if you have your load out set up wrong for the battle you are in, you just have to slog through the battle and hope the loadout is good for the next fightOverall, I enjoyed the experience of playing this game, but got to the point where it was no longer fun to play, so I put it down and I will not finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a very unique blend of point & click and turn-based RPG mechanics. When I think of point & click adventure games, I think of the time spent collecting items and trying to combine or use them to solve puzzles. But since the game is also an RPG, you can also find equipment or consumables that might help you in battle, but are otherwise not necessary to advance the plot. And since the story is one big heist, time is of the essence and trying to brute force your way is a bad idea.You control three characters, each with a set number of AP (actions points) needed for most of your interactions with the environment (activating a mechanism, looting a body, etc). There are also actions that can only be done by a specific character, including mini-games associated with their talents (lockpicking, hacking, feat of strength). Depending on your decisions, you can waste your AP on something you don't need (or even nothing at all).If you have no AP left, you can end your turn to recover them, but the danger level slowly increases after each turn, which can reduce the mental state of your team (bringing handicaps if it gets too low) or trigger a battle. You'll have to play smart if you want to succeed, even if you are willing to spend time to collect weapons or upgrades.There are also a few branching paths in the second half of the game. They don't impact the story in a meaningful way, but they give you multiple ways to solve a problem, each with exclusive scenes and dialogue, adding some replay value.Overall, the "adventure" aspect makes me think of one big escape game, between the time management and the amount of puzzles, which is great in my book! ... Although that might also be because the architecture of this world is downright insane. Does the story take place in Racoon City?The battle system is easy to understand, yet engaging. Your main goal is to exploit the weakness of your enemy (pierce for humans, tech for drones, etc) to break their guard, then deal massive damage. If you are familiar with the break mechanic of Octopath Traveler, you'll know exactly what to expect.There are also plenty of status effects (both positive and negative) that your characters and enemies can inflict. For exemple, you can mark your enemies to temporarily increase your hit rates and damage, or try to knock them unconscious to interrupt a charged attack. And like the rest of the game, each action require a set number of AP, meaning you'll have to take a break from time to time to regain them. You'll have to think about the best course of action for each round, instead of blindly spamming your strongest attacks.There are some good ideas, but the execution is not perfect. My main complaint is the lack of variety, as each chapter only has three or four enemy types with little variation. And unless the party is split, it's really easy to keep your characters in good shape, both physically and mentally. Combined with the lack of rewards outside of XP, random encounters just feel like a waste of time, especially after reaching the level cap.Finally, I love the comic book style and the over-the-top chara-design. It makes the game stand out while fitting the dystopian setting, satirical tone and dark humor.Unfortunaly, the story itself isn't anything special. It's not bad, but it's nothing you haven't seen before, and while the aftermath of the final battle is cathartic, the rest of the ending is underwhelming. I feel like an epilogue is missing after the credits. Still, I enjoyed the characters and the world, so if there are plans for a sequel, I'll definitely check it out.If you are a fan of RPGs and adventure games, give it a shot. It's a refreshing take on both genres, and while it could be improved, it's still a enjoyable way to spend 14 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun mix of point and click adventure and turn based combat.  The voice acting is quite good as well, not something I expected from an idie game. After you get abilities that let you self heal and recover composure (sanity) then you can last forever.  The final boss is significantly harder than any other fight in the game, so don't neglect your combat abilities.  You really don't need to put too many points into non combat abilities as you can still get past all the mini games even at the lowest level.  Overall, very enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is that kind of games which no one has heard about. Why you should give it a try:- Sci-Fi story where bugler, combat medic and the IT-guy meet each other and plan to do a little, almost inconspicuous crime on Saturday night, nothing can go wrong, right?- The game has very unique and fascinating art-style.- First location (near bar) looks great.- Whole game main trio been goofing around. - Approximately 90% game’s been voiced, awesome!
