_childDocuments_.review: First things first, buy this on sale if the price is too much for a 15-18 hour video game. I enjoyed this game from start to end. Yet even though I enjoyed the story, game play, characters, music, and style there are issues that will make or break this game. Firstly the story can grab you but certain key story beats were not written well or seemingly forgotten. It seems as if they were rushed to conclude the game in 3 chapters. Perhaps the creators lost steam in finishing this project with a bang. But if you decide to play this fun game just know this will feel like the first part of a larger story. I hope they are able to make a sequel or put out free or at least cheap dlc. But they should have sent out a product that was a bit more refined with a more satisfying conclusion. Although considering I bought this at $15 I can't complain. I got an enjoyable experience, that I don't regret playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I give this game a 9/10. I loved the atmosphere and visuals of the whole game. Believe it or not, this game made me use my brain, not a whole lot of it but still. As much as I like this game though, it has it's own flaws. Most people would say that Act 1 is great, Act 2 is good, and Act 3 is tedious, and all of this is correct. I've never been a fan of point and click esque games, but this one is great, and if you ever have trouble with finding something to click on, a character even has a skill to use that highlights those things for you.Even though I praise this game so highly, the combat later on gets tedious. The first ending boss to the first Act is fitting, and is a great fight, even up to it. The second Act just has that same boss copy pasted *right before* the final second Act boss. The boss after that though is still fun in its own way if you could see it. The last Act though, just kind of derails the fun aspect of most of the game, making you go to the same rooms and areas constantly to do things and get items/continue the story. The final boss though, has two phases, with no break in-between. At least in the second Act it gives you one.Ending is kinda mid, and leaves quite a few holes for questions with absolutely no way to get answers unless they make a second game or dlc. Of course if they did do that, I would buy it, hands down. Even after bashing it, I still love this game, and would recommend it to anyone who even has the slightest interest in it as they won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: If you like looking around to solve puzzles you might like this game. If you just look on the internet to know what to do, don't waste your time as 80% of the game is figuring how to move forward in the story. 10% mini games, which I didn't really like and 10% combat which is super easy. The game is 3 chapters, there are moments when you chose between two options on how you are going to solve your situation. I played the game twice to see all the options.P.S. There's a bug with the gloves if you have them equipped and your lock picking skill is already maxed it's going to be harder to lock pick locks.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the art style was pretty cool and the story was probably neat but I found it impossible to pass even the first mini-game for Shelly. I would get 3 points every time then the reaction of the arrow would change drastically, slowing down so i wouldn't be able to fit it in the window. Combat is easy enough and the dialogue is ok but there's just not enough explanation in the mini-game tutorials for me to recommend it to anyone. 4/10 It's whatever.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a real unique treat, blending both point-and-click as well as RPG elements quite well in my opinion. It's story and characters are fleshed out and well voice acted, it's puzzles feel good to figure out, It has a pretty good amount of content for an indie game. It's not perfect, but I think it is worth the price tag, especially if its on sale. (Also the most positive negative review complains that the boss fights are strenuous and unfair and, while they obviously have the right to hold that opinion and the bosses will get harder overtime, I don't believe them to be unfair by any stretch. Just remember to upgrade Patch Up and to spread consumable items equally among your teams and you'll most likely be just fine.)
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how I missed this game: It honestly scratches my Final Fantasy/RPG turn-based combat itch better than almost anything else on the market today. It's an amazing game that cannot easily be described: A Action Point Based, Point-and-Click Adventure Game, with a Turn Based JRPG style combat system in a dystopian future British environment with enough character that it oozes out its pores?If you liked Disco Elysium, you should already be clicking "buy", if you like turn-based game, you should seriously consider it, if you just like interesting and off-beat stories and characters, you might have bought it already.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute thrill, until the 3rd chapter. After what felt like the billionth fight in a row with no rest for you or your characters to explore the room..... You get 7 ap, which you use both in the map and in battle. Guess what doesn't recover between battles unless you use a special "end turn" button on the map. But wait, it gets better. Every time you hit that button, you have a chance to get a new wave of enemies. And on the 1st and 2nd chapter, it's at 25-30% of the time. Chapter 3? Every. Single. Time. So you have to manage pulling down the beefiest enemies the game has to offer and come out of combat with your characters with some kind of AP so you aren't in an endless loop of battle.Which it wouldn't be so bad if you could dump skill points directly into boosting a characters AP pool. Or if enemies gave more experience as the game went on to offset the serious increase to enemy toughness.The puzzles are not even remotely hard in and of themselves. A couple expect you to take some extremely serious leaps in the logic though. Chapter 2's final couple areas had a few of those. And as others have pointed out, there is a serious tedium to the hunt and click aspect of the game for it's puzzles. Pixel hunters are not fun. For anyone. Ever. Stop putting them in games.The combat itself is about as basic as it gets, but the weapons need a serious overhaul or a way to improve them. The main character? Not a single change in his Melee weapon since the prologue. It still does very minimal damage too. The other 2? They've gotten some upgraded stuff but it's mostly garbage.Love the artstyle and setting, on first glance I had some Disco Elysium vibes. Definitely want to see more in this vein, but it needs some serious overhauling, and the play testers that signed off on more than a few of these systems should be fired. If you can get this for 10 or less, pick it up. Anything more is a ripoff.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Point and click games are my favourite and I love the blend of that in this game with the turn-based action. This game is fast paced which is enjoyable in this style of game, there's no slowly walking to investigate something it just skips right to it. I'm early into the game but so far I am enjoying it a lot. One issue I have found at the moment is sometimes you can click an option. For example left clicking on a computer to open up emails and for some reason it doesn't respond, find myself having to double or even continuously clicking.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Really a great throwback to the RPGs I grew up with - stuff like the later Final Fantasy games, Golden Sun, etc. Central gameplay loop is Final Fantasy-esque party of 3 combat punctuated by lengthy and interesting point and click puzzle segments. The voice acting is great, and the music is really top notch. There are a couple of small visual issues (Sally's leg clips through the back of her skirt) but otherwise the visuals are great, very reminiscent of Disco Elysium. Overall, amazing game, I want more stuff like this to be made, and I really hope the game is long. I haven't finished it yet, but I really want like a classic Final Fantasy 50+ hour version of one of these games. The top tier writing and setting and art make you (despite the depressing setting) want to wallow in the place the game creates.
_childDocuments_.name: Sunday Gold

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable experience, even if the game is unfinished.Takes about 15h to reach the "end", so at a small discount, this game is gold :)I recommend!To sum up the experience: bland RPG and fighting mechanics (dont come for those, you'll be disappointed) but stunning artwork and funny characters and dialogues in a dystopian guy ritchie's movie.Enjoy!For more details on what s really good:- it s beautifully drawn, voiced and animated!- the universe you play in is like Snatch and Altered Carbon had a baby- the characters you play are well written, funny, cocky, strong, scared psychos who have almost the same goal in mind- the story is really ramping up, getting crazier and exciting (for the first 12h out of 15h), which is good enough for me thanks to the first 3 pointsAnd for what makes me say that the game is unfinished (as in they put it out there way before they were actually done with it):- the figthing mechanics are unbalanced (80% of the skills are useless in combat, so you only use the same ones again and again for 15h)- the enemie pool is slim and repetitive- you loot a lot of consommable you dont need because the fights are too easy- you loot a lot of equipment you dont need because... the fights are too easy- the boss' figths are bland (gimmecky, lots of HP... so you just need to hack at them, no real tactic is needed)- the last Act doesnt end, it kind of stops right after killing the boss, there is not even a scene where the "heroes" talk about what happened and where they are at now that everything is over. They are not even getting back at the pub together for a pint of beer! Oi Mate! What a disgrace!

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday gold is a mix of persona 5 and an old school point and click game. Most of the gameplay is mixed three boxes, a turn based jrpg like combat system, puzzles, and turn based exploration system. The combat is like a persona game, if you have played it then you have already mastered this combat system, its not that deep but its enjoyable, just like the persona games this combat greatly benefits from having nice visuals along with nice sounds to make the ok combat into a enjoyable time. The issue with the combat system is that most of the combat is random fights that require little skill to win, its just the same fight over and over again at random times every time you end a turn in exploration mode, its not fun and a slog after the first mission, the game just needed more fights that were planned. The exploration mode uses ap to do actions, kinda like dnd. This system was obviously made to made point and click exploration more interesting and require some thinking for the moves you make. While its fun for the first mission it slowly turns into a slog and requires little strategy in planning someones turn, because the only drawback for ending a turn is combat nothing else. This turn based system could be interesting if more consequences where added into the game in response to ending turns, theirs literately a mental bar similar to games like darkest dungeon that is barley used in the game. Since turns dont matter you also loot everything which means you gain a ton of items and consumables which in turn makes the fights even easier. So all parts of this system are very flawed mostly due to the difficulty and the easy restrictions on ending turns. The puzzles are actually fun, but the exploration uses way to many, the last level has never ending puzzles, i just wish puzzles were used for optional content rather them being used constantly to progress the main story. Though the gameplay is disappointing, the rest of the game is very very good. Voice acting is amazing, and along with the great writing it really immerses you into this near future world. Characters are all very funny and have very good chemistry, they just really fit well into this world. Game looks great, reminds me of disco Elysium mixed with personas comic ascetic. Music is also great and makes the combat alot more fun. This games story is obviously a critique of rampant captalism and what people can get with massive amounts of money. It mostly shows the absurdity of our captalist societies, how as a society we can see the mistreatment of workers and people under this system but dont do anything about it because of how oppresion is portrayed to us by the media that is ran by these same oppressors. While it does do a good job at showing this part, i wanted more from it as a whole, i was expecting a larger story around this subject, but near the end it moved towards a more personal story about the villain. Though it went in this direction it was still good but i just wanted more. In the end, Sunday gold is a mixed bag, while it has excellent visuals, characters, and music, it is bogged down by its gameplay systems that are underdeveloped resulting in a slog after 10 hours of gameplay. I would recommend this on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a game that perplexes me, it oddly has the extremely similar flaws to that of We Happy Few.The theme is unique to current events through satire in a "what if" scenario.The characters whilst on a noble journey are not "good" people, yet have their own motives and are accurately portrayed throughout the story to remind their companions about such. Extremely interesting and makes me wish this game had more time for development so players could learn their backstories individually rather than one-liners and exposition dumps.The gameplay at its core is decent, but once you reach the later part of the game (most notably Chapter 3) it starts to get extremely boring when enemies are just time sinks and puzzles that have you jumping back and forth in the same rooms. I immediately knew that I was gonna be spending more time looking at the camera transitions rather than solving the puzzles when I unlocked three ways to enter adjacent or farther rooms in several branching rooms. It's just like a college student writing an essay and half-winging it on the last part of their work after being fatigued, it felt lazy and rushed that makes me believe they intentionally made the final boss as difficult as it was.Boss Spoiler:Decent title just held back by longevity.

_childDocuments_.review: The whole game being turn based was a nice touch.  Basically you get some action points to do with as you please more or less.  When they're out you can End Turn to refill whilst the enemy do their thing OR you can use items to gain extra points, maybe with side effects.  Each character has their own specialities so some things you have to do with them but most things you can juggle them around depending on what action points you have left.   Combat was mostly fun.   Loved the story.  The main characters are all decent enough, even if the main bad guy is a tad predictable and sterotypey.  All the voice acting was great, voices fit the characters to a T.  Warning for the squeamish, (I don't think this is a spoiler cos it's in the demo and previews) this game features mechanically altered dogs and people.  The art style isn't such that it would be upsetting to everyone but it might put some off.  Having said that it's an adult game for adults. Has a bit of a Disco Elysium vibe. _childDocuments_.review: A great RPG game with point and click puzzles!Love the artstyle, which has a dark but vibrant atmosphere!Soundstrack is great, but the voice acting in this is top notch! The bantering between the crew, ex-crew, and enemies really kept me engaged and made me want to explore everything!The combat is pretty straight forward (just think of a lighter version of Octopath Traveler, where you should focus on breaking guard and capitalizing on it) and the puzzles are pretty simple, albeit I had a few head scratching moments, but what makes it come together is that you have to manage your AP which is shared in both combat and puzzles/exploration. There is also a composure system (Think of Darkest Dungeon sanity system) where the more your composure drops, either through enemy attacks or in game events, the more the game works against you, ie: Rushed turns, debuffs, etc.There is definitely an item management as resources are somewhat limited, but you should be fine so long as you're not being wasteful.I would not say this game is rather long nor grindy, as I was able to finish it within 12hrs and was lvl 12-13 on the last boss. There is also a decent amount of back tracking involved for both progression and optional side stuff.All in all, I had a great time with Sunday Gold. It is a short-ish but challenging rpg game and I definitely recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Sunday Gold is a thrifty mash-up of point & click adventure gaming and turn-based RPG. It's dripping with style, with striking visuals, snappy combat sequences, a soundtrack that'll get stuck in your head and voice acting that brings the game's cast of big personalities to life. Those are the highlights. The bad news is that Sunday Gold also manages to combine the most frustrating parts of adventure games with the most annoying parts of turn-based RPGs. The only thing more frustrating than being stuck on a puzzle is having your attempts to solve it interrupted by random battle sequences. More than once, I ended up in a frustrating loop where I'd lack the action points to solve a problem, hit the end turn button, get a random battle, and come out of that battle without enough action points to move forward in the sequence. At that point, I'd have to hit the end turn button and roll the dice on another random encounter. There's a fun skill tree for you to customise your party as they gain experience, but I hit the level cap around the end of the second act - which made the combat encounters in the back part of the game feel increasingly tedious. I really wanted to like this one more than I did, and for what it's worth I did end up finishing it despite the frustrations I ended up having with Sunday Gold. I'd still recommend to anyone who finds the comic art look or pitch of the game enticing, but I wouldn't hesitate to throw in a few caveats.

_childDocuments_.review:
Once bustling and full of life, the city of London is in a dark and dismal state. Unemployment and homelessness are at an all-time high. Ethical boundaries are being stretched to their limit and corrupt billionaire, Kenny Hogan, is up to no good. It's up to ragtag band of criminals Frank, Sally, and Gavin, to put a wrench in Kenny Hogan's plans and bring him to his knees. But this is no simple job and there'll be a smattering of obstacles they'll have to face along the way...

Sunday Gold is a point-and-click, turn-based adventure game set in grim, dystopian future. Play as a ragtag trio of criminals to hunt down and expose the dark secrets of an evil mega-corporation and the malevolent billionaire behind it.

name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II
detailed_description: Reviews and Accolades OCTOPATH TRAVELER II Prologue Demo A free demo is now available! You can choose any of the eight protagonists, play for three hours, and carry over your saved game data to the full game. Travel beyond starting areas is restricted, but you can explore those corners of Solistia to your heart's content. About the Game The story takes place in Solistia, a land comprising an eastern and western continent divided by the sea. It is a bustling era, wherein large vessels navigate busy sea routes and the power of steam gives birth to new technologies. Some people thrill to glamorous stars of the stage and industry, while others are brought to tears by war, plague, and poverty. In this faraway realm, eight travelers hailing from different regions venture forth for their own reasons. Step into their shoes and explore the land as you see fit, using their unique talents to aid you along your journey. Embark on an adventure all your own. Begin your adventure as one of eight new travelers, each with their own origins, motivations, and unique skills. The series’ HD-2D graphics, a fusion of retro pixel art and 3DCG, have reached even greater heights. The story takes place in Solistia, where diverse cultures thrive from east to west and the industries of the new era flourish. You can sail the seas and explore every corner of a world that changes from day to night. Each traveler has a unique set of Path Actions they can use to battle townspeople, obtain items, take others along in their travels, and more. Where will you go? What will you do? Every path is yours to take. Familiar mechanics from the original game have been preserved, like the freedom to develop your travelers’ jobs and skills, as well as the Break and Boost system that made battles so exhilarating. New mechanics have also been added. Toggle between day and night with the push of a button to transform towns and the people within them. Path Actions will also vary by the time of day, enabling you to further explore the world. A new type of tale starring two travelers who now walk the same path. Each traveler possesses a unique latent power, which can be used to turn the tide of battle. Board canoes to cross rivers or sail the sea on a large vessel to voyage to every corner of the realm.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like the first one but better. Not to say this is completely superior to the first; that one has a slightly more enjoyable cast overall and a stronger lategame imo, but a lot of tweaks to the systems and structure work out in the sequel's favor. There are character specific EX skills, monster summons are infinite, latent power is new, thief/dancer/merchant swapped elements to fit more thematically, and the story structures flow better since each traveler's path doesn't follow the same chapter 1-4 flow, just to name a few. However, it can be too similar at times, such as the 8 main jobs being identical bar a couple move changes here and there. Basically if you liked Octopath 1, you'll like this one too, but it's not different enough to warrant a purchase if the formula was wearing thin for you near the end of the original. Btw my playtime is a bloated from grinding to level 99 and farming equipment I didn’t need lol

_childDocuments_.review: Big buyer's remorse on this. I got it because I felt a bite of nostalgia for the old JRPGs I used to play many years ago and figured I'd give this guy a go, intrigued by the concept of taking old-school art direction and bringing it into the present times. I've played through the first chapters of a bunch of stories and I'm struggling to keep on with the grindfest.So, the issues:- Extremely cheesy writing and stories. I didn't have high expectations, but this is beyond bad and probably viable only to children. Characters are super flat and stereotypical, and they do stupid or senseless things for the plot's sake.- Bland world. All the towns I've visited so far look like the generic JRPG town, connected by generic roads. Hardly anything memorable in any of them.- Grindy gameplay. Can't understand why one would stick with random encounters breaking world exploration outside of mere nostalgia. It was arguably one of the weakest aspects of games like FF6. If you enjoy fighting the same group of enemies 20 times and beating them with the same sequence of actions over and over, you'll enjoy this.- Narrative inconsistency. The heroes are all do-gooders on a ridiculous level (we have the warrior that detests war, the capitalist merchant that abhors personal profit, the assassin that hates blood, the inquisitor that despises inquisition, etc) and between quests where you save everyone the game has you mugging, beating up and extorting random NPCs from towns. Thise misdeeds are completely untied from the main narrative and have no consequence whatsoever. Like, why? - Unremarkable presentation. They picked the pixel sprites from the FF6 era and slapped them on a pseudo-3d environment with a depth of field effect, which is kind of corny on its own. There's also an effect with moving clouds overhead casting shadows on the world. That's it. They didn't bother animating or adding detail to anything the characters do. In a scene, characters were sitting at a table, and they were simply in their standing positions, clipping into the chairs. The SNES had memory limitations so the simplistic animations had their reason, but this is a modern game with a 60 euros tag and this just feels like lack of effort.The pros:- Pretty music, even tho it doesn't hold a candle to the older Uematsu works. Not nearly as dramatic, but JRPG music is kind of always good.- Intriguing combat system. Very customizable, very old-era FF like, smooth and satisfying combos. The only issue is that you'll need many hours of grinding before unlocking the cool stuff. In conclusion, this guy is way overpriced for what it is, a kinda shallow nostalgia trip into the era of SNES JRPG games. I'd only recommend it to people who miss the endless random encounter grinding or don't mind a very simplistic adventure tale with sparkly graphics and sound. But then, I think emulating an old SNES like FF6 or Chrono Trigger or something, would probably be preferrable and much cheaper.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: 5 | Narrative: 5 | Graphics: 5 | Soundtrack: 5 | X-Factor: 4Overall: 5I am incredibly biased.I love this game. It's one of those games that'll leave you feeling empty upon completion, because you foolishly went ahead and completed such a masterpiece of a game. This game builds upon the already amazing core that Octopath Traveler was, arguably improving upon the story, fighting, character depth (with a few exceptions), and post-game. Of course, just like any game, OT2 isn't without its flaws, but everything that the game has done right shines so brilliantly that I can't help but put this game on a pedestal. The voice-acting was great (both the JP and ENG vas were for the most part, all fantastic. WHY didn't you make Temenos sound like a twink Square Enix :c). The world is beautiful. It feels like 2.5D pushed to its absolute limits in the best way possible. And the music? Wow. After playing many games of this genre, it truly is a gem to find a game that has music that checks off all the bars of "sounds great, doesn't get repetitive, fits the atmosphere, and makes you *feel* something." OT2's OST has you covered on all fronts there. The turn-based fighting in OT2 is unironically the most satisfying and exhilarating combat system I've ever played in a JRPG. By a long stretch. Can you make battles fast and feel overpowered without making the gameplay trivialised? Yep. Are there multiple unique battle mechanics going on simultaneously to make the fights more interesting? Yep. Can you run actual strategies with your four party members that feel great to pull off? Yep. Need I say more? I usually play JRPGs for the story, and fighting tends to be a by-product of getting through the story faster. However. I enjoyed every battle I fought in this game. _childDocuments_.review: my recommendation comes with a caviatthe high praise this game (and the franchise) is gettin is beyond meyes, part 2 is slightly "better" than part 1, but it's still not great...not even "good"why you ask? the crux lies in the name. the concept beeing 8 characters, each sporting their own systems and stories, which as you might have guessed already comes to the detriment of a plot and cohesion. part 2 tries to bring the "party" closer together; there are some incombat comments that aknowledge to existance of the other party members and very rarely out of combat "interactions" between the cast; yet it's still hard to describe how disconnected and strange the whole thing feels.how does your party come together? you literaly go up to a new character (optionaly you can play their personal story chapter 1 asap) and they ask if they can come along...that's it. and that's also the programm for the rest of the game.neither does it make sense, nor does it feel immersive. it's better than part 1 where this whole party-thing was an utter mess, but it's so far from "good" that there's a lot of work ahead if they ever want to make this a realy good rpg-franchise. this weird design also progresses into the gameplay. you start with a character at level 1, do their story, just to meet the next char at level 1 do their story, rince and repeat. meanwhile you cross whole continents mostly in lvl 5 to 11 areas..."repetative" is the name of the game. which also extends to out of combat character skills, which are a good idea, but also suffer for the concept of 8 (characters), since many skills overlap and thus are pretty much pointless.this whole cycle repeats pretty much throughout the whole game, beeing it chapter 1 or each character's progressing chapters. it's just bad and disconnected.on the other side the turnbased combat mechanics are great. the progression mechanics (job-system and gear options) are great. the production value is amazing. the game looks and sounds (VO and OST) even better than part 1. the world feels realy diverse and designed (even the menues) with class. if i had one piece of advice to give to the developers it would be to get away from beeing forced to have 8 characters. make it 4, do them properly, design their interactions (narrative and gameplay), and bring in the name Octopath by other means (or just pick another name).i've played many rpg and jrpg, starting with NES back in the day. along the way western and eastern rpgs realized that to improve the feel of these singel player game you make the npcs, the party, feel more "alive"; one major step in this direction was the original Baldur's Gate franchise, but there were also plenty of jrpgs doing this...and it has kinda become a (logical) standart. in this context Octopath 1 and 2 just fail...there's no sugarcoating this. it's gotten better, but it's still just plain abysmal.why does my magic-scholar seeking revenge for the death of his family travel the world with a little girl wanting to be dancing star? why does the turbo-capitalist/socialist decide to help out the assasin seeking freedom and revenge...what's the girl with owl doing in the same group? it's almost funny how strange it is that these characters have little to no interaction while hopping from one live-changin event to another. it's a solid turnbased jrpg, which suffers from a disfunctional party-system, a disconnected plot and quantity over quality; i'd probably recommend getting it on a discount...and i hope the devs take a step back and reconsider their approach to party and story design.

_childDocuments_.review: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Title: A Masterpiece of Adventure UnveiledReview:Octopath Traveler 2 has left me utterly captivated, and my 5 out of 5 rating is a testament to the exceptional experience it delivers across every aspect. The gameplay in Octopath Traveler 2 is nothing short of phenomenal. The intricately woven narrative, combined with the freedom to explore an expansive open world, allows for a truly immersive and personalized adventure. Each character's unique story adds layers to the overall narrative, creating a rich tapestry that kept me engaged from start to finish. The open world design is a masterclass in environmental storytelling. The diverse landscapes, bustling towns, and hidden treasures create a sense of wonder and discovery. Whether following the main story or embarking on side quests, every corner of the world feels meticulously crafted and alive. The combat system in Octopath Traveler 2 is a perfect blend of strategy and dynamism. The fast-paced turn-based battles keep you on your toes, requiring quick thinking and strategic planning. The synergy between characters and the ability to chain attacks add a layer of depth that kept combat consistently engaging throughout my journey.In essence,  has not only met but exceeded my expectations. If you're a fan of captivating adventures, intricate narratives, and strategic combat,  is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterpiece of a JRPG that combines the best elements of the timeless, genre-defining classics (Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire, etc.) with contemporary features that add tremendous depth. The game really respects your time as it never felt like any one task took too long or was too arduous (towards the end of first gathering the eight playable characters, around the 10-15 hour mark for me, I was gettting a bit bored, but that was really the only time in my 65 hour playthrough I felt that way). Absolutely worth full price if you love JRPGs, but it also comes up on sale and I waited for a decent one.Classic JRPG in depth stories with many twists and turns, but all of the main story lines and even some side quests are voice acted, and well.  You can sit back and listen to the dialogue proceed automatically or skip through it, switching back and forth at will, which is great for me because sometimes I want to be engrossed in the story, other times I would rather be speed reading and getting through it as quickly as possible, and other times I would rather be fiddling about my house with the story proceeding in the background.Classic party turn-based combat but with puzzle like elements that require some thought, on the many unique bosses anyway, rather than spamming your best abilities (although there's plenty of that as well for random encounters while exploring and leveling). Each of the eight characters has a unique starting job and can have one of 11 other secondary jobs equipped, which can be swapped at will out of combat once they are unlocked. Each job has a unique set of abilities and passives to learn. This results in a great balance between customizability and simplicity.The music feels nostalgic and classic but with contemporary composition and audio quality. Many different acoustic instruments are featured across the some 60+? different songs in the game. It might be the single most outstanding feature of the game.The world feels full, with many, many npcs who you can interact with in a variety of ways unique to each of the playable characters. For example, you can steal an npc's items at night or purchase the same items during the day; you can politely ask for information from an npc during the day or bribe the same information from them at night, etc. If you're a completionist or have completionist tendencies, this can be a little tedious because every new town (and there's well over a dozen) you go to has anywhere from 5-20 different npcs to interact with. Pretty much all of this kind of interaction is optional and not voice acted, but overall its a great feature that adds a lot of hidden depth to the game.The main quests are very on the rails, i.e. the game tells you where to go and what to do. The many side quests though are not.  You have to use the clues you're given to figure them out using the various unique ways to interact with npcs.  Or just google them of course, but I'd recommend saving that for near end game, its rewarding to figure out or happen upon a solution to the side quests.The art is amazing. In the overworld it's you're classic pixelated sprites, but in combat the enemies are all beautifully drawn and literally larger than life.I honestly rarely finish games, I can't think of another in the prior ten years besides Divinity: Original Sin 2 and Chained Echos (another amazing contemporary JRPG). That includes the first in this series, which I got 25ish hours into and just could not keep going. Huge props to these devs for taking the great parts from the first one, fixing every single major complaint about it, and making this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I must...  recommend  to fans of classic console JRPGs. I previously did not recommend it, and I shall leave my reasoning for NOT recommending it up front, and then get onto the reasons to recommend it. To begin with: No mouse cursor.This is 2023. There is  excuse for a game developed in 2023,  to not have full mouse-and-keyboard controls. I want to  and with it, This is inexcusible. No matter how good the game itself is, this is inexcusible. I don't own a gamepad, I have no interest in owning a gamepad. Unbelievable that this game doesn't have full mouse and keyboard support.And preempting the inevitable: yes, I know there's a menu option that lets you use the mouse to select the next up and next down menu options:  I require being able to move a mouse  on my screen, in two dimensions - Z and X axis, updown/leftright, to a menu option, and  with my left mouse button to select it.Well, to start with, instead of making like every other game out there and completely throwing everything out in favor of a Fresh New Thing... Octopath II basically uses the same combat system from Octopath I. They added some things, but it's fundamentally the same thing, so if you remember the old dance of 'experiment with different weapons and elements to see what cracks this bad guy's shell, then hammer him with it,' you're up and running inside of five minutes.  (Looking balefully at you, Mass Effect...)Otherwise, it's a cheerful, lil-bit campy, return-to-form, like a Final Fantasy III/6J-era return to sprites for people who missed those things. I like the fact that they don't dance around the existence of brothels or corrupt noble lords who like a new girl every night, for example. I'm still getting stuck-in to the story and all, but so far I have an amnesiac apothecary axe-murderer in my party, a cheerful, bubbly dog-girl savage who turns monsters into vittles mid-combat, and a film noir knife-and-sword murderess thief who complains about the scent of blood, yet has no problem murdering her way across two continents in my party.

_childDocuments_.review: An easy recommend if you have any interest in JRPGs. The original Octopath Traveller was solid, this improves on it in basically every way. Satisfying combat and exploration. Lovely soundtrack and nice visual design. Nothing is missable, you can go in blind and not worry about messing up your characters. Incidentally, the story of this game is not related to the first game at all with the exception of a few Easter egg character appearances. I would play the first game first anyway, but this is absolutely a stand alone experience.A common complaint of the first game was that the eight characters didn't feel like they were really travelling together, due to their disconnected stories. That's not been entirely fixed here, but now there are "crossed paths" quests involving pairs of characters and a cool final chapter where all eight are involved. It definitely helps the party feel more coherent.There aren't too many quality turn-based RPGs anymore, even Final Fantasy is an action RPG now. If you like playing these games at your own pace, definitely consider this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very good game with some issues.I usually start to get bored with these types of games at the 40 - 50 hour mark. But this one kept me engaged throughout the 80 hours I put in. This is attributable to the 8 main stories of which all were good.I had 4 issues with the game that I did not enjoy.1) The graphics look like a smeared finger painting. (Very Blurry) Fortunately, there was a mod that got rid of the blurriness and at that point it was like a brand new game and looked great.2) The implementation of the character's special ability was clunky, For instance, there was a time where I had to give someone who was sick in bed some medicine. Instead of just giving it to her from the party, I had to individually select the one and only character that could give the medicine. Then, I had to make sure it was the right time of day so the option is available. (What does day or night have to do with giving someone medicine)? Finally, I then had to choose another menu where the command "soothe" is available. It was like this for all the characters.3) The boss fights in many cases were just frustrating as opposed to fun. The reason being that in many of the fights, the bosses have 2 forms. So you spend a good amount of time defeating the first form only to lose to the second. Guess what? You have to fight the first form all over again. These fights are long and repeating portions you have already beat was not enjoyable. My advice towards the latter half of the game is to be seriously over leveled. I had characters leveled into their 60's and was still losing boss fights. Who knows, maybe I'm just not very good. :)4) I wish the stories could have been played out from beginning to end without having to stop and switch character stories due to level restrictions. The game forces you to start a brand new story with a brand new character and lose all the momentum you had going from the previous story.Overall though, if you like JRPG's, this is one of the better ones.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2, like its predecessor, is a real masterpiece. It perfectly captures the feeling of old-school JRPGs, but with all the modern quality of life changes that make it less of a chore to play (except maybe random encounters, but that's fine) and the benefit of decades of development in video game story quality. All of the characters are appealing in their own way, and the tonal shift between some characters makes for a very satisfying, if slightly disjointed, experience. The stories range from amazing to decent. Unlike in some middle chapters of Octopath Traveler I, I never felt like I wanted the plot to hurry up in Octopath Traveler 2. Also, the music. THE MUSIC. If you can believe it, OT2's soundtrack is even better than OT1's. If you're a fan of old school JRPGs, this game is a must buy, even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I love RPGs but this is too slow and too tedious.  Writing seems really lackluster. You have multiple people with stories that dont really seem interconnected. I save a random guy in the snow. "Hey ill join you!"  What? how do you even know if we are going in the same direction? How about a cleric that just sees you passing by and asks you to help him defeat people you've never seen before? Motives seem flimsyI picked Ochette as my first char and this is unpleasant to play. The capture mechanic is fine but not being able to target?  Multiple times I try to heal and because it targets randomly, I heal the person with full hp multiple times.  You might say, well, you'll get better captures later.  Ok, but I have to enjoy the game enough to get to that point. Also looking at a monster capture index, I can see there are 5 identical captures that all perform that same healing skill, except they give different items on preparing them into food. Not just with healing but lots of captures have these identical attacks with minor differences in power. This to me is some illusion of variety that is  just a sprite swap.Let's talk about the exploring.  Loot and chest implementation is lazy. You go from point A to point B in pretty much a straight line and there will be a fork in the path specifically for an enclosed area with a single chest. You didn't stumble upon a chest and find cool loot, it was just sitting there in the open with nothing else around it.  That's all there is to the world. _childDocuments_.review: I said this would be GOTY 2023 the day it was announced, and I'm happy to say that this is genuinely one of the best JRPGs ever made. I'm only 20 hours in, and I would already passionately argue for this. And that's not just recency bias speaking, it's *that* good. Team Asano just doesn't miss. Yet another vast world with gorgeous visuals and an absolutely jawdroppingly fantastic soundtrack, alongside eight unique protagonists, each with their own stories. Their main objectives remain theirs alone (which I personally don't mind), but there are new crossed path stories which intertwine some of their tales. Plus, it's very likely that all of their objectives will tie together in the end, like how the first Octopath did its storytelling.The turn-based combat remains crisp with the delightfully crafted Break/Boost mechanic, alongside some improvements to how the jobs play, plus the introduction to Latent Powers, which can be used to turn the tide of battle or press an already existing advantage.I could go on and on about how Octopath Traveler II is the best thing since the first Octopath Traveler, but I don't want to drag this review any longer (for now at least). Easily one of the best purchases I've made. Must-have if you enjoy turn-based combat, or just videogames in general.

_childDocuments_.review: The amount of quality and care that went into Octopath Traveler II compared to the first is night and day.  A huge step up from it's predecessor in most every regard.While I considered myself a fan of the first, Octopath Traveler II has wildly exceeded any expectations I had, and is a title I now consider a JRPG classic.  Each of the Traveler's tales are filled with intrigue, save for one that did have to build up it's "slice of life" story to reach a compelling end.  Additionally, the characters interact far more as well.  At any time you can view banter between characters in the journal, no matter your team composition.  Characters also call out to each other in combat, either singing their companions praise, or showing their care.The HD-2D style has never looked better.  Beautiful character animations, as well as a lot of dynamic camera work really emphasize bigger moments in both the story beats as well as combat.  No longer is every "advanced job" hidden behind mid to endgame optional bosses, but rather tend to be available fairly early, save for 2.   Character customization in general feels great as well, with the classes being shaken up, some better, some worse, but still puts a fresh spin on them. The day and night cycle was not a feature I initially was interested in, but fairly quickly did I find a lot of excitement surrounding it, as my Travelers path actions drastically changed, and my party could accomplish more each time I hit a city.  Shortly after, I also began to realize that it was key for solving some of the sidequests, which also feel much more improved, rewarding those that pay attention to the game's environments and NPC details discovered through said path actions.All in all, I'm very pleased with my time spent with Octopath Traveler II, and would strongly recommend it to anyone interested in JRPGs, and would even say it's worth checking out to those who may not have had the best time with first entry.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually around the 70 hour mark in an RPG I look forward to the end of a good story.  Octopath Traveler 2 is the first game I've played in a very long time that I don't want  the story to end.  Enjoying it very much! Incredible masterpiece from Square.  I love just about everything about this game. I only experienced a very tiny slowdown in the middle of the game, unsure of where to go.  Once that obstacle was tackled I had no end of choices.  They've come a long way in character development from OT1.  Still some characters that usually get left behind.  I still always have to bring the scholar, and almost never the dancer.  I think the weaker classes could have used some skills to make them more useful.  Temenos is the cleric, I almost never use him in his chosen role, I use Cassti instead.  The only real negative for me.  They could have possibly eliminated grinding a bit better, not that there is a lot of it, perhaps 10% of game play time.  But at 80 hours I have a 20 level difference between my highest and least used characters.  I thin this is ok mostly.  It's not like the level 40 characters are useless in a party with level 60 characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Re-reviewed: Octopath II represents an evolution of the series—both good and bad. The developers expanded on the visuals in a way that feels like a natural extension of the original. The story strives to be bigger, and loses a little of the intimate feeling of the original, but is still ultimately quite satisfying. The difficulty curve is substantially more shallow than its predecessor, and thus perhaps more accessible. But the spirit is very much here, and newly-released bonus content definitely more than scratches the itch for a true challenge. Finally, that music. It's another outstanding score from Nishiki. Overall, like its predecessor, this game is exactly what it wants to be. It's an homage to the games of 30 years ago, but done in a modern way. It's got style, substance, and heart. There's no upselling, no microtransactions, no battle pass. It is my kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is a MUST play for turn-based RPG fans - having played OT1 is also a plus but not necessary since the story is mostly separate; although you'll be missing some references / call-backs to the first game.OT 2 improves on the core mechanics of the first game with some much needed QoL changes. The OST is amazing and the story of each character is really well done albeit not being equal to each other - this cannot be said however for the "main" story of the game which feels lackluster and is the same criticism that the first game has. Think of it as the game having 8 different stories (With very minor interactions between the characters during the said story chapter) and one connected main story that ties up everything at the end.I cannot recommend this game to everyone - it's mostly story driven and can bore people who prefer action-RPGs. For those who stick around though, you're in for a treat!

_childDocuments_.review: The combat improves from the first game, adding some additional layers that make combat engaging. The story suffers from the same problems as the first game. Most of the individual stories are just that - individual stories that don't involve all the travelers. The best improvement came in the form of "crossed paths" where there was actual character building and interactions between the main characters. Dungeons could do with some puzzles every now and then, instead of a single path branching to items. The final boss introduces a couple of mechanics that were genuinely awesome and I would have loved to see them expanded upon in the rest of the game. The game isn't perfect, but it was enjoyable and worth the money. If you liked the first game then you will probably like this one as well.

_childDocuments_.review: It felt strategic and satisfying, and the best part is it only gets better-- all the way up until the game's final moments, may I add. I had countless moments where I would just sit and think 2 or 3 turns ahead to cook up a strategy for big juicy damage. The times where those strategies worked were some of the best feelings I've ever had playing a video game. The amount of options to customize your team and the freedom to create wild build also is incredibly welcomed-- especially the latent power system, which is new to this game. Each traveler has access to a secondary job to help customize their playstyle, but they all have their unique latent power that differentiates them and makes sure they aren't made obsolete by another traveler. Combat is easily my favorite part of this game.  Random encounters always get annoying for me eventually and to be honest it felt like there were a decent amount of them. Fortunately, the combat was so fun that I felt like I wanted to fight for most of those encounters, and in the other times I popped on a skill that reduced encounters, which is very welcome and made me enjoy overworld exploration much much more. On the topic of encounters, there thankfully wasn't too much grinding. The way the game spaces out the traveler stories makes for pretty solid progression if you switch out your party members often. I think I only spent 4-5 hours total out of my 115 hr playtime strictly grinding. I'm fine with the HD-2D graphics, and there are some moments where the game looks really beautiful. Sprite animation is intentional and fluid, and battle effects are really pleasing to look at. Not astounding, but certainly nothing bad. One of the best OSTs I've heard, ever, in anything. Each song is beautifully crafted to fit the setting it plays in. There of course are reused, generic songs that play a lot, but even they sound good. Slight spoiler (I guess), . There's basically nothing to complain about here-- sometimes it feels like I paid $60 for an album with a game on the side and I love it.  I  say not every story was created equally, but in the end I found each traveler's story to be good or even great (besides one). Coming off some games with thoughtful and interesting writing, there were certainly moments that had me questioning "wtf is this." Since the stories progress in chapters (40-50 minute chunks of story), a lot of the time characters have unusual development that make the writing feel really poor and rushed. There might be a side character that is introduced to help develop our protagonist who undergoes a complete character arc in the same chapter. It makes the side character feel super artificial, like they were engineered and produced in a factory specifically to develop our protag in 30 minutes.And, I think, inherently, the way this game is structured can lead to some disappointing or downright upsetting moments like those. Obviously, the game's structure is incredibly important and is what makes this game special. But if the game wasn't structured the way it was, this would be really easy to fix. The biggest example of this, for me, was one of Throne's chapters that had branching paths (slight spoils ahead).  To me, this made the game feel very disjointed and unresponsive to the way I chose to play the game, and it took me out of an otherwise intriguing story. Again, it's because of the way the game is structured, , I just can't ignore how these moments hurt my overall enjoyment at parts.I kind of just ♥♥♥♥ on the story a ton, but let me make it clear that it also left me moved and full. The times I do play JRPGs, which, again, are rare, I play long, long games with overarching stories and memorable characters-- this game is not an exception. I grew to love each and every character (except one) in their own ways. As cheesy as it is, you really are along for the ride on their journey through Solisita. Again, I thought (nearly) every story, overall, was well done and had satisfying conclusions. The variety in the traveler stories were also good, there's a good mix of happy-go-lucky fun and insufferable trauma. There are plenty of moments of joy, sadness, anger, and everything in-between, and the lore actually is quite expansive and well thought out (again, it doesn't always play out smoothly, but in the end you can appreciate it). Seeing the way the travelers' individual stories came together, and how they ended was really satisfying.It was in the game's final moments when I really realized how special of an adventure I just played through-- there is no other game that contains an experience like this. There is no other game that, despite it's large flaws, has left me this astounded and satisfied. There is no other game like Octopath Traveler II.On paper, my number scores might look... not great. I would rate it higher if I could, but unfortunately numbers don't care how I feel. Trust me, I feel like this game is worth your time and will bring you enjoyment. The experience is much more than just a score, and I implore you to start your journey.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the previous Octopath Traveler, I purchased this game with concerns that it maintained its quality while improving its flaws. Fortunately, this was done in spades. Not only has the quality of music and combat remained intact, everything has been given a touch up.The combat, though still challenging in some areas, allowed for more versatility with the expansion of job systems and latent powers. This allows for more challenge in later fights, where the player must understand their skills and class combinations to come out on top.In terms of level design, the landscape got a face lift. Dungeons were more varied, so it isn't just cave #13. This was achieved with more in-depth application of assets, increased quality of paths, and the abandonment of the 90 degree turn being the sole method of transportation.In terms of story quality, the worst story in the entire cast in Octopath Traveler 2 is more compelling than the best story of Octopath Traveler 1. There are points where I have even laughed over the interactions between characters. And the overall charm of these characters makes it difficult not to get lost in the story.There are many other things this game has improved over its predecessor, but to listing them all here would be redundant considering most others have talked about them as well. All in all, this game is worth it at the price, but if you are willing to wait for it, the game is especially worth it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first one, you'll like this one. It's mostly more of the same, but they add some additional things to increase interactions between characters. However the glaring issue of the main story lines excluding your whole party still remains. Honestly I don't really know how they'd solve that issue without trying to come up with an infinite number of possible dialogue options per scenario purely dependent on who's in your party at the time, so I don't really fault them for that though it was a major criticism at the time. I do find most of the characters more likable this time around aside from one or two. The battle system is pretty much the exact same other than a few extra skills and abilities here and there. They did improve on the out of battle actions for all of the characters and gave two per character so everyone is useful in some capacity or other whether it's night or day time.I would also say the story lines of all of the characters are all just as compelling as before as well. A few are better (Throne > Therion for example) and a few are worse (Chastii < Alfyn (sp)) Overall though it's a beautiful game and they've done nothing but improve on the visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: TL DR: If you liked Octopath Traveler (OT) 1, you gonna love OT2. If you've never touched OT1, you can freely jump into OT2 (no pre-requisite), and you should, because OT is probably becoming a classic JRPG.Really, OT2 basically polished everything from OT1.- Prettier graphics.- Improved combat mechanics with good added features.- Added interesting feature of day/night cycle that affect character path actions as well as combat.- Maintained its notable strong point in OT1: Great music scores.- New set of character stories of similar quality to OT1.- Characters now actually acknowledge each other's existence somewhat, with duo chapter stories and a final all party chapter to enforce the fact that they actually travel together.The only down-point I found is that though everything became better, there is no groundbreaking changes anywhere.For a game called OT2, I expected some bigger leaps from OT1, but OT2 feels too similar to OT1 and is pretty much a big expansion rather than a complete sequel.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler II is by far one of the best RPGs I have played in quite some time, the first game was quite special to me and the second one absolutely achieved that same place the first one did. From the little choices to the big the game continuously surprises you and innovates on the previous title's combat, story, music, and aesthetic. Spending time in this world again and journeying with the travelers was a pleasure. _childDocuments_.review: I'm 12 hours in so far, and this may be one of the best JRPGs I've ever played. OT2 takes everything great about the original and hones it for the better. The graphics, animations, and writing are all vastly improved. The way classes work has been tweaked as well, mostly for the better. I haven't delved into the new system for the secondary classes enough to give a verdict on that. Currently, I have 5 of the 8 travelers, but I already like all of them so much I'm struggling to determine my go-to main party. In the original, I pretty much had my set party from the get-go. Also, the composer from the original is back for the sequel. Not only do they create new motifs and themes for the new characters, but there are new arrangements of tracks from the original that are gorgeous (the new arrangement of "Determination" in the opening of Hikari's story is just one example.) If you loved the original Octopath Traveler, this one is even better. If you're new to the series, the story is pretty disconnected from the original so far, so you could start with this one. If you like JRPGs, this game is a must-play. Honestly, if you enjoy video games, this is a must-play.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: After 73 hours of trance-like gameplay until I got 100% completion, I'll say this, Octopath Traaveler II is one of the best games I've ever played. I was overjoyed learning that a second game had come out after beating the first and let me say, this game improved on everything I has dissatisfied with from Octopath I. The story(?) of the first game was one of the stories of all time. But Octopath II has actual engaging storylines for each character that didn't feel like they paid a high intern to write a fantasy story(I'm looking at you Tressa). I started with Osvald because the idea behind his story intrigued me and I'm glad that I did! He may not have the most complex story out of the line up, but Square Enix delievered a revenge story that surpasses Primrose's by far. I really enjoyed all of the other stories, Temenos and Castii's stories are tied for my favorites. Onwards to gameplay, I love the feeling that Octopath brings with it's gameplay, it's highly rewarding to those who come up with strategies that blend all of the character's strenghts together. I thought that having job guilds in this game was a nice touch, and how the secret jobs in Octopath II don't just completely dwarf the main 8 in power. Sure you can break the game pretty early on and hit the damage cap within your first 10 hours, but it's more fun to just experiment and learn what every abilty does to theory craft the best way to defeat the next story boss.All in all I love this game to death, and I think that everyone should give it a shot(Or at least the free demo which gives you 12 hours to explore the game before you buy it).
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: Cannot recommend this game, no matter how much I try.Just like the first game, it's 8 completely separate stories, and not once do they ever come together in a meaningful way. Every character is just "meh" at best. The one good thing this game has (just like the first) is the soundtrack.The whole Day/Night "cycle" is a sham. You can sit there and just spam a button to make it day and night over and over again. Yeah, because that's immersive. All this does is allows access to different skills for each character...skills that are just recycled from the first game (like Bribe, Seduce, etc). The game is so ridiculously easy (you can even check the forums for this one). It's bad when you have to run from 80% of the battles or else you overlevel everything and it becomes a snoozefest. The fact that you have to escape battles just to keep the game in "balance" is a joke.If you absolutely LOVED the first game, then sure, buy this on sale. If not, avoid this and spend the money on a game that actually has some care (and story) to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Another fateful journey, another game vying for my favorite. At 130 hours of play (and probably a bit more to go), Square Enix has done it again with OCTOPATH. Where the first OCTOPATH was a traditional fantasy with warring kingdoms, fantastical beasts, and evil gods, OCTOPATH 2 is a more modern fantasy covering themes of betrayal, greed, and wrongful accusations (with plenty of the first themes thrown in for good measure).Pros:- The characters are as deep as each needs to be, and each of their stories is compelling. - Yasunori Nishiki has created yet another soundtrack that I'll be playing for a while to come- Improvements on the story cohesiveness. While OCTOPATH was 8 separate stories with mostly overlap in place, OCTOPATH 2 makes sure to weave each story past the others, even giving some side quests that tie specific characters directly together.- Day/Night system. It's just a nice little update over the first game. Now, you have twice the music as each area has a day theme and a night theme. It also helps you tune the difficulty as you like and opens up new ways of looking at a story.Cons:- It's only 130 hours. They did a fantastic job of wrapping things up in that time, but I want it to keep going.- In all seriousness, my only complaint is that one particular travel method is helpful twice and then never again. I suspect that's on purpose, but still.

_childDocuments_.review: still obviously playing this for quite a bit but I will list the things they improved upon compared to the original thus far1. the characters actually interact in combat and acknowledge each others existence. They also interact in specific duo chapters, they are no longer just there with no dialogue with each other. Even in the original the only time it was acknowledged there was even a party story-wise was the post game lol. They fixed this.2. The stories of this game versus the 1st one are WAY better I personally liked Therion's in the original but for the most part here? I actually care about the plot of all of the characters they even made me ACTUALLY LIKE THE PRIEST'S a lot. Temenos is a gem of a character.3. this is a small thing but the starting chapter in 1 was always if you started with 1 you got 1 and it was balanced around having 1 member. Now if you had 2 it was balanced on that and so on. They changed this so all chapter 1's are unique and you cannot bring the other party members with you. Instead for several of them you get temporary party members either for the whole chapter mostly or for a bit to grind levels with real fast. They even gave those temp members their own skill pool and unique dialogue. I actually really like this. 4. The added day and night system is fun and there are in fact more abilities for all characters outside of combat (and some in) from it. They still mostly gravitate towards the 4 actions in the original but with some twists. Getting info, obtaining items from npc's, knocking people out, and recruiting temp npcs to use in combat. none of this changed but the way it was implemented makes each character feel a bit more unique in how they do these things more so than 1.on top of this they added unique ways the 4 characters who can recruit people do so by giving either passive buffs like merchant selling things or battle buffs like the dancer combo with whoever she has to do a song ability on top of it. Not all of the recruiters have these unique abilities to combo with the NPC but its neat to see.5. The Hunter character now has UNLIMITED uses of all monsters yes you read that right all monster abilities can be spammed forever as long as you don't turn them into food and keep them. This makes her SUPER versatile and really fun to use because of it.6. You can now have duplicates of the base jobs other than the original. You want 4 merchants for some reason? you can do that by getting 3 licenses and using the base merchant. You do have to master the skills multiple times on various chars to get more licenses but it is a thing you can do. In the original it was limited to 1 per job at a time, that is still the case with the extra jobs not attached to any characters defaultly but that's fine its just nice to have that kind of versatility in builds to mess around with combinations.7. Somehow the OST is even BETTER than the first game I loved the first's music but this one man it blows it away and they even have different versions of all non battle themes for day and night its really nice!8. Rebalancing was done to all jobs to make them more useful and also nerf a few of the super strong ones for better balancing. Some skills were moved to a different class some were removed and just fully changed for instance merchant no longer has as much weapon versatility with hired help 2 of the original weapon types are now gone so they can't do that anymore. Unless you want to spend a load of money for the veteran to hit all enemies with all weapon types not as efficient or really doable early game though. On the other hand the dancer now actually feels MUCH more useful than before having an ability to lower shield gauge REGARDLESS of their weakness and overall improvements to the skills they have to not JUST be all about buffs they can now fight too and lost some of the buffs nobody really used anyway.9. there is now a boat you can purchase when you get enough money like most jrpgs that let you reach new areas you could not before and access secrets. Bosses, loot, entire dungeons, quests, etc. this was not at all in the first game.10. The unique talent bar that now charges for each character and does a different action is really fun think limit breaks but you can choose when to use them instead of being forced to use them when they activate. It adds more versatility to the cast on what job you should specialize in to make the synergy work out. I really like them as they all fit the character they are attached to.11. Almost all if not all enemies now actually have attack animations of sorts. In the original it was traditional old school jrpg where the enemy flashes then an effect plays. That still happens but they actually have attack frames instead of just 1 sprite animation standing there. This of course includes bosses and even minor mook enemies. I was surprised they gave the normal monsters animations at all but they did. A welcome addition.Also to add on to this the civilians animations now match the protags when they are wielding weapons instead of generic civilian sprite animation cool thing.12. another small thing but the bosses actually talk during combat. This seems trivial but in the original it was just dialogue boxes, Hell the character the boss is associated with will sometimes even have lines during combat and unique lines when attacking, getting hit, or fully charging BP. Small things but nice to see that add up to a really fun experience!thus far that is all I can think of but when I fully finish the game I will be back with more. I heavily recommend buying this though its very well done!

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is an improvement over the first game, which is quite an achievement because the first game was excellent.The most memorable experience I had in OT2 (no spoilers) was when I entered a new area I hadn't visited before and it was night, even though the previous area had been daylight. The button that switches the area between night and day was not working. The music changed, becoming low and somber. While running along, I entered a random battle, but the music did not change. The enemy was really creepy. After killing it everything returned to normal. When I left the area and then returned, it was still normal, as if the horrifying encounter never happened. That was just a masterful use of game mechanics, music and foreshadowing. There was no narrative or any other warning this would happen. Well done! You scared the hell out of me.OT2 uses the same formula as the first game where you experience 8 stories. The gameplay and graphics have been improved.My only complaint (as a filthy casual gamer) is that there is no difficulty setting and no way to switch off random encounters. It's been 36 years since Final Fantasy 1, I would like the option of actually playing a game instead of running into brick walls every 50 steps! We should be allowed to grind when we want and to travel when we want. Forced random encounters make progress very slow and annoying.I am aware of Evasive Maneuvers but that only reduces the encounter rate. If it switched off random encounters altogether, that would be ideal. More games need to follow the example of Bravely Default 1 and include a menu option to opt out of random battles.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this one pretty much cements Octopath as the premiere JRPG series running to date, given that Final Fantasy has strayed into action/cut scene territory for good. The pacing is a little non standard and a lack of enemy power scaling forces some early sequences to be far too easy given that you can progress in one of eight possible directions at any given time, but that doesn't lessen the enjoyment here one bit. The story is top notch and is broken into small and digestible bits with frequent save opportunities. The graphics remain phenomenal and the voice acting is solid, particularly given that characters have all sorts of custom animations and battle cries even in really obscure situations using non-standard classes. The music is superb and has subtle variations from day to night in each area that really set the tone well. Everything about this is what you want from a modern take on a classic game play. Also, kudos to Square Enix for being the only remaining company that takes the time to do enough quality control on an RPG before release that it doesn't have to drop endless patches with hundreds of bullet points spelling out corrections for its quests. Everything is perfect from day one.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute masterpiece, which gets absurdly good in many ways.This game got absolutly robbed of nominations and tbh straight up winning the RPG category. First starting with the presentation, it has beyond gorgeous graphics, both from a technical sense and artistically. It trumps every almost pixel art game in the water. The OST is full of bangers and masterfully done.The storylines are all very interesting (bar one) and governed from a singular thread carrying the plot forward, though it may not appear as such at first. 7 of 8 characters are amazing from the start, the last one I grew to appreciate over the course of her chapters.Combat is fantastic from the build variety you can set up your characters with, to the actual combat mechanics and enemy variety, boss fights were always a treat, and balance well done too as it never required more than a few dozen minutes of grinding at worst, and only 2 or 3 times over a 70 hour playthrough.The social interactions with almost any random NPC in the game puts games with a much larger scope and budget to shame as well.I loved both Sea of Stars and Chained Echoes and would recommend those two to anyone, similar games in many aspects, but Octopath 2 is hovering miles above both.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; It's a game that would be a 10/10 for a hardcore JRPG fan, but some quality-control issues make it an 8, with the first being a 6 or a 7 and the average being a 5.Generally, everything from the first game has been improved in some way. Gameplay, job customization, music, voice acting, story telling, quests, side-quests, world design, dialogue, pretty much everything has been taken a step up from the first Octopath. Gameplay is much the same as the first, but with new additions that spice it up. Latent Powers and the new guild license system all add a new layer of depth to an already-great battle system. For those who don't know, altars and subjobs have been changed to class guilds and licenses (akin to asterisks, or job stones, or whatever), with each class guild giving you up to three licenses for each job. This means you can have a party of four warriors or two merchants and two clerics, or any combination of jobs. You're no longer restricted to only having one character per subjob.In addition to that, followers have been enhanced and given new depth as well. Agnea, the Dancer, can have her dances augmented by her followers for special effects like granting additional BP, or letting them reflect attacks. Partitio, the Merchant, can hire NPCs to not only perform various attacks, but for out-of-combat bonuses as well. Things like earning more money from sales, getting discounts on purchases, earning more money via the Collect skill, or giving a small chance to receive purchases entirely for free. Yes, I did savescum to proc the 1% chance to get the boat for free, because I think it's kind-of charming that they let you do that, even if it wasn't really worth the time and effort to save the 100k.All the world-building elements have been enhanced as well. Characters all interact more and even have quests together, voice acting and dialogue is generally a step up from the last game, and almost every single NPC has meticulously detailed backstory with every town having entire arcs and stories set up that you can only discover by scrutinizing them, which I love to pieces.The only real problem is that there are some glaring quality-control issues that only surface several hours into the game. The most notorious is mistranslated skill descriptions. The first ones you'll run into are Enervating Slash and Resilience; The former says it removes positive effects on the target, while the latter says it enhances all of the character's incoming healing. They actually remove all of your positive effects for a power boost, and boost all your outgoing healing respectively.There are also some pretty bad audio balancing issues. Several characters lines are not balanced with respect to other characters or background music. Ori from Partitio's chapter 2 is probably the first example you'll encounter and is much louder than anyone else, with her lines crackling her microphone on occasion. There are also some who are too quiet, like in Temenos and Throne's crossover quest.Overall it's a great game, though.

_childDocuments_.review: The original game was the first draft of a formula: a battle engine revolving around breaking enemies by attacking their weaknesses and saving up Boost Points to strengthen your moves; eight unrelated travelers on eight unrelated journeys, finding themselves slowly dragged into the machinations of a single villain; a gorgeous art style; an entire world to explore, with secrets to find and stories to hear; the greatest VGM OST since Chrono Trigger. THIS game barely alters said formula; in that sense, it plays everything safe. That said, it also executes on the formula PERFECTLY, with stronger characters, stronger stories, more secrets, even crazier bosses and character classes, and jaw-dropping music and graphics. If the third sequel is as stagnant as this one, I'll be concerned, but right now, this is the perfect Octopath Traveler.
