_childDocuments_.review: Hate to not like this game - but the pacing of the game is pretty slow. Decent amount of natural grind to the game. Story pacing is slow and uninteresting. The dialogue is pretty difficult to listen to. The RPG combat elements have an interesting foundation - but just didn't connect for me. If the enemies in the game scaled to your party better, it might be more interesting - but 90% of the fights in this game are one-sided beat downs that take you far too much time to execute. You never really feel threatened as the player and thus the system is largely uninteresting. The gameplay loop is extremely repetitive with no difficulty anywhere to be seen. You spend your time ferrying your squad through an exhausting number of random encounters to reach really poorly written story segments that drag on longer than they are welcome. I will confess - I did not make it deep into the jobs system that is available in the game and only hoovered up 6 of the companions - but I just could not see how they were going to ultimately make the combat interesting, and it looks like I was a good 20-30 hours of grind away from being able to evaluate it.This is not even including the large amount of faffing about you can do in town using your character's skills to steal stuff you don't need or find rumors about stuff that you don't want to know.Glad people have been enjoying it - but definitely not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love music, this game is worth playing for that alone. Underrated feature - THE BATTLE MUSIC IS NOT ANNOYING. I'm a massive fan of OST (I had a decently large YT channel dedicated to it until - ironically - Square Enix shut me down) and this is easily the best one I've heard so far this decade.I haven't gotten super far into the game yet, but I already feel like I've got my money's worth, even at full price. The story is well-written, well-presented, and the English VA is excellent. It's also so far very concise, unlike your typical wordy, flowery, lengthy JRPG dialogue. There are random encounters, but the encounter rate feels perfectly tuned. The areas you explore (as far as I've seen) are pleasantly compact and not maze-like, but there are plenty of secrets hidden throughout. The character customization is simplistic but the battle system is fun enough. Octo 2 has addressed *almost* everything wrong with the first. The only things it missed were shared party XP and no longer being tied to an old style save system. Otherwise the game delivered on the conveniences and QoL that I think is mandatory for modern games. In regards to the story, characters, looks, and music the game is aces all around. It may honestly have one of the best game OST's ever and I really don't feel like that is a stretch. All the classes got some adjustments and whether or not you like those is largely going to be personal preference, for the most part I did. The cast is much more endearing and likeable then then original bunch, whom I liked about half of. Their stories are gripping and they interact far more than they did in the original. The world is beautiful and the dollhouse maps are varied and fun to explore. The combat continues to feel good and be fun to play, frankly a lesson Final Fantasy should take from this game, but they already burned that series to the ground. Thankfully for those of us that long for the FF of old stuff like Octopath exists and after 2 I will most certainly be playing an Octopath 3. Overall an 8.5 or a 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Were you a fan of the previous Octopath Traveler? Then you'll definitely enjoy this. That being said, if you were NOT a fan of the original, this isn't really doing anything so new that it brings in fans who weren't already sold on the concept. It's minor innovations on a pre-established formula set forth by it's predecessor and doesn't stray too far from that road. As such, it's a 100% recommendation from me if you were a fan of the original. If you weren't though, then unfortunately I don't think enough has changed here to ultimately convert anyone. For those who were fans though, here is a brief (non-spoilery) list of the improvements you can expect to find here:-Another slammin' soundtrack (arguably better)-Significantly better VO (I'm on the English dub, cannot speak for the Japanese version)-Slight updates to the combat system to keep things fresh enough for another round-More interaction between the characters that the previous game was sorely lacking-As a result of the above character interactions, the story has a bigger impact and feels less disjointed-Adding different path actions based on if it's night/day gives you more ways to interact with the world-Robbing everyone is still as fun as ever

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I have such conflicting feelings about this game.  Most of the game is fun, with interesting stories and a boat load of jobs, skills and equipment for you to mix, match and play however you want.  When you play through that 95% of the game, you genuinely feel like the developers *want* to create a fun game and have succeeded in doing so.But then you run up to the final bosses of each story, and you realize the developers absolutely abhor you.  The story bosses are a completely gimmicky mess that veer into one of two directions: either you get lucky with the *correct* party setup and just steamroll over them; or you guess incorrectly, use the *wrong* members, jobs, or accessories and it becomes basically impossible.  Then once you inevitably guess wrong and wipe, the game forces you to go all the way back to the last town to switch up your party, replay a bunch of incredibly boring fights, skip a ton of boring cut scenes you've already seen, before giving you another go.If the devs are so lacking in talent that they have to resort to gimmicks and setup checks, then they should at least have the decency to put the final save point / party change point right in front of the boss.  Making you teleport all the way back to change party members, trek through 3 maps and skip 5 cut scenes just to take another swing at the boss is just downright player hating.Leaving this down vote here so I can remind myself to think very, very hard when Octopath 3 comes along eventually.

Steam Curator: There is definitely a lot of features and gameplay mechanics to utilise in this game to justify a solid playthrough, especially if you are a fan of turn based FF style games. Several classes and subclasses to choose from, plenty of skills to unlock, attack boosting and unique ultimate abilities that unlock even more creative ways to deal damage to your enemies. _childDocuments_.review: There's no mixed option so I guess I'm hitting downMinor story spoilersThe game works very well functionally, mechanics are well thought out, the multiple classes allow for a diverse set of comps and the end game bosses find ways to shake up the core mechanics and keep things interesting.But like solid mechanics are only 1 half of an rpg.The individual stories can be hit or miss, its subjective, but at the end it doesn't matter all too much due to the games structure. Since the game only encourages you to find other party members, but at no point requires you to actually accept them to your party, the games 8 stories play out as if you only have the one character. This goes against the games end chapter, which implies a sort of "found family" connection to the characters, despite their minimal interaction. On that note, the travel banter from Octopath 1 makes a return. The banter being inconsequential, unvoiced, optional dialogue that allows for slight interaction between party members during chapters. The quality of the dialogue is also subjective, but runs into the same problem as before, that being, after the banter ends you just have to go back to pretending the other party members don't exist. A solid improvement over the first game would be the introduction of the crossed paths. After certain requirements are met, 2 characters will go on a side story that expands on the world and provides much needed character interaction. Of course there are only 8 of these crossed paths in the game's 64 chapters, and the crossed paths are between 2 characters and 2 characters only. A nice addition, but by no means a selling point. The games world building is a bit sloppy as well. The quirky mountain village that Ochette visits is also the home to a genocidal cult the tries to kill Temenos. Partitio's run down mining village is also a hub to an active slave trade. The Kingdom of Ku is a japanese-inspired warring imperialist state that is so powerful it can threaten a kingdom located on a entirely separate continent and no one else. These details are rarely, if ever, mentioned outside of the particular characters story. While there are thin connections that run through each of the 8 stories, they often don't lead to much. That is until they are all offloaded onto the player during the final chapter. And that just returns back to the main issue which is that octopath traveler is just a fundementally awful way to tell a story. The game wants to build up to a grand epic finale, the 8 travelers fighting against the eternal shadow that's been pulling strings from the beginning. But why? yes the world ending is a bad thing but why is anyone doing this? Once Osvlad gets revenge on Harvey, why is he still hanging around? Jobs done, pack up, revenge over. Agnea's story is about becoming a star and bringing smiles to peoples faces, why is she fighting the god of darkness? The game responds, "who cares, they've been good friends this whole time". Don't get it twisted, the epilogue and end game are extremely enjoyable, but it relies entirely on the player accepting the fact that the game said, "all of these characters ideals line up with no conflict and they are good friends who care deeply about one another" and putting in the bare minimum. Fixing this would be hard, as creating separate dialogue accounting for all possible party combinations would take over 16 million scenarios. A better option would be having each character follow a set path when you choose them at the beginning. ex: picking Ochette first would always have you meet Throne, Temenos, Osvald, etc in that order. while picking Hikari first would have you meet Castti, Agnie, etc. This solution would allow for the player to still have a sense of freedom, while laying out the structure to tell a proper story. Characters could be picked up at different levels in different areas, and the different paths each characters take allows for greater replayability. There would have to be some sacrifices, but it could work.Much like the first game, Octopath 2 provides well though out mechanics, engaging bossfights, and fascinating worlds to explore, but is a game who's story leaves much to be desired. it's alright/10

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Highly polished JRPG with excellent visuals, combat, customization, worldbuilding, and music. Minor story and pacing issues. OT2's gimmick is playing a standalone RPG story quest for each of the 8 main characters. The party size is 4, so you bring along 3 other characters as you work through the current protagonist's adventure. (When you're simply exploring or doing side content, you can play with any 4 characters in your party.) The main characters' 8 stories run parallel to one another, but they eventually join together at the endgame as you fight "the man behind the curtain". It's almost impossible to write 8 memorable stories, but Square Enix came close. 6 of 8 stories are excellent and feature pathos, comedy, and mystery. I loved the different flavours of heroism in these stories! The remaining two characters were dull. I skipped through most of their dialogue. However, considering the insane ambition of the game's premise, 6/8 is a great success ratio. OT2's overarching story is a slow burn. (You won't start connecting the dots between the 8 main characters until you've played for a few dozen hours). Thankfully, it has a memorable payoff in the endgame and epilogue.I must give props to the world design. OT2 features 8 richly-designed regions (one for each party member). it's so much fun to explore the map. Every location is chock-full of detail; you're rewarded for taking your time. The exploration is enhanced by OT2's unique look. The visuals combine pixel graphics with modern shading and lighting effects. The end result is a beautiful aesthetic that can compete with classic and contemporary JRPGs.OT2's biggest strength is its battle system. It's deep, challenging, and strategic. To defeat the toughest bosses, you need to think several turns ahead, synergize your party's abilities, optimize your loadout, etc.   I appreciate that the strength of the player's strategy is just as important as party level. There are nearly limitless customization possibilities in OT2. You can modify your party formation, secondary jobs, support skills, equipment, etc. The game is very well-balanced, so each player can develop a unique and effective playstyle.There is a huge amount of optional content in this game (side quests, optional dungeons + bosses, hidden locales) and all of it is high-quality. However, the side quests could have been more ambitious.Yasunori Nishiki created an epic score for OT2. It's over 7 hours long! Each track elevates the corresponding locale, story beat, or battle. One final note: OT2 is a very long game and pacing can be an issue. There were a couple of times in my playthrough where I was either overleveled or underleveled for my main story quests. When underleveled, I needed to grind trash mobs for a couple of hours. When overleveled, the random encounters started to feel like a chore.

_childDocuments_.review: So I might only have a few hours on Steam, but I've beaten it twice on switch, including the final boss, so I'd say I'm more than qualified to comment on it. The only difference I know of is it runs better on pc. This is the best RPG I've ever played. I'd give it a 9/10 or a 10/10. No, I'm not a connoisseur of the genre, but I really cannot sing the praises of this game enough. The production value is off the charts. I am a huge fan of the 2.5 D visual style and this game capitalises on it extremely well to produce a simple but beautiful environment. It looks especially great in 120fps on PC. THE MUSIC! Yasunori Nishiki composed the soundtrack for this game and the first one, and I am pleased to say he is my most listened-to artist of all time on Spotify. The songs are intense, atmospheric, and unstoppably catchy. If you watch video-game content and particularly Nintendo content on YouTube you've heard at least one track from this game, even if you don't realise. Some favourites of mine include Hikari's theme, Partitio's theme, Agnea's theme, For the dawn, Normal battle II, and a bunch of others I won't name for spoiler reasons. the story is formulaic, yes. However, in Octopath II, the team pushed the boat out and decided to experiment with the formula to improve the pacing of each character's story and the results are great. While I still think Primrose has the best individual plot of any Octopath character, the general quality here is far higher than in the first game and there are really no stinkers. Every character is compelling and supremely likeable. The overarching story is more fleshed out with Crossed-path chapters leading up to it, although it still isn't a focus of the experience. That's not a critique though. Octopath Traveller isn't a large epic tale like your average JRPG, it's an anthology of short stories. In Octopath II we have a series of short tales all connected by the general theme of hope & nihilism. Go in expecting this and you'll have a much better time. Oh and I haven't even mentioned the battle system. I don't really like menu combat. It's boring and unrealistic. I LOVE the system in this game. It's focused on optimisation and efficiency. Planning and strategy? not too complex but endlessly deep. Job system? unique and highly re-playable. Grinding? entirely optional! sure, the game recommends level 45 for each final chapter, but with a good strategy and a bit of practice you can easily do it before level 30, especially with good gear.Pros:> amazing soundtrack> Great characters, I love all of their plots. > interesting and deep battle system that is highly re-playable and actually makes you activate the neurons> Visuals are beautiful, especially on PC where the resolution and FPS aren't limited> improved in essentially every way from Octopath ICons:while I love this game to bits, I have a few very specific nitpicks:> what is the point of the protagonist mechanic? an absolutely tiny complaint overall but one that still carries over from the first game. let me switch all my characters from the beginning. It's the whole point of the game. >speaking of switching, the "formation" mechanic in the last part of the game... really should just be the system for the whole game. Do we really need taverns? (except to restore rep ofc). I know that sounds a bit radical but I genuinely can't think of a good reason to not just let us take all 8 characters in the party, even if only 4 can participate in a battle. again, the game is called OCTOpath, not QUADropath. I would say keep taverns but make them optional.> If there's a third game, I hope path actions are expanded on a bit. I'm not a fan of pure RNG or a level cap to decide their success. I don't necessarily have a good alternate suggestion but I think it could be improved. conclusion: if you like good video game music, are a fan of interesting menu combat, or just like the idea of a victorian era JRPG this game is great. If you haven't played an Octopath game, this is the one to try. If you played the first one and liked it, you will like this one! If you played the first one and didn't like it, there's a good chance you may like this one! They improved heavily on the weak areas of O.P. I, and enhanced its strengths.

Less of an OTII issue and more of a general problem. But I think this one does it well enough.The stories are... okay. _childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is an instant classic, monumentally fantastic JRPG, and I recommend it on the same level that I recommend Final Fantasy 6 and Golden Sun. It is Amazing, however I can see that there is still room for improvement.Octopath traveler 2 is better than Octopath traveler 1 in every single aspect. Dialogue, voice acting, writing, combat, exploration, items, world building and cohesion, connective plot, Characters, the literal only thing I can't bring myself to say Octopath 2 did better is the music because the music is absolutely amazing in both titles.Most of the character's stories (Hikari's sucks) are actually interesting and compelling plot lines that made me want to see them through to the end. The connective tissue between these character's stories is much more present and makes them feel more tied together. There are a lot of very subtle references to things that occur in other character's stories or the places they go that make them feel like they're actually happening in the world. There much more character interaction, having 4 additional mini stories featuring groups of 2, and a lot of travel banter that is actually quite relevant and worth paying attention to. Towards the end of the game however we get to see all 8 of the characters interact and sadly it made me realize that if they could have had something of that level throughout the rest of the game it would probably be the best RPG I've ever played.The combat is similar to the first game and you'll find no complaints from me there, I loved the flow of combat in the original. However, to freshen it up there is this new layer of strategy with some more mechanical depth that is very welcome. Every character in the game is given something unique to them and it just works, it's great!The first game left me with a sour taste in my mouth at the ending because of how unresolved everything felt, but thankfully they were able to wrap things up in a MUCH better way. When I finished the first game I never wanted to play another game made by this studio again. I'm not quite sure what got me so excited for this one, but I'm glad I decided to give them another chance, because now I can't wait to see what they make next.

_childDocuments_.review: The TL;DR: Octopath 2 is a great experience only marred by a few blemishes, some related to gameplay, some not. Play it if you love JRPGs; read this review if you're curious about some nitpicks.I encourage reading other reviews for insight into what makes the game good. This review isn't about that. Instead I want to offer feedback on aspects of the game that I thought were poor or lacking in quality, and that I want to see improved in a DLC or sequel. Four criticisms in total, two major followed by two minor, (indirect spoiler warning):1) Agnea's story. With eight individual stories in the game, some are bound to be better than others. But Agnea's chapters are particularly poor because they clash with the rest of the setting and the gameplay. Why is any part of Agnea's story resolved through combat? Excluding a few exceptions, no part of her story naturally demanded combat in-universe. It could have been solved through talking. But combat "has" to be there because octopath 2 is a JRPG and not a visual novel. This infringes on an otherwise solid immersive experience, where things (mostly) happen because they make sense. Note that some of this criticism applies to Partitio's story as well, but less egregiously so. These stories should likely have been altered or even swapped out.2) The translation. There's no mincing words here. The translation (Japanese to English) is terrible. In benign cases, the English script only replaces one word for another with similar meaning. But a significant amount of the time, the way characters express themselves is so different to the original Japanese script that you end up with full tonal shifts or personality changes that the original creators could not possibly have intended. Translations like this must be avoided; they insult the people pouring their hearts and souls into making characters that players are supposed to love and care for.3) More content and / or more customization. Although the gameplay in Octopath 2 is great, it can end up feeling monotone. There are not many classes in the game, and those classes do not have very many abilities. This means that once you've played a class for even a short period of time, you've seen everything it has to offer. I wish classes had greater depth, or that there were more classes, so as to encourage experimentation and avoid long-term staleness. I do not want X class to be doing the same thing at hour 40 that they were doing at hour 2. 4) Visually (Un)attractive characters. With Octopath 2 it is clear that Square Enix is continuing the trend of conservative female character designs with little to no sex appeal. I would simply like to voice dissatisfaction with this choice.Although I've been critical in this review, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Octopath 2. I still think it is a great experience, and a must-play if you enjoyed the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically this game is like a dream come true of all of the great mechanics from your favorite classic sprite based JRPGs (FF5, FFTactics, Chrono Trigger, Xenogears, etc) but with the FX, 2.5D graphics, and UI design of a modern game. The first game was one of my favorite games to come out that year and one of the only games that I went out of my way to do the super boss for due to the mechanics and tactics being that satisfying to play. 2 just takes everything that it did and made them better, the stories were more varied and interesting, the characters more complex, the minor mechanical inconveniences improved upon by buffing weaker classes, making each character more unique with Latent abilities, and improvements when interacting with the world. My one major gripe with the first one was the lack of your party members interacting with each other, and while they have improved that with this one by including the Duo side stories, more banter options, and the ability to see banters that were missed due to party composition, I still think that they have more they could be doing with it. I love each of the stories but I just feel that they would be improved by interweaving them more. Also... Minor spoilers for Casti's chapter five: The fact that after you defeat the boss they ask her "How does it feel to take a life" When she had the secondary job of warrior and has actively helped other characters on their quest for murder is just... Jarring. I get that they wanted to make her a pacifist... But when it just isn't supported mechanically it just created a severe dissonance between the narrative and the mechanics of the game. I felt much the same when dealing with Agnea's story as well, though it doesn't frame her as quite so deliberately a pacifist.Even with those relatively minor gripes it was still a 9/10 game for me. I have played about 80 hours so far and I have no doubt that I will play at least 20-40 more and have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler II has a lot of good things going for it. It does have that nostalgia feel you crave, but completely falls flat everywhere else. Good Points: --Good general feeling with battle system--Walking around, exploring new areas, awesome.--Overall it's a cool game, but not a great game.Bad Points: --Character stories are boring and copy paste with each other. Read dialogue, fight boss..... Read dialogue, fight boss..... Read dialogue fight 3 bosses. --Boss difficult comes down to how many turns they get. Basically they will speed up frantically when the boss has low health and start getting 4 turns a round. That's not how you adjust difficulty in a game. It's extremely lazy. --This game has almost no boss mechanics. --High level bosses are basically HP sponges with nothing to offer. If you are high level enough they can't really do anything to you and you just have to wait until their hp is gone. Which is super boring gameplay.--I don't care about all eight people and all eight stories. After awhile it gets boring and I can't bring myself to level up the characters I don't want to play just to finish their story. At least with a traditional RPG, you can kinda deal with it. The story is there, then gone and move on. Oh no not this game. You have to go all the way through all the trash storyline you don't care about. Octopath 1 was terribleOctopath 2 was just less terrible

_childDocuments_.review: After 100%ing this game I can honestly say it was an absolute blast to play for almost the entire time. The music, combat improvements, updated job systems, story, small character quips and moments, etc., all made for an enjoyable experience that had me hooked from the first minute til the end.Story wise, outside of Agnea's story (which I wasn't a huge fan of), the individual arcs were amazing, and there were a few times where I found myself saying wtf just happened that was crazy. The cohesion between the characters is heavily improved upon from the first game, and it actually makes out a unified endgame threat that excites you. The true final boss was amazing, and the mechanics they incorporate were awesome (the music slapped too). The only other knock I have, is that the leveling after ~65 (when you're trying to prep for the "secret" boss) takes forever. Yes, you can cheese with Dancer's and Alrond, but it still took a good 10 hours or so to get everyone leveled, cause x100 exp RNG can be harsh to work with.All in all, if you are a fan of the Octopath 1 or JRPG'S similar to this, you have to play this game. If you're on the fence about getting this game, then there's no shame in waiting to get it on sale and playing it then. Even if you're super casual and play it just for the stories/music/combat, I'm sure there will be at least one or two stories that really keep you coming back.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is very good at it's high points, it's low points are unfortunately much more copious than it's high points.  Some of the good points:⦁	Hunter's no longer the worst class in the game as Provokes can be used infinitely without wasting the monster and the starting creature while weak can always remove at least one shield point most of the time.  Early on Hunter's also a decent source of money.⦁	The stories of Ochette, Temenos, Osvald, Throne, and Hikari have a really strong story that once you get to the final chapter you see how they all interconnect.  The characters are all interesting and varied, they feel like the game's true party.⦁	The addition of the crossroads stories and banter are a welcomed addition to try and connect the characters together better.'⦁	Ochette and the Beastlings are a welcomed addition to the lore of the game, though I wish it explained more how they managed to avoid falling to darkness.There's a couple of major issues that the game has that drags it down starting with the inherited ones from prior games:⦁	Lack of Experience Sharing with new and inactive characters.  This is a major problem that's still in the game as you must complete all 8 character's stories completely to beat the game, and that means you need to level up both groups individually to level 50 in order to be high enough level to complete the story.⦁	The main characters don't have strong motivations to stick together starting out, and none of the main stories of the characters require other characters.  The crossroads do help, but they really should be something that needs to be done in order to further a given character's main quest.⦁	Finished too soon, the genuinely interesting and passionate storylines about the principle 5 characters they really end right as they get interesting and really would'be been better with another chapter or two.  The interesting cillains die too quickly and don't make reappearances till laterThe new problems this specific game has:⦁	Agnea and Partitio feel completely unconnected to the story of the game, their personal quests have nothing to do with the main villain of the game nor do they have a strong motivation to stay with the group.⦁	Castii's story is too predictable and could've been better if it was a Typhoid Mary sort of story.  While there's connections with the main story, it shows a lack of passion for this specific character's story and motivations.⦁	Banter is unvoiced which lessens it's impact, and sometimes the banter is about unrelated things rather than more interesting questions like Ochette asking Temenos about the origin of her species never happens and is a missed opportunity.  The banter between the principle 5 characters really should've been them trying to puzzle out what's going on in the story.  The developers should take some notes from |Tales of Berseria| on how to do Banter.⦁	The game's overarching plot point is ironically weaker and less interesting than the individual characters villains (like Harvey).  The game's actual villains are revealed last second and don't really make much sense given the narrative.   They're not really shown to be evil until that point, and one of the actual villains is only ever seen in a flashback and has no place in the actual story.  You don't even fight them while they're disguised, or have them mock you before running away, nothing.  You only learn that they're evil because an area you were already in manifests a journal that acts as a confession of wrongdoing which really feels out of place.⦁	The secondary characters from a character's story don't really have much of an impact in the other character's stories, even those that stick around like the hunter's talking Animal Companion really ought to be able to contribute something to conversations or banter but don't.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a much improved game from the first entry, but there's issues still here that have been exacerbated to some extent. If you don't like/tolerate grinding, stay away from this game or look up some guides to push through the character stories. Good ---Writing Quality. Great characters. Every character is at least likable, if not lovable. Their personalities will keep you invested and their banter is much more natural than the cast of the first game. Most of the stories are well written. I don't think the Dancer's story fits very well with this game and probably should've been changed for something else. With the nature of the stories in this game being much darker overall than the first, the Dancer's story stands out like a sore thumb. It's also the most generically told of the bunch. Most of the stories are predictable/tropey, if you've played any amount of JRPGs, but the Dancer's story was the only one I actively called every plot twist from near the beginning of their journey and found to be completely trite. Every other story was decent to great (The Merchant and Scholar stories were my personal favorites). Combat. It continues the break system from the first game but gives you plenty of options and ways to optimize your party within that system. Good system. Not a ton of change here outside of minor improvements. Classes. Good variety in the classes, including the hidden jobs. Some are game-breakingly powerful if you go through the effort of optimizing your characters and giving them appropriate sub-jobs and unlocked skills. Art. Same 2D-HD engine as the first game, but with better particle effects, more angled shots, etc. This might be because I played the first game on Switch, but the particle effects stood out a lot more vs the first game. Just a better use of the engine to show off the beautiful pixel art throughout the game. Music. The soundtrack is fire. Filled with great battle tracks and many excellent motiffs that you likely won't be tired of if you're playing this at a reasonable pace. If it's the only thing you're playing every day, you might tire of the battle themes, since there's only a few. Neutral ---Side quests. Some of these are good, and some are a waste of time. A lot of them aren't very engaging and might require you to look up solutions, unless you're very attentive or spend an extra couple of hours seeking out the answers for yourself. A lack of guidance on these quests can be cool, but sometimes there's *no* guidance, and that can be an issue. They made a better balance here than the first game, but they still need work to balance making side quests too hand-holdy vs like finding a needle in a haystack. Cons ---Grinding. Okay, you're probably thinking "it's a JRPG. It's gonna have grind!". Well, yes, but this is excessive grind. I'm a regular MMO player (FF14) and I find this to be a grindy game. I've beaten all the Etrian Odyssey games, dabbled in Disgaea, etc. I know grind. This is excessive. Of my 70 hours playing (I was alt-tabbed out of the game for 25+ hours, so my total time is a bit high) about 15-20 hours of my playthrough was pure grinding against mobs. I used all the XP boosting items and abilities, equipped the Octopuff and Cait accessories to have them appear more often, and even used the end-game strat of hiring a specific NPC to boost the XP output from battle. The grinding is just too much, all the way through the end game and will likely require 2-3 extra play sessions of your total game time to just be properly leveled for the final boss. It's recommended level is 70+ for the fight. The next highest dungeon is lower 50s. This is akin to the FF3 grind for the Crystal Tower where you just grind for levels due to the boss' damage output. Overall, pretty good game. Just be aware of the grind if you plan on playing this. Overall a solid 8/10 pre-end game grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, well, well...I wrote my review for Octopath Traveler after I got a 100% completion. I did get this game on release and got 100% in like 80-ish hours but didn't write a review for some reason. Not that it was forgettable or anything, it was quite opposite, especially with certain character lines and insanely crafted soundtrack. After the recent release of the soundtrack on streaming platforms, I wanted to write a few words.Octopath Traveler II, just like the original game, offers a huge world you can explore, even more expansively than the original. You get the same main jobs as in the original (Warrior, Merchant, Thief, Dancer, Apothecary, Hunter, Cleric, Scholar), and get to look at the world from all those perspectives. Stories of the characters are much more compelling as standalone stories, and this time, you get to see an overarching final compared to the original's subtle and optional resolution. And just like in Bravely or Final Fantasy series, you don't need to play previous entries to understand the game. There are reoccuring names and themes, but it's just like how a character named Cid appears in every Final Fantasy.The world of Solistia is very well-crafted, and each character helps you explore it in the smoothest way. There was not a single moment I was overwhelmed with lore. You get to see religion, economic shifts, academic pursuits, entertainment, and so on. Characters themselves are quite interesting, and definitely not one-dimensional like the original's some characters. For example Temenos is a high ranking cleric in the church, just like Ophilia from the original; however, Temenos has flaws and complex relationships compared to Ophilia's lovey-dovey starry eyed good girl persona. Characters' personalities also reflect on their path actions, which are methods you can perform on NPCs to obtain items, get help in battle, get information and get them out of your way. There are 16 total path actions and the wide variety of these methods give you the option to roleplay. You can be an honest person and ask them for items or purchase them, or you can be a jerk and beat them up for it. The choice is yours!The turn-based combat is the main gameplay loop with its own unique touch introduced in the original: break & boost system, where you target enemy weaknesses to break the enemy and use boost points to enhance your skills. In this entry, the game offers a "Latent Power" mechanic, where you get a special power unique to the character that can allow a wide variety of in-battle effects. And the job system, just like in the original, offers many, many combinations, and with the latent powers, it becomes even crazier.There are many other things to adore in this game. Day-Night cycle offers different path actions for characters, enhances battles, changes encounters. Sprites are much livelier than the original, every enemy has attacking animations. Each weapon has a unique sprite in battle. And the music... It definitely wouldn't be an exaggeration if someone said this is the best video game soundtrack of all time. From character themes, overworld music, boss themes, transitions during scenes and battles and many more. You will definitely be humming some of the tracks.I find the price tag a bit too much, but it's worth every penny. If you want to wait for a sale, it's completely understandable. If you don't, you won't regret it either.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100 hours, what can I say? I grew up with Final Fantasy games. FF 2 & 3 on the Super Nintendo, then the pivotal FF 7, 8, 9 and 10. These were how I fell in love with games growing up. Then Square Enix left behind that type of game, and created new Final Fantasy's in name only. The old design of slow paced, turn based combat was gone. The commitment to eye popping visuals along the journey, seem to have been lost as well.The first Octopath Traveler reminded me of the games I loved growing up. Although, it was too grindy and the stories disjointed. I played 100+ hours of the game on the switch. Now the sequel has come out and improved on every aspect of the game. The new day/night cycle is great, the town actions engaging you out of combat for hours, the new abilities and classes. The fantastic new stories, which are much, much improved.The game was a joy to play. Even with small qualms (obtuse quests, silly end-game bosses). The game had a surprising way to keep mixing up the formula where another 100 hours passed by. I really hope they create a third. Whoever is in charge of this series has the heart of the old vanguard.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler II is a JRPG masterpiece that fixes nearly every single issue the original had, as well as adding high levels of additional polish and features that elevates the sequel in essentially every aspect.Now, I'm quite a fan of games with job systems and high levels of party customization, so I was inherently drawn to games like Bravely Default and Octopath. Before this game's release, Octopath Traveler 1 (the original) became my favorite single player game of all time, despite the many criticisms that game had. One of the biggest issues people had with the original game was that it was essentially 8 mini narratives rather than one cohesive story; there were some light crossovers lore-wise and such but you could in essence play the entire game 1 character at a time with no other party members and not miss anything. The result is a game with high levels of freedom and exploration in how you interact with the world, but it did feel pretty limited in how the narrative came across (as well as jarring in certain situations where it made 0 sense for characters to be traveling together).That freedom is still present in Octopath Traveler II, but they've done a significantly better job blending narratives together and making the party seem like a cohesive unit with motivation to travel together. It's not 100% perfect, but it feels much more natural, not only in how each story is crafted, but other, small areas as well (such as the "Crossed Paths" and the character quips in battle). I will omit a great deal due to spoiler reasons, but feeling the party's attachment to one another felt much more real in this title, which made certain narrative elements much more enjoyable/emotional. The 8 characters themselves are also extremely likeable, and I felt a significant attachment to each of them and what they were working toward. Not all of the stories had the same "stakes" necessarily, but they were all told in a way that really made you root for each of them, and the characters themselves had significant growth that felt rewarding to experience, especially since it felt so much more like they were growing together. From a gameplay perspective, it's a case of "don't fix what's not broken". The break and boost system from the original game is already wonderful, improving traditional turn-based gameplay significantly, and Octopath II doesn't make needless changes to it. Rather, it's been elevated to have a few more options up your sleeve that make the flow of battles much more interesting. The obvious addition is "Latent Power", a feature that gives each traveler their own unique battle ability that can be utilized separately from any other. This makes team composition that much more enjoyable, as making characters have unique traits to them changes who you might have filling which role. There are other gameplay changes that add higher levels of customizability, such as EX skills and how certain jobs work/grow (I'm being intentionally vague since discovering these is part of the fun). This is all without mentioning the encounters themselves; the original game had plenty of interesting fights, but II takes it to another level with battle-specific obstacles to overcome. Oftentimes these unique battle gimmicks work really well as narrative tie-ins as well; a great example of this is a particular fight for the apothecary's story (those who've played the game probably know what I'm referring to). The pressure to overcome not just a boss's HP, but other external elements make every turn count, and battles felt constantly interesting.Outside of just battling, path actions have returned and have also been elevated. Octopath Traveler II introduces a day/night system, changing areas slightly based on time of day and also allowing for the use of 8 new path actions in the overworld, totaling 16 different (but related) skills to use in solving sidequests, exploring areas, or just for world building. Here's a situation: an NPC is blocking a door to a good item. In the original Octopath you had 2 options:1: Challenge as the warrior if your level was high enough.2: Provoke your beasts as the hunter and lose reputation on failure.Both of those options are still present, but there's 2 MORE options to solve this conundrum too now:3: Simply ambush as the thief. Prevents the need to enter combat (assuming your level is high enough).4: Knock them unconscious with the apothecary. Rather than a level requirement, the obstacle instead requires a certain item instead (used specifically for these situations).This doesn't sound like too much, but it adds a lot more flexibility to your team-comp as well, so you don't feel like you're missing out on something by not having some method of guiding NPCs or such; there's way more options to cover your bases. Additionally, both Challenging/Provoking feel like less of a chore now, since Challenging rewards the warrior with exclusive in-battle skills and Provoking beasts is no longer treated as a limited-use interaction; captured beasts will stay with you indefinitely until you turn your helpful companions into food (Ochette is brutal). All of the path actions feel this way, and there's genuine benefits to most of them...except maybe purchase (sorry Partitio, I'm always gonna go on a thievery spree in every new town!)All of these on their own are enough improvements, but there's so many other little things that add up significantly. UI interactions are streamlined more, character's have more fluid animations in and out of battle, weapons have their own unique battle sprites, cutscenes have dynamic camera usage, areas seem more unique and beautiful in how they utilize the HD-2D engine, and so much more. Each character's path is much less formulaic than the original, which always fell into the exact same pattern (chapter narrative -> dungeon -> boss -> repeat). And this is without mentioning the MUSIC. The soundtrack of both games is absolutely phenomenal; Yasunori Nishiki once again knocks it out of the park. Plus, if you have played the first one, there's a good number of musical nods to the original game as well.Overall, if you're looking for a solid, polished, classic JRPG experience in a world you can lose yourself in, this game has all of that and more. You can really feel the love that went into crafting this world, and it really feels like they nailed the kind of storytelling they set out to do when making the original (which, once again, I still love with all my heart). It's certainly worth at least giving the demo a chance, since you can pick up right from where you left off.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: I forgot until this game how much I loved the original Final Fantasy games as a kid back in the 1990's.As much as I love the FF7 remake and the modern FF games, Octopath Traveller II reminds me of the *best* parts of Mystic Quest on the old SNES (yes, yes, I know Mystic Quest was ranked poorly among FF games, but it did have great music, and great atmospheric graphics, which are similar in OT II).This game really, really has an excellent aesthetic unity to it, with music, backgrounds, and sprites combining to create a magical, optimistic, youthful world.And it's a world that strikes a good balance between complexity and simplicity: unlike modern JRPG's that sometimes try to have countless mini-games and gimmicks, OT II has a narrow focus on quests and turn-based combat. Sprinkled in are bits of problem solving where there may be multiple ways to get an NPC to stop blocking a door, or ways to craft items you can't afford. And all along, there are 8 party characters to collect and learn about, and a surprising amount of lore beneath the surface that you can only get by using certain skills on NPCs and completing side quests.All that said, the game does have a couple of issues for me:#1 - The early combat scales badly. Until you get four party members, some areas are fairly hard despite being near your level. I know other reviews bring up the combat difficulty, and while I think it's harder than some may claim, that difficulty is front-loaded a bit. I wish the game scaled according to the number of party members, because it's not hard per-se to find other party members, but it does take a bit of time.#2 - On the opposite tack, once you get four party members and level up somewhat, a bunch of areas of the game are nothing but a walking simulator with annoying pop-up enemies to insta-kill. I direly wish the game changed all starting areas other than the one you began in to have a bit tougher enemies. While the world of the game looks and really is a bit larger than I expected, a bunch of areas are clearly just empty prologue zones meant for the starting point of the 7 characters I didn't pick at the start of a new game. The result is that chunks of the game near those other starts remains at level 1 or level 5 or level 16 danger permanently (at least they have thus far) and will never be anything but a nuisance until such time as I start a new game in them and experience them in those prologues. #3- The primary job/secondary job system works mostly well. I'm already beginning to try a few house rules, though, to limit myself, because taking 3 Warrior licenses for secondary job is a lot when it comes to battles. The dual-class system of primary/secondary jobs is very very open and free, which I mostly like, but it's particularly weird that in combat, the secondary job is basically fully accessible for its skills and combat gear. It's just weird to have virtually no limitations, such that I can take the Scribe primary character and give him a Warrior secondary job and get all the same support skills for combat and use the same Warrior weapons. It's weird that dual-classing really has no limits combat-wise (the primary job is always what you have for overworld skills, though, so there's at least that).#4 - One last gripe about combat itself: like the JRPGs of old, sometimes the best path forward is to grind the first few steps in a zone near or slightly above your level until you can actually face a particular boss. This is a minor gripe, and one inherent to this type of game, but I wish, again, that the difficulty scaling for combat worked differently because its so up and down that I am either getting dunked, or dunking on, most engagements, to the point that I have to scour the world map for the one area actually at my level where I can grind to get stronger in reasonable-ish amounts of time.#5 - The story is slightly weak in spots. A lot of story sections are fine, and the random lore is great, but a few things are naive to the point of absurdity. I mean, Partitio's love of economics is great... but his intentions are so pure and his various crises so black-and-white that it does feel strange. And it happens for one or two other characters I've seen, too, in a few spots. And I get it that it's a classic JRPG game, but the boundless optimism feels just slightly off for me, and maybe that has more to do with me aging than with the game itself. Probably, I'd feel the same way going back to Mystic Quest. But already in the original FF7 there was more of a gritty, muddled world of ethics at times, which I do miss occasionally; I love a youthful, optimistic world within the game, but only to a point, and it does tip over that point a few times so far for me.#6 - Last gripe, and this one is small, but: I love the over-world NPC-targeting abilities, which are both fun and comedy gold, but the game is a bit weird with the reputation system. Like, totally glad it would give me negative rep for provoking someone, but why does failing to glean info from a NPC result in negative rep? My scholar is just looking at the guy for crying out loud... he gets negative rep for failing to read their lore, but my warrior char can walk into someone's own home, duel them, leave them unconscious, and that's totally fine? The reputation system in this is hilarious but also oddly designed. Mugging people and provoking people should definitely *always* be negative rep events. Reading someone via the scholar should never effect rep at all. Buying goods off someone that are only re-sellable should be positive rep each time because Partitio ends up losing money on the deal unless there's some trick I'm missing. Lastly, a few neutral-ish things:#1 - Day-night cycle is gorgeous, and has music tones that change perfectly for each area according to if its day or night, but it's a bit strange I can freely change the time of day, and a slight nuisance that over-world abilities for NPC interactions *change* according to time of day. I sometimes forget and try to bribe someone and have to go back to night time after almost accidentally dueling them.#2 - Some abilities are balanced badly. Scholar seems to get info on an NPC for free way more easily than I'd have to pay (sometimes decent money, too) to have that same info. Bribes should scale a bit better. It's somewhat neutral because I get that it might just be my playstyle, but a few of the over-world abilities look imbalanced.Overall, I can see why this is Overwhelmingly Positive for reviews on Steam. It's a great game, and is faithful to the classic JRPG format of Square/Enix going back 30+ years now. As a fan of Mystic Quest, and the first few FFs on the NES before that, this is a game that I enjoy on every level, from the nostalgia, to the actual gameplay, to the beautiful presentation quality.But its episodic structure creates some issues with the random monster encounters and the lay-out of the game world, leading to areas feeling practically like dead-space if you didn't start near them. Novel concept there, but the trade-off to its 'jump in as any of the 8 characters' approach is that they needed to add scaling for the danger levels for those other starting areas when you don't start in them, and they really didn't. Even 23-ish hours later, I still am going to explore probably 2 more portions of the map that are at level 1 or level 8 or level 16 even though every main char in my party is lvl 37 or 38. I still have to get those other 2 chars and I know from the pattern so far that they will require me walking through some lvl 1 zones yet.Great game, and just one or two small design issues that seem like they could have been better thought-through, particularly with combat scaling in the 7 start zones that you didn't begin in for each playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, if you liked the first Octopath Traveler, you'll most likely enjoy this one.  If you were on the fence about the first, you may like this.  There are some cool changes (secondary job system is nice), but there are a few things I have issues with.First I'll start with what I love...  the day/night cycle.  Each area has a different sound track based on day or night.  Your characters have different actions...  and the townspeople are in different areas.  Also, as expected, enemies are harder at night.  Secondary job system is much preferable to totally switching job.  Like that a LOT.  You can also have multiple "licenses" for certain jobs, so you can have, say, multiple secondary Clerics in your group.What I don't like...  the English voiceovers are garbage for the most part.  Some are so awful I skip dialogue just so I don't have to listen to them (I'm looking at you, Partitio...  the 16 year old who sounds 40).  The stories are very cliche so far.  There have been very little unique to them yet, and I'm only missing one of the characters.I still recommend the game, but if you've played enough other games you'll be thinking to yourself "Yup, I've seen this story line before".Also, is the Beastling Village supposed to be called the Beasting Village?  I feel like that's a typo...  but what do I know.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler II provides 8 amazing characters, 8 amazing stories, and one amazing game.What I loved:1. The characters - I seriously love all the voice actors of each character. they fit so well. They all have great personalities too.2. The stories - All have great backstory, some gives a light tone (ex. Partitio, Agnea), but are stressful and dark (Castti, Osvald) Each have an individual story. A path they must walk, it's very interesting to see what they encounter.3. The Design - Bosses look so damn good, the characters we control look so damn good. 4. The music - WOW, just wow. It is unfortunate how underrated OT music is. The music perfectly fits each character, each scenarios, each battle so well. Sometimes it is the same music but with a different shade. A few great examples would be Agnea, Temenos, and Hikari.5. The combat - I thought turn based was kind of dying, but I guess I'm wrong. OT2 did it perfectly, the hit sound, the charge sound. It feels incredibly satisfying, not too fast, not too slow.6. The graphic - The lighting is perfect in this game with its 2d/3d mixed. Resulting in greatness.What I did not like:1. Lack of character connection - Same as OT1, as each have their own story. The characters are together, but they feel so apart most of the time. Having side stories to connect them did not help so much.2. Side Quest: I personally find side quests in OT2 to be like finding an easter egg. It is so hard to do without an actual guide, which I do not like to look at as my first playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is a good improvement on the first game. The game has very similar mechanics but they are expanded upon or refined and feel less clunky than the first. _childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the first OT game - beautiful graphics, great soundtrack, interesting class system. The lack of character interaction was a bit annoying, however, as well as lackluster cutscenes and some story content that fell pretty flat. That said, I went into OT2 expecting more of the same, hopefully with a bit more polish.What I got was more of the best parts of the first game - the soundtrack is somehow even better, the visuals are just as great - plus new features, some welcome QOL things, and a lot of work towards fixing the flaws of the first game. The day/night cycle allows travelers to have multiple path actions, latent/EX powers add a bit of variety to combat, the characters actually interact with each other (voice lines in combat, shared stories), the cutscene camera work is way more dynamic, and the travelers' stories are more cohesively, rather than a last-minute endgame series of references. It also feels like they toned back the need for any grinding to stay on-level with story content.It is still a JRPG, so if you're not a fan of random encounters or other traditional mechanics, this may not be for you, but if you enjoy that kind of thing (and especially if you liked the first game), this one is well worth the price. Great game.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start a warning. This game has a lot of grinding, as in running around fighting random creatures to make artificial numbers go up because the game set them there. If that turns you off like it typically turns me off, this may not be for you.Another issue I have are some of the bosses. Not all of them mind you, but ♥♥♥♥ me some of the bosses are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. We are talking taking away boosting abilities (Basic game function that can be effected by a status effect), nerfing all healing for a boss fight, giving the boss a ♥♥♥♥ ton of attacks (They swing first after you stun them), and giving a status effect that ♥♥♥♥♥ up boost, Spells, and health randomly you can't cleanse. But, what is good?Everything else basically.The characters: All unique in their own way, even if several have a bit similar stories. But in here we have:A friendly Inquisitor who is not afraid to let faith falter a bit.A Scholar who is utterly devoted to mathematics and things he can prove.A Beastkin hunter who is obsessed with food in a charming way (No fat jokes, just eating).A Thief done with the life they have.A girl who wants to become a famous dancer.A Warrior prince who tires of war and wants his people to prosper.An Amnesiac Apothecary finding her past.And a merchant interested in making coin and sharing it.All unique, all interesting, all with their own stories that the rest of the cast can comment on. Speaking of:The stories: Like the last game, these stories are separate, uniting mostly in some foreshadowed Big Bad (I think, haven't made it to the end but the game is not subtle about it.) That said, it works well here. The stories are all unique because they don't need a uniting theme or plot, so they can tell their own story. And that's a real benefit to the game because these stories are great on their own. Though not spoiling anything.Combat: A bundle of fun. Each class has a specific role. From casting enemy wide spells with scholar, buffing the party with Dancer, Light and healing with Cleric. And almost all have a weapon attached as well to make them work well. Enemy defences are well defined, though tip: Pick the scholar as your starting character. Your locked to your starter in the party and he is near esential with his ability to find enemy weaknesses automatically or with an cheap spell. MUCH better than guessing and checking. But the rest of the party has good auto abilities as well, from summoning allies, creating potent concoctions, being able to learn new attacks in duels, and more. Each character feels unique and complex. And there's reasons to pick all. Only complaint is, again, arbitrary levels for missions, not required but you'll have a much harder time if you ignore them.Music: Fantastic, fits all times.Art: Only complaint is nose design at times, otherwise 10/10Should you buy it: Do it. Unless you hate the grind.

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt really special to me, and it kind of encapsulates a lot of the reasons why I grew up loving the genre. I enjoyed Octopath I quite a lot, in spite of the shortcomings it had. Octopath II however became one of my favourite JRPG's I've played in a long long time. All of the stories feel very varied in tone, often in surprising ways to what my first impressions were, and there's even a fair share of twists that tripped me up along the way. What surprised me particularly is that no story ever felt like a drag. I played them in a similar way to the first, that being doing everyone's earlier chapter, then everyone's next part, and so on. However the formula for chapter progression feels a bit more unique this time, which made hopping back and forth that much more of a pleasure to find out what would happen next. The game also feels a lot more cohesive than the first, especially in terms of tying it all together.There's so much flavour in the game too, with towns and the NPC's. Every NPC has some little story or background you can find out about them, and seeing these reflected in their items, dialogue or even their role in the town/quest/whatever they're involved in, was a special joy for me. Even a good handful of sidequests managed to get me invested in whatever little stories or issues were going on.Combat feels great as expected, and the addition of an increased battle speed option is a much welcome addition. Jobs and skills feel quite similar to the first but with a lot of tweaks and new additions to give it a fresh feel. There's also a huge amount of bosses in the game, and every single time I see the spritework it just brings a smile to my face. Some of them are even sort of puzzly or gimmicky, which force you to play with an unusual approach. A special mention goes to a couple of endgame fights  The only downside I can say is there were times I felt like I'd gotten somewhat overpowered without really grinding, and even held back on some bosses because I wanted to see what they'd do next.The music is on another level, and was honestly one of the parts of the game I most looked forward to prior to the release. Every character theme feels perfectly crafted for the traveller, and the variation of battle themes, town themes, and different versions of the character themes just hits the musical sweet spot deep within me. Special mention to Agnea's Theme, and also .I have to gush over just how fun it is to explore in this game and find new things. Choosing when to risk going into higher danger level areas for some treasure, or finding new caves and dungeons with the excitement of seeing what cool new boss laid at the end of it, or big new equipment for one of your many travellers. Even just the loop of entering a new town and going to , lawfully buy from everyone, find out their information and scout for abilities for Hikari, or new partners for Agnea, Partitio or Temenos - it become something I missed when I inevitably reached the last town in the game. Well, granted I can see this being a little tedious for some people, not that it's mandatory of course.I was really excited for this game, and honestly I'm just really happy that I enjoyed it as much as I did. It was a fantastic time. I'll be listening to the soundtrack and excitedly waiting a 3rd entry in the series for the foreseeable future.

_childDocuments_.review: OCTOPATH has a very special place in my heart. From its Story to its gamplay to its Art Style, it all just resonates so well with me. I can mull over team compositions, builds and gear options for hours on end. I can lose myself in the beautiful worlds. I can bang my head into the difficult bosses over and over until they're finally toppled. I was thrilled when the sequel was announced.Many of the rough edges of the first entry have been addressed in the sequel. The Characters now have more intertwining stories at certain point in their journey. The linearity has been broken up with some characters actually being given a choice as to which branch to go for first. New mechanics have been added, like Latent Power, to differentiate the characters more in combat. And finally a lot of returning mechanics have received an overhaul to make them more approachable and more useful, which has had VERY positive effects on my buildcrafting - I felt like I had a lot of options to make meaningful additions with every character that joined my team.OCTOPATH 2 is one of the few games I have a realistic chance to get 100% in which is very rare for me, becaause I tend to just move on when I've done everything I wanted, rarely do I want to do everything, but this game has sucked me in so much I feel like I can actually do it.I highly recommend playing this game if you like a more or less "traditional" RPG with turn based, strategy-heavy combat. Even if you didn't like the first one, the sequel has done a lot to improve on its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's important to first point out, while Octopath 2 is a definite improvement over the first game, it still only expands and improves upon the fundamental framework of the first game. It isn't trying to be a completely new experience, but more of a "we figured out more what we want to do with our game design that already exists" kinda deal.That being said, Octopath 2 is probably one of the most solid games to come from Square Enix in decades. It truly feels like this is what the first game should of been all along, to the point where it's upsetting this game has to share it's name with a first title that has people wary of both this franchise and graphical style. While I'm not the biggest 2D-HD fan, I think Octopath 2 looks pretty fantastic due it not being a switch launch title, and the extremely upped presentation.I can't sing this game's praises enough. If you're a fan of SNES-Style RPGS, and thought the original Octopath would be so much better with a more varied and focused direction, then do yourself a favor and give this game a shot. It's truly a fantastic game in every way.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )Octopath Traveler II's approach to being a sequel is very much about refining existing ideas. Nothing here will be very unfamiliar to anyone who played the original game, but nearly all of it is more fleshed out and generally higher quality. Although I liked OT1 a lot, I was disappointed by its eight stories being almost entirely unconnected and found little need to even think about some of the characters until the final dungeon suddenly required the use of everyone. OT2, thankfully, takes those common criticisms to heart and focuses heavily on linking its stories together. Side stories featuring two characters are the most noticeable change. After advancing both involved characters to a certain point in their stories, a new mission starring both of them will appear somewhere on the map. These are largely unrelated to each character's main objectives, but they help build relationships between your party members while also featuring the abilities of characters you might not be using much. The events really help it feel like you have a coherent party journeying together in a way that OT1 failed to do, and even better, these stories hint at and build towards a larger plot that links all eight main branches. It's easily the best new feature. The other features Square chose to highlight - the night/day system, boats, and latent powers - are fun additions, but don't radically change anything about the game. Night and day changes give you a little bit more to explore in each area and set up some clever ministories for NPCs. Boats allow treasures to be placed on easily seen islands that can only be reached by finding a less obvious dock. Latent powers give you powerful combat abilities with long charge times, although some character's powers are much more obviously useful than others. All of these are good additions, but I needed to re-read the game's store page to even remember that they weren't in OT1. That's an endorsement of how easily they fit into OT's other systems, at least. I found the writing and combat to generally be stronger than in OT1 as well. Neither of these were major problems in the first game, but I can hardly remember anything about half of that game's characters and even less about its world or most of its fights. Although Partitio's story fell almost completely flat for me, the others were all fun and had memorable moments in each chapter. Major bosses almost always have something unique or cool about them, and even Partitio's boring story has some good fights at the end. Still, you'll find some of the best writing and combat in missable optional locations. There are loads of dungeons to the side of main paths with tough fights at the end, and you'll find the setups for quite a few good short stories if you learn the background of NPCs in each town.--------For more reviews, see

_childDocuments_.review: Big improvements in many little ways over the original; it truly makes the original feel like a beta.I only have two major criticisms of this game: inconsistency in writing quality (both in dialogue and overall plot structure), and the lack of acknowledgement of the party in individual storylines.For the first: while I am fine with the Travelers having different levels of stakes and grandeur in their plots, for some reason this also tended to correlate with the quality of the writing within the game. Hikari's chapters were dense with interesting characters expressed through fairly grounded and genuine dialogue. His story wasn't exactly breaking new ground (none of them were), but it was executed exceptionally well from start to finish. A lot of Agnea's chapters were permeated with outlandish or exceptionally cliched dialogue. Osvald had the strongest start with his first three chapters, but his antagonist was essentially a parody of a Saturday morning cartoon villain, which made it difficult to take anything seriously.The second: this could have easily been remedied with maybe one or two extra recorded lines for about half of the chapters, and very mild rewrites for scenes for one or two of them. These would be used if there's more than just the protagonist of that chapter present in the party, which is far more likely to be the case than not. As it stands, a lot of the scenes have baffling dialogue were it is implied or explicitly stated that the character is alone when they are not.Besides that, this game was a treat to play. It's rare I have a game that puts me in the "I could be playing *insert game* right now" state when I'm doing most other things, but this game did it for me, especially in the second half. It has the best combat out of any turn-based 4vX RPG I've played, especially with the bonuses given for breaking an enemy, ending the battle in the first round, and ending the battle without being attacked making even grinding fun, when each battle becomes a quick little puzzle in terms of figuring out how to meet all three of those requirements.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first Octopath Traveler on the Switch when it was first released and I loved it. The gameplay, visual styling, and soundtrack all came together for a enjoyable experience in one of my first forays into this style of JRPG.The main drawbacks of the first game included a disconnect between the characters (how do 8 people come together on a shared journey and not interact?), lack of content outside the eight stories (once you completed all 8, there is little incentive to finish the game unless you are a completionist), and not much strategy to the fights beyond a select few overpowered builds (hello 1-HP Olberic).Despite those shortcomings, I still loved the first game.And I love the second game as well, because every one of my criticisms have been addressed. Characters interact with each other and feel like a group traveling together, content has been expanded to include different branches on an single character's story and includes crossover stories, and new jobs have been added that expand the gameplay strategies.Everything else returns from the first game, all that is left is for you to try it out yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: My second favorite JRPG of all time, after Chrono Trigger. Doesn't stray far from the classic JRPG formula, but does so in some interesting ways.-It's a HUGE open world, full of side quests and secrets. I put in 100 hours and still didn't see everything.-Contains typical JRPG levels of melodrama and cliches; still, I can't help but love the characters. They're written with heart.-Nonlinear story with flexibility in how to complete it. Though each character has a separate story, there are combined quests and "travel banter" to tie the stories together satisfyingly.-Each character can pick a second job, leading to rich strategic decisions and variety in party composition.-This is the first JRPG that made me unironically think "oh yay, another random encounter!" Because XP is a precious resource, and because the "boost" and "break" systems require thinking, making even the small battles interesting. If you're not into that sort of thing... be warned, this game contains hours and hours of random encounters.-Every character has a unique way of interacting with NPCs, and every NPC has a story and personality beyond "I heard a rumor that monsters are coming back". The ability to recruit NPCs in combat is especially fun.-Lovely Gothic environments (with the Wild West and feudal Japan thrown in for good measure).Emerald, may your rocks no longer freeze.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid 8.5/10 of a game. If you enjoyed the first one, you will like this. If you didn't, highly unlikely you will care for it. Although there are improvements in most areas, they don't change the basic formula. -I do have some gripes about the storylines here and there. Some npc characters don't get enough explanation in the end. But there is some very well done foreshadowing and some excellent twists. There are also mysteries in which the answer is never stated but enough clues are there to deduce the answer yourself. -If you're thorough and enjoy exploring, you will break the battle system half-way through and random encounters are over in one turn for half the game. It is still an interesting turn-based system, it just has balance issues. -There is a nice stretch at the end of the game where the full party is actually acknowledged as being present. More of this is needed. A theoretical OT3 should be purely this. Move away from the 'character is alone for everything but battles' style of chapter storytelling. It is just jarring.-As was the case with OT1, the tone can shift in extreme ways. The game can shift from a golden hearted child-like view to some dark, depraved material well beyond the boundaries you may believe the game had set. I like this element. -One thing I loved about this game was the ability to discern the background of hundreds of NPCs across the entire game. They are often mini-stories in their own way and does a lot to flesh out the people within a town. -The soundtrack is amazing.I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I finished Octopath 2, I can say without a doubt that this is better than the first game in every conceivable way.The combat system is great, no surprises there. The first Octopath already has a good foundation for the combat, and Octopath 2 further improves that by adding more interesting abilities and special latent powers to make every character feel more unique and powerful. The characters are also a major improvement from the first game. They are more interesting and unique compared to the first game.The game itself looks absolutely gorgeous. The 8 main characters all look amazing, and they are animated and voice acted even more compared to the first Octopath. I am simply in love with their character design, and they connect with me even more than I thought they would. I was initially uninterested with some of the characters like Temenos, Throne, and even Ochette, but they won me over at the end.The story, while still disjointed for the most part, are also a major improvement to the first. Each seperate travelers have a much better written story and their chapters are no longer formulaic and predictable. The biggest improvement however is the final ending chapter where they actually interact and fight a final boss which is in my opinion was better than Galdera in the first game. They also bothered to actually give us an ending epilogue that just puts a smile on my face. If only the first Octopath did this, too.If you don't mind grinding for a bit, and look past the anthology styled story (I still wish it was one big interconnecting narrative than this) I think this game is worth your time, which is not what I would've said about the first one.9/10 and this game is already a personal contender for GOTY.
