_childDocuments_.review: I played the original Octopath and quite liked the concept and ideas they had, new things that were really interesting and fun to try, good character stories etc. Octopath 2 feels so empty by comparison, the stories feel like overused tropes, some of the characters motivations make zero sense, I've finished the game completely and can say that out of all 8 stories, maybe a few are actually worth going through. I would say maybe wait for a sale if you're interested, but don't expect any groundbreaking or wildly interesting stories from this one. Graphics & Mechanics wise the game is still great in that department, the weakness system is still a bit frustrating sometimes, and random battles happen WAY too often even with Evasive Maneuvers equipped to reduce the encounter rate.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing Octopath Traveler 2. It's got elements from the original game (break/boost mechanic, subjobs, path actions), but also has new additions (latent powers, the day/night cycle) that made the game more interesting. If you liked the original Octopath Traveler, you will definitely like OT2. If you found the combat slow, there's a 2x speed battle option For those that thought the plot in the first game was middling/disjointed, you'll find that OT2's is much better in that regard.If you're really not sure whether you'd like the game, you should play the demo. It's 3 hours, and the save carries over to the full game! Give it a try :)the sad part: no more meming with 8x Bewildering Grace in a row
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler was one of my favorite JRPGs (and one of my favorite games) of all-time, and OT2 carries on that legacy so well. It looks and plays beautifully, and there is charm around every corner. You don't at all need to have played the first one to play this game, and both games stand on their own merits. The additions of sailing, day/night cycles, and small quality of life improvements are appreciated, and I think this would really shine on the Steam Deck as well (I'm playing this on my PC but loved the portability of the original Octopath Traveler on Switch). Can't recommend this game highly enough, and can't wait to play it more and more! It's easily a 100 hour game if you let it be, and I suggest playing it in short bursts to enjoy it fully.

_childDocuments_.review: The best JRPG I have ever played. It has a beautiful art style with an absurd amount of small details, one of the best soundtracks you could ever hope for and strategic and fun gameplay. Simply a great game.All 8 travelers are likeable and their stories are interesting. Each one comes with special abilities that only they have and all of them are good. There is no such thing as weak link here. Every character is good and with a bit of thinking they are amazing. Their lines of dialogue are also fully voiced (well almost fully, about 95%) and the voice actors do a great job in giving these characters even more personality.Progression feels natural and fun and rewards exploring and trying different things. You'll find a lot of great items exactly when you need them and can play the game pretty much without visiting the stores until you finish all their stories, because everything you need can be acquired by just running around, exploring and fighting. The dungeons look very distinct from each other and offer great opportunities to grind and some of them come with extra bosses, which are all unique with very different mechanics, strengths and weaknesses.The secret super boss is an amazing challenge. It's a super hard fight that can't be beaten by brute force. You have to have a strategy or you'll have your butt kicked to the curb.Visually, the game is stunning. The art style is amazing and though it took me a while to get used to it I absolutely fell in love with this 2D HD art style. You have your classic old school character sprites in a beautiful HD environment with many, many, many small details and it looks simply great. But the best part for me is the boss sprites. So many distinct bosses all in a pixely art style that just fits their mechanics perfectly.The sound design has exceeded my wildest expectations. Everything from the voice lines, the ambience music, SFX sounds and especially all the different fight themes is incredible. The clear highlights are obviously the boss themes. All final bosses have their own music, the super boss has a song that puts an unexpectedly emotional note to the fight and the final final boss theme, which also has lyrics, is very distinct from every other song in the game and elevates the fight from good to amazing.You'll have a hard time playing this game and not enjoying yourself. There aren't any major flaws and the small imperfections are easily overlooked amidst everything this game does right. I played this game once on Steam and got 130 hours and once on the Nintendo Switch with another 90 hours and the game has a lot of replay value for fights alone, so the price of 60§ is very reasonable too.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is  a worthy successor to the original, incorporating the tactical, turn-based combat, side characters full of life and flavor text, and satisfyingly challenging boss fights. The sequel brings with it a day/night cycle, allowing each traveler to have two sets of abilities, and affecting the flow of battles. Also new to the sequel is the Latent Power gauge, (functioning like a Limit Break or Overdrive for long-time Square Enix fans) allowing for powerful combinations and turning around challenging battles when used correctly. The story includes a number of nods and references to the original without requiring the player to have completed or even played the first game to fully understand the events as they unfold.That said, RPG fans looking for a richer narrative experience may be disappointed by some of the campy plot-lines of a few travelers. In some cases, the main villain of a character's arc is apparent from the outset, leaving the dramatic reveal wholly dissatisfying. However, this gamer found callbacks to such tales as The Seven Samurai, The Count of Monte Cristo, and other classic tales to be endearing enough for the game to be forgiven. The game remains beautiful and stylistic, and mechanically satisfying to "play with the flavors" of adjusting your party. A must-have for those that enjoy older RPGs with a modern touch.

_childDocuments_.review: Outstanding: Music, environment (charming art, lots of variety), battle system, boss battles, interface/controls Average: Storylines (the way they progress is a bit simplistic, doesn't keep you hooked, but pretty creative overall)Below average: The gimmick of having multiple characters who each have their own storyline is creative and makes for a lot of content, but it also means you lose the thread of why you're doing what you're doing, and there is no grand scheme that connects all the separate stories. They try to address this a little by having a "main character" but the only effect is that you can't switch this character of your party, which doesn't really affect much. The other characters need just as much attention because you need to level them up too. Overall: amazing game, well worth playing

_childDocuments_.review: 100% Recommend. If you enjoyed the first one, you'll really like this one. Even if you weren't fully on board with the first one, this one is a huge upgrade. Every aspect of this game that I've encountered is an improvement. I'm going to post a few choice improvements down below that aren't spoilers and are focused instead on mechanics:1) Secret jobs aren't nearly as game-breaking in most aspects as OT1, though they are beefy still.2) A lot of the core class mechanics that I found iffy or irritating in the previous game (Like, how Apothecary used skills, and Captured beasts having use limits) have been fixed in this one.3) The mix of day/night path abilities is awesome, and opens up some cool combos and teambuilding.4) The EX abilities are a cool way to distinguish the character's core class and make them distinct in it outside of another character picking it up as a secondary.5) The character stories have a wider range in tone, which is very enjoyable.6) Octopuffs.7) Boats.8) Latent power mechanic is also interesting. I'm not super fond of some of them, but it's definitely another cool way that characters distinguish themselves from each other.9) Crossed Paths. One of my only real complaints about OT1 was how outside the travel banter the 8 characters were essentially wholly disjointed. This alleviates this at least somewhat.10) So many things about different core abilities and path abilities. The fact that the Dancer and Merchant get bonus passive effects from their follower npc is incredible, Captured Monsters being infinite use, and turning extra ones you capture into consumable items is fantastic, the warrior being able to steal skills from people he challenges, the different ways you can go about acquiring items and information based on who is doing it (risky % based versions, or auto-success versions that require specific level to even try), Apothecary being able to mix-and-match their Combat Medicine instead of just "expend items to get x effect". And so so much more.Seriously, if you liked the first one, get this one, now.Side note: this is one of the few games I play where I don't completely turn off the music. Almost every single song is on point.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is a great game that improves a lot on what its predecessor did. However there are some things for me that hold it back a bit. My first problem is how interconnected the stories are. There is very little increase in content compared to the first. All you get is 2 characters of the 8 hanging out for 2 chapters in side stories as well as all of them interacting for a bit at the end for the final boss. Their main stories do not cross at all which is disappointing. The second problem i had with the game is that its way too easy. The merchant class is completely broken with the ability to hire 4 people to do 4 attacks the do damage between 35k to 40k dmg to all enemies. All you have to do to use this ability is pay 30,000 which may seem like a lot until you start robbing all the citizens of their items and sell them. In the end I'd rate the game an 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It narrowly gets a no from me, mostly due to how the game falls off and becomes repetitive fast.Know that this game leans heavily on its turn-based combat, the stories are short and often exaggerated as well as senseless.While it leans on the combat that part of the game is also a weak-side unfortunately, the random battles are cumbersome and boring. The saving grace making it palatable is the ability to speed up the battles and that the battles overall goes fast. The powerscaling however is very badly handled and the bossfights end up playing out exactly the same way over and over and over again. The system is set up in such a way that buffs and debuffs is the end all be all, average allies does maybe 500 damage per attack but properly set up my damage dealer that normally does 1000 damage per hit can popoff over 40000 damage in one attack.On top of the above frustration of the battle-system and powerscalling letting us down the stories are also really weak. They have potential but end up missing the strikezone most of the time. For example, one of the stories is mainly about corruption, but who corrupted the character, how and why is is not just glanced over but entirely left out.  The story is supposed to be done but it just leaves a bad aftertaste, like the precourse is somehow supposed to be the main meal and most stories have critical flaws of this extent. Either being incredibly exaggerated, nonsensical or just overreaching. There is one great story in there (mostly character driven) and the rest according to me is mediocre at best.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful throwback to classic JRPG with enough modern amenities to make it worth anyone's time.The music is phenomenal and the addition of day and nighttime versions of each song to complement the addition of it to the gameplay really makes it easy to appreciate the subtleties of each composition.The gameplay is still just as fun as the original Octopath Traveler and the break/BP system takes the best part of the Bravely Default games and rewards you for taking the time to strategize and maximize your damage output during the windows of vulnerability you develop in each battle.The sprite work remains amazing throughout with a special nod to each boss sprite and their over animated and large features. Between the larger artwork and the sweeping musical score setting the stage, each boss fight is a delight.The addition of the "Crossed Paths" stories starring pairs of the 8 travelers also help the group feel much more cohesive than in the last game, helping to develop the natural connections between them and make them feel like a genuine team of characters that are travelling together and invested in each other's plights.Genuinely, the best modern take on a classic JRPG that I have played since the Trails in the Sky games a few years back. If you have any interest in these games, this is the best one in years. Please play it and let's make sure we speak with our money and let Acquire and Square know how much we appreciate it when they make a genuinely amazing tribute to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough! This is one of the greatest RPGs ever made. You can come up with setups that wipe bosses nearly instantaneously! It's great.The music, art direction, and graphical style are top notch. Voice acting is very well done as well.You don't need to play the first game to enjoy this one; this game is much improved over that entry (I loved that one too, but it's much more flawed).Definitely don't sleep on this game! If you're interested, check it out! And make sure you do the true ending after all 8 traveler stories!

_childDocuments_.review: Having obtained 100% on this game, there's a few things to gush about. I love the turn-based combat and it allows for quite a bit of strategy; which opens up even further as you find additional jobs scattered throughout the world. The music is stellar (though I have my favorites) and each character has their strengths in combat and with interactions. The beauty of pixel art is on full-blast and I stopped at some of the scenes to just take in the view. I legitimately loved the ultra-hard optional boss fight because after level 50, there isn't much challenge. I couldn't stop playing the game until I had completed everything.However, I felt some things were lacking.- The stories. They felt unconnected, though it was fun to find the references between them (and some are well-hidden), having the entire party go through a chapter but be ignored during story sections was a tad irksome. Also, some stories will not resonate with you. Agnea did not for me, but after reading up about how it connects I can appreciate it a tad more. I chose Hikari and loved that entire arc. (Castti was another favorite for me.)- The world. It is big, there are roads, but it feels quite empty outside of the cities. Most times its a way to get from point A to point B. There is scant story between actual cities, though lorewise it makes sense (what with monsters and all. Also, you'll want to get the ship.)That being said, I found it well-worth the price, and I have hope in the future that Octopath Traveler 3 will be an even greater work.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best turn-based RPGs I've ever played.  The pixel art is beautiful and is a perfect demonstration of why art style trumps ultra realism and cutting edge graphics.  The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in a long time, with many songs that I find myself listening to outside the game.  Story-wise, this is better than the first Octopath Traveler and it finds a good balance between lighthearted story threads, and more serious threads about betrayal, revenge, evil, etc.  Gameplay-wise, this game never got old for me with the deep RPG mechanics and tailoring your equipment, jobs, and stats to suit your style.  You have tons of armor and weapons that suit a physical attacker, magic attack, speed and evasion, defense, etc.  In battles, the new latent power system adds yet another layer of strategy and depth beyond the first game.  Thinking ahead a few turns to queue-up the right buffs, debuffs, BPs, etc. can lead to almost broken character builds that devastate the party.  However, even with these strategies, the game offers some difficult bosses that will challenge you.  In terms of flaws, I didn't like that the encounter rate reduction feature was locked behind an ability that takes up one of your 4 ability slots.  I think it would have been better as a quality of life feature to just offer an item that did the same thing, since the encounter rate is a bit high, and it can be annoying especially when back-tracking through easier areas.  I think it is also worth highlighting that this game does a great job of making NPC interactions more enjoyable.  Depending on the characters in your party, you can risk stealing high level weapons and armor, you can recruit support characters who can assist you in battle, buy items (if you don't want to steal them...), or learn about the NPC to discover news items or unlock better equipment in the weapons shop.  Overall, this is the best Square Enix game I've played in a long time and I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: I never finished Octopath Traveler 1 despite how very much i wanted to like it. It felt tedious very quickly and i struggled to care for most of the characters and their story. Im very happy to say that Octopath Traveler 2 improves on every aspect of the first game and im loving it.PROS:-All characters are interesting, immediately memorable and with very engaging stories. Some arent as epic as others (i.e. Agnea dreams of becoming a star dancer and writing the best song, while Hikari has an evil sharingan power hes trying to keep in check while also trying to save his kingdom from his brother who murdered their father the emperor and wants to wage war to the world)-All party combinations are viable and every character can cover any role depending on how to set them up. The multiclass job system is incredible and works perfectly. Some combos are better than others but all are very much viable.-Social skills of characters offer a city exploration minigame of sorts thats very rewarding. If you explore the cities on both day/night you will drown in money and items and only ever bother buying healing items from shops.-Art style direction is absolutely gorgeous.CONS:-You cant take your starting character out of the party. This is both annoying for social situations and very disruptive to the gameplay as you often find yourself in a pokemon-like situation where your protagonist is a powerhouse destroying everything while everyone else just there to leech xp. -The random battles are too many (just like in the first one) and it gets tiresome really fast trying to explore only to enter combat every 10 steps. There are some ways to mitigate this but it would be nice if some max-repel item existed.-The city social skills take a lot of time. The best party combo i found for socializing was Casti,Agnea,Throne,Osvald as Casti/Osvald/Throne could loot everything in a city during the day and Agnea/Osvald could loot everything in the city during the night. Sucks for me that Hikari was my protagonist so i couldnt do this setup till his story was over.-Enemy weaknesses very often make no sense. Maybe thats pokemon logic bleeding in but i would expect a water monster to be weak to electricity and not fire. My advise: -Get this game. It has some very small flaws but is overall amazing.-Start with Osvald as both his day and night actions are incredibly useful and he never feels like a burden.-Keep tabs on high level zones so you can explore them later, its easy to forget about that lvl16 cave you found when you were lvl5 and now you're lvl35 and whatever was in it is worthless.-Always be +5 lvls of the zone you are exploring unless you are hard min-maxing. _childDocuments_.review: - Same art style as the first installment in the series.- Same superb composer has produced another gorgeous soundtrack for this game.- Truly wild difficulty imbalances- Uninteresting bosses- New battle mechanics don't add anything to the experience- Egregious narrative imbalances- Overly short and poorly-designed dungeon- Story so poorly written that I was skipping every cutscene after twenty hours of gameplayOkay, so let's start with the good stuff. Artistically, the game follows in the footsteps of its predecessor, and that is exactly what is called for. The brilliant art style remains intact, and we have eight gorgeous new regions of the world to explore.Similarly, the first game's composer is back, and he has crafted a score that is just as brilliant as the first game's.So far, so good. Unfortunately, the rest of the game absolutely falls apart.The game's new mechanics don't really add anything to the experience. The day/night cycle is at best ignorable, and when it's not, it's annoying (ex. a quest giver only shows up at night; a door is only unlocked at night; etc.). "Latent powers" are wholly uninteresting, not just because the powers themselves are droll, but because the mechanic is essentially limit breaks, which have already been done to death by hundreds of RPGs across the past two and a half decades.Break and boost are still present, but the game doesn't use them well. Bosses fall into one of two camps: big bags of HP; secondary monsters create break "locks" on the boss. In 50 hours of gameplay, I didn't run into any other boss types.This brings me to the narrative balance, which is, in fact, attrociously unbalanced. People often misunderstand the term "narrative balance," so let me be clear: this is how well the game manages the osscillation between story mode and exploration mode. Games that put the player through very long stretches of either tend to grow tedious. The first title in the series nailed this balance perfectly. However, this title is a mess. Some chapters don't have any dungeon at all, consisting entirely of one long, unbroken stream of bad writing. When dungeons do appear, they tend to be short, sometimes ridiculously short, and therefore fail to generate any sense of exploration. There are numerous other structural problems: bosses that don't have save points before them and needing pay high fares to sail off an island if you choose to start there, just to name a few.I felt that this game's line writing was significantly worse than the first installment's. It could be that the two are equally bad, but that, due to the narrative imbalance, the gruelling story sequence make my actual experience of the story that much more tedious. Regardless, I got so tired of reading and hearing vapid, insipid, unispired dialogue that I started skipping the story sequences entirely around the 20-hour mark and simply reading the textual summaries of those scenes in the game's main menu. Side note: How, in 2023, could any writer with half a brain craft a story (one of the eight stories) that is essentially a paean to laissez faire capitalism?And the game hasn't gotten unfun enough yet. That superb, impeccable difficulty balance they achieved with the first title? Yeah, they threw that away for installment two. Most of the early game bosses are laughably easy, which is forgivable, since it's the early game. They turn unremarkable in the mid-game, when it becomes clear that the designers are going to reuse the same two aforementioned boss mechanics ad nauseum. However, the real "treat" is waiting for you in the late-game, where chapters appear that are marked as "level 45," but which contain bosses capable of utterly trashing a level-62-average party. I checked all my equipment, all my accessories, and, stumped, looked up how one is supposed to defeat these monstrocities. The answer: take them out quickly before they can use their attacks on you. ... ... THAT IS NOT STRATEGY. THAT IS JUST CRAPPY GAME DESIGN.Yeah, I'm considering re-enacting my personal ban on Square Enix.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit disappointed in the first Octopath, but this game fixes basically every issue I had while leaving everything that worked untouched. The gameplay is almost identical to the first game, which is fine because it was by far the best part and if they changed the break/boost system I would have cried. The world is much more interesting and feels like a real place rather than a big utilitarian circle all the characters live in one slice of. The stories and characters themselves are also so much better written. With maybe one exception (agnea) none of the characters are nearly as one-note as the first game. The stories themselves still have the issue of there only being 1 real character with 3 people awkwardly phasing in and out of existence at the game's whims, but a lot of small changes like more frequent party banter and characters calling each other in battle offset this enough to not bother me as much as the first game. Also Ochette is in the game and she is awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10. As a fan of the first one, this one still managed to surpass it in every way. Designers really knew how to cater to us. Octopath Traveler 3 is now my most anticipated game.Biggest advice I have (aside from buy it): appreciate the game for what it is and what it's trying to do, instead of trying to force it into what /you/ think it should be. No you aren't going to get Tales-style skits or full team cutscenes, but you get a lot more. It's just a different shape of storytelling.Random thoughts:- Obligatory: the music is perfection.- Quality of life elements. Game respects your time. (no need to grind, 2x game speed, abilities to reduce encounters, fast travel, plenty of items to boost xp/job xp gain, instant day/night switch).- The stories! I liked them all. I don't want to go into too many spoilers, but the way the game manages its themes is quite creative and something you can't really appreciate until you get to the end. I thought the way it was done in this game was far far better than in the first title. Suffice to say - it's worth it to make it to the end! The game nails the "congrats you just beat a huge jrpg" vibes.- Combat. Better than any other JRPG out there. The abilities, the boosting, the big damage numbers, the boss pixel art, the voice lines. Very satisfying.- Side quests that aren't just "go here and kill this enemy/fetch this item". Requires you to think outside the box / remember random NPCs you picked up before.- Party crafting. I feel like half of the fun of this game is deciding how you want to set up your parties, which jobs you want to assign, which role to give to each character. The game puts limits in the right places so everyone can't just be anything, but enough flexibility that you can feel creative with how you did things.- Game runs and looks beautiful on PC with upscaling and high refresh rate.- At least one really hard boss that makes you feel like your party crafting was worth it.Only drawback I would say is that there might come a time when things "click" for you and you have made 1-2 of your party members Destroyer of Worlds and you will absolutely steamroll any chapter 4 + optional lvl 50+ bosses (aside from one), to the point that you will miss entire elements to boss fights. I wish that they gave these bosses more HP or introduce a mechanic that lets you scale difficulty, but hey, I can always watch the fights on youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath 1 tried but ultimately failed to live up to being the spiritual successor to Live-A-Live. Octopath 2 may as well be considered a complete do over. No you do not need to play Octopath 1 at all as Octopath 2 kind of invalidates its existence. Octopath 2 basically perfects the idea of every party member being the main character of their own storyline, and said storylines are far more engaging than those of Octopath 1. Also while the individual character stories are just that, individual, the game does do a decent job of making it feel like this is a group of people travelling together and helping each other out with their problems. This is aided by the new cross-episodes that take 2 characters from the total 8 from your party and pair them together to go on escapades together, as well as sometimes party members may chime in with their thoughts during single characters individual episodes.The combat of Octopath was already excellent and is mostly unchanged from the originals. The vast majority of the game is side content found throughout the world like dungeons and hidden bosses. Choosing to do these or not is the difference between a 50 hour playthrough or a 120 hour playthrough.Overall I consider Octopath 2 to be a must play for any fan of JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: When making a game you could call 'retro', there are two approaches:1: Make this exactly as it could have been Back Then, with the ultimate achievement being making a hack to get it to actually run on the original hardware.There is nothing wrong with this approach, but it's not my favorite. Inevitably, it leads to more compromises than necessary, and while I am absolutely a nostalgia-addicted loon the fact of the matter is that there have been a lot of improvements in the industry since the SNES.2: Recapture the FEELING of what it was like, back then, to play X game for the first time.This is what Octopath Traveler 2 does, and what I value most.Having played both games concurrently like a madman, I can tell you now: Octopath Traveler 2 is a massive improvement over Octopath 1, which is a very good game. Octopath 2 is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece. It perfectly captures the feeling of starting Final Fantasy VI (we called it III) on the SNES as a child, of having this massive expansive world to explore with a sprawling story and an awesome setting and a great aesthetic - but it captures that feeling TODAY.This doesn't play at all like a super nintendo game,  This game incorporates improvements and innovations in the turn-based JRPG genre in the twenty-five years since then, .So what is this game?Eight playable characters that each have their own unique story, four optional 'hidden' classes that add a ton of gameplay variety, the best new soundtrack in a game in years (this belongs right next to Mario RPG and Yoshi's Island for memorability and excellence), a ton of optional dungeons and cool rewards and character build variety, impressive depth in combat ranging from random encounters to boss fights...If you've played Octopath 1, this has a TON of improvements over it, too. The characters' stories no longer include your other characters you've unlocked (so they feel more "their" story, as opposed to later chapters where it feels more like all the characters are there together) and overall there has been a TON of work to make it feel less like "these are eight different people on tangentially-related solo adventures" and much more like "This is a fun adventuring party of disparate individuals who travel together".Also, this is possibly the best JRPG party ever. I liked Octopath 1, but every character of every class is a straight upgrade over the previous game's version as a character.They've even taken the jobs that were very meh in Octopath 1 and given them a chance to excel, here! EXCELLENT work. Buy this game, I want this series to continue forever. This game will not disappoint you if you love JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Since this is the first game that I’ve 100%’d in a very long time, I felt compelled to write a review of this game.Octopath Traveler 2, improves on the formula introduced in the first game, and has created a much more engaging environment. The updated battle mechanics with latent abilities, adds an entirely new level of flexibility to play exactly how you want to. This is probably my favorite battle system to date, as it feels like the player is not limited on what they can do. The developers allow combinations of abilities that create overall fun and powerful synergies. I truly believe that a player could play through the game with any combination of jobs, provided they had a sustainable party composition.I will say that I found the story of this game to be incredibly lack-luster. I feel like a lot of the storylines are cliché and the cast has a very unnatural and forced relationship. Some of the dialogue of ‘party banter’ does improve on this slightly, however overall it’s very disconnected. I would discourage someone playing through this game solely for the story.The fights in Octopath Traveler 2 are extremely well paced, especially for a JRPG, with all of the final chapters of characters having memorable fights. I would encourage anyone to fight all of the bosses in the game, as this is where I felt the game shined. The fights challenged me; solving the situations that were unfavorable and overcoming the fight was a super satisfying feeling, and was a good mental exercise. The optional bosses, albeit difficult, are very much worth the time to play through though frustrating. I have not experienced long fights like a couple of the ones encountered in this game with several phases and changes to mechanics. Even though they were long, I had a ton of fun finishing them.Overall I would recommend this game as long as you are not solely looking for a good storyline. I completed this game over a span of a few days, and I don’t feel as if it was particularly grindy. I would like to note, the leveling process feels pretty well paced for your first party, with very little grind. I personally did not want to go through the whole process again starting a party from scratch,  so I looked around for a good leveling method and the devs basically give you a method that is very reliable and will level up your new party fast.Leveling Method I used: Lastly, if you played Octopath Traveler 1 and did not enjoy it, I would not let that discourage you from this game. The improvements made from the first game really do take the franchise to the next level.If you end up purchasing the game, I really hope you enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: You can literally steal candy from a little child. In front of his mother. And then you can steal from the mother too. And then beat her up in front her child. And to top it off, you can do that all inside a church. You can also force old people to fight for you and steal from the little kids.This game is a masterpiece!What a fantastic game. I had such a good time with it. It scratches all my nostalgic 90's RPG itches. The developers did a great job of building on the foundation of Octopath Traveler 1. This game doesn't really change much but what it does makes it a MUCH better experience, it's like they took the parts that worked on the original, made them better and worked on the parts that didn't. It's almost everything we could've wanted out of a sequel. It's gonna be hard replaying the first game, as 2 is just that much better overall. It's an amazing (even if flawed) JRPG with little/no grinding, and also one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.I can't stress how good this game looks, seriously, it's like how you imagine your childhood favorites looked through nostalgia goggles. Basically the only pixel art game that I can call gorgeous. I sometimes wish Final Fantasy had never gone 3D and instead had gone the 2DHD art direction. The 2D-HD is a style that instantly makes the game a must-try for every pixel-art lover, and a beautiful game to try anyway for people loving more modern art. I also loved the voice acting with the podcast settings. It's hard to describe but it's such an enriching touch to an artistically curated 2D-HD series.This game's scope is epic, like truly epic. The variety in the towns and dungeon design is stellar; and there's so much of it. There are really crazy secrets hiding in the places you least expect them. The game actually takes from the indie horror genre in fun ways. The game does not hold your hand on secrets; it's really up to you to find them. This was extremely appealing to me.The characters are fantastic. It's a shame there are so many people who dislike the 8 different storylines, as I loved it and I think it's a very interesting way to compile multiple stories into 1 video game. If you didn't know, the game divorces them into 8 separate stories, think each character is the protagonist of their own story and they're all on the road together, telling each other what they were up to at taverns or camp fires. This means each character really shines in their story, but has less overlap up front. All eight of them are VERY distinct both in characterization and gameplay features, and unlike the first game there are built in crossover stories and a lot more side dialogue with party members bantering. Whether it's your thief in a human trafficking scam, revenge driven scholar avenging his family, your lighthearted country girl dancer, your blindly optimistic merchant, there's a lot of character work going on. Most people won't connect with all 8 perfectly, but you'll find ones you love. The pacing is also much better. Every chapter has its own structure that makes sense for that character's story. Some chapters are split into multiple towns, some don't have boss fights at all, many don't involve dungeons, and some don't have story and is just straight to a boss fight. In general, there is no rigidity and you won't know what to expect from the chapter until you actually play it unlike the first game where you knew it'd be the same thing every single chapter. The game varies up what you're doing enough to not feel like a slog. I will also mention that the writing and stories were much better than the first. Each story on its own is solid but perhaps not earth shattering, and some are deadly serious while others are consistently casual and light-hearted. There were some that were very high stakes and some that were very low, and it felt a little unbalanced in that regard, but all the stories were a joy to play through. The end of the game has a dedicated story where all eight stories cross over and is a strong closer.You also have a lot more main character interaction with the extra paired chapters, being able to read party conversation in the menu after and a much more extensive final chapter. The interactions the different party members have with each other, the funny little moments together and the trust that they have in one another are such a big improvement over the first game. There's really such a big difference between having a group of characters that feels like they play off each other, and a group of 8 npcs who don't talk to each other.The game has a combat system that is 95% the same as Octopath Traveler 1. It has the BP gauge as well as shield points for enemies (aside from HP and SP/MP like most RPGs have). You also had all the different jobs, the JP, the skills, and all that good stuff from the first as well. They added the latent power gauge, which gives the travelers special abilities when the gauge is filled, sort of like a limit break type of thing. The latent power abilities vary by character, and the gauge adds another layer of strategy to what is already a pretty strategy-minded system. There was a loud group of haters who complained Octopath 1 was too grindy, but if you really use your BP and enemy shield points to your advantage and have your party set up to compliment each other, you can play through without much trouble. Octopath 2 is no different. Only thing I didn't like, and I just dislike this about all RPGs that do it, is that reserve members (characters not in the active party) don't get experience. This leads to things becoming unbalanced very easily if you're not actively switching characters out, but that also requires you to change how you fight.Yes, the game is time consuming. It's one of those games you can easily sink more than 50 hours into and not even realize it. But, the experience of playing is SO well worth the time overall. It made my 36 years old’s heart WEEP with more than one story. I was absolutely enthralled, this should be talked about in the same league of FF6 and Chrono Trigger. It looks amazing, it sounds amazing, there is so much love and work put into everything. So many secrets, so many options, almost every NPC has something interesting about them. It's massive and well written. It's just so very good. It may not be everyone's cup of tea but it's certainly worth every penny of the $59.99. 50+ hours of gameplay is more than acceptable. Octopath 2 makes 1 seem like a proof of concept, and I'm really glad I played the sequel. If you're on the fence after not liking the first much maybe give this one a try. For everyone else, what the hell are you waiting for?10/10 Would commit atrocities by fighting grandmas and stealing from little kids again.

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredible journey! Finally beat the final boss and [REDACTED] super [REDACTED] boss. It was a long road, and Octopath Traveler II is what I may classify as a perfect sequel. My reason for this is that it keeps all the original mechanics and game play in check, and yet improves and adjusts things that could have been better from the first game. An example of this is the removal of the purple chests. They were only accessible if you had the thief in your party in the first game. The purple chests have been removed and do not exist in OP2. The character stories are much better formed (i.e. not the same linearity that all the paths in the first one had). Osvald starts in prison on a remote island in the middle of the northern frozen sea. No one has ever escaped from there. The motivations of the characters and antagonists was streamline in a way that worked exceptionally well.And as a new mechanic, there are dual stories (i.e. Osvald and Partitio later on get a storyline about them and their encounters together). Finally, finding the final boss and [REDACTED] are much more viable and aren't impossible to discover without the internet. Biggest tip is to pay attention to NPC's and their information from Inquire or Scrutinize. It may be more useful that you may think at first. Cheers Octopath Traveler II! You are a wonderful experience for anyone willing to take the adventure!!

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath II builds upon the foundation the original game made and ends up making one of, if not one of the best modern JRPGs in recent memory. Whereas the first one had many minor flaws that built upon themselves over time, this one fixes so many of those gripes and adds onto them to give you a full and proper experience.The story is great, not only trying to connect the separate stories into one more coherent narrative but also making each one more unique despite the common tropes. A more diverse cast, with greater characterisation and more engaging plot beats to make it truly feel alive. What helps is that rather than being stuck in the 4-chapter formula, each plot can have you choose which order you do a chapter in or has more/less chapters than others.The gameplay is the biggest improvement, as each job not only is made better by having a more diverse skillset, but characters also come with unique powers and abilities, making them  somewhat important besides their jobs. Latent powers give each traveller something to bring to the team, and a wider range of passive and active abilities allow them to make both path actions and combat options much, much more customisable and enjoyable. Add the day/night cycle bringing its own challenges, some much needed QoL and none of them feel worse to play than others!While the graphics remain relatively the same, the presentation and display of them has improved too. Towns feel more alive, roads more organic to traverse, things more fun to explore. The continents feel alive and the music makes it only better.I can't emphasise enough, go play this game. It is GOTY worthy or at least worthy enough to be the best JRPG of the year. A love letter to the classic 16-bit FF games, complete with the modern benefits and design choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly the best JRPG I've ever played!The most striking feature is of course the art, music and voice acting, but what you may not see on the surface in trailers and videos is the ridiculous attention to detail.10-15hrs into the game you can give any of your characters a sub-class "job", of which there are 12 in total. So you can spec a healer to also be a warrior. But the detail is in the fact that each characters artwork changes to reflect their job, and their voice lines match their new abilities and even the weapons have distinct unique art! Multiple variants of Sword, Axe, Spear and more that you may only see flash on screen for a moment during an attack makes the game just ooze high production values.The pacing is excellent. As each story chapter displays what level is associated, you'll find yourself naturally hoping around the world to do different chapters as you level up, with very little need for grinding for the first 20-25hrs. At this point there does become a noticeable gap between levels in the story, mostly around the jump from Chapter 3 to 4 but nothing major, and it coincides with unlocking a new way to travel the world so you find yourself with a lot more exploration opportunities. It's at this point you can start diving into dungeons, doing side quests and finding rare enemies and items. So the "grinding" never really felt tedious or repetitive, it was more a way to pivot you off the story path, and onto an exploration path for a while. Enemy variety is huge, as mentioned the game opens up further at about the 20hr mark and I was stunned to see a whole new theatre of enemies with unique look and feel, as well as abilities. The character Ochette is practically a Pokémon hunter, where she can catch enemies and utilize them in battle, which encourages explorations as you'll find yourself looking for the strongest variants of the element or weapon type these monsters use. Of course, the game plays with eight characters in a sort of "vignette" style story telling, where you pick someone and hear their tale play out in whatever part of the world they are in. While the stories for the most part a really interesting (its to everyone's taste but I think we'll all find one or two not to our liking as much) this is probably where the game falls down slightly, in the fact that the party doesn't really feel like a team. They'll add some quips or "banter" about what's happening but for the most part each story is very disconnected from each other, so much so that cutscenes will play featuring only one character exploring a ruin on their own, then a fight happens and your party are all there, and then another cutscene and they're gone. So for me that'd be one aspect that doesn't quite feel right. Occasionally there are side chapters where two characters buddy up together for a bit, and these were some of my favourite chapters, albeit a bit short.Anyways, to prevent going any longer, the game is excellent. The eight classes, stories, and unique gameplay associated with them (crafting for the healer, taming animals for the hunter, unique opportunities for the merchant which I don't want to spoil) - it makes the game feel really fleshed out. I'm 40 hrs in, there's still large dungeons to tackle, parts of the map I haven't explored and three classes I haven't even found yet! Also the music is so good! Loving the game, works great on Steam Deck with max settings too!

_childDocuments_.review: The narrative structure is akin to a literary octopus, with eight tentacles of plot weaving in and out of each other. While this can sometimes feel as though you’re trying to watch eight television shows simultaneously, the individual stories are engaging, filled with the kind of drama, humor, and heart that can make even a pixelated character feel like an old friend. The interweaving tales provide a rich tapestry of lore that rewards players who enjoy piecing together a larger narrative puzzle. is a love letter to the JRPG genre, penned with the care of an artisan and the flair of a poet. It manages to strike a delicate balance between homage and innovation, delivering a game that feels both familiar and fresh. While the fragmented storytelling may not be to everyone’s taste, the overall package is as satisfying as finding an extra onion ring in your order of fries. For fans of the genre, it’s a journey well worth embarking on, promising dozens of hours of adventure, strategy, and the occasional urge to weep openly at its beauty!

_childDocuments_.review: I was a really big fan of the first game, and was really looking forward to this one as well.  And it seems they took the safe route.  It's literally just more of the same.  Both the good and the bad.  The combat is still amazing, the art style is still beautiful, and there's so much content in this game.  Though they also kept in a bunch of little things I didn't like from the first one.  Once again, every chapter, the featured character completely treats the rest of the party as if they don't exist.  They tried to compensate with this with Tales Of series style skits, but they aren't even voice acted, which Tales is, so there's not much excuse.  They did introduce side chapters that feature two party members, but it's just not really what I was hoping for.  And I get it, to have dialog witten for every possible combination of characters for any given chapter would be a large ask, but they could at least be standing there present.  But if you go for the final boss, there is a lot of dialog between all 8 characters, but it's just so late in the game.  They also locked you into your first character pick again, which I didn't like.  Because of this, your "main" character is going to be greatly outleveling all your other characters that you can swap out. And I don't really see a purpose in doing this.  That character's story plays out no differently if it was your first or last character pick.  Also locked away till the tail end of the game is the ability to swap out characters from the menu at any time.  If you were going to allow this, it should have been available from the beginning.  And I know a lot of this review is negative, but it's like, this amazing game could have been even more so.  So I'm just lamenting the lost potential.  Despite all my nitpicking, I still highly recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty much a classic RPG as you would expect, but improved in many ways not only from those games of yore, but from the first entry of the saga itself. I just HAD to 100% it to the very end and I had a BLAST at it! :)The first Octopath, amazing as it was, had some issues that made it be a bit far from perfect. For example, you never felt like the party connected with each other, well... because they really didn't. It was like playing small stories that were all but interconnected, so the characters felt stale in regards to one another even if they were awesome and/or interesting by themselves. Then Octopath II came in and somehow managed to keep the "eight paths" unique to each other whilst finding the way to make the other travelers you play as have a say, a soul and a stage. The travel banter they have sheds light to their characters (hidden and true), plus things get even better amongst one another once you reach the end of the game -- and you'll have to buy this and see what I mean for yourself.Fights, as they come, are an improvement on classic RPGS and Octopath I as a whole. They can get pretty challenging if you come thinking it's just "get better gear and smackdown", but you actually have to think if the gear you got will combine well with what build you're having your travelers follow. And there are a LOT of options: a fun mix-and-match of skills, gear and strategies you can pull off to reach the end of the game with relative ease or a challenge brought upon yourself for underestimating it.And when you think it's all said and done, you got more challenges coming: one is  and the .Pretty much a 9.5/10. My ONLY gripe with the game is that the music isn't as awesome as the first entry in the series (don't get me wrong: it's FANTASTIC, but the music from Octopath I was superior), but it quickly became one of the best classic RPG experiences I have ever had in all my life.What're you waiting for? Play it! You won't be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore my playtime, I 100%'d this game on Switch. Bought it on sale on Steam to experience it again and to support the series.This is possibly my favorite RPG. It's definitely somewhere in my top 5 favorite games.Basically this took everything about Octopath Traveller and made it better. Fixed the vast majority of the issues I had with it (which were few to be clear, I loved the first game too) and expanded on the systems it introduced. Each character having a different path action depending on the time of day really adds to the versatility of each character and is probably my favorite change. The stories of each character are still mostly self-contained but also intertwine far better than they did in the original, with increased party banter opportunities to build that sense of camaraderie. The characters themselves are fleshed out pretty well for the duration of the story being told, and they're incredibly memorable. I unreservedly recommend this game to anyone with a hankering for a fantastic story and a damn good RPG to back it up.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many games whose sequels just do not live up to the hype. Octopath Traveler 2 is NOT one of those games. This game has made it so the first game, which I have on Switch, is downright unplayable. This game improves on every aspect of the original. The combat and story, key parts of any RPG, are absolutely wonderful! This is one of those games I wished I bought at full price because that is how much I love and wish to support the creators of this game. Beware, slight spoilers ahead...The characters are so well fleshed out and best of all, ACTUALLY INTERACT WITH ONE ANOTHER! This was a huge peeve of mine back in OT1 where the group of 8 felt super distant. There is voiced dialogue and chapters with multiple of the travelers and when I first saw such a thing existed, I was so damn happy.If that wasn't enough, the developers added more depth to the combat, specifically with the Latent Power Gauge. This new feature adds so much more complexity to the games, because sure you can just destroy everyone with raw numbers, but there is a damn addictive delight you get when the strategy you came up with is executed perfectly, leaving all of you enemies destroyed with either magic or melee.The music was great too. My absolute favorites was Partitio's theme and I can't wait for the full soundtrack to drop on Spotify, while it is not as amazing as the first one I would wager, there are still some bangers hidden in there that will really get you jamming to them.And the last thing I will tough upon is the graphics. I've never been a believer of "Good Graphics = Realistic Graphics", and this is the game I would put on a pedestal because I can only call it beautiful. The camera and animations make the world feel 3D instead of 2D, but the 2D nature of the environment or characters do not at all take away from the breathtaking views. The boss enemies are cool as hell, and locales you visit are so diverse and fun, the dungeons and mobs are intriguing to boot!Overall, this is probably one of the best games I have played in a while. It has been a long time since a game has reverted me back to when I was an elementary school kid, desperate for the day to end so I can pour hours and hours into this game. It was my first playthough and I 100% the game, and I rarely looked at guides until I got stumped at one particular boss. If you made it this far, I promise you this: You will not regret buying this game. I wish this game all the success and I pray to god that the developers get the rewards they so deserve because this game is a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: WITH THESE HANDS, I can definitively say that this is just the first game, but BETTER in every single way. From characters, to music, to mechanics and content, OCTOPATH TRAVELER 2 is an amazing journey from start to finish. Just about every issue with the first game has been resolved and the experience improved, one of the biggest ones for me being dialogue and cut-scenes which now have an auto and 2x speed mode, meaning you can just sit back and watch and listen to the story. Speaking of listen, the voice acting is VASTLY improved compared to the first. I played the entire game in English, and despite some funny translation things (common in this genre really), I was engaged with the voice actors 100% and was drawn into these wonderful characters.And then the MUSIC. Some things can't be explained well, and just how good the music is, is one of them. While amazing on its own, Yasunori Nishiki created an OST that shines the most in the game itself. From the transitions between overworld to battles, the characters theme rolling into the boss battle themes, and the new transitions from high beat day music to wonderful solemn night tracks, at no point does the music feel overbearing or intrusive. And above all is the the more complex ranges the music has now, with the Main Theme in particular being a larger arranged version of the original theme. Another note for the music is the inclusion of leading vocals into the night tracks and into some songs in a certain characters journey. Hard to explain why, but man do those tracks hit the spot. The OST is just amazing and Squenix needs to hurry on the official release.As I'm posting this, I have JUST finished the game. While there is still a couple things to do to 100% this game, I will have to take some time to really digest the experience and will likely add on to to this review after I have thought on it. BUT, I suggest people to play this themselves and enjoy it, its better on your own. ALSO YOU DON'T HAVE TO PLAY OCTOPATH 1!! There are references to the first, BUT it has no direct connection to the first. Its better to play the superior product with all its improvements rather than waste time on what is really a CLASSIC JRPG, with all its flaws.TBC.....

_childDocuments_.review: I write this review immediately after completing the game and wow; it is fantastic. For those looking for a brief summery I would say that if you enjoy turned based combat and don't get easily irritated by random encounters than this game is worth giving a shot. For those who have heard about the lack of story in the original Octopath Traveler, you need not be worried for the each and every story in this game was good at worst, and fantastic at best. My recommendation on which path to start with, outside of what you find most interesting, would be either Osvald, Throné, Castti or Temenos as these are some of the best in my opinion. However, a fair warning: All of the stories I just mentioned, as well as a few other ones, go to some pretty dark places, so if you are not comfortable with more gruesome stories than the game may not be for you. Aside from the story, the games combat is very fun and engaging. For some of the harder fights near the end, I was really stressing and having to plan out the moves and amount of resources that each character would expend in one turn. most of the game is not very difficult but some of the bosses at the end of character stories can be brutal if you are not prepared. On top of the engaging battle system and well written story, the games art style is unique and beautiful. The art style is called HD-2D, for those who don't know, and it combines high quality 2D sprites and a beautiful 3D world. Beyond the general atheistic, all of the different job outfits look incredible and the monster designs are interesting to look at. The various attack affects are also beautiful and and another level to the combat.In addition to all of the aforementioned qualities, the game has what is easily one of the best soundtracks I have heard in any video game full stop. This games soundtrack was so good that I was motivated to do unnecessary side quests just to obtain the disks in game so that I could listen to them again. In short, the people at Square are masters of both storytelling and music in video games.I only really have two major grievances with the game: The first, you can only level up four out of the eight characters at a time. While, on the surface this might not sound like a problem, it becomes one later into the game. After I completed the first four stories, I had to go back and start the other four. However, because I had already unlocked every area in the game, I was not earning passive exp for my characters when traveling from place to place. This essentially meant that I had to spend a few hours grinding to get them to the correct level to progress their quests.  The second, there is not as much cross party interaction as I would have liked. Outside of the four crossed path stories and the occasional party banter there is little to no interaction between your party members until close to the end of the game. For me, that was enough. I still felt that my party was a collective, a team working towards a common goal. However, I still think that there was room for more.Overall: This game has a fantastic and flashy combat system, beautiful eye-candy graphics, and phenomenal soundtrack, and a fantastic story. If you enjoy JRPGs this is a must buy. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, here we go.As a classic JRPG fan, Octopath II (and by extension, Octopath) is a love letter to the genre, and a fantastic, modern take on the formula. With stunning and beautiful classic 2D pixel art adapted to a 3D atmosphere just like its predecessor, alongside gorgeous music and a compelling and easy-to-fall-into story line comprised of eight different paths and eight different and unique characters, my love for Octopath II knows little to no bounds.There's too much for me to say about how much I adore Octopath II. The characters are interesting and intriguing as they are lovable and memorable, and the stories they tell are just as intriguing as the characters themselves. The music is just, absolutely gorgeous, and have some of my favourite battle and ambient themes of all time. I don't even have to mention the graphics again, but I will because god, this game is just so, so gorgeous. I could go on and on about what i love about this game, and why I have 93.9 (and there will definitely be more) hours in this game, because honest to god, I just like replaying it. I'll 100% it someday.Everything you could ever love from the first Octopath was taken, and improved in Octopath II. If you loved the first game, I will guarantee that you will love the second.If you're a classic JRPG fan like I am, of old school turn-based RPGS such as the earlier Final Fantasy games, you will love Octopath.

_childDocuments_.review: I never reviewed it, but I loved Octopath Traveler 1. I enjoyed most of the stories and I loved the stradegies afforded by the combat system, that set it apart from the other turn based rpgs I have played.That being said Octopath Traveler 2, while it doesn't do anything super crazy or different from the first game, does what the first game does, but better. Practically every concept introduced within Octopath Traveler 1 has been reexamined, iterated on, and overall improved.For the story, without any spoilers (As of writing this review I have only done a handful of chapter 3's and most of everyone's chapter 2's), however from what I have seen from the stories, they are so much more engaging. While there were one or two stories in the first game I just never jived with. There isn't a story in Octopath 2 that I am at the very least, invested in in some capacity.For exploration, the new mechanic to change day and night basically doubles the amount of things you can do in each town. Having two path actions per character that are available at different times of the day also add layers to who you should bring along for a given task.For Battle, the star of the show is the Latent Power mechanic, as well as the reshuffling and changes made to the classes we know from Octopath 1 to make them, at least to me, more interesting. I find myself using the classes that I didn't use as much in the first game here because they feel so much more intuitive and powerful to play in this one.Not to mention there is loads more interaction between the cast than in Octopath 1, the smallest and most significant being the battle interactions each character has. It feels like you're building a team, where as in the first game there was little to no interaction between the cast until the very end. Its not the *only* thing. But I'll leave the rest of those interactions for you to discover for yourselfAnd the Music? Its Octopath Traveler! Need I say more? The entire soundtrack is a banger.While I haven't beaten the game quiite yet. I am madly enjoying it.

Very small and straight forward layouts with some NPCs for you to use path actions on, that has not changed in this game.Pros:Cons:Stories in Octopath Traveler tend to be on the simpler side, what makes them engaging is the execution and the mature themes that they explore.Pros:Cons:I really enjoyed the backstory, story and personalities of all the characters except Agnea. _childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler II not only surpasses the original game, but improves so much that it makes the first game seem like a proof of concept. The combat was definitely the best part of the original game and that's the thing that is arguably changed the least, but that's not bad at all! The shield break system remains one of the most addicting and fun system in any turn based RPG, on the same level as Shin Megami Tensei's press turn. It's even better than the original with fixed balancing and the addition of character's talent gauges that give each character a unique meter move, some I used far more than others but they were all very interesting.The major improvement on the original is the stories and characters, the original had good stories but pretty generic fantasy tropes. The stories are much improved now with different chapter structures, less obvious stories, and a better cast of characters than the original. There's also a lot more traveler interactions than in the original with the major contributor being the cross paths chapters between two travelers, all really fun that build relationships between the characters. The XP gain was also a massive fix than the original, with A LOT less grinding required which is a welcome addition since the game still took me 75 hours to beat.(SPOILERS IN THIS SECTION) My only real complaint is the final chapter, not that it was bad or anything but some characters from the main story were just randomly evil the whole time and it didn't feel natural at all.Overall, Octopath II is one of the best turn based RPGs I have ever played with fun gameplay, stories, characters, visuals, and music (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the music is still fantastic) and any big fan of the genre should pick up this game immediately.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming from someone that got into the franchise through a friend.I've never played any JRPGs before I played the Octopath Traveler first game (prequel to this one), and I must say I thoroughly enjoyed that experience. I had some small issues with the first game of which most came down to the user convenience.Was a huge fan regardless and that made my choice for playing II obvious, it needed to happen.When I first picked this up I was looking forward to the same story, combat and MUSIC (don't forget the OST) experience I had with the first game.Now I must say... this game found every single point of user convenience I lacked in the first game and even added more (I didn't even know I missed this in the first game).Just for this I believe this experience was just so great, them literally improving all of my small gripes with the first game felt super nice. Devs deserve a lot of respect just for this alone.That was not all however, the story also felt a lot more intertwined than the first game, which was a different take, but definitely welcome. Personally I believe the story can still be improved upon for a (hopefully) third game, as this sotry had moments where I was drawn in but just as much had chapters where I was a bit detached as it didn't do much for me. Don't take this as a negative point, it's still good, I've just come to expect a lot I guess and that's on me, not on the game.Combat feels good, impactful and sometimes strategy is still necessary, which I can appreciate. There's some challenges in this game (much like the last game) that had me retry a couple times before being succesful, and that's what makes it exciting in my opninion. Although at some points later on in the game there were a couple fights were I downright handicapped myself by excluding one class as it was too easy to brute-force bosses. Despite this I would still say combat is satisfying and challenging enough.Overall this game was an improvement to the first game on a lot of fields, and that's already a tremendous feat, as to me personally even the first game was a very good game.Very happy with the purchase, and if you like the genre I'd say it's probably a must.If you don't know the genre I believe starting out with Octopath Traveler (I) would be a good introduction, it's got me interested for sure and I'll be back for any continuations FOR SURE.

_childDocuments_.review: Title: A Lyrical Sequel to a Classic Journey - OCTOPATH TRAVELER II Review"OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" follows in the footsteps of its predecessor, expanding on the unique blend of nostalgia, innovation, and storytelling that captivated players in the original game. Developed by Acquire and Square Enix, this sequel offers a familiar yet refreshed experience that pays homage to classic RPGs while introducing new elements to keep the journey engaging.Visually, "OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" retains the striking 'HD-2D' art style that defined the original game. The meticulously crafted pixel art landscapes and character sprites create a visually stunning world that feels like a living, breathing homage to the golden age of 16-bit RPGs. The dynamic lighting effects and environmental details showcase a level of artistry that elevates the game beyond mere nostalgia.True to its name, the game features a new cast of eight protagonists, each with their own unique stories and motivations. The narrative structure, where players can choose the order in which they tackle each character's story, returns, providing a sense of freedom and replayability. The character development and individual story arcs are once again a highlight, offering a deep dive into the personal struggles and triumphs of each protagonist.Combat in "OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" builds upon the original's turn-based mechanics. The Boost Point system returns, allowing players to enhance their actions strategically. The addition of new job classes and abilities further enriches the tactical possibilities, encouraging experimentation with party compositions and strategies. The depth of the battle system ensures that encounters remain challenging and rewarding.The soundtrack, composed by Yasunori Nishiki, is a masterpiece that complements the game's atmosphere perfectly. The evocative melodies and orchestral arrangements enhance the emotional impact of key moments, creating an immersive audio experience that resonates with the player long after the game is turned off.While "OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" successfully builds upon its predecessor's strengths, it's not without its minor flaws. Some players might find the episodic storytelling structure to be less cohesive compared to more linear narratives, and the pixel art style, while charming, may not appeal to everyone's visual preferences.In conclusion, "OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" is a worthy successor that honors the legacy of the original while introducing meaningful improvements and innovations. With its captivating visuals, deep storytelling, and refined gameplay mechanics, the game stands as a testament to the enduring charm of classic RPGs. Whether you're a fan of the original or a newcomer to the series, "OCTOPATH TRAVELER II" is a journey well worth embarking upon.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:-All around improvement over the original. If you enjoyed the first, everything you liked is back and better-Main cast has a little more spice to them (for the most part). They're still very clearly pure-of-heart-good-guys, but Temenos and Osvald have way more going for them than the fairly plain characterisation Ophelia and Cyrus had in the original, for example.-Not that you'll need it for the main game, but grinding has been improved a lot. 100% here is a lot less demanding than the original, and even if you do want to go the extra mile, it's easier to do so.The bad:-Villain writing is very classic JRPG. There's a significant amount of bad guys who are evil and want power with no nuance to it. I'd argue that things are even more black and white in this game than in the original, which is saying something.-Crossed paths are good but there's still not an awful lot of interaction between the cast. For the most part you're still playing 8 individual stories that are tangentially related. If that was your biggest gripe with the first game, that's not really fixed here.-Difficulty balancing is pretty haywire. I'm honestly not sure what the "intended" path is, since it's really easy to overlevel if you explore everything, and easy to underlevel if you flee from everything. It's still fun, but I'd say it's even less challenging than the original, which many people already thought was too easy.Overall it's still arguably one of the best JRPGs released in recent years, so if you like the genre, you'll get your money's worth here.

I can see that the developers are actually trying to make the story better and more interesting this time.
