_childDocuments_.review: This game is . I liked 1 quite a bit, but it felt like it lacked a bit of identity/spirit that sort of left a milquetoast taste in my mouth. This game is not that. Octopath Traveler 2 genuinely takes an overwhelming majority of SE's library and makes them look amateurish; even the legendary classics that I also have enjoyed significantly do not hold a candle to this game.The overall visual presentation for the game is stellar and has grown rather significantly from its time in OT1. Every area in the game stands out as highly distinct in my mind and the world truly feels much more diverse than it was in the first game which sort of trapped itself in having similar aesthetics for just about everywhere in the game. Animations are cool as hell and firing off a fully boosted attack that you've been setting up has a significant sense of impact, especially if the gameplay effects are similarly major. There's a lot I could mention in overall visuals, but I'm not that good at properly describing this sort of thing.One of the absolute biggest things that changed with 2 for me is absolutely the soundtrack. OT1 does have some extremely memorable tracks in places, but overall a lot of the music was a bit forgettable. Yasunori Nishiki went  with this game. There is almost not a single track on the OST for 2 that is not memorable to me in some way (which was definitely not the case with OT1, I can't actually recall any region bgms or, god forbid, protagonist leitmotifs without pulling up the soundtrack) and just about every single weak area of OT1's soundtrack was MASSIVELY improved. On top of that, the parts of OT1's soundtrack that were memorable have equivalents in OT2 that are just as good if not significantly better than their counterparts from the first game. This game's soundtrack easily is one of the best ones I have heard in -ANY- Square Enix title, and I'm well aware how blasphemous that may come off as.The world itself is incredibly rich. Just about every single plotline had me extremely engrossed in the events that occurred, and even beyond that even one-off side quests and NPC bios from inspections with travel actions revealed rather interesting characters that have plausible backstories with more than enough information to infer further and apply imagination which gives the game a much stronger feeling of just being -alive-. The game does get rather dark at times and discusses some rather uncomfortable subjects, but it's not really so much as to be deterring (speaking as someone who is very easily disturbed by heavy philosophical topics and other similar things). They also went out of their way to ensure that the party in OT2 feels much more like a group of people and less of a group of eight characters that experience their own stories completely on their own, which was one of the biggest weaknesses of OT1's main story writing. Interactions/banter are a lot more common in this game by comparison.Class design in this one feels a lot more thought out, and just about every job has more than enough tools to have a fairly well-rounded kit which was something classes struggled with a bit in OT1. As a sort of consequence, OT2 is an easier game overall than the first game, but I personally don't really find that to be much of an issue since most of the ways of snapping the game in half over your knee are honestly just the game rewarding you for proper party planning, setup, and execution. You could look up strategies or what have you, but I largely played this game blindly and ended up coming up with my own ways to approach problems. Sure, one of the main ones I used ended up being a pretty commonly recommended one on the internet, but just the fact that I was able to simply just figure it out is something I consider to be a positive.There's plenty of side content and areas to explore if you ever get tired of focusing on main plot lines and I easily spent 30+ hours just wandering around the world and expanding my horizons and finding new places and people. It's not really required, though, if you aren't really interested in that sort of thing.In general, if you are even somewhat of a fan of classic JRPGs, or maybe even not someone who dabbles into that part of the RPG genre, Octopath Traveler 2 is absolutely worth your time. This game is genuinely one of the best RPGs I have ever played, and I play a  of JRPGs.  It is genuinely incredible. If you were underwhelmed by Octopath Traveler, do not let that deter you from this game because it is leagues beyond that game in just about every way it fell short. This is just my own personal opinion, but I consider this game to stand tall above just about every FF in that series and all of its progeny sub-franchises. Acquire and SE's development team(s) for this series have created something that embodies just about everything I like about Squaresoft's older conventional JRPGs and doesn't just live up to those standards, it meets them and In conclusion, I honestly just have to re-iterate: This is one of the best games I have ever played in my life.  Do not let the Metacritic score deter you. It is a genuine one-in-ten-thousand masterpiece.(Edit: I goofed the formatting. Whoops!)

_childDocuments_.review: I am currently 73 hours into Octopath Traveler II. Usually, after investing this amount of time into a game, I would start feeling a bit fatigued, ready to wrap it up and leave it behind me. As it stands, I have finished only three of the eight character storylines, but that doesn't daunt me the slightest, because I'm still hungry for more. The game is just that exceptionally good.I liked the first game very much, but the sequel manages to improve upon the original so much that the original almost feels like a proof of concept compared to this. The stories I have finished so far are gripping and compelling. Castti, the compassionate healer haunted by a shrouded past; Osvald, the scholar seeking retribution after a monstrous betrayal; even Hikari, who I at first assumed to be just another cliched brooding warrior prince, got me invested in seeing his quest through.I never beat the true final boss of the first game. Not because it was challenging. It was, but that wasn't the problem. The problem was that every time I tried, I had to waste time on a pointless and trivial boss rush, so I stopped wanting to even try. I already managed to stumble upon the true final boss of the sequel once, and after deciding to give it a try for morbid curiosity, I was happy to see that it just let me get into the boss fight right away.Of course, I was wiped out in three turns. It was clear that I have no business here quite yet, that I should first gather all the tools the game has to offer and master how to use them, and come back when I'm well and truly ready. That said, I appreciate it that a game this lengthy shows that despite its length, it respects my time. It trusts me to make that mistake without forcing me to spend 20 minutes steamrolling through pushover boss rematches to show that I'm ready to make that mistake.Also, the original game's true final boss felt a bit disconnected from the rest of the narrative. In the sequel, though, all the stories have hints of something behind the scenes. There's always some great corrupting presence, catalyzing the evil that the party has to fight. I am not sure yet if this monstrosity is the presence the stories are hinting towards, but it most certainly feels so.Octopath Traveler II is a stellar example of its genre. A story that meshes together more coherently than its predecessor, in a world full of nooks and crannies to explore, in the context of what's simply a well designed party-based RPG that would be fun to play even if you stripped away everything else but the fights and the party management. A strong candidate for my personal GOTY.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first Octopath Traveler game.  I didn't expect Octopath 2 to meet every standard set by the first, but I also didn't expect those standards to fall in the ways they did.  In many ways, this was an enjoyable experience, but key areas dragged it down for me to not recommend it.The most important aspect of a game like this, for me, is the story.  The story feels like a shallow outline written by an uninspired new Californian writer, if that makes sense, especially when there are specific and jarring references to "capitalism" critique, unconventional relationships, and 'might makes right' villain motivations, all of which can be done just fine with a cleverer and more subtle treatment, mind you, but it is done here with the depth of a 15-year-old alt-lifestyle groupie.Villains are laughably one note, evil for the sake of evil, basically.  And of the ones that have some sort of redemption arc, the reasoning for their change is explained with one or two lines of dialogue and flakier than my corn-based breakfast.  The playable characters are inconsistent in their values and broken with respect to their logical perspectives in certain situations.The merchant was especially bothersome to me.  He was even shown in his own storyline that simply giving people wealth was not a viable solution to poverty, and yet his story revolves around doing exactly this without consequence (and not even with his own financial risk!).  Contrast this with the merchant in the first game, whose story revolved around learning about people's needs and desires rather than fooling them into thinking they needed things they didn't.  Imagine!  A MERCHANT character making money selling goods to people who need them and IMPROVING the lives of the people whom they are CAPITALIZING from.  It's as if the merchant in the first game was a protagonist and also A MERCHANT.The nuts and bolts of a game like this is the battle system, and I actually LIKE the battle system.  It is essentially more of the same from the first game.....     except....    there are broken abilities that make much of the battles in the game pointless.  Hikari and two of the merchant support abilities make random encounters a bore.  With mildly sufficient equipment, he effectively will one shot the enemies at the beginning of battle at no cost of resources.  So basically, as you walk around, a random encounter is just a nuisance for Hikari to slap across the face and you continue about your business.  Worse, resources aren't much of a worry for ANY character with one of the apothecary's support abilities, which restores 30% of HP and MP after each battle.  This encourages the player to slam every encounter with the strongest attacks immediately just to get it done, because those resources will be replaced.  It breaks the tension of exploring any area. (It also makes inns pointless)  For sure, the first game had synergies with certain abilities that trivialized battles, but it took more effort to find them and implement them.  You felt at least mildly smart for figuring them out.  In Octopath 2, it feels like thought and effort are overrated.Even the achievements are trimmed down to trivialize the accomplishment of achieving them.I will say that the sound and visual art of this game is as much a treat as the first, so no shade thrown on those artists.All things considered, this game just feels like a hashed-out, lower effort release rather than a project made from a place of passion.   If you want some extra frosting on your Octopath Traveler experience, this game is fine as a source of empty calories.  Otherwise, buy it on sale.  If you are looking for some meat, this will leave you disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. If you liked the first game at all then buy this one. Everything the first game does well, this one does better. Everything the first game fell short on, this game improved upon. The path actions are more fleshed out, stories are more interesting, and animations and voice lines are peak. New systems make everything feel fresh and the different abilities are way more fun to use. I especially found magic a lot more interesting to toy around with.  Team building is more difficult, which is purposeful and makes you feel good when a team really comes together to deal lots of damage. The secondary jobs have been expanded upon heavily and are much more engaging to toy around with (For example, Hikari probably isn't the best choice for Armsmaster!) Latent powers and EX skills give each character their own distinct feel too, which means even more possibilities. Other improvements to the combat aren't even directly related to the actual combat. Each move has its own unique animation and voice line tied to it, so combat doesn't really get old. This is made even more impressive when you realize the developers went to the length of having it done for every character, which sounds like a no brainer, but really who is making their Agnea a warrior? Doesn't matter, she has voice lines for every job and every skill. Additionally, each weapon has its own sprite so you can literally see the characters wielding the weapons they have equipped which is such a cool touch. But even if you do get bored of the animations or are trying to grind some levels or something, the game does have a double speed option that can be toggled with the push of a button during combat. Lastly, characters talk to each other during combat, getting worried when an ally has low HP, thanking them when getting healed, or congratulating each other when defeating an enemy. During boss fights the characters involved in that boss' story even shout at the enemy or have full on conversations mid-fight. All of this just makes combat a more fun and engaging experience and really brings the characters to life. Speaking of bringing the characters to life, the stories were compelling, and I found myself wondering where some of them would go. Obviously some were more straightforward than others, but the diversity in the cast made it feel like that was just the way that character was meant to deal with their problems (Ochette and Agnea I'm looking at you).  Not to say that some stories didn't try and present any themes or make any points, but some were more compelling or thought provoking than others. Stories like Temenos' and Throné's left me wanting more, gave me questions, and had me thinking. These ideas carried into the post-game bosses and really tied the whole story together for me. The plot twists surprised me as well. Specifically the best chapters were: Throné - Chapter 4Partitio - Chapter 3Osvald - Chapter 1/2 & 5Temenos - All of itAnd lastly the music, visuals, and voice acting. Yasunori Nishiki did the music again and it is exceptional. When a character is hyping themselves up before a big fight or giving an emotional monologue the music really brings it all together and makes you feel something. The visuals are stunning. Improvements to shading and models makes this game truly beautiful. I found myself appreciating them the most when the game was at dawn or dusk. And to be honest, the voice acting is pretty incredible. I find most Japanese media that gets English dubs to sound amateur, but this really blew me out of the water. Hearing Castti shout, "THESE HANDS!" or "NO MERCY, ONLY PAIN!" when using full BP always sent a shiver down my spine. In conclusion, I believe this game to be a masterpiece of game design and a true showcase of what a game can and should be. This game set out to be a turn based, story driven, modern JRPG and it went above and beyond. This is pretty much the best game in this genre. Now we just have to hope that this IP isn't just going to gacha hell, and that we actually get an Octopath Traveler 3.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game, time well spent.Gameplay:The content isn't repetitve, never had to grind in this game. Builds are very versatile, opportunities endless. There's an extra boss - the only thing that actually requires grinding, my endgame party with 70lvl x4 and 50lvl x4 characters felt too weak for it.Graphics&Sound:Simply glorious, you always get this warm and cozy feeling when playing this game. I especially like the transitions from day to night and the other way around. The way the melody goes on but with different instruments, simply a bliss. There's no epic soundtrack like Olberic's from Octopath Traveller I, and I liked the last boss's song from the first game better. Nevertheless it's still really good.Story:Maybe I don't consume enough media to be this "seen-it-all-and-its-cliche" guy, but I loved the story. At first I didn't like the characters - their voices even, but I grew to like them. Some stories are plain better than others, but that's the only downside - not all stories are equal. The final battle is now a part of the main plot, unlike the first part where it's technically a side quest. Travel banter and character interactions is fun. Also the sidequests actually have consequences even in the ending cutscenes.Cons:Long commute in some cases - fights happen every N steps, so sometimes it's annoying because you are very much overleveled and overpowered, have no interest in EXP or other rewards from the area, but you still get the random encounters and they take time and break the storytelling.Final areas' enemies are the same - I've noticed as I was cleaning 4th or 5th character's final level that enemies in their last chapter areas are the same - same golems, elementals and other cliche JRPG mobs. Also they don't make sense storywise sometimes - you are in a crowded city or in an empty castle, but you still get random encounters with some golems and elementals which is strange.No clear indications for stats - I had to google to find that some things potency is dependant on your elemental defence. Or that there's no point in going above 999 in a stat. Or that some buffs scale off your elemental attack on a physical attack.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll list some of my problems with Octopath Traveler 1 and how Octopath Traveler 2 fixed these. When I finished the game on the Nintendo Switch, I thought of it as a 7/10 game barring the Switch limitations. Its a really good game don't get the rating wrong, but there were enough issues I had that had it lowered. I did wish there was more voice acting in Octopath Traveler 1 when playing through it and Octopath Traveler 2 has voice lines throughout the game! The next problem is that the travelers never really interacted with each other outside of travel banter and the only instance of it was the secret boss at the end of Octopath Traveler 1 from what I can recall. Octopath Traveler 2 fixes that with the addition of Crossed Stories where two travelers interact with each other and new combat lines. The last problem is that it was a bit of a grindfest in Octopath Traveler 1 and in Octopath Traveler 2, they have plenty of ways to expedite the grind.Octopath Traveler 2 is objectively a really good sequel in the series. You do not have to worry about playing Octopath Traveler 1 before playing Octopath Traveler 2 as they are completely disjointed stories aside from the secret superboss. The soundtrack and beautiful pixel art are just as expected from playing Octopath 1 which means that they are amazing! I would argue that the soundtrack blends more with the context they are played in more than Octopath 1. The combat is the same Octopath 1 but they iterated on it by implementing a meter for each traveler and giving each traveler two unique skills that only they can learn. In addition, there are some job class changes that make each class feel better to use. These unique skills can help give an edge in combat and each traveler's special meter can help turn the tides of battle to your favor! The stories of each traveler are really well developed standing by themselves and have their own unique theme that all add up to one big theme that all the travelers' stories can add up to collectively. Even the side stories can have some relevancy to the overall plot of Octopath 2 which is neat. Score: 9.5/10Although this was a significant improvement from Octopath Traveler 1, there are some problems that still exist like idle members not getting exp though this is a subjective topic and is not as much of a problem since there are ways to expedite exp/jp gain. Even if you haven't played Octopath Traveler 1, I'd recommend to play Octopath Traveler 2. It was such a good time playing through this game and the stories can make you feel emotional if you decide to get attached to the characters. This is definitely a must play in 2023!I need an Octopuff plushie.

_childDocuments_.review: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II is one of the greatest JRPGs of all time.I adored the original OCTOPATH TRAVELER, and the sequel is everything that I could've hoped for. Each story immediately grabbed my attention and held it throughout, from Agnea's lighthearted wishes for stardom to Osvald's much darker plot for revenge, and the resolutions to each not only felt satisfying in a standalone sense, but each tied very well into the overarching major plot extremely well— not a new feat for the series, contrary to popular belief, but one that I nonetheless feel was done much more satisfyingly here compared to the previous entry. The new Crossed Paths make for interesting new scenarios involving two characters directly working together and interacting, which I definitely feel scratches the itch of those wishing for more interaction between characters. I won't spoil how everything all comes together in the end, but I will make one thing very clear: I cried during the credits. Not something that happens often for me, but Team Asano has found a way to do that to me twice within the past year (the other time being with LIVE A LIVE's remake on Switch). Absolutely lovely madlads over there.The gameplay mechanics have been refined, upgraded, and otherwise made practically perfect— the Break and Boost combat is still as addictive as ever, the Path Action system continues to encourage exploration of every nook and cranny in each town (including new nighttime Path Actions!), and the characters overall feel much more balanced this go-round, all without taking away anything that made them fun in the first entry! Being a big fan of Merchant in the first entry I chose Partitio, and I was delighted that he was not only just as fun to use as Tressa from the first game, but the rest of the gang was incredibly enjoyable as well, with some of the more complex classes like Hunter and Apothecary getting fantastic reworks so that the Beast Lore and Concoct systems respectively are much easier to use. With the first game I felt like I had to push newcomers towards Tressa in fear that they'd pick someone else and end up dropping it because of their imbalances, but in 2 you can really pick anyone and have a blast without prior knowledge of the game, which is exactly what I was hoping for! (Still don't regret picking Partitio though, gotta love the funny Texan money man.) The soundtrack is possibly Yasunori Nishiki's best work yet, continuing in the thematic style of the first game's soundtrack but getting very experimental with instrumentation and vocals in ways that the original didn't quite explore. The overworld themes had me excited for the next adventure, the nighttime themes had me relaxed and serene, and of course, the battle themes will have me tapping my foot for years to come. I won't get into too many specifics on the soundtrack since that touches on spoilers, but I will say that the saxophone in Partitio's theme was unexpected but works extremely well.The world of Solistia is beautifully varied in culture and environment, allowing for a much more distinct look and feel for each of the storylines— you'll be going back and forth between the lush countryside of the Leaflands to the streets of the bustling New Delsta in a flash, and it's always a joy to look at no matter where your journey takes you. It's a beautiful celebration of how far the HD-2D visual style has come over the years, and whether you've followed every new Team Asano release or are just jumping in for the first time with Octopath 2 (which is totally okay to do, it's not connected to the first entry story-wise!), you're in for a treat."The places you go… The deeds you do… The tales whose hero you become… Every road is yours to take."(Reader's note: The hour count on this review does not reflect actual playtime, as I beat the game on a Switch copy before buying a Steam copy. Yes, this game is so good I bought it for full price twice, and have over 100 hours on both copies. I swear I'm very normal.)

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath 2 is great. It takes everything that made the original Octopath Traveler interesting, and improves upon it in every way.2023 is shaping up to be a great year for JRPGsPROS:- Octopath 2 is an open world RPG done right. Octopath 1's world felt like a donut with branches coming off it, where as this one feels much more fleshed out and like an actual world spread across multiple continents.- Tons of hidden and optional areas to explore.- Tons of well designed larger than life bosses, both for the story and optional ones you may just come across at random when exploring- With all the character actions available, towns and npcs really come to life.- I love the little boats you pull out of nowhere when you get into water. The water/land dynamic makes for some interesting map designs as well.- Excellent pixel art throughout the game. Characters, bosses, backdrops, all look fantastic.- Beautiful music, many memorable tracks. Partitio's theme is especially good.- An especially well crafted and balanced turn based battle system.- A very well done job/ability system. It is fun to progress your characters and create builds.- The characters are likable and much more memorable in comparison to Octopath 1.- The stories are also much better and well written compared to the first game. They all are interesting and stand alone on their own, but also end up coming together and being related in different ways for the finale. CONS:- There is a train boss! ..but you cannot suplex it..- The job and ability menus are unnecessarily annoying to navigate up until you finish all the character stories, and then they suddenly make last minute improvements to it. Why couldn't it have been that way for the whole game?- Sometimes when you are going back and forth between different character's chapters, the story telling feels less smooth and more like running back and forth to hit the next trigger.- There are too many reasons to fight at night.. a character that buff your party automatically at night, a character that debuffs all the enemies automatically at night, a job ability that gives you boosted EXP at night.. but there are no reasons to fight in the day. So a lot of the game is experienced in the dark sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: When Octopath Traveler came out on the Switch, I felt like it was unfinished. I theorised that there would be a PC release thanks to the game's use of unreal engine, and hoped that such a release would tie up some of the loose ends the original release had. Imagine my shock when the PC version changed nothing at all, and still charged full price! Imagine my shock when the sequel surpassed the original in every way, and even had a lower price!In terms of gameplay, the game sits fairly high on my list of JRPGs that manage to have an actual interesting combat system. This was the case with the first game as well, but the problems that game had made it feel like a waste of time once you'd finished it all. I'd strongly encourage anyone to try the demo if you're interested in the game at all.Regarding story, Octopath Traveler II is not necessarily deep, nor does it really have a lot of character dialogue for how long the game is, but the characters have much more care put into their presentation than the first game. I'd rate it as perfectly serviceable.The game's soundtrack does a lot to pull you into any given scenario. Perhaps a bit too much, as there were some cutscenes toward the end that had characters mumbling at a volume that made them inaudible under the swelling dramatic score. But this only happened a couple of times, and the music is good enough that occasionally hearing it a bit too much isn't all that problematic.Octopath Traveler II feels like a proper realisation of the game that its predecessor was an unfinished prototype of. Overall, I would wholeheartedly recommend the game to anyone interested in the genre. There's a lot to love here, and where I once had no hope for this series I'm now eager to see what they do next. Hopefully it'll be something a bit more different, though.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I am hesitant to pick up a game using the old pix-elated sprites from Final Fantasy games of NES and SNES especially when dealing with titles such as Pathfinder Kingmaker, Wrath of the Righteous, the upcoming Rogue Trader and other type RPGS/SRPGS. I picked up Octopath 2 on sale and it brought back all the Nostalgia of playing Final Fantasy 4 and 6 and what made those games great.  The voice acting, the day/night path actions really fleshes out the characters well in terms of similar affinity to those I loved in Final Fantasy Series combined with a compelling story(s).  I chose Osvald as my primary traveling protagonist and really enjoying his playthru.  The addition of 2nd jobs also provides an added dimension of multiclassing.  Although my avatar is updated in both fights and the menu, the overworld map sprite seems to retain my former be-ragged appearance of looking like a vagrant. The ability to recruit random NPCs is also welcomed and provides another aspect of team customization.As a minor spoiler I am still early in the game to not know if we obtain a home base of sorts similar to the airships/flying castles that we can upgrade, however I would recommend this game for those wanting a good RPG with a well written story arc, memorable characters, and Final Fantasy Steam Punk feels.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hands down a must play. The way I realised this is that even though I could critique some aspects of the story, the random battles, the character bonding moments, the quality of quests etc (except the music, the music is objectively in a platinum league of astounding quality) the thing  noticed was....I kept on playing, I kept on wanting to play more, I didn't get bored, I didn't feel like things felt familiar or stale. And that's the mark of a good RPG. The story is decent and in line with traditional RPGs albeit it gets dark in some places. I did feel a sense of camaraderie among the companions but not as much as Dragon's Quest or a Persona does, but each character is interesting and I like the small touches (funny dialogue in bars and them talking to each other during combat). The combat system is great and the job system really makes it so that I never really had a 'favourite' group of 4 fighters, but rather I had 8 bad assess from which I needed to choose 4 according to the needs of the area/boss. The final boss fight was satisfying and felt like a good balance of trial/error and incremental improvement to push you to learn the system more and more. The music....oh my god the MUSIC! I had finished playing Sea of Stars before I played Octo 2, and SOS has an incredible soundtrack, Octo is in the same league, I am going to be listening to this OST on repeat for months to come. Even if you don't want to play the game, listen to the soundtrack!Overall it's a 9/10. It's an excellent game. Is it a special game? Mostly no, but a little bit yes. For me a 'special' RPG is one that you are willing to play again, despite knowing it's going to ask a big chunk of time from you, you're still willing to play it again for the experience. I'd do that for Chrono Trigger, Persona 4/5, FFVII, Dragon Quest 8 etc. but for Octo 2 would I do it? mostly no...but 25% yes I would. So at least we can say it's an excellent game and a little bit special! :D Get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic old-school-style JRPG.  Really takes me back to the FFVII / Chrono Trigger days - superb in-depth game mechanics, great voice acting (even on the English side), an amazing Score, beautiful retro-pixel-style visuals, and good stories all walks of life.I would change a couple things though:1.  Despite the ending story being well done, the end-game "tie-in" of all 8 characters stories and lead-in to the final chapter felt a tad rushed and less seamless than desired.  It was fairly sudden and a lot of the lore was buried in voice-less/scene-less journal texts.   The whole "Avengers" team assembly build up at the end to "fight the evil" was just too quick and needed more story, more gameplay, more everything with the 8 characters spending more time together as a group.  Fighting with all 8 characters was also super out of left-field for someone who hasn't played OT1.  It would have been nice to have fights like that earlier on so I would have known it was even a thing that was coming.  (Pro-tip if you're reading this:  You need to level all characters in this game to finish it, so don't ignore ones you're less interested in).2.  The level 90-99 experience grind needs to be reduced.  Getting all 8 characters to level mid 70s was not bad, but even using all EXP boost strategies (extra bonus skills, accessories, caits, the Alr*** summon), the grind from 90-99 is an incredible SLOG.  I eventually gave up with my core team around 91-95 and my B team 70-80 and finished the game as such.3.  Without spoiling anything, with the final chapter's "event" that happens - NPCs throughout the world act as if nothing unusual is amiss.  None of their dialogue changes, they're still out and about playing music and oblivious.  Very weird.  I remember even back in the FFVII days when major events, all the local NPC dialogue changed up to reflect it.  The fact that this game didn't do that really down-played the final chapter and made it feel less fleshed out.  It was slightly immersion-breaking to the story.4.  The Altars are easily missed.  I had my core team up to level 90-95, ready to take on the final chapter, before I realized (after looking online), that the dang Altars are labeled on your mini-map when you're in a zone.  I had only accidentally stumbled upon 1 the entire game.  I would change those mini map symbols to be more distinguishable or inject some more obvious tutorial to the player to allow them to at least easily find the FIRST altar, so they know more are out there.  5.  I finished the game and never used NUTS.  I learned about nuts after browsing Reddit, and wow... what a incredible thing to have missed the entire game.  Why are these not made more obvious to the player?  They come off as in-fight bonus items, when in fact they are PERMANENT out-of-fight items???    I can't be the only one who never knew.  The use of these items needs to be made more obvious to the player, or again, maybe inject an obvious tutorial to get you to use the first one and see how it works.Otherwise, this game is fantastic.  I didn't even finish all side-quests/unlocks and there's still so much game play left.  I would strongly recommend one thing if you pick up this game:Get a nice drink, sit back, and take your sweet time.  Enjoy the story, the voice acting, the music, and game-play.   When you're finished, you'll be left with a feeling you've had back in the day after finishing one of those classic JRPGs that have stuck with you to this day.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. Here are my thoughts as someone who played a lot of JRPGs and dropped OT1 after 7 hours lol:Pros:- Captures the feeling of old school RPGs perfectly. It feels like I'm playing a brand new RPG from my childhood days, bringing in that sense of nostalgia and wonder to the game.- Music is godlike (as all Square RPGs do), accompanied by gorgeous visuals that blends 2D SNES-era graphics and high-fidelity 3D perfectly.- Freeform party building system where everyone can be anything as long as you have the proper subjobs and support skills, means there's no hard "holy trinity" for the party, allowing for some wacky builds that is unique to Octopath Traveler.- Latent Power is not just an "ultimate" ability and served to bring more depth into the battle strategy, which is a nice change of pace compared to other RPGs that only makes ultimate-like mechanics a system 2 nuclear/panic button you press once in a while.- Day and night system is an actual core mechanic gameplay and story-wise rather than just aesthetics.- All of the characters have interesting personalities and equally interesting motives for their stories. I find myself enjoying the travel banters and the dialogues in the story more than the first game.- Hikari, Temenos, and Ochette's stories are the highlight of the game.Mixed:- This game focuses more on strategy, party building, gear hunting via dungeon crawling, and support skills rather than stat growths and leveling. So if you're coming into this game thinking you're gonna breeze through the game with the stuff you bought at the local stores just because you're 10 levels above the recommended level for the chapter, you'll be deeply disappointed. Take it as a plus or minus, it's up to personal taste. I'm leaning more towards plus tbh.- Osvald and Throne's stories are a bit too edgy for my taste, but they're kind of alright.- Overall the stories have a lot of noticeable plot holes, but they're forgivable due to the scale of the game.Cons:- The difficulty is not adjusted properly. Way too hard at the early game and way too easy at the endgame. I had to install a mod that increases all enemies' health and shield points by the last few chapters in the game so that I could get an enjoyment out of the endgame without one-shotting the bosses because the endgame gears, jobs, and support skills were ridiculously overpowered.- Since you can just one shot all the random encounters with the optimal strategy for your party, it's just repeating that same routine for every random encounter, making them tedious by the endgame. Not to mention that some endgame dungeons have increased encounter rate, making them very frustrating to navigate through.- Castii, Partitio and Agnea's stories are wasted potential. One has a great premise but is very poorly executed, and the other two is just so detached from the overall plot it might as well be a chain of side quests. The only saving grace these three had is that their characters are at least interesting unlike in OT1 where some of the characters are boring as hell, which I've already mentioned before.Overall, the game is a very solid 8/10 for me. I love this game so much, but there's some baggage that I have to put through in order to enjoy this game. Play this game with the gameplay-first mindset and you wouldn't be moaning too much at the shortcomings this game has.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. Octopath 1 was an amazing game, but all of the little improvements that Octopath 2 brings make it blow its predecessor out of the water. The day/night cycle (with dynamic music to accompany it) adds an extra layer of depth to the game that makes exploring just that much more fun, having an extra 5th chapter for every character along with crossed paths adds depth to the characters' already incredible stories, and the addition of  Latent Powers gives the characters even more uniqueness and entices you to try them out. The break and boost battle system returns with the same 8 regular classes, but there are different secret classes this time around which are pretty neat. Not to mention, the soundtrack is just as good as the first, if not better. I also really enjoyed how all of the stories are tied together in the end; paying attention to story events and keeping track of unanswered questions gets rewarded. All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the first.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I found OT 2, I played OT: CotC, and as someone who was completely new to the series, it was more than overwhelming to get a firm grasp of what was going on. I had my fair share of turn-based games, so I wasn't entirely inexperienced. However, when I came across OT 2, I was a bit wary of the gameplay after I stopped playing the previous one. What caught my interest, which inevitably convinced me to give this one a chance, was the game's modifications, QoL, and other improvements that differed from the first game. I don't regret buying this game, as I was blown away by the gameplay, visuals, stories, and the music (especially the music). This is definitely a game you should experience yourself, rather than having me explain every aspect. If you're into turn-based games and have been looking for one for a while now, then this is well worth the price. Though, if you're not into them but want to try it out, then wait until it's on sale. To those that are worried about completing one playthrough and then not picking it up afterwards cause you're bored, I can somewhat agree with you that there's very little content after you finish the game. On the other hand, you can always do a run with a different character or come up with a new team idea than the previous ones you had.

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is an upgrade over the first game. In fact, if you haven't played the first game I recommend just jumping to this one. They don't share a story anyways and this game has some good quality of life improvements. I like a lot of aspects of this game. it's got an open world design where you can go almost anywhere at any time but you may not survive some areas that are higher level early on. You can start as any of the 8 characters. You can choose to do each of the stories in any order (or skip any you don't like) while exploring the world.I only completed the 4 stories of the characters i decided to keep in my party. That's because Octopath Traveler 2 has the same problem I had with the first game. Each character has ~5 chapters. Each chapter follows the formula of story dump, dungeon, boss, more story. Each character's story is completely separate from each other. So to go through all 8 stories is to have giant dialogue dumps 40+ times and for me it was just too much. I enjoyed the 4 stories I played, but I also played Octopath Traveler 1 in at the beginning of the year and the story dump formula got old for me. I wish the game had some kind of cohesive narrative to bring the 8 characters together as opposed to just 8 strangers who are doing their own thing outside of combat. That being said, Octopath Traveler 2 is one of the better JRPG's to come out recently and I feel like the turn based system is fun. The customization options for your party keep it interesting. Personally I prefer Bravely Default 2's systems but Team Asano has been doing amazing work for traditional turn based JRPG fans. Overall, I do recommend the game. Just be aware of the dialogue heavy stories and know there isn't a grand narrative but 8 smaller narratives.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok....so I want to say the game is good.Music - amazing.Mechanics amazing (however I found the game to be too easy but I admit I am usually someone who knows how to play these kinda games, there was one boss that was actually challenging wish there was more of that, but to be fair most of square enix rpgs have been "easy" if you "know your way around". A difficult mode would've made these game "chef's kiss".The game is very entertaining and absorbs time easily, without feeling drained or exhausted.But I have to say the major disappointment about the game is...the story....to me was extremely un-layered and just cheesy "feel good vibes" extremely basic narrative...nothing lore-esque about it.There's something about the story/dialogue that is just way too simple pimple, I don't even think children will find it interesting. It's like the a really boring netflix show or something...nothing exciting...no compelling lore to wiki and obsess over at all...if anything you might find yourself skipping dialogue easily cause there's too many "talking about the weather - hehe" dialogues...Is it worth 80 dollars.....mmmm.....it's not terrible, but the story definitely makes is the angle that cheapens the game immensely. While the characters are lovable....their stories lack depth, and they become "a cliche" tied to their "role" in the game too fast - no dimension.Which is compared to the old school final fantasy series....that is the big major difference to be honest...but Square Enix has been releasing really poor quality games for a while now imo, this made me "hopeful", as they recaptured what was fun about their classic RPG releases.Here's to hoping they're not just going to milk good concept poorly! _childDocuments_.review: This is one of very few game I would consider to be a masterpiece in its own right.  I have not a single bad word to say about it. Visually is incredible. The Music and Setting are are masterful.The characters are generally well written and goal orientated.The plot lines are above average even if a little simplistic at times.Dialogue for the most part is good. Locations are a visual treat with huge diversity in backgrounds and environments.Enemy diversity is great and well thought out. Combat is actually pretty deep, there is a lot of tweaking players can do to achieve massively different results with various job combinations and abilities and characters, and i mean a lot. Itemisation matters a fair bit. Especially for the super boss. Looting and exploring is nice, small detours but not excessive to get cool and sometimes really strong loot without massively inconveniencing you is really good. The map size is good and tons of locations to visit, explore and complete. Side quests are impactful and rather well designed with nice story tie ins and break up the main story a bit. I really cannot recommend this game enough. If I had some negatives to talk about of which I dont have many and some would be pretty nitpicky but ill list them anyways: 1. Dialogue in places can be a little be weak, unnecessary or drawn out.2. Some side quests are truly incredibly vague to the point you are likely going to have to look them up the vast majority are self explanatory but some are just like "wut?where?huh?"3. Some of the main characters are just considerably or massively better than others simply because of job/item combinations that some cannot access simply due to their base job. 4. Some characters are better to start with than others, its not necessarily a negative as such, but it can encourage starting a path you might not want to simply because of how efficient it can be to progress early.5. Agnea is a character is quite an annoying character and the least satisfying story line. 6. The lack of a bestiary, especially for ochette, as ochette becomes a staple shield breaker but if you dont know which enemies have which abilities can be a pain to work out where and which ones you need, even if not for ochette simply to see which enemies are in what locations etc. In conclusion the game is incredible. Get it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game somehow took everything about the first game and improved on it in big ways! The cast is of course as like-able as  before, but the writing behind their stories and the events that transpire feel much better written and more lengthy, adding to the overall content of the game. The visuals, map layout and overall design feels like such a huge step up, with so many stand out areas and environments with such lovingly crafted detail. _childDocuments_.review: Time Value to Money: Around 70 hours for a first run. What this game does well:It builds on small moments to create a crescendo with stellar animations and a top shelf sound track. Every character feels multi-sided allowing for growth. RPG elements: e.g. "Will I mug, steal, or purchase this item?"Banter between the crew often has plot substance in addition to playfulness. Overarching story builds up into a tangible story thread. What it does poorly:The Random Encounter is tuned to be about every 5 seconds without a trait which gives you a normal rate of 10 - 15 seconds.  This is tedious as almost no grinding is required.Pacing:  By the end of the game I was far too over leveled at around 60, despite fleeing from every encounter save for bosses the last 20 hours of play. Fleeing for 20 hours because you're already so OP & resource rich with twenty hours left isn't a fun combat experience. Difficulty: Not a single game over or failed encounter. It starts off a bit interesting as one has no party members, limited skills, and almost no resources but quickly becomes orders of magnitudes easier.. . . : This can be silence. This should be silence. 95% of all ". . ." are accompanied by anime grunting noises and ". . ." is written a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really knows what it wants to be and doesn't care if people don't like what they're doing. They did little to change Octopath II's core from it's predecessor, however they've sprinkled little improvements throughout the experience to make it feel fresh and new, however I couldn't help but feel deja vu in some parts like I've played this exact scenario in 2018. Game takes a very dark turn, touching on some topics and themes I wouldn't expect an RPG to touch on anymore, especially when Octopath 2018 played it very safe with narrative. II feels like Team Asano was allowed to spread their wings and fly. The new 3DCG they're calling it leads to some cinematic set pieces I feel only modern technology can create while still giving a nostalgic feel from the Super Famicom era. Music has been cranked to 11, though I wouldn't expect any different from Yasunori Nishiku. All in all if you know you like these kinds of games chances are you'll find something to enjoy in Octopath II.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a semi open world JRPG. Graphical style is similar to Final Fantasy pixel remasters, with added 3D effect. Gameplay reminds of those classic Square RPGs. Battles happen mostly randomly and they are turn based, similar to Final Fantasy X. I highly prefer real turn based battles over real-time or active time battle (ATB), so that's definitely a plus. Random battles feels a bit odd and outdated concept, though. The game has story sequences separated by semi open world exploration, where you're mostly free to travel in the world following paths. You start with a single character and when you begin traveling, you encounter and unlock different characters with their own stories. I think you can unlock every character, it's just a matter or which order. Every character has a fixed main job and possible customizable side job. As said, battles are turn-based. There's a huge emphasis on breaking the enemy's block by exploiting their vulnerabilities. It's actually quite satisfying when you get the combo right, one character breaks the block and the other deals massive damage.Good:+ Looks good+ Great soundtrack+ Story seems good+ Turn-based battles+ Less cringy than some modern JRPGs+ Voice actingBad:- Random battles- Characters not that memorable

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 improves upon OT1 in visual design, exploration, and combat, with the music being as awesome as ever. It manages to shake up the formulaic story progression found in the first game, which is refreshing.The story starts off perfect (easy GotY material) then decides to go off the deep end 70% through. While the game attempts to improve upon the interconnectedness of the characters, it is still sorely lacking in many areas. Additionally, the way the 8 stories connect feels forced, especially compared to OT1.The EN localisation is abhorrent. Over 10% of the skills in this game are horribly mistranslated, often to the opposite of what they actually do. The story is similarly butchered, with mistranslations abound and liberties taken far beyond what is acceptable.The music of Octopath is a technical masterpiece. In OT1, character motifs transition seamlessly into boss music, a technique that is still present. With the new day-night mechanic, we have 2 separate tracks for many areas, both of which transition smoothly into each other at every point.Octopath has my favourite pixel art design of all time, along with particle effects that are a joy to look at. Also, character sprites now move a lot more, breathing life into battles.There is so much content. The way the world is joined together, along with the myriad of dungeons scattered throughout, make exploring this world feel like a much-improved version of OT1’s exploration.The new Path Actions add a lot of depth to gameplay and exploration, and the side quests were a joy to figure out (when the localisation wasn't butchering the hints).Secondary jobs now come with side quests to acquire legendary gear and additional job permits (i.e. items allowing you to simultaneously have the same secondary job on multiple characters). Special secondary jobs are also more varied in how they’re unlocked (as opposed to fighting a boss like in OT1).Still, I wish they had included CotC’s mechanic where the world map kept track of the chests you’ve opened and Path Actions you’ve cleared in each area. It would have made searching for NPCs easier, with the only solutions now being a) using a guide and b) searching every inch of the map and hoping you get lucky. A bestiary would also have been useful.There are many more options and strategies available now. Every time I unlocked a new EX Skill, I lost myself in the endless possibilities of how it could synergise with other skills and characters to make an insane combo. The journey to build a set of unique monsters/skills for Ochette/Hikari was also really fun.But.A good set of synergistic skills needs good enemies, which is where this game suffers.You're almost never responding meaningfully to the enemies' actions, and there's no point in taking advantage of the amazing synergies between skills when most mid/late game bosses die in 1.5 hits.There were only a handful of fights where I felt adequately challenged, with all else being "solved" by putting damage buffs on 1 person, defence debuffs on the enemy, and pressing the highest damaging ability.Combat was really fun and challenging in CotC, which also had the QoL of having numbers on skills/items, so I don't know why OT2 is like this. Hard to believe that the designers of CotC's amazing boss and arena fights were responsible for this series of boring stompfests.Overlevelling is a major issue. I had flashbacks to Pokémon and Elden Ring, where I overlevelled everything by virtue of being an exploration completionist.You can’t even safely run from trash mobs, because the flee success rate seems linked to level. Your choices here are to overlevel by killing them or waste time failing to run away 5 times in a row.The plot, worldbuilding, characters, themes, and (JP) dialogue were absolutely perfect at the start, and subversion of expectations was spectacular for the first half. However, the story began falling off past that point, then gave me Game of Thrones Season 8 PTSD at the end.They reused plotlines and arcs from OT1 and CotC:Almost every single character is one-dimensional—especially the villains. Villains don't all need to be Jaime Lannister, but when every bad guy is going, “Oh me bad guy because world bad destroy world hahaha”, it gets old. There were a few well-written, complex characters in Triangle Strategy, so I don’t know why OT2’s characters are more one-dimensional than even OT1’s.They tried to add interconnectedness between the travellers with Extra Stories and Travel Banter, but they don’t interact with each other outside of that. Travellers should really feature in main stories not their own—otherwise, it feels disjointed insofar as the OCTOPATH theme is concerned, such as how Temenos’s story was .Unlike how every character's story in OT1 connected together meaningfully at the end, that connection in OT2 felt very forced, such as how (MAJOR OT2 spoilers)  were those characters’ only link to the overarching plotline.There was a LOT of buildup in the story, most of which went nowhere. I’m not talking a few loose ends—I’m talking worse than Game of Thrones Season 8. “Who is that person? What did they want? Why did they do that? What does this mean?” All asked; never answered. It feels like OT2’s story was cut or rushed, or maybe they’re DLC/sequel-baiting.I’m changing this review to negative if it turns out they cut OT2’s story to place in CotC.I’m pretty sure the localisers who butchered OT2 also handled Triangle Strategy’s localisation, which mistranslated “Armlet” to “Amulet” and “take over the city” to “sack the city”, which is like translating “restrain him” to “rob and rape him”.They clearly feel that the English-speaking audience is filled with pearl-clutching Karens, as evidenced by how Temenos being called a dog is localised as “hound”, which fails to recognise that insults are meant to be insulting—not awkward. Or how they PG-13’d Agnea’s sister talking about Agnea’s boobs, changing that conversation to a euphemistic cringefest involving the word “talent”.The localisers also believe that English-speakers are mentally inept, as they translated プラットじいさん (Grandpa Platt) and プラットばあさん (Grandma Platt) to “Platt” and “Platt’s Wife”. To them, English-speakers are too stupid to understand that the couple running the orphanage aren’t the orphans' biological grandparents simply because they have "Grandpa" and "Grandma" in their name, so the solution is obviously sexism, where they reduce a woman’s identity to her relation to her husband. Good job.Speaking of mental ineptitude, this is the second Octopath world where they decided to ♥♥♥♥ up the speech of the Huntress’s homeland. When they aren’t busy making H’aanit speken like she wille to the 15th Century returnen, they’re making the beastmen sound like they have a mental disability. This is a problem, because a) they speak like innocent children in Japanese, and b) . Amazing.The goal of localisation is to improve natural readability at the cost of accuracy, but there’s a reason “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it".Octopath Traveler 2's early game was absolutely fantastic in damn near every single way. Yet, while the aesthetics and exploration remained strong throughout, the combat became a cakewalk, and the story left too much unfinished and unresolved.

_childDocuments_.review: This really is just the same game as the previous Octopath Traveler. I suppose if you expect more of that, then this is a perfectly good game. However, it seems many people in the reviews here have misspoken when they claim that this game resolves a lot of the shortcomings of the previous one. Unlike, say, actual old Final Fantasy games (particularly VI), there is no meaningful interaction with the world whatsoever. I mean, I can mug everyone in the entire town and they act like nothing has happened. There is no point in talking to any of the NPCs, because you'll glean no secrets. It's all just filler. Each dungeon and thru-area is highly formulaic. You always know you'll find the one random chest kinda off to the side. There's no need to really explore, you won't find any secrets, not like the classic FF games. Art direction and physical design of everything is splendid. They really got that right. But like the previous game, all the actual substance isn't really there. "Where's the beef?"

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the non-bad things out of the way Graphics and sound fit, no complains there. Combat system is solid, progression system works....done. Now for the bad. In short: they have neither learned from nor improved upon the issues of the first game.There is neither. You have 8 solo characters that have absolutely nothing in common and that have virtually no interaction either. You have 8 mini stories that are outright crap. Stories are cut into chapters and intentionally made so you don't play 1 characters  story without interruption. There is no connection between either story and the chapter design is...sh*t. Enter area, get popup, confirm you wanna do the chapter, get hit by walls of text, use the characters path action at least once, get hit by more walls of text and occasionally you get to fight a bit...story chapter done. How low can the developers of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest fall ?.....is like 90% of the game. Every single character story chapter revolves around the characters path action. There isn't a single side quest you can finish without using at least 1 path action, several can't even be started without. And even the skills for 2 jobs (inventor and armsmaster) are locked behind path action. This leaves you with the "choice": pick a party that has all relevant actions..or constantly switch members...but neither is actually an option. Choosing a party with all actions leaves you with like 1 party setup, constantly switching fails because path actions are not limited to towns where you can change party members and more (example at the end).  Adding day and night means you have 2 options for each result for day and night (e.g. 2x steal for day, 2x steal for night)...except it doesn't work. The game does not allow you to beat up children (sadnes...). The warrior's day action knocks out NPC blocking your path...by beating them up...can't use it on children. Can be worse... The priests night action gains information..by beating the NPC up...again can't use it on kids. Only way to get info from kids during the night is ...bribing them with the warrior which wastes money. Even better is the scholar who has a "steal" night action...by beating the target up. => not on kids. Only way to get items from kids during night time is the dancer...but her path action depends on her level. There is the next problem: only the characters in your active party get xp. So you can't just switch in the dancer for her path action...nope, you have to lvl her first.The promised example: A sidequest requires you to get a new lens for a lighthouse. Every normal game allows you to talk to the NPC and offer to buy it...not this pile of **. You have to use path action...and out of the 4 steal path action only the one from the merchant is allowed to be used. So you run back to town, switch in the merchant, run to the docks, board your ship, sail across the sea to the island, walk up the island to the lighthouse, buy the damn lens and go back to town to switch out the merchant.....truely great design....

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveller 2 is a decent turn based JRPG. It has okay story, satisfying combat, and a lot of content. There is also a unique interaction mechanic with NPCs that increases the game's depth. My main gripe is that it has random encounters. You would think that a modern JRPG would move away from random encounters like all the recent JRPG games, but Octopath Traveller 2 continues to use this annoying mechanic. Random encounters are annoying when you just want to explore or move to another place and also make the pacing in the game really choppy when you are invested in the story. Grinding in the game is also a hassle because your characters level up individually and not all together. There are 8 characters in total, but you can only have 4 characters at a time, which makes it a hassle to grind and use different characters. I would also like more variety in skills between characters that would making team compositions more interesting. All in all, if random encounters bother you, don't pick this game up, because it can ruin your experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good, modern JRPG which improves upon its predecessor. The characters somewhat copy the jobs from the previous game, but they introduce new stories, which is the more important part. I loved Octopath Traveler I to death, and this game makes me feel like I am experiencing the whole game all over again.Although the jobs are mostly recycled from the first game, they added new abilities which makes this game a little more different. The game also feels a bit easier than the previous game, which I appreciate since the first game had some unnecessary difficulty curves at the start of it. However, I'm used to the Octopath formula, so I might just be used to the combat system.I've gone two hours into the game and I don't see any "step downs" whatsoever. Therefore, if I can suggest the first game, I would suggest the second game even more!

_childDocuments_.review: You can change the time of day with the press of a button, bringing about changes to the world and your characters. It also progresses naturally if you let it. Was constantly taking screenshots and marvelling at the world design. The music is colourful and emotive, and the way it changes depending on the time of day never got old. Being able to interact with every npc in the world in multiple ways was fun on OT1 and still is on OT2, but characters now have two path actions they can perform depending on the time of day. Like on OT1, the battles consist of exploiting an enemy's weaknesses to break them, stunning them and giving you a chance to deal heavy damage. This "breaking" mechanic makes battles more three-dimensional than a traditional JRPG. Each character has a plethora of specialised skills they can use and can also adopt a secondary class, allowing them to use even more. Characters can mix and match with any class in the game, allowing you to execute some incredible strategies during battle.  Battles can be very difficult based on your approach. There are also two frighteningly hard endgame bosses that will pull down your pants and suck you off. Overall the stories on this game are a lot better than on OT1. They are slow at times and extremely anime-like, but if you're into that: great! At the very least they allow you to skip any dialogue or cutscene you don't care for. It dragged a bit sometimes, but like I said at least you're allowed to skip it. Annoying, especially when your characters are way more powerful than everything around you. I'm not saying the game is easy; but if you play your cards right, you can get extremely powerful very quickly. There is also one way to become basically immortal, which I won't mention. This is my biggest criticism, and if you're the kind of gamer who only enjoys "hard" games, then you won't enjoy OT2.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game mostly because I was bored and had nothing else to play at the moment. It is a serviceable JRPG, but certainly not worth the asking price. Wait until it's on sale.To go into further details: the random encounters are too frequent, until you finally get a skill to reduce how much of them you get, at which point the encounter rate becomes somewhat bearable.After that, though, the grind remains, since the characters who are not in your party do not gain experience.What purpose this serves beyond extending the game's playtime, I do not know.The core gameplay is decent, though I tended to find myself only using a small selection of skills even in boss battles. Many of them are simply not worth looking at, which is a big problem when there are so few to choose from. I liked that most characters had a way to use skills other than their own (with Oscar and Throné being the exception) since it added some of the variety that the core skills lacked. The hidden jobs do help to alleviate that issue, but they arrive much too late into the game to be enough in that regard. Octopath as a series desperately needs more skill variety.The story varies from mediocre to hilariously bad. What it almost always is, though, is trite and cliché, with Throné's arguably being an exception mainly through contrived twists. The various character's stories are not linked by anything but the final arc and some short chapters that star two characters together. One could say that they have learned from the first game in that regard, but I say they've done the minimal effort they could to address that problem, and it shows.The music and the graphics are pretty good, and I don't have much else to say on that front. Good character design, very nice pixel-art. The area design is alright, though I suspect most of them will fade from my memory quickly now that I'm done with the game.Overall, the game is mediocre nostalgia-bait, much like the first one. It's a shame. The few innovations it brings in terms of art-style and gameplay are wasted on it. Still, I have hope to see the potential of these ideas realized in the future. For now, though, this game is just a way to keep boredom at bay for a while, and as such, is definitely not worth its full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just begun to dip my toes into this fantastic game but I felt compelled to leave my first impressions. Having played the first Octopath Traveler, it seems like a lot of the failings of that game have been corrected here. I can't express how delighted I've been being introduced to each of the main characters and their stories thus far. Each character has a fairly dynamic personality where they don't feel like they're just occupying a stereotype. I mean sure, there's a few plots that are essentially cliches like The Count of Monte Cristo, the amnesiac with a dark past, or the wrongfully convicted prisoner, but these all feel well executed. There are also gems like Temenos the Cleric who is unlike any other kind of white mage archetypal character I've seen in any JRPG.  He's a morally good character, yet his personality and actions would make him seem as if he's neutral or secretly bad. It's actually quite fascinating. I've also noticed a lot of quality of life updates this time around, such as combat speed multipliers, characters having two role actions, and the "grind" feels a bit lessened than previously. Other than that, it's still roughly the same type of game as before which is perfectly fine because the art style is beautiful and the combat feels great. I'd definitely recommend it to fans of JRPGs and ESPECIALLY those who played the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: OCTOPATH TRAVELER II

_childDocuments_.review: Octopath Traveler 2 is a fantastic game that builds upon the first version's flaws, though doesnt resolve all of them.The game is outstanding in the Graphics, Music, and Gameplay departments. You'll find few better JRPGs in these categories.Where it continues to find fault is in the multiple character story arcs. Unfortunately having 8 characters that do not mesh together apart from weak unvoiced and overall lackluster cutscenes that are completely avoidable. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:  Octodad Legends 13 - Happily spent the money I saved from skipping Lightfall to buy this absolute gem.legendary OST, charming world and characters, mechanically solid and fulfilling game play of average strategic complexity, beautiful graphics and 2d sprite work, fleshed out world full of things to explore with some very welcome surprises, good writing with an excellent localization, brief but sufficiently set-up conclusion, satisfying send-off. Lots of nods to the classics. .Good game.s'cold----Disclaimer, I have one functioning braincell and am adept at picking up heavy objects and little else. This is a feely-weely review and any degree of objective analysis is beyond my miniscule scope.I enjoyed Octopath I to a degree but it didn't have enough holding power for me. The novelty of combat wore off after the first couple dozen levels, the path action system added a degree of tedium to town sequences that already felt a bit hollow and difficult to get through with how shallow a fair few of the NPCs can be. The towns themselves felt more like set-pieces than actual locations with history and purpose. Coupled with the disconnected and occasionally simplistic character arcs, I had a hard time motivating myself to progress past the chapter 2 mark for most of the cast and eventually set the game aside. Also Alfyn rubbed me the wrong way and I have no idea why. He seems like a nice enough fella. Out of curiosity, and wanting to give the series another shot, I popped in to check the reviews and feedback on II and could quickly tell that it was a pretty safe buy. And hoo-ey do I not regret that purchase one bit.This is an incredibly charming and well constructed sequel that seems to, insofar as I can tell, improve on every aspect of its predecessor while making up for the original's shortcomings. The characters all have a unique charisma and charm, performing with appropriate gravitas for each of their respective arcs. You won't find any complex relationships or character building but you've got 12 competently written stories and some brief, entertaining inter-party banter peppered throughout and you'll be very familiar with the cast by the end.My favorite characters tend to land in the edgier/grittier writing area, so while Osvald and Throné were right up my alley, I really enjoyed Ochette, Partitio and Agnea's tales. There wasn't a single story that felt flat or uninteresting, even the lower stakes ones. The emotional impact of some of those story beats and boss fights along with the incredible music really hit me hard. Additionally, the supporting cast you meet on these arcs and even in some of the optional side quests generally tend to be more memorable and charming than your standard npc fare. Props to ya' boy Crick. The music is stellar. Yasunori Nishiki churns out another very impressive soundtrack while making some stylistic and instrumental homages to old 16bit era tracks by Uematsu, Shimomura, Mitsuda and Kikuta.The quality of his compositions here have improved quite a bit from the first game. The tracks cover a range of sounds and dynamic levels and assist the emotional impact of key moments so much that I'd almost dare to say the music carries the game by itself if the rest of the package wasn't so solid. A few of my favorites being the haunting 'Shadow' theme, Hikari, Castti, Osvald and Ochette's themes, the character arc end boss theme and the unique phase 2 themes, Agnea's in particular. Also a big standing ovation for the standard boss song. That track absolutely slaps and got me fired up every time the character-specific overtures started to play, something I distinctly remember loving about 1.Combat has a little bit more depth and balance than Octopath I, and kept me engaged from start to finish. Aided heavily by improved 2d sprite and 3d animations, sound design, a couple more mechanics and better overall class balance. Path actions have been improved with the day/night system, making team building much easier. (Though somehow I still managed to build a core team that completely lacked any "guide" actions.)They function essentially the same as they did in 1, but in tandem with a more fleshed out world and characters I was much more invested in, made town sequences an enjoyable experience instead of the tedium that I remember from 1. Eventually I found myself actively scouring towns for info and items while keeping an eye out for those key 'specialist' npcs that are needed for the myriad side quests.It was great to learn a little about each town and its inhabitants and watch the world and npcs change and open up as I completed more of each character's stories.The conclusion, while a bit brief, was sufficiently bread-crumbed throughout all 12 story lines and felt natural and satisfying. Overall I couldn't be more satisfied with my time spent with this game. If I had to give any advice it would be 'don't worry about class balance, pick a starting character that appeals the most to your tastes and take your time with this game. There is a lot to take in here and the more time you spend exploring, interacting with the world, and taking a moment to enjoy the music, the environment and the characters, the more you will get out of it.' I'm eager to get back in and polish off the last few side quests I have and figure out how to track down that .It's also inspired me to go back and give Octopath I a proper full playthrough. 9/10 Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I have seen some garbage sequels and remakes within the past few years so my expectation for Octopath 2 was low. To my surprise this is indeed a fantastic RPG. I played the original Octopath a couple of years back and while flawed it's still definitely a great game. But the sequel is even better. If you have played the original Octopath there's a good chance that you will enjoy this sequel and if you have not played the original but enjoy RPG's you might like this as well. You can expect more of the same as the original Octopath but only better with refined combat, camera angles and effects, engaging characters/story arc, beautiful world exploration and fairly challenging and fun dungeons to get lost in to. I am having trouble putting down the controller. That's how good it is. While I was disappointed with Square Enix RPG offerings in the past few years I have to give them credit for producing this amazing game. If there is one thing that I would criticize Octopath 2 is that there are some strange altered script and censorship on the localized English translation. That is something I definitely dislike and stopped me from buying other remakes of previous RPG's under the Square Enix umbrella. Because of few censorship I'll give this game an 8.5/10. It would've deserved 9.5/10 if they remained faithful to the original script.All in all if you're a RPG nut this is highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a jewel of the genre. I have played most of Square Enix titles from SNes and I am thrilled that they were able to put together the same feel but with modern tech. Music is rich orchestral music, tailor made for every character and important scenes. Graphics keep this 2d feel about them but effects like lighting, fog, 2d layers take advantage of every new technology. Battle system is very good, with some variants to the classics that make it dynamic and thrilling.The bad things I found are extremely personal. - You can Mug, Steal, Duel, most of the NPCs that only have one line of dialog. Even important people form the story, like the father that just told the son he is proud and should go in an adventure, as soon as the dialog is finished, you can steal what he is carrying, or fight him for it.- Some character objectives seems childish, like "eliminate poverty on the world"- When playing the main chapter of the stories, you do so with that character alone, disregarding the others. I'm guessing as you progress on the game there will be a main story line for all of them together, but this breaks the feeling of a party throught the beggining, is like you go somewhere with your character, you help them get there, and then just watch as he/she struggles through it.- Characters joining the party do so "just because adventure". The writers did not spend ANY time into making the stories to intertwine better here. Is just "hey I see you travel, let's travel", "alright, travel and adventure it is!"Overall this game is probably 8/10 for me, but just because we have so many games now a days, that the bar is so high. For reference, I would give the latest Baldur's Gate a solid 9, and I can't think of any game that is a 10 right now.
