_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game as a long time fan of Mortal Kombat and a fighting game enthusiast. That being said, this game is missing a lot, a disturbing amount. The story of the game is quite fun and is over 4 hours of cut scenes. Like 11, it felt like a movie with parts I get to play. The timeline reset story is fine and I enjoy most of the characters and how they are portrayed. I do miss the conflicts and changes of sides during the previous on going story line. Starting at the beginning again means some characters will be missing from the roster. No Noob Sibot, No robo smoke or Sub-Zero and several more. But the beauty of starting over allows for new ways to introduces those characters. speaking of introducing characters there are ZERO new characters as of currently. The only hope we have is for DLC to bring in new characters but I would assume they would use that for third party characters like Omni-man and bringing in characters that didn't make it in on release like Ermac and Quan Chi whom by the way are fully put together, working characters that are in the story mode but are not playable. Also on the character front, say good-bye to some of your favs because they have been pushed aside as 'Kameo' characters, who you pick along side your playable character who can be used for small boosts, hits and combos but have no use as characters otherwise. The list includes Jax, Sonya, Kano, Sektor, Cyrax, Motaro and frickin' GORO, and more. What makes little sense is that some of the Kameo characters are also playable, Scorpion, Sub-Zero and Kung Lao all have both Kameo and Playable character fighters. I'm so bummed that I cant play some of my favorites now that they have been demoted to kameo characters. Mortal Kombat 11 had 25 playable characters on launch while Mortal Kombat 1 has 23 playable characters and 16 wasted Kameo characters. I can only hope they will add some of them as both Kameo and playable. Also characters I hope for are maybe coming based on rumors like Cassie Cage and Noob Sibot but no confirmation. You can also say good-bye to the possibility of the Kollecter being playable, as he is the shop merchant in the story game mode invasions. At the very end of the story *SPOILERS* Liu Kang brings in other elder god, time lords from other timelines to fight off the army of Shang Tsung's time lords and undead foes. during this segment and ensuing fights there are all kinds of characters that we will never get to play who have full move sets, Like a female version of Kano or a merge between Sub-Zero and Scorpion a Sonya who uses Kitana's blades and MANY MANY MORE! Its like they're teasing us with custom characters and playable fighters who we will never get to play. That is unless they add any of this in the future. We can hold out hope I guess.I know I've talked a lot of negative but there is also a lot to love about this game. Its plays well, combos are fun to pull off, hearing people rage into their microphones when I win. Just some of the few things you can love about this game. Again the story is super entertaining and friendly to old and new Mortal Kombat players alike. And with the story ending in a large cliff hanger (where Jax is missing his arms, very cool) who knows if we'll see more in a DLC or free update. I have high hopes for the future of MK1. Started rocky but a possible uphill climb to perfection.    Current Condition 9/24/2023:  6.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Mortal Kombat... The franchise that seemingly always has great entries, but always releases with loads of issues and controversy. I remember when MK11 came out and the game didn't even function on PC. You would enter the customization menu, and the game would always crash about 5 minutes in while you were designing your load-out or character. Eventually, they fixed that. That was only one of the many issues.But what did MK11 have at release that MK1 does not have? It had:- A great story (once the cutscene bugs were fixed)- Loads of customization options- The roster was adequate even with some of the less popular characters- Better, more interesting redesigns of MKX characters- Drastic visual and graphic improvements from MKX- More balanced game-play than MK1 does currently- Constantly rotating towers that were simply in the menu and provided awesome rewards- Great Kombat Packs and guest characters- etc.MK11, however:- Created controversy over "sexy" characters- Laggy, buggy, glitchy, terrible port to PC at the start- Busted cutscenes- Crashing issues- Awful Krypt design (more of an opinion)- Mictransaction galore- X-ray visuals were replaced with the awful, jelly filled fatal blows- Roster still wasn't that great compared to others- etc.Overall, MK11 had it's problems but they were eventually sorted out and the game easily became one of the best in the franchise due to it's massive popularity.Compared to MK1, here are some changes - MK1 has:- Less customization, BORING customization, with similar mictransaction goofiness (but less egregious, I might add)- A better release roster with promising Kombat Packs on the horizon- Kameo fighters that ruin the gameplay by adding extra mechanics to balance- Awful balance among the characters both primary and kameo fighters- Seasonal color palettes that, since release, are just orange all around which means there are less "skins" to collect and just color changes- Our regular towers have reverted to MKX's design, so they're less interesting- Slower progression, seemingly- Online for the PC port is awful, haven't even gotten a chance to really play it, personally- A better story to enjoy- Lag issues, very similar to any modern game releasing, but this is ridiculous for MK at this point- Slower, boring, uninspired invasion system that could have just been replaced with a Krypt had they expanded on the tower- Medium difficulty is super easyI have more to add to this. I really do, but I don't want to sit here and just dog on MK1. I think the game is good and I think it's worth it if you really need to get your MK fix, but there are other fighting games out there to play right now, too.Even then, you could always redownload MK11 or even MKX to enjoy some MK as Netherrealm (hopefully) fixes some of the major issues and as they continue to develop the game. I have no doubt that the game will be a much better game near the end of it's cycle, just like MKX and MK11, but I'm sad that this game, the only game I've been excited about in a long time, is hardly worth my time. I log in to play a few invasion fights and then I turn it off after about 45 minutes.Don't buy MK1 unless you're desperate to check it out, but keep it under the refund time-frame in case you don't enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that the gameplay is good. I have generally have no complaints about that. I am the farthest thing away from being proficient in fighting games, but even without having that experience, I can tell this is quality. Or at least that it's better than MK11. All the characters feel easy to control, the combos are (relatively) simple to pull off, and I've genuinely had a good time playing it.However, this is where my praise of the game begins to taper out. Because despite the fun I have had with this game, knowing what I know now, I would have saved my money and spent it elsewhere. This is a good game, do not forget that if you continue to read further, but understand that there are series things wrong about this game that you NEED to take into consideration before buying this. Like, oh i dunno, the fact that i got scammed. Literally.I pre-ordered the Premium version of this game, it came around to about 110 USD. That's not the exact range, it's a ballpark. This was the most I have ever spent on a single game in my entire life. And what did I get for buying the pRiEmIuM eDiTiOn? Only one kombat pack. That's it. Every other Premium Edition of a game I have every bought has included all DLC. Now, you could say it was my fault for misinterpreting what was said on the promotional material and that i should have read the fine print and blah blah blah blah. And I'll give you that, I should have looked into it more. But at face value, it looked like they were including all of the DLCs with the Premium Version of the game. If they said it wasn't included, it was not easily visible. You might also notice something too. About how the version of the game that I am talking about is nowhere to be found. That is because they removed that version of the game, and posted a new version, that is 10-20 dollars cheaper. And it only includes Khaos Reigns and Kombat pack 2. It does not include Kombat pack 1.And that's not where the complaints end either. Kombat pack 1 is not free from my ire either. Because it only contains 6 characters. (I'll get to the cameo system and it's characters, believe me) And exactly how long did it take them to release these characters? Within 4 months? 2 maybe? How about all at once, like how you'd expect a DLC pack to release it's content? Your wrong, whatever your answer was. Because we had to wait a year for 6 characters to be released. The only compliment I can extend to Netherrealm is that AT LEAST THEY'RE MORE ACTIVE THAN MOJANG. I only learned after the fact that Netherrealm does a release schedual for the DLC characters, but I heard that they released these things within a reasonable time frame. GTA 6 WILL come out before we even hear about confirmation on a Kombat Pack 3.And Khaos Reigns. All you need to do is just glance at the reviews for it and see that something has gone horribly wrong, and that I am not a lone critic. The actual game itself while i'm writing this review, is 50 USD. The Khaos Reigns DLC is also 50 USD. Price tags set expectations, and with a price tag like that, one would expect the DLC to hold the same amount of quality and the same amount of content as the base game. However Netherrealm is not most people, and they don't expect you to be most people either. Because they expect you to be an absolute bozo who is willing to spend 50 dollars on 3 hours of content that NO ONE EVEN LIKED. I have been reading reviews for 45 minutes, and all i see are thumbs down, and three people who only picked thumbs up as a joke. It's like Netherrealm looked at what Call of Duty did with their overpriced DLC and said, "Hmmm, yes, SOME OF THAT PLEASE!!"And dear Super Earth, the Cameo system. Listen, i'm not skilled at this game by means. I'm new to fighting games, I have to look up guides on youtube on good combos, I struggle doing air moves, and I still have no idea what frame data is aside from the name. But the Cameo system was second most difficult thing I was struggling with during my time playing this nightmare. It is just so, so, sooooooooo difficult for me to figure out how to naturally use these characters that actually helps me out during the match. Shoot, it's difficult enough to find one that synergies with my actual character without looking up guides and stuff. And that's just my thoughts on using the Cameo Characters. Because I have a whole other complaint with them. Satans Hooves, why the god would you pick such an annoying way to under utilize your characters? Because I want to play as the cameo characters. Straight up, why can I not play as the Cameo Characters?Like, I understand not wanting to let characters fade away and be forgotten, but i'd rather not know what i'm missing out on honestly. Because you're telling me that Sareena gets put into Cameo status, and not Ashrah? You're telling me that Lei Mei has more of a right on the proper roster than someone like Jax? I want someone from Netherrealm to look me in my eyes and tell me that Tanya is cooler than Shujinko. AND DON'T EVEN GET ME STARTED ON MOTARO, YOU KNOW, THE CYBORG CENTAUR WITH A LASER SCORPION TAIL!! GODDD WHYYY?! WHY WASN'T HE AN ACTUAL PLAYABLE CHARACTER?!?!?!!And now we finally get to the most egregious thing about this game. The Climax of the show. The final nail in the coffin that got me to say, "screw it!" and actually write up a gods honest review. This is the worst optimized game I have ever played. It takes up 100 something gigs on my computer, refused to load on an external hard drive, crashes every time i load up Towers of Time, takes forever for the shaders to load, EATS my fuggin ram like a hungry HUNGRY HIPPOPOTAMUS, to the point that it will refuse to launch at times, stutters randomly during playing, and takes forever to load during anything, such as booting up the game, online matches, and even something as simple as switching between different costumes for the characters. AND THE WORST PART IS THAT THESE PROBLEMS NEVER LEFT. I PLAYED AT LAUNCH, EXPERIENCED ALL OF THIS, STOPPED PLAYING FOR A YEAR, **GOT A NEW COMPUTER,** AND STILL HAD ALL OF THESE PROBLEMS. Maybe it's just a me problem, maybe i'm just cursed, maybe no one else has had the same tech problems I have had with this game like I have. I say wait 10 years, or at least until they drop the price by like 30 dollars, AND THEN BUY THE GAME ON A BARGAIN SALE, IF YOU BUY IT AT ALL. Otherwise, get acquainted with Eiichiro Oda's literature, maybe study up on the filmography of Gore Verbinski, I don't know. That's my advice if you want to buy this game. But if you really want some advice? Want a solid review of the game? Then let me tell you this.-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------TL;DRDEAR GOD, JESUS, BUDDHA, THE JADE EMPORER, ODIN, OSIRIS, ANUBUS, AHURA MAZDA, OBELISH, TURBANED ZARATHUSTRA, MARIA, SIR GIDEON OFNIR THE ALL-KNOWING, AND THE SEALED EXODIA!!! name: Phoenix Springs
detailed_description: After the reporter Iris Dormer reconnects with her estranged brother, she finds herself in Phoenix Springs, a desert oasis home to an enigmatic community. As she explores ancient ruins and interrogates a rich cast of characters, she must uncover the mysteries that connect the place, the myths, and herself. Inspired by classic point-and-click games , Phoenix Springs updates the genre for the modern player with intuitive controls and a streamlined UI. Conduct your investigation by collecting clues and leads in your inventory rather than physical objects. Connect these clues with the environment or mention them in conversations to progress. Discard false leads and red herrings as you solve logical puzzles designed to challenge and delight fans of story-rich interactive experiences. Fully voice-acted Hand-drawn art and animations Streamlined UI Immersive neo-noir universe Challenging puzzles

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by being blunt, I liked Phoenix Springs. This is an interesting point-and-click adventure game. But, I’m worried that this is something that most people will not enjoy for one clear reason: the story is puzzling. Think of this as if you're watching a Lynch film. I finished the game, but I still can't properly describe what transpired. Some will love that, while many will find that annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This game blew my mind. Frankly, the aftertaste is similar to that of finishing a great novel. This relatively short piece of art channels favorite themes of Kazuo Ishiguro, Don DeLillo, and even, to some extent, Italo Calvino. It explores the frailty of memory, death and what lies beyond, and the dangerous symbiosis of longevity with technology on an entirely different level. I dare say this video game handles these themes even better than some other mediums traditionally considered more suitable for deep and profound exploration. The gameplay is reminiscent of old-school point-and-click adventures, heavily reliant on text, but it has a twist. While at its core it remains a "quest", it delves more into the protagonist’s inner monologue audibly rather than textually. For example, all exchanges between characters are narrated by a single actress, and they sound like this: “The man has a weighty stare. I asked him about the missing flowers, but he doesn’t seem to know. His mind wanders off somewhere far beyond any reach”. Her voice is somewhat monotonous, distant, unemotional, and it’s an amazing trick that drastically deepens the immersion (and probably reduces development costs, hehe). Also, there’s no inventory in this game. All we have is literally a mindmap, so no more antenna trouts or banana lockpicks for you! The visual style is also something rarely seen in video games, bordering on fauvism aesthetics with a touch of pop art boldness (yes). Also, it has a strong noirish feel (perspectives! shadows! negative space!) because, first and foremost, this is a detective story — the main heroine needs to find her little brother. But somewhere along the road, it transforms into a lucid, vibrant, synesthetic journey into the subconscious, and isn’t that the best thing imaginable? I loved every bit of this game, and sooner rather than later, my friends will hate me because I’ll buzz their ears off with how great Phoenix Springs is. You should try it too.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, an emotionally compelling game with a unique prospective with distinct art style and game mechanics to match. If the trailers catch your interest at all, I suggest you give this game a try.I do agree that Phoenix Springs falls into the trappings of the hyper-specific solutions of the point & click genre. And the second half feels like a completely different game altogether. I'm still not sure whether I feel like the first half of the story is setting the player up to understand the second, or if they land as two different games entirely.What I do know is over the course of a few days, I played through the game 4 times. And am still finding connections and conversations I did not on my previous play through's. If you love finding out what indie games can do, I'd really suggest this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Mysteries and point and clicks feel like natural fits for one another. Both are fundamentally about hunting for clues and fitting together the bits and pieces into a coherent narrative. Both ask the player to trace logic that may not be immediately intuitive, but which can be solved if the player is willing to look a bit askance at the clues they’ve been given. Both also potentially fall victim to the player being asked to reproduce the devs’ logic rather than their own, and for an outcome to necessitate a certain understanding of what’s been provided so far. For Phoenix Springs to be a point and click mystery using text rather than objects, then, is a natural choice, and one that makes the game a fascinating exploration into the mystery of life and death itself. Phoenix Springs is, as the intro suggests, a point and click mystery game. After reconnecting with her long-lost brother, former journalist Iris Dormer seeks to understand the story of her brother’s life and why he warns her not to go to Phoenix Springs. To do so, she must investigate the mystery of Phoenix Springs itself. Describing the story as uncovering the mystery of Iris’ brother is, admittedly, doing a bit of a disservice to both the story and the world in which it’s set. This is a game less about understanding one particular story, and more about recontextualising the dystopia in which it’s set. Phoenix Springs’ dystopia is one of a world disconnected from reality, where truth and meaning have ceased to be anything real, and are instead window-dressing for a world hell-bent on its own destruction. So it’s an examination of our world, told through the lens of a fantasy world to make it feel a bit more palatable. With that context, then, it’s easier to understand that the fundamental mystery is not Leo Dormer per se, but that examination of how a people so disconnected from reality as those of Phoenix Springs came to be. Throughout the narrative, we’re given clues — the devaluing of academia and ethics, the hyperfixation on the body and the possibilities of techno-immortality — though realistically, we the players already know the answer, and are just along for the ride. Equally, the setting is painted in vague, meandering brushstrokes, making it clear that our focus should be on the people and their response to the destruction of their world, rather than the mechanics of the world’s destruction.This creates an interesting dichotomy where, on the one hand, I’m propelled through the game by my curiosity at how this game is going to tell a story I already know, while on the other, I’m left with the knowledge that, for all its touting of its novelty, Phoenix Springs isn’t doing anything I haven’t seen before. I’ve explored many dystopias, and I’ve seen many where the dystopia is a set dressing for self-examination. Phoenix Springs is one of many narratives telling this same story, even if it does it well.One of the elements Phoenix Springs emphasises is its gameplay and its use of text and interlinking ideas rather than items to solve its various puzzles. Phoenix Springs is not a game with an inventory, per se, but rather, a cloud of thoughts populating Iris’ head, waiting to be linked with one another and the world around her. These thoughts serve the same function as items would in other point and click games, though here, the substitution of thoughts for items complements the theme and feel of the game nicely. While there is a certain degree of novelty to having thoughts rather than objects, on the whole, the use of words had less impact on the gameplay than the game might have hoped. I still went with my age-old tactic of using the most logical thing in my inventory on a problem, trying the less likely things, then throwing everything in my inventory at the problem to see what would stick. In practice, this meant asking dead-eyed NPCs about the life, universe, and everything, just to see which specific phrase might trigger the next step of my investigation. While the text-based approach fit the game well and made it more interesting as a whole, it also isn’t a revolutionising of a point and click mystery. Where Phoenix Springs truly excels, though, and where it does feel deeply unique is in the look and feel of it. Both its visual art and sound design are stunning, with the art looking like no other game I’ve played. Where the story has perhaps been better told in other games, and the game mechanics are less unique than the game maybe wants them to be, when placed in combination with its art and sound, Phoenix Springs becomes a unique and mesmerising experience. On the whole, as a game, Phoenix Springs is a perfectly decent execution of its concept. That I’m saying its story has been better told by other games is less a slight on Phoenix Springs, and more a commentary on how much time I’ve spent in dystopias. Similarly, while its text-based clue system may not be as unique as I’d hoped, it is still satisfying to put clues together, and to watch words fade and others appear in their place. Solving mysteries will always trigger a delighted little tickle, even if how that mystery is solved is through throwing clues into a bin and jumbling it about until something interesting pops out. What makes Phoenix Springs stand out is its art and its dedication to crafting a complete experience. While the story and gameplay may lag at points, spending time just admiring the art feels like time not wasted. It is time spent being in the world, and is perhaps the epitome of the lesson the player is meant to take away from the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful nonsensical experience. The detective side of the game is incredibly well done, with point and click mechanics that focus on collecting words rather then things and using them to find your brother.  Those parts were the highlight and had me hook, line and sinker.Once you get to Phoenix Springs however, I struggled to continue. The game becomes a never ending slog of characters saying things that don't make sense, finding clues in places I'd never think to look and searching for what exactly? Its never really clear and the game revels in that ambiguity.If you love the point and click genre and/or adore David Lynch movies, maybe you'll find something special here. Without strong affection for one or both of those, I wouldn't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Played start to finish in a bit over three hours. The writing is excellent, the art style is awesome, the puzzle mechanic is wonderful, and it all those excellent pieces get mixed together into mud. There's just something about the way that the game world is designed that makes it feel like sorting through a needle stack to find a piece of hay. Take, for example, an early scene at the University. There are something like nine screens you can travel through and hundreds of items to click on. Each clicked item lets you "Talk to", "Look at", or "Use", leading to hundreds of possible interactions. Beyond that, you can use any idea you have unlocked with any item, leading to a feeling of endless interactability. Yet, there is almost always (seemingly) a single solution to every puzzle, so most of the time the interactions feel like they lead you nowhere, and get increasingly frustrating as the game goes on. This puzzle system works extremely well in the confined areas of the start of the game, but near the mid point, when you suddenly have access to dozens of locations, this feels more like a pixel hunt than an adventure game. All that said, I probably still would have left the game with a generally positive outlook (I found the ending to be extremely powerful), except for the puzzles in the titular location. Without spoiling anything (although keeping an eye towards saving you some frustration), there is a puzzle that seems to broadcast that you are solving it in the wrong manner but requires you to do the same series of interactions *four* times in a row. These interactions involve a multi-minute walk across the map (click out of frustration, I did learn here that you can double click to run), to do the same thing four times. This was probably 15% of my total play time and completely soured me on the experience. There's definitely a lot to like about Phoenix Springs, especially if you are a fan of arthouse cinema, but the frustrating puzzle designs, especially in the latter half of the game, really take the wind out of the sails.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with Phoenix Springs for sure! In particular the artwork, sound design, voiceover work, and overall atmosphere were beautifully done and engaging. I think it may be divisive for players in that there is quite a lot of walking from place to place, backtracking, back and forth. And while it was tiresome at times, it does reflect quite closely and drive home the game's plot and themes about repetition and monotony. If the linearity of life to death becomes obsolete and rebirth is possible, then it becomes an endless, confusing cycle.I think the walking around was maybe exacerbated for me because I didn't realize there was a way to run until I finished the game (lol). However, I played on Steam Deck, and while everything was playable (with the little trackpad as a mouse), I wonder if the run never triggered. I feel like I definitely double clicked at least a few times when trying to go somewhere, but hey, maybe I didn't.Anyway, def enjoyed the game and appreciated its take on the point-and-click adventure genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly captures the dreamlike vibe of avant-garde movies from the '70s, while still carving out an identity all its own. The experience is polished in basically every area. Both the writing and the visuals are sharp, with consistently immersive sound design, and mechanical narration delivery that manages to never become grating. As a point-and-click adventure lover, I also appreciate how different the puzzles were; they're not necessarily tough, because brute force remains viable for the most part, but their solutions encourage a fittingly abstract thought process. If I have to complain, I do think that the figurative "inventory" of subjects could've been incorporated more seamlessly. Rather than always unlocking/removing subjects after a dialogue sequence or interaction, making you sit through the repetitive screen and sound effects, that could be happening in the background--during the dialogue sequence or interaction.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very conditional recommend. Phoenix Springs is a good game for people who liked Immortality or Kentucky Route Zero but want something even more surreal and opaque. If you want answers, this game will not give them to you. But it does have some interesting thoughts on immortality, memory, and technology to turn around in your head. And it is very beautiful.As far as the point-and-click puzzle gameplay, I was a bit disappointed. I liked it quite a lot in the early game, but once you get to the titular Phoenix Springs, the logic starts to get really weird and personally, many of the solutions would not have occurred to me in a million years. Maybe my brain's screwed on wrong. Wouldn't be the first time. There is a developer-written guide linked in the menu, thankfully. But overall, I still like the unique spin on the genre with replacing the physical inventory with an inventory of words and concepts.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic game! Excellent world building, impactful writing and dialogue, stunning art, and rewarding puzzles. Quite literally everything you could want from a modern point and click game that feels very honest to the genre in the 90s. At the risk of sounding cliche comparing this to other games, I feel like Phoenix Springs is a mix between The Case of the Golden Idol and Season: A Letter to the Future. Great to play over a weekend or with friends who like to unravel mysteries.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: An ambitious point-and-click mystery game that tells a linear story through complicated artistic metaphors that are surprisingly not pretentious. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, until the ending. Where the game just abruptly ends closing the game at 3 hours only. The reason I bring up the hours it took to finish the game is due to the feeling of unfulfillment I had in the end. For a $20 game that is highly linear and quite literally depends on the story in order to stand on its own two feet it fails to do so. Because many questions are left unanswered, many metaphors are just tossed into the air without a validation of their meaning causing many of them to become a red herring. I was enthralled by this story, I listened DEEPLY to every single opinion or fact IRIS said because she was written competently, a great example that is spoiler-free is "she's sunbathing, lizard-like". I have no idea why but that comment has latched onto my head. Iris sees the world in such a fascinating way that I was never bored with her. And yet, I'm disappointed because we don't get a full circle with her, The game ends abruptly and roll credits. While I can piece together the story, it still wouldn't answer all the questions the game brings up. Aside from the bad taste the ending left in me I still recommend the game, The soundtrack is beautiful, unique and calming. The puzzles while mostly easy are fun and are integrated surprisingly well with the story, many point-and-click games sometimes push a puzzle as a roadblock, yet Phoenix Springs rewards you for paying attention to the comments made by Iris and the bizarre characters you meet. Rather than having you make leaps of logic to create progress in the story.  The gorgeous art style.    In conclusion for a niche unique point-and-click experience, I cannot possibly recommend this more. Though the game is short, and its shortness does harm the quality of the experience, the journey it provides is wonderful. I just wish they answered more questions than raising them, perhaps if this sells well we'll have DLC or a sequel. I'm already a fan of this studio and cannot wait to see more from them. 4/5
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Point and click games are hard to get right, additionally, they are largely thankless work as they don't sell well. So i commend the devs for making this. This was a good game. The art work is enticing, enough to drag in a seasoned point and click player and give it a shot, despite how much garbage there is on the market. There is also some pretty profound dialogue in this game. Overall it is interesting enough to keep you playing, Takes about 3-5 hours to complete.There are problems too, in fairness to any potential buyer, there is a lot of back and forth and retracing your steps, and the puzzles are a little esoteric at times. I think the game design itself fell over a little bit when you get to phoenix springs in this regard.Overall, recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I was on a search for a puzzle-based game when I came across 'Phoenix Springs'. It took a second to get into the rhythm of the game but after that I was hooked. While historically I haven't been interested in narrative-based games, this story took me by surprise. The characters feel distant but distinct, even the seemingly vapid ones create depth and meaning to the story. From the games I've played I find the narrative gets in the way of playing, but this time I was hanging onto every word.The commands are simple and hints readily available if need be. The tension built throughout the game, a constant push and pull, is intoxicating. While I wish the game was longer, the artistic style is a reason alone to purchase the game and if you want to be left thinking for days to come, 'Phoenix Springs' might just be the game for you. 4.5/5
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't played a point and click in a long time but picked up this one because a friend recommended it. Haven't completed it yet but loved the 3 hours I spent playing it so far. Amazing art style, excellent writing and voice acting, great sound design, the gameplay never felt tedious as it's often the case with this type of games. A shame this is not getting more attention.Edit: I finished the game and would definitely recommend checking it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I expected surrealism and a loose narrative style. Oh boy, did I get what I asked for.The game is gorgeous, the voice actor is great and the game play is a simple connect-the-dots detective style that is mostly there to carry the story, which loosely reminded me of the same existentialist tropes found in 'A Scanner Darkly' and 'Under the Silver Lake'.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Striking and strange. A game that maybe is more on the "artsy" side but has seemed to worm its way into my brain. I think about Iris and Leo CONSTANTLY. I think about the crying one and the silent one. I think about the DJ and the people dancing for 53 hours straight. Although it's short on a single play through I can tell I missed a billion things. The atmosphere is weird and beautiful and I wish only to spend more time figuring more out. Understanding more of the world both in and out of the Oasis. It's all so strange.I love it. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This is a slam dunk for me. I had the same feeling playing this game as I did reading surrealist fiction by Cesar Aira or Hiroko Oyamada. The detective mechanics and the sense of expansive wonder are not unlike in Chants of Sennaar. The visual and aural design are absolutely off-the-charts, like jaw-on-the-floor. Can't recommend this highly enough. Can't wait for what's next from the team. This is great art.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Springs is a point-and-click game that goes far beyond the classics. There is no classic inventory of objects to combine, but you progress by matching clues. The mechanics are original. More surprising than the gameplay, however, is the art direction. Phoenix Springs is a visually stunning adventure that I recommend to everyone. Especially for those who love the surreal genre. At times I felt as if I had been catapulted into a Murakami book.Read full review here:
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This hit all the right notes for me. Surreal nonsense and puzzles.There was a few times I had to look up a solution when I feel like I shouldn't have had to but that happens to me a lot in puzzle games and I might just be stupid. The trick to having fun with these kind of games is to figure out when it's okay to just look it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I review on Steam because I so desperately want other people to play it. Phoenix Springs is a gorgeous game in every way. It's art style, characters, world, and storytelling will stick with you for a long time after you reach the credits. It's weird, beautiful, and just the right level of challenging. If you like mysteries and point-and-click adventure games, I cannot recommend Phoenix Springs enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Springs can't be described any other way than, an experience. I was intrigued by the hand drawn artwork and the futuristic atmosphere and went into this knowing very little of what to expect. So I was both pleasantly and frustratingly surprised at how easy the concept was to grasp but how challenging it was to connect some of the dots. Iris is an interesting character. I found her to be a bit robotic in the beginning but I started to connect with her as the game wore on. She's trying to find out what happened to her brother and each level leads her closer to him and deeper into a world that...let's say the more you know the more you realize you don't know. It was so satisfying when the pieces of the story started to come together and, though the pace is pretty slow to start, it really ramps up at the end. I even like the achievement system of connecting Iris' ideas and reflections, which really encourages you to have her leave no stone unturned. This isn't a game for everyone, you really have to enjoy putting in detective work and retreading your steps sometimes multiple times to solve the mystery, but if you enjoy the point and click style of game play, I think you'll be pleased with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I was impressed by the sound design in the trailer, but disappointed by sound design in game.  There are ambient sounds but relatively little music.  And while it is fully voice acted, it's all one voice actress, who narrates everything, including dialogue.  The sound quality of the voice acting is noticeably lower in game than the trailer.YMMV on the cryptic story, but it was a bit of a miss for me.  It's okay if I didn't understand what was really going on, but I would at least like a clearer understanding of what it's trying to say.At least the visual design is excellent.  What you see is what you get there.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Springs starts out as a rather quotidian point and click 'guess the clue' game. This warms you up and shows you how the game is played. But after the train ride (no spoilers) it becomes non-linear, poetic, otherworldly, spiritual, dreamlike. I thoroughly enjoyed this transition into the 'alternate reality' and the games' final scene, which though intelligible, is inconclusive. The art work is gorgeous. I wish more games were designed this way.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. This is really one of those gaming experiences that you know you will remember forever.Phoenix Springs is incredibly unique. The game's atmosphere rivals some all time greats with the combination of visuals, music, and voice. Its gameplay is simple, yet still gives you amazing "ah ha" moments as you solve puzzles. The story is as ambitious as a science fiction epic, yet somehow feels more important told through this game's mellow and mystifying short tale.Please play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: FULL REVIEW:  [Croatian]A mesmerizingly beautiful, albeit confusing, project that shines the most in its mystical opening hour. It plays out like a mixture of Lynch & Bakshi, and the cyberpunk angle makes it stand out, as well as voice acting that's out of this world, and the third person narration helps keep the player at a cold distance. Some technical issues and an anticlimactic ending keep it from true greatness, however.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend, but I gotta admit, my journey with the game didn't start so smooth: I was stuck at the very first screen. A familiar feeling from playing Point&Clicks years (decades?) ago emerged, as I caught myself brute forcing my way forward. I wanted answers and I wanted them fast, and that's really not what the game is asking of you. It seems to want you to be patient, to listen, to pause & come back, and I couldn't help but oblige. It felt very fresh, even though it's such a classic mechanic. The art style is incredibly compelling to me, but I also loved the voice acting, the music & the setting of the story. Finding a solution is always rewarded with a gorgeous cut-scene. It also doesn't make things clearer than they need to be. I highly recommend surrendering to it and trying not to find meaning in every little corner.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Phantasmagorical. Oneiric. Less of a point&click and more of an art house piece where the further down the rabbit hole you go the more the conventions of the genre fall apart. Seduced by the stylistic choices, I felt let down by the premise at the beginning, got frustrated by the gameplay by the middle and became extremely puzzled by the end, but at no point was I anything less than enthralled. I still don't know whether the game become more streamlined by the third act or if the rules of its narrative finally clicked for me to start making a twisted sort of sense. However, I do know that this is the cleverest thing I have seen in the medium lately, and I was happy to see the story become increasingly more surreal while never becoming pretentious - a tough balancing act. The game says very little outright and that might not be for everyone.But it is for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I love its animation. Haven't seen a game portrayed like this. This is literally art. As someone who likes point-and-click mystery/adventure games, this one is worth its price, I'd say.Very unique & also has its eerie vibe while not being uncomfortable.The gameplay, "remember to remember," is a take that I haven't seen on games. It's an experience to behold.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Very much worth playing. It is a point-and-click mystery, specially the first part of the game. Thereon has some more soul searching quests, but it remains a classic point-and-click in its gaming nature. It has a special graphical style and a differnt mood from your typical adventure, but it remains very recommendable game, particularly to the adventure game afficionado but, overall,   a drawing experience to every gamer
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I love the amount of dialogue from the character, connecting two items nearly always unique line of dialogue even if it's wrong (and given I have less than half the achievements from my playthrough, there must be a lot more!). Art style is a thing of beauty, pictures/trailer is representative of the whole game.The story is very ambiguous, there were times where I thought I'd finally understood an idea, an underlying theme, etc. which then had no continuation or closure to build upon it, so I had to cast it out, much like the red herrings for the puzzles you encounter. This constant battle wading through a whirlwind of ideas is one I felt I shared with the character.By the time the credits rolled, I felt further than ever from knowing the truth; but nor did I feel entitled to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gorgeous: the art, the animation, the ambiances and (too rare) musics, everything comes beautifully together to create an amazing experience.It is also a short ( 3-4 hours )and cryptic point&click game, in its story and storytelling. The player has to put the pieces of this strange world and its mechanism together by himself. It remind me of Returnal (storywise, not gameplay-wise!) in a very good way, that leaves some place to interpretation and guessing.A strong recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: The hand drawn graphic style is great. Instead of the usual item collecting and figuring out where to use them like most point and clicks, you collect clues and connect them to progress. This feels like the perfect game for fall. A chilly afternoon spent solving a mystery with your beverage of choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I'm on my 2nd play through (I was a Kickstarter backer so I got to play the DRM-free version all of last week)First of all I can't believe I get to see my name in the end credits of such a work of art. Thanks for the extra key devs!!Now I will say that the mystery is so dense I didn't get it all the first time so it won't be for everyone. But I think I'm starting to piece it together and HOLY CRAP!! Now I will still prbably need a 10 hour long youtube video to explain it to me but I haven't been excited about a game like Phoenix Springs for a long time!
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Full Walkthrough - Fresh, unique and exciting, Phoenix Springs pulls you through a compelling mystery with excellent writing, impeccable design, and an inventive take on the point-and-click genre. Every aspect of its presentation is considered, culminating in a cinematic experience that is more than the sum of its parts, and worth every second you spend with it.Rating - 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game 6/10.A bit to hard for me. The game is so pretty, but I think It's too expensive for the amount of story. It's very artful and poetic. I think it was OK, but I don't think I will play it again. There was alot of nonsence talking, that did not make things easier, just making me more confused. Sometimes you would have to do actions 2 or 3 times in a row, making me think I did something wrong. I'd like the main-character to make more clues when you're stuck, instead of me having to read the "tips"-page and jump to another window.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Point-and-click games have never been in my repertoire. In fact, I’ve avoided them almost my entire life. What I want to congratulate Calligram Studios on with Phoenix Springs is the visual representation and marketing of the game. It’s been a great year of games especially those I had a chance to review where the main protagonist is a female lead from Caravan SandWitch, Arranger: A Role Puzzling Adventure, Mika and the Witchs Mountain, and Été. Phoenix Springs is in great company.The visuals connected me to something deeper. The hand-drawn style, combined with the green-and-yellow color palette, pulled me into the world of Phoenix Springs. Together with the eerie sound design and minimalist inventory, the game offers a uniquely charming indie experience.Phoenix Springs is a must-play indie game with rich artistic illustration, haunting sound design, and a noir world that has already made it a critically acclaimed hit of 2024. It's become my must-play and on of the best games of 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely Art to me. And very impressive art as well.Though, I think it falters on one painful point: The UX/Feedback is poor to the point where frustration diminishes the quality of the experience sometimes. It's minimalistic, which is nice and more immersive, but often also very unclear. It's often slightly confusing where you can walk to, like they're random invisible spots on your screen, no path, door, arch, whatever. But worse, interaction sometimes feels like randomly trying things until something goes 'click'. Not too often, but you'll get stuck for a while.An example: At a point you'll need to do something twice or more, but the game never shows any clue that you should, and you can't progress if you don't. This happened a few times and I think it may have been done on purpose, to emphasize certain components of the story. I'm on the fence. I think even in Art, you don't want to discourage or impede the player to much by breaking the basic rules of your own game.Buuut the good devs were aware of this and provided a wonderfully mostly spoiler-free walkthrough on their website. Super nice, thanks you guys!That said, I think Phoenix Springs is a fantastic work and I will probably play it again, because I don't think I fully understood what I just saw...
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Phoenix Springs is a beautiful game with great voice acting and a compelling world built through breadcrumbs that will ultimately leave you with more questions than answers.Phoenix Springs is the debut title from Calligram Studios. It is a point-and-click adventure where you play Iris, a reporter looking for her brother, Leo. To locate him, you’ll need to search your environment for clues that lead you closer and closer to him while exploring his connection to the mysterious Phoenix Springs.The core mechanic at play here is the gathering of action words. As you click around to speak to the characters in the world and take a look at items, you will gather words that can help you move the plot forward. Your brother is always at the centre of your word bank, but you’ll gather places, things, concepts and more to move through the world and get closer to him.You can use the word bank in combination with “talk to” and “look at” action. At the start, I found myself at times confused about exactly how to use the word bank in combination with the third “use” action, but after a few fumbles, I figured it out.Right off the bat, it would be a disservice to not dive in and talk about the style of Phoenix Springs.To get closer to finding your brother, you’ll mouse around visually stunning maquettes. The game world looks like it was drawn and colored with markers reminding me a lot of early Detective Comics but with a more futuristic look to it. Up close, the art is even more striking, especially when we get to see the faces of characters in close-up moments. We lose a lot of the character detail in parts of the world where the camera is pulled back – but this brave choice strikes me as deliberate and allows the player to feast their eyes on the beautiful painted backgrounds from the team. The lines are always clean and the detail is always awe-striking.The game colour-wise leans heavily on yellows, blacks and greens with punches of red. The art direction is strong and I hope that the game is recognized for Best Art Direction as we approach the end of year award season.Beyond the beautiful art, the game has great voice-acting from Alex Anderson Crow. It’s subtle, increasingly despondent and brooding. Her performance combined with the world-building does the most to move the narrative forward.The game is divided into about half a dozen major areas varying in size. There’s a nice mix of sizes in these areas. Half were quite small and the other half were several times larger than the smaller ones. The tiny ones are easy to crack the codes on. The two larger set pieces, especially the trip to the titular Phoenix Springs, have many nooks and crannies. Even though part of the fun of this is one is poking around the world to see what you can find, I wish the game would have done a slightly better job at signposting for the player. Some paths weren’t immediately obvious. Beyond at times questioning where to go, a few parts of the map in one of the game sections had sub-sections with similar names. This made it tough to navigate without deliberate traversal focus.Phoenix Springs can be played in a few hours depending on how quickly you can solve some of the game’s tougher puzzles. Some of them are more clever than others – but your satisfaction with this one will depend if you need a story to end by telling you exactly what’s going on. Without spoiling the major plot points, the game does a great job through environmental storytelling at alluding to what’s happened to Leo and the world around you. But even in the end, what the game is trying to say will be left up to you to interpret.This game is a head-scratching psychedelic near-future neo-noir mystery with a beautiful art style. Just don’t expect it to spoonfeed you the game’s message.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me a lot of Kentucky Route Zero in the way in which it presents you with a reality that's just different enough from ours to feel completely engrossing, but also in the way it unfinchingly tells its story. Great environments (special mention to the transitions from noon to sunset) and outstanding voice acting. The writing is also impressive. Great game overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. It hits a really specific place in much of what I love, from ambience and tone, to setting and story. The narrative of this game is absolutely fantastic, the way it is told is fantastic. I have seen and read some criticism of this game that, to me, feels rooted in a real lack of curiosity and at times that's been disappointing to see. I feel like there is a great deal for a lot of people to love in this game.Sure, there are moments "puzzle wise" that I think don't work as well as I'm sure the Devs would hope, but there is an included guide. Some may see that as a bad thing to need to include but I personally see it as a good thing, allowing you to enjoy the game at your own ability and understanding. If you can't figure something out then use the tips and get back to enjoying the experience.If you like when a game gives you an experience, and gives you moments and questions to really think about and sink your teeth into them Phoenix Springs is absolutely right for you. A truly outstanding experience
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: It is a short game, leaving me with more questions than answers. These questions however, are asked in one of the most visually stunning and unique worlds I have seen in any game. The voiceacting and mesmerizing soundtrack has something hypnotic about it. I find the games core mechanic of collecting leads and combining them with any other element interesting, yet not fully realized to its potential. I found myself trying everything without much of a plan on two occasions, which was close to being frustrating, but not the biggest deal as trial and error will always reveal something interesting.Beautiful game with interesting themes that I would love to see explored further at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Played through the magical Phoenix Springs (twice) this week. A sleek, dreamlike noir that'll never give it to you straight. It's a captivating work, with mysteries I still feel desperate to solve. Some of the best writing and art direction I've seen in years. What a treat from Calligram Studio. An incredible debut. Cannot wait for whatever they plan for us next.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost - Phoenix Springs is absolutely *gorgeous* - I fell head over heals in love with each and every frame of this game. Beautifully drawn, colored, animated, and paced. Absolutely classic.And then.. THEN there's the absolute ground breaking rethinking of the point-and-click adventure - the detective mind-map exploration may be the best implementation of [inventory item 1] + [object] I've played. Point and click master work. I've already completed the game outside of Steam, but woahhh is it nice to see achievements popping up from my exploration.. and.. *seventy eight of them* whattttt is this! :DA+++ absolutely love this game, so so so very glad to have stumbled across it. Do yourself a favor and give it a spin.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: I only have a vague understanding of what happened. A thin, ghostly vision of someone else's memory, but:I love how the narration is paced. I love the main character's voice. I was entranced. I don't know if I love the way the game made me feel. I might have observed something deeply personal that was not meant for me. Great game, I will play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Phoenix Springs

_childDocuments_.review: Lose yourself in the mystery of Phoenix Springs, a modern point-and-click set in a striking neo-noir world. It begins with an investigation: find your brother Leo. You already know where it ends.

name: Under The Waves
detailed_description: Under The Waves is a narrative-driven adventure game about the engulfing power of grief. Set in the depths of the North Sea in a techno-futuristic 1970s, professional diver Stan is struggling to overcome a life-changing loss and embrace a new future. The isolation of the deep sea is a fitting manifestation of his state of mind, and as Stan retreads further into his self-imposed solitude, he starts to experience strange events far beneath the waves. He will eventually have to make a difficult choice... A love letter to the oceans, Under The Waves invites you to dive into a gorgeous underwater world, brought to life in a poetic blend of cinematic visuals and poignant storytelling. Live a gripping story through Stan’s eyes and guide him through an unforeseen series of events that will bring him deeper and deeper into the abyss, the reflection of his own psyche. Wander the vast seabed piloting Stan’s submarine and encounter the beautiful wildlife, Stan’s only company while he’s trapped in his own mind. Explore caves, wrecks, and underwater plants with Stan’s special wetsuit, following the mysterious manifestations of his memories, to find a way back to the surface and save his life. Collect materials and craft equipment that will help Stan navigate further on this self-discovery expedition. You will have to dare get off the beaten track to experience mesmerizing moments and reveal more about the tragic past he is trying to escape... KEY FEATURES A surreal voyage under the waves — Live a poetic underwater adventure about a man trying to overcome his traumatic past and save his own life, both literally and figuratively. Will Stan ever reach the surface again? Explore the depths of the sea – Pilot your submarine over the abyss and swim your way through caves, wrecks, and submerged plants in search of backstory pieces, salvageable waste, collectibles, and more. Craft equipment to help Stan explore further. Witness the beauty of the ocean – Dive through gorgeous underwater environments, from unfathomable depths to retro-futuristic facilities, immersed in a contemplative ambiance brought to life by an atmospheric soundtrack. A unique setting full of mysteries - Discover an alternate reality of the year 1979 where retro, science-fiction, and fantasy flow together in beautifully-rendered graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: WHAT IT IS NOT:· A RPG: no leveling system, no perks, no character improvement.· A survival game: no bars to fill except oxygen, crafting on its bare bones (just to keep you underwater and advance to the next phase of the game).· An action game: the experience is not about fighting anything underwater.WHAT IT IS:· A narrative storytelling game (as advertised).· A very solid diving game: you really feel exploring the darkness of the sea.· A trip to the depths of the human sorrow.· An entertaining experience.I hope this helps.
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: In Under the Waves you play as professional diver Stan who has suffered the loss of a loved one and taken a job with a questionable oil company to escape to the solitude of an underwater maintenance station. It’s a narrative driven exploration game, where you explore both the ocean and the protagonist’s soul. It’s very slow – taking up pace towards the end when it’s also partly ecological thriller - and it’s absolutely brilliant.The game has stellar voice acting, Stan’s model is very detailed and beautifully animated and most of all the underwater scenery and visuals are outstanding. I’ve been a diver for 40 years and the way the colors wash out with increasing depth, the lighting, the limited visibility, the atmosphere, the topography, the wrecks – it’s all done very, very well. Also, the way you control Stan as a diver just feels natural. I first struggled with the different ways you control Stan and the submarine but after a bit of learning I started to appreciate the precise and logical controls of the sub as well.Then there are the dream sequences which are visual masterpieces, eerie and atmospheric, taking place in submerged highways, houses, or shopping malls. Proving once again that not resolution or details or ray tracing make for great visuals but mostly art direction.This is not a game for everyone, it relies on atmosphere and empathy – there’s a lot of tension but no real action. Some of the tasks may feel menial but to those who love the ocean and who can bath in the atmosphere (pardon the pun) it’ll bring joy to discover the wrecks and caves, small treasure and (hopelessly) try to clean up the ocean. But most important is that you can relate to Stan’s trauma and for this I guess it’s almost mandatory to be a parent. That’s why I say it’s a game for adults – not because of explicit content but required life experience.Few games have touched me like this – Firewatch comes to mind, which – of the games I know - is probably the most similar one, also combining emotional struggles with environmental beauty and disaster.On the technical side the game ran very well on my upper middle-class system (Radeon 6800 XT) at 2560x1440 with “ultra” setting. I’ve encountered a few bugs with achievements not unlocking, chest icons staying on the map although the chests were already opened, and I had a total of 3 crashes. These minor annoyances may have been fixed by now, the 1.02 patch literary came in after I finished and quit the game. There’s just one thing that’s a pity and I don’t understand how it could pass QA – the lip sync (English) is completely off, sometimes by almost a second. I’m very sensitive in this regard and since the voice acting is so strong and the character’s face quite expressive this partially destroys the atmosphere and immersion. An easy way out would have been to have no lip movement at all, so that it’s just the inner voice but in its current state it’s quite a distraction. I do hope they can fix it.Finally, a word about the displayed wildlife, which may not be very accurate for the North Sea, but each discovery gives a passionate diver goosebumps. When I stumbled upon the Giant Squid I got so excited I almost smashed the sub trying to get a photo. And there’s a magical situation with Humpback whales resting upright without moving.Still, Blue Sharks are pelagic and don’t behave like Reef Sharks (the Blue Shark marks the spot …), Conger Eels don’t swim around during daytime, nor in groups, Basking Sharks will rather be found close to the surface etc. etc. With all the environmental awareness, I’d have appreciated a more realistic approach regarding the animals.So, if you’re ready for a long dive, love the ocean, and are open for a slow and emotional journey with quite a few heart-breaking moments do yourself a favor and play this. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: T.L.D.R - This is NOT Subnautica or an action game. It is a story ( sad story ) set underwater. Great graphics and interesting game play and mini games as the story slowly unfolds. You can not die, unless by your own stupidity. Review-If you want an underwater action game then DON'T buy this. If you like story based games and underwater activities then grab this one.Yes the controls can be a bit weird at time. You can go external view when piloting the mini sub. I found that when in a tight space it was better to go cockpit view as the external camera would clip in the terrain.The story is a slow burn and the game starts at day 3 (day 1 and 2 being a sort of tutorial) You will get an idea of what the story is about by this stage. There is also an Eco story and message going on throughout.Beautiful underwater graphics and animation of marine creatures as you explore the area you have been assigned to as an undersea tech for an oil company. In addition to the daily tasks and missions assign over the course of your 7 days under the sea ( it skips 10 days to advance story) you can have a go at some fun mini games. one being a punch bag that you have to time your punches as it gets faster and the other playing a guitar that you have to hit and hold keys as the song plays.All in all this is a relaxing stress free game with NO jump scares or bloody gore. Yes some dead creatures will appear now and then. this is the nature of life but nothing gruesome.You may also shed a few tears at a couple of points depending on your emotional levels.There are 2 endings to this game depending on your choices. Luckily you don't have to play the whole game through again to see the other ending as all main choices that give these are in the last chapter.Thanks for reading this far. I hope you enjoy the game if you do buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: - REVIEW -A deeply emotional Journey through the sea. Less "Subnautica" and more "Gone Home".The character(s) are portrayed very well and you will get emotionally attached to them and feel what they feel.Gameplay wise it is bascially your average "walking simulator" but with the addition of the special environment and the resulting travel methods - diving and your little sub.Also some very light crafting mechanics, though you can and likely will rarely use them.Graphics and performance are great. Under The Waves has a pretty special, slightly "comicy" look, especially when it comes to the characters.It fits the game well and performs top notch.The underwater flora and fauna looks very good, so does the water itself.I discovered zero stutter, bugs, framerate drops, tearing or anything alike. I would recommend playing it with a controller - the 360 degree movement within the water felt kind of unnatural with mouse/keyboard.The price tag is absolutely fair, it felt like it has just the right length for an emotional campaign like this. No filler, a little bit of optional exploration, but always with a clear path ahead if you wish to follow the story.I would absolutely recommend playing it. - 87/100 ---- MILD SPOILERS! ---The game touches some very sensitive topics within the great theme of loss. It does so very polite and thoughtful, but for some people - especially parents - it might create an uneasy feeling throughout the story. If you feel you are sensitive in that area, you might want to keep that in mind.Thank you very much for reading, stay safe und have fun with the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Can't turn off motion blur, depth of field, chromatic aberration nor film grain.Update: You can turn off motion blur and depth of field at least if you go into the game's configuration folder and create a file named "Engine.ini". Then, inside that file, copy and paste this:[SystemSettings]r.MotionBlurQuality=0r.DepthOfFieldQuality=0And then save the file. The game should now run without those two.Update 2: After one month, it's finally possible to disable film grain and chromatic aberration!Still, there aren't any options for motion blur and depth of field so you can use my tips above if you want to disable those.

_childDocuments_.review: Diving headfirst into , I was initially expecting a 'Subnautica'-like experience but with a more somber narrative twist. What I encountered, however, was an absolute emotional roller-coaster that left me utterly floored.  is a narrative-driven adventure, casting you in the role of Stan, a professional diver struggling with deep-rooted grief. The deep sea's isolating atmosphere serves as a metaphor to Stan's own inner state of mind, resulting in a heart-wrenching choice he must eventually make.Within the game's breathtaking underwater world, you're granted the freedom to roam and explore the depths freely, capturing stunning images of marine creatures while immersing yourself in an unforgettable story line. The narrative, though undeniably gut-wrenching, is a must-experience, offering a terrifyingly realistic portrayal of the all-encompassing power of grief and the destructive impact of human greed on our oceans.Crafting mechanics add depth to the gameplay, allowing you to assemble essential items through discovered blueprints and gathered materials during your exploration. Additionally, the game presents collectibles hidden within old shipwrecks, offering a chance to interact with these items within your life module and uncover their lore. You are still able to search for these collectibles even after you've completed the main story line, thoughtfully marked on your map, eliminating the need for tedious location hunting.All said and done,  captivated me completely, rendering me speechless and leaving my face streaked with tears. It ignited within me an intense desire to raise awareness about ocean conservation. I can't recommend this game enough; it's a powerful reminder of the urgency to protect our oceans and care for one another. Dive in and experience this life-changing journey for yourself – it's an adventure you won't want to miss.

_childDocuments_.review: The weird lens distortion, even indoors and the grainy effect among many other post-processing effects cannot be disabled and it just makes my eyes hurt while playing this game.All those image post processing effects on the camera don't make the game feel more immersive or the art style more distinct, it makes it look horrible and unplayable. Even if it has a good story to it, it's unacceptable in 2023 to have so little control in graphics options to not be able to disable all these things.P.S. Character animations are pretty bad too, but I don't mind it as much as forcing the game to look in a particular way and you have no way to adjust it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very nice and heartfelt title but bear in mind that this is mainly a *NARRATIVE* game beyond anything else, the survival and exploration elements being extras. It's immersive and has gorgeous visuals but is (very) slow paced, to the point where I'd argue it's essentially on rails, even if you have the freedom to swim in apparently whatever direction. After having finished it I'd recommend just following the prompts and not deviate too far from the path to enjoy the story and not waste too much time gathering stuff that is ultimately useless.

_childDocuments_.review: Under the Waves is pretty average I'd say, the music and visuals are superb, but the gameplay and story are meh and I experienced a decent amount of bugs as well. The submarine driving and exploration were definitely my favorite aspects, checking out the deep sea wrecks and wild life is enjoyable. Everything is just so slow in this game, you move slow, the character talks slow, the gameplay is slow... it can go from being chill and relaxing to boring at times. The story just kinda feels like you understand it within 5 minutes and just doesn't really go anywhere and is very predictable. The crafting and collecting of items is nice and good incentive but my map bugged out and some boxes that I already grabbed wouldn't go away, so that kinda ruined the clear the whole map goal. There's alot of issues like achievements don't all work, visuals bugs, forced letterboxing"black bars", audio settings not working ect, really killed the mood. I just love anything in the ocean and the atmosphere while just being in the sub is awesome, just feel the game falls flat in most other areas. The real "message" of the game about the horrible state of pollution in the oceans is also pretty heavy handed and kinda preaching to the choir at this point. If you crave underwater experiences it's worth while but I'd wait for a sale it's not very polished atm and it's short. 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the following may read like nitpicking, but atmosphere is a huge part of this game, and accurate details of the undersea environment and habitat technology contribute to the sense of being grounded in realism. 1. Submersibles do not burn fuel, they're battery operated. Change fuel icon to battery and dialogue referencing refueling to say recharging. If you're thinking "But what about diesel electric submarines?" those run their generators to recharge their battery banks only while surfaced. While submerged they operate purely on batteries. 2. Radio doesn't work underwater, save for ELF which is too low bandwidth for anything but Morse. Change references to radio in dialogue to "hydrophones" or "hydroaccoustic transmitters". 3. Add swishing noise synced to arm movement when walking, doesn't sound or move like he's underwater. Visual distortion effect behind him would add to this.4. Add internal lighting to habitat as seen from outside. Internal lighting should appear red tinted, like the Moon submersible's internal lighting5. Specify O2 bio generators contain algae. Terrestrial plants would not be used for such a purpose. Seems cribbed from Nemo's Garden, the purpose of which is growing food, not life support. Algae is 200 times more efficient than even trees at processing CO2 into O2. Can be as simple as internal green glow added to domes. Plants inside appear to be red algae, if this is already canon then disregard complaint #5. 6. I appreciate there's at least a lockout chamber on the Moon submersible to explain how you enter or exit while submerged. But it needs a pause during lockout cycling, and a sound effect for compressed air purging the water + some bubbles from the hatch. Still a step up over Subnautica. 7. "Life Module" (Habitat) has a lockout chamber the game refers to as an airlock. Airlocks lock air in, as in space stations. Lockout chambers lock water out. 8. The bathroom is positioned such that one must walk through it like a hallway to get to the bedroom. This is problematic in an undersea habitat as you want to confine humid air and bad smells as much as possible. Realistically the bathroom is always located in the wet porch area for this reason. At the very least the two sections should trade places so you only go into the bathroom when you need to use it, rather than whenever you need to reach your bedroom. Probably not fixable as the modeling is already done, but FIY. At least you included a sliding acrylic humidity barrier, but his bedroom would still constantly smell bad. 9. Minor gripe, but the protag wears his wetsuit to bed?Please correct the easy to fix ones that only really require changes to the dialogue and minor sound design changes. That will be sufficient to change this review to a recommend. -Narcosis technical consultant/writer, marine engineering autist
