_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this to players who are interested in a more chill, narrative driven, emotional journey. Are there things about the game I wish were different or more fleshed out? Sure. But, at the end of the day, the game was enjoyable and had a strong enough story to keep me engaged. Overall score: 7.5/10Recommend: YESTime to beat: 15 hrsAchievements completed: 90%Pros:1 - the game is a visual treat2 - driving around your mini sub, "Moon", is quite enjoyable. I enjoyed the controls of it, the way it animated, and upgrading it.3 - exploration is decent fun4 - story is enjoyable. it's a bit depressing, emotional, but it's still good5 - game does a good job at making you feel alone and isolated at the bottom of the sea. I enjoyed the guitar and boxing mini-games to pass the time. Manipulating your face in front of the mirror provided a good laugh too!Cons:1 - whole game is pressing B on things (for the most part). Probably could have benefited from fleshing out some of the interactions to be more engaging, interesting, or, at the very least, not have the icon "B" hover over everything. Would be more immersive if there were more subtle cues. Yes, turning wheels and pulling levers is generally not pressing "B", which is good, but everything else pretty much is. I think seeing the "B" cue constantly on the screen just gets old and hurts immersion. One example, the geodes. Maybe you needed some sort of drill to pop them off, and they slowly fall towards the seabed floor. You have to swim towards them to collect them, and maybe you DO press "B", but the letter "B" is not displayed on the screen. Maybe the geode just illuminates ever so slightly (a very subtle thing) once you're close enough to grab them. 2 - Lip-syncing animations are very bad. It's distracting how bad they are. I couldn't figure out if they were just going for a certain aesthetic or just did a really bad job. Either way, it's distracting and could have used some polish. The rest of the game is animated so nicely, it stood out like a sore thumb. 3 - I spent all this time collecting resources, fabricating things, upgrading my sub, and I honestly don't think I needed to do ANY of it. The game is too easy in this sense. Everything you need already exists and is available in the world. There's no reason to craft anything. Game could have benefited greatly from leaning more heavily into this and not having so many things so readily available out in the world. 4 - I really loved how the game gave you a choice at the end. It would have been nice if you had other choices to make as you played the game that could alter the story, further alter the ending, etc. etc. 5 - game desperately needed some combat. Not saying it needed to be focal point of game (IMO exploration should have been), but when entering the private sectors, would have been nice touch to have to deal with combat drones or something that required combat. Like when you went to the server room. Instead of a dead body, maybe there are people actively trying to destroy the data that you need to fight. Would have added a real nice wrinkle to the game. 6 - there is nothing to fear while playing the game. None of the animal life attack you. It would have been nice if you had to figure out ways to avoid sharks, orcas, etc., or distract them, in order to get to loot. 7 - even the main "enemy" in the game (not sure if the game ever gave it a name, but it is some kind of supernatural enemy that is trying to stop you) is not scary in the least bit (but most certainly COULD have been). It's easily dealt with, easy avoidable, even in the moments where the game is trying to create suspense. One easy solution is if you took health damage (or Moon took damage) if you were caught inside of it. It would at least make it so you wanted to avoid it. Would also be cool if the more you got stuck inside it's "web", the more it could read your mind, and the more intense your "hallucinations" were. This could encourage you to interact with it, but only so much (as you don't want to die), in order to have more meaningful and deeper interactions with Pearl. But for those who wanted to maintain their sanity, they could avoid it, and focus more on Emma. This would be a spectrum, a sanity spectrum have you, that would directly impact dialogue options, story arcs, and the ending. Would add replay-ability to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have thalassophobia, which is a fear of deep water, so I typically avoid games that involve dangers such as diving, sailing, and yes, even big puddles. But something about Under the Waves really caught my eye, helped in large part to the pedigree at Quantic Dream – I have fond memories of Heavy Rain and Detroit: Become Human. Under the Waves did not disappoint. The atmosphere is pitch perfect. You play as Stan, a man broken by grief. You have taken a solitary job at the bottom of the north sea, while you struggle with a recent life-changing event. But the longer Stan spends in the depths, the stranger his experiences get. The mood can sway between light and playful and then snap to dark, spooky, and full of intrigue. The plot is a slow, incremental burn, with the final scene consisting of quite a shocking decision to be made.  The entire game takes place underwater. You navigate a sizeable map through either swimming or in a small submarine called ‘Moon’. Both control very well, which were aspects I had trepidations over. Over the course of three weeks, you’ll carry out routine tasks, as well as partaking in exploration, photography, collecting, crafting, upgrading, and the occasional minigame (playing the guitar or boxing). Most missions are a simple take on getting from a to b, with puzzles only really consisting of finding the right entrance and locating switches and levers. It has a repetition to it but I never found it outstayed its welcome. For the most part, bobbing around in a little sub looking for sunken treasure was relaxing and rewarding. I didn’t know this before I played but no creature will cause you harm. The game is full of sharks, whales, orcas, turtles, octopuses, eels, crabs - even a giant squid, if you can find it - but they just swim away if you get too close. Your submarine can take damage or run out of fuel, and when swimming around, you may get the odd occasion where your oxygen is low, but the game is generous with fuel, repair kits, and oxygen boosts, so you should never be in any real danger. Just get in a habit of checking your equipment and crafting some resources before each time you head out and you’ll be fine.  I beat the game and collected almost everything, at a relaxed pace, in around twelve hours. The game does have some issues though. I played on my MSI GF65, which has an i7 and an RTX3060, and I ran the game on ultra, but I found it had an infrequent and somewhat idiosyncratic stutter to it, which never really went away. It isn’t awful but certainly noticeable. I also had two crashes where the game just shut down. On top of that, I seemed to encounter a few bugs regarding the map and the final item I had to eventually give up on recovering. A chest icon appeared on the map but when I went there, the chest wasn’t there and I spent an embarrassing amount of time trying to locate it. There were also other chests that I did find but sometimes the icon would remain on the map. So the game has a few bugs, but nothing that took away from the experience. Overall, I had a blast with this. The plot and small cast of characters were nothing new but it all worked. The atmosphere, visuals, gameplay all were fantastic. The extras were distributed, at least for me, in just the right amount so that I wanted to get stuck in. And the ending will stay with me for some time, but that will be in part due to what my disturbed viewers settled on picking. If you love indies and a narrative focused adventure, then I highly recommend Under the Waves.

The technical issues are there and do break immersion. I will add one more point! There is no way to change the controls! When you start the game, you are prompted to choose  the type of controller you want to use. I thought it is a joke, so I was a little bit sloppy with my choice thinking that the game will detect the controller automatically or that I can change it later in the game, like every pc port of a console game that I played so far. The world is immersive when the bugs don't take their toll on the game. The story got me hooked. I liked the futuristig setting. The music is beatiful. Graphics are Ok. The tasks are very boring. They feel more like chores than adventurous tasks.  Voice acting is ok. There are some lip syncing issues. Depression is not a topic for a game in my opinion. There is no fun in that! The face of Stan is very ugly. I'm sorry for his wife! I will revisit this game later! I don't raise my hopes that the tasks will be redisigned because this is part of the main core of the game. But I would like to see most of the bugs fixed, because restarting the game because of them is not pleasant! At least they introduced in an update the frequently autosaves which alleviates the pain! P. S. one gamebreaking bug that I encountered is "zero gravity"! After turning the telvision off and leaving the table I start falling through the map never stoping. I think this has to do with the fact that I changed the views during television and suddenly Stan disappeared. After I left the table he was outside his base falling through the map! I game to escape reality, not to feel bad about the game I'm playing. Activism has no place in gaming, even for topics which I fully support.To be fair, I should have done a little more research. _childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of games playing under water, especially if they're about diving as well. And the game does give the feeling you have, when you're deep under water and only can rely on your gear. When the sight is limited and that feeling and sound of pressure all around you. But that's basically all the game can offer. The gameplay is pretty boring. It tries to be more than a walking simulator by throwing in mechanics like crafting and the exploration, but it doesn't really add to the experience. Instead it feels like it's just streched out, especially with the big map, to make the game longer, without offering actual content. The animations and graphics in general aren't really good either. And then there are dream sequences thrown in. Sequences like that are just annoying. They can make sense in movies, but in games they are not needed. They just stretch the game out even more.I can't recommend the game, even though I bought it with a discount it's just too expensive for what it has to offer. If you cut the game down to a 2hrs experience and sell it for 1/3 of the price, it would be a whole other story.
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: As an immersive exploration game: very good. As a story: not that deep or thought provoking. As a survival game: easy mode.Let me first start with the positives:+ The graphics and music is very good and immersive. At times it's quiet to increase the tension.+ The makers of Subnautica should take notes on how to make a story driven game set under the sea.+ There are fun mini games. You can play the guitar, punch a punching bag, take pictures, and it's funny that you can make faces in the mirror. It enliven things a bit when it gets too depressing.+ Game runs well. Encountered a "Fatal Error" crash only once.+ They paid attention to small details like how your sub gets dented when you crash into things. However, I still wonder how aquatic plants can grow in an environment that can't be reached by sunlight (i.e. inside pipes).+ Unlike Subnautica, this game has a map with icons! Such a great "innovation" to add one to a game based around open world exploration instead of having other people mod it in for you.+ Lots of logs to read which gives some interesting tidbits about marine animals. It can also help a casual player to catch up to the story when they don't have the time to play this game in one or two sittings.Depends:+ - There is this film grain texture that made me thought that there's something wrong with my graphics card. Eventually I just get used to it. I guess it's the "artist's vision". Game could've been the same with or without it. Can there be a toggle for this filter?+ - While there are survival elements like gathering materials and crafting items/upgrades, items are so plentiful and at times are already there right when you needed them that it totally negates any tension. At times I think the devs are scared that players will have to repeat a day/load a save. I guess it's fine as long as I treat this game as an interactive movie instead of a survival game.+ - Minor pop ins.+ - Got to the ending at 9 and so hours. Limited replayability and linear story but as long as you're in for an immersive and story driven experience then I think this game is apt.+ - While the story is mostly about dealing with grief, to me it felt that it lacks.. depth. I was expecting some existential themes that'll really question one's purpose or something philosophically profound that'll keep me awake at night but that's on me.Negatives:- Lips not being in sync with the audio.- Despite the game being about taking care of the environment and not leaving trash behind, your character throws spent casings when he use certain items.- Now this one is a big bug that softlocked my game's progress. Ending related spoilers: Overall, I think the game's good. It's my first time playing this so called walking simulator games and this is a good introduction. Might try other games and I hope they'll have the same immersive environment as this game but have a more thought provoking story.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games which are story led, you should like this. The theme throughout is two-fold, grief and environmental protection. It's very linear story line, there is very little deviation from it, choice or control apart from . However, there is an 'exploration' element to the game and you get plenty of time to do so. The achievements are quite easy to unlock too, if you were determined, you should be able to get 100% fairly easily. Here's the good and the not so good:✔️ Great environment, very atmospheric, makes you feel like you are in a huge oceanic space. I played on ultra settings with an i9 and RTX 4080. Remained at 100fps throughout.✔️ The voice acting is reasonable throughout.✔️ The soundtrack and score are excellent - an absolute highlight to the whole experience.✔️ The story line is interesting, there's no killing or shooting at all which is very refreshing.✔️ The wildlife doesn't attack you which is more realistic and aligns with the environmentally friendly approach the game has.✔️ The sea creatures look reasonable.✔️ There is plenty of life in the ocean, every direction you look, there is something swimming about. They have created a hugely diverse environment in terms of movement.✔️ The visual approach is very cinematic, everything from the camera angles through to being able to turn off the HUD and change angles during some cut scenes. ✔️ I played with a controller and that worked well for me.✔️ Took me 17 hours to collect everything, do everything and complete the game. Which I thought was reasonable.👎 A bit buggy - boarding the 'Moon' or the submarine is clunky and careless in terms of the animation. Some interactions were frustrating because I couldn't position the character easily in front to create the prompt to interact.👎 The cinematic angles are great ... in the big environments. But in the closed in sections (there are quite a few) the camera angles are a huge hindrance to the whole experience. The camera can go all over the place and at terrible angles making game play far more difficult than it needed to be.👎 Facial animations are brilliant, I found coordination with the vocal emotions didn't tie together smoothly.👎 The logbook is bugged. Part of the story is reading collections in the log book, but the text wonders down and you can't scroll to read more which is a huge shame and something I would have expected to have been sorted for release.👎 Animal animations are a bit awkward. In tighter spaces, they also clip in and out of the scenery too which impacts the immersion. 👎 Control mechanics are different for swimming and for control of the submarine which makes things a bit tricky. You have to change from one to the other quite a bit throughout. 3/5
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: Very immersive, visual, and emotional game. The game is short and it is a quick play through but the story is great and will leave you attached to the main character. The visuals are a little artsy and not HD realistic but it is not so artsy that it takes away from the immersion of the underwater environment. Definitely worth a play if you want a game with relatively chill game play but certainly not boring or forgettable.
_childDocuments_.name: Under The Waves

_childDocuments_.review: An emotional story about a man looking for a meaning after a traumatic loss. Trying to flee the world into a dark and lonely ocean of pollution. Finding a personal truth when venturing into the deepest dark of the ocean and his mind. An unusual game where it's slow pacing is built onto the story. Making you reflect on the things of life. The Serene silence of the ocean, either makes you wonder where it all went wrong. Great atmosphere, great gameplay. Although did met with some random crashes. (after specific cinematics). Although there isn't much to do, there is an ocean to explore. Look for lost treasure and enjoy the animals that roam there. Definitely worth it if you are a fan of friendly sharks! (and oceans)

_childDocuments_.review: a very good game that has somehow managed to blend and tackle the tough and heavy topics of ocean pollution and grief. the ocean exploration is easily my favourite part, the sub controls do take some getting used to though. the enviroment is beautifully done and all the aquatic species are amazing to see. i enjoyed the story telling overall and the voice acting is decent. I would love to see the devs make another game but set in the deep ocean. id say overall for me its  a solid 7.5/10 the last 2 missions knock half a point off for driving me insane trying to pilot the sub in such twisty turney places.  if you like the idea of swimming around the ocean and diving wrecks whilst also completing missions and collecting trash to upgrade stuff then definetly give this a go. the story itself is an added bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: A mixed bag.  But because the ending mostly worked I'm going positive.The metaphor is obvious straight from the trailer, the visual art and style is very good.  The characters constant narration and self explanation gets pretty annoying.  Its mostly told with all the subtlety of a sledge hammer.  The style and atmosphere carry you through it to the big finale which ultimately does land.Its not really going to explain any of the narrative.  Its not really about the world around you just the characters journey.  So if your expecting all loose ends to be neatly tied, well your going to be disappointed.The camera and off kilter angles and darkness may look nice but navigating right underwater wrecks with your dinky flashlight really did give me a headache and was not at all enjoyable.  I mean call it achieving a sense of claustraphobia if you like but its still not fun. Most of the game isn't that though.

_childDocuments_.review: As soon as I stumbled upon the trailer to Under The Waves, I knew I needed to give it a shot. Upon completing this game, I'd like to share with you some of my thoughts. Using a controller, I would describe the control scheme/camera as one of this games major achievements. Seriously, I can not praise it enough, I've played countless scuba type games and in this regard this game might be my favorite. The 3rd person free camera paired with the excellent 3d space maneuverability allows for an extremely intuitive and satisfying experience. That goes especially true for the divers controls and I found simply swimming around a unique joy. This holds true for the submarine as well, but not to the same extent, though the submarine has its own strong suits. Notably, being able to semi change the control scheme to the strafe mode at any moment is much appreciated while maneuvering in tight spaces. Simply put, the controls of this game are intuitive and just feel good to engage with.On the topic of the camera again, I must say bravo! Being able to position the camera around the diver and the sub independent from their movement just produces such a cinematic experience. Paired with the beautifully stylized graphics, It feels like I am watching a movie that I control. By the way, great decision to let you bring said hud down, allowing the stunning graphics to speak for them self. On top of that, I think the distance of the camera from the diver helps you feel sufficiently small in an environment of giant creatures and vast open water.  I really enjoyed the scale of the world and how full the environment felt. It is obvious that the developers in this game passionately but their soul into the world and experience they were trying to deliver. The environment and exploration deserve praise as well! One small thing I really enjoyed was how seamless the transition between diver and sub, which made the game a bit more immersive for me. The world has tons of unique and interesting areas/elements that made exploring feel so rich and fascinating. On top of that, said exploration is rewarded with tons of items/upgrades to find, which is fulfilling. Not to mention just the general wonder that comes from exploring an ocean environment and being privy to the incredible creatures that inhabit them.The Story of Under the Waves is ambitious and succeeds in a lot of areas. However it has a few flaws. I love the dark and mysterious tone they were going for, as that sort of story feeling is my personal favorite. In my opinion however, the story and tone are held back by the pacing, which subject to drastic changes in speed. This can make the story come off a bit abrasive. On top of that, every story note is sufficiently explored(Especially the sort of dark mysterious things that come to light), while some beats seem to be reiterated a bit too much. Regardless, I still think the overall narrative is interesting and fulfilling, and I admit their were times where i was definitely gripped. Given some practice and learning, I expect some excellent narratives from these developers in the future. While I have more thoughts, this review is starting to drag on, and as such I will conclude with this. To the player:For $30, this game offers and immersive and captivating experience. I am a certified scuba diver in real life, and I can attest that this game captures a lot of the same wonder I get while actual diving, which is an amazing achievement. I highly recommend you pick it up and give it a shot!To the Parallel Studio:I thoroughly enjoyed your game! From playing it, it is obvious to me that you posses both the passion and skill to produce art worth experiencing. I hope that you continue to hone your abilities and improve, as I believe you have the potential to join the ranks of the truly great indie studios. You have earned a fan and I can't wait to see what ever you try next. I expect great things. Thank you.P.S.Consider opening a patron, as I suspect many would like to support your efforts further as I do.

_childDocuments_.review: This game drew me in, immersed me in curiosity and wonder, chilled my bones with the consequences of human indifference to our environment, and then crushed my heart with the progression of the story at the center of it all. In a way, the game itself is much like the ocean: mysterious, alluring, stunning, foreboding, and most of all... DEEP.11/10 story. One of the few narrative-driven games I've played that left me staring at the rolling credits just absorbing and contemplating everything. This will definitely be a staple in my collection and would recommend anyone who loves a good story mixed with free exploration and interesting missions. Give it time, the first few days in-game are sluggish, but be patient and allow the story to pick up. I promise it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Under the Waves is plain boring from start till end (spoiler: I've watched the end on Youtube, couldn't risk wasting more of my time). The narrative where the main character is grieving his daughter just got on my nerves, outside of what I couldn't find any interest in the dull gameplay where you just spend your time pushing buttons and solving simple puzzles. The games tries to follow a genre that was opened by masterpieces such as Firewatch or Soma (I can't recommend enough playing those titles!) but using the worst gameplay ever and very boring cut scenes that we don't seem to be able to skip. So yes, there's this good intention of talking about climate and how we screw the oceans using gigantic oil refineries, but you know what? Maybe you should just save yourself (and the planet) a couple of GPU cycles by closing this game and go clean some rubbish on the nearest beach instead of playing :)

_childDocuments_.review: Great story about a parent coping with severe loss and the way the mind manifests realities in those situations. Alternatively, his loss creates some kind of connection to an intelligence deep below and these aren't hallucinations at all! Pretty thought provoking either way one looks at it.As a parent and having lost a few very close friends during my own journey, the grief Stan displays and his stammering and constant failure to find the right words hit me far closer to home than expected - well done!

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game.  Poignant lesson to the story, as I am a recent widow this hit home hard in a good way. Under the Waves was a really nice journey to go one with the protagonist, an important one that we will all go one in one way or another in life. Grief. The game itself was a bit short, even for the completionist in me that tried to do all the extra stuff first. I personally would have preferred a longer game, with perhaps more tedium to extend where the story couldn't (ala mortuary assistant and its repetition). That said, I recommend a playthrough. Is the price right? Yes and no... W/ inflation and everything considered, 29.99 as a start is fair. Given frequent sales, just wait for a deal if that is steep, I was happy I did! I would like a sequel, or prequel, as the main story itself was very personal and touching, yet the world built here and hinted at could(should) be grander!

_childDocuments_.review: First off, lovely watery soundtrack.I do love an under water game (Subnautica and expansion). This game captures the beauty of the underwater world. There is the beautiful story of trying to look after the ocean running throughout whilst a personal story is also there which feels awkward even though you are alone onboard.It took one death and a little while to get the hang of oxygen. You know, running out of oxygen capsules under water is not recommended. Once you get around that, it's a beautiful world full of beauty and jobs.Highly recommended to get away from your everyday shooting, high pressure games. It's a relaxing world down there even if the overall story is a sad and grim one.Just completed the game. You gotta love Stan, poor fella. Stuck between a rock and a hard place.It's a sad story with an up turn. It's optimistic whilst feeling sad along the way. It's very rare to feel any emotion in games apart from the need to survive but this has other story lines that you don't expect. Despite being a short game (compared to most) it's enjoyable. I think the ending could have been shown a bit better. Seems to be missing a final hurrah, if you know what I mean (without explaining what's missing)....Overall, it's a lovely painful, life affirming game.

While everything is perfect what the games delivers, it is a shame that they didn't make more out of it:1) Longer story2) more and deeper crafting opportunities3) more "freedom" while playing through the story (more kind of exploration)4) bigger map with some different biomesWould love to see a successor.

_childDocuments_.review: Immersing players in the captivating world beneath the waves, "Under the Waves" fulfills the dream of exploring the underwater realm in a way that goes beyond mere gameplay. This game seamlessly weaves together a dark and poignant narrative with engaging story elements, tasks, adventures, and exploration.The narrative unfolds with a sense of depth, conveying both the beauty and challenges of life beneath the surface. The game skillfully balances suspense with a strangely calming environment, providing players with a unique and immersive experience. Whether you're delving into the mysteries of the deep or simply enjoying the occasional evening of relaxation, "Under the Waves" offers a versatile and enjoyable gaming experience.One of the standout features is the incorporation of tasks and adventure elements that add layers of complexity to the gameplay. From collecting equipment to crafting, the game offers a comprehensive and rewarding experience. The interplay of survival instincts adds an additional layer of intensity, making each decision and action feel significant to the overarching narrative.For those who appreciate the occasional escape into the gaming world, particularly within the realms of suspense and underwater exploration, "Under the Waves" comes highly recommended. The combination of a well-crafted storyline, atmospheric environment, and diverse gameplay elements makes it a standout choice for anyone seeking a gaming experience that transcends the ordinary. So, dive in, explore the depths, and discover the wonders that "Under the Waves" has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved Under the Waves. The story was emotional, heavy, and well-written.The music was phenomenal. The voice acting was great. Stan was very well done. The game gives you a steady flow of main missions and a handful of side quests that will send you pretty straight to the end. But I really enjoyed the swimming and exploration moments during the downtime. You can either just go explore while you're completing those main quests or some days will give you "free time" where you can go back out and explore some more on your own. The map is a really good size. Big enough where you feel like you're really exploring and discovering new areas and landmarks. But not too big where there's a ton of empty space. I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of games like Firewatch, The Invincible, etc. I was able to 100% it in just under 16 hours and it was a great game to stream. I played this on my steam deck with a PS5 controller and I didn't have any trouble. The game ran smoothly and worked perfectly. Can't wait to play more games from these devs!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a relatively short game, and can be completed in 5 hours or less.  It consists of drinking coffee, driving your submersible around the ocean, and doing various tasks for a petroleum corporation.  You can pick up plastic, clean up oil, and take some photos of things if you want - but these are mostly unnecessary.  The story itself is... Well, it's a story about how corporations can't be bothered to follow proper safety protocols and the dangers of being in a state of pure isolation when your mind is obviously not in a great place.  The strange dream-like worlds you'll experience are obviously dreams to the player, yet our character seems to struggle with it.  There's an obvious disconnect between us and them, and I do wish they'd of done a better job with this part.  Overall I feel like the story really fails to capture any real sense of caring for the character or your mission.The game loop is there, although it feels rather minimal.  The ocean is pretty large but there's little incentive to actually explore.  There are cool things to find, but it ultimately doesn't contribute in any sensible way to the story, adventure, or ending.  The submersible is a blast to play though.  The on-foot sections are much slower and borderline irritating at times.Voice acting is superb.  Sound effects and music are great, and the music alone was enough to make me happy with this purchase.  Graphically the game is beautiful.  The ocean really does feel alive with the various sea life in the game.  The environments are cleverly crafted and there were only a few times I felt lost or disoriented.While the game never sucked me in, it was certainly an experience I'm glad I had.  I'd suggest waiting for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of walking simulators and story-rich games, as well as almost anything that takes place underwater, like Subnautica. However, unlike Subnautica, I genuinely wanted to continue playing Under The Waves since it didn't rely heavily on spending an exorbitant amount of time scrounging for resources located every which-where across the map.This game told a genuinely captivating story that I loved, and really had me feeling things, which compounded onto its storytelling. I loved this game so much that I felt driven to hunt down all of the achievements (with a little help from the Internet), and they weren't really so much out of the way, in my opinion.The character's lips didn't match up with what was ever being said, and some objects seemed to be "ragdolling" often enough, but I'm used to that, so it didn't pull me away from what I loved about it.Money well-spent for me!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with a touching, meaningful and melancholy story. It is beautifully told through an unsuspecting lens but delivers on the message nicely. The setting is beautiful, the art style is an excellent match for the style of game that this is (not hyper realistic, focused on a fantasy/sci-fi story). I'm recommending this game but I did feel like there were some issues that detract from the overall experience, and I've shared them below. First, some of the movement mechanics feel a little unfinished/unpolished - there is a lot of drifting and sometimes it feels like you are swimming in an invisible molasses soup (or into an invisible wall). It is not horribly distracting from the overall experience but it was certainly frustrating at times. Secondly, for being a game about grief, they sure like to rail on fossil fuels and the energy industry. SEVERAL times throughout the game I was distracted from the larger message by little jabs and statements about the evils of the industry. I get it, these industries have done harm to the ocean/world - but it feels out of place to make these statements in this game and in the settings they were made.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that could have been great but ruined by so many inconsistences and narrative immaturity : - You're working for some kind of oil rig conglomerate but you (and your boss) were environmental activists... Will someone please fire the HR manager of this company ? - The whole environmental plot is awfully and immaturely written (spoiler : oil extracting companies are evil). - It also doesn't mix well with the grieving part of the game, making it seems that two plots were forced into a single game. - You're married to a still active environmental activist but she never criticize you for doing maintenance in an underwater oil rig. - Everything you do in the game ends up triggering an environmental catastrophe. - Who sends a grief-ridden depressed ex-environmental activist guy to work alone in a deep sea station for an oil company ? Please rehire the HR manager and fire him again- The grief plot ends up with "I'm going home" but they're never were any progress in grief (It seems to get worse actually)And so on...

_childDocuments_.review: I completed the game in about 16 hours. I don't normally write reviews, but I wanted to in this case because I could feel the love that has been put into this game. I have some limited experience scuba diving, and was amazed by how well the game captures the experience. The diving/swimming animations for the main character were done through motion capture, so they look realistic and natural. The sound design was also exceptionally well done. Things tend to sound different underwater (louder and closer, and less directional) and the developers captured this feeling exactly. The sounds of sea life in the environment, the way you hear yourself breathing through a regulator, the bubbling noises, everything worked perfectly together and was extremely immersive. (There was also this dual sense of freedom and claustrophobia, which basically captured how I felt diving as well). Things I loved: - The sound design, including both the music soundtrack (it's REALLY GOOD), the ambient environmental noises, etc.  - How immersive it is- The small details that help create immersion - The - The story. It - The fact that the devs made changes based on feedback (for example, it was requested that the mini map icons disappear after you pick up a collectable so you can see which ones you had already picked up and which ones were left to get- this patch happened while I was playing and was SO much better)- The free camera worked amazingly well. Really cool to be able to see all the diver animations in detail and explore the environment freely. - The environment design. It's really good, down to the varying visibility, the light/darkness, the sea life, the landscape (seascape?), everything. Just an absolute joy to look at. Things I liked less/minor quibbles: - Unsure if this is a bug or a mistake on my part, but I - I was actually terrible at  ... let's just say this is a skill issue but it would be nice to be able to turn down the sensitivity on the controls a bit to adjust maybe. Not a big deal. I played with controller and definitely recommend doing so over keyboard/mouse. - A couple of lip sync issues with the dialogue when you're looking at the main character's face. This is so minor it was a non-issue. Really scrambling for things to say in this section. Issues/bugs (mostly for the devs if they read this): - The game crashed once after exiting an area on I think day 16. No big deal, it had saved at that point so I didn't lose any progress. - Encountered a couple of bugs that required me to exit to main menu and resume from there (for example, once on day 17 I stopped being able to move my character ). They did not persist after restarting from menu so it wasn't a big problem. tl;dr This is a game that has had a lot of love put into it and you can feel it. I would absolutely recommend this.

It does have a very impressive and immersive deep sea atmosphere. But the setting is symbolic, to a large degree - this is not a sandbox game or even a game with much freedom to explore at all. I think this may disappoint some players, but I do think the story is well told and well staged.

_childDocuments_.review:
Under The Waves is a narrative-driven adventure game about the engulfing power of grief.

Set in the depths of the North Sea in a techno-futuristic 1970s, professional diver Stan is struggling to overcome a life-changing loss and embrace a new future. The isolation of the deep sea is a fitting manifestation of his state of mind, and as Stan retreads further into his self-imposed solitude, he starts to experience strange events far beneath the waves. He will eventually have to make a difficult choice... stay lost in the depths forever, or break free to the surface and to the rest of his life.

name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind
detailed_description: JOIN OUR COMMUNITY About the Game Desktop Dungeons: Rewind is a modern remastering of the award-winning, bite-sized, tactical dungeon crawler. Founding a new kingdom isn’t easy: it takes cunning, manpower, and lots and lots of gold. How will you pay for the outrageously overpriced taverns and banks? Better descend into the dungeons and steal riches from the deadly inhabitants any way you can. Embark on an adventure - Choose from a diverse cast of replaceable adventures. Explore bite-sized dungeons. Heal by exploring - Reveal hidden terrain to regain health and mana. But plan your route carefully or you’ll have nothing left to face the final enemy. Die. Rewind. And try again. - New to DDR, your death is no longer quite so inevitable. After death, you can replay a dungeon from an earlier point to try a different strategy. Build your kingdom - Trade monstrous trophies for gold and upgrade your settlement to attract the most skilled adventurers. Show your friends who’s boss - Daily online challenges. Discover everything that earned Desktop Dungeons a cult following: innovative game design, hundreds of hours of content, daily online challenges, the amazing soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky and Grant Kirkhope, all the DLC, and more! Desktop Dungeons: Rewind is similar to titles like Runestone Keeper, Into the Breach, and Dicey Dungeons.

_childDocuments_.review: I have about 730 hrs in the original and also did a bunch of playtesting for this remake. Desktop Dungeons is one of my favorite games of all time, and it's so great to have a remastered version for its 10-year anniversary.IF YOU ARE NEW TO DESKTOP DUNGEONS: This is a no-brainer recommendation. This game, while simple on the surface, is strategically deep and very unique - nothing else quite scratches the itch for me. There is a learning curve, but it's worth it!IF YOU ARE FAMILIAR WITH THE GAME: First of all, you can import your old kingdom if you link your account, so no re-grinding! Second, while the game is mostly the same, there are a few very smart adjustments. The first thing you'll probably notice is the new dungeon layout that is better suited to widescreen resolutions. There are also tweaks to classes like Fighter and Berserker. And of course, there's the namesake Rewind feature.Like me, you may be turned off by DD:R's UI at first. It is very, very different from the original. When you're used to seeing the entire dungeon at once, it feels jarring to start zoomed in. Instead of having the most important UI items clustered together on one side of the screen, they are spread out across the perimeter. But give it a chance - it grew on me, and I think it will grow on you too. It should definitely be an improvement for new players -  there are subtleties like enemies facing towards you when they will strike first, and combat prediction now extends to all status effects.I have one major complaint: No custom keybindings. This is an accessibility issue, and it frankly is unacceptable that a remastered game released in 2023 lacks it. It should have been one of the core features. Hopefully it is implemented down the road.Overall though, I'm so happy this game has gotten remastered. More than anything, I hope it brings in lots of new players and revitalizes the community!

_childDocuments_.review: Not a true review, but a big kudos to QCF for giving this  out to players of the original.  Super classy move, guys.  Big thank you!As for the game, if you've played the OG Desktop Dungeons, you'll be extremely familiar with the mechanics of the game.  The graphics got a very obvious overhaul - for better or for worse - but the gameplay remains exactly the same, offering players new and old the same plate of tactical deliciousness that the original had.  If it bites you, you'll find yourself spending countless hours clicking away at this brain-teaser of a dungeon crawler.But that doesn't tell you much, so let's just go over exactly what this is - it's a tile-based dungeon crawler that is made for bite-sized runs.  Play it for 20 minutes or for several hours at a time, the randomly-generated dungeons ensure there's plenty of replayability and the town building/upgrading will keep you diving for treasure.  Unlike other tile-based crawlers, instead of being an omniscient overseer of the map, you have an avatar and how/when you move/attack is vital to the way the game works. Exploring undiscovered tiles heals you and replenishes your mana, but every step you take away from an enemy you've damaged means they'll be healing (enemies never move, but ignoring them is usually temporary at best).  There are all sorts of spells and other ways to mitigate this to allow you to tactically run from a fight and return to it with less penalties, but dungeon crawling is a delicate balance of tactical decisions you'll need to make rather than being full-on risk/reward.It looks like the same classes and races are here (each combo giving you a different set of bonuses or abilities for your run) and the mind-bending puzzle mode also makes a return.  The inventory system and the info panels also got a makeover - again, for better or for worse - and I haven't yet discovered all of the changes made here yet.  Though I do have to note that you can no longer long-click to access your glyphs which is a bit annoying.At first blush, the game feels bigger somehow, but the change to a new engine makes it feel less like a desktop distraction (like the OG game or the old LucasArts Desktop Adventures games... member those?) and more like a fully-fledged 'game'.  Not a big deal, but a lot of my time with the original was spent multitasking and you can always run this in a window for the same effect.  Either way, the dungeons seem to have a larger scope than before with more room to plan out your approach than before and plenty of opportunities for converting glyphs where the original felt super tight on that front.  Maybe it'll get tighter with more time under my belt.At any rate, I'm pleased that the devs didn't try to reinvent the wheel here.  They expanded the original rather than modernizing it which is telling me they know exactly why people played the first game to begin with.  To me it feels like they're bringing it ten years into the future and not mucking with the formula.  "Modern audiences" can go somewhere else.Haven't played the first game? As of this writing, it is being given away for free. If you're on the fence, go play it, then come back if you're jonesing for more.  Edit: I also just confirmed that you can sync your old saves to this game, so even more reason to go try it out and keep all your progress!(Some edits to correct some stuff after giving the game more time.)

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this remaster over the original. I liked the original Desktop Dungeons very much, and although this game includes the great gameplay systems and humor of the original, the old version is still perfectly playable and better in every way.The elegant pen and paper boardgame style of the original has been replaced by a mobile game interface and graphics. The new 3D models and environments are competently made, however they ruin the visual clarity the original had, especially when you zoom out to get an overview of your tactical options. Because of the extra visual clutter of 3D models it's a lot more difficult to identify enemy types and other things at a glance.The original game showed the whole dungeon in one screen, this remaster allows zooming in and out. Zooming out all the way makes things hard to see, while zooming in spins the camera in a bizarre  not-quite-isometric rotation. This slightly rotated camera serves no purpose other than to make the game more difficult to look at.The new UI is abysmal. Instead of presenting all important information in the same panel like the original did, in this remaster important elements of the UI are spread out all over the screen. Information you need to keep track of and compare is presented in different corners of your monitor making you have to swivel your head like you're watching a tennis match. Why was this game made? Did anybody ask for this? As a standalone game it might have had potential after some UI improvements. As a remaster of the original Desktop Dungeons it's a big downgrade.

_childDocuments_.review: Dear reader, hang tight, as this will be a long one.Desktop Dungeons and I go way back, and I have many fond memories of this gem, being familiar with it since the early Alphas,  dating way back from circa 2010. Ever since then, the seeds of its genre bending, non-conforming, innovative gameplay were already planted,becoming fully realized in 2013, refining many of the systems and mechanics seen in said Alpha.Now, in brilliant fashion, we see yet another polished iteration of the game, Desktop Dungeons Rewind, a prety clever addition to the title that I'll explain further down the review.Now, enough with the reverie. What even is this thing!?As I mentioned, Desktop Dungeons Rewind (henceforth simply DDR, for brevity) doesn't conform to a set genre, but rather, the interplay between many aspects of established genres is what makes the game tick. You have top down dungeons with random layouts (with set rules toensure it is beatable) from roguelikes, playable classes and fantasy races from most RPGs (each with unique traits), as well as equipment, inventories and other such staples, but in a very unique way of going about it.Another layer that makes the weird and wonderful DDR sandwich is resource management, but not in the way you might be used to - you are not building a base to survive relentless waves of monsters; resource management is key to be able to outlast and beat enemies.Health, Magic, Experience, Spells, Equipment and even the exploration of the dungeon itself are resources.Each "dungeon" can roughly fit in one screen (though there are multiple floors, in many cases) and the overall objective is winning by beating the boss (or, in some cases, bosses) and exiting the dungeon triumphant. Monsters are distributed in such a way that their levels range from 1 all the way to 10 (the bosses). This aspect of the game could be considered something of a puzzle game; different dungeons have different denizens with their own innate abilities and statistics that need to be taken into account with each engagement.Combat is entirely tactical and deterministic, with the combat predictor being a large part of how enemies are approached, and utilizing everything at one's disposal (and even knowing when to let go of such things) ends up "clicking" and leads to an incredible feeling of clarity. There are so many options, synergies, and individual equipment pieces with varied effects that the ever elusive elation of emergent play happens here naturally.When defeated, the player is given the option to try the run again, "rewinding" time to roughly the halfway point, restoring the state of play and allowing the player to redo mistakes.Besides dungeon spelunking, the player has some light management aspects to contend with, mostly allowing for meta progression unlocks that range from items, classes, races and more, allowing for a more customizable, front loaded approach to future expeditions, aswell as practical puzzles for the struggling player (I wholeheartly recommend any newcomer to try them).All in all, the game is a one of a kind experience that cannot be contained or defined in simple terms,  a kind of beautiful genre chimera that one can't help but love once its ingenuity and heart become clear to the player.

It seems they expect you to already know plenty about the game. Gods' preferences are not recorded for seeing later. You can't see what building upgrades will give you before you buy them. At one point I completed a set of puzzles and never got the reward. The game never mentions anything about saving so I assumed it automatically saved as I went as many games do nowadays. Unfortunately dungeon runs are not saved when you close the game so I lost all my progress in the middle of an adventure. I like the game, but I wish it would communicate better with me, and I played a good deal of the original; the experience should be worse for new players.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna preface this by saying that I'm averse to change, and I've got more than a thousand hours in Enhanced Edition, not including the time I played the beta before the official Steam release. (And not even touching on the time I've spent playing the free alpha!) TLDR of this review is "get the original instead."1) Attacking in Rewind includes an animation that takes way too long. While it's possible to enable "animation cancelling" in the settings, this simply allows you to start a second action (such as another attack) while the animation is playing, meaning it'll simply jump to the next animation. This is opposed to the default behavior where you're not really able to do anything until the animation is over. While the animation can help newer players understand attack order a bit better (actually showing certain enemies attacking before or after the player does), it's distracting and it slows down the game. In the base game, what few animations that do exist are kept minimal and nigh-instantaneous.2) Some critically important combat prediction info (most notably, whether Death Protection will be expended) isn't presented in as clear-cut a way in this game. The combat preview does cause your Death Protection to turn yellow and gain strikethrough when hovering over an enemy that will remove it when attacked, but this information isn't present on the part of the screen where the rest of the combat prediction information is located. In Enhanced Edition, the combat prediction included a word or phrase to sum up the result of the combat, and a big red "BARELY ALIVE" being plastered right in the middle of the combat info is definitely a lot more helpful.3) The camera resets to the zoomed-in position at the beginning of every dungeon run. While the zoom-in gives you a better view of the "glorious 3D" and the aforementioned animations, it keeps you from knowing your location relative to the walls of the map, and it prevents you from seeing other important information that might come pre-revealed (such as enemies of equal or lower level if you're a Fighter, or glyphs if you're a Wizard). So, I always have to scroll out as the first thing I do every time I start a new run, which is... annoying.I have a few other reasons for preferring Enhanced Edition over Rewind, but most of those would have no bearing on a person who's never played either game before and is trying to decide which game to play.I wanted to like Rewind. And it does have its merits, including but not limited to the titular rewind mechanic (I can't tell you how many adventurers I've lost to misclick). But overall, I can't recommend this game in good conscience when the original game is right there in all its building-pokey, dungeon-clicky glory.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a longtime fan of Desktop Dungeons, all the way back to the alpha. One of my buddies and I used to trade a USB flash drive with a copy of the alpha version on and we would try to get high scores. The remake from nearly a decade ago was the perfect upgrade in terms of complexity, progression, art, and playability. I was initially delighted I got a copy of the 3D remake, but have been quite disappointed by the experience. In fact, I would go as far as to say this is the worst version of the game so far, including the alpha. Please note this is only after 10 hours of review, but as someone who has played the previous two games for hundreds of hours combined, I would say that I can give a fair estimate to the gameplay loop as it is nearly identical to the previous iterations.For starters, the 3D graphics are a nice idea, but they are incredibly bland. The animations are overly simplistic and the in-game models lack the personality the 2D portraits have. This game completely misses the mark when it comes to the 3D transition as it actually takes away from the visual identity of the previous game. Not only that, but the 3D perspective actually makes the gameplay worse by introducing the game at a slight angle in order to show the 3D models. This means you now have to pan a camera around. Not only that, but each map you go on is now just a floating square in space. Previously each map was a static screen, yet it had a nice and simple look to it with visually clean sprites and backgrounds. Now the models look horrible up close and the maps are dull and lifeless.The gameplay is unchanged from the previous games with a few minor changes that either worsen the experience or do not fundamentally alter the experience in a way that treads new ground for the series. The biggest differences I could find were that the inventory system has been modified slightly but not in a way that changes anything more than the previous game, as inventory management worked essentially the same. The new mechanic, the Rewind mechanic, is a mixed bag for me. Basically, once you die, the game rewinds your playthrough to a point not too far away from where you died. Basically, it gives you a very generous second chance that is far enough back that you can make a smarter series of choices. It's optional, but always is prompted on a death. It feels like it panders to newbies a bit too much, as the series is known to be quite difficult and requires really careful planning of each action in the most challenging levels. It's a nice feature I suppose, but I think it goes against what the series is known for. I believe there may be a few new items too, but I cannot confirm.Overall, I would say that this game does not really warrant a purchase. It seems kind of pointless to get this game when all the levels and challenges are unchanged from the previous game. It plays much worse than the previous entries and lacks the soul the previous game had. Honestly, the more I played this, the more I wanted to play the older games. Until they add more to make this game unique to previous entries, it's not worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I have over 600 hours in the original Desktop Dungeons game. The UI for Rewind is clunky. The 3D graphics and maps are more difficult to read, and I don't find the animations that interesting.  I also found the original game's controls very quick and easy to use, while Rewind's controls (mouse as well as keyboard shortcuts) to be cumbersome and lacking. I'm honestly very surprised the Devs went in this direction. With the MASSIVE success that many retro games / indy studios have, I feel like they could have expanded Desktop Dungeons or done a DD-2 with similar / updated pixel graphics and it would have been very charming. The 3D version is just not fun. The daily challenge is a cool concept but is also hampered by the poor UI and map display. Bring back the leaderboards and daily challenges from the OG game, please.  TLDR: If you want a puzzle-RPG, try the original Desktop Dungeon. It's a hidden 10/10 masterpiece. This "rewind" remake is an inferior product.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the original Desktop Dungeons.  And the majority of what I enjoyed is still here, in this remaster - the gameplay is still really sharp and clever, massively emphasizing puzzling out strategies and careful resource management. I don't even hate the new style - but it is absolutely lacking in the personality of the original, and more importantly than that, is way less clear and transparent with information.  Being able to immediately and clearly understand your situation is absolutely critical to this game.I'd rather have the gameplay and balance updates ported back to the original Desktop Dungeons, and I'd advise anyone interested in this game (and it is a good game!) to just play the original Enhanced Edition instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing this with two things:1) The devs gave a free key to anyone who owned the original Desktop Dungeons, and that's mighty cool of them.2) The amount of time I have in this is not representative compared to the amount of time I spent playing Desktop Dungeons in total, or the pre-release test build, and neither does my playtime in the original Desktop Dungeons, as Steam was not the primary platform on which I played it. I easily clocked in a thousand hours since 2011. I am not reviewing Rewind as a standalone game, but comparing it to what came before.The presentation of Rewind is absolutely hideous. The original game used a wonderful, expressive hand-drawn tileset that was easy to tell apart at a glance. You could view the entire play field without problems, and you had a full overview over everything. In Rewind, that clarity goes out the window. While the user interface does technically provide you with more, and *more clear* information compared to Desktop Dungeons, it's also gigantic, hideous, lacks any charm, can't be scaled down, and worse yet, blocks the playing field. Despite Rewind being released for the PC, it looks and feels like a low-effort mobile game port. The playing field itself can't also all be viewed at once conveniently. Zooming out to be able to see the whole game field makes the 3D models of enemies difficult to distinguish from one another, and the user interface ends up blocking the upper-left corner of the field, so you need to scroll the map around to be able to see anyway. It is a pain to play, and the only environment on which I could possibly imagine wanting to play this version of the game is a phone.I understand that a lot of the decisions made for this game were due to the problems the team created by choosing the resolution they did in 2011, and yes, the original game does have some problems relating to that. The original game is virtually unplayable on 4K monitors, etc etc. I get that. But this? This ain't it.As it stands, there is not a single thing I like in Rewind over the original, and I cannot under any circumstance recommend it while the original is still around.I'm sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Still one of the best puzzle-rogues of all time! Just needs some more QoL improvements to reach true excellence. What follows below, applies to both Rewind and DD.***Please don't enter the game expecting a dungeon crawler: this is a puzzle game where each turn can spell victory or defeat, so you might agonize over a single attack for minutes. You've been warned.A couple design decisions could be considered questionable: for example, I never liked how the Gods' punishments and effects are made purposefully obscure, especially in a tight game like this where a God punishment can be run-breaking.If you are like me and like more complete information, don't hesitate to keep this page open while playing.Other than this, I'm not a fan of "Preparation" because it adds a roguelite element to the game that feels unnecessary. Gladly, the devs are well aware that this might be an issue for some players and have a "Purist" achievement for each dungeon that involves not bringing with you any prep item, so this is a minor complaint in the end.Overall, I think Desktop Dungeons is still a great game, and you'll definitely get your money worth out of this. Just bear in mind the puzzle nature of the game before buying :)

_childDocuments_.review: Think of this as a rogue-like puzzler dressed as an rpg/strategy game. You pick a race/class, bring some items, and start at level 1 on a map made within parameters. Some maps are better suited to certain classes or strategies, but each map is an individual experience. You fight through, level up (maybe all the way to 10) and you win or you die. If you win, you get some cash to unlock stuff in your town before trying new maps with new strategies or old maps with new classes.Big thing to be aware of: There are two versions. There is an OG and this new 3D version. The OG has much higher reviews (88% overall) than this, newer version (76% overall) at the time I'm writing this. Which is better?The OG is the one I bought and that has my heart (250+ hours), but this one has it's place. I got it for free since I own the original (a kind move by the company!) and I've enjoyed going back and winning some achievements again.The perks of this version -Rewind - There is a rewind if you die. In the original, I have accidentally double clicked to my death. It sucked, but there was a sense of danger and achievement when things went right. This is a tough game. If someone wanted a more casual experience, the rewind feature exists in this one. There's no such thing in the first. Personally, I've used it once or twice, but I usually just get mad and restart. I feel like I lost if I have to use it so I don't.3D graphics - The original was all 2D and fit in a small window. This version has graphics where you can zoom in or out. Some people will vastly prefer this. For me, it was meh. I didn't play the OG for the graphics and I prefer the old look. It's not a massive turn off, but I immediately zoom out when I start a map and then never play with the zoom feature again. I'd prefer if it was zoomed out to see the whole map from the start. There are some QoL improvements to make things easier to see and discern, but the graphics update didn't do anything for me.Balancing - The games are mostly the same, but there were a few tweaks here and there. It used to be you could hold down on the mouse and select from a wheel, but this one doesn't have that. The inventory is reworked so that things are given a weight value instead of organizing them around slots. Some things are better, some things aren't, but nothing really offends me or compels me to stand and sing. The intro was done a little differently to make it more friendly, if I remember correctly.**************** Bottom Line ***************************Should I buy this or the original? If you like challenging puzzles with more than one road to success, I think both are viable. The Rewind version will look newer and be a little more forgiving. The old one is more compact and looks retro, but I bet it could run on a supercharged potato. I like the retro look myself. I've played the OG more myself, but I've had fun revisiting the game on this one. I think a lot of people were mad it was the same thing and yet not so they downvoted this when it came out. The company gave it out to people who owned the original for free (like me!) and I've gotten 45 hours of fun out of revisiting it, so hooray! Thanks!******* Strategy advice ************YOU HAVE TO LEARN THE SYSTEM TO BE SUCCESSFUL! Exploring heals hp and mana for you AND the baddies. "The Black Space" is like a resource. There are times to look around and times to carefully consider your clicks. That is all.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to admit flat out, I am biased.I am one of the people that preordered the original 12-13 years ago and anxiously awaited each step of development. _childDocuments_.review: I first played the original desktop dungeons way back in 2013, around the time it came out. I thought it was pretty neat, but I wasn't any good at it. Got completely stonewalled fairly early into the hard dungeons, then didn't think about it for almost a decade.I returned to the original a few weeks ago, completely oblivious to the impending release of Rewind. Got much deeper into it this time, but that was more a matter of relying on guides than my own skill improving.I mention all of this because it's more relevant to Rewind than you might imagine. In case you haven't learned this already, this is *not* a sequel. It's a soft remake, with easily the largest change being the new visual style. The rest of the changes are small enough that you can still use almost all of the same guides from the original to improve at this one.That might sound disparaging, as if I'm suggesting that the changes are insignificant. But that's not quite right. The changes are small, yes. But in a game this complex, with this many intersecting components, small things can cast long shadows.I'll admit I've somewhat lost my train of thought here. The end point I'm trying to make is that Rewind is a significant improvement over the original. I recommend it highly as a result.
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the original Desktop Dungeons, this remaster is a downgrade, but still probably worth playing if you're a new player who enjoys a deep, satisfying, puzzle-like experience. The strategy and depth the game offers is still present, but... - The 3d models are nice, and so are the animations, but having the map be scrollable/zoomed in feels pointless. Not being able to see the entire map at once makes it so you can't easily see what resources/shops/enemies you have available. - In addition, the visual design for enemies, shops, and a lot of other things aren't as clear as in the original game; shops and subdungeons in particular seem to blend into the environment way too much. The items being at the bottom are also not nearly as visually appealing as the old system (The old one had a nice D&D style "Glue item here" theme going on, and it also didn't clutter the screen as much).- The UI for showing your health/enemy health, as well as combat simulation, is a bit annoying. While its nice that you can see fairly easily what debuffs/buffs you're getting on your next hit, I feel all the information (enemy hp, your hp, attack type, resistances, etc), is spread too far apart. I'm constantly moving my eyes left and right to check the HP thresholds of myself and the enemy.- Theres some UX issues as well w/ the main world hub; the most annoying one is the lack of a back button in the tavern after selecting a dungeon. You can't select the eastern dungeons afterwards, as the initial dungeon info is blocking it... - Crashes seem to be happen occasionally; the triple quests w/ the goatglades sometimes crashes in between dungeons, meaning your earlier run was essentially wasted. ? The rewind mechanic is interesting; it allows for a free "scouting" of the dungeon if you want to use it that way, or as a backup option if you mess up an attack. + I appreciate the balance and QOL changes that were made; the addition of showing enemies 1 tile into the fog was a nice addition, and some of the underperforming classes were also buffed. + Some original DLC (goatglade) was added in for free! They also gave the entire game for free for original owners, which is nice. Now, while it seems like i'm complaining a lot, its more because the original game was really really good. I had a few hundred hours in the original + the extreme edition mod. And all of good dialogue/dungeon design/puzzles/content are still there. It just feels disappointing that this remaster doesn't feel as polished as the original.

_childDocuments_.review: So... I played the alpha a lot and I have more than 400 hours in the original full release version. This is one of my favorite games of all time. _childDocuments_.review: My play time on this title isn't a complete picture of my many hours spent playing the previous installment of this game. Much praise to the developers for giving owners of Desktop Dungeons this remaster for free, that is a very nice gesture.That being said, having played Desktop Dungeons for a long time I cannot in good faith recommend this remaster, while I do like the balance changes, the same cannot be said for the UI changes, which is an integral part of the game.The information you want is all over the screen, whereas in the previous installment of the game it was in a fixed location and fairly compact. It wasn't perfect then either, but it was better than having everything spread across the screen.I also don't think the 3D-models and slanted view of the map does anything but make things look confusing. If you play for long enough to get to the hard dungeons, it's pretty important to have a clear overview of your options, and most of your decisions are made based on this information.And lastly, as others have pointed out, the unique art is no longer present, instead replaced with what I consider fairly lazy art. for example, if you were to pick a race (Kin in DD:Rewind), all the classes they could be would have unique art, whereas for this game I only saw a mannequin face for the different kin, and nothing else. _childDocuments_.review: I bought the original Desktop Dungeons years and years ago. Not only is it an amazing game that you can sink a lot of time into in small intervals, but there are also a number of reasons I've kept it close at hand for years. -It can run on anything, but has a massive amount of content. -It can run on tablets. -If you own it you can play it in web browsers, this was great when I was in college and sitting around for a few hours. Not only this, but the devs actually care about what the community wants. A few of us called for the implementation of the codex from the original, and these guys listed out perfectly valid reasons as to why that was difficult to implement. They then implemented it anyways. In addition, they gave the Remasters to the owners of the original for FREE. I can't say enough good things about the game. If you like fantasy, dugneoncrawling, roguelikes, and puzzles, this is a game you can get for as much as a burger, and will pick up and play for years. Good luck beating it though, because it's hard as hell in a good way!
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: A remaster of my no. 1 most played Steam game. Desktop Dungeons is simply the best puzzle game on Steam (I haven't played all puzzle games on Steam, you're going to have to take it on faith). The remaster itself is... eh, okay? Nevertheless, I suppose a so-so remaster of one of the best puzzle games of all times still deserves a thumbs up.Pros:- Now in fullscreen- Combat prediction is much more detailed (less number crunching for you)- Rewind option lets you retry a failed run once- Some weak classes got a much-needed buff- Goat Glade got reworked into a building that can recreate any item, a big boon for high-level playersCons:- The art style is not as charming as the original pseudo tabletop look, including the character portraits- UI is harder to parse, information is scattered across the screen- It's almost impossible to see the entire map without something blocking your view- No new content except minor tweaks- The magnificient (but mostly superfluous) in-game compendium was cut- Reminders of what quest you're on and how the gods work have also been removed, and those were much less superfluous- Not compatible with the excellent, albeit perhaps too extreme "Extreme Edition" mod (although save files are transferable between both version and the Extreme Edition mod also retrofits Rewind's tweaks to the original).
_childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I'm Lekon. You may know me from.... this game! Yup, that's me, the Lost God of Goats. You may wonder how this happened but suffice to say... I can't talk about it.Anyways, my children shall gnaw upon your fields. You shall weep and gnash teeth, at least until you get the hang of the game. It's tough but you will learn how it works! At first it's tough, yes, but eventually you're doing level slingshots through popcorn monsters and death protection abusing to kill a boss 7 levels higher than you just to show off. And it feels just as awesome the tenth time as the first time you get the math just right. This is a hell of a game I've been playing in various forms for over a decade and yeah, I'm biased, I'm IN the game, so of course I want you to play it. Go, Play! Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Desktop Dungeons since the days when it wasn't even on steam yet, and aesthetics aside - though I actually like the new graphics myself - this is the best the game has ever been. _childDocuments_.name: Desktop Dungeons: Rewind

_childDocuments_.review: One of my all time favorite strategy/puzzle games!This is a really unique game with a TON of mechanical depth.  I've played the non-remake version for hundreds of hours and I feel like there is still more to learn.I've seen some people compare this game to a pure puzzle game, but one of the beautiful things about this game is how much choice you have over how to approach any given challenge.  DD is all about adapting to your circumstances - trying to figure out how you can use what you have found to deal with the problems you run into.  Every resource in the game has tons of versatility and every threat can be approached in many ways - it never feels like you are just trying to find the "one solution" to a run.This game has a TON of really varied content, too.  The dungeons all feel really varied, but still manage to be approachable with a wide range of builds.  Every class feels pretty distinct, and some of them have hugely unique playstyles.The new rewind mechanic is a great addition to the game and makes learning as a new player way easier.  When you die, you now get one chance to go back and try to correct your mistakes - it's great to have such a direct chance to learn from your mistakes!Strongly recommend trying this out if you like strategy/puzzle games at all!
