_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg offers a reprieve from massive or self-serious releases with a casual pace and charming art style. Surprisingly, this game reminded me of Stardew. Just imagine instead of farming in the valley, you're in a resort town with a focus on beating the dungeons and socializing with members of the adventurer's guild. In between dungeon attempts you'll get to know the locals and other visitors as well, revealing their stories and weaving them together in an overarching plot.The structure of the world and gameplay are quite accommodating to the player, reducing as much friction as possible, which made for a relaxing adventure game that you can easily hop in and out of. If you do prefer a challenge though, you can always turn up the difficulty or attempt dungeons while under-leveled.This is a modest game that executes its intent well. Give it a go if you feel like you're in a rut with bigger releases.On a more personal note, I enjoyed ripping around with the magic snowboard a lot. If this game does receive some kind of follow up, I do hope they build on it for more dynamic movement in combat and the premise of winter/adventure sports combined with magic.

_childDocuments_.review: The main character is interesting and it made me listen attentively to her inner thoughts.Overall a pretty interesting story with incredible NPCs.I found the combat to be a bit finicky at first but quickly got used to it and it remained challenging throughout.The game often auto-saves and there's no penalty for dying, which removes a lot of stress from a game with an otherwise intense combat system.Speaking of challenge, the "New Game+" was a ton of fun! It didn't just increase enemy stats, but introduced newer and more difficult attack patterns, which added a lot of replay value.Although not too difficult, the puzzles were engaging.An amazing game that I will be recommending to everyone I know.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate describing a piece of artwork by its similarities to other properties, but the influences that made this game are worn well on its sleeve, so I will hate it a little bit less this time.Dungeons of Hinterberg is the culmination of a Zelda-Persona-Celeste smoothie. With a whole bunch of bite-sized Zelda-esque dungeons to explore, the social link and day-to-day mechanics of Persona, and a plot that fits in line with games like Celeste, this game manages to nail the niche of short and sweet, but with a compelling story, interesting combat, and the magic and attack conduit systems that keep things interesting. My only real gripe with the game is that there are a few segments that made me motion sick, but they're few and far enough between that I'll let it rest. Good game. Lovely time. Enjoy your slay!

_childDocuments_.review: Solid cozy game. I buy a lot of games and I don't complete the majority. I finished this one. The aesthetic and music is on point. It's clear it was made with care by a small team. The combat is fun and the levels are creative. The story won't surprise you but it fits the mood perfectly. I played on the hardest difficulty and if you've played games like this before you should do so too to keep the progression interesting. The run time is about 25 hours for a single playthrough where I visited most little chests and secrets. I maxed out friendship with probably 3/4ths of the cast. There is a New Game + with some extra goodies. And I will give them props for letting you choose if you want to reset all friendships in the second playthrough or keep your progression. I don't think this was available on release. Additions like that are the sign of a good developer. Changes I'd recommend.* Add a sound cue for the parry. (Yes just like in Windwaker). It's very hard to see the visual prompt in the chaos of spells. Parry with slo mo feels very fun and I'd like to be able to do it more. * Add an "auto advance" to the dialogue. I want to read the dialog but I also don't want to press X all the time. Fast Forward is great but skips things entirely.* Making climbing smoother by not requiring the camera to be pointed directly at the next hold. Or even do an auto jump to where ever the stick is pointing next. * The camera sometimes goes nuts when you use a power like blade spin and lock on at the same time. It's pretty funny to have the camera jobble around 2 inches from the enemy but it'd be a little smoother for combat if the camera stayed back a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an interresting mix which is fun to play:- Story: told through the dialogs (so no big wall of text to read, just a few dialog lines). I found it engaging, and well written (characterization, backstory, character voice/motivation). - Exploration: explore a location to find all the dungeon. In practice this means trying to figure out where on the mountain there is a dungeon you haven't visited yet, not difficult but its easy to get turned around. You'll also want to collect many artifact left around the mountain- Puzzle: In each dungeon you solves puzzles using either your magic power or activating switches to move forward. The game of incrementally introducing mechanic that are used later in more complex puzzles. When you are stuck, most of the time it just means you missed an interactive elements (remember to look up). Difficulty is fairly accesible, but does require engaging your brain.- Battle: you'll encounter ennemies within the dungeon that you need to defeat to move forward. There also a few on the mountain, mostly acting as a checkpoint to ensure you have the level for the ennemies within the dungeon further ahead- Time Management: each day you decide with which friend you spent your evening, you helps boost some stat and may provide artifact. Those decision can have massive impact on your player build.I enjoyed this game a lot, the mix of battle / puzzle in the dungeon prevent it from being boring. As you advance, you'll also find that you find some time to best combine all the skills and artifacts to max you damage and defense.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a serious gamer who likes fast paced action, it stresses me out haha. But this game so far is great, I'm playing on vacation mode and I can control how much action my character gets into. There's a lot of rabbit holes you can go down and explore tons of things. I think the only thing annoying is how the days are broken up. You have morning, afternoon, evening, and night. and you can only really do one task at each. Morning and night you can't do anything for those time chunks. But afternoon and evening you can run around but you can only do one task like hang out with someone or do a dungeon. It's just slightly annoying is all. Over all, for the casual gamer this is a great buy. Fun puzzles, exploring and you have great control on combat level.

_childDocuments_.review: Pleasantly surprised by this game! The puzzle's aren't really that difficult but in a doesn't-take-too-long kind of way with combat encounters sprinkled throughout.Combat feels fine and the game lets you focus your strengths into whatever play style you want. _childDocuments_.review: Cozy and familiar, yet also unlike anything I've played before. Much like how Persona combined social sim mechanics with a JRPG and found great success, this game, too, finds success by combining those social sim mechanics with Zelda-style dungeon crawling. The social mechanics don't go as deep as Persona, but I still appreciate them being there and enjoyed my time with all of the characters. Makes me wonder what other genres might do well with a Persona-esque remix...It has the feel of an indie studio's first game, yet it also is far more ambitious than what most indies would dare attempt. There are precious few fully 3D Zelda-likes, so I'm glad we at least have this game as an example of how an indie can do it well. The dungeons are plentiful, clever, and always full of surprises. They don't have the length or complexity of a typical Zelda dungeon, but they're still very interesting and fun to complete. I greatly enjoyed how each dungeon stands apart from each other, how they all introduce some unique gimmick that makes them memorable and unpredictable. Special mention goes to the snowy area for having the most fun and creative mechanics and level design in the game (Glacial Galaxy had me in genuine awe).The vacation / theme park framing of the game's events greatly appeals to me personally, as I love the whole "MMO-esque" atmosphere of being just one adventurer among many. It gives what you're doing a strong communal feel, which pairs nicely with the social mechanics, The "commercialization of magic" theme is very reminiscent of games by Aggro Crab (who helped make this game too, btw), but this game handles its social commentary with a bit more nuance. Sure, treating the sudden appearance of magic and monsters as a tourist trap is tacky and exploitative, but the game still takes time to consider what good it has done for the villagers and the tourists (the protagonist Luisa is herself a tourist, after all). The game examines its themes from all angles, which does not diminish the efficacy of the game's core message but rather adds greater weight to Luisa's actions. There were a few moments where I honestly had second thoughts on whether what Luisa was doing was the right thing, which I think is an indicator of some pretty strong storytelling.It's a well-rounded experience that shows great potential for a sequel!

Weapons with more damage and armor with more armor is fine, but all the small boosts to magic/physical damage don't feel noticeable and I find myself just picking whatever because it doesn't seem to matter.- The game has different areas with different weather/special abilities per zone. Probably would have beaten the game already if this wasn't the case.- Ran worse on steam deck than I anticipated, but I did not spend too much time optimizingSummary: Despite the things I don't love, it's a thoughtful and delightful game that deserves a look. _childDocuments_.review: 10/10 An indie gem.Between exploring a fun new world with great narrative storytelling and quirky characters to carry your interest, this is definitely a game to check out. The game has wonderful puzzles that won't leave you staring at the screen for an hour. Most of the puzzles are easy to put together and the context clues are easy enough to spot to carry the combat/dungeon crawling at a good pace.26 different dungeons! While they're all pre-generated, they each have a unique themed world with puzzles. Once you complete a dungeon, there is not really a reason to go back into it unless you're an achievement hunter and missed a collectible coin (which is needed to purchase new aesthetics) or some chests.The worst part of this game for me was the controls. I played PS5 controller and it felt very clunky and took time to muscle memory my way through combat. I hate the way the control decides to lock onto combat characters and often kept it off. There's not a huge penalty to dying, so the combat is pretty much button mashing with some skill to it between magic/sword/charged skills. I'd say the controls are similar to Tales of jrpg series or Elden Ring with the overlapping L2 & R2 skills.This is a great game for a casual narrative being told through a mostly linear storyline with some options to deviate based on who you want to make friends in town.I completed the game on tough mode (highly recommend, normal felt lackluster) in about 20 hours and 33 in game days to give you a sense of how long it will take.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fun surprise this game turned out to be. Dungeons of Hinterberg mixes dungeon crawling with social aspects and fun little puzzles. And this mixture is the heart of the game. On their own, all the pieces are good but not great, but together they form a very enjoyable experience. As Tourist Luisa you stay at the town of Hinterberg and in the morning of each day, you travel to one of 4 very distinct Zones, search for chest and materials, fight some monsters and do some small puzzles. Placed and sometimes hidden in these Zones are Dungeons, which give the player a more creative mix of the overworld elements, with some really fun puzzles and gimmicks. Since each zones has it own 2 unique Powers, there is a good amount of variety with the puzzles, even if they are never too complex. Combat sections help with the pacing between puzzles, even if it is the weakest aspect of the game. I was really surprised with the amount of ideas the dungeons present, even if the 2 powers per region and the limited pallets would let you think otherwise. For 25 of them, it is really impressive. After exploring and finishing dungeons, you return to the town of Hinterberg and do some shopping, upgrading and socialising. Similar to Persona for example, you meet a bunch of different people with their own story and reason for living or visiting Hinterberg. They also provide multiple reward for meeting them a few times, like equipment, unique upgrades or new special attacks. The Mix of exploring, fighting, puzzles and story works great together, especially since the player can often choose what and how much they want to do each in game day. Combined with the fresh setting, the game provides a very chill and fun experience.The more open and relaxed approach also helps with the games biggest weakness, its rather simple nature. The puzzles are fun and diverse, but rarely challenging. Same goes for the combat, which could have used some combos and more mechanics to stay interesting the whole game trough. Some special attacks give some freedom with the way the player fights, so do the amulets you can equip, but the combat still mostly consists of some light and heavy attacks, maybe a magic power here and there, and those special attacks. Not bad, but also not really great. The game is also more on the easy side, even on the hardest difficulty. And since there is no time limit or missable characters in the town parts, the social aspect is also not exactly complex and doesn't need careful planing.But this game is more than the sum of its parts, they work great together, as a relaxing, fun and charming experience. Don't expect complex combat, a long and lore heavy narrative, super challenging puzzles or intense time management. It is clearly meant to be a chill escape with a lot of variety and a unique setting. A vacation with a big extra of magical realism and a lot of heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons of Hinterberg

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg is a lovely blend of style and nostalgia. The Melee combat at its core is a little lackluster, but it's heightened by various swappable accessories, swappable skills/abilities, and each of its four regions having their own two unique spells as well. Enemies are never too difficult, and sometimes fights have just a little bit extra to keep you thinking. Each of its regions are not only entirely unique visually, but they each have their own way of presenting gameplay to the player. I won't spoil them at all, because aside from the story, they really are their own character to be experienced.There's A LOT more I could say about this game, but I feel like I would be spoiling something no matter what I say. I'm sure there are individuals out there slamming this game because they have inexplicable hatred in their hearts, but I can say with concrete certainty that you could play this game for 40+ hours like I did and not even get a remote inkling of the things that these people will tell you is "wrong" with it. I had to actively search online to find out where I would have been presented with the things they take issue with.

_childDocuments_.review: i feel like dungeons of hinterberg is a difficult game to talk about without making it sound derivative. it has that very mechanically simply action rpg style combat as something like kingdom hearts. it has daily social sim activities tucked between dungeon crawling segments like persona. it has overworlds dotted with puzzle-filled dungeons that are solved with clever application of magical powers you acquire throughout your adventures like a zeldabut it's the meld of these, and the clever usage of them that stands out. it's like good soup, there's v rarely any exotic ingredient that elevates it. it's all in the amount and implementation of these various mechanics that make a great gamemicrobird uses tricks like perspective changes or theming dungeons around a very limited application of your powers in order to give you rewarding puzzles and interactions that don't wear out their welcome. the simple mechanics actually become a strength in this instance because they become an easily mastered foundation from which to engage with the often clever puzzles. there were more than a few instances where i had to take a step back and really think about how to solve them, but it was never because of mechanicsin that way, the game does an excellent job staying on theme. it's nice to take a vacation. it shouldn't be frictionless and the best vacations are ones where you actually try to engage and interact with the area or community you're visiting. yet it's also important to let go, keep things chill and live in the moment. if that's an experience that really speaks to you then this is a great game for you

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but I feel like with how much I enjoyed my time in this game and how little I'm hearing about it online I want to do my part and add a review.This game is a lighter dungeon crawler RPG  with puzzles and some borrowed social and time management mechanics from the modern Persona games. You dive dungeons by day, exploring the areas around Hinterberg, and then you cap the day off with some rest, recovery and socializing in the town during the evenings. You get to meet both locals and other travelers and get to be a small part of their time in Hinterberbg. There's a focus through the story about reflecting about the costs of tourism on the local towns and cities and impact on those who live there; how they find themselves overrun with people staying for a little while, maybe not acting the best  and then leaving the place worse for the wear. While it doesn't really offer a solution on this (as if there is one) it's a story beat that they hit on a lot and one you can definitely spend some time reflecting on yourself. The soundtrack was lovely and the fact that it was included at the time of purchase was a nice bonus, I think a couple of the music tracks will probably end up on my music playlists. I think the dot shading art style was unique and fresh, and I found basically no bugs, just a great level of polish from a smaller team. The puzzles were petty intuitive and I rarely if ever had to look up guides, the mechanics never really over stayed their welcome and the ability to just go to different zones every in-game day helped keep them feeling fresher for longer.  Steam deck performance was pretty solid with only a few minor drops below the 60 FPS and mostly in the parts where a lot of the zone was visible. My complaints if any are pretty minor. I do think combat was a bit stiff at times and didn't evolve as much as I would have liked it to, I imagine it was an intentional choice but sometimes the game would stutter while dishing out high numbers of hits, which again would be an odd choice, maybe it was an attempt to add some weight to the combat? At some point it did just kinda blend into the flow so It stopped being something I was thinking about. Even though the combat was stiff, I think the game only really needing 17 hours to complete  means that the run time is short enough where the stiffness does not turn into staleness Another minor complaint of mine pertained to the social links. I didn't get to see the ends of probably about half of the social links. I think reflecting on this it's because I don't really think there's enough dungeons and rest spots in the overworld to achieve max social links without just burning multiple days to add extra evenings. I absolutely could have just continued to waste the days to see through the end of the links so I'm willing to chalk it up to more of a skill issue on my part. Maybe allowing me to leave my room at night to spend time with those social links instead of just watching TV / Reading a book in my room could have helped give more chances to complete these social links. I know it's very unlikely that this game will get a sequel but I really do like the setting they've built with the modern era combining with magic, it's not one we see very often and the characters in the game definitely mention dungeons in other parts of the world multiple times, so there's definitely room to work with if a sequel were to be built. All in all, I do highly recommend this game. While I think Dungeons of Hinterberg  may not be the game of the year and it may not be one of the largest scoped games that is released this year,  it's a game that I'm going to remember fondly and recommend. It's definitely a game that I think slots in as a pallet cleanser, something small to play between big releases.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg is an absolute gem! You're Luisa, arriving in a small, idyllic European village in order to get away from a life of stress and inconvenience. Beside it's quaint feel and carefree nature, the village has also gained attention from tourists after magical dungeons appeared three years prior; making the location a huge tourist attraction for better and worse (depending on who's being asked. Gameplay/CombatDoH, at it's core, is a very simple hack and slash. However, with the addition of charms (combat modifiers), weapon enchantments, magic, and special combat abilities it's easy to find depth if you're looking for that. The spells too are a joy to use, and change depending on which of the four biomes of the game you're in. The can be a super fun snowboard of light, a gooey box, a ball of lightning and more. Each them also have really solid environmental and combat usability! For example, the gooey block can be climbed on, or used to encase enemies for easy dispatch! The snowboard can be used for easier traversal, or just to mow down enemies!Relationship SimThe relationship sim aspect is also fun, especially because the majority of the characters are genuinely compelling, and their stories meld so well with the overall narrative.  Rewards for completing relationship ranks are also really good on balance. You'll often get boosts to various stats, legendary equipment, or even very powerful gameplay modifiers. Frankly, you're really missing out by skipping this aspect of the experience.Dungeons/PuzzlesThe last thing I'll talk about are the dungeons, and they are all so fun! Each one was so unique and I was constantly being surprised by clever (but not brain-busting) puzzles and mechanics. Puzzle mechanics, especially, deserve praise, because each time I thought I had a dungeon or a biome figured out for it's "gimmick," the game totally proves me wrong! I was always itching to get back out to experience the next dungeon!All in all, Dungeons of Hinterberg is a monumental achievement from a such a small team, and anybody who feels like they need a little vacation of their own should join Luisa on hers! You won't be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I think I like for the vibes more than the content - a lot of relatable themes about figuring out what you wanna do with your life mixed in with environmental and social statements on the encroachment of capitalism in every part of our lives, set in a vibrant and beautiful world with a fun cast of characters and enough content to keep you playing for a good long while but not so much as to wear out its welcome.Ironically, though, I think the "dungeons" ended up being the least engaging part of the game - the puzzles within rarely make you actually think too hard, and the combat never moves past serviceable even if it's, y'know, fun enough - the big bosses that occasionally show up are a nice enough twist, but they're usually pretty gimmicky, so, ehh. And the game's got some weird balancing - I rarely found a use for money other than to upgrade my armor, since doing a solid amount of exploring pretty much guarantees you'll find better gear than you can buy, the gift-giving system seems vestigial (I gave gifts like, once or twice ever and maxed every relationship just fine - though I will say, there's way way more social link scenes available than you'll have time to experience in a standard playthrough, I dragged the game out an extra 25 days just finishing them all). And, like, this is just a personal gripe but - why no jump button? Why the weird auto-jump? Yes I know old zelda games do that but I still don't know -why-. 'Cause I swear I had more deaths just from Luisa deciding to yeet herself off a ledge as I approached it than I did for any other reason. Oh yeah, the game is super easy, at least on standard difficulty. Maybe that's why the dungeons felt like the least engaging element.But exploring the main hub maps is a delight, and the actual social aspect of the game in town was something I ended up looking forward to just as much 'cause I did feel the characters were all generally pleasant to hang out with - except Julian, that guy kinda sucks but, whatever. And the game is consistently really pretty to look at - even if i had some minor performance hiccups from time to time, whatever. I really enjoyed my time in Hinterberg and while I'm not sure it's a game with much replay value, it was a pleasant and engaging time while it lasted and I'm glad to have played it.

There are a couple of miss-able achievements, so check out a guide before proceeding. You'll enjoy yourself with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg is a strange fusion of multiple game concepts, but it . All days basically follow the same schedule: you get up in the morning and have a little chat, then go out to explore, slay monsters and do dungeons in the afternoon, and choose whether you spend your evening alone or with company. Then you'll go to bed and do it all over again. A story segment will occasionally disrupt this pattern, but not for long. None of the things that you do are especially complicated. The combat is basic (and a bit stiff, but I got used to that quickly); it doesn't evolve a lot, aside from adding effects to your weapon and finding new attack skills to use. There's enemy variety, but not a whole lot of it. Each region comes with two magic spells for both exploration and combat--but you can only use them in their specific zones, so there's no mix-and-matching available. The social system is simple. The writing is straightforward. But every component is executed well and sits on top of the very unique setting to form a compelling whole. The UI is informative and easy to use. The graphics are nicely stylised and the framerate was rock-solid aside from two or three stutters--although I'd prefer a larger draw distance for generic NPCs and overworld loot. The world is fun to explore and the size of each zone is just right. The music is pleasant to listen to and sets the mood well. The characters aren't very deep, but all of them can get a chance to shine. ()Special credit must go to the puzzles; these are the absolute highlight of the game for me. Well-designed, well-paced, intuitive and never overwhelming, with very few moments where I was stuck for over a minute. I'm not great with puzzles, but these were a lot of fun to solve. ( There are a few options, the most prominent being no death during combat. There's no way to get a hint for puzzles though. I hope to see that kind of feature in more games in the future.) is the operative word here; I enjoyed the game loop a lot. I often have trouble finishing games nowadays, but I couldn't put this one down until I'd 100% completed it. Definitely pick this one up, either at full price or on sale if you'd like. There's around 30 hours of great content here. I wouldn't mind a DLC or a sequel either.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a joy to play, and I'm sad it's over.  The game cycle of dungeon run, social/shopping and repeat was overall relaxing, with a few somewhat challenging parts. Maybe I didn't invest enough into the magic skills, so in combat I hardly used them, but the Attack Conduit skills were a regular thing; very effective and fun.  I wish more options were available though.The dungeon environments are varied and play off different themes & mechanics in a very Super Mario 64/Galaxy type way.  Some are longer than others, with a couple being over a little too soon I thought.My complaints of this great game are all about me wanting more, basically. You are on vacation, and there is some nice graphics and generally cozy atmosphere, but thats it. A Short Hike starts and drops you immediately into an open world where you can go anywhere at any time.  There's a vibe to it and I've seen plenty of other games capture that vibe that it may as well be its own genre at this point. Alba: Wild Life Adventure, TOEM, Smushi Come Home, even breathe of the wild has that vibe. This game is not in that genre. The open would is merely a tool to traverse to the next dungeon with some puzzles used as obstacles, and roadblocks any time you wanted to go explore this way.Also the elements of Persona are very light.IT IS NOT a bad game. I am a dead broke artist sorry devs usually I would support you regardless.Music is pretty dope though.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: (I can only recommend it)Great and very fun Indie hack and slash game, with good story and great puzzles.It feels polished and thoughtfull with a love for details, eventhough some edges are a bit rough and there are some missed opportunities.The Good (a great package)- The combat system is fun and easy to learn but offers a lot of details that can be tweeked to your prefered style.- The puzzles are great and EXTREMLY well balanced. The concepts needed for the puzzles are introduced gradually and get more complicated with each step. So you are never overwhelmed by the puzzles but still have to use your brain to solved. - The story is great and deals with a lot of relevant topics (not going to go into more details because spoilers). The world and story unfold naturally while interacting with different characters. Giving each relation ship meaning.- Story, puzzles and combat integrate well and even interact with each other. So all in all it feels like a well rounded package.The Bad (mostly little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥)- Mostly balancing and timing of events.- As the world grows you get some additonal abilities and things to do, that are hinted at the beginning, but not explained and you are left wondering what to do with the item you just picked up. (trash for me)- Money becomes useless in the endgame, as you get a LOT of it and at least I didn't have anything left to spend it on.The Neutral (some I found or didn't like personally)- Some low low level enemies are harder than some powerful enemies. (Could be my fighting stly)- No encyclopedia of enemies. (Or I didn't find it because it was part of some relationship I didn't finish)- No long range weapons or weapon variety. (Other characters use different weapons)- No customization options ASIDE from the sword.ConclusionA really great game for an Indie studio and a game that had more heart and thought put into it, than I have seen from bug publishers in a while, There is definitiv potential for more, but overall a great package and I can only recoomend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg is a charming, if a little bit short, action/adventure game that I found myself enjoying so much that I couldn't really put it down until I was done. You go through 25 dungeons in the game that are well designed and don't over stay their welcome. The dungeons are mostly puzzle based with some combat sprinkled in. I can't say the game was difficult at all, but if you enjoy Zelda games, this is a great game to pick up. Some of the dungeon puzzled stumped me from time to time, but I managed to pull through, even though I think I cheesed one without realizing it at the time.The story is nothing groundbreaking, but is exceptionally charming with a cast of characters I found myself liking. _childDocuments_.review: I think the most important thing to keep in mind is that the game is more of a Puzzle game than anything else.  I don't think any of the trailers do it proper justice with emphasizing that your dungeon delving experience is going to be more about solving puzzles than fighting monsters.Now, I don't think it's a bad thing at all.  It fits the game's narrative quite well, and the puzzles are mostly solid throughout your experience.  I think some of the later puzzles do get a bit tedious, but overall the vast majority are nicely designed.While the puzzles are a fairly large focus of the game, I think the interaction with various NPCs is one of the more satisfying elements.  Talking to NPCs will improve stats, and relationship status.  You can go into your log to see upcoming rewards for talking to them, which isn't the most intuitive method.  I wish I could just look at their icon on the map for a quick look.  Ah well, not too big of a deal.The combat is mostly ok, but it's not very deep at all.  I don't want to say it's shallow, as you have standard attacks, magic, and special attacks.  You can combine these for some cool fights, but there's a relatively small collection of enemies.  It'll either click with you, or it won't.  I don't think there's much of a middle ground, but everything else about the game more than makes up for it.OF course, you don't always have to head into dungeons to fight stuff.  You can also find various locations to relax and enjoy the scenery.  Watch some tv or read a book at the end of the night.  Any choice you make lends itself towards the narrative, which means everything you do will matter.It's a delightful game full of charm, passion, and interesting locations.

_childDocuments_.review: In a word, it's  A humble game with a grounded take on what magic in the modern-day world would look like. 4 overworlds and 25 dungeons to explore, a combat system that's simplified but highly customizable, and a colorful story about a small town turned tourist hotspot, complete with vivid landscapes and atmospheric music. The gameplay loop is pretty satisfying and always gives you something to do next, so it's easy to stay and play a while.The meat of the gameplay is exploration and combat. Each area provides you with a pair of spells to grant an edge in combat and solve environmental puzzles. Combat consists of light/heavy sword attacks, dodging, spells, and (later on) Attack Circuits that grant special attacks. You also have Charms that you can equip for effects ranging from stat boosts to bonus effects on kills, with a good handful of unique effects. I played in Normal difficulty and didn't find the combat particularly challenging as long as I kept my gear up-to-date, but you can get overwhelmed quickly if you don't watch your backside. Most of the puzzles weren't complicated, although I occasionally had to stop and think about a handful.One of this game's strengths is the variety of the dungeons. Each one feels distinct, despite dungeons of the same overworld sharing the same environments. There's a large variety of mechanics beyond the spells: one dungeon has mini-planets that bring me back to Super Mario Galaxy, while another has mind-bending isometric puzzles like Monument Valley. Lots of features that each appear in a handful of dungeons, some only appearing in a single dungeon. Each dungeon felt new in some way.The game's other major strength is its worldbuilding. It's a pretty realistic take on what would happen if dungeons showed up in today's world. Nearby towns capitalize and turn into tourism hubs, filled with everyone from sightseers and novelty seekers to professionals and stars who do dungeons for a living. Monsters and magic become akin to bungee-jumping - a thrill-seeking hobby with manageable risk. You'll get to hear from a lot of people. A professor studying the local phenomena, and a young girl working multiple jobs just for the chance to be here. A local shopkeeper and the owner of the brand-line gear store next door. A handful of pro slayers, each with their own reason for being here. You'll hear a lot of opinions about Hinterberg and the magic that dwells within. Getting to experience magic is, well, magical. Shouldn't everyone get to experience this? The dungeons bring jobs and tourism, but how do the residents feel? How much has Hinterberg changed in the eyes of those who have known it? How far will people go to profit off of the dungeons? How well does anyone understand magic, anyway? Amongst all the slaying and spell-casting, there are quite a few moments of thoughtful reflection on breaking free from a stagnant lifestyle and finding a sense of adventure.The main story took ~20 hours for full completion. I spent some extra time to collect everything and max out NPC relationships, which took ~3 more hours. It was definitely worth $30 imo, but even better if you can catch it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly comfy low-stakes hack & slash game that invokes feelings similar to Persona with its social aspects in the evening with some light zelda-esque action in the dungeons during the day.The game itself places a heavy emphasis on taking a vacation away from modern life and work by reminding you that Louisa, and some of the other characters, are there on vacation to get away from their normal day-to-day, with its chill relaxing atmosphere and encouraging you to take time off and use the days to relax and/or socialize with others.Dungeoneering is the primary focus of the game with each dungeon taking around 15-45 minutes depending on how much you overthink some of the puzzles. For the most part, the puzzles are isolated enough that you shouldn't have to bash your head off a wall for too long to figure them out. There are 4 explorable regions each containing their own set of dungeons which provide their own set of magical abilities to help you traverse and explore the dungeons or region itself. Since each set of magical abilities is locked to a specific region, it helps the dungeons mesh together in each region as you are only expected to have skills A & B and not C & D.The only real complaint I have is that depending on the dialogue options you choose during story sessions, it can come off as Louisa jumping to conclusions using information learned on the option you didn't select. The museum segment comes to mind for the most jarring example of this. While you still have the information to piece it together yourself, it can be somewhat jarring for Louisa to suddenly reach the same conclusion without access to that information. Of course, it's also possible that's just my poor reading skills and memory at work too...Overall I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to others.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons of Hinterberg is a magical adventure. It's a game about a journey of self-discovery through the beautiful landscapes of Hinterberg.It's a beautifully crafted game; the art style is cartoonish, but don't let it fool you because the game can have its challenges in the hard mode.Each day you choose which dungeon you'll tackle in the morning or where you want to rest. After slaying, you get to do your shopping in the afternoon, and finally the story progresses through your encounters speaking with a diverse cast of characters and getting to know them in the evening.That's where this game shines; it offers multiple experiences in one solid package for fans of Dungeon Crawler, puzzles, arena fights, and RPG elements.I've had a blast playing it, and my only downside is that you can't continue at the end.But like the main character, your journey ends with a sense of accomplishment.

_childDocuments_.review: A game full of soul. Definitely one of my favorite games so far this year and my top indie game. What makes a game special is if you feel you're better off having played the game, and it's definitely the case here.What to expect: 25 dungeons in 4 handcrafted maps with exploration. Each dungeon should take 15-30 minutes to complete. There's combat with a single sword option, but you have multiple magic and special attack options. To be clear, the focus of the dungeons are their design and puzzles with combat sprinkled in instead of the other way around (except for boss dungeons). Each day is split into two main parts: going to one of the 4 maps where you choose to do a dungeon or to relax (to increase some stats) with the second part being back in town where you choose to relax solo (to also increase some stats) or to spend time with one of the cast of characters to hear their story and unlock equipment/services/etc. You can only do one dungeon and hang out with one person per day. The game recommended using a controller, but I had no problem using KB+M.Downsides: I don't recall exactly, but by the 8th or so dungeon you've encountered all the enemies (except bosses). There's no different skins for your equipment; the way you look at the start of the game doesn't change. There are about 16 characters you can befriend in the game and it can take 5-6 nights to fully max out a relationship with a character. With 25 dungeons, if you want to max out multiple characters you'll either be replaying dungeons or immediately heading back to town as there's no way to skip going out to the maps each day. It's annoying having to spend 2 minutes each day heading to the open maps and clicking to get back to town and going through the loading screens.

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly more of a 3D puzzle platformer than a "dungeon crawler", despite the name. But the name contrasted with that visual vibe ought to tell you that on its own. It's small pieces of different gaming genres butted up against each other, but with no continuity  between them. You are now in mode 1: talking to story people. You are now in mode 2: the simplistic overworld you take to get to: Mode 3: the levels (the game calls these dungeons but they are puzzle levels with very little combat worked in there). This game got me really thinking about how games are made. I can see the scope-shrinking decisions they made here. How, sure, you can "do" all these things, but you basically just choose the thing from a menu and then teleport to the thing you chose. This isn't an open world where you explore, level up, play a role, and dive into some dungeons, even though that is "literally" what you are doing. The connective tissue between all these things is what makes an RPG immersive, and that is exactly the aspect of this game they clearly isolated as the thing to specifically not build, which dropped the development scope by a lot, no doubt, but also makes this game definitely NOT an open world dungeon crawling RPG. In exchange for your time, you are going to get much more of a puzzle platforming experience. That's fine, that's cool. But if you are trying to do some real role playing and dungeon crawling, this is literally not what you are looking for.

Combat is simple but deep enough to remain fun throughout, with all the different skills (attack conduits) and build-altering charms. Highly recommend you give this one a try. Played entirely on steam deck so far, runs great.

_childDocuments_.review: With only five hours in I cannot give a comprehensive review but I can say I do very much recommend it. The premise of a real world resort that allows everyday tourists to delve into dungeons and fight monsters is of course something fun and novel. It works well with the mix of action RPG and life-sim mechanics. The core of the game play loop is a mix of combat and puzzle solving akin to the Legend of Zelda series. Combat has a bit of a Souls-lite feel that is very forgiving for players that do not want a full Souls style challenge. You have a lot of room to customize you play-style with upgrades for weapons and gear as well. The art style is one you will either love or hate with a very pastel palette that gives it a bit of comfort and charm. Almost like playing a Sunday morning cartoon or anime. Finally their is the day to day life-sim mechanics similar to the Persona series where the relationships you choose to cultivate and how you spend your time outside of the dungeon impacts the growth of the protagonist. I will of course update this with more time in.

name: Affogato
detailed_description: Join Us On Discord! About the Game Affogato is a RPG revolving around a sorceress juggling with the running of her new café, managing her debts, meeting customers from all walks of life and ultimately helping them overcome their greatest fears and secrets by burrowing deep into their minds. Enjoy a story rich RPG featuring an innovative 'reverse tower defense' mechanic and beautiful anime graphics. Make critical decisions to help your customers defeat their inner demons by entering their minds and leading them to safety through challenging card-based reverse tower defense levels. Choose your routes and cards wisely or lose your customers forever! Get to know customers from all walks of life. Lend them a listening ear, hear their stories, step into their minds and help them resolve their troubles. Forge special bonds with those you feel an affinity toward and become the approachable sorceress you've always aspired to be. Plan each day with care and manage your time wisely. Will you focus on bringing in moolah for your café, honing your skills as a barista, learning stronger spells or bridging closer bonds with your customers? Remember that the clock is ticking and that every decision you make costs time in Affogato! Making a good cup of coffee is the cornerstone of being a barista. To be a truly great barista, however, you need to understand your customers and figure out which brews are perfect for them. Affogato features realistic coffeemaking simulation. Master the art of making great coffee and you can unlock hidden conversations and storylines!

_childDocuments_.review: I wish steam had a neutral review, because on the one hand I want to recommend this but there's also some major issues going into it that I feel need to be warned beforehand. I won't bore you with too many details because quite frankly everyone else has reviewed the game far better than i'm, capable of... Instead, I will outline my issues with the game and why i've left this review, and I hope that you take it into consideration before buying it.This game oozes charm, style and it's generally written nicely to present a fun experience. The soundtrack is outstanding, artstyle clean and interesting. And the gameplay honestly starts extremely strong too, the whole reverse tower defence system and coffee minigame are great and I was looking forward to seeing how the game would build on these....Sadly, it's these two mechanics in question that are why i'm leaving a negative review. Not because I don't recommend, I really do, but because I cannot recommend the game outside of some very specific caveats and conditions.First let's talk about the game's core gameplay system, its reverse tower defence mode. Because quite frankly, even on normal it quickly becomes punishingly hard. The developers clearly have specific builds and card combinations in mind and if you have not discovered them or do not want to use them then you're really, really not going to have a good time. By the time you've reached the second story boss, unless you're running one of these combinations then these fights are going to grind down into an unbearable, unenjoyable slog at best and an impossible fight at worst.Coupled with limited time windows to complete stories and character interactions or personal stat boosts taking up potential currency grind time I could genuinely see instances where people effectively lock themselves out and are required to reload earlier saves or drop the difficulty.I inherently disagree with this design, if you're like me and enjoy finding a team that works and then comfortably sitting on it for a while? You're in for a bad time. If you just want to experiment and not be beholden to the very obvious combos and teams the developers had in mind? You're in for a bad time. These encounters are designed in a manner that stifle expression and freedom, players should be free to explore their own creative deck builds or express their teams in any manner they desires and still be able to scrape through on the standard difficulty.So, why not just drop the difficulty (which you can do freely)? Well, because easy is effectively "story mode" and sucks almost all interaction from this game mode. It's too easy, you're either forced to adopt teams the developers had in mind and struggle through some extreme difficulty spikes on normal or bore yourself to death with being unkillable on easy. There's no inbetween, and that's just poor balancing that needs to be addressed through the inclusion of more difficulty options. A fight should feel fair and engaging, and you're either forced with boring or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (god forbid knowing what hard is like).So that's my first major warning, is that if you're looking at this game and just want a comfy time without the game being trivially easy? Look elsewhere, because a game that has an achievement for resetting a stage at least 10 times before completing it, that over 30% of players own is indicative that the developers really need to learn how to balance their difficulty appropriately.The second issue I have is in regards to the coffee making aspect. After all, you run a coffee shop, and you make friends and will often be required to make brews for them. However this aspect of the game feels extremely neglected, and the writers really fumbled on this one.You are heavily encouraged by the game to go off order, make alterations to the drinks, season them differently to suit your friends tastes. This will likely then come with a healthy friendship boost that allows you to skip some gift giving or timewasting with them in order to continue their side stories.The issue with this, is that the game never actually even hints to what these characters actually like. It's never sewn into the dialogue naturally, or at all for that matter, and the amount your can customise your beverages is pretty extensive.So what it feels like is that you're fumbling around in the dark, and making a choice to just ignore what the game is encouraging you to do and make their drink normal for a standard friendship boost, or randomly guess what you think they might like at which point you're probably going to get it wrong and miss that friendship boost. And in a time management game, that feels like you're being punished because the game isn't rewarding you for reading what the character is saying and using intuition to customise their drink.If anything, the game punishes this. And this is where I have to give my second major warning and complaint about the game.See, one of the characters you can befriend mentions that people gift her cakes and snacks (in a positive tone) and this is before you ever make her a drink. Then when she does order a drink, she orders a pretty sweet one.Me, thinking that the game had finally dropped a hint about what the character liked, I seasoned it with chocolate to make it a bit sweeter. Nope, wrong answer, no friendship gain for you.Frustrated I reloaded a save to experiment and made her the drink normally. At this point she is happy with what you've provided and mentions lemons with her drink and how she loves it.Okay that's great, because you actually have two different options for lemon when seasoning. So I reload and try again, putting a lemon slice with her drink. Wrong answer, no friendship gain for you.Reload, and then try lemon juice instead? Wrong answer, no friendship gain for you.This entire coffee making system feels extremely half baked and poorly done, and the writing team really fumbled when it comes to things like this. If you wanted to pick up a game so you can pay attention to what people are saying, then try and make a coffee with alterations based on what you picked up? Wrong game, because the game will never say what they like and if they do then I guarantee it'll be the wrong choice because the writers didn't stop and think "hey we said this character likes lemons and there's multiple lemon customisation options, should we maybe reward players for serving that?". They won't, and it's extremely frustrating that they don't.Overall I still recommend the game... ish. I'm still going through it and if more complaints like these continue to crop up this could quickly go from a maybe to a no. But right now, these two are something you should really be cautious of before picking it up.----------------------------EDIT: Further thoughts down in the comments.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels way too bare bones, almost like a proof of concept rather than a game. It's missing a lot of quality of life in terms of menu options and fine-tuning in gameplay. A lot of the times I find myself having to use the singular strategy that can actually built up penta, maybe paired with a the one required card that you need otherwise you can't win the TD section. It plays similar to Loop Hero, except you place units rather than upgrades, except this is way less in depth than that game. Functionally it actually plays out like a puzzle game, which I wouldn't mind if you didn't have to reset all the way back on every single mistake which can be as simple as forgetting to flip one tile in a certain direction.Art and sound are great, but presentation is probably the only real redeeming feature. A pretty picture for a pretty hollow game. Narratively it's just really uninteresting. I can feel inklings of a good story in the character plotlines, in particular the hints of interwovenness between Keke, Sera, Dave and the cop guy (I forgot his name) has potential, but in the end it's all really disconnected from one anothere, and none of the separate story lines are very interesting. Dave has some potential with the study of multiple patients but in the end it's all so shallow. Lindsay story was alright, Keke probably the best of the bunch. The rest really nothing worth talking about. It feels a little too precise to get all the story lines in one run, and there's no new game plus, so getting all witch cards requires some planning out I'm not willing to do with this game.There is a lot of "flavor text" I don't know what to call it. More than anything it's filler text. There's some new blogs and articles and you can talk to Mephista for stories, tidbits and "jokes" (istg this is a mistranslation and is supposed to be rumours because NONE of those were jokes). But it's all so meaningless? It's just fluff, it barely has personality. I'm willing to bet a lot of it was AI generated, just to fill out an otherwise empty overworld.The socialising gameplay is also really nothing to write home about. You have some stats that you can improve visiting some stores, and you can make money running your coffee shop (which by the way you should simply not do as you just more money than you need simply playing the game and it offers no events whatsoever outside of a stat boost which apparently was only added afterwards, so it's just not valuable). You only really want to visit the hot pot place on weekends, and some of the others on events. Talk to a character every evening or you most likely won't get all quests done (I didn't). But it all feels very meaningless, at best it's a hollistic puzzle in order to get all witch cards in one run, but gameplay-wise it's all ineffective and there's no strong motivators to do anything. Literally only a few characters have hard stat roadblocks and it's just a specific stat per character. it's just not in-depth enough, there's nothing to it.The most redeeming part of the game is surprisingly the coffee making. it's fun figuring out what coffee a customer wants in order to trigger a hidden little cut scene. it's comfy and pleasant. it's, again, not very in-depth, but it's cozy enough. There's enough options to keep you intrigued at trying them all, although none of it really leads to all that much.In the long run this actually plays out more like an atelier game than it does a persona game, flow-wise, you've got your little hub where you alchemy and you're performing chores on a time basis, meeting characters and "gathering" in the meantime. The thing is. All the main story questlines are nearly mandatory? They put a deadline on them, but almost all of them are forced procs in the morning in your coffee store which you can't prevent? Like idk. This game just feels like an incredibly rushed endeavour and an attempt to appeal to people wanting something with persona-esque social links. This just needed more time in the oven. There's something here, but this is just not it.edit: i forgor to mention that there's also several soft-locking bugs, such as skipping text on the final fight just leading to a black screen? Similarly the auto-save into continue pipeline can lead to a black screen in the end-game, although i'm not entirely sure what caused it. Not in really a bug, but in the gameplay sections your characters get scrambled really easily and there's no way to really fix it. When they rejoin groups after being split sometimes they will just keep rejoining and splitting in place, causing that to also essentially softlock. They're all in all not the worst, i don't care very much for these, but they do exist and they can be hindering.

_childDocuments_.review: So I finished the game today, and the best I can say about this game is that it's very...mixed.Pros:- Gorgeous artwork. UI and character design are all fantastic, but the tarot cards are the real standouts- Soundtrack is wonderful, if limited- Reverse tower defence is a fun gameplay aspect- Characters are generally interesting, bar Ema (seriously, I find her so unlikable)Cons:- Writing is all over the place. The first arc starts strong and feels like you're investigating a mystery. The second arc is a slog on the other hand and just drags through a poorly paced plot. The third arc is better, if rushed. And the fourth arc is also good, if again a little on the rushed side- Remember how I said reverse TD was fun? It is, but it feels like you spend very little of your time playing these stages. To make matters worse, there is basically a meta where you have to play certain cards in a certain order. This isn't so bad in the initial levels, but the difficulty ramps up in later levels and you have to play perfectly. I just wasn't having fun during the final boss fight at all- Coffee shop is underutilised. I liked the idea of running the coffee shop and ensuring you had enough to pay for your rent; that was a nice innovation on the Persona time management system. But it's half-baked. You get so much money through story missions that I felt encouraged to do anything BUT open the coffee shop. I think an interesting way to integrate the coffee shop into the core gameplay would have been to allow the coffees to be power-ups in levels. Eg espresso restores some penta, Frost Nova slows down enemy attack speed etc. That would have helped with the balance as well- Social stats. I hate these in Persona and I hate them here. They serve no purpose other than to be an arbitrary roadblock that artificially lengthens the game. If these are in a sequel, PLEASE let them give some kind of mechanical advantage - it's so annoying having to raise my Intelligence to speak to the girl that the MC initiated the conversation with in the first place???- No NG+ as far as I can see. So you have to restart all over again if you want to get the social links you missed. If I did miss that option, please let me knowThis game is a 5/10 and it's a shame Steam doesn't allow for neutral reviews. I'd recommend this game but only on sale. I appreciate it is cheap anyway, but the lack of balancing and slowly declining level design really undermine a good foundation. For what it's worth, there is potential here and I'm interested in seeing a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Affogato: A Quirky Blend of RPG Genres!ヽ(´• ω •`)、Step into the magical world of Arorua in Affogato, a game that offers a unique concoction of role-playing elements. As a sorceress turned café owner, you're thrust into a whirlwind of responsibilities and adventures. The game's standout feature is its reverse tower defense mechanic, which adds a twist to traditional RPG gameplay. While Affogato brings a fresh perspective to the table, it isn't without its share of hiccups.Set in the enchanting city of Arorua, Affogato introduces players to a sorceress managing a café with dreams and debts. This dynamic, coupled with meeting a diverse array of customers, forms the heart of the game. Each customer has their own story and struggles, and it's your task to plunge into their minds and guide them through card-based reverse tower defense challenges. This intriguing concept adds depth to the gameplay, encouraging strategic decision-making to rescue their inner selves. However, while the narrative direction is commendable, it occasionally stumbles over its ambition, creating a mixed bag of emotions for players.Visually, Affogato shines with its anime-inspired graphics, blending vibrant colors and enchanting character designs. The jazz-infused music complements the atmosphere, engaging players further in the magical world. Nevertheless, the game does have its rough edges, with some aspects feeling underdeveloped. The controls during battle can be clunky, causing occasional frustration. Additionally, the translation and UI issues dampen the overall experience.The barista simulation aspect, where crafting the perfect cup of coffee for each customer holds a special place, enhances immersion. This mechanic, reminiscent of titles like Va-11 Hall-A, introduces a layer of personalization to interactions, deepening the player's bond with the game world. However, this gameplay mechanic is not exempt from flaws. Forced coffee-making orders and lack of detailed card descriptions somewhat hinder the flow and strategic potential of the system.Affogato's brave venture into cross-genre territory is evident in its blend of management, visual novel, and tower defense elements. The narrative's attempt to tackle sensitive themes, such as the first story arc dealing with suicide, is a double-edged sword. While it aims to add depth, it might unintentionally alienate certain players due to the potential emotional impact.In conclusion, Affogato offers a rich cocktail of gameplay elements that seek to create an unforgettable experience. The innovative reverse tower defense concept and charming anime aesthetics stand as the game's highlights. However, it's important to acknowledge the game's rough edges, such as control issues and translation problems, which hinder the overall enjoyment. If you're open to embracing a new blend of RPG elements and can overlook some shortcomings, Affogato might be worth a visit to the magical streets of Arorua. Just remember to approach it with an open mind and a dash of patience.Are you interested in finding some amazing STEAM games to play? Well, we have a fantastic suggestion specially for you! We invite you to join us, Nyanco-chan, on our YouTube & Steam Curator channel called Nyanco Channel. On this channel, we share reviews and recommendations for really cool STEAM games. You'll come across a bunch of enjoyable games that are sure to catch your attention. So, why not give it a try?

_childDocuments_.review: While not a masterpiece, in my book Affogato is sufficiently endearing and engaging.Presentation is on the level. Great artwork all around, hands down. Music isn't particualrly memorable, but it's doing its job just fine. Just about every character is voiced, some minor NPCs being the exception, which strongly elevates the experience.The story is not much more than serviceable, but the way I see it, this is pretty easy to forgive thanks to the character interactions being quite enjoyable. The writing is alright, but an extra editing pass to eliminate some minor typos here and there wouldn't hurt. What's not great is that certain scenes contain utterly pointless choices; the chance to select between "Sure." and "No problem." is not appreciated. It's just not.Now, the gameplay is a mixed bag. Definitely do not go in expecting that managing a cafe and/or brewing coffee will be the focus of the game, because they are anything but. Again, there's nothing to complain about in terms of presentation, but the substance just isn't there.On the other hand, Affogato has reverse tower defense sections to offer, and these are a fair bit more elaborate. Admittedly, I'd vastly prefer a classic tower defense game, not its reverse variety, but that's me. I feel the game would benefit a lot from having a more robust upgrade system for the deployable units, but that's pretty much my only grievance here. The difficulty can be adjusted whenever, so whether you seek a challenge or just want to focus on the story, you'll get the option that fits you.Overall, what we have here is a pretty entertaining VN/reverse tower defense hybrid. If this sounds like an agreeable mix, consider giving Affogato a taste.

_childDocuments_.review: So this game as it is has some really great features, but there are definitely some things that need to be updated, balanced, or changed.First of all, this game is a reverse tower defense/time management style game similar to Persona. It has great music, good voiceover, and a really cute style. At first, this concept seemed awesome and I was very excited to play through the game! However, I discovered that I started to enjoy the game less the more I played for several reasons:- I agree with several of the people here that mentioned that the game has a serious difficulty spike around the second boss, and on normal mode I found myself having to restart and replay stages up to 10 times to defeat it, which is a lot for "normal" mode. On the last/second last boss, I ended up having to revert to "easy" mode, and even on easy mode the game was pretty difficult. I honestly couldn't bring myself to finish the game because I had played stages so many times that I got burnt out; which sucks, because I wanted to see how the story ended. As is, this game is soul crushingly hard, and I honestly just quit. Even Darkest Dungeon and games of the like I still played through over and over again, even when slews of people were dying. This game is honestly harder.Also, just a technical thing, I couldn't for the life of me select which unit to recall in battle. Like, there isn't a way to cycle through all of your units and then select the one I wanted, so I have to keep pressing the button hoping that the one I want to recall is selected. If this feature is in the game, then I couldn't figure it out. I also wanted to be able to zoom out on the map a little more, especially the really large maps later in the game.- The coffee making aspect really threw me off; at first when it was introduced, I thought we would go through a "diner dash" situation where we would have a bunch of customers come in and we'd have to quickly make their orders as they liked them. I was really looking forward to this type of gameplay, but I realized that the coffee making aspect is just to help improve relationships, and it feels a little lazy at that, especially when the main story has you making a billion Americanos and Lattes because that's all people want. An entire menu of coffee options, and all people want are Americanos and Lattes XD.I'd really love to see an actual "work day" where you manage your coffee shop and serve customers; that just makes sense to me when you have it so embedded in the game instead being a coffeeshop owner where your demon sidekick does everything in the background for you.- The game feels weirdly short to have a relationship aspect similar to Persona; because ideally you would want to explore everyone's stories. I don't know if that's even possible in this game unless you have perfect time management skills; There are different ways if improving your 3 stats in the game, but they don't feel impactful at all. I wish the game were a little better at showing you when the best times would be to visit each location for stat upgrades because it can be a little vague. I almost wish that your personal stats would reflect in the tower defense stages in addition to relationship building.- Also, there is absolutely no threat of not paying your rest. The game gives you SOOOO much money through the story that you cannot possibly not have enough to not pay rent, so I don't understand why the game makes it so important.When playing most games, you always go through a bit of "trial and error", but then figure out something that you like or something that works, and you roll with it. In Affogato, I felt like I had to do "trial and error" even down to the end of the game because nothing works and I still keep dying. Trial and error is only fun for so long before it becomes discouraging.Overall, this game has so much potential; and with a few tweaks it could be great, but as is, I found myself no longer motivated to finish a 15hr game. A 15 HOUR GAME. I've played games for 1,000s of hours, and I can't bring myself to finish a 15 hr game that I initially enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: Revising review a bit because I got to play way more of the game. It is EXCELLENT. The music gives off 90s city pop and TVB movie vibes. The music is so good on its own that I bought the soundtrack to support the devs, and now it's my default work music. My friend actually just let Affogato hang out in the street to enjoy the theme. I cannot recommend buying the soundtrack enough. The gameplay is challenging and with some techniques you can turn a simple game of reverse tower-defense into gigabrain RTS territory of micromanagement. The story is the best I've seen in a while, putting triple A games to shame. Some of the lines just strike you deep to the point of haunting. And to put the cherry on top, the translations are surprisingly good. Often in these small projects, the core game is held back by a bad translation job (see - Depersonalization). You don't see that here, minus the occasional mistake. All in all, I've had it wishlisted since the demo and the game has exceeded all my expectations by a mile. The devs have been very communicative and you can tell that this is not just a product, it is a passion project with tons of heart behind it. I hope it blows up despite the unfortunate launch window (sandwiched between AC6 and Baldur's Gate 3) and gets the recognition it deserves, because this is a 10/10 from me. GOTY so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Rough around the edges, but I'm enjoying it so far.I greatly enjoyed the music with its jazz tones mixed with dance. Adaptive music added to the battles is a fantastic touch I can't praise enough, with a 1x, 2x, and paused version of the battle theme. Music player in the phone is nice, but I wish I could set it to play random or make playlists.The overworld artstyle feels derived from Arknights while having a certain own take on the style. The character portraits are well drawn in a style I can't quite identify the inspirations of.I can certainly feel Va-11 Hall-A inspirations, like the articles available on the phone (the comments are a welcome addition to it, I wish Affogato made comments about the articles after reading them, though), drinks making (altho this may be closer to coffee talk, which I have yet to play) and returning to the room at the end of the day, which may be a Persona thing. Speaking of which, the fact there is a looming calendar date, plus use of tarot card reminds me of it, especially with there being 3 social stats which bars you from progressing relationships and the free-roam city is similar to Persona, if only there was a quick travel home tho.The unique menu items have fun little descriptions, I wish that side bar was a little less clunky by maybe using categories or having it focus on the opened recipe instead.Mephista is funny, altho this may come at a cost of the tone given the first story arc is about suicide.Lindsay has my favourite outfit I've seen so far, but she basically has Fluttershy's personality, minus the animals (plus for me, but might make you hate her).Natalie is your typical burnt out journalist, and I think is quite a mood.Issues so far:Lack of a content warning for suicidal thoughts, and POV of someone jumping off a building. As someone that's been there, that scene was slightly terrifying... (I'm way past it now bShop customisation could have benefited from a separate menu, rather than simply using items in your bagForced to follow a specific order to make certain coffee, for example if you add milk to an Espresso, it makes 'Caffe Latte' and stops you from creating 'Caffe Mocha' despite both using milk.Affogato's walk animation looks awkward since her hands swing faster than she takes her steps.UI translations have been a bit sub-par, 'reorganise' and 'restart' are too similarCard descriptions don't include stats, or what their children/spawned cards do.Counter for how much mana the hermit has generated would be nice.Lack of sound FX when beating a boss really takes you out of the moment.Clunky controls in battle:Writing issues:I have no clue why we are shown the start of the Aoi demon fight at the start of the game, it feels like it shows no narrative purpose and spoils that entire section since we are already shown: That she made a contract and why she made the contract.

_childDocuments_.review: Barista-witch-therapist and her archdemon bestie dive into the minds of everyone in the city to solve their problems and exorcise...other demons. Great character vignettes, if a somewhat predictable overarching plot. The dialogue includes some very funny shout-outs and fourth-wall leans and outright breaks it once or twice. I liked how Affogato handled darker material, and that despite the dark themes, it doesn't take itself too seriously. Music is decent, chibi graphics were very cute. I wish there was more interaction with the coffee-making, and more on how to perfect recipes for each person. My only real complaint is the UX - the menus don't always wrap around and it's annoying to hit down 7 times, and I had a lot of issues with unit selection during tower assault stages because there's no zoom and for whatever reason the controls are hypersensitive. There were times I wouldn't even be touching the controller and turned my mouse off and the camera would still be randomly panning to the left. For how novel Affogato is though, it was worth it. And it's MA-GEN-TA.

_childDocuments_.review: Having spent roughly 5 hours with Affogato, I can confidently say that fans of deck-builders, Persona, and/or coffee absolutely owe it to themselves to check out this game. While I haven't finished the campaign, the core gameplay loop has come into focus and it's definitely enjoyable and, occasionally, addictive.Affogato puts you in the shoes of a transient witch who can't help but help others, often getting herself run out of town in the process once it's discovered she's a practitioner of the dark arts. I won't spoil anything for those who have yet to play, but the story is interesting despite borrowing pretty liberally from Persona 5. Speaking of Persona, the influence of Atlus' JRPG juggernaut is felt pretty heavily in the presentation, menus, music, and overall atmosphere of the game. Definitely not a bad thing, and it's nice to see an indie developer put forward a project that so clearly wears its inspirations on its sleeve but does so in a way that's homage rather than shameless imitation.The core gameplay loop is that of a deck-builder mixed with what I would call "reverse tower defense". If you imagine Slay the Spire meets Loop Hero, you're not too far off. Outside of the actual combat sections players get to manage a coffee shop during the day, complete with some Cooking Mama-style coffee making sections. My one gripe is I wish that there were more opportunities to make coffee, as I found these sections to be the most relaxing and charming parts of the whole experience.The visuals are decent and have their own style, but the amount of chibi/kawaii type characters and designs might be grating for some. It also is definitely at odds with the subject matter of the story, which takes you to some pretty dark places (including suicide, suicidal ideation, etc.).The steady power creep of unlocking new cards in your deck, upgrading existing cards, and experimenting with loadouts is very fun and rewarding, and I can absolutely see myself playing through to the end and then immediately restarting to try different battle strategies. If I had to give this one a score I would say it's a solid 7.8/10, and developer Befun Studio are definitely a team to watch.
