_childDocuments_.review: 12.6h (100% achievement, finished the game) 8.1h No. Yes (15 achievements). No. is a story-driven game focusing on the lives of the residents in a small village. You'll be able to control some of the residents and make their life choices while trying to cope with the loss of a village member.- Story that was told from a different point of view, focusing on each person's interest and goals- It's up to you to control the characters to finish their quests or not- It can be hard to listen to two conversations that happen at the same time- No fast-forward support for the second playthroughIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650's environment is drawn in 3D, with low-poly characters and little details. This works well since you mostly see the characters in a top-down format, and you can see their expression through the portrait in their profile. The UI was similar to  with you controlling the characters, with a focus on the quests. Instead of clicking on any object to assign the characters, you'll click on the part of their profile - whether their needs or goal - and instruct the character from there.Despite the slice-of-life theme, I didn't find the story to be particularly boring. The soft voiceover does a good job of portraying the atmosphere, and the interactions between the characters are short. Moreover, most conversations will lead to another objective that will be summarized in your profile.The story is mostly task-driven, with hardly any conflict with each other. Characters mostly deal with the grief of the loss of a village member, and the tasks will mostly focus on grieving and moving on. Some will be affected greatly, while some will get back stronger. It's a story of how the villagers move on.Despite that, I found the change to be too subtle. It might be because it was hard to keep tabs on all characters at once, but I wasn't particularly attached to a character. The ones who grieve mostly take a lot of time being alone with you having to direct some characters to help them... or not, your choice. Eventually, they'll back up on their own even if you don't do anything. I still like the ending, though. The game does a good job in its presentation. The scene where a light that moves throughout the village, accompanied by touching music sets up a nice atmosphere for the ending. However, since I didn't feel attached to the characters, it had less impact on me.The game has an illusion of choice. Throughout the game, you'll be tasked to do some quests, choosing between several options. Most of them lead to the same result, while the ones that matter mostly won't affect much on the overall story. It'll only make a change for the ending of the character, which wasn't much highlighted in the story. was played in a top-down view, in an interface similar to . You can move between the areas, rotate the camera, and assign a character to do something. The only difference is that the actions that you can do are mostly limited. I like the limitation since it means I don't have to be overwhelmed micromanaging the characters later on.You'll start controlling one character. As you progress, you'll control more characters, totaling 5 characters. This might make the gameplay hectic, but luckily, some characters have fewer tasks to do than the rest, so you only have to focus on 3 characters at once most of the time.That being said, it still can be pretty hectic. Characters will talk to each other sometimes, and when there is more than one conversation going on at once, you'll face two options: 1) Make all conversations run at the same time, which obviously can be hard to focus or 2) Wait until the conversation finish before starting the other, which will make other character to stop doing anything until the conversation finishes. Imagine if you have 3 conversations going on at the same time. The last conversation might start 2-3 hours later, even though you need them to do a lot of things. Moreover, you need to make sure that you are not moving your screen to where the conversation that you want to pause is since that's how you trigger the conversation.As I said before, you'll be faced with some decisions in the game. Sometimes, a character will have a lot of tasks that they can't do with the given time, and you need to prioritize which one to do. Some of them will lead to the character's ending, although honestly, I don't find them to matter that much. The relationship between the characters is nice, but it wasn't highlighted enough to make you care about them.I finished the game in ~8.1h. I'm pretty sure there were some offline times when my internet disconnected, although I'm not sure how long. I spent the rest of my playtime sweeping the achievements that I missed. There might be a fast-forward button, but it was too slow, especially when you want to fast-forward through the night. Moreover, you can't skip the cutscenes. That cutscene where the character moved on is cool, but not when you see them more than once.As for the difficulty, it won't be hard to finish it since it's a narrative-based game. You don't have to replay the game for the other endings either - I don't find it to be that worthy to watch. is a game with a good narrative. I know I'm complaining a lot in the review, but the game wasn't bad narrative-wise. I like that it manages to keep me busy throughout the game, and despite being focused on the daily life of the characters, the quests don't feel too monotonous. Furthermore, the game does a good job of setting up the atmosphere. If you enjoy story-based games, you'll like this one, although since the story isn't that outstanding, I suggest picking it up on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the game so my heart is a little heavy now, but wanted to write a review before I got too far away from the game.  The story deals with a small town dealing with grief.  The problem is that everyone is dealing with theirs in different ways so it all seems to be hurting more than helping.  As the player, you learn the story and do tasks and take care of characters, or not.  Your choices affect the events and relationships between the characters.  At times, I found it hard to juggle and I missed some things.  At others, I felt like there weren’t enough tasks and was waiting around for time to pass, but not wanting to fast forward (which you can do).  In the end, I felt like I dealt with most of the relationship issues I wanted to, even if I did not accomplish every event.  So I was happy with my ending even though when it comes to mourning, there are no quick fix happy endings.  I thought the voiceovers were very well done and the graphics were very nice.  The music was beautiful.  There is one save and it saves on exit so you can’t change fate, but don’t lose progress upon exiting the game.  It works.  In the end, I thought this was a very well made game dealing with serious topics.  I am glad I played it.  I don’t feel like I want to replay it soon, but given the choices and tasks, replayability is definitely an option.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very emotional but wonderful journey about a community that loses one of its members and which impact that has on everyone and how they deal with the grieve.  13 hours 2/10 1,5 No, but you don't need a guide No Kinda, however, you can turn back time to earlier days (not forward, only to earlier days, so don't go too far back) to get missing achievements. I would recommend doing this after you finish the first playthrough.  No No No No A tiny bit, I struggled with the achievement "The Little Things" but I just needed a bit of luck to get the objective done. No difficulty setting NoOhh "Closer the Distance" you broke me into so many pieces but also got me invested in the story so much and let me fall in love with all the details the developers added.. and that all at once. This was a journey, a wonderful journey but a very sad one and I cried so many times while playing this gem of a game. I have played the first  from Osmotic Studios and that one told me already that this studio is so good in telling stories. That one tells a story about the dangers of our online activities. Not everybody's cup of tea... However, the story in Closer the Distance is one about losing a relative unexpectedly and what that does with a family, but also within a (small) community. Normally it takes me at least some time to get closer to a character to get so emotional. However, Osmotic Studios did such a great job in storytelling that when the main character dies very early on in the game, I instantly became emotional. In this game, you play as Angie, the person who has died. You are kinda the ghost of Angie that tries so hard to help her loved ones move on. Tries to fix what is broken within the small community of Yesterby, what she already tried to do so much when she was alive, but she can't let go after she died. This is done in a sims-like gameplay. You start with only having some control over her younger sister because she is the only one who can hear Angie's voice. You can already see some of the wishes of the other people in the small community of Yesterby and you will unravel more of their wishes and mood swings in the days/weeks/months after Angie passed away. A little into the game you'll also get a bit of control over some of the other characters. This way you try to complete their wishes for what to do next and what is going on. I love how they choose to go with a Sims-like game style. Lately so many announced sims-likes got canceled while I desperately looking for something that plays just like The Sims, but on Steam with Steam achievements (and not 50 DLCs). This was such an awesome game, and a great way how they told such a heavy and emotional story. With so many different characters and their own life goals, dreams, and quirks. And did I already mention how much love and attention there went into all the little details?? This goes from portraits of the families hanging in their houses to the sounds of characters sounding more echoey in some locations where that makes more sense, to the beautiful music this game adds. Especially by a character who will join a little later. This is very out of character for me, but I won't go too much into detail about the achievements in this game, as most of them are beautiful stories that will play out in the game and I don't want to ruin their stories by already telling you about them. I would recommend playing through the game blind the first time and just exploring those stories you're most interested in. You can always go back to earlier days (but this will delete the progress you made after that day). So I highly recommend just playing through the game once and then going back in time to mop up the missing achievements. I had to replay a specific day a few times because I kept having a little bad luck with one of the wishes, however even the third time I played through a day, I still saw new dialog options which was so surprising to me. A lot of the story you already know by then and can easily speed up time to get past them, but to get surprised with even new scenes was amazing. I give Closer the Distance 4,5 out of 5 stars.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I hold a generally favourable opinion of Closer the Distance, as the game masterfully depicts the impact of profound loss and the burden of grief upon a small, tight-knit community.In my opinion, however, an emotional, narrative-based game such as this is burdened by the micromanagement nightmare of playing through the eyes of a wandering spirit. You're tasked with simultaneously tending to the physical and emotional needs of fourteen characters, all whilst carefully juggling their individual relationships and personal objectives. It feels somewhat like multi-boxing the Sims.I couldn't shake the feeling that the game would have packed more of a punch if it were to maintain the same focus on tending to the needs of the townsfolk, yet limited itself to the perspective of just one character. Managing such a large ensemble of personalities made it difficult to form a meaningful connection with any of them.That said, I'll award bonus points for hiring The Witcher 3's Geralt as a voice actor. Nice touch.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to players, who don't care too much about outcomes from their actions and play visual novels for fun.Otherwise, there are many complexities for people, who want to get the good enough ending and are hyperprotective of their small pixel people.There are some problems that I find annoying (for me personally):- Conversations take hours and you have to skip them if you want to watch over all the characters. I care about all of them too much, and it is impossible for me to care for them equally and listen to all of their conversations at the same time.- Some characters are high maintenance. That's life, but for me it added more headache than needed.- The UI was not user-friendly when I tried to find out where an action takes place—you won't know the location until you actually perform the action. You might figure out the location when you scroll around and see a white arrow. Found this out around 3 days after in a game time.- The walk speed of all the characters is equally slow. I have seen that some people have bicycles around their houses - why couldn't they use them? Even ride sheep, if that could help them do their tasks faster.- This game has freezed my computer around 4 times in total. I don't think this speaks greatly about the optimization.I am not sure that these points might be fixed with patches in the future, because this is the point - life just happens. And you learn to cope with it. But I hope, that at least some things, like needs could be patched up. This absolutely would help more players enjoy this game. PS: The needs system doesn't make sense to me — you have to manage their hunger, but not their bathroom needs. Every action takes hours, which undermines the realism the game is aiming for. Why add the unnesessary ones then and cut time?
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: If you like story-driven games, you should definitely try Closer the Distance!What I particularly like is that the game manages to tell a really difficult story with a certain lightness. No feelings are hidden or denied. I can easily put myself in the shoes of the characters, which is due to the good dialog (I play in German) and the really excellent music. What I also like is that you have the opportunity to follow so many different characters. It shows that a tragic event like this can affect a whole community. The different ways in which everyone is affected is also well done.The right artwork/design also adds to the atmosphere. Everything has a gray and sad shimmer to it, but still remains very beautiful.An advantage of the game design is that you can leave the dialog if you feel the need to accompany other characters. At the same time, important events are marked so you can't miss them.I haven't finished the whole story yet, but I'm really trying to get more details about the backgrounds of the characters and the town. Especially how the community works together and how their stories are connected.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting game to recommend for me, especially because the fans of the emotional games like these (such as myself) seek these out on our own and it's very hard to convince other's that aren't already established fans. But Closer the Distance is a very successful and even faithful meld of The Sims and Life is Strange. The crux of the game is grieving, and the sombre tone will remain the same throughout the entire game. There isn't a way to make everyone truly happy, but it's a game to help people move on from losing a loved one as best as you can, even if you fail. The music of this game is incredibly well done in terms of fitting the atmosphere. The voice work and cast is phenomenal for a game this small. You might find some talents behind major video game. (eg. The town carpenter is Geralt). PS: Certain cutscenes are unskippable, if a dev is reading the reviews people consider adding a skip function to all cutscenes.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I am not a fan of the 'emotional' genre, as such games usually feel superficial to me. Like okay, we feel the feels, but what's the point? But I'm so happy I've given this game a go. Had to replay the first half for a couple of times before moving on to the ending, and it helped me get the point. It's like shock therapy for someone with attachment issues (me). And I understand that this game is probably targeted at young adults, but it felt really really mature to me. Absolutely loved it, although it crushed my soul a little

_childDocuments_.review: A heads up, but this game delves into topics like death, grief, etc., so you have been forewarned. :o is an emotional, story-driven, life sim developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Skybound Games.  The village of Yesterby is shaken to the core when news reaches its people that Angela, a teenage girl, was killed in a car accident.  Of course, it's Angela's (Angie, for short) family, especially Conny (her younger sister), who is most shaken by the news, but it affects most of the citizens as well since they all were close to Angie.  Although Angie is gone, her spirit watches over Yesterby, and in particular, she reaches out to Conny, telling her that she wants to help the people mourn and eventually move on.  In a way, you can say that Angie is the narrator while Conny is the main character.  However, Angie's spirit also reaches out to a few notable citizens, like Galya (Angie's doctor) and Zek and River, Angie's best friends.  That's the basic story synopsis, so I'll stop here to avoid spoilers and all that.In regards to the gameplay, it is a life sim, so you take control of playable characters, like Conny.  However, there are plenty of NPCs, too.  Playable characters will be given tasks, some of which are mandatory while others are optional.  As to the optional tasks, they appear at night when Angie is talking to Conny.  The tasks appear as small balls of light, and clicking on one will initiate the backstory as well as the corresponding task.  Of course, characters can succeed or fail at tasks, depending on their physical and emotional states.  There are even tasks for NPCs, and depending on their interactions with playable characters, again, they can either succeed or fail with their tasks.  As for gameplay controls, you can either use the mouse or controller.  (For review purposes, I used my mouse.)  You can zoom in and out of places as well as click on tasks, people, objects, etc.  There is a tutorial that explains the controls, so you'll quickly get the hang of the game.  You can play either in windowed (with many screen resolution options) or full screen mode as well as choose anywhere from low to high graphics settings.  (Again, for review purposes, I chose to play on medium graphics settings.)  The game takes place over the course of 15 in-game days or so, and you can rewind a day if you need to.  Finally, there are plenty of Steam achievements, a few of which can be quite challenging to obtain.Now that I've gone over the story and gameplay, I'll move onto my thoughts.  I must admit that I wasn't aware of this game until quite recently although I am familiar with its publisher, Skybound Games.  When the call came for reviewers and such to try out the game, I definitely wanted a chance to play it.  (It may be difficult to believe, but I used to play quite a lot of life sims way back.  I admit that it has been a while, though. :o)  Thankfully, a review key for this game was provided.  Without further delay, I'll first talk about the story.  It wastes no time, as it starts off with Pia, Angie's mom, angry that Angie is late, and Axel, her husband, and Conny have to calm her down.  Of course, there's no way that Pia would have known then what happened to Angie, so when the news hits, it absolutely devastates her, as it does the rest of her family.  The story is quite emotional and can be very depressing at times.  It deals with heavy topics, such as loss and how to cope with it.  I like how you not only get to see the impact of Angie's death on her family but on all the citizens of Yesterby.  They react in various ways, and that's totally normal since not everyone will react to death in the same way.  Also, I like how Angie's spirit watches over the people and how she wants to help them through Conny and a few of the others, so that Yesterby can move on.  There is definitely resolution, and Conny's story will usually end in the same way.  However, for other characters, it may vary, depending on which tasks are done and/or if they're done successfully.Since I just touched upon this, I'll next move onto the gameplay.  I enjoyed the life sim elements here, as not only do you need to complete tasks but you have to check the characters' health and such.  Of course, they have physical needs, such as sleeping and eating, as well as emotional needs, like getting into a daily routine or feeling like they accomplished something.  It can be quite challenging at times to monitor the characters' needs since they can affect how well they're able to complete tasks.  I found this especially challenging for the boat house. :o  Also, I should note that it isn't possible to complete all of the possible tasks in one playthrough, so you'll probably either have to start a new playthrough or rewind a day if you want to get certain tasks that you might miss the first time.  As for the basic gameplay, it requires a lot of clicking and such to move the characters around, so I would recommend using a mouse.  In regards to Steam achievements, it is possible to obtain all of them but only through more than one playthrough.  I will note that even though most of them are quite doable, I found a couple of them to be challenging since either the characters' needs have to be monitored constantly or they have to be in the right place at the right time.  Thus, it took me a little longer than expected to get a review out since I wanted to obtain all of the achievements first. ^^In regards to the art, it is stunning.  It has this 3-D style that really makes it stand out.  It's definitely different from the 2-D, anime-style games that I usually play and review.  The style makes Yesterby and its citizens come to life, and the colors are used well.  Also, there are lots of animations, bringing another element to the game that makes it feel alive.With the music, the tracks were such a joy to listen to.  They have this country, laid-back feel to them (and this is coming from someone who tends to dislike country music).  The lyrics are beautiful to listen to, gripping at your heartstrings.  Especially, the guitar playing is wonderful.Overall, would I recommend ?  If you enjoy emotional, story-driven life sims and don't mind the occasionally challenging task or two, then this game is totally worth checking out.  I liked visiting the village of Yesterby and getting to know its citizens as they all talk about their connections to Angie.  The people help each other to grieve and eventually, to push forward with their lives.  For the asking price, I'd say it's worth getting, as it took me almost 25 hours to obtain all of the achievements.  I had to replay a few times because a couple of achievements kept giving me difficulty. :o  Still, I'd say that it's worth getting, and for me, this game has motivated me to get back into playing more life sims.Finally, I want to give a major thank you to Skybound Games for the review copy.  I had a wonderful experience getting to know Yesterby and its people, all of the problems they had to face, etc.  I hope that there are more future games, like , on Steam. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: If you have recently lost someone close to you, you will either love Closer the Distance dearly, or it may send you to a level of depression I cannot be held responsible for. It’s heavy, it’s real, and it is not friendly. Closer the Distance is agonizing. It’s a beautiful story, and I’m so glad I experienced it, but I would be lying if I said there weren’t times where I wondered what could possibly be the point of making something this depressing. My eyes are itchy, my chest is heavy, and I don’t feel any better or wiser than I did before I started. So with that warning, and please, please heed it, I recommend Closer the Distance to all who are in need of grieving.

_childDocuments_.review: Closer the Distance is one of the more beautiful games I have played in a long time. The design, visual and auditory, is spectacular and both create a powerful ambiance that perfectly suits the game's themes.The gameplay itself was not always my favorite. Managing the Sims-esque moodlets/needs of the characters was sometimes difficult given the pace that some of the games days require to try to complete goals and tasks. There were certainly characters that I felt I had let down by the end, largely because I was trying to juggle so many plates in a compressed timeframe.But really, the gameplay isn't the point of Closer the Distance. The story is sober, touching, painful, and beautiful all at once. It presents a tapestry of the different ways that people grieve, and it doesn't shy away from the pain that comes with both healing and failing to heal. In my playthrough (or at least my first playthrough) I got to watch some strained families come together in ways that would let them move forward. I also watched one particularly hard hit individual drag down her closest partner, isolating him from his friends and insisting that he share her misery.Closer the Distance is far from trite or cliche. The story does not blindly insist that everything will be okay, that the ones we've lost are always with us agreeing with our every decision, or that loss isn't really loss at all. The characters and the story feel the grief, the longing, the anger, and the absence all the way through. Some find peace more easily, others, it's clear, will always carry the scars. The game offers a frank, beautiful look at the meaning of community, the nature of love, and the kaleidoscopic web of entanglements by which we impact the lives of those around us. It gives weight both to the major choices in life (whether to proceed with a business venture or to leave home, etc.), as well as the little moments that color reality (watching old favorite TV shows or taking a sun bath). A raw, honest humanity resounds through the story and leaves behind a picture of life that most media shies away from, embracing the heaviness and hurt that coexist with the beauty of of life, love, and community.Closer the Distance is a heavy experience. It is saturated with powerful feelings and moments that will hurt. It can also, sometimes, be a frustrating game where the mechanics will stand in the way of accomplishing everything you would like. But it is, above all, a beautiful, touching experience that compellingly covers one of the hardest parts of human life. I strongly recommend this game for those who feel that they can overcome the emotional challenge that it comes with.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely like this game. I found it be an interesting experiment in combining narrative design and life-sim mechanics. Taking the systems of a game like The Sims and giving it a more structured narrative with complex characters and a meaningful plot about grief. The art style is minimal but pleasant and the sound and music are atmospheric and contribute to the story. All the characters are fully-voiced, which definitely does a lot of the work in making them realized. Overall, the storytelling is rich and multi-layered with strong themes and the characters show significant growth. I'd love to see this concept with a wider scope and more polish, but I recommend this experience, particularly to anyone who enjoys narrative driven games.3.8 (76%)
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. It is a interactive novel where you experience the story of individuals learning how to cope with grief and loss. It was definitely a healing game for me. I loved how intentional the dialogue felt, and I was immersed in the world of Yesterby. Making a game based on such a sensitive topic, I think the creators did wonderfully. At times, I wanted to be able to complete all of the task of each character, and I am sure the character wanted everything to go perfectly as well. But both the character and the player learn that not everything goes your way, and that is ok. Beautiful cozy game and highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Closer the Distance explores grief, loss, and (re)connection in the small town of Yesterby. You control several characters across the game as you navigate events, completing story-related tasks as well as basic needs-based elements. You can choose what task you want that person to pursue or not, though some choices become committed and you cannot override them.The story is emotional and beautifully written, with a soundtrack that really enhances the narrative element. My first playthrough was just shy of twelve (12) hours and I plan to replay to make different choices, or pursue them in a different order, to see how that may change the narrative element. Because of the nature of the story I feel it has replay-ability, especially if you didn't complete all the achievements on the first run. I'm curious to see if there's a path to completing all the achievements in a single playthrough. I have only one con and it's that if you can pet the dog, it wasn't immediately obvious. I'll need to double check if that's an option.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most accurate and complex portrayals of grief. Doesn't try to pathologize grief, but instead understands it as messy, complex, and deeply personal. As well, the game allows the player to choose the path different characters will take, instead of putting grief into rigid "right" and "wrong" boxes.There is no one correct way to grieve. It is different for every person, and it impacts every moment of life; every relationship and decision made.This is a beautifully haunting game. An unguided narrative through a topic that is not often discussed in our real lives.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: The art and music are lovely but the game is set up so that the story is the main element and the story is a snoozefest. It touches on a lot of complex topics and then doesn't explore them at all. I think they were going for something like Life is Strange vibes, but that game is significantly longer and only asks you to invest in about 3 characters. This game is just spread too thin. It would be hard to tell a compelling story about, for example, alcoholism and grief in under 2 minutes and they didn't manage to here.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty unique game. It’s akin to The Sims in that it’s a life sim about managing people in a small town called Yesterby, but it has a somber story heavy focus to it with the town grieving after losing one of their own in an accident. There’s about a dozen different characters walking around and it’s impressive how well it’s simulated as they go about their day and constantly talk to each other on their own. While you don’t actually get to control everyone, you’ll interact with the entire town through dialogue conversations (that are paused so they aren’t missed and can easily switch to them), and it makes them all feel distinct from each other as you watch them try to process their grief and help tend to their wishes. The only thing that seemed a bit unnecessary was the needs aspect, it’s not really a hindrance but since the game is always timed, you kinda just end up having to ignore it with the characters you control if you want to focus on talking and advancing the story

_childDocuments_.review: Love the writing, the melancholic atmosphere and music, the voice acting and navigating the characters' emotional stories, equipped with a list of things that one could do to help and a thoughtful description of their complex emotional states. _childDocuments_.review: This game is intense and tragic, depicting the overwhelming feeling of grief. However, it's also a beautiful story about how to let go. _childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its heavy-sounding subject matter, I was completely charmed by this narrative-focused drama. The idea of a main character influencing the people left behind after her death really speaks to the imagination. Humankind has pondered the mysteries of death for ages; we can fear it or we can embrace it, and this game isn’t afraid to explore grief, loss, and depression without becoming too bleak or overly religious in the process. It’s hard to say a game dealing with these emotions is “fun,” but in some ways it truly is, confronting you with your own helplessness when dealing with others, because you can’t suddenly force people to behave differently simply because you want them to. As a simulation of life, "Closer the Distance" very much succeeds. Certainly it plays on the feels, becoming a bit dramatic now and again with its artistic cutscenes, trying very hard to make you cry. But overall, this is a narrative that fits in with novels like "Reservoir 13", "Everything I Never Told You" and "The Lovely Bones" – all dramas about a community dealing with grief and picking up the pieces after a traumatic event. If people still don’t believe video games can be art, they really should play this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I find it rare to, especially in the last couple of years, find great writing in a game where characters feel alive, real and relatable. Closer the Distance has some of the best collective feel from all the games in recent memory for me personally. Especially how well the subject of loss and how it affects each of us differently. All in all it is a love letter to people who have experienced loss and struggle with moving on. Especially the ending, where most games don’t know how to end, ending was the most moving part of the game where the writing and I believe personal experience really shined. One neat detail I love about the game is the design of the needs system. Every person has different needs to be taken care of. In that sense it is a lot more deeper than The Sims and just looking at the needs of the person, you can tell who they are. Without needing to read their history or bio. Like an introvert who needs their alone time and routine to calm down. Or a person who needs to keep herself busy helping others, so she does not blame herself.There are a couple of small points I think the game could have polished better. The game introduces a character in the middle of the game who arrives into the town. Presenting later what sort of feels like the most important decision in the game. But in the end that decision does not have a real impact, unless you choose one certain option - at least I did not notice while doing all the endings. Also for his own presence and goal in the game, there is not really much the game gave him to do. Most critique I would give the game is pacing - the time you have to complete tasks is too short - and the needs system is quite demanding for a story driven game. To make sure you get to complete every task, you have to skip dialogues and let them play in parallel because of the loss of time. Your timing has to be almost perfect and you have to hope rain doesn’t ruin your day when you need to take a run. I'm afraid that for most of the casual players the game can be too stressful and demanding and they might not experience the story because of that. This is even emphasized by the fact that the most impactful activities have to be done in just a couple of days where everything has to be perfectly planned and then you have a couple of days basically just waiting with nothing to do, but just wait for the next story to wrap up. I think even the story would have benefited with more breathing room in between and with a more relaxing vibe (or like casual difficulty). But all in all, this is the best game and best story I have played in years and I can imagine so many more stories using this game and system design. Stories from all over the world. Somehow I even ended up imagining WWI stories from trenches handled in this design, the vibe of the game seems perfect for a somber story like that. So here is hoping that this is not the last story this team will introduce to us - and it would be cool if the one traveler would be the only thing connecting them.And I wish good luck to Osmotic Studios for their future projects ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty darn good. It has the Sims like experience plus the drama of a Life Is Strange. The voice acting is great. It really makes ya feel for the characters and the emotions that they are portraying. Even had me tear up a bit. Each character has goals, needs etc. It's our job to make sure the main character at least gets thru this. Graphically the game works for what it's goin' for. It's not AAA and it doesn't need to be. It does put some AAA games to shame tho when it comes to the voice acting, narrative and the drama it presents. Gameplay Impressions:

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure at first but the more I play it the more I'm enjoying it. It's fundamentally a story, kind of like a TV show... but you know what everyone's thinking and feeling, and you get to control some of them. The connections between your characters are meaningful and you feel good for completing people's wishes. It's magical, and at the moment there really is only one game like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: It makes me wonder if the writer (or the entire dev team) has ever experienced profound loss in their lives, because the way the mom and the dad react to the untimely death of their daughter is completely unrealistic. People lose their minds when they hear something like that. They can't contain their emotions, even the most stoic person will be at a loss for words. They won't just go to a different room and act like nothing happened. This is seriously unrealistic and weird. The way they initially react to these horrible news took me out of the game entirely. This is not how people act when someone dies unexpectedly. They wail, they get angry, they collapse physically. It takes them weeks, or even months to put together a coherent sentence.One of the most memorable moments of my entire life was when my father received a call from my uncle telling him that my grandfather had passed away. It still remains the only moment that I have ever seen my father broken down like that. And he was expecting it! Grandpa had cancer and genuinely wasn't doing well. Yet my father was bawling and desperately hugging my mother like I had never seen before. Can you imagine what his reaction would be if I, his young and healthy son, were to die unexpectedly? And like I said, this is not a personality thing. Literally everyone loses their minds when a loved one dies. I don't think I can fully immerse myself in this game because it doesn't seem like the characters' daughter or their sister or their girlfriend etc. died; it's as if their two-week-old pet fish died. Sorry Osmotic, I liked Orwell but this is just badly written so far. Will update if I change my mind.Edit: The writing doesn't get better an hour in, and I got spoilers  If you care about believable characters in a story, this is not the game for you. Also, the gameplay is lackluster, it's basically simplified Sims that had the potential to focus on the themes of the story but does not. For example, it's difficult to take care of yourself when you're grieving, but here the gameplay is very inconsistent. It would've been better to simply focus on the vitals: e.g. making dinner for a character who was close to Angela while playing as a character who wasn't as much affected. This is what real people do for their community when someone dies. Every character has their own bars to fill and it isn't entirely clear why they care about these abstract things when it hasn't even been 24 hours since their daughter/sister/girlfriend/patient died. I am sure this makes sense to somebody who saw a grieving person (which is why I don't understand how hard the ball was dropped by the devs, no disrespect intended). I was lucky enough to never experience such grief, yet, but I have seen many people go through it. Like I said before, they shut down. You have to help them. The concept is solid with this game but it's just... the atmosphere is not there. Why am I going around as the sister of the deceased and asking the little boy across town if he's alright? His parents should be asking ME if I am alright. And why doesn't anyone tell me to rest and grieve while I'm going around town asking if the 80-year-old grandma if she felt bad about my own sister dying? It's just weird. It rips me out of the setting. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who cares too much about his project is a nice touch; that's good writing, I have no issues with that. The wife of the doctor who is gleefully obsessed with making a wreath for the deceased? Weird.For what it's worth, the graphics and the sound design is nice but games like these depend on the writing and the atmosphere; this game just does not have it.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible storytelling that really examines how different people approach grief. I enjoyed the ability to control different characters but  I agree with the critiques that the pacing sometimes felt either too stagnant near the end or too overwhelming in the middle. Overall, the gameplay felt really unique and it really felt like you had to choose between which characters to help. Looking forward to more games like this :)
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Really amazing narrative, interesting portrayals of how people handle grief very differently and having those differences be baked into the meters (distraction vs diligence vs solitude for 3 different characters). It's a beautiful game with very real reactions to loss and thoughts on how to move forward, and how moving forward looks different for everyone. Have already recommended this one to a few people.Some slight performance issues where things start to lag or glitch out if you don't save and close the game completely every once in a while. There are also some small gameplay problems with "cutscene" dialogue overlapping each other if there are 4 characters in the same area and events overlapping because some of them cannot be predicted in advance. Bit difficult to juggle so many characters in a reasonable amount of time--could benefit from a slightly longer day cycle or something like that. But overall lovely game.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely swimming in atmosphere. The town is gorgeous, the music is moving, the people and interactions feel genuine and interesting. I'm in two minds about the gameplay though. A sims-like game with a story? Sign me up! But it's the story I stayed for, not the gameplay mechanics. Characters have need bars, but fulfilling them doesn't actually seem to benefit the characters you control at all - or at least it's never explained how it does. You seem better off ignoring them so that you can fulfil quests, many of which are quite tightly timed. I failed more than one due to vague deadlines and attempting to let my characters fulfil their needs, which was frustrating, and in some cases didn't understand why I'd failed at all (I assume they were overridden by other events). My other problem was conversations between characters - and there are lots - last for hours. You get an alert and the conversation gets put on hold until you switch you it. As lots of people will want to have conversations at the same time, including many for quests, you either leave everyone frozen while you listen or you skip some of them, which I didn't want to do because they were brilliant. My biggest wishes for the game would be for it to pause time while conversations happen (which would allow you to listen to more conversations and allow the characters more time to take care of themselves) and to explain the effect of need bars better (if there is any). As a side note, possibly as a result of my choices, the main character, Conny, spent the last several days in absolute depression, rocking back and forth on the bed or in front of the fridge. No one tried to help her. Especially when she was the only character I could control, this seemed a bit bleak. Poor Conny.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: A melancholic, touching narrative game.Setting itself up as a life-sim game this title manages to tell a beautiful, bittersweet story about loss, grief, community and growth. Being able to control some of the characters, and to see the wants, needs and goals of all of them, makes you feel very connected and immersed in their lives and relationships; it also works well in giving the player a direction and a sense of progression through the story.The narrative is very strong: the writing is full of emotion but tactful, every line feels important; the characters are fleshed out and don't feel stereotypical; the events shown are compelling and tackle sensitive topics, but their presentation is mature and never feels melodramatic.The visuals are delicate and tasteful, same for the score.The controls and UI work fine, although it could use some more keybord shortcuts.Overall an excellent experience if you're looking for an impactful story driven game, totally recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really interesting, can't say it's "fun" to play given that it's all about each characters individual grief journey. That being said, it is a great game with lots to do in it for the characters you'll slowly unlock. It's very similar to The SIms, with taking care of each characters individual needs. It even gives me a hint of Life is Strange with the story, and choosing actions that change certain outcomes.I'll say, if you've lost someone recently like I have, or if you're still deep in your grieving process, I'd recommend waiting to play. The whole game involves losing someone, and although the story and lessons are great, that doesn't mean you may be personally ready for them.With that all being said, it really is a nicely done game. I've yet to finish it, but I think I've played enough to leave a review. It may take me longer to finish the game due to how emotional it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This plot-driven life simulator moved me more than I anticipated. Your decisions matter - mine led to me missing several achievements - although I'm not sure how deeply these decisions can influence the direction of the story. You may have to replay the game to find out. That said, I did enjoy the whole experience and hanging out with those characters, their fears and hopes and preoccupations, and I found myself rooting for them. A fun game.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Closer the Distance begins with a tragedy in the tight-knit community of Yesterby. Angela, a teenager with her whole life ahead of her has died in a tragic accident, leaving her sister Conny and her parents Pia and Axel shocked, in addition to the rest of the town. From what you get to learn about Angela before the accident, she was like any other teenager; wanting to see the world and be free of her seemingly pre-ordained life in the small town. She made me think of many a heroine from John Green’s works, especially Alaska Young.You get to know the residents of Yesterby quickly, Doctor Galya and her partner Leigh, Leigh’s son Bodhi, the enterprising Jasper and his wife Blanche and their children River and Eli, town carpenter Melville and his son Zek, who was also Angela’s boyfriend, and village stalwart Henrietta. Osmotic took great care in making sure these NPCs weren’t carbon copies of each other, each was unique with their own reactions and coping mechanisms to Angela’s death.There’s an element of The Sims in Closer the Distance, as you can monitor health, hunger, sleep, self-care, and a few other categories for every person in the town. It also varies from character to character, with ‘Play’ being one of the meters for youngster Eli and ‘Health’ being one for Galya. Using this mechanic in a game about grief was inspired. The characters were so shockingly human that I tried to ensure everyone was fed and taking care of themselves (the mom in me), but I realized that I couldn’t. I wouldn’t be able to make everyone better on my timetable; I needed to wait for theirs.To get down to brass tacks, Closer the Distance is unique and a shining example of games as art. It’s an exploration of community, showing how grief can twist and strain or even strengthen bonds, and how hard it can be to let go, especially if you’re not ready for it. I wasn’t ready to say my final goodbyes to Angela when it happened, but Conny was, and that’s really all that mattered.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this if you enjoyed the emotional gut-punch that was Life Is Strange. The story focuses on a town that has recently been struck by tragedy and each protagonist you play, deals with it in his or her own way. There's a Sims-like element introduced, but it's really more gimmicky than an essential part of the game. Really, we're gonna cook for 3 hours when there's a show boat to be finished?I thought the story itself was great. It shows grief, confrontation and acceptance on a relatively small scale. Don't go into this expecting a lot of action and shocking events, for you will be disappointed.The music in this game is fantastic - I can't stretch that enough. Acoustic guitars and just really pretty, small songs.My only two gripes were the voice-acting and how abruptly it all ended. I won't spoil anything about the latter, but the voice-acting was really disproportionate. There are some big names here, including everyone's favourite Witcher, Doug Cockle and some big names from the Horizon-series and they perform really well. Some of the voice actors however are simply less experienced and you can tell. It never gets terrible, but some artistic choices are dubious.Overall, I would rate the experience a solid 7/10. It's definitely worth the 18 bucks it goes for now.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: The way you have to take care of everyone's mental and physical health through sims-esque menus is very well done. The decisions on whether to take care of the person or use the person to ensure someone else feels better. It's a hard balance. It makes me grieve for my own family members that have passed. Reminded me of when I struggled to understand whether to give myself space or push forward to make sure my family's grief wasn't as strong.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just beautiful, not only in design and soundtrack, but also in its story. I know a lot is happening but that is the point of the whole situation. Everyone is going through it differently and this is shown by those many conversations you have at the same time. I am normally not an emotional person but the ending got me ugly-crying. I am looking forward to see more games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: Good narrative game with a very unique concept, but the formula is still new and raw! I'd give it a 7/10 and would fully recommend you pick it up for its unique experience.I hope that the developers continue to refine the formula, because this type of storytelling has huge potential!Closer the Distance is an emotional choice-based narrative experience about grief and change. By mixing Sims-like needs and wants, choice-based gameplay and a narrative which keeps on moving with or without your input, it delivers a personal story in way that I've never seen before.- A small-scale, emotional plotline told in a way never told before in a game- Very binge-able. Wanting to play through "just one more day" led me to finish it in two sittings- Well polished core gameplay loop with very few bugs- Generally, each character behaved believably and distinctly when faced with a difficult situation- The game responded to my actions and brought them up in dialogue between characters- Good theme song- Fast-forward and pause buttons were very useful quality of life additions- Good clean UI and a really effective art style to match- Some characters felt shallow or redundant- Voice acting and writing wasn't of consistent quality- Sound muffling effects would happen even when in the same room as the characters- No epilogue meant I couldn't see the impact of my playthrough on the characters- Achieving 20/23 achievements in one playthrough led me to believe the game was more about the illusion of choice (unverified, achievements may not reflect the reality)- If I accidentally triggered two events simultaneously, I had to jump between them otherwise I miss out on important information which broke the flow- Frustration as some character actions were locked for me without any indication of why- The walk speed was unbearably slow at times, especially given the size of the island. It led to more frustration with time-sensitive tasks.- Pacing towards the end was rough. Too sudden and too slow at the same time- I never saw any negative consequences to someone's needs falling low
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: A touching story about loss and coping with it, with sprinkles of topics like decomposition of community, erosion of tiny towns as well as sparking hope for the future to come. Beautifully made, well acted, well written and with lots of heart and a very open concept. It has some snags, like the final days being stripped of control... But decisions DO matter and lots of things you would like to see will come undone, if not pressured hard enough. A great game with great idea behind it.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review: What a delightfully unique title. Massive fan of narrative games, especially with poignant meaningful stories, and this is up there with the best of them. I have never seen a presentation style like this (The Sims meets Life is Strange, basically), but it is a compelling proposition as a fan of both games, and the cozy vibes are immaculate. Definitely a game to enjoy with a hot cup of coffee or tea.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

_childDocuments_.review:
Closer the Distance is a deeply moving, slice-of-life sim that tells a story about the connections between family and friends in the face of tragedy. 

Following a fatal car accident, players take on the role of Angela, a young girl from the town of Yesterby, who finds herself watching over her loved ones as they navigate the grieving process. 

Using her ethereal ability to influence the townspeople she once knew, Angela’s choices will ultimately determine the fate of Yesterby.
_childDocuments_.name: Closer the Distance

name: Crow Country
detailed_description: A survival horror game, where you’ll test yourself against puzzles and riddles as you investigate the eerie tranquility of the abandoned theme park. Don’t be deceived by the whimsical surroundings, something is awfully wrong in Crow Country. As you unlock new areas, backtrack and discover more, you gradually piece together why Edward really shut down his park and where he mysteriously disappeared to. You’ve heard some pretty disturbing rumors, but they couldn’t possibly be true…..right? For visitors to the park who are more interested in spotting crows and taking in the sights, Exploration Mode allows you to journey on without the fear of being attacked by the mysterious monsters roaming Crow Country. If you knew what those monsters really are….. Just how far would someone go to follow their ambition? Are some sins too wicked for redemption? A tale of reckless hubris and human greed, and now at the center of it all... you. Who are you really, Mara Forest?
