_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this: the mystery, the aesthetic, the puzzles, and all the little design choices seemed to be directly targeting me, specifically.  What I mean is, Crow Country feels like it took all the things I like from the games that inspired it, and left out the things I don't like.It's spooky, and occasionally startles you, but it's never truly frightening or disgusting, at least it never crosses the line of what I personally would consider truly frightening or disgusting, but it does occasionally approach that line- a line that games that this is inspired by frequently crossed with wild abandon.  (FYI: no, I would however never even consider letting a child play or watch this game being played.)  The environment and especially the sounds are perfectly designed to let you know when you can relax (such as safe rooms) and when to brace for threats or surprises.  It also pauses, and specifically and importantly: it pauses the action when you are reading or in your inventory.The puzzles have a Myst-like quality so far as there being notes and clues everywhere, so if you're observant and bother to write your own notes about where things are and anything that seems like it could be important, then you'll have no issues at any point in the game solving the puzzles, and you'll feel like a genius.  It goes so far as to keep track of all the puzzle-related notes you've found, and put binders of them in the safe rooms so that you can go back and remind yourself of important information without having to scour the map for a specific note that you saw.... somewhere...The game also never breaks your trust.  What I mean is, the game establishes patterns for how it will function, and doesn't break those patterns. I would be more specific, but I'd prefer people figure out the rules for themselves. I will say that I'm happy with the choices that the devs made here- because this is a game, and it needs to have rules that the player can pick up on, and breaking those rules to shock or frighten the player is not worth the betrayal of the player's trust that the game will follow its own rules.This was brilliant, and I hope that it is successful enough, and the devs enjoyed making it enough, that they will make more games like it!

_childDocuments_.review: A bite sized take on a classic horror game. If you liked playing the early Resident Evil games or Silent Hill games, this game is for you. _childDocuments_.review: A charming, recognizable art style, great story, fun characters in spades, who manage to intrigue even with their relatively short time spent on screen and in conversation with the player, which is highly commendable. The soundtrack is a great, if somewhat muted work of ambience, which straddles the line between music and hair-raising, quasi-musical tonalities (quasi-musical, for they are scarcely recognizable as such at times) incredibly well. Along with the actual ambient sounds, and the aforementioned spectacular art and animation, it manages to create an atmosphere as thick as the fog that surrounds its Haunted Hilltop.This is SFB Games' first foray into any kind of horror, but boy do I hope it isn't their last! They went directly for the jugular with Survival Horror, one of the more difficult kinds to pull of, and yet they passed the trial with flying colors. For my entire 9 hours of playtime I was fascinated, confused, freaked out or scared in some form and always interested as to what would come next and how the game's unique theme park aesthetic would surprise me. But Crow Country also managed to have something many pieces of horror lack in today's day and age: coherence. It is way too often that I see developers so insecure of their art, that they decide that the only way to make a well-liked horror game is to throw in cheap jumpscares or vaguely grim imagery that seems to have little to do with any on-screen happenings; but not Crow Country!The game even manages to sprinkle in some tasteful comedy for good measure, which manages to marry both Leon S. Kennedy's endearing confusion and naivete from Resident Evil 2, along with his unfettered bravado from Resident Evil 4, and put both into Mara Forrest, the Crow Country's wonderful, female protagonist.If you enjoy slightly more oldschool survival horror, such as rose-engine's masterful sleeper hit "Signalis" from 2022, then you  will love Crow Country in equal measure – of that I am sure!

_childDocuments_.review: I always thought the term "drenched in atmosphere" was a bit overzealous when describing the tone of a work, but I think that might come close to describing the core appeal of . An indie survival horror game that works modern shader techniques to the bone, 's biggest appeal is its visuals. Using great camera angles, strong shaders, and dynamic lightning, this game looks like you're playing a pre-rendered background straight out the PSC era... except you can rotate the camera around 360 degrees. The exceptional detail with which  depicts its rotting amusement park world is nothing short of an achievement in art design. Luckily,  is more than just a pretty face, as it's also a competent survival horror game with some genuine genre innovations.To reiterate,  looks incredible. The actual artstyle here is good, but the camera, lighting and shaders all come together to give the game a peerless aesthetic.  Point blank, I don't think any other "PSX-like" game actually looks this authentically like the pre-rendered backgrounds of  or . On top of this, the setting of a theme park is pretty inspired. Each location is crammed with detail and soaked a rotting atmosphere that you almost feel on your skin and taste in your mouth. You explore abandoned rides, confectionery areas, and fairways, each of which has it's own flavor and purpose in the wider park. While the map is small, each room is carefully picked to maximise atmosphere or detail. In general, detail is the name of the game, as the game has tons of strong aesthetic touches to elevate itself. For example, the main enemies (called "guests") let out these horrible wails when shot. If they're knocked to the ground, then they'll writhe in pain before bleeding out. If Mara walks over them, they let out a death rattle as she crushes their ribs. This level of detail is everywhere in , giving you solid feedback for every action you take. Combined with a strong soundtrack, these aesthetic touches really elevate the game.The story follows police agent Mara Forest, who's been called to the abandoned theme park of Crow Country in search of its owner. Mara soon finds that the park is overrun with horrible mutants, and begin unravelling a tale of gold mining, strange bacteria, and conflicting loyalties. While the characters of  aren't exactly complex, the story itself is a satisfying little mystery. The game has a lot of good reveals, and is told in a non-linear manner through notes and diary entries. Often, the game lets you figure out key plot points long before they're explained to you directly, which is a great sign for a compelling mystery. I think the game lays it on a little thick with the foreshadowing for some plot points though, including a major endgame reveal that I predicted twenty minutes in. It got to the point where I was convinced the plot was setting up a red herring, only to actually go down that route. It's still a good tale, and the ending has a great reveal, but I think easing up on some of the hints would be good. The actual structure of  revolves around non-linear exploration and puzzle solving with hints laid out in notes. These hints are scattered all over the park, and often delivered with information that does not fully link up with where you currently are. This often means that the game rewards you for paying attention, with puzzles that are effectively explained but devoid of context at the time you see them. You often have all the hints you need to solve a puzzle, with only the most optional ones being obscure, and the game leaves it up to you to connect the dots together with the information you have. In general the game's puzzles are satisfying, and I really enjoyed how nonlinear exploring the park was. Once you get two or three major items, you can kind of go anywhere, which lets you tackle objectives in whatever order you please. This non linearity is excellent, and the wealth of accessibility options ((such as no inventory management) mean that I could genuinely recommend this as someone's first survival horror title.The only major place where  falls flat is in the combat. On paper, the combat has a lot of great ideas. Unlike every other survival horror,  has no lock on, allowing you to manually aim your guns. Not only does this create some good tension as you line up your shots, but it also allows guns to be used for purposes other than combat, such as shooting crates to trade resources or at world objects to solve puzzles. While the enemies look intimidating, and give great feedback when shot, no enemy poses a real threat. None of them have much health, and the game soaks you in pickups and ammo. Mara is pretty speedy and reloads lightning quick, which means backpedalling out of danger and reloading is always an option. I consider myself a pretty solid survival horror veteran, and I never came close to dying once, which is a genuine shame. There are optional boss "fights", but often they were over before they began. This was true of older survival horror titles too, but I would have preferred if  kicked things up a notch for the difficulty. Perhaps a "true hardmode" difficulty could be made that increases enemy damage and speed could be implemented?I really can't recommend  enough if you love survival horror games. The atmosphere on display here is stunning, and it comes packed with a great place to explore, a solid story to dissect, and some great gameplay ideas to carry the genre forward into the modern day.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful little game! A love letter to the old PS2 days that still retains some niceties from modern games. The game is pretty well a more accessible entry to the survival horror genre. You have the option of gaining hints via an in-game system, a non-combat mode for people that just want to enjoy the story and aesthetic (or hard mode), and the ability to use both joysticks or an old-school D-pad type control scheme to play.I am certain this game will scratch that itch for both newcomers and well-acquainted players of the genre and I highly recommend it.The save dialogue sums it up rather well so far:"Staring into the flames... I feel something. It's a curious mixture of hope and dread. Maybe everything will be okay, and maybe it won't."

_childDocuments_.review: + Very strong abandoned theme park atmosphere that evokes childhood nostalgia.+ Great horror sound design inspired by the greats. The music is also nice.+ An overall "analogue" aesthetic that helps ground the game in its intended era (1990).+ Graphics inspired by the pre-rendered backgrounds of yore, but executed in real-time 3D, with full horizontal camera rotation. This leads to a perspective and style of aiming that hasn't really been done before, and it is well done.~ The decision to use rounded designs and chibi proportions in a survival horror game does make the game feel a bit harmless at times due to shape language. Objects with sharp, ragged edges tend to be a lot more terrifying than soft, rounded things. But I also love how the game looks. It suits the theme park vibe; it's not supposed to be a terrifying place by itself, rather it is spooky because of the events that caused it to become abandoned and crawling with monsters. That juxtaposition is in itself unsettling and I imagine was part of the intent. The monsters are also still freaky enough to feel threatening, thanks to their erratic animations and bloody appearance. So it's still a spooky game, but don't go in expecting Silent Hill levels of fear and mastery over psychological horror.+ Good control options. Can use either tank controls (harder) or modern controls (easier). The path of least resistance felt better for this game, but it also made the game quite easy, so I may do a second playthrough using only the tank controls. Also, you can disable the HUD elements entirely and the game remains 100% playable that way.+ Hint system implemented in the form of a fortune-telling machine you can physically interact with, which doesn't hurt immersion. You get 10 uses, which should be more than enough for anyone to finish the game without ever needing to open up a walkthrough.+ Intuitive map system that helps you remember where things are, without obnoxiously telling you where to go.+ Effective "jump scares" (not the bad kind, trust me they are not cheap, annoying or overused at all).- The regular notes could have used more styling. It didn't feel like I was reading a sheet of paper I just found, it felt more like reading a video game text box pop-up with a transparent background.Fairly enjoyable dialogue for the most part, but I felt that there was too much of it for how simple the story is. There are also too many notes and tutorial notes scattered everywhere, diminishing the feeling of isolation and horror a bit. Some of the notes may have made some of the puzzles too easy, sometimes outright giving you the solution to a later puzzle,  but overall, it's not a big deal.The story could have had more subtlety or mystery, letting us piece things together ourselves, or it could have used symbolism for more mature themes. Instead, what you see is what you get: you know exactly what's going on at all times. However, I can appreciate that the game doesn't bite off more than it can chew, as it could have felt pretentious if executed poorly. Instead, the story feels somewhat cute and nostalgic; it's like the story an imaginative innocent child growing up in the 90s could have genuinely come up with after having visited a theme park, but told in game form by a talented team.While it results in a story that isn't super deep or interesting, it was still enjoyable to experience because of the great art direction. There's nothing wrong with having a story that anyone can understand, and I think this game would make a great introduction to the survival horror genre for kids, even if those who grew up in the 90s and early 2000s will also find a lot to love here, and are likely the main target audience.Overall, this game is an easy recommendation. If like me, this game's visual style caught your attention at first glance, then you will most likely enjoy it. I hope the devs continue to make games in the future, as there was a clear vision and passion put into this game, and I appreciate that a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I'm one big scaredy-cat when it comes to horror games but I have to admit, this is one of the best and pleasant (if you can call horror pleasant) survival horror experiences I've ever had. I don't know where would I begin with my praises. I loved the PS1 inspired aesthetics, the awesome spooky atmosphere, excellent sound design and music, the tight and surprisingly varied design of all the areas, not forgetting the great puzzles. All and all, an extremely well designed package.

_childDocuments_.review: + unrivaled horror atmosphere+ lo-fi graphics delight with nostalgia+ enemy designs are great with lots of variety+ huge emphasis on puzzles, backtracking+ end-game bonuses make another playthrough worth it- combat is fickle  - very short and very easyCrow Country is a time capsule from the 90s: you'll find things here you haven't seen since back then, most of the game's design sensibilities just don't exist anymore. Sure, indie survival horror games trying to emulate some of the genre's earliest hits are a dime a dozen, but not many of them compare so favorably as Crow Country does. What it does best is its atmosphere, but many aspects of the game are so ahead of its contemporaries that it's immediately one of the best in the genre, at least the current modern take on the genre.The story is really nice, with clear inspiration from movies like The Gate, The Fly, and more. It's not cliche but does take some major plot beats from other sources. It can feel a little bit heavy in the tail end of the game, especially near the ending, where it dumps loads of exposition on the player. It's not dripfed at a steady pace; in fact, for the first half of the game you kind of have no idea what's going on. Which is maybe a good thing as it lends itself to mystery really well, although I did find it hard to be invested at first when you have so little to go by. You go into it knowing you're exploring a closed amusement park with some monsters and that's kind of it. It's fresh in a sense because there's no prior canon or info to go off of and instead you learn what it's about as the protagonist does, too.What Crow Country does best is nail that 90s survival horror vibe. The game is markedly lo-fi with filters making it look like an old PS1 title. Characters are low-poly, gouraud shaded, animations are clunky, there's a depressing fog enveloping everything, enemies are nondescript and hard to make out... I love it, it feels right at home with some of the genre greats like Resident Evil, Clock Tower, Silent Hill. I know focusing on how a game looks shouldn't be of much consideration but it looks like marketing screenshots of pre-rendered scenes printed for magazine yet it's all ingame. It's an artistic decision to make it look as "bad" as it does, but it emulates 90s graphics sensibilities super convincingly. Bravo!Combat is not so good but as is true of the genre, it's de-emphasized in favor of puzzle solving and backtracking. Every time I had to participate in combat, it felt frustrating to control and land pinpoint shots, especially since there's no melee option (until a 2nd playthrough, at least). It was better every time to avoid enemies by running around or tricking their pathfinding to your advantage. The puzzles, though, are excellent and varied. Some are headscratchers but most were obvious. They can be both obvious and clever, though, because even if many of them were easy, they were fun to solve and involved steps I wouldn't have thought of, at least.Resources are so plentiful yet your inventory has a very small restriction on how much you can carry. It was a common situation where I had 40 handgun bullets and passed by maybe 40 more on my travels with no way to mark their location on my map, or a box to store them in. Making it frustrating is that if you have 39 handgun bullets and pick up a box of 8, it truncates to 40 bullets meaning you've lost 7 to the void. Oversights like this just lead to frustration because it shouldn't work like that at all.Difficulty is basically non-existent. With supplies being so ample and enemies so easy to dodge, most of your hits will be from traps or by rushing things and not taking your time. About the halfway point I became aware of the S-rank requirements of 10 heals or less, so I stopped healing and instead beat the rest of the game in danger status. And yet I had no issues at all. Enemies pose no real threat other than the bosses. The game desperately needs a hard mode making enemies either more aggressive, or restricting how many items are available to you.The game is very short: I clocked 6.5 hours to get all achievements, then I spent another hour playing with the post-game unlocks which included a "treasure hunt" of shooting all crystal crows on the map. Granted I had a blast the entire time, I do wish it was longer and the map was larger. If you were going for a casual minimalist playthrough without going for a 100%, I could see it being 4-5 hours instead. Again, it sorely needs a hard mode so at the very least you can get another playthrough out of it.I assure you that if you have even the slightest bit of survival horror blood in you, Crow Country is like travelling back in time to the 90s to witness the genre's heyday all over again, it's that good. I hope we see more either from Crow Country or this developer again because there's some real talent here and it shows.Capping max TDP to 7w can keep 60fps pretty much consistently. I say pretty much because I wonder if there's some memory issue with certain shaders or effects. In many areas with enemies, 7w can keep 60fps no problem, but the moment you have the flashlight on in conjunction with enemies on screen, it does fluctuate to the low 50s. Likewise if you have a save point in a room with flashlight on. Upping TDP to 8w, 9w, 10w doesn't really improve things; uncapping still doesn't keep 60fps.If you keep flashlight off, 7w can do it for the whole game until the final boss, where you then hit 30~40fps and no configuration can bring it much higher. It becomes a very big stuttery mess in the final boss room, your mileage may vary. It's weird behavior I'd have assumed wouldn't happen considering how low-fi the game is.

_childDocuments_.review: 1990. A special agent Mara Forest (don't forget, don't mess it up) arrives at the scene. She's looking for Edward Crow, the owner of a theme park called Crow Country. Is Mara's look a tribute to Suzi from the Sphere Hunter? She definitely has the same haircut. Anyway, what we have here is an eldritch sci-fi story about gold, monsters, and an injured girl. Sadly, the story doesn't develop naturally, opting for an exposition dump at the end. The notes and talks are lacking, yet it's neat regardless. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, having a cutesy sense of humour, which only sometimes goes full clown. All in all, it remains somewhat sombre and weird throughout. A bubble art dragon from Ecstatica watches you from behind the glass, a grandfather clock points a shotgun at you. You pop open a mermaid for her battery and burn a fairy's head for her key.The unique presentation is so lo-fi it's hi-fi, these game's high-class and tasteful visuals are rare and unique, making for one atmospheric adventure. These backgrounds are a work of art, too, no doubt. Simpler character models leave room for imagination, hence their cutesy look adds to the dwindling fear factor. I find innocent-looking things harbouring malicious intents a rather scary phenomenon under the right circumstances. Little Big Adventure was unnerving at times, like when a friendly-looking elephant plushy clubbed Twinsen to death. It felt like a betrayal. Overall, the survival horror stylisation is impeccable. Alas, it's only stylisation. I wouldn't call Crow Country a survival horror. It isn't terrifying, only slightly discomforting, and it's not challenging enough to say you fight for your life. But it's rather peculiar still.The mechanics are also nothing but stylisation. The game gives you a ton of resources, you can get complacent. Healing, ammo, gun upgrades - all in droves. If you're in for the guns, it has all the classics: pistol, shotgun, flamethrower, magnum. Allegedly! I never found the last two, but it didn't matter, in the long run. It's an easy game, my stingy ass slipped through while only using a pistol and grenades. Keys, notes, puzzle items take priority, for CC is more about puzzles and exploration. Crow Country doesn't write down codes for you. Everything is cryptic, everything is locked. It's up to you to blast the game open. And it forces you to pay attention. The lack of highlighting coupled with muddy visuals makes finding things tricky, but hey, the locations are tiny and the map is really helpful. The loot is somewhat randomised or maybe trash cans only give you resources when you lack them? Seems so.Thus, attentive scavenging becomes an integral, enjoyable part of your exploration routine. A plethora of secrets and shortcuts also add to the sense of discovery. You'll find lots of items and interactions hidden in the environments, including objects to shoot. Like explosive barrels, electrical generators that can shock you or your enemy, bear traps, crates, jars, and barrels. The traps get more devious and abundant with time, you'll see that they're the main source of health loss here. But healing items are scattered all over the place. Not to mention unlimited saves in abundant save rooms, positioned on every corner. It's a confined, intimate world, which makes backtracking a relaxing ordeal. It is a leisurely stroll through an amusing theme park, after all. I suppose it's my problem that I was looking for hardcore RE experience that was never there.Once again, it's a game of puzzles and hazards, less so murder. The monsters, even when there's a bunch of them, don't have a menacing presence. Sure, they "smell like an infected wound", they're "broken, shaking, falling apart", they're "in no shape to continue living"... quite literally, in practice, a kid could tear them apart with their bare hands. There's no glory in killing. Conceptually, it's Silent Hill-ish, I guess? The roster is fine. Flayed crow people, cronenbergs, creepy crawlies, bubbling puddles of flesh, and brittle bone giants... all more pitiful than fearsome, all easily avoidable. Even though packs of enemies spawn in the places you visited, creating some clutter, I probably killed no more than a dozen, and those - for convenience, not survival.It's a shame since I found the local elegant aiming system fun. You don't just aim in a general direction but can freely move your reticle, being able to target different body parts, decapitate, etc. It adds more control, and therefore depth, to combat encounters. Bullets also lose power with range, so it's beneficial to stay close, which would be a neat risk-reward system if simply shooting fast wasn't the most effective tactic. What else is there? I hope I didn't come off as a hater. Like, uh, there's some replayability! Quite a merit, right? You even unlock bonus items and challenges upon completion. But no, thanks, it's a one-and-done for me. Still, it's alright for the price. Clever puzzles and unique visuals elevate it above mediocrity. To conclude, Kendrick is a godlike prodigy. Sorry, I got bored talking about the game and would rather argue with a Drake fan in the comments.P.S. I've heard the inclusion of a hard mode is a possibility. That would be a game-changer. Oh wait, it's out NOW... I keep telling myself to never buy games at launch.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: This game was fantastic. I loved every minute of it. It took me 6.5 hours to beat with getting only 8 out of 15 in-game secrets and 9 out of 15 achievements but I honestly wish I spent more time in my first playthrough getting as much more as possible because I just want to spend more time with my first experiences. So, if I had one thing to say about this game, it'd be to spend as much time soaking it all in on your first go.(I just want to preface by saying I played the game with a PS5 controller so some of the things I say are based on controller and not on KB&M).The things that I loved about the game:-Aesthetically nostalgic. The late 90s style is done perfectly. Giving the player the ability to rotate the camera instead of using static cameras lets you really appreciate all the work put into the art. Also, others may not like this but I appreciate that pick-upable items like medkits and ammo blend with the art style instead of sticking out like a sore thumb. "Hey, is that a medkit or just part of the background?" Well, just walk over and press X or whatever the keyboard keybind is and find out! Majority of the time, it actually is a medkit or ammo so don't feel turned off by it.-The story and dialogue. It's just like the right amount of goofy. Everything the main character says to herself and to others is just goofy and I love it. I don't know any other way to describe it. It doesn't take itself overtly serious and it shouldn't. Don't forget to exhaust your dialogues!-The secrets. I love me some good secrets and I don't think games nowadays do it enough justice. Go collect these trophies to get a secret! Go do all these side missions to get a secret! Go find all the poop stains TO GET A SECRET! Like go to hell with all that. Crow Country does it just right. Play the correct piano songs to unlock the paintings. You may be stumped for a good bit but once you see the trick it becomes so simple and feels rewarding. One puzzle stumped me for so long I had to have some friends help me and once we figured it out I felt so stupid because it was so simple. But I loved it.Things that I feel could be better:-Combat. Now, the way shooting is done I love. It's cool to have that free aim to aim where ever you want and although funky with the camera perspective, it's not too hard to get use to. BUT! It does feel like it only runs on the X and Y axis(horizontal and vertical planes). When trying to move diagonally while aim, I found that I was just aiming straight down quickly while moving slowly left or right instead of just following a smooth diagonal path. So then I'd have to aim back up to line of the shot. It just doesn't feel smooth trying to aim diagonally so you're better off just moving left or right, lining up with the enemy and then going up or down(if needed) to put the crosshair on them. I can understand why though. When I played, I used the analog stick instead of the D-pad. The game has both a classic style control scheme(tank controls) and a modern control(not tank controls) scheme but the aiming itself is most likely based off the classic control scheme which uses the D-pad. Thus, horizontal and vertical emphasis.The other thing about combat is that you really don't need to engage in it. Monsters will only really engage with you if you get too close but it's easy enough to just run away and disengage with them. They'll only follow you if you stay within their aggro range so I found myself just zigzagging through enemies because there was no point in killing them. I got hurt more by the various traps that come into play as you progress the game than to monsters. I had max ammo for the majority of my playthrough and only really killed an enemy if I had to backtrack through the area a bunch of times. Being an inspired horror game, it detracts from the horror aspect when your enemies are so non-engaging and you're never put into a situation where you feel like your back is against the wall.That's about it. I can't think of anything more to say at this time as I've probably spent like an hour trying to come up with things to mention and now my brain is mush. TL;DR - Loved the game. Art, dialogue, secrets. Liked combat but could be better. 8.5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pleasant jaunt of a game. Movement is generally pretty satisfying, and it really feels nice as a survival horror experience. A bit of a breezy experience. The atmosphere of the game is honestly a bit relaxing, a bit tense at a few key points, but just walking around gives me a sense of tranquility, even outside of the Exploration mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This is genuinely one of the better throwbacks to the genre I've played in years. I really enjoy how it feels less like a PS1 game and more like a classic DOS/Win 3.1 game like Ecstatica or LittleBigAdventure. It's such a peculiar styling that it genuinely got me more into the atmosphere than if it were just wiggly polygons on wonky vertexes and overloaded dithering.Control is top notch as well, not a missed note in terms of giving the player enough options to maneuver in combat (and avoid it entirely if you want). Only real thing I have is I'm not huge on the waving of the aim reticle when doing more precise aiming, but that's moreso a me thing if anything.Really my one big misgiving with recent Survival Horror titles often being too heavy on the Key-Door-Switch puzzles, especially when it feels like it goes against the world the puzzles are in. This one definitely had moments where I had to grab a guide and it kinda sucked me out with some of the longer tasks.Thankfully the game is short, about 5 and a half hours in a single sitting for what I played and it's still very much well worth your time if you're hankering for a throwback survival horror game that actually makes an attempt to do it well.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where I wish I could review without giving a recommendation either way. It's definitely not bad by any means, I'd place it more on mediocre. The artstyle, ideas and effort put into the game is palpable and I commend the devs on those grounds, but unfortunately it just felt slapped together to me. Initial excitement slowly gave way to confusion and boredom, quite a lot of the puzzles weren't that engaging, the story got too flimsy and I wasn't a fan of combat (tank control-style aim without any lock-on nor a melee weapon or kick to destroy boxes/containers, not to mention enemy design getting boring quick). It's also one of the shortest games I've played to date, under 6 hours. Part of me wishes there was more to experience, but I was also pretty done by the end of it. Overall it was an okay time, even starting off pretty interesting, but ultimately grew into a forgettable experience. There is some level of charm to it, but if I knew what my experience now was going to be, I honestly wouldn't have bought it. Giving this a thumbs down only because every review thusfar is positive and I want to shine a light on another perspective of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: What a Damn good game.Crow Country revitalizes the old school Survival Horror Video game formula by not only looking the part and feeling like it too! But also by having the fun gameplay and puzzle solving while including modern game design that take away all those little outdated and clunky mechanics from games back in the day due to either limited hardware or poor design choice.First off I love how this game looks, it captures perfectly the early PS1 era graphics with some extra added rounded polygons to give everything this smooth look. The theme of the whole game fits so well with the gameplay too. The sound Design and Overall Soundtrack is amazing as well. The little sound effects remind me of a combination of Resident Evil and Silent Hill while the OST does the same with the safe room reminding me more like something you would hear in FF7. Such a great blend of Midis it makes the whole experience feel so authentic to what its replicating and does it so perfectly. The game also made me feel eerie and uneasy in certain areas with the creepy soundtrack and even made me jump a few times!The puzzles are all fun to solve! Not incredibly complicated and all over the place! The whole game is like a big Jigsaw Puzzle with Combat added into the mix. Such a great blend that it never feels tiring or annoying having to solve a puzzle but it feels more exciting and fun as the game world constantly encourages and rewards you for exploration and interactivity with everything around your vicinity. There's a different Dialogue for every single thing you can touch along with almost everything in the world being interactable and Mara (the main character) always has something to say weather it be a simple comment or something funny and witty. The Devs even hid items around the map depending on where your camera is angled, such a smart way to make a simple mechanic interactive and rewarding. The game starts off pretty relaxed when you first arrive in the park with the game easing you into the place with little hints spread across the world warning you about the things you can find or run into then amping up the enemy encounters and difficulty the more you progress throughout the story. The story as well is also interesting and gives you extra encouragement to find out more and read the newspapers you can find around the map. Everything about this game is just done so well its hard not to recommend.  The story is good, the gameplay loop is fun, the Details are everywhere and the passion is there, just go ahead and buy this game already because you're in for an awesome rewarding experience!

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciate the aesthetic and charm of this game and of how well it represents what PS1 games looked and felt like. It's fairly short, even for a blind first-time playthrough, but I have cleared RE3 (original and remake) faster so that shouldn't be a deterrent. In fact, this is definitely a speedrun friendly game for those invested in the idea. The story was definitely a bit vague outside of the obvious motives, which is fine. It didn't need to be terribly deep, but the portions left to one's imagination are neat and I wouldn't mind if they did something with that in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and atmospheric homage to early Resident Evil and Silent Hill. The art style is dope. The story is actually pretty decent which I wasn't expecting. Scratches that RE style puzzle-vania type itch. Good secrets. Good music. Good puzzles. Good jokes. The weapons feel really nice - although it took a little adjusting to get used to with a controller, which I used to play. I ended up completing the campaign with all secrets at just under 7 hours. Well worth the time and price. I will replay for sure. I want that S Rank and that platinum trophy. A+!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. Lots of fun little secrets, nice atmosphere and a dev team hopefully determined to keep improving the game for a while still.It's kind of a micro-survival horror, which is common for indie games of the genre. Still it's a little disappointing that there weren't any real bosses, only five technically, and I don't even consider three of them bosses at all. The game is also very easy, due in large part to the fact that there are no fast enemies or ones with projectiles.Everything in the game just slowly shuffles towards you not-so-menacingly to try and hit you with feather-light melee attacks. Effectively infinite ammo too as whenever you're critically low, you can go back to your car or get more from vending machines, so there's no point in managing your resources.The stars of the show is the protagonist and the theme park itself, not exactly the combat.I'd say if you're an avid fan of such games, give it a try, and if you aren't, you'll probably still find some enjoyment out of it, albeit probably at a much lower price point.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of survival horror games, I had high hopes for this one. The premise – an abandoned theme park overrun by bloodthirsty, grotesque creatures, not unlike the one in  – was undeniably intriguing. All in all, I wasn’t disappointed, so this deserves a thumbs up from me, but I wasn’t completely satisfied, either.First of all, the difficulty: if you enjoy a good challenge with some cryptic puzzles, you’ll definitely love  as sometimes it’s downright punishing. OK, to be fair, this is a PS1-style horror and back in the day these games were hard as hell, so the developers managed to replicate this aspect quite well. Also, you can choose to play as a pure exploration game, with no combat and no enemies, which is nice to have, I think. But be warned if you go for the normal or hard mode: resources are absurdly scarce, and the enemies are relentless, with traps waiting for you everywhere. A survival horror game should make you feel vulnerable, and boy, you certainly get this here!Then there’s the aiming. Sure, oldschool action-adventures often used clunky mechanics, but here the controls for aiming are so terrible that even after hours of play, I struggled to consistently land shots. Why don’t we have mouse support, I wonder? And why can’t we have a melee weapon by default? In the second half of the story I saved every five minutes, trying to avoid having to use my guns as much as possible…As for the atmosphere, it’s genuinely impressive. Slowly but surely everything gets darker, more sinister around you, and all the chaos creates a palpable sense of dread. The fact that I could only see a bit of the environment around the protagonist always kept me on edge, fearing what might be lurking after the next corner. I also liked the plot, although it felt a bit messy at times, but still, it was OK with a few interesting characters.Ultimately, I can only recommend this to oldschool, retro survival horror fans, the really, really hardcore ones, mainly due to the clunky mechanics. If you liked the classic  and  titles, you’ll probably find something to appreciate here.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very good!  At first it seems strange for a survival horror game.  You start with a pistol that has (somewhat) infinitely replenishable ammo, which early on seems to lower the stakes, however because you need to shoot things for certain puzzles / traps it seems like a necessary choice by the devs, and once you unlock other weapons it becomes more of a balance for the ammo for those guns.  It's about a 6 hour long game, the puzzles are really well made and if they give you trouble there are hints scattered around the map, so if you wander around you'll likely find a solution.  The story was really great, I won't spoil but the twist certainly scared me.  Sadly it isn't super replayable, there aren't too many challenges or side modes that I think would add to the game, so you can experience most everything on your first playthrough depending on your end rank.  That's not a huge negative though!  It's great for what it does.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country delivers a chilling and faithful recreation of the PS1-era Resident Evil experience. The devs have masterfully captured the classic PlayStation aesthetic, with pseudo pre-rendered background feel that sets a hauntingly atmospheric stage. While the core gameplay mechanics receive a welcome modernization, the spirit of classic Resident Evil remains – complete with tank controls (although their use is not necessary).The gameplay loop is both simple and engaging. Players navigate the desolate and infected Crow Country theme park, now overrun by violent, mutated humanoids. Resource management, a cornerstone of survival horror, plays a crucial role. As Mara, you'll constantly assess your limited ammo and health supplies. However, Crow Country offers a touch more leniency than its inspirations, with resources occasionally respawning throughout the environment. Puzzles are cleverly woven into the environment, often relying on visual storytelling and strategically placed hints to guide players towards solutions.Crow Country excels in both its narrative and environmental design. The abandoned theme park serves as a well-crafted stage, offering diverse and haunting locales. Each area is brimming with unique details and interactive objects that pull you deeper into the unsettling atmosphere. Scattered notes throughout the park unveil a rich backstory and lore, while well-written characters manage to inject touches of humor and charm into the dark events that transpired at Crow Country. The overarching narrative, centered around themes of hubris and loss, is very compelling. The soundtrack flawlessly complements the experience. Layers of ambient synths and soundscapes create a chilling sense of isolation and tension, while the save room music offers a subtle counterpoint of hope and safety. The sound design serves to further enhance the overall experience.Crow Country is a must-play for fans of classic survival horror, particularly those who fondly remember the PS1 era. It expertly captures the essence of the genre while offering a modern and engaging experience. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully executed game all around. Gameplay, ambiance, story... I found myself constantly thinking back and having realizations about subtle details that impress me even now. All kinds of little things that just perfectly sold me on the experience. The moment-to-moment gunplay is immensely satisfying as well; I'm glad I took the time to acclimate myself to the tank controls and experience it to its fullest. Not even constantly walking into chandeliers could dampen my enjoyment.Projects like this are keeping the survival horror genre alive and well, and I couldn't be happier to see it.

The isometric angle can mess up some of your shots but enemies aren’t bullet sponges or move very fast so it’s easy to recover. Highly recommend picking this up if you are able to.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another prime example of why steam reviews are utter garbage and would be better described as more of a YouTuber popularity contest instead of an accurate indicator of a game's quality. I'm also getting kind of sick of indie devs blatantly trying to profit off people's need for nostalgia with these crappy PS1 filters. Why are there so many crappy PS1 "horror" games now? That's all this really is after all, bad 3D modeling and a ps1 filter...which for a game that describes itself as survival horror was.... certainly a choice. I mean does anyone even remember what the original Silent Hill looked like? It wasn't this weird Playskool aesthetic, it was creepy and uncanny, everything this clearly wants to be but isn't. If you want to use a PS1 filter fine, but no PS1 game ever had this bad of 3D modeling...it looks more like a Nintendo game in that regard. I get some people like this art style, but for a horror game? I'd rather have 2d than this I think. It clashes a bit and isn't really all that interesting imo. The gameplay is also mid. Controls are awful and you can't change them because reasons apparently. Just because you couldn't remap controls on PS1 doesn't mean we don't need that option in 2024 ffs. Normal walk speed is atrocious and God help you if you get your health chunked to less than half because you'll be at a snails pace. Probs not an issue on easy or normal but on hard it sucks due to the severe lack of resources.Also WHY are breakable objects the primary way of getting resources when you don't have a melee option?? All out of bullets and one hit away from death but can clearly see a health pack in a glass bottle? Bet you want that huh? Too bad! No bullets, guess you better snail walk across the map and pray you find one just sitting out in the open. Just a baffling decision. It clearly takes inspiration from RE4 in that regard, but like, you had a knife and could always slow jog in Re4 classic.Idk, don't let nostalgia and steam reviews trick you into thinking this thing is some masterpiece. It's derivative at best and sloppy at worst. If you want a good indie survival horror experience, buy Conscript instead. That game  had a good deeper message and actually made me feel a bit gross with myself after the credits rolled (and during the game) which is a Hallmark of a good horror/war story. It's a shame this title got all the attention instead.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is how you'd expect it to be, the style and care of old videogames with modern systems and gameplay. The story is interesting, and possibly the scariest part of the game. There isn't cheap horror, is the setting of it all that is haunting. It is a short game in the best sense possible, and there are some systems focused on replayability, giving a different experience.My only complaint with the game is that it is way too easy, it seems the gameplay (without the story) should be about choosing which enemies to kill and managing resources as in old Resident Evil games, but you are never in a position where an any enemy really blocks your path. I hope this changes in the Hard mode, and that players expecting this kind of challenge are the scope of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: What a phenomenal title; it is such a genuine love-letter to the classic survival horrors that clearly inspired its conception, but strays far enough away from any definitive style that it is allowed to forge its own identity. With noteably modernisations to allow for approachability where the classics tend to feel more cumbersome for a modern audience, and a brilliant story that doesn't fall into complicated or convoluted plot threads, this is a great game for survival horror newbies to find some footing in the genre, while still offering enough that veterans will have a good time as well. If you're a fan of horror games at all, do yourself a favour and play this one.

_childDocuments_.review: A survival horror game that takes inspiration from PS1 era survival horror games and absolutely knocks it out the park in terms of sound design and atmosphere while still doing its own thing.First off, Crow Country is probably one of the most accessible survival horror games I've seen. Normal difficulty is quite forgiving with the plethora of items lying around and all the tips that are discoverable in the form of sign postings to bring would-be newcomers up to speed with expectations or inherent understanding that veteran players of the genre would approach the game. Even then, if it's still too difficult, there's also an Exploration mode, eliminating enemy aggression altogether. This game is now going to be my go-to whenever someone new to the genre asks me for recommendations. It's perfect for getting your feet wet with the genre.In terms of atmosphere, this game is immaculate. Steeped in a visual design that emulates pre-rendered objects and backgrounds, is this sense of noisiness. Areas are littered with bits of trash, discarded cups and popcorn buckets, dusty and unused construction materials, creating this sense of business that grounds the pretense that this amusement park used to be bustling with people -- a better time. An the sense of emptiness in the wake of that adds to the feeling of eerieness and unease. It especially contrasts in the more themed areas of the park where the garbage all over the place really drives home the sense that the park was largely abandoned fairly quickly. Overall the I think the aim of the visual style is executed perfectly.Gameplay-wise Crow Country plays very much like, well, a survival horror game. You have resources that you need to manage and need to actively make the conscious decision to either engage adversaries or run away from them, often only dispatching ones that would get in the way of repeated traversal of areas you might revisit. Combat involves a risk/reward tradeoff, as the closer you are to enemies the more damage your bullets do. Movement is tight and very well within the expected range you'd expect a protagonist of a survival horror to move. One thing of note is that I would consider Crow Country to be slightly more puzzle-oriented than the conventional survival horror game. This isn't a bad thing; I'd argue it's a differentiating factor for the game, because the way the puzzle routing is structured works very well. When paying attention, all puzzles link into one another quite cleanly in a way that feels satisfying. All in all, the gameplay is very polished and refined.One thing I can't believe, is that the game is only 19$ US for how well put together it is. Frankly, I think the devs are a little nuts. This is easily worth more.A lot of love went into this game and I can tell. And while I don't know if SFB Games plans to consider making other survival horror games in the future, I'll definitely be there to try them out if that comes to pass.Thank you for making such a delightful game.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game, but it may not be for everyone, even those who enjoy the genre. If you're interested in the store description at all, then it's definitely worth checking out. I'm going to highlight some of the things that people might dislike in order to help you make a more informed decision. Crow Country is rather short, maybe too short for the price tag - I completed it in just over 6 hours while thoroughly exploring and backtracking. However it does offer strong replay value, with many hidden secrets, a scoring system, and new items and challenges that get unlocked upon beating the game. I'm definitely going to go back in for more.The real charm of the game is the graphics and the overall presentation. I grew up in the Gamecube/PS2 era so I dont have any nostalgia for this style of graphics, but regardless it still evoked that classic, retro feel for me.Every room is meticulously crafted to have a specific mood and feel to it, and the rooms change as you progress through the game.The important parts of the story are directly told to the player, but there's tons of extra documents scattered throughout the park that you can look for that help to flesh out the characters and the history of the park. In my thorough search, I missed 4 of the 15 secret items, so there's definitely a good challenge in finding everything.The puzzles and key item progression are all rather straightforwards. Serviceable, to where anyone could solve them given enough time, but left me wanting a bit more of a challenge, but I did still enjoy them all.There's also an in-game hint counter that you can use up to 10 times in case you get stuck or lost. I ended up using it twice myself, but only to confirm that I was looking in the right spots. You can definitely complete the game without using them once, so I see them as a good accessibility option.There is one "puzzle" I want to mention specifically though. While optional for a weapon upgrade, the solution is purely brute force, *and* contradictory to the clues given. For anyone wanting to know what it is going into it, the "puzzle" is in the , and the "solution" is to  There are interactables in the room that would seem like hints, but they're all entirely irrelevant. I'm hesitant to call this setpiece a bad inclusion, but it is something I would say needed more work. The combat is a bit too easy, and most of my healing was from environmental damage. I also finished the game with nearly capped resources when fighting my last enemies, and the only times I went below "caution" health was in the puzzle mentioned above. Granted, I explored , but I never felt like I was really needing to manage resources whatsoever. The lack of a difficulty slider, besides "enemies" and "no enemies", is also something to make note of if you want a challenge. The enemies can be strafed around with no challenge at all, at least when using modern movement. The tank controls, while significantly slower, are probably the best way to play the game. I don't find myself getting scared easily, and Crow Country was no exception. There were a few times I was naturally jumpscared, but the extent of the horror was in exploration and finding new enemies.Despite all of the games flaws, it was an amazing experience, and I ended up finishing in one long sitting. I'll definitely be looking forwards to future releases from SFB Games.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr I loved the game start to finish only part of the game that I thought was actually unenjoyable and bad was the mushroom puzzle due to it having a lot of rng that can change how many healing you have to use.Gameplay feels great. Obviously best to use a controller, but controller wise it feels like a very responsive modern game while still having a control scheme in the default that lets you play same as the older games, like RE1, Parasite Eve, etc. Controls are intuitive and intelligent, the flow to map from inventory is very comfortable. You can obviously just hit select, too, but being able to just tap LB -> RB feels very convenient. Having the aiming reticle exist is such a big +. I hated the older survival horror games where you vaguely magic a bullet into a general direction. Here, there is actual precise targeting, and it leads to a lot of very interesting interactions with the world outside of combat. Crowquest was extremely fun, and a lot of puzzles that require use of your guns is cool, too.I just wish melee was a thing (barring the bonus item); but judging by the tutorial notes, I can tell it was very deliberate to make you decide on whether or not you want to burn a resource to check what's inside a container; on my S run, I did actually find myself low on ammo a few times and restrained myself from breaking things. If I could just run up and knife it, the item economy would be even worse. But, to be fair, I still think the item economy is really bad, even in Murder of Crows. I do not feel like Murder of Crows honestly changes too much. There are slightly less loot sources, and now you can get single rounds instead of whole boxes which replace some spawns, that's about it. The only real motivator for feeling threatened is the scoring system; which it would be more threatening on sight if you actually saw what was being taken into consideration for that score. Would really suggest showing the rules of the different game modes imo.Loot is extremely plentiful, and I never really feel bad burning ammo to mow the lawn. The enemies are just not a threat.All being said I had a nonstop blast with the game, and as soon as I beat the game I went for my S run...then crows quest...and then my murder of crows run...and the whole time I was having more fun with this game that most games I've played.I think puzzles are really good but imbalanced. I will admit, I do love playing a second run and being able to "sequence break" the game by having knowledge you canonically shouldn't have. The game does drastically change as a result, and it's pretty easy to know the map like the back of your hand in a short amount of time because of how specific and detailed the different zones are. On the first run, there was maybe 2 puzzles that I got stuck on. One was the Mushroom Puzzle, because the hints on the wall gave the impression that you only want to eat the safe ones, and ignore or figure out how to get rid of the poisonous ones.Puzzle 1 I had a problem with, this is the one I actually hated in the game and have a big issue with just existing.Puzzle 2 I had a problem with:Otherwise, I do understand why there are a  of simple puzzles. On a first playthrough, they are simple puzzles you simply don't fully understand yet, and then an event happens to distract you from being able to fully comprehend what's going on, despite it being extremely simple. I think puzzles are overall extremely well paced and progress from simple to complex in a very entertaining way! The octopus puzzle is probably my favorite one because of it's subtlety. You will see the actual hint long before you know it's a hint Premise  is infinitely better than Resident Evil. Mara is an amazing character with a lot of soft humor that still feels accurate to the setting for the character's perception.  The enemies are very cool to me; I think the introductions to them are extremely unnerving and work very well with the enemy unique ambiance. the Spindle, for example. When you first enter back in the square, and hear the atmosphere, you won't be able to see Spindle immediately. So it's just incredibly unnerving and unique music and then you just see this big ♥♥♥♥. They do this a lot, and every time it's really cool to me. Big story stuff here. I don't really have many comments on the story. If you follow the staff notes, and listen to all of the dialogue, you should get an extremely intuitive and good picture. The story was a very fun background to all of the events; but the world building I think easily trumps it. The creators behind this game KNOW how to create worlds, and I can't wait to see more from them on something else. I'll be watching!!!!This game is an extremely easy recommend at full price, I'd still buy it at 40; already gifted it to a few friends and they love it, too. Buy it!!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Even though I had fun with this game and stuck with it to the end, my recommendation is to wait for a sale. The game does have its charms and aspects I enjoyed, but it feels like there is something I disliked for each part I liked. It's also not a long game, about 5 hours or less on normal, which was what I played. I should note that I wasn't playing optimally and was occasionally wandering around looking for secrets or lore. I'm not someone who wants $1 per hour of gameplay or something like that because I believe that short games can be worth the price if they are really good, but I always scrutinize a game more heavily if they are under 10 hours or so as a general principle.Lets start with the good. I mainly have three points for this section which are the setting, ascetics, and the puzzles. With the location being a theme park, it allows for a decent verity of locations to explore and the types of obstacles and puzzles to solve. The devs put effort into making each area feel different and identifiable and thus make it easier to locate specific points you want to go to, even though it's map size is on the smaller side so you shouldn't have trouble navigating. It's easy to see from the store page that the ascetic design is meant to emulate PS1/early 3D games and they made sure to ingrain it into many aspects from level design to gameplay. Character models are low detail/poly, compared to the environment, and help contrast against the enemies who have much more detail and grotesque designs. The puzzles were often times nice little breaks from running around the map and fighting enemies; even though none really caused me to get stuck from its difficulty. Puzzles can range from simple ones which just require the information/resources within a room, to a few that span the entire map and might require visiting multiple locations and reading various notes to solve. There are some parts that I would call okay or passable, which I should note are not major marks against it, but they are areas that I felt like could have been improved easily. The main culprit being the combat which is a multi-layered situation, and the controls. The game wants you to do two things during combat: aim for the head and let them get close which will deal more damage. However, your aim will have constant sway which makes it hard to aim because its fairly significant sway, and enemies often times have unpredictably jerky head movement which can even move to near 90 degree angles. With that said, it sounds like this should be a negative, but it isn't because of the following gameplay mechanics. You're disincentive from combat because you gain nothing for killing enemies, and they'll respawn eventually so you can't even permanently clear a room, only temporarily. It's only worth it to kill enemies if it's a boss, or if it's blocking something, otherwise you just run past them which is easy. Furthermore, because you're now stockpiling ammo, the game's loot system decides to just give you nothing when searching crates and trash bins because it's trying to keep you from having too much ammo, even though there is a max carry limit for each ammo type. Controls are a bit more simple to explain. Don't play this on keyboard and mouse, it feels awful, and it's clearly designed for a controller. If you do play with a controller, it's fine; even though I wish some of the duplicate button inputs were instead used for giving the map a dedicated button. I'll also re-mention the game length because it is short for $20 US, but it tries to make up for it with unlockables, secrets, and challenges that you can try out on subsequent playthroughs after your first complete run.Unfortunately, this is the point where I need to point out the issues. I'll keep this contained to my two major complaints which are the notes system, and the story to some extent. The notes system is just bad, and feels like a placeholder. All notes are tracked in a notebook in every save room which means that you must run back to a save room whenever you want to reference them, unless you write them down or take a picture of them, but this isn't the bad part. Every note is just text on a plain background with a number, and all the notes in the game are sorted according to their number. However, it seems like there is no thought put into why they're placed into the spot they are in the notebook because you have to cycle through them each time you're searching for a specific note with instructions or a code. This isn't bad in the beginning but becomes awful late game because note 1 might be from the start, note 2 is end game, note 3 is somewhere in the middle, and so on. I spent a decent amount of time just cycling through notes because I didn't memorize the exact number of the note I needed and there are 40 of them, and since they are all text on a plain background, I had to read enough of each one to determine if it was the one I needed or not. There is no way to filter it, or change its sorting, you are just stuck shuffling through each and every one. This one major flaw kept taking me out of the experience and lessened my enjoyment. While I do have the story in the flaws section, it's not nearly as egregious as the previous. It's more that the story was losing me by the end, and especially during a specific plot revelation during the end. The characters are fine if simple and do a little bit of work to flesh out the setting, but I just didn't care for them mostly. I think only one character helps you directly and the rest just spout exposition or lore you already discovered in a note an hour earlier. Aside from characters, my issue with the story is in how the park relates to it, and the final revelation about the monsters.  It's honestly not that bad, but it was just something that was nagging me once I thought about it. As for the monster reveal,  When I reached what I considered late game, the notes issues, and general waning interest gave me a little difficulty in wanting to finish it, but I did because I was still having some fun with it. Admittedly, I think I should have played this all in one go instead of taking multi-day breaks in between playing it for a hour or so; that may have helped me keep my motivation for playing this.I do want to mention one more thing before I write my conclusion, and it's that I was mentally comparing this to another indie survival horror game while playing, and that game was Signalis. Unfortunately, I think this caused the various issues with Crow Country to be more apparent, since I think Signalis is the better game after beating Crow Country. Especially because they are both retro styled survival horror games that both cost the same amount, $20 US.To wrap this up. Crow Country is a fine game with some good, a lot okay, and some bad aspects throughout. I had fun with it and liked a decent amount of the puzzles and level design/environment, but it's held back by its flaws and odd design decisions. If it's on sale and your interested, I would say to pick it up since the devs were trying to make something unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Modern Survival Horror Masterpiece. Takes a lot of tropes from all kinds of horror games and videos and films. Yet merges them all so seemlessly, so effectively and passionately that it stands on it's own. The smooth gameplay and animations kept me playing, the great sound design and enemy design kept me scared and the narrative kept me guessing, creating a captivating mystery. But I could still piece it together for a real sense of satisfying closure in the end. (With a great bone chilling addition to it that I love "2106")Crow Country is terrifying and so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun. HIGHLY recommend especially for horror fans. Sometimes it's better to not know.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country understands everything that makes classic survival horror games appealing, while still being deeply original. From the interconnected map, to the heavy atmosphere, to the strategy of which enemies to kill and which to run past, to the horror of not knowing what will be around the next corner (all while having a cute art style), I love every moment of it.It even has a ranking system, unlockable items and tons of secrets like a retro survival horror game should have.If you're intimidated by old survival horror games, Crow Country also works as an excellent entry point with accessibility features, a hint system, and dynamic difficulty somewhat akin to RE4.Crow Country is a modern masterpiece in my opinion, and I recommend it to anyone with an interest in horror.

_childDocuments_.review: Must-play for PSX survival horror fans.Even though fight is a bit wonky sometimes (most of the time felt too easy on the medium difficulty level, also one of the enemies got me stuck next to the wall), the mechanics are ok. You can also play in adventure mode, without any monsters.I feel like Crow Country is a really strong adventure game. Puzzles are interesting and non-repetitive. There are a lot of secrets to be found and you will find good reasons to replay this game.I LOVED aesthetics and graphics, music and sound design is also quite well done.Overall, I really enjoyed this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a tight well paced survival horror game. While a bit on the easy side I found the combat to be satisfying enough after I turned down the default sensitivity on my controller. The real meat and potatoes is the exploring the amusement park itself and the puzzles. The puzzles are legitimately good. Some just boil down to finding a note with the code on it, which is par for the course, but the best ones really do require you to think about what is being asked and engage with the game on it's own terms. The optional puzzles for some of the secrets are definitely the hardest and require some out of the box thinking and as such are the most satisfying. There was really only one puzzle that I felt was too obscure for it's own good but even then the method of finding the answer was satisfying and intuitive in it's own way.As of this writing I have finished my first playthrough with a time of 8 hours and a rank of A+ and I'm ready to go through for round two for some new game plus goodies. I do hope the title continues to get some updates added in the future as I find the game charming, funny, and often times clever. Give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a solid throwback at classic survival horror games like Silent Hill and Resident Evil. A fantastic art style and overall great atmosphere help it make up for gameplay that lacks challenge and tension a great survival horror experience promises to deliver. A must play for fans and those who are new to the genre!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a fantastic throwback to the PlayStation 1 days, with graphics and a vibe that will remind you of classic Resident Evil. The story is engaging with a great plot twist and some genuinely funny dialogues that keep things lighthearted. The survival horror element is spot on, with plenty of enemies to keep you entertained. I'm looking forward to trying out the hard mode when it comes out. If you're into survival horror with a retro feel, I definitely recommend giving Crow Country a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for an oldschool Survival Horror game then you have come to the right place! It's easy to see that it's inspired by old  Resident Evil and Silent Hill games. At first the story may seem cliche but it has a really nice twist at the end.There is lots of puzzles and they are nicely balanced, not hard but also not braindead easy. Sadly not all of them are well done, looking at you Mushroom puzzle.As i said before oldschool survival horror so the controls are clunky, you will travel from room to room looking for key items and fighting/avoiding enemies.What else can i say?The game is really great! I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: SFB games really nailed the retro aspect of the game, whether it's for the music, ambiance or visual. The game is not very long you can extend your game time with the hard mode and the collectibles which are pretty fun to do. As a survival horror game, we can go through all the usual elements: ammunition management, puzzle, weapon upgrades, hidden items. There is not a lot of innovation on this side, but the game should be played for it's PS1 style before all.The game is really worth the try
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A great little game for a weekend. I actually really enjoyed the twist of the story, and the game is breezy enough to 100% just for fun.Nothing negative to say except for 2 "Puzzles"   ***Spoilers***1: The Mushroom Puzzle. I think the mushrooms that are safe should heal you, while not counting towards your ranking, making it an actual puzzle rather than just "Eat all the mushrooms".2: Getting the Shotgun. This one is probably more on me, but maybe some text with the Plastic Gun could be changed. I took way to long to figure out that I had to use the Handgun to shoot the targets. Getting the puzzle right is no problem, it was figuring out that I didn't need to "Fix" the plastic gun, I just needed to shoot the targets with my actual Handgun. Having played a lot of Survival Horror games, I figured I needed to fix the thing instead shooting my lovely stockpile of ammo into it. It made every gamer instinct in me recoil in disgust, LOL.Highly recomend, great job!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game more. the story is amazing. i was always itching to find out what would happen next. it made almost any part of the game that could've been considered bad, good. the atmosphere of the game with the audio and visual effects pulls you into the game and feel any emotions or tension needed. the puzzles are interesting and unique, each one completely different than the last. the combat is forgiving and can even be avoided entirely, but won't hesitate to challenge you if you let it. this game is amazing, and i completely recommend it to anyone looking for a semi horror game with the best story you haven't read. if they somehow made a sequel to this game, i'd buy it in a heartbeat.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A very focused, condensed survival-horror experience that takes all the familiar trappings of classic survival-horror games like Resident Evil or Silent Hill and strips it down to the bare essentials of strange puzzles with key items and traversing a zone that you will become intimately familiar with as you blast hostile monsters, or don't and navigate around them. The puzzles can be weird with opaque solutions, but the experience of living in the Crow Country theme park and getting embroiled within its mystery and intrigue involving the people behind the park itself and the origin of its hostile creatures.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute banger. Do not get spoiled on this one. Not super long, so replay value to get S-Rank is there (yes you get something for doing well). If you're a Resident Evil or Silent Hill veteran, this isn't very hard. You can beat it in under 5 hours if  you get hooked like I did, and I got A+ rank on my first playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is pleasant and refreshing horror game. The story is great and easy to follow, with certain twists explaining what seemingly felt like plot-holes early on.I greatly appreciate that every item is used more than once, and Mara doesn't just go "welp this served its purpose" and leaves their things all around. _childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

I got a bit stuck a few times because I just forgot certain things existed, like a computer terminal I saw earlier, but mostly the puzzles were just right for me. _childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game all around! The atmosphere was great and made my first playthrough tense and terrifying! The following play throughs were a fun rush and I couldn't stop playing this game! The hardest mode "murder of crows" puts a spin on your previous learned material and brings you back to the old RE days. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking to find a great scare with lovable graphics and design.
