_childDocuments_.review: With a blend of graphics and gameplay that harkens back to the PSX's golden days, Crow Country not only stirs up nostalgia but also carves its own path as a unique and successful game. It offers a fresh perspective on the survival horror genre, setting itself apart from the crowd.For those who fondly remember the era of survival horror games on the original PlayStation, Crow Country will feel like a warm reunion. It's a game that embraces the hallmarks of the genre: tank controls, save rooms, fixed camera angles, and tight gameplay that beckons you to explore and solve the mysteries scattered around for better equipment.Immerse yourself in the role of special agent Mara Forest, taking on a mission of utmost importance. Your task is to uncover the truth behind the enigmatic Edward Crow, the owner of Crow Country amusement park, who mysteriously vanished two years ago after the park's sudden closure.In true Murphy's Law fashion, everything that can go wrong does, and Mara finds herself amid mysterious zombie-like creatures lurking in every corner of the park, and that's where our adventure begins.As you explore the park, you'll encounter a complex structure filled with traps, secret passages, and a variety of critical items. These elements, reminiscent of games in the same genre, add depth and challenge to the gameplay. In true Resident Evil fashion, you'll need to navigate various attractions, evade enemies, and collect a range of trinkets to unlock new areas. The thrill of these challenges will keep you on the edge of your seat, eager to see what's next.Crow Country amusement park has all the Raccoon City hallmarks, as you'll need to find masks, batteries, keys, a joystick, gasoline, and even acid.As always, the overall loop is very satisfying. Games like this live or die by how cohesive and interconnected the areas are and how enjoyable it feels to solve riddles to open up new regions without clear direction. The sense of accomplishment when you finally crack a problematic puzzle is gratifying.Crow Country shines in this sense with its repetitive puzzles, interesting gameplay touches, and organic, well-thought-out map that has you searching for clues around every corner. It's nothing too complicated and follows a consistent difficulty level throughout.Crow Country excels in creating an immersive atmosphere. The park is shrouded in a palpable sense of dread, heightened by a haunting soundtrack that echoes the eerie soundscapes of Signalis and Alisa. The detailed backgrounds and subtle animations further enhance the game's moody atmosphere, with the lighting playing a crucial role in setting the tone.In terms of narrative, while the main story writing is on a certain level without too much nuance, the overall line and its resolution are commendable. Interacting with items or notes scattered around the environment also reveals some fascinating background stories and events in the game. Many of these descriptions can be deciphered not just to fulfill a decorating task but instead to reveal a mystery - a new weapon, a weapon-specific attachment (Laser Pointer), or an upgrade to an existing gun, for example - or to reveal more about the motivation of a named character in the game.There are some excellent additions to the tried-and-true formula in Crow Country. For example, in some areas, you'll find fortune teller kiosks, which you can consult several times in a game to get clues about what to do next. The first clue will maintain a degree of ambiguity, but if you need another clue, the next one will be much clearer. In this way, you can get tips on what to do in places where you are currently stuck in the game. In addition, notebooks are placed in the save rooms - these collate all the staff notes/information you've found so far and are very useful for determining how to solve a particular puzzle or where to go depending on which location is open. You can also choose between two difficulties when starting the game, 'survival horror' or 'exploration,' which ensures that you don't get attacked by any of the game's enemies and instead focus on solving puzzles and exploring the park. In short, those who don't like challenges and want to explore the story will find what they want here.Like Signals, Crow Country doesn't have as restrictive a viewpoint as its esoteric counterpart, but it uses free aiming for its shooting mechanics. But pairing this gameplay with fixed camera environments leads to mixed results. At times, you'll find yourself dragging the crosshair into ridiculous places. You have equipment here, such as your standard pistol or shotgun. You pull out your weapon of choice, and a crosshair appears where you can freely aim at any target. It's cumbersome but functional, and as we'll discuss later, enemy behavior serves this particular mechanic, but dodging enemies in the environment often becomes the more attractive option.The game is set in an amusement park, which gives Crow Country many options for where it can place you without sticking strictly to one central theme. You'll find yourself in the clutches of a haunted mansion, a dungeon, or even a sinister sea world. Diversity will be one of the factors that will allow you to progress without getting bored. There are mechanics such as rummaging through boxes or kicking vending machines to find supplies such as medicine kits, grenades, ammunition, or antidotes, which will keep you in constant search. We also have the luxury of eliminating enemies by interacting with fuel barrels and wall-mounted electrical boxes.Like the original Resident Evil series inspired by the game, enemies in Crow Country roam often and don't actively interact with you unless you're nearby. While they're not precisely stationary, each one moves gruelingly, and you must get close to their line of sight to anger them. Due to their placement, running away from them is often a good option, but occasionally, clearing up allows you to move around freely.Crow Country is a lovingly built, most extraordinary hits mix of retro horror ideas remixed and polished to create a perfect light-hearted memory of what those games were all about. It's derivative by design but in a way that feels more like a competitor to the source material as much as a copy. Obviously, for fans of old horror and modern retro PSX scares, this is an excellent addition to the genre, but Crow Country is also a great game in its own right.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Short version:Great game. I want another one.Long version (spoiler free):Everything from the art style to sound design is full of charm. I played the game on normal (survival horror) mode, which I admit was surprisingly easy. I personally didn't find this a negative, and the devs have added a more difficult mode for those wanting that kind of an experience (I will likely do a run on it, too). There is also a full on exploration mode, which I think is really nice of the devs to put in. It did feel a bit hand-holding at times, but I don't think it was to the point of being patronizing. While some of it was pretty obvious, and it may have taken away some element of discovery, I think it just added to the fact the devs clearly wanted to make the game very accessible.The gameplay feels good and fluid, the controls are very responsive. Its like playing an old classic horror game without the clunkiness often associated with them. I personally loved that the game did not take itself too seriously, but the silliness never compromised the atmosphere.That's the most prevalent feature of the game in my opinion. The charm. Its everywhere. And I love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game, great to play with a controller. Really brings the feeling of an old PS1 Resident Evil-like game. Characters were fun, music was great, gameplay was on par with the time it's trying to mimic.I even liked it enough to do an entire second run, trying for 100% No-hit. Unfortunately I fell just short of an S+ Rank, but it was a great time.Overall this game is a definite recommendation from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: solid game, it's visually beautiful for what it's going for. When I realized i could move the camera, my mind was blown, I thought the game was in a fixed camera like the classic Resident evil games. the game also doesn't treat you like an idiot when it comes to the story, all the clues are laid out for you and your character also picks up on that too. ***SPOILERS***my one gripe is that there aren't any alternate endings as far as i can tell. the way some character interactions are set up, it made me feel like i can change the story outcome, but it's the same ending regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine the graphics of Final Fantasy 7 with the gameplay of Silent Hill and you basically get Crow Country. Keep in mind that this is basically an indie title made by very few people.The puzzles will make you think a bit, but aren't too hard - I actually did find all secrets except for one (which I simply missed due to perspective). If you're stuck, the game has a hint system, which can be used up to 10x.Aiming is pretty awful. But other than that, combat is not particularly challenging. The focus clearly is more on the puzzles. It has spooky moments, but is otherwise not exactly an intense horror game.The entire area of the game isn't huge and is limited to a theme park - It took me 6 hours to finish the game incl. all secrets the first time. Quite ok, but I did hope to get beyond the theme park.Overall I liked it and I'd certainly get a sequel if one is ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: i really, really love this game!!! i've been looking forward to it for a while and i'm so happy i finally got to play it in full!! the best way i can describe it is really cute in a horrifying way. i love the characters (especially tolman and julie!) and the monster design is definitely terrifying. i was definitely scared to turn corners and go thru dark hallways. i love the atmosphere, the soundtrack, pretty much everything. it's super reminiscent of and clearly inspired by classic survival horror, but also has enough of its own personality to set it apart from those classics. i ADORE this game and i'll be playing it over and over again!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: okay so this game isn't scary, but thats okay. Its extremely engaging and just over all enjoyable. People complain about tank /bad controls don't realize that it's the point. its a puzzle game, and fighting is something you have to do in order to survive, not something that should be the most fun, fluid combat system for you to max out your style gauge on
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a blast from the past using a polygon art style that is akin to Final Fantasy 7 that was released back in 1997 on the playstation 1, that will be a draw for many people to feel that nostalgia through how the game presents itself. The game is a short one but it sets out to do everything it wanted to do in that short time, the story was fun and serviceable and had some predictable twists if you’re paying attention to dialogue. After that the gameplay is paying homage to the classic horror puzzle genre many people have grown to love like the old Resident Evil games, Parasite Eve, or Dino Crisis. You’re put in the large amusement park of “Crow Country” playing as protag Mara. You’ll be running all over the park solving puzzles and collecting one item that will eventually help you get more items to open that one door you’ve been passing by but couldn’t open. The gameplay loop is familiar and it works pretty well here. If you have played the classic horror puzzle games I had previously mentioned in my review then you know how the “gunplay” works here, it’s slow and a bit clunky but that’s on purpose, you don’t have to fight every monster you see and don’t have shoot evert trap everything can be easily ran passed if you so choose. I don’t have much to say about the game beyond what I've already said. If you like those classic hor/puz games and that polygon style of ff7 you’ll likely have a lot of fun playing this game. It’s short and simple and a quick bit of fun. I don’t smoke cigarettes, and I don’t drink coffee.  TL;DR FUN GAME THAT PLAYS OFF THE CLASSIC HORROR PUZZLE GENRE IF YOU LIKE THE FF7 POLYGON STYLE OF OLD YOU'LL LIKE IT
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a 10/10, at least for me.The style and atmosphere really brings to mind the survival horror vibes of old while having it's own identity. It was always exciting to see what the next area would bring! The story has also super engaging and was amazing to experience and learn throughout the playthrough! It really drew me into the experience and the world of Crow Country, and offered many interesting surprises and revelations!Puzzles were created in a way where if you were focused and observant, then every puzzle was absolutely solvable, nothing random or obtuse. On top of all of that, the replay value of the game as well is increased with the ranking system and fun unlockables! The funny dialogue at times was also a nice touch!Super awesome game all around, no complaints, everyone play it please :D
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent survival-horror game. The puzzles are well designed, though the game is basically nothing but puzzles. The gameplay itself is also simple, there's effectively no reason to play this game rather than Silent Hill or Resident Evil if you haven't played those games yet. The story is simple and the plot twists are simple. I enjoy that there is a lot of attention to detail to the environment, and it seems like a well-crafted world. You will have to play this game with a pen and paper since the game won't write codes for you, and some puzzles are easier with it. There's one puzzle in particular that is extremely poorly crafted (the mushroom one) that unfortunately comes early in the game, but the rest are fine despite this mishap.The "message" the game tries to deliver you is way too in-your-face and obvious for me to enjoy it personally. I'm referring specifically to the statement it has on society. It had good pacing until the end when it just sort of spells it all out for you. I like to speculate, but it's not possible here.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A simply beautiful game that harkens back to the Resident Evils and Silent Hills of yesteryear, while providing an experience and control scheme more palatable to gamers with modern sensibilities. Everything about this game is just perfect. The combat, the visuals, the environment, the sound, the atmosphere, it all comes together to make a truly unsettling and proper survival horror experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little survival horror game, would recommend. As someone who grew up in the N64/PS1 era, this game felt like home. It's in that wonderful category of retro style graphics I would describe as how I remember it looking rather than what it actually looked like. Especially when it comes to the camera and controls.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: FANTASTIC PS1 Era-Inspired Survival Horror experience. Quite a complete package and packed to the brim with secrets, substance and style. Modern control scheme with the ability to play the "authentic experience" tank-style controls (on a controller with a stick AND a d-pad) without even having to open the settings is awesome and well thought-out! A surprisingly deep and complex plot unveils itself as you open the park up more and more. The game carries itself with humble self-awareness leading to some pretty good gags and some anti-conditioning pranks for genre veterans that really help this game feel like a love letter to the games that made survival horror what it is today.I have to give props to the sound design and anyone that worked on sfx, it's used well in this game and every rattle or groan the enemies make doesn't sound cheesy or immersion-breaking. Surprisingly lengthy and with high replay value, Crow Country is worth the price tag in that you ABSOLUTELY get you money's worth of entertainment if you enjoy the horror genre at all (or even puzzle games), and also support indie creators that get to create the things THEY want to. This is one of my favorite indie titles in memory, and the cozy CRT vibes it gives will certainly be revisited by me time and time again.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Classic style survival horror with FF7/PS1 graphics, what's not to love? A fun, well paced and well designed game that I will return to from time to time. Shooting took some getting used to and at first I didn't really enjoy it but it grew on me. The music is phenomenal, especially Fairytale Town. Indie's are keeping survival horror alive and this is one of the best non RE/SH game I've played.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: runs flawlessly on the steam deckI beat the game in 5.3 hours in my first casual playthrough. It's a fantastic game and one of the best survival horror games ive played in some time. I did not get every secret and ending up with a B+ rank. I was able to get some cool unlocks that allow for replay-ability which im excited to do. Very happy to have bought this day one and i really hope there is a sequel
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect survival horror if you find the likes of resident evil a bit too muchLess emphasis on inventory management while leaning more into exploration and puzzle solving fits into a good niche in the genre. A great little story that, while fairly predictable about halfway through, is still delivered well.Emulates the ps1 aesthetic while keeping the advantages of modern game design. It's been executed just perfectly the whole way through. You wont regret this one
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing survival horror game with PS1 graphics taking inspiration from Resident Evil and Silent Hill. Go through a theme park that only gets more and more creepy as you make your way through some fun puzzles and uncover the mystery of what is happening. Beat the game in one sitting and actually got stuck in a few places. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys survival horror and some secret hunting. Though some of the secrets I looked up because I still have no idea how you were suppose to discover some of them with out, granted that was only 2 but still they seemed completely arbitrary. Maybe I didn't read some notes hard enough but who knows.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: They really nailed the old school graphical aesthetics of this game. If you believe that modern horror games have to have hyper realistic graphics to be scary this game may really change your mind. The atmosphere is consistently creepy. The enemy designs are creepy. The music and sounds are creepy. Love that there is an option to use tank controls like the original RE games. It feels like this developer really put their heart and soul and admiration for original RE and SH games into this game. Totally recommend if this type of game is your vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a ton of fun! Total flashback to playing on the old CRT in your parents house. The puzzles are simple if you are smart, making it a little short like people have been saying, but if you are like me then itll be hours of entertainment.  If you have a steam deck its a must buy, the smaller screen really helps.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, bite-sized Resident Evil in an aesthetic I didn't know I needed in my life. The graphics are if Twinsen explored Silent hill, but with the vibe of a Five Night at Freddy's Funko Pop. Part of me wishes it was a little longer, but another part of me is delighted that it didn't overstay its welcome. 3.75/5.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Really damn good. I had some issues with the awkward camera angle, and the overly twitchy aiming, but the incredible atmosphere, story, and overall audiovisual presentation was seriously next level. The story in this game is presented better than most AAA titles.Play this NOW if you like survival horror, metroidvania style exploration, or games with fascinating lore and worldbuilding.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan of Resident Evil or Silent Hill, this game blends all aspects and invents a fun and interesting game. The puzzles are forgiving but yet challenging at the same time. Most of the combat is optional (except for bosses) and makes it a fun and enjoyable experience for people who are new to the genre and veterans of this genre. If you haven't already added this to your cart, do it now.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Game is very good, it's got all the good stuff you would want from a game similar to old RE and Silent Hill.  My only problems with the game is it's too easy, the enemies don't feel very threatening, inventory management is non existent as the game lets you hold everything you pick up so you don't really have to do any prior plannings in dealing with situations the game lays out.  Also small gripe is as of writing you can't have tank controls on controller set to stick instead of dpad which is lame.  If you like old RE, you should for sure get this game, it doesn't need much else to explain from there as you will get that fix from this, it's just it feels like those games but made a lot more casualized as it's only set back.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Very tight and fun survival horror game! A perfect example of the genre presented in a sort of toy form. I mean that as a compliment! It's short and mostly easy. It's atmosphere and artstyle don't really install fear but they are charming. It's like a PG horror movie from the 80s? When you could do blood and like a few swears and maybe even kill a guy or two but mostly it was a lighthearted adventure. It's a really good adventure! I would easily recommend this to fans of the genre as well as folks just curious about it. Good game!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Basing it's roots on Classical Survival Horror with a twist in it's isometric 3D View, I can attest that the game has a nice albeit short experience of fun. It's design and uniqueness is interesting for a single play-through, but I wouldn't be too keen for future endeavors as the game is easy as is on it's medium difficulty and there aren't a lot of scary moments except a few pop-ups. What captivates though is the cheesiness, exquisite atmosphere and to it's quirkness which sells this game for what's it's worth. (Also that Shout-out to BRASIL is Sublime.)
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Do you enjoy classic survival horror games? How about the sense of foreboding that comes with exploring an abandoned family fun center? Nostalgia for Playstation 1 graphics? Then Crow Country is the game for you. A third person survival horror throwback game where you fill the shoes of Mara Forrest on her mission to find Edward Crow, owner of the Crow Country amusement park.Potentially the best indie survival horror game since Signalis. I highly recommend everyone play the demo if they are on the fence about Crow Country. It will convince you. The vibes coming from this game are near immacualte.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: So far I love the atmosphere, the exploration and puzzles but the game really needs a fix with the enemies, they need to be a little bit faster and definitely more agressive, so far I used my pistol bullets only on puzzles or bottles, I shooted some enemies just for experimentation, not because they were a real threat.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely charming in its story and presentation, and the soundtrack is stellar. I even got some little spooks during my gameplay, loved it!It's a bit short though, but like any good survival horror inspired games it gives you many incentives to replay it (story choices, secrets, bonus weapons...). And replay it I surely wil!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Cool little game, definitely recommend to fans of Silent Hill and Resident Evil. The developer was kind enough to add in some optional modifiers and modes for those who want to experience the game in a more relaxed way (giving the player multiple "lives" and a mode where enemies aren't aggressive). A single playthrough should last around 5-6 hours, and of course there are several hidden secrets and items you can unlock which encourage subsequent playthroughs. Whether that's worth $20 is up to you. Personally I think the price is a *tad* high given the amount of content the game contains, but if it ever goes on sale for like $10-15 I'd heartily recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Simple, quality survival horror with a beautiful visual style, great soundtrack, and intriguing story. Not very difficult if you're a seasoned veteran of the genre but still a fun challenge that's very worth experiencing, especially with all the other points I mentioned in mind. Great puzzles overall; I personally found one or two to be too obtuse for my liking but I'm not exactly the best in the world at puzzles lol. Anyway, please buy this game. It deserves all the praise it's been getting and more.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a fan classical survival horror games, this game is for you. Interesting art direction, challenging but fair puzzles, great level design and a pretty good story with a memorable and charismatic protagonist. The only downside is the combat. It is clunky even for titles this game is adhering to. Also, the game is too easy when it comes to resources, but hard difficulty is on the way, so that might change. And the last minor nitpick - ths game needs to be played with a controller. You can play with keyboard and mouse, but key bindings are bizarre and cannot be changed.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Just a quick Mini-review. Amazing game. Could not put it down. This is such a classic gaming experience. You get everything in one nice package. No in-game store, No horrible unnecessary side quests. No "hold up" to progress padding. No intruding cut scenes, No day one performance patch. No 3rd party launcher to access the game you bought. _childDocuments_.review: Recently, I reviewed the survival horror masterpiece, SIGNALIS, and I considered it to be one of the best fantasies of disempowerment. It was a wonderfully crafted game with a story that was deep and intricate, and the gameplay forced strategic thinking and surgical precision, and I personally enjoyed every second of it.On the other hand, Crow Country is a much simpler game. Much like SIGNALIS, it is molded in the classic survival horror formula, but here, the execution of its elements are simpler. Instead of spreading progression out through multiple maps, Crow Country mostly takes place in one map. Instead of a deep, thoughtful story with thematic interpretations, Crow Country's story is fairly simple and straightforward. None of this makes the game bad at all; in fact, Crow Country is meant to be a more accessible take on the same formula.Much like SIGNALIS, the presentation of Crow Country is pretty simple. Character models are fairly low-fidelity, looking like action figures straight out of the 90s era, which kind of reminds me of the character models seen in Playstation 1 games, which is pretty good. Enough detail exists in the models for there to be cohesion in what they are meant to be, but enough detail is missing for the mind to fill in.The environment design is easily one of the game's biggest strengths. The setting of the Crow Country theme park reminds me heavily of Silent Hill, probably because of the heavy use of fog and dreary lighting. The theme park feels more like an abandoned town; empty of any life that would normally fill it with noise. The music helps enhance the atmosphere, making the game feel more distinctly like Resident Evil, with deep orchestral-sounding hums and occasional grunge.The sound effects are also really good. Every weapon sounds incredibly powerful, with meaty bangs and chunky reload sounds. The enemies mostly use incredibly low grunts and sometimes sludgy sounds to signify their presence in the level. Even the heart monitor in the inventory screen has really good sound design, and it changes based off the player's health status.In terms of gameplay, Crow Country is again molded in the classic survival formula, but with some changes to make it accessible. Instead of limited inventory, the only limit the player has is on how much of each type of ammo they can carry at a time; otherwise, they can carry pretty much everything without worrying about having to do a lot of backtracking. This also means that item boxes don't exist, reducing the backtracking required of the player.Most of the game is spent running around looking for key items to use in a variety of puzzles, and the puzzles are okay. They don't ask much from the player; often they just require them to remember a code and use it on a keypad. Since the map is relatively small, the backtracking itself is less of a hassle, with the main obstacles being whatever enemies are still alive. And thankfully, if the player is stuck, there is a hint system that tells the player what they should try doing.Combat of the game is also incredibly simple. There is no lock-on aim; instead, the player must manually aim their weapon and land shots on enemies. Aiming for the head does the most damage, but it can be quite difficult to land the shot when the enemy is moving towards you with their limbs twitching. For the most part, it is well-designed, and encourages once again a thoughtful approach to combat; however, resources are less limited, and it can be easy to fill up on them relatively quickly, so often times, I saw myself just using the ammo because I knew I would find more really quickly. As such, the tension of combat comes less from having to make the thoughtful decision between fight or flight, and more on trying to land shots on the enemy instead.Overall, I'd describe the gameplay of Crow Country as a more accessible take on survival horror, and there's even a difficulty that removes the enemies, allowing the player to just explore the game to their own leisure. What's quite interesting to me is that even in that difficulty, the player is still expected to use their weapon, since some puzzles actually require them to still use it. The pistol then becomes more of a tool first, and I am quite fond of this approach.Despite this approach, exploration is not compromised. The game heavily incentivizes exploration, as there are tons of treasures to find if you are a puzzle wiz and have a keen eye. I actually like this approach, since the player is strung along to discover things themselves, and the puzzles here are more interesting as well.The story of the game is very simple. You control Mara Forest, an investigator searching for Edward Crow, whose missing persons report was filed by Natalie Crow. Along the way, you encounter a small variety of characters, most of them searching for Edward Crow for their own reasons. The cast of characters are all really good, and they're all decently memorable. I also found Mara to be well characterized; she's stubborn, but also quite caring, and a later twist in the game recontextualizes a lot of the dialogue she has, though I won't spoil it at all. In a world where most indie horror games often have very complex backstories, often unnecessarily so, it's refreshing to see a game where the story itself is actually simple. Even the backstory is well laid out to avoid confusion, and enough is still left up for interpretation.Crow Country is another example of a game to me that proves that old survival horror games were actually good, and that it isn't nostalgia that made them good; they were well-designed from the very start. It's nice to see how indie developers are proving this, and it's something that I wish to see more of. Though I understand that game design will continue to evolve, I hope that older game design won't all be considered outdated, and Crow Country, along with many other indie games replicating the older times of gaming, is one of the best examples of this.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing I only have 6 hours in Crow Country on Steam, but I've played quite a bit more on Switch. This game is pretty incredible with a few little weird hiccups here and there, but there's two things a survival horror game needs to be in my opinion: Good, and Two (2) hours long. Crow Country is both. The plot was surprisingly good, and I was stuck thinking about it for like a week after beating it, The music is top notch as well, really cant say enough good things about the music. The enemies are varied and threatening but not obnoxiously so. It's not the hardest game in the world but on your first run its pretty tough. And its short, therefore replayable. I'm slow at these games so my first run might have been somewhere around 4 hours maybe. And to help its replayability its pretty open ended in the middle. Once you learn the order that things need to be done in there's a little period where things feel a little free form and its nice. A few puzzles have multiple solutions and when me and my brother discussed it we realized we had each solved like half the puzzles differently and never knew about the other solution which was cool. On all fronts that matter its easily a 9.8/10 video gameMy negatives are minor though. There's a notoriously confusing puzzle, not in the way you solve it but why it's solved that way, and a weapon upgrade is locked behind it, So even though an S rank doesn't require you do *all* of the secrets it still kinda sucks that you'll likely end subsequent runs with one weapon not upgraded and one secret not done just because its annoying to do. Sorta related is that ranks don't take clear time into account, and as a result you don't get a clear time on your report card at the end, which not everyone will care about but its a little odd. And the other thing may just be me but the camera angle when coming out of certain doors is a little nefarious and leads to the doorway hiding enemies that are directly in front of you on the ground. By default aiming your gun centers the camera behind you too so you cant line the camera up sideways and shoot things, and there isn't another camera center button. And I guess in that regard you could complain that the game doesn't use fixed camera and tank controls but I personally love how Mara feels to control and I don't mind the camera movement because generally its very good. It just has its moments is allBut yeah, all in all this is a big recommend, if you're a survival horror fan you should play this. I compare it favorably to Signalis if that helps you at all

_childDocuments_.review: I love love love Crow Country. The art style harkening back to old PS1 era survival horrors, the excellent writing of Mara akin to Heather from Silent Hill 3, and the delightful set dressing of the entire game in a hokey theme park, it's just a perfect game for the spooky season. This is a must play.For fellow photosensitive folks, there are only occasional moments such as when you're saving where there is a bright flash. _childDocuments_.review: An exciting, horrifying, and aesthetically pleasing PS1-era survival horror throwback game. Very rarely do I find a game that I purchase and play without any hesitation. I was hooked all the way through. If you're a fan of the era of horror this game is hearkening to, then you should just buy the game already. Experience it for yourself. It's no flawless masterpiece, but it's a lovingly crafted master work just begging to be experienced.It's worth pointing out that Crow Country has some flaws. Quite frankly I didn't find the game all that horrifying from start to finish. Scares were paced out well, but there should've been more. With the game's great visual style and captivating 3D models, I was expecting a bit more from certain assets that didn't really do much. The creepiness of the game's setting and overall presentation hooked me at first, but it waned as I continued playing. I did get scared a few times, but those moments felt unfortunately fleeting. That's not to say this game isn't scary, but I just wish it was scarier. A few pop-up scares got me to jump, and I found that the atmospheric soundtrack paired well with certain unsettling rooms. It helps that the flashlight isn't that helpful. For whatever reason the only flashlight available in Crow Country was a gas station pen light. These are minor issues, though. If anything, this might be a positive for players who aren't that good with horror: this is pretty light, overall. Creepy, unsettling, definitely scary at times, but not overwhelmingly so, which should help players stick with the game if they can brave through the beautifully dreadful amusement park.A major criticism of mine, however, was the writing. Crow Country has a very good trailer which drops some intriguing plot hints, but I found myself disappointed by the actual game's plot. It starts off strong: Mara Forest, our protagonist, heads to Crow Country to do some good, old fashioned police work. However, she makes it clear at the start that she isn't just here because it's her duty as a police officer. There's something else compelling her to explore Crow Country, and I absolutely love that as a plot hook.What follows... isn't all that interesting. Things get revealed, and I don't want to spoil anything, but most everything is predictable. There was , which was interesting, but wasn't enough. While the story was creative, it didn't do enough to keep from being predictable. If you've played a survival horror game, you're probably able to guess why Crow Country is the way it is after you get that first bit of exposition. However, the characters are well written. Mara is a fun protagonist, her dialogue ranges from playful to curt, which helps her feel real. A few other key characters play off one another in such a way as to make their relationship feel real. Some characters don't have much going on, but I still found myself enjoying reading their dialogue. But, there isn't much dialogue in the game. But please, don't let my disappointment with the story dissuade your purchase. There are some fascinating bits of background details, and I found myself appreciating the less important bits of writing (notes, journal entries) since they helped illustrate the game's world and character backstories. The first few Resident Evil games do this really well too, where some notes paint unsettling pictures and stick with you. There's a few notes from this game that will stick with me for a while. Lastly, this game is pretty easy. I finished the game with plenty of healing items and ammo to spare. A few game tips which tell you exactly what the best playstyle is are found pretty early in the game. I struggled the most with the random traps laid throughout the park as you progress. At first there's a few traps placed around the large park quite sporadically, so they're not a problem. Eventually though, you can't walk three steps without getting hurt by something if you're not careful. This sometimes felt cheap, but I adjusted to said traps and they eventually became a minor nuisance. But still, without those traps I would've used far less healing items and ammunition.Crow Country isn't perfect, but if this were to have been a PS1 game, it would've at the very least developed a cult following. This game's proof that you don't need to reinvent the wheel to say you've created something amazing. Sometimes all you need to do is refine the wheel and slap on a vibrant coat of paint to draw in a crowd. A passion project made with love such as this should not be passed up. Sure, the story's not the best, and there's definitely scarier games out there, but Crow Country is the rare game whose quality can be felt deep in the curious observer's heart. Give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I practically never leave reviews for games but Crow Country was so fantastic that not only did I feel compelled to complete it in a single long sitting, but to be a completionist about it AND now scream about it from the rooftops!The low poly and classic render method brought nostalgia whilst modern minds gave puzzles, progression and storytelling that experienced polish. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing through Crow Country. This 3rd Person isometric game is an homage to PSOne era survival horror titles like Resident Evil and Silent Hill (both of which are really evident in the gameplay design and sound respectively). The game takes place in the titular theme park, which was closed down following an accident some two years prior. You play Mara, a young woman that breaks into the park to hunt down its owner, Edward Crow (for reasons that become clear over the course of the game). Though relatively compact, each of the park's zones must gradually be opened up by solving puzzles and hunting down key items: this makes progression and exploration feel really satisfying, particularly since each key can be used in multiple places, yielding lots of goodies and secrets. There's a nice blend of interesting puzzles, from straight-forward observation to slightly more cryptic clue-deciphering: everything makes sense, and if you get stuck, referring to your collection of Staff Memos (which appears in each safe room) usually helps! Despite its cutesy low-poly models, parts of the game are deliciously tense, and there are a couple of well-placed jumpscares too. I really enjoyed the story, which is entertaining without being overbearing.Combat was my least favourite part, solely because of the awkward button-mapping (with no option to rebind). Aiming is done with R1, and shooting with B: this can feel really unintuitive, and is only compounded by Mara's inability to move when aiming. Enemies are bullet sponges unless you can score a near point-blank headshot, too: this encourages you to be careful when fighting, though I found my tendency to explore every millimetre meant I had plenty of resources left over by the end. Thankfully, enemies are never abundant enough to cause headaches...far more troublesome were the late-game traps!This was an entertaining, atmospheric play that I enjoyed even more than I expected. Heartily recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: -[FIRST IMPRESSIONS]-   Crow Country is a game that grabbed my attention the moment I saw it.As a major fan of the Silent Hill series and the graphical style of 90s gaming, I was already very excited to try the demo SFB Games kindly provided. I played the demo for all of about 5 minutes before I was sold on the art style as well as the sound design. If a demo can sell a game before you find your first save room, that says something. -[STORY/GAMEPLAY]-   In the year 1990, you assume the role of one Mara Forest, a girl with a gun as well as a file containing information on a missing person, Edward Crow, founder of Crow Country. Mara makes for a finely crafted protagonist with an unintrusive nor overbearing presence that does not invade the player's sense of agency, whilst still retaining a clear and distinct personality with quirks seen through various interactions that make her an enjoyable, even memorable character to experience the game through. With the sole goal of locating the missing Edward Crow, Mara must traverse an abandoned theme park full of dangerous enemies, charming (if not all too difficult) puzzles, mysterious staff notes, phone calls and environmental cues that raise many questions and precious few answers. That is, at least, until it all starts to click.  You'll make use of items found throughout the park, you'll leave some where they are in case you need them later. You'll find maps and keys and piece together just why exactly this park was shut down, locked from the outside. You'll collect a small armory of weapons with which you will combat your fellow park-goers. Ammo is not necessarily hard to come by, but you may find yourself opting to avoid some altercations in favor of keeping a lucky few bullets for something more worth the resources. This is doubly true in the Murder of Crows mode, which sees you not "finding" ammo so much as scrambling for it, as well as ramping up the enemy aggression in a mode more suited for people who enjoy resource management, who like each and every trigger pull and spent casing to feel like a decision to be made.  Echoing caws, memorable music and chilling ambiance, the unsettling cries and groans of guests, Crow country is packed full of an incredible use of sound to instill and exemplify fear and uncertainty in tandem with its graphical simplicity, much like the cult classics from which it takes its roots. SFB Games fused a comforting familiarity with awe inspiring creativity in their world and story to bring to us a fresh and invigorating re-imagining of the survival horror classics of years past, such as the Silent Hill and Resident Evil franchises as well as the hints of Amnesia: The Dark Descent story archetypes that I felt bleeding through the colorful visitors, both friendly and not, that you'll meet on your tour of the park. -[POSTGAME CONTENT]-  I will keep this segment as spoiler-free as possible, though I will say that the postgame content unlocks would be better off discovered on your own. Nonetheless, for the curious I will talk briefly about them here. Upon the defeat of the final boss, the end cutscene will play out. Afterwards, the screen fades to black before Mara reemerges from the dark into a spotlight where the game will then evaluate your performance, tracking the number of healing items you have used, how many secrets you have found, how many hints you have used and finally, how many lives you used if you play with the  "Extra Lives" function.   These factors affect the rank you are given for the playthrough, and there are unlockable rewards given for B, A, and S ranking the game that can be permanently toggled on or off in subsequent playthroughs. Completion of the game at any rank allows you to toggle the "Crow Quest" setting in subsequent playthroughs, adding 42 breakable crystal crows around the map with a cute reward for finding them all locked behind a door that is now in the first save room. Having done an A rank playthrough, An S rank playthrough using my B and A rank unlocks, Crow Quest as well as having plans to play the Murder of Crows mode, the game has a nice handful of things to do after completing the gameif you're the type who likes replayability. -[MY SINGLE COMPLAINT]-  I suggest that anybody reading this review before having played the game skip this segment, as I don't want to plant any ideas or opinions in anyone's head that would impact their enjoyment of the game. Instead, I wish to bring this one complaint to a place where it may be seen and maybe even taken into consideration in updates or tweaks to the game later on. Just maybe.-  -[CLOSING THOUGHTS]-  Crow Country is a game well worth its asking price, something I find notable as a person who often justifies the price of games mostly with how many hours of content it buys. However, Crow Country is short and sweet, having taken me 8.5 hours to complete on a first playthrough (which I later came to find was on the slower side), but still left me feeling like I had played a profoundly worthwhile, well-crafted experience. SFB Games clearly made Crow Country with love, it is evident throughout the entire game, and I'd love to see more like it. More wishful thinking, but I would love to see an update or paid dlc with an "Extra Episode" type of mode like what is seen in the Resident Evil 2 remake. Perhaps with some larger guns and set after the main game in some kind of government-involved park cleanup or in some implied future events.But even if this game were left entirely as is, never to be updated again, It would remain a fond memory of a very, very good survival horror experience. Just play it already. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is absolutely wonderful and I loved every second of it. _childDocuments_.review: The setting and mystery are the backbone of the game - much like other games from SfB the aesthetic really shines. The world of Crow Country is plausible, filled with little details and elements that make the whole thing come to life. All of the strange, wacky theme park rides and weird puzzles make for a kind of fun-house experience that's very charming.The characters and dialogue are entertaining and finding all the secrets of the game through their various perspectives is a lot of fun, especially unravelling the main character's story.The puzzles are fun and well constructed, except that One Puzzle - I hope the developers will revise this puzzle slightly because it's such a down point from everything else. There are a number of other puzzles where there's a puzzle-based solution and a brute force solution, so it's confusing that this one seems to only provide a brute force solution.Some points you might like to be aware of before buying:Although the game is pitched as a survival horror, I'm not sure that I ever felt I was in real trouble. Med kits and ammo are relatively plentiful, and enemies rarely felt unbeatable. For me that's actually a bonus because horror is not my genre, but hard mode is in the pipeline as of review - if you're more of a veteran you might like to try this mode from the start.On the other hand, if you want even less survival horror, you can turn these elements off entirely with story mode.My first playthrough was 6.5hrs - the game is very fine tuned so those hours are free of bloat, making for a very satisfying experience, but if you were looking for something longer this might not be it.Overall I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pure nostalgia. That would be an adequate motive to try out the game.However, a recommendation based on such concept as the sole reason of playing, would merely be unfair to the developers. PS1 era inspired horror games are becoming more prevalent, but attaining desired feeling of "nostalgia" is not easy to come by. Crow Country presents you the fragments of the past, bringing you back to your childhood, as an impeccable, complete experience from the graphics to the sound elements and manages to captivate you with a story, which is still a regular discussion topic on the dedicated subreddit. Despite having a storyline quite straight-forward, every step I took left me wondering with what I was yet to encounter, evoking emotions of despair and comfort simultaneously. The game encourages the player to check every corner of the map and rewards for doing so. The puzzles are well-made, including references contributing to the main premise of the story, and easy to comprehend, just require paying attention to the notes and the environment.As an instance of survival horror genre, the game was leaning more on the story side than survival with the abundance of healing items and ammo supply. While this might have not satisfied the expectations of some players longing more for a survival - action gameplay, I believe these feedbacks were relieved with the release of hard mode.Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone seeking a unique yet familiar experience.Actually you know what, the game has a perfect description of itself."It's a curious mixture of hope and dread."

_childDocuments_.review: [Steam Deck][Survival difficulty]+ Graphically, it wears its PS1 inspiration on its sleeve, but with an added flavour of FF7-style character models, and it's a combination which works surprisingly well. The game is really atmospheric, there are a lot of details in the environments and the monsters can be legitimately spooky in encounters.+ The music appropriately builds up the creepy atmosphere and the sound effects are very well done. Some enemies have a particular sound that drowns the soundscape a bit to signal their presence nearby and it nicely raises the tension and keeps you on your toes.+ Crow Country itself is amazing as a setting, an abandoned theme park dripping with creepiness and crow automatons. It's divided into clearly recognisable areas and the level design is inspired overall. It feels like a (sur)real place, but is also fun to explore from a game-play perspective. On that, the map system functions really well, displaying all the needed information clearly, which keeps exploration and puzzle-solving fun.+ At the heart of the abandoned theme park is an interesting mystery, which resolves in a pretty cool way and relies on an interesting cast of well written characters. Mara Forest, your playable character, is particularly well written, with a distinct, relatable sense of humour and a mysterious connection to the game's antagonist which unfolds as you progress.+ The puzzles were all pretty great to solve, engaging and fun. Hints, and sometimes even solutions, are peppered throughout the environment, rewarding exploration if you're stuck. There's also a hint system through a fortune-telling crow which you can use a limited number of times per play-through.+ Combat is solid enough; took me a while to get used to the aiming, probably one of the PS1 inspirations that could have stayed behind IMHO. You have the classic survival horror weapons and grenades to make your way through a variety of spooky enemies. Ammo can be scarce, but the game offers you a hand through various mechanics. You can return back to your car to resupply on ammo, or you can search trash cans and vending machines, which tend to give you resources when you're in dire need and refill after a while. + The game does help you out a lot, either with combat or puzzles, the survival difficulty mode skews on the easy side compared to other survival horrors. This, however, makes it a perfect entry-level survival horror experience. Really great as your first time playing this kind of game. And there is also a Hard mode if you're a seasoned veteran and you wish to up the difficulty. The game is also short, but I feel it's an appropriate length and it absolutely doesn't overstay its welcome. Plus, it probably makes speed-running more accessible for a larger group of players. Again, a perfect introduction to the survival horror genre.+ Runs flawlessly on the Steam Deck, really great way to play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a modern classicCrow Country evokes feelings of nostalgia while crafting a survival horror experience that feels new and refreshing.Gameplay:I couldn't help but binge-play this game while on the edge of my seat wondering what new secret or monstrosity I would uncover behind the next corner. The enemy designs were unnerving, making me hesitate before each headshot costing me dearly. I felt like I was playing a remastered hidden gem from the PS1 era of video games as Crow Country perfectly captured the aesthetic of the era. While the weapon selection is sadly limited, the controls for aiming and the limited ammo more than make up for it. You not only focus on making each shot count but need to be mindful of the distance between you and your enemy. Finding the perfect distance ensures you get the most damage possible per shot while avoiding being torn to bits. I found myself dancing the fine line between combat-savvy and foolhardy in a few of the later enemy confrontations.Story:***(Spoiler Warning)***The mystery that enfolds at the theme Park Crow Country is one that is slowly pieced together throughout your journey leading to a startling and satisfying conclusion.   Mara's perspective on the events of the game and her environment help add depth to her character and bring a welcome relief to the tense atmosphere that can permeate some of the more treacherous levels. I found myself taken aback as I slowly began to piece together Mara's backstory and true intentions. My favorite scene from this game is descending down the ladder to the bottom of the roots as it was the perfect visual to behold with a musical score that underlined the finality of Elaine's descent. Finally confronting Edward Crow and having the secrets of the roots laid bare made every step of the journey worthwhile.  Conclusion:Crow Country is well worth the price of admission for its creative vision and wonderful storyline.The thoughtful attention to visual aesthetic and the staples of the survival horror genre make this an experience welcoming to fans both new and old. With its level of replayability, I know I will be revisiting Crow Country Theme Park soon after my first visit.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a pretty interesting little game. Going into it completely blind, it's a pretty friction-less experience when compared to a classic Resident Evil or Silent Hill game.  The combat is something between classic Silent Hill and a modern Resident Evil game, since you switch between a movement mode and a shooting mode, and while in shooting mode can manually aim your guns to hit enemy weak points. The game offers both a more modern "relative" control scheme like Silent Hill 4, as well as a tank control scheme like more classic games. The only gripe I have with this setup is that instead of switching between the two in the options, the directional pad appears to permanently set to tank controls and the joystick to relative. If your controller has an analog swap button this isn't a problem, but for certain controllers this makes tank controls unusable. The puzzles are straightforward, almost to a fault. Some of the interactive ones were neat, like the piano/painting puzzle and the swan puzzle. Others, like the forest fairy in the theater, less so. Changing your brain to thinking of interacting with the world only with your handgun is a bit of a different perspective and threw me off of a few incredibly obvious solutions. The item balancing is fine, it's a bit of enforced scarcity where certain item drops are based on your current healing/ammo count but it can feel bad when you're playing really well and then go out of your way not to open boxes to avoid pointlessly using up pistol ammo for no payoff.The first play through is enjoyable, and can be pretty easily beaten blind in a single sitting, but there's not too much for replay value when compared to a classic Silent Hill game. The ranking system is a little anemic and the combat, while novel, feels a bit rough around the edges. Give it a shot if you like survival horror games. You can play a good chunk of it in the demo if you're unsure, so no reason to hesitate.6.5/10 bretty good

_childDocuments_.review: We seem to be in the middle of survival horror revival period, with both high profile and niche indie titles revisiting this niche subgenre of action adventure games. There have been some great titles released over the past 7 years and quite a few solid ones. But there’ve also been some stinkers and a few titles that cared more about the aesthetics of the genre, not its design. From the early previews and the demo, I expected Crow Country to land among the latter. Thankfully, the game turned out to be considerably better than that.Being a true survival horror game, you can expect one interconnected world you can explore, finding key items, passwords and new weapons and upgrades that help you progress through the story. Resources are limited and avoiding combat is a valid option for the majority of the situations. The game world is relatively small, but the game commits to the metroidvania-like design and has only one true point of no return close to the end, so until that point you can revisit any room you’ve been to previously. Which combines wonderfully with how the game world is updated as the story progresses, with new enemies and traps added in unexpected places. Traps in general are a great addition to the usual genre gameplay and I really liked how they spiced things up.The most unique aspect of the title, I suppose, is the top down view with a Final Fantasy VII or Little Big Adventure reminiscent art style. And while I’m happy about being proven wrong that this approach isn’t the focus of the game anyway, it does feel like a detriment overall. Action in the game doesn’t feel good. Neither does it feel bad, but the way camera and controls work isn’t very helpful. You could argue about the difficulty of creating a top down/isometric survival horror and claim that it’s impossible to make it work well. But Heaven Dust and its sequel exist and show how it can be done better. Still, the iffy combat isn’t a deal breaker for this game.There was one surprise I did not expect at all – the story. Even in very high budget survival horror/survival action titles the plot and the characters tend to be quite weak and the only consistent good example people liked to point at was Silent Hill (it has not been a good example for decades by now). But both characters and the plot in Crow Country have nothing to do with the usual trappings of adult psychological horror and despite that the storytelling is extremely well done. It’s an odd story and a bit farcical at times, but wonderfully written and delivered as long as you give it a bit of time. It easily grows on you and will give you several unexpected twists by the end.I did not expect Crow Country to be fun. Interesting, stylish, curious – sure. But it was actually fun. New game plus unlockables make revisiting the game faster and more entertaining. There’s a special mode with no combat for those who want to experience only the story and puzzles. So there’s really no reason not to try give it at least a couple of hours and see if you like it. I did. And while it’s not a glowing recommendation, a lot of other “good enough” indie survival horror titles I’ve played over the past several years would’ve been lost or ignored if they were to release during the peak of the genre in the late 90s to early 00s. But not Crow Country – I feel that it would’ve found its audience and remained a fondly remembered game to this day.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not mistake Crow Country as just a Resident Evil tribute. This game is highly unique in it's quality of writing, it's pacing, and it's fun. The story, and setting is highly intriguing and unpredictable. The puzzle solving options, and potential for mastery on repeat playthroughs are vast. The graphics support the storytelling, and puzzles with their exaggeration. Making puzzle solving elements clear, while hiding important resources in plain sight. It also doesn't rely on excessive gore to scare the player. instead relying on it's previously mentioned intriguing setting, and writing to spark your imagination. The game maintains a perfect mood throughout, with the player always being afraid of the implications of their surroundings, and the well being of their favorite characters. but it never paralyzes the player, making unable to continue.No other exploration-survival horror does it as good as Crow Country.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think this is inherently a bad game, but compared to many of the pretty spectacular survival horror releases we've seen in the last few years I can't justify recommending it. We've seen the likes of Signalis, Tormented Souls, and Alisa to name a few. If you're gaming on a budget, I'd recommend any of those over Crow Country.To break it down, Crow Country really sticks the landing on aesthetics and has some clever puzzles, but aside from that it struggles in many other aspects that I consider essential to the survival horror genre. There's no two ways about it, the game is way too easy. Something worth noting is that there's a story mode that lets you simply experience the game without the survival horror/combat elements (and I'm assuming solve all the puzzles since I never played it). The unfortunate reality is that enemy encounters have basically no effort put into them apart from the optional boss fights. This is likely a result of implementing a mode where there is no combat. Enemies simply appear in areas, gradually increase in quantity, and eventually traps are thrown in for good measure.The enemies in survival horror games play a huge role in world building, and equally important is the way the game forces you to interact with them. In Crow Country, the game rarely makes us reckon with the enemies, they're simply obstacles and often in a very literal sense. As the game progresses it feels like someone's just turning up the dial for "enemy density" rather than difficulty, and the environments are cluttered with enemies without really feeling dangerous. Combat in general isn't much to write home about and aiming and shooting your gun feels awkward, though anyone with even modest amount of survival horror experience will breeze through the game.When it comes to the story I was pleasantly surprised by the number of characters you interact with, though none of them are too interesting. Without getting into spoilers, there are a few twists that might leave you with more questions than answers. There's plenty of lore sprinkled throughout the game but none of the ideas held my attention for very long. The park itself is a treat visually, though it eventually begins to feel very small in the latter half of the game. Once you uncover more of the story, it also feels as if the setting was chosen simply for the aesthetic as its connection to plot is fairly arbitrary. Near the end you get a huge lore dump and basically have to decide for yourself if you care or not.To end on a high note, the game looks very charming and it's obvious that a lot of effort went into the visuals and environments (especially given that the camera can be fully rotated in every room, allowing you to see everything). For my part, I finished the game once and likely won't ever touch it again. If you feel compelled to get it, I'd wait at least until it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is exactly the game it's trying to be, a nod to PS1-era survival horror games.  It's not straight horror though, as it's pretty funny at times but it does have horror atmosphere.  I love the visuals and bought the game because of them and was stunned to find out the developers were from the Detective Grimoire games which are a completely different art style all together.  My only complaint about the visuals is the camera feels too zoomed in in a lot of areas.Basic combat and enemy encounters are rather mediocre, though that's a symptom more of the game's design focus than a deterrent to the game's quality.  There's the right amount of simple to medium level puzzling and the backtracking feels largely satisfying due to various shortcuts between areas that feel natural.  You're going to backtrack a lot so it not feeling tedious is important.Really like the little secrets and incidental dialogue for examining stuff as well.  Thoughts on the story/plot are neutral, neither particularity interesting or terrible.  Not the greatest use of notes, feels like there are too many scattered about and it hurts the atmosphere a bit.Crow Country is an example of a small-scope game done well.  It's long as it needs to be and not padded out like 95% of all games.  An excellent homage to games of the past that shows you don't have to reinvent the wheel to make a game feel fresh.  Recommended to anyone that ever played and enjoyed OG Resident Evil-type games.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of survival horror, Crow County was not very stressful, which was refreshing. It can be a little much. You can just run past them, or use your potentially massive stockpile of ammo, so it's not a big deal.If you hate the combat all together, you can literally just turn it off and treat Crow Country as just a puzzle game. Something for everybody.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a neat little gem that doesn't tread any new ground in survival horror but it doesn't really need to. It's not overly difficult and puzzles are creative and simplistic. The story is surprisingly engaging and the combat is satisfying. Crow Country works great for those looking to step into the survival horror genre and there's plenty of fun to be had for vets as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is an excellently assembled survival horror game that would be perfect for newcomers to the genre, while still providing some excellent touches for oldheads to enjoy.The gameplay itself is very streamlined, focusing on making the tank controls and limited firearm combat as smooth as they can. I'd even go as far as to say the game is easy, even on its hardcore difficulty mode, due in part to how forgiving the map's layout is and how simple the gameplay can be. This isn't a point against it though, since it's focusing on providing an atmospheric experience instead, something it EXCELS at.Everything about this art direction is gorgeous, from your highly-stylized psx character model to the lavishly detailed environments that somehow manage to feel like resident evil pre-renders despite maintaining full camera control. The storyline is sensible, the characters are memorable despite limited appearances, and there's plenty of reward for poking around and exploring these detailed environments. At times too much reward even, haha, for a survival horror game I never really felt at risk of running out of supplies and ammunition. That may just be my familiarity with the genre though, since I was naturally gravitating towards min-maxing my resource spending in a way I don't think the game wanted to demand of me.Overall, highly reccomend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: A strikingly cool low-fi survival horror, it harkens to the best days of the PS1 with its low-poly aesthetic, while taking cues from many adventure and horror games and offering an experience firmly grounded in modern design ethos (despite the narrative taking place in the 90's).The survival experience is fairly basic but extremely well made: a dense and winding space that opens progressively through shortcuts and simple lock and key and logic puzzles, peppered with some enemies and traps to get in your way. It manages a tense atmosphere through its mostly tight spaces, the evocative enemy designs, and the surprisingly well told and haunting story that ends up being thematically relevant to our own concerns, with a dash of cosmic horror to spice it up.It also takes from the best in the genre its attitude towards speedrunning: your first playthrough will allow you to peel apart the different layers at your leisure, while subsequent attemps will likely be more focused on efficiency to attempt reaching the elusive higher ranks. The game's length lends itself to playing over and over, with a first playthrough likely taking around 5 hours and subsequent focused runs between 1 and 2 apiece.Overall, an excellent compact take on the genre that horror fans should definitely check out, along with old school adventure gamers, as the game offers a combatless mode to focus exclusively on the narrative, a fantastically accessible design and overall cool move, in service to a great story that ought to be played by many. Go for it!

_childDocuments_.review: Have you eaten up every Resident Evil and Silent Hill inspired horror title you can on sale in the Steam store? Are you a SIGNALIS fan and looking for something a little more comfy while scratching that retro survival horror itch?  Can't wait for Tormented Souls 2, Post Trauma or Samurai Unicorn? You SHOULD spend that hard earned money on Crow Country!An important one for many people nowadays: THIS GAME IS FREE OF POLITICS AND MODERN GAMING WOES. Unless I missed something insignificant or did not go over the developer's social media with a fine enough toothed comb, there should be nothing here to make you regret your purchase.If you're a survival horror veteran, you may find the danger level of this game a little on the easier side, but only marginally. Monsters still hit like a truck, and there are more traps in this game than even The Evil Within (a major accomplishment in my humble opinion); those poison gas spitting crow heads, I tell ya!The atmosphere is just top notch, and maybe I was expecting a story that was kid-friendly with the classic Final Fantasy VII aesthetic, there is mild swearing, loads of "cutesy" body-horror, and an ending that left me feeling satisfied but in a strange state of melancholy? Hard to explain without spoilers, it's rather bittersweet.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: It's easy to say that Crow Country is a game from the past in the form of a mashup between the PS1's Resident Evil's gameplay and Final Fantasy 7's aesthetic. It would be an accurate representation: but Crow Country's use of nostalgia just sets the basis for a wonderful experience that keeps you tense without focusing on jump scares. The story is typical for the genre yet has reasonable side characters that I wish there was a little more of, but also has a good set of lore and makes you wonder what truly is happening at the park. Exploration is good and allows you to find items and secrets without needing a guide to it. Those looking to be hand held will find minor tools to help, but the game is much better when you're figuring things out yourself. The combat is alright, but the base speed of Mara is too fast for my liking: you can run by a lot of the challenges that the game presents, and I think the combat is effective even with the interesting camera angle. When pushed into a corner you do get the panic that you'd expect. Did I feel like I was in trouble a lot of the time? No, but I also realize that having played a lot of games like this, I may be asking too much from the game. But that doesn't overshadow the creepiness the game presents. The game gets those uneasy vibes without being in your face about: it lets things fester, and does some tricks to keep you off your game, especially as the game progresses. In the end, Crow Country is a blast from the past while still having nice changes from that formula that makes it different enough to stand out. It's a game that most everyone, even those who may not have had good experiences with Survival Horror in the past, will enjoy. :
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true love letter to classic survival horror games. It has that fantastic pacing I always look for in these games, a very fun interconnected map, fun and stressful gun-play, resource management that never impeded my progress but made me think about how to use my ammo. The enemy variety was also quite impressive, this game has quite a few interesting enemy types.The story was very intriguing and always kept me engaged. The characters are pretty unique and memorable for the most part. I do think one of the plot-twists was a bit predictable but I still love how it played out in the end and I think the amount of storytelling in this 7 hour game was really commendable.I only have a couple small complaints: the enemies sometimes get a bit janky with the level geometry. At most this made me lose a bit of immersion but ultimately it wasn't a big issue, just something that could be fixed up a bit. I also think one or two puzzles were a bit unintuitive, mainly the second storeroom secret. At the end of the day it's just a secret collectible so it's not a big deal but it did mess up my pacing a bit.Final verdict: please play this if you like survival horror games like Silent Hill and Resident Evil. I can't describe how refreshing it felt to play a new game of this genre in 2024. I'm gonna keep an eye on this studio, I need to see what they do next.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a decent time with this, enough to warrant the price tag.  It has the elements of the old PS1 horror games and it feels nice to zip through the puzzles.I do think it misses the overall atmosphere of being a horror game though.  Like one aspect is that as you progress the game will repopulate areas with enemies and traps but there doesn't feel like there's any reason for it other than the devs just think they need to have stuff to get in your way, even though by that point you're just running around avoiding everything as there's not much point.The underlying premise of the narrative is fine, but it's very short, abrupt with little buildup with everything getting dropped in the last 5 minutes of the game for the most part.Gameplay is mostly visual puzzles with some find the clue in a different part.  Gunplay is clunky but that may also be very much the point given the inspiration material.Again overall I thought it was a fun little game but if you're looking for something really horror related then this won't really fit that.

_childDocuments_.review: It will be a struggle to put into words how much I enjoyed this game. It ticked so many boxes for me, it was a game built for me basically - I grew up on the original survival horror games, and adore older generation gaming graphics. They are my favourite! This game ignited so much nostalgia, but brought it to a modern era. I loved sinking into this game, getting lost in it's world and tale for hours. I'm looking forward to playing it more - lots of replayability in this! The puzzles were the perfect level of challenge, some caught me for quite a while but there was so much to explore, that I could come back to them later without feeling too stuck. The referencing in this game, little homages, commentary and humour in this game are perfection, it made me laugh, cry and be terrified in it's atmosphere and storytelling. The designs and environments created are phenomenal, it has a cute style and yet so much creep factor in the creature design! The characters are so touching! They all have such individuality in their personalities. Playing with the controller was my preferred setting, very customisable to suit your playstyle. The mechanics were very different compared to other games but I adjusted and really enjoyed it - I think it does help to be accustomed to old school survival horror, definitely gives an upper hand to players of this game. I definitely would play more games like this! If there are sequels to this game sign me up!Thank you so much for making this game, I have not come across a game like this for so long, and it means so much to me to experience it! It really means a lot that I am able to feel the way I do about this game.

_childDocuments_.review: In short - buy it and play it!The game is underselling itself and could easily cost the same as new resident evil games.It's a return to old school survival horrors with a good amount of quality of life improvments, but just like silent hill games, it's the best to play in blind.
