_childDocuments_.review: It's really great resident-evil-like: atmosphere, story and visual style all great BUT... I found the survival horror part of it more annoying than scary or challenging. Enemies and traps seem to be random and appear in previously empty areas. When you have to traverse it a lot you want to clear some areas and expect it to stay cleared. Now you would find random enemies AND traps again. The trap "looks like a regular bandage but actually is a bomb" was especially annoying.. Just why...So in the middle of the "survival" experience I decided to switch to "adventure" because I was more interested in the story and puzzles and didn't want to deal with the unfair enemies and traps for the entire game.So not perfect, but still worthy to check out.

_childDocuments_.review: TL'DR: 8.5/10 indie resident-evil-1-esque horror. Plays great, interesting character dialogue that isn't shoehorned, and sometimes a good staged spook moment.Gameplay: 4.5/5 - Aiming is fun and reminiscent of older titles in a charming way. Very fluid and nothing ever feels cheap or unfair. Trap disarming / avoiding baddies can get monotonous and tedious instead of fun at times. Very satisifying to nail a baddie with a trap.Biggest Critique: There are not enough punishing moments to really invoke fear into the player. Resident Evil had ways you definitely could mess up a puzzle and get yourself killed if you didn't think ahead, and that is what I think this title is missing. The stakes never felt that high because you can pretty much steamroll through anything spooky as long as you can hit your shots with pistol and save your big ammo for mini-bosses and bosses. I never had a moment where the game humbled me once I got the shotgun. The monsters were my ♥♥♥♥♥. If there was some more severe punishments (like the bookcase room, that is a good example of the kind of thing the game needed more of) for failure or more moments to keep us sharting our drawers.Score: 8.5/10 - Buy it and try it.

_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A must play for fans of old school survival horror. Crow Country is the complete package, with a smart, compelling narrative, excellent puzzles, tense old school atmosphere, and a fresh take on combat that blends re1 and re4 style shooting. The run time leaves a little bit to be desired but if you're like me, the secrets littered throughout the map, as well as the scoring system and the unlockable weapons will have you coming back for a second play through. Crow Country is a mystery well worth solving and is absolutely worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: CAW!~Its pedigree is clear and its structure is strong. "Spooky amusement park" is probably the best horror trope because it can really be anything and lends itself to having tight corridors and specialized areas with strange methods of gaining access. I think that the devs took full advantage of the trope with a kooky story. The graphics, but especially the character models are very reminiscent of PS1-era graphics. Aiming feels pretty tanky even if movement doesn't thanks to full analog control. If you prefer tank controls for movement, the D-pad will provide that. If you know what you're doing, you can absolutely blow through this game with all secrets found. This is one game that's very distinct in its difficulties. You have "I'm just here for the story", "How it's meant to be played", and "No freebies". Good luck.  I appreciate that you're not penalized for saving in terms of your completion rank. Feel free to save after you do anything and savescum if you get hit.The film grain effect works, though I find myself wishing I could turn it off after a while. Sound effects are the loudest things in game by far, especially the "CAW!" that plays when you open the game. The characters all have their places in the story and have mostly reasonable motivations, but they're a little one-note. The story is dispensed pretty evenly throughout the story, but it still results in an info dump at the end. Also, I think that there should be some acknowledgment for ignoring all those calls. Sorry, I'm phone-shy.

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country plays smoother than butter, looks more rotten than weeks-old chicken and has wit drier than plain toast.Not many games manage to mix tight mechanics and controls, a strikingly unique visual style and pithy writing into one package, but SFB games has managed just that.The puzzles are a genuine delight to solve, complemented by interesting area discovery and high-stakes survival horror gunplay. I loved writing notes and taking screenshots to unlock every door and follow every head.So much character is given to Mara Forest through her dialogue and her inner monologue when interacting with the world. I laughed several times at her reactions to examining items in the world, which fill her with a playful curiosity that separate Crow Country's tone from more serious games in the genre.Get. This. Game! 🐦‍⬛

Either way I would still 100% recommend it to anyone slightly interested in indie survival horror. It's up there with like Signalis and Evil Tonight etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Nostalgic survival-horror with a rather different twist to the usual zombie fare. Kept me thoroughly engrossed and eager to unravel the story. Rather short and completeable over one weekend, but satisfying enough to leave me feeling contented by the end.The controls (barely any support for KB&M) and abundance of respawning enemies + traps make for some troublesome sections.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game. I appreciate the inclusion of tank controls, but the reach and aggression of enemies tends to be too high to be able to actually use them. I did feel like I was wresting with the camera every now and then, but it was generally a small enough issue that I didn't give up any hits to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a love letter to people who love resident evil. The game keeps you locked into suspense and curious til the very end.  You find yourself in a maze of locked doors, and puzzles trying to find the owner of the theme park while evading terrifying creatures who roam this theme park. It's a fantastic introductory game for people who want desperately to play a horror game but normally are too scared!It's graphics are incredibly nostalgic and feel authentic to a playstation console experience.The gameplay is fun and tricky, at times if you panic it can be difficult to make shots, but there's always running!!The puzzles are just the right kind of difficult, not too hard but not too easy.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: genuinely one of my favourite horror games ive played. It grabbed my attention so hard i finished the whole thing in a day. The environments are fantastic. The atmosphere is great. Although it can be quite challenging in murder of crows mode where it's more chaotic, the combat is good and the aiming style is interesting. i really enjoy the monster designs as well, and the explanation at the end of the game for their existence made me feel bad for them. The music is also amazing, and its some of my favourite music in a video game ever. The slight detuning of the instruments and the bitcrushing effects made it feel very nostalgic but still eerie. I think my favourite off the soundtrack and a good example of what i mean is the Fairytale Town theme! overall VERY solid game :)
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This masterpiece for me is a straight up 9/10. I really enjoyed the visuals, the subtle humor, the scares and the combat was also really fun. The puzzles kept me engaged and so did the story. This is a MUST play for any survival horror fan. It is also one of the more easier/casual games allowing easy entry for casual players and also includes a exploration mode that removes combat. My only one gripe about this game is the excessive amount of traps as the game progresses. Although it keeps the player always on their toes about their movement. to conclude, this is one of the best survival horror games i've played since Resident Evil 2 Remake.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Floored by how good this game is. The aesthetics, creature design, sound design, and weird worldbuilding/twists are all impeccable. I've never had a survival horror game's story surprise me as much as this one. It's a short game, legit creepy, and packed with optional secrets and puzzles if you really want to poke around. Cannot wait to see what these devs make next.I should mention, I got a key for this game, and the price COULD be considered a bit steep for how short it is. That being said, there seems to be some replay value, and the overall quality more than makes up for the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is not just a throw back to the Early 3D days of survival horror. It's also a really good survival horror game! The combat has just the right amount of clunkyness and responsiveness to be challenging but not frustrating. There puzzles are all very clever, and were all manageable without looking online. Most of all, this game has done a better job than any survival horror in mixing the grounded, biological horror of Resident Evil, with the psychological horror of Silent Hill, without having to dive into the supernatural. There's a great mystery that drove me to keep playing to figure out what it was all about, and I was not disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely tribute to Survival Horror games of old, hearkening back to classics like Silent Hill and Resident Evil, with the influence from the latter clearly showing. A very unexpected, yet incredibly welcome influence that the game draws upon though is the Final Fantasy VII, with the models and character designs taking inspiration from the limited and somewhat dated models of the JRPG classic. This does not detract from the experience though, and you quickly adapt to the characters and their personalities as you traverse through the spooky and haunted halls of the Crow themed amusement park. As someone who holds adoration for the early Resident Evil games, and especially for Final Fantasy VII as well, this was an absolute gem to play. If you like classic survival horror games, yet perhaps don't like the somewhat convoluted plot lines of its many modern contemporaries, then this 5-6 hour game is absolutely for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Classic Survival Horror fans will be very pleased with this game. It has some good modern twists with the option for analogue movement and camera control, at the same time with tank controls with the camera focusing on your character as you turn as well. While playing normal mode, there was a pretty generous amount of ammo lying around, but you'll realize that the later enemies can be kinda spongy in health, so you should take advantage of the traps around the environment to make use of your ammo. The last thing for sure are the puzzles. They're not the most complicated, but they are very clever in the prompt you're given and how you solve them. Overall, even if you don't play classic survival horror games, it'll still be enjoyable. Definitely 8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with Crow Country the moment I tried the demo back in 2023. Back then I thought it was an excellent throwback to 90s horror games, and that still rings true in Crow Country's full release. Rich with a style and atmosphere that evokes memories of PS1 era games such as Resident Evil/Silent Hill, full of really neat puzzles in a well-designed interconnected map that's all enjoyable to engage with. They perfectly nailed what they were trying to go for here.As a note, I should add that like some of the games Crow Country hearkens back to, you can very easily blast through it in a VERY short amount of time in subsequent playthroughs once you know what to do. I'm actually pretty cool with this, since in my opinion it makes the game feel more genuine in what it succeeds in being, which is a classic style horror game that any fan of the genre should sincerely consider checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: It tries to be a ps1 style survival horror game but there is no real horror and the puzzles at some points can be missed if you dont search every inch of a room (water pump) There is an NPC that breaks the 4th wall by making fun of the fact that he wants you to complete the puzzle. Combat is too clunky even for survival horror and it gets annoying as the game feels the need to add more crap to move around. If you want to play a better game play My Friendly Neighborhood
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game in the style of the original Resident Evil games. The graphics are great in that charming retro way. The game is tense with surprises every time you return to an area. The story is pretty solid as well.Love to see indie games bringing back these kinds of games largely forgotten in the Triple-A gaming world.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country is a horror game oozing with charm, mixing the blatant old-school visual style of the classic horror titles of past decades, and applying its own unique style layered on top of it. Fans of old Resident Evil titles will be right at home here, with plenty of puzzles to solve, eldritch monsters to battle against and a ticking tension bomb of survival as you explore the depths of Crow Country. There's even a pretty interesting story weaved in with a very appropriate mix of seriousness and the sort of 90's-goofiness that you might come to expect. Hard to fault it for what it tries to do really, it's a strong recommendation for anyone who likes this kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow country is a charming survival horror experience that understands what made the original Resident Evil good and fun to play.Anyone who enjoys classic survival horror experiences will most certainly have a lot of fun with this game.Despite the limitations of a somewhat small game world, the game packs so much in many areas, and works hard to make the section memorable for you as a player.While the art style is weird and unique, resembling the original FF7 more than anything, it is extremely surprising that the developers managed to create such a scary atmosphere with such an art style.And while the combat system may take some getting used to, it adds to the tense situations, and quite frankly, is a very nice take on the combat mechanics of small classic survival horror games.It could have had more to it, but the simplicity works real well for the game, and any more would start making it more complex of a game, something that could be explored in a sequel perhaps. But no worries, the enemy movement and the manual reload aspect will still keep you on your toes when combat starts!The puzzles in this game are fun, I would say they are not the best, perhaps a couple of them were too vague to solve with the hints, but they were optional.To cut it short.It is a really fun game that understands the mechanics it has real well and manages to use all the aspects of the game really well, and that delivers a really satisfying experience in the end, and any classic survival horror fan is bound to love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A silly, well structured and accessible PS1-style survival horror.Most of the difficulty in the game comes from its puzzle solving; you can outright turn off the monsters if horror doesn't suit you. There's also both tank controls as well as modern controls in case you're not fond of the former.What I love from this game though is the charming and silly moments from character interactions with the environment and each other. Mara especially is my favorite. There are moments when the story takes itself seriously but it's not an oppressive atmosphere like Resident Evil or similar titles. I had a big smile on my face pretty much my entire playthrough.Highly recommend!!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: This was such an engaging game with its amusement park setting which made for fun puzzles and scenarios in addition to its likable characters and survival horror elements and I can't stress how much enjoyment I got out of it from start to finish. You start off not knowing much about the events which have transpired that led to your purple-haired protagonist, Mara Forest, exploring the abandoned remains of the amusement park known as Crow Country, in search of the missing Edward Crow, founder of Crow Country. I found the mystery aspect of it so cool with how you'd slowly figure out more about the plot as you proceeded with the game from reading articles scattered throughout the game along with dialogue shared with its small cast of characters, with some twists for good measure. The game also made such good use of its setting being an amusement park which made for a lot of variety in terms of the types of puzzles they had available ranging from arithmetic puzzles to puzzles that would require you to interact with the actual amusement park rides as well as obtaining clues through staff notes which made for a more organic experience rather than it seeming like an obvious clue to the puzzle. The puzzles weren't super difficult to solve either and mostly required being observant of clues in your surroundings and notes you've obtained rather than using pure wit but I really did wish the puzzles were more challenging though they were definitely creative.The survival horror aspect was also fun with how they incorporated having traps laid out all over the park which could either be used to your advantage to attack enemies or could be disarmed by expending a bullet from your already limited amount of ammo, and it got more difficult as the game progressed with how more types of traps are installed and more enemies are introduced into those areas. In addition, they also had wooden crates and translucent containers you could shoot through to gain access to the items stored inside them which could be a gamble especially in terms of the crates due to not knowing what items are hidden inside, if there even are any, for the price of a bullet. And when you think you already know the game well enough, they trick you with another mechanic where they lay out items mimicking ammo/health items that could poison/injure you instead, which certainly made it really chaotic by the end of the game but I enjoyed that aspect thoroughly! XD However, even with how brutal the game is, it has save rooms, and you'll get access to more save rooms with the key items you obtain as you progress through the game which kinda made the increase in enemies and traps at the latter half of the game not as difficult as it should be especially with how short the game is.  Regardless, it was still a super fun and exciting game in terms of its premise, plot, puzzles and survival horror mechanics and I can't wait to play more games similar to Crow Country! I give it an 8.5/10!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Right up there with Signalis, Conscript, and My Friendly Neighborhood with the elite survival horror throwbacks. The story, the humor, the PS1 graphical style that's a throwback to the blocky days of Final Fantasy VII...all of it is *chef's kiss*. The only issue is that it's not ever really scary. Enemies are slow and easy to dance around, ammo and healing is plentiful...but the vibes? They are immaculate.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A great entry-level horror game that is also easily the most wholesome horror game I have ever played. I can't recommend this enough for people who enjoy Resident Evil style games and classic survival-horror systems. The game is fairly modernized to be more palpable for those resistant to more obtuse mechanics of games like this, and is an overall low-challenging game in terms of combat and puzzles. The polish, dialogue, and charm of the game certainly makes up for the low-difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A quick review for a concise game. Crow Country is an excellent survival horror title that pushes the genre's envelopes in a couple ways. The standout aspects for me were the visual presentation, the character interactions, along with the sheer number of good puzzles. The retro style and isometric perspective are quickly evident by seeing a simple screenshot, but the details put into animation and sound effect work bring it all together. It's a game set in a theme park that feels like it was built from toys out of someone's old attic. I really loved the pacing of the story and how it was delivered through character interactions. The characters come and go, showing up in new spots from time to time. The combat is sure as hell clunky, but that's par for the course in this genre. The star of the show with regards to gameplay is the puzzle and map design. The theme park is one tight intertwining puzzle box for the player to solve that hits a lot of familiar notes and some new ones too. Like I said, Crow Country's a concise experience but more importantly, it's a dense and satisfying one. My first playthrough on the standard difficulty took about 6-7 hours and that was finding and figuring out all the secrets. I don't see too much replayability here, but one more playthrough on the hardest difficulty, trying to get that S+ rating could be in my future.Check out my full review of Crow Country
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute love letter to the PS1 era and the horror genre. Personally, the length of the game was perfect especially since it has multiple playthroughs available with different modifiers. The music is wonderful, the art direction is perfect, and the writing is genuinely both hilarious and intriguing.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough of Crow Country and it is more or less exactly what I had hoped it would be.A very competent PS1-styled Survival Horror Game with an intriguing story that doesn't overstay its welcome.If that is something you crave, this is the perfect game to satisfy that itch.As a small caveat, I sadly encountered a few bugs while playing the game; at least one resulting in me not being able to pick up one of the games "secret" items and another one drowning out all sounds by what felt like a falsly triggered sound effect playing on an endless loop.While they didn't massively influenced my experience I still hope that these bugs, even if they are few and far between, get patched out in the future.Nevertheless, Crow Country is still a game I wholeheartedly recommend to fans of the genre as well as newcommers alike.UPDATE:The bugs I experienced were fixed by the Anti-"Xenophpobia" Update.With these patched out, I can recommend Crow Country unconditionally.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Great indie horror gem.+ Somewhat Silent Hill mixed with Resident Evil feel, unique retro art style, fun puzzles, interesting story to follow, great monster design, absolutely top notch music and heavily silent hill inspired sound design.- A bit short, camera can be an issue during combat, npc dialogue a bit silly sometimes, aiming takes getting used to.Overall definitely recommend! Great job developers!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting much from this game other than the well done visuals and PS1 aesthetic, but I was pleasantly surprised by how entertaining the story and most of the puzzles were! Yes the game is simple but it doesn't feel "cheap." I was genuinely stumped on at least 2 puzzles and though I never died it wasn't a free ride either. You got resource management all throughout the game which gives you a sense of strategy and forces you to not spam your guns lol. Also I really liked that there is some New Game+ added as well for a bit of replayability :)
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals in this game are absolutely top-tier, It’s full of charming little details throughout, and the dialogue in this is so cute, every part of this game just feels like it was made with such genuine love. The story is simple but enjoyable, fits the game perfectly without trying to do too much. the puzzles are a bit hit-or-miss imo; some are so straightforward that they lack challenge, but do become more complex and enjoyable as you progress. Combat though can be a little janky at times, but doesn’t detract too much from the great experience i had. I’d definitely recommend! The unique art style alone deserves more appreciation in gaming!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Complexity of the game increases the further u progress, so you never know what dangers u might encounter ahead of you. The enemy variety is quite rich in comparison to the size of the game (around 5-7 hours). The player gets rewarded for looking into every nook and cranny by giving them special rewards, so there's barely any time wasted looking around the amusment park.The progression is open-ended in a sense that finding a key item will allow you to access multiple seperate areas at once and while the world is small, it's filled with interactive environments that can help you as well as harm you, so it's best to be careful at all times.I think a lot of people will agree about this game's style resembling the pre rendered backgrounds present during the 90s in the best way possible. The music is quite atmospheric as well as charming, due to the game allowing itself to be silly at times, not always relying on pressuring the player and letting them just have fun.I dont really have anything bad to say about this game, i only wish they added a bit more replay value like higher difficulties or different modes.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: "Staring into the flames...I feel something."Crow Country is an AMAZINGLY made survival horror game that hooks you in and doesn't let go till the last second of it.Its a love letter to Silent hill and Resident Evil, down to some manurisms from characters and obviously the gameplay controls (even having old school tank controls!). With many secrets to found and an interesting mystery that doesn't let up till the final moments, this game had me GLUED TO THE DAMN CROW MONITOR FOR 6 CROW HOURS TILL I WAS DONE WITH IT.So go out, break into this abandoned theme park, and "... maybe everything will be ok""and maybe it won't."
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing callback to ps1 survival with great modernizations. If you are into horror at all do yourself a treat and buy this game as it is extremely accessible. The art style is amazing very much inspired by silent hill ps1 but it also feels like a modern take on that style with the free camera and non pre rendered backgrounds that feel pre rendered if that makes sense.Puzzles are challenging but not too obtuse.Story is very interesting and engaging!And most of all it’s horrifying!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A modern day survival horror classic! A super fun title for people looking for an entry point into the genre or veteran's pf the genre. The artstyle is a superb throwback to classic titles with polygonal models and pre-rendered backgrounds, but with the insane effort of none of the background being pre-rendered and it all being completely modelled, allowing for adjustable camera work and some visuals I can only describe as a delight.The characters are all a lot of fun to interact with, escpecially our lead Mara Forest as she's far from a blank slate protagonist and hearing her thoughts on a ton of aspects is great in gradually really building up to a solid idea of her as a person. It all works well to the games central mystery focused story, which kept me guessing the entire way and having to reconsider already thought established ideas consistently, all leading up to a story which I will not forget for some time.I cannot recommend enough for anyone looking for a game which has a real spark of life for the horror genre and especially as an indie voice! In an area which has become a bit overrun with cheap jumpscares and titles which don't offer much for people looking for a good story and gameplay to match, Crow Country is a shining beacon of indie horror and survival horror in general!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country does a good job at nodding to the PS1 era of games, and evoking the nostalgia for anyone who grew up in that time (or those who just really like retro styled games). The puzzles are challenging enough, the atmosphere is perfect, the story is direct, but the option to learn more about the park, and the characters is there in the form of books, notes, and journals, lots to read. The combat isn't overly challenging, but for me that wasn't a big deal. I'm having lots of fun playing it! Would recommend to anyone who enjoys this style of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, I think the story is pretty good. Difficulty has something to be desired but the benefit of that is that it's a good first survival horror game for newcomers. It's also not terrifying either but still has that tension that comes along with survival horror which makes it pretty accessible.Atmosphere is pretty good and the music is made by Ockeroid, which is also good, obviously.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country nails the PS1 survival horror aesthetic, while streamlining the typical experience for a short and concise trip through a well-designed world. This game trims most of the fat that usually comes with the genre. Inventory management is nonexistent and ammo is abundant. Monster designs are god-tier, but there is not much of a challenge in dispatching them. The map can tell you where secrets and unsolved puzzles are, so there are never moments where you need to spend hours backtracking or examining every pixel like in some survival horror games.SFB Games have crafted a short and tight experience that looks like a crisp '90s survival horror sans CRT filter, with modern and smooth gun-play between relatively simple puzzles. The story kept me wanting to read all the lore items and exhaust character dialogue, and Mara's quips make her a very likable protagonist. Easily recommended to survival horror and/or PS1 fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: On of the best games I've played all year. The story was fantastic and the retro presentation is just what I needed! Don't dismiss this game as just another attempt to trade off people's nostalgia for the past. This game is genuinely good on it's own merits. It's a bit on the short side, but I can never fault a game for getting in there, doing it's thing very well, and then getting out before it overstays it's welcome. Besides, if I'm saying it's a bit short, it's only because I liked the game so much I would have played it for twice the amount of time!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; A spooky survival horror throwback that does it all right. This was a fun, cute little game that reminded me of some of the early PS1 survival horror titles I played as a kid. It doesn't really do anything new or innovative, but it does the old formula really well. The storytelling, the graphics, the mechanics, it's all an homage to its forerunners, and it's done beautifully.There are a couple of places where the narrative feels a bit bare, or where dialog seems a little abrupt (meeting the lawyer, for example, left me wondering if I had missed a scene or a line of dialog somewhere), but it's rare and really doesn't take away from the experience. On the plus side, the dialog (particularly the protagonist's inner-monologue) has a few spots that DEFINITELY take aim at those illustrious forerunners, in a fun and tongue-in-cheek kind of way. It's not quite an easter egg, but it'll cause some grins from genre veterans and newcomers alike, and it's neither so frequent nor so goofy as to not fit the setting.My only actual gripe with the game is that it's shorter than I expected. I have ~8 hours on it at the moment, and I've already beaten one playthrough. It's a small studio, though, and for the quality of what they put out in this game, it's definitely worth the price. You're definitely going to want a controller for this one, too. It's playable with keyboard, but it's really designed with a controller in mind. If the devs do more like this one (please do more like this one!!!), I'll be ready and waiting!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: what a good game!!! the story and characters kept me invested from the beginning because of the little clues the writing drops for you about what's going on in crow country, i loved the mystery and how it wrapped up so well at the end! i think the puzzles were just difficult enough that you felt accomplished for solving them but easy enough that we didn't really get stuck on anything, which is a mistake i think a lot of horror games can make (getting too frustrated/stuck on puzzles can ruin the scariness). The monsters were so fun and there were some really spooky moments, this is such a clever game definitely do yourself a favor and play this!!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: You’ll watch the trailer and think you’ve discovered the next best retro-inspired throwback survival horror game. This is mostly due to the enhanced PS1 graphical style and overall presentation. However, it’ll only take an hour or two to dispel this illusion. Like many hyped games, the overwhelmingly positive reviews are more about the idea of the game, rather than the actual game itself.Sadly, the story is not very compelling or even that interesting. Instead of hinting elements of the narrative throughout the game, the story is all revealed at the very end of the game. At that point, you'll just want the credits to roll and reclaim the space on your computer by uninstalling it. Areas of the map are also not revealed gradually or in a way that makes sense based on the items you have like more classic games in the genre (Resident Evil or Silent Hill). The atmosphere of the park isn't even that moody or spooky despite attempts to adjust the lighting throughout the game.Enemy-wise there are freaks popping out from walls and puddles of sludge and humanoid mutants that move (slowly) towards you. However, there is never a point in time when you’ll feel challenged by any of these enemies. They can all be avoided with great ease and never really capture a sense of danger that is found in (good) survival horror games. Even the bosses (both optional and required) are a walk in the park. Drop a grenade and the battle is already half over.  The biggest jump scares come from these annoying chandeliers that fall on and damage your character. At best, this game feels like a sequence of half-baked mini puzzles from OG FF7. It’s probably best enjoyed by people who like PS1 aesthetics but don’t actually like or have experience with survival horror games from that time. If you want a game from now that actually captures that vibe, check out Alisa instead. I'd even argue that "chibi Resident Evil" aka Heaven Dust is a better option than this.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommend. Went in thinking this would just be a fun, if shallow, little throwback but was pleasantly surprised by the story and the atmosphere. Not the scariest game you're going to play but it's got great vibes. I loved the commitment to the retro style and a lot of the puzzles were pretty solid.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: I recently finished playing Crow Country on my Asus ROG Ally (Ryzen Z1 Extreme model), and it performed great on the 15W power setting.This was a really fun and concise experience. The story had the potential to go completely off the rails, but it stayed grounded in a way that perfectly complemented the setting. It was an absolute treat to unravel the narrative throughout the playthrough. The game leans toward the easier side, so if possible, I highly recommend playing on the hardest difficulty available. Also, try to avoid using any hints from the crow mechanic—just dive in, explore thoroughly, and read everything you come across. You’ll enjoy it even more that way!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow country is everything I wanted and more, it has a classic old-school horror game vibe but plays like a more polished modern game. The story was paced well and kept me guessing up until the games final moments. The beautiful environment draws attention and has alot of details which paired with the amazing OST will set the perfect atmosphere as you explore the abandoned theme park.100% recommend enjoyers of the horror genre to pick up this gem, you won't regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man I definitely recommend this. Survival horror thats not all that difficult but vibes and story are on point. Doesn't outstay its welcome. Leaves you feeling satisfied but also wanting more. I know I've definitely missed some secrets, but thats okay, im sure youtube will have the answers.Highly recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Crow Country was excellent, even as someone whos never beaten a survival horror game before. It's not the most challenging game, but it was fun, engaging and kept me moving from puzzle to puzzle, room to room like a good book I couldn't put down. There's plenty of post game content from the looks of it, and a few more mysteries I didn't solve in my initial run left to figure out as well. Highly recommended to both veterans of the genre and newcomers who want to get a stable footing into the genre. A+
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: The first Resident Evil-esque game I've played and I absolutely love it, spent a good part of the last 2 days playing through the game twice to get all the achievements and will probably play through it again some time in the future. It has a very good mix of puzzling and combat, and I only ever got stumped by a puzzle once, even with a hint, and even then it was because I missed a fairly obvious object that was sitting right in front of me. Combat feels very good and is very fair, I would recommend playing on 'Murder of Crows' difficulty for a good challenge, since it really ups the tension; wondering if you should engage in a fight or try to run past enemies, and then running into a trap on the ground and getting hit anyways.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A short but sweet experience, well worth it for the atmosphere and aesthetics alone. Easily recommended to those in the mood for survival horror and/or a particularly well made PS1-era throwback game. Worth noting that it's pretty easy if you're experienced in the survival horror genre, but a Hard Mode is planned for a future update.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Resident Evil and Silent Hill-like. Captures the look of a pre-rendered CG background from the Playstation era and yet you can still move the camera freely. Apart from showing off, this is a lovely way to add additional depth to exploration. This does however, undermine the use of the tank controls option, as it then can be very easy to miss certain pickups from just the camera not moving. Otherwise, a wonderful time. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Crow Country

_childDocuments_.review: A great little throwback to Survival horror, but more in heart than in mind.The art style is really cool and neat, absolutely loved it. Music is wonderfully ambient with saves room music, cool grungy/metal synth music like Silent Hill.Mechanically, it removes the most grating parts of the old survival horror genre, like tedious inventory management, suicide runs, chest runs to stash crap. It's also a little TOO overt with tips and tricks, telling you stuff that's obvious for most gamers, and spoils some surprises by trying to help a little too much. The awkward auto-aim is gone, now requiring manual aim like in RE4 - targeting key parts of enemies while they run at you. The story is pretty interesting and has very cool twists that I haven't seen in the genre before. I won't say more to not spoil you, but I was pretty involved and interested the whole way through. It's simple to follow, few characters that are all present and put context to the story.My first playthrough was done at around 5 hours, which is pretty average for the survival horror genre. The game has some 2nd playthrough features, but no NG+, though it wouldn't add much to the experience anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: I never write reviews, but Crow Country has compelled me to share my thoughts. I'll try not to ramble (I will ramble, I'm sorry).Personally, it's a 10/10. Gorgeous visuals evoking PS1 aesthetics, complete with clean animations and UI reminiscent of 90s PlayStation classics. Fun, yet coherent writing that drives a compelling narrative and a cast of distinct characters. I found the horror surprisingly effective, there were plenty of good scares. Certain traps had me yelping more often than I care to admit. Solid survival horror gameplay that will please newcomers and oldschool survival horror fans alike. Crow Country, on a PS4 controller, feels fantastic. It's worth noting I have yet to try mouse and keyboard.The game isn't incredibly long, but I consider its 5-6 hour runtime a strength. The world and characters are beautiful and intriguing, the story had me hooked from beginning to end. I think it was all tied up quite nicely. I never felt like I was wasting time or tiring of the environments. If you're thourough and an obsessive loot hoarder like myself, you'll enjoy your grand backtracks for that box of shells or a grenade you swear you left behind. The pacing, even as a frequent backtracker, never felt slowed at any point, and I wonder if this is in part due to the lack of item storage or inventory management. Items can sometimes be hard to spot and, in turn, it can be difficult to remember every item you left behind for pickup later, so you might find yourself wandering at times. I won't go into detail, but there are other ways that Crow Country prevents all the backtracking and exploring from feeling samey as well. It'll keep you on your toes! Plus, with completion rank rewards and plenty of secrets to uncover, Crow Country has some solid replay value.I can personally see this game becoming another annual replay for myself, alongside RE1 HD Remake. It's charming, nostalgic, yet fresh--an all around good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. Everything about this game is a throwback to the old survival horror days of Resident Evil on PS1, the graphics, the gameplay, everything. The crunchy, pixelated graphics lends itself well to the atmosphere of the game; sometimes the less you can see of something, the better, as your mind works to fill in the gaps. The gameplay is spot on as well, as the puzzle solving that you have to do in order to advance through the game is clever but not frustrating. Additionally, you have 15 secrets to obtain, with varying difficulty for each secret (although none are too extraordinarily difficult). The story is simple but decent, as it takes a different angle for explaining the causes of the "guests" than most other survival horror games do. Beyond that, the main antagonist is pretty well done, and I found myself empathizing with him after figuring the plot out. It's nice to see an antagonist have the level of depth that they do, especially for such a short game. Once you have completed the story, there are additional modes and challenges that you can go back and do, which are solid additions to the base game and increase the longevity of your experience. I only have a couple of minor issues with the story in the game, and they aren't drastic enough to take away from your initial experience. Firstly, I wanted more explanation of the main story. While I won't spoil the ending, I found myself wanting to know more about what happens at the end, and for the protagonist to simply say "shut up, I don't want to know" was pretty unsatisfying. Hopefully the developers come out with another game in this universe that explains it more or adds on to the story. Secondly, I found myself wanting more lore for stuff outside of the main plot. While the game does a good job of sprinkling in lore tidbits here and there for you to find and they're pretty satisfying, there were some spots in the game that some additional lore would be nice. Maybe I'm a brainlet and didn't pay enough attention but there's certain things in the game that have a couple bits of lore and then it just stops, namely Ophelia. She's mentioned a couple times in the park, and then when you find  There's a couple of other times this happens, but you don't notice it until after you finish the game. Lastly (major spoilers ahead)  Overall I think this is a solid 9/10 experience, pick it up, you won't be disappointed.

name: Dicefolk
detailed_description: Dicefolk is a tactical roguelite game based on customizable dice and monster-catching mechanics. On your adventure as a Chimera Summoner, you'll meet dozens of unique and powerful creatures that you can recruit to create the perfect team. Play as Alea, a young Dicefolk hero who discovers her ability to befriend Chimera and fight back against evil forces threatening humanity’s extinction. Embark on a thrilling quest to save humanity from the grasp of an evil sorcerer. Build a team from over 100 unique, hand-drawn Chimera to suit your playstyle. Unlock all the talismans to uncover the mystical secrets behind the Chimeras’ existence. With a large variety of Chimeras to befriend and command, you'll need to strategize and adapt your playstyle to suit each battle. From tough tanks to speedy attackers, each Chimera brings a unique set of abilities to the table. Your tactical choices will determine your success in battle! It’s all up to you! Customize your dice for maximum influence over your Chimeras’ attacks and abilities. Control the order in which battles play out and choose when parties take action. Dicefolk defies RNG and gives you unprecedented influence on the roll of the dice! Each playthrough offers its own rewards, and the Chimeras you encounter in one run can be entirely different than those you find in another. With different Chimeras comes different strategies to assemble your team for the perfect run!

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me but since Steam doesn't have an option for neutral review I guess I'd have to leave a negative one.The main reason for it being - game simply lacks depth and variety.Despite there being so many different chimeras, different factions with supposedly different playstyles your run would pretty much always look the same.You're always looting the whole map, you're always buying your two die In shops, you're pretty much doing the same stuff on the battlefield - attack and spin, well maybe sometimes more inclined to spinning over attacking and vice versa.Runs just don't feel different enough:- you don't get enough decisions;- chineras mostly split in two categories - bad and good ones, not really considering your build;- item pool is pretty small and I feel like every run I'd see more than 50% of the pool;- no rarity or tiers for items (like boss specific f.e.) makes very unexciting to get one too;Balancing the game with very little decision to make also makes your game really easy - you pretty much can't fail making a build and only can die to execution error.And sure there is trial mod (aka ascensions) which are byw done in a cool manner when enemies become stronger but you also get benefits.But by the time of this review I've beaten trial level 6 and haven't lost a single time (11 or 12 wins back to back).That being said I do want to highlight that on all the other fronts game is really nice - most charming artstyle, comfy music, lots of little animations for different debuffs, like sleeping states drawn for every chimera! Or every chimera making a unique sound taking damage.You can really see lots of loved poured into the project and I do appreciate it.But still it's a GAME. And most important thing in a game will always be gameplay. Which feels shallow and lacking - its like there is missing a system or two to seal the deal and make the game really great.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely baffled to how little attention this game gets. This game has some of the best synergies in gameplay I have ever seen in a rogue-like. The world of Dicefolk is filled with "Chimeras", monsters with all kinds of weird designs and abilities. These creatures suddenly went hostile when an evil god named Salem took control of them. You play as Alea, a young hero who takes ont he task to defeat Salem. You are equipped with a talisman that lets you take control of chimeras.The gameplay is a mix of rogue-like, deckbuilder and monster tamer. You play through three zones and each zone has multiple nodes for you to discover. Most nodes are hidden when you enter a zone and you have to defeat enemies to reveal more of the map. You start with three dummy creatures which are strong enough to defeat early enemies but what you really want are chimeras.These can be found in statues, there are three in each zone and you can pick one chimera from these three statues (like picking a starter in pokemon). These chimeras always have a special ability. These abilities are activated under specific conditions, when the creature attacks, when it gets attacked or if another ally takes damage and so on. You usally look for abilities that complement each other for your strategy. For an example, there is a creature that attacks back if it got attacked and another that attacks when one of your creatures attacks.This way you can always attack back when your chimera gets hit.Combat in this game works a bit different to other creature battlers. Instead of having a bunch of abilities for your creatures, you use dice here. You start with three dice and can get more later. Each side of a die has various symbols that define what you can do. Swords let you attack, shields block one attack, crossed swords let you and the enemy attack each other and many more. A key gameplay mechanic is also rotation. You always fight with a team of three chimeras and enemies  also have up to three creatures. But only the monster in the front can normally attack and take damage, so you can rotate creatures around with your dice to change who can attack or who takes damage. This way you can split damage between your creatures while maxing out damage on enemies.The enemy team also uses dice but you can decide the order in which what die is used. This gives players great control what they want tdo despite the random element od dice rolling. I think this  is a great way to combine RNG with tactical decisions.Damage on your creatures is kept between battles but there are often ways to heal inside and outside in battle.One aspect for healing is equipment. Each chimera has slots for items just like in Pokemon but the number of item slots can be increased on special nodes like the campfire. A chimera can have up to five items. These items can provide healing more attack power or even provide completely new abilities. Equipment is the key to refining your build, they pair greatly with the individual abilities of your chimeras. As you progress through the zones you will also find the dice merchant. Thi sguy offers new dice but also improves yur existing dice by swapping out sides with new ones. This way you can increase the chances to roll what you need and is another great way to control the RNg of this game.As you progress through the game you will unlock new talismans. These act as "creature" decks. Each talisman has their own pool of chimeras that they can pull from when they offer you one at statues. These are often themed around specific gameplay mechanics like being aggressive with attacks and attack power or playing more mobile with many rotations for your team to activate abilities. A great way to try out different strategies and playstyles.Once you beat the game with all four base talismans you unlock the door to the final boss, Salem. By playing with the various talismans you will also unlock more chimeras, new equipment and even new gameplay mechanics. There are so many cool combinations and strategies that you can try out.And beating the game unlocks trial mode, which works similiar to ascensions in other rogue-likes. They increase the diffciulty by adding more challenging rules to the game but unlike other games you also get a possitive rule change like getting free rerolls. It's interesting to see a difficulty system that does not just increase the difficulty further but makes things interesting by giving you something in return too.The last patch also intriduced a new challenge mode that lets you play a run with very specific rules, starting equipment and creatures. Beating these challenge runs unlocks new items for you to try out.There is a lot to discover and I really love how all the mechanics fit perfectly together to support your strategies. It's like a neat little puzzle box that you try to solve.
_childDocuments_.name: Dicefolk

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with this game when it first released its demo. I just completed my first run to make sure it lived up to its promise, and I'm happy to report that it exceeded my expectations.Dicefolk's biggest draw for me was its unique battle system in which you control both your team's and your opponents' actions via dice that are rerolled every turn. The strategy then becomes about playing those dice in the most optimal order. A large attack may be coming your way, but maybe if you rotate the enemy team to a sleeping sloth before playing that attack, it gets wasted. Maybe the enemy is about to heal, so you swap them into their full-health unit and laugh at the stupid AI for doing exactly what you told it to do. It's very satisfying and constantly makes you feel clever. I've never played a game that tackles combat like this.I also love the way that you recruit your chimera. Every map (of which there are three throughout a run) gives you only one chimera, but there are three opportunities to get it. What this means is that you always get a selection of three random chimera, but each one is unveiled to you one at a time. Do you take the first thing you see for an immediate boost in power, or do you try to fight through and see them all before making a decision? It's a great risk/reward system.With a counted 106 chimera in the compendium and only getting 3-4 a run, Dicefolk promises to offer a lot of variety in its team composition for many runs to come. Honestly, throughout my first run, I couldn't point to any flaws in design that would cause me to not recommend this. Maybe something will crop up on multiple repeat playthroughs, but so far, this game has aced it for me. Definitely give this game a shot if you're a fan of roguelikes, monster-tamers, or board games in general.EDIT: So I've played this a lot since launch day, and am even happier to report that it's got great replay value. I just completed Trial XI (for Slay the Spire fans, essentially Dicefolk's Ascension 20) and am still finding new synergies and busted combos that make the game feel very satisfying. Now that I've seen most of the bestiary, I can confirm the designs are all killer too. No notes for this game. It's simply one of my favourite monster-tamers and my favourite roguelikes. Go play it.

_childDocuments_.review: so much potential but just not quite there. for context ive finished the game and am climbing through the tiers of the trial difficulty. it really is a great game concept but as a someone whos looking for a roguelike experience this genuinely feels like an early access game when it comes to the roguelike elements and specifically around the lack of build defining choices.The core gameplay is great - lots of thought provoking decision making in the moment to moment combat. The art and music are captivating and really engaging. However I have had considerable issue with the lack of variety in this game. The classes have their own list of chimeras and each of them are clearly at different powerlevels. This issue is exacerbated with how you only have the option of having 3 of them within your party and only get to pick a single one from each area (there is one more way to pick but it's utterly random from the roster). This means that most of the time you will resort to a no brainer pick when presented with options (This includes equipment as you will likely see over 60% of the options in each run). This results in many runs effectively being the exact same thing - which to be honest isn't a bad thing but with the way the classes are structured - despite the massive roster of creatures - everything will feel samey because you will always pick the safe options when presented with so little choices.To the developers - you have built a fantastic foundation but please continue to work on the class system and overall roguelike decision making. I would personally suggest removing the class locked systems altogether to give players more variety and instead have classes based around starting game defining equipments or special dices specific for that class. Another option would be the idea of being able to collect more creatures but being able to swap them in and out or even being able to select your three creatures from the start to let players focus on equipment (can add rarities, an upgrade system etc). Lastly please consider add rerolls of some kind to shops - i've had many runs where I've been bricked trying to run a mana build without getting a single mana dice or mana items (This just makes certain archetypes unplayable) until the 2nd or 3rd area of the game. I would love to continue playing this game if these issues are addressed! This really hurts because to be honest - the game is so unique but I just can't recommend the game for players like me who are invested in this genre as the lack of variety utterly ruins the experience given the price point. In saying that - if you are looking for a casual roguelike game and this looks appealing to you please don't let this deter you!

_childDocuments_.review: Man, this is a tough one. It is a good game, chimeras are well balanced, there are different strats and builds to mess around for a bit. Main mechanic of controlling both yours and your opponen's actions is clever. That said, the game has 2 big cons for me:1) There just isn't enough variety for a game of a genre like this one. I gets repetitive pretty fast. No big decisions to be made, no events that shake things up a bit. Once you see all he faactions and enemies, runs get pretty similar from each other. 2) The game is very, very easy. If you are a rogue like vet like me, you will probably not lose a single game. I have played 12 and haven't lost yet. Ascensions give you boh a penalty and a benefit, so the game doesn't get much harder either. As a result, I'm in a place where the only purpose of playing is to unlock every chimera and item, while I keep climbing the ascensions in the hope that, at some point, the game actually gets a bit more challenging, having not much fun in the process. I do like that there are many things to unlock, but if the difficulty is a cakewalk it just feels like a chore to me. It would have been much better to have less things to unlock (meaning more in the base game) but with an earlier ramp up in the difficulty that made the game more fun and challenging.As it is, the game seems much more enjoyable for people that come for the creature collection aspect that for fans of roguelikes. It also seems more appropiate for players not familiar with this genre, given how easy it is. But for people that are searching for a replayable and challenging roguelike to put a lot of hours in, there might be better options around there.

_childDocuments_.review: Has its flaws and feels a bit shallow at times, but is honestly a lot of fun. The mechanic of controlling the order of what your enemy does makes this more of a strategic puzzle game of sorts and is 100% the main selling point of the game. I was put off by the idea at first, but once I tried out the demo I found myself really enjoying it. The creature designs are also pretty great.The game has decent progression as each run gets you closer to unlocking a new chimera, potential item to purchase during runs, and/or new areas. Honestly, while later chimera's are usually a bit stronger with what I experienced so far, some of them are only good in specific circumstances or combinations and are less reliable then some of the older options (at least for consistency). For the most part though, you can use any of them to win since each individual run is quite easy. I have so far played through 8~9 runs in the full game and 2 test runs through the demo. I have only lost 1 run, on the final boss of said run, after getting no synergies and no decent items the whole time and still was a mere 12 damage from victory. I have beaten every other attempted run easily including my very first. This isn't to say I'm a tactical genius, but rather that the game is pretty forgiving and easy (without feeling boring; at least 8 hours in) unless you get really unlucky or make really dumb decisions repeatedly.Each successful run, in my experience, is between 45min~1hr. A little short, but at the same time is probably a good amount of time to prevent each run from overstaying its welcome.The DLC is inexpensive at 5 dollars and adds some cool critters, though it feels like it should have been included with the base game considering the game's somewhat lighter content.All in-all, the game does enough right and is unique enough to be worth playing and investing some time in. It could have a little more depth, but what it is, is already really solid. I recommend at least checking out the demo and seeing what you think.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to state that as of the time of writing this review, I'm only about 4-ish hours in, and I've only beaten the game 5 or 6 times.If I could, I would definitely leave a neutral review, but since I can't, I will leave a positive one because I believe in the game and there are some very solid fundamentals in play here. I'm going to start with the positives.PROS:* The game is challenging enough, and you do have to put some thought into your plays and your composition to make it to the end of a run.* The monster design is solid all around, lots of great designs (even though a few here and there are just... not really that good)* Items are mostly great and there are lots of different ways to win, several different monsters and mechanics are viable.* The "Ascension" system in the game seems solid so far as well, adding both good and bad modifiers to your runs.* The four "classes" play fairly differently, giving you a different roster of monsters to work with, which complement each other fairly well without pigeon-holing you into just one viable build.Now, there are some things here that I feel can only come from one not really playing many games in the genre or being fairly new to game development, which might as well be the case, so I'm going to point them out, but mostly because I really like the core concept and I think this game has everything to become a real gem.CONS:* SO. MANY. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. % TRIGGER. ITEMS AND SKILLS. My ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ god, it's atrocious how many items have "Do X, 10% of the time" or skills that are "Do Y, 50% of the time". This feels absolutely horrible and makes it very hard to plan your run and turn. This is supposed to be a tactical/turn based/strategy game and this sort of RNG on top of dice rolling is just... No. Please don't.* It feels like a lot of the monsters were meant to have evolutions or some sort of progression but they just... don't. An evolution system or a way to further customize monsters would be amazing, but right now they are all the same stat block with exactly one passive skill attached to it, which quickly makes monsters feel bland and... samey. Same attack, roughly the same HP, one passive skill. That's it. * Despite finding a handful of viable strategies already, there are far too many monsters who are just straight up useless outside of very niche item combinations and builds, which you can take with a grain of salt since I'm not even done unlocking everything._________________As I mentioned, I'm fairly early into the game, and maybe I'll play enough to unlock everything, and if the opinions above change, I will come back and edit it accordingly. As of right now, I really wanted to express these opinions as I might not have the time to do so later and this game made me care, despite it's flaws, it's been a fun short ride and hopefully I'll get to experience more of it in the upcoming days.tl;dr: Initial impressions are mixed, but if the devs address the attrocious RNG based items and abilities and give some of the monsters a glow up, this could be an absolutely fantastic game down the road.________________Edit: Revisiting the game later, now with the DLC and more content, and yeah, they didn't address anything that was wrong with the game, they just added more stuff on top, so take from that what you will. The RNG is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brutal and the monster design is... Fine at best. It's a serviceable game, the challenges for example don't even let you know what level of "ascension" you'll be in, there's just so much that makes it seem like the devs never actually played or playtested it for obvious frustrations.Overall I think it's a 6/10,so I'll leave it as a positive even thought it's closer to mixed than positive in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit pained to leave a negative review for this.  It's cute, it's got creatures that you collect, it's very evocative for the first few hours, BUT it's missing the heart of what makes a good roguelike.  The other negative reviews have been accurately pointing this out and the devs either won't or can't make the changes necessary to really shake the game up and make it into a much better game.Primarily, it still feels like it's in early access with major issues that remain unaddressed: * difficulty is too low and the final boss is laughable (the fight before him is almost always much harder)* there are no 'decisions' during the run - you see everything and get everything* creatures and items are in no way balanced with a few 'good' ones and a wide array of useless* the item pool is incredibly limited and not tiered (you'll see the same drops over and over)* run difficulty is determined by the RNG favoring you with 'good' or 'bad' creatures and stores* the different "creature family" talismen wind up feeling very similar* the spinning mechanic seems like it will be pivotal (ha) but you use it less and less once you get your team set upThe core concept is good, but the execution is not.  That said, the game is still enjoyable.  It's got charm.  It's got decent creature visual design.  If you're not deep into roguelikes, you may even love the game.  As such, I'm going to say: vets of roguelikes: 5/10, newbies or creature collector fans: 7-8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I received a free copy of this game from the developer, but I would gladly pay for it several times over. On its surface, Dicefolk may look like a standard roguelite dice-battler, but its systems carry a surprising amount of depth. There are lots of monsters to unlock and discover, each with their own abilities that can be upgraded if you find this game's version of a shiny. Being able to equip each and every monster with pieces of unique equipment adds to the strategy, and that's before even getting into the dice which can be customized and added to.Other reviews have complained about the gameplay becoming stale after a while, and I suppose I could see how it might once you invest a significant amount of time into it. Some monsters could use a balancing pass, as well. Some are basically useless, while there are a few that can absolutely carry a run. But right now, I find each run to be fun and tactical. It feels great to win, and losing doesn't feel like it's just down to bad RNG. I'd definitely recommend this one for anyone who likes roguelite deckbuilders or even anyone who likes creature battlers and wants something that strays away from the standard formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Dicefolk is a game that immediately attracted for its gameplay and cute artstyle when I play the demo. The fact that you also select what the enemies dices does and can try to mitigate damage and other negative effect that way is so clever. I was also always a fan of dice game and throwing dice so getting to personalise the dice face was also a joy. Unfortunately, as you can see with my playtime, I barely played 4 hours and I'm already getting bored. Simply put, there is not enough variety for a rogue like. Neither with enemies, your own chimera(the little pokemon-type creatures that fight for you), nor with objects. Then there the fact that many chimeras simply sucks. Not only because many of them are just straight up bad but others also only shine in a specific team composition. If you don't have the chimeras that synergize with them, many of them become useless, which dwindle an already limited pool of creatures. The second stage is especially difficult because it contain so many bad chimeras. I know luck play a role in all rogue-like, but never I restarted so many runs because of bad rolls on chimeras and object. The fact that apart from unlocking new things you don't really get to progress between the runs reinforce that feeling of luck dependence, since that normally how those games balance this aspect.  Play the demo, see if you like the gameplay, and then decide if you can play this, and exactly this(with very few upgrades and evolution), for the next ten hours or so. Otherwise, I would suggest to play something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Dicefolk is a simple game that's deceptively complex. The primary mechanic that sets it apart from its competitors is that you control the actions of both your team and the enemy team through partially randomized dice - therefore, the strategy mainly revolves around trying to execute all of the actions in a way that minimizes your damage taken and maximizes your damage dealt. On top of this, your team can be comprised of many, many different monsters, each with unique abilities. You can also put equipment on them, but admittedly a lot of the equipment I've found is for seemingly really niche builds.This game is very fun and IMO worth the asking price. You can easily get more than 20 hours from it, and that's $1/hr in my currency. Especially if you enjoy theorycrafting, there's a LOT of customization available in this game between the different monsters, dice, and equipment. So much so that it's almost overwhelming. The only thing it's missing, at least for what I would consider the ideal roguelite, is more meta progression. As someone else said in another review, it'd be much more fulfilling if you could unlock new skills or increase the power of your monsters permanently every time you play. I'm aware meta progression is not a staple of the genre - but the reason I say it for this game is because it has a massive cast of monsters, and adding meta progression would give incentive to play a team more than once, which is at the moment a little difficult to justify when there's so much customization. Of course, this is all just my opinion. Ultimately, putting aside what I think the game could add, what it currently IS is still worth your time if you like the genre. It's relatively cheap, fun, and easy to pick up for quick 30-45 minute games. I really do recommend it. Also, the music slaps.
_childDocuments_.name: Dicefolk

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't exactly bad. It's fine, but it has some glaring issues that make it tough to recommend. The gameplay variety is severely lacking, there's a very small pool of builds you can actually do and rather quickly the game becomes dull. The item variety is small and most items are just numerical buffs that don't feel particularly exciting or impactful. However, I find the biggest issue to be the potential for growth during runs. You can only ever grow your build so strong, partially due to you only essentially getting 3 chances to upgrade your core build during a run in the form of adding a new chimera to your team. And partially due to there being very few items that can create fun and interesting synergies should the RNG align properly. This all leads to every run essentially feeling the same, you never get to experience that particular roguelike fun where the RNG aligns perfectly and you get some god build that allows you to storm your way through a run. This does have the upside of very few runs collapsing because your RNG screws you. But those extreme highs and lows are part of the fun of this genre.Overall the game isn't bad, I wish I didn't have to leave a negative review because it is fun for the first few hours. But very quickly it becomes stale and you find yourself realizing that virtually every single run plays the same. If it goes on sale for under $10 it might be worth it as a weekend time killer, but for now, I can't really recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a concept I've never seen before: you roll two sets of dice, your allies and your opponents. Trying to make optimal plays for your allies while simultaneously trying to make your opponent's sequence of moves the most sub-optimal really stretches the brain muscles.  For the monster collecting aspect, there's over a hundred spirits with unique abilities, and as you can only obtain 3 to 4 each run, each run is wildly different. You piece together a strategy using the spirits and relics found. You're given three chances per area to choose a spirit from a Shrine to add to your team in a risk/reward system. If you grab the first offering, the remaining two Shrines give gold and health pick ups to keep your run alive. But if wait until the second or third offering, you might find a spirit that synergizes with your current strategy. And the spirits have a chance to be shiny, with improved abilities. That's another pull to wait. They are a joy to find, but then you might perish in the battles because you took too long to pick an ally.It is disappointing there isn't a bench. Sometimes I have a team that flawlessly complements each other built before the third area, which means the shrines are dead. You either pick a new spirit to replace one of your members and lose that perfect complement. And one of your buddies that carried you through hell is gone for good. Or... you lose out on those essential health pick ups.As for a difficulty slider, it has Trial Mode which is similar to Slay the Spire's ascension system.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had a ton of fun with this game. People have made plenty of comparisons to Slay the Spire, but it's really its own thing. Rather than just deal with enemy intents like in StS, you actually control the order that they do their moves -- and you have plenty of ways of manipulating what actions they'll even take on a given turn. That makes the combat feel way more engaging than in something like StS, where the enemy intents generally force you into obvious responses. "Oh, they're going to hit me for 20 damage? Better make sure I end the turn with 20 block." By contrast, here you might roll several dice and see that an enemy is going to swap positions with one of its allies, and whichever one is in the lead will permanently increases its attack power, and one of them will do an attack against one of your guys. That's a lot more thinking involved to determine what the best order is for the enemy -- and that's without even considering your own dice and the special rules of each of your own guys. Speaking of which, there's a lot of variety in the different pokemon-esque companions that you recruit in each run. I've seen some complaints about the random nature of finding 'chimeras' (what they call your allies), but the truth is that I've managed to beat the final boss with a wide plethora of them. There's also different starter talismans that let you enter a run with a vague idea of what kind of build you want to get into (such as attacking as much as possible, or creating synergy with rotating your leader for free damage, etc.). The only other big complaint I've seen is people saying there's a lack of content, to which I'm utterly confused. Counting the trial and special modes, there's like 30+ difficulty levels that add new twists and turns to how the game is played, and completing each one adds new items and chimeras for you to unlock in future runs. And given that a single run can take anywhere from 30 minutes to 1 hour, this is a great game to pick up and play when you just want something to keep you engaged without it turning into a 2 hour+ affair to finish. If you somehow lose a run, it never really feels bad since it's not like you wasted a ton of time trying to get to the final boss. All in all, I actually like this game even more than Slay the Spire, which is probably the best compliment I can give an indie dev.
