_childDocuments_.review: Very fun little game with unique and engaging combat. Being able to control enemies' actions felt fresh and added depth to an otherwise simple-looking game. The game is at its best in the first hours when trying each faction for the first time. Most negative reviews point to the lack of variety, which leads to the game feeling the same the second time you play a faction. I certainly agree with this, as there are only a few chimeras that are actually viable if you want to win. Some straight-up feel unusable.This especially becomes clear once you unlock the end game, "trial mode." With the incrementing added challenge, you have to play optimally rather than just making any build work. I'd like to believe the devs know this, so I wish they made it so you always start with a chimera shrine to recruit your first unit from the get-go.I get that random is the name of the game for roguelike, but having the shrine at the very start would have eliminated all the time I wasted restarting my run until I got a viable starting chimera. A quick restart button would have been great too.It honestly wouldn't even hurt if you could just pick a starting chimera from the whole pool. This would have been a more reliable way of ensuring players could do different builds, as they wouldn't waste time being stuck with non-viable chimeras.Some chimeras are very clearly fit to be a support, so it just doesn't make sense to leave it all to rng when you could be stuck with all support units.Not having rerolls at the shop really hurts making builds too. Plenty of my runs ended with me having excess gold and not perfecting my build. I never had a run where I felt like I completed the exodia.Overall, the game is easy, even up to the last modifier of the trial, but I personally don't think it really needs more challenge. I think the biggest strength of the game is making different builds. Its shortcoming is the lack of more viable builds. I've certainly repeated the same strategies throughout my playthrough.I finished all of the trials, but I started feeling fatigued halfway through. This certainly made it feel disappointing once I finished, and there wasn't any real reward for it. At this point, I feel I've already experienced all the game has to offer, but I honestly expected to play the game for less. I'm certainly satisfied with the game as a whole.Lastly, I was also disappointed when I found out there was no achievement for defeating the final boss at the very first turn.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I don't write many review, but I really recommend you don't get this game.I usually buy every new roguelike/lite that comes out, seeing flaws in every one along with redeemable qualities in each. Dicefolk falls completely flat across the board other than marketing.My time listed at 6.2 hours isn't accurate, because I cooked dinner and ate while the game was open, and took a few breaks since I downloaded it. A more accurate time spent in game would be 3 hours, and I beat every single of the 4 runs on my first try with the different talisman (think like different characters). And also, on the last and 4th character, I went to fight the secret end boss (think The Heart in StS); and i beat it without any issues without even knowing it would be there, so no preparationI understand that most roguelikes have ascensions modes, and this one does too, but being able to go in blindly and play the game the same way each time really shines light on how poor the game is designed. And frankly, even if the game was to be made harder, I probably wouldn't play it any more.If you're reading this and decide to get the game anyway, let me tell you how the game will go.You'll start your first playthrough and see cute characters with unique abilites, and you'll go "wow, there's probably some really cool combos". Then you'll get thrown equipments and items that have generic stat boosts, which you'll usually just hoard on one character that you choose as your carry. Then you'll buy every dice upgrade regardless of what they are, and you'll run through every boss usually exploiting some broken mechanic that was handed to you.The fights lack creativity and thinking, the overworld lacks creativity and thinking, and the "decisions" presented to you are so obvious to make that it lacks any creativity and thinking.Genuinely if you still want to play it, I recommend you buy it on a day you're completely free, so that you can just beat the entire game with all 4 talisman in 2 hours and refund the game entirely

_childDocuments_.review: A rogue-like strategy based around finding Chimera, resolving dice and team rotation. The interesting part is that you will be playing against yourself, using the dice of your enemy.Overall, it's a short and easy game. With 3 worlds to cross (and a shorter ultimate 4th world), being able to find each boss in 5-10 minutes make every run easily possible within an hour to blast through.The Chimera are charming with fluid idle animations. The battle animations, on the other side, are pretty bad. Everyone has that same default attack motion tween in which your Chimera just drags itself into the enemy.You get interesting starter specialization routes, with each field having their own unique bunch of Chimera.Unfortunately, the balance is horrible. Some Chimera are strong enough to defeat waves on their own, while others have way too much setup for the most marginable reward imaginable, making them mediocre at best after slapping some meta equipment on their slots.The gameplay is fun and you can end up with amazing synergies in your team thanks to the expanded customization.It's worth a play... but there's definitely room for patching and content updates.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Very early into the game so this is not the most accurate review as you can imagine, but i think for smaller and very recent games like this one every voice matters, (plus if someone czan play the game for 30 minutes and leave a negative review saying that its entirely luck based i thiink its fair game tell about the pros of the game instead) will probably update it down the line tooDicefolk is a creature battler roguelike, easiest comparison would be Slay The Spire but instead of cards for a deck you gather pokemon for your team, combat has some interesting mechanics, namely the titular dice that youre rolling represent actions of both you and your enemy that will happen during the turn, taking cue from games like Into The Breach, Dicefolk lets you play around your enemies intentions, but goes one step further and lets you decide when those intentions materialise: put simply you control when your enemy moves, attacks or buffs, those things *must* happen on the turn but its your choice if your opponents crushing attack deals 0 damage because your Chimera is under a shield or it obliterates your vital damage dealer and ruins the run entirely. This makes every turn a fun little puzzleof positioning and timing.Game executes a simple yet very charming style, the chimera designs are cute and interesting to look at, each of them comes equipped with their set of stats and a passive that will dictate its position in the team and the overall strategy you employ, you can build a team around buffing one strong chimera that will oneshot most enemies if a combo is executed well, go for a shield run where your creatures will deal less damage yet be invincible to most attacks, naturally there are poison and magic builds as wellMetaprogression is nice as well, you unlock new events, new locations to visit, new chimera for your team and new enemies to face in the next runs, improving both the challenge and variety, i imagine you could sink a couple hundred hours into the gameWhich, of course, brings us to the drawbacks, of which there is one - the game does not seem to have too much replay value. First of all the combat gameplay is rather simplistic - most of the actions you adn your enemies perform are rotations and attacks, chimera passives are also mainly tied to these two things, which means that most of the combos you can make will be different on paper, but will not play that much differently. I should mention, however, that the game allows you to buy new and customizing existing dice, so this is somewhat mitigated by you being able to either make your deck more consistent or unlock brand new actions for your team. That there is only a couple dozen chimeras per class with some of them overlapping means that you also wont see too big of a variety of creatuers, the fact that you mostly battle these same chimeras as your enemies does not help that either.As a final message i hope the message here is clear: the main drawback of the game is that theres not enough of it, which should be saying at least something about the quality of the experience. In the state that the game is in at the moment it probably will not become your go-to rogueliek you sink thousands of hours in, but the hundreds you can give it will be quite fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The “Creature Collector” genre is in bit of a renaissance at the moment. Nothing has yet to usurp the influence of Pokemon over the concept, even when Nintendo has been treating the IP with negligent hands and its own fanbase with contempt. They’ve got ‘F*ck you” Money after all. Yet that hasn’t topped games like Monster Sanctuary or Cassette Beasts, and now Dicefolk from making themselves a seat at that table.It’s essential these games have remarkable art direction and indelible character design. For me, the draw of the genre is discovering facets of ourselves in the world and fellow lifeforms around us. A sentiment reflected in the saying, ‘What is here, is also there.” A single facet of that profound reality. A universal notion that predates the advent of agrarian culture. A notion borne from the subterranean altars of ancient bear skulls and fertility cults. Wondering after the strange manifestations of life in order to understand it and ourselves better. Interactive enneagrams. The animal kingdom, in a sense and in praxis, shows how baffling life (and death) can be. At its core, indescribable, ineffable nonsense. Where all one can do is imbue things with meaning and order. The grace of apoptosis. Baked into the lore of Dicefolk is the Greek conception of Fate and the dynamism between Necessity and Fortune. Necessity is the karmic consequences of the confluence of our actions. It must be confronted before one can carry on properly with their lives. Necessary, in other words. As it relates to Dicefolk, it’s the procession of decisions made with one’s dice that leads to an inevitable outcome that we may or may not perceive. It’s common enough to foresee if one is cognizant of their actions.Fortune is the order of the shadows. The fickle hands of whimsy and play. It’s up to the game if you’re to get run-altering drops of gear, or a timely bonfire to heal your chimeras. Speaking of, the Chimera designs are at once legible and charming, clever even. Suffused in aesthetics with the mechanics of the game itself. Dicefolk doesn’t have the luxury of limelight, what with nowadays arguably being a golden age of indie gaming, nor the luxury of being the earliest bird. For as beloved as Pokemon is, it’s aged like a musty vault of oats, infested with the ergot of hideous textures and phoned-in mechanics(’Who wants to get lunch?’). Nintendo and Gamefreak feel it’s not necessary to change so long as their fortune holds out. Regardless of how uninspired the Pokemon designs or the gameplay becomes. With this all in mind, Dicefolk and its creators at Tiny Ghoul and Leap realized their vision. A lovely fractal of competence, class, and creativity that Gamefreak would stand to learn a lot from.

_childDocuments_.review: Dicefolks is a great addition to the roguelike deckbuilding genre. It's not really a deckbuilding game but it has a similar feel, except you choose chimera (they're like monsters or creatures, you know what I mean). Each chimera has a different ability and stats and you can equip them with items to add additional considerations in battles. Battles are turn based except you choose when each action, yours and your opponent's happen. These actions are determined by dice rolls and include things like attacking, swapping who's in the lead, guarding and so on.Dicefolk feels like great roguelike deckbuilders in the synergies that can happen with your chimeras. The game is good at not overwhelming you with different potential strategies and it's pretty easy to understand how different abilities will work together. The meta progression is great, with something new being unlocked after almost every run. My only gripe would be that the runs are a little long for my taste in a game like this. For context, I usually took 45 minutes to an hour for a successful run. But honestly I didn't ever feel like the game was tedious. The creature designs and art style are fun and there are a plenty of things to unlock to keep you coming back for another run. If you like this genre, and especially enjoyed Wildfrost or Dicey Dungeons, which I think are Dicefolk's closest relatives, you'll like this game.

This new mode gives the enemy one more dice and lets you reroll once. I didn't enjoy this mode at all, it completely destroys the game balance of the basic game. I think this is because in the first biome the enemy usually only has two dice, adding one more is a huge advantage. Rerolling doesn't help much at this point because starting out you have lots of garbage stuff on you dice.Overall I enjoyed the game but I don't think there is enough content here. I'm not going to play the entended trial mode because I don't enjoy it at all. There are no leaderboards, no challenges except the extended trial mode that I dislike.

_childDocuments_.review: Dicefolk is a fun, well-polished take on roguelite, dice-building, and party management mechanics. Thematically, it's Mesoamerican Pokemon. To me, this combination is delightful.* Giving the player control of enemy actions is a fun strategic element.* Each additional level of Trial Mode gives benefits to both the player  the enemies. Asymmetric power keeps the difficulty from feeling overbearing.* The dice elements are simple and easy to understand.* Three party members is perfect. It gives you variety and guarantees that all team members can see action (if you want them to).* The difficulty curve isn't smooth. The two final trials are much harder than preceding trials.* Dice options are limited, so you lose variability on this front.* Runs are ~1 hr long* Lore is doled out one snippet at a time for ~20 runs. It's not super deep, but there's definitely a story there.* Combat takes some tactical thinking, but it's only a couple layers deep.* It's most like Slice & Dice, in my experience. Both are all about die-rolling for combat abilities. I appreciate Dicefolks' bent toward customization of the dice, but I think Slice & Dice has more replayability because of its limits to party management (and plethora of modes).* The party juggling reminds me of Roguebook. Dicefolk is way more polished/finished. But Roguebook is a deckbuilder and cards provide more variety than dice, so it's not a perfect comparison.* Dice will invite comparison to Dicey Dungeons. DD has better music (IMO), but Dicefolk is way less RNG-dependent at higher difficulties.This game is great for sprinkling a few runs throughout the week without eating up a huge amount of time or brainpower. It won't be a forever game for me like FTL, Monster Train or Slay the Spire and that's okay. In fact, I love this game precisely because it provides a great puzzle experience without demanding  much.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )Dicefolk is a rougelite monster battler that takes obvious influence from both Slay the Spire and Pokemon. You fight rotation battles a la Pokemon's Generation V/Black and White, but the actions of monsters on both sides are controlled by dice. You click the die you want to activate and may also get to chose who is targeted by it depending on the action. You can always chose not to use some of your own dice, but all of the monster dice have to be used each round, so battles tend to be order of operations puzzles where you need to use the monster powers in the least effective way possible. Almost every monster also has a special ability like getting free attacks under certain circumstances or suffering a penalty to compensate for amazing basic stats, so you've got to pay attention to how those interact with the battle as well. Unlike the climbing maps of Slay the Spire, Dicefolk's map lets you freely move between all the nodes available. Each level provides at least two opportunities to swap in new team members. One of those chances comes from the three statues on the map, which will give you an additional choice of monster for each one you activate. You could choose whatever the first one spawns and get a new monster quickly, or you could wait until you've activated all three and have a better chance of getting one that really fits with your team. Later statues have better odds of spawning rare or shiny ("incandescent") monsters with improved abilities, so there's extra incentive to wait. Your other chance comes from a guaranteed event that lets you spend money to buy a single monster that's randomly chosen before you make the purchase, so it won't always be one you'll want. Most of the fun of the game comes from those monster collection events and the other events that help build out your strategy. Each map also has two shops that provide improvements to your dice faces or even additional dice to use each turn as well as single use items and passive equipment. Still other events give you direct stat boosts, ways to increase how much equipment you can use at once, or choices between some or all of the above. You can make some very powerful monsters if you make good use of these events, and healing is easy enough to come by that I found it almost always worthwhile to clear each floor. Unfortunately, that last sentence also hints at the game's biggest issue. I found that building out one ridiculously boosted monster and doing every event on each floor was a dominant strategy. That might not be a problem if the ways of making one strong monster were as varied as the ways of making a strong deck in StS, but here it seems like the key is almost always just about getting your leader's strength as high as possible and finding some ways to get regen. It follows a very similar pattern with StS where you have to reach the final boss door with every character before you're actually allowed to fight that boss, but unlike StS, I reached the door on my first try with all but one character and then beat the boss on my first try all but one time as well. The lack of difficulty might be a less immediate issue if you're new to the genre, but the effective strategies are so simple that I think a new player would still find them pretty quickly. To its credit, Dicefolk does do a few innovative things to try to mitigate that problem as you keep playing. It has an ascension mode like every roguelite, but this one is unique in that both you and the enemies get a buff with each level. This helps runs start to feel unique again since each successive win leads to further modifiers, but since you've already won the game many times by the point you're able to access ascension, it's almost certainly coming after the fatigue has started to set in. Winning runs also leads to new monsters unlocking and new events, and of course you can change between different characters, but most of these have little real impact on your strategy after the first floor.

_childDocuments_.review: "Dicefolk" on Steam carves its niche within the tactical roguelite and creature-collecting genre, mixing traditional roguelike elements with a unique dice-rolling combat system that allows for an engaging player experience.Pros:- Innovative Combat System: The game's combat mechanics stand out for their complexity and strategic depth. Players use dice to control the actions of their team of Chimeras and their opponents, offering a layer of strategy that goes beyond simple turn-based battles.- Diverse Chimera Collection: "Dicefolk" features a wide range of Chimeras, each with unique abilities and playstyles, from resilient tanks to swift attackers.- Engaging Roguelike Elements: The game incorporates roguelike elements effectively, ensuring that no two runs are the same and maintaining a high level of replayability. With the chance to unlock new Chimeras, equipment, and even game-enhancing talismans, players are continually presented with fresh challenges and discoveries.Cons:- Repetitive Enemy Encounters: While the game offers a variety of enemies, at it's core it is the same each time.- Difficulty Balance: In my playthrough I noticed that the games difficult jumps pretty strongly instead of having a good gradual pace.- Underpowered Chimeras and Equipment:  The game has some work on balancing as some chimeras and equipment feel essentially negligible while some way to strong without a solid foundation as to why."Dicefolk" presents a compelling blend of tactical combat, creature collection, and roguelike progression, wrapped in an accessible yet deep strategic package. Despite its minor hiccups with balance and variety, the game rolls a winning combo of 5/6for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: So I beat the last trial mode for one of the classes, which took me about 20 hours total, so I assume I’ve cleared the hardest difficulty (so far) for the game which I think gives me an informed opinion! Dicefolk has your basic roguelite format- there are enemies, you kill enemies, you collect randomized loot and allies to customize how you kill enemies, rinse and repeat. There’s three main acts and a final boss act and games run between 40 to 60 minutes (a lot of that will be animation time though, even on the fastest setting). That’s all boilerplate.The way you kill enemies is via commands like ‘attack’, ‘guard’, ‘rotate’, and so on. You have a party of 3 little critters and fight up to 3 other enemy critters. Your commands are dictated by dice that have the commands on them, and you can modify the dice to suit what synergizes with your critter abilities. There’s a lot of little dinguses in this game! So that's cool, plenty of content on that front.Despite adhering to dice, I almost never found myself cursing RNG. There’s a lot of methods of counterplay (and even a reroll option on later difficulties) so very surprisingly I never felt that the randomness of the dice hurt my ability or led to unfair situations (at least often enough for me to care). Rather, since some very powerful abilities were rare, I was more often excited to roll a powerful dice than I was getting stuck with a dud set of dice, which is an impressive feat for the game given how much randomness there is going on behind the hood! All that being said, especially on the last few trials, you will absolutely get gobsmacked not by dice RNG, but by enemy RNG. It’s a bit unfortunate there are some team compositions that will render your team 100% dead, particularly when it comes to things like the thorn mechanic. That comes with the territory, though. I will say enemy variety is a BIT lacking. It gets a bit tiring having to face the same early game monsters over and over again. Art and sound design are pretty good. All the critters have little custom sounds and a few different animations, though the basic interface is very simple so there’s no much wow factor there. Music is decent, the UI is (mostly) functional enough. It could really use a battle log function or something though, since often there’s so much going on at once it’s hard to tell what exactly killed your critter (especially annoying on later difficulties where your beasts are at 1 HP a lot). Not much of a story, so I’m not even going to cover it.My biggest complaint would probably be that the early trials (the easiest difficulties) aren’t just mandatory but are also EXTREMELY easy. This game functionally has a five to six hour tutorial since you’re almost guaranteed to blow through the first runs you do. I think that was by design, in order to not turn people off, but for me it was the opposite and I was almost put off by how unchallenging the game was. It got better at the hardest difficulties but the game is so slow sometimes that chugging through the baby modes really put me to sleep! But since I paid about 20 bucks and got about 20 hours of gameplay out of it, with maybe another 20 if I try to 100% it, I’d say it’s generally worth the money. I think the premise maybe could have used a bit more time to cook, since games start to feel real samey given that most of your dice are going to be pretty much the same from run to run, but it’s a serviceable enough product. Solid 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope to write a more in-depth review sooner or later, but for now: Dicefolk is a very engaging, battle-focused roguelike with creature collecting elements. Unlike most creature collectors, you'll only have your creatures on a per-run basis as opposed to keeping them long-term, so I hesitate to call it a true creature collector, but it is nonetheless highly enjoyable.The core gameplay loop is using your three creatures (and periodically replacing them) to attack the enemy creatures, with rolling dice that you can customize throughout your adventure and change the faces of (they're functionally d6s except with actions instead of numbers, so you can have something like "attack the enemy" on a face, and "guard against an attack" on another). I loved the demo, and I'm loving the core gameplay loop still -- it's an extremely solid game that is just generally really enjoyable to play.The creatures are extremely important in this kind of game, even if it's not a true creature collector, and they certainly don't disappoint. Each one feels unique and it's super fun to build up strong synergies between them. The art style is one I personally enjoy, and I think the designs are all really solid. As with so many creature collection games, this one has its own rare-color-variant, in this case called Iridescents, but in this game they provide a significant power boost. For example, if you creature may have an ability that requires it to be in the lead position to activate, instead it may trigger from anywhere if it's iridescent. It's a fun power boost, but also doesn't really feel like it's balanced to where they're absolutely necessary or anything.Overall, the game has felt extremely good and I have almost entirely positives to say about it. Almost. While not quite a negative, I will say that the story cutscenes have felt... out of place to me. It's not a genre where I really expect to have story in my face, and what they showed me felt... I don't want to say 'bland' exactly, but it didn't feel like it really meaningfully contributed to the overall quality of the game at all to me. It feels irrelevant, I guess, and I'm generally the type of gamer that appreciates lore in games. Idk, it's not a huge deal or anything, as it's maybe a minute of cutscenes across two instances thus far in 6+ hours of gameplay, but it was something that stuck with me as being the sole element in the game that just kinda felt out of place, like it was checking a box on a checklist rather than really belonging. But again, not a big deal, just a minor "huh?" kind of thing. The demo is free and gets you into the gameplay really quickly -- you lose nothing but maybe 10-20min of your time by trying it out, so take my word for it and just try it. I feel pretty confident in saying you'll be glad you did.

_childDocuments_.review: The strength of the game is certainly its innovative and extremely deep combat system. You have the unique ability to sequence both your team's actions and the enemy team's actions. Sometimes the difference between the victory and defeat is figuring out whether it is advantageous for the enemy to attack before or after you swap the positions of your creatures. Add to this, a wide variety of triggered effects -- both as innate passives on your creatures and on pieces of gear you equip --  and figuring out the optimal sequencing in battle is a fascinating tactical puzzle. The game also does a great job of ensuring replay-ability and variety across runs. The game includes four factions, each of which feels quite distinct and have their own style of teambuilding. My first run was with the Warrior faction, and I relied heavily on a chimera who triggered free attacks whenever an ally attacked. By equipping this chimera with a trio of powerful relics, the frequency of his attacks carried me to victory. Then in my second run, I played as the Storm faction and gathered a team of chimeras who triggered a variety of abilities whenever I changed the positioning of my chimeras on the field during combat. By combining these passive abilities with equipment abilities that also triggered on repositioning, I was able to cleverly time the movements of my chimeras into and out of the front row of combat to generate exciting cascades of cool buffs and damaging abilities. On my third run, I began by recruiting a chimera who cast a magic spell that froze enemies in their place ... and on my fourth run, I watched my enemies whither away while inflicted with huge volumes of poison ...Despite the strategic depth, the game does a good job of starting simple and layering on complexity. Although there are eventually a huge number of team-building possibilities available, the game starts you off with a relatively straightforward set of chimeras that you can recruit and then you gradually unlock additional strategic options after each run. Ultimately, as someone who enjoys both team-building RPGs and rogue-lite games, Dicefolk is easily worth the purchase price.

name: Yomawari: Lost in the Dark
detailed_description: A young girl awakens in a dark, unfamiliar forest with no recollection of how she got there. As she searches for the way out, she crosses paths with a mysterious individual who reveals to her that she’s been cursed. In order to break the curse, she needs to explore the streets of her town at night to seek out her lost memories. However, malevolent ghosts lurk within the shadows, and the girl must avoid them by running, hiding, and shutting her eyes if she hopes to survive long enough to break her curse. The Night Continues: Another chapter of the atmospheric horror series has emerged from the shadows! With a new story set in a frighteningly familiar world, new and returning fans alike can dive right in. Home Sweet Haunt: Eerie sound design and shadowy environments set the stage for gruesome and terrifying ghosts never seen before in the series. New Fear, New Me: For the first time in Yomawari, you can customize your character’s appearance by changing her hairstyle, hair color, clothes, and accessories. See No Evil: Do whatever it takes to survive the terrors of the night. Unveil secrets and specters alike using your flashlight. Find clues while listening to the sound of your heartbeat to detect nearby ghosts, and utilize a new mechanic, closing your eyes, to avoid the gaze of the evil spirits watching you.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of the series, go ahead and get it, but honestly it's the weakest of the series.Long story short this 3rd entry in the series is long and empty.While the past entries also had similar problems, this one is worse... but it's still a decent game. There's a lot of questionable stuff, but in the end it is still a decent storied game.Each "chapter" in the story has a mini-boss and they are annoyingly long despite it requiring to do the same simple action over and over again.The world feels empty during the "chapter" section since it narrows the pathway and prevents any kind of exploring. Maybe the past entries lacked direction confusing the player, but this one shoves the player in the direction too much for the whole chapter that it becomes tedious. It might also be the reason why the main character (player) talks so much regarding the situation (i.e. "Oh, a key. Maybe I can open the fence at X"). I can tolerate tedious repetition on the final boss/area but repeating for each "chapter" made me get more and more frustrated by tiny QoL inconveniences.For some reason they decided to take out returning to the house from the menu so you have to walk extra miles just to save the game. Not only that but the world feels more cramped and empty at the same time. The non-chapter specific enemies are 80% rehashed and provides no synergy with the new mechanic of "closing your eyes", which btw makes you move at a slugs pace slowing down the already slow pacing.Despite the bad stuff, it does still maintain the good atmosphere and sound. Story is not as amazing, but still good enough. I definitely liked the way they split the *chapters* and how the player visits them.So overall I'd say this game is a 7/10, and recommend to fans but hesitate for new people.I've yet to complete the collection, but not really looking forward to it compared to past entries...UPDATE: Finished the collection, and realized how static the enemies are. Each path feels the exact same every time, making it more tedious to traverse the large map.I have also changed this review to a thumbs up, since I can't say the game itself is bad by itself. Just quite disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: Solidly decent so far. As other reviews have and will no doubt mention, the game has been a bit empty at times between objectives. The game most certainly reuses assets from the previous titles. The school from what I can recall has some absolutely identical areas, and the town itself has at least assets that have been reused if not specific zones from my recollection. Just like the previous titles however, the game is awesome at atmosphere. What little of the story I've experienced so far has left me intrigued enough to continue as well! This game proves the series strengths once again such as its complete grip on sound design. The directional sound is on point, and the general usage of audio cues is very good. None of the events feel forced or inorganic either. Everything I've run into feels very unique, and tends to come completely unexpectedly. These are the things I absolutely loved in the previous entries and I'm glad they still seem to be as strong as before. The major issue with the game is one of pricing. I would suggest buying this game on a sale when possible, or buying either of the previous two titles (at the time this review is written they are on sale). They are both extremely solid and the first title is cheaper than Lost in the Dark.All that being said, I do think that the game justifies its worth for those who were fans of the other entries, and potentially even for new fans, with the caveat that the other entries are both cheaper on sale or off sale, and that you are willing to deal with a little bit of tedious wandering. Definitely worth my own money thus far however!

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed it for being more Yomawari, but...it's definitely the weakest in the series. The atmosphere, scares, and story are all a step down.  (really there's not much story to speak of till the very end) The general town areas use all the same enemies from 2, and are completely uninteresting.  The specific chapter areas tend to have more new stuff, but a lot of the mechanics and challenges end up feeling kind of tedious.  The boss encounters go on for quite a while, while not changing much throughout.  A few special interactions with story segments towards the end add a little interest, but it feels like too little, too late to drum up much excitement for the finale, which while better than the rest of the chapters, definitely pales in comparison to the high bar set by Midnight Shadows.Overall, I'll give it a thumbs up, but you should really only bother if you played and greatly enjoyed the first 2 games, and are hungry for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently, I am right before/at the final boss of the true end. I'm unsure whether I want to finish the game, so I'll write my review now.Short version: The game has more content than the previous entry (at least in terms of hours needed to get though the story) but the gameplay it offers is much worse. It feels tedious to play. The spirits you face don't seem to have much of a connection to the main plot at all, and seem to be there to pad out the game's length. Not worth it for the price.Long version: I played the first two games on the Switch - there's a bundle available with both "Night Alone" and "Midnight Shadows". The first game is already a good time, and I enjoyed how every encounter with a major spirit have you a better picture of the overall conflict and story. "Midnight Shadows" improves the presentation and adds a lot of story scenes and character interaction. It just has a much more fleshed out story."Lost in the Dark", however, feels like a step backwards. While they added the whole "close your eyes" mechanic as a new interaction with the various spirits, they also removed the badge system of "Midnight Shadows", which I had enjoyed quite a bit.Progression wise, you have several items you find that give you hints on where to go to recover your memories. You can visit these places more or less in any order you want. Each of the places has a spirit encounter. Some feel more fleshed out than others, and there are some interesting ones that stand out a bit. After banishing or dealing with the spirit in some way, you find an important item that helps you remember your past. A problem here is that the items are always found in the same order, no matter the order in which you tackle the various spirits. This leads to some finds not making much sense.Overall I feel like the game is too long for what it's trying to do, or just not well enough designed. The game just feels less cohesive than its predecessor. And considering the big pricetag, I would not recommend this game unless you desperately want more Yomawari. Even then, be prepared to be somewhat disappointed.If you have a Nintendo Switch, I'd recommend getting the bundle of the first two games. Otherwise, perhaps the complete Yomawari bundle or the NIS Horror Bundle might be worth it with a big discount.

_childDocuments_.review: As of this review, I have 100% completed the game and got every achievement.Like the previous two Yomawari games, this game is an atmospheric horror game that focuses on Japanese folklore. Gameplay is exploration through various locations to progress a story while surviving ghosts and collecting items. I won't go into too much detail about things here to avoid spoilers, but there are a few interesting ideas this time around. These ideas freshen up the gameplay a bit, but do feel a bit experimental. They pop up in certain parts of the game but don't come up again after that. The game is also much more open than the previous entries. In the previous games, the map seemed open, but was heavily restricted by where the story needed you to go. For this game, as long as you find specific items around the town, you can access areas in whatever order you'd like.I want to also point out some flaws with the gameplay. The game is fine on the first exploration for each area, but when it comes to backtracking, it leaves a bit to be desired. Checkpoints, which allow you to "fast-travel" to other checkpoints, are few and far between. This wouldn't be much of a problem- if the character wasn't so slow. More often than not, I wanted some form of faster movement like a bicycle, at least for post-game or something. I found myself just running into enemies so that I could respawn at a checkpoint, since it was faster to just respawn than to have to run all the way to one. As for the story, it covers themes similar to those from the previous games, but they feel better handled this time around, at least to me. The story especially ramps up towards the end. It has some twists that they hint at throughout the game, but you wouldn't be able to guess without putting in more thought. A really solid plot overall.Giving my overall thoughts, this is a pretty solid game. It takes the Yomawari formula and improves on it, with a much more open design compared to its predecessors and some unique gameplay ideas. Backtracking is this game's biggest weakness however- and if you're a completionist, it might feel like a slog to fully complete. I would definitely recommend this to a series veteran. But if you haven't played a Yomawari game before, I'd recommend checking out this series' second game, Midnight Shadows first before dipping your toes into this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of this series and completed the previous two titles. I think this is a decent game for those who are new to the series. But there are some issues as a fan.StoryAt first, I felt it was lacking compared to the previous "Midnight Shadows." However, it gets better as the story progresses. Everything that happens in the story has a meaning.I especially liked how you recover true memories and the subsequent climax. I hope the detail will be explained in the novel like the other two.MusicThis game features two OSTs and is the first in the series to have title music. Both are as good as the prequels, which give you a sense of helplessness, a feeling that the future of a protagonist is grim no matter the effort.I think they are very good at representing the protagonist and Kotori whose fates are toyed with by a curse.SystemAlthough this game has a lot of reused assets from previous titles and most ghosts are the same, there are some improvements and changes.Closing eyes, higher resolution, wider and more natural lighting by the flashlight, a lot of side-quests, and non-linear stamina gauge replenishment make stamina management more important. Also, pebbles work on most enemies if you throw them BEFORE the ghosts notice you.I am not against reusing assets. But for a completely new town, more new ghosts would have been natural from a world-building perspective.Like “The Firefly Diary” and "A Rose in the Twilight," this game is very good at creating an atmosphere. I felt a strong "early Heisei-era Japanese countryside" vibe.Overall, this game has the same soul as its predecessors, along with a good story and a bitter end.I really wish more people knew about the Yomawari series.

_childDocuments_.review: Just wrapped this one up after getting stuck before the true ending, and I gotta say I agree with what a lot of the other reviews here are saying: if you're a fan of the series already, this one's another good installment but definitely not the best if you're looking for what Yomawari as a series boils down to at its core. It still maintains that lovely "spooky but not scary" atmosphere that the previous two hold so well, and it's been a while since I've played so I don't recall exactly how many of the spirits are recycled, but there's plenty of fun new ones here.This one is structured in a more "linear" fashion the others, but I only mean that in reference to each specific sub-area that you have to go through to progress the story. The (mostly) open exploration is still there, as is the benefits of retracing your steps to visit areas you've already been through now & again to see if you missed anything, or if there's anything new there. In the first two games it was clear that many of the spirits were based directly off of Japanese myth and yokai, but I'm not sure how much that carries through into this one - but original ideas are still really neat!This one's also got something more of a story than the previous installments, I think. It's certainly more driven and focused, with everything you do being guided by that main story & what you "need" to do next, but - the story ended up hitting me in ways I wasn't expecting! Literally as soon as you get into the main portion of the game, you know that you're trying to recover lost memories, but it wasn't until way later that I realized that that's because the entirety of this game deals with the long-lasting effects of Also, yeah, Kotori's a very neat character, and surprisingly deep, & I can see why everyone on the community page loves her so much.So in short, yeah, if you already like Yomawari, this one's definitely good to pick up! But probably on sale, though. If you're new to the series, instead start with the first two - they still hold up super well, since it's a formula that goes pretty much unchanged throughout.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only been playing for 7 hours and haven't completed the game, but so far the experience has been very enjoyable.The game is a step up from the previous games in total playtime (I completed Night Alone in just over 4 hours, still loved it) however some of this is to the game's fault. Early on in the game it can be confusing on where to go or what to explore next, and while the game gives you multiple ways to proceed in the story which usually is about finding story relevant items in special places in a different order, but to prevent players from proceeding into areas they shouldn't be able to, several areas are coated in fog. If you step into these areas, you are swiftly hunted by a spirit and will die in seconds. In order to clear the fog you must discover the memories in the area you can explore, which can be confusing as there is no map indicator of which areas are foggy (oftentimes leading to me trying to revisit areas to see if fog cleared only to see no change) and I believe that the other games did area progression better in some cases with Night Alone directly telling you where to go in the protagonist's diary or objectives but this itself isn't a deal breaker for me though. I love exploration in horror games and although most boons for exploring are collectable items, I still very much love each one I find and do appreciate how this progression system makes you explore around the world for the keys to proceed.I think the story for this game so far is on par with Night Alone and in some points even reaches Midnight Shadows' heaviness in story while also having slight rises and dips in certain areas. The opening of the game hits hard in Lost in the Dark and I really did get immersed and empathize with the protagonist. Then some areas I believe stretch a little too far, if you've gotten to this point  however I was a bit preoccupied so maybe the problem is me and this area is better than I say so feel free to disagree.Even with all its flaws, I still really love this game so far and might be one of the first people who would hoist signs up requesting a fourth one. I do think the price is a little steep especially compared to the prices of the previous games, I would probably give it a $5-$15 cut although I'm not in control or have proper understanding of those so I can't say what is or isn't good for the game price wise. All in all so far I would give this game an 8/10, really love the characters and all the dialogue from the protagonist, the themes are amazing, story is interesting and the gameplay is pretty engaging despite its shortcomings in places. I'd recommend this to anyone who is a fan of the series. However if you're just starting out I'd recommend Night Alone or Midnight Shadows mainly due to the price, but if you can look past that, I'd recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the story that makes it so I can't recommend it positively. it's not that it's told poorly, but that it's the sort of story I can't deal with having to play through a game for ~20 hours to seeThat out of the way, there are other good and bad things that aren't nearly as subjective.First, the atmosphere is on point as ever. Just as creepy and unnerving as you'd come to expect from the series. The sound direction is pretty good, but could have utilized 3D audio more. The boss encounters many seem to have disliked, and I really only think the true final boss encounter was a problem. Everything else was reasonable and the ones that were more problematic had good checkpoint placement. Personally, I think they were one of the best aspects of the game. The other one being choosing a cat over a dog. Just really frantic fun! The exploration was mostly fine, but a few times I was extremely lost on what I was supposed to be doing, one time because the UI design left out a point that needed to be interacted with, so I didn't realize I could/should. If this were a secret, like a certain invisible sphere, then that's one thing. But it was needed to progress through the game. Another time...I just hadn't yet happened upon something that required me doing something that you normally do not do in this game. I do miss the hiding in objects function, but the holding your hands over your eyes function was neat in its own ways.Still, they got rid of most of the things that made exploration and dealing with ghosts more of a thing. It basically boiled down to run/close your eyes. Wasn't as much strategy as the previous games. This was a disappointment. It also lacked the "equipment" system, which meant less things to find that make it more fun to explore. It's nice to be able to customize the MC some, but disappointed you didn't find things like hair accessories/outfits to dress up with. You had what you had, and the selection never changed.  Really could have done more with that.I really can't think of much more to talk about, if you didn't feel like you wasted your life on the game when you beat Midnight Together, it will probably be an enjoyable experience, as long as you have enjoyed the sort of gameplay of the yomawari series thus far. Just, the final true boss encounter is one to be ready to spend some time with...

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow five years have already passed since the last Yomawari release and besides the time passing too quickly, I enjoyed that game a good bit. Super atmospheric, a large world to explore, and some decent puzzles too. This one though? Ehhhh....The atmosphere is easily the game’s best point. It is quite literally the same as it was five years ago: limited lighting, grainy world design, absolutely creepy yokai roaming about, and ambient sound design in place of a traditional soundtrack. For the type of story being told here, all of this works in the game’s favor.That said, I was a bit disappointed that there’s really nothing “new” to differentiate the feel from the last release. It uses the same audio and graphical assets, has a very similar world design, and somehow feels a bit more empty.One of the things I praised in the last release was that large world with plenty of stuff to find. This game has some of that, but it doesn’t quite match the extent of the former and honestly, it became boring to have to trek across identical, empty areas just to get to the next story objective.I won’t make the case that Midnight Shadows was super involved gameplay-wise, but I can’t help but feel that Lost in the Dark took it even further down. Most of the gameplay involves running around, picking up items to get you to the next area, and then repeating. In fact, the first two “dungeons” or whatever were literally me searching however many rooms for a key or other item, picking it up and bringing it to unlock or activate something, and then repeating that in the newly unlocked area.It’s back and forth busywork and maybe I’ve become less tolerant of such gameplay over the years, but the last one had a bit of this too, it just didn’t feel like to this extent. When you do get to a cool part - the boss encounters - those last maybe a few minutes before you have to cycle through the next hour or so of searching and pressing your one button to interact with things.I ran the game at 4k 60 fps with no issues to speak of, although the settings are limited to just simple window and resolution options. Controls are simple enough that you can get away with doing keyboard and mouse, but it plays way better on controller and that is what I opted to use for my playthrough.I cannot in good faith recommend Yomawari: Lost in the Dark. The last game - Midnight Shadows - may have been fun enough, but this is somehow worse while adding nothing really new. Great atmosphere, but with the same assets. A large open world to explore, but nothing really rewarding to find. A decently interesting story, but matched with some seriously tedious gameplay that left me bored after just a couple hours. Maybe in a bundle or on deep sale - but for now it’s not worth it.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Yomawari: Lost in the Dark is the third installment of the Yomawari series. Although the art-style is cute, the contrasting horror elements featured to give life to Japanese urban legends and superstitions showcase its unique charm. Like its predecessors, the series is set in a small town surrounded by different areas. Each area is unique and showcases different types of stories that the consumer gets to experience. I personally loved the main story of the game. The game starts with the protagonist contracting a curse and needs her memories to remember how to break the curse before the following morning. The strategic use of storytelling to play around this theme was excellently executed and I loved the twists that I encountered along the way.If I were to compare it with the previous entries in the series, I would say that there was a lack of  Overall, I love this series and its style of storytelling. I look forward to seeing more entries in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start this review by adressing the elephant in the room : the price.Even if I enjoyed the game (and the franchise as a whole), I can't in good faith excuse the 40 dollars price tag.I still bought it on the release, but at best with this game, you'll look at around 15-20h length if you go for completion.Unless you're a big fan of the Yomawari games like me and need it right now, wait for at least a 25% sale.Now that it's out of the way, what to say about the 3rd installment of the Yomawari series?This one felt more focused on the story, which is both a good point and a bad point.The good point is that you get more involved with the characters at play and the heroine (who is customisable this time), the bad point, however, is that some story beats really slow down the pacing of the game to have the character basically repeat what you just saw but in a dialogue format.Difficulty wise, it felt a bit easier than 1 and 2, with the addition of a new mechanic "closing your eyes" which replaces the "hiding" mechanic from the first 2 games. It roughly serves the same goal, but makes it more proactive.For the gameplay, and more precisely, the exploration, this one is structured a bit differently. The town and streets by itself felt slightly emptier which makes going from point A to B less tedious. The more difference comes from the fact that the game isn't linear this time. You'll have to explore the town to find your memories back, and when finding a specific item, it'll unlock a new zone which works a bit like a "dungeon" or "instance" and feels more contained. This allows the game to focus on a specific gimmick for each "dungeon" which makes them more unique and quite enjoyable.For the technical aspect, it's still top notch. The sprites and the various places you'll visit are always a treat to look at and the ambiant sounds really put you in the mood.To wrap this up, I'd say, if you've already played 1 and 2, you'll probably like this one too. If you haven't played 1 and 2, this one is also a good start since they're not really connected and feels more polished than the others.

_childDocuments_.review: The third game in the Yomawari franchise combines some of the best stuff from the first and the second with less of the growing pains of the second. The game was a pleasure to run through, enjoyable all the way through, maybe the final encounter was a bit rough.PROS:-A beautiful world to run through, with many areas I enjoyed running through when exploring for secrets.-A wonderful soundscape. The game lacks a soundtrack, but the title theme strikes my heartstrings. I enjoyed wandering the map and listening to small details, not to mention the monster's notable sounds.-While I recognize older enemy designs, I enjoy the new ones and how the sounds they make add tension and character. The subtle noises of the tightening ropes of one enemy will linger in my mind.-I don't play many horror games, but I've played the entire series, sharing it with friends. It has a deep place in my heart.-The encounters with the "Boss Ghosts" were spectacles, definitely the writing complexity of the first with the size and complexity of the second game, minus the 'drawn out'edness. I enjoyed each gimmick they brought.-The "post game" is full of wonderful revisits for the prior mentioned "bosses".-The taking away of "hiding spots" and adding the "eye cover" mechanic was a much needed remix of the mechanic. Spiced up encounters with old monsters and new.-The whole plot. Has multiple meanings and I love it.CONS:-The tinnitus ring of the fear/stress mechanic, while a nice touch, got old after the first few hours.-The spider "jumpscare" is rubbish and predictable. It lingers too long for what it is.-While NIS's artbooks are notorious for being rubbish, this one pales in comparison to the first. (Concerns DLC)-If you have a fear of multiple eyes or 'close together holes', It'd trigger you, but it's a horro game so... Expected, I suppose?

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly my most anticipated game of 2022. I'm a fan of the series and the new entry was another great specimen of storytelling. I like the tragic backstories of the spirits and the way the protagonist overcomes difficulties. The new character customization feature was a nice touch. The sound design is top notch. Ambient sounds dominate and music is kept to minimum - effective for creating an eerie mood. Don't let the cutesy visual style fool you to think this is a game for kids.I had some minor technical issues at launch (full screen switching to windowed when alt tabbing: fixed by selecting borderless window, game not launching on PC after playing on Steam Deck: fixed by verifying game files, dogs in shopping district getting temporarily stuck when going after biscuit) but aside from these it was a smooth sailing all the way up to 100% completion.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're new to the franchise, the first game is the best, so play that first. All games deliver on being cute stealth-based collectathons with dark and occasionally disturbing storylines, wrapped in an atmospheric horror blanket (and the odd shameless cheap jumpscare.)For returning fans, I broadly enjoyed 3 more than 2- 2 had a tighter, darker story (arguably too dark,) and more collectibles and post-game stuff, but for me 3 has a more interesting story, more interesting mechanics (big ups to closing your eyes and sneaking rather than hiding in bushes,) and is the only one of the franchise I even got CLOSE to 100% completion on.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely an improvement from the older games, they remove most of the items you probably never gonna use i.e. Torch, Firefly, garbage bag(since you can just close your eyes) and also improvement to the puzzle in the game, not just super obvious puzzle. now you actually need to use your brain sometimes(it still not too hard to understand though) The boss in this game are much more creative than ever, including sub boss you find throughout the story line. this make the game more engaging along with the story in this game, which is also wayy longer and deeper than previous game so there is more to uncovered and explore. _childDocuments_.review: Listen, if you're looking at this game and not the first game in the series, there is a good chance you already know what you are getting into. If you haven't played *Labyrinth of Refrain: Coven of Dusk*, turn back and go play the first game in this "series" would be my recommendation. Although a little less developed compared to this sequel, the game serves an introduction into NIS's take on a traditional grid-based dungeon crawler. If you really want to dive into the series, hunt down and play *The Witch and the Hundred Knight* in this strange timeline, but know Hundred Knight and its sequel are action rpgs with very different gameplay from the Labyrinth games. If you do want to dive in, be warned, this series is not a typical NIS rpg like their poster child Disgaea. The Labyrinth games have very dark themes and subject matter brought up, and quite frankly awful things happen to the characters within these games, all while hiding behind the cutesy art of Takehito Harada. The story of these games are ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and I highly recommend them because of it.If you have played Labyrinth of Refrain, and didn't drop off the game as soon as you hit the second dungeon, then I can easily recommend Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society. This game takes everything that was learned in Refrain and makes it much, MUCH, bigger. More classes, more mechanics, more dungeons, and of course, a even more complex and demented story. If you were blindsided by just how *bleak* and *mean* things got for the cast of Refrain, Galleria isn't that much different, albeit that I braced for it this time around. In my opinion, Galleria is at it's best when the story starts to spiral out of control, and with it's much larger cast than Refrain, in the addition to just having more story cutscenes in general, Galleria has time to fully go wild during your long play through.At it's core, Galleria is another grid-based dungeon crawler with an emphasis on telling a complex story, something unique to the genre. Problem being, despite my praise of the story the actual mechanics of this crawlers isn't anything special. 95% of your playtime will likely be easily defeating random battles with little strategy while the other 5% will be the absolute difficulty cliffs of some of the bosses later in the game. Party building is a somewhat frustrating practice that, while greatly improved from the first game with the ability to select what skills a character has "active" and change them when needed during the still tedious reincarnation process, you still need to plan well in advance or start from scratch to get truly good characters. Additionally, like the first game, the massive roster of characters you need to build up to (capping at 40 characters participating in combat) means you either will spend many hours doing inventory management and character building, or automate everything you can via auto-equip and have a written plan for character progression. This game also introduces randomly generated dungeons floors, which will take up most of the latter half of the game. These floors re-randomize each time you return, and definitely overstay their welcome by the final area, which will have you taking on a colossal one. Not to say the dungeoneering is bad, on the contrary, Galleria has a ton of new and exciting ways to navigate the dungeon compare to the already interesting dungeons of the first game. Breaking walls returns as well as new features like underwater tiles and time limited areas. When you actually are not in combat, the act of exploring the dungeon is fun, and it feels like you can stay in dungeons much longer than the first game without having to return constantly.Overall, with how the game is designed, unless you are feeling confident and are not afraid to spend many extra hours grinding, I would look up a guide when stuck on a boss or challenge and possibly build advice if you feel outclasses. Random item drops containing very powerful and important items return and it can be frustrating to learn how much grinding some of them can take. You'll also need to complete some very specific sidequests if you want to finish the story, and with how unreliable the loot/quest items can be to drop, it might be nice to know ahead of time what to keep or grind for.Despite my problems with the gameplay, which is still much better than Refrain (especially reincarnations), I give a hard recommendation to Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society. If you choose to dive in, expect a very good Visual Novel with a good but sometimes frustrating Dungeon Crawler RPG attached to it. It's a game with a lot of good twists and turns that I don't really want to spoil, and it definitely is on the longer side, but I think anyone who is either a fan of the dungeon crawler genre or is looking for a dark and complex story shouldn't pass it up.

_childDocuments_.review: So... I REALLY want to like this game. I really do but it is a convoluted, massive, unexplained mess of everything that respects no ones time.Pros: Fantastic Story: I cannot stress this enough, the twists and turns are just amazing and have kept me on my toes from start to now.Art: The art is beautiful too, lots of character designs are just gorgeous and work so well. If you like tiddies there are a lot of them in there too... for reasons.Voice Acting: Some of the voice acting has just made me tear up and cry over a few of the charactersNeutral:Character Creation: There are a LOT of options here. Personalities, Favourites (do they do anything? who knows. See tutorials) and you unlock a lot more as you game. There are 24 classes, two sets of 12 that are slightly different (the game does not tell you outright how to switch between them. It's Triangle on a controller.Cons:UI: The UI is a mess. It barely has any information and uses hundreds of disparate icons to try and explain things that go nowhere. The sort functions are incredibly weak and barely existent. The equipment system is clunky and a royal pain in every way. There's an optimize feature but you have no way of telling how it even works if it even works. It will constantly pick worse equipment for characters and classes for no real reason.Gameplay: Lots of variety, lots of things to do... and do... and do... and do..... When you get to your second set of 120ish random floors. Then there's more... Minor Mechanical Spoiler: Side Quests: There are a lot here. They're basically fetch quests. Insanely long grindy fetch quests that rely 100% on RNG. Need 10 of an item? get ready to do the same 5 floors in a dungeon for 3-4 hours. Maybe it'll take 6, maybe it'll take 1. Who knows. The story required side quests at least have a decent drop rate but a lot of the best gear is locked behind these requests.Boring items: The whole point of the game is art. You find art, you find rare relics, you find all sorts of interesting things that do all sorts of interesting stuff... but not one of them has any sort of flavour. There are no pictures, no descriptions, nothing... it's just an icon in your inventory and a slot in your bag. You even carry around a CATALOG of these items and have no way to access it to or anything, it's just another icon to stare at pointlessly. This is especially disappointing from NIS who have a habit of making very creative descriptions.Skill System: This is... a lot of issues with the UI here. The worst part is you are constantly resetting your characters back to level 1 to power them up but of course this resets all your skills so you have to do them all again. A lot of the skills make absolutely no sense "When an enemy has 1hp do exactly 1 damage" What? why? How is this important? Tutorials: This is another UI issue in that a lot of the mechanics just aren't explained. Luck? too bad. Pursuit attacks? what are those. SP Abilities: Good luck figuring it out on your own. Just so much that should have been better explained.Spread sheeting: This is more of a personal beef but any game where I need to spend several hours making any sort of spreadsheet or pouring over them to make sure my characters are powerful enough to fight some of the BS bosses the game has. It becomes really important because some skills and classes can make your build effectively worse... to the point where you just need to start over on them.Conclusion: I'm just going to find a youtube video of the ending from someone who has more time to waste than me. I'm 90 hours in and I migth need another 90-120 just to beat the last dungeon. So... nope.

_childDocuments_.review: StoryThis game's story GOES places. I mean, it looks all cute and cuddly on the surface, but those content warnings aren't for show. It's hard not to get emotionally invested, honestly ... It's kind of Kafkaesque to begin with, and just when you think you've gotten into the groove, it starts doing some straight up David Lynch stuff, or at least it feels that way. It does seem to largely explain the mind-screwage eventually, with some of the typical anime/visual novel style heavy handedness and quite a bit of charm and flair, which is not particularly Lynchian (he rarely explains much), but it's been some time since I felt as discombobulated (in a great way) by a video game's script. Its use of the formal elements of the medium and subverted expectations to intentionally pull the rug out from under the audience and leave it devastated, confused, and needing to go deeper is kind of a master class ... I mean, it doesn't quite have the philosophical depth of Pathologic 2, and definitely lacks the budget of a Kojima blockbuster, but what it manages to pull off with just a (fully voiced) visual novel interspersed with hours of seemingly disconnected dungeon-crawling is impressive. Eventually, the crawling and the story feel like part of one large and somewhat twisted puzzle-box mystery. The specifics are almost less important than the confidence of execution. Without any spoilers, I will warn that this game is NOT over when the credits roll for the first time. It's not too difficult to activate the second cycle, but you do need to do something very specific, at which point you will be able to start your "new game plus" / "post-game" - which is really just the continuations of the story and more game - think Nier Automata. It's essentially one story broken up into several "campaigns." If you've reached the credits and are feeling like the game was smaller and shorter than you expected, have no fear ... if it's more dungeons and floors that you want, it will oblige ... oh boy will it oblige ... and the same goes for story as well. ** I will take a few meaningless, imaginary points off for a bit of gratuitous fan-service and the dialogue sexualizing a teenage girl at a few key points ... I do think the latter can be read more generously as a reflection on the character's anxieties as a vulnerable young woman in a fairly typically medievalish sexist society, and it does effectively read on that level to an extent. So I am not entirely ready to condemn it as pervy or gratuitous. But, like the first game (albeit much less often), it sometimes just gets raunchy for the sake of being raunchy, and that's rarely my personal cup of tea. Hardly detracts from the frankly stellar overall writing and character development.GameplayI played the first one of this series on the PS4 a few years ago, and while I never quite finished it (something new and shiny came along and distracted me, I think), I loved every minute of it that I did play, so this was a no brainer for me. Hence, if you enjoyed the gameplay of Labyrinth of Refrain, you will largely feel at home here. Some might say it's too similar (in fact, a lot of the mechanics and art assets, specifically some of enemies and pretty much all of the puppet soldier art, are straight up reused), but there is no need to fix what ain't broken, and as this rather lengthy experience goes on, it continues to slowly build on that foundation and remix the established formula in what I felt to be interesting ways. If you've not played the original, well, it's like a modernized Wizardry, which is very much like Etrian Odyssey, or Persona Q, or SMT Strange Journey / Soul Hackers ... that sort of vibe. The two biggest components are dungeon exploration and party building and management. Combat is essentially a byproduct of the latter - if you build your party effectively, you'll rarely struggle too much even on nightmare world difficulty ... most of the time. Either way, it does effectively give one the joy of constantly tweaking and optimizing, upgrading weapons, trying out different brigade configurations with different covens and coven compositions, and so on. Navigating the labyrinth is generally good fun and neither too challenging nor so simple as to be boring - it's a lot of vertical thinking, resource management, and strategic risk taking, along with the usual genre staples like illusory walls, moving floors, teleporter tiles, switches, and so on. There are occasional procedurally generated floor blocks in certain sequences of the game, but they are still regularly broken up by bespoke, hand designed floors, and aren't particularly tedious, even featuring some unique choices and events on occasion. Aside from all that, there are a few welcome quality of life features that take a lot of the tedium out of the difficulty these kinds of games sometimes hit you with and are worth a mention. A party wipe does not result in losing hard progress, so even if you do screw up, you'll only lose some currency and rapport (which is a background thing that isn't worth micromanaging too much). The XP stockpile feature is back from the previous game and offers a very nice risk reward balance as well as a convenient way to quickly power level new puppet soldiers. The meat system, wherein enemies drop XP granting items after every battle, also makes it easy to bring new party members up to snuff. Just stockpile the meat until you need to make a new puppet, and then just cram all of it down it's throat at once and watch those levels go up. I do find that wiping as a result of an accidental fall can be quite frustrating at times, but it does offer a real sense of danger to the pitfalls, and the relatively forgiving wipe consequences take some of the sting out (of course, if you've stockpiled hundreds of thousands of XP and lose it all, it can cause that sinking Dark Souls feeling of "I lost all my souls to gravity" But again, it's risk and reward. English Voice ActingGood. Madame Martha and Eureka can get a bit grating sometimes, simply because of the exagerrated cadences the actors were clearly directed to maintain ... most of the time ... but those cadences do serve a purpose, and both characters are enjoyable all the way through. ArtworkExcellent character and monster designs. Great VN portraits and backdrops. Nice textures on the dungeons. Solidly stylish UI. A bit too fan servicy for my taste on the puppet soldier art, but the art itself is still good regardless. Music is great, vibes are good ... or very bad, but , like, intentionally so.   OverallIf you're into jrpgs or rpgs in general but aren't a huge drpg / gridder / blobber person, I think this one has some real crossover potential and is still worth a try. If you're into drpgs / wizardry clones, etc. this is a no brainer - both this game and its predecessor form one of the best series in the genre to come out of Japan in recent memory, and an easy contender with all the greats, including, in my opinion, SMT Strange Journey. If you're a hardcore Call of Duty player, or if you really need high end graphics and fully animated cutscenes, this is probably not it, though.
