_childDocuments_.review: I quite enjoyed Labyrinth of Refrain despite a few issues and I was hoping for a similar experience with the new addition to the series. However, I cannot recommend this game.The first part of the game is quite enjoyable but it then transforms into something bizarre. Listen developers far and wide, RNG is not fun. RNG levels are shallow creations compared to human designed levels. The majority of the dungeon levels after Aluna are just RNG. This leads to weird situations where you can fall through the world and wipe the party and so on.Furthermore, if you play this game only do the minimum in the first part of the game to just complete it because you will lose everything. This is more like two short games in one rather than a single game.Finally, the story is just bad. This is common with dungeon crawlers; however, this game has a completely chopped up story with all kinds of lose ends and weird dead ends.For those who care, the game is long but not because of content and quality. It is the latter part of the game with RNG hell that makes it long and repetitive. The game also has very weird programming issues. Such as no proper exit game from the save screen, weird moments where you are forced to watch all of the credits, no immediate ability to save and quite the game after starting second half/second game within the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Labyrinth of Galleria is a game for a very specific kind of person. I find that a lot of RPGs nowadays pride themselves as being something you can finish in a (compared to AAA games) short amount of time, have minimal-to-no grinding, a lot of QOL, and an easy to understand story.Galleria, to me, isn't one of those games. You will be spending a lot of time grinding. You will be spending upwards of 40 to 60 hours playing the game if you aren't the most well versed with dungeon crawlers or turn based games. You will be doing annoying things over and over with no shortening. The story is obtuse and full of timeline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that will make your head hurt.That is why I am recommending it. Galleria is a BOLD game. It tells a story I have never seen anything like, with turns I could never see coming and a lot I could through genius foreshadowing. Your characters' stats will climb into the thousands as you deal with stronger and stronger and complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss fights. It's a cathartic and addicting game that's not afraid to appeal to a very specific demographic that I am a part of. If you're part of it too, I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, Labyrinth of Galleria is a very good game that quickly rose to the top of my list of favorite games from 2023. Although there are some aspects that could be improved, the overall experience is still outstanding. The music is amazing, exploring is incredibly rewarding and enjoyable, the combat is satisfying, and the story is captivating. The game does an excellent job of drawing you into the character of Eureka and the world of Labyrinth, making you want to continue delving deeper into the dungeon to uncover more of the story.I believe it is a must-play for fans of traditional dungeon crawlers, as these types of games are becoming rarer and rarer. While we have franchises like Mary Skelter from Idea Factory, Etrian Odyssey from Atlus, and Labyrinth of Refrain from recent years, and there are also hidden gems which unfortunately have not received as much attention. I truly hope that the traditional first-person dungeon-crawler genre will regain popularity soon. I think Labyrinth of Galleria does an excellent job of showcasing that there is still so much untapped potential in these types of games.Full review at :

_childDocuments_.review: Labyrinth of Galleria, a witchy sequel?Just completed everything last night and I must say I enjoyed my time with it, all 100 hours of it. The story was surprisingly good and protagonists were interesting, one bit of a dimwit but in a endearing way. Localisation is excellent and I didn't see any glaring errors. The story is divided into 3 acts, the finale being hit more like an optional post-game similar to DQXI. The story is primarily told in a VN format which is around 1/3 of the game, gameplay making up for the remaining equation.Gameplay loop is quite good and addictive. You basically explore handcrafted dungeons which are well designed. I think they're about as good as Ethan Odyssey series. You gain abilities that let you jump, swim and smash walls. Exploration is great here and it's very satisfying to fill in the maps. As for combat, it's decent. There's 3 difficulties to select. Easy / normal is a cakewalk in general. Nightmare is recommended if you are looking for decent challenge and want to engage with mechanics. Party customisation is better than Refrain but still not up to the level of EO. Pacts are basically your classes that you can customize with skills from other pacts. Puppets serve as equipment layered on by additional equipment slots. Skills are fairly standard such as taunt, buffs / debuffs, covers, counters and ailment. Ailments do work on bosses but they are more resistant. There's a summoning mechanic that spawn machina that does various stuff but it's not very well explained and requires trial and error to figure it out. Often, it's difficult to tell what's going on during combat especially late game when you have +15 puppets. Combat log helps but there's no way to look up what kind of abilities or status description being used by enemies. At least, the game isn't too difficult and you can mostly just brute force your way through encounters even on higher difficulty.In later acts, the game mix it up with some randomly generated dungeons which aren't as interesting but at least you can simply skip them outright if you're sufficiently powerful. Hope you enjoy that 3605 floors of random dungeons. Well, it's not as bad as it sounds since there's shortcuts that you can use to skip up to hundreds of floors.Few sections were bit tedious requiring you to farm some shiny treasures in order to complete all sidequests. One of final bosses requires a special pact & special weapons to defeat which can be hit of a hassle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does NOT respect your time. AT ALL.Forewarning to anyone thinking of playing this game:  The first playthrough you get with credits is simply part one, and the second slough playthrough you do to get to the credits sequence is part 2. Part 3 forces you through what I can only call rng dungeon hell with new enemies, new hazards in the dungeon and tons of bosses that the game expects you to want to subject yourself to because they believe the story is so precious and top notch that you will of course want to waste another 60-100 hours soul transferring, exploring for just the right items and shuffling together brigades to beat.This game feels like it is from an earlier era of gaming brought to the modern era with barely any of the QoL innovations of today added in. Story is good, but not good enough that it is fed to you in between long stretches of rng dungeon crawling and foraging for elusive items that ramps up in difficulty the more you progress to the point where you can have all your characters at max level and still feel weak. _childDocuments_.review: Why? In short, : Firstly, the game introduces a fetch-quest system early into progression (say 10 hours in), but fails to teach you that the fetch quests are required at all. Mind you, only the fetch quests from the first part of the game are required. During the second part of the game, none of the quests are outright required, but about 5 of them are near-mandatory, as they grant you special equipment to defeat that story segment's final boss. If you slept on the first part's quests, then you'll eventually reach the ending (say, 30-50 hours along) & find out you needed to complete all of the available quests up to this point in order to UNLOCK a final, mandatory fetch-quest. Failure to complete that final quest (and by extension, the other requisite quests) will lead to your progress in the game halted.With the fetch-quests alone, the game fails to convey its expectations to the player, which can lead to any unprepared player needing to back-track through the game for an indeterminite amount of time in order to find all the neccessary drops. This is obviously not a pleasant surprise. .But wait! That's not the only time you might have said issue. If you push through the game to reach the final boss of the second part of the story, then you'll quickly find out that said boss is immune to all types of damage. Surprise! Let me repeat that to really drive it home: the boss of the second part of the story is immune to all types of damage. You can only kill it via damage from a VERY SMALL subset of weapons, or you need to use a special spell to remove the boss's immunities. But guess what, the aformentioned spell & most of the previously mentioned weapons can only be aquired by completing a secondary fetch-quest chain in order to aquire a key which opens unique chests containing the necessary loot. Once again, if you sleep on those quests you'll regret it. Your progression in the game will be halted by RNG - and it will absolutely ruin the pacing of the story.Heck, even if you're not playing the game for the story, you'll still feel like you can only progress after forcing RNG to be in your favor. Meaning no new maps, new abilities, etc until you complete an arbitrary checklist.Now let's put all of that to the side for a second, and talk about another issue.Another thing to note is that the game can feel pretty aimless toward the end of the first act. You'll eventually reach a point where you aren't unlocking any new regions to explore, and you'll be forced to back-track repeatedly with each new ability you learn. This got tedious in my eyes. To be honest with you, I LOVE metroidvainias because of their sporadic moments of "wait, that was always connected to this place!?", but I never really had those moments in this game (and I suppose it's my bad for having unfair expectations on the game - I admittedly don't play many dungeon crawlers). But even with that being said, I think the game can take slight, distant inspiration from metroidvainias in the following way: by de-coupling all of the movement abilities from the story. In other words, making it so that the player can unlock any movement ability as soon as they stumble upon the right place, instead of expecting the player to reach a certain threshold in the story BEFORE allowing them to unlock said ability. Let me give you an example. During the first part of the story, I spent a lot of time exploring ahead, so to speak. I'd often wander around & avoid the story fights because I was more interested in collecting all the abilities first (which again, is the metroidvainia mindset & not something you can do in this game). Well, at one point I managed to reach the location necessary for unlocking a water-walking ability, but I couldn't actually obtain the ability for I hadn't completed enough of the story. And unfortunately enough, the game made no special indication that anything of value was at that spot, so I promptly ignored it & moved on. This led to a jarring experience whenever I finally progressed far enough to unlock the water-walking ability, for I assumed that specific place wasn't important, and so I never thought to double-check it.I admit that's in-part another "me" problem, but this still plays into the aimlessness of the game. The game doesn't try very hard to tell you where you need to go. Whenever the game gives you any sort of direction, it's often vague, such as "Find another ancient relic," or "Do what needs to be done." Furthermore, the game does add "!" icons to the map to mark important spots, but some icons only show up once you've progressed far enough into the story - and some of the icons appear sooner than they should, which caused me to become desensitized to them.For example, several "!" icons are used to mark the spot where you found a magic button, of sorts. Well, the tooltip for those icons claims you saw a cutscene at those locations far before you're actually able to see said cutscenes, which was yet another point of confusion for me. I believe that verbatim, the tooltip reads "Saw visions of the surface." And I promise you, that will make zero sense to you when you first see one of those buttons.Now, in the spirit of picking on the game, I'm going to put far less effort into the 2nd half of this review, just as they did with the game.- the 2nd part of the game contains 2 randomly generated dungeons (each has approximately 100 floors), which just feel like "content for the sake of it"-- it also contains a couple of hand-crafted dungeons, which are far more memorable- the final part of the game (postgame) contains 1 randomly generated dungeon (having a whopping 3651 floors)-- it contains one other hand-crafted dungeon, which is a forgettable slog of samey rooms- a few of the enemies' designs felt overly-gratuitous. I'm usually fine with horny-style monsters, but if the game wanted me to take it more seriously, then I'd prefer if they didn't make a monster that looks like a chick pointing her arse-cheeks at me (aka the sweet liddy)- the bestiary has several copy/pasted generic descriptions for monsters. they do little to world-build, and often amount to "this is a monster made out of magic. ooooooh~"- several spells & special abilities feel worthless, as casting said abilities requires everyone in a specific squad to participate, meaning you could potentially waste 3 mages' turns in order to cast a single-target heal spell, for example- inventory management is a huge headache. they needed some way to dispose of/ sell items in bulk- the story touches on royally dark topics: self harm, suicide, sexual harassment, cannibalism (and more). I found exploring the darker refreshing, though it certainly won't be everyone's cup of tea This game did not deserve such a wonderful, heartbreaking story. The story was the saving grace of the game (in my opinion), and I wager the story would see more success if it were an anime or light novel instead. Even if you like the dungeon crawler genre, the game will still throw a lot of samey "content for the sake of content" in your face, which will try the patience of any playerIf you, like me, are here because you've played the Disgaea series & wanted something different, well I truly discourage you from trying this game out.For those curious, here are my time-stamp completion estimates. Note, I started using a guide toward the second half of the game (since I kept getting lost). Just keep that in mind.- completion of the 1st part of the game (30-50 hours into a playthrough)- completion of the 2nd part of the game (80-110 hours into a playthrough)- completion of the postgame (130 hours total)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a partial, short review (as I've just finished the 'first' part of the game and barely started ).Labyrinth of Galleria is a very special game and, while universally well-received, I don't think it's for everyone. As the name implies, the game has way more to offer than first meets the eye - in fact, I'd say most of the substance is found many, many hours into it.Overall gameplay is quite complex, but I don't find it overbearing. The first half of the game is easily doable without tons of grinding, but after that, the difficulty curve goes up exponentially, and so does the time investment.Without a single doubt, I think the strongest aspect of this game is the story: it's a wild, wild ride. _childDocuments_.review: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society is worth the money, time and pain it takes to finish the game. It really, really does ask a lot of you but I was absolutely determined to answer it in full.I'm the sort of person that buys game long after launch and during sales. There's no shortage of things to fill your time so waiting for discounts is nothing to me. I bought Galleria not even an hour after it came out. Unfortunately I was all too familiar with the previous games in the Witch series and knew I just couldn't fit it into my schedule hence why it took me almost the whole rest of the year to get to it.I loved both Hundred Knight and Labyrinth of Refrain, both of them had terrificly memorable stories and interesting gameplay systems. The addictively rich slivers of story fed between sessions of wonderful(and also tedious) exploration kept me coming for more long after the midnight oil should have run out hence why I was so intimidated with starting Galleria. I knew for a damn fact that I'd get hooked and pulled deep into the rabbit hole. I was so very right. The game is contending for my GOTY spot against both FFXVI and AC6.The whole story unfolds much like a mystery with the first half being almost entirely setup and the second half unravelling question upon question upon. The writing is tight and effective and its setting and characters brimmed with charm. On its surface Galleria looks much gentler and more lighthearted compared to the previous Witch games but sure enough the waters ran deep as there was much, much more darkness and tragedy lurking below. The comedy is much less slapstick too so those deep running streaks of tragedy stood out all the more since you're given plenty of opportunity to warm up to everyone before the suffering sets in. There's plenty of twists and turns to keep you at your seat but ultimately it's your empathy for the characters that will keep you driven. I can't exactly pinpoint any moments that punched me in the gut the way Hundred Knight and Refrain did but I can tell you that it never dried out on both sweet and bitter flavors. No matter how tedious and daunting that final stretch of game proved to be, I was absolutely determined to see it end on some sweetness after all that pain it puts everyone through.In terms of gameplay, Galleria’s mechanics are absolutely a step up from Refrain. Your options for building your party and tools for dungeon exploration have been expanded on wonderfully. You won’t actually see the full potential of the former until you’ve cleared the first half of the game though and frankly the exploration tools are wasted in the second half. With regards to party building and battles they’ve added a few new combat mechanics and given you more control on customizing your characters’ abilities in combat. If you want to breeze through the game and skip out on grinding, I most certainly did that by tuning skills, magic and team compositions and ran through the first half at risk of wiping out against elite field enemies. Seeing more story sooner was one part of my motivation but the other part was wanting to unlock the “multi-classing” aspect of the customization faster since that’s where the experimentation gets real interesting. They did a very good job of gating your builds so there was always more room getting opened up to play around with up till the very end.The exploration was well thought out for the first half – tightly gated and always teasing you with peeks at what’s coming and reminders to re-explore sections you’ve been to. I’ve seen people remark on the samey-ness of the visuals but I did think that was appropriate for these particular dungeons, especially in light of the fact that the game had a lot of major content cut due to the developer’s near-bankruptcy budget constraints. Those cuts become so very, very apparent in the second half of the game. Gone were the delightfully crafted dungeons and in came procedural generation – especially bland procedural generation, ones they saw fit to give you exploration shortcuts for. Apparently there were meant to be just as many of those uniquely themed dungeons that Refrain had for the 2nd half but those dreams were sent into the abyss. Mind you that there’s still a ton of gameplay content to be found but the traces of those grand ambitions do give you much to lament on. You don’t get much opportunity to make use your full dungeon exploration toolset until the very end where they become necessary for survival. The final two dungeons were slogs to get through but the concepts behind them were certainly interesting. I’d want to chalk up that tediousness to wanting to put the players in the same mindset as your player characters but it was more than a little bit excessive. Thankfully my putting off playing the game blessed me with the patches that made that bitterness go down more easily but I can’t help but feel they were being a tad cheeky with how they patched the true final boss. Honestly though, I think I’d be extra mad at them if I could have just cheesed the final boss after all that slogging through to get there.One of my major traumas from playing Refrain were the “normal” final boss and the true final boss fights. Galleria, just like Refrain, has story bosses you could easily steam roll if you were having fun exploring and unlocking stuff. And just like Refrain it has ridiculous difficulty spikes for the elder beings that demand you to go back and grind your team and equipment up for. I’m certain that a third of my play time went into the space between both final bosses here. It was tiring and frustrating and though I do admire their decision to make both of them feel like colossi standing in your way, I really do not want to ever have to repeat my preparations or attempts at taking it down in hypothetical sequel. A tip for those of you going in, that true final boss is a DPS check that does every kind of damage and you should pick a god and pray that it doesn’t decide to try wiping you out twice in the same turn.Finally, my thoughts on the end. Like I said before, I’m certain that slog to the true final boss was meant to put you in the headspace of your main character. You are literally asked to make sacrifices to get there and I did feel I earned that last measure of sweetness to be claimed. I don’t want to spoil it too much but that whole final stretch came with plenty of bitterness, not just for Galleria but also for Refrain. There’s a ray of hope at the end of it for both entries that I’d want to see paid off in a sequel because it’d be too cruel in so many ways to leave it here with Galleria. I’d love to see an anime adaptation of Galleria because I do feel the ending sequence could have been presented so much more tenderly and be made that much more heartbreaking. Here’s hoping they find their way to delivering the sweetness that the characters deserve in one more Witch game.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Most fun I've been having with a dungeon crawler in quite some time.The VN segments are nice, the dungeon is interesting, enemy variety is good as well. Over all I'm still only scratching the surface of this game, but I need to review one of the games I nominated for the Steam awards ... so, here I am. ;)(Also: Real playtime is at about 21 hours slowly accumulated over half a year while playing on the go in offline mode on Steam Deck.)
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful party-based dungeon crawler with plenty of content!Like most of it's kin it has some seriously challenging moments. And has moments where it does not hold your hand.Tied together with management style gameplay the game demands you to explore thoroughly to progress and you can easily find yourself spending half an hour or more scouring each floor for secrets.An all-together well formed game, the addition of voiced dialogue and plenty quirky characters make the inbetween dungeon crawl moments feel more meaningful, even if the story only truely opens up in the later stages.7.8/10!A surprisingly high score considering how critical I can be.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: So this is a turn based rpg that will make a mess of you. but since a mess is on the table why not make a mess of the dungeon. so the name of the game is uneasy. any random baddie can spawn in with extra stats skills loots powers. but you have to take him down first. get lucky remove his head with a well placed attack. or get unlucky and get split in two. if dark souls were a dungeon crawler :) the luck stat can be stacked .. but it changes as lady luck has no memory :) im not sure why the achievements are the way they are. almost half the folks who have this game have every single achievement for it ? i guess it sucks you in :)
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Labyrinth of Refrain, you will find that this also scratches that same itch. I cannot recommend it enough. I do have two complaints, though, namely 1.) The dungeon environments are a bit of a downgrade from the first game (way too much mossy cobblestone, and 2.) figuring out if you are going to wipe or be wiped by new enemies feels a bit impossible, especially when some of them refuse to take any dmg from a majority of dmg types.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun and good story. The story has a lot of unexpected turns and is generally understandable when compared some JRPGs.Dungeons are big and beautiful, although the art gets repetitive. They're not too punishing like classic dungeon crawlers and there's plenty to explore. If you're looking for dungeons with darkness, spinners, and invisible teleporters, look elsewhere.I wasn't expecting to like the procedurally generated dungeons, but they were actually enjoyable. Partiuclarly, the final dungeon in Section 3 of the game was more fun than I expected. Lots of good loot, crippling handicaps, and a looming super FOE made it more exciting.Lots of grinding if you want and mixing and matching the skills from various classes (facets) is a lot of fun once you unlock the soul transfer ability. You will need to do transfer a few times to beat some of the bosses. Combat itself isn't too complicated and exploiting the stun mechanic is the key to success. I mostly auto-battled for 99% of the game, which can get tedious, but there's ways to speed it up in the option. Monster art is good.The game has three endings, and the first section of the game is almost like a tutorial. At the very least, you should go through the first two sections. There's a lot of good story in the second section. Section 3 has a little bit of expansion on the story, but you wouldn't miss much if the size of the final dungeon intimidates you.As for the negatives, I wish there was an unlimited inventory. Like the first game, the final boss of Section 2 requires very specific equipment. I ended up referring to a gamefaq.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the game.it surprised me in many ways. The artwork, music, character design, and voice acting create a great atmosphere for an exciting, unusual, and often dramatic story that really drew me in.The dungeon crawling and character mechanics were also very enjoyable, with a lot of leveling and a wide range of options for classes, skills, attributes, and items to consider.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: There's so much to do and customize it's really overwhelming but in a good way. The story is so amazing there's twists all along the way and they catch me by surprise often. I was really invested the whole time and sometimes I rushed through the labyrinth part just to get to the next cutscene. The story is the best part, imo.You can get through a lot of the game just by using basic attacks depending on your team setup but I don't think that's a bad thing. I think more of the fun comes from customizing your team so they can be really powerful. ❤️
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: A very strong recommend, if you like dungeon crawlers. It's almost a strict improvement over the first game mechanically, and the plot and atmosphere are still wonderful. My only complaint is that I got mentally stunlocked by the soul transfer screen and had to break out a spreadsheet to satisfy my autism...EDIT: I retract my very strong recommend (although it's still very good). It's also mostly an improvement. A lot of this is better than the first game, but the game is dogged 1 major thing:The procedurely generated dungeons are not fun and too long. When I wrote this review I only knew about the first, and I thought it was an optional grind area. There are 3, they are mandatory, and they are most of the dungeon in the game. You'll see 90% of the hand crafted areas in your first 30 hours, and from then on it's just "find the elevator". Really makes the crawling part less interesting, and in retrospect I really don't understand why they couldn't have just... made more normal levels.There is also 1 questionably designed boss, and the way more confusing soul transfer, but overall I'm still a big fan. But play the first game first, then come back to this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard recommendation. On one hand you have a much better story then you would expect given the slow start. On the other you have a legitimate dungeon crawler that you can spend countless hours in. The problem is this game doesn't respect your time in the slightest.The dungeons are huge and require a ton of backtracking. Quests are vague and you can easily not only get lost for hours but lock yourself into a bad ending. There are more classes then ever but the required skills to make them good need lots of grinding and reincarnating into other classes for the right skills. This leads to most of the classes not even being very good. The covens are worse now since you can transfer spells leading to more grinding. The second half of the game you restart from scratch and do it all over again. There are multiple randomly generated dungeons. The actual combat's difficulty is in the setup. One you get classes/equipment you can just hit auto attack 99% of the time.But if you sit through that you get a hell of a story. Or just watch it on YouTube.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: So, while I love this game I must put in a word of caution.  The story of this game is similar in tone to Labyrinth of Refrain, the previous game in this series.  If you haven't played Refrain you don't need to in order to play Galleria but you need to know what you are getting yourself into.This game looks and plays like the popular Etrian Odyssey series.  If you liked Etrian Odyssey you will find this game fun but the character creation a bit simplistic.  At first the story seems to be a typical JRPG much like Etrian Odyssey, annoyingly perky female protagonist and all.  Do not let that lull you into thinking that this is a light, fluffy cookie cutter story.Mild spoilers warning.  Much like many Tales of games, things go insane around the "halfway point" and become very dark indeed.    While it is never graphically disturbing the game does reference abusive relationships, torture, rape and murder.  Characters can and do die in horrible ways.  If these things might disturb you then please go play one of the Etrian Odyssey titles, they are excellent games with much lighter stories.  If you are feeling up for a dark story with a hope of redemption this game is a solid choice (though I would recommend a guide occasionally to reduce frustration).
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: First of all the UI in this game is terrible, for example I spent more than an hour disassembling hundreds of my items one by one because there just isn't an option to do it in stacks, also soul transferring skill management over and over of an entire brigade without any templates is too time consuming (2 games and it wasn't addressed even though it is easily fixable)Story is nice but you can really get lost in the timeline - you get a scene and need to guess/estimate of when it is occurring and it gets overwhelming.But overall I enjoyed the game and the mechanics especially the final dungeon people were complaining about, it was actually my favorite part of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: At many points, you think that this game just doesn't end....I still do not know what certain functions do. Steep learning curve but doable in multiple ways.Having finished both games, I liked the story of the first more but the battle mechanics of the second are far better. I look forward to the next one.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Behold, dear reader, the twisted labyrinth that is Galleria. The Moon Society beckons, and one young girl named Eureka heeds the call, venturing deep into the unknown depths beneath an ancient manor. With naught but a troupe of enchanted puppets by her side, she delves ever deeper into the madness that lies ahead.This dungeon-crawling RPG is not for the faint of heart, for the combat system is both complex and customizable. Up to 40 units can be managed in five covens, each with their own unique abilities and strengths. And yet, even as the battles rage on, a captivating story unfolds, one that blends humor and horror in equal measure. Your choices will shape the outcome, for the game boasts multiple endings.Labyrinth of Galleria is a sequel to the acclaimed Labyrinth of Refrain: Coven of Dusk, but it stands on its own as a masterpiece of the genre. Its gameplay mechanics are deep and varied, its dungeon exploration challenging and rewarding. The art style is charming, and the voice acting brings the characters to life.But beware, for the darkness that lurks in the shadows can be overwhelming. The game is dense, its tutorials and menus numerous. Its objectives are not always clear, and the pacing can be erratic. And yet, for those brave enough to venture forth, the rewards are great. For within the labyrinth lies a mystery that is both disturbing and alluring, a tale that will haunt your dreams and linger long after the game is done.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the lousiest combat system I have seen in any game ever, which drags the entire experience down. The illustrations are nice, the voice overs are good, the story is engaging enough, but the gameplay is garbage. The exploration itself is ok, but the battles in between are SO boring (and there are LOTS of battles). There is no strategizing, you beat everything by just attacking. Abilities are useless. There are hundreds tiny cogs that change numbers slightly, but none of it is explained well and most of it doesnt even matter.For the price tag of 50€ this title delivers mediocre indie quality. Don't waste your money here.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: The story is well-written, dark, and interesting.Art design is excellent.The dungeon crawling is fun, with well designed dungeons, a good sense of danger, and a manageable difficulty curve.This is a grindy game, no avoiding that (well, sort of: cheat engine works like a charm).I was a huge fan of Labyrinth of Refrain, and replayed it a couple weeks before this one came out. I think Refrain is the better game, with the edge in terms of story, dungeon design, and music. This one is not far behind though, and I think they are both pretty underappreciated.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Keep in mind I only have 30 hours in by the time of this reviewPros:- Well designed dungeon crawling, streamlines a lot of the usual chores and allows to explore without much enemy intervention unless you want it- Great art, beautiful character design- Story is interesting. Characters are vibrant and well written.- Easy and fun to play overallCons:- Music is repetitive and there are only a few tracks, had to turn it off. This is coming from a big Tenpei Sato fan.- It's all mostly the same dungeon with color swaps, so far. No visual variety.- Battles feel like a slot machine- Story is hinting at rape and other dark themes that are a bit too much for me, could get worse or notI recommend it. Don't expect Disgaea levels of polish tho, this obviously has less budget.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed my time with the game and recommend it to other who likes the DRPG genre niche. Straight up improvement over the first game, with I would argue a more likable protagonist(s) albeit a slightly weaker and disjointed story overall. Aside from minor mistranslated skill descriptions, Localization is on point too. I've got nothing better to say about the game that other have not already.I do recommend, however, using a guide when playing as it is easy to get lost/stuck. The game provides absolutely zero guidance and some of the mechanics are super obtuse and obfuscated. Just swallow your pride instead of getting lost on where to go for hours like me.Only other real criticism that I have for the game is that the game should have ended 30 hours ago. It definitely overstayed its welcome and stretched a little bit too far. The last dungeon was awesome in concept but by the time I reached it, I was basically just speed-running as I was ready to just get the game done.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: The final climb, daunting as it is, is one of my favorite parts of any dungeon crawler.  Every shortcut turns the next few floors into a stealth game as your team is currently as strong as tissue paper, waiting to slowly get your strength back.  But spend too long on a floor and you might get chased by an unstoppable, plodding ghost, or see entire chunks of the level disappear.  The more you put into this game's mechanics, the more you get out, the more you can *squeeze* every advantage necessary to win.  It's great.  A true successor to the first game, even if the story is basically carried by the strength of the two main characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: fun exploration, in-depth character building with numerous options and an intriguing story with numerous twists and turns make this one of the best DRPGs you can play right now, even despite it's long runtime (somewhere around 95~ hours for me to finish the main story, and then 107 hours total to achieve the true ending)
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted Labyrinth of Refrain but more and that's exactly what I got.While there were what felt like many subtle improvements I was a little miffed that the dungeon themeing wasn't as strong in this one. The first each one felt like their own world and had a mini-story all its own and now they're much more homogenized.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the previous game or love team-building dungeon crawling or just curious about this game. PLAY IT!! This game is so fun. I'm having a blast exploring the labyrinths, its level design is good and rewards people who explore more. I also absolutely in love with all the characters so far. The voice acting for English is great too. And most importantly EUREKA IS SO CUTE!!!! MY HEART~
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant dungeon crawler that mixes old-school design with modern storytelling and sensibilities. Honestly, it's probably one of Nippon Ichi's best games. The only real complaint I have is that it drags a bit in the middle because of some cryptic event flag hunting, it's annoying to have to re-equip skills each time your characters reincarnate, and also the final dungeon required to reach the true ending is a bit of a slog.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: It's  on par with it's predecessor Labyrinth of Refrain , a fun and solid Dungeon crawler nothing to miss out.Edit: After playing through the whole game I had to correct my review. Although Galleria has a little less Dungeon diversity, the great story and interesting new mechanics make up for it plentiful. Also the game keeps you much longer at bay and is challenging without being frustrating. 9/10 definitely recommended for people who like dungeon crawlers.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Fun so far, and I suspect I'm relatively close to a tipping point in the story, but the handheld/vita UI with minimal details is starting to piss me off. Inventory/equipment management is pretty boring and unenjoyable as a result, which is an issue when your party can conceivably have dozens of puppets by endgame (the auto equip function doesn't seem to be very good). The encounters are also pretty binary; either auto attack fests where you can't be bothered to input commands or encounters where you risk puppets getting one-shot from the first turn. I will probably need the story to start picking up (as I suspect it will) within the next 5-10 hours to finish this.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore the time played, I've been playing it on a different platform.Gameplay wise, a marked improvement on Labyrinth of Refrain in most ways. It's hardly the most strategic of dungeon crawlers, but it's still fun and satisfying to figure out your party lineup, there are a lot of viable and meme setups. Most aspects are generally well explained in tutorials.The dungeon layouts are far more complex than Refrain, you REALLY have to pay attention to things you see and areas that might be suspicious as you go. No spoilers, the story has a similar but different feel to Refrain; some of its content is light-hearted, some of it extremely heavy. It doesn't treat the player like an idiot in any part of the experience.I haven't finished it yet, but there seems to be a significant amount of content, at an estimate probably somewhere in the 50 - 60 hours range [post-finished edit, I significantly underestimated; I finished it at just under 90 hours. There's a lot in this game], perhaps longer depending on difficulty setting and how much grinding you feel like doing.The port is also excellent. Easy swapping between input methods, no technical issues that I've had whatsoever, not a lot of options but still enough and not many are really necessary. Mouse input actually feels like mouse input, not an emulated controller. You can even play the entire game with just a mouse.I absolutely recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the main story at 82 hours without the use of a guide. The post game content is probably twice as long lol.If your like me and believe game length should factor in on your purchase. This game is well worth the cost of admission. If you don't factor in the total time you will spend playing a game, Then wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Fun cutesy game with alot of different mechanics to explore.  Honestly have barely scratched the surface of the game, so this is little more than my first Impressions.So far I have had none of the bugs / crashes reported by others.  But I will agree that even though there are alot of tutorials, somethings you will run across before you stumble across the tutorial that explains it, and there are some things I have stumbled across that i never found any explanation for and had to fumble around with to figure out on my own (sealed equipment for example)All in all a lot to explore both map wise, and game mechanics.  If like me, you are new to this series(?) there is something of a learning curve, but TBH I like that in these kinds of games.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good dungeon crawler. I liked the first game a lot, and this game expands on things while being fairly standalone. Finally finishing it with my current playtime, it does suffer from some bad pacing with the requests you have to do later. The end/postgame team building is a real hoot though, and the true ending is great. This has to be one of my favorite JRPG plots period.
_childDocuments_.name: Labyrinth of Galleria: The Moon Society

_childDocuments_.review: Three hours in im enjoying this 'sequel' already. I never tried 'steam' version of previous titlesome said it's poor port but this one is clearly playable with keyboard and mouseGalleria clearly hints that you need to explore every inch of tiles in the dungeonit's not explained before in refrain making you miss certain important key items or 'secret' enemiesIf this game built like the previous game I advise to explore every single tiles as some enemy might be impossible to beat without certain requirement and they don't tell you what it isthat is the case for refrain and idk if galleria is more relaxed or punishing.See it for yourself!

_childDocuments_.review: So far the game is better than the first. A lot of stale kind of dungeon exploration has been gutted and replaced with what the first started with. Layers and layers of a Labyrinth, very fun to explore pitfalls, breaking walls. This series is at its best when the Labyrinth feels like Campanula. Characters are good too. Solid 10/10 gameplay so far.

name: Black & White
detailed_description: JOIN THE COMMUNITY ON THE CUBE GAME DISCORD About the Game 'Black & White' is the second game released by ZeroCreation after 'Lay a Beauty to Rest: Dark Peach Blossom Spring'. The game type is visual novel + war chess game. It is like a painting with symmetrical composition, presenting a dystopian world of black and white. 'Black & White' has more than 250,000 words of game text. This is a 'not dystopian' dystopian story. Players will observe the memories of the twelve main characters as they are observing, and continue to communicate with the mysterious girl. - 'The opposite of justice is not evil, but another kind of justice.' This sentence is the most crucial theme of 'Black & White'. In the world of Black & White, you can trust the White Church camp that symbolizes order, fairness, and reason. You can also identify with the Black Cinder Crow camp, which symbolizes freedom, culture, and sensibility. On one side are priests with white hair, possessed by insects, and different personalities. On one side are historical figures who have returned from the dead, died tragically, and are romantic. How would you choose? The art style of 'Black & White' is extremely unique, and all the UI and characters in the game present a contradictory intention. There are nearly 100 characters and more than 400 CG or story maps in the game. We not only carefully sculpted the vertical paintings and CGs of each character with an extremely serious attitude. A branch plot is also set up for each of the twelve characters, and the branch plot will present a large number of story maps in a manner similar to comic interpretation. Compared with our previous work, 'Black & Whitef' has optimized the animation. While ensuring high-quality static art, some art can be animated and lifelike, which can make players feel better. Enter this world! We also put a lot of effort into this game in terms of sound, and strive to achieve the top level of domestic two-dimensional games. Lin Fangzhou, Harper, Xu Luyang and other three composers are mainly responsible for the soundtrack of '', and the sound effects are also produced by special sound engineers, who will control every link. The dubbing director of 'Black & White' is Mr. Mori Zhongren, and the dubbing actors have invited Hanser, Tao Dian, and many dubbing actors from Yuesheng Dubbing Club to cooperate. There are a large number of turn-based war chess level elements in 'Black & White'. We hope that through the war chess level, people can be more immersed in the characters and worldview, understand the plot, and at the same time, we hope to bring more fun to players who like war chess. There are more than 30 level maps in the game, including moving in subways, wilderness, urban areas and other venues. In the first half of the game, players need to constantly unlock the character story, and at the same time clear the less difficult and guiding story levels. In the second half of the game, after players collect 12 characters, players can freely assign characters to form a team, clear 28 challenge levels, and unlock more follow-up plots and game achievements in the challenge levels. The game adopts weak cultivation, in the process of playing the level. Players can unlock new skills of characters by achieving achievements or unlocking plots, and match different gameplay combinations.

_childDocuments_.review: Great aesthetic and storyline, heavily reminiscent of Drakengard 3/DoD3 (why did drakengard 3 resonate so much more strongly with China...? lol). The SRPG parts feel a lot more like what I expect from "War Chess", your units don't have MP, don't level or have complex stats, and have 3 skills they can choose from each turn. Most HP counts are around 4-6 and a strong skill will do 2 damage, so it feels a lot more like a puzzle than a Final Fantasy Tactics kinda thing. Already some really interesting unit ideas, one unit moves a pet unit around and makes a debuff field between them, another can stick their pet unit onto friendlies to deal more damage.Playing with Unity AutoTranslate, it's not too bad. The battle mechanics are absolutely simple enough to understand easily with machine translation. Official English seems to be upcoming, but I got tired of holding my breath.
_childDocuments_.name: Black & White

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a peculiar narrative style, its story is rather intriguing, and it has some good written characters (although not all of them are written equally good, to be honest). I also have to give credit to the setting, the idea of "everyone has their own truth", gray morality, etc. is executed rather well there. A pity that the gameplay (SRPG) part is mostly there just for the sake of it, it doesn't affect the story in any way, and on top of that doesn't present any significant challenge even during the so-called "challenging" battles. Still, it's not that bad either and may serve as some kind of a break from reading the VN parts.I hope that the future sequel will take into account all the controversial aspects of the original game and make it all better and more enjoyable.

detailed_description: Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key Digital Deluxe Edition In this set: - The main game - 'Another Look' Costume Set A set of 22 costumes, 2 different color variations of the default character outfit for each of the 11 party members. - 'Back to Summer' Costume Set A set of 2 costumes for Ryza, namely the 'Summer Adventure!' costume and 'Sea Breeze Blouse' costume that were introduced in previous games. - Gem Pack 100,000 Gems that can be used for Item Duplication and other purposes. Gems become available as you progress through the game and learn 'Duplication' or 'Item Rebuilding' in the Skill Tree. - Key Pack 20 Pristine Keys that can be used for Key Creation and other purposes. Pristine Keys become available as you progress through the game. Note: Costumes can be changed in the 'Changing Room' from the diary on the desk in the atelier. The respective character must be in your party. Please visit the official website for more information. Other editions featuring this product are also available for purchase. Please avoid making redundant purchases. Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key Ultimate Edition In this set: - Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key Digital Deluxe Edition - Atelier Ryza 3 Season Pass Access to 6 DLCs that will be added in the future. - Season Pass Bonus: 'GUST Collaboration' Costume Set A set of 2 costumes for Ryza based on young Plachta's and Ramizel's outfits from Atelier Sophie 2. Included in the Season Pass: 1. 'Endless Summer Splash!' Costume Set 2. 'Far East Travelers' Costume Set 3. Recipe Expansion Pack 'Alchemy Mysteries' 4. Recipe Expansion Pack 'Art of Adventure' 5. Additional Area 'Rosca Island' 6. Gust Extra BGM Pack Note: The Season Pass Bonus and item 1 will be released on the same day as the game. Items 2 to 4 are planned to be released before the end of May 2023, and items 5 and 6 are planned to be released before the end of June 2023. The content of the Season Pass and release dates are subject to change without notice. Please visit the official website for more information. Item 1 is a set of 11 swimsuits, one for each party member. Item 2 is a set of 9 Far Eastern-themed costumes, one each for Ryza, Klaudia, Lent, Tao, Patricia, Bos, Federica, Dian, and Kala. Items 3 and 4 add new recipes and items that can be used in synthesis and combat. Item 5 adds a new region and World Quests unique to that region. This content requires the game clear data in order to play. Item 6 adds more than 400 in-game BGM tracks from older Gust titles, including ones from Atelier Ryza 2. In-game BGM can be changed by selecting 'BGM' from the diary on the desk in the atelier. Costumes can be changed in the 'Changing Room' from the diary on the desk in the atelier. The respective character must be in your party. Other products featuring the base game and/or similar content are also available for purchase. The Season Pass and all items included in it can be purchased separately at a later date (except a bonus). Please avoid making redundant purchases. About the Game The story begins when a group of islands called Kark Isles appear near Ryza's—the protagonist's—hometown. Seeing this as a threat to their home, Ryza and her friends investigate the isles and discover ruins with a huge gate. Just as Ryza approaches the gate, a strange voice echoes in her head, telling her to reach the Code of the Universe. What is it that lies beyond the gate, and what does the 'Code of the Universe' mean? In hopes of finding a way to save their home, Ryza and her friends set off on a great adventure that revolves around a Key and the roots of alchemy. - Explore a vast open field! In this title, multiple maps are connected seamlessly, allowing players to move between different areas without the loading screen transition. Enjoy exploring in a vast, living world with a greater degree of freedom. - A total of 11 party members! Reunite with characters from previous games and meet new key characters essential to the story. Embark on your adventure with a wide range of friends—one of the largest in the series. - Use the 'Keys' with unknown powers to unlock various gameplay features! In the heart of this title will be the new 'Key' system. Keys have various types and effects that can be used in exploration, synthesis, and combat. Make good use of them while adventuring to enjoy a more satisfying, smoother experience! Note: Please visit the official website for more information. Other editions featuring this product are also available for purchase. Please avoid making redundant purchases.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A beautiful game that doesn't quite live up to it's predecessors. Gameplay has been refined to new heights, but a disappointing lack of character development and nothingburger of a story make this one less than the sum of it's parts.If you haven't played the first two games, go do that before you even think of touching this one. All of the most important character arcs for the core cast happen in those two games, leaving most of them without much to work through in this game. It's certainly great to be able to spend more time with these wonderful characters, but they're almost all resting on their laurels at this point, with most character quests being limited to short scenes where they pat each other on the back over how far they've already come. None of the series' handful of romantic parings get a definitive resolution here either, so temper your expectations accordingly. The story serves as a pretext to reunite the main characters and send them on a new adventure, but really lacks the same sense of urgency or consequence the previous games had. In Ryza 1, you were trying to save your home from a seemingly unstoppable natural disaster. In Ryza 2, you were doing everything in your power to save a precious companion and help them return home. In Ryza 3, you go on a meandering, often directionless journey to turn off a long dead civilization's emergency broadcast system. It's implied that the sudden appearance of the new Kark Isles might be destabilizing Ryza's hometown of Kurken Island, but there's no real timetable or any indication the stakes are getting higher as the game progresses. There just isn't a strong or immediate emotional hook this time to keep things interesting. In terms of gameplay though, this is easily the best in the series. The existing combat system has been fine-tuned to perfection with the added ability to block at any time, allowing you to mitigate damage with good timing. Alchemy has been given a shot in the arm as well with the addition of the key system, which allows you to add new effects and elements to existing recipes in order to create more varied concoctions. Each of the game's four regions can now be explored continuously without scene transitions or loading screens, including the entire overworld map of Ryza 1 as an added bonus. The only thing I did not like here is that there seems to be some kind of adaptive difficulty or level scaling at play for enemies. I encountered situations where common enemies often had exponentially more health than the story bosses they were standing right next to. I enjoy grinding out the best equipment and items possible with alchemy as soon as possible, but the scaling at work here made it a bit less satisfying than in the previous games.As a final note, the localization of this game is very disappointing. The English script frequently suffers from strange word choices and grammatical errors. I wish the publisher had spent more time and effort on this front, but I can kind of understand why they didn't. This series is not broadly well known, and a vocal minority of perverts are making sure that many people's first exposure to it is the 'Ryza Thighza' meme. These games are actually very sweet and wholesome with only a tiny amount of very tame fan service. Anyone looking for actual 'echi' content is not going to be satisfied, and anyone disgusted by lewdness might give these games a wide berth because of their undeserved reputation. I know it's pointless to talk about and people are going to meme for the lulz, but I really wish these games had the all popularity and success they truly deserve at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are reading this and wondering if you should skip the first 2 games. Do not skip them. Go play Ryza 1 right now. Ryza 3 is unfathomably large compared to the previous games. Also, there is a sky? I never noticed the sky before. I've been walking for over an hour just to reach the first quest checkpoint. The environment feels more like Genshin where I can just kind of go whereever. At one point I was riding a dolphin? They crammed a lot of stuff in here. The banter between characters is as awesomely innocuous as ever. Like just deliciously forgettable nonsense and overly polite and friendly niceties. Please inject this game directly into my calcified veins I complained about Ryza 1 and 2 being too easy, so that all the crafting options felt unecessary. I said I would have preferred if they let me play on very hard on the first playthough. Ok, so now on Ryza 3 you can start on Very hard, and I got absolutely destroyed by hedgehogs in the starting area. They killed me in 20 seconds. Since this is my goodbye to Ryza, I feel like I have to power through this. Apparently, Very hard is indeed VERY hard lolOk, in my defence, I was trying to fight before the game even allowed me to use items. The fights are still hard and it's definitely wayy more fun. Because I have to squeeze everything I can about the low quality materials I have and use every item I can create to beat basic mobs of enemies. This feels way more like the game was intended. A subtle change in the fighting system now is that AP increases faster than you can spend it, which makes the Aggressive mode more useful than it ever was before. In previous games, Aggressive mode would be almost always detrimental, except if you were at lvl5 tactics with too much AP to spend. In this game, it seems the Aggressive mode is quite useful. However, I also think that on Very hard I'm probably not playing the same game anymore. Graphics took a while to get right. But I managed to get 60fps by running windowed in 1080p and then upscaling to 1440 with Lossless Scaling app.The colors are so bright in this game it kind of hurts. Environments are shockingly large now. Kinda feels like I'm in the real world this time. Ryza's jogging animation is better than Ryza 2, but still not quite as perfect as Ryza 1. At least her walking and sprinting animations are somewhat normal now

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review, I have 100% completed this game and unlocked every achievement.I have played and fully completed Ryza 1 & 2 as well, and was so beyond excited for Atelier Ryza 3. For the most part, the game didn’t disappoint.The environments and explorable areas are *way* larger than before, even more so than Ryza 2. In fact, the entirety of Ryza 1’s map is just the FIRST AREA of this game. It’s actually mind blowing how much content they packed into this one.Ryza’s Alchemy takes a logical next step in allowing you to modify and adjust recipe material loops with secret keys and link morph, making for the most detailed, intricate, and comprehensive crafting system in the Ryza trilogy.The combat is the absolute best its ever been, an evolution on Ryza 2’s system, with a much cleaner UI, quicker action, more characters, and secret keys to really mix things up. And of course, the soundtrack is once again absolutely superb. Hearing the new versions of Ryza, Klaudia and Patricia’s themes made me smile so wide.While there is so much to love about this game, there were unfortunately a few things I was genuinely disappointed with. I don’t think the story is as good this time around, which is a shame for Ryza’s final outing, though I will say the character redesigns and new characters – like Federica – are really great.The game’s ending, and therefore the conclusion to Ryza’s story, disappointed me and left me feeling very unsatisfied. I don’t want to post spoilers here, but there were some character developments I was expecting to happen that just felt right and natural, that at the end of it all just… didn’t happen.It left me with a bad taste in my mouth while watching the credits.Also Serri appears in the game for a whole 3 seconds and she’s like my favourite character in the Ryza series and pretty much the only main character that didn’t return in this final game wtf Gust why you do this to my girl…In short, Ryza 3 is a fantastic game with a personally unsatisfying story and ending. Its such a shame, because this was the last hurrah for Ryza and her friends, and in my opinion these wonderful characters (klaudia & ryza especially) deserved a little better.I still think this is the best of the three from a gameplay perspective, but Ryza 2 is probably my favourite overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This should be the title.Only buy this game if you enjoyed playing Ryza 1 and 2 and you want to play more Ryza. If not, don't bother or wait a year later so that all patches and updates are in. TLDR: This game is disappointing. 3/5 (its ok at best). I have finished the game. It's still disappointing. There is fun to be had for sure specially if you like 1 and 2 but the flaws are way more noticeable for me which led to disappointment. Story: Don't expect too much. Its more or less the same as 1 and 2.Gameplay: Combat overall is the same as Ryza 2 so if you like that then you might will like Ryza 3 combat. Its probably larger than Ryza 1 and 2 combined (the world, not the thighs). Unfortunately, the size of the world is all there is to it. Exploring the world is not rewarding. It seems like the devs tried to have an open world game and then gave up half way or they ran out of budget (which probably explains why the UI is the way it is). Ryza 3's world is the most disappointing part of the game and this is the main feature (compared to 1 and 2).What's wrong with the map/world:- Not enough enemy variety. Majority of the enemies are palette swaps. I find this acceptable in the previous games since the world is not big but considering the size of Ryza 3 (not the thighs). There is also no optional super boss hiding somewhere in the map. In Ryza 1, they at least have those elemental super boss just chilling in their spots which they could probably add in Ryza 3 but they did not.- Terrible treasure chest contents. There are a lot of treasure chest scattered around but you are better off ignoring them. Most of them contain items that can be found anywhere else. This makes exploring the large world disappointing. I found 1 treasure chest containing a recipe and that recipe was pretty much nothing by that point in the game. Some of the treasure chest are so far out the way and only contain low quality items.They could have at least added some treasure chests that contain good items hiding behind a super boss.- There are many areas in Ryza 3 that feel like filler or padding. For example, the areas in Ryza 1 are back, but they are only involved in like 1 or 2 side quests or none at all. This would not be bad if there are at least some special enemies or items there but there is nothing.- Lots of Invisible walls. You think you can jump across a fence but turns out you can't. The large map gives you an illusion of being open but its more like a large hallway. This is easily noticeable in towns. It gets really annoying when you can just jump over a fence instead of going around the fence.UI: I need people to look past Ryza's thighs (It's hard I know) and admit that . The UI is worse than Ryza 1 and Ryza 2. That's right. The 3rd installment of the series has worse UI than that of the 1st game released years ago. The developers fell for the Minimalist UI crap common to open-world games. Ryza 3 even has the compass at the top-center of screen with quest markers like Bethesda games. They went so minimalist that certain basic UI elements are now gone.What's wrong with the UI:- In Ryza 1 and 2, the Gathering Tool you have equipped can be seen in the corner of the screen.. You need to press a button just to see which gathering tool you have. How can such a Basic UI element went missing? Who knows.- In Ryza 2, opening the Gathering Tool wheel near a gathering point will display all possible items that can be obtained.  You need to switch gathering tools just to see the possible items.-In Ryza 1 and 2, you can see the time of day in the corner of the screen.  Want to know what time is it? Just look at the sky, I guess. Another basic UI element that went missing.-In Ryza 1 and 2, there is an option to switch the confirm button to X or Circle (yes I'm using dualshock).  You need to remap the buttons if you want to switch. The problem is that this is not reflected during combat. It will still show Circle for the basic attack while you are pressing X.This is the 3rd game...-In Ryza 1 and 2, the Equipment screen can be selected in 1 menu.In Ryza 3, the Equipment screen is now behind 2 menus. You need to go to Menu > Battle preparations > Equipment. Why hide one of the most used option behind 2 menus?-Missing icon labels. If you are wondering what category your items are, you need to simply press the option button (or whatever you call it) however, there is no label. Never played 1 and 2? Good luck guessing the what the icon means.-Some Quests wont appear in the Quest Log. Ryza 3 introduces Random quests. This quests just appear at random while you are walking around. These quests does not appear in the quest log. They instead appear at the right side of your screen.It's kinda funny that they went for the minimalist UI when the right side of the screen now has a Quest list. There is also a floating cursor in the screen pointing you to the next quest objective.Also, certain NPCs will give you a fetch quest that will not be listed anywhere. I hope you have a notepad ready or have a good memory.I have other complaints but this will get too long.As for some positive things to say: -You can now see the remaining Basket space in the corner of the screen unlike the previous games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the best iteration of Ryza. But the Ryza series took a lot of steps backwards, so it's ultimately 2 steps back and 2 step forward.First off, the positives.This game's maps are very beautiful, the entire region is interconnected without invisible borders that cuts the regions into smaller inorganic rooms. Apart from the island in your starting area, you're able to walk from any point in the region to another without needing to go through a loading screen. Movement is faster and feels great to accommodate bigger maps. There are also warp points scattered everywhere for quick fast travels.They also got rid of the biggest most mundane chore in the Ryza series alchemy system by removing most of the recipe morphs and cutting the rest of the morphs to be very short. So you don't need to morph through 10 recipes to get the best stats for your item only to find out you're missing a material and forcing you to restart your progress.And now for the negatives.Despite having huge beautiful maps, the world is extremely empty. There are no points of interests or worthwhile reward for exploring the maps at all. You already have access to most of the materials within the starting area of each region. There are chests scattered everywhere, which could've been used as a great incentive to explore but all the rewards from chests are low quality common ingredients that becomes instantly outclassed after an hour or two of playtime.Combat is the same copy and pasted button masher from Ryza 2 but with worse UI that somehow displays less information. There's even less depth as a result. Not that it matters anyway because of how easy this game is. I started playing the game on Charismatic difficulty and everything melts like butter once I got access to half decent gear. Enemies only start to put up a fight when I switch to Legendary.Raising characters is still as terrible as ever. Every character starts off as a blank slate and you unlock passives and character defining skills by doing chores. And this game is extremely close to making character raising system engaging. Separate from the skill system, there are character events scattered throughout the world. These events are infinitely more fun to find and do because they provide a small little story which lets you get to know the characters better. However, for completing these written character events, you're rewarded with negligible amount of SP instead of something worthwhile like new skills. Instead, unlocking new skills is locked behind mundane chores that were ripped from a random quest generator. And despite having Secret Keys in its name, the key system is extremely negligible. You only need to get involved with the key system a few times for main quests, outside of that, you don't need keys at all. And I'm actually glad because the key system is terrible. To obtain the actual keys that you use for various purposes, you need to craft a blank key and use them on landmarks and monsters to get the actual keys. Keys are used as consumables to:1) buff characters in battle2) enhance crafting3) open resource nodes4) open new areasThe main problem is this system is a huge RNGfest. The blank keys have certain rarities attached to them. Having only the highest rarity is not actually good because there are some good key effects locked behind lower rarities, main example being adding certain element to your crafted item. And the drop table varies between monsters and rarities without the game telling you any information.Keys can enhance characters' performance during battle but the game is already easy enough without it and it's more cost effective to just craft better equipment and items because they provide much bigger boost and aren't expendable like keys.Resource nodes can give higher quality materials but they literally don't matter given how easy it is already to get items to 999 quality. The nodes sometimes provide new crafting recipes, these recipes are the only reason to open nodes up. But the drop rates for these recipes are low and there's only a set amount per region and you have no way of telling whether you already unlocked all the recipes from that region or not.The new areas you open up with keys have the same issue as the rest of the maps: they don't offer anything new. There are no new materials, the chests are useless, there's no reason to explore.I feel like the developers focused too much on developing the new movement and map system and neglected everything else. I hope that Ryza 3 is a stepping stone for future Atelier series and the newer games won't suffer the same neglect as Ryza 3. For now, just play Sophie 2 for a good modern Atelier experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe this game's quality, I'd say it slightly improves the strong points of Ryza's previous outings, but doesn't do anything to address their flaws.For the pros, the graphics are amazing (this is the game's biggest strength). The world is big and full of places to explore. The story is good by Atelier standards; that is, it's nothing special but it's okay. Atelier has always been more character-driven than plot-driven, and the characters are well-written and likeable here. The music is beautiful, though not always particularly memorable.For the bad? As with Ryza's last two adventures, the game is pathetically easy. Once you learn the basics of alchemy, you'll craft some decent gear and proceed to absolutely annihilate every single encounter in no time. This is true even if you pick Very Hard difficulty.The lack of difficulty is especially bad because it ruins the main draw of the Atelier series: alchemy. What makes these games satisfying is when you encounter a challenging obstacle, like a tough boss, then figure out how to make an item that allows you to come back and overcome the problem much more easily. When the combat never has any challenge, you rarely feel any motivation to synthesize, other than for the sake of filling out your item compendium.Combat has next to no strategy involved; you just mash the attack button, then use as many skills as you can afford until you run out of AP. None of the encounters encourage any other strategy. If you've made an okay set of gear, this will literally carry you through the entire game.Although there's a big world to explore, there aren't that many rewards for doing so. If you look around, you might find treasure chests, but the items they contain are mediocre at best. Again, if you're half-decent at alchemy, you'll have that item but better already.There are also glaring balance issues. The most blatant one is the Ultra Purity exploit, which allows you to easily obtain as many gems as you need. Gems can be used to duplicate and rebuild items, making alchemy even more trivial. There were easy gem tricks in the previous games, but none were as simple, accessible, and effective as this one. I have no idea how this oversight ever made it out of the game's unreleased beta versions.If you liked Atelier Ryza 1 and 2, you'll probably like this too. But if, like me, you thought these games were boring and lacked challenge, prepare to be disappointed once again.If you want a better Atelier experience, I'd strongly recommend Atelier Sophie 2 over this.
