_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 3 is intensely strange as a game and takes the "there's not much content for this game" feeling that Ryza 2 has and makes it even worse. They've decided to go Open World for this one, which is somewhat of a departure from where the other two went.It feels like with all 3 games they're mixing the previous games into it. Not just with how it plays, but every single part of the previous games - from the weapons, the recipes you have to make, the skills you pick up, the items you use, the enemies you fight. All 3 games it's identical. And this one takes it a step further and even has the entire map of the first game available from the start. It's now (mostly) seamless which is an interesting idea but it's completely devoid of content, just an enormous desert of nothing new and the same collectibles.I feel like this is how a lot of the open world of the game feels. I'm finding the items I found in Ryza 1/2. I'm killing the enemies I killed in Ryza 1/2. And I'm running through very large very empty areas to do all this. It's also PACKED with invisible walls. God they're everywhere. Why can't I jump over this 50cm fence? Who knows! There's a garden in the first location that is infuriating because there's a ton of very small hedges it just won't let you jump over so you have to navigate all around them. And a village in the final area that's filled with ladders that is extremely hard to navigate because there's only a few points you can jump over/down from where you are.Honestly if it was a realism thing I'd be okay. Sure, don't let me jump 50 meters to my death, absolutely. But there's plenty of enormous jumps it WILL let you make. There's really no pattern to what might be an invisible wall and what won't be.The skill tree in this game compared to the other one is huge and very varied. I sort of like that it has so much variety but at the same time if you don't go towards some of the stuff in the tree you miss out on extremely important mechanics/items and I just don't think these should be locked away behind random chance, especially not the core crystal expansion and item rebuilding, two very important mechanics.The central gimmick of this one over the other two is the key system. When you're fighting enemies and they get below about 60% health you can create a key. They have various affects, including opening doors/chests across the game, buffing you in combat and helping along some recipes. For the most part the regular chests have nothing in them though, there's legitimately none in the entire game that are worth while so opening barriers to pick them up is sort of a waste.However - there are 'storage points' in the game. They show up as crystals that you can go and interact with. If you use a rare key on a rare storage point it gives you a new recipe. This is the only way to get a ton of really important recipes and the game never ever tells you this. The first few storage you interact with use up precious key charges (yes, they run out) and give you a random assortment of absolute rubbish so you'll think "ugh what's the point". It's a frustrating mechanic and the amount of times I've seen people post about the game saying "Did you know this??" is pretty high. There's at least two quests I couldn't complete because I straight up could NOT get the recipes that I needed. It's just a terrible mechanic.The translation of the game is awful as well. It's not QUITE machine translation bad, but it does feel like it's been run through a machine translation then someone has gone back and fixed it up a bit. There's a lot of super awkward sentences in the story and many parts where it's really hard to tell what they're actually talking about. The story also has a ton of repeated content, I feel like I went to see Ryza's parents to say bye about thirty times. When these two things are mixed it starts to make me lose connection with what's even going on. There's an absolute TON of character cutscenes as well, marked on every map. Because of the bad translation and repeated content these feel wasted. Any other game i'd have loved a load of time hearing my characters chat but in this I just found myself skipping the things when I accidentally triggered them.There's a lot of parts of the story that don't jive with the actual gameplay too. It makes out you're leaving town for months, but the game only takes place over a single summer and you can fast travel all over at any point all the time. So when Ryza tells her parents she's going away THREE DIFFERENT TIMES it just feels weird because of the way the rest of the game plays. She's been gone at week, at best. The way the story treats this (you have a few tearful style homecomings) just feels absolutely baffling.And the PC controls are awful. V brings up the map. The digging on your mount only works if you try and dismount when you find a dig spot (the game says to press the left mouse button. This does not work). Quests are F. G is the item menu.No idea why any of that is the default.It would be fine, but the previous two games were absolutely fine to play on PC, why the regression?The game feels like 60 hours of content stretched really thinly over a 30 hour game, filled with bizarre design choices.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most engaging crafting systems in RPG I've played ... until I found that creating infinite "dust" (a currency to copy crafted items) is allowed by the game (It seems like it's by design, but this design seems to be an huge oversight). _childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 3 (Something Something Key) is the third game in a trilogy, and I want to start by saying that I highly recommend playing all three games. The Ryza trilogy is also part of a much larger franchise, yet its gameplay is a pretty drastic departure from the rest of the series. This is both a blessing and a curse, however, as it means that anyone familiar with other Atelier games will probably want to do some research into some streams or something to see if this looks like it's worth a try, but if you're like me and don't know or don't like most of the rest of the series, the accessible easy-to-learn crafting and the fast-paced real time battles might make this one of the best in the series.Never heard of this series? Then none of that context will help. Atelier Ryza is a game that focuses on storytelling in typical JRPG fashion; fight bad guys and get stronger to progress, but unlike Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy, your equipment is never found or earned, but always crafted. Story progress unlocks new areas, new areas have better stuff to craft with, better ingredients make better pizza.The first two Ryza games are quite a bit better than the third in terms of gameplay and engagement. Ryza 3 does a nice job tying up the end of the story and is still absolutely worth playing if you liked the others. It has a much more open world, more "fluid" gathering animations, and about twice as many playable characters as the previous games. The problem with the larger scale, though, is that you have a huge open world, four times larger than Ryza 1's map, yet only as much content and story as the other games, so it just feels excessive and empty. The additional characters are another example of excess in design. You have more than enough characters to hypothetically form two whole parties with bodies to spare, yet you'll only ever need enough for one. Is it worth it to spend extra time and resources developing all the characters fully? Probably not.I have a lot of minor complaints about Ryza 3 when comparing it side-by-side with the Ryza 2, but with over 100 hours spent on just one playthrough, they clearly did something right. Play it for the story!

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 1: 4/10Atelier Ryza 2: 5/10Atelier Ryza 3: 6/10The first Atelier series I've started and finished, I'd say it met the expectations I had for it. True to its trailer and screenshots, the Atelier Ryza series is a casual experience of saving the land with the help of the friends you make along the way. Despite my number rating, I would recommend this game for those looking for a pleasant experience and easy-to-follow story. This is NOT a game for those looking for a gameplay experience, or those who dislike reading as there is a lot of JP dialogue/ EN text.I'll start positive. Ryza 3 is definitely the strongest of the Ryza series: offering smooth exploration, gathering, crafting, and battles compared to the 1st and 2nd games. Pacing of the main story, if ignoring most side content, is well paced. Characters are as lovable as they've been in previous games filled with banter, alchemic miracles, and overcoming adversity. Easily, more than half of my playtime was spent on alchemy crafting alone. On the negative side of things however, Ryza 3 suffers in the same way the previous games do: alchemy in battle is absurdly powerful, alchemy crafting is broken with a few choice perks, difficulty is near meaningless, no replayability, near no endgame. The worst offender in the alchemy system is that Neutralizers can usually be looped into themselves, making for an easy early 999 quality item effectively putting you in the end game even on the highest difficulty. This trivializes all fights, including bosses, as they usually die in a few item uses. Unique to Ryza 3, another terrible decision is the Super Trait: Ultra Purity which easily trivializes gem reduction and duplication leading to easy gearing and mindless alchemy. You could purposely avoid items and exploits to make fights and alchemy artificially harder, but why would you? Ignoring gameplay and immersion for a moment, the story is only told through dialogue. For a game made in 2023, by Koei Tecmo, with similar competition such as the Tales series, the quality of storytelling does not meet modern standards. There are only TWO uniquely animated scenes in the main story and even then it's mostly dialogue with no animation worth mentioning. Not unique to Ryza, this is a problem with the JRPG genre in general, and especially those that use rigid game engines like this that seemingly restrict animated movement. Lastly, in my personal opinion, there is no need to play the first two games as there is nothing mentioned there that is not mentioned constantly in Ryza 3. Whatever main story took place in Ryza 1 or 2, have virtually no mention in Ryza 3 or contribute nearly-nothing to the main story. The only thing that transfers over is the established world building and some characters. The world building doesn't change. The character dynamics don't change. You're not missing anything if you have an open mind. If you are looking for a very casual experience of a simple story with friends having a more-exciting-than-usual summer, I'd recommend it to you. Otherwise, steer clear as you'll be disappointed. I went into this knowing what to expect, and receive it I did.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a "this game is bad, don't buy" review. Ryza 3 is still fun, but it's just so underwhelming compared to the first two that I definitely wouldn't recommend unless you love pointlessly big open worlds.Ryza 3's biggest plus is that the game looks beautiful! They did an amazing job improving graphics and making the gameplay smoother in some ways, like how you can run while collecting items on the ground, or how you climb vines automatically (though the auto climb sucks with ladders...)Everything else that's good about the game is basically just Ryza 1 and Ryza 2 features. The alchemy is basically the same from Ryza 2, you just now have keys instead of the drops. Combat is also largely the same, though it felt more fun to turn on aggressive mode every now and then compared to Ryza 2.All the other new features just feel so bad to use. Keys are RNG trash. They seem powerful, but they're limited use so I'd rather just... Not waste them. It's at least ignorable if you're just going through the main story, but they're required for the plat trophy and it instantly makes them go from a pointless feature to a bad feature (screw the roles trophy...)Supply points are also up there. You need keys to open them, and many recipes are locked behind them. Just make me recipe morph for those recipes, this was highly unnecessary and unfun!Super traits are another feature, though these are just unfun but ignorable. They're powerful effects that you can put on items, but they can only be transferred from raw ingredients to items. All it does is adds more features to a game that already has so many pointlessly overpowered features that it makes it more annoying to make any decisions.The game also features 4 big open worlds and they are just so pointlessly big. It makes it actively annoying to search for that one ingredient you're missing in a recipe, and it made it take longer to do all the sidequest that are normally shoved into the one town since they're now scattered all over the maps. There was absolutely no benefit whatsoever to adding so many large zones that are each the scale of Ryza 1's whole map. This could've just as easily been a game taking place exclusively in Sardonica or Nemed with a one or two other small zones for the finale.The two new spirit beasts also go underutilized for some reason. They're completely optional, so they just seem like massive afterthoughts. You need them for the plat trophy, and so far I've only gotten some garbage chests as additional rewards from them.Ryza 3 is just another game that felt the need to make a big open world and failed to deliver. It tried to make some big changes (which I appreciate, as I hate it when a game series just pumps out the same garbage over and over with a fresh coat of paint) but it completely missed the mark and made a game that is just Ryza 2 but worse.If you loved the first two games and just want to see the conclusion of the Ryza trilogy, this game is at least worth it on sale. Unless exploring is your favorite thing to do in Ryza, this game is the worst of the three.

_childDocuments_.review: It has been 4 years, since the events of the first game of the Secret series, both in game and both in real life. Time for Ryza and friends to return, for one last summer, one last adventure...New game needs new gimmick, to separate itself from the first game. Last game it was the ruins exploration, now it is the secret keys. It is  a really fun, creative new system, especially since it is incorporated in the story, it is created by alchemy and it has a lot of uses. The only downgrade is the rng, but at one point, you can mass produce more keys than a sweatshop factory, so it will not mater.Alchemy system also got updated, with the keys and the new link morph system,and, in my opinion, it became the best in the series.The combat did not change too much, but it became much easier than in the previous games, taking away a lot of the early game challange.Unlike the previous games, the game became open world, with load screens only between the big regions. And to be honest, this is not as good as i hoped it will be. Exploring the game world takes a lot of time and many times, you can't explore parts of the region, because you are constrained by not having specific traversal items, since you get them alter at the game. But, when you return to said area, it will feel like, waiting did not worth it, since everything you can find in these areas are basically the same tier, as other things in the region. So other than exploring a new cool part of the world, it is not too rewarding. Another big problem here, is that the world is empty. I mean, yeah there are treause chests (with meh treasures in them), and a ton of monsters and resource nodes, but that is it. No activities, just some random, radiant quests, but they become boring fast. YOu can get some secret recipies from treausre nodes but that requires you to have Super Rare keys, so again, it just adds to the late game grind.This is where the game got the biggest  upgrade. It looks way better than the previous 2 games, while keepeing the same art style. The music uses a lot of tracks from previous games, and some new tracks. They are integrated really well into the game world, and it always matches the mood of the game.Voice acting, well, japanese voice acting industry is on a way different level, than the rest of the world, so from a game series with budget like this, it is expected to be really great. Both returning and new voice actors are perfect matches for their charaters, and put their whoel talent into makeing them alive.The ambient and combat sound design is also a great match for the game. As in the previous installements.The story is a perfect way to finish the Ryza trilogy. Wholesome, cute, funny, and it takes care of a lot of things, that were in the air sicne the first game.My only problem here is the ending. Without spoilers, basically it ends like the second game. We knew this is the last, but instead of a "The end" ending, we got one that feels more like "The end?" or "To be continued".11 character main cast. This is the biggest in Atelier history. Our old friends, from previous games return, with new characters in tow. Their storylines all get some concolusion, and we see some minor characters make their return too, though they did dirty with Roma and Pamila, by making their quests like just they are some random NPC-s.My biggest beef here is Clifford and Serri. Other than some mentions, we do not see them return, other than being in the frame of the epilogue for 1 second. They were important characters, especially Serri to the oren lore. They would have deserved some closure, at least in the form of a quest or something.As i said, the game world became much bigger and open world. So there is a lot to explore and a lot of lore to learn, trough quests and hidden memoires. And, one of the biggest update here are the monsters. We get new monsters models, not just reskins of the old ones, which makes the game feel more diverse and interesting.This was never a strong point in the series. There is new game plus, there is a harder difficulty that unlcoks after finishing the game once, but that is it. Well, it can be good to return, and replay the game, after a couple of years, to once again set off to an adventure with the characters, but, if you fully finish the game once, there is nothing new in a second replay.Sadly there are some bugs. Though, if you look up online, you can solve the issues, so there are no real, gamebreaking ones.Every farewell is a sad one, including this one. Atelier Ryza 3 is a pretty great concolusion of the series, but, looking at how successful the Secret series were, compared to other entries in the Atelier franchise, i would no be surprised to see the gang return in one way or another in either a new series or in a Ryza 4, the aftermath game...If you are a fan of the series, you will have a great time with this game, if you are new here, go and play the first Ryza game first.

_childDocuments_.review: In the midst of unfinished AAA game releases of 2023, I can safely say that Atelier Ryza 3 wasn't a part of those games. As a matter of fact, I feel like Ryza 3 is more than finished; It is a polished version of what makes previous Atelier Ryza games so great. It makes me wonder how can a game such as this one keep improvising with each release. It really makes me happy seeing how far the developers at Gust have improvised their Atelier games over the decades. Now let me talk about a few improvements that were made on this from its predecessor:- I see improvements on all character models except for Ryza herself, which I will be explaining later. Characters are more expressive in this game and that made cutscenes look a lot less like a puppet show and more of a well-animated 3D anime.- You can travel seamlessly between locations on the map. No more loading screens and having to press 'A' on my Xbox controller every time I want to move to a new location.- The environment felt more believable and alive. I also noticed that they applied foliage sway on objects like plants and grasses. And these objects will also sway if you walk/run on top of it. Small detail but a very welcome one.- Movement is a lot faster. You can basically zoom through the entire location very quickly if it wasn't for the enemies roaming around.- Gathering is instantaneous, especially for materials that you pick up off the ground- You can pet the dogs and cats. The only issue I have with this is that they basically copied the same model throughout the entire map (not a big issue though).Now let me also talk about a few issues that I have with the game:- Stuttering at certain times. Though it is not that big of an issue for me since it happened only when I was about to enter a new location on the map. Remember that this game does not have loading screens and traveling between locations is basically instantaneous.- Ryza character model looks like a paper. I know that's just my opinion but the older Ryza games did Ryza models better.- I have no issue with instantaneous materials gathering but I only wished that they put a much clearer sound effect telling me that I've picked up the materials. At certain times I feel like I picked up material but wasn't sure because the only indication that you'll get is at the bottom left corner of your screen telling you that you've picked up the item. All in all, I truly recommend it, especially to players who've played the previous installments in the series. If it wasn't for Zelda: TOTK, Ryza 3 would've been my best game of the year 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion after 24 hours:Good:- I'm pretty satisfied with the game so far overall, if you liked the first 2 it's mostly more of the same.Bad, mostly minor nitpicks:- Infrequently the translations/subtitles come off as extremely literal and in rare cases unintelligible word-salad; there are occasionally typos.- Some of the crafting trait effects are still unclear as to what exactly they do and there's no early target dummy to test it yourself.- If you use a controller you're going to see Xbox buttons regardless of which controller you're using.- The adjustable camera distance during adventure resets to default after any area transition including battles.- The breadth of idle chatter the group has during exploration is pretty limited and repeats itself fairly often.- There's important info you can't review tutorials for or are never explained despite the robust in-game manual (key crafting uses regenerate when you go back to base; basic attacks in relation to Tactics level are never explained again after the first time).- There are hundreds of loot chests and 90% of them seem absolutely worthless.***Final thoughts after finishing the main story, 120+ hours:I tried to do 100% quest completion (I think I missed one Lent quest, I couldn't figure out where to find another of a specific enemy type it needed).- Even on Very Hard the game becomes trivial after you make really good core items, for me it was around level 70 where I could just end any combat without trouble at all. The game was hardest during the beginning before you synthesized anything.- Super Traits are too powerful.- The DLC for extra recipes seems insane considering base game recipes will let you beat anything with no trouble. The DLC gives you extra gather nodes too, I can only imagine it makes things even easier.- Big thing I leaned for traits: the descriptions are purposely vague because the effect is dependent on what the item targets; i.e. if you put healing on an item that targets enemies the enemies will get healed.Kala is my favorite character.***The post-game voice actor Extra features are worth listening to, I enjoyed them a lot.They just added Legendary difficulty which is 2 above Very Hard. I think I'll try it but it sounds boring since you can take your overpowered equipment over from regular New Game.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 3 is an easy recommendation to people who have played the previous two games in the  series. Story details from the previous games are heavily referenced and returning characters build on the bonds forged on the last adventures. The Atelier games are RPGs that balance combat, crafting (synthesizing) and gathering. You HAVE to make everything; weapons, gear, accessories, traveling equipment, consumables, etc. It'd be strange if you spent more time in combat than synthesizing. The synthesis system in the Atelier Ryza games is pretty fun. You follow a recipe that requires a specific ingredient or an ingredient of a certain category/element. The ingredients themselves have traits that can be inherited into the final product.The main new mechanic in Ryza 3 is the Key Creation system, you basically can create these keys in-combat from weakened enemies or from fast travel locations. These keys (depending on rarity and RNG) can provide buffs in several aspects of the game. You can use one mid-combat, use one while gathering, use it during synthesis, etc. It's a little overwhelming at first and it took me a while to understand how powerful keys were, but I thought it was interesting. As for the rest of the game, I'm not a fan of how much Ryza 3 leans towards "Open World". The maps in-game are large and there's a lot to explore, however, I found that a lot of the ingredients would repeat themselves too often. Honestly, I don't think they knew what to do with so much space. By the time I finished the main story, I think I uncovered 1/3 of the landmarks (fast travel locations) across all regions. Even after uncovering all of these landmarks (for 100% achievements), there seemed to be a lot of NOTHING going on aside from the occasional dungeon that hosts a quest or two. While I appreciate them adding the Ryza 1 areas, they were barely used too. As for the story, I'm split down the middle. Personally, I don't find it satisfying because . Contrary to this, I really like the characters. Everyone in the cast has a personal struggle and it's great to see how the characters rely on each other. Though, I feel like they overdo it sometimes with the character quests. I don't like getting bombarded with slice of life cutscenes when I'm progressing through the main quest or just want to go back to the atelier to craft something. Ryza 2 had a similar issue and that felt 10x worse ... so I guess they eased up on it a bit since then. Combat is immaculate, it was very fun and I never got bored. I think the combat system has come a long way since Ryza 1. My favorite parts are the skill combos, swapping characters mid-fight, and the option to change which abilities trigger from Action Orders and when. It kept things from getting dull. Klaudia is best bard! Those are my overall thoughts on Ryza 3. I'm kinda sad that Ryza's series has come to an end, but definitely looking forward to what Atelier Yumia has to offer in 2025. I hope a lot of my issues with the "open world" stuff in Ryza 3 are addressed then.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Atelier game by an absolute mile. Not even remotely close. It's a huge game (something like 4x the size of Ryza 1 and 2) and alchemy always gives you incentive to explore. The story has a lot more going on than previous installments and relies less on the sort of independent slice of life events they used. Tons of quality of life features like faster gathering, tracking materials, etc. Combat feels fun and rewards you for spending time crafting the best stuff. Old characters have less development since they've already kind of gone through their arcs but the new characters pick up the slack. Overall great experience.Biggest issues are the localization (which has some pretty glaring issues early on, with straight up typos and grammar mistakes, but does get a bit better. still not acceptable to have a localization of this quality) and the fact that it drags a bit towards the end after you've unlocked the final recipes. If you go out of your way to make the highest quality stuff, you'll blast through the final parts even on the highest difficulty. Still, fully recommend it. If Koei Tecmo gives Gust more time to develop games like this, and puts effort into future localizations along with bringing back English VA, the Atelier series could really break out of its niche. The series feels close to moving from "good for hardcore JRPG fans" to "good for anyone who enjoys RPGs."

_childDocuments_.review: Obligatory "I wish Steam had a 'meh' rating."Atelier Thighza 3 is by no means a  game, but it felt like downgrade from the previous two. The zones are needlessly big and contain a lot of areas that serve no purpose besides extra gathering spots, creating quite a bit of bloat in the exploration. Something about the art style of this game felt , telling myself "I remember Ryza 2 looking better than this" when I launched it for the first time.The story was fine. I liked the new characters and return of some old, but after a certain point everybody but the original cast gets shoved away. Ryza 2 is my favorite of the trilogy, and it was very disheartening to know how minimal of a part most of the characters from there played if at all. Atelier is recognized more for character interactions over story, but this fell a little short compared to other entries. I wish Klaudia and Ryza went somewhere, felt very strange to just pretend that nothing that Klaudia expressed from the previous game ever happened.If you're the type to go for 100% achievements, this one is a bit of a RNG nightmare. Some of them are centered around key forming, which is just an RNG-fest of trying to get specific effects. This whole system was scarcely explained.PC port is pretty mediocre, but I haven't played any GUST game that didn't give me a fair share of problems. I'd recommend getting it on another platform.Overall it is worth a play if you're a fan of Ryza, but don't set your expectations too high. The end of their journey is satisfactory, and I hope we eventually see Ryza again with her apprentice starring as the protagonist in the future.

That being said Atelier Ryza and its sequel 2 were good. They were big improvements on the franchise and all its mechanics in general (also add in Sophie 2). Ryza 3 blows those games out of the water. Like I said if Ryza 1, 2 and Sophie 2 were good, this game is great. Its the first atelier game in a long time I didn't feel too overpowered for the enemies just by crafting good gear and weapons right off the bat. Enemy balance feels better where you can definitely break the game and be overpowered but you're not just steam rolling everything in its path and waiting to start a new game+ like previous titles. Link morph is an awesome addition to the synthesis system and felt like a way to get more involved with elements and traits like the Sophie 2 system but without the cumbersome puzzle mechanic.The story is even better. Especially with the icons around to really show you where to have little events with party members. Inclusion of quests to show you the culture of the area were also a nice touch. I'm not the biggest fan of the randomized quests which pop up, but they aren't killing the game for me.Overall this is the best game in the Ryza series and a great way to end the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 3 is the pinnacle of the trilogy without a shadow of a doubt, and makes for a very fitting conclusion in that sense. The sense of scale of the world downright dwarfs Ryza 1 & 2, and the Atelier series finally has a fully loaded in interconnected world with no separate loading smaller chunks of areas; and there's even multiple massive areas to explore instead of just one. You are also given so much creative freedom in general compared to the previous entries. For the environments, you're very rarely restricted on where you can go, and you can go anywhere as long as you have the appropriate item to reach it (You are given the vast majority of the exploration items very early on too). For skills and synthesis, you can get ANY skill you want in any order as long as you have the required SP to do so (and branch out the skill tree). Along with that, the titular "Secret Keys" can enhance your items in various ways if you're smart, and can potentially make up for a lack of quality materials to get very good stats earlier on. A big criticism I had with Ryza 1 was how railroaded the game felt both exploration wise and synthesis wise, so Ryza 3 addresses all my complaints and then some. This also helps Ryza feel more in line with the older Atelier games like the Mysterious trilogy which also similarly had lots of creative freedom and exploration despite the smaller areas and scope.Speaking of that, if you've played Atelier Firis before, it seems to me that Ryza 3 accomplishes what that game set out to do and fell short on. Much like this game, Firis was more focused on larger open environments. However, areas were still separated by loading screens, and Firis' movement speed was pitifully slow with limited fast travel options making getting around to be a chore at times. Ryza's ability to fast travel instantly anywhere with rideable animals that move very fast give just the right amount of pacing, and does Firis' ideas justice. Even other minor things like random sidequests you find by talking to people were also in Firis. Honestly, the fact this game is just not separated by smaller areas loading in helps the pacing a lot.The combat has also been very refined from Ryza 2 which I already had very little issues with in the first place. Attack animations are very quick, snappy, and satisfying to just watch. You also earn AP & CC much quicker in this game, so it helps to speed up the fighting when you're grinding for materials. If you wanted more depth though, then that also is delivered. The aforementioned Secret Keys are also used in combat to give various stat buffs, and can be equipped on characters as gear to also give buffs. This along with the new Order Drives and up to 5 party members being able to be used in active battle gives a nice healthy dose of freshness to the mostly similar combat, making it more fun to go through.The only truly negative things I have to say about Ryza 3 is that the soundtrack is not nearly as good or memorable as Ryza 2, maybe even Ryza 1. It's still not bad by any means, but considering Atelier's pedigree of fantastic OSTs, I think it fell short in most instances. (EDIT: I found out the reason I felt this way about the music was because the main composer for this game was Kazuki Yanagawa who is usually the head composer for the Atelier series as a whole. Hayato Asano was the head composer of Ryza 1 and 2 which explains why it sounds so different. Upon further listening, I don't think the soundtrack for Ryza 3 is necessarily worse, but I did experience some tonal whiplash when I was expecting Hayato Asano's style.)Also, when trying to discover landmarks, the world map is covered in clouds until you walk right up to the nearest landmark, and a portion of the clouds are uncovered. This can sometimes make finding the appropriate path to the landmark needlessly confusing as the environments are so much bigger than before with many alternate paths. This means you can sometimes just take the wrong path into a dead end or just flat out not know where the entrance to the area is until you look everywhere first. The map is always uncovered on the mini-map which does help, but it's very zoomed in and doesn't always help you out when you need it.In short, Ryza 3 surpassed my already high expectations of Ryza 2 and fixed just about any issue I had with the Ryza trilogy in particular. The game does assume you already played the last 2 games because it explains very little and has lots of callbacks, so if you haven't played the other two, play those. Otherwise, Ryza 3 is a no-brainer to purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the game and sitting on my opinions, I've decided to edit this review. Atelier Ryza 3 is for sure a purchase for people who played Ryza 1 and 2. I for one didn't enjoy the 2nd game, but I found my Ryza 3 experience very enjoyable. Movement and exploration is far more fluid, and the music is great. Synthesis is the most fun of the three games in the trilogy. More recipes are off the beaten path IMO in this game as well. Ryza 3 suffers from enemy design and ingredient collection unfortunately. Like all of the games before, areas could do with one or two more unique enemies, rather than recolors (unless we're talking about punis). I feel as if GUST hasn't been able to make an engaging difficult combat experience in their games, and Ryza 3 is no different. Enemies have no unique abilities and pose zero threat. I know this is Atelier, but there should be better ways to gain an advantage in combat other than synthesis. Its about time GUST gets more creative with combat. The open zones are great and give a liberating feeling, but ingredients are sorely lacking. I love the map design, but they lack any unique resources for me to explore the nooks and crannies. Sometimes ingredients are limited to one zone, when they could be spread out a little more to help with gathering. This wasn't a problem in the previous games, but now that the maps are larger this problem has shown its face. Diving has been a largely forgotten mechanic, and I only used it for exploration once. The map suffers from side quest and event bloat. Looking at the end game map just makes me shudder at the thought of being a completionist. The events are beyond boring and have no purpose. The events are so short they don't even properly show character interaction; They just serve to interrupt your exploration. As for side quests, don't bother. I have never encountered a side quest worth my time, as most just fill your inventory with quality 60 junk. As for the story, I haven't encountered a more forgettable plot. Dusk stories were driven by their world and setting. Mysterious stories were driven by the MC personalities and goals. Ryza stories have always been lacking in this regard, and Ryza 3 is no exception. Thank god that there's a skip button. Overall, Ryza 3 is very ambitious with its changes to combat and exploration. Despite this, there are many issues that have arisen or haven't been fixed that lead to a flawed experience. Even so, Ryza 3 still retains what I love: music, synthesis, and a laid back atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 3 has improved on everything in Ryza 2, in my opinion, and the PC port actually runs very well.  I do recommend the game to both new players and veteran Atelier fans if you like the gathering, crafting, exploring, semi-turn-based combat, and/or the anime-style.  It isn't exactly groundbreaking or innovating, but it's a good and fun game nonetheless.Graphics are nice eye candy but nothing groundbreaking.  Very vibrant world with decent art direction and texturing.  I particularly like the character shading techniques, but none of it is quite on the level of certain other anime-styled games.  At the time of writing, however, disable the depth of field to fix the weirdly bright and blurry environment.  The rest of the graphics look great.Keyboard + mouse controls feel a bit floaty and off here and there (it's roughly what you'd expect from a primarily-controller focused game ported to PC)), but overall they are actually decent, and you have the ability to rebind keys fairly well for different modes and menus.  Could be better, but it's perfectly playable.Gameplay is exactly what you'd expect of an Atelier series game—if you liked it before, you'll like it now, and if you didn't, you probably won't change your mind.  However, it does improve a lot from Ryza 2.  Combat feels a lot better as well as many other mechanics.  You'll be gathering a lot of materials and crafting a lot of items, and if you like that sort of thing, the gameplay loop is very fun.  Again, the devs played it a bit safe with mechanic additions, and that's probably a good thing.It runs very well so far with a solid 120 FPS at max settings on a 3090.  I haven't had any frame drops or other issues with it.  The game does *not* support ultrawide displays at either 21:9 or 32:9.  You can set a custom resolution in the settings.ini file, but the UI will be stretched, and using a hex value editor to fix it breaks the minimap.  Game is also running well on Steam Deck; however, there is some freezing here and there.Finally, to address some of the comments on sex appeal and censorship: yes, the game still has physics on all outfits that would show it (not plate armor or leather, for example), and while photo mode does disable Ryza's model when too close, you can also just move her around to zoom in closer—works fine for me.  It's misinformation, and the Atelier series has never exactly been fanservice-y.  You can enjoy Atelier Thighza 3 perfectly fine.Once again, I do recommend the game if it sounds interesting to you.  It is a very good, fun, and enjoyable game for its genre and the audience it is made for.  If you don't like the genre and theme and/or are positivity-challenged, obviously I don't recommend it—it isn't made for you.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the previous Ryza games, you know what the basic gameplay is like. Ryza 3 is lacking a bit of polish on release with some awkward translations and some technical issues at the start of the game (turn off the depth of field option). These will most likely be fixed in upcoming patches. In terms of gameplay, Ryza 3 is another step forward for the series. With Link Morph and the secret keys, there's even more customization possible with the alchemy system than ever before. Exploration is smoother than ever in a semi-open world and the map is huge. The entire main map from the first Ryza game is just one of the areas in Ryza 3.The game's story is good as well. I do still feel that the first Ryza game has the best story of the three, but this game's story is solid overall. There were some parts that I didn't feel very invested in (i.e. the Sardonica arc) but the rest was engaging. You get to see the characters grow some more, and now the main cast are all adults. The characters from the previous games get satisfying conclusions to their arcs, and the remaining plot threads are all addressed. The new characters are also likable and get a decent amount of development, though they're not the focus. It does leave me feeling a bit bittersweet because even though I spent 88 hours beating this game, it still feels like it's over a bit too soon. The ending was satisfying, but I would have liked the journey to continue a little longer. I guess that's appropriate though since this is a game about endings.

_childDocuments_.review: A great send-off to the Secret trilogy and to Ryza herself. While there’s certainly things that could have been improved, overall it’s a culmination of everything that made the first two great with brand new things packed in as well. With the current sale for Lunar New Year going on I’d recommend picking it up, moreso if you’ve played the first two (and if you haven’t, they’re also on sale and I have reviews out for them too), but really it’s just a nice finale to the series and something I could see myself coming back to in the future.- : The alchemy has been expanded upon in some ways, but also reduced in others. To start off, all the systems you’ve come to know and love are unlockable from the start, just locked behind a decent chunk of SP in the skill tree. This includes but is not limited to Item Rebuilding, Rebuild Levels, and Item Duplication. Unfortunately the Essences from Ryza 2 do not make a return, but that’s nothing major. Ryza 3 prefers to have you hit the ground running, with a ton of recipes unlocked from the start and not a lot of recipes unlocked by morphing, most of them are unlocked from the skill tree. Honestly I much prefer this method as it essentially means as long as you have the materials. The super traits system is a cool new take on the traits system. Basically, sometimes the materials near a landmark will be special and have a super trait, which can be transferred to your items upon synthesis. These have honestly just an incredible amount of range of what they can do, but they’re very powerful. - : The real-time turn-based combat returns yet again, but this time it’s better than ever. The combat in Ryza 3 essentially expands upon Ryza 2’s system. You’ve got 3 on-fielders and 2 back-liners (up from 1 in Ryza 2 and 0 in Ryza 1), which can swap in at any time after a cooldown.You’ve got the skill chains, action orders, core items (in which they’ve changed the Core Crystal upgrade system to be several upgrades of miscellaneous types instead of just 5 general upgrades), and the new key system, which can be used in battle as well, which I’ll cover in another section because the keys are used in several parts of the game.- : The graphics (and performance) continue to get better with every installment. Not much to say here really, all the environments and models look great, each area really has it’s own theme.- : Ryza 3 is almost definitely the easiest game of the three to ‘break’. The new super traits system as well as almost full freedom very quickly allows you to get overpowered gear and items FAST. Not to mention you can get ‘infinite’ gems and complete the skill tree in record time. The difficulty options are nice to have, but with just a bit of planning I was using like 4 items to bully every enemy and boss even on the hardest difficulty I was able to select.- : Not that bad, honestly. A full playthrough will bring you pretty close to the $1:1 hour ratio that is the ‘goal’, and the missing parts of that are easily made up for with the quality of content in the game. - : The story continues a year after Ryza 2 as a mysterious set of islands have appeared near Kurken Island, so you’d think that the majority of the game would be investigating these islands. Wrong. The archipelago is actually pretty small and you explore the whole area pretty quickly into the game, with only one thing at the end of your look around that leaves you with questions. Ryza and co. then travel through a few areas in search of a single thing. Yeah, one thing, that they aren’t even sure what exactly it is. It feels like they kind of forgot what they were doing in the first place. I will say, however, that the plot itself is pretty good, but it just kind of forgets where it’s going sometimes. There’s a lot of areas left unexplored or even mentioned in the story, which is backed up by some World Quests and Character Quests, which does help fill in the world a bit more. Overall I wouldn’t say it’s a bad story, but again, it really just forgets what the goal is sometimes, and really only gets back to the original plan about two-thirds through.- : Here it is, the title of the game, the Secret Keys. Keys are created via either a Hollow (bad) or Pristine (good) key at landmarks (your fast travel waypoints in this game), and have a randomized set of effects that apply to numerous parts of the game. You can equip certain keys as Symbols to your characters which can provide stat boosts or change their role (which provides a special buff), activate them in the open world to increase gathering quality/quantity or open locked doors to get to chests, use (or create) them mid-battle via Key Modification (or Key Creation), which lets you infinitely combo basic attacks to gain massive amounts of AP to use your skills for a limited item, and most importantly use them during Synthesis to get some extra buffs on your gear. Now this all sounds great, doesn’t it? Well the thing is - I didn’t really use the keys that much. Outside of the story progression, occasional time I ended up in front of a locked door, or some party quests or tricky fights to use keys in battle or synthesis, there wasn’t any time I thought to myself ‘Ah! I should use a key’ Maybe when you play you’ll do something more worthwhile with them but to me it was a bit of a let-down how much the game hyped them up with all the tutorials just for them to not really stand out.- : Overall the completion is pretty easy, but there are a few things that can trip you up, such as manifesting all roles or completing the requests of the sword master brothers. Nothing is missable except maybe for a glitch I heard about, . At the very end of your completion journey there’s just gonna be those few achievements so I recommend using the  to clear up any confusion. - : Honestly, exploration is the biggest downside about the game for me. Ryza 3 is semi-open world (as opposed to segmented open world like the first two), as in you can travel across the entire map without a single loading screen, but the map also isn’t just a giant circle, it’s essentially a bunch of linear paths with a few large open areas every so often. Combine this with the fact that the map is so large, having not only the entirety of the Ryza 1 map, but also 3 entirely new regions (and even a part of Ryza 2’s map in a free DLC), which means they have to spread materials out more, which means that most of the areas you’ll almost never return to save for when there’s a quest objective to go there or you need one material you managed to miss the first time around. The fact that it’s open world also doesn’t help with locating items, as when you try and find it in the in-game guide, it just tells you the landmark it’s closest to, which can be a pretty large area with a few different climates, so I ended up resorting to YouTube or GameFAQs for other people’s documentation of item locations. - : Characters are overall pretty good, and you’ve got a total of 11 party members to pick from, which is absurd. But really the reason this is in cons is kind of just a nitpick, but Clifford and Serri from Ryza 2 are the only characters out of all of Ryza’s companions to not be present in this game, which as a huge Clifford/Serri fan, I find quite offensive.<Section shortened because hitting character limit lol>- : TL;DR Keyboard controls didn’t look bad the few times I accidentally went to them.- : TL;DR Same NG+ system as previous two games, except only 2 new difficulties.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm putting in this review right after clearing the story, rather than after 100%ing the game like I did for the first two. I still plan and aim to 100% the game, don't get me wrong. Getting straight to the point:This game is a much better experience than Ryza 2, in my opinion. There are only a few downsides when comparing, but they are small things like UI features and Synthesis animations. Unlike the earlier games, this one is open-world. The map is absolutely huge, it's bigger than the first and second combined and then some, with the DLC adding in new areas as well. But this won't be reviewing the dlcs. When it comes to the gameplay loop, the story, the visuals, the characters, it's phenomenal. The combat is much faster than the earlier games, you gain AP at a faster pace, which in turn leads to faster combos. Your other characters also earn CC at a reasonable rate while you're not in control of them. This game wraps up the trilogy in a nice bow, finalizing the stories of the new characters as well as the existing characters, storylines that have been ongoing since the first game. When playing the first game, I didn't think it could get better, then I played Ryza 2 and changed my mind. And you know what, it happened again. Atelier Ryza 3 deserves all of the praise it gets. It was a wonderful experience, all in all, with the trilogy landing itself in my list of favorite video game stories.EDIT: As of hitting 54 hours into the game, I have 100%'ed Ryza 3, now making all three of the Atelier Ryza games 100%. Everything I said above, I agree with still. If you've never played the Ryza series and want to jump in, start with 1 for the story, as its still a good experience. If you're on the fence about buying Ryza 3 after playing the others, I highly recommend it as, in my opinion, it's the best game in the Ryza trilogy.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR It's not a bad game, but really disappointing. The core gameplay was enjoyable, but everything else was mediocre. At an eventual deep discount, it's worth playing to finish the trilogy, but if you only play Ryza 1 and stop there, you're not missing much. While visually stunning, the open world was devoid of almost anything interesting in terms of gameplay. It's understandable that returning areas like Kurken Island needed to be patched together, but even in new areas, there were a lot of linear sections. Ryza's movement in the field is also very limited, and there are a lot of invisible walls that have no reason to exist. Why can I only jump down some cliffs or over some fences? Exploration isn't rewarded at all. Chests are always full of garbage, usually a single synthesis ingredient that you can already collect, and not even a high quality one. Reaching the edge of the map just gives you access to more gathering points for the same ingredients (and some nice views). In some cases, I even felt that exploring before progressing the story took away some of the impact. The lore was good, but the story itself was just okay. The minor twist in the ending was pretty obvious. After the writing in Ryza 2 fell short of the first game, I didn't expect the story of this game to be great. The epilogue was nice, though, as I think it neatly wrapped up the arcs of some characters.I do think that there were either too many characters, or not enough. With eleven playable characters already, I don't see why that couldn't have been thirteen to include two playables missing from Ryza 2. But at the same time, some of the characters in this game were just plot devices and did not have to be playable. The localization was also a weak point. I think that a different localization team was employed for this game compared to Ryza 1 and 2, and it shows. It's been a while since I played the previous games in the trilogy, so while I can't really comment on the perception by some that the dialogue felt flat and out-of-character (though it certainly sounded strange at times), I can report that the English translation had enough errors and awkward grammar to the point of being a little distracting.As for the rest of the gameplay, most fights were too easy, even on the highest difficulty available for a first playthrough. I didn't upgrade my equipment as frequently as I could have or employ the new secret key mechanic that often and was still able to mow through every boss fight with ease. I had more issues with random triple battles. Moreover, the story relevant synthesis tasks were really simple (like, five ingredient simple) and almost pointless. The hardest synthesis task in the game was just a sidequest that involved creating purposefully low-quality items. For a third game in a trilogy, I don't think it's wrong to expect more of a challenge.Random quests were fine, but boring. Unlike the first game, or even the second one, there were no interesting NPC storylines that you can follow throughout the game. That was something I liked a lot about Ryza 1 and it's disappointing that it has regressed to this point. You can pet the cats and dogs, if you're into that. And sometimes NPCs will react if you run through them instead of phasing out of existence. So those are two improvements over the previous games.Overall, this game was a decent time waster. The core gameplay loop of gathering and synthesizing still works (and therefore doesn't need to be discussed), but the supporting elements that should exist to differentiate Ryza 3 from a crap-tier freemium gacha game are very weak. Which I suppose makes a lot of sense given what followed it.

_childDocuments_.review: The (as of now) final game in the Secret series, Atelier Ryza 3 is, in every way, an improvement on the previous game. In many ways, it actually makes the past game even better! While the last game felt, at times, a bit pointless, this one feels as the natural conclusion to what came before, focusing on the whole journey since the first game, using and expanding everything that worked on the second game, while also putting the weaker elements plot-wise to the sidelines. This time, I felt the characters felt like the natural evolution of what they were on the first two games, and the new characters are actually better integrated to the overall plot.However, that also means that if you didn't like the previous games, this is probably not for you. The gameplay was improved, but the core of the systems wasn't changed too heavily. Plot also keeps the same general beats and feels. In the end, it's a nice, feel-good game that, at times, feel a bit padded, but overall still a experience I enjoyed. If you liked the previous games, go for it. If you didn't play them, I feel like with this Atelier sub-series in special, it's better to play the previous games first.

_childDocuments_.review: Gust went absolutely all-out for the final game in the Atelier Ryza trilogy. I wasn't a huge fan of the scaling enemies at first, but I understand why they did it, since it's a (mostly) open-world game. I say mostly, because there are multiple regions for you to explore, and you unlock them by advancing the story. Once you reach them, though, you can go pretty much anywhere. On top of that, there are also a ton of party members to choose from.All-in-all, while there's a bit of jank here and there, I'd personally say that this is the best game in the trilogy. Hopefully all of the money they've made from these games and their new gacha will allow Gust to make new (non-gacha) Atelier games in the future. Fortunately, there's a ton of other Ateliers to tide me over until that happens.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not done with the game, necessarily but.. I've seen enough to generally understand how I feel about it. It's an unfortunate departure from the more focused adventure of Ryza 2 and returns to the much more open ended style of Ryza 1.. which I hated, because that lack of focus and drive made it a chore to get through. This series thrives best when there's a clear goal, a carrot on the stick to help the gameplay cycle of craft>explore>gather>fight feel rewarding and paced well. This one is so big and so open ended that, like Ryza 1, there's less direction in what you should be doing and therefore nothing to keep the pace addicting and constant. This issue is compounded by the sheer size of the world, because while it's really cool that the world is so big and all, it's just that much more tedious and difficult to find the materials you want to find. On top of that, 90% of the materials you can gather in every area are the same in EVERY area, so finding the less common stuff is just that much more annoyingly difficult. The world is just needlessly big, and then random quests instead of the godsend quest board that made its return in Ryza 2 just.. sucks ass. It's annoying that every 100 feet you run, a random quest will pop up, prompting you to do it or miss out on rewards, which vary from materials to cole(money) to Skill Points needed to progress the skill tree.WHICH, on that topic, the skill tree manages to be so much worse than in Ryza 2. Like with the gameplay and exploration and pacing, the skill tree manages to be open ended, giving you no direction in what you unlock and what order you choose to do so. The problem here is that a lot of KEY features are literally hidden by tree paths that only reveal themselves after you've purchased a skill, and sometimes they won't even appear until you've purchased rather far into that path. So finding a key feature you want or need becomes a chore in itself, and grinding for SP is much slower this time around as crafting rewards a lot less SP than before, and much more is required to unlock things. I'd like to make the third tier of weapons, but I can't because I haven't unlocked the gold ingot recipe yet. In Ryza 2, you did this by crafting through the first two ingots. Not in this one, now most recipes are locked behind the skill tree or apparently rng nodes? I haven't found those yet. :/The key system too is.. not great. It adds a weird RNG gacha element to the game where you can make keys out of enemies or locations, but what they do is random. I don't know, this game is better than Ryza 1, but is a huge step back from Ryza 2 and Sophie 2...

_childDocuments_.review: is not only the worst game in the trilogy, but it's also the first game I've played from start to finish that I would not consider good (although my sample size is pretty small, so take it with a grain of salt). While there were many features in this game that really improved on the mechanics of the first two games and smoothed out my experience, the actual game is rather mediocre and underwhelming compared to the two that came before it. Since there's not much time to spend on talking about it here, instead I'm just going to give the three big reasons why I think this game was a complete and total downgrade from Ryza 2.First of all, there's the  Now this isn't a huge deal because it doesn't hinder my enjoyment of the game by any means, and I do understand that it can be tough localizing the game into different languages. But it does feel a bit worrisome because it isn't something that should be happening on here, especially for a high-budget game and considering that the other two games didn't have this problem. And a little side note here since it does fall into this category: the interface is the worst it's ever been. I'm referring to the font style/size and how difficult it is to read it all. And I'm not just talking about the dialogue on the side, I mean that the game as a whole has a poor contrast to the light font style they stuck with. It's fine if they use Century Gothic as a main typeface but they can't compromise visibility to save space on the screen and have it such an eyesore to read things.Next, there's the  I'm not talking about the game's story, I mean that Ryza 3 tries to add so much content into the game without finding a way to put them in, that when you actually come across it, they're so confusing and pointless that you can just ignore it and you won't have a problem at all. I don't know if its because they had less time to work on this game based on how high in demand the game was, or maybe they were just being sidetracked on developing Resleraina, but it really does seem like there's way too much of a focus on style over substance in this game. Even though the map is much bigger, there's almost a third of the map that has no purpose in the main story and can be ignored until post-game. There's more pointless features too, like how the chests try to lure you into finding a way to "complete" the game when there really is no reward for it other than useless trash. Or how about puni raising? What about the keys that aren't ultra rare? These features are so complex that it frustrates me when I realize that it's all just crap outside of achievement grinding. They could've put this to use, but no, they didn't put an incentive to them.And last, . Fitting for a protagonist whose main character trait is being ordinary, right? But I digress. And this accounts for everything from the underwhelming and forgettable soundtrack (aside from a few select tracks) to the annoying quests that this game tries to shove into your face to try to divert your attention away from the main plot, until it turns into a massive, jumbled mess. Or how about the fact that the quests they do have are so tedious and unsatisfying? Let's also talk about how the cutscenes are so dull and tedious compared to how they were in Ryza 1 and 2. Not to mention that goats in this game are ubiquitous and yet instead of giving them attention and adding something like, perhaps, letting us pet them or talk to them, or even have a side quest for them, they're just demoted to background objects that make you lament about how much wasted potential they were. I loved the goat quest in Ryza 1, I was hoping they could expand in the third game, but they did nothing. Zilch. And on top of ALL of this, the difficulty is just plain trivial. There's the early game, which is a bit harder than the first two, but after the Cleria region you can easily synthesize your way to the max and destroy everything till the game is over. I tried looking back at the first two games to see if I was just getting more familiar with the mechanics, but nope, those games still had a reasonable difficulty curve unlike this game, which is virtually nonexistent two hours in. For a game that tries to end the trilogy, it just ended up being so boring that it made me regret ever investing my time into this series.All in all, these three things permeated the entire game from the start to the finish, and they became so prominent in the postgame that it becomes more apparent that this is just a downright inferior video game. It's a rather mixed bag, and while I wouldn't say it's terrible, it's too complicated and too research-dependent for me to enjoy the game. That being said I don't want to trash this game entirely, as it does, story-wise, end the franchise on a satisfying note, and there are many signs that it feels like Gust is trying to bring something new and innovative to the table. Like I said earlier, the world map, the key system, the interface changes. Of course, they were subject to various results, but at least I can respect it for what it is. It was a nice experiment, but it did not work well with the game itself. Overall, this game is a  UNLESS you're devoted to completing the trilogy or UNLESS you want to complete the RNG-dependent achievements of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, not the best out of the trilogy of Atelier Ryza games. Can't speak when comparing it to other games from the Atelier series, but it still isn't a bad game.My major complaint is that the developers still haven't fixed the glaring RPG issues from the previous two titles, and that was useless treasure and a useless economy system with Cole and the shops. One of the main staples of an RPG is to collect whatever passes for currency/ies in that game, and trade them in for better equipment or consumable items that are USEFUL to the player. With the shops selling subpar items, the only thing that was even worth buying were the collectible decorations you can buy. That's it. As for the treasure chests, the quality of the ingredients given were so low that it made searching for the treasure chests pointless, even in late game areas. These chests didn't even have scaling quality based on how far in the game you encountered them. It'd be like if you played any JRPG and found a bronze sword (usually the first type of weapon seen) in a chest in the end game dungeon. It was insulting to say the least. Especially since several chests were unobtainable until you've progressed far enough into the story, just to get an item from a chest that were worse than things you found literally the moment you started the game.Despite the huge complaint I just made, the rest of the game was fairly well done. Yes, the difficulty is quite low, even on the highest difficulty setting, but that is to be expected from this type of game that focuses less on the combat and more on the story. Great soundtracks, great story progression that felt like it wrapped the series up well, and great voice acting. Some of the new game mechanics were quite tedious or useless, but still unique and interesting all the same.Overall, I'd barely give this game a passing grade of a 6/10. Good game to waste some time with and have fun. But not necessarily worth putting much time into or getting serious over. Definitely better as a relax and chill sort of game. If in the future the developers fix some of the issues I've listed here, then I might update this review to reflect this, as I'm sure that there will DLC and content adjustments coming out in the near future.

Problems with lip movement matching, or characters getting stuck steps or not climbing ladders happened frequently enough to be noticed, but not to be that bothersome.The new characters are really cool and the returning characters are great. The character quests give a little more interaction between the party and Ryza herself, and the World Quests changing the World itself is actually really nice.All in all, fantastic game, though it is a little expensive, especially if you also consider the DLC. _childDocuments_.review: Probably the best of the Ryza trilogy, and quite possibly the best Atelier game.  Pretty much everything they execute on is a home run.  Fun new characters?  Check.  Cool new locations?  Massive interconnected maps to gather and battle through?  Check!  The only thing I wasn't 100% on was the story.  While it wasn't bad by any means, I think the names they gave some stuff and jargon associated with a lot of these terms was a bit too wordy.  Luckily they have a glossary to help out with this.I also love how cinematic they've made going in and out of battles.  The opening segment in this game is probably the most unique and fun to an atelier game period.  Everything in general LOOKS amazing, too.  If I remember correctly, Sophie 2 was a big upgrade from Ryza 2, but this was an even bigger step up from that!  I think my favorite little aspect of this game was how expressive some of these characters got.  The facial expressions are incredible!  And finally, this game does a really good job at wrapping up Ryza's story, bringing in characters and plot points from previous games to culminate in the ultimate end to our honest alchemist's tale.  If you haven't played these games before, I highly suggest you start.  Ryza 1 is the perfect place to start.  And this is the perfect way this series ends up!

_childDocuments_.review: I really love Atelier Ryza 1 and 2. The second built on the lore of the first game and even gave NPCs voice lines. It made alchemy 1000 times easier with the skill tree system. However, in Ryza 3, the plot seems rushed. It doesn't explain the history behind whatever ancient civilization they were exploring long enough until the end of the game. Also, it feels that Ryza 3 heavily relies on the past 2 games to make itself good especially since it keeps mentioning them all the time.They opened this world map system where I had trouble getting to certain places due to the fact the entire map doesn't show. The mini map system if I remember in the old games showed the entire map each time so it was easy to navigate.Even the exploration items had very little use aside from the farming tools. The Air Drop was only used in the beginning of this game as well as the swinging band thing. I opened All Crystal Connection and didn't see a single red/yellow crystal so what was the point of that?Finally, the characters while it's easy to tell their personalities, I didn't get to know enough about them. I really liked the fact that for the characters stories in Ryza 2, they go into depth of the relationships between them and Ryza. It's enough to make a small story about them for the game. For example, Klaudia misses Ryza in the 2nd game a lot, and they mention it and it gets fixed. I won't explain how in case of spoilers. But in Ryza 3, there's only short interactions between Klaudia and the other characters. It's around like 2 minutes of conversation each time.  They're still good but I like Ryza 2 more.tldr: plot holes, relies on past 2 games too much instead of being original, waste of making good exploration items, lack of character relationships but still good character stories, and play Ryza 1 and 2 and skip 3

_childDocuments_.review: If you really enjoyed Ryza 1 and 2, most of the *core* gameplay is still the same or better. I am not reccomending this game, because everything around the core gameplay, is absolutely terrible. My play sessions last only 30 min or less because I keep getting so frustrated and hopping off to take a break.The movement feels absolutely terrible. If you have sprint on, you will constantly overshoot gathering nodes, if you have sprint off, you walk at a literal snail's pace. Also, no consistency between Ryza doing a sliding stop when you let go of the movement stick, or properly just full stopping. Even worse than that, however, is the UI. This could be one of the worst UI/UX experiences I have had in a modern game. In an effort to minimalize the UI as much as possible, it is near impossible to find any of the information you are looking for. Everything is super tiny font, pushed to the far edges of the screen, and goes away almost immediately. The "area map" requires 3 button presses to access(very slow btw), and even when you get to it, it is obfuscated until you find some random ass landmark in the area. Absolutely EVERYTHING that isn't the core gameplay (alchemy system, combat) is significantly worse than previous titles.

_childDocuments_.review: More Ryza, just what I neededI feel like the game needed more dev time, there's many small things which could have been fixed with just a few months more: typos or grammatical errors in the english TL, cutscenes staying locked on one animation for longer than they should, parts where they could have put a bit more love into it (for example, opening the Door for the first time on the Islands, there's no animation or anything?), and just overall jankyness with animations, movement, UI, etcThe open world, while being a nice change from the previous games, brings with it a lot of oddities as well - sometimes you're stopped by an invisible wall when it should be fine to jump off, objects appearing only when close to them, dolphins just disappearing when swimming into shore on themIn general though it was enjoyable, I never felt like I was facing an impossible enemy, was relatively chill and the callbacks to Ryza 1 and 2 were cuteSummer's finally ended.

_childDocuments_.review: PEAK RYZAProbably the by far the biggest budget release in all Atelier series. Content is rich, there's short story/event everywhere. There's full motion capture in some cut-scenes (which I don't remember seeing in any of the previous games?).The inclusion of Ryza 1's full map into the game is really nice, you can have a nostalgia trip without going back to Ryza 1. You can feel the love for the series from the development team.Gameplay wise, I can see a lot of quality of life improvements right away, for example, pick up ingredients . Synthesis process become more complex but also more flexible. Battle is as smooth as ever. The newly introduced key chain feature can be overwhelming at the beginning, but it become very useful once you know what you're doing.The only complain I have:The level required for monster to start running away from you is extremely high. It gets very annoying when you're trying to explore the map but constantly being chased by monsters.Overall:One of the best in the atelier series, I can't decide if I like Sophie 2 or this one more, they're both great in their own way.

_childDocuments_.review: Barrel!This game makes me wish there was a "Mixed" review option.The final game in the Ryza series, R3 certainly improved every aspect of the gameplay and visual department; that much is for sure. I can only hope future Atelier games are on this engine because it is incredible! Every second I spent playing was a second I enjoyed, and as someone who's played quite a few Atelier games, every little QoL change (picking up items while moving, cleaner movement, sneaky loading screens that trick you into thinking there's none) would blow my mind ever time I saw them!Although I have my personal gripes towards the character designs for the Ryza games, specifically of the female cast, I still enjoyed their characters and thought they were lovely. But then we come to the crux of the matter, and why I wish I could give a mixed review as, for me at least, it's a deal breaker. The English localization... Kinda blows. You can at least tell it wasn't just machine translated, but it feels like they needed one or two more Quality Checks before release. All the dialogue is readable, sure... but it all just feels . People say things in ways no sane human being would ever say, and it's hard to not notice every little oddity in the dialogue. It just baffles me, since Ryza 1&2 had incredible English localizations! And it really sucks because it's such a glaring issue in what is arguably the best playing Atelier game to date. If you see this and want to give a try, give it the ol' Steam 1.9hr Shuffle.Plus, story wise, you do need to play the last two games for any context.

Gather this and come back. Defeat this monster and come back. Nothing that makes it interesting like explore the secrets of this dungeon for example.Alchemy:The mechanic is good. It's fun at the start but it takes too long to do alchemy in my opinion. It get's boring at some point and it takes this way too long to unlock your skill tree or create good equipment.Fighting:They give you new mechanics for battle every few levels to make an attempt to keep it fresh.But the problem is that the base of battle keeps the same and too repetitive. No camera freedom and it is more a cutscene that is shown over and over again.Also the further you come in the game the longer the battles become and you can't wash the repetitive things clean with adding more repetitive mechanics that makes it feel even a longer fight.It made me at some point avoid fighting instead of collecting materials that way.Conclusion:Story is fun music is good. The background is insanely blurry and doesn't run well. Even if the technical issues are fixed the battles are just bad. I can handle action games, I've played all the souls games, but combining the dissociating nature of JRPG battles with frantic battles that prevent tactical game-play results in the worst of both worlds.The boring combat of older Atelier games was acceptable because the crafting was the focus of the games. The formerly bland fighting of the pre-Ryza games is now made bafflingly irritating as party members do whatever they want and the tactical skill choices is replaced with undefined icons. The only new feature I actually like, the active defense, was ruined when monsters started attacking from off-screen. I've played Atelier games since the first Atelier Iris, but if they continue like this I won't be playing any more.
