_childDocuments_.review: The best of the Ryza series mechanically, but certainly suffers from a few things. Some people enjoy sequence breaking in the Atelier series, but Ryza 3 takes that to a whole new extreme with the open world, where you can easily get things like endgame traits before even finishing the second story boss, and have gear that is 90% of the way to perfect before that point too. The balance between gameplay and story is also shot to hell too, as you aren't really so much alternating between stories and alchemy, due to how there's not really a loop of that in the same way as previous Atelier games. Also open world syndrome,  with vast areas being totally underutilised, and repetitive random quests, aswell as useless treasure chests spattered all over. Hopefully in games going forwards, if they choose to retain the open world, it will be reduced in scope and increased in depth. Ultimately still plenty of fun for anyone who loves the series though. It has everything you'd expect, and is by a landslide the best of the Ryza games in terms of combat and alchemy, even if it lacks things like the alchemy notebook that was present in Sophie 2, using Ryza 2's SP system instead. Feels like a fitting conclusion to the Secret arc too. Wouldn't mind if they kept some connections going forward though, even if it was just making reference to the games being in a shared world or such, and maybe having a character or two pop up purely as a small sidequest rather than being an important party NPC in future games. Kind of like Logy in Mysterious.

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be described as quantity over quality. It's still a good game, but definitely feels like a downgrade compared to Atelier Sophie 2 across all aspects.Ryza 3 does keep all aspects of the two previous games, so if you liked Ryza 1 and 2, you will mostly like Ryza 3 too because it basically inherits everything while also adding a few new mechanics, but overall it's more of the same.The maps are huge in this game and looks amazing in the beginning, but I think it actually made the exploration experience way worse after playing for a while because the maps feel very empty with a bunch of useless items scattered around. Not only that, but the enemy variety is really low and their position in the map is very weird where there are multiple group of the same repeated enemies very close to each other. Treasure chests are also really bad in this game, giving useless items and don't feel rewarding to make the effort to fully explore the big maps.UI is also worse than the previous games. Everything look way more simple and bland, and some useful stuff was even removed in this game, like the indicator of which tool Ryza is currently equipped for exploring. It also doesn't include many QoL additions seen in Sophie 2, like the map overlay when exploring.The story was very uninteresting in my opinion and I had a hard time reading all text and felt like skipping most dialogue. It didn't feel immersive and nothing really happens. Maybe because it's the third game with the same characters and the same world and they didn't have anything else to develop for these set of characters other than an excuse to reunite all of them again, but the most critical part is how the main quest story progress goes. In this game I felt that basically all story missions were just going to a certain location on the map to watch some dialogue and then repeat again for the next mission. There was almost no main missions requiring to make a new complex item from a recipe or defeat some difficult enemy. The alchemy and combat quests were left to some random NPC side quests that appear on the map and are pretty much useless quests that can be completed in a minute. It feels like Ryza 3 doesn't give the player the motivation or the challenge to get stronger and to develop new alchemy items. It also doesn't give the player the motivation or reason to explore all areas of the map. It's totally possible to beat the game without exploring even half of the total map of the game because there are no missions requiring the player to go to those places. You can go to those places, of course, and discover new scenes and items, but it's all side content.Combat is pretty much the same as the previous games, which I'm not a big fan. I think the combat feels slow, lacks depth since it's mostly button mashing without strategy and the enemies are spongy. Being ATB combat also means that you don't have full control of the entire party, leaving the companions to the CPU, which is not ideal. I think this new Ryza combat system fails the item and resource management aspect that make Atelier games fun.Same goes for alchemy. It doesn't feel rewarding. Everything is incredibly easy and the traits don't feel that useful compared to other Atelier games. I also think the new progressing system in this game was poorly implemented, giving really low amount of SP given to unlock new recipes and locking many new item recipes behind the discovery of a certain item and not giving a single hint of where it is until the player discovers it for the first time. In many times, I felt this enters an infinite loop requiring the player to search info on the internet. For example, when you need to make something and you don't have the required item to make it, it's blacked out and doesn't give you any info on where that can be to gather it, then you discover that item's location which is locked because you have to upgrade your gathering tools, and then the item to upgrade the gathering tool is a recipe from the skill tree, which you have no idea where in the skill tree it is, just to find after you have already spent all your SP into other skills that don't lead to that recipe. It's not natural progression like in the other Atelier games where you unlocked stuff by following instructions from a guide book with clear objectives and collected items that are connected to the main quests.The graphics have been improved and some animations too. It still looks outdated compared to most anime games these days, but the artwork is done so well that it doesn't really matter. The PC Port is also excellent and runs at maximum settings 1440p@60fps very stable on a RTX 2060 Super. Zero issues, no crashes, no bugs, no glitches.I'm a big fan of the Atelier and have played all games since Atelier Rorona. But unfortunately I did not like the Ryza series. I wasn't a big fan of the first two Ryza games too, so I think it's my own fault for forcing myself to keep playing the third game of the trilogy that I did not even like.I think this game is a complete downgrade over the older Atelier games and Sophie 2. Not a big fan of the new ATB combat system and alchemy system, the storyline and soundtrack are also really weak compared to the other trilogies. Ryza 3 made things even worse by delivering a huge but empty map which made exploration feel like a chore and less rewarding. The progression system feels disconnected from the main story missions which by the way are basically go to certain location to talk to someone, leaving alchemy and unlocking new content to side and optional quests.I really love the Atelier series and I hope Gust keeps making traditional Atelier games like Sophie 2.It saddens me to give a negative review for an Atelier game, but nothing about the Ryza trilogy really clicked with me. I'm glad it has finally ended after 3 games with the same protagonist opening a path for a brand new game that goes back to the series roots, but the thighs success really worries me that they will follow the Ryza combat/exploration formula in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Skip to the end for my thoughts on Ryza 3 itself, but first, just want to get something off my chest regarding the current state of JRPGs and the willingness to include what ESRB terms "suggestive themes" in console games nowadays.I was a Nintendo gamer since the N64 when I was a kid. My tastes in games were influenced by it and carried on since then. I saw an article about “Operation Rainfall” when I was checking up on The Legend of Zelda Skyward Sword on IGN back in 2011, and noticed a game Nintendo made called Xenoblade Chronicles. After playing it in 2012, I was hooked on JRPGs, and didn’t realize until then that they offered the experiences that appeal to teenagers and young adults, but in video game form.So I’ve already written this in my review of Blue Reflection: Second Light, but I’ll write it again: JRPGs are the best at capturing the feeling of Young Adult novels and giving a well rounded entertainment experience for that same feeling. I’ve played many of Gust’s games since the Nintendo Switch generation, taking notice that Nintendo was making efforts to finally offer console quality JRPGs to its audience and to promote them along with third party JRPGs. I’ve noticed an evolution in Gust’s quality since then too.For the Ryza series in particular, I noticed something else, something that boosted its popularity. Her character design and attire. I do think there is a critical moment going on with JRPGs and their appeal. I see it with Sony’s attempts to stifle it, and zealots on Twitter and in game journalism analyzing, scrutinizing, and harassing games and anime that display the “suggestive themes” dimensions of entertainment and the human experience.This is strange to me, because other forms of entertainment do not have this issue. Go watch something like “The Summer I Turned Pretty” for an example of a popular young adult show, for instance. Go to Youtube, Twitch, TikTok, TV shows like The Bachelor/Bachelorette, music videos and performances,hell, social media in general, or real life, and people are enthusiastically using visual mediums to flex their muscles, to show their stuff, to show their skin in style, to relish in that dimension of the human experience.So what does that have to do with Ryza 3? This game hints, compared to previous entries, that JRPG developers are unsure of whether they should continue embracing content that celebrates the “suggestive themes” dimension of entertainment. I even saw it with Xenoblade Chronicles 3 too. So those two games do have suggestive themes in some form, but they use creative ways to also “tone themselves down” as if that were necessary. Stuff like “black leggings” or in Ryza 3’s case, giant ribbons or elongated capes, to hide certain parts of the human body. Outfits that are “less risqué” (). Or even, spray painting black paint on body parts, even in DLC costumes. I see it with Forspoken and Final Fantasy XVI, where instead of being leaders in providing the T-Rated experience and rounding out the entertainment offering on Playstation like they used to, Square Enix is instead following a checklist of things to try to conform to the "new" flavor of Playstation, those games instead go “M Rated HBO Show” and have no "fun" suggestive themes to speak of.I do think Sony Interactive has something to do with it. Some games actually get modified for Playstation only and release complete on PC and Switch. I have to think that Sony also coerced Square Enix to conform to their flavor of entertainment, which does away with suggestive themes and leaves only bloody violence and hardcore “mature” sex and no fun or cuteness. And I think that Japanese developers broadly are at a point where they’re wondering if they should conform too, or if it’s safe to create entertainment like they want.Here’s what I think: conforming to Sony Interactive’s style/flavor/brand of entertainment is misguided and could lead to many people losing interest or enthusiasm in video games as an entertainment medium. Or, it could be a severe opportunity lost. With Western developers conforming around certain styles, flavors, “HBO mature show”, there should be an opportunity for Japanese games to lead in providing what’s missing. The ones who made it this far after the turmoil of companies shutting down or collapsing have every reason to continue producing things their unique way. They should recognize that the human experience includes “suggestive themes” and entertainment in other mediums still embraces that. If video games don’t provide it, people are one click away from other mediums that do. I think it's an important point for Gust games too, whose brand is to create anime styled T rated games. They should not be conforming to Sony’s misguided neutering of suggestive themes or Twitter zealots and their harassment or twisted logic that only allows Baldur’s Gate 3’s sexuality to be Okay but not the "Japanese" kind (but in fairness to Baldur's Gate 3 it is a breath of fresh air because it has that quirkiness that others in the West refuse to make but it’s too hardcore for my tastes (BEAR?!?!?!)).Japanese game developers should be leaders in providing the T-rated, young adult content in all its dimensions. Despite all that I wrote though, I do appreciate that the suggestive themes aren't gone altogether in console JRPGs (in fact, in Ryza 3 the romance part of it is even more direct than before for certain couples), and I recognize that when it comes to the attire of female characters  or the use of sexuality in gameplay that they are just trying to carefully navigate what may be a social trend, however much I disagree that it's a broad trend in the tastes of potential customers rather than over-zealous people on social media looking for something to ridicule for virtue signaling. Oh yeah, as for the Ryza 3 game itself, it’s very fun and I found myself more engaged to the crafting than before. In previous games I was able to half-ass it but in this one I had to plan and think out traits and quality. There's also an inventive new mechanic called recipe morph. For instance, turning a fire bomb into an ice bomb. It has several large, open maps despite the advertising/trailer making it look like the “Kark Isles” were going to be the only open world area. Seriously, it’s a grand, world hopping adventure with a large cast of fun characters, and even takes some ideas from AAA games such as random quests out in the world. I know the quality of the games themselves are going to increase from here on, no mistake about that. But that flavor, the "suggestive themes", the honest display of the young adult experience, I really hope that "suggestive themes" don't get neutered even more, and I am holding my breath to see if Persona 6 conforms to the current flavor of what is "appropriate for Playstation" like I suspect Final Fantasy XVI did. But for the time being, that is all, Ryza 3 is a very high quality JRPG that has caught up to others and even surpasses some with color, charm, and multiple maps fun to explore.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Where to start. I cant stop praising Gust for continuing to make the series at such a high level of quality and evolving in iterative sequels while holding onto the core of what people like. Ryza tranistioned Atelier to a more traditional JRPG fairly ok, but in Ryza 2 they found the perfect blend of new more standard JRPG fare and Atelier slice-of-life goodness. Ryza 3 goes a bit more towards the big JRPG, and feels like an attempt to make Atelier AAA, so to speak. There's tremendous polish in things like the animations or how you tranisition into battles that take place on the actual spot you encounter the enemy and fade back into exploration instantly. The flow of combat is now insanely satifying, think Ryza 2's system on crack. They Key system is a fun addition and it has infinite uses to tie it into every aspect of the game. You can use them for combat, exploration and synthesis, so every player has a reason to interact with it, and every part of the loop feels more tied together. I also can't believe how big the map is. It seems like its about Ryza 2 size at first + a new Emerged Island area that feels Breath of The Wildy, then a couple hours in, bam, THERES AN ENTIRE SECOND MAP with it's own central city like Baird from Ryza 2. My only criticism is that it feels too wide and too shallow in those regards. I think game devs in general should focus in packing space more densely with content and making the cities and town feel lived in. With memorable small time npcs that feel like more than just repeated window dressing. (Ryza 2 had a few that felt like the named small npcs in early Trails Games) It feels like too much space nobody asked for that doesnt have enough interesting things about it at least so far. Ryza 2's map was enough guys, make cooler smallerm places, no need to go this overboard. Still, as always the evolution of Atelier continues to be a nice sight to behold. I hope the next one is more chill, more slice of lifey and while I have nothing against cool open spaces to explore, scaling things down and making them more dense and rich instead of just bigger could be nice.That's my only criticism and it's not just of Ryza 3, but modern AAA games in general, which Ryza 3 feels like its trying to reach for. The polish is appreciated, no need for giant spaces and busywork, that's the part of AAA I dont wat Gust imitating.Everything else is awesome so far. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key...So, this is the end? Well, yes, it ends, but...Let's explore the ups and downs of the game (+, +/-, -, ?):+ The AR formula works perfectly here (gathering, synth, gems...)+ The OST is once again great!+ There's some outstanding character development in the game*. I especially love how Bos and Lent get to shine in the story.+ I got to see  again.+ The gameplay is satisfying.+ Lila is still the coolest badass character. I need more of her. 3 games and her boobs were never discussed. Love that! For real, I really like how appearances are never a topic and no one is made fun of based on their looks.+ I love the atmosphere of these games, and this game makes me feel really relaxed.+/- I have no idea how I feel about the story. I guess it exists.**+/- This is the easiest game in the series. There's no challenge. Is it bad thou? Maybe not?+/- I know I need more Serri, but none of Clifford. Got neither.+/- The locations are beautiful, but most of them are meaningless to the story.-* 2/3 new characters are really boring and meaningless. Federica and Dian seem important, but are mostly meaningless. The same kinda goes with Kala, but at least she has an interesting personality, and she can provide some insight to the history of the world.- The chest rewards are useless 99% of the time.- You like side-quest? Well, there are bunch of random ones just popping up whenever you move locations. Most of them are for nothing, and the rewards are usually bad and not worth the effort. This is really annoying to a person like me who "has to complete a side-quest whenever possible".- Oh Tao, and other characters I never use, I guess, you're here? -**I had pretty high hopes about the  mystery, but it ended up being almost nothing.-- The key system is terrible. There's almost no reason to waste time early in the game, and later, it doesn't really matter. AND IT'S THE MAIN THING HERE! I loathe this system that blocks the natural exploration and reward gameplay.? The board system isn't bad, but what do I do with the remaining SP I keep getting...?? I hit the max level when I was about 60% done with the game...? The graphics glitz out every now and then.AR 3 is the weakest in the series, and I feel this game was supposed to be a grande finale, but it ended up being "just a game". I did like my time with these characters in this beautiful world, but there was a lot of "things just happen/exist" here too. It's still satisfying, but as a stand alone title, it's not much. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Ryza 1 & 2, you'll most likely still get enough enjoyment out of 3 for me to recommend it. However, if I were to describe my impressions of Ryza 3, the first expressions that come to my mind are something like "quantity > quality", "meaningless bloat" and "spread too thin". In this review I'll focus only on the negative stuff.I've only played 4 Atelier games so far: Sophie 1 and the Ryza trilogy, with Ryza 2 being by far my favorite and the only entry which I felt got the Atelier formula and gameplay loop down perfectly for me. Compared to that, I think Ryza 3 is a big stepdown and is easily my least favorite Atelier I've played up to this point. It is the first entry that I got so burnt out on that I started skipping all of the side content just to get to the ending as soon as possible out of fear of losing my interest completely and dropping the game.The biggest elephant in the room is the open world. At first I thought that this might be an interesting experiment as open world and exploration fits pretty well with the gathering style RPGs that Atelier games are. The idea looked promising. The execution is beyond terrible. Exploration is a pointless waste of time you shouldn't even bother with. You get access to pretty much all of every region's gatherable ingredients right at its start so no matter which nook and cranny you explore, you'll never find a new one. Treasure chests are a joke, I've found and opened 100+ of them and haven't found a single one that was worth more than the 3 seconds you've spent opening it. And that's pretty much it. The world may look really nice, sure, but the same gatherables over and over and pointless chests are the only thing you'll ever find there. Oh and also randomly generated MMO quests with the same types of rewards over and over. And randomly generated drop points of loot. Randomly generated loot with random properties. Opened by randomly generated keys, again, with random properties. There's also some stuff about building your own Ateliers, but that's only at several predetermined locations. And the choice there is just between 3 different buffs. Later you get to upgrade them, but that's just something you do all at once whenever you unlock this feature and doesn't involve any choice, just adds more buffs and like 2 extra rooms to the building. Again, cool idea, but the execution is as deep as a puddle.The key system is a new gameplay system that affects crafting, character customization, combat and "exploration". Never really got into it, most likely because of the fact that it's completely RNG based when rolling individual keys and their properties. I don't think this kind of system belongs in a game like Atelier and I hope it was just a one off experiment.Outside of gameplay, my impressions of the story elements also aren't entirely positive. I'd say the main plot has an interesting enough idea as far as Atelier main plots I've seen so far go (which to be honest is not a high bar but this is not the focus of the series). I think Ryza 3 does only a "good enough" job when it comes to setting up the slightly melancholic atmosphere of a "final adventure". When I look at Gust's Blue Reflection series or even the previous Ryza games, I'd hope for a bit more than a passing grade for the final entry of the trilogy full of farewells, since I consider Gust to be masters in the melancholy department. But maybe they just wanted to keep the ending upbeat instead of leaning too far into sad or bittersweet. I guess that's what Blue Reflection is for, so I'll give them a pass on that one.But much like the open world, I also felt burned out by the characters quite a bit. Most of their arcs are complete after previous entries and I feel that the game is too obssesed with this idea of showing "how far they've come", "how mature they are" and "look at these kids all grown up after 3 games". To the point where most of the dialogue is just characters mentioning this, along with generally being nice, affirming each other over and over and over and showing their "competency" with very little character conflicts and developments. A lot of the lines start feeling like unnecessary bloat and you really wouldn't miss anything if you skipped 70 % of them. It often reminded me of the same problems some of the games from the Trails series have when too many characters get together at the end of every arc and just clutter the dialogues with pointless affirmation.TLDR: If you liked Ryza 1 & 2 a lot, I think you'll still enjoy 3. But you should take care not to do unnecessary stuff you don't find interesting as it is much easier to burn out on this one. It does just a good enough job to close the final chapter, but I'm definitely more than ready to move on from the Ryza trilogy and start at a new beginning with a completely new cast, world and mechanics (well other than the mobile gacha unfortunately).

_childDocuments_.review: Following up from one of the more impressive entries in the series (even if the alchemy itself was very weak)...This game unexpectedly felt like a marriage between the first ryza (what it did well/its atmosphere, for that matter) and atelier firis, the 18th game. All in all I think it falls a little short of the enjoyment and streamlined nature of Ryza 2 but I liked it a ton. The primary con is that this game is absurdly grindy, whether you start abusive alchemy loops early on or not. With the whole island from the first game available to explore, there is just so much miscellaneous stuff to do (largely fetch quests, I'll admit). You will probably enjoy the game a great deal more by sidelining this optional flavour content.As far as pluses, this game has an insane amount of voiced content, impressively so. The only notable things that aren't voiced are the landmark cutscenes and the DLC. The soundtrack keeps to the standard of the second game and the combat remains a bit more involved than the first game. The openness was *EXTREMELY* unexpected since Firis did not seem to go over well with the core fanbase or for new players (though it is my favourite to this day). I am pretty happy they decided to resurrect a lot of that open roaming at a whim. I'll emphasize this doesn't feel like "x game but with an open world", it feels a great deal like Firis specifically. With that also comes pretty obtuse recipe discovery, but eh. In terms of plot and worldbuilding, this game ties up an amazing amount of plot threads from the prior games (particularly 2) that tend to be forgotten a bit in previous trilogies. I was impressed when three loose plot threads came to mind about 12 hours in and they were all addressed within an hour, lol. And not just as throwaway lines (Clifford and Serri were certainly abandoned from the plot at large, but ah well. We know what they're doing still I suppose).The first game is pretty reasonably clearable (to platinum completion, all optional content, staring at every piece of scenery possible) in like 30 hours. It is remarkably short and they still failed to voice nearly everything except the core scenario. It set up an alchemy system that is very approachable but also probably my least favourite since...mana khemia. All three games are roughly in keeping with this, and oddly 2 and 3 introduce some very simple ways to break the game wide open very early with alchemy mechanics. I think Ryza 1 was an extremely rushed project that only got ~40% of the way through properly before they crammed to get the product out. This game feels like what they were aiming for but a lot more polished, particularly all the kurken island and character content. Slap onto this landmarks, extreme openness with what areas are available instead of feeding one after another very gradually through the main story, 5 trillion side quests, and dozens of hours of filler followed by a dozen hours of honestly compelling character/lore interactions, and it is 10x better of a game. Things that hold it back from 2 IMO are:- Streamlining: The game is padded with a comical amount of fetch quests, grinding, collectathons, scattered cutscenes that lead nowhere (and plenty that do lead somewhere, but they tend to be back-loaded), and extraneous new features. Ryza 2 is a pretty damned perfect balance of polishing its haggard predecessor and introducing fun new content and mechanics without wasting your time everywhere. By the time the fatigue sets in everything is well on its way and I liked the flow better than most of the games since the PS3 gen started. I can't speak for how Ryza 3 feels while ignoring all this content and playing it straight through the main story, but I imagine that's the ideal way to experience it and it would stack up favourably with 2. - Scaling: I like to meticulously tune myself to the game's difficulty scaling so I don't roll over everything with a cheese bomb early. This game has a bit of an issue with their being nice FOE-ish encounters early (which I always welcome) but towards the mid-lategame everything feels very weak and at best just spongy. It's obviously the common compromise we see with open world games that want everything available at a given time to also be approachable, but that's a pretty tall ask when you unleash the entire map in like 4 chunks. - Environments: Ryza 1 has some pretty neat new locations opening up and there's anticipation for what each new area will look like. The final field is awesome. Ryza 2 has exceedingly colourful dungeons that remind me a bit of Lydie & Suelle (granted a lot of that colour is having a token ice dungeon, token volcano dungeon, etc. zelda style). This game...has plenty of forests. Mines. Rivers. Thinking back, I was pretty letdown by the uniformity of it all. Realism isn't really a plus in a fantasy world...Every time I saw huge swaths of fog on the world map I was expecting something grand and fantastical but it was usually just another forest or mine, lol. It's not egregious but it is one factor that weighs down all the optional world content. The underworld is awesome in this game as in the last two, so they certainly did well with that. - Character Designs: It's toridamono again. They're just Azur Lane characters. It's jarring and off-putting but everything else about the series stays pretty intact thankfully. In contrast to the plain atmosphere transitions between fields, the music changes were great...it is customary for this series to have music design that far outpaces the actual atmosphere. I just wish the fields better conveyed what they intended. TLDRThe game is bloated which is a minor downgrade from Ryza 2, but it is still amazing. I almost wish this game sucked instead of Ryza 1 so it was easier to introduce the series to people. As it stands I would encourage people to skip ryza 1 in whatever capacity possible, whether by reading a synopsis, throwing a Let's Play on in the background, and jumping straight into Ryza 2 to get a good, accurate gauge of the series as a whole. Beyond that, I imagine Ryza 3 is as polarizing as Firis with its open world qualities, though this inclusion is plagued with more problems/tedium than when it appeared in Firis IMO. If you've played through 2 and you enjoyed it then 100% play this game, ideally rushing through story and character content. If you haven't started the Ryzas at all, see above and please don't think too harshly of the series. Ryza 1 is the biggest disappointment I've experienced with the series in a decade and 2+3 address the issues there very cleanly (besides character designs). The alchemy system is definitely on the weaker side but still an alright indicator of how it will feel in earlier games. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: I have 100% completions in 1 and 2, 3 was too much of a chore to get everything.There's a bit too much RNG involved with the side quests, whereas in 1 and 2 they were guaranteed to spawn, in 3 you have some really random RNG requirements to clear side quests for spawns.  The spawns have rare spawn rates which you need to use keys to increase upon, and thus you have to farm keys.  To farm keys you have to farm jewels, to farm jewels you have to farm overpowered crafted items.I was able to craft overpowered weapons about 10 hours into the game that I basically kept for the remainder.  Bosses and monsters are very easy, the only limit is how long it takes to get across the map and traversal is very tedious and slow.  There are a few jump-sequences required and the platforming in this game is just plain awful.  The UI also has some weird inconsistencies, (the forums have lots of complaints about this).  I'm running this off a nvme SSD, RTX 3090, 5900x, and loading the map takes a decent amount of time for whatever reason.The good: crafting is great, Ryza is back, very large world to explore.The bad: much more of a grind compared to previous titles.  If you like grinding side quests (fetch 10 of this... etc)., you'll enjoy the side quests and side stories.  Feels artificially long due to distances between quest markers.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I liked Ryza 3 and would recommend it to anyone who's played Ryza 1 and 2, though I don't think it's as strong as an ending as I was hoping for.Now let's do this in Pros/Cons format to better organize my thoughts:PROS:+ Crafting system returns from the previous games and is just as fun to break as it's always been.+ Combat is quick and has been slightly tweaked since Ryza 2 to make it just a bit more intuitive.+ The world is gorgeous to both look at and explore. It's not exactly "open world" but it's open enough and with 4 different explorable regions, you'll never get bored of the scenery.+ The returning characters get to conclude their character arcs and we get some good payoffs.CONS:- I do think the ending goes on just a tad too long. It's mostly go from point A to point B and then back to the Atelier to synth a new key item, then repeat the process.- The newer characters are fun...but they aren't very well developed. Which to be fair, they're competing against characters we've known for 3 games now.- Recipe Morph is almost non-existent in this one. Very few items can be created through Recipe Morphing so it's much harder to rebuild late game items.

_childDocuments_.review: ONLY RECOMMEND TO PEOPLE WHO WOULD PUT GAME STORY OVER GAMEPLAY.ONLY RECOMMEND TO PEOPLE WHO ALREADY PLAY RYZA 1 AND 2.This game's value is significantly lowered for people ignorance of the story hand have no connection with the world, the character and the story of the two previous games, even though there is story recap, it's no where near experience their story by yourself.The game really invested in invoking nostalgia feeling so the previous two game is a must, else it will quickly feel tedious because they stopped the game for a cutscene and start talking about something you have no connection with, especially when you explore regions appeared in the first game. There is also small mentions/ appearances of characters in second game, what would make you jump 'OMG it's <insert character name>' are completely voided otherwise.The story is about a group of rebellious kids grow up to be dependable adults, sometimes it can give player feeling of jealousy of what they achieved, but if you look at them like a parent would, it is strangely heart warming.Story in this particular game is rather bland  compare to the first two and requires a lot of insight about story about the first two game to process and understand the plots (I'm giving spoilers here but it is very subtle, hope to not ruin anyone's experience: 'the Kurken Island earthwakes', 'life mission of Ryza's master', 'Lent's reason of travelling', 'Bos's reason of training', 'the seed and flower', 'the starchild', 'Fi', etc.), which make the nostalgia part even more important if you want to enjoy this otherwise-would-be-grind-fest game.A lot of people talk about how the game world is too big, personally I think the size of the world is fine, it really emphasis on how much the group has grown from exploring their own island to exploring other continents, and they do give you more mobility options in this one. The biomes are unique and interesting, even though a majority of monsters are re-used, it give the world some consistency. Talking about consistency, it would be better if the materials gathered from areas in first game stay the same in this one, I had so much trouble finding the Rose for Tao's perfume that I know grow a lot on the way to the tower in the first game.In the end, It was a good wrap-up for Ryza's story with her friends. Sad to see it ended, but better stop when it is still good. As usual, Gust always nail the last cutscene and outro. Good story overall. I am looking forward to the story of the next alchemist.

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Ryza 3 is a wonderful sequel and conclusion to the title character's series, with a sprawling world that is larger and more beautiful than its past two predecessors combined, yet also manages to become an absolutely empty shell of an open world.Gathering feels so much better now. No longer are we bound to locked-in animations of bending down to snatch materials. It only happens sometimes. For the most part, you smoothly go from picking one item to the next without an animation even as you're running. Until you get to tools, which is like 4/5ths of the amount of gathering you do.You will often find yourself pausing at a resource that requires a tool, and doing a good ole circle to check which material is offered from which tool. Another peeve I had, harvesting with a tool often requires you to stand RIGHT BESIDE the resource. You're inside the harvestable bush? Sorry, better back out, circle around, and inch forward a little until the resources pop up again. I can't tell you how many times I've run donuts around an item because you can't hack at it unless you're at a certain angle.The hideout system is a great addition borrowed from Atelier Firis, but instead of a mobile atelier you carry around and slap down at designated locations, in Ryza 3, you can build stationary ateliers in each major location of the game. There are several types of ateliers that provide unique bonuses, and you can later build upon to grant additional bonus effects to. It feels so nice to have a place to return to and really sells the adventure aspect. Ryza, and you by extension, essentially leaves a mark in the world doing so.However, I did have a big gripe with it. Much later in the game, you can expand the atelier. This is the 'build upon' part I mentioned earlier. The inspiration and impetus for this is Ryza thinking it's getting cramped, because of your growing party size. Before, everyone stays within the foyer of your atelier hideout. After building additional rooms— you guessed it! Everyone continues to stay within the foyer. Come on, Gust. The NPCs and living world are a step down from the second game. Everyone is essentially a mannequin.The most major letdown about Ryza 3 is the story. I know, I know. We're here to watch cute characters do alchemy and go on adventures, but that isn't an excuse. The plot managed to be so convoluted and nonexistent at the same time. A third of the total character dialogues are "Hey, remember what we did in Ryza 1 and 2?" That's because the cast completed their character arcs in the second game! The only one in 3 with any semblance of a character arc are the new ones (naturally, since they are new) and Tao.Look, the story sucks. I would have forgiven Ryza 3 having an unpolished story if it was more gameplay than story, but over half the game is just cut-scenes of characters talking, and it isn't interesting. I've never been more thankful for a second monitor while the game was on auto-talk. Hey, at least a lot of hinted ships from the past two games set sail, which was a pleasant and wholesome surprise though.Events face the same problems the second game and Sophie did. Cut-scenes are queued, so you can be adventuring with a new character for hours, and another character in your party will later come up and be like "Hey, nice to meet you!" Or a character mentioning their hesitation traveling somewhere soon, when you've already been in that place for ages now. It's so jarring.There is so much space to explore in this game. It's probably the largest and most ambitious yet, but only because it's also vastly empty and painfully under utilized. I wish so much games that don't need an open world would stop making open worlds, and Ryza 3 is one such example. I'm begging developers here. Making a big open world game without adding a proportional amount of things to do doesn't make it fun, all it does is accentuate how empty it is. Not to mention you're baited into exploring nooks and crannies on the map for chests, but since items inside the chests aren't affected by quality and quant multipliers from the skill tree, the materials are WORSE than what you harvest in the field.All of these grievances make sense, once you find out that Ryza is getting an anime adaptation, that the third game was hastily created as promotional material for it. That's great and all, why couldn't we get a fun game to go along with it?I didn't face any technical issues and that's a lot to ask for from Koei-freaking-Tecmo, and just the triple A industry as of late. The crafting is top-notch if you're type to spend hours and hours on maxing out traits. The icing on the top is a new Super Trait mechanic, which is a superb addition for adding an extra layer of OP-ness for every synthesis. You can essentially become god very early on thanks to neutralizers having a material loop. A colored neutralizer can go into the same color neutralizers, allowing you to max stats and traits very easily.One thing to keep in mind that I didn't realize until later on: Super Traits. Super Traits can only be applied once. For example, you have a material with the Overpower super trait. You use that material in a neutralizer synthesis. Only those neutralizers will have that super trait active. BUT trying to apply the Overpower super trait from the neutralizers to another synthesis item won't work. It had to have been from the original material with the super trait. Careful so you don't lose a high value Super Trait!I had a lot to complain about with Ryza 3, but at the end of the day, I had a lot of fun and sank HOURS into synthesizing into ungodly powerful items. It's exactly what I wanted in a crafting game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza 3 is an excellent conclusion to the Secret Trilogy and a must-play for any Atelier enthusiast, especially if you enjoyed the previous two Ryza games. This game brings back all the elements that made Ryza 1&2 great, while expanding the world to explore with new ingredients and recipes to play with.One of the standout features of Ryza 3 is the new "key" system, which complements the battle, alchemy, and exploration systems, giving players more degrees of freedom to beat all the challenges the game has to offer. However, the difficulty could be trivialized even in the maximum difficulty without needing a lot of investment in the mechanics.The game's OST brings a lot of the great songs from past games, adding some adequate but not ground-breaking score for Gust standards. Additionally, the endings for all the character arcs are satisfactory and provide a fulfilling conclusion to the Secret Trilogy.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent ending to one of my favorite trilogies in gaming. It's a game that feels nostalgic at the start, and inevitably melancholy by the end. I loved going on one final adventure, traveling to new places with Ryza's friends.I love that you can break the game to pieces completely right at the start if you want to. I held off for a while, but it's great that you can. The alchemy in this game is the best it's been in the whole trilogy. The music, too, is amazing. And I gotta say, the new characters are fantastic. As you'd expect from the end of a trilogy, there are a lot of great story payoffs that I wouldn't want to spoil. There's only one storyline that left me unsatisfied, but they can still fix it by following up on it in a future game. Other than that, the game would be a 10/10, amazing experience for me, but... there's one other big blemish on it and sadly I can't not mention it. That is, the very, very poor quality of the English localization. It has lots and lots of mistakes. Context errors, straight up grammatical nightmares that don't make any sense. It's ok at times, but at other times, you can't even follow the plot because the text is barely comprehensible. I think the localization needed a lot more time, QA and polish, and I get that it's the first time they make a worldwide simultaneous release for this series but they should feel ashamed to put out a product in this state. I've seen other people complain about it too, so hopefully Koei Tecmo are listening and will fix it eventually.

_childDocuments_.review: +This is the biggest, most beautiful Atelier game in the entire series without question.  Certainly the best game in the series from a technical point of view, which is a very good sign for the future of the franchise.  I'm already excited for the next mainline entry!  (Also, I like the addition of Super Traits, which are only accessible from base ingredients.  It ends up making items more unique, since you can't simply give the same Super Trait to everything)-I have little nitpicks here and there, but my main complaint is the same as 2: I didn't want to play as Ryza AGAIN.  Ryza's story happened in 1.  It was great.  Everybody went through their character arcs and everything was neatly tied up.  Normally, we'd get to explore the next game with a new protagonist and new cast, and maybe we'd get to see our old friends on the side through new lenses to see what they've been up to since the previous game.  But not this time: Ryza 1 sold too well.  So it was starting to get old playing mostly the same party in 2, but by the end of 3...not my favorite, that's for sure.Overall, I had a lot of fun in this game and in the  Ryza trilogy as a whole, but I am very, very much looking forward to the next adventure being something new.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're here then I'm assuming you played the other Ryza games already, if not then you should go read reviews for those games instead as this is essentially the same game as the others.The best bits of this game are the alchemy (obviously), exploration and environments, and lots of nice quality of life bits to make things less tedious.The main story is exactly what you expect from a modern Atelier game, it exists and that's it. It's never really fleshed out much and is mostly made up of piece meal individual stories. It is nice to see how the characters have evolved over the course of 3 games but they're still not much more than two dimensional anime tropes.The worst bit is by far the combat. The game is extremely trivial in terms of difficulty if you spend even a small amount of time focused on creating equipment and a few bombs. You have all these features - swapping between party members, swapping out with reserve members, order drives, fatal drives, and managing AP and CC - yet none of those actually matter at all. This is more so later in the game but all you need to do is give Ryza some overpowered bombs (which its far easier to do in this game) and suddenly you can one shot everything on the hardest difficulty as soon as combat starts.Overall if its not your first Atelier game, and this shouldn't be, then you're getting exactly what you expect and its still a fun series despite its flaws. thighs/10

_childDocuments_.review: Gust went sick-o mode on this one. The technical issues can get pretty rough but hopefully they'll iron them out in the coming months. Performance with the steam overlay on is dreadful for some reason and screenshots break. I've been crashing a fair amount today however I'm using the atelier-sync-fix and haven't played without it so it's not clear to me if the crashes are normal or due to that.That aside, this feels the most worth your money at full price out of Ryza games and seems like it'll just make 1 and 2 obsolete. The huge maps with minimal loading screens / teleports is such an awesome experience for these games and really gives it a grand feeling. I've only mainly been in the first map and some of the colors / scenery in it are absolutely beautiful. It gives off the impression of having 10x the resources allocated to it than 1 and 2 did.I came into 1 for the thighs, got hooked on the crafting, went into 2 for more thighs and Klaudia + much more fun combat, and then went into this one just expecting more of the same but am having my expectations blown out of the water pretty frequently despite some of the issues I'm having to deal with. Love it.EDIT: Clarification before the rest of this; I have been playing solely on Windows using a Windows fork of atelier-sync-fix: , which I compiled myself with VS. Ran into a consistent crash at the end of a mandatory conversation, so I removed atelier-sync-fix. Crash no longer occured and haven't seen one since. Still not sure if that is the sole cause but it seems like it might make things less stable. Performance surprisingly is not much worse without it, I had just assumed it would be as big of a gain as it was on Ryza 2 and went with it from the start. Playing on 4k max settings on my 5700XT and I don't know what the framerate it is but it feels only slightly worse. So, for anyone curious about atfix, maybe try it and lean towards avoiding it if it's not much better. It's possible I didn't compile it correctly as well and so maybe I'm totally at fault.EDIT2: I'm getting intermittent crashes when accessing the Guide / Help in the game, but otherwise things are running well and stable, plus they even just toned down the DoF a little bit in an update last night / this morning. The crashes occur even completely vanilla with no overlays of any kind, so I believe that 100% is on the game's part. Which is a pretty rough crash as often you'll be synthesizing a lot and then you take a look in the Guide for a material or to get more info on an object, then you've crashed and lost potentially a lot of progress as autosave probably didn't kick in if you haven't left the same location and so you would need to manually save somewhat regularly.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a yes, but with pretty severe caveats that may make the game a no for you personally.  Be careful.Atelier Ryza 3 is the finale of this "Secrets" trilogy, and with it the ATB based combat, large tool and movement oriented maps (this one is open world-ish), molecule node model crafting, and Ryza herself as the protagonist for 3 games in a row.I'll start with bugs and technical issues, since they're pretty bad compared with pre-Sophie 2 games; and this one is even worse than Sophie 2.  Some of this is Linux/Deck only, some affects Windows users too.  Like all Atelier games (on all platforms), there are sync problems which most people get around by installing a fan made patch (look up Atelier Sync Fix on github).  I just used my standard forced frame rate limiter (DXVK_FRAME_RATE=60 %command%) and had no trouble, but the sync fix is probably better to set up.  Like all Atelier games, it uses proprietary patent encumbered video codecs so the videos will only play on ProtonGE on Linux; videos don't play on standard Proton.  Like Atelier Sophie 2, the game still has the infinite loading screen and far more random crashes than previous titles (like Sophie 1 or the Dusk games), this affects all users but affects Linux users more.  Running ProtonGE 7-47 let me avoid MOST of these hangs.  Running the current (at the time of this post 7-53) ProtonGE or Proton Experimental will cause the game to crash after loading the startup video.  I still had ProtonGE 7-47 installed, and that worked, I don't know which GE version brought in the startup crash (Linux only issue).  When viewing an item or monster from the game's encyclopedia, the game will crash after cancelling out of that screen (also Linux only most likely as I haven't seen anyone mention it on Windows).  This makes tracking down items far harder.  The game has pretty hefty performance flaws and a lack of optimization, which is probably the early adopter tax; however Koei-Tecmo don't have a great track record of fixing things post release.The world is mostly open world, there are 4 main areas and two additional smaller maps (one being Kurken Island, which is separate from the surrounding areas).  You have seemless transitions between what were separate zones before.  The game tracks "regions" for determining what items or foes are available, which are areas around a point of interest (which also act as fast travel points).  You can't tell which parts are considered one region, which can make it tough to track down rare materials.  You continue Ryza 2's introduction of travel tools, so the spirit beast is back, along with the emerald band and water drops that allow you to reach new areas.  Movement is a bit more streamlined, but the open world nature makes it feel a bit more lifeless than Ryza 2.  The game had other open world-isms such as randomized quests popping up, which are basically the same as what was on the request board in previous titles, but now appear while exploring.  Their popup pollutes your UI, and the UI blurs what's behind it which makes these random quests really annoying to run into.  Enemies scale with your level (through a range that covers most of your playthrough unless you do a bunch of grinding), which means that you almost never have enemies run away when you greatly outlevel them; the only way to scare off foes from gathering nodes is by using the spirit beast.While Ryza 3 brings in some new quality of life, it also removes some from Ryza 2.  You can do hand pickup node collection while moving now.  Most of the time, it won't block your flow of movement!  Tools still require you to stop.  Node preview only shows your equipped tool now, not all items harvestable.  You have to take the time to look at each node and see if there are any new items available.  This makes things really frustrating with the enemies constantly aggroed on you.  Like Ryza 2 (but not Ryza 1), when deconstructing items for gems, the chosen item filter resets to the top of the list.  This makes it far more annoying to go through and get rid of your lower value items one type at a time.Combat is an extension of Ryza 2's, except now you can more easily combo attacks.  The combat camera is zoomed in really close to your character, which makes things really hard to see where attacks are coming from to block.  It also increases the vertigo and motion sickness risk.  I spent most of my combat playthrough looking at the skill box to know when to combo effectively.  You have a LOT of characters (11 of them!), and can only bring 5 to battle (3 front line and 2 swap-in characters).  You'll likely just want to craft up gear for the ones you like most through the first playthrough, unfortunately some of the more interesting characters come far too late in the story to want to invest too much into.  You have CC charge upgrades too, with Ryza, Klaudia, new character Frederica, and  having CC reduction making them great swap-in characters to spam bombs later on in the fight.  Tao continues to have very low skill costs and low weight (recovery) times so he's good as an opener (as are to a lesser extent  and Bos).The final boss also has a really frustrating mechanic.  The story is just OK, it's awkward at spots and some aspects don't make much sense.  KT used a different localization firm and it shows.  The character interactions are good though.  Bos joins you this time, and there are 3 new characters for Ryza 3.  A number of returning characters as well, from both 1 and 2.  Some characters have nice new outfits, others do not.Crafting continues with the Ryza standard type of system.  General crafting is even easier than Ryza 2's, you have far fewer recipe morphs this time.  None of your weapons or armor use morphs, so you don't have the long chains where you can build up huge stat boosts as in Ryza 1 or 2.  The new mechanic this time are link morphs, where you can activate it and put an item into one of the core (required) spots, and it'll change the behavior of that node and completely change the tree attached to it.  This can lead to new recipe morphs or fun things like dual elemental bombs.  You can also get a buff item that does damage to your party, or applies a debuff so be careful!  This makes it far more complex, but also more frustrating as you can't really see what would happen to the tree until you activate the link morph.  You also have "super traits", which require a special node to allow and can only be passed on by raw items, not crafted intermediary items.Overall, I did enjoy the game but it's definitely not my favorite Atelier (Escha & Logy still takes that throne, with Sophie 2, Ryza 2, and Shallie close behind).  The open world I feel hurt the game more than helped, and the open world traps that many games fall into (random quest popups, the lack of differentiated areas for knowing where to gather, scaling foes, uninspired collectibles/chests) make things less interesting.  The crafting this time around was less interesting, while being simultaneously easier and harder (if you use link morphs).  The English translation was a downgrade from previous titles, and the story falls apart a bit toward the mid-end game.  I'm hoping that some of the tech issues are fixed, as I'm hesitant to recommend this game to SteamDeck or Linux users in its current state.  Even Windows users experience some of the tech issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier is always a day-one play for me as a series, so perhaps I'm a bit biased when I always give them positive reviews.The usual Atelier rules apply as always. It's a series where you'll spend more time picking flowers and making items than you will actually fighting anything, and the other half of your time is watching cutscenes, usually rather low-stakes ones that help create a comfy, feel-good emotion. The Secret Trilogy (Ryza, Ryza 2, and Ryza 3) would probably be a good jumping-in point for people who are used to more normal JRPGs though, as this trilogy has overall simpler alchemy, and the active-time-ish style of combat might appeal to JRPG veterans.Ryza 3 tries to experiment a bit more with what can be done in the Atelier formula, like the other entries of the Secret Trilogy before it. The world is mostly subdivided into 4 huge maps with mostly seamless transitions from one end of the other. Running the distance from the Secret Hideout to the holy tower in the first game without a single loading screen was pretty impressive, and quality-of-life adjustments allow you to more easily gather materials while moving without losing much momentum. I will say that the localization is a little spotty in some places, but other than that I feel like it's a worthy sendoff to one of the Atelier franchise's most experimental trilogies.I have a tendency to ramble, especially when talking about a series I love as much as Atelier. If you like Atelier, or the thought of a game where you can lose hours upon hours just making a better bomb to throw at forest critters or a tougher stick to hit things with, I would highly recommend playing this. Probably play Ryza 1 and 2 first though, because, whereas there is a recap video in the game available, I feel Ryza 3 is best experienced with nostalgia from playing the first 2. Thanks for reading this far, and may we all continue to synthesize items as long as we live!
_childDocuments_.name: Atelier Ryza 3: Alchemist of the End & the Secret Key

_childDocuments_.review: The finale of Ryza's trilogy and easily the best. General improvements, new QoL and features abound, from the *extensive* open world regions to neat new alchemy systems. The game felt like a significant step forward in pretty much every way, and I've loved playing it.I do want to complain about some translation issues that suddenly cropped up, though. Not sure why they seem to have underperformed there. It's not even remotely so bad that you won't enjoy the game, but there will be the occasional moment where you wonder if a dialogue line was accurate or if this thing has the wrong name for some reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything you liked about the last 2 Ryza games with the addition of several new systems revolving around "keys". They can be used as equipment to give stats, used as actual keys to open doors, door-like walls, and certain types of chests, used in synthesis to give all sorts of effects, and used in combat to give temporary buffs and remove the AP cap allowing for longer chains of abilities.  I did not care for these keys. The category of effects you get can be manipulated somewhat, but the effects themselves seem to be entirely random, so if you're looking for a specific effect, you may need to look for some time. This will only really matter for the achievement hunters though, as in all Ryza games simply making seeds and using super high quality ingredients to create a giant bomb for Ryza to throw will trivialize the game, even on the highest difficulty. Aside from that for combat: there is additional customization to the characters order system where you are able to decide which order is given, and under what conditions. There is also a system where you get points for each order completed, and can use those points to use an additional skill from anyone in the team, even if they are not in the party.  For synthesis: There are now "super traits", and "link morphs." Link morphs allow you to take the effect of an item and change it to do something else. Effects are things like a bomb doing fire damage. You could change that to ice damage, or various other things. This applies to weapons and armor as well. Super traits are basically just an extra trait, but with one limiting condition - they cannot be transferred from synthesized ingredients, meaning you must find the super traits you want on base level ingredients that match one of the categories of the item you want the super trait on. This makes creating the perfect items a bit harder, as simply finding all the traits you want and putting them on a philo stone won't work. So there is a bit of extra RNG involved in everything but generally, someone who just wants to beat the game won't contend with it much. Another solid game by Gust and a fair ending to Ryza's story. If you haven't played a Ryza game before, just play them all. The Secret trilogy will be hard to top.

_childDocuments_.review: I only played Atelier Ryza 1 and 2 for this review so please bear with me if I do not explains some details very well.First, I commend Gust and Koei Tecmo for their success in this game by making an Atelier game with an open world concept. Two things that are noteworthy here: the concept and PC performance.For the concept, it makes sense that doing alchemy does not limit to only Kurken Island, hence Ryza's party decides to go to different regions. However, in relation to the plot, especially the end of the story, the game made less sense for me. Speaking of endings, I liked this adventure story with some explosive events, and certainly the best ending to the Ryza series. Better play it for you to discover when you compare it to the first 2 Atelier Ryza games.For the PC performance, despite an open world rendering, still performs 30 fps and above FOR AN OPEN WORLD game. Probably this is because, this is an anime game more or less. Nevertheless, this proves that an open world does not need to be too graphically demanding.Soundtracks are also good that they entice relaxation and adventure.The boss fights can be challenging especially, but doable as long as you know what to do every turn.Overall, I recommend this game especially if you just want to relax yourself after all of these dire situations.

_childDocuments_.review: It's everything you loved about Atelier Ryza but refined. Combat feels about as good as ever. You get into the game play loop a lot faster than in previous titles with old characters come back within the first hour and new characters on the horizon. The game is particularly effective at paying off the effort players have put in to the previous two titles, with flashbacks showing just how much Ryza & co. have grown and changed. It's heartwarming to see their younger selves next to their older selves, and it's even more affecting knowing that this is their last adventure.What can I say: It's Gust firing on all cylinders. They managed to bottle lightning with Ryza and - so far - this is shaping up to be a pitch perfect send off of her.

_childDocuments_.review: The thickest thighs waifu is back!Feels like the first game in general. You begin in Kurken Island and then you expand your adventure in the other areas as the first game. Everything in this game remembers the summer.Is great to see how Ryza has grown. Now she is an adult, in her twenties, and everyone else has grown too. Specially Tao, and even Bos, which he is a playable character too. Sound is great, uses melodies from the 1st game also. Combat system remains the same. There are some good details like Ryza gets dirty (in her thighs LoL xD) when she passes through narrow places. But also there are some unpolished things unfortunately: Her movement animations feels robotic, and when she walks and changes direction there is no 360 degrees movement but 8 direction like old games. Besides, it doesn't excel like other games from Gust. There is no details in the technical side. Compared with Atelier Sophie 2, this looks not as beautiful. Looks simpler. For example, in Sophie 2 there were great details like shadows projecting from her clothes over herself and the shadows changed if you moved around. That was a great detail level back then. But Ryza 3 is not as detailed. It's not like is the most important thing, but given that Gust had worked very hard with previous games, then it's only natural to expect no less.In terms of new mechanics, it's a bit confusing how to use the magic keys, or rather... they are useless. The only thing I fing useful is in combat, and not all of them, just some of them only. The keys that allows to access to hidden areas, it's confusing too: I have keys with the element required, but I can't enter whatsoever. This new mechanics I didn't like it.On Steam Deck runs fine, only the intro CGI cutscene doesn't play. I have played over 30 hours and all the cinematics are played with the engine, not CGI, so it's ok to play on the Steam Deck even though says is not compatible.Despite the downsides, I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly stunning graphics ( I played with anti-aliasing off and it looks phenomenal) , great action, good looking costumes for Ryza (if you buy the dlc), likable characters, nice battle system, and yes plenty of fan service ( despite the fake speculation that went on)! The only drawback I can think of is that they reuse some of the music from previous titles. I think this series is like the comfort food of RPGs. _childDocuments_.review:
Ryza and her friends are living their lives on Kurken Island when news of a sudden appearance of a mysterious group of islands in nearby waters arrives.
To find a way to save her island, Ryza and her friends will set off on final adventure surrounding the "roots of alchemy."

The stage for this adventure is a vast open field!
The field is made up of multiple maps that are connected seamlessly. Enjoy this adventure in a vast and ‘living’ field that is one of the largest in the Atelier series.

You can do many things with the key!
Obtain various types of keys which can be used in different instances of exploration, synthesis, and battle. Each key has a different effect, so use it to enjoy the adventure conveniently!

name: MechWarrior 5: Clans
detailed_description: In MECHWARRIOR 5: CLANS, players take on the role of a newly graduated pilot from the Smoke Jaguar cadet program, thrust into the heart of the Clan Invasion of the Inner Sphere during Operation Revival. This pivotal moment in the MechWarrior universe sees players leading a five-mech 'Star' squad across numerous planets with diverse biomes, engaging in an expansive campaign filled with immersive gameplay and intricate combat encounters. Armed with customizable BattleMechs featuring cutting-edge technologies, players explore a wealth of tactical options and strategic possibilities. The game leverages the power of the Unreal Engine to deliver stunning environmental details and visceral destruction, making every battle against the tyrants of the Inner Sphere an epic experience. As the first Clan-based MechWarrior game in nearly three decades, it combines a captivating narrative with well-crafted characters and moral dilemmas, culminating in a dynamic and adaptive combat experience enhanced by a revamped MechLab, Hardpoint, and OmniPod system. Experience the Clan Invasion from the perspective of Clan Smoke Jaguar as you lead your Star through engaging missions and combat, with cinematics unlike anything seen before in MechWarrior Strategic adaptability is key to victory and more accessible than ever with the new Battle Grid, Command Wheel, and Streamlined Controls Customize your 'Mechs with advanced Clan weapon systems, equipment, and upgrades for mission-specific battles, and advance your pilots with the new pilot progression system Experience MechWarrior like never before with a fully standalone campaign featuring detailed environments and dynamic destruction using the latest Unreal Engine and new Tech Updates Play with up to 4 other players as you protect and lead your Star through complex missions and thrilling combat

_childDocuments_.review: Put it this way, if you like Mechwarrior 5: Mercs, but felt you wanted more story (and saw how each Mercs DLC was getting better in story), well look no further then Clans here as it's basically all the lessons learned in Mercs to give a proper story driven campaign. So that's basically what you get, no sandbox, but a linear (with a minor branch point near the end) story about the Clan Invasions of the inner Sphere from the Smoke Jaguar's perspective.. And boy is it fun!... Yea, some will complain there's only 16 mechs, but in reality that's really all the mechs the Clans did bring for the invasion in Lore. if i recall, there are still 2 mechs missing, but the major favorite clan mechs from the Timber Wolf (aka Mad Cat) to the awesome 100t Dire Wolf mech are all here in their full omnimech glory. Obviously if you come from Mercs you gonna be spoiled with all the mods your use to having like YAML, Pilot overhaul, etc.. since now your back to vanilla, but overall it's not that bad, the bugs/issues people have said they encounter, in my almost 42 hours to beat the story I really didn't encounter any of that and nothing game breaking. I did encounter some sound bugs in the "in-game cutscenes" where nothing would play and there are some points within a mission where no music will play (which is a shame cause the music is just as good as Mercs, less "rock" oriented though) and there would also be a little " fpsstutter" every time new enemies would spawn, which can be  tad annoying, seems to happen more in "cockpit" view rather then "drone" view, which me I'm more of a drone view kind of person when playing mechwarrior. Outside of those issues, it was basically smooth sailing, on average with my RTX 4090 and CPU I averageed 160-170 FPS. The one knock I will say, and this is sadly by design which I confirmed on their discord is while the cinematics are beautiful, they are not formated for an Ultra widescreen view, so my beautiful LG 39 inch monitor was seeing all those excellent cinematics in letter box format which stunk a bit honestly from an immersion standpoint, but gameplay was fine it full advantage of my ultra screen monitor. My hope is future DLC may support it for cinematics, but we'll see i guess. Bottom line, if you enjoyed Mercs, but are ok with no "sandbox" gameplay (at least for now, perhaps future DLC will introduce those elements), then by all means check this out, you won't regret it. Keep in mind, there is really no replay value (you can easily play both branches in the story by saving just before, and it's near the end game, so it's not long after that point the game is finished)... and personally I don't count the sim pod where you replay the missions you did, but with certain challenges added in as replay value at all.  So after you've beaten the story, you'll proabably end up going back to Mercs like I have, heh.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for a Clans MW since MW4 Vengeance.Combat is tight, weapons feel powerful and chunky, movement is exactly like I remember it. Hopefully future mechs don't get locked behind paid DLC, but I'm assuming that's exactly what will happen. No Daishi, which is a massive disappointment.The story is stupid. It's exactly what you'd expect from a MechWarrior game. The voice acting is hysterical at best, cringy at worst. The models of the characters are awful, facial animations are TES Oblivion levels of dead, but absolutely none of that matters. That's not why I'm here, Im here to play with mechs.There is no instant action, which is such a massive oversight. MW5 Mercenaries had one out the gate, which was awesome. It's a damn shame you have to endure the stupid story and it's (mercifully skip-able) cutscenes to play with mechs. But when you do get to customize and fight in your chosen mech it's absolutely a good time.Do I think this is worth full price? Nope. Wait for it to go on sale. This game is lacking a lot of the content I was hoping for, but it's a good game. If you ignore the awful story and acting.

At first I was worried how to get the Mechs since in Mercenaries you could cobble together your own, but in this one as you play every mission or two you unlock the next mech, slowly getting heavier and heavier mechs. For those of you worried 'there aren't enough mechs' please check the mechbay for OMNI BUILD. It lets you change the weapons loadout of the mech to be substantially different all on the same mech. Overall I'm enjoying it. I do miss the open sandbox of Mercenaries, but this has so much more lore and story to it that it makes up for it.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some bugs. I have a ryzem 5600x, rx5700xt, and 32 gb of ram. Even with fresh driver installs, the game initially crashed my entire computer within 5 minutes, regardless of if I was actively playing, or just in the initial menu screen. Cpu and GPU temps stayed normal. It took me about an hour of experimenting, and discovered that whatever reason, running the game at my native resolution (whether full screen or windowed) was causing the crash. I dialed my resolution settings down from 1920x1080 down to 1600x900 and was able to up all my graphics setting back up to high. At that point I quit experimenting because I just wanted play, and it was now stable.Gameplay: pretty much the same as mercs. If you liked that, you'll like this. There is a lack of mechs on offer true, but you can mix and match hard point configurations to come up with your own variants, which is pretty cool. (I am currently using a Hellbringer outfitted like an Orion!) The difficulty on normal is usually fine, but at one point I dialed it down to "story mode" because some of the missions are just absolute slogs (looking at YOU "disciplinary action")Story: probably the best in the franchise. The voice acting and cutscene animations are pretty good, and the mission briefings gave me flashbacks of MechWarrior 3. I feel they've also done a good job showing the brutality of smoke jaguars without making them cartoonishly evil. Pgi has stayed faithful to clan language, culture and customs, and letting the scene explain what's going on without having to literally explain it. They do a lot of "show, don't tell" which is exactly how to handle story telling in this medium.Overall it's a solid entry that I am enjoying immensely.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a recommend but maybe wait a few days for patches. There's some audio issues with the cutscenes(sounds very low quality) and one of the pilots' VO also sounds like it was recorded with a really bad mic.I know some folks are complaining about the limited mechlab but canonically it makes sense for what it is. The ability to add armor to specific locations on the mech is quite nice since the AI likes to target your arms a lot since those are where your weapons are located.After a few patches this will be a solid 8-8.5/10 for me. The environments are much more detailed & the story driven campaign makes me feel like I am taking part in a huge invasion. It's quite a step-up in quality from MW5 Mercs but with a caveat: no sandbox mode. So if you want a 25 hour ish long campaign with an interesting story & interesting characters, then it might be your cup of tea.

_childDocuments_.review: Like MWO and MW5: Mercs, my biggest complaint is that this game uses the same, blocky "Vanilla" designs for the 'mechs.  It also still strays away from the MechWarrior "togs" that are worn by MechWarriors in the lore, instead putting the characters in full body suits.  Other than that, the gameplay is very enjoyable and it seems like the story line follows the progression of the lore pretty well.  It is a shame that the story centers around a crusader clan, instead of a warden...but Smoke Jaguar has never before been a playable faction, so I suppose it is only fair.  Despite my own opinions on content, I do recommend this game for those who enjoy the BattleTech franchise.  At only six hours in, I am looking forward to seeing how the individual story develops...even though I know that Smoke Jaguar will never be ilClan (thanks to Victor Steiner-Davion).

Feel like it's because it's loading textures while playing.There is some quality missing from battles to make them more atmospheric - i feel like there is not enough wreckage, for example all components so far like hands just disappear, and on the model it has a clean cut (edited-not all mechs, light mechs seem to have this issue), instead of some metal wreck.I really like the repair system, feels way more forgiving, making me take my losses as they come (no need to keep buying replacement gear every time you lose an arm). _childDocuments_.review: This is basically a beta release with the full story, but none of the QA properly done yet.If you have a computer with the system requirements around the recommended level, then in the strongest terms I can use, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME YET.Unless you're a diehard Battletech fan, it's not worth it. It's a 50/50 shot on whether a 30 series card will work without issues. 20 series cards more or less can't run the game without turning the graphics down to minimum. 10 series cards flat out lock up when trying to load the game.It isn't worth commenting on the games other merits until they fix the performance problems, the game cannot be fairly judged in the state it's in.Piranha, fix the game.
