_childDocuments_.review: This is a children's game, but for adults. If the Simpsons, Adult-Swim and X-Com had an orgy, 'Highwater Bruno Ganz' would be the baby's name. This is like Power Rangers. You see their heads move, but this game's expletive subtitles read f**k, sh*t or c**k. Definitely not a game for minors, especially with references to the Fibonacci sequence, Eadweard Muybridge and Georges Méliès. But if you enjoy turn based killings with serene, although potty-mouthed Euro-centric yet bizarre calming touring music, then look no further.Here, you can enjoy linear based game play with no real exploration or map; forced slow pop-up dialogue and credits; no manual game saves; one difficulty setting; no RPG-style leveling up or retention; limited to no weapon selection or diversity; random character combat; unexplained or difficult to decipher game play battles, perks or special abilities; very short story, and etc. Be careful of paid reviews with thumbs-up obliviously, because there's not much else to see here. Knowing and traveling most of the world, this seems a bit Swedish, Dutch or German. With the gaming world expanding across the globe, and with international programmers coming out of the woodwork to make some cash, I wish there was a neutral selection rating, because I cannot in good conscious recommend this game. But I would also hate to down-rate some else's vision and hard-work they spent time and effort to share with others. Although in the spirit of not being close minded, and knowing that the world is much bigger than one country, I will uprate it, because I admit, the game was somewhat fun and is good for wasting a few hours. However, be careful of what you wishlist for.

_childDocuments_.review: "[...] there’s still time to enjoy the view." That's why I bought this game.Except for there is not much to see when you are traveling with your boat. The surroundings are very minimal, basic and often feel copy-pasted. There wasn't much to enjoy the view. The graphic art style is great though.Long story short - would I recommend playing it - No. If you are interested in my why keep reading.Camera controls:Often I'm annoyed about the camera angle and camera controls in general. Depending on your last camera angle (before entering a cutscene) you might not be able to see half of the dialogue. Happened to me a few times. And in combat your view can be fully blocked because you can't control the camera anymore when its the enemie's turn. Suddenly you're not able to see what's happening in combat because the surroundings are blocking your view when the enemy moves.Combat:The fights are sometimes too often in a row in my opinion. Especially because I tend to struggle with them. Probably #Skillissue I know... But I feel like I was missing some information in combat a few times. Like it took me some attempts to understand that I can push trees diagonally as well. Or the indicator in which direction characters will be pushed (especially when pushing more than just one around with a single move). Either it wasn't there for each character or the indicator wasn't visible enough. And I still have no idea what green tiles in combat means.Dialogue:The further I progressed in the story I feel more annoyed about all the dialogues.Also I hate that half of the dialogues is just a video and I have no control about it at all. I can't decide when to confirm the text. That's a mandatory accessibility feature for me. Not everybody reads text at the same speed. There's a high chance that people will either be bored because they read faster or not able to read half of it because their reading speed is too slow.Map:What's the purpose of a map when you can't see where you are? Maybe it's just me that has an other understanding of a map. I only used it to see my next objective. In my opinion the map is more confusing than really useful and funcioning as you would expect a map to be.Overall this game doesn't feel polished. At least I haven't encountered any bugs; or I didn't notice any, so that's a plus I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: Highwater ties in with the earlier two games they've made, nevertheless you can perfectly play it as a standalone. While prior knowledge is not necessary, I must admit that I enjoy puzzling out the entire dystopian universe that Demagog Studio has put together so far. But I digress.In this chapter of the chronology, you will mostly play as Nikos – a young guy with an insane plan and a challenging goal. His dream is to board the rocket that is leaving for Mars along with his group of friends. After all, this is where the wealthy people reside now, and with Earth being flooded due to the Great Climate Catastrophe and resources becoming scarcer, Nikos believes that it is worth the risk and gamble. This journey could mean a better future for him and his friends.Although the overall storyline was decent, it felt like it was not well developed compared to the earlier games. For instance, I feel like I know more about Nikos' yellow dinghy, Argo - which is named after the ship from a Greek story than I do about Nikos' companions. This just doesn't feel right to me, I genuinely feel like I should know these people more in-depth; Like who are they, how did they end up here, and how do I know them?Moreover, if you think you can skip the slow dialogue and focus solely on the gameplay… Then I'm afraid I have bad news for you. Certain parts of the game are predetermined, which means you cannot speed it up by button smashing. Believe me, I’ve tried. As a slightly faster reader, I found that rather frustrating. At least it lets you skip cutscenes, so you don’t have to go through those over and over again if you decide to replay a chapters. Exploring and piloting the dinghy are two of the three main activities in the game. It's like a walking simulator, but with a boat. However, I was disappointed with the dinghy's slow speed, which stayed the same throughout the game. Additionally, you can't stray too far from your path, which takes away from the fun of exploring or fooling around just for the sake of fooling around. Overall, the exploration part of the game lacks excitement – you can collect items sometimes which can be bothersome. Consider the following scenario: You’ve been asked to find and bring a basketball. It may seem like a simple task, right? But what if I told you that, when you found it and wanted to bring it to your boat, the basketball was so heavy that it delayed your pace to the point where a snail could overtake you? This happened multiple times with multiple objects and frankly was annoying.At other times, as part of exploring, there are conversations in the game where you may have to select an answer. However, it does not seem to affect the game's outcome in any way. Frankly, it feels out of place, and I'm not sure why it's included in the game.The final main activity in the game is turn-based combat with a puzzle twist. While the concept is cool with the added puzzle element, I am not a fan of strategy games, so for me, it overstayed its welcome, especially as the game progresses. There are far too many battles to my liking, and I would prefer more story, lore, and/or exploration instead.The battlefield is structured in a grid-like pattern. Your pre-chosen party members, as well as the enemies, will be on this grid. Each character in the game has unique abilities, attacks, and movement techniques – this means the enemies too. The game follows a turn-based system, a bit like chess; you take turns and hope to defeat your opponents before they defeat you. As you progress through the game, you will find items that can enhance your character's speed, attack, defense, or even a new weapon.Now, you must wonder why I mentioned there is a little puzzle twist. Sometimes, on the battlefield, you’ll find items that you can use to your advantage. This could be a shopping cart, a tree, a rack, and so on. In the early stages of the game, I ran into an angry butcher. I guess it’s fair to say I had a little bit of beef with him, and we went to battle. I soon realized that I would not be able to defeat him using the normal turn-based strategy. He was much stronger than me and probably could’ve beat me in two hits, all while I did nothing but a small scratch on his health. I had to find another way, and I did, and I liked it. It's nice to have an element of thinking outside of the box included, it made it a little more exciting and interesting. A first look at the gameplay: The game's visuals are incredibly stunning, especially the low-resolution art style. The serene blue seas and lush green islands make it a place of beauty as these shades complement the game and theme perfectly. One of the most captivating places in the game is the Humbolt Botanical Gardens; its pink and purple hues, along with the darker blue, are mesmerizing. It is undoubtedly my favourite part of the entire Highwaters world. However, I also felt that the game world and all the locations felt a little empty, and the reason for this was not explained. Perhaps the creators missed an opportunity to add more depth to the setting; they could have gone further to make it more interesting.The game once again includes a radio station, this one cleverly named Radio Highwater. Just like the earlier games, it harmonizes with the visuals effectively as it tells the story through the host and the songs – which will be the only voices you will hear in the game, except for a few in-game performances. All dialogues are presented as speech bubbles that require reading. I noticed a major difference in this game compared to the others. In the previous games, I could listen to the host or a song until the end without any interruption or getting cut off. However, in this game, I had to stop my boat sometimes to hear the whole song or avoid getting interrupted by something like a cutscene. The overall quality of the radio Highwater didn't feel as strong as the stations of the previous games. This is unfortunate because the radio stations are what distinguish this series of games and set them apart from others.Well, here we are, at the end of the review. This time around I don’t have much left to say. To be honest, I am disappointed and cannot give this a thumbs up, at all. And while I applaud Demagog Studio's efforts, I know they can do better, especially given their past performances. I had high hopes for Highwater because I appreciate the game's core concept and the narrative that runs across these games. However, it fell short on many levels. Despite this, I’ve grown to love the universe and its ongoing lore, and I can’t wait for the next chapter of the story as I'm still craving more.Thank you so much for reading and see you in the next review!with love,TchiiIf you enjoyed reading my review, kindly give it a thumbs up. Your support would mean a lot to me.Disclosure: I received a free copy of the game, and I wasn't paid to write this review. The opinions expressed in the review are based on my personal experience, and they are not influenced in any way.Consider giving a follow to the list below for more first looks, reviews, or recommendations.||||

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. This is the third game in this IP, which features Golf Club Nostalgia (formerly Golf Club Wasteland) and The Cub. This entry is the prequel to the events of the other two games. There are two extra stories that you can play after you finish the base game:  and . ARC offers an in depth playthrough of a cutscene from the base game, and Aftermath deals with the people you leave behind from the base game.Anyway, as mentioned this is the prequel to the other two games in the series and not only dives deeper into how Earth became toxic for humanity, but also explores the events leading up to people leaving for Mars through the eyes of Nikos and his band of adventurers who are set on making it onto a rocket that will be heading to Mars. Additionally, story points include touching on how the children who were left behind were able to survive (and if you've played The Cub, you know they thrived). This was a fun and quirky story that did a good job of fleshing out the world you have come to know via the previous games. I'd say there is still more to be had, and I can see Demagog Studio making a few more games in the IP.Beyond the core story, this game is a meta machine and leans heavily into a comical and sarcastic look at society and politics while also managing to be very spot on in the way it views these things and how it presents those views. I really enjoyed this aspect of the game a lot.Where Golf Club Wasteland was inspired by Angry Birds and The Cub was inspired by various platformers, this game takes its inspiration from turn-based semi open world RPGs. I think it's cool that the devs try a different style with each entry. It's not perfect: the turn-based battle sequences are very slow paced and you have no control over your party composition; but the actual application of said battles and the inclusion of special abilities, limited use buffs, and a small variety of weapons does work fine. The world exploration is limited, but also nice. You will travel around in your little rubber motorboat, the "Argo", and will find various areas to disembark and explore. Mostly, the exploration will allow you to find buff items, weapons, and bits of lore in the form of books, newspapers, and the occasional random item. There are also places with phot prompts to take snapshots of in game. Beyond that, exploration will take you to the next story/quest areas. These various locations are marked on your minimap and are easy to navigate to.The game does a good job of not making you backtrack too much. Where that would be necessary, it will simply teleport you back for all intents and purposes. So, the tedium is thankfully missing.The graphics are consistent with this developer's previous work. Very colorful world juxtaposed with the detritus of a dying world. There is a good amount of detail with the various assets they crafted, and it is a visually pleasing game through and through. Most dialogue is written, but the radio host from the other games is here as well, manning the mic for HPR (Highwater Pirate Radio) this time around, and they included both more songs and more news segments for this game than with past entries. It's a fun thing and pretty much something to expect from all Demagog games moving forward. Fortunately, you can tell they enjoy having the radio stations in their games.While I wouldn't characterize this game as a must play, I would say that if you have played the other two games, you should definitely also play this one. It's fun, and what flaws it has can be forgiven due to the overall charm and cool factor the game and series has. I think grabbing this one on sale is the way to go.

_childDocuments_.review: A very chill game with beautiful music and a heavenly atmosphere, despite the grim setting itself.  Turn based combat is a nice touch that doesn't require much strategy but is a novel approach since this game wouldn't work as well as a straight up 3rd person platformer, so goofy / jumpy violence was never going to work here and what they've chosen instead works well. _childDocuments_.review: Reviewing this game is going to be tricky as some of the design decisions and faults can annoy people a lot while others can really love the game for its strong points and what it’s trying to do. I was very hesitant on getting this so soon based on the mixed reception but I’m glad I went ahead with it after completing Highwater.So what’s the gameplay basically? The loop is generally using your boat to get to the next destination. The journey is supported by the same radio host from The Cub with some music mixed in between. There are short cutscenes that don’t overstay their welcome. You can also explore (optional) areas to find collectibles, weapons and boosters. Collectibles are magazines or books with a cover and title to set the mood (so no real reading material). Weapons can be character specific and boosters are consumable items used during battles only (heal, better movement, hit harder etc). The fights are your typical strategy RPG like Fire Emblem or Final Fantasy Tactics. So the game is mostly going from A to B with a lot of focus on fighting and exploring. Exploration is kept light hearted, everything you can interact with is hard to miss. The fights are not as complex as the games I mentioned and there is no progression system like level up or learning new skills. Skills are usually bound by the weapons you have equipped and there are some exclusive character skills.So what’s so good about this game? The style is strong with this one. Some of the landscapes seen while travelling are so pretty with a great use of color. The game is great at showing you what humans are dealing with, how everyone is coping and how desperate they can become (it’s depressing). The battle system is actually VERY good. Although I didn’t expect anything close to Fire Emblem, it’s still complex enough, satisfying and it made me think a few times due to the objects you can interact with along with some of the achievements. Speaking of the achievements, they’re terrific. Some are clear from the get go. Others make you guess and keep you on your toes but once you encounter the moment you’re supposed to do something, you’ll know when the achievements will trigger. As long as you keep notes of the achievements (read them to remember) and explore all areas, then they’re doable and fun to get. I got them 100% blindly without using a single guide. The game also has a good pacing for the most part and the length (7.8 hours in my case) feels just right. There is chapter select and you can check your collectibles from the menu. The game saves automatically after leaving an area, completing a fight or picking up an item. So you never feel like you’re forced to play longer than you want. The performance, 1440p resolution and loading times are excellent.I’m going to deal with the negatives a bit differently this time. First I’m going to focus on the negatives that I noticed and then talk about the negatives experienced by others. To me it was the overall lack of polish in terms of UI, bugs and graphics. All of these are not that bad but you do notice them. The UI can be lacking or unclear. For instance, I didn’t find out where I can check enemy movement before attacking. Sometimes it is unclear where you can attack when the color of the tile is mixed with a different tile to indicate something else. When equipping weapons, the grey color to show you who can equip what is so light, that you can easily miss it and wonder why certain characters can’t equip something. The bugs are mostly some rare visual bugs or when your party gets in your way while exploring. They can cause you to get stuck. While the style is good, the graphics could have been better. Some of the environments and objects are too blocky and it felt odd that you couldn’t control the camera while exploring or using your boat. With the graphics, perhaps it’s because of its mobile roots since this was a Netflix exclusive for a while. Others didn’t like the game’s map, the lack of character backstory or strong characters in general. The map is not typical and not really helpful in the grand scheme of things but it’s not needed at all because the game gives you the illusion of exploring ‘islands’ but it’s not really the case. If you go too far to the left or right, the controls are taken away from you temporarily to put you on the main road. The mini radar literally shows you where you can go and how close you are. The map is there to give you a general sense of direction but it’s mostly to make you feel how it’s pointless and there is no real infrastructure due to the story. The story is not really about the characters. It’s more about showing you how this can happen to anyone and how it feels, not the characters being memorable.This is a game that could have used some more polish but I still loved it. I’ve completed it within 4 straight days and I leave satisfied. €20 feels like a bit too much but the €12 I paid is fine. I could have played the Netflix version for free but I’m glad I got it on PC for the performance etc. Give the game a try if you like the lore of Demagog games and are a fan of strategy RPG while keeping expectations in check in terms of scope.

_childDocuments_.review: Highwater is great.  You and a rotating, motley crew, explore the ruins of Earth after an ecological disaster and every once in a while get in an Xcom style battle.  The Earth is flooded, you ride around in your inflatable raft, The Argo, and listen to Highwater Pirate Radio (The precursor to the excellent Radio Nostalgia from Mars, from Highwaters sister games, The Cub and Golf Club Nostalgia) and it is just as fantastic as in the other games from this developer.  The stylized graphics look great, the sound design is fantastic and the characters are wonderful.  I enjoyed playing this game a great deal, and I look forward to whatever is next from Demagog.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Highwater, the second entry of the Demagog franchise, and the third one I've played. Formerly an exclusive on Netflix for whole 6 people, the game is now released on Steam for all of us to play.The story is set after the environmental disaster and floods took place but before humanity's departure to Mars, and the game takes the form of third person exploration instead of two dimensional sidescrolling Golf Club: Wasteland or The Cub chose to adapt.The main plot of the story is very straightforward, a band of refugees are trying to get inside a rocket to escape to Mars, their last chance at salvation. but the developers must felt a certain amount of pressure lengthening the game with the core plot this simple because the writing here is subpar to be honest. all characters, for some reason have this overly chill, laidback attitude that's almost nihilistic. there's no sense of urgency and the game encourages this vibe by putting slow paced boat rides and indie folk music. Insurgents are referred to as a serious threat but they're depicted as an incompetent laughingstocks who don't even think to confiscate crowbars from their captives when you meet them, and there's a bandit Viking gang which I suspect is only put there to insert humor aspects into the game which I felt just dumb and off putting. Subtle worldbuilding that comes with collectibles feels stale now, while I agree with the most of the points the same message of technology ridden society sucks megacorpos bad multibillionaires evil is being preached to players without any difference in tone for 3 whole games at this point. Also some of the early areas are cheaply paced lore dumps and just riddled with collectibles. Okay, Elon Musk is an insufferable egomaniac, I GET IT. The predecessor of Radio Nostalgia, Highwater Pirate Radio, still exists with the same host but with not enough caller stories to fill the gaps between songs and public announcements it feels much less genuine than the one from Golf Club.Turn based combat, tolarable, but hardly enjoyable especially with Josephine being too overpowered with her chain attacks paired with ranged attacks from other characters. it's so easy you don't even need to spend the consumables given to you. The last boss is a pure joke, with only 2 weak enemies serving as guards your goofy band of rejects will effectively make a pinata out of the boss.I also experienced few glitches, easy to spot ones like dialogues getting attributed to wrong characters and two word balloons spawning outside of the screen boundaries. A lack of QA on their part.I admire their effort in trying new approach to expand their IP but sadly this installment failed to meet my expectations set by their other games. recommended only for people who are really invested in this franchise. 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It should be a perfect game for me. Exploring a post apocolyptic flooded world on a power boat, searching little islands for some lore and the occasional turn based tactical skirmish all while listening to some chill tunes  on the radio. It all sounds appealing but I just found the implementation here to be a bit of let down. The games controls seems a bit wonky, the horizontal camera pan is reversed (at least for my brain) and although the game offers re-mapping changing this particular aspect seems to be an oversight.The world is mostly empty, the islands are all kind of samey, and the lore is never really that interesting. So exploration just feels unsatisfying.The tactics bits are fine and I appreciate the even have an undo button but it just lacks a bit of dept and feels very repetitive after a couple of battles.The radio DJ can provide a bit of world building at times but mostly its just kind of bland indie music that wasn't really to my taste.So overall although I get the game is going for chill but it kind of just comes off as boring.Regardless I think it would be harsh to give it a bad review since its not necessarily a bad game. Just wasn't my taste and I'm just more disappointed than anything. So despite everything I've said I'm still giving it a thumbs up, I'm sure other players will be able to get more out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I was excited when it was first announced, and it kinda sat on my backshelf for a while, but now that i've played it all in one go (about five hours) I find myself woefully disappointed. I can't even tell if the devs cared that much, i'm sure they did, but theres just so many bugs and such they could have caught simply by playing the game through right before launch. The story is kind of all over the place with a pretty whatever ending, not worth the time spent or payoff. And the combat is frankly a joke and a waste of time basically the whole way through, either being the most trivial of logic puzzles or being utterly trivialized by characters you get halfway through the game. The characters aren't really that compelling either, despite experiencing them for five solid hours I didn't really feel like I actually got to know them, or care about them. The views really had nothing to look at, a couple pretty vistas and nothing more. And I swear the game wasn't translated properly. At one point out of nowhere a singer just starts singing in spanish with no hints of any spanish speaking anywhere in the game at all? At the end of the day, was not a good experience. I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: After some thinking, I've decided to recommend this game, but  please bear in mind that this is a very reluctant thumbs up, as Highwater is quite a mixed bag of positives and negatives. It has interesting ideas and cool concepts, but it falls short in its execution.The story has some nice hooks and a really well-crafted narrative arc, but the backdrop is your run-of-the-mill post-apocalyptic world and the characters feel flat. The interesting thing is that they feel distinctive enough during gameplay, as each one of them has different movesets and mechanics, but the developers have failed to translate this diversity into the dialogue.Take Nikos, our main protagonist, for example, who behaves like a support during combat encounters. He can taunt our enemies to draw them away from his friends, he can interrupt attacks with the flash of his camera, and use a fishing rod to pull targets towards him with, setting them up for a combo or placing them in the way of environmental hazards. However, his kind-hearted nature and need to protect others is never explored or even shown in the cutscenes. To be fair, he does give some food to an orphanage in the first act of the campaign, but then leaves the children behind without a second thought, so I don't know if this counts as an example of his supportive nature.Or have a look at Josephine, one of our main DPSs. She has a fun (and rather OP) trait called Bloodlust, which gives her another turn after every meele kill. This rewards aggressive in-your-face fighting when we control her, yet when it comes to dialouge, her recklessness is nowhere to be found. She is just as mild and well-tempered as the rest of our crew.The gameplay also has its ups and downs. Cruising around in our boat while listening to Highwater Pirate Radio can be chill, and there are also a few set pieces that look jaw-dropping, even with the not very detailed graphics. As a high voltage electrical engineer, I found the flooded wind turbines to be the most breathtaking part, but there are a few other locations that are well worth a look too.But aside from discovering these aforementioned locations, there is not much else to do as the turn-based combat begins to feel repetitive and uninspired after the first hour or so. To be fair, there are a few fun encounters towards the end of the campaign, but we have to make our way through a lot of slow and dull fights to get there.It is also worth mentioning that the Steam store page boasts about the clever use of the environment in these battles, but in reality these options are either absent or they make the encounter trivial. For example there is a map where you have to defend three generators, which the enemies can approach from two chokeholds, full of environmental hazards. I lost two out of my five characters in the first round of this encounter and still managed to win at the first attempt, thanks to the hazards doing my work for me and killing most of the targets.All in all I see the potential in Highwater but I think it's important to point out the flaws in its execution. If you really like turn based combat or climate fiction, you should give it a try, otherwise I would say wait for a sale maybe.

_childDocuments_.review:
Amid the Great Climate Catastrophe, the flooded region of Hightower has become a kind of safe zone between the two dry regions: the nearly global ravaged land of the War Zone, and the fortified city of Alphaville, where the ultra-rich live behind giant walls.

With life on Earth becoming untenable for humans, and rumors of an escape to Mars floating around, Nikos begins a perilous journey, picking up friends along the way. First to Hightower, then beyond to cross the impenetrable border of Alphaville, battling insurgents and stealing food along the way. Will Nikos and his friends manage to sneak into the rocket in time?

Highwater is a story-driven 3D adventure game with isometric turn-based combat set in a flooded post-apocalyptic urban environment. Navigate the world by boat, discover islands, and find new allies to help battle foes in turn-based combat.

name: Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2
detailed_description: A year has passed since the events of Fuga: Melodies of Steel. The war was fought and won. Life went on. That is, until the children are summoned to Pharaoh to aid with the investigation of the recovered Taranis. During their survey, the Taranis suddenly goes haywire and sets out on a deadly rampage, trapping and absconding with a number of their party. The remaining children and Malt board their erstwhile enemy—the dread tank Tarascus—to chase after the Taranis and save their friends. Revamped tactical battle system! New additions to the battle system based on player feedback such as the reworked Soul Cannon and newly implemented Managarm allows for cutting-edge tactical gameplay! Fight battles how you see fit! Plot your path forward on the branching routes of the battlefield. The new airship support system allows for even more options! Make every decision count! The choices you make affect the Judgment Gauges, ultimately changing how events play out. You are the author of your own story. The weight of despair, rage, and loss will shake you to your core in Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2—the RPG of hard choices and tough decisions! *It's not necessary to play Fuga: Melodies of Steel to enjoy Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2.

_childDocuments_.review: War is hell.One would think a game where using furry animal children as ammunition for a giant cannon would be a little more funny: launching a screaming kindergarten girl at enemy forces while the opposing general asks what in the name of Mr. Rogers is wrong with you.Instead, it's one of the most gut-wrenching outcomes possible in the game, one you will do anything to circumvent if you've anything resembling a soul. The formula from the original Fuga hasn't really changed too much. Each party member specializes in one of three weapons- the swift but weak machine gun, the jack of all trades grenade launcher, and the no-subtlety-included cannon. You can only have three members manning weapons at once, with one back up member supporting each 'gunner' with varying effects.Combat is very simple at first glance. Most (90%) of enemies can be delayed by enough hits from one or more of the three weapon types, helpfully indicated by the clock icons hovering over an enemy. Smack them with the right weapons, and you can delay their turn, allowing you time to pick off enemies, heal, recharge, or any number of tactical decisions.As before, the entire party shares a HP and SP meter. Judging when to use skills that consume precious sp will be a major issue throughout the game- there are multiple recovery spots that refill hp, sp, or both, but getting to them sometimes means passing up the chance to get materials to upgrade your tank or experience for your crew.Upgrading the tank requires time during intermissions and increasingly precious materials, and so the real difficulty of FUGA begins to rear it's head- resource and time management. Battles can leave your crew- composed of children, I should reiterate- fearful, injured, or depressed, which all require mental and physical care. Beyond that, each crew member has their own desires as to what they want to do- sleeping, farming, upgrading, cooking, etc.- and satisfying these requests not only results in more experience, but increases their morale, allowing them to eventually enter a super mode in which their strengths are magnified.Beyond that are the links between crew members. Here, friendship translates not only into warm and fuzzy feelings, but also bursts of massive destruction that can turn the tides of more difficult battles, as well as increased benefits when they act as support to each other. Link attacks all share a common theme of doing tremendous amounts of damage, but also have additional effects you will need to reserve for the right moment to best capitalize on- some link attacks restore crucial HP or SP, while another might leave enemies engulfed in flames or delay every enemies' turn.Managing all the above upgrades, healing, and interaction all draws from a limited pool of AP each intermission. 20 to be exact. Balancing this along with the limited funds you'll accrue from fighting and exploring ruins means you'll have to decide where to build on and where to cut corners, to avoid getting into desperate situations that require one of two last resorts- the Managram and the Soul Cannon.The Managram deals massive damage to all foes, with two costs- no experience is gained from the battle, and the selected crew member used as ammo is rendered unconscious until they rest during an intermission. This serves as a second-to-last resort; expensive but far preferable to it's bigger, nastier brother: the Soul Cannon.The Soul Cannon activates when your tank takes a critical amount of damage, but FUGA 2 goes a step further than the original. Before, the Soul Cannon became an OPTION to use when things were looking grim- the choice as to when to fire, and who to sacrifice was entirely up to the player.In FUGA 2, your resident pragmatic AI takes the nail-biting decision of choosing who to sacrifice out of your hands by selecting someone at random, with no regard to their level, placement as a gunner, or how desperately you don't want them to die. Once selected, a countdown begins to firing, during which you will need to find a way to end the battle before one of your allies is consumed to save the rest. The Managram, while not an immediate "I Win" button, may be the lesser of two evils in such situations.This is not to say that said AI- Hax- will load a kid into the cannon the moment your tank's paint job gets scuffed. During intermissions, you may have an opportunity to offer up a prayer to the soul cannon, which can lower the threshold at which it begins the firing sequence. More immediately, however, you can use skills and items to restore HP, thus preventing yourself from ever reaching a point that you're forced into desperate measures.And then there's Malt.Malt is the guy through whom you make choices that affect Empathy and Resolution, with Empathy being realizing that you are, in fact, a bunch of children who have been thrust into another war, cutting slack in such regards, and generally putting others lives and well-being first. Resolution is about results, and if that means ignoring a smoldering town to pursue an enemy or being a hardened drill sergeant to make sure your crew survives the next encounter, so be it.The gameplay punishes poor decision making, but not so severely as more masochistic titles like Darkest Dungeon. If you're looking for solid tactical gameplay with the occasional emotional gutpunch, look no further.

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel to using furry children as live ammunition game.CC2 delivers another fantastic entry in the Little Tail Bronx series.Fun new systems to play with, and a slightly annoying graphical bug aboard your steel clad home remains unfixed. Visuals cute, story really good, music is great, game is great. As story focused as a game like this is, the only other minor gripe I would have is that the recap doesn't really do a very solid job of re-capping anything. It's a clip show with dialogue playing out the events of the prior game. This of course isn't a problem if you have played the first game, and I would recommend you do so anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my  if you want to know more about the first game.One year after the events of FUGA 1, what’s left of the kid-heroes are forced to embark on a new quest, this time against their former, faithful war machine gone rogue fr yet-unknown reasons. Between sentient war remnants resurrected by ancient technology, and a new enemy that threatens Gasco once again, the kids’ work is far from done yet.FUGA 2 is set in the floating archipelago of islands formed after the conclusion of the first game. Despite the war being over, recent events plummeted the region into chaos nonetheless. The ‘ancient tech going FUBAR’ trope is a nice excuse to reuse a lot of the assets and enemies seen in the first game, despite there being novel additions with a focus on Ancient war technology. A few new characters are introduced, but most of the main cast will be the same, with consistently well-written and distinct personalities, and an abundance of interactions.The writing of dialogues and story is of good make, despite some weird sentences due to the translation from Japanese. The plot is engaging and has some clever twists, however the way characters react is predictable and some dialogues can’t help but feel cheesy, dipped in shounen anime shenanigans like “the power of friendship beats everything” and the likes. Still, good enough.The linear path ahead, in each chapter, will be divided in various branches, each hosting a number of loot caches, enemy encounters and special events. Although these paths are fixed, you can’t know what enemies you’ll face, and the decision on which one to take will be yours: remember that higher risk means higher rewards under all aspects, from items to XP and cash. Taking the hardest ones will see you strapped for HP and MP, and your crew usually demolished, debuffed and fatigued, but on the other hand you’ll have plenty of cash and material for upgrades at the next Intermission, regular breaks to recuperate and manage your crew. What FUGA lacks in freedom of direction when exploring the world, it makes up for in events variety and the surprise factor.Combat works in a turn-based fashion, with your mobile fortress having three weapon types available: machine guns, launchers and cannons, each of them with different action speeds, accuracy, damage and effectiveness against specific enemies. For instance, taking out airborne enemies will require an MG’s precision, while you’ll want to use cannons for heavier enemies, but not before stripping out their armor with special attacks. Each of the kids has a specific weapon assigned to them, and a unique roster of abilities: some youngsters are more inclined to a support role, others pure damage, or debuffing your foes. The hot-swap function, available every three turns, allows dynamically changing the available guns and kids so that you can have the formation that works best against the current enemy. Based on their affinity, cultivated during intermission phases and also by fighting together, children may have morale surges that trigger their special passive abilities, and also unlock Link Attacks with their favorite battle partners, often inflicting damage to all enemies alongside potent passive effects. Battles are highly tactical and dynamic, as you’ll have to know what each kid does best, and use that feature at the right moment, while also juggling the tank’s HP, MP and eventual debuffs your crew may have, like Fear reducing accuracy or Depression, making them unable to act until the next Intermission, to name some. It sounds complex, but the game does a great job in gradually introducing the mechanics in a seamless, friendly way. Boss fights are the zenith of this system, and a true test of your preparation and tactical prowess.Intermission phases are crucial to absolve a number of functions. During these times, you’ll be able to upgrade the tank using parts salvaged from enemies and random loot, or bought at shops. Cook for your crew to grant long-lasting buffs, manage the crops and farm to have materials, select individual kids to manually talk to each other, and pay attention to the Wish Diary that will grant morale boosts, extra XP if enough desires are fulfilled. You'll have only 20 Action Points each phase, and actions have varying costs: optimizing and prioritizing them for the maximum efficiency is critical - choose wisely. This system gives a much-needed respite from combat, breaks the main gameplay loop, and gives a new dimension to the strategic elements - a great addition.Alongside the paths you’ll sometimes encounter greater activities that consist of minigames of their own. For instance, Ruins morph the gameplay into a 2D platformer-puzzle of sorts, having the kids navigate old ruins, avoiding or killing enemies, and managing bullets as a key resource to destroy obstacles and operate machinery, in FUGA 2 with added elemental effects, compared to the previous chapters. Finding the Treasure Key, not getting your kids mauled by traps and finding all items will result in a higher rating. Settlements feature dialogues with civilians that influence Malt, the leader of the group,’s Disposition towards either a ruthless commander or a gentle soul, unlocking unique passive abilities as a result. Other than that, you’ll be able to buy and sell materials, better seeds / cattle and consumables.

_childDocuments_.review: An improvement nearly across the board over the original. This is very much "Fuga 1, but more" and I'm very happy about it.The basic gameplay is the same, however they've added several new enemy types and revamped old ones that spice up encounters and make some of them really annoying (in a good way... I think). The new "pack attack" mechanic forces you to delay or eliminate enemies of the same type before they can band together for a very damaging attack. Ally abilities have been changed around and altered significantly, and even their weapons have changed in some cases. You'll need a different mindset when tackling this game compared to the first, and it's not unwelcome.Malt is now properly the main character of the story, providing an anchor for the main cast. You make Malt decide between Empathetic or Resolute actions, which unlock gameplay bonuses as you gain more of each meter. The dialogue is much improved over the first game's. Though there are some conversations that slip back into the "one character says one line of dialogue at a time as we go through the cast" problem of the first game, at least they react to each others' lines this time around.I found the story itself to be an overall improvement over the original, though for better or worse this is another case where some things were not changed. At times I found it to retread ground from the first game, but I didn't see it as a wholly bad thing. As I approached the end I was worried it was going to fall apart and my praise of the early story for naught, but it actually came together wonderfully. I walked away from the story more than satisfied.I can't wait to see where CyberConnect2 takes this series next.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review I have not yet completed the game, and afterward I'll give try to write a more complete review, but so far it's very clear that this game is everything that was promised and more. To call it simply an upgrade from its previous iteration is missing the big picture. Fuga 2 completes the first game in a way I can hardly explain, but not only that it opens up the entire series to new depths that continually excites me every time I discover it does indeed go deeper than it already has.If you have not yet played the original Fuga, then I highly recommend you start with that game before playing this one. Fuga 2 is incredibly story-focused, and as a direct continuation from the events of the first game you won't be able to appreciate just how much the writing is able to tug your heart strings. Although sometimes it feels as if the writing could see a little improvement, the developers' ability to effortlessly balance sharing moments with cute furry children alongside their bravery in the face of emotional stress from dealing with constant battle, loss and fatigue, being able to personally help forge and engage with the bonds that tie the crew together, and picking at the mysterious plot threads that tie the story together really drew me into the game in a way I don't often get to see other games pull off. Plus, I just like seeing how much has been built up from what was established for the world and characters in the previous game.The worst thing you can say about the gameplay is that it's almost completely identical to the first game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. If you enjoyed the previous game, then you'll appreciate the extra features and rebalanced combat system that keeps the game interesting.What I love is most that each of these new features feel like such a natural extension to the game. A lot of effort went into giving each piece of content a purpose, though as of now I'm still waiting to see where they're going with Malt's new Leadership mechanics.Aesthetically, this game is as beautiful as ever. The art, the music, even the GUI are masterfully crafted and with such a unique and polished charm that is reminiscent of nostalgic console RPGs of yore. It really feels like I'm picking up an old classic like Valkyria Chronicles or Fire Emblem and discovering for the first time why gamers fell in love with it. These devs deserve some love, so please pick it up and give it a try. This is a quality game that you don't see most other Steam titles quite able to measure up to.

_childDocuments_.review: This game series is quite solid. You didn't disappoint me with the first one, which was a pleasant surprise, and this sequel is also great. It was fun. Yes. Perfect? Not for everyone. Was it worth it? Yeah, although I think they should have sold it for $30 at release, because the game, while great, is a budget game that should be treated as a budget game. Fuga 2 has a ton of competition in the $40+ bracket. I honestly think it has difficulty competing because much cheaper games are out there. Fuga, and games like it, only are loved because their story exists. They often take away, leaving us begging for the completion of the story, and the fulfillment must pay off. This one does. However, upon completion, such games lose value for a time. This might seem like a bad thing, but it isn't because this game fulfilled its obligation to pay off the story. Did they sequel bait? Sure, but Fuga 2 is fulfilling, and that's what matters. In a world where I recently suffered the plotholes and unfinished ideas of Visions of Mana, and the terrible payoff of some platformer games, I am thankful that Fuga put in some serious effort.It's an RPG where your tank kids each have a gun but share a health and energy pool. Save the world from the evil ancient human boy with bad tank that and save your friends.Here are my only gripes:Your game needs English dubs, because I do believe it could catch a bigger audience with them.You need to release Tail Concerto and Solotolobo for Steam. You have some strong difficulty jumps at moments. although they are manageable.You also deserve bigger recognition for your games.You should have sold it for $10 less, although that's just my personal theory on marketing your game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have never played a "little tail bronx" series game before its ok, no one has lol just jump in. The series is actually over 25 years old and more of a passion project for the developer rather than a mass market IP.  Within you will find a rather unique blend of steam punk, Japanese pretending to be french, an over the top detailed world and at a surface level furries i guess...although they are actually humans. Deepest lore. Just like the previous games in the series, Tail Concerto, Solar to robo and Little Tail, the gameplay is...typically Japanese. Stuck in the 1990s. Basic, bare bones and sorely lacking vs any modern western offerings. Fuga gameplay is your typical press turn affair. Attack/Defend/Special. Rock/Paper/Scissors. Not really a bad thing, just don't expect any big brain gameplay haha. Its all about the world building, art and character stories....Which are all great. The world is packed with detail, the characters have lots of interactions with each other and the world around them. Its not quite got the epic soundtrack like Solar to Robo but i do like me some steam punk faux french mystic japan tank driving. Im pretty sure there are dozens of art books and novels of lore about this setting. If you are ok with lots of story and shallow gameplay this isn't a bad purchase at all. And yes, you can still launch those furry kids out the cannon for the god emperor haha

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun JRPG experience that serves as a solid follow-up to the iconic Fuga: Melodies of Steel.Story is somewhat like the original game in terms of the morality and hardships of war, while the gameplay mechanics have been expanded somewhat while still maintaining the core loop of switching child soldiers in battle, delaying enemy attacks with machine gun/grenade launcher/cannon match-ups while raising affinity, upgrading the giant tank and doing farming chores and resource expeditions during intermissions.In Fuga 1, the Soul Cannon was an optional resource to use for overcoming a difficult boss fight: When the tank HP drops below half, you can choose to instantly vaporize the boss by sacrificing one of the children to the Soul Cannon.In Fuga 2, the Soul Cannon will automatically select a child to be harvested if the tank HP drops below a certain benchmark, and your only options are to either defeat the boss in a set number of turns or use the Managarm, an alternate weapon that merely knocks out of the children instead of killing them outright. Or, you can spend six intermission action points to pray to the Soul Cannon and disable the automatic selection outright, which is convenient.The story about the perils of revenge isn't exactly a novel concept, but I respect the characters and the developers enough to approach the story as it is, blatant sequel hooks aside.

_childDocuments_.review: Fuga 2 takes everything I loved about the first game and basically improves on it (well, maybe not so much the story).This is the kind of sequel where playing its predecessor first will definitely enhance your experience. Yes, there’s a recap of the first game’s story in the main menu, but Fuga 1 and 2 really deserve to be played back-to-back since the sequel focuses on the same group of kids.In terms of difficulty, you can tell that CC2 really wanted to up the stakes with the sequel. Battles will feel harder than the first game to begin with, but again, if you have prior knowledge of the combat, you shouldn’t have much of a problem.But the main draw of the increased difficulty comes in the form of the reworked Soul Cannon system. Basically, if the Taranis is at less than 50% HP (or lower thresholds depending on how many times you pray to the Soul Cannon before bosses), one of the kids is randomly selected to be shot out of it after a 20-turn timer expires.I imagine most people will probably nope out and reload if they’re going for the True Ending, but this new system can make for some very tight saves if you’re taking too much of a beating and can still beat a boss while that timer is ticking down.While the new additions may not be for everyone, Fuga 2 is pretty much everything I could’ve ever wanted in a sequel to a game about cute little French furry children who take the fight to “totally not dog Nazis” in a tank that might as well be a giant Metal Slug.
_childDocuments_.name: Fuga: Melodies of Steel 2

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel to the first Fuga game, it's an enhanced version of the first game generally with a few new mechanics, and a slightly more involved system of choice and consequence.Visually it looks about the same, UI, character design, world setting; it's all very similar to the first.  Music and sound is also much the same, even down to Japanese and French as the only voice options.The characters are a year older, and since they were (sometimes very young) children in the first game, there's a fair bit of growth and change between them.  This includes how they generally look, their personalities and mindsets, and changes in how they interact with each other and how they play as game characters.  Several characters have different skills, roles, or even weapons which can throw you off a bit from the first game.  Only Malt, Boron, and Mei are relatively unchanged, other characters are slightly to extremely different from their role in the first.  Some changes represent their character growth (especially Sheena), others reflect upon the needs of the group (such as Chick).Combat is basically the same, except that you now have additional leader skills Malt can do randomly, which are based around a new choice and consequence system.  Difficulty is close to the same, with some spikes and valleys just like the first game.  Chapter 9 and 10 are pretty spikey, with a lot of long, dangerous, and drawn out resource draining fights while a few other chapters are less so.Storywise it's a bit more mixed.  I like some of the story aspects, but also felt some fell flat a bit.  It's not as cohesive as the first game's war story.  Overall it's a little darker, with a few more twists.  You do find out the reason the Taranis was built to be operated by children if you read the lore notes which was a bit of a mystery in the first.A few new features are:* The Soul Cannon is a bigger threat, and not a last resort thing you never want to use.  When you reach a certain HP threshold chapter 3 and on, you will have a character randomly chosen (a small number of story significant characters can never be chosen until the resolution of their story) and you have 20 turns (remember each action is considered a turn) to kill your foe or the Soul Cannon will fire, killing that character.* There's a Managarm cannon as a new addition.  This can be used in any battle to do massive damage but will cost you the XP and knock out a character you choose to power it.  The character is not lost, but cannot be used until the next intermission when you spend 5 AP to have them sleep.* There's a morality system, several decisions will give you an option for Empathy or Resolution.  Empathy emphasizes supporting your teammates, helping out citizens, and provides more defensive leadership skills.  Resolution emphasizes working toward a goal, and provide more offensive leadership skills.  Endings are determined by your placement on this morality meter.Overall, it's more of the same, but better gameplay wise.  Story is more mixed but it does explain some of the lore and mysteries from the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: You kinda need to play the first game otherwise much of the narrative context will be lost and the beats won't hit as hard but if you have, Fuga 2 is a great follow-up and improves in basically every meaningful way on its predecessor with much snappier plot pacing and a story that constantly evolves with new developments, better UI streamlining and more interesting combat balance with the new Soul Cannon creating a lot of tension and recovery items being far more limited. I think the game is a little harder as a result but you really shouldn't play this without playing the first anyway so that's probably fine?Great sequel, looking forward to being obsessed with the third game too.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Fuga 1, Fuga 2 is a better game in nearly every way.  You should definitely play it.If you haven't played Fuga 1, go do that first; this game is a direct sequel, and you'll want the context of the first game.  If a game about tactical, turn-based tank combat and furry kids being sent to war sounds at all interesting to you, go check it out.If you're curious specifically how it's improved:  Characters have new abilities and are significantly rebalanced; there's a wider variety of enemies and the game keeps introducing new mechanics for them further in the game; the story is paced better and not all rushed at the end; and there are a variety of new systems introduced, like airship travel, an empathy vs. resolution alignment system, and a new superweapon, the Managarm, that is guaranteed to win a fight but knocks a child unconscious and causes you to lose all XP for that fight.Possibly the most interesting change is a bit of an early-game spoiler, but if you don't mind: If I were to make  complaint, it would be that I don't think the soundtrack is as good as the first game.  It's still good, with some beautiful vocal themes, and I'll be listening to it outside of the game, but it doesn't have quite the same energy that the first game's soundtrack did.

_childDocuments_.review: Fuga: Melodies of Steel was my game of the year for 2021.It was a game I wasn't expecting to get a sequel, but here we are.Lemme say out of the gate that presentation is as good as the first game, with improvements across the board. Music, art, characters... everything is top tier, at least to me.Story is as gripping as the first game, as it did make me invested in everything that is going on with the plot, even if it does have a faint bit of sequelitis about it. Twists and turns happened throughout that kept me on the edge of my seat. That being said, it is best if you played the first one from start to finish with the best ending, as that is cannon and this game picks up a year after all that chaos in the original.The gameplay really stands out, as past characters have been given altered kits, and the mechanics are as well rounded as the first game, but this game has a bit more of a punch when it comes to it. I found myself switching out more often, using items and scrapping the bottom of the barrel for resources, I interacted with options I didn't use in the first game. And the rework to the Soul Cannon as well as the Managarm added into the mix actually made some bosses intense, with me having to use the Managarm several times in the game, for both bosses and elites when I picked a fight I couldn't win in the long run.Overall, fantastic game. Improvements across the board to the entire formula, and I am happy that I got this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A sequel that makes minor but all positive changes to what was originally already solid tactical game with good artwork.Fuga 2 has the same gameplay as the original title, fate again has the children aboard a powerful tank chasing down the one they used in the previous game that has been commandeered by someone who has also taken some of cast hostage. You fight 1-3 waves of various enemies making use of each characters weapon type (machine gun, grenade launcher, or cannon), their base damage, speed, and crit skills, their unique skills that use the tank's SP, and the passive bonus each character gives when placed in a support role for one of the three active gunners that can be something like additional damage or HP regeneration. Enemies may be be easier to hit with a certain type of weapon or hitting them with certain attacks may delay their turns. Between battles your tank travels across the chapter's terrain giving you options of taking easier or more dangerous paths that will likely have more items and less regenerating supplies but more items and experience. Reaching certain points in each chapter allows you to spend AP to have the characters talk to raise their affinity with each other for stronger support bonuses, cook meals for stat improvements, grow food to cook those meals, upgrade weapons, sleep for an XP boost and to recover injured characters, speak to depressed characters to help them recover, etc.The main changes from the previous game are that some of the characters abilities and weapon types have changed, partially to avoid some easily exploitable strategies and due to having one old character not playable for this game. An airship can be run into on the map that you can pay to drop replenishing supplies for you, pay to bomb enemy targets on the map so you won't have to fight them, buy and sell items at a shop, or you can pay to transport your tank back so that you can travel alternate paths for more more items and experience. The soul cannon of the first game that allowed you to sacrifice a character to win a battle has been changed, no longer being just a pointless inclusion no one would have a desire to ever use. In normal fights the soul cannon is replaced with a different powerful attack that will injure one of the characters and remove them from the battle and cause you to receive no experience for the fight. When fighting bosses the new AI inside of your tank will automatically activate the soul cannon if you reach a certain percentage of health where a character is then random chosen to be sacrificed unless you can win the battle in a set number of turns. While I never even came close to having the soul cannon used (or even activated) this is certainly a more interesting method of use than in the previous game and there are events that can only show up in certain chapter if particular characters are alive or dead, so you can see them repercussions from losing a character aside from just gameplay ones. A new addition is the ability to build up empathy or resolve points based on conversation choices that allow the main character access to passive bonuses that can be activated in battle when you pass certain thresholds, depending on if you are focusing on building one up or a combination of both you can also see different events while traveling.The only problems that remain are the nonsensical way some information is given. Your abilities and support bonuses just don't make clear what they are actually doing and you really need to try things out to see what is good or not as it just writing nonsense like does a large amount or gigantic amount of damage is meaningless especially when comparing different skills that can be somewhere between level 1-3 where they get better but see no description change when it comes to damage. You also run into merchants that just say that they have stuff and you can either pay some money to get some thing, some more money to get more things, or pay nothing to be given an item that would have been part of what they can sell for free. I can't understand why anyone thought this was a good idea or something that even makes sense, one of Malt's responses of refusal even seems to be him saying he would need to see the supplies before paying for anything.Fuga still has good different tactical gameplay and good music, and the sequel hasn't made any large changes but it has made some minor improvements and good additions.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: I admit, I was somewhat skeptical about what this game would be like after seeing the Secret Movie in the first game. However, from the first minute to the very end I saw that my fears were entirely unfounded. This sequel matches or surpasses the first game in just about every aspect.The plot to the game initially isn't quite as interesting as in the first, but it does eventually prove equally as captivating in the mysteries it poses and the lore it expounds upon. But above all, Fuga is a series foremost about emotional storytelling, and this game's focus on loss and grief certainly hits just as powerful as anything from the first. One thing I did appreciate about the first game is how it focused on the twelve children in almost equal measure, maybe excepting Britz for story reasons. Now that Malt is THE main character of the story it feels like some others, such as Socks and Boron, fall by the wayside in terms of character growth. Even Malt's actions seem somewhat out of character for him, as if only to drive the plot forward, but does resolve itself in a satisfying enough way. On the plus side, we do get newcomer Vanilla who is an absolutely amazing character! The villain is also quite interesting. At first I thought he was super sinister and got really invested in him, then he became kind of plain and boring, but then THAT THING happens and the villain becomes really incredible again. Also, those two grandpas... I never thought I'd EVER end up liking those two characters, but over the course of the game I found myself growing SO attached to those lovable oldies.On the topic of gameplay, things are massively improved here. While some of the characters retain their weapons of choice from the first game, some have switched things up and mounted a new gun, helping to keep things fresh. Skills have also seen a change where everyone learns half the number of skills (5 down from 10) but each skill has three levels, becoming more powerful as the gunner levels up. Enemies, too, have a few new tricks up their sleeves. The tank can now be afflicted with a number of new status ailments, making battling these new foes all the more tactical and challenging. I also like how you aren't just drowning in Energy Cells and Repair Kits this time around. Seriously, the first game is a cakewalk compared to what this one has to offer. Lastly, the Soul Cannon... In the first game you never needed to use it and it felt inconsequential as a result. Not to spoil anything, but the Soul Cannon's implementation in this game is MUCH better.The music is, as you'd expect, spot on. The main theme "Wherever the Wind Takes Us" is my new favorite song in the entire series. The reuse of one song in particular during two fights in the final chapter put a big smile on my face. The track playing in chapter four hit me in the nostalgia harder than anything ever has in my entire life. Yeah, it's good. Also, I love all the new voice lines the children have gotten. Even the new takes on the same lines from the first game. What's more, they now get a cool megaphone filter when you attack an enemy with a skill. With that kind of A+ sound design it's no wonder that Mei's anguished whimpers during the boss battle in chapter one left permanent emotional scars on my soul.I love this game, I really do. I love the first one, too. You should play both. And get excited for the third game, I know I am!

_childDocuments_.review: An upgrade over the first game in every conceivable way. Aggressive play is now a lot more viable and rewarding, and there's more player freedom in general to pick out different tactics. I do think the plot stumbles in a few places, but on the whole, this even darker-toned sequel does so many things right in the gameplay and tone department that it more than makes up for it.Enthusiastically recommended. _childDocuments_.review: Do you like turn based JRPG combat? Then you should absolutely play this game, it has some of the best around. Do you not like turn based JRPG combat? You should play this anyways, it might change your mind. It has you juggling a large group of characters, each of which use one of 3 weapon types with their own spin on it, in and out of three active turrets on your supertank. Effectively you have a party of three active characters (plus three support characters, each assigned to one of the active roles) at a time all operating off of the same hp/mp bar for the tank. You can rotate who is in what slot on the fly giving a huge degree of flexibility in how you can approach a situation.Of course Fuga has a lot to love about it besides just the combat, though that is the main thing you will be doing in it. The cast of characters are all likable, the art is charming, and the story hits some good emotional beats. Said story follows a group of children as they pilot a supertank to fight against a new threat to save their friends and their country, struggling along the way with the pursuit of revenge. Also they're all french and furries.One thing to note is that this game is a sequel, and while it has a recap on the main menu for the first game it doesn't do a great job of telling you what all happened. Fortunately Fuga 1 is also an extremely good game, and well worth your time so if you're interested in this but haven't played the first then you should really go fix that. They even updated it with the QoL features they put in the second!

_childDocuments_.review: Fuga: Memories of Steel 2 is the direct sequel of the first game and part of a planned trilogy developed by CyberConnect2. This series is part of a universe that originally started with a ‘90s game called , which presented a world populated by dog and cat people. The first Fuga introduced an alternative version of France invaded by Bermans soldiers who captured people and turned them into slaves. Our protagonists, a group of children from a small village, managed to find an ancient powerful tank and use it to fight back in order to save their beloved families. This is essentially the first game plotline, but there is much more to it and Fuga 2 includes a recap for those who are new to the series. Unfortunately, this recap is very confusing, so I would suggest just looking for a YouTube recap to get a better idea of what happened during the first game, if you are not planning to play it. Playing the first game is recommended only if you would like to connect more with the protagonists themselves, but in terms of gameplay Fuga 2 is a better game overall. The game starts one year after the war against the Berman Empire, won by our young group of protagonists. Some of them are now summoned by the authorities to do some tests on the Taranis, the powerful tank they used to fight against the Bermans. Unfortunately, the Taranis suddenly traps the kids inside and escapes. The rest of the children, guided by their leader, Malt, decide to drive the Tarascus, a special tank used by the main antagonist during the first game, to chase the Taranis and save their friends. During this journey our protagonists will face brutal challenges and emotionally shocking moments in a captivating story that will certainly be appreciated by those who love fantasy war-themed animes with supernatural elements.The most important story and gameplay factor is that our protagonists can use the Soul Cannon, a powerful weapon capable of defeating any foe by sacrificing a child. Although the first Fuga, just like this sequel, features multiple endings also based on the number of children alive, the game doesn’t keep track of them and there is only one canon ending where everyone survives. I don’t know the developers’ intention here, but if feels weird seeing some children die in the first game (and the others being shocked) while in the second game they are all back alive. It’s a pity because the story could have been deeper if only the player’s progress and various endings could be transferred onto the next games (like in  and  games). That also makes the entire concept of the Soul Cannon less meaningful, because children die if you use it and you probably won’t get the best ending, but in the next game you will find them alive as if nothing happened.In terms of gameplay, Fuga 2 is a classic RPG with turn-based combat. You move the tank through a linear route that sometimes splits up into multiple paths of variable difficulty and rewards. Each point of the route will feature an event, such as a battle, a chance to refill your tank HP/SP or a moment to spend some quality time inside your tank, upgrading it or simply socializing with the crew. Additionally, there is a new feature that allows fast travel between already-explored sections (maybe try a different path) through an airship. Turn-based battles are essentially the same ones from the first game, with only minor improvements. Two children can control each part of the tank (such as the cannon or the machine gun), with the rest being available as backup. Swapping them is fundamental because they have different skills and linked abilities if the duo has a high level of affinity. Sometimes they can also enter Hero Mode, which doubles the inflicted damage. All enemies have weaknesses based on the type of weapon you use; if you use the correct weapon you can delay their turn multiple times. As mentioned, the Soul Cannon can be used against powerful bosses by sacrificing one child. Personally I never found myself in the position to use it, also because it’s much easier to retry a boss fight instead of losing a child forever. Plus, this time there is a new weapon: The Managarm. This cannon works like the Soul Cannon, but deals less damage while only temporarily incapacitating one child. The trade-off is that you don’t get any experience from battle if you use it, and experience is very important for your characters to level up and obtain new skills. Combat is generally very easy if you follow the normal path and not that hard if you follow the most difficult one, with only few boss battles being really challenging.When you are not fighting you will always be in your tank, spending time with the rest of the crew. You spend AP to talk during these intermissions, as well for doing any upgrade to the different areas of the tank or for doing any other activity such as cooking, farming or sleeping. Making the children talk to each other is extremely important as it increases their bond level (with benefits during battles) and unlocks Link Events (basically short dialogue scenes). Sometimes you will also be able to visit towns and speak to different NPCs who will inform you about the state of the world, buy your stuff and sell their own stuff. A new addition also sees Malt, the group leader, having two traits, Empathy and Resolution, which are affected by the choices you make during certain dialogues. This will unlock Leader Skills (very useful during battles) and change some of Malt’s replies, but overall it’s a pretty basic system.Visually the game is wonderful as always, but it is clear that multiple assets from the first game have been reused, like those for the tank interior and the user interface. It’s the same for the music and sound effects, which are pretty much borrowed from the previous game. I would have loved to see more changes in these departments, considering this is an indie game being sold with a price slightly above average.Even if it is almost identical to its predecessor, Fuga: Memories of Steel 2 works perfectly thanks to well-written dialogues, an interesting cast of characters (you would feel more attached to them if you’ve played the first game) and small new additions that improve the experience. While combat is generally simple and easy, the story is always captivating and enjoyable, especially if you love war themed animes.

_childDocuments_.review: A good follow-up for Fuga: Melodies of Steel 1. A lot of the same basic concepts and mechanics, but several new variations and a change-up to several enemy types and the skill sets of your characters. Perhaps it was having just completed the first of the two games, and being fairly used to turn and timeline based strategy games, but this one felt somehow easier? Being able to shop for tank parts rather than have to barter up/down for them like in game 1 made it so I seemed ahead of the curve in many spots. However, I am not discounting some of the downright dirty moves some of these enemies have been given such as HP/SP Drain, Counterattack, or the familiar Depression and Injury debuffs. A very aggressive playstyle is warranted to ensure some of these more powerful enemies do not get a chance. I was constantly low on SP, but the resolution choice skill line granting a chance for a small SP restore when below 1/3, and a support pairing restoring 1-3 SP on basic attacks(based on affinity level) always kept me afloat.Again, as with the first game the second play-through felt worth it to finish upgrading and maxing out the tank. And while I managed all the steam achievements in 2 go-arounds, I did need another partial run to get a few more Affinity level 10's due to the secret gears on the main menu requiring more than the 30 for the achievement. Also, as with the first game, I took specific prompts seriously and made sure a key character had plenty of high affinity bonds with other characters. And out of habit refused to make use of the super-weapon options. Though I did have one close call with under 10 actions left till one of my crew, picked at random by the tank's new onboard AI, would have been spaghettified into pure soul energy and blasted at the enemy. Zealously keep HP high during bosses folks, or the boss battle can suddenly become a timed event!Again, glad the achievements do not include the 'Bad Endings' as a requirement for steam 100%, even if my in game journal is lacking all of the possible bad ending scenes of some, to specific members, to all of the crew being dead at the end of the game. Would be a bit too much of a chore to "Truly" 100% everything, but after 38 hours I got the secret main menu scene, so that is good enough for me.I would totally support future games from this developer/studio, and to be fair 38 hours of great/engaging content is more than many so called AAA studios can offer these days.
