_childDocuments_.review: I've never seen what would have otherwise been a fun game get dragged down so hard by its level design. Really though, this game could have been a top 10 for me in 2023. BUT, the lifeless, tedious, monotonous level design sucked all of my joy out of the game. If you're reading this you've probably heard more than once that Boltgun needs a minimap or a compass... this is true, but in the end it's still a band-aid for the game's biggest issue which is gawdawful level design. You see, good level design doesn't require a minimap. They find ways to make levels flow while still allowing for player exploration. Old school Doom has labyrinthine levels AND an automap, but ultimately it wasn't necessary as the individual areas within a level were unique enough that you always had a rough idea where you were. Quake didn't have a minimap but didn't need it as the levels did a good job of guiding the players to their objective... also most of the Quake levels took between 5 or 10 minutes to complete. In Boltgun, you have the worst of both worlds where you have copy/paste level sections to make it almost impossible to know where you are, no automap, and levels can take anywhere between 20 and 30 minutes if you don't know where you're going So to all the people out there saying, "Boltgun doesn't need an automap! Getting lost is part of the experience. Modern games hold yer hands too much!" f*** off. Getting lost and wandering about aimlessly isn't fun. Give me an automap that's toggleable and feel free to get lost all you want. To the devs, dear God, please add a compass or an automap. And fire your lead level design because my 5 year old son could design a better level than that person.

You'd be better off buying Dusk, Hrot, Ion Fury, Ultrakill, Cultic, or Amid Evil of you want a solid retro inspired fps experience. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's not  good as I hoped; but still pretty fun and a delight to play. That's mostly due to how juicy the weapons feel and how pretty everything looks - the visceral sound of the boltgun hitting a target and making them explode into bloody chunks... pretty satisfying.My main complaint would probably the level and encounter design. Especially egregious after playing Quake 2, where fighting and exploration just meld together into a coherent whole; here some encounters wall you in until you PURGE all the heretics and daemons from the area, and I'm really not a fan of such design. It wasn't cool in DOOM 2016, it's not cool here.And the levels feel less like interconnected areas but more like hallways that connect one PURGE area to another. Ok, it's not  bad; it still has this classic Doom feeling of finding keys and opening doors, circling around to open another door with a new key, etc. But I found it pretty easy to get lost and there is no map - nor any other way to navigate other than good ol' orientation and the occasional wall markings.Still - the general combat feels good enough that you're mostly willing to forgive these faults. It's simplified quite a bit - reloading is almost instant, the chainsword attack is very powerful and comes with a homing charge to make sure you hit, and the enemy AI is simple and predictable, with almost nonexistent dodging. And it works.Actually, scratch that. It  works. I played the game on Hard difficulty ("Emperor's Mercy") and some parts of the game were a joke, some were quite annoying to get past. The general exploration is ridiculously simple, mostly killing off human cultists and some minor daemons with an occasional Chaos Space Marine or two... but during the PURGE segments you're be hit with a seemingly endless deluge of all sorts of enemies, including bosses. Not going to lie; I didn't enjoy the boss fights at all. They were difficult, and not in a fun way. During the final encounter I had to save scum because I was just sick of the cycle of fight - get hit - run around trying to find a medkit - seek out the boss again. And if you've cleared the area of healing items you're probably screwed.What I really enjoyed about the game, though, is its interpretation of W40K. I'm not that much into it, but I do enjoy the setting - and it's important to point out that it is meant to be . The Imperium of Man is not a force of good. You're supposed to take a lot of things with a grain of salt and just embrace the goofiness of it all. And the game delivers well on this front. You're accompanied by a servo-skull that's a huge dork and its comments often remind you just how silly the entire W40K lore is... right before you press dat T button to say something like "YOU'LL HONOUR THE EMPEROR WITH YOUR DEATHS!!!" and let them know the Emperor's Mercy.Don't get me wrong - the game was pretty fun to play. It's just that the fun was sometimes soiled by moments of frustration; and the frustration was rather strong. Maybe setting the difficulty to Medium ("My Armour is Contempt") would've mitigated the issue somewhat. But even then, only 11% of players have beaten the game at all, even on the lowest difficulty, so maybe the frustration points are more serious than I'm making it seem.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of both warhammer and boomer shooters this should have been a free win for Boltgun. However, the longer I've been playing this game the more glaring its fundamental flaws are becoming.There's multiple areas of gamedesign that are important to crafting a competent retro shooter and Boltgun fails at most of them. Movement and leveldesign, the core of every succesful run and gun type of game fall flat for a mayority of the game. Most enemies require the player to permanently run in order to avoid significant damage but running feels sluggish due to excessive inertia and not enough grip. This often hampers the flow of combat especially when theres a lot of deadly abysses in combination with narrow bridges. The mechanic to lock on and charge straight into enemies via melee attacks seems like a great way to counter balance some of this sluggishness. Zooming from cultist to cultist while splattering them into a pulp of gore is incredibly fun. But soon most enemies get too tough to effectively kill with your chainsword removing this boost in agility as the game progresses. And portal sections that are unecessarily complicated to navigate don't help either.The next pillar of a good boomer shooter is usually the tools you are given to dispatch whatever enemies the game throws at you. However, if you're looking for well balanced weapons that each fill their own niche throughout the game like in Ion Fury or Culthic you'll be dissapointed. Instead a third of your arsenal consists of basically identical weapons. No matter if you use the boltgun, Heavy boltgun or vulkite caliver you get three weapos that all deal low damage at a rapid speed with basically no difference in handling or situational utility.. Then there's a category of weapons that just feels odd to use. The melta gun hits like a truck which is nice. However, it also runs out of ammo rapidly while simultaneously making you do quickmaths because for some reason it reduces your ammo counter in increments of 5 with every singular shot. And no, this is not due to some sort of alt fire mode because there is no such thing.  The plasma rifle, while dealing decent DPS is more often than not more dangerous to its weilder than enemies due to excessive friendly fire. Especially in close quarters swarming with nurglings this gun makes you feel like your own worst enemy when it should be a prime candidate to slaughter tons of small enemies with AOE. Then there's the vengeance launcher which  somehow introduces delayed damage  in a genre that is known for split second decisionmaking a reflex based gameplay. And lets just not talk about the shotgun which I only ever used when runnung out of every other type of ammo. Every single weapon in Amid Evil is more interesting than the entire aresenal of guns Boltgun has to offer. Especially when factoring in alternative firemodes which Boltguns arsenal is completely lacking with the exception of temporary damage buffs.And finally, to make the underwhelming experience complete the game manages to mess up the third pillar of any good Boomer Shooter which is enemy design and variety, There's basically only two types of enemy you'll encounter. Glass cannons that explode into a million pieces of gore if you ever so slightly touch them. These guys are "overkilled" by most of your weapons meaning that using anything other than the standard Boltgun feels like a waste of ammo and sometimes even an unecessary risk (*cough* plasma rifle *cough*). Enemy type number two is the bullet sponge and oh boy are there a lot of them. Maybe it has to do with the difficulty I chose (the games equivalent of hard) but at around the 5 hour mark the game seems to be filled with chaosmarine terminators, greater plague toads and these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ teleporting bird mages. In order to kill them emptying an entire magazine or two into them is not enough. You'll often find yourself dumping the entire stock of ammo of every single on of the guns that are reasonably fun to use into the first wave of enemies only to impotently boop your shotgun at the remaining horde of demons. It was a scenario just like that when I was no longer willing to spend 10-15 minutes of tickling another identical boss monster bird person to death and quit the game instead.So what positive thing is there to say. First of all I really enjoyed the visuals. A lot of boomer shooters use their retro presentation as an excuse for bad art direction but Boltgun isn't one of them. The designs feel very in line with the established warhammer aesthetic even when they don't dare to do anything that's really new. But that's alright, gotta save necrons, nids and orcs for a later day I guess. The soundtrack is of a pretty high quality and fits the retro arcade theme wel while most guns and sound effects sound well produced and meatyl. Personally I would have prefered the music to lean a bit more into the Warhammer fantasy, Maybe some heavy metal mixed with gregorian chants but I can see why they went with a soundtrack that is more suitable for the period of gaming history they want to emulate. And maybe my standards are too high when it comes to boomer shooter soundtracks but  I blame Andrew Hulshult for that. This relatively high production value is elevated with a very fair price of 15~20 USD. Many boomer shooters are far less visually impressive and not built on a license as strong as Warhammer but will cost almost the same on release. Verdict: I should have loved this game but didn't. If you want a similarly priced game that is superior in pretty much every aspect to Boltgun go play Amid Evil instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Warhammer 40K Boltgun a bad game? No.Do I recommend Warhammer 40K Boltgun? Also no.Warhammer 40K Boltgun is probably the best single player Warhammer 40K FPS game available, but when you consider the competition that's not exactly saying much. The game is a solid but average retro shooter that I suspect gets a much greater appreciation thanks to it's W40K paintjob than it's level or game design.You're not asked to do much in this game, simply move from point A to point B and shoot anything in between. Enemy AI is basic, and pretty much all attempts at difficulty revolve around locking the player in a contained area and spawning more enemies. Each level has secrets to find, but these are just the same reoccurring power ups which are often just put in plain sight. There's no real incentive to explore or look around levels, and this is reinforced with the unimaginative level design which seems to be concentrated about funnelling you into the next encounter.Weapons feel solid to use, but they are also very limited in gameplay mechanics to differentiate themselves. You have the titular boltgun, a shotgun, a heavy bolter which is basically the boltgun that doesnt reload, a plasma gun for slow fire/high damage attacks, an almost pointless grenade launcher, a meltagun for low ammo high damage, and two beam type weapons. There is a system for enemy armour values against your weapon strength, but you can pretty much ignore this in most scenarios. You also get limited use grenades and the game is generous enough that you can use these fairly freely.The game is split into three chapters and you for some reason lose your weapons between each chapter. Not a huge issue but an annoying one. The first chapter seems to be the best one in terms of pacing, design, and atmosphere while the remaining two feel a lot more dull and forgettable. I found myself struggling to work up the interest to continue playing this game in those chapters and ultimately had to force myself to finish the game.As mentioned, Warhammer 40K Boltgun is not a bad game per se, but apart from it's Warhammer 40K skin it doesn't really do anything to make itself stand out. If you're looking for a retro shooter with more depth and style I'd recommend Dusk, or if you're after a retro style game with far better atmosphere I'd suggest Lunacid and if you're desperate for a Warhammer 40K shooter, well Darktide has finally started to sort itself out and you can use a boltgun in that, I wouldn't bother with Boltgun until it's at least on a deep sale, and maybe not even then.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: Aah, if only this game had come out in the 1990s, it certainly would have been a smash hit and probably boosted the WH40k franchise's popularity considerably.There's really nothing much to say about Boltgun; it's a retro-style FPS (boomer shooter) where you either shoot or chainsword your enemies into oblivion. The sight of their gibs flying around as you wipe them out certainly warms the nostalgic cockles of my heart.Having played Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine nearly a decade ago, I was mildly surprised to see that Boltgun takes place in the world of Graia. But playing as an Ultramarine, the sole survivor of a doomed drop pod landing, brought back many fond memories. As always, the Emperor protects. Amusingly, if you time yourself correctly, you can even get your enemies to fight one another. True Chaos in the making.The levels are well-designed (24 across three chapters in the base game), and the handy servo-skull guide keeps you from getting lost. In fact, the only time I had to use a video walkthrough was for Furnace of Damnation, the 23rd level, as it was a bit confusing midway.Lore-wise, though not an issue with the game itself, it raises an eyebrow to know how a lone Ultramarine can go up against Great Unclean Ones and Lords of Change, which are the game's secondary bosses. Greater Daemons, which have annihilated entire civilisations, armies, and worlds but fall (after admittedly hard battles) to a Loyalist Astartes. Well, at least the Nurglings take the time to moon you before attacking.Forges of Corruption is no less enjoyable, though what it lacks in the number of levels (five) it compensates for the length thereof. Of course, the DLC contains new weapons & enemies for those discerning servants of the Golden Throne. I must admit, the fifth level is ridiculously enjoyable. Gibs galore.The Horde Mode is as is, though the downside IMO is that when you've wiped out a majority of the foes in a round, some of the smaller ones may have escaped your attention, ranging from the rank-and-file cultist to the pint-sized Nurgling, which forces you to hunt for them in order to finish the round.The selection of weapons is similarly enjoyable. I was initially disappointed that you couldn't keep the weapons at the start of a new chapter, nor do their upgrades carry over at the start of a new level, but I eventually learned to adapt and see them as challenges. Similarly, the pseudo-retro soundtrack is most suited to the game.I certainly got my money's worth with Boltgun; so much so that I bought the DLC seven levels into the game. Those who enjoy the mindless slaughter, do get this game. At least you can kill in the God-Emperor of Mankind's name.

_childDocuments_.review: Boltgun is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be, what it wants to emulate, and who it's for.Currently going through on the hardest difficulty, and this is how I'm feeling after about 2 1/2 hours.The visuals are pretty solid. I'm not a huge 40k fan or anything, but the environments have always been super cool, and this game does great respect to those. Gothic architecture always goes great with mass murder. The enemy and character art are great, I love the little goobers that just show you their butt before it gets filled with the Emperor's Holy Might (bullets) (do NOT misconstrue what I'm saying here). The only minor gripe I have with this game visually is that there are some maps that look cluttered, and enemies are occasionally a little hard to distinguish from the background. But I am also an idiot soSound design is great and the soundtrack is very fitting. The weapons are punchy and it's extremely satisfying to watch those DISGUSTING CHAOS turn into DISGUSTING GIBS. Again, only issue I have is a small one. Please avoid this spoiler if you wish to avoid a bad opinion: The only overarching thing for me that I can point out as a "negative" is that it's purely combat. Which is totally fine, since you kind of expect that in this kind of game. My favorite franchise is DMC so I'm used to turning my brain off and watch Funny Bad Guy get turned into Funny Bad Guy: Paste Edition, but (at least on the hardest difficulty) the combat really starts to wear on me when I get to the 3rd massive encounter of 6 waves with very tough enemies. To me, this is best played in 1-2 level bursts, then coming back later.Solid 3/5 type beat. For $22, I'd say it's quite worth it for someone looking for a pretty familiar boomer shooter experience in a very visually interesting world. A great palette cleanser after the disaster that I've watched unfold over at Darktide. If I had a Deck, I personally think this would be a great pick for the console for my 1-2 level bursts.

_childDocuments_.review: I will first say this is most likely my first game in the Warhammer 40,000 universe so I don't really understand, or even care, about all the lore around it. I bought the game because it is advertised as a "boomer shooter" (I like those) and because it looks good, I guess.The game is OK.I think this game does what boomer shooters do: fast movement, powerful weapons, a lot of blood. It does that alright. Expecting any kind of innovative gameplay will leave you disappointed. Saying that progression through the level is completely linear would be wrong, but you can't get lost either. Most of the time you are just "moving forward" and shooting things. If you have nothing to shoot, you might be moving in wrong direction. There are a few exceptions to this, like backtracking to get back to the door after getting a key.Secrets are like 80% disappointing and require you to just go around all the corners of the current place/arena you are in. The other 20% feel more like secrets because they aren't immediately obvious, you don't accidentally stumble upon them, and require activating a wall or a bit of platforming, for example.You are given PLENTY of ammo on literally every corner so ammo starvation is never a problem (at least on normal difficulty). You can actually fairly easy kill most things with the Boltgun (first weapon you are given), except for the most spongy foes, and bosses.All in all I think it's a great game to wind-down to in the evening; where I can just run around and shoot things without too much thinking.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: I dont understand the hype, or even the compromising "it's good but not great" comments and reviews.  This game is honestly straight up objectively bad, and I'll explain why.I love this genre, it's prob my fav, and I have played it all since the 90s.  All the dooms, all the modern games, and all the modern clones like:ProdeusUltrakillAmid EvilDuskMothergunshipIon FuryNecromundaAnd they're all better.-For starters, this game has run off by default, and if you aren't running, you aren't going to dodge anything.  Nobody should hold down shift.  At least they put the option to toggle it.-Arenas are clunky, and blocky.  Not a lot of open space to circle-strafe, not a lot of room for backing up.  Many walls, blocks, bumps.  You'll find yourself constantly clipping and getting stuck against something, or hitting something and losing your momentum.  The vaulting isn't good enough to integrate with your combat-Weapon ammo and abilities are too limited.  You only get 3 grenades.  I dont see any way of increasing this capacity.  Weapon ammo is also pretty limited.  And every gun has a reload.  Shotgun is painfully one shell at a time.  Reload has no place in games like these, but thats more personal preference I will admit.-No upgrade system or character progression?!  Come on, in this day and age, weapon upgrade systems, mod pathways, attachment options, etc need to be present in a game like this.  Especially given the base damage of every weapon I have encountered so far is very low.-Damage is too low for the mobs.  I am only playing on medium, and it takes 4+ shots to kill little frogs (which are smaller than humans), and the chaos terminators, etc.  Bullet-sponges are fine in games like these, but certainly "trash mobs" (the frogs that spit), shouldn't be 4+ hit mobs in an arena that constantly spawns dozens of guys all around you.  And on medium.  Lol I can clear all doom games on Nightmare but I am dying on level 3 in this?  Not a skill problem, a design flaw.-Level design is also weak.  Linear is fine.  Secrets are strangely placed.  At times it's not clear where you need to go, what is a door and what isn't.  It's easy to miss terminals.-The talking skull needs a voice, or get rid of it.  Constantly looking at the top corner of the screen to read paragraphs of text during combat especially is bad design.  -Ammo and otherpicks need to make a DIFFERENT sound when you're at full, trying to pick them up. Again, unless you READ where it says "full", it makes the same normal pickup sound, and you keep going for the pickups thinking you need more.Every game has it's flaws, and any one of these grips would be acceptable and nitpicky without the totality of them.  But all together it makes for a weak game, and a weak title in this genre.  Look above at my list, all of them are better than this and most at the same price or cheaper.  If you like 40K, get Necromunda instead.  It's a better version of this.The gore is good at least.  40k theme is good too.  Gun sound effects are solid.  Music is good, but doesn't play long enough or frequently enough.  At the very least, arena design and gun damage needs an overhaul for this to be a good game.  And there needs to be weapon upgrades/mods/progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the positive reviews are ironically spot on. This does feel like a Warhammer game produced by blind devotion to the Omnissiah, as the Mechanicum is also not capable of creating anything original, only sub-par knockoffs of existing designs. The graphics are probably the standout feature in this game. The sprites are incredibly well made and look gorgeous. Sadly the same can't be said for the rest of the game.The maps feel lazy and repetitive. Lot's of geometry just randomly clips into other geometry, as if haphazardly placed without a thought given to the architecture of the buildings, corridors or alleyways they are meant to compose into. There is also strong fluctuation in the level of detail. Some things look incredibly flat and lifeless, yet at the same time you've got overly detailed ducts and pipes running across ceilings that could get away with 1/3 of the polygons spent on them.Level design also feels next to non-existent. I don't generally agree that games like these need an in-game map, to reference where you are (as some other reviews are asking for). But the levels in this game feel so poorly designed that it is almost necessary. They neither feel like they are funnelling me down the proper correct path (as you would have in something like Doom 2016), nor do they offer any interconnectivity and exploitability (as something like a WRATH: Aeon of Ruin offers). It's just one samey looking room connected to the next, with litte to distinguish them from one another or to act as landmarks for orientation.Gunplay is fairly solid, however switching weapons takes forever, as does reloading. So it felt quite punishing to swap between the weapons I had unlocked.The chain-sword also felt hella awkward. It can be super satisfying in some situations, but generally it just feels very meh to use. Performance is another major issue. Comparable games in this style easily run with 200+ fps on my system, while this game struggles to maintain 150 with frequent drops down to low double digits. I suspect it has to do with loading of enemies or map-chunks. Which is quite mind-boggling, when you consider that the entirety of the game-files can comfortably fit into a mid-range PC's memory three times over.Overall it feels like the devs took bits and pieces from the boomer-shooter scene, without really having any understanding of what makes or breaks these kind of games. There is definitely potential in the game, but it needs quite a bit of polishing, rethinking of core mechanics and the hiring of a competent level designer.All in all, just another MEH Warhammer game. So if you are the type of person who likes Warhammer video games, I'm sure you'll feel right at home.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr It's made with love and has a great first chapter, but it drastically overstays its welcome and it suffers from both unintuitive level design and a critical lack of enemy variety.The reveal trailer for Boltgun features a man moving out of his house, raking through old boxes of 40k stuff before finding a fake floppy disk of Boltgun, at which point he flashes back to playing it in his youth. In a sense, it was prophetic. Boltgun feels a lot like replaying a game from your childhood and realizing it's not quite as good as you thought it was when you were 4. It's a surprising magic to capture for a game that came out in 2023.The first chapter of this game is wonderful, I will admit. Planetside on a Forge World you're given free reign to jump, shoot, slash and smash through Chaos hordes in lovingly rendered PSX-ified versions of mainstay 40k setpieces. Both the 3D worlds and the 2D spritework of you and your enemies are GORGEOUS, truly done with love. If the entire game were like this - or if chapter 1 was the only chapter - I'd be slightly kinder to the game. With only the Boltgun, Shotgun, Plasma Gun and Heavy Bolter on your side it's a rare moment in this game that actually feels like a balanced, enjoyable experience. When Chapter 2 started, I was PUMPED to get more of this game in my veins....You may notice that I said I'd only be slightly kinder to the game. There's more than a few reasons for that and they pop up even in Chapter 1. For starters, the music is absolutely forgettable. I'd hesitate to even call it 'good', and so many tracks blend together I actually don't have an estimate of how many the game has in total. Of particularly note is the same repetitive droning techno song that plays every time a Purge event starts. I enjoyed it the first two times, but by the 40th time I actually began to loathe it. I don't see myself replaying this game, but if I ever do it'll be with the music off. There are ambient tracks in Inquisitor with more life to them, for god's sake.But that's just a minor gripe. A far more pressing issue is the game's critical lack of variety in every single aspect. Music, yes, but levels weapons and enemies too. Taking a leaf out of DOOM's book, nearly every level boils down to "find 1-3 coloured keys and exit". The problem here is that the levels are formulaic, samey, repetitive. Both visually and in format. Really, the level design and pacing suffers from issues that weren't present in most original boomer shooters and have LONG been solved by the new wave. You can only keycard hunt in samey, uninspired corridors/warehouses for so long before it all starts to blend together. It doesn't help that later levels are decidedly unintuitive, often featuring routes where "the way forward" is anything but. That the environments are so samey doesn't help either.As for weapons... In truth, Boltgun actually has a healthy variety on this front: Boltgun, Shotgun, Plasma Gun, Heavy Boltgun, Vengeance Launcher, Melta Gun, Volkite Caliver and Grav-Cannon. The problem here is that most of them aren't worth using. Your starting Boltgun is so ridiculously effective at any range and ammo for it is so plentiful that using any of the other weapons just feels folly. Pick one of the above weapons to be your designated Big Guy Killer and use the Boltgun for most things. If you find a Machine Spirit pickup the Boltgun gets a significant damage increase, only compounding the issue.Don't bother with the Shotgun, in defiance of the boomer shooter law that all shotguns must be god-forged weapons, this game's Shotgun is a wimpy ineffective weapon that's not even useful for trash mobs due to your ability to simply hit F and bulldoze through them with your body. It doesn't even SOUND good. I challenged myself to use every weapon where possible and it was an exercise in frustration, especially due to the encounter design which we'll get to later.Perhaps most jarringly is the Chainsword, this game's sole melee option and replacement for Doom Glory Kills. It's... Useless? It takes too long to kill a single trash mob (which again, you can charge through) and is useless on anything with armor. You can even mash the attack button to grind enemies into paste for... no point. The chainsword does not confer extra health or ammo, it is simply there. Set dressing in all but name.I wish I had more to say about the enemies, but I'm just disappointed. Having leaned too hard into being a 90s FPS, Boltgun features about 12 variations on "guy who slowwalks at you and shoots", three boss enemies and about 3 melee-only enemies. They are completely uninspired and drab, and there are some startling omissions for a Chaos-oriented game. Daemonettes and Bloodletters would've been welcome in this game, but their respective gods are absent - it's just Nurgle, Tzeentch and Undivided. Save for Pink Horrors (who often explode into two Blue Horrors on death), they all lack for meaningful gimmicks and they pose little threat most of the time.Most of the time.Perhaps this game's biggest pitfall is the encounter design. Not so much an issue in Chapter 1, but by the middle of Chapter 2 the game has exhausted its bag of New Stuff and resolves to simply throw more harder enemies at you in confined spaces where dodging isn't much of an option. I died a few times later on through no real fault of my own, I simply made the mistake of having 100 health and no armor before walking into a tight corridor that had three plasma gun cultists in it. The Purge events succumb to this too, bombarding you with enemies in a vain attempt to appear meaningfully difficult. Sad part is? Most of the time they succeed. Malus Caedo is simply too fast to be threatened in a wide open space, and there's a reason all of my deaths were in transitory areas. It reeks of a development team who loved 90s shooters but didn't quite get them on a design level.Have you ever seen a comedian tell a funny joke, get their roaring laughter, and keep going to a silent hall? That's this game. I laughed in Chapter 1, there were 6 more hours ahead.Ultimately, I wish I could review this game fondly. Rare are the games that make me /sad/ to negatively review them. But while Boltgun is clearly made with love, it's not *well* made. For every plus (Rahul Kohli's amazing VA, the taunt button, the respect paid to the source material, the titular weapon) there are about 50 negatives.Who knows, maybe the blatantly teased Khorne DLC coming later will fix most of these issues, but I doubt it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a piece of ♥♥♥♥ mechanically. If you really care about texture work or environments and jack off to that ♥♥♥♥ this game would be for you. However as a game it has very basic enemy behavior, it's either stand still and shoot at the player, shoot then strafe left or right, or just run right at the player. The level design makes areas look exactly same in nearly every level and this gets worse with added verticality to every subsequent level makes navigation and exploration become tedious and monotonous. _childDocuments_.review: Once the 40k fanboys cool down from orgasm, you will see the review score on this game come down.EDIT: Review score dropped as predicted LOLIt is a passable boomer shooter that will put a smile of 40k fans faces, so you can't say it doesn't do what it sets out to, but it doesn't do anything beyond that.• No minimap, and levels can lead you in circles• Performance issues even on hardware well above recommended specs• Braindead AI• Tons of ammo pickups, although you're almost always maxed-out• "Secrets" are a joke• Very minimal damage feedback; you can't even tell you're getting hit half the time• Takes way too long to get all the guns. WAY too long• "Toughness" stat from the tabletop poorly translates to shooter game and is a nuisance• Little enemy variety and they reuse the same bosses over and over.Buy it only once it's 50% off, and if you're a big boomer shooter boomer — there are many better games in this genre out there right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game. If you are even a remote fan of the 40K universe and/or DOOM you will very much enjoy this game. Great weapons, gameplay, and characters from the 40K universe. Anyone familiar with the lore will instantly recognize many of the game aspects.Weapons are very fun and satisfying to use, especially the namesake Bolter or Boltgun. They are also upgradable adding yet another fun element to the combat.Level design is good but can get a bit repetitive. The gameplay makes up for this though and you never feel it is tedious with just enough variety to keep any veteran FPS player occupied. Campaign length is just about right. I think I'm right about at the mid point, 12.5 hours in. Of course other players may finish quicker but I'm the type that has to look in virtually every nook and cranny.My only gripe is that I wish the chainsword, a very important weapon in the game, was not so clunky and animated a bit better. I think the original DOOM did a better job of this with the chainsaw. The chainsword can a bit clunky and awkward to use. The animation could use a few more frames.I bought the game on sale and for the price I paid, I think I got a really good deal. The game is refined, polished, bug free (from what I saw) and priced appropriately.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not familiar with the Warhammer license but I have played Space Marine on the Xbox which this game is kind of a sequel to.  This game is a fun but has some pacing issues.  For starters the game looks and feels great, the weapons especially feel good to use.  Being a Space Marine and feeling the heft of his steps and how heavy he is when he drops from a great height is superb.  What I did not like was the padding and how levels take forever to complete, once after you finish a tough fight and think the level is over, there's another huge fight.  Lastly some of the enemies are annoying to deal with, from the Aspiring Champions who get a second wind when they get knocked down, to the Plague toads and Nurglings swarming the player.  I do recommend this game but know there is some frustrating game design.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun for the first few hourse but then its charm just windles. The levels aren't as memorable as Doom or Quake, and that's fine, but there isn't anything in them that make them stand out. The secrets aren't supper hidden except for one or two in each level, but the secrets aren't as rewarding as you might expect. After the first chapter it just looses its hook, and this is proven by the contrast of people that have finished the first chapter and the ones who have finish the second chapter. It was an ok game but there are better boomer shooters out there. I played up until the end of chapter 2 but I really didn't feel like continuing anymore, I wasn't really having fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing for like 1 hour and I already love it. High framerate with only chug being in high enemy areas, the soundtrack kicks ass, the guns feel good to use and it feels like Doom Slayer got inducted into the Adeptus Astartes. The game also has fun minor attention to detail things like your marine reading scriptures when you AFK (Whaddya waiting for, Christmas?).Weapons have STR values like on tabletop and enemies have a displayed toughness indicator. True to form using a STR 3 shotgun against a toughness 4 Chaos Marine is less effective (you could still do it) and it makes classic boom-shoot weapon switching a mechanic. The minor lore accuracies are also nice, as pink horrors actually split into blue ones true to tabletop. All in all game runs well, sounds great, feels fun to play and I'd highly recommend. Ah, finally a Warhammer FPS that isn't bogged down by bad decisions. If I had one recommendation for the devs it would be to slightly optimize the FPS in large firefights, but other than that I am fully satisfied by this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to enjoy this game, it's simply not that fun. Is it a blast the first hour? Sure. Do the glaring issues start to become too hard to ignore after that...? Absolutely.Levels are too big and sprawling with no minimap.Enemies all "feel" the same and are not super fun to fight (you will have seen most of what the game has to offer in enemy variety within the first hour)A TON of enemies don't have real "queue" sounds that help you differentiate between them or to know when they're close. Feels like shooting cardboard cutouts. Do the weapons feel nice? Sure. But with the enemies feeling the way they do to fight, every time, time after time... everything eventually feels like a tedious chore. Especially when certain enemies are bullet sponges for no reason.But my biggest gripe and disappointment? Almost no music. Hear me out, there is music in this game, but most of the time, there isn't a real track playing. It's just awkward ambiance and environment sounds. The same few tracks play for all the "purge" sequences and boss sequences I've encountered so far. A pounding synthwave/choir blend would have been perfect to set the grim dark tone, even some 80s/90s flavored rock, but not this.A real shame considering how cool the trailer made it out to be. All hype no bite.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty good game! The shooting is fun and the weapons feel great to use, especially the standard Bolter you get at the start. Weapons also seem very impactful due to the sound design and the shower of blood and gore whenever you blow apart an enemy. Visually it has a great sense of style, thanks to the pixelated sprite-based looks. The enemy designs are varied and their animations are detailed. There are some very distinct and interesting looking areas as well.However, for me personally there were 2 main issues holding this back from being great. The first one being the level design: it was a bit too confusing at times for my tastes (especially with no map). I found myself wandering through multiple parts of same-y looking levels, while trying to find the right button to use or door to open. Secondly there were some difficulty spikes that, at times, really hampered my overall enjoyment of the game. The biggest one that comes to mind is the boss at the end of act II: a small arena, lots of enemies that only get replaced with stronger ones once you kill them and a very limited amount of pickups. There are also some areas where you get attacked by different types of enemies from all sides. That coupled with some of the battle arenas being quite vertical in design, made for a chaotic and sometimes frustrating experience. All-in-all it was still a very enjoyable shooter and I do recommend it. Especially if you're better suited for these types of games than I am.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: I am not a Warhammer fan, this is the first ever product of its name I have touched. I am, however, extremely fond of boomer shooters, like muslims to Mecca I used to revisit my childhood classics yearly along with some of the better .WADs or mappacks for other games.This certainly passes for a boomer shooter, but that's all there is to it. It feels like the devs have been passed a checklist of the bare minimums that make up a shooter of the kind and just fulfilled the necessary quotas without giving much more thought to it afterwards. They could have done so much more and it is a shame they did not.I wouldn't ever trust the devs to keep a secret due to the fact they have no idea what a secret is. The placement of secrets is so mundane, no hidden walls, no switches, no intricacies requiring thought and exploration, just walk into a container in the middle of the pathway and grab the item within to see a Secret Picked Up notification. They're literally put in your way so you cannot miss them, you could try speedrunning some boring levels and find that you'll naturally somehow find all but one secret in a level without effort.Another gripe I have is with the attempted pacing which is at odds with the AI's capacity, the level design and the weapon design, i.e. the damage. The levels are segmented into arenas, symmetrical most of the time, wherein a purge commences, which is basically a swarm of enemies spawning in the player is tasked with removing. This would be more fun if it didn't boil down to chasing down and looking for the enemies who are having trouble navigating the terrain.The maps aren't memorable at all, no incentive to explore, no secret stashes with weapons to obtain if you look hard enough, nothing. just copypasted corridors aligned symmetrically. Some places you may get lost due to how same-y everything looks.The weapons, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ do they  They are beefy, the sound, animations, headbob, recoil, everything makes you feel like a damn titan, that paired with the fact that each step is a stomping thud after thud is just perfect, BUT, the enemies are hitsponges, the weapons don't hold much utilitarian use like in Doom Eternal, wherein each weapon is useful for each respective mob. Some mobs are nonsensically stronger than those who you'd logically assume to be stronger, e.g. the frog thing vs. a chaos terminator (or whatever the mob's called). The longer you play, the more you realize the dissonance between how beefy, strong and brutal everything sounds and feels to how effective, damage-dealing it really is.It's also extremely easy (playing second to last difficulty, as is the shibboleth for boomershooters since Doom & Duke), I almost completed the first chapter without any deaths, I first died fighting the first boss, I wish I could say I like the game given that I paid 19.79€, I can only say it's  at best and wait for a significant discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface that in the end, I really hated the Game but overall it is still a good Game!So in June 2023 I played this Game for around ~1 hour and then I had enough. But this was not the Game's fault, I was probably just fed up with Boomer Shooters. (Kind of still am I guess. At least for the moment.)Now I finally gave it another go. Also glad that I waited so I could play the Forges of Corruption DLC right after.For Boomer Shooters you can't write an essay anymore, we all know where the influences lie and what those Games are all about. And yes, even though Civvie11 disagrees, I still call it a Boomer Shooter...First off, this is just an extremely good feeling Game. It feels so crunchy and punchy when you shoot something (the crunchiness is comparable to Cultic). This goes to say, sound design is also excellent, because without the punchy sounds it wouldn't feel that great.The overall Atmosphere of the Game is also pretty good. Locations are varied and most of the time the environments are interesting to look at.What I was mixed on was the Music. In some parts it felt fitting, in other parts it felt kind of strange and as if it wasn't fitting the game(play) at all. Serviceable I guess.I also liked the feeling of your character/Space Marine. You really feel like a hulking tank but way more nimble than in Space Marine 1 or 2 for that matter.For example you can run very fast, you can dash (almost never used it), you have a very high and very far reaching jump and you can clamber up ledges.Many Boomer Shooter rise or fall with their weapon roster and I can say that all of the weapons in Boltgun and the DLC are really good and fun to use.Regarding Secrets in the Game: Well, some secrets are no real secrets because they are basically right in your face and some other secrets are really secret. But since the levels were so huge, I really didn't want to look for them all (though I found most of them anyways).I didn't have many bugs. I had one area where the sound and music was stuttering for a complete section and even a restart didn't help but apart from that and a few minor graphical glitches, it was fine. The Game ran at a steady 60fps for me (specs on my Profile).Storywise there is not much to say. You play a Space Marine and you kill stuff. Cutscenes were rare and not that interesting but had a nice pixel style to it. I kind of liked that there were a few nods/"easter eggs" regarding Space Marine. Nice little touch.So, I played the whole Maingame and the whole of the DLC on Exterminatus (highest difficulty).And I don't know if it was because of the difficulty, but at the End of Chapter 2 of the Maingame, the Game started to overstay it's welcome a little bit.The levels got bigger and bigger and basically you just kill waves and waves of enemies.This can be fun for a while but here it also felt very tedious. I also had to take a break after 1-2 levels because I kind of got exhausted many times.After finishing the Maingame, I jumped into the DLC Forges of Corruption which I will say a few words here and not on the DLC page.The DLC was a SLOGFEST on Exterminatus. I already wanted to end the Game in the middle section of the Base Game but well, sometimes I like to torment myself.In the DLC I was just not feeling it anymore. Almost ENDLESS Waves and Arenas full of enemies that seemingly never stop spawning and the levels (most of them) felt like they were double the length as in the maingame.It was definitely more challenging but also way more annoying. In the end I was just exhausted but not in a good way. Some of these later arenas take 10-15 minutes to clear and there are multiple in one level. Also in my head I was just like PLEASE FOR THE LOVE OF ALL THAT IS HOLY STOP SPAWNING MORE ENEMIES and then there were more and more and more and I just didn't have fun anymore.After finishing the DLC I at least got an achievement that only 0.6% of players (as of writing this review) have for completing it on Exterminatus but yeah, for me this was not it.I would like to see a Boltgun 2 someday but I don't want more content for this Game. Oh and yeah, the free Update - Horde Mode - gets a nope from me as you probably could've guessed. Nice addition but yeah, I had my fair share of hordes and hordes of enemies in the Maingame and DLC.Overall still a good Game.......

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being an avid fan of Warhammer 40k, when Boltgun first appeared on my radar, I looked the other way.  Aesthetic of the promotional materials didn’t appeal to me at a glance and VERY EXCITED narration of the trailer made me pause the video and forget about it rather quickly. That was until the game finally released and WH40k community got about as excited as the trailer guy sounded. Curious as to what the fuzz is about, I dug into Boltgun proper and while it is not all gold down there, I sure did enjoy time spent playing in the mud.Widely dubbed as Warhammer 40,000 boomer shooter, Boltgun is a fast-paced FPS starring hordes of enemies strewn across numerous arenas and a sizeable arsenal with which to paint the town red in the most literal way. The game was developed by Auroch Digital and published by Focus Entertainment, I am confident more indie-inclined among you already recognise the latter. From the get-go I can already assure those wary of WH40k’s notoriously “hit or miss” releases. Not only Boltgun is a hit, I’m tempted to state it does a surprisingly good job at appealing to the general audience while also being faithful to its universe. That alone is a no small feat (I am looking at you, Dawn of War 3).Storywise Boltgun remains true to its retro shooter roots, namely there isn’t much of it to speak of. After short intro cutscene all of the pieces are set – the player is to embody power armoured boots of a veteran Space Marine, sent at the behest of an Inqusitor to combat daemonic corruption. Even if Ultramarines, servo-skulls and Ordo Maleus are foreign language to you, it doesn’t require much knowledge to jump straight into WH40k’s rendition of Doom. Despite its intent on accessibility for wider audience, Boltgun sneaks in a fair share of fine details meant for the fans of the universe. Chief among them that the game ties directly to Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine, but it is also the little things – such as armour points being called contempt, a literal take on Armour of Contempt, an idea of hating evil so much as to shield one’s mind from its corrupting influence. Not bad for a footnote story told mostly through cutscenes at the end of each episode.Lore shenanigans aside, this title’s main selling point made its way even into the title – Boltgun. This magnificent edifice of war is capable of firing mass-reactive explosive rounds at full auto, causing even the most robust cultist to explode into gibs when hit twice. And that’s just the starting gun. There are 7 other guns to join the arsenal as the player progresses through the game, each one of remaining viable as new weapons are unlocked. This is in no small part thanks to power level mechanic: every enemy has a designated armour value and the player’s weapon needs to match it to deal optimal damage. A shotgun blast will turn a daemon with physique of ugly infant to pulp, however a fully armoured Chaos Space Marine will require something with a bit more of a punch, like a plasma rifle, to reduce all that pesky defence to atoms.Speaking of the punch, in terms of audio effects Boltgun is amazing. Every weapon sounds and looks like something a transhuman supersoldier would wield – it is heavy, meaty and deafeningly loud (I reduced sound effect settings to third of the others to be able to hear soundtrack during my second playthrough). Same goes for Space Marine armour – sprinting is accompanied with loud thuds and there is even camera bobbing up and down a little to add further feedback to weight of the character. That is, until you proceed to start jumping as if gravity was a scam (you can sprint backwards too for some reason). My only bone to pick is that weapon and enemy sound cues, while vital to gameplay, were so overwhelming that at times I questioned if there is any music in the game at all.No less interesting are the visuals of the game. Despite their pixelated looks (the effect is received via filter which may be reduced to achieve modern-looking graphics), the interiors are in many places incredibly detailed and they do well to relay gothic aesthetic of WH40k’s technology. True to the spirit of modern rendition of oldschool, all enemies and some environmental details imitate sprite graphics, resulting in organic blend of 2D and 3D. Supposing that you get to see said details, as Boltgun adores obstructing the player’s sight – interiors are often dark and foggy, highly reducing field of view and a red filter covers vision during daemonic invasions. Paired with the fact that some guns take up nearly half of the screen, at times your aim will be driven mostly by an educated guess and subsequent screaming.For all the fondness I may have for WH40k and boomer shooters, Boltgun surely does not go without its share of caveats. To begin with, it is not really a boomer shooter, besides the pixelated graphics. The player’s character is ridiculously mobile, there are no hitscanners in the game, keys often loop the player back into the level rather than open new areas and the game in general is best compared to 2016 Doom. Beyond a shadow of doubt it is a respectable source of inspiration, however Boltgun in my eyes is a modern shooter paying homage to old-school rather than actually being retro itself. Nonetheless, given how boomer shooters are a prevalent trend throughout last decade I can understand why Boltgun would like to encourage association.Probably my biggest issue with the game is the damage feedback. Many of the enemy attacks have splash damage, meaning that this title repeatedly indicated hits from behind for oncoming projectiles. Furthermore, I failed to observe any difference between feedback from attack which barely scraped my armour, when compared to one that halved my health. On the less vexing note, some aspects of Boltgun are simply odd to me. Falling into a bottomless pit has the player put safely back into the middle of the action with only a fraction of health lost, unless there is an obvious threat down there, like working machinery which will kill the player instantly. One would argue that bottomless pit is a clear indicator of danger too, alas there is this peculiar inconsistency instead. No less strange are the secrets, which in Boltgun lingo designate power-ups found throughout the game. Many of which are nestled comfortably in the middle of a major arena in preparation for the big fight to come, enough said that I found over 80% of them during my first playthrough without looking much.This one is a matter of taste, however Boltgun is fairly easy even when played on the highest difficulty. In most cases it offers overabundant supplies of health and ammo and only the last chapter of the game managed to give me an occasional pause during my rampage. In a genre notorious for absurd top difficulty, some may find it lacking.All things considered, I’ve had a blast playing Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun. While it is by no means a perfect or groundbreaking game, it soundly delivers a solid, entertaining piece of FPS action. If shooters hold any water to you, by all means do try this game. Should you happen to be WH40k fan at the same time, I reckon you’ve probably beaten the game already. In case you didn’t, it is a gun-wielding power fantasy made in our favourite flavour, highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Review at 3 hours, just after the first boss fight in the library.It's... okay. Its not $30 AUD okay.Everything done great here has it's flaws.Scenic level design is damn near perfect. Distance and scale is shown well. Detail is the lo-fi equivalent to Spacehulk DeathWing. Ships fly across the sun. Titans are in the distance. But then it goes and makes any text unreadable and the level components repetative.The intro cutscene is a brilliant throwback to old school pixel art animation and a damn sight better than a static image blurred and claimed to be animated. No negative there, its just good.Levels have a good flow and lead back to themselves most times in a logical and comfortable manner. Arenas tend to be multipath spaghetti (in a good way) but the AI can't navigate it well. This leads to a wave starting and you wandering around trying to find any enemies.Finding keys is good and you always know where the door is but secrets are just sorta thrown around. They tend to be in a box at the back of a room or a ledge off to the side. Every time. They aren't rewards, just power ups.The power ups are fun, powerful and last 30 seconds. You tend to find them at the end of the fight so they aren't useful...The gear power ups are amazing. Mechanicus and ammo box. They disable at the end of the map. Balanced and unfortunate.Guns are appropriately damaging but some of the sounds are underwhelming. The damage model is great, using inspiration from the tabletop strength and toughness rules. Boltgun is 4, shotgun is 3, plasma 7, heavy 5. Enemies have toughness, Humans 2 or 3, marines 4, termies higher, keeper of secrets 7. Meaning plasma is mostly wasted on lower stuff and the shotgun is almost always useless compared to the boltgun.When the enemies are placed in the map they are placed well. Unfortunately they tend to just spawn in when you walk to a specific point. Knowing where the enemy is and picking targets is satisfying as anything, too bad the game only lets you do it sometimes.Hidden paths and areas are placed well and have certain visual tells to lead the player into them. A left side path beyond the right side obvious main entrance will lead to the last 1% of kills for completionists. A box with a ladder can be climbed to lead you to an overlook so you can ambush the next group. But the actual secrets are seemingly just a powerup in a crate most of the time. On the first level there is a wall you can open for a power up you don't need. On the second there is a door that you can turn around to see and fight some marines to get a power up to fight the marines.There are red barrels to shoot in convenient locations but then the giant shells laying everywhere don't explode.There are chaos icons everywhere and tend to look fitting. You cannot destroy them for some reason.There is warp f---ery in logical places and they look amazing. But the screen turns red for some ungodly reason and makes it hard to see during arena fights. It reminds me of the old red jam for damage indicators. Developers, I don't need to be told that a wave is incoming by making it hard to see.Pro: Terminators teleport in as jumpscares. Con: Random cultists teleport in as regular enemies to fight. Makes no sense.Enemies are very well designed so far. Everything has totally different feels to them. Attack patterns, damages, risk factors and weapons to target them effectively. Then they get trapped in corridors as you jump around to go to different levels. Completely breaking the flow of combat.You get given heaps of grenades, usually when you don't need them. But you can only carry 2 timed and 1 impact and unknown vortex. Same with ammo, same with health, same with small armour pickups.Everything in the game is like that.-------------------------------------------------In conclusion. A refreshing splash in the face of a lot of other developers. But far from perfect.It's... okay. Its not $30 AUD okay. Get it on special. The 10% on release is not enough for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic boomer shooter. It owes as much to Doom (1993) as it does to Doom (2016). You very much have to keep on your toes and constantly moving. If you sit still long enough to scratch your nose, you're probably going to die. The maps are pretty well varied. It's not all future space cathedrals, but there is a lot of that. All 8 of the guns have their uses, and you're given way more than enough ammo to consistently use your favorite gun in most cases.One interesting feature is that the game renders at hi-rez, then deliberately applies a filter to pixelate and alias everything for a retro aesthetic. You can turn it off if you so wish, but i found it charming.My one complaint is that the game desperately needs a map. I got hopelessly lost more times than I could count and ended up wandering around in hopes of stumbling on the next area. A couple times I even had to resort to Youtube videos just to figure out where the hell the game wanted me to go.

There's a lot of things the game fails to capture in terms of pace, enemy diversity, level design, and sense of progression compared to other shooters of the genre like Dusk, which many consider the golden standard for these kinds of games. I may buy it again in the future but for the price point, even 20% off its not enough for me to get into it.

_childDocuments_.review: As other negative reviews have stated, I really want to like the game.  I would love a boomer shooter with a warhammer 40k coat of paint.  This is not that.  It is close, on the surface level it has a checklist of the correct elements.  However, it lacks the subtle design choices that make the gameplay flow of the greats work.  Below I will discuss the two most crippling.  As someone who has sunk hundreds of hours into GZDoom and Ion Fury let me tell you, the details matter.  If you read this and think "why does it have to be exactly the same as the game you've already played?" I get it.  But read what I'm gonna say and think about how many things about the gameplay this does NOT cover.-Sound Design:Sound is your radar in games without a radar.  It is essential that sound be used to tell you what is going on in the environment without you having to look.  In Boltgun, the noise of your own gun drowns everything out.  This is wrong.  The noise of your own gun is the least important sound.  You need some feedback that you did in fact shoot but that is all.  The most important noises are the noises that relate to what your enemy is doing.  Especially the noise they make upon first spawning, while dying, and while shooting at you.  You should be able to identify distinct noises for every enemy type.  This is important because it lets you keep a mental tally of what enemies are around and what attacks are coming your way.  Boltgun does not do this.  Most of the enemy spawn and death noises are a mixed bag of low growls, and the only really strong sounding weapons are the firearms (often the actual least threatening).  The worse offender for this is the plasma rifle renegade, whose attacks are devastating but quite quiet (this enemy also has a very drab and hard to identify sprite, not good for such a high value target).  This is not only bad for game design but also bad as a 40k game.  The devs seem to know that bombastic battlecries and insane screeching are part of the 40k aesthetic, but not a single chaos marine will scream "CORPSE-WORSHIPER!" at you at the top of their lungs.  And the screamers of Tzeentch!  Where is the scream?????  Another huge issue with this has to do with armor of contempt, the temporary invincibility ability the player has which activates when taking lethal damage and recharged by killing enemies.  It has NO sounds for when it activates, when it runs out, or when it's fully charged.  This ability is essential to high level play.  It is a travesty that you have to rely on an animation and icons in the corner of your very busy screen to use it.Preventable Damage:Boomer shooters are like math problems.  There is a finite amount of ammo and weapons in the level.  This means that if you do not play well it is possible to reach a situation in which it is nearly impossible to complete the level.  You've simply wasted too much ammo and health.  In this way the game is challenge of attrition.  Individual fights may not be hard, but if they cost you a few too many hitpoints you may need to use a health item early in a hard fight later, making your chances of success lower.  So it is important for high level play that all damage be preventable.  Boltgun violates this in a couple ways.  First, many enemies fire scattering projectiles.  Movement is the key to not being damaged by projectiles, as in they must be dodged (if you are curious, the key to avoiding hitscan enemies is killing the enemy or taking cover before it can shoot which is why most of the hitscanners in doom are the weakest enemies and all have long delays before shooting, but there is no hitscan in boltgun).  But when the projectiles fill the air at random, from multiple sides, not taking damage becomes nearly impossible as you cannot predict where the shots will come from.  In doom, for example, all projectile firing enemies have distinct "dances" that you can do to flawlessly put damage on them while avoiding all damage yourself.  The challenge therefore comes from being flanked, and the response from the player is positioning and target prioritization.  This isn't the case in Boltgun, encouraging you to instead stick to cover.  But there are lots of rushdown enemies too and therein lies problem two, melee animations are extremely fast and bad looking.  In other boomer shooters, melee animations have a long windup of "safe time" before the damage comes out.  Typically, this means you can avoid the damage unless you are cornered or not paying attention.  This is a much more thoughtful setup than the way it works in Boltgun, where the enemy seems to damage you just by brushing against you.  To be fair, not all the enemies are equally bad with this and the new lightning claw terminator seems better than the base game enemies.  But overall it remains a problem.There are other topics I could mention like the arena based map design, limited ammo capacity, focus on teleporting waves instead of organic encounters that are more in line with a game like Doom Eternal (which I intensely dislike) than an actual boomer shooter.  But this will do for now.  You might think, "hey, isn't it unfair to compare it to doom, a timeless classic with decades of map-making to refine its gameplay?" but I'd say no.  There are games like Ion Fury that clearly learned from the classics.  This clearly learned from current trends instead.In short, just play Ion Fury instead

_childDocuments_.review: 2 hours in, I love this game.  3 hours in, I’m completely over it. 4 hours in and I'm thinking about the finite span of human life.If two hours of pure fun is worth half a GW mini to you, go for it.  If not...The maybe constructive part: what I cannot understand is that the game makes itself as accessible as possible, even to the point where you can play on the hardest difficulty completely invulnerable, and yet there are no waypoints, map, directions from Mr. Skull, or even ‘following the lights’ like most FPS games.  I played Wolfenstein 3D and Doom as a kid, and let me tell you, nobody liked those games for the complexity of their level designs.  This game has the action, and everything that gets in the way of it should be considered chaff by the devs.  I will check back in if the DLC has SOME kind of directional assistance.  If you wrongly remember the 90's as a time when we didn't need directions in our shooters, I have two words for you: idspispopd/noclip.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game in every aspect. Plays as snappy and fun as Destiny 2. It does everything just as good as Destiny except level design. Like, the level design is horrid. Everything is the same grim-dark palette, which fits the world's great aesthetic, but there needs to be a way to hint at where you are supposed to go. Like, you decided it's perfectly fine to use such a tired level design trope as "Yellow Paint on Jump-able Edges," but a green light near the exit of an encounter area was too "holding our hands?"  You can always hit the hint key (default N) to get a projected path on the ground of where you are supposed to go, but the path fades after a few seconds, and your Ghost does its irritating, non-talking talking sound loop even more.  The levels are too big, especially with so few enemy types. Lotta variety, mind you, just only 5 different tactics spread across a couple of dozen sprites. Gameplay is top-notch. Soundtrack shines on a few occasions. Sound design needs more polish. Same for UX. Level design is a trash heap.

_childDocuments_.review: Boltgun is a decent shooter but lacks depth. Many aspects of the game feel under developed, mainly the lore. There is an understanding that this is a retro shooter but that is no excuse to provide a lacking experience otherwise. As someone who know very little about the Warhammer 40k Universe, this game has nearly no lore to offer to get engrosed in the role of being a Marine. There are nearly no cutscenes and the cutscenes that there are very static and short. There is ingame dialog coming from the Sorcerer but it is text only and presented during heated combat especially if you are playing on max difficulty which just means you are going to miss the small bit of lore that is left over beyond the 3 short cutscenes. If this game is supposed to mirror a game like Doom, Doom 2016 and Eternal both had splendid lore delivery via well acted dialogues and extra bits of readings. I also enjoyed the secrets in Doom way more than in this game. I wish the secrets were more elaborate, but I prevailed and I am glad I did. Many were super easy to find while others were hidden insanely well (took me 3 hours for one of them). The secrets and 100% kills is probably what I enjoyed the most even though I almost gave up on them after realizing how shallow the game is, the secrets could have been a lot better in some aspects.Story aside, there are also combat aspects that feel under developed. The units start feeling repetitive with no new ones ever really showing up. Bosses are also frequently reused. There also is nothing explaining what the secret abilities do, unless you find the main menu 'Help' option which I found after my 100% Kills & Secrets playthrough.Performance is also terrible for whatever reason in this retro shooter (note: streaming might be a factor but other more demanding games are fine). There are many full frame freezes while playing on my AMD 5800X3D + RTX 4090. Additionally, for having such simple geometry, some of the hitboxes don't line up and your sticky grenades get stuck to them.None the less, I overall enjoyed the game. It took me around ~40 hours to 100% Kills and secrets at the hardest difficulty. Some of the secret rooms were particularly hard to find.

_childDocuments_.review: Edited after finishing chapter 1 on Exterminatus: this game is exactly what I was expecting of it. Nothing more, nothing less. A boomer-shooter Warhammer-styled game. Not deep, but very entertaining, especially if you're a fan of the franchise / genre. A good game, but it's obviously console-focused, which affects difficulty in weird way, making enemies easier. The only bad thing about is that you need to collect the same power-ups, like the ones improving your ammo, on each level and it gets yeeted on the next one. Also, the "secrets" in this game are ass. Like, hilariously, taking a little detour and finding a power-up is a "secret".It might be worth pointing out that the game DOES NOT want you to die and it is obvious: the health, armour, and ammo pickups are extremely abundant even on the highest difficulty. Oh, and there's no fall damage, and falling into bottomless pits barely does anything to you.If you want more challenge - go try Cultic.(1st review, right after purchase, down below)-------Why, oh why isn't there a freaking Warhammer 40k game where I can play as a right and proper Chaos Marine? Well, at least I find solace in the fact that Khorne cares not from where the blood flows. ONLY that it flows! And here it flows freely! I shall take the instruments of the so-called "righteous", despoil them, and brandish as my own! Who are those heretics and why are they shooting at me? If you can't distinguish your own, then you, weaklings, are going to end up as decoration for my spikes! Skulls for the Skull Throne! This one, after 2 missions on Exterminatus, got me SO PUMPED that I'm absolutely sure that I'll finish it 100%.Lots and LOTS of gratuitous gore-galore, pixelated goodness and chainsword action. _childDocuments_.review: First things first - you don't have to be Warhammer-pilled to appreciate Boltgun.I imagine that 99% of people reading this are - in fact - Warhammer fans, but I wanted to state this fact for anyone not familiar with 40k at all, or just know some part of it.I've finished 2 playthroughs - one on Exterminatus (highest difficulty) and one on Low just to grab the remaining secrets (I've tried my best to get as many as I can without searching the web - but that's another topic that I'll cover below).Gameplay of Boltgun is fun and this genre is all about fun.There are many weapons to choose from (however I haven't used all of them on a regular basis) and plenty of different enemy types.It can get a bit repetetive at the end, so I'd say play 4-5 maps and take a pause, because it can be a bit boring for some people.I cannot say much about other difficulties than Exterminatus, but this one provides a challenge - even if you are experienced player like me.I've been playing shooters for about 20-ish years now and chapter 3 wasn't a walk in the park. If you like difficult shooters - I strongly advise picking Exterminatus.Some people say that there are too many enemies, but they are playing Fortnite and should be considered heretics. Don't listen to them /sTaunt - that's a nice feature with many, many voice lines written to make it fun, but what's its purpose really?I have no idea. If you're streaming or feeling goofy - it's great, but I wish it did something gameplay-wise like taunting lesser enemies to charge at you, so you can kill multiple of them with you dash or shotgun/melta. I don't know, just bouncing off my idea.Concern #1 - accessibility settings.By the Holy Terra - I have no clue why they decided to put infinite ammo/all weapons/all levels/invulnerability settings in the game. Perhaps for a typical game journalist that struggle even on the lowest difficulty.Almost every game in this genre has cheats, but devs decided to include them in the options.I was trying to find some information on the web, but without any success. Why they did it? It'll remain a mystery it seems.And now the neat part - you can play with "journalist settings" and still get the achievements.For 99% of people it won't be something bad, but as an achievement hunter - it pisses me off. I play on the highest difficulty, spend a lot of time and someone does it while using cheats with the same effect. I do check how many people have achievements, and it's simply not fair, but again - I'm in minority and my approach is a bit different than for a stereotypical player.Concern #2 - melee is worthless in later levels, some enemies are bullet sponges (mainly Nugle-related ones, but that's KINDA lore accurate I guess?) and some of the weapons seem to be under-powered. I used Heavy Boltgun/Plasma/Grav most of the time.Concern #3 - there are arena type fights in most of the levels, and some of those "arenas" are VERY big. It would be great to see a marker on let's say - last 5 enemies. I've spend some time searching for mobs tucked away in the corners in a couple of encounters.Level design is not on id Software level, but it's not bad either.Again - some people/heretics are complaining and want a map. A MAP?! Why?! HERESY!I was lost only ONCE. There are plenty of visual clues where to go (like slime, braziers or candles), maps are not some crazy maze-like nightmare fuels and if you are lost you can use a nifty path feature (under "N" by default). During my second playthrough I was abusing it to see how it performs and there was one situation where it wasn't showing me where to go properly, but otherwise it did it's job well.Secrets are well hidden (there are 147 of them in the base game), but not super obscure like in original DOOMs (no humping every single wall is needed) or even DUSK and most of them provide a nice buff that will come in handy in higher difficulties, so look around.Nothing special - really. It does it's job, but it's not something that I will listen to on a daily basis like I do with DUSK, DOOM or FromSotware games.Sufficent. There's nothing more to add here. There's some story going on, but nothing very interesting. This is not a story-driven genre after all.Before you laugh that this game looks like garbage - it's intended to look like this (Captain Obvious for the rescue!)There are some "retro" settings and you can manipulate the pixelization and colours - just like in DUSK. A nice touch in my opionion.I appreciate the amount of gore (reminds me of Brutal DOOM), but you can turn it down if you want somehow.Sprites look good, weapon animations are great and you can clearly see from which era in gaming Boltgun was taking notes.Boltgun is fun game that can be appreciated by "normies" that don't live and breathe Warhammer 40k.There are 27 levels in the base game and 5 (longer ones) in the DLC (Forges of Corruption is the only DLC at the time of writing this review and it's harder than the base game - just letting you know).Boltgun has some flaws, but really nothing major in my opinion.It's worth buying on a discount if you're not a Warhammer fan, and if you are - you're spending too much on plastic anyway.FOR THE EMPEROR!

_childDocuments_.review: It is the 41st Millennium. For more than a hundred centuries the Emperor of Mankind has sat immobile on the Golden Throne of Earth. He is the master of mankind by the will of the gods and master of a million worlds by the might of His inexhaustible armies. He is a rotting carcass writhing invisibly with power from the Dark Age of Technology. He is the Carrion Lord of the vast Imperium of Man for whom a thousand souls are sacrificed every day so that He may never truly die.Yet even in His deathless state, the Emperor continues His eternal vigilance. Mighty battlefleets cross the daemon-infested miasma of the Warp, the only route between distant stars, their way lit by the Astronomican, the psychic manifestation of the Emperor's will. Vast armies give battle in His name on uncounted worlds. Greatest amongst His soldiers are the Adeptus Astartes, the Space Marines, bio-engineered super-warriors. Their comrades in arms are legion: the Imperial Guard and countless planetary defence forces, the ever-vigilant Inquisition and the Tech-priests of the Adeptus Mechanicus to name only a few. But for all their multitudes, they are barely enough to hold off the ever-present threat to humanity from aliens, heretics, mutants -- and far, far worse.To be a man in such times is to be one amongst untold billions. It is to live in the cruelest and most bloody regime imaginable. These are the tales of those times. Forget the power of technology and science, for so much has been forgotten, never to be relearned. Forget the promise of progress and understanding, for in the grim dark future there is only war. There is no peace amongst the stars, only an eternity of carnage and slaughter, and the laughter of thirsting gods.
