_childDocuments_.review: Honestly the gameplay is really good but there are so many design choices that I just can't get past.  Particle effects are impossible to see through and constantly stack on top of each other.  Enemies are massively bullet spongy.  As in it can easily take over ten minutes to kill a Lord of Change.  Tying your weapons strength based on the number of secrets you find is annoying for speed running.  I'm finding issues with collision on pillars and walls constantly bringing me to a dead stop in the middle of an intense fight when I'm only walking alongside it.  Enemy damage is seemingly random.  I'll be hit by a generic dude who dies in one bullet for 4 damage then the next bullet from the same guy does 80.  Don't even get me started on the wall hacks these enemies have.  Having smart AI that tracks the player behind cover is fine if the damage is at least consistent.  I never feel like I'm being killed by something fair (other than the obvious I got too aggressive times) or half the time I won't even know what killed me or where it came from.  There is a lot of great ideas and mechanics behind the game, but overall it could really use a few patches.  Aspiring Champions alone are easily a reason enough to avoid for now.UPDATE:I am now a few more hours into the game and I have to say it's worse. I've made it to my first Great Unclean One and I'm confused at where the fun is supposed to be in fighting 50 Nurglings and the Unclean One at the same time in an arena full of pillars to limit your movement and block your shots.  Half of the weapons feel unusable at this stage.  Shotgun does no damage to anyone who doesn't die in one hit.  Heavy Bolter is super cool but limiting movement in this game is the fastest way to get swarmed.  Plasma guns splash damage seemingly hits me from like 30 feet away but if I shoot the ground 10 inches from an enemy they just shrug it off. I can't fully understand why they gave collision to every enemy as well. The Deathwatch core rulebook describes Space Marines as being around 3 meters tall and weighing between 500 to 1000 kg.  So tell me why a normal human, or even a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Nurgling can stop me dead in my tracks without the charge.  I understand for balance purposes why my footsteps don't just crush these fools but at least let me walk through them. So many terribly designed enemies.  Plague Toads, Champions, and every single Boss/Mini boss. I can't fully comprehend how so many people are ranting and raving over this game when it has like a 6% for just completing the game on the easiest difficulty.  I love Warhammer and I love boomer shooters but this games reviews are clearly being carried by the Warhammer fanboys who've put .5 to 2 hours into the game, gave it a good review, and then quit to never return.  It's so promising in the first few levels and then everything just plummets around chapter 4 or 5 of the first level.The games only 20 bucks.  That's literally the most positive thing I can say about it.  If you're a huge Warhammer/boomer shooter fan and don't care that you may not finish the game, or if you're like me and willing to bash your skull against its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ until something different happens then by all means you will get your times worth out of it at least.  I plan to keep running against this brick wall til I at least beat it but I absolutely can't recommend this when there are so many much better games in this genre already available and this one feels like a 5 (maybe a 6 if I'm being generous) out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: BOLTGUN!It’s a violent, old school, boomnshoot that makes the Warhammer fans happy by not being garbage!BOLTGUN!It is a game that makes the bolters seem heavy and powerful, not feeble like so many games!BOLTGUN!It is basically Doom 2016 in its design ethos, using sprites to make it seem older than it is!BOLTGUN!It has no single large flaw, but so many annoying little problems that it is bloody frustrating at times and makes you want to play something else.So, the much hyped Warhammer 40k: Boltgun. An FPS that places you in the armour of one of the Ultramarines and demands you do very violent things to the forces of Chaos for 10 or so hours. It simultaneously shows a great attention to detail in its construction and provides some VERY meaty shooting, but it is also let down by so many design flaws that at times it makes you wonder what they were thinking while making it. It is a generally advisable game for a long weekend, but if you are looking for some top quality old school shooting there are far better options out there.Critiquing a game like Boltgun for someone like me is somewhat tough. I’ve played a LOT of these old school FPS games and I’ve been playing them for a long time. As such there is a quality standard I have for what could be seen as good or bad. Boltgun is clearly a very good game, it is just deeply flawed in some fundamental areas that, for a long time “boomshoot” fan it may not be advisable. For more fair-weather fans, this may seem like a pedantic splitting of hairs, but they are big issues in the eyes of some. This does beg the question for the potential buyer: what is your threshold for flawed design?Before I dig into the gameplay there is the fact that Boltgun is a licenced product. A Warhammer 40k licenced product. To skip over a lot of text regarding the history of the universe in videogame form, I’ll just say that, yes Boltgun is a good use of the 40k licence. It sits up beside titles like Dawn of War or Space Marine in its quality and respect for the licence. I’ve seen some hardcore obsessives comb over the details in this game and they seem quite satisfied with what is happening, who is doing what and why the events are occurring. In this regard I guess that should be enough of a reason for hardcore 40k fans to lap it up.This reverence in the licence goes beyond simple aesthetic and mechanically carries across to the gameplay. Rather that drape a Warhammer skin over a pre-existing title, Boltgun goes and does the old “it really makes you feel like a Space Marine!” shtick.Space Marines are not normal (or even innocent) men. They are what happens if you took Arnold Schwarzenegger at his peak and multiplied his mass and strength by 6, only for him to take a Panzer III and wear it as a shirt and turn its cannon into a fully automatic rifle. You are a heavy monstrosity and the game always lets you know this with the endless thudding of your feel or the huge crash as you hit the ground. Granted your jump is a little floaty considering the idea of how heavy you are supposed to be, but the general fantasy is maintained.The greatest part of the game’s authentic push comes with the weapons and combat. If you have an understanding of how 40k weapons work you will know, like the marines themselves, everything is larger than life. A boltgun itself is not a rifle, it is a fully automatic grenade launcher built from wrought iron. Thankfully, Boltgun takes these concepts and makes them flesh in game. The melee chainsword is a monster that can rip even the biggest enemies apart if you keep revving it. The basic boltgun, rather than being a peashooter, utterly gibs the basic foes in a single shot. The plasma gun feels like you are carrying a microwave that throws superheated material that you REALLY should not be holding. Linking to this is the enemy roster, which is vast and satisfying to fight. While it simply sticks to fighting the Chaos forces, the minions of Slaanesh and Nurgle bolster the ranks nicely and give a huge number of beings to slaughter, ranging from the (likely purposefully) absolutely infuriating Nurglings all the way to the huge boss like Lords of Change. Almost every encounter feels like a good challenge due to the variation on display and things rarely stagnate thankfully.So as a Warhammer product Boltgun delivers nicely!As a regular old school shooter? Ehhhhh… almost.For all of its qualities there are numerous flaws in the game. Listing them would be absurd as, while I was playing, I noted at least two or three problems per fight. These were never huge, game ruining issues, but they were the kind of things that drove down a classic experience into the more middle of the road slog that peppered the market in the mid-2000s: It is less a title with a fatal blow and more a death by a thousand cuts situation. Things like the animation lags that cause weapon swaps and reloads to seem delayed, enemy melee animations that don’t synch with the damage, some strange float in the air control, secrets not actually being secrets and just powerups that call themselves secrets, inconsistent mantling on surfaces (this isn’t a boomshoot with that lads!), enemies that blend into the background, difficult to navigate maps, incoherent difficulty curve, autosaves that place you in instant death situations etc. If there were any of these single issues in another game they would be bundled into the flaws and may even have whole paragraphs written about them, only to be brushed off as “but this is only a small issue in a great title.” Here these issues are so numerous that it makes it somewhat hard to fully recommend Boltgun as it frustraits just as much as it pleases.If I had to point to one area that highlights the issues, it would be the servoskull you have to assist you. Aside from having a floating head that you accidentally fire at from time to time, it is supposed to assist you in your journey. It does so less in helping you navigate maps or giving useful advice, more in that it gives irreverent comments in the corner of the screen, out of the way so you can’t read it. Even then, when it does do something debatably useful, it is usually highlighting a medipack in the open when you are at full health. It COULD have been a useful companion considering the repetitive nature of some of the maps where you can easily get lost, but alas it is more a burden than a help.In conclusion you are likely going to be one of two people looking at Boltgun:A Warhammer fan looking for a good use of the licence. In this case, go nuts! This is a really good use of the Space Marines.ORYou are looking to get a new, old-school shooter. In this case, only buy it if it hits bargain bin levels of discount. There are so many titles in this genre these days that Boltgun is more a wet weekend time killer than an essential play. Go grab Dusk first, or Ion Fury, or Amid Evil, or or or etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm by no means a Warhammer expert, but I've enjoyed a couple of the games I've played, and Boltgun is no exception. The story is you're a space marine sent to kill a bunch of things. I know the lore goes deeper than that, but for someone like me, it was unobtrusive and set up the premise of playing a heavyweight super soldier with an arsenal of great weapons. The gameplay is nothing we haven't seen before, but it's straight forward and fun, in no small part thanks to the outstanding presentation. I know 2D sprites on a 3d plane is hit or miss with some people, but I love it, and I found myself enamored with the detailed pixel art. It helps that it's super gory too; the eponymous boltgun, your bread and butter, pulverizes normal enemies into a pulp. The rest of the arsenal is also a lot of fun to mess around with, with some of my favorites being the plasma rifle, the vengeance launcher, and the gravity cannon. Much stink was made at launch about the often obtuse level design, and thankfully the devs have implemented a navigation tool that is 100% optional. I turned it on and immediately had a better time; while the levels are cool, they really could have been more intuitively designed. See something like Amid Evil for an example of how to do huge levels in an easily legible way. Still, with Nav turned on I found myself enjoying the relentless pacing.Other accessibility options exist too, and don't seem to affect achievement unlocks. Things like infinite health/ ammo, all weapons unlocked, and all levels unlocked are really nice additions. Again, like the nav, they're completely optional, but I wound up toggling a few of them during the game's final boss, which falls into the Doom Eternal trap of being a rather arduous slog against an enemy with ridiculous amounts of health, as well as infinitely spawning enemies.Special mention should be made to the soundtrack, which, instead of overt heavy metal homaging the 90s, is instead a weird industrial/ darkwave mix. It suits the fascist, blood thirsty nature of the player character well, and almost gives things a mild horror vibe at times. The weapons all have fantastic sound accompanying the great gore and weapon effects.Boltgun has benefited a lot from the updates made since launch, and now it's something I can say I really enjoyed. The generous optional accessibility options are a really nice touch, and I could see a sequel ironing out some of the rougher spots of the game (mainly the very dense level design) and becoming a small classic. As is, this isn't really anything new, but it's a case of "if it ain't broke, don't fix it."

The game needs a map option for people playing for the first time- Enemies become repetitive. Once you face a great unclean one, you have now seen every enemy in the game. Congrats.- NO ORCS OR TYRANIDS ONLY CHAOS (which is fine to me but could be seen as a flaw)- I know pistol start is a common theme in retro shooters but like. COME. ON. how many times u gonna take my guns?(small gripe)- Certain guns are useless with the machine spirit. Ricochet shotgun, I am looking at you.- Purge sequences can become very repetitive quickly. Especially given the lack of enemy variation.- Overall repetitive nature of some of the levelsIn saying ALL of this if you are a fan of retro shooters and 40k BUY THIS GAME!if you are into JUST retro shooters or JUST 40k i would recommend waiting for a sale. _childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: The style, sound design, and visuals carry this game HARD with everything else ranging from so-so to sluggish. Which is abysmal for the price point.The most I got out of this game were the first couple of levels as that's when the punchiness of the mechanics, visuals, and sound design mask the rather dry gameplay. Everything afterwards dragged its feet with the gameplay loop becoming stale.Sure, the combat is impactful and it is thoroughly satisfying to mow down enemies one by one. The problem is that it never changes during the entire course of the game. Different weapons and enemies don't matter when it all comes down to which enemy is tougher and which weapon deals more damage. It's way too rudimentary to be engaging long term.The level design doesn't help things since it's hopelessly linear and cramped for the most part. It's frustrating since it feels like the game never fully plays to its strengths.Music sucks too. The only good tracks are the menu & credits theme. Everything else is this kind of droning synth-y garbage with no variation. I get that its purpose is to set the grim-dark mood but other Warhammer games have proven that this can be done without sounding like mashing keys with maximum distortion.That being said the game isn't awful. It's serviceable for the genre. Dull is only mildly repulsive after all.But at this point I've played so many games that serviceable isn't cutting it. Not worth the price, dissappointingly mediocre. 5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: + All round well made boomer-shooter + Great atmosphere, music and artwork + Guns feel chunky and satisfying + Warhammer 40k fans will definitely get the most out of the experienceCons: - Not unusual to get stuck inside geometry - Way too easy, hardest difficulty is absolutely stuffed with ammo and health pickups - Could do with more sound effects for enemies as they can be hard to find sometimes and can sneak up on you (Looking at you, Aspiring Champion) - Could do with a mapBoltgun is all around a good game, it was pretty fun and feels almost like a mix between classic Doom and the modern Doom games in gameplay style. Good mindless fun, every level has an interesting design that makes them very memorable, great enemy variety although they could be a bit more aggressive. I played on the hardest difficulty and had very little trouble with enemies, hardest mode feels like the Hurt Me Plenty mode on Doom which is basically medium/normal difficulty. The game inundates you with ammo and health even on the hardest mode, I had so much health, armour and ammo that 90% of the time it was all around me and I couldn't pick it up because I already had too much.I noticed some people saying the levels weren't well designed, I disagree, I think they're overall well made although a map would come in handy in some of the earlier levels that can be a bit confusing. The game does a decent job of making sure you're always pointed in the right direction.If you like both boomer-shooters and Warhammer, this game is worth it, although definitely play on the hardest mode if you are used to Doom's difficulty, even if you don't normally play Doom on high difficulties. If you just like boomer-shooters and are specifically looking for a challenge, this is probably not going to do it for you. If you like boomer-shooters and just want to unwind and shoot demons, pick it up on sale I'd say.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s fairly common knowledge among long-time fans of the series that there just really aren’t that many good Warhammer 40k games. You got Dawn of War, Space Marine, Mechanicus….. and that’s about it. Maybe Darktide. Most of these games are over a decade old and aren’t the best thing to recommend to people anymore.But what if we made a game that was intentionally designed to be old? Enter Warhammer 40k: Boltgun.Riding the high of the 2020 resurgence of the “Boomer Shooter”, FPS games designed to be more reminiscent of the simple but effective formula of 90s FPS games. No regenerating health, no hiding behind cover. Just you, your guns, a whole lot of enemies, and your typical olympic track star speed to evade them.I believe Boltgun is worth your time and money, especially considering how cheap it is. But it’s always best to make an informed purchase. That’s what I’m here to do!As aforementioned, Boltgun is part of the “Boomer Shooter” genre of FPS, which are FPS games designed to appear and somewhat play like old 90s FPS staples such as Doom and Quake, but with modernized movement and controls. Boltgun definitely gets this idea; arenas are large and designed to run around full sprint while mowing down your enemies, and you have a total of 9 different weapons to unlock throughout the game as convenient spinning pickups. However, every good game has a core mechanic that sets it apart from the rest. In this case, much to the delight of myself and other fans of 40k, Boltgun excels at emulating an FPS experience that is extremely similar to the IRL tabletop gameplay. Every weapon you can wield has a “Strength” value, and every enemy has a “Toughness” value, both of which can be conveniently seen at all times on the UI. If your weapon’s Strength is greater than your enemy’s Toughness, you do more damage per shot! If it’s equal, you do okay damage. If it’s lower, you do noticeably less damage. Every weapon in the game has a different gimmick that sets it apart and makes it useful compared to the rest. The weapon the game is named after, the Boltgun, has a Strength of 4 and a very deep ammo reserve. This makes it excellent for chewing through cannon fodder enemies, but struggles significantly against heavily armored enemies. Comparatively, the Plasma Gun and Meltagun have a Strength of 7, making them extremely effective against every enemy, but they possess either a low rate of fire or very low ammo reserves, meaning you can’t be wasting them on random mid-level enemies.Just like all “Movement Shooters”, Boltgun demands you avoid damage through strafing and running rather than hiding behind cover. Every enemy attack that isn’t melee is a form of projectile that can be avoided with good enough reactions or speed. Some enemies track better than others, and so you must strafe rather than just try to outrun. Some just spew hundreds of rounds, forcing you to keep moving or else they’ll catch up with you.Another staple of the BS FPS formula are secrets and power-ups. Every map contains an array of power-ups that only last until the end of the level. One example of this is special ammo for the Boltgun that makes it fire faster, penetrate walls or add an AOE. Another is the Vortex Grenade, which when thrown creates a small black hole that rapidly damages and sucks in any enemies around it. But the most impactful power-up you can find is the Machine Spirit, which empowers whatever weapon you are holding when you pick it up. Some of the secrets are genuinely just impossible to find without a guide (Just like Doom), but there’s usually a few easy ones to make up for it. I can usually reliably find the Machine Spirit every level.Overall, the gameplay is responsive, engaging, and multi-layered; the best kind of FPS gameplay you can get. Varying enemy toughness requiring you to switch weapons is great moment-to-moment engagement that keeps you on your toes, and the multiple different types of environments you venture through help keep the game fresh even when fighting the same enemies. Remember Doom: The Imp never changed from start to finish, but the places you fought it in did!However, one critical flaw I must make known is that Boltgun lacks any form of map. While the environments are relatively straight forward, sometimes you loop around to the same “hub” room with a key for a new door and need to remember where that door actually is. It’s only a bit annoying and time consuming, but be prepared to actually pay attention to where you’re going so you don’t get lost.Another staple of the Boomer Shooter genre is an intentional lack of focus on the story. It’s still there, of course. It just barely matters. You play as Malum Caedo, a Space Marine of the Ultramarines chapter, tasked with purging the Chaos filth off a Forge World. Don’t know 40k lore? Don’t know what any of that means? Doesn’t matter! Point and shoot at the bad guys. It’s as easy as that! Boltgun has a very good grasp of the world of Warhammer 40k and the “grimdark” feeling it pioneered. The combination of technology and religious zealotry is on full display through excessively large cathedral designs, overcomplicated iron techno-junk, and of course the chaos corruption and vandalism covering it all.The low-poly nature of the environments help to emulate Quake, which is clearly the main inspiration for most of the gameplay (As it is so practically all FPS), but the enemies are a nice unique 2D claymation spin on the sprites you normally see in these kinds of games. It reminds me very heavily of Doom 64, which had far different and rather memorable redesigns of the classic Doom enemy ensemble.Weapon effects, enemy attacks, and particles are very distinct and prominent, though the sheer AMOUNT of effects can sometimes cause a bit of blindness by making it impossible to tell living enemies from the pure carnage going on around them. This is compounded by the speed of the game, which sometimes results in confusing scrambles where you just spray and pray and hope for the best.I have no complaints, but also no compliments about the audio. The music is okay, but not even slightly memorable. The guns do sound satisfyingly chunky, but not quite enough to really resonate. It’s good and performs its job satisfactorily.I typically don’t have any problems running Boltgun on my PC. However, on random occasions, the game will suffer a sort of stutter-freeze where every two or so seconds, the entire game will freeze for a split-second. This will happen repeatedly. I don’t really know what causes it, or how to solve it, but restarting a few times seems to fix it.Boltgun is an excellent retro “Boomer Shooter” that perfectly emulates the lore and appeal of the Warhammer 40k universe while still being approachable enough that non-fans can enjoy it too. While it does have some momentary annoyances, like the complete lack of a map, it is a majority fun experience. It comes with a satisfying amount of content, an enjoyable weapon roster, and iconic enemies, all with a 40k coat of paint. I've replayed it three times and enjoyed it each time!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game because a shooter game set in the Warhammer 40k Universe is such a solid idea that I am surprised it hasn't been attempted more often outside of games like Space Marine or Spacehulk, but there was just too much holding this game back from being good. First and foremost I just have to say that this game claiming to be a boomer shooter is a bit misleading or at the very least something brought to contention; a Boomer shooter is meant to be a game that despite having a start and a finish line of sorts; the pathway to get there is non-linear, meaning you can go to certain areas at your own pace as you wish and get creative in how you get there; keycards while in existence were not always as required as much as people may think. This game is more akin to an Early 2000's wave shooter that is in actuality a lot more linearly designed than the game makes you think. Sure keys play a role akin to your Duke Nukem or your Doom or what have you but they are given such special emphasis in the game that entire pathways of a level are dedicated to you getting to those keys and going back to the door you just found. And it gets particularly grating as time goes on in this game because of the obvious linearity. It's not a bad that a game be linear; but it is bad when the game sets up the expectation for more nuanced level design than that. By wave shooters I mean that most of the game's levels will have you stop dead in your tracks and fight on built for Multiplayer style levels that lead you to just fight waves of enemies and it isn't very fun at all; and there is a reason no one is nostalgic for it because it is just a time wasting thing that ultimately people who care far too much about multiplayer shooters to care for, so don't expect early 2000's wave shooters come back anytime soon.I found the music also particularly annoying and unbecoming of a boomer shooter as well as a 40k game, the weird Dubstep action movie type music clashes heavily with the Gothic themeing of the game's world both set up in the opening cutscene. It comes off as a game that in all honesty wants to ring in the 40k fans, the modern shooter fans and the people obsessed with boomer shooter speedruns on YouTube to try and bring this up to the fray and it kind of clashes into a game that ultimately doesn't know what it wants to be.

But as you play  these little issues become major annoyances that all too frequently break up the gameplay flow.I'm only on Chapter 2 and it feels like a slog.Maybe i need to give it a break and come back to it?Maybe Darktide's fluid melee & gun based combat spoilt me too much (much better game combat wise, with much better variety) as i just can't get into this clunky mess.If you want something vague 40k shaped and shooty buy this.If you want something with a boltgun that makes you feel like you are firing a boltgun its just not this. I'd even recommend buying Doom 2016 over this as the Heavy Rifle rocket mod feels more like a Boltgun than this games Bolter.As for enemies, theres no satisfaction in slaughtering them. _childDocuments_.review: Strap on your power armor and rev up your chainsword, because Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun is here to deliver a nostalgia-fueled blast from the past that will leave you grinning like a Bloodthirster on a caffeine high.Imagine DOOM and Warhammer 40K had a baby, and that baby grew up eating nothing but protein shakes and metal albums. That's Boltgun for you. It's a frenetic, over-the-top shooter where you play as a Space Marine who, clearly, never learned the meaning of "subtlety." The game's plot is as straightforward as an Ork's battle plan: see bad guy, shoot bad guy, repeat until everything is a delightful mess of pixelated gore.The graphics? Pure retro gold. It's like they ripped the 90s from a CRT monitor and injected it straight into your eyeballs. You'll be mowing down heretics and demons in beautifully blocky glory, all while listening to a soundtrack that makes you want to headbang like it's 1993.The weapons are satisfyingly chunky, and the sound effects are meatier than a Squat's dinner. Every trigger pull feels like a thunderous declaration of "I AM THE EMPEROR'S FURY!" Enemies explode with the kind of enthusiasm usually reserved for fireworks displays or particularly enthusiastic New Year's Eve parties.If you're looking for a game that's all about depth and strategy, this is not it. But if you want a no-holds-barred, adrenaline-pumping joyride through the grimdark future, Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun is the game for you. Just be prepared to laugh maniacally as you leave a trail of destruction in your wake. And remember: in the grim darkness of the far future, there is only bolter fire. Lots and lots of bolter fire.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: A solid boomer shooter entry, you feel powerful and the game gives you a power fantasy you'd expect to get from being one of the Emperor's finest. Guns hit hard and sound chunky though bigger and tougher enemies can take a alarming amount of punishment sometimes.Visuals look great, the art design is some of the best we've gotten in 40k titles so far, up there with Chaos Gate and the OG Space Marine title.Sound is fantastic, the stomping of you just running around makes you sound so mean and there are a large variety of Taunts that can be performed that give a surprising amount of personality to your marine. I'd like more sound cues from the various enemies but the ones in place work i suppose.(In doom every enemy had a different alert sound letting you know without seeing just what was around the next corner)Controls are SOLID and tight i only ever felt like i was out of control when i'd use the charge ability as you tend to skid, and don't use it on any kind of incline or it'll stop short, overall not a terribly useful ability unless you are fighting a bunch of little guys tbh.The weapon variety is solid and most feel like they not only serve a role but have substantial punch but feel very "purpose" oriented, you don't really have a standard "workhorse" weapon so busting out the right tool for the right task can be important.The badNo map. WHY? why is there no map function in a game featuring maze like at times levels and back tracking to locked doors? this is probably the biggest issue besides the frustrating teleporter room early in the game.Mini bosses: they're kind of lame ngl. Lords of change and great unclean ones who just seem to be tanky and thats about all they have going for them, the huge amount of minions they'll call in will give you a harder time than the boss itself.Weapon levels. Each weapon has this sort of level indicator on it and...i still don't quite get the point. Bigger number is better of course but most of the higher tier weapons already do more damage anyway? its like having a number to explain that a rocket launcher is better than the pistol. No ♥♥♥♥ its better.A better mechanic would have been anti-armor or something to give something besides a arbitrary number to indicate what would be the best weapon for a task, or just let the players figure it out like 99% of other titles.TLDR a solid entry into the boomer shooter genre and a solid 40k game overall. _childDocuments_.review: In a world where we get half a dozen amazing boomer shooters each year. Boltgun just doesn't do enough to stand out from others over the past few years: But Boltgun does have some great stuff. Its best feature is its level design. Some are truly massive, very vertical, and varied. Even without a map, it's easy to navigate. There are some enemies that require some tactics. There's a demon that will split when dead into two smaller ones unless you blow up its corpse and a Chaos Marine that is b-lines you like a Warhammer fan on their next figurine purchase. If he hits you, when he dies, he resurrects, adding real tension, especially when they do insane damage.But there are two sins against the boomer shooter code that Boltgun commits, reusing bosses way too much. It's a short ten-hour game yet it runs out of new enemies and bosses basically by the first episode, three hours in. You fight the first boss again before the next one, and then as "mini-bosses" again. Boltgun also has way too much combat, which is the first time I felt that while playing a boomer shooter. It's nearly non-stop and with the lack of variety, it just feels like you're playing Diablo or Destiny, aka a grindfest. You don't even get to see the BFG until you're in the final episode :(But the biggest sin is weapon feel. Every boomer shooter has to deal with how to stop players from using only the shotgun. Doom Eternal solved it with limited ammo and the chainsaw. Fashion Police Squad made weapons be tied to enemies. Here the weapons and enemies have a ranking. If they match, your weapon does standard damage. Higher or lower and you do more or less. Ranks go from 2-8. The shotgun is a 3. See the problem. So when you run out of high-ranking weapon ammo for the RPG, laser, and plasma weapons. You get stuck with a flaccid gun in both damage, sound, and visual feedback. The good weapons you get are sadly really late into the playthrough and have low ammo. There's a melt gun that lives up to its name, but it has 6 shots which is less than the BFG, which is a laser blackhole. which is super dope btw. Overall the weapon balance is all over the place and I'm too lazy to explain why most are lackluster, like why does their rocket launcher have an explosion radius the size of a baby puddle?But you do get lots of blood and if you're a fan of Warhammer, this is not bad... for a Warhammer game.I don't care for the branding and just wanted a great boomer shooter, instead I got an average one.This is one of those it's on the edge of the recommending scale, even though I sound like I hated it. It's just so average I lean to not recommend, when it doesn't do something interesting.If you've played every boomer shooter, or need a mental break from a stressful life, you could do worse. You could play StarfieldYou like scores?Is 7/10 or a 5/10 average? See why scores are pointless

_childDocuments_.review: I got this day one because I wanted to support the devs. Personally though I think most should wait until it's deeper on sale because while fun in small bursts, the levels quickly feel tedious. It's easy to get lost and have to waste time backtracking because there's no level map to pull up like in Doom so you just have to look for arrows in the level telling you which way to go, which is lazy as ♥♥♥♥ level design in my opinion. I also don't like being stripped of my weapons at the beginning of each new episode. I know that's how these games worked back in the day but it feels pointless and just makes earlier levels in episodes 2 and 3 more frustrating because you have fewer guns to rotate through in major arenas. I love the audio design, although a little more music variety would've been nice and maybe some more enemy sound effects to telegraph to the player that they're nearby or above/below. The guns feel great to shoot, and the controls overall are decent and feel appropriately weighty for a Space Marine. The chainsword felt weak and not useful in most situations which is a bummer cus it's cool in theory. The secrets also aren't that exciting so I don't feel motivated to replay levels to 100 percent them or beat them on higher difficulties so it just doesn't feel like a very robust package. However, the gore and overall tone of the game are excellent and this definitely scratches the old school arena shooter itch I was having! If you're a Warhammer or Doom fan it's definitely worth playing at some point but you may wanna hold off until it's more on sale. Or not, do you!

_childDocuments_.review: Boltgun looked very promising, but ultimately it felt disappointing:Controls are smooth and probably the only place where I had no complaints. Visuals were good for most part, although levels very quickly start to blend into each other. Different types of cultist are also difficult to distinguish at a glance, especially on darker levels or when you are trying to stay mobile. Which means that it can be hard to distinguish the harmless from the deadly enemies (see below).The actual levels vary between the maze-like, that can be fun to navigate, and long linear corridors that you just sprint through while dispatching occasional enemies. Annoyingly, the more complex areas often result in your running around trying to find that one damn cultist that you need to kill to end the current encounter and allow you to progress. Besides magic walls barring your progress until you've finished an encounter, you'll also find yourself hunting down keys needed to unlock gates. The problem with those keys is that tend to feel like they were placed in the levels at random. In one notable instance you can walk in a nearly straight (and fairly short) line to/from the key to the gate it unlocks, which makes one question why you even had to pick up a key in the first place.Enemy design is also puzzling. Not in the "each enemy is a puzzle you have to solve" kind of way, but rather "why is one dude with a Heavy Stubber more of a threat then several Chaos Space Marines put together?". As it turns out, Chaos Space Marines just tend to stand around, occasionally fire their weapons, and very occasionally throw a grenade, neither of which pose much of a threat. Chaos Terminators are slightly more threatening, but their seemingly taking a coffee break between every salvo leaves them wide open to having their their excessive health bars wittled down by whatever weapon you can be arsed to point in their general direction. Chaos Marinee Champions do pose a threat, due to their high melee damage and ability to re-spawn, but they are also quite rare, tend to start far away, and (like most other enemies) cannot jump. Flamer demons are also notable in this regard, since their "bullets" move so absurdly slow that you are more likely to run into them due to sheer carelessness or forgetfulness, than you are likely to be hit by them due to a failure to evade incoming fire. If you are not standing directly in front of those enemies, then you can just stroll out of the way, with plenty of time to finish your coffee on the way. It does not help that enemy AI is also extremely simple, to the point where you can snipe enemies at a long distance without them ever reacting to being hit (and ultimately killed) by distant bolter fire.Ultimately just types of two enemies stand out as being threatening, both being enemies you that fight from the very start of the game: The first are cultists with plasguns, since they not only tend to blend in with other cultists but are also capable of shaving off a quite significant chunk of your health with next to no wind-up. Turning a corner and immediately taking a plasma bolt to the face is not my idea of fun. The second are pink horrors, who would be nearly harmless if not for the fact that their shots track over a long range. That alone makes them significantly more threatening that nearly every other (non-boss) enemy. Bosses are somewhat threatening, but this is chiefly due to their exceedingly deep health-pools; boss battles feel more like battles of attrition than a skill based challenge.This is based on playing on "hard" difficulty, since enemies were so toothless on "medium" difficulty that I nearly dropped the game after the first couple of levels. But even then, difficulty only spikes in arena areas, and only due to the sheer amount of enemies that spawn, often spawning behind you and in areas that you had cleaned out already. Deaths are mostly due to slow attrition in those overly long encounters, where your health gets whittled down by stray bullets, rather than due to actual mistakes on your part.Sound design is also lackluster: Enemies lack distinguishing sound cues, or any audio cues at all, meaning that enemies frequently sneak up on you without warning, and while your weapons for most part have meaty sounds, grenades in particular sound sound more akin to popping a balloon than detonating high explosives. Your ever-present AI companion also does little more than raise the noise-floor, while their subtitles are placed/sized in such a manner (in the top left corner) that you frequently miss what is being said due to focusing on what is happening in front of you.Of the four weapons I encountered in the first chapter, I would consider two to be practical: The Boltgun and the Heavy Boltgun, both of which were my go-to for the majority of my playtime. The shotgun is useful against some enemies, but suffers from too wide of a spread, too slow a rate of fire, and a too slow a reload speed to be useful in most encounters. Meanwhile the plasma gun had to be shelved for most of the game due to posing a bigger threat to my health than any enemy, despite not doing that much damage to tankier enemies. On occasion it could be used against distant enemies, but enemies getting close to you would immediately render the plasgun a bigger threat to your health those enemies ever were, should you accidentally shoot one of them at too close a range.Ultimately playing Boltgun just felt like a chore, and that is why I decided to drop it after getting to chapter 2, after about 10 levels.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty phenomenal. The boltgun itself is amazing, almost to the detriment of the other weapons in your arsenal. I love the detail of the maps, the environment is soaked in 40k goodness. But a map would be nice. The other issue is with the wave mechanic of purge areas. The maps lead to large arenas where enemies will swarm you. Until they die, you can't move on from the area. But it sends them in waves. Other than those 2 issues, I absoluely love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes a good first impression due to solid shooting mechanics and 40K lore but hits a wall very quickly. I've only played 2 hours but I feel it's triple that and I don't mean that as a positive. Level design is non-existent, you just move from one killing arena to the next through connected hallways. Enemy variety and gameplay flow was already stale and boring by the third level and I found myself zoning out and dying more due to that than the difficulty of the game itself. There's no interesting landmarks or exploration and I was shocked to see power ups sitting in plain sight and met with a "SECRET FOUND" when you pick it up. What? That's just pure laziness and a cheap attempt at player satisfaction. A secret is, well, you know, a secret? It's like if somebody tells you a "secret" that water is wet. This game feels like what happens if you read what a boomer shooter is on paper but you have never actually taken the time to play and learn the design principles. This game feels like all the uninspired first mods that would be made for Doom and Quake. That's all well and good for a free mod but it's not acceptable for a $30 commercial product. There's good core gunplay here I just hope they do something more interesting with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great sort of love letter to '90s style shooters, by way of Warhammer 40,000. The game looks and sounds fantastic, weapons feel really good, the level designs are consistently interesting, the enemy types provide varied challenges, and the little nods to both FPS history and 40K tabletop games are charming throughout. I'm not partial to the game's arena sections, but they're not bad. The arenas seem to be designed for you to run around in, Doom 2016 style, but the slightly bullet-spongey enemies, large number of incoming projectiles, and kinda awkward weapon switching behaviour often encourage you to find a relatively defensible area and hunker down instead. These arenas often include strong powerups, like double damage, that would encourage the more aggressive approach, but they're frequently tucked into places you're not likely to explore until the enemies are clear. These arenas are still mostly a lot of fun, but it can feel like you're not making full use of the lovingly crafted retro-modern level architecture.The exploration / corridor segments though? Those I really, really enjoy. The level design is great, managing to channel that old school maze vibe without actually being difficult to navigate (with just a couple exceptions). They pack in a lot of surprise and delight, with unexpected features, varied scales, and a lot of nods to actual tabletop terrain you might have if you're a 40K or Kill Team player. The game is not short on these exploration segments and, in my opinion, they're where it really shines.There was one boss fight that kinda sucked, and I wouldn't complain about a punchier Meltagun, a slightly bigger item pickup radius, or a little more enemy variety (or just fewer toads), but overall I had a really good time with this one and would recommend it to anyone who's into fast-paced, old school shooters and/or Warhammer 40k.

_childDocuments_.review: In general I feel like this game is lackluster compared to Cultic or even Doom, hell for all its faults, even Prodeus manages to provide a more focused and well designed experience, and the main problem imo is the level design. It really does feel like the evil twin version of Cultic where it's designed by a cynical committee trying to cash into the boomer shooter trend instead of being made by one passionate dude who knows his games, or like, a sub-par map pack for an otherwise good shooter. The game feels overall not fun to play, even though all the building blocks are there.Warhammer games tend to have this problem where the developers need to strike a compromise between the ginormous architecture while not making them feel barren and lifeless in a world where humans are as populous and meaningless as germs; Space Marine had a similar problem, while games like Darktide or Necromunda or even (sorta) Inquisitor Martyr manage to sidestep this by putting you in cramped, lived in environments that tend to be full of enemies by virtue of them being mostly enemy bases or encampments or just overran. It's not impossible to set up a game in the 40k universe without constant ginormous battles going on, but it requires a very tight, very focused and very purposeful level design, and the levels I managed to play are instead sprawling, confusing, mostly empty urban areas with enemies sprinkled around that you can see and snipe a mile away with your very precise and very powerful weapons.On top of this lackluster map design, the game doesn't have an automap, which feels wrong not only because it's just been a standard for the genre for over 30 years at this point, but also you are accompanied by a servoskull whose only function seems to be hovering over one of the gajillion health pickups you don't need because you're already at max health and scream like, "oh hey! a health drop! praise the emperor!". This game had not one but two incredibly convenient ways to provide some sort of guidance to the player, and it chose none, and I'm not sure if this is a misguided attempt at making it feel "oldschool", but it really feels half assed in this regard.As an example, in one of the earlier levels, you're faced with two paths into a semi-circular hallway full of enemies. You kill everyone, and regardless of the entrance you chose to this hallway, you'll reach the other end. You'll backtrack, assuming wherever it is you need to go is somewhere along that hallway, only to go back to where you entered. You'll see two glowing energy generator things in two awkward elevated areas, maybe you need to destroy those? Maybe there's like a pressure plate somewhere? Maybe you need to find a secret door? A switch? Well, after spending a solid 10 minutes running up and down this area, I realized I was supposed to go back where I came from, back through the wall with very clear "you can ledge grab here" yellow paint, and open a door before this section, for which I picked a key without even noticing. I also came across locked doors that I must have grabbed a key for because after a while I managed to open them, although I have no idea when and how I picked a key for those (I couldn't see any indication I had picked any keys on my UI although maybe I overlooked it I guess? I don't know).See what I mean? Confusing or abstract map design is one thing, but when you're lacking the basest player guidance (and the little there is kinda makes you think you shouldn't be backtracking when you should be) it's just easy to lose the thread of what you're supposed to do and what you need to keep track of. And there's absolutely zero reason for Boltgun to be this way.Enemies I'd say are mostly fine, but they usually either fall on "dies in one shot" or "massive bullet sponges". Some of them do hit a good balance, like the chaos guys that split in two when killed, and I know chaos marines or terminators are supposed to be tanky, but fighting them is reduced to "just stand in front of them and unload for a few seconds while they're locked into their pain state".I managed to unlock three weapons: a boltgun, a shotgun, and a plasma gun. They all work like they should, they are satisfying to shoot, they feel nice, but except in the very few occasions where you're thrust into close quarter areas there's no reason why you wouldn't simply pew-pew at the mobs from a distance instead of closing in with a shotgun. You're given a ton of ammo for it, and the enemies will just sit there and shoot at you so you'll return in kind, which makes combat feel underwhelming. You also get a chainsaw lunge, which will one hit the weakest enemies while on the tankier ones it'll leave you right in front of them doing minimal damage unless you puposefully do a lunge at the RIGHT time, like a lamer version of a glory kill. Again, no reason to do it other than because you want to do something badass I guess, but enemies will die anyway (with no extra drops or anything as far as I saw) so it feels pointless.Sure, you can wade through enemy groups and do lunge kills and unleash stupid amounts of firepower on heretics, but again, more often than not it feels something you choose to do because the game is boring otherwise, more than because you are thrust in hectic do-or-die situations. It's almost like you're forcing yourself to play in a particular way not because you have to, but because you are trying to make a boring game fun. It's like if, for example, instead of locking you in an arena with monsters constantly threatening your position, Doom 2016 just... put them out there, at a distance, on a wide open area, and gave you a perfectly accurate chaingun for you to potshot them from afar, all the while showering you with health and ammo. You can make it fun, but I'm sure you can make hammering your ♥♥♥♥ fun if you want it bad enough. Even when the game actively locks you into an arena and tints your vision red and tells you to PURGE ALL THE HERETICS I was just sitting on a ledge, enemies in the open below me, and started killing them until I just like, shrugged and was like "well I guess I'll close in and make things a little fun or something I dunno". After easily dispatching them, I explored the area where I found a boltgun powerup, a rage powerup and a new weapon I didn't need at any point because I was able to just pistol them while they were standing around.I played 3 or 4 levels, and I just don't think I want to play it more, or that I'll come back to it. For the price it's a reasonable offering, but for the neat graphics and satisfying weapons, it is a very shallow feeling game to play, with little guidance, not much flow to the levels, and very cheesable mobs. All the technical bits are there, but a boomer shooter lives and dies by its level design and the flow of action, and this game fails at both.Hey, it's cheap, and it is a passable effort so you can try it for yourself. I just did not have an enjoyable time playing it. 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I suspect most of the praise for  comes from people who either haven't played many other "Boomer Shooters" or are simply fans of the IP first and foremost and therefore look past all of its many,  shortcomings. Either way  is a very mediocre FPS game, at best.  Its level design is extremely basic and often straddles the line between being a subpar linear affair or feeling like a rat trapped in a claustrophobic maze. Signposting is poor to boot and you'd think with the 40K license you'd see some stunning vistas and environments but this potential is entirely squandered as well. Combat arenas aren't very interesting at all and offer no engaging gameplay opportunities (aside from shooting the numerous red barrels that are littered throughout, I suppose). This is made all the worse because mechanically speaking  never introduces any new options either. I played it on the highest difficulty and the only challenge it provides is that it turns enemies into walking bullet sponges. It never forces you to adapt to situations differently. It's retro to a fault and doesn't hold a candle to OG's such as DOOM or Blood in areas like level design or gunplay (which I'd argue are the two main staples of the genre).  Performance is also woeful and has no right to be this shoddy when the visuals (albeit stylistic) are otherwise rather basic. Especially considering you're stuck in boxed environments for most of the time. Similar titles such as Prodeus or Viscerafest fare much better in this regard. So if you have any experience with the genre then I would steer clear of this and instead look elsewhere to get your shooty fix (Slayers X, Cultic, INCISION, Ion Fury, Voidborn, Turbo Overkill, Viscerafest, etc just to name a few).   is host to a ton of underlying design issues that make it stale after about an hour or two. At the very least this means that you'll be able to try it out yourself and still get a refund as you'd have seen everything the game has to offer within that time.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game a few hours before it launched, and then refunded it a few days later after playing about two hours.I greatly enjoy retro shooters, and there are things this one does right and things this one does wrong.  While all the reviews are currently jubilantly positive, I'll bring some other views.The game is a good power fantasy, and is a true 40k game - with all the good and bad that brings.  The titular Boltgun is a very satisfying weapon to use.But the arsenal, overall, is kind of disappointing, to be honest.  The shotgun is not very useful, and only seems to one-shot enemies that the boltgun already one-shots, missing out one-shots against many key targets you'd really like to delete faster.  The plasma gun's damage is quite disappointing, IMO.  A lot of the later weapons are just different types of beams.  There's no flamers or lasguns or anything from the arsenals of other factions of even just the Imperium.The downside to being 40k (or maybe an upside if you're a fan) is the usual; your protagonist is a Space Marine whose only personality trait is loving the Emperor and being excessively wordy in taunts.  If the only thought in your mind is PRAISE THE EMPEROR! then you'll love it.  I don't care for the Imperium (or really any faction) in 40k, so the ironic fascism, xenophobia, and religious zealotry is just annoying at best.The vaunted chainsword melee is, while really cool (you can tap the button to continue to do damage until a target dies), not really good.  It can be used for mobility, but its actual killing ability is weak and if you want to use it as a weapon it locks you in place for other enemies to hit you.There are numerous enemy types, as well, many of which are functionally (or visually) interchangeable.  Most enemies seem to either die in one hit or take an absolute ton of damage.  I suppose it makes sense for demons to be tanky, but sometimes it gets a little annoying.The fights and level design are both visually impressive but started to feel repetitive to me very quickly.  Whereas Doom can make fights feel very interesting by mixing up the spacing of fights, Boltgun's enemy design doesn't really allow that.  There are weak melee enemies and then enemies that shoot and make it a bit of a bullet-hell, narrowing the type of combat scenarios allowed.  Maybe it opens up later in the game, but I got to map seven and just felt bored of it all.There are numerous power-ups that don't tell you their effect; they may or may not make a screen overlay, and their icons only occasionally make sense, like a visually larger magazine for your gun or a box of ammo to refill all your guns past max.  Others are just tokens and even if you know the many, many intricacies of 40k they don't really explain themselves.  I actually thought some were just collectibles for a long time.All in all, while it's fun blasting things apart with a boltgun, that was the only enjoyment I found in it, and the novelty wore off quickly.  It could be something you'd enjoy, but I think unless you're a die-hard 40k fan, it will grow old for you, too.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy this game as a fan of this style of shooter, but honestly it has too many issues to be fully worth the time.Firstly whats good is how it incorporates 40K stuff, I don't know loads about 40k but you can tell its very reverential of the quirks and the lore of the game, the taunt button is great and the weapon strengths is a nice addition at least aesthetically.Another quite good part is the grenade button, a nice modern addition thats does change the style of combat too much from what it is inspired by.However there are quite afew issues, mainly the levels are just too big. A lot of people compare this game to DOOM but I'd argue its closer to Star Wars Dark Forces (although not in quality) or even Quake. The levels are just too big for a game that is meant to be fast paced, and there is no map. When this first came out I remember loads of people making fun of people complaining about the lack of a map, saying 'oh you just need games that hold your hand this is a real game(TM) for real gamers(TM). Thing is though, classic DOOM and Quake had maps. In this you spend so much time wandering around confused and then just occasionally picking off a couple of enemies, it kills the pacing.The weapon balancing in terms of how they feel is pretty off also. The Boltgun itself is fantastic and by far the most fun to use, which is an issue as it makes using any other gun a slog. The shotgun feels particularly underpowered, lets be honest its impossible not to compare it to the DOOM 2 super shotgun (best gun in any game ever imo).A further issue I felt was the optimisation, part the reason I enjoy the old raycast/ binary space partitioning shooters (as well as early 3D ones like Quake) is that they can run on anything, yet this considering its old school graphics did not run brilliantly on my computer and for no real reasonThe music is a bit bland, especially during the very sluggishly paced parts makes things not very intersting. If you want to make things more hype I recommend listening to some Yeat or Ken Carson in the background, rage rap music I find always fits well with this style of game.So in all, I would say that if you are a 40K fan I would recommend but maybe wait for a sale to get your full monies worth as it does have its tedious parts, if you are looking for one of these retro style shooters there are better games out there, maybe if you've run out buy it in a few years on sale.

This is a game that I highly recommend for longtime Warhammer 40k fans, newcomers to the franchise, or anyone who loves classic retro fps "boomer shooters" that have their inspirations from classics like Doom or Quake.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful, push-through, rainbow-grim, carnage campaign. Adheres to the retro gaming aesthetic and the retro 40k aesthetic (we all know 2nd ed was best) simultaneously to deliver the very same doom-esque game we all talked about precisely 30 years ago (2nd ed was released in 1993).There are some aspects of retro gaming I don't miss, including getting lost in unusually quiet labyrinths every time you find a key and have to search back for some obscurely coloured door. Perhaps true to the tabletop, there is a limited amount of terrain and architecture features, often recycled, which can sometimes make navigating the map to find every little secret, like many of us cherished in the new doom series, a little fatiguing.None the less the "purges" are insane, the feeling is spot on, and the game plays like heaven. I almost wonder if they shouldn't have attached an assault pack to the protagonist (an anonymised veteran beaky) because of the insane acrobatic that can be achieved in the grim dark halls. I routinely flew up levels, lept up ledges, and could bounce around better than the screamers could. All the while, the powerarmour footsteps clunk away, perhaps touching the ground every ten metres or so.I haven't had so much fun since brutal doom nor felt more self-assured that my disdain for primaris is entirely justified.

_childDocuments_.review: I would have recommended this since the artwork is fantastic along with the enemy designs and sounds. But the game is borderline miserable as a FPS the second you step off regular difficulty. The main problem is the "toughness" system that apes off the table top. What is toughness? its an armor modifier for enemies and your weapons. On lower difficulties its barely an issue with the titular boltgun ripping through most enemies.On harder difficulties however it becomes a nightmare of balancing. Lower grunts and enemies have low toughness, so the damage output is about what you expect with an FPS. However, really quickly you will run into chaos champions and plague toads that will absorb an absurd amount of ammo from your lower toughness weapons. This isn't as much as a problem in the first act because the scaling is suited to give you weak weapons/enemies and work its way up. I was having pretty good fun for the first act, but the high toughness enemies were kind of annoying to deal with. Then came the second act.Despite it not being a boomer shooter, it still keeps the boomer shooter rules of resetting your weapon collection at the start of the new act. This means you're back to a boltgun on the first level of act 2. That wouldn't be an issue until you realize you're running into mid/late game enemies from act 1 again in the first level. You're forced to use your low toughness weapons on harder enemies that will suck up all of your ammo to kill. This becomes a long game of attrition rather than fast paced action, ultimately becoming extremely boring and frustrating to play. This is also ignoring the charge/chainsword is completely worthless on harder difficulties because of the same mechanic.Overall if you like to play games on easy difficulty go ahead and grab this, otherwise avoid it like the plague.

_childDocuments_.review: For reference I played on the normal difficulty.It's pretty good for everything except the gameplay. It's just running around holding down left click. Enemies either die in 1 hit or 80, and the enemies don't really get more complex from the few you see at the start. They either shoot you or run at you, there's little in-between, yet some enemies just have an insane amount of health for how little they contribute to fights. The first time I encountered one of the chaos marines I was expecting some kind of intense match-up but the only thing it did differently was that it could throw grenades, rarely and inaccurately. If it wasn't the first enemy to soak up bullets, I would have been much more disappointed in how underwhelming it was, especially considering they're just slightly less common basic enemies. The theme that's immediately established in the beginning of the first level is that the player character is a walking tank. You kill enemies in one shot, enemies don't do that much damage to you, and dodging bullets is fairly easy. Coming off of that I expected the game to be a sort of power fantasy. Where you're basically the DOOM slayer but in the Warhammer universe. The rest of the first chapter instead drove home how I felt like the DOOM slayer, but if he was only allowed to fight using NERF guns.Speaking of feeling like I'm not doing enough damage half the time;The gun upgrade powerup seems to do nothing for a few of the weapons. The first time I got it I hoped that it would stick around, since there's a power level number next to the weapon on the HUD, but it only lasts for the one level, and you only get one in each level, if you do get one at all. There's no permanent weapon upgrade mechanic which is a shame because the base weapons feel way too weak most of the time. It feels like the boost the weapons get from the upgrade powerup should be the default state of the weapon. Every weapon just feels way too weak, and a great example of this is in the shotgun. There's very little reason to use the shotgun. It has a slow fire rate and a tight pellet spread. Normally that would mean that the damage should be high; to use it as a source of High burst damage. However, the shotgun's pellets each do the same damage as one shot from the boltgun, and each shell fires 8 pellets. Seeing as how the boltgun fires pellets fairly quickly, the shotgun only slightly beats out the boltgun in DPS, and that's implying that you're hitting every shot, which the game disincentivizes, what with all the enemies and projectiles flying around. Shotguns in games like this should fall under one of two categories: Having a wide spread and lesser individual pellet damage, or having a tight spread and higher pellet damage. One befits crowd control, and one benefits using it to deal burst damage. The shotgun in this game has a tight spread and low pellet damage, so it fails as a shotgun. If the developers can't design a good shotgun, then they should have taken more time to make the weapons feel better.

_childDocuments_.review: A 40K set combination of "boomer" shooter and Doom Eternal with good movement and weapon feel and a good art style though with a variety of more minor problems and AI and stage design issues that stop it from being great.Boltgun often feels closer to Doom Eternal than to the older "boomer" style shooters I often saw it compared to with its arena style battles sections (or purge sections), the allowed amount of verticality, long range engagements you can find yourself in, movement speed, some enemies dropping health and armor when killed, and with a weapon strength and armor toughness system that makes certain weapons much more effective against specific targets giving you a system where you try to use the gun best suited for the enemy type to a greater extent than you would otherwise have to.The plot has you going up against cultists, Chaos Space Marines, and the demon forces of Nurgle and Tzeentch. The game might play in a way that surprises people who know less about the setting and thought the Space Marine character would be slow and tanky only to find themselves playing as an extremely agile character who can sprint in all directions even with a heavy weapon, takes massive leaps when you jump and can pull themselves up ledges, and who can take a lot of damage very quickly if you aren't careful. Dodging and keeping enemies at range is often what you will be doing as they can have strong melee or AoE attacks, and your own weapons or the environment can have AoE attacks that will easily damage you and your enemy. Holding down sprint or leaving it toggled on is how I played the game 99% of the time and making use of jumps and quick direction changes was the only way to avoid a lot of attacks, even more so with how well enemies will shoot to lead into the direction of your current movements. There are times when it can feel more like playing a bullet-hell shmup as well as an FPS.The difficulty modes seem to effect things like the damage you take and enemy number or what spawns without making changes to your weapon strength or enemy toughness levels. If you start at a low difficulty and raise it later replay the game on a higher setting this does allow you to get used to enemies and what weapons work best in certain situations as it isn't weakening them on the lower levels.For being the first gun you get the Boltgun is a fairly satisfying and potentially powerful weapon as you find the hidden (and sometimes not so hidden) secrets in a level that often give it damage and ammo capacity upgrades. The shotgun, heavy boltgun, multi-melta (DLC chapter or turn all gun option on only), gravity gun, and rocket launcher (DLC chapter or turn all gun option on only) are also all very satisfying to use, though even some of the squishier looking enemies tend to have a higher toughness than the shotgun's low power and with many of the weaker enemies dying in one or two shots of the boltgun I probably found the shotgun less useful than the other weapons despite how satisfying it feels to use. Though even trying to use the shotgun on a more armored target has the visual effect that shows your attack mostly just bouncing off to let you know it didn't work well on top of the information given with the enemy health-bar and toughness rating.The sound design makes the weapons more enjoyable to use and while not every stage is that interesting of a location the art style and use of color makes things easy to read, stand out, and often pleasing to look at.Chapters can be fairly long but you are able to save or quick save wherever you are so you don't have to replay an entire level if you are killed. Some of the stages can become confusing to navigate but the game was eventually patches where a button press causes your servo skull companion to lay out a course for you that shows you where to go by drawing an easy to follow path along the floor (less easy to follow in some areas due to it not being able to be shown on certain environments or when verticality comes up).There is a taunt button that, while I don't believe it causes any effects on your enemies, does allow your character to shout a Warhammery line of dialogue and there is a very large number of recorded taunts for him to yell that were entertaining to use if nothing else.For all that it does well, there are a lot of things I thought it did poorly or that were just odd decisions.When you get to purge arena style fights with waves of enemies spawning some of these locations are large enough where I had trouble getting the last remaining enemies of a wave or at the end of a segment to either come to me or for me to track them down to move on. A few of these areas, more so in the DLC chapter, also tended to just run me almost completely out of ammo in everything. When enemy does become scarce than you can run into issues where some of the enemies and weapons capture that powerful feel of the guns and visceral feel of them but then some enemies like the Chaos Marines and the higher health demons can just feel like bullet sponges that can both feel like a bit of a chore to whittle down their health bars and they tend to have less satisfying deaths compared to charging through or using the shotgun against weaker targets.There are tiny 2 health and armor pickups everywhere that are often doing little to help you and that start to take away from the visual design of the game. They are both tedious to collect, become easy to ignore, and if playing on the two more difficult settings you might well find yourself losing 100-200 health/armor with one bad move which just makes it all the more annoying that they weren't just replaced with more of the larger health and armor pickups or some new middle ground between them. Grenades also start to have a similar feel where you can only hold two frag grenades and one krak grenade but they are just scattered all over the place, often both types sitting together, frequently with another set almost right next to each other. Ammo is scattered around and you might need or just find yourself backtracking or running circles around an area picking up everything to get ready for or to rearm after a purge section and it would be nice to just have a faster less tedious way to rearm instead of needing to take the time to do that.Due to the size of some of the maps and arena sections it is often very possible and the best strategy to just stay still sniping enemies from afar that can do little or nothing in response or to just back up into a corner as enemies slowly funnel into your sights as they all reach you at different times and can often seem to get stuck on walls or each other. Some enemies seem to be in areas that they aren't allowed to leave in larger sections, and in arena sections even though enemies can follow you you are often so much faster and have access to the verticality of your jumps that it is easy to outpace them in many situations and to shoot them as they try to reach you again.The chainsword and charge are somewhat odd offensive tools I never got the hang of. The charge soon can't even do enough damage to defeat some humanoid enemies, and while the chainsword can do damage and lunge you at foes to temporarily stun lock them it can easily get you into trouble when you try to use it on or near an enemy with a shotgun or explosive weapon that you couldn't identify in that half second before you made the decision to use it. I'm not going to say the chainsword is bad, as even on hard I did use it by itself to kill the first Lord of Change boss in a few seconds but I never found it or the charge that useful...Full Review: Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: The actual game plays well in terms of technical aspects. I play it on Steam Deck and it is just fine there, eating a low-medium amount of battery life. The story is adequate.  You feel sufficiently enveloped in the setting. It has a few easter eggs that seem out of love, like Cacti that resemble the ones from very old editions of White Dwarf.  The game experience is frustrating. The map layout can be very confusing, leaving you lost for much of the time and the Servoskull is unhelpful. Sure that's funny for the "non-Euclidean geometry" level thematic to Tzeentch/Chaos but it gets annoying. Too often I'm looping around trying to figure where to go, and I don't particularly like how most levels have this mechanic with a key. For six or so ten minute sessions in a row I would play and then quit this particular map because it was a lot of a walking through portals, falling to bridges, and getting disoriented with no end in sight. This repeated three more times with a desert level. The graphical details can be hard to distinguish or get muddied together in a grimdark pixel mess where you're not sure where to aim. Some of the enemies feel unbalanced, as for example an Aspiring Champion is much more threatening than a Champion or some of the boss levels. It feels hard to just "chill" with this game. Call it a "skill issue" if you want. I can recommend it for people particularly into Warhammer 40,000 as a setting, holding over between Space Marine and Space Marine II as it sort of continues the former, and for people who very much like the Doom clone style of game play. It doesn't feel right to give a general recommendation because the map progression is just too frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, as much as I hate to say it, especially after my considerable pre-release hype, this game kinda just made me sad. For all the style Boltgun has, all the obvious care that was shown in terms of art direction and sound design, as an actual  I feel it misses the mark quite considerably. As has already been pointed out in a number of other reviews, I think much of the positive feedback surrounding this game was written prematurely, by people who had only played for a few hours at most and were, maybe, largely reviewing based on aesthetic rather than playability. I finished the game on the hardest difficulty (Exterminatus) in a little over eleven hours. Not going for 100% completion or anything, but not speedrunning either. Suffice it to say, it's not an especially lengthy experience. And yet, fewer than 10% of players have finished the game on *any* difficulty. Fewer than 15% have even finished chapter two! That's a whole load of people that likely aren't going to be commenting on, or possibly even noticing:And that's certainly not an exhaustive list. Now, having said all of that, the right kind of person will probably still enjoy this game for what it is. I didn't think it was  bad. So... what is there, if anything, to like about Boltgun? Well, for all my complaints, actually quite a bit I think, depending on what you're looking for. As I said, it's got a great sense of visual style, and was clearly developed with love and care with regard to the source material. The dev team clearly has some pretty big 40K fans on it. Along similar lines, it's got satisfying weapons with (mostly) solid feedback, a good soundtrack, and  voice acting. I think if you're a big 40k fan yourself and are just interested in taking in the sights and sounds, appreciating the setting and the nice art and all that, you'll probably enjoy yourself. Just lower the difficulty and have a chill time blasting heretics into fine red mist.Conversely, are you a fan of the genre, and like it when your boomer shooters are difficult but still feel fair? I'd recommend looking elsewhere. Go play Dusk. Go play Ion Fury. Go play Amid Evil. Cultic, Prodeus, HROT, Blood, Heretic. Go replay friggin DOOM. Any of those will feel far better than banging your head into a metaphorical wall for 10 hours.
