_childDocuments_.review: The work done by Captain Titus in the events of the famous Space Marine storyline, finally got a soft-mini sequel in the form of Boltgun. Finally, we see the Ultramarines return to the forge world Graia, to end the heretical fallout from Inquisitor Dargon's disastrous experimentation with an energy source from the Warp. Boltgun has little plot, but what it does tell in its absolutely gorgeous, stylized and masterfully presented 2d, pixel-art driven cutscenes is worth playing through. While the game does lean toward the retro, you can alter just how retro it looks and plays via display options and the accessibility tab (also a glorified cheat menu for the less able bodied players or those just bad at these sort of "boomer shooters"). At times, I forgot I was playing a 40k game and was transported back into the peak nostalgia of playing Doom WADs growing up. Doom was a trend setter in so many ways, it didn't normalize things such as speedrunning and the sharing of in-engine rendered recordings of said speeruns, it had completely innovated the concept as its own. To this day, there are a bulk of amazing total conversion WADs for Doom (if you don't know what a WAD is you may be too young for this game, genuinely) and among the most beloved is Brutal Doom and Project Brutality, which this game borrows heavily from.Despite everything, Boltgun feels surprisingly great to play. It emulates an older engine but with none of the limitations besides the occasional crash on a certain early bossfight, that I only encountered once. Only Doom Eternal had managed to get me into something I can best describe as "doom hypnosis", but this game succeeded in doing such too. As a result, I actually beat the main game in a few sittings within the same day and have no regrets for such. The arena mode is also spectacular, albeit borrowing a lot from the trials of Doom 2016. I enjoyed the sprint function being of the speed it was, which really emulated the sense of speed I loved most about Doom Eternal. This game emulates far greater games and ends up being far more competent than anyone would have expected as a result. As far as boomer-shooters go, it may not be the most special thing out there. The environments run out of tilesets and assets quickly and the last 2/3s of the game is basically just the foundry level from Doom 2016 ongoing forever, but I really enjoyed the beginning areas of the first two chapters, a snowy mountain top and a desert canyon respectively. Everyone says the DLC is even better, albeit much shorter, with only five levels for its chapter. I will save my impressions on that for another review on the DLC item itself.Overall, I really enjoyed Boltgun for what it offers. A simple, one time romp in a beloved franchise that has frankly, been prostituted shamelessly by Games Workshop to subpar studios to make subpar games. For once, this game is just unironically above average, which makes it solid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gold by 40k standards. At a very affordable price, I think this is definitely worth a few playthroughs. My only genuine complaints are that the soundtrack is repetitive. While there are two tracks I found amazing, I wish the rest of the game had at least, a new song per level. And some have complained before that some tracks feel almost AI generated or AI-assisted, but I honestly think that is just because the soundtrack itself is on the generic side.The thing is, even the bad 40k games have spectacular soundtracks. So it was a let down to see that the soundtrack didn't match the euphoria of seeing a Chaos cultist's guts cling to the ceiling before plopping down with drips of blood. The gibs and blood are visceral, impactful, perhaps almost on par with Brutal Doom's and they even stay! The only time I saw blood decals disappear was when stacking literal hundreds of bodies in Arena's 12 rounds and even then, the gibs stayed! Love to see a game take advantage of the simpler graphics to ensure the bloody representation of a 40k fight is best preserved by formerly sentient carrion littering the battlespace. Seeing hundreds of bodies surrounding a singular point of victory in Dawn of War 1 was the champion of this for a long while and finally, Boltgun and hopefully Space Marine 2, will be the new heroes of this effect.While the environments and music can become repetitive quickly, the sprites and true-to-lore designs make it all worth it. Not to mention, the fact you can taunt mid-combat with some truly catchy quotes from the Ultramarine you play as, adds a fair amount to the vibe and overall feeling of the game. Every fledgling 40k fan once read the zealous quotes from the wikias for its impeccable, dogmatic diction and general creativity. And old fans surely remember the many battle cries from Dawn of War, while being able to emulate the angry-anglo accents behind them that were dialed up to a 100 on the cheese level.Finally, some real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 40k foodIt is like a nice cup of warm recaff served black. Bitter in its simpleness, but the bitterness is what wakes you up and get the job done.♥♥♥♥ the Nurglings and Plague Toads though, absolute bullet sponge scum.

_childDocuments_.review: The general gameplay is fun and the guns are stellar so far but, there's been multiple maps that I've found that were just too easy to get lost in. I found myself spending at least 20+ minutes on certain maps just running along the walls to look for an exit that may or may not have been there. The Survo-skull guide is more annoying than helpful. There's also an audio issue with the game if you play with Controller (my preferred way for shooter games like this), in which you have to make sure that you don't plug in the controller until the game has booted and run for at least a minute or the sound will become static and cut out all the time. And even then once you think it's fixed, the issue will return if you happen to click out of the game screen and then you have to restart the process all over again. I love this game and want to finish it because I'm a huge 40K nerd, but I can't recommend it to anyone unless it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: OVERALL 4/10I'm a big fan of Warhammer video games ever since playing Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine and this game pissed me off >:(. I would also like to point out that I have at best GLOSSED OVER the surface of the lore and even I can tell this game is at best OSTENSIBLY WH40K (imagine Superman eating green kryptonite like candy, THAT degree of inconsistency).GRAPHICS 9/10The graphics ARE well-designed and follow the Warhammer 40K conventions almost perfectly. HOWEVER I do take issue with the SHOTGUN ("Most GUARDSMEN that use shotguns"  and later weapons which I am pretty sure are NOT REALLY or at best TANGENTIALLY canon ("Volkite Weapons in the present time are exceedingly rare, and are scarcely ever seen amongst the Chapters of the Adeptus Astartes in the 41st Millennium." .SOUND/MUSIC 10/10Once again, I have no issue with the soundtrack or sound effects. They are well done and work together to bring the Warhammer 40K world to life. Good job team!CONTROLS "It's complicated" >w> /10TECHNICALLY the controls are responsive even though I found aiming somewhat difficult / annoying, though that COULD have been my mouse so I shall give them the benefit of the doubt. The issues I have with the CONTROLS relate directly to the GAMEPLAY.PLOT 8/10From what I saw it is standard Warhammer 40K fare. My only issue is ONE (1) Space Marine going toe-to-toe with innumerable Chaos Marines and Chaos CHAMPIONS, not even including all of the demons (lmao, as if ;p) and the less than inspired writing.GAMEPLAY 3/10This game is not even remotely Warhammer 40K. Your avatar moves WAY too quickly and smoothly for someone wearing bulky full power armour. You practically glide through the environment like Doom Guy (and not even Doom Guy was this fast and smooth like butter).There is no sense of impact whatsoever. Enemies run through hails of gunfire without a check in their step unless you hit them with a "rocket" eg. plasma gun (also, they don't really work like that). You would figure someone getting hit with a BOLTGUN (a "machine gun" that fires exploding bullets "A .75 caliber weapon, the boltgun works similarly to a grenade launcher firing a relatively small explosive"  would find forward motion somewhat difficult.On that note, enemies move WAY too fast. Almost everything in this game flies at you at a full sprint and glides around tight corners with nary a check in their step (the same goes for Chaos Champions in full power armour by the way). While that might work in other settings it doesn't work in 40K (in which case don't call it 40K).Speaking of enemies moving WAY too fast. The designers were a little slap-happy with the teleportation / enemy spawning. While I can appreciate demons gating in to such a chaos infested area, mortal enemies like chaos champions and chaos terminators as well as greater demons spamming themselves into reality stretches the imagination in WH40K (summoning ONE [1] greater demon is a feat unto itself that usually goes wrong when the defenceless human cultists are discovered and shredded nigh-instantaneously, "Summoning such a creature demands a high price, for it takes a tremendous amount of psychic energy for a Greater Daemon to achieve corporeality in the material universe. The price is always a sacrifice, the death or possession of a living being that acts as a gateway from the Immaterium into the material realm." .I was thoroughly annoyed at the addition of the shotgun. They could have easily replaced that with the Meltagun (I have heard it said that "It’s kinda like a heat shotgun In it’s function"  which would have made more sense lore-wise AND would have looked far cooler. ALSO! The shotgun is so weak and ammo in general is so plentiful it's barely worth using (unlike your eponymous Boltgun which is always useful and better in every way).The maps are far too large, leaving you running around looking for the exit. I get the feeling they were going for a Quake deathmatch-style / Doom 1 TO 3 design ethos but the size of ONE (1) arena dwarfs every map I remember playing in Quake 2 (MeMoRiEsSsSsS!). Every map I played was like a bunch of Quake death match arenas glued together with Doom style corridors and rooms into one colossal Doom style dungeon (the game even revolves around finding keys like Doom 1 and 2).SPEAKING OF WHICH!!! The large levels add to one of the game's major design flaws. EVERY gun is like a sniper rifle (including your BOLTGUN, a "machine gun" that shoot exploding bullets >w>, Press (X) to doubt, X). While enemies spray and pray "cones" of slow-moving bullets from a distance allowing you to dodge their bullets (in 40K? X) your guns hit their mark every time from virtual kilometres of distance, try to have some sense of internal consistency >w>.This game is Warhammer 40K in name only and should have been called something else. It's like Mad Max: Fury Road, the only reason they used the name was ride the coattails of a superior franchise. With a complete re-skinning and revision to the avatar movement, I would have no issue with this game (it's like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ real-time pixel-and-sprite Superhot that wants to be Quake and Doom [slow moving bullets you can dodge...]). As it is, I sort of do >:|.FINAL VERDICT = In need of improvement. I lost interest after running around the massive library level looking for the door.This might very well be the FIRST game I request a refund for. I shall ruminate on this regard...

_childDocuments_.review: WH40K Boltgun (2023) represents a retro-inspired first-person shooter (FPS) game, developed by the company Auroch Digital and published by the company Focus Entertainment.++ Be it the gravity of the power armor, an overheating plasma gun, or the depiction of the servants of the four chaos gods, all of them contribute to the creation of an authentic WH40K atmosphere. Solid weapon feedback enhances the immersion, while the variety of enemy combinations keeps up the challenge. And I appreciate the fact that most cultists are killed with just one bolter shot; it pays respect to the technical background of the weapon.o Dear developers, you have a broad spectrum of successor chapters at your disposal. And yet, I am forced to play as one of the Imperial poster boys from Ultramar once more. I get it, they have tons of lore behind them and the casuals love their smurf guard. But, how about throwing light at an underdog, for example the Sons of the Crow. As a successor chapter of the Raven Guard they are specialised in the field of infiltration; suits your underlying scenario as far as I can tell.- It seems the corruption of the chaos gods among Graia’s population runs deeper than originally anticipated. Occasionally, the cultists stand around absent-minded, despite a genetically transformed freak with a chainsword slaughtering everyone around them. The Inquisition was right after all, consuming too much Slaanesh porn rots your brain.Then we have the ranged troops suffering from severe short sightedness, which causes them to get into close combat, or not reacting at all when being fired at from afar. Papa Nurgle really loves his myopia diseases.Not only WH40K fans but FPS gamers in general will enjoy Boltgun’s gameplay and presentation. And I have to admit, throwing insults at minions of the ruinous powers, while my chainsword works itself through their corrupted shells, puts a smile on my face.Estimated time for 100% completion: +30 hoursSingleplayer achievements: 21Multiplayer achievements: none

_childDocuments_.review: Even after a short time with Boltgun, I am impressed. For the price, it's an excellent game. Despite not being particularly fond of DOOM-style shooters, this is a satisfying experience regardless of the unmistakable appeal of it being set in the 40k universe. The only drawback is the shotgun, which underperforms on greater difficulties compared to your other options, but this is a minor issue. I highly recommend giving this game a go! (Doubly so if you love the Emperor)

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a very promising start to it- the look and the feel elicited the memories of classic shooters, and with a combination of attention to detail and stellar sound design, you really feel like you are a space marine, an unstoppable killing machine wearing an entire fridge and who hits like an 18 wheeler. But unfortunately, I feel like the game overstays its welcome. After Chapter 1, you have essentially encountered every enemy and weapon there is to find in this game, and the game itself eventually gets lazy with level designs and just decides to throw one HUGE wave of enemies at you after another. Assuming you can even find your way forward, since the maps are so confusingly designed and there is no mini map or anything,Tl:dr The game is great in the first chapter, but very quickly becomes a boring slog through endless mobs of enemies and labyrinthine tunnels. If you're a fan of 40k, this is definitely for you. If not, wait for a sale to pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I can comment on the game play at 2 1/2 hours of game play - it's good. It's really, really good. It nails the 40K aesthetic perfectly, completely capturing what it would feel like to be a Space Marine. The game escalates pretty quickly, but I never felt under-powered (so far) even when a freakin' Chaos Space Marine Terminator teleported in while (what felt like) a dozen Pink and Blue Horrors of Tzeentch swarmed me. I love that armor is called Contempt too. The level design feels so good too. But god I hate those Nurglings. They thematically as annoying as you'd imagine they'd be from the lore. I cannot wait for the Spacehulk mod... or any of the mods... if this game gets a good modding community around it I'm gonna gonna need to spend $60 on Space Marine 2.

_childDocuments_.review: I get why people like it. I just don't think I'm one of those people. I recently went on a "boomer shooter" kick. I saw this was out, and it looked really enticing. Instead, I found Amid Evil heavily reduced in price. Tried it, thought it was ok. Still had my eye on this. Then I again bought Dusk. Again - just thought it was ok. Still looked at this. Then I remembered I had Quake. And I started a new save file in Quake and thoroughly enjoyed my experience - played all the way to the end. I even played some of the extra levels that used to be mods that are now included with it. I thought it was fantastic. ... but I couldn't get away from what people were saying about this game, and the art style made me eventually cave and buy this. And ... I'm just a little disappointed. It's fun for a while, and you can tell the devs have a heart for Warhammer and boomer shooters - but this fails in that the game is basically a DOOM: Eternal clone without the heart. Just, wide open area, run around shooting everything, shoot your way to the next wide open area, rinse, repeat. And the secrets aren't very difficult to find - so it doesn't scratch the puzzle itch either. This might be for you if you're into the Warhammer lore and were just waiting for a proper shooter with the 40K banner. But, if not, and you've never played it before, check out Quake. It's the best at what it did. The levels have lots of secrets that are still easy to miss, and the combat loop is superb and even still holds up to this day. And the extra, player-made levels are the iciing on the cake once you finish the main "story."Side note, I know the devs worked to give us an experience, but imho it just doesn't stack up to what's already out there. If you enjoy it, no need to flame me. Just do you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is literally all I wanted from a 40k shooter for years, satisfying and fairly accurate weaponry, detailed environments and enemies, interesting usage of various new and old game mechanics and a fantastic soundtrack. The Heavy Bolter sounds, and even *feels* how it should, the regular Boltgun punches through chaff enemies in a single shot, and the plasma gun actually blows up weaker enemies unlike in the predecessor "Space Marine" where it was a glorified paintball gun. Fantastic game, excellent value for the price

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun ReviewBy Thom Stone on HIGH Devastating new weaponry, nightmarish new areas, loathsome new enemies.LOW Some levels feel like deja vu. Purges are even more tiresome than in the base game.WTF Navigation mode is nice, but still no map?Editor’s Note: This review covers only the Forges of Corruption DLC. For a deeper look at the core Boltgun systems and content, please see the original review.Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun was released last year and received many accolades for its fresh take on the ’90s-style genre, reflecting the pixelated glory of early FPS games like Doom or Star Wars: Dark Forces while meeting modern standards for things like framerates, sound design and UI.Last month, Auroch Digital released Forges of Corruption, which includes a new campaign that is equal in length and quality to one of the chapters of the base game. They simultaneously released a patch which included new achievements, a new Horde Mode, a navigation mode and general quality of life improvements.For those who don’t know, Warhammer 40,000 began as a TTRPG back in the late ’80s, so before playing Boltgun I only knew of the IP from legions of miniature Space Marines on display at various board game retailers. Now, after eight hours of playing as a Space Marine, I’m much more interested in the whole universe.I started by going through some of Boltgun‘s base game to get a feel for it, and after about an hour and a half it was clear that I didn’t need to understand its backstory to enjoy annihilating every last heretic on the planet Graia. When I then booted up the DLC, I was briefed by Inquisitor Seibel about the overtaking of an Imperial forge on Graia and my mission was to take it back for the Empire.The cutscene ended with an image worthy of a power metal album cover — Mallum Caedo (the Space Marine embodied by the player) standing on a burning hill, looking determinedly at the horizon — needless to say, it got me hyped to lay waste to the Manufactorum.I was glad to find that I was in for more stomping around as a Space Marine, taking out hordes of disgusting, slime-spewing demons and all sorts of heretics with a huge arsenal of weapons to choose from. Like the base game, the player gains more weapons as they progress, giving a sense of becoming more powerful even though there are no RPG elements of upgrading weapons or armor. By the time I got the new missile launcher, I felt like I could take anything on, even my first damage-sponge boss known as a Great Unclean One, with relative ease.Most of my favorite weapons were less conventional, like the Vengeance Launcher (a grenade launcher loaded with tiny grenades that stick to enemies before they explode) and I still preferred anything over the shotgun, as it was weak against the new enemies and took far too long to reload.My new favorite level soon became Escalating Chaos, which featured an eerie purple canyon and included some light platforming challenges. Overall, the color palette was muted, which worked for establishing a dystopian atmosphere but started to become monotonous in more than a few areas. This leads me to one of my main qualms with the DLC — many levels, enemies and mechanics felt as if they had been copied and pasted.In the sewer sections and some of the arenas, I often asked myself, “Haven’t I been here before?” Also, by the end, I had grown so sick of the “Purge” sections (where players must eliminate big baddies and regular enemies spawn until they’re gone) as they became so challenging even on Medium difficulty that I found myself wishing I could just cheese my way out so that I could get back to making progress.My last objective in this DLC was to destroy the Daemon Forge, at which point the developers pulled out all the stops with three big baddies and droves of regular enemies teleporting to my location all at the same time, and I was barely able to beat two before I died on my fifth or sixth try. Eventually, I tried to adjust the difficulty and found that there wasn’t an option to do so mid-game, but I was able to turn on invulnerability — I’m not proud to admit it, but I had to just to finish the campaign.Ultimately though, I encountered many of the same problems in the DLC that were present in the base game — the difficulty spikes are fierce and there’s not much variety here beyond running, gunning and finding keys.Despite the lack of DLC freshness, Forges of Corruption was engaging enough to hold my attention and enjoyable as hell most of the time, but I think it would be great if Auroch added multiplayer in future Boltgun patches or DLC — I would imagine playing with fellow Space Marines, whether it be deathmatch or co-op mode, would be a blast.While both the core campaign and this DLC would use a little tweaking, there’s no doubt that they remain exciting, engaging plays that come recommended. As Incommodus the Servo Skull says, PURGE THE HERETICS!Rating: 7 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: You're here to slay heretics and drink Promethium. And you're all out of Promethium.No, seriously, the game lacks Flamers. Which might mark it up for oecumenical inspection for the Sororitas main that I am. The Holy Trinity of Bolter, Melta and Flamer exists for a reason !..Anyways, Boltgun is Brutal Doom's more Brutal cousin. It's loud, over-the-top and absurdly violent, and it's gorgeous, and glorious. The gunplay is incredibly satisfying, the weapon variety (bar heretical omissions) is top-notch, the level variety is pretty nice (especially considering this is a 40k game !).My main complaints would be the lack of grand orchestral themes for boss themes (but that's being nitpicky ... Old Doom games didn't have it either) and the fact that enemy variety, considering the 40k universe, in kinda lacking : I'd have liked some Blood Letters and Daemonettes for my Chaos ... Or just some Orks sprinkled along with the local fauna, as they've been on Graia for a while (but that's being nitpicky as well).So. By Imperial Edict, this game is considered excellent and recommended as part of all Astra Militarum drills and Schola Progenium courses. (Pending review for heretical lack of flamer.)

_childDocuments_.review: is Warhammer 40,000’s take on the retro shooter craze of the New 10s and Boring 20s, looking to use the weight of its franchise to make up for its shortcomings elsewhere. The visceral appeal of being a Space Marine and ripping through crowds of foes is a timeless draw for fans of the franchise, and when the experience is even  competent? Throne on Terra, that’s cause for celebration.The first and most important note is that Focus Interactive, creators of the well-received  3rd-person shooter, love the franchise. The second is that they’re pretty good at this whole game development thing, and will try to make the end product enjoyable for the player. While a working knowledge of the setting in general, and  in particular, is encouraged for a better idea of what’s going on, it’s not necessary if you’re just here to wreak havoc.Returning to Forge World Graia, you are tasked with recovering a shard of the heretical power source previously used by Drogan and the forces of Chaos, in order to halt a full daemonic invasion of the system while it is recovering from the previous disaster; alternatively, you are Doomguy’s even-more-angry super solder 2nd cousin and turn everything that looks at you into chunky tomato soup with a series of increasingly ridiculous weapons, while the game thinks you care about its story.The basic gameplay loop of charging through stages, collecting weapons, and rendering your foes into their component organs is, for the most part, simple and satisfying. You can run at breakneck speeds, leap over barriers and mantle up most surfaces, and have generally good mobility while handling your multitudinous arsenal. does take some inspiration from the tabletop game, giving each weapon a Strength rating and each enemy a Toughness rating, and if the Strength of the gun doesn’t meet or surpass the Toughness of your target, it will deal considerably less damage. While that usually means each gun has clearly-defined roles, like the Plasma Gun being one of the best options for heavily-armored units and the Shotgun chiefly used to wipe out Cultists and lesser daemons, some of them are deceptively powerful and can punch far above their weight. Each stage has a hidden (or “hidden”) pickup that will empower the weapon you’re holding until the end of the stage, allowing more flexibility or focusing even further on the weapon’s niche: for example, the basic Boltgun gains enough Strength to threaten just about everything, where the Heavy Bolter allows you to move at full speed while firing.Focus took the unusual route of making nearly every weapon, both yours and the enemy’s, projectile instead of hitscan. While this does allow some impressive situations where the game becomes a minor first-person bullet hell, it also gives you the theoretical option of dodging almost everything (and swearing like a sailor when those hitscan attacks crop up).However, the game has a problem with feedback. While movement and gunplay are fine, damage the player takes isn’t as well signaled; there are damage indicators around your crosshair in each of the 4 cardinal directions relative, which will show red or blue depending on if you’re taking health or armor damage. There are no pain grunts or HUD indicators when you take large amounts of damage at once, and your screen only begins to show the telltale Red Ring of Danger when your health falls to around 50, out of a standard maximum of 200 (250 with crumb pickups). It’s quite possible, even easy, to lose track of your health in the more frenetic combat arenas, and find yourself dead from a hard-hitting melee unit that came up behind you with little warning and dealt 2/3 of your health in a single blow that you mistook for just another bullet filling the air.The overall map designs are atmospheric, but not very well laid-out; seeing the different parts of a Forge World shows the love and detail that Focus put into the window dressing, but traipsing through sprawling, samey corridors is even worse when you’re given no navigational tools whatsoever. For the most part it’s not hard to figure out where the game wants you to go, but that’s very little assurance when you’re 10 minutes into blundering through what you thought was a new hallway while your robotic mission control blithely asks if you’re lost.On the other hand, the art direction is great. It can’t be said enough: Focus  Warhammer 40K, and all of the items, enemies, and environments fit the setting like a glove. The music is largely forgettable, generic rock riffs with a little Gothic choir sprinkled in; the sound effects are great, with the real stars of the show (the guns) all having the punch you would expect from them, and the enemy barks are good, if lacking in variety.All told, I’m split on . For Warhammer fans, in a constant battle with the Star Wars fandom for the coveted crown of “Most Abused Housewife”, it’s not only better than the trash they’re used to getting from licensed games, but it’s actually , and made by a company that’s proven they care just as much about Warhammer as the fans buying their product.  gives them exactly what they expect and crave: a decent shooter where you kill heretics for the Emperor (even if you're stuck playing an Ultramarine).For those with no interest (or passing interest) in the franchise probably won’t be as wowed by the end result, which doesn’t really bring anything phenomenal to the table. Still, it’s a matter of cost perspective; I’ve blown $22 on worse ~9-10 hour jaunts, and though that’s a bit steep compared to other boomer shooters, a good sale could bring that down to something worth the time away from the grill.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, it has great style and it feels fun to run around and blast demons and xenos...However, the pacing and difficulty is all over the place. You'll have long stretches of the game where it's not challenging at all and your just gathering up loose power ups scattered throughout the level, you'll then be funneled into a large area room where hordes of enemies will be thrown at you and it becomes nearly impossible as enemies teleport in behind you and just blast you in the back. Compounding the frustration of this, you can only heal by finding health that's pre-set on the map, or what little drops from enemies... so you end up having to reload saves time and time again because you got blasted by an enemy in the back that wasn't there 1 second ago and lost half your health; and ran out of health items in the area. Enemies also feel far too bullet spongy... which is sad for game titled after a gun that shoots explosive cannon rounds.

_childDocuments_.review: In the previews, "Warhammer 40k: Boltgun" just looked interesting. Due to my strong connection to boomer shooters, I've decided to give this a go.What I did not expect though: How much I'd grow to like it. This is one excellent entry into the franchise! I'm currently playing on Hard, but I might give Exterminatus a try in the future. Positives: - It's a semi-sequel to "Space Marine" and that alone is enough to count it as a positive. - The sound design! Oh, man, it's oh so satisfying at every end. The hollow metal sound a shell makes when it hits the ground, the meaty explosions when you decimate enemies, the weapons discharging, the electronic whispers of your Servo Skull - absolute music to my ears! Probably the biggest positive I can give. - Very smooth controls that give you all the momentum and speed you'll ever need. - Graphics are pretty detailed to that old school aesthetic. Bonus points for having enemies as sprites. - Having a taunt button adds to the overall experience playing as a sophisticated, highly genetically altered killing machine in the name of the Emperor.Neutral:- The music itself is just ok.- Finding Secrets is good, but often they're not really that hidden. Negatives: - The boss design ranges from questionable to downright irritating.- Losing all your weapons between overarching chapters? Come on...Though, overall, this is (so far) the best boomer shooter I've played this year! No doubt one of the best Warhammer 40k games, too. A really good time, especially when you're into this franchise. Yet, it's also disconnected enough, that beginners can find something worthwhile. "I AM THE EMPEROR'S EDGE!"
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't want to read the essay, scroll down to at least get my main takeaway if you're not sure about trying the game.---------------The only things I really appreciated in Boltgun are gunplay and visuals. Most of the guns feel satisfying to use, there is an incentive to actually utilise all of them because of the system that make certain enemies weak against a specific kind of weapon. The only negative here is a shotgun, which is just too slow and doesn't reward it with enough damage output. Also, guns sound very solid and blowing up enemies to pieces gives very nice audio-visual feedback that enhanced this aspect. Game also looks fantastic, sprites are nice, I really liked gun models, and some of the visual effects shooting the guns have. Eenvironments (though felt copy-pasted to some extend) presents you with a nice atmosphere, look good and crispy and overall serves well the WH40K setting. There were a few moments when I just stopped playing to simply appreciate my surroundings.Things that just didn't work so well:level design - apart from visuals that felt somewhat varied (not too much tho), the design itself is just too one dimensional, there is no ingeniuity, just go, purge the arena, go further, another purge, go little more, you're done. This isn't inherently bad, but to do that for 10 hours straight or so just feels like a chore (tbf, there are a few moments when there's something more to it, where you have to apply some 'spatial logic'(yes, I made that up) to figure out the next move but they are very few and far between sadly). I didn't even expect dusk's craziness or selaco's/hedon's maze-like intricateness (of which too much can also be a bad thing), but it's just too bland overall and I was still disappointed.Soundtrack and parts of sound design are just... not good. Apart from technical oversights like very evident point of looping in the tracks, or mixing that's all over the place (very uneven sound levels of certain parts of audio fx vs the others), OST is just not memorable, doesn't create any exciting moments, and very often feels out of place. In the 1st chapter there's a lot of what feels like someone's not so great attempt at making choir/orchestral based music, later on you there was more emphasis on making not so great attempt at atmoshperic ambience mixed with some industrial and synthwave-y stuff, but all of that is just very subpar to most of the music you can find (usually similar genre-wise) in other boomer shooters, and the worst of all, it just doesn't empower you in any way, doesn't make your adrenaline rush it's just... there (I stopped paying much attention to it after few hours). Main theme is kinda cool, but you only hear it in the menu so, yeah.Combat - I didn't appreciate melee enemies spawning out of thin air right behind your back (pretty sure never died because of that, but still annoying), aspiring champions in narrow corridors ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ suck (ofc vengeance launcher stops them, and there's way to avoid their zoomies but it's another annoying thing if you don't have ammo or space to move aside), also toads are way too tanky. AI is kinda bad as well, even bosses can just sit there and not aggro you cause they're lil bit too far which makes them laughably easy to beat (played on hard). Ofc they put on some challenge they don't get stuck etc. but nothing to write home about. Also the amount of enemies in purge sections are kinda a mess, sometimes there are so few that purge lasts 2-3 minutes or you have to literally look for them. Other times it takes forever and it starts to feel like a chore because of how heavy this game leans on being an arena shooter. There's nothing wrong with arena sections even in boomer shooters ofc, but if you have so many of them it just feels like a lazy design choice (and other aspects of level design don't do much to elevate the overall experience). Oh, and hitboxes are kinda janky as well.Coming back to bosses - there is just 3-4 of them recycled over and over, and are just not fun tbh. Regular enemies have some variety to them and in this regard Boltgun does a good job. ok, you know what enough yapping, here's my main takeaway:Unfortunately in this day and age, with so many amazing retro-esque/boomer shooters for similar price or less, I just cannot fully recommend Boltgun. Maybe if you played all the other noteworthy titles (dusk, ion fury, cultic, prodeus, project warlock, hedon to just name a few. I would also add selaco - even though it's a different type of shooter really, but more because of the sheer quality, ingenuity and attention to details it has to offer) and you're curious, or you're some certified 40K freak, and doesn't have too much of an experience with such games it'll be fine, just remember that after 1st chapter this game kinda goes downhill (still, it's ok, there are just way better options out there). I really appreciate devs for making this game, and I know they put a lot of effort into creating it. Given that it was their first endeavour in the genre which is actually really hard to pull off. I applaud their dedication and would say they did a pretty good job. I still recommend it to certain kinds of people or to anyone if they're not scared by the negatives underlined by this or other reviews (well, duh, it's your money, if you're really interested in the game nothing will stop you). I also hope the devs will use all the criticism and experience from making Boltgun to make something truly outstanding in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: Game would be great if it wasn't so darned confusing on so many levels.The level design falls apart after the first chapter, quickly becoming confusing. _childDocuments_.review: Boltgun is a game I am conflicted about. Friend bought this for me as payment for a comission I am still working on.I love Doom. I love Doom 2016. I love Doom Eternal. I played Brutal Doom a lot a few years back. These types of games are really really fun for me. What am I leading up to here? Well to be fully honest, the game... lacks something for me. I cant pin it down.There is something in it thats missing. It feels like it lacks... a certain punchines.The moment I load up the game, I dont get this feeling of "Hell yea lets kill demons" like I do in Doom. I Boltgun I get the feeling of "Ok load in, kill mobs, get to the end. Done." This might be due to me not being familiar with the 40k universe and sure I can see how that would be important to know if you wanna be fully immersed.But I would also say that as a noob and newcomer to 40k which I 100% am, it also works against Boltgun. I see the mobs and... yea they are mobs. Some stronger, some less so. Some downright annoying by design and others straight up murk you if you dont pay attention for a second. This is the same in Doom but in Doom the context is simple: Its Demons from Hell.In Boltgun you dont have context as a newbie apart from the names. Lesser Plaguetoad. Greater Plaguetoad. Yea they mean what they mean and they are what they are. Once you fought them, you get what they are 100%. And by that I mean you get its a plaguetoad. But what in the fresh hell is a plaguetoad??Or these almost bunny looking abominations in blue and pink? Sometimes the pink one splits in two after death, other times they dont. It probably is explained somewhere but I dont got time to read up on 40 pages of 40k lore for 40 different enemy types (It probably doesnt have 40 enemy types, I just thought its funny to write it that way).And so in turn, just seeing the sprites meakes me go in to kill... the sprites. I got no connection to it. No idea what they are apart from their name and that honestly sucks. Cause Id love to know more. But with the game more focused on its gameplay, that wont happen here.-In addition ot the above, here is where I go into missing punch. The gameplay overall is good. Its not great or terrible. Its good. A SMG is a SMG. A shotty is a shooty. And so on.  But in come the powerups and for a majority of them I barely even know what they do. I can assume it for some, but for 80% of them I just got no idea. I know some give you a buff. Others special ammo which does more damage... or at least I hope its that! Others give you instakill and others again buff your health and armor. But then there are artifacts where I just dont know what they do.-Overall, the game isnt bad. Its not. Its interesting and can be fun. But I feel this is more for the 40k nerds than for people who dont know 40k. And I say nerd in a lighthearted manner. Yall love the universe, I aint gonna trashtalk you for it. I mean I respect what the game is trying to do so much that I am even giving it a positive review despite me not really finding much enjoyment in it. -Will I play it again? Probably. Ill try at least. I wanna see what the game got to offer, maybe eventually it will click. But so far, I cant say it has.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly can't recommend this game, and that makes me sad.Quick run-down: It tries too hard to be a boomer-shooter... flaws and all. The game suffers tremendously from trying to replicate old winding, maze-like, "wait... is that the way forward? I can't tell" boomer shooter map design. This is not a good thing. Most maps are multi-layered in some way, allowing you to drop down into prior areas once you've ascended. This is good! What's not good is how hard they tested to make sure you can't skip any areas. Taking advantage of advanced movement to skip sections has always been a hallmark of boomer shooters, and the fact that the designers don't want you to have fun moving around the map is saddening. The number of times I rummaged around a particular area on a map thinking, "Oh wow, there HAS to be a secret back there" only to get stuck was far too many. Worse, many "secrets" are often just... placed out in the open. They're more power-ups (and in fact are) than they are "secrets." The game suffers from not telling you much of anything. Again, this is in the style of old boomer shooters where you just got new weapons/upgrades with little to no information. It would be forgivable if there was some in-game codex, digital manual, or if they were intuitive. Your options are unintuitive. You give some clues through marketing and gameplay that you should use weapons with a higher strength (number on your gun) than the target's toughness (number on enemy's healthbar) to do more damgae. This tells you "use S4 to beat T3. Use S5 to beat T4, etc." Unfortunately, THIS IS ACTUALLY RARELY GOOD ADVICE. The shotgun is particularly effective against larger, high-toughness targets as they have more area to get hit by shotgun pellets; the plasma gun's poor ammo-count makes it bad for dealing with the targets it should beat simply because the "bullets-to-kill" ratio isn't *quite* good enough. This leads to... Some enemies are a pain to bring down, especially when you don't have the arms to do so. I understand Nurgle Daemons are supposed to be tough MF'ers, but the unfortunate optimal solution to dealing with them is to often stay very far away and just slowly plink them with bolter shots. This slows down the game, making it feels like a pain to progress. Boomer shooters are regularly about strafe-movement to dodge enemy shots and move around while getting up-close-and-personal to deal with problems while carefully dancing away from enemies. The lethality of enemies on anything higher than "Easy" coupled with bullet-spongey enemies (below) leads me to be unable to use movement to my advantage. I often find that I would rather take cover than actually play this boomer shooter like a boomer shooter. I can rarely tell when my character gets hurt. Very often I'll come out of a bloodbath feeling unscathed only to realize I have 20 HP and no Contempt (armor) left. It leaves me wondering where it all when, and what I could have possibly done to address that health loss. This, also unfortunately, leads to the problem... If I hit a checkpoint with 20 health and no armor, and immediately after the checkpoint it spawns 4 chaos space marines and a terminator in a cramped hallway, I am effectively soft-locked and cannot progress. I die over, and over, and over again trying to get through it without taking any damage this time, and might only be able to succeed after an hour of trying. The only thing worse than this is when I encounter the same issue, except there was no checkpoint and I'm sent hurtling back 10-15 minutes of progress.Despite all of the above, I really want to like the game. The guns seem really cool, and feel great to use when you get into it. The fact that this ONE upside makes me want to come back despite ALL of the above means there is something here. But, alas, I really can't recommend it. Sorry Auroch.

_childDocuments_.review: I have finished my first play-through, I came away fairly positive with some caveats.I played on Exterminatus (hardest) difficulty, as my first impression of the game was that it was too easy on the lower difficulties. I think the game IS fun. And when everything comes together, the game absolutely slaps. The harder difficulty is actually more annoying than it is hard. I would recommend you actually just play on the second hardest. The weapons are fine, shotgun is a travesty, yet i would say the gunplay is still fun. Enemies and your weapons are typically all projectiles, there is very few if any hit scanning weapon dmg. Unfortunately, a lot of environment and design repetition. Bosses are re-used. Bosses can be easy to cheese depending on which boss room you are fighting in. They are typically more of a hindrance than a fun fight. In that respect, bosses are fairly disappointing. Arena rooms are too blocky in their design for circle strafe gunfights, this opens up a lot in chapter 2 and then chapter 3 goes back to more of the same in chapter 1 with more verticality in the arena design. this doesn't help much on Exterminatus as you will be swamped with nurglings and other such enemies which charge you down. The environment aesthetic and atmosphere is unmistakably 40k, so in a general sense they are fun to play through but since they're very same looking and the game doesn't give you a map, expect to get lost will varying frequency.I think the game is fun but not amazing. Would recommend you buy it on sale, unless you're a big 40k head then i would say you are gonna get the space marine power fantasy in full here.

_childDocuments_.review: In the modern sphere of boomer shooters this game is a solid 5/10. The graphics are good, but with how fast paced the gameplay is visuals will turn into a muddy blur and it becomes incredibly hard to discern the enemies, and projectiles from the scenery. The enemies lack rhythm in their attacks and movement. They have almost frame perfect attack timing so using cover feels useless. The enemies also tend to slide around making it frustrating to try and predict their movements. The weapons look, and feel great to use, but there is little difference in their time to kill and there is no change on their effectiveness depending on the enemy types so you might as well stick with the bolter you get at the start of the game. The enemies are all essentially reskins of two class 1. little guy who moves fast and dies in one shot, or 2. big guy who moves slow and takes a lot of hits. The levels are chock full of items so much so that you'll only be able to pick up about 10% of them, except for arenas when you actually might need them. those are usually barren of anything useful. For being bound to right click you'd think that the chainsword attack would have some use, but it does the least amount of damage out of any of the weapons while locking you in place during use so you might as well never use it. Over all in the now crowded market of boomer shooters this game does nothing to stand out except having the 40k brand attached to it, and for $20 you could buy at least 3 other games just like it except better.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun

_childDocuments_.review: Solid, straight-forward, bang bang shooter. - Movement is nice and chunky, suitable for a power armor wielding big boy - and you're pretty quick, can grab ledges etc.- Weapons are all useful, with map-based powerups and upgrades (temporary, alas). Ammo is balanced to be both always available, but you never have quite enough to just run with 2 weapons. Forces you to switch it up. - Map navigation is usually straightforward with plenty of fighting sprinkled in between bigger arenas, with your little servoskull support will give you hints and pointers if you get lost long enough. Some areas do be a bit too samey and key paths/buttons can blend into the backgrounds. Not too much maze-hunting though.- Map variety is alright between industrial, cathedrals and nature + some weirder ones. It's 40k, so maps tend to lean into those flavors.- Enemy variety is *decent*, and I wish they'd put in the expansion enemies and weapons in the base campaign too. You got your cultists with various guns, your standard tzeentch and nurgle daemon roster and like 3 flavors of generic chaos space marines. _childDocuments_.review: This is a decent old school fps. Is it that great though looking at the 93% positive reviews? Hell no.I recommend it but only for die hard fans of old school fps. I'd rate it a 65 /100.But first what's positive:-level design is usually good-it has some nice set pieces-soundtrack is all right-gunplay is mostly fun-finally a new old school fps with quick saves and quick loades and both are super fast, in fact loading times in general are pretty fast in this oneNow the bad stuff:-First of all this being a Warhammer game is already a downside for me. Warhammer lore and design is just so boring and generic imo. -Then the bit of story this game has is shown in (ugly) cutscenes where mostly there is just some woman talking. The game doesn't explain any of the lore and I just had no clue what the story was about. Of course story isn't important in an old school fps but if you wanna have a story in it make it understandable.-The game gives you so much ammo for almost every weapon like constantly at a point where I had full ammo for every weapon after every fight pretty much. Ammo is supposed to be the most important ressource in an old school fps. But in this game it's not really a ressource, it's abundance. Another really annoying part is that the max ammo you can carry for each weapon is so low. Why not make it the other way around? Give me a high max ammo count but don't give me ammo every 3 seconds so exploration would actually be rewarded and ammo would be an actual ressource to care about.-Enemies are either canon fodder or bullet sponges. However this gets better later on when you get better weapons.-Boss fights are so unfun. Why? Because devs decided it's a good idea to infinitly spawn enemies in the boss arena. Also bosses have way to much hp. This all means that, at least on the highest difficulty, there is really just one strategy which works for boss fights: Mostly ignore the regular enemies, I mean whats the point of killing them when they will just respawn. Instead go for the boss and throw a vortex grenade at him, then just unload a strong weapon like the heavy bolter and the boss is done very fast and easily. Except the last boss which is just ridiculously hard mostly because he basically respawns multiple times, has even more hp, and you only have 2 vortex grenades available there.-The rewards for secrets are mostly useless. You either get a powerup which aren't that useful usually, or an upgrade for a weapon of your choice (but the upgrade only lasts for the current level and there is only one upgrade item per level; so this upgrade system seems pointless for me) or a a bit of a stronger ammo type for the boltgun which isn't a big deal either. Well, usually in an old school fps you get some rare ammo in secrets which always feels very rewarding but here as ammo is redundant the secrets are as well.-This game uses arena fights where enemies keep spawning in (finite number except in boss fights) way too often. I mean don't get me wrong, this concept is fun in the new Doom games but I don't want this in the actual retro fps or at least not that often.-Performance often got around 40 for me which is ridiculous looking at the graphic quality.-Some weapons, especially the shotgun are really underpowered and basically only usable against the canon fodder enemies.-You can't see your stats (kills and secrets until you finish a level. WHY?-Poor damage indicators, melee enemies often don't even have an attack animation, so it's super hard to tell when you get hit, you literally have to look at your hp to see itEDIT: with an update the devs added a screen to show you the level stats and also improved damage indicators. So those negative points are now gone.

_childDocuments_.review: Death by a thousand cuts.This isn't a bad game. But there's a lot of bad in it.-Movement feels good-The shooting also feels good-The graphics also look good-Can't dash mid air-Weapon/enemy levels feel unnecessary and make the combat annoying especially in boss fights -Damage feedback is non-existent. You'll run around shooting things and have fun and then suddenly drop dead because you didn't notice you were low on health and got sniped from behind.-Reloading... in a game brandishing itself as a boomer shooter why the hell do you have to reload your weapons?-Furthermore, if you're expecting something like Doom, don't bother. This plays a lot like a retro version of the modern Wolfenstein games.-The music...exists? Not only does it get drowned out by the gameplay, what is there doesn't sound that good. Mostly ambience.-The levels are a drag. They all play the same and with spongy enemies and sometimes confusing level design it makes them a slog to go through.-No map of any kind. If you get lost, either pray for luck to be on your side or look up a walkthrough.-You loose all your weapons and their upgrades between episodes. Not all things from old shooters should be copied, it just ruins any semblance of progression.£18.99 feels way overpriced. Maybe £7-10, but not £18.99I got the game day 1 but I'm struggling to even finish it.I hope I'll finish it eventually, but not yet. If you're a Warhammer 40K fan you'll probably enjoy it (along with other positive reviewers) but if you're just a normal gamer maybe go look for some other games. But if you're dead set on getting this game, then get it on a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay mostly consists of going from arena to arena battling huge numbers of enemies in enclosed spaces. Some of these Arenas are fun, some are tedious and grindy. _childDocuments_.review: Classic Doom works because the hitscan enemies are easily manipulated, and the stronger enemies have telegraphed attacks that you can strafe. Modern Doom works because the weapon variety gives you answers for any situation, and the fast-paced combat and constant damage are mitigated by systems that allow you to recover health and ammo mid-combat.Boltgun is trying to be both, matching the aesthetic and straightforward gameplay of classic Doom with the speed and performance of modern Doom, but it executes on both very poorly, forgetting what worked best for each era. The result is an uneven mess of bullet sponge enemies, weak weaponry, a lack of resource generating options, and terrible movement. The player only feels empowered due to how hilariously enemies explode from even your most basic weaponry. As soon as you face any other enemy type, your combat options are incredibly limited. Dying for the eighteenth time to a toad that can hitscan attack you with its tongue from half an arena away, with no way to dodge, shows the developer's lack of experience in the genre, and hopefully their next effort bears fruit that's less bitter.

_childDocuments_.review: As a member of the popular (and overused)  Ultramarines chapter, you’re sent on a suicidal (so, standard) mission on the forge-world of Graia to cleanse a Mechanicus assembly plant from the influence of Chaos forces. Boltgun isn’t at all a lore-heavy title, despite stemming from one of the most lore-heavy fandoms around. It’s shooting, purging and dodging hails of warp-fire without much preamble all the way through. The entirety of lore consists in brief animated panels at the start and end of each chapter; aside your faithful servoskull’s one-liners and some bosses’ dialogues, there won't be any more lore to absorb - which is kind of a shame, considering how interesting and rich 40K’s universe is - but for this genre it’s fine.The levels feature a selection of iconic 40K environments, ranging from desolate wastelands ridden with wreckage of Emperor-knows what conflict, to the sprawling underground forge-worlds off the Mechanicus - and their labyrinthine maintenance tunnels you’ll definitely get lost into. There’s a good amount of detail in the making of environments, the entrails of your pummeled enemies being only the last coat of paint to the fairly-elaborate locales. The sense of how enormous the infrastructure and places are is conveyed very well: levels are definitely large in most cases, and with good verticality. You’ll explore mostly on foot, with the occasional use of machinery, like elevators, or Jump Packs (jetpacks) that however, only act as a “static” movement boost and can’t be brought around. Fear not, as your mobility will still be quite exceptional, with your Space Marine being able to sprint, leap great distances and grapple to most ledges for easy climbing. You’re immune to fall damage, too, in good old-school FPS tradition. Levels are sprawling and the absence of a map / clear direction can be detrimental in some cases, as in larger ones you’ll definitely get lost big time. Secrets here aren’t your classic DOOM-like sliding wall nor any obscure puzzle or destructible prop: any and all hidden upgrades or goodie caches will be simply laying around in some remote corner, or behind some clever parkour. There are generally six per level, and finding them all provides no benefit other than achievements, if you’re one of those “achievement madmen”, that is.What you’ll be doing most of the time is - you guessed it - purging heretics, the 43rd millennium’s favorite pastime galaxy-wide. To spread the Word of the Emperor you’ll have nine blessed constructs of the Omnnissah, ranging from the “simple” (it’s a damn 40mm cannon, son…) Bolter to the more devastating Plasma Gun or the exotic Volkite Caliver and Gravity Cannon, to name some. Each of these is perfectly capable of reducing your enemies to literal red paste, however some may be more effective than others depending on the situation: each foe has a Toughness rating (armor) and you’ll ideally use weapons with higher Strength (piercing power) to inflict full or even bonus damage in case their armor is low enough. Combat feels exciting, high-stakes (on higher difficulties) and satisfyingly brutal, with relatively low time-to-kill for both yourself and the enemies - in most cases, standing still is a death sentence (exceptions definitely apply if you find a great spot, though).Consumables include Frag and Krak grenades in limited numbers - refills are plentiful all around though - to deal with respectively globs of weaklings or single high–armor foes. Last but not least your Chainsword will enable instant-dash attacks to any nearby foe, granting you damage reduction while tearing them to pieces. Cool as that may sound, on the higher difficulties, other enemies will make Swiss cheese out of you while you spend precious seconds hacking at that single target, so that’s not really something viable, especially when the reward for a melee kill is just a few pieces of extra armor - not worth the risk.Generally you’ll be circle-strafing in arenas dodging heaps of bullets, but in plenty of linear sections a more careful approach, sniping targets from afar when possible and conserving resources is not a bad idea at all - it all depends on your playstyle, mostly everything is viable as long as you stay alive in the process.Bosses are disappointing. While they feature some iconic foes a normal Space Marine would never defeat on its own, like a Great Unclean One to make an example, their attack patterns are limited, they’re slow and only threatening because often supported by a enormous amount of trash mobs. Once they’re cleared, the only thing left is a lumbering HP sponge that poses little threat to our swift blue agent of the Emperor. The fact the same three bosses are recycled several times without variation also adds insult to injury.The only form of permanent character progression are the weapons you’ll progressively acquire, and even those will be reset at the end of each chapter, for whatever reason. Upgrades are all temporary and range from special ammo for your bolter (that, admittedly, doesn’t feel so special as it boosts damage marginally while adding no other real advantage), the Machine Spirit Blessing that overhauls the currently-held weapon for a while, and the Emperor’s Blessings, respectively boosting weapon damage, melee damage and damage resistance. Last but not least the extremely rare Vortex Grenade will heavily damage bosses and utterly obliterate anything else in a large radius, but only one can be carried and often they’re hidden in obscure places - better save them up.

_childDocuments_.review: A few YouTubers I follow recommended this before launch, praising it as something like "40k-flavored DOOM done right". Unfortunately, now that I've finished this game, I'm questioning how much they were paid to shill this disaster. Everything about this game is wrong: the level design is terrible and feels completely random most of the time, most weapons don't have distinct uses or aren't worth using, braindead enemy AI just charges right at you (regardless of terrain), the music is terrible and sounds randomly generated, and bullet sponge bosses are recycled to an obnoxious degree. Put simply, this game isn't worth playing and I don't recommend it.Looking at the developer's catalog on Steam, it appears that they've never made a FPS game before, and it really shows with Boltgun. The first two levels felt like a mediocre DOOM mod but that's probably the highest praise this game deserves. Levels have no coherent structural design, no environmental clues for where to go, and have "secrets" either hidden in plain sight or have timed powerups that are irrelevant after you're cleared the area. Worst of all, perhaps to hide their incompetence, there's no map! Going back to DOOM again, they got that right back in 1993 with a quick-to-load 2D overhead map that you could actually continue to play the game on while viewing it. Perhaps the devs didn't include a map on purpose so that people couldn't see how hideous their level design was. Chapter 1 is tolerable but feels like a bad DOOM mod, Chapter 2 turns into a MC Escher painting, and Chapter 3 was designed by a madman. Assuming they're a human and this wasn't mapped by AI, I'm genuinely concerned for the sanity of the person who designed Chapter 3, and I hope their family is checking on them.The only weapon that feels right is the titular Boltgun which unfortunately falls off after the first chapter. The shotgun is basically a scattershot boltgun but the cone is too wide to be useful in most cases (a bad shotgun in a FPS game should be reason enough to not recommend this). The plasma gun is supposed to be the rocket launcher stand-in but the AoE is too small, the fire rate is too slow, and you're animation locked after firing. The heavy bolter is decent against charging enemies because of the small knockback but it either needs to fire faster or do more damage to be worth using otherwise. The Vengeance Launcher is a revolver that fires bolts that explode on a delay but its mostly useless because the initial hit does no damage and the explosion damage isn't worth the wait. The Melta Gun does excellent damage in a huge AoE but only carries eight shots worth of ammo. This is clearly supposed to be your boss deleter but you end up magdumping and then running around the arena looking for more ammo for it almost immediately. The last two weapons, the Volkite Caliver and the Grav Cannon, are just continuous fire infinite range lasers, with the latter having a small pulling AoE at the end of it, making for a really boring BFG replacement.Boltgun wants to look like a Build engine game, wants to play like DOOM 1993 combined with DOOM 2016, and wants to emulate Halo's player movement, but none of that really pans out. I was really looking forward to Boltgun but it's a complete mess that isn't fun to play most of the time. If you're looking specifically for a 40k FPS game, Darktide has improved greatly since launch and is worth the extra money over this. This is a poorly made product trying to appeal to nostalgia, yet another "boomer shooter" that blends into the Very Positive background noise on Steam.To end on a positive note, here are some completely free DOOM (1993) mods you should play instead of spending $20 on this UE4 student project: GMOTA, Combined Arms, and High Noon Drifter are weapon mods that have ridiculous variety without getting into power fantasy territory (like Russian Overkill). Project Brutality is a conversion mod of Brutal Doom, adding dozens of new monsters and weapons with tons of options for difficulty and power scaling. Reelism 2 is total conversion where you fight through frantic arenas to get cash to spend in town on upgrades and better guns to fight through higher difficulty arenas. If you're looking for megawads to play through with these weapons, check out Ancient Aliens, The Brotherhood of Ruin, and Vanguard (or any Cacoward receiver is a safe bet). There's a massive catalog of free content created for DOOM 1 & 2 over the past three decades that you should check out instead of Boltgun.

_childDocuments_.review: Bolt Gun is the whole package: a slick and highly polished 40K Boomershooter.  It has deliciously chunky Gun-play, complete with a "hold to slow time and aim" chainsword melee.  It's got satisfying traversal physics and mechanics paired with great level design. The ever intriguing 40K Universe is obviously a big help, the art direction and story are a great and enjoyable representation of the ludicrously over the top Grim-Dark setting.  Plays like a grab bag of elements from modern and classic GZDoom/Quake/Build engine games. Like Doom itself Boltgun features tightly designed "linear but exploratory" levels, albeit much larger than even most community WADs.  This comes complete with key hunting, pre-defined combat encounters, and levels taking  30 - 60 minutes to get through first time.  The levels lead into each other, making the game feel like a journey through the story location (which is great!).  My only real nitpick is that on the highest difficulty, I didn't die until the second last mission of chapter 1, It doesn't seem as finely tuned a difficulty as something like Doom Eternal's Nightmare, or even some of the high difficulties in Doom mods like Project Brutality, REKKR, Ashes 2063 etc.  However the difficulty does ramp up as you progress. I just would have preferred a difficulty setting that kicks you in the teeth right from the start, and ramps up from there.  I hope we get some additional difficulty modes in updates or DLC.Speaking of DLC....  could we please get some actual WORTHWHILE DLC for this game.  Games Workshop games hardly ever have good DLC and it's a shame.  I would love to see additional chapter DLC with new enemies to fight.  Imagine fighting Tyranid and Genestealer Cultists on a Space Hulk, or Drukhari in the Jungle.  Aeldari on a crazy Forge World.. whatever.  I could do without Orks.. it's ALWAYS Orks but I know that's probably one of the more likely DLC plans.Highly recommended for 40k fans, this is one of the best games to ever be released in the setting.  Also recommended for Boomer-shooter players, this is one of the best to come out in recent years.  For anyone else, it's a great game, a great intro to 40K, a great FPS in general (Retro or otherwise).  It's easily the best FPS of the year so far. I was only planning to check it out and play it later when I didn't have so many games on the go already... But Boltgun just keeps pulling me back.  That is the sign of excellence for me, when I literally cant help but boot a game up when it comes time to play something.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - This game is fine, even pretty decent at times, but I wouldn't recommend this at full price unless you know you're going to enjoy it.  The core of the game is solid, the aesthetics are great but lacks variety, and the game's balance is a little wonky and can be tedious at times to slog through.  I'd recommend playing in short three-hour-maximum bursts as not to burn yourself out.  There are much better retro-style FPS games out there to play.Gameplay (6/10)-Despite the insistence of the marketing, this isn't a boomer-shooter.  Sure, it's retro-styled, but the only thing boomer-shooter-y is the graphics.-In general, the difficulty varies from 'kind of easy' to 'surprisingly difficult' without any real consistency or reasonable building-up.  Be prepared to save before every large room just in case.-The guns vary from good solid workhorses that will carry you through half the game, to somewhat useful, to incredibly niche if not outright useless.  Good feel to them and they all work, but some of them might need a buff of sorts.  The titular BOLTGUN! is almost too good for most circumstances, doing comparable damage to other guns.-The missions are decent enough but just a little too long, and dare I say there's too many missions.  You could easily cut out a third of the game out and it would vastly improve.-Enemy variety is good, but unfortunately at the end of the first act you've seen all the non-boss enemies, so it gets stale after a while.-Some enemies are just way, WAY too tanky to be fun to fight against, or have broken mechanics, or both.-Enemy melee attacks strike on the first frame of the animation, before they look like they've even hit you, which feels cheap, if not an outright mistake.-Level design is honestly pretty bland, and feels very video-gamey.  Like they designed it to be a video game level first.  And even then, the levels are kind of bad at signposting where you're supposed to go.-Also, no map?  Really?-The campaign will take you about 12 hours to get through, which doesn't sound long, but for a retro-style FPS is a fairly long time.  Unfortunately the game doesn't quite manage to make those extra hours feel much different so it gets very samey.-The servo-skull is nice, but I wish his dialogue was a) actually audible speech, bit-crunched as it might be, and b) had the subtitles more in the centre of the screen.  Trying to read possibly important information in the top-right corner of the screen while in the middle of a firefight is just bad design.-Feedback from being hit is pretty rubbish sometimes, and it can be hard to tell a) what's hit you and b) how powerful the attack is.  You get roughly the same feedback from an attack that deals a tiny amount of damage versus one that knocks out half your health/armour.-All powerups are secrets, and all secrets are powerups.  They're not usually that secret, especially for a 'boomer shooter'.Aesthetics (7/10)-Faithful to 40k's artstyle while also having the chunky pixel textures.-The weapon sound design is good, each gun sounds punchy and heavy, and the visceral sounds of violence from your shots is satisfying.-Sound design in general with the game is a bit weird though.  Everything going off at once means it's hard to parse what's going on sometimes.  Possibly an issue with me playing with TV speakers, might be better with headphones, will amend this after my second playthrough if so.-I do appreciate that the enemies kind of look like the models rather than an attempt at realism. The animations could do with a couple extra frames but that's not a dealbreaker.-Environmental design is decent but seriously lacking in variety; there's only really three different types of environment across the whole game.-Rare for me to say, but I honestly wish Caedo talked more without player input.  All of his lines of dialogue are locked behind a taunt button.  Given the effort the voice actor put into the role, it's a shame we don't hear it more.-Actually, I wish we had more dialogue in general.  It's kind of surprising that the only things cultists say is 'UH!' whenever they spot a giant hulking 8-foot-tall transhuman warrior, or that the Chaos Space Marines don't taunt the player for being a corpse-worshipper.  The bosses even have dialogue, but it's all said through the servo-skull's subtitles; you could easily have a voice line and subtitles on screen and it'd be much more immersive.-I love the cutscene artstyle even if it feels a little disjointed from the gameplay artstyle.Story (??/10)  [spoilers but also not really because it doesn't matter]-It's kind of hard to write about the story in this game since it's so bare-bones, but also really isn't important.-It's nice that it's a direct followup to Space Marine, arguably the best non-strategy 40k game out there so far.  Playing Space Marine isn't... strictly necessary but if you're a Warhammer fan playing Boltgun you've probably played Space Marine anyway.-It's a servicable story in the more literal sense - it services the need of the game, which is to get you from point A to point B with as much violence as possible within.-That's... really all I can say about it.  It's okay.Overall, this game is... okay?  Mid at worst, kinda fun at best.  Probably not worth the AU$30 I spent on it, length of play notwithstanding, and I'm not sure how much I'll end up playing it in the future, but honestly, I'm just happy the game works and is functional right out of the gate.  Probably one of the better 40k games out there, but competition isn't fierce and otherwise the game is fine.  If you're looking for a good, true-to-form boomshoot experience that came out roughly the same time as this, I'd recommend 'Slayers X: Terminal Aftermath: Vengance of the Slayer'* instead.Bonus Round: random Warhammer Nerd Nitpicks!-Why is the Meltagun Strength 7?  It's been strength 8 since I started playing in 2008, and not for nothing but it's recently gone UP in strength.  Probably for balance reasons, but still, if they're pulling the mechanic of Strength vs Toughness, why not be accurate with it?-For that matter, why does the meltagun not just instantly vapourise Aspiring Champions and Chaos Terminators?  Outside of invulnerable saves or bad rolling, it's pretty consistently done that since I've been playing.-Chaos Space Marines shouldn't be so easy to kill and so underwhelming in their attacks.  They should pose a serious threat to the main character (who is a Veteran, not a Captain) and be introduced way later, much like the Champions and Terminators.  Probably wouldn't be fun to fight them like that, but still.-The plasma gun damaging you on overcharge is a cute nod, but the fact it doesn't do any extra damage when it does overcharge is a missed opportunity.-I really feel like the Volkite weapon should cause an actual detonation when it kills an enemy rather than insta-gibbing them, but that's less important.-The plasma gun takes up the same ecological niche as rocket launchers in other boomer-shooters.  You know what might have been a better choice for that?  A missile launcher.  Which Space Marines have.*Vengeance was misspelled intentionally.  Trust me, Slayers X is a good game, it just LOOKS like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
