_childDocuments_.review: Ever come across that one obscure little game, decide to play it and unconsciously get reminded why you loved playing video games in the first place?This is one of those games. It's a mixture of several genres, and borrows from many classic and newer games but it is wickedly stylized, immensely fun and unique on it own.Game design and designers have become bland and uninspired as of late, and it takes playing one of these "little" charming games to remember the joy of experiencing a really good game, crafted with purpose and a little inspiration.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I cast a decoy spell, then dodge roll behind a shambling monstrosity and beat its head in with a lead pipe. Then I run out a nearby door and slap it with an explosive arcane trap as I pass, killing the backup that stupidly lumbers after me after seeing what I did to the back of its friend's skull. I loot their corpses for plants to turn into paralysing agents and acid bombs, then re-equip my Norse shield for the next fight. My frilly blue dress is stained with blood and the rings on my fingers make me itch for violence. The lady in my peripheral vision laughs at me again. I don't mind. ----All is well with the witch leader who incinerated me on sight when I first got here. The beef has been squashed, and I now cordially toss her all my spare change and rotting limbs, and in return she makes my bones into steel. There's still a big, lumbering problem in the dining hall, who is apparently so juiced that it takes three paralysing grenades to even make him flex his traps. He has dashed my skull into the nice shiny floors a few too many times. Along with that, if I even slightly approach his buddy Mozart while dodging his swings, the guy immediately stops playing Serenade No. 13, stands up, and starts striding towards me like I punched his grandma. I can't even see him unless he is reflected in a mirror, I have no way to harm him, and the big man still scares me. ♥♥♥♥ the dining hall. I need to become one with the mirror.----Later, I exit the witch basement, so high off bad juju and spirit dust that local furniture is floating through the ceiling and being replaced by bloodied, caged mannequins. I crawl through a hole in the mirror to reach Nowhere, a serene, starry ether plane where business is booming. I sell photographs of spirits to a man who can't remember his name. In return, he deals me ghostly trinkets, and loads of cash money american dollars. You see, I've found my calling in this dream, not even four nights in. Ghoul hustling. I'm a dealer of the damned. A haunt huckster. A poltergeist peddler. A shade smuggler. And as this bandaged junkie keeps satisfying his memory-fix off my photographs, I get richer and richer, AND I get free passage throughout the mansion with the mirror's portal network. If I use any more magic at this point, my soul will rot from the inside out though, so I'm kind of stuck with my trusty pipe, and that's bad news for the rest of the mansion.----I'm still in a dream, snake eater. I've been popping flash bulbs into most spirits in the house, and getting profit in earnest to keep me going strong throughout the rest of the house, letting me explore more. The paranoid butcher in the basement that was hired to dissect bodies now dissects bodies for fun. Despite this man openly confessing to me that he kidnaps children to take apart in the dream to be a better surgeon IRL, I continue to talk to him. He goes berserk at the drop of a hat, and after many throwing knives, invisible witch branch sucker punches, and clutch closet dodges, he goes down.  I now mix his blood in the sacrifice altar so that I can keep my trusty lead pipe with me next time I mess up and wake up in here. My next destination is the hedge maze outside the house. A devout man in a Crusader's helmet tells me not to associate with witches or their spells lest I be cast down in the eyes of the Lord. Little does he know, I'm so high off the Coven's arcane bath salts that the hedges around me are made of meat. Despite this, I do in fact carry a bible, and Matthew 4:10 is my greatest weapon against the paranormal next to flash photography. I ignore him, he's a hater. I catch a child rummaging through the body of one of my kills. One of the Wretch's little scavengers again. I crack it over the head with my pipe, and it goes limp. My turf, my business, my loot. That should send him a message. My vision blurs constantly, so I drink more coffee.---While I shoulder-check my way through my fellow asylum patients and rummage through dressers, I'm finding more out about Mostyn House, and the dream that keeps me trapped rotting in my bed in the waking world, while I fight for my life in a shared consciousness with other patients.  Alfred Mostyn, a Welsh coal mogul, had this house built as a country home, and then died from pneumonia along with his daughter. Before the final member of the family, Peter, also passed, he gifted this house to an American physician and his daughter Margaret... the same woman who's been guiding me through this nightmare, and one of my few allies here. Hang on, if she owned this place along with her father, what's she doing wading through the dreamscape with the asylum patients? Before I can return to the foyer to talk to Margaret and catch myself up on her story, the floor begins to shake as footsteps rapidly approach. The tallest chambermaid I have ever seen sprints towards me, and proceeds to beat me over the head with a candelabra. As I back away to apply first aid, I am jumped by a skeletal apparition. Before I can pull out my lens piece and escalate gang violence with a snapshot, it sprays me with so much ghost coke that my tolerance gives out, and my skin crumbles into ash.----I wake up in the bed again, my hand already gripping my lead pipe and camera. I have lost everything else, but that's fine, for what else need I remember, in a place like this? My memory is sharp, and my friends are just a mirror away. I know my way around this mansion, even as it shifts to disorient, and I will build my empire again. I have abominations to concuss, witchcraft to study, and a story of bloody tragedy to unravel. ----I'd recommend this game if you're interested by what you saw in the trailer. I promise it is even more than it seems. This game mixes so many genres and it all blends, introducing all of its mechanics to you at a reasonable pace and allowing you to make the most of them as you scrounge for resources to figure out strategies to deal with each section of the house. The combat is definitely janky, but I found that an enjoyable challenge to work around, and as you get more familiar with your weapons, items and rings, you find ways to circumvent obstacles and tip encounters to your favor. The atmosphere is downright oppressive at times, especially with the well-done sanity mechanic, which leaves you toeing the line of madness to reveal hidden secrets and benefits from being at a high curse level. The game rewards a sharp eye and frequent checks of your inventory, map and notes. The soundtrack and environments are surreal and you never feel fully safe. The game also opens up as you play, with a massive map, an arena mode, minigames, a NG+ hook, and a smaller roguelike microcosm inside the game, which is fitting considering the story. Speaking of which, the story goes places far beyond the initial 'escape the house and dream' goal, with a lot to say on ethics, industry, and surprisingly, abuse. The worldbuilding is surprisingly deep, and the many notes you find throughout your playthrough help piece together how the world operates and how people have adapted to the setting. I only wish there was a wiki for the game where I could see all the characters' dialogue to better piece together the history of Mostyn House and the many people and factions inhabiting it, though I guess the NG+ is there for a reason. Not only is the game replayable with the vast amount of gear and playstyle options you have at your disposal, but multiple endings and a fresh view on the world will change the way you see many characters from start to finish. I plan to replay it at some point, but I need a breather for now. Make no mistake, this is a fully finished game with a lot of love put into it, which is more than many triple A games can say for this price. A worthy tribute to classic adventure games, and a solid entry that stands up well on its own. Hats off to Moonless Formless for one of the most engrossing games I've played this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often say this about any media, because everyone else is saying it all the time, but this game is immensely underrated. At the time of review it's sitting at 70 reviews and a peak concurrent player count of 42 people. That is insane to me. This is a full game. Other people are selling what amounts to , as a full game, and this is a full game.Things this game has: * A map that is absolutely much bigger than it initially seems. When I thought I had sussed out the game's limits and what the core gameplay loop consisted of, it sucker punched me with how far it could stretch the grounds of its premise. * A fully fleshed out action RPG system that allows you to tailor the gameplay to how you want to play. You don't wanna fight and want a full horror stealth experience? You can mostly do that. You wanna facetank every enemy while smacking them with an electric baton? You can do that. You wanna dress up as a clown and throw firebombs at people til they die? That's a pretty strong build. And the game is so dynamic and the enemies are so diverse that you don't have to stick to one build, in fact, you are strongly encouraged to switch "classes" on the fly like you are playing Final Fantasy X-2 and you've got all the dresspheres.* A STORY. A real actual story with meaningful twists and characters with motivations. And there were points where I was like... that's a plot hole. And then the game would reveal to me, no it wasn't. Actually we thought this through. And there's stuff that is both really surprising and yet not out of left field, and stuff that is satisfying because you can guess it ahead of time and it's great.* Straight up two separate roguelite zones that are I believe completely optional for those who love rolling for truly randomized loot so they can min-max.* Minigames. An arena mode. All this junk that absolutely doesn't have to be there but it being there makes this game feel so much bigger and grander.* A dog companion. And you can sit down in a chair and pet the dog while you read.This game takes a lot of reference from Rule of Rose (including one piece of armor which seems to be an explicit reference to RoR's protagonist's costume), which is a classic horror game that I really adore. It takes reference from American McGee's Alice. From Resident Evil and Silent Hill. From Bioshock. From Clocktower. From Dark Souls and Bloodborne and Hollow Knight. And it blends all those up in blood soup and adds its own flair, not content to just be referential. It stands on its own, heightened rather than dragged down by its heritage. This is a full game. I feel like we see games like this less and less these days.I bought this thinking this would be a fun halloween romp I'd play for a day and get bored of. Nope. Went all the way to the end. One end, of four. This is a full game. Do I have to keep saying that?  is a true hidden gem, and I hope people will find it and try it.

_childDocuments_.review: Indie devs doing what AAA rarely do anymore. So, let me start by saying that I found this game completely by accident, scrolling down the horror games section looking for something Markiplier played once, and I saw this weird looking yet highly reviewed game. My experience with Astlibra led me to be immediately interested.I haven't played much yet, but I already wanna get out of job to play some more. I'm also playing other AAA titles like Dragon's Dogma 2 and Horizon Forbidden West, and this has so far managed to get me thinking more about my hobby than those two.I'll try to explain how this game works and what it's about: It's a blend of roguelike elements with survival horror and Dark Souls. Whoever did this loves old school survival horror, as the whole game feels like a love letter towards two niche classics: the original Clock Tower and Rule of Rose. You play as a teen girl who seems to suffer from a yet to be diagnosed ailment, and was sent to an asylum for "treatment". On her first night there, she awakens inside her dreams, which happen to be a shared dream between the patients of the asylum. She learns not only that this surreal version of the place is inhabited by hostile creatures, but that she's unable to wake up from it and the more she stays there, the less human she'll become until she turns into another one of those creatures. With the aid of a young witch and a cast of unnerving yet charming characters, she'll explore the mansion and try to find a way out of the dream.Every time you die in the dream, your returned to the room you awaken in, as not even death can save you. The general layout of the mansion and key places seem to be in fixed locations, but the rest changes, meaning that you can't count on familiarizing yourself with the rooms to make it out. That said, certain loot DOES seem to spawn more frequently inside certain room types (e.g. Med kits on Restrooms).  In Soulslike fashion, you'll lose all but your key items and relics (permanent equipable buffs), but as you explore you'll be able to "remember" items, meaning you get to pick which of the items you found this run remain when you die. Combat so far isn't super polished as enemies are fast and have big hit boxes, but it evens out with the fact that you can attack and dodge all you want.Early on, the game plays like Clock Tower with combat elements: you need to stealth your way into the mansion, plan your fights, and avoid stronger enemies. Unlike what the 2.5D game would have you think, enemies are as capable of traversing the mansion as you do, and things like shooting a gun, breaking a vase or ringing the bell will not only alert the enemies in your room but those in nearby ones as well, and they can and WILL chase you across rooms. Thankfully the stealth speed is fast compared to other games and you also have endless sprint.Things get spiced up with the magic system. You can find or craft scrolls that her consumed to cast spells with interesting effects like anti damage barriers, door seals or even the classic fireballs. The caveat is that every time you consume a scroll, you also gain Curse, which is a status that can only be cured by black candles. The more Curse you build up, the more paranormal events and weird stuff happens around the mansion, until eventually the curse starts consuming your life like poison.Eventually you'll find permanent equipment that persists between runs like armor and relics that will give you powerful effects and you'll be able to craft synergies that will in turn make areas of the mansion easier and lead you deeper into it.I've read that there's still other features I haven't discovered and even new things to find during New Game Plus so, if you don't mind the clunkiness of combat and janky but effective visuals, grab this game that considering my early experience and content I've yet to discover, should be way up the list of horror games. Let's support devs like this, who aren't afraid of making new ideas work.

_childDocuments_.review: I found out about Withering Rooms from Punchy's GDQ speedrun and I'm forever thankful to him. It's a horror metroidvania with procedural elements, I guess? And also a profound ARPG if you consider late Castlevania games as such. Stylistically, WR possesses traits of Sanitarium, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, and American McGee's Alice. Still in a league of its own, it bleeds profusely over the world it animates. You wake up in a corrupted Dream as a girl with bad posture, a clinical patient named Nightingale. A silent child in a screeching night with no end. The Dream isn't an evil phenomenon like Elm Street, only a violated miracle comprised of looping incorporeal processes. Bubbling with cruel ideas, the setting goes balls-to-the-wall, incorporating character-driven Lovecraftian sci-fi about human vices, trans-dimensional interpretation, and cycles of abuse. Defying thematic cohesiveness, the game invents its own theme of chaotic insanity. The setting takes root in Aztec culture and Byzantine mazes, all wrapped up in 1900s clinical horror.Washing away the meaning of things, burrowed deep within the heart of the Dream is the Curse. Its spiffing scorn permeates the grimy scenes of eclectic depravity. Being its guest, you shall burn alive, dredge knee-deep in poison sludge, and get eviscerated with a rusty sickle. So far, the Dream is unique to Mostyn House, which went from being a country retreat to a cholera clinic, then our trap - the asylum. Swarming with monsters and secret passages, the Lament Configuration twists itself each night on all layers of unreality. While the real-world bodies of its comatose explorers rot in beds, becoming nightmare creatures. Death in this existential deadlock is a fluke, your real body rots all the same. The suffering is tangible yet normalised. You won't see empathy from the desensitised factions, conflicting in a crackhouse world. Most inhabitants whose minds are still intact only push you around. By doing their bidding, and by your will, the Dream shapes into 4 endings.Its pliant nature isn't fully reflected in the game's randomiser. It's more of a theme. The overall map structure shifts slightly, it mostly impacts monster placement and loot. This could get monotonous if not for the constant growth. Initially, you get a few floors to roam, a lame Overlook's hedge maze. Then the world blows up, sprawls, endlessly choking on its own trauma, and protrudes its entrails further, with shortcuts, pits to jump into, sights to see. Dilapidated backgrounds bathe in crispy lighting, the visuals are explicit and raw, overtly Satanic, with slick animations and stark enemy designs stimulating the ultra-violence. When the Curse meter rises, reality peels off with it. Walls bleed, dressers turn sacks of spasming meat. Oppressive ambience, unnerving giggles, hidden chests, and panic-inducing hallucinations ensue! Alas, you won't be as amused when the meter fills. A massive chunk of Curse Rot damage suddenly hitting my face during an odd fight was the main cause of my strokes.Panting, you scour around the mansion and its outskirts like a mouse, appearing from behind wardrobes and disappearing in mirrors. A bottom-feeder's min-max involves more than leaving a tart for later. The early power creep lies in discovering blood altars and travel points, slotting your item wheels with explosives along the way. Bring people's organs to blood altars to remember valuable items, build your permanent arsenal step by step. Death takes all that is forgotten, so embrace the "use it or lose it" mindset for resources and consumables. And there's no reason to grind. The game is separated into 4 chapters with progressively better loot in corpses and furniture. When you uncover most fast-travel mirrors, death recovery takes mere minutes. As long as you're running somewhere terrible, you make progress. I think running is better than the local stealth system. You can crouch under a table, but I only used it to evade shots and charges. Let the bodies hit the floor. Everyone's mortal, lootable, and the killing feels great! Granted, combat tends to go out of hand. One moment I'm on my merry way when, in a second, my army of knight armour and human-sized dolls gets incinerated by an SS flamethrower hulk.Next time, holding a Bible and a scythe, blindfolded, you pump a Byzantine titan full of paralytic agent. An axeman curses you in Greek while a witch of Salem giggles in the corner. Toss a grenade, slash her face, shotgun the Greek. Swap to the camera! Flash a ghost, run, get jumped by a nurse with a necrosis needle, roll, fireball, run outta the room to get sandwiched between a stone eye and a body bag slug! Still can't wake up. But can bulk up! WR's wide array of customisation options begins in its progression system. To level up your stats, initially, you offer organs to a witch. Or should you use a machine to harden your body with organ grease instead? Later, infuse yourself with ancient blood you found on a dusty skeleton, why not? It's more simple than it looks. The system constantly shifts like a dream, but it's intuitive and impactful. The stats should be familiar to everyone. Vigour, poise, resistances, curse tolerance, luck, perception, that useless inner light, and more... there’s room for self-expression. I went full-luck procs with a drop of vampirism, effortlessly facetanking all enemies and bosses by the end.I had to get crafty to make it work in NG+, but the level reset is free, you see. Consider this: the "rebirth" involves tearing off Nightingale flesh chunk by chunk, then reattaching it for whichever build you desire. Meanwhile, without any such requirements, the agreeable gear system provides a lion's share of your stats and important transformational effects. There's a heap of swords and whips to try on almost a hundred enemy types, each sporting a set of cheeky moves imbued with status effects. But you're spoiled for counters. Choose your synergetic dresses and rings with care, fashionably swapping outfits according to the situation at hand. Cursed or not, it's still a dream, so your drips can be as outrageous as you want. WR is pregnant with gunslinger hats, golden armour, and vampire tuxedos. It even has... 2 guns. But it's a classic combo - a revolver and a pump-action. Stab or pump, you have to be quick, aim accurately, and self-bandage timely. Staying lucid to pepper the crowd with acid jars and fireworks in-between. What else? The puzzles are clever.Withering Rooms is obviously the fruit of many sleepless nights. I was bewitched and couldn't play anything else. Not until I was done enjoying melting every face available, exhausting every dialogue option with those I couldn't melt. I took their plights personally, which is a testament to the abnormal writing of this game. The visuals you can see, but that part is the jack in the box I can't convey without spoilers. I would never list to you all the intricacies forming this spectacular danse macabre anyway. In my case, it effortlessly eclipsed all competition for 2 weeks. Upon completion, I went for the NG+. Hard as nails, with a dress made of star meat and a sparkly sword, it was so different! I still prefer ending C, though. You may think differently, but you'll get involved to your ears. Because Withering Rooms is thoughtful, polished, well-balanced. It's mad as a Hatter and it's a barrel o' fun.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Under-rated gem, appreciated by those who love to dig for a deep dark challenge.Withing Rooms =75% Dark Souls levelling system, weapons, armour, and general difficulty15% Silent Hill designed enemies, atmosphere and art direction10% Castlevania music, sound effects, and 2D level design100% AwesomeSauce. Positives: + The story was easy to follow and interesting, original, game has multiple endings+ Grand sense of exploration and wonder.  Playing at 3am in the dark, absolutely lost in a forest with zombie horses and bloody body bags chasing you when you have a sliver of life, never felt so tense and good.+ Sound effects are creepy and on point.  From the clanging crystal sounds of the outdoor cage area to the general creepy sounds when you are cursed status gave me goosebumps + The music is haunting and beautiful, eerie piano playing throughout, weird smooth jazz, unfitting drum and bass, always fresh and original+ There are 89 monsters in the game, and the game was constantly introducing new creeps during my whole 20 hours of playing. Nothing ever felt stale. The enemies are superbly designed, gorey, gooey, slimy, spiky, disgusting and morbid this game has it all.+ A plethora of different builds and hundreds of items and ways to outfit your character. My build was built on poise and violence, heavy attacks with with bloody pipe with a heavy gold suit of armour.+ A plethora of interesting morbid characters to meet with an abundance of fun side quests+ Secrets aplentyNegatives:- Some quests in the first half of the game are not explained too well, the directions are not 100% clear. I managed to get through by exploring every nook and cranny of the entire play area.  The game is fun though, so I didn't mind. Some people might get frustrated.- Might be too difficult for some players. You have to upgrade your character properly and stick with a certain build or you will become lunch meat quick.- The combat could be a little more interesting, with more moves such as jumping, sliding, etcI obtained all 54 achievements and would still play more if my backlog wasn't so huge. Lets hope for a sequel Withering Rooms 2 soon!9.5 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect in almost every respect. This isn't something I can remember ever saying about any other game within my memory. Maybe something like Okami? If you like video games, if you like survival horror, if you hate randomization and want to see an example of it being done perfectly, this is the right game for your dollar. I said 'almost every respect', so before I gush about this game,  I'll say up front what isn't perfect. Some of the balancing for melee combat seems to be poorly thought out, there are some optimization problems (no way should I be experiencing framerate drops on a 3080 and I9), and some of the environmental traps, particularly portraits that cast silence spells and wall spears in the labyrinth, are hard to see/impossible to do anything but duck and walk past. It can also be mildly demoralizing to clear Mostyn and the grounds of monsters, only to die and have to do it all over again. But that's just the nature of a roguelike, and it always starts to be fun again when you get into it. That's all I have for negatives. Let's get to the gushing.Withering Rooms is an action-heavy semi-roguelite survival horror adventure game. You play as Nightingale, a 15-year old girl who finds herself within the confines and grounds of Mostyn House, a traditional spooky Welsh manor. If you die in your explorations, the house's rooms reset themselves and you wake up on a different night. That's the basic gist of the gameplay, and I wouldn't want to say anything more that would run the risk of ruining the fun of finding out what's actually going on or the fascinating rules of the bizarre setting, or of meeting the strange and almost uniformly endearing residents of the house. It's got both the air of a Silent Hill, with odd people saying odd things in an off-putting way, and the classically British concept of a great country house full of eccentric characters. They're kind of all pretty horrible, including Nightingale herself, but when I think back, I can't remember one of them I don't think of fondly. As you learn more about what Mostyn house is and what's happening there, you'll come to understand how all of the characters came to be how they are, and to do the cruel and horrible things they've done.There are a variety of gameplay paths. Melee is apparently doable but very difficult. Magic and later on guns are easy mode, but come with the restrictions of limited ammunition and, for magic, the accumulation of curse damage. I haven't tried stealth, but it's also an option. There's a new game+ mode (which I've just begun as of writing) which apparently offers further challenges. There are many (tasteful, Nightingale is 15) costume options, so if you're into playing dress-up, that's very much an option. I found a classy black dress and hat and stuck with it, but I'm sure a lot of you will be into experimenting. What I'm saying is that you'll never be railroaded, bored, or forced to do something you find boring or unpleasant.Withering Rooms is full of more subtle and loving references to the survival horror genre than I could list, as well as survival horror-adjacent adventure game outliers like Harvester, to which there's also some clear homage. But that shouldn't suggest it's derivative. The story and setting are unique and imaginative, 'Lovecraftian' without the boring cliches that usually come with that appellation, and it kept me interested in the nature of the setting and narrative right up until the somewhat shocking ending. Somewhat shockingly, it's even got some clearly-articulated and non-invasive 'progressive social commentary', if you're into that kind of thing. And they didn't even need a consultancy firm. The soundtrack is also incredible, and it's notable that the game is unafraid to use silence/ambience when needed, in common with its survival horror influences. I think the soundtrack was mostly composed by the developer, although feel free to correct me if I'm wrong. If they released it on vinyl I would buy it.This is the kind of game that keeps me from being demoralized with games. I've basically stopped playing AAA games developed in any Western country, and it's great that labors of love like Withering Rooms are still being made by talented, dedicated auteurs who want to do more than just foist a corporate agenda on what they see as a mass of bovine consumers with no thoughts or opinions, nor any right to have them. Withering Rooms respects you, it respects your time, and most importantly, it both loves and respects video games. And isn't that what we all want?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a real hidden gem.A friend has gifted me this game ages ago and it sat in the backlog for a while, and seeing "action roguelike" and "procedural generation" I was kinda turned off and only gave it a try thinking I'll play it for an evening and remove from the backlog forever. I was hooked 20 minutes later after the prologue.The worldbuilidng is really interesting and goes deeper and deeper with fresh ideas and plot-twists, and even ng+ has some new story in it.Mechanics-wise game is also quite unique and it didn't feel like a roguelike to me tbh. There's a set world which you open up gradually, and once you reach a "checkpoint" - that's it, you can return there at any moment, so the progression does not reset with death really. Same with items - some are just stuck with you forever after you get them, and some you can just "remember", so they also stay after death. So after maybe the first hour of exploring the game you can make a build, which stays with you after death.The music is also great! Although sometimes the placing is really weird - like, my favourite track in the game is just in one transition screen which you pass by like 2 times in the whole game. You exit the screen - music's over. Weird, but I'm still happy it was there.So yeah, highly recommend if you like unique experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Withering Rooms is a massive hidden gem. It very clearly had a ton of passion and thought put into it, and I played nonstop till I reached 100%. It's a love letter to classic PS2 survival horror without the jank that's usually associated with the genre. There is a truly STAGGERING amount of content and replayability, The amount and variety of new areas, new mechanics, new enemies, and secrets constantly drip fed throughout the game had my jaw on the floor.The music is great, the tone is great, the horror is very effective, it's full of charm, and there's an awesome feeling of progression as you work your way up from slinking around hiding from monsters, to becoming a proficient killing machine. The puzzles are super clever and challenging without being obtuse.The story also deserves to be highlighted. I have not seen a ton of roguelike/roguelite games with a great story, but Withering Rooms' story really blew me away. A genuinely very creative concept with so much mystery, and an impressive level of internal consistency within its universe. The magical/supernatural aspects are explored and explained in lots of depth, and with very little use of Macguffins or "don't think about it too hard it's magic." If you like piecing together lore from various notes and dialogue, you'll love it.It's not for everyone as combat is relatively simple, so if you expect Souls or Devil May Cry, it might not be for you (though there is a surprising amount of versatility for different builds!) but if you're a fan of classic survival horror games like Clock Tower or Rule of Rose, I can't recommend it highly enough. One of the best indie games I've played, and it's still only in early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This one's a sleeper. A good slow burn.The combat is clunky - that's OK. It's intentional. Like how tank controls were back in the PSX era of survival Horror. It adds to the sense of panic you should rightly be feeling when you get caught off guard. Indeed, this is more a game about careful preparation, of turning the tides in your favor before you make the first move.The atmosphere is thick, the music is aces, the vibe is immaculate.If you like survival horror, you will enjoy this little gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially torrented the game thinking I'd play a bit, get bored, and uninstall. I LOVED IT. I bought the game and binged it. Even having beaten it I still think about the game and want more. It's a wonderful game. I've seen some reviews or discussion about it being too hard, and I totally disagree. Play like a coward and make use of all your tools and you'll be fine. By the end of my game, going into NG+, I hadn't died. I got close though. I'd also recommend specializing or picking at most two damage types to focus on. I went with high poise, melee centric with some magic investment. I initially was disappointed in it, but the steel pipe was my excalibur. If you're going for a bleed or backstab build I'd recommend the knife with attack speed. One other criticism I saw was that dying was too consequential. I don't think so at all, just make sure you're keeping your best, non-consumable gear, and grind using the coffins. Heck, there's a couple npcs that gather materials for you even if you've cleared the night.Anyway, the music, atmosphere, mechanics, and setting are amazing. I wish the best for the devs

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface this by saying that I ALMOST skipped over this game by thinking it's just another horror sneaking indie game. And while it is, it's SO much more than that.Withering Rooms is a game that's insane in scope for something made by a single developer. My first playthrough clocked in at about 18 hours (the Steam playtime may be shorter on my profile because the demo let me carry on my progress), but there's New Game Plus to go with a new quest and ending. It's a game that just keeps getting bigger and bigger and bigger - The map ends up being massive with unique locations and around 90 unique enemies and a few bosses. Gameplay-wise, the game lets you customize your playstyle a lot - while the core combat basics can be described as Souls-like adjacant, overall I wouldn't say this game fits that category. Between ranged weapons, magic that relies on the Curse meter as some sort of anti-mana and a non-unified character progression, it breaks out from the confines of the Souls systems and I say this positively as a huge fan of these games. I've beaten it as a mellee build which is completely viable (if a bit janky), but my experimentation has led me to believe there is a lot to try out there. Summon armors to help you, throw every status at your enemies, gun them down, throw bombs at them and so on. There's a lot of options. And don't get turned off by the "roguelike" tag either - while it has elements of it, dying does reset the map but you get to keep a GOOD chunk of your items (this is part of progression and by the end of the game this can hit 30 items or so) and your story progress doesn't reset.Story-wise, it took a few interesting turns here and there and my only complaint would be that with so many characters it can be hard to keep track of who's even important and the lack of voice-acting does make the character stand out less but I still enjoyed it and considered the three basic ending options for a bit so I did give a damn in the end.The game IS a bit janky though, but I had no crashes or big slowdowns short of one or two areas and my computer is mid-range of now. Overall, if this game seems interesting in the slightest to you - try the demo out. This is an easy recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: From the trailer I thought: "Man, this game looks like Clock Tower meets Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Dark Souls"From playing the game I thought: "Man, this game plays like Clock Tower meets Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Dark Souls"I feel in love instantly, because growing up as a kid the kind of games I loved were Horror, Survival Horror and Action Adventure games, Those are all games that I loved with a passion. If they had some Rule of Rose or Haunting Ground twist in there I'd be playing a game that I wish I created!

_childDocuments_.review: Lovecraft + resident evil + roguelike + general weirdness = a great time.  Imagine Silent Hill 2, Bloodborne, Salt and Sanctuary, Resident Evil 1 and Binding of Isaac had an unholy baby and you get Withering Rooms.  It's as unique and bizarre as it sounds.This game has a great feel, weird stuff happens, becoming cursed leads to more weirdness, you have to explore and work things out for yourself.  The walls dripping with blood isn't even close to the weirdness you'll see in the first hour of play.  It's a lot of fun.The only fault is that the music is sometimes completely at odds with the visuals.edit: Don't be afraid to die.  Don't be afraid to engage in combat.  Both are how you become stronger, both are necessary, both are integral to the story of the game.  I made the mistake of trying to avoid dying and combat and it leads to frustration.  Embrace both, then grind up the organs of NPCs and grease yourself up!

_childDocuments_.review: Back in the day I would often find Bullfrog, Westwood Studios and Sierra Entertainment titles in the bargain bin at Toys R Us. They were cheap and ran on my crappy PC, but they were also really, really high quality games. Space Quest 6, Little Big Adventure, Dungeon Keeper, Theme Hospital, Syndicate, etc. these were games that steadily grew in popularity over time, mostly because of how deeply they influenced other titles and developers. Withering Rooms is one such game.There are a lot of indie rogue-likes out there, and more than enough 'Metroidvania' titles, but not many of them have a distinct 3D look to them. I've played through a lot of Dead Cells and Axiom Verge, gander at some of the more recent Metroidvania style games...they are either highly-tuned, 2D games...or throwback pixel art. The setting of a lot of Metroidvania titles also seem to flip-flop between Sci-Fi / Fantasy and dungeon-exploring horror. I'm not complaining, but what made Symphony of the Night and Super Metroid all-time great games was really their art direction and sound design. Withering Rooms has an impeccable sense of both and this is what makes the game stand out.The enemies and characters feel like a cross between clay animation and puppetry; enemy models have a menacing presence, but also a snapping peculiarity that makes every encounter just a little bit more 'odd' as well as typically scary. The early industrial setting of Withering Rooms is probably its main draw: the firearms and jury-rigged projectiles ensure you're never overwhelmingly comfortable fighting enemies. The melee combat is 'souls-like' in its variety and 'weighty' action. The interiors and backgrounds of the game are drab, gothic and gruesome but, once I got far enough into the game I was surprised to see some scenes with levity. I've never played a game I would consider a great example of 'folk horror' until this one.The sound effects and the soundtrack, without question, are the best I've heard in years. Metal Hellsinger, a Sonic game...a bunch of JRPG remixes? All that music nominated for the Steam Awards in 2022 was good, but they absolutely were not novel. The music of Withering Rooms occupies a special zone between a joyful haunted house and a György Ligeti piece; it's completely one-of-a-kind.I can't recommend this title enough and I can't wait for more 'nodes' and areas to be added. Withering Rooms is certainly an occult classic of gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: A very well-crafted and excellent horror souls-esque game!You would like this if you happen to enjoy Souls-likes, have an appreciation for survival-horror classics and most of all have enjoyed Silent Hill way back in the day.This is essentially a 2.5D Souls-like with rogue-lite elements, each iteration of your gameplay is a sequence of a dream, when you die, you wake up in your bed at the start of the dream with the layout of the estate generated slightly different. Upon your death, you do in fact lose most everything that isn't marked permanent, with those few items remaining that you've chosen to make permanent by "remembering" it, for your next dream. While this may seem too punishing at first, you'll quickly find yourself becoming more comfortable with the game's style and mechanics, to the point that awakening in a new dream is more of a convenient boon than a hindrance.The horror elements are properly disturbing and spooky, the setting, writing and atmosphere are very compelling. The combat, while a bit clunky, feels good to master especially with a proper build. The levels don't drag on, there are dozens of armor/weapons for different builds, dozens of items/consumables as well as a very welcome variety of enemies with a proper bestiary, with four possible endings to cap it off.I would VERY highly recommend this game if any of the aforementioned at all has appealed to you, press on and you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is being slept on. You play as Nightingale, a girl with kyphosis who is stuck inside a dream. Go play the demo (it's free). The LORE, dialogues and setting are unironically really interesting and keeps me wanting to learn more. The combat is pretty much like a 2D souls game, with metroidvania exploration. Just like souls games, the LORE explains why you wake again when you die, and dying has consequences. Thankfully the game gives you a lot of options to mitigate dying and make it less painful.The game offers an insane amount of different types of armors and weapons for clinically insane fashion-souls enjoyers. Your character can look anywhere between a silent hill nurse and a f*ing hobo, nobody can judge you inside the dream.My only complaint was that it was getting too easy by chapter 4, but then I found a secret ultra hard mode that introduces a nemesis-like enemy and I'm back in love with it.So yeah it's gud play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I can safely say that this game is one of the best Indie projects on the platform and easily deserves to be recognized among the greats of the horror genre. But don't worry, when you die you still keep your levels, upgrades, and any items that are "permanent" or "remembered" after making an offering to a shrine. From the fantastically written side cast to the page turning story, this is genuinely something i could see replaying to get all the content and different endings available. Is this game good? Frankly no, it's a masterpiece. Buy it now and support this dev, they are dedicated to delivering the best experience possible and very active in the community. With the imminent release into 1.0 I hope for a successful launch and look forward to the devs next project, whatever it may be.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm massively impressed. In a sea of derivative and generic haunted house horror games  this really stands out. It cherry-picks mechanics from old classic survival horror games Clock Tower, Fatal Frame, Silent Hill and Eternal Darkness and blends them all together in  a truly striking manner.  It's alive, unique , very atmospheric, delightfully creepy, truly beautiful to look at and wonderfully written.  A tale of a dream that's a place, of witches and vengeful undead that plays out almost like a puzzle box as all truly great locations in survival horror games do. Not since the original Resident evil game have I encountered such an expertly and intricately crafted venue for such shenanagins.   The 2.5D graphics are really well done , with some truly impressive flourishes and the soundtrack is superb: It starts with some fantastically morbid baroque music and  then quickly slides into the darkly psychedelic.  The game mechanics are clear, simple but create a world of possibility, strategy and possible solutions for any given problem.  When you add the semi rogue-like , almost bloodborne-esque death mechanics and the procedurally generated maps that create an ever shifting play area, not to mention the excellent bestiary it makes for a truly unique experience. The puzzle mechanics  are just right, the story is very interesting and for several other reasons "Withering Rooms" reminds me of my time in Yharnam. The controls are fluid, responsive and both the hiding and combat are very smooth and well done.  All in all an absolutely stunning piece of work and nothing that I've seen so far would even suggest that this game is actually in early access. There's a talented team here, whose future games I will follow with great interest as I don't think that it's overkill to say that this is pretty much, for my tastes, the best horror game you can buy on steam right now. The price is criminally low too. If you like intelligent horror games, then you are almost assured to enjoy this. I normally don't review a game until I've spent more time  with it, but I am just so knocked out by this that my enthusiasm forced me to break my rule. Destined for greatness.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I Beat it a few weeks ago. I still think about this game regularly. Definitely going to be in my top 3 games of the year.  If you're interest AT ALL, just get it.Sometimes when I play a game I think “Do I  actually like this?” 95% of the time I have to ask myself that question, I end up realizing I don’t like the game and I’m trying too hard to like it. This games was a very rare 5% where I ended up liking… no… loving it.The reason why I originally didn’t know if I liked this game is because it has a pretty fair amount of clunk to its combat. I absolutely hate clunky combat. However, for some very strange reason, I actually like it in the game. As another steam review I saw brought up, overcoming the clunky combat is actually somehow enjoyable. I don’t get it, but it’s somehow true. It’s the thing that originally made me almost stop playing, but then I stuck with it and like it a lot. I don’t think that’s ever happened to me before with combat in a game. Really weird.Also this game has very “meh” animations. That being said, this game is made by 1 guy. For being made by 1 guy it’s absolutely insane. There’s like over 90 enemies with multiple attacks and a bunch of other NPC’s. So this can be more than forgiven.Outside of the gripes above, I LOVE everything else about this game so far. The story is very interesting , the characters have great depth, it’s scary, the enemies have great character design, the music is great, the atmosphere is on point, it has great ideas that it executes well, it keeps slowly feeding you new interesting mechanics and concepts, and it’s sense of discovery and progression is awesome. Best of all, the game is simply very unique. I really haven’t played anything quite like it, and it’s when games like this come along I remember why I love video games. It’s awesome that there are these people out there still driven to take big chances and make unique experiences and pour their heart into it (like this developer clearly has).Anyways, I just beat Chapter 1 and I was going to wait to review this game until I beat it, but I want to review it now as it deserves more positive reviews and it’s very under appreciated.If you like the look of what you see on the store page, just buy it. Support developers that actually make complete and unique experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Real hidden gem here. Good exploration with a lot of surprises, fun resource management, and surviving is tense and has stakes. The game's central "curse" mechanic is really cool and has a lot of visual effects on the environment. The story is more interesting than I expected and the writing has strong character. Combat's janky, but the game doesn't expect you to be perfect and you are allowed to die on boss fights without losing your items, so it's alright. I do think there's a bit of missed opportunity in the survival mechanics (the game gives you a lot of options to distract or avoid enemies, but I felt it was less work and more profitable to just kill them), but it's nice that the game doesn't force you into one playstyle and those options are there if you want them.There's a lot more content than I expected with quite a few unique enemies and weapons/armor/spells meant for different builds. NG+ is also very substantial with a lot of changes and a new story goal. Just a really impressive work all around from a solo dev, glad I heard about this one.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since I've played a horror game that not only scratches that old school survival horror itch, but also does something truly unique with the format. A randomly generated, sidescrolling horror game that somehow doesn't feel hacked together OR needlessly repetitive? This game is a unicorn - a spooky, blood-soaked unicorn, covered in rags, ready to murder me.I'm not terribly far into the game, but I can tell there are plenty of interesting items and little secrets to find. I am discovering new weapons, enemies, and strategies at a pleasantly regular pace, and the creepy vibe has not worn off yet. These two factors indicate a strong understanding of what makes a good survival horror title work, and the influences of the dev are on full display here, which (I would assume) include games such as Clock Tower and Resident Evil.The presentation is quite good for an indie title - visually, the game has a cohesive look and feel, accompanied by a solid musical score with a surprising amount of variety. The creature designs are interesting, each with their own backstories, and reminiscent of enemies found in titles like Silent Hill and numerous other classics. The writing is also great - there are plenty of documents scattered around, as well as characters who have lots to say about where you are and what is going on. The story is, so far, interesting and notably well told (something that is sadly uncommon among other indie horror titles).The gameplay is in a good place right now, though I'd imagine there are many tweaks and new toys to implement. It's tough to make a survival horror game with this much combat, as you don't want the player to be too capable, nor do you want actually playing the game to feel like a chore. Preparation is the name of the game, rather than grinding levels. Withering Rooms strikes a nice balance, though I have to say that first boss battle was pretty rough. I'll chalk it up to my own skill, or lack thereof, for now.Last note: the game is in Early Access, and as such, expect some bugs here and there. I have discovered a few minor bugs on my own - nothing that reloading a save couldn't fix. There is a bug reporting function within the game, and the dev is active (and attentive!) on Discord. This is a big deal, and a huge positive mark. As long as we continue to see frequent updates, (which, based on what I've seen, I do not doubt that we will) this title is going to really shine once it hits version 1.0.Overall, I've been enjoying my time with Withering Rooms. I'm making steady progress, the thrill of discovery is still present, and I'm genuinely having a great time getting spooked by the various horrible creatures within. TLDR: As a horror fan, this is  worth a buy, as long as you are okay with a few bugs here and there during the EA period. The look and feel are top notch, and the concept is a winner, and something truly unique in the survival horror space.EDIT: I am taking a break from this game and am (anxiously) awaiting its final release so that I may dive in for a totally fresh playthrough with all finished content added. I am confident it will be worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: After 19.8 hours I finished my first playthrough of Withering Rooms.Let me tell you right now, I will play New Game+ (something which I rarely do) and thus you probably already guessed: This Game gets a recommend from me.Withering Room is a 2.5D Roguelike/Roguelite (it has both Elements) Dark Souls inspired (I know, we all can't hear it anymore) Horror Game.The Game is not scary but it has a great creepy and eerie atmosphere.Basically when you die, you just re-awaken, the map layout gets randomized (even though there are a few fixed points), you can find a few items that are permanent as soon as you find them (some key items and armor for example) and some items you have to find again, except when you found a shrine (which you can activate with materials) and then you can choose a few items that stay with you permanently.Let me just ramble a little bit here.The Voice Acting in the beginning for a few monsters was actually kind of bad but after a while it grew on me.This is a thread for this Game, many things grew on me.Graphically at first I thought it doesn't look great but definitely decent, apparently it didn't run well on Ultra (optimization issue) so I had to turn it down to high. Don't know if there really was a difference.The Animations were also not that great but it did the job.Also the Combat felt kind of clunky. Enemies don't telegraph their attacks well, they turn way too fast and they have extreme tracking (they predict your input I think).I did a complete Melee Run, at first it was way too hard and clunky (but it gets better, even though it is kind of repetitive and stupid; you just either mash your Attack Button or Hold it for a Heavy Attack, that's it) and the dodging didn't feel that good.That all sounds kind of mediocre but let's get to the good stuff.First off, Sound Design was really good.The Music I didn't care for at first, then sometimes it felt kind of out of place (too modern in places) but it also grew on me and I could really appreciate it. It was fitting most of the time and some tracks even stuck in my head.There is a ton of enemy variety in this Game which kept it kinda fresh, even though (at least with my build) it was just running up to them and hitting Attack.(I had a vampirism melee build with a pipe, so I just facetanked everything.)What this Game does really well is the feeling of progression and it became kind of addicting with a good gameplay loop.In the beginning I was a bit frustrated because 9 1/2 hours in I just had one death and then a very long run and then it happened. I had soooo much stuff and lost it all. BUT I learned that you get items back really quick and you become kind of strong the longer you play.Overall I died 10 times in my first playthrough, MOST of the time it was my fault because I got overconfident or went unprepared because I couldn't bother to stock up on Healing Items, but there were also a few cheap moments.The puzzles were pretty easy and the combat challenges also became quite easy the further you get.Still for my first playthrough I had already quite a bit of fun.So yeah, Credits rolled (not even a minute, so yeah, kudos to a very small team apparently) and it puts you right into NG+.Later on I will jump back in again and do at least 1 or 2 more endings before I lay Withering Room to rest.Still, very surprising Game that probably will grow on you...Addendum: 35.9 hours and I had to 100% the Game. Yes, it's that good. Be warned, one Ending can be a little tough to get. But this flew kind of under the Radar, I want more people to play this!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know where this game came from but I'm glad I found it, because it would have been an absolute tragedy to miss out on what has been one of the best games of the year. It's a real hidden gem.Withering Rooms is a finely-crafted, rogue-lightish, sometimes spooky, sometimes strange, brain-scrambler with well-made characters and weirdness that comes out in droves. You know you're having a good time when the walls start bleeding.The gameplay is a challenging and addictive 2D action RPG with multiple avenues of advancement, and it strikes a good balance between hammering the player and also letting them grow and course-correct. Player dies. Items get lost. Player recovers. Player tweaks skills to finally overcome that shrieky, squealy, dripping, bloody baghead monster the next time they encounter it. Eventually, you can min-max yourself into an unkillable 15-year-old death machine.Add on top of this the multiple endings, a new game+ with new surprises, and countless ways to customize your ever-growing arsenal of powers, and you have a game with some of the best replay value in its genre. It'll definitely keep you busy for a while, and it was never boring to start a new run for another ending.The sound music is also on another level compared to most games. A huge amount of care went into composition and placement, and there is nothing but quality everywhere you listen.I'm not sure what the dev is doing right now, but I really hope it's making another game. Definitely pick this one up... it'll hypnotize you.

_childDocuments_.review: クロックタワーよりブラッドボーンに近いです。1周クリア後でも新しいコンテンツが多い。 I rarely give games glowing reviews. This game stands out, a lot. It's not just "Clock Tower". I'd say it's maybe 30% unique/new, 50% Bloodborne, 10% Dark Souls, 4% Resident Evil 1, 3% Clock Tower 1/2, 2% Silent Hill 2, 1% Fatal Frame. It doesn't feel like an indie game (quality and content-wise). I honestly didn't expect to be this impressed. Best game I've seen/played in the last few years.It's probably the closest we'll ever get to a GOOD new Bloodborne (or Clock Tower). Withering Rooms >>>>> any new Silent Hill/Resident Evil/Sony remake. Many people seem to look at this and assume it's only Clock Tower with no combat. It's so much more than that.The game was completeable from day 1 of Early Access, but over the past few years the dev has continued to add tons of new areas, content and adjustments for FREE (I know people like to hear that word).Haven't played recently b/c busy, but I always intend to play more. My 44 hours doesn't include the new stuff added in the past year.Found this game while searching for interesting stuff on Steam, during an indie fest around early 2023 or late 2022? Had it on wishlist and saw it released as Early Access. I was hesitant to buy it, because there are so many similar-looking games that are uninspired clones of something else. Wasn't sure if I'd like it. But the customer reviews made it sound unique and well-designed, so I gave it a try.It's actually . I can't emphasize this enough.I thought it'd be similar to Neverending Nightmares, but it's very different. Imagine Clock Tower 1 with heavy Bloodborne influence, and hints of Resident Evil 1, Silent Hill and Fatal Frame. The combat is like 2d Dark Souls. For those worried about difficulty, you can choose between default and "narrative".Note that I only mention the above games to give a clearer idea of what Withering Rooms is similar to. It stands on its own as a fresh, unique and very well-designed experience.- Lots of weapons, consumables, magic, equipment, abilities. Lots to experiment with.- Stat levelling system that you can allocate points to increase survival, resistance and even speed of all character motion.- Weapons have different stats and different attack animations. There are stealth options, so you can play that way, if you want. There are also shields.Combat may feel a little clunky at first, but it's satisfying to master. The dev has repeatedly made it easier and more responsive. It's not a full-on action game, but there are encounters with multiple monsters. Just don't expect to overpower them easily. Survival is priority. Stockpiling consumables and equipment makes it easier to survive. A good run goes a long way.Everything seems very well-designed and thought-out. You can recycle everything into something useful. There are systems in place for everything scenario.If you die, you lose items on you that aren't currently "saved". As you progress, you unlock ways to overcome this. The location of non-essential rooms and their contents also get shuffled/randomized. But There are also progression elements that carry over even if you die, so you won't feel like you're stuck and not progressing.Art direction seems really good. I haven't had a single problem with the art. Very atmospheric.  Movement and animation seem perfectly fine. Feels weighty and satisfying. Most modern games can't even get that right nowadays.Sound effects are crisp, clear and very atmospheric. Music is REALLY good. Most recent game soundtracks are too ambient and boring, but this game's BGM is really great.I often get irritated/depressed at how most recent games/films/etc often fail at so many basic aspects of art, sound/game design, etc. But this game seems really well-made. I say this as a 2d/3d artist/animator myself. I'm very fussy about quality.You know how everyone complains that RE7 only has 1 enemy and Callisto Protocol has around 3? This game has 30-40+ unique enemies, with different abilities, patterns, etc. Not exaggerating. I was shocked at how many unique enemies there are. Lots of bosses, too.Lots of interesting, quirky characters, both allies and enemies. They all seem to have their own interests and ambitions. Like the Souls series, their affiliation may change throughout the game.The writing doesn't feel annoying at all. Unlike most fictional media nowadays, it doesn't try to lecture or educate you on how ignorant you are. Conversations aren't fully voiced, but there are voices here and there. The voice acting seems mostly fine and natural, which is also VERY RARE for English games/localizations.There's tons and tons of lore. The world is really fleshed out in detail. The best part is it barely interferes with the gameplay or pacing, much like the Souls games. You can simply not choose the extra talk options, or not read the documents you pick up. Despite this, you can still feel the atmosphere and weight of the situation at hand.I want to say it's very "immersive", but I feel like that's an overused term now.It's way longer than I expected. Whenever I thought I was getting close to the end (as you'd expect from a relatively cheap, small indie title), the world kept opening up. This was before the dev added way more content, too.Back before tons of content was added, my first playthrough was  There are multiple endings and even some choices that may make a significant difference to the world/characters. Also New Game+, which unlocks even more completely new content!!Nothing major. I ran into a few bugs and had a few other concerns/criticisms, but they were all promptly fixed. The only thing I can really complain about is how you can sometimes go through doors or interact with the background by accident while trying to do something else. But if you're extra careful, this probably won't happen.Stuff that already got fixed:- Rebalanced/adjusted combat/controls (many times).- Item sets, categories, shortcut wheel, etc to help streamline menu navigation.- Enemies can enter rooms as you exit, which can look a little janky. This was adjusted so that they enter/exit much more quickly.- Outfits are now separated into mix'n'match parts instead of full-body sets.- Lots of bugs, and more.Very highly recommended. Best game I've played in the past few years. This and Alisa are probably the only recent survival horror games I liked. I'd personally love to see more games like this, maybe with 3d gameplay.Lately I've been thinking about why I feel this game is much better than Elden Ring:- Unique, fresh experience. ER felt too much like Souls.- Much better game design than ER. Everything is recyclable, so you always have incentive to keep exploring.- Doesn't have upgrade systems locked to the same locations like ER does, meaning more freedom.- Huge amount of content that possibly rivals ER. There are SO MANY unique enemies.- NG+ is very different. Many people don't feel motivated to play ER more than once.- Way better music and sound design.- More interesting setting, lore and maybe NPCs. FromSoft games tend to be vague with the lore on purpose (which is fine). But they tend to use the same concepts/setup for every game, similar to the Dark Pictures Anthology devs. This game is a breath of fresh air away from that.

_childDocuments_.review: Concept: A Souls-esque side-scrolling metroidvania inside a cursed dream full of blood and metaphors.Execution: It looks and plays like a bad Flash game, with floaty controls, bizarre hitboxes and none of the precision needed for Souls-esque gameplay to work. Additionally, it feels like most mechanics were cobbled together by two or three people without asking each other how they should function.For instance, magic requires that you craft scrolls, fine. But it ALSO requires mana. And mana ALSO makes you melt when you spend too much of it, but you also need to be in the "not melting, but very low mana"-zone to progress in certain areas, but tiny black blobs on the floor, poorly-defined AoE effects, many spells, some trivial activities(like dodge rolling if you're wearnig the wrong item, or running, similarly), can also affect it. But relatively early in the game you have access to items that slowly tick your mana up and down, so keeping it in that "good zone" is a tiresome chore. Truly a wretched mechanic.I could probably have forgiven stuff like that and completely ignored the magic if the combat was good but the combat is... a floaty, trashy mess? Enemy swings will sometimes stunlock you because their hitboxes are big enough to score multiple hits, while also dragging you around, sometimes you can roll through enemies when they attack, sometimes you can't, sometimes pressing a movement key immediately after rolling makes you roll again instead of turning you around, there are invisible Poise bars regulating knockdowns and stun states. Thrown weapons and spells have unclear ranges that you can only find out by spending your very limited ammo.The soulslike mechanic of restarting after you die is also just... intensely dull. I'd rather just have been able to save the game, because all it amounts to is asking me to waste more time because it deletes your entire inventory except for a few "remembered" items. No enemies or items are randomized each time, so it is LITERALLY doing the same thing over and over again, the most mindless, soulless grindy experience imaginable.I think the way to make Withering Rooms good would be a combination of tossing the entire Soulslike idea out of the window, into the bin it goes, it's garbage, adds nothing to the game, and tightening up the combat mechanics. Especially in their current incarnation they completely implode when it's more than a 1v1 fight, especially if you have summons, since some enemies and summons appear unable to attack each other, but try anyway, locking them into permanent loops, enemies sometimes block each others' attacks, etc. and multiple enemies can often stunlock you unavoidably. In some places it appears intended to split enemies up and drag them apart, but in some areas enemies are locked into their room and refuse to leave it, so it's not always viable. It's also a "1D" fighter, in that there's only left and right, no up and down, no platforms, no jumping, nothing, to add a bit more spice to things.The tiny percentage changes to stats from armor and helmets(you can wear one of each, but for some reason they have less of an effect, individually, than rings that you can wear four of), should also be modified because it's extremely dull to find a new suit of armor and "oh boy, it's +1% to Scrungliness."It also seems to imply that there's an option for a ranged build, but having gotten about halfway through the game before getting bored of it, I've yet to find any ranged weapons except for truly wretched and pointless throwing knives, and one-use throwables. Seems like a trap option.I would rather be locked up in a REAL sanatorium for dying cholera patients than play this game more.

_childDocuments_.review: The game makes a lot of hay about all these girls sent to an asylum for misbehaving but once they're there and introduced to a wondrous dream where they can't die and magic is real they almost all decide to become psychotic witches and start murdering people. Whatever misbehavior was an old school euphemism for, I suspect people were right to send girls to an asylum for that.Also the back half of the game is absolutely bloated and drawn out with enemies with equally bloated stats but you can always leg it to a merchant and will always have enough money to restock medkits and consumables so it just feels like the soulless ARPG drudgery of shooting at a big fat health bar and mashing the health potion button whenever you get wrecked all just lasting WAY too long. It's not like I have a tactic available to me to meaningfully mitigate damage anyway. Even the ones you could pretend worked would just draw the fight out longer and cost more than chomping medkits.And the roguelite part is a wash. It was supposed to make horror game pathing no longer a solved problem but now it's just an even longer, even more boring Dark Souls corpse run spread across an entire level collecting your old power back piecemeal before you can start killing again.Just to add one more thing: A lot of people are expecting Souls here but the game does not want to give you the Souls dodge. You CANNOT just mash attack and roll through enemy swings here. You aren't fast enough. The dev does not want you doing that for free (And this isn't a bad choice but it is a confounding one for several reviewers). You MUST use a resource or some other trick to try to dance like that, which means there is a hard limit to it. And for several reasons beyond just that, melee combat is not viable long term after around act 1.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 | Gripping story | Unique Experiences | A true hidden gem.Withering Rooms is one of the most incredible games I've ever experienced for an Indie Game. Imagine elements of Silent Hill, Souls-like game combat, blasphemous-like whilst all remaining tolerable, manageable & possible to defeat by ANY gamer despite the difficulty at times. The game features a variety of combat styles & progresses the further you delve into the game to which you can figure out your own "builds/preference styles" as you explore/unlock. Dying within this game you will lose "everything within reason" and have to restart with "nothing" however it isn't as bad at it seems I assure you. There is multiple ways to help aid these scenarios the more you play. The enemies are of a vast variety giving you plenty of different and unique experiences throughout your journey into Withering Rooms as well as boss fights with an option to respawn once you die in a boss fight WITHOUT restarting. The lore/exploration is nothing shy of phenomenal & the MASS variety of items, weapons, consumables & buffed items you can find is excellent. There's such a wide variety of just about everything to this game polishing it off to absolute perfection. Withering Rooms solidify's itself as a true 10/10 for me & to discover there is multiple ending options AND MORE content within NG+....this just blew my mind. The developer deserves SO much credit and respect. I cannot recommend this enough. Just don't expect it to be easy. It will challenge you.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible indie game by a single developer at a great price.  No need to wait for a discount.  If the genre tags look appealing but you are left wondering 'did this actually get properly stitched together?'  The answer is a resounding yes.  This is not a perfect 10/10 game but easily 8++ if the genres are appealing to you.  Every aspect (sound, atmosphere, gameplay, puzzles, story, challenge, etc) is well polished with none of the modern ubisoft-style hand holding inside an environment that urges you to continue exploring (carefully)... all while your expectations of the game's size and diversity continue to be eclipsed as you progress.Also big shout-out to the developers website (that can be found by googling the name of the game) -- it may as well be a proper wiki straight from the developer and even has hints available to progress the game (spoiler tag'd by default) if you get stuck. _childDocuments_.review: A Clock Tower-y rogue/survival horror style game set in a victorian era haunted mansion. Withering Rooms does a lot of things right. Graphically it looks very good, with the house being well detailed with distinctive paintings and furniture to the cholera zombies and ghosts infesting the grounds. There's a lot to look at. There is a significantly heavy use of grey in the palette, but you're not going into this for a sunny adventure, now are you?Sound is very important and you can keenly hear where enemies are walking in relation to you, which is quite helpful. Music is fitting and the voicework is also quite good.Now, it's worth mentioning this game is difficult. You can essentially level your character through offerings to a witch for small increases, although the offerings are at times gatekept by certain foes, so you'll need to think about how to invest in your character going forward. This can be tricky as you're not really privy to all the play options this game has at first. There is a 'narrative' mode which I've yet to try, but this is supposed to make it more playable/easier.This brings me to my only real complain about Withering Rooms and perhaps why it seems rather difficult. The combat is... not the best. While the creator does mention this is not Dark Souls and you have options to hide around many set pieces, your character is agonizingly slow to attack, dodge, or raise a shield. Combat control inputs just don't feel responsive at all. Almost every enemy is faster than you (when they feel like attacking, sometimes they just stand there absently at times during a battle) and you need to take them down for various coins/offering pieces. I felt like my character's defensive options were a bit underpowered because of the sluggishness and it didn't necessarily matter what I did. You get stuck in long attack swing animations frequently and I lacked meaningful options to play it smarter or safer, especially in the beginning when your gear options are poor or you're in the process of restocking after a failed prior game.You can get some one shot spells and items to help, but not all of them seem to be that useful. It's also worth noting that hiding isn't perfect- I'm not sure what the pattern is, but even outside of combat, sometimes enemies just inexplicably double back and suddenly know where to look for you. I have no idea why this is.As a reminder, like many rogue style games, the beginning of any playthrough from a previous run is often more monotonous than fun. Restocking items is a chore and without new gear to monkey around with, repeated starting runs can be less than enjoyable. You can 'Remember' several items from a previous run, but I usually had these to the ones I felt were always necessary/useful.Generally speaking, I've liked this title and it has some strong points, but the gameplay doesn't feel like it's where it needs to be yet outside of a general flow. I think if some of the sloggish pacing were eased up on, I'd feel a bit more positive about it. For now, it's got some definite strong facets, but there's some play elements I'm not 100% about. Still, it's at least worth trying and the developer is still tooling with it as of this writing. Hopefully, it will continue to improve.4/2/23 Edit: Actually, I'm going to kick in another complaint here. It's more apparent in the second act, but this game has annoying leaps of logic sometimes. I get that there's an inspiration from Silent Hill at play, but when you find lightbulbs in a tin can in that game, that's not something you want as a take away. Storywise, this hasn't been an issue, but there are some gameplay elements that are just baffling and unintuitive.For example, in the second act, you encounter bear traps on the ground. Obvious enough peril. But how to navigate dealing with them? Strike them with your weapon to set them off? Seems rational, but no. Alright, so the enemy in that room walks slowly and can go through them without harm. Makes sense you could do the same, right? Wrong. Turns out you're supposed to roll through them. Keep in mind, rolling does not protect you from damage whatsoever, if you don't equip a specific ring that curses you for invincibility frames. But here and without the ring? That's the solution. How does rolling through bear traps in this case not deal damage, let alone seem like a way to break your neck, become the solution over more logical steps? There's talk of throwing pottery shards at them, but we're right back to 'why don't weapons set these off'?Secondly, some of these puzzles are... downright esoteric. I'm sorry, but the constellation and organ music puzzle in act 2 are not satisfying. They work off of this vague coordinate based clue and frankly, the actual solution seems more like a stretch and not something I would have ever guessed. Concerning the star puzzle in particular, I was able to interpret the implied meaning to almost two dozen different potential solutions that seemed like they would have made sense. Had I not hopped onto the discord to ask, my gameplay of this would have just stopped because you can't do anything else without getting it right. It just feels like unnecessarily vague logic and it felt like 'it works because that's what the game says' rather than making much sense. According to the achievements at the time of this writing, not even a fifth of all players for this title have even beaten the second level. These need adjustment, either with more thorough clues or just entirely re-done puzzles. I still consider this game more positive than not, but these logic puzzles don't necessarily flow well.
