_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally much of a horror game player, so when the developer originally contacted me about Withering Rooms, I thought maybe I’d have a quick look at it and decide to pass.  The game turned out to be pretty interesting - it generally avoids a bunch of cheap jump scares and instead uses the theme as a substrate for some cool lore & game systems (if you've ever played Darkwood, it's basically that approach).Overall, the game is a sort of 2.5d survival horror that is somewhat reminiscent of Resident Evil.  You're trying to manage resources and strike a balance between sneaking past scary creatures or taking the calculated risk of fighting them directly.  It's somewhat rogue-lite in how the rooms are randomly generated each night, and you lose the majority of your items if you die.  However, much of your core progression is permanent and your character generally becomes more capable over time.I later found out that some of the world structure and traversal is similar to the earlier Clock Tower games, though the smoother gameplay, addition of combat (which I believe existed in Clock Tower 3?) and interesting resource management conundrums help to set Withering Rooms apart.One of the more interesting systems the game has is "Cursedness".  Casting spells, being hit by certain enemies, etc. can curse you.  The more cursed you get, the more the game changes (though I’ll leave it to you to see how far that goes).  Of course, as hinted by the name, being cursed is definitely something to be wary of - though it’s absolutely worthy of experimentation.  It's sort of like a much-better-implemented version of Bloodborne's Insight mechanic.The moment-to-moment pacing of the game has this sort of “leave you to your own devices and let you get immersed” feel that I really enjoyed in Dark Souls, Elden Ring, etc.  There isn’t much hand-holding and being overly reckless can lead to death in an instant.  Conversely, an observant and deliberate approach will pay off in spades.  Careful use of the peek feature, setting traps, and managing your resources can get you far.Regarding the earlier mention of Dark Souls; while Withering Rooms’ combat isn’t quite as complex as a Souls game, successfully surviving enemy encounters is similarly satisfying.  That being said; despite how invincible you may feel once you get settled in, combat is always a risky proposition - there’s a lot of value in sneaking around rather than engaging every random enemy.The soundscape is evocative of old-school games with dark and scary/brooding atmospheres.  I don’t think I have a great way to describe this (not being well-versed in the terminology for styles and genres of sound or music), but it’s what you would expect from the older Resident Evil games, Hexen/Heretic, etc.  It’s sort of this even mix of comfortable familiarity and uneasy strangeness.  It’s the flavor of old-school that you hear in Elden Ring’s menu sounds, or some of the sounds that were in the Dark Souls 2 network test (and unfortunately replaced in the game’s release).Additionally, the game’s music does a good job of alternating between the various themes that give the game its charm and taking a moment to step back into a quiet ambiance that gives you plenty of room to get lost in planning your next move, speculate about the game’s story, and let the spooky atmosphere get to you (especially when cursed).Even though I’ve only played up to the beginning of Chapter 2 as of the time of this review (via a preview copy provided by the developer), I’m enjoying what I know of the story so far, and itching to know more of what’s going on.  While a certain major milestone revealed a significant amount of what’s going on, there’s definitely a bigger picture that I haven’t yet grasped.  I don’t want to risk spoiling anything, but I can at least say I’m especially intrigued by what seems to be going on with the mansion you’re trapped in (a generic-sounding statement that will make a lot of sense once you’ve hit a bit of time to dig in).

_childDocuments_.review: Very wonderful! Gameplay, Atmosphere, World, & Exploration feels just as good as the trailer. The weird animations fit the theme imo. Plus there are cool secrets & mechanics like the curse system. It changes the world & slowly kills you. I was jump scared when shopping at a merchant & accidently bought the wrong item also... All I could do was laugh. Enemies strangely make you feel helpless but like they're still removable at the same time. It's a really interesting mix of souls like & survivor horror gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished it yet but this is one hell of a crazy and creative game.Think of a Bloodborne setting with a somehow mix between Survival Horror and Souls-like elements, with Rule of Rose, Clock Tower, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Remothered, Haunting Grounds, and even a bit of Fatal Frame, vibes.You go through a ever changing (each night actually) Manor and its surroundings, stuck into a neverending dream where people mutates into monstruous things because they're actually stuck in the dream world, but they're still living in the real world (although in a coma). You quickly get a taste of what is to expect in this game and the horror vibes make you stay cautious about your surroundings. Lots of items to find and lots of ways to play (although the gameplay is a bit clunky and slowish, but I think it's kinda reminiscent of oldschool survival horror on PSX/PS2, so I find it fair!), but you'll have to be careful about not dying because you'll lose a lot of your items for your next run (I didn't say all the items because there's a game mechanic for that actually.)It's really awesome, and the game still delivers with new monsters, new areas and new story plot the further you dive into the game.I mean, the game manages to be a better Silent Hill than what's Konami has in their bag.And we don't have Bloodborne on PC but Withering Room is the "kinda bloodborne setting" at home and I'm glad this game exists.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy roguelikes/roguelites and bought this based on the demo, which I liked. The atmosphere is great.The problem is that once you get past the very early stages that you see in the demo, the monsters immediately get twice as spongy, and there are multiple hostiles at a time, and they hit a lot harder. The demo isn't really representative of what you're getting.The melee controls are too clunky to do what you need them to do. Basically imagine Mortal Kombat 1, except your character is a lot slower and moves a lot less smoothly, and you can only punch or roll. A better comparison perhaps would be what you'd see in an old flash game from the 2000's.There are spells and better weapons and so on, but the thing is, you need to defeat the above mentioned hostiles to start finding them.I really like a number of things about the game - love the atmopshere, love the curse mechanic and the idea of the spirit world. The story seems great. But too much of the gameplay relies on this really shoddy melee combat system and the balance just doesn't work for me. I can't get past it. If the game felt fluid and your characters movements were fluid, I would love it. But they're not and that's that. I wouldn't recommend this even on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying this is not at all my type of game. I don't play spooky games or sidescrollers at all, but I could not stop playing this game. With a great story and challenging puzzles, this game's innovative class system lets you solve your conflicts in many ways. I could not recommend this game enough. You don't have to wait for a sale, if you are on the fence buy it. My favorite things about this game:1) If you are not dumb, you will never die. You don't lose your things, but with the remembrance system, you can keep more and more items even if you do die.2) For each act the is a new inventory cap for every item, and if you don't have your inventory maxed it is always available in the store. If you plan right you can always have spells and consumables.3) As you play, you unlock custom loadouts that can be switched mid-battle. You can start a fight with a spell in a witch build with 376% spell power, then swap to your poise monster blender build when they are close!4) Random Dungeon rings! (Gives me bloodborne glyph-hunting memories)

_childDocuments_.review: I hate roguelikes. I hate roguelites. I can, sort of, play some roguelites if the roguelite elements are really, really 'lite' and unobtrusive. About the limit for death penalty that I prefer, is the Dark Souls series. Any more than that, like item impermanence, or level-up impermanence, I can't stand that sort of thing.I'm here to make the case that even if you hate roguelikes and roguelites, but you enjoy RPGs, or Metroidvanias, or any game that rewards careful planning, a methodical approach, and being thoughtful about your character build, then this game is absolutely for you. If you're someone who does like roguelikes and roguelites, so much the better. Note, this review will be completely about gameplay, and will only mention things like art direction or sound design when they have a meaningful impact on said gameplay; yes, the game is very pretty and it sounds very good, and credit to the people responsible for that, but those just aren't the meat of this game. This review will be as spoiler-free as possible.First, I want to tackle the thing that triggers me about roguelikes in general, and that is impermanence. Yes, there is a hefty amount of that in this game, but that will mostly revolve around losing consumables and other similarly expendable resources, like currency, if you die. There are mechanisms in the gameplay that allow you to 'save' your area progress, your quest progress, and even a few pieces of equipment (though, in the early game, you will have to be very selective about what you want to keep if you die, and what you're okay with risking losing to a death). Any level-ups you do are permanent, even if you die, and there are quite a few currency resources that are permanent, and many pieces of equipment that are also permanent by default. That said, dying still sucks in this game. Don't die. Fortunately, the game makes it very easy to not die. At least, the game makes it proportionally easier to not die based on how many resources you have, which works in kind of an inverse risk-reward dynamic; in other words, if you have few resources, you're much more likely to die, and lose what little you have. If you have a lot of resources, you're pretty unlikely to die, unless you do something stupid. The thing is though, if you don't die, you can actually 'snowball' really, really hard, and basically clear entire maps of enemies with ease, and once all the threats are eliminated, they stay dead unless you die (in most cases; no spoilers), so you can explore in relative safety. Dying when you have a bunch of spell scrolls, healing items, etc. sucks, as it can take time to recoup your losses, but the important part is that you can recoup them.

_childDocuments_.review: [Ending C][Steam Deck]+ To start off, don't be intimidated by the rogue-lite mechanics. The game offers plenty of ways to compensate, among them a multitude of very viable builds that you can play with, a way of saving before each boss fight allowing retries without losing anything, a very cool fast-travel system, and a myriad of varied tools that you can use to defeat or avoid enemies. The rogue-lite elements still pose a challenge, but the game takes great care to never make them frustrating. And they're nicely integrated with the lore and the world, a pocket-universe-like Dream where each death reshuffles the layouts of your surroundings.+ The game very much encourages you to role-play if you want to rise up to its challenge. Thankfully, most builds are viable and pretty strong. I played a bleed build, which was pretty fun, but magic is certainly really strong, poison builds can be loads of fun and projectile builds can carry hard as well. Essentially, anything but a plain melee build is not only fun, but also efficient to varying degrees. As for how you craft your build, you level-up in a Souls-like fashion with certain attributes gated by level, you can have rings with various perks and stats, amulets which are similar but only have one slot, and armour and clothing with stats and perks of various kinds. Add artefacts, charms, a decent number of melee weapons and a bunch of consumables that are insanely useful and you have a great number of customisation options and ways to approach every encounter.+ The curse system is also very inspired. Each spell you can cast has a toll that fills your curse bar a bit. If you get it filled to the maximum, you suffer from curse rot which drains your health quickly, but can be stopped with a specific item. However, being cursed to certain degrees reveals hidden elements of the world, from access to important NPCs to loot of all kinds. It's really well done and often spooky. It reminds me of Bloodborne's Insight, but Withering Rooms has a better implementation of the concept honestly.+ There is a surprising amount of content in this game. Worth mentioning are an arena with multiple encounters which give an alternate path of levelling up, a couple of side-quests and the ability to grind charms by repeating the encounters after its completion. On top of that you can add a labyrinth dungeon which offers yet another path to level-up, as well as a way for the player to grind for rings with random stats in order to min-max their build.+ Puzzles were pretty great, a good mix of fun and challenging to solve for me.+ The soundtrack is quite good, very varied but always a great fit and contributing greatly to the atmosphere. Some catchy tunes in there as well.+ The art direction is cleanly eerie and the PS2-era style graphics are quite effective at creating a creepy and atmospheric Mostyn mansion and its adjacent locations which you'll explore in the game's four chapters.+ The world and the lore also managed to pull me in quite easily. It has some interesting similarities with Bloodborne in that there is a Dream which is a pocket universe within which blood plays an extremely important role, but that's sort of where the similarities end. The game has its own spin on the concepts and it's well presented through the lore text, which you'll find plenty of while exploring. There are multiple iterations of the Dream, its origin is mysterious and interesting and blood and organs have various terrifying uses which the cast of characters (and you) make use of throughout a pretty compelling story and plot.+ Runs beautifully on the Steam Deck, only a few performance drops here and there but thankfully not in gameplay intensive moments.- Text size is pretty small on the Deck though. My eyes eventually adjusted, but I don't think I did them any favours >.<- Combat is indeed a bit janky, with hits not having the impact you'd like to feel and dodges being less reliable than you might think, but I got used to that fairly quickly and, honestly, the depth of the build-crafting more than makes up for it to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Withering Rooms is the kind of game you don’t get every day. Back when the title was still in Early Access, one of the ways the developer described this game was somewhere along the lines of “If Clock Tower was an action RPG”. Which… fits and, even more surprisingly, works incredibly well. This game is so strange, yet so fascinating and inventive. Its influences are recognizable, yet its mood is immaculate… And while I didn’t enjoy every second of the game and do find faults with some of its aspects, it was also one of the most inspiring gaming experiences I’ve had in quite a while.Let me attempt to describe how this game actually works. This is a side scrolling action RPG, with melee, ranged and magic attacks available and working as a somewhat simplified approach of the combat system one would find in a From Software’s “Souls” game. The layouts of the “dungeons” that are available for exploration during each of the game’s chapters are randomized every time you die, with rooms and their content moving around a set location, but never fully randomized. Inventory is also lost upon death, but as you continue playing you will be able to “remember” more and more items between deaths. And of course, there is also a system of leveling up that will help even the odds against some of the more difficult problems the game would throw at you. Curiously, and more in line with Clock Tower, stealth and traps also play an important part and while it is possible to just kill all enemies on the map, often times the game expects you to be smart and adaptable, hiding and running away when needed, leading enemies into traps and utilizing every tool you have.One of the most memorable and coolest central mechanics of the game is the idea of the “Curse”. When comparing to other game concepts, I’d say this is a middle ground between the Sanity of Eternal Darkness and Insight of Bloodborne. Except, unlike the cool looking but purely negative impact of insanity from the former, and rather limited stylistic and gameplay impact of the latter, Curse is a resource you will learn to manage through the game. All magic curses you, lots of enemies curse you and as you get cursed, the locations change, becoming more distorted and creepy. Becoming fully cursed is deadly, as your health starts to gradually (and rather quickly) drain until you cleanse the curse or die. However, being cursed also reveals a lot of hidden elements that benefit you, lots of weapons and tools you have work better with curse and not being cursed at all puts you at quite a disadvantage. Meaning that you always need to consider managing this resource, sometimes even more closely than health, and it never gets old or uninteresting.Another big reason for how interesting everything is lies in the presentation and storytelling. Despite being, from the technological perspective, rather plain, the game oozes creepy charm and its hard to not love how amazing the style is. The soundtrack is absolutely incredible too, so don’t be surprised if you find yourself humming along the tunes for different rooms and locations. The story is really well told and is genuinely interesting to slowly unravel. And out of all different types of “Lovecraft inspired” weird fiction/cosmic horror game stories, Withering Rooms is definitely among the more interesting ones. The game even builds its “new game plus” into the story in a really simple, but fun way, so don’t stop playing once you’ve finished the game once.Now, that isn’t to say that you will definitely enjoy every part of the game. I feel like some parts of the combat are intentionally underpowered in a way, that eventually becomes frustrating, against the huge health pools of some enemies. And while stealth is a viable and often necessary option, you do need to kill at least some enemies and level up to go against bosses which you cannot skip. The side scrolling roguelite structure of the world also means that some of the locations eventually turn into very long hallways that start looking a little tired after a while. Since this game only has two layers of depth to the levels with the “front” layer and the “back” layer of rooms you can enter, some of which can be interconnected, but are usually only entered from the front layer. And some of the sections genuinely feel like huge difficulty spikes, if I’m completely honest. Though, to counter that the game has a “Storytelling” difficulty mode that you can switch to and from at any point of the game – it does “re-roll” the world, but additionally feels like a completely valid way of experiencing the game. So if you do get to a point, where you start constantly struggling, I would still urge you to finish the game even if on the story-focused difficulty, it’s absolutely worth it.Because of that last option with difficulty switching, I can’t think of a reason not to recommend Withering Rooms to anyone who is even at least mildly interested in what this game promises in its trailers. It’s an unforgettable experience, with an incredible vibe, great soundtrack and lots of fun mechanics. Seriously, don’t miss out on such a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a completely underrated. Its level design structure to backtrack is done exceptionally well and its curse function is incredibly unique that adds to the environment and combat mechanics. The game is loaded with an insane amount of items, including simply rings that have multiple strengths and weaknesses. The enemy variety is pretty large, and the game oozes with scary atmosphere, especially when you get cursed, and as you are heavily cursed the music and environment changes.The melee combat isn't its strong suit but I find it suitable, notably it being a horror game. The game also allows you to use spells which come with with negatively boost your curse meter. Once the curse better is filled, your life will drain. The game has a different weapons that have their own strengths. In this game you can bleed out or get poisoned and you can utilize that to with your own tools.  The game has its own level up system which encourages you to kill to get fingers, organs, and such to level up. The story is somewhat interesting but I haven't followed it too closely. The game is simply fun to play and explore. The soundtrack is definitely eerie which suits the game incredibly well and while I haven't finished it, there is a new game plus mode and multiple ends for this game. It is a game I can see myself playing through a second time to some degree. It is somewhat of a permadeath game, you will lose items but there are ways to keep items in multiple playthroughs. Main bosses of course will be beat and you will keep the keys you had in your last playthrough so not everything is done from scratch again. Very highly, highly recommended for fans of atmospheric games, fans of horror games, fans of metroidvania, and fans of simply good games.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m posting this after completing all the darkened bestiary pages and finishing a few runs. One of my favorite things about this game is the way the environment changes with cursedness. A hallway could go from looking very well put together with nice harpsichord music to the walls bleeding and the tunes changing to ticking and scratching, adding to the tension. I’m a fan of optimizing builds to get the most damage output, and there were no shortage of outfit combinations nor weapon/projectile/tool/offhand items to try out. I loved meeting the characters of this game, and the way everyone has their own unique personality. There were Dark Souls’ vibes to the dialogue. It really feels like discovering something new every step of the way. Even when replaying the game, there continues to be new things to uncover. Well worth the price. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is quite literally one of the best horror games I’ve played. I love the concept of exploring a haunted mansion where, if you die, things get randomized and switch around. The customization of nightingale is amazing and the versatility for weapons, projectiles, and spells is incredible and keeps combat fresh. If you like games like don’t starve and binding of Isaac, you’ll definitely like this game. Death means you restart, but there are a plethora of ways to keep your items and the maps never reset in such a dramatic way that you lose your footing. The story and lore is incredibly interesting as well; this is one of the few games where I actually exhaust all dialogue and read all documents because they’ve piqued my interest. If you struggle with the consequences of dying and/or find the combat too difficult, there’s a wonderful narrative difficulty that allows you to fully enjoy the story without all the intensity. The only thing I want is a guide where to find all the clothing and weapons because this game is not so popular yet to have full guides. However, the creator has a made a comprehensive list of all the items, collectibles, and even story hints, which just shows the dedication. I can’t recommend this game enough, 10/10 on every count!
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good rogue-lite metroidvania game. Most of things are done right.The dark world is amazing. Curse mechanics fits in it very nicely. You get curse(debuff) when you use a spell or get specific damage. The world changes dynamically according to how cursed you're. The locations you can go are very big and wide. You must explorer many locations each of which has very unique atmosphere. The more you explorer, the stronger you become. This is essential part of metroidvania and this game's done very right. Exploration is quite fun in this game.Fighting is not fun at all. All enemies/boss fights are the same. You can kill them all using powerful items. The only concern is enemy resistance. That's all. Plus, the big con is that you become invincible for a short time when you're in danger. This allows you to recover your health so you never get one shotted. This game balance is very bad and not fun for those who seek challenging gameplay like me. If combat is fun and each boss fights is unique like GRIME, this game must be one of the best games in its genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game. I described it to a friend in this sort of way:-Character and hiding of Clock Tower-Spencer Mansion-esque from Resident Evil-Monster Design of Silent Hill-Leveling of a RPG-Exploration of Metroidvania-Setting of Amnesia-Roguelike Horror of World of Horror-Dodge-rolling of a Soulslike (haha)It's a strange game that comes together in a fantastic and addicting mix. I started playing it and haven't been able to stop. It's incredibly deep with a lot to do after beating it with multiple endings and things unlocked in NG+. It has an interesting story, a variety of play styles, great monster design, good visuals, and relatively simple but fitting music. I really can't recommend enough giving this one a try. It's a great time and I'm still finding things to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Dang, Moonless Formless. This game is a banger. An obvious love letter to old school survival horror, this game brings that slick side-scrolling, mansion exploring gameplay to some pretty good 3D graphics. The RPG elements blend incredibly well with the gameplay, and there is a great balance of searching, fighting, crafting, and using resources to purchase and level up.This game combines so many ideas without becoming a horrible mess, and I'm so glad for it. Right now I'm running a magic build, but I might try to become a melee tank and see how it goes.So far I've managed to kill a boss with curse rot, survive after getting cure rotted during a boss fight, died 5 times in row with no progress, only to clear a majority of the mansion on the next run. I've practiced fighting the various creatures, and gotten much better.Get this bad boy. It's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually hate roguelikes because I find the concept of playing reshuffled levels over and over daunting and dull, especially since many indie developers employ roguelike mechanics to pad out otherwise boring games.That said, this game is definitely the exception. The story is great and the gameplay is fun, yet challenging and evolves at a steady pace. Unlike other rogueikes, there's an actual sense of progression.It's like if Dark Souls, The Coma, Silent Hill and Resident Evil had a baby.Also, bonus points that it was made by a solo dev who has an obvious passion for retro horror games. He even created his own FAQ walkthrough page for the game, which is just more evidence of how much he considered the player experience. Like, just adding things like being able to change note font to typeface and adding optional tutorial rooms to get used to new game mechanics seem like minor things, but show just how considerate the developer is.This game is an indie gem, like the Stardew Valley for horror survival games. This game deserves more coverage and an award of some kind. If it's ever nominated for a Steam award, I'm definitely voting for it. It's definitely one of the best horror survival games I've ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique game. Despite what you may have read, it isn't much of a rogue-like. This is a relatively linear game with some randomness in-between. This isn't a bad thing, mind. Since so much of the game revolves around back-tracking and environmental awareness, the minor changes from run to run can totally ruin your planning if you're not paying attention.This game isn't short either. It's fully-featured with multiple endings, a post-game, and more. I don't know what else to say. If the screenshots look interesting to you, it's worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a privilege to play this indie game, titles like this make searching through Steam discovery queue worth it.Gameplay is similar to Souls games in 2.5D space, you got them dodge rolls, different weapons, leveling up, so on. While the game offers hiding spot from the horrors, you will most of the time end up duking it out with them instead. Hiding spots are mostly a way to dodge, when going left/right doesn't work.You lose all but "memorised" items upon death (not in boss fights) and the areas shuffle a bit in layout, loot and enemies. While this, especially early, makes things seem challenging, the more you play and get accustomed to rules and strategies, the more manageable things become. My only deaths were in the first chapter of the game (not counting bosses), though very late-game had some close calls.The game has a lot more going for it than is initially apparent in terms of story and gameplay aspects, so I do suggest sticking with it. My favorite part was early half of the game when I was trying out new weapons and strategies, before I had started focusing on a specific build.+ Intriguing story+ Fantastic theme+ Good OST+ Build variety+ Lots of content+ Replay value* There's so much content, at times I felt it's a bit bloated in certain parts- Jank, had more than one boss seemingly getting stuck while I whittled them down and some specific attacks didn't seem to connect with rare few enemies as they should have- Bugs, all minor, but enough for me to mention them here briefly- Balance, any ranged build appears to enable cheese tactics, while melee, at least on paper, seems difficult in comparison. I played ranged, but I do see melee having some nasty tricks of their own, like specific DOTs and stuns. Ranged > Melee is a common problem within the genre, however- Ending(s), while good, lacked some "oomph"While I usually would be put off my a game that resembles a "Souls" game due to having played too many at this point, Withering Rooms offers a refreshing experience that kept me hooked from start to finish, despite the issues mentioned.There is also a demo available, for those interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

Will this final(?) item allow me to enter the room and grab the last documents?The trailers make the game look sillier than it is. It has its silly moments but that's not on purpose.The game is cold blooded like the games it takes its inspirations from.I love how the story is told. It makes you feel implicated and worried. Thanks to the soundtrack also.The game doesn't hold you by the hand but it's not punishing like a Soulsborne game. The game wants you to survive somehow. It's a roguelite after all. You can make long runs early enough.But when you die, you'll feel cold. You'll feel it.The game has downsides too. I'm not gonna lie. I know it won't reach the replayability of some other roguelites like Rogue Legacy 2 or In celebration of violence but it wasn't designed to pretend playing in the same room.The game was developped by one person.To the dev and everyone involved in the game.... I love your work!I LOVE THIS GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: I can give a thumbs up to Withering Rooms because i feel like for the amount of content, the $18 sale delivered. Mind you there are a few critiques i have. First and foremost, the ambiance and environment of this game is fantastic. Always making me feel spooked out as I wait for the next enemy to pop out and curse me even more into madness. Nostalgia also plays into a factor, really honing in on the ps2 era of silent hill and the like. The rogue-like mechanics with perma-perks and leveling keeps the game fresh and forces you to constantly think about what you are next steps are. The narrative is also a set of writting. This game has scratched a horror itch i've been wanting itched for a bit of time. And the length of content is quite exceptional for how incredibly small the team was. However, the one thing that falls short and i believe was overlooked in one way or another, was the combat system, which is a bit concerning because the game had been in early access for a while, but hasn't really met much change. The combat is what you'd expect of a hack and roll gameplay. However, longevity in your run is very dependent on caution and understanding of when to back of. Because as soon as you die, you lose out on everything not marked as saved (which is limited for a while). It is here that the game because almost unagreeably hard, as you dont have the ingredients to make healing items, the coin to buy wares and potentially some items that made the run easier. With the rooms also shifting its enemies and content, it very much becomes a run and grab so you dont have to lose health to make health items that only give you a little back. One other issue aside from this is the notion of iframes and dark souls-esque declarations, but the attack range or the duration of the attack is too long. Or is too quick. Quicker than the player. Many times i found myself having the best gear set up, but having the battle boil down to the amount of healing items i have, dictate the outcome of the battle. Regardless of skill and dodging, and knowledge of the fight. I really think the team needs to revisit either the way the player can work to mitigate or negate full damage, or the enemies attacks need to be reworked. Not nerfed, but definitely revised. I'd give this game a 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: i don't have enough words to express how much i love this game! the gameplay loop is so fun, the soundtrack is enthralling and the story is fresh and captivating! the fact that both the ost and the game itself were made by just one person blows my mind. also, as a lifelong survival horror fan, i can tell how the developer's love for the genre permeates in so many aspects of the game... it somehow manages to pay homage to many classic survival horror titles while also being its own thing. nowadays we see so many titles that are marketed as a love letter to the survival horror genre, but at the end of the day they just replicate old formulas and call it a day. this game takes the risk and dances to its own tune without forgetting nor straight up copying the legacy that came before it, and i respect that so much!!!i am seeing people complaining about clunkiness in combat, but it didn't bother me that much. besides, what's a traditional survival horror without a bit of jank? as sh horror fans we've really been in the trenches of clunk along the years, so at this point it shouldn't phase us anymore, hahahaha. what's important is that, from my perspective, that "jankiness" does not take away from the experience.i really hope that this game gets the recognition it deserves and gains more visibility in the sh community. for my part, im already recommending it to all my friends that also love the genre! it really is criminally underrated... i hope it becomes as big as it deserves.i don't say this lightly, but this game has become one my favorites next to the likes of rule of rose, galerians and haunting ground. please give withering rooms an opportunity, it deserves it!

_childDocuments_.review: The story and the atmosphere are the big highlights here. Little touches in the background really amp up the creepiness. Discovering secret paths and unconventional ways of accessing new rooms, or safely traveling between rooms you already had access to, is my favorite part.

_childDocuments_.review: I talk about a lot of things I love in this game but I haven't spoiled everything. I have refrained from talking about plenty of things. This a very interesting game. It's a little bit janky but it's very playable. The aesthetic of the Asylum is interesting. I won't spoil anything but the game literally has lore behind why the building's style is a bit strange. Ha - EXCUSES! But no, it's cool and makes sense. The game is set in a dream world version of the asylum, so the real thing would no doubt look relatively normal. It's a bit like what some people call a McMansion. A mcmansion is a house, especially a large one that does not adhere to standard building practices because form was focused on above function. In some cases, it refers to a building that was built to look like a building from an old era but doesn't do it perfectly so it looks strange. I love old buildings. Spoiler: The enemies look cool, especially the witches and initiates. The intelligence of the enemies scared me. You can hide under tables and beds, but there's a not uncommon chance that enemies will check where you are hiding and attack you. The dialogue from the enemies is creepy and the voice acting is very good. The enemies can also leave one room and enter another. I witnessed one enemy get up from it's bed after I attacked it, leave the room, enter my room and sleep under my bed. The guy with the pistol can also leave the room while you are peeking into the room he starts in. Enemies with a gun can accidentally miss you and kill another enemy - I love that. Some enemies are pretty easy to kill with an axe. Based on my experience, don't be too shy about attacking sleeping enemies or some other basic enemies like the maid. Somehow despite being pretty bad at fighting enemies, I found it easier to kill them when I gave up on pure stealth and attacked them like I was on bath salts. I also enjoyed attacking enemies then leaving the room so they can't attack me until they follow me out. You need to be stealthy at times but you can't just hide forever. Use a lantern as soon as you can in the basement because it will make your life much easier. It took me a long time to realise I had a lantern in my inventory. I bought it and then just didn't use it for 20 minutes.I do not 100% understand the lore yet - I haven't completed the game - but I do understand a decent amount of what is happening. I cannot remember names so when a character is mentioned I just think "Oh yeah... that guy I read about and completely forgot". With my almost amnesiac-like memory, it is like I am a patient of the asylum myself.The music is repetitive at times but it is mostly alright.The creepy vibe is very well done with random things that can happen like silhouettes in the foreground, giant faces appearing in windows and plenty of other things to keep you creeped out and entertained.So yeah, this is a great game. I always prefer hiding and doing stealthy things in games. I have to get out of my comfort zone and attack enemies but I still enjoy the game a lot. I hope the developer makes more horror games. This is one of the best games in existence in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam's rating system is woefully incapable of communicating just how strongly I recommend this game. Withering Rooms is without a doubt one of the greatest games I have ever played.Gameplay-wise, Withering Rooms is a very Souls-inspired action RPG with great customization and satisfying progression. Exploration is great. The difficulty is just right, with options for those who want more or less challenge. The replay value is off the charts with new game+ introducing new mechanics and challenges. The atmosphere is excellently spooky and the story and characters are as compelling as they are cryptic. Last, but certainly not least, the soundtrack is absolutely .I got all of the achievements and saw basically everything the game had to offer in about 50 hours. Then I kept playing for over 100 more because I was still enjoying the game so much. That is an insane amount of enjoyment for $25. And the fact that this was the work of a single person, the good ol' One Dude in a Basement(TM), absolutely blows my mind. Moonless Formless' team of one has talent to rival the largest AAA development teams, and this masterpiece is a testament to that.This game cannot be praised enough and I strongly recommend it to anyone who enjoys the horror sub-genre and/or Souls-like games. The demo is a great way to give it a shot, as it lets you play the first half of chapter 1, and you can continue your demo save file in the full game. So go on and give it a try!I will likely replay this game many more times in the future as I eagerly await whatever Moonless Formless creates next.

_childDocuments_.review: A very special blend of Castlevania, Resident Evil, Silent Hill,  and Alice in Wonderland.Give this game a shot, it may surprise you. After an hour with the demo I was hooked and bought it, 50 hours later I got the true ending and loved it to bits. If you enjoy horror game aesthetics, or stuff like American McGee's Alice this is a great blend of that with some Castlevania exploration and combat. Its a roguelike, but there are a lot of permanent upgrades and you can find shrines throughout the world that after making an offering lets you "remember" 1 more item to persist beyond death. The map layout is static, room order will be shuffled as well as cosmetic decorations but the world as a whole stays the same. So the roguelike nature really takes a pretty small toll on the game, if you are turned off by that tag just know it doesn't affect things much. The atmosphere is great, full of spooks and uneasy areas, there is a curse meter which raises when hit with certain attacks or when using magic yourself and it does a bit of a Bloodborne insight thing where it changes the world around you. Going from a normal victorian hallway to a Silent Hill hellscape. This meter when full also lets you perceive things you normally cant see like ghosts and traps and such. The story is weird and creative and a joy to unravel through talking to NPC's and finding notes, I felt driven by narrative just as much as I was gameplay progression. The game starts out simple and combat may take some getting used to, its a bit rigid and you have to learn timing and spacing, when to backhop, run, roll through enemies. You'll also make use of some stealth to hide under tables and let stronger foes pass, as the game goes on you can dig more into a build of choice roughly split up between melee, magic, and throwables/guns. Theres some good itemization here, with interesting offhand items to use, some risk vs reward using the curse meter and all the usual stat boost stuff you get in a Castelvania-like. Resouces play a big roll here, there are lots of healing items needed to get through the game along with spells requiring consumables to make and throwables/ammo being limited. This is one of the reasons I think it upholds a good illusion of difficulty. On paper looking back at my stats, I only had 4 deaths and those were all at the beginning. After a bit I hit a sort of critical mass and finished the game without another death, there is a oneshot protection mechanic built in where you are put in a danger state after reaching "0" where you have a second or 2 to use a heal. But I wouldn't say the game felt like a breeze or anything. I still had to keep switching out gear to be efficient with whatever I was fighting. And I was churning through resources, its just I was accruing them at an equal rate, hence the good illusion of difficulty. There is a lot of content here to go through, if you really want to explore and see everything the map is pretty big and lots of enemies to fight (89 types). There are 4 endings, a pretty solid NG+ and hardmode, and some fun items behind filling out the bestiary on hardmode. Graphics are good enough to sell its atmosphere, lighting can be pretty nice and spooky as some areas are very dark in a way you cant just turn gamma up for they require one of the light sources you can get in game. Animations are a little stiff but not bad, the soundtrack is so good I ended up buying the OST. All in all a really great game with some heart in it, and a surprising amount of content and fun items to find. Give the demo a whirl if it interests you it gives a pretty good snapshot of the game, and watch the video on the store page for a preview of some of the more powerful weapons you can get later. I think its worth it at full price, its a game I can walk away from feeling good about tossing a coin to a passionate indie developer and get a lot of fun hours out of it. I look forward to future works.

_childDocuments_.review: Holy heck is this game good. Having just finished Chapter 1, I'd have been (almost) content if that was the end of the game there. It meshes together elements of Clock Tower with a fair amount of Soulsborne(!), not to mention some loving nods to a number of other survival horror classics (which I'd list, but that would be ruining the fun).There's an element of rogue-likeness to it, which initially deterred me, but it doesn't hinder the core elements of the gameplay - namely a feeling of progression in terms of exploration and story. The rooms may switch around if you die, but the overall world remains in a fixed layout, and for that I'm extremely appreciative because it can sit there in your thoughts and just...occupy a space. The overall presentation, narrative and puzzle-solving have also consistently surprised and impressed me. The writing, too, is exquisite without tipping into pretentiousness.I know this probably sounds like an unrealistically glowing review, but this game just resonated with me so perfectly. You know how you get an idea in your head for a game that you would love to exist, but you'd never be able to invest the time or resources to make it? For me, Withering Rooms is about as close as it gets.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely whips. Holy crap.Withering Rooms is a 2.5D throwback to Haunting Grounds, Rule Of Rose, Silent Hill, and some of the other titans from the playstation survival horror boom. It uses stock 3D assets and it uses them with the deftness of a surgeon maneuvering a knife. There's some jank to the controls, and that's to be expected given that this is a one person project mixing survival horror and action and soulslike progression, but the jank is basically a feature once you get used to it. Cheesing fights feels good. Heck, this whole game feels good.And the combat isn't even its strength. Withering Rooms uses solid audio design and strong writing to tell an absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ story of occultism and cosmic horror. There's only three endings (that I'm aware of), but there's a lot of small decisions you can make and a ton of side content that I wasn't able to fully explore, since the path to Grand Central glitched out on me (Mind Control room didn't spawn, and nothing in the Antenna Room could be interacted with even though I had the cylinder). The side content that I *did* explore was easily half of my playtime, and this is a game with a New Game+ on top of that, so if you really vibe with it you could be playing it for a while.Between this and You Will Die Here Tonight, indie survival horror has never been healthier as a scene. Withering Rooms is a dang good game, and if you like classic jank, genuine unease, and completely wild plot twists in a story that's both grounded and gonzo, you should absolutely give it a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A ridiculously good Metroidvania / Survival Horror / Roguelike game that hits all the right notes.--Notes:--+ Story is very thrilling, despite the COMPLETE lack of voicework for the most part. There's a lot of twists, turns, reoccurring characters throughout the dream that get you invested via their oddities. Nightingale herself is even a character, despite having zero actual words she says.+ Gameplay I'll be breaking down in greater detail below, but the game loop is honestly very simple and tight: If you don't die, enemies you kill in an area stay dead, each area has collectible items that can greatly enhance your gameplay and help turn the tide of battle, enemies are varied and offer different, unique fighting styles that can challenge set playstyles more than others or make certain ones harder to execute like how some enemies will be resistant to physical attacks but not bleed or poison, or maybe they are weak to curse or fire, etc. You go from room to room, clearing enemies, collecting things, crafting consumables, clear more rooms, etc. It's simple and fun.+ The RNG isn't too intrusive for world generation, lots of static places.+ Visually this game has two things that put it into it's own unique category. On one hand, I think the game looks similar to unity asset flips we've seen in the past, most noticeable in the characters, but past the first in game chapter you get exposed to more and more of this game's unique flair. You see, as your curse rises, the world changes and the rooms, literally, wither which offers up ONE new enemy [Missed opportunity] but also changes the feel of the world.* Withering as a mechanic from curse also adds a risk/reward as you are more likely to find items you lost on previous nights when you die. The game is keeping track of what you had when you die, and the only way to remember specific items is for you to kill bosses and activate shrines that cost loot from enemies, which is then divided up further via the upgrade system which typically costs the same enemy resources to level you up. When you die, you drop everything not remembered, including those enemy drops that allow you to level. Giving yourself a high curse and running through areas you have been to already will let you pick up weapons, consumables, items you had the night you died. The issue with this mechanic is that resources are plentiful and there is no actual risk if you don't stay at high curse when fighting normal enemies, as it's totally possible to kill every enemy in an area prior to getting to the withering, then just running around empty corridors picking up everything new, which blows. There is one unique enemy that spawns when you are in the withered areas but he's honestly a pushover even in the early game using either statues or flat out fast weapons.- Combat is the worst part of the game. For the most part, there isn't that many weapons you gain access to AND are worth using, either because they are simply too slow or their stats are too bad to even be worth using, let alone cases where you don't even get a weapon to spawn at all. There is a ton of physical only and bleed weapons but basically none for fire or poison which makes those elements naturally suck far more, and while there is a single lightning weapon it is only in the last act of the game so players WILL miss it and that's probably intended given how strong it is. The issue with combat is that while there is technically 3 fighting styles; melee, ranged and magic. Ranged and magic are by far more limited than melee, which would be fine if they had a high variety of high damage things at their disposal, but for the most part they are either too utility focused [Magic] or still require a ton of hits to take down enemies [Ranged.] To talk bluntly on ranged, there IS no early game ranged weapon that works in a way that is consistent, instead you are left with throwing knives that do no damage that you have to retrieve, and you can only hold 4, and throwing pots until the final act. Throwing pots vary wildly in usefulness as the acid damage they deal CAN be useful but trying to land the pot without dealing massive damage to yourself is basically impossible, and then once you get to the final act you get access to the Revolver and Shotgun which renders throwing knives even more useless as both the Revolver and Shotgun will completely outclass every melee weapon you have and almost every ranged option by the time you get them, with only specific enemies being quicker to take out with curse pots, poison pots or acid if it's an automaton. Magic is a bit better, as it offers several different elements and ways to kill which is better, such as Curse Ball which became my go to fave for several high health enemies who lacked resistance to curse, Armored which gives you 25 shields to a max of 200 bonus HP, Harvest Field which lets you siphon health off of enemies every tick, or Fireball / Enchant / Possession Book which let you deal just more damage and add active meat shields to the fight, but then you have Dummy which is pretty useless as it takes so long to cast and enemies will kill the dummy so quickly it is useless as a meat shield, or the awkward cursed door which does basically nothing as a lot of enemies won't leave their rooms. Magic has a max of roughly 3 weapons so outside of spells you have 3 highly inefficient weapons that give you curse damage every time you cast, like spells, but deal far less damage and have far less utility. In particular the tree branch wand works like the rock from Friday the 13th on the NES, where it literally just goes over enemies heads making it useless on all but the tallest of creatures. The time that magic felt the strongest for me was by the end of the game where the spell curse toll for casting spells was basically nonexistent meaning I actually had the ability to cast Fireball more than twice without getting curse rotted and losing HP every second until I burned a candle. Circling back to melee, the strongest melee weapons are the ones that you can abuse the luck stat rings with as ALL the melee weapons, base, deal pitiful damage, and that would be fine if there was more variety that was valid, but for the most part you will be pumping the speed stat so that you aren't hit out of your attacks all the time while pumping health so you can just damage trade enemies to death, and once you attacks get fast enough from a high enough speed you will literallly stunlock all but the hardiest of foes to death, so it's just boring. The combat just doesn't feel very good at all mechanically, with none of the playstyles being that interesting.* I feel like a crossbow or bow for the early game would drastically spice up ranged combat, and a handful of two handed melee weapons / buffs to shields would spice up melee. The problem with early game is that ALL your options are very limited and so you'll be stuck with the axe for basically 3 acts before you get your hands on another weapon that is both 1) Strong enough to be worth using and 2) Fast enough that you won't be constantly hit out of your attacks. Shields in particular are basically useless as the time investment to put up a shield is such that you can't do it in response to an enemy so you basically have to raise the shield after you have stopped attacking and hold it there for over a second to make sure the block counted, it's just not responsive at all. Magic being more limited is fine because it's on the spells and not necessarily the wands, but having more useful wands and buffing some of the weaker spells [Or adding new, pure utility spells like a fast travel to Nowhere or a spell to cast a light above your head or one to add a fast travel point to a location temporarily] would do wonders, and that tree branch wand is COMPLETELY unacceptable given how good curse damage can be.Conclusion: You can dress up Nightingale like a Victorian Barbie, I'd love a sequel in some form9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting survival horror game that I find captivating and a lot of fun to play.   The best mechanics in the game are ones you'll encounter early on: you always come back to life when you die, but you don't come back with all the things you've gathered.  You have to use shrines to "remember" items, armor, weapons, spells, etc. If you "remember" an item, then it'll spawn with you when you come back to life. If you don't "remember" it, then it's lost on death. The other best system is the sanity system, which is called "curse".  As you become more cursed through using spells or fighting horrifying enemies, the world changes in real time and becomes more and more horrific.  But there's *benefits* to this happening, such as finding items you lost before when you died, being able to see shortcuts and hidden secrets, and being able to better see ghosts (who are dangerous, but otherwise only visible in a camera or in mirrors). While the combat might feel a bit janky at first, there's a wide breadth of what you're able to do and build around by the final chapters, from melee to guns to magic, with a good amount of armor and rings to support different builds. The combat is similar to Bloodborne meets SIlent HIll in 2D.  It's a bit slower and more methodical, and by the end of the game it's not very difficult, but it's fun to engage with. The plot is the only weak point, as it reveals itself rather early on and there isn't much that is mysterious or engaging after the early reveals. However there is a lot to discover here and if it clicks for you then you'll have a lot to dig into as you go through the game. From monster design to the overall aesthetic to the discover and combat, I absolutely love this game and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Silent hill, Resident evil, Clocktower.... Boil e'm, mash e'm stick e'm in a survival horror rpg where death punishes you with a new layout. This ABSOLUTELY gets a yes from me. Complimented with upgrades, items you can keep after death, equipment loadouts to suit your playstyle and great atmosphere and music. I just entered part 3 last night and still am not done with my first playthrough after the time i've put into this so far. There is a LOT in this game. So turn the lights down low, grab a Jill sandwich and take a ride into the Withering Rooms!

_childDocuments_.review: At first I thought this is something like a side scroller Resident Evil with randomization.Turns out it is much more akin to Bloodborne. The atmosphere is fantastic, the scenario is really weird but interesting (It does the "weird other world" style very well), the soundtrack and sound design is really good and I adore the way the areas change depending on your cursed stat.The only thing I would criticze is the unresponsive and floaty combat, which is quite bad for a game with that much fighting in it. Thankfully you can easily brute force your way through most of what I encountered so far by simply combining certain gear items and spaming healing items.Careful, it says "Roguelike" in the tags, but it doesn't feel or plays like one at all. You lose all non-important items (including gear) when you die but you get ways to permanently protect items you want to keep. On respawn all containers also respawn with random stuff in it.Edit: Finished it by now and, yep, really good game with combat that is not as good as it should be. Still fun, though. The story itsself was ... interesting. Sadly I can't go into detail on the world itsself due to spoiler reasons, but the scenario is an insanely good idea.It got a new game plus with some extra stuff. It doesn't force you into the extra stuff or upscaled enemies, the choice is yours at any time.A word of warning: The atmosphere shifts dramatically over the course of the game and loses a lot of its early intensity due to the combat focus (Monsters lose a lot of their scaryness if you hit them with an axe in the face). That is not a bad thing, it is just different.The same goes for the story. It reveals its core mystery early on, thus you know how but not why, which shifts the story telling dynamic and mystery.Edit: By now I somehow managed to get all the achievements after about 27 hours (according to Steam but I afked a bit). They were fair and didn't require grinding (it helped that you can do most endings in like an hour from start to finish in NG+). Just one particular monster was difficult to find as it seemingly shows only up randomly in a particular place.It was well worth it for me, but I am a sucker for creepy, uncanny horror, good music and soulslike elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: The game is full of soul: very cool horror graphics and a setting which changes based on your 'curse' level, interesting builds you can create: magic, melee, build, poison etc., and most importantly a engaging and developed story. Also, the game is not a roguelike in the truest sense of the word. I  would say it even encourages you to not die and keep playing on the same night. I think this approach also makes it more satisfying since you can stat planning your action before entering rooms. Also ,exploring besides the main story points rewards you greatly.Overall, in today's landscape of games that kind of feel like a do-over of another title, this game actually offers something fresh that got me hooked instantly. If you find the premise even a little bit interesting, I highly recommend it .
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that captivated me from the beginning was the soundtrack. From the opening title screen it lured me in like a moth to a flame. Also the controls and combat system is also easy to learn, but difficult to master. Absolutely surreal music and production behind everything audio in this game--from the SFX to the actual music and scary ambience. Since I'm in Japan, the out-of-this-world music itself just adds to the atmosphere and duality between fantasy and reality, which makes it even more surreal for me. There are also LOTS of subtle references to other horror games and franchises in the genre; Silent Hill, Resident Evil, Parasite Eve, just to name the big three off the top of my head. The combat, enemy AI, challenging but fair premises of the game is also a huge plus. The diversity with different styles and builds, elements, as well as the MASSIVE gear pieces one can attain with weapons, jewelry, charms, necklaces, amulets, armor pieces, etc is on another level.All in all, yes, I love this game and everything about it thus far. Reading the patch notes and changes the past almost year, it really seems that the game developer (YES ONLY ONE who is based in Seattle), really cares about this product and it's fanbase. This one single game developer and music producer just outshone multi billion dollar game developers and gave me a product that I immensely enjoy playing. The different builds and challenges are what will keep me playing for MANY MORE HOURS, possibly hundreds more. (take notes EA, blizzard, this is how you do it.)
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly didn’t expect this game to be much but I was so wrong. It’s phenomenal! So much variety in enemies, weapons, spells, etc. Very well done! Plays more like a metroidvania than a procedurally generated game (like Dead Cells, Hades etc) in my humble opinion but nails both for sure. Handcrafted too, not your run of the mill procedural crap. Interesting puzzles that had me go to Google but when I found out the answer, realized it was me and not the game! Still shocked at how well done the enemies are done. A lot of them have very interesting attack patterns, are visually pleasing, and some of them are spectacles! Just can’t say enough great things about the game, it’s absolutely worth it. Also, this isn’t your typical rogue-like where you will die over and over and over again. Not to say that the game is easy because the combat can be challenging but the runs are long and you’ll go a while before you die. In my opinion, it’s very possible to complete the game without dying more than a handful of times if you manage your inventory correctly and use the coffin feature. Anyway, just see for yourself if you are mildly interested in metrodvania/procedurally generated games with tons of variety throughout most aspects of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best souls-like sidescrollers and in general a fantastic game. Everything from the story, music, setting, progression, locations, and horror atmosphere is extremely well designed. Many take issue with the combat, and while it definitely feels clunky at the beginning it makes a lot of sense as to why it's designed the way it is. There's a decent variety of builds and weapons, multiple endings, and a substantial new game plus that has its own unique game content and ending. Fauna was right, this is truly the dark souls of sidescrolling horror roguelites.

_childDocuments_.review: Explore a mysterious mansion, haunted by strange friends and frightful fiends.  Enter unsettling alliances with the denizens of this twisted dreamscape.  Awaken from defeat to find the halls have shifted, the house now foreign yet familiar.  Crawl through filthy tunnels in search of cursed artifacts, but mind the ominous cost of the gifts they bestow.  Welcome to the withering rooms of Mostyn House.I enjoyed exploring the first floor of the mansion, finding a key that let me out into a dark courtyard area, and encountering a coven of witches that offered to recruit me.  I thought they seemed pretty suspicious, but they didn’t immediately attempt to slice me up like some of the things I encountered, so it may be an inescapable bargain to brave deeper into the mansion.  The foul denizens stalking the halls can be super menacing, very effectively sending a chill up my spine even when I think I’m safely hidden in a closet or under a table.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: I was lucky enough to be granted earlier access to the early access version of this game.  At it's core, it's a great rougelite survival game, featuring a few distinct "builds" you could focus on.  The complexity of the game continually ramps as you proceed, offering new stats to increase, new ways to level, and new areas to explore.  But really, the draw for me is the vibe:  Clearly the Clocktower influence is at play, but for me the biggest influences can be found in PS1 and PS2 era horror games like Silent Hill.  The story of the mansion and the characters within it has kept me intrigued for hours, as I continue to attempt "runs" deeper and deeper into the madness within.

_childDocuments_.review: So... I want to be guarded in what I say about this game. It feels like a good game, but it's not quite the game I wanted and expected. That doesn't mean it's a bad game; it just means I'm not the target audience. I started to lose interest as soon as I found the cleaver, the first weapon.I feel like horror games tend to go downhill when they give you weapons (that's my opinion, and you're free to disagree) because it reduces the power of the monsters and the fear factor they engender. I prefer games like Little Nightmares or Alien Isolation where the goal is to hide, distract, and evade. I was hoping here for more of a run-and-hide mechanic and wasn't really looking for a game where you had to debate whether the goal was to sneak around the monster or find a way to kill it. I'm not a fan of real combat in these kinds of games since I tend to find it unbalanced. Since this wasn't the kind of game I wanted to play, I felt my motivation wane to keep playing.I admit I did struggle with the keyboard controls, which I found hard on my hands, but I managed to get around this by using a controller.That said, the graphics are really good, the story is intriguing and the atmosphere is satisfyingly creepy. I'm probably not going to play much more right now but I might come back to it at some point. I'm planning on following the rest of the game on a 'lets play' but for the right audience, I think this could be an awesome game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a 2d Dark Souls or even souls-like. Withering Rooms is more like a very simple metroidvania in which you find the necessary item to move forward and do just that. There aren't really "builds" that you can do, you just switch for the better weapon (the one that deals more damage) and that's it. There's some magic but I found it kinda lackluster. The meat of the game, combat, feels very stiff and is not fun. Whack, roll, whack, roll, and the character feels janky. Withering Rooms might've been a decent game in a world where there is no competition in this genre. Here it's just not enough in any area.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly janky and horribly unbalanced. There is a mechanic in the 2nd half of the game that allows enemies to drain your max HP every single hit they do. To get your max hp back, you have to basically either die or restart your run, in a roguelite game, losing any items you haven't specifically chosen to save (you only get a limited amount.) I don't understand why the (solo) dev would in any way think that is a good idea to implement in a video game.The first 2 chapters were fun, the last 2 chapters completely invalidated that. The further it dragged on the more boring it became. The game should've ended upon leaving Mostyn House, the entire 2nd part of the game is legitimately bad to the point where I can not reccommend anyone waste their time with this game.Do not buy this game, it's just not good. Not even on sale.

Pressing TAB to get to the main map while paused still works so I'm using that. However, having the Minimap broken now is super annoying.
