_childDocuments_.review: Best way to describe it is: it's the love child of Dark Souls and Silent Hill carried to a term by a metroidvania surrogate. It shouldn't work, it should be a hot mess. But it's perfect, a perfect mutant child of disparate genres and I hope it has many similar siblings in the future. Hint hint Moonless Formless! If you struggle with those previous mentioned games with 3d due to motion sickness (or just wanting to murder the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera soooo much as you try to see past a screen full of giant crotch) but you still want something that feels similar - this is your game!Just make sure you do the main quests involving the basement as soon as you can. The game is not a lot of fun until you unlock the ability to level so BASEMENT! ASAP! Just hide and wait horror game style if you can't take the monsters - but don't delay on that objective, it's the thing that opens the game up and makes it fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to love this game soooooo bad.  Played for 13 hours and made to Chapter 3.  However, it turns out a played it wrong in that if you miss your opportunity to level up in Chapters 1 and 2, you miss your chance FOREVER.  I basically can't progress anywhere in chapter 3 because I am 1) underleveled, and 2) have no consumables because you lose them all when you die.  Literally can't make it out of the first hallway in Chapter 3.  I realize that "get gud" is the response here.  But this game isn't like that... it is impossible to not take damage the way that the combat system works.  Anyways this game was really fun and very addicting for about 13 hours and then I hit a brick wall.  I realize I could start it over again and "do it right" by following a guide or something.  But a guide shouldn't be necessary for a game like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is cool af! I really don't like roguelikes or 'roguelight's, but there are so many hidden mechanics, metroidvania elements, and such an interesting story, that I am hooked on this game. It draws a lot from the first four silent hill games. I love exploring the world. When you think you've done everything in an area, you find out there's completely new stuff going on and secrets to find. My favorite roguelight for sure. A GOTY contender in my book.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A nice sucker punch attempt by Moonless Formless to make a survival horror game with a rogue-like twist. I found a particular innovation to be very intriguing, namely the curse mechanic. I'm partial to having a "madness meter" that has a physical impact on the world like the one implemented here. Some more secrets and hidden paths while cursed were very neat ideas.There are a lot of thoughtful concepts that were poured into this game; some hit, some miss. I hope for a new instalment where Moonless takes what makes the game unique - the curse mechanic - and expands on it even more.Even though I enjoyed the game, I still wish it had some more voice acting, but you can't expect everything from an indie developer. Kudos to an interesting ride, and thanks for your hard work.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10,Absoulutely great game.It's been a while since the last time I beat a game in one playthrough. For most games, I just play a part of them, get tired, and abandon it until months later, but this game totally captivated me."To be honest, a game about main characters having to fight their way to find a way out of a dream world is not a new concept, but Withering Rooms still manages to provide a unique perspective and fascinating story. Witches and magic, guns and technology, this game combines two different themes very well, which provides players with a lot of play styles to choose from.Additionally, Withering Rooms has a new game+ mode, which allows players to encounter new monsters and delve further into the  later game , you can choose a dog to follow you and help you with combat ,you can even pet it ,what a good game!Overall ,it's pure fun to play Withering Rooms ,players of horror survival games would definitely love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Horror RPG that feels like a metroidvania with roguelite aspects including permanent progression. It comes with a slow, tactical approach to combat (I don't know if this will change later), stealth, solid atmosphere & mystery and fantastic music.This game is fun, unique and criminally underlooked. The entire first chapter can be played through the demo, lasting two to three hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Withering rooms is a survival horror, rogue and souks like metriodvania. You heard right, a lot going on but damn does it create something special. It took a few deaths for it's unique style to click but once it did the gameplay is hard to put down, incredibly satisfying. It's clever, ambitious, methodical, thoughtful and hand crafted design really pulled together something spectacular, especially from a solo dev. The side scrolling really allows this game to be what it's intended to be. If you have a love for at least two of the mentioned genres above, like planning and a critical thought approach to combat this slow burn is for you. I look forward to more in the likes of DLC. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game, acts like a bit of a mixture between a Roguelike and a Souls-like. My only real nitpick is that it's far too easy, you can essentially just out heal almost all damage, very easy to get coins to buy extra heals and once you get Ranged weapons, the game is a peace of cake, and there's only one boss in the game that I'd consider difficult.Despite that, I would still highly recommend this, fun game play, good story and decent characters, absolutely love the atmosphere as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Withering Rooms is an absolute gem, from its world building and story down to the gameplay, complexity and creativity. The eerie designs and outstanding soundtrack deserve nothing but praise. As a mix of Roguelike and Metroidvania, Withering Rooms finds the perfect balance between resetting your progress and permanent upgrades.The clunky, imprecise controls on the other hand made me curse so much it'd put the game's omnipresent curse mechanic to shame. Also, I was a bit disappointed by melee being completely inferior to a proper magic build and many items – armor in particular – seeming quite useless compared to others you might find much earlier in the game.Don't get me wrong, though. This is one of the best and most compelling games I've played in ages. I've finished it four times, got all achievements and unlocked everything, but I would gladly sink another 50 hours into it if there was anything left to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: With so many games looking for attention hard to choose but the reviews really sold me on this gem. It is as good as has been said. Then found out solo dev and am in awe. Even got me reading all text which I won't do unless its a great game. Even if you don't like horror or creepy imagery its worth it as it so much more than that. Cant wait for last chapter.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up on a whim for Halloween and I'm so glad I did. Fantastic game which is well worth your time. Amazing vibes and fun build variety. Combat takes some getting used to. Its supposed to feel sluggish because this game is more about resource management.  One thing the reviews rarely mention is how this game is way bigger than you first expect. Especially if you like to explore. Secrets, side quests, optional bosses, mini games and optional zones behind optional zones. You can beeline to the exit, get a full game and still miss some of my favourite parts. 10/10 would recommendTextbook example of a hidden indie gem
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I booted this up thinking I'd just try it out for a few minutes before getting to other games in my backlog, but Withering Rooms immediately hooked me. The atmosphere is great, with a wonderfully eerie soundtrack bolstering it, and the writing throughout is surprisingly succinct and gripping for it mostly being through dialogue boxes and item descriptions. The gameplay is slow and measured but that's obviously the intent; it's a little unforgiving but it's very fair and if you prepare well, as I did, you'll never experience any genuine frustration. Do yourself a favour and get this!!! Wonderful game
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible horror 2d, roguelite, vania-ish game. Anyone who's a fan of horror, grim worlds, souls games, etc. should absolutely give this one a play. The high achievement completion rate makes me think there's either not as many players as it deserves, or it's so engrossing that most people play through more than once.I really have nothing bad to say about it. The final "D" ending is very tough, as it requires an item that greatly increases enemy difficulty, but it's that much more fair and fun on a NG+ play. The lore is particularly fascinating to me. It all lies entirely within a realm of believable fantasy, set in the late 1800s and early 1900s. It's grim, dirty, bloody, scary for a while (and occasionally it ramps up again), and tons of fun.The music is absolutely on point, perfect for the periods it takes place in, and present/absent as necessary to set the correct moods. The puzzles are good, generally not too hard, not too easy. Progression is clear and delineated at no-going-back points. Body horror is all around, but maybe not to the extent of Silent Hill or something like that. It has its own 1800s rooted style that's very effective.It's got cute costumes, various builds you can enter into, respecs, arena mode to fight or practice whatever you want, extras for going above and beyond the normal playthroughs, all the things a great horror game should have.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I'll be cursed, this is really good. Lots of cool details, quite complex mechanically but the systems so far appear to work well together.Losing the inventory on death sounds like a really bad design decision, but nope, it's not a big deal and arguably works better than the DS-style system. Makes the resource management really fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: (Haven't beaten the game yet, I'm on chapter 2 at the time of writing this)Really cool and unique horror game. Has more of an emphasis on combat than a traditional horror game, and boy is the combat fun. It has a little bit of jank to it (in traditional horror game combat fashion), but not too much to the point of being frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've ever played for me, it's like it was made with my exact tastes in mind. If you love horror, souls-likes, metroidvanias and rpgs there's definitely something for you in withering rooms. I was especially surprised by how much i liked the story and lore which is usually something I don't care a lot about.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant game that introduces many new ideas, and surprisingly they all work. Every item is interesting in the game and evolves how you play. And there is a lot more in the game than expected.One of the more refreshing parts of the game is how death is handled to create tension. When dying you lose all items, but with enough exceptions the game doesn't lose momentum (you can avoid the penalty with bosses, and can choose items to keep). And it makes you feel alright splurging the many consumables the game offers to survive.More could be said, its a rich experience. if your on the fence the free demo basically lets you play the regular game for a good while!
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Only spent an hour, but was completely engrossed.  You could tell this was a passion project. The attacks feel meaningful and weighty, the gameplay is straightforward and tense, the story is well written.  I can't wait to play more.Edit: 10 hours in and it's gotten only better.  Will def attempt all achievements in this game at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Straight up, no chaser.  You drop 60 bucks on a game and you get some propped-up, stuffed shirt that gets boring in three hours or is littered with so many constantly revisited tropes and archetypes that have been boring you for ten years.  Then you get this game out of a bundle for three dollars and you immediately see everything that's wrong with the majority of corporate developers.  No ♥♥♥♥♥♥' love.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun, gem of a game. Starts off as a survival horror, where running and hiding are your best options, but slowly becomes an insane mini souls-like where your new goal is to become as overpowered as possible. Many different builds, dungeons that drop randomized loot (which, if you're like me, will keep you looking for the god-roll to push you from overpowered to broken), and a bunch of new mechanics that only reveal themselves in NG+ encourage multiple playthroughs. There's a little bit of jank; some animations are weird, dodging can be finicky, etc., but it is overall a very fun game.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I was going through my library and realized this game deserved a review.A very good little game. While the movement/combat feels a little bit sluggish, I pretty sure it's intended. The game has a Very good art style and a large variety of possibilities for different builds, and a great creepy atmosphere. Very much worth the price point.Also has a new game+ system going on if you want to get all endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Hidden gem, with tons of content (different play styles, lots of enemies with their gimmicks, a mysterious and interesting story and so on...). Furthermore the game is also challenging (through battles / bosses but also through puzzles)Lastly, the game encourages to do multiple runs to see different endings. Can only recommend !
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: The game is made for everyone. You can be terrible at action games, but still enjoy this game, no matter the difficulty. This is because this game has numerous weapons and ways to best the enemy. There are melee weapons, projectiles and magic. Based on your specialty, you can gain specialization in any of them. Although, it must be noted that, projectile is very useful where magic does not work. So, make sure to upgrade this. The game has good dodging mechanics and there are items that provide immunity to projectile damage. Although, I personally feel, melee attacks requires skill. I prefer magic and projectiles. Furthermore, before every boss fight the game allows you to save before a mirror, so that you don't need to restart the night. You can also use stealth to bypass enemy you don't want to engage with and there is a stick that makes you invisible. So this is the best action/horror game I've ever played, that balances everything well and is for every kind of player. It's just sad the game does not receive enough recognition. Maybe, if people like Markiplier or Pewdiepie played this game, people would have known more about it. The game lacks marketing and I came across it while browsing steam out of boredom. Not everyone browses steam. Most people buy games based on YouTube recommendation from YouTubers like Markiplier. Not to mention, Steam does not provide advertisement for small game developers. So, their product is less known. I hope, the company will improve the advertisement of this game, so that it gets easily recommended, without browsing. Using magic has some side effects. You get cursed and need to use warding candles to undo your curse. There's also ring that reduces curse. Getting cursed isn't bad though. To see certain things you need to be cursed. It is like Alice in Wonderland + Harry Potter + Silent Hill horror elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Great 2,5D horror game. The view from the side felt a bit off and I was hesitated to buy this game, but there is a demo. Downloaded it, fell in love and got the game.When you try it, don't get frustrated when you die. Some of your items are permanent and you can mark up to a few to be saved after death. Some enemies are not worth the hassle and running/hiding is nearly always an option.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily the best modern indie horror game I have played.  This creates a dilemma. If you’re looking for a 2.5D soulslike experience, this is not it.  The game's combat system emulates modern action RPG mechanics and real time combat (soulslike) but the hitboxes and hurtboxes are inconsistent and defensive maneuvers are unreliable, making this feels more like an RPG as you need to win by attrition.   If you want a modern indie horror game that offers something different from the typical digital haunted house experience, this game excels all of them while seamlessly incorporating David Lynch Twin Peaks era characters, classic art, classic literature, bundled with a flavor of legacy horror games such as Silent Hill and Clock Tower.  I love the style and art, and the nods to older horror games like Clock Tower and Silent Hill are well done. The combat is more engaging than in other games in the genre, though it falls short when compared to true action RPGs.  This is a great game in this regard.This game combat presentation is similar to contemporary game Corpse Keeper, which leans heavily into roguelike mechanics.    I like both games quite a bit, but this is the better game because it doesn't rely solely on flawed 2D combat.  This game roguelike mechanics are not that hardcore. Although I haven’t finished the game yet, I’d rate it somewhere between a 7/10 and a 9/10.  Regardless, it’s definitely a game worth recommending.  I can see this game easily standing the test of time, and getting direct or spiritual sequels.  It may not be a masterpiece, but it comes close.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I think I might have accidentally dampened my experience by building a magic character (which makes the game far too easy) but this is easily one of the best survival horror games I've played. Gets all the resource management aspects right which is always the most fun part of survival horror for me. Excellent atmosphere and music with fun enemy designs. Rougelite elements are incredibly light to the point where it becomes irrelevant but it does add a bit of extra tension to the early parts of the game which was fun. Understands that combat should be janky to create more tension. Highly recommend to any fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably one of the best horror games I've ever played, when it comes to specifically the horror. The atmosphere is done so well, the paranoia, the mystery from the story, the way curse interacts with your environment having you constantly questioning what is real even after dozens of gameplay hours. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game. The combat is extremely clunky and unforgiving, and the beginning of the game is really tough as a result, but it's extremely easy to be overpowered with a decent build, so the difficulty tapers off quickly once you start working towards something. Up until around late chapter 2/early chapter 3 is gonna be suffering though. Other then that, this game is just so good that I can't even think of all the ways I want to gush about it. If you like the atmosphere and themes that Silent Hill games give, you want to play this. This game also has one of the best soundtracks ever.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Great 15-25-hour game with replay value. If you like Resident Evil/Biohazard and if you like souls-like games to a light degree, this game holds a great place in the middle. My experience: I beat the game once in about 20 hours. While it is a "rogue-like" with a mechanic that resets all the mobs and the room locations for each area upon death, my only deaths occured in the first few hours of the game, where it definitely has the strongest horror, no hope, vibes. After that, due to the strong arsenal of tools and items made available to you, death is pretty avoidable, so I didn't experience much of the rogue-like elements. Even without resetting the mobs to grind items, money, or materials, intentionally, I felt myself a bit OP by the end thanks to certain projectiles and magic. The variety is great and they give you tools to deal with everything. Certain new mobs appear overwhelming at first, but quickly reveal a weakness. Bosses are where the game's difficulty really shines if you haven't drawn the right roll in a game of rock paper scissors. I almost died multiple times when walking into boss rooms too abruptly, but even then, the game has items to help insure you for death if you really want to throw caution to the wind.The plot is intriguing enough to keep me engaged and the multiple ending options are welcoming. Leveling up is satisfying and the items are intuitive and actually useful in most cases. The mini-map, fast travel system, weapon diversity, enemy variety, and creepy feel make the game totally worth anyone even remotely interested in either the horror, souls-like, or adventure genre. My ONE piece of constructive criticism, which may be a necessary evil, is that you (or at least I) had to constantly pull up the item wheel or inventory menu to craft or swap things in and out during longer battles and encounters. I found myself using everything I could to survive since death means resetting the dream, which I avoided like the plague. Pulling up the item wheel gives you infinite time to think and plan in high-tension moments and slows the pace and fluidity of combat, but I don't know necessarily know what would have been better than that for this game - it's just that it was a bit of a pain, at times, to have to constantly bust out the item wheel to see "welp what can I do now to live and beat this baddie...anything?"Long story short, great game, totally worth the time and money investment. Very satisfying, very fun, very creepy.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Withering Rooms is an extraordinary accomplishment, competent on virtually every front and excellent on many. This appears to be the first release by Moonless Formless, and one I'm confident players will cherish and remember. Hopefully there aHorror games rarely let you wear the face of the horror you fight and master its tricks. Withering Rooms does, and that's a major part of what's sold it for me. You can inflict the same horrifying curse rot you experience upon your foes, you can be the edgy little witch or blood gremlin and that rules, both from an aesthetic and gameplay perspective. You get to be powerful, but never powerful enough that you're totally without threats. Withering Rooms is incredibly fair to the player. Boss rooms have shrines that allow you to avoid fully dying if you lose the fight, fast travel is readily available, and resources are pretty plentiful. A first playthrough will be challenging, with several points where you need to adapt your build or your playstyle and learn how to deal with a troublesome enemy. Subsequent playthroughs are much easier, but between NG+, an arena that you can scale to your liking, and an artifact which activates hard mode, there's a ton of replayability and room for challenge.The real thrust of what made the narrative interesting to me are the vibes, the world, and the plotting. You don't encounter a game that successfully draws from Rule of Rose every day, but this Victorian nightmare in Wales does so brilliantly in the cozy, elegant furniture contrasted against the twisted forms of humanity lost. The function of the dream is fascinating to dig into, and for having clear influences Withering Rooms feels entirely its own. The strange political battles between major players in the dream especially stick with me.UI and UX are great. You'll be in menus frequently, so it helps that they're quick to navigate, easy to read, and a shortcut menu is included to cut down on interruptions. I encountered no noticeable bugs and just occasional framerate dips in rooms with lots of NPCs (only like 3 of these in the whole game). Most of the problems I ran into, like long walks back to fast travel mirrors, had solutions that I just missed.The only thing I can really be critical of is that the game occasionally suffers from how unique it is. Builds that depend on low HP or high curse involve a lot of waiting around that gets tedious. Magic and ranged builds can involve a lot of running back to vendors to get supplies, and the hiding mechanic almost never feels useful to me. There are often built in solutions to problems, signaling foresight on the developers part, but they're often enough bandaid-y like needing to farm randomized rings for a certain stat.Even after beating the game 3 times, Withering Rooms is still fun and I'm gonna keep playing it. I'd recommend it even at full price. There's more than your money's worth here and I'm confident this game won't disappoint.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: There's something very compelling about the whole survival not-quite-horror resource hoarding paired with the roguelite trapping and souls-y combat: You start off struggling, using everything you find to get a little further, to find more resources...and then you find a level up person, lock in a couple pieces of critical equipment that are better than what you start with, find more permanent upgrades, and suddenly the enemies aren't a trouble anymore. This cycle repeats a couple of times over and it's very satisfying to experienceGreat game, hope to find more like it
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves way more attention! Enough has been said about how it's a Metroidvania with Dark Souls/Clock Tower/Silent Hill vibes, so I'll just give you my overall thoughts about my experience so far:The story is unique, and dare I say Lovecraftian? Trust me when I say that the more that you play, the more intrigued you will be! You learn most of the story through documents, books, letters, and little things that the NPCs say, so it's similar to Soulsborne games in that sense. Without giving too much away, the sense of progression in this game is great. There are many viable builds you can put together, with tons of different pieces of armor, weapons, and rings that you can find all throughout the map! Also, The music and graphics are really well done. I hear a lot of Silent Hill/Resident Evil influences in the soundtrack. It has its own flair and style though. The graphics are charming, and the overall level and character design is excellent! There is much more variety to the levels than I ever could have thought when first starting out.Honestly, the only downside to this game that I can think of right now is that the combat is pretty damn clunky. For better or worse, it reminds me a lot of early PS1-era survival horror. That being said, your character is literally a young girl, so it kind of makes sense that you wouldn't be very good at fighting! All in all, get this game and stick with it for an hour or so. Once it clicks, you'll be hooked - trust me! Great job, Moonless Formless! I'm a fan!
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'll try not to spoil too much, but I'm at a point now where I thought I was at the end of the game and ‘rushed’ my melee build.... now a new area has popped up and the mechanics and builds are starting to click for me as I unlock more and more gear.  The story has also evolved in ways I wasn't expecting. This game really is a breath of fresh air in how it combines different genres and mechanics. In my opinion it's not that scary, but the atmosphere and setting are great and completely satisfying. For me, it's not as clunky as some reviews claim - it really reminds me of Dark Souls 1 with its tempo and animations - in a good way! So yes, grab it and enjoy this familiar yet very new gaming experience. As a wise man said: Müsst ihr ist.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game punches well above its weight in scope and originality. For those with roguelike fatigue give this game a chance. The mechanic feels more like an additive instead of a forced feature. The eerie effects they implement alongside a curse stat is great and made me jump more than a few times. If you enjoy spooky atmospheric games with a bit of action this is definitely one to check out.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: To note, this game is ROUGH. It clearly is a indie game and I've actually soft locked myself once while playing due to being 'too good' at it. Regardless however. I find this game's concept and ideas quite interesting. The game play is somewhat clunky, the puzzles however are expertly done and require actual thought when they aren't simply math related. The only major issue is the combat, which can be rather repetitive if you just decide to stab everything to death with a kitchen knife rather then engaging with the stealth mechanics. The issue with those being you can only properly level and get stats through killing monsters, so sneaking by anything unless its to save resources is quite useless. The story and world they build is interesting and very dark, and the mechanic around being Cursed is something you actually must manage, as you can miss secrets while not cursed, but items are more common and places to hide are plentiful.Overall, the game simply needs polish which it seems to be getting through frequent updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A shockingly rare treat. It plays more like a metroidvania than a true blue roguelike but there are elements of a roguelike inside it. Not a jumpscare horror game but rather a survival horror with a scary ambiance. It has a good story sprinkled in bits throughout the game which requires the player to slowly piece everything together. Overall a great game that currently stands unique in the market.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: If you told me that one of the best games of the year is a 20+ hour epic, survival-horror roguelike, with interesting story and branching choices with 4 different endings ―accompanied by Soulslike combat for good measure― and all of it done by a single developer. I'd tell you to start taking your meds again
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game on a lark due to it's great horror themed trailer, cheap price, and desire to support a solo dev and I think this is lowkey one of the best games of the year--definitely the best Indie game, and I have a hard time seeing another game top it.Made by one dude (with music and voices provided by others), they simply get what makes a game like this fun. It's a love letter and fantastic expounding upon Castlevania, Soulsborne, and other rougelite indies without feeling derivative in the slightest. The game can even be a little frightening despite the "cheaper" look, with devious uses of the 2.5D perspective; when it first happened (you'll know it when you see it) I was cackling alongside the dev. Just great, smart stuff.On the surface, it's not something I would typically want to try: the cheap look, the rougelike tag on Steam, the animations and models looking a bit stiff or canned. The horror element is nice, but is that enough to carry a $25 game?What a fool I was. Smart uses of the 2.5D--and later, fixed camera--perspectives made even the strongest run a little tense, never knowing if I'll get bled too quickly or find that ring I really wanted last time. The scares were smart; the hiding mechanic is fun; the story was well written; the music was fantastic and varied; the enemy designs were amazing; the rougelite elements were LIGHT but impactful... I could honestly go on for pages about every little thing I loved but that's boring. The amount of love, polish, care, and expertise that went into this (surprisingly long and varied) indie is a new bar to clear. The only reason I'm not giving it a perfect score it due to some unavoidable rougelite tedium and a few bugs, including one that's preventing me from playing it on NG+. Hopefully it gets patched soon because I'm dying to see all the new toys and enemies Moonless Formless scattered.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Best indie game I've played all year and for that matter in a good while period. Basically gave me the vibes of a roguelite sidescrolling version of a mix between Bloodborne and the American McGee Alice In Wonderland game. If that combination sounds appealing to you, then definitely give this game a go. I was very satisfied with my purchase from beginning to end. The story is really bizarre and intereting, the art direction is awesome, the soundtrack is a total vibe, and the overall gameplay from the puzzles to character customization is overall solid and satisfying. I think the only real complaint I have is that the combat itself is a bit janky, but I kind of get the impression that might've been intentional so as to emphasize the RPG aspect of it more by making it really difficult if not seemingly impossible to avoid attacks from certain enemies (particularly late game) and in turn forcing you to level up your character's stats to better deal with them rather than relying on skill alone. In other words, I don't really see how (despite it having a Bloodborne vibe to it) someone could possibly do a no-hit run in this game. Anyways, despite that rather minor complaint, I again really loved this game and found it to be a total gem and really impressive quality for an indie game from such a small studio (I actually don't know if this was made by more than 1 person total besides the voice actors...if that's true, wow that's impressive). All in all, definitely my indie game of the year for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: So this game has gone from being completely unknown to me, to a game that I picked up in the steam sale that has quickly become one of my favourite games of all time. I'll admit, Silent Hill 2 is my favourite game of all time, so I definitely fall into a bit of a niche and this game was basically made for people like me, but that doesn't take away from just how good this game actually is. Great story line, solid game play, interesting roguelite play loop, great character design, great audio and pretty much everything else about this game is great... Combat can be a little frustrating at times and I've definitely lost my cool more than once, but with so many different ways to play the game there's always a way around something. The only negative from me is the terror mechanic. If you become terrified there's basically no counter, your character just runs around screaming getting mercilessly pummelled by enemies until she dies. Luckily this doesn't happen too often, but it's a majorly frustrating way to die, especially when you're carrying loads from a successful night. The game won't be everyone's cup of tea, but it is definitely mine... It's also set in Wales too and even has a lot of Welsh language sitting in the background which is pretty epic. This is the third (technically fourth) horror game I can think of that's set in Wales - Koudelka, Maid of Sker, Sker Ritual and now Withering Rooms.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Not really a roguelike. Not really a horror game. Actually a souls-inspired ARPG. Extremely, comprehensively janky in a good way; even though the game is fairly easy combat always feels like a scramble. A lot of really interesting and well-designed systems. The big weakness is the weak writing- the story is actually very interesting and has a lot of cool ideas but it's largely told through dialogue and found documents which are just flat-out poorly written. With a script rewrite this could be one of my favorite games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is made with passions and lots of love. You can see the limitations due to budget but still the quality of this game is top notch. Truly one of the best rougelike-horror game out there. - The model, atmosphere, themes and settings are all beautiful and dynamics. The game will immerse you into its own world.- Fighting mechanics are quite janky. It could use some more refine but they are super entertain nonetheless. The game gives you tons of options so that you can build your own doomgirl.- Story itself is the gem. Complex but worth following and entertain. Will make you scratch your head at first but then you will easily connect all the dots. - The puzzles are not hard at all. They only require you to pay a tiny bit of attention and read the requirement.- There aren't a lot of dialogues but most of them are decent and they give you pieces of story and lore.- Voice acting are barely existent but the game doesn't need them anyway.- Sounds in this game is really good and quite memorable. You know it's a good horror game when the game utillize good sounds to scare you instead of only using cheap jumpscares.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting to get so addicted to it, it's amazing in many ways, and didn't made me run to try and get a walkthrough when I was stuck, actually made me want to discover the secrets and puzzles. Also...  the candle being able to clean your curse levels, is that a Silent Hill 4 reference? If so, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a refreshing face, a mixture of horror (but not that scary, more of dark "vibes") and combat. The game seems clunky at first but develops more depth as you go in, its clunkiness has a sort of charm seen in older games. The roguelike elements are pretty light, you lose most everything upon death and reset and all rooms reset and move around, but the types of rooms you'll see are consistent. Its one of those games where you slowly build into your preferred playstyle instead of a clear "pick this if you want this playstyle". Having beaten the game and gotten the "true ending", I feel like there isn't much as much replayability as a true roguelike, as this game is meant to be a long playthrough to get through it once, and subsequent playthroughs are a little faster, but you still have to go through some motions to progress the story (including watching cutscenes and talking to NPCs and doing their quests, solving the same puzzles) which detracts it from the roguelike experience. As a game and experience as a whole, I'd say it is pretty fun and challenging, though perhaps overstays its welcome just a little bit. Dying also feels very punishing in the sense of being time consuming.I'd give it a 7.5/10, definitely a unique game and story that's worth a full playthrough, but imo doesn't offer enough incentive/QoL to warrant repeated playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful ❤️love letter❤️ to the "Survival Horror" genre like the old Resident Evil, Rule of Rose, Eternal Darkness and etc, mixed with Rogue-lite elements...I can only see this game getting more attention as it is very well crafted with love and care 😇The beautiful Victorian horror lore and gameplay elements are seamlessly combined, which encourage you to adapt your build, tactics, and manage resources in different ways. Some say the combats are clunky, but I feel it is intentionally designed so to force players to do the "resource management" which is one of the essential elements of the "Survival Horror" genre.You're not going to beat the bosses with "level 1 deprived build", like souls-like just with pure player skill (Don't get me wrong, I love souls-like), but rather with long-term skills of resource management decisions and wits/knowledge.What are you waiting for? _childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. I don't know where to begin to sing its praises. The game is a lite rouglelike mixture of your average survival horror and metroidvania. You can finish the whole thing without dying. Very easily, actually. The game gives you lots of options to survive, and if you are still struggling, you can just grind your level until you are strong enough to brute force your problem. The game is also very generous with the items and equipment drops, which I like. Not everything needs to be "dark souls" difficult. Some balancing needs to be done on the second half of the game, though, imho. The story punched way above its weight; I wasn't expecting anything "deep" or big, but the more you play and uncover, the more interesting it becomes. I really enjoyed the world and the lore they created, and I think that was the main thing that grabbed my attention when I played the game. There are lots of endings that tie up the whole plot in whatever way you feel satisfied with them. Combat is clunky and slow, but I like the way it feels. You have to dedicate your character to an attack, and learning how to survive against enemies is fun. Luckily, the game has lots of different enemies to deal with, so you can have new challenges before the whole thing becomes stale. The soundtrack is nice, nothing to write home about. It matches the atmosphere and makes the experience better, so that is all I could ask for. Overall, I am very happy with this purchase. I would recommend anyone give it a try, at least. If the game doesn't grab your attention in 2 hours, you can always get a get a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant and unique take on a horror roguelite. It takes the best aspects of a roguelite - the massive replayability and different builds - and mixes it with an interesting story-driven game, creating a perfect hybrid that feels like a usual adventure game from time to time but with a twist. The game is divided by chapters, once you advance a chapter you can't go back, and there's a loop mechanic (hence the roguelite). If you die you'll lose every item that is not permanent and the map will 'shuffle' itself, but you easily can do a deathless run if you're careful, the game is pretty generous, giving you so many tools to help you. The combat itself is super fun, it's very reminiscent of a soulslike with the dodges and attack patterns, there's a bunch of different status to get used to, and sometimes you'll be able to adapt and cheat bosses by abusing your gadgets. You can do a mage build and invoke a bunch of guards while burning everything, you can do a poison build and slowly watch enemies die, you can do a melee build and bleed enemies to death, you can do a projectile build and shoot everything. The possibilities are great and they all feel powerful once you get the strongest strategy and upgrade the right attributes.The main plot of the game is a bit convoluted but I enjoyed it, the characters are very likeable, there are tons of plottwists too. There are 4 different endings, a good amount of side quests and the game rewards exploration with special items and bits of lore. It's definitely a horror game too, some segments are at least spooky and all of the designs are gruesome, enemies vary from zombies-like, monsters and even ghosts.The visuals may seem a bit dated, but I enjoy it a lot because it reminds me of old PS2-era games like Haunting Ground. The sometimes janky feel of the game seems to fit on this aesthetic too. The sound design is awesome and the soundtrack works a lot creating this oddly specific vintage dream-horror atmosphere.I cannot recommend this game enough, it's very fun and way too underrated. It's not that kind of game that'll change your life, but it's a memorable quality time with lots to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely recommend this game and its soundtrack! I should note that the game has an unbalanced gameplay that can lead to overplaying due to boring running around and abusive battles, so it's a diamond in the rough! What I mean about the combat system is that the game allows you to suppress monsters with your power, followed by repetitive restoration of HP and curse. This is boring and needs to be replaced with more understandable and polished fighting techniques! Also, in my opinion, there is a lack of consistency in visual styles - there is not enough correct dosage of cosmic Lovecraftian motifs, Alice Through the Looking-Glass, dark fantasy and so on! I like this game and that's why I wrote a lot of criticism! This is an original and in some moments brilliant game that will definitely leave an impression! The game has several endings, a huge number of items and mechanics, and there is endgame content (Game+ and not only)! Thank you for these emotions! I wish the developers to achieve a level of excellence in their next project, as their hard work cannot be overlooked!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games ever made. It is an absolutely incredible experience that I would highly recommend to anyone seeking a content-packed masterpiece of atmospheric horror rogue-lite with clever but workable puzzles and souls-like combat elements. I cannot express my praise and admiration for this game enough; I am obsessed with it. I have no idea why no one is talking about this creative genius and his fever-dream of a game!Pros:-Very dark and creepy atmosphere-Best insanity (curse) mechanic I have seen in gaming-Loads of secrets, including meaningful NG+ content-Large boss variety-Good souls-like combat and build variety-Creepy awesome lore-Go from survival horror to creepy power fantasy*Phenomenal concept and achievement, especially for a solo devCons:-Combat animations and timing are a bit janky (if you're making a souls-like, you want this to be extremely tight)-You tend to either be completely underlevelled or massively OP.-Some items seem purposeless eg. Troy's Head (I could be at fault here)-Would benefit from high quality voiced NPCs (it would improve the atmosphere)-Losing all your stuff is terribly disheartening (you can get it back if you get enough curse)-Toward the end, the looting gets really boring.Overall, I adore this game, strongly recommend it and I gleefully look forward to seeing this developer's future work. They have a real gift.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts out feeling like a horror game like Clock Tower, hiding from enemies and sneaking around to avoid them, having them chase you through multiple rooms as you desperately try to find a hiding spot, finding and using items to distract and avoid monsters.Then you find some weapons. Weak weapons at first: a cleaver, some throwing knives, a few bottles of acid. Though weak, you may cleverly use what weapons you find to take out one of the larger monsters using hit & run tactics. Maybe kill monsters that can chase you while avoiding ones that can't leave their room. So it starts feeling less like Clock Tower and more like Resident Evil, going from horror to survival horror with smart use of items to take out your enemies.Eventually, you gain the ability to level up your stats. You start finding armor and rings with stat bonuses catered to certain playstyles. You find different weapons with different movesets, and material to upgrade your gear. The mask falls off: this is actually an action RPG. Farm some materials and spec into a build, and soon those monsters you once ran away from now melt on the spot to your +3 harvest spell. Not like Clock Tower or Resident Evil, more like Salt & Sanctuary without the platforming. On reflection though, that transition from helplessness to almost overpowered worked quite well following the traditional survival horror power curve, and the horror aspects helped add to the tension when encountering new enemies your build might not be strong enough to face head on.Overall, a thoroughly enjoyable and interesting horror-themed 2D Souls-like.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a hidden gem and will probably be the best game I end up playing this year. Like with a lot of modern games there is obviously some Dark Souls inspiration here (no surprise), but what makes Withering Rooms unique compared to similar games is how the game is fully designed around it's very punishing death mechanic.When you die you lose most of your non-key items, which includes weapons, rings, spells and consumables, and additionally every room you explored get shuffled to a different location. You can save some of your items between lives by finding and activating blood shrines, but since item save slots are limited you are going to have to make some tough choices on what you think you might need and what you are willing to lose.I have a feeling this mechanic has already broken many players item hoarding habits, because while item stacks only take up one save slot, even valuable consumables like healing have to considered against items that are important for your build. The fact that you can't save everything plays a significant role in how you play the game and even how you build your character.Beyond the gameplay, while some of the art has a "stock asset" feel I still feel the art is not bad overall, even in the situation that some of the assets weren't made in-house. Also the story is good, and despite being a story game I feel it's very replayable, to the point that I'm considering replaying it myself after I'm finished.One problem I have had with the game is the performance. The game runs fine most of the time, but I've had some bad framerates occasionally, even in places where performance drops shouldn't happen like the menus. Lowering the graphics to medium fixed the problem for me (although that didn't work the first time I tried it.)Overall, it's a unique game with a punishing, yet well thought-out death mechanic. I strongly recommend it, especially if you like challenging videogames but don't want to play another generic "Souls-like". It's more unique than something like Lies of Pi, which while I felt was a good starting point for a Dark Souls inspired game to be more than just a ripoff, I feel Withering Rooms has more of the originality that I want to see from these types of games.-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------edit: At the time I wrote this review I had just started chapter 3, and while I still feel what I wrote holds up I forgot to talk about the horror aspects of the game. Honestly I didn't feel the game was all that scary at the time. The later chapters definitely bring out more of the scariness, and there is a good ramp-up to it as well. By the end of the game I was experiencing more dread and paranoia, the best comparison being Silent Hill.Despite this, I feel the story gets a bit too campy towards the end of it. Up until chapter 4 I was actually pretty invested, but near the end I stopped finding the characters and plot in general to be very believable, and additionally I thought the ending decision was a bit forced. Ultimately I still like how the story was presented, and since the credits list only one developer I can't say I'm not impressed with it anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: There are not enough words in the English language for me to adequately express the reasons as to why you, the reader, should buy this game. As of the writing of this review, I have 44.5 hours on record, and I have barely scratched the surface of everything this game has to offer.. I am on my first NG+ playthrough, with many more to come, as there are multiple endings all entwined together through the story's "multiple timelines" narrative. Having said that, let me delve a little deeper as to the reasons why I've been playing this game obsessively. Picture Silent Hill, but with an RPG twist, with some Dark Souls mechanics and story-work, and rogue-like elements, all packaged up in a neat little bundle with quaint yet effective graphics that draw you into the world with a rich story and themes.The rogue-like progression is rewarding - it's not too long after being a lost lamb in the world struggling to beat up one single enemy that you are handily dispatching those that would give you a fair deal of trouble mere hours ago. But don't get cocky, because just as you feel ready to take on the world and the gods themselves (literal gods), someone comes to slap you down and remind you that you are just a cog in the machine that is this game. Not egregiously, mind you, but just enough to send you back to the spawn point. And as to the death mechanic...After each death, you are revived in a designated safe room with the rooms and item boxes/items re-arranged. What you keep on you after death depends on what you've remembered at the few remembrance shrines throughout the game, and those items help you to get further as you progress through the levels. A not-quite unique, but very well executed mechanic. The story is rich and deep, revealing more of itself in subsequent playthroughs through notes, NPC's, as well as new NPCs on subsequent playthroughs that further extend the story. The end of the first playthrough is not the end, as I'm discovering, and there are many more locations, almost a game within the game, after you've reached the end of the first "iteration" (that word is gonna come up a lot in the game).The NPCs are fairly milquetoast, though with stories of their own that tie into the greater world that the game presents. The combat, depending on your playstyle, is either really bad or okay. You have a number of ways to deal damage; melee, projectiles (guns, bombs, etc.), and spells. All of these can be replenished through a crafting system introduced a little ways into the first playthrough, and you'll find it exceedingly useful, as some healing items can be crafted as well. The enemies you use these weapons on are varied and creatively put together, coming with their own bestiary entries wherein one can find their strengths and weaknesses. Due to the rogue-like nature of the game, as stated earlier, enemies that once terrified you and kept you from exploring a room or area for fear of dying, can be brushed aside some time later after leveling and/or attaining new equipment.Oh yeah, and there's a leveling mechanic, too.This is, despite it's length, a very brief explanation of the game for the unititiated. For $25 full price, it's worth it. On sale, it's a steal. Buy it, play it, love it.

_childDocuments_.review: I tend to gravitate towards run-based roguelikelike type games. The Silent Hill-esqe aesthetic drew me in and the metroidvania style progression kept me coming back.  You will gradually unlock shortcuts to various areas of the house, the rooms of which are scrambled after each death.  The combat feels very slow and almost Dark Souls animation priority methodical. Your character is not a powerhouse, though through upgrades and spells you can definitely hold your own.  I'd say this is a vibes game first and foremost but it has enough interesting ideas and tweaks to the run based genre to be worth a look, even if you're someone who has hundreds of hours in dozens of other run based games.  It doesn't have the tail of most of the other heavy hitter games of the genre, but I am enjoying my time with it and am even pleasantly surprised by the story threads that pull the progression along. It's definitely made me realize how much more room there is for horror in the procedural run based space.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely feels like something made from a solo dev lmao, but it's very charming like a 2.5D version of the kinda horror game thing you'd find while browsing randomly on Newgrounds back in the day and get captivated to try and complete, which I'm currently in the middle of chapter 3 so my view may change at the end but so far its been a fun time for what it is.Well worth your time at full price and definitely for sure on sale if you can look past the gameplay jank and how brutal the first few hours are until you figure out how combat is supposed to be handled and start getting the tools to really mitigate what you lose upon death (and you will die. a lot.)EDIT: Finished my first run after about 12 hours and I still stand by my recommendation. _childDocuments_.review: Don’t usually write reviews, but this has so few, it’s criminal.It’s 2.5D horror side-scroller with genuinely superb occult world-building (with things like opening and closing any door 3 times moving to a secret room). You explore the environment completing objectives, doing side-quests, acquiring items and lore, and fighting creepy monsters. When you die, the layout changes (a bit) and you keep quest items and equipment that you mark (a certain number) for the next run. Story is surprisingly engaging so things flow forward naturally in-game.A lot of credit has to be given to the developer for implementing a host of “anti-frustration features” that do not make the game easier, but simply prevent one from throwing their controller while playing games in general. You can keep an increasing numbers of items from one run to the next. You take a lot of damage but are reduced to 1hp and given some invulnerability on the final hit. The environment is not fully random but semi (you always know where everything is) so that makes exploration genuinely worthwhile. Puzzles can be skipped with a purchasable item. The dev clearly plays a lot of games, and should earn this game an easy recommend.One area where you shouldn’t go in expecting much is the combat. It’s surprisingly clunky with slow animations, zero hit connection on enemies and very little feedback.- Anti-frustration features- Superb, genuinely interesting occult world-building.- Great variety of items and enemies.- Good visuals.- Super-clunky combat

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid gamer with a penchant for both the eerie and the intricate, my time wandering the shifting halls of Mostyn House has been nothing short of captivating. Developed by the solo dev powerhouse Moonless Formless, this 2.5D horror RPG masterfully combines elements from classic survival horror with modern roguelike mechanics, offering a fresh yet nostalgic experience.Graphics and Atmosphere:The game’s Victorian mansion, with its beautifully rendered, ever-changing layout, offers a sense of dread and anticipation with each new night. The Unity engine brings this dimly lit world to life, with shadows and flickering lights that keep you on edge—a perfect homage to the genre's roots.Gameplay:Withering Rooms is challenging, with a steep learning curve that respects the player’s ability to adapt and strategize. The mix of weapon gathering, artifact crafting, and real-time combat encourages a tactical approach rarely seen in today’s faster-paced titles. Each playthrough feels unique thanks to the procedural generation, ensuring that no two adventures are the same.Inspirations:Withering Rooms intricately weaves together the essence of various gaming genres and eras, creating a rich tapestry that appeals to both nostalgic players and modern adventurers. At its core, the game channels the atmospheric tension and intricate level design reminiscent of early survival horror games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, where every corridor turned could lead to sudden terror or crucial resources. This hybrid approach is further enriched by a crafting system that nods to the resource management found, where players must think critically about what they carry into the shadows. Additionally, the game’s use of magic and artifacts introduces a layer of strategic depth akin to the spell and item combinations, encouraging players to experiment with different approaches to combat and exploration.By blending these varied influences, Withering Rooms not only honors the mechanics that have shaped the survival horror and roguelike genres but also evolves them, offering a complex, engaging gameplay experience that challenges players to adapt and overcome in a world where the past haunts the present.Conclusion:Withering Rooms is a testament to the creative heights one can achieve in indie game development. While it may pose a considerable challenge, the thrill of overcoming fearsome foes and unraveling the mysteries of Mostyn House is immensely rewarding. For those who cherish the thrill of classic horror mixed with inventive gameplay, Withering Rooms is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally do not write reviews for games, but this one was so good that it would be a disservice not to. Withering Rooms is a truly fantastic game that pulls from many other games and genres while maintaining a wholly unique feel and aesthetic. It truly excels in all aspects in a way few games do. The gameplay is fun and engaging (though it may feel a bit "jank" at first), with many ways to build your character. The aesthetics are great, as the already interesting Victorian mansion gets twisted into a nightmarish space by your rising curse. The music is one of a kind, the normal tracks slowly becoming more strange and esoteric as the world around you does. The story and worldbuilding is top notch, and made me want to know what was going to happen next and how my actions effect the world. Additionally, the characters within the world are great, and have their own intersecting motivations and schemes that are only fully revealed in the later stages of the game.Overall, this game is not just good, it is an underrated masterpiece. I would highly recommend buying this game at its full price, it is more than worth it and you will be supporting the work of a developer who truly made an amazing piece of art.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a masterpiece, and one to not sleep on if you are a fan of horror games such as Silent Hill, or a fan of exploration games like Castlevania/Metroid (Metroidvanias)! Mix those together, and that is what Withering Rooms is! It has been a long time since I have tried to get every achievement in a game on Steam, but I couldn't stop until I got them all for this gem! I just finished it up, and I honestly wish there were more! I am a HUGE fan of this game, and the Devs did a terrific job! Big kudos to them, you should be proud of yourselves!I went full melee in all of my 5 playthroughs, and I can tell you right now, it can be difficult. I am not one to play Souls type games, but for some reason, even though the combat is very similar, I COULD NOT stop playing this. I am pretty inclined to try building a ranged loadout, as well as a magic one, just to see how powerful those builds can be, and to see how they play out in combat. I have read that both of these builds are easier than melee, but I went with melee to see how challenging the game could be, and it really can be rough at times. Luckily, you can create a sort of save state before boss fights, so you can gauge if you are strong/skillful enough to get through them without having to lose progress. This is a great touch, and adds some accessibility to Players.I wanted to know the story, and then I wanted to know how each ending was. Getting Ending D was a CHALLENGE, and I am glad that there was end game content that made you work for it. I DO have to say though, I wish the endings were a bit longer. For how rough it was to get Ending D, I really was hoping that it was going to be jaw dropping. You DO learn some more lore, but it is basically as short as the other 3 endings. That's ok though, it was worth going for it just to see how challenging this game can be, as to get it, you have to "Burden" yourself, which makes all the enemies in the game much, much harder, as well as add a new threat that hunts you down.The atmospheres are very creepy, and when you become a certain amount of "Cursed", the environments change from lit and sort of peaceful (for the most part), to grotesque and eerie. This is why I compared it to Silent Hill. It just has the vibe of when you hear the siren go off, and everything around you changes. As for the "Cursed" status effect, think Eternal Darkness, but on a smaller scale. Not a bad thing at all, but Eternal Darkness REALLY messed with your head in so many ways. In Withering Rooms, being too "Cursed" not only changes the aesthetic of the game, but also causes creepy noises to be heard, and little things like shadows appearing in the foreground, and it can really mess with your head in tense moments! LOVE IT!There is a lot of equipment in this game, and all of it can be very useful in how you build out Nightingale. There are melee/magic/ranged weapons, and then you have offhand items (such as shields, or items that are helpful like a lantern), talismans, rings, headgear and outfits. Each of these give stat increases that can change how your loadout works, as well as negative effects to balance them out. Some may grant you a percentage increase to melee, but also lower your curse/poison/bleed/etc. resistances. It is imperative to pay attention to what you have equipped, as lowering a status resistance too much can be fatal! Curse by far is the worst to have low resistance to, as being too cursed gives you a status effect called Curse Rot, which not only drains your health, but also prevents you from performing certain actions, or using certain weapons/items. You are also able to level up gear and such to a total of +5 once you get certain items, and these levels make them more powerful.You level up in this game, and can allocate points towards permanent stat increases. There are multiple ways to go about leveling up, in the form of different offerings for different NPCs. It gets much easier to acquire these items once you have played through the game at least once, BUT the caveat being you can only level up a certain amount of times before you must finish the game. After finishing the game, you can level up more, increasing your chances of survival on each new playthrough. I was around level 120 when I finished earning my last achievement. There is also an NPC that can be found that allows you to respec, so if you want to change up your build, you just have to pay a small fee. I am glad this is an option, because in the beginning of the game, you really need to spread out your stats. Once I got use to the game, and got good melee gear, I re-allocated my points into things like melee power, health and speed.If any of this sounds like your kind of game, I HIGHLY recommend getting it! I definitely got my money's worth!

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. It's sort of a mix of the really old Clock Tower and older Silent Hill games. The story is a bit esoteric and the setting feels more like the main character than the people themselves. I finally completed it last night and felt a bit sad that it was over.Only cons I can say(which aren't cons to me) is that the combat has some serious old school jank feeling(Dark Souls or modern RE game this is not) but that just made the game feel even more special to me. You will take some hits in combat, and the magic system is really cool in the sense that you have to trade your sanity as a cost every cast, while also trying not to hit your limit(and avoiding enemies that also hit your sanity). The only actual con I can think of is how there are these weird hard item limit caps where if you have X amount of items you can't buy more(which seems reasonable) but that limit seems to also include if said item was used in the crafting of something you currently have. For example, for magical crafting items, it seems like there is a limit somewhere between 15-20, but even if you have 0 in your inventory, if you have casts made and queued up for a magical spell that includes those reagents, tough ♥♥♥♥ you can't buy them. This does result in a bit of tedious backtracking to go buy some more after you blow your casts.Even saying that though, if you like weird/spooky settings more than "scary" or jump scares and a penchant for older horror games. This is a no brainer. Initially the price tag turned me off, but by the halfway point when I realized the game was far longer than I thought, I didn't regret the purchase at all. Pretty sure this is like a solo dev mostly too. Just a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game and would highly recommend it if you are into horror games with some Bloodborne and American McGee's Alice flavor thrown on top.The game has a decent enough story with a world that remains largely interesting throughout. Most of the NPCs and locations are enjoyable, though I do feel later on in the game the npcs begin to feel more lazily implemented. In the first half of the game, NPCs generally have several topics they can discuss, but by the second half of the game nearly every NPC you talk to will only say one sentence or essentially say "I don't have anything to talk about"/"I dont want to talk" when choosing the talk option. I feel there was a lot of missed opportunity with NPCs and how they interact with each other, and its a shame that I didn't feel the same enjoyment from the world building in the second half as I did in the first.The game is labeled as a "Roguelike", but I question if it was the right decision to do so. The game is barely a "roguelike", and it's more of a linear narrative game where it has a lose-progress death mechanic similar to a typical From Software Title. The game is broken up into a few chapters called "Nights", and each one acts as a narrative gate to the next section of the game. Upon death, most of your items are lost and any progress you made throughout the specific night/chapter you are on will be reset. Some players might find this to be a punishing mechanic, but  it can truthfully be circumvented rather easily and you will reach a point in the game (very early on) where unless you AFK infront of an enemy, it will be nearly impossible for you to die. - There is an item that you can buy to revive you when your health reaches zero. This item will always be restocked by the shopkeeper that sells it anytime you lose the one you have. You can easily run away from any danger the moment you lose the item due to revival and immediately buy a new one. This alone makes it not possible to die to normal mobs.- Every boss room contains a candle that you can light. If you remain in the room with the candle lit, if you die to the boss you will immediately revive at the candle and lose zero progress. You can keep relighting the candle and reattempting the boss as many times as you like with zero consequence.- There are so many healing items in the game and nearly every single one of them will be infinitely restocked at shopkeepers anytime you run out of them. Add on to this that the game pauses anytime you open inventory, and you can just about always safely select the healing item you need and use it without being punished.- There is a mechanic to select items that you desire to carry over into the next night. By the end of the game you can easily have over 25+ items that you selected to be basically "permanent" items. Equipment/weaponscan also be upgraded and when done will mark that equipment as permanent as well.- Add onto all of this, the procedural generation that happens between nights is very lite and doesn't alter too much besides loot drops and maybe some mix up to the ordering of rooms in a single hallway section of the house; however the general layout of the house is the same, enemy placement is the same, npc placement is the same, etc. So there is very few surprises that can catch you offguard when restarting the night. There is also a mechanic in the game that lets you restart/loop the night to farm items whenever you want, so you are guaranteed to always have an endless supply of items that you need. I looped several times just for the sake of seeing if the feel of the levels were the same, and they indeed were.- Even if you do manage to die, the game has systems where you can find loot from a previous death when opening chests. Though this is tedious as it is luck based and random, so youll have to loot through several chests and potentially loop the night a few times to get everything back.With all of this, it basically makes the "roguelike" aspects of this questionable and feels like its more of a time-wasting mechanic rather than any meaningful roguelike mechanic that serves to alter or strengthen the enjoyment of the game. I truly believed this game would have benefit from changing this mechanic to drop your items on death and you can make a death run to retrieve the items, similar to running to collect dropped souls when you die in Dark Souls. I think this would feel less punishing for people who struggle with combat while also retaining the spirit of the game without need for wasting players' time. That being said, I only ever died in the first chapter of this game, and afterwards I never died again. By the end game I was so broken I could kill the hardest bosses in the game within a handful of seconds without them even laying a single tick of damage on me; so all of this is didn't really affect me and is a minor nitpick overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Rare is it that I review games on steam. Withering Rooms deserves it. I've not finished the game ( taking my time on Chapter 3 out of, I believe, 4 ) and am impressed beyond all rational doubt. It's a WitchSim, it's a Soulslike, it's a Metroidvania. Those are titles I would apply to the game, but it feels unfair to categorize it in such a limited way. Withering Rooms has its own identity, and I strongly recommend that anyone with even a passing interest in the Horror or Weird genres pick it up and play it.Fascinating story, gratifying mechanics and unapologetic style. I love this game.If I had to pick on something that I disliked, it's how melee combat feels and works. I think the game was designed with magic in mind - and that's fine and good - but melee builds feel a little more limited in their scope despite a number of items doing their best to prop it up.... But given that I find the magic so fun to use, that's less of a negative and more of an augment to how I play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The store page here doesn't really do the game justice: there is a lot to love here.Sort of a souls-y side scroller with some stealth/horror mechanics. Where the game excels: there are countless ways to solve combat problems. It's almost never right to just run in and start swinging at an enemy, the game incentivizes you to try to use your massive tool kit of consumables, equipment and spells.The actual hand-to-hand combat feels clunky and unfair but once you get the idea that you gotta use your items, things get easier. I think there's a really unique game here that deserves more recognition.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most beautifully crafted games I have ever played. The atmosphere is the perfect amount of creepy, the weapon choices vary and the lore is deep. Withering Rooms takes some of your favorite horror aspects from Resident Evil by giving you a room system that requires the player to return to previous locations in order to proceed in the game. They manage this all while making it a rogue-like. If you die, the rooms and loot are randomized, this sounds unbalanced but it works beautifully. I don't write reviews, but seeing this game with only 500 reviews is criminal. Seriously, give this game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Where to even begin with this one. I had no expectations going into it. My brother recommended it to me on a whim. Initially I treated it a stealth horror game because that's how it starts. You are a fragile young girl with a meat cleaver and there are undead horrors about. I now play the game more like elden ring, wandering around the manor and surrounding wilderness and vaporizing anything that looks at me wrong. The story is the type where the more invested you are and the deeper you look the more you'll find to like. It's a good time and a fantastic cosmic horror story.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure if this game was gonna be worth $25, given how it looked like a quick, short game about a witch being lost in a mansion. Turns out I was very wrong. The game is deceptive in the beginning but as you play, you'll see the world and gameplay expand like crazy. You'll get a good idea of just how big this game's world is by looking at the Bestiary count.The best part about the game is that it's actually really fun. It's a rogue-like side-scroller with somewhat janky movement, but the amount of weapons and spells you get, as well as the buffs you get from various accessories and items, make this game almost too addicting once you're hooked in.Definitely worth the $25.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Only 3 hours in and i'm hooked.It's a very good mix of the old Resident Evil game (fight and resources management) on sega saturn and Dark Souls mechanics (NPC interaction, questing and resources management)-The atmosphere the art and music is on point.-Resources management and crafting is fun.-Merchant and 'service providers' is fun.-Cursed state mechanic. Fun and challenging to balance your cursed level for benefits.-Gimmicky items and tools to extend your survival, run away or win a fightThe fighting is a bit stiff but as i said it is a reminder of the feeling of stress you would get when cornered in that old Resident Evil game.Every night that you die you lose everything but your level. It permanently increase the game difficulty (more/new ennemies) but there is a game mechanic where you can save a pool of items and equipment. This pool can be expanded and there is some way to reset your night without dying, at a cost, until you die for good then it reset the cost.Also there is some permanent equipment unlock and mechanics unlock that persist throughout your runs.Don't miss out on this one, even at full price. If you are a fan of roguelikes and Dark Soulish atmosphere/mechanics this game is for you.Also there is lore.-Lore?-YES. LOOOOORE.
