_childDocuments_.review: Whenever I get tired with the lack of creativity and originality in the gaming industry, something like this comes along and breathes life over me - and more importantly, the industry itself. Whatever expectations you have for this game from looking at the clips/screenshots/description, I PROMISE you they will be vastly exceeded.PROS. Stunning visuals. Gorgeous / horrific enemy and character design.. LOTS OF DIFFERENT ENEMIES that really showcase the devs imagination. . Similarly gorgeous and horrific environments, equally as varied.. Very clever and immersive use of lighting throughout the entire game.. Wildly Unique and engaging story, told 66% by dialogue and 33% by lore fragments throughout the environment. Just a general weird kooky unique vibe to everything.. Great quick-button system. Story mode for those who are ♥♥♥♥ at combatNEGS. Weapons / Spells / Armour / Modifiers are WAY too varied. This may be a plus to some but I feel like they could have narrowed down all of these a fair chunk without it affecting freedom of combat in the slightest. It makes inventory management clunky.. Inventory management is clunky. Skill tree is similarly too varied, ties in to above.. Could be deemed unfair and punishing by some.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Tier (higher is better)GS | Withering RoomsA-Amazing game. Really great use of limited resources - considering that it was made by ONE PERSON - and also a great story and a really fitting soundtrack.This game is action-"horror" + rogue-like random level regeneration / partial resource loss on death (but you can incrementally save more resources each death and your character stats / your game quest progress are saved) + souls-like combat elements.It has unbelievable depth and is addicting as heck to play.It boggles my mind that this is not more popular.Also of note it HAS an alternative "story" difficulty option for those interested.Video on store page misrepresents the vibe and feel of the game a bit; it has great, varied and melodic music, and is very cozy.If you want to know how it actually looks and feels, I highly recommend watching your favorite streamer play the first couple of hours (I was instantly hooked).In my opinion, one of the best true indie games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic Roguelite (there is progression)+ Great story+ Fun combat mechanics with pros and cons via the curse system+ A large amount of possible builds, all involving melee, magic, or projectiles (i.e. guns), and all fantastic+ A respec system for leveling+ Lots of deep little secrets+ Longer than you'd think it would be+ Post game content in form (currently) of the Burden book (hard mode)+ A True Ending. Don't look anything up until you finish the game the first time.+/- Melee very taxing early game, but this is mitigated mid game where you unlock stronger level up options- Projectiles unavailable until mid-late game. I'm betting this was not initially available in Early Access and then became an idea later.I would love to see more of this. Looking forward to yall's next game, if yall make one.
_childDocuments_.name: Withering Rooms

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. Level up, collect outfits, cast spells, find a build that fits your play style, and explore a mansion of insanity. When you die you lose anything not bound to your memory and wake up from your bed. Some items are bound by default, and you can unlock a crap ton of slots to add more things to your memory. The game has 4 endings and a NG+ and a massive amount of side content that you can sink a lot of extra time into to get a lot of stuff to help you beat the game. Overall a good time for the player and a terrible time for Nightingale.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Easy recommendation to anyone who thought that the store page was worth glancing at.It's like a side-scroller with elements of resident evil, silent hill, bloodborne, little nightmares, and more than a handful of other cool ideas.The game encourages you to tackle its problems with whatever mixture stealth, skill, and/or tricks you want as exploring its world will continue to provide you with new active/passive tools to try out. The sheer amount of options seems to provide as much build variety as Dark Souls although with more limited move sets. However, the choices actually feels interesting AND the game has QoL features to make swapping between them trivial, so you can easily experiment.It's also a roguelite but they do some pretty interesting things with what it does with it.Like they have mechanics for making retrieving anything you lost easier, you get the ability to craft items which will let you save things between runs so that your build isn't destroyed(the above things are also thematically appropriate).Also, my favorite feature that sold me on it after the monster design is that casting spells is strong but has a cost of both crafting components AND you acquire corruption. Get corrupted enough and you start to die, HOWEVER, the more you're corrupted, the more the world shifts around you ALA Bloodborn's Insight system.Even after 19 hours of play, the game is stays fresh by offering interesting places to explore, monsters to vanquish or get murdered by, and even some new mechanics occasionally. Also, even though the character has powered up, it still feels like a survival horror game, which addresses my main complaint with the Resident Evil series where it shifts from a B horror movie to a B action movie half-way through.I definitely recommend it to anyone interested in it and I think you'll learn whether you like it or not well within Steam's refund window.

_childDocuments_.review: By now I've finished my first playthrough, and I'm already starting my first NG+ run, so I've figured it was time to write a proper review.  Withering Rooms is a strange and obscure blend of genres, from survival-horror, to a slightly soulsy action RPG, a metroidvania with a slight pinch of rogue-lite and quite possibly the most underrated game ever made.  But I still don't really know how to approach a review for this game. So I will try to get the elephant out of the room first. You will probably see the screenshots, and maybe see a trailer. The game certainly may not make a good first impression, it looks weird and janky, and well, it is. I won't try to convince you otherwise but for me it was part of the charm once you get into it. But this certainly not one of the games from the endless dump of asset-flipping indie horrors on steam. Discovery and experimentation are what, personally, is the true joy of Withering Rooms. So Describing the game pretty much feels like spoiling the experience.  The thing is, this is a decepively mechanical game. In fact, I could probably spend a whole paragraph explaining to you how doors work and the unique interactions with other systems and the emergent gameplay possibilities. Or the rest of this review  rambling about the clever Curse ‘resource’, one of the games main risk-reward mechanic. While not quite an highly systemic game there are many emergent gameplay elements present, it encourages you to be creative and try different things.  Some of these mechanics the game will tell you, others you will maybe find out experimenting on your own. That being said, it is entirely possible to play this game in what would be the equivalent of the ‘Dark Souls, two-handed greatsword for the entire game’ approach. But I still think the best way to play it is to just do a bit of everything and not be afraid to experiment and use your resources.  This is a permadeath game, but not as punishing as the label expects. There is a lot of permanent items and character progression, with a high degree of player agency. But still, I've learned that you should definitely, play it safe and approach resources with a ‘you use it or you lose it’ mentality. This is a survival-horror game, after all.  There is a also a great amount of content here, with a lot of side content, build possibilities, variety of ‘biomes’ with different mechanics and the huge amount of unique enemies with varied weaknesses and strengths. It is very rewarding to learn and explore the world, adapting your play style to each situation.   There is also the story, which is a delight in it's own right. I also won't say much about it as I feel just talking about it would be a bit too much for this review, the other reviews have described the appeal better than I can. What I can say is that it's told in a surprisingly straight forward way, with characters and clear development of the world. The world has strict rules and finding out about it's inner logic is honestly fascinating.   The fantastic atmosphere also helps, the game has definitely has a cool vibe, with great horror moments and timing. It has caught me off guard a couple of times, but also knows how to pull  back to relax  and have some fun. With over 100 unique tracks the music also sets the tone perfectly.  It also has a substantial amount of quality of life features, avoiding a lot of what I can vaguely describe as “indie roguelike ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥” of annoying or frustrating design, most of these features getting unlocked and expanded as you progress. On top of that there are fun NG+ hooks adding to a great amount of replayability, there is a whole lot of game to this game. This review has gotten way longer than I thought, so yeah, that is what I can say is Withering Rooms. In more simple words, it is my favorite indie horror game ever made. Confident, weird and unique, but also, extremely addicting. I've been playing games for over 20 years, and sometimes it feels like the magic is gone, this game is for me a reminder of the joy in all of that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly cool. It takes familiar aspects from a large number of games and weaves them into something that seems largely unique. I would call this a roguelite, horror-inspired action rpg. The horror is constant and heavily themed, but without the obnoxious scoring or spooky jumpscare nonsense. It steps back and lets the atmosphere do the work which I appreciate immensely (partially because sudden loud noises kinda make me jump. I think it's due to living with somebody who is chronically ill)The models and textures can look rough at times, but I feel like that's a reasonable complaint to have of an early access game. There is a lot of love and character in the designs and environments that shine through regardless. The roguelike elements aren't too abrasive, and you can do quite a bit in one playthrough if you're familiar enough with the mechanics. You can actually pick and choose a limited amount of items to keep so after enough progress you're barely losing anything on a per death basis. The rogue aspect seems to almost exclusively refer to loot drops and enemy respawns which, I'm fine with. It feels like it's more preoccupied with being an entertaining game moment to moment than with the microprogression familiar to the genre.Combat is kind of... strange? I think it's because they're trying to do a metered, weighty attack system in a two dimensional space. normal enemies have stagger windows, and you can dodge and block with varying degrees of success. I still haven't found a counter for the charge move that is alarmingly common in one of the later areas of the game but perhaps there's a specific item to address that. The sanity gimmick is pretty interesting and I like the real time changes in the scenery. The amount of time put into the transitions and the characters and the (kind of sparse?) but interesting seeming lore shows somebody cares. Rather than slapdash taking horror meme fodder and throwing it in the game, the world and environment actually feel semi cohesive. It borrows aspects of clock tower, silent hill, and soulslikes without ever feeling like it fits comfortably into either of those, while having its own unique-for-the-modern-era victorian style to it. I like collecting clothing and weapons. Dressup for any game is a plus and I think shows how much effort the developer is putting into the game.I haven't finished the game yet but it is promising for what it is, and worth it as is.

_childDocuments_.review: Withering Rooms presents a masterful synthesis of Survival Horror and Souls-like RPGs with a dash of randomness and an incredibly compelling story with expansive and interesting lore. The atmosphere is fun and spooky while still carrying dramatic weight, and the safe room tunes are as good as any classic RE or Silent Hill entry's.Sure, there's the occasional bug (and the game crashed on me maybe 6-8 times in my ~25 hours of playing), but the design and vision of the game are sharp and more than make up for these technical shortcomings. Withering Rooms has the makings of an underappreciated cult classic, but I hope it finds a greater audience because it's really something special.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has had considerable updates since my initial review so I'm updating it.I love this game, it encourages you to solve combat through smart means. It's not until later in the game will you be able to survive trading blows and even then it is one of the more resource draining processes. My favourite method of dealing with foes being cursing doors and then luring enemies through them.The major letdown in combat are the boss fights and [spoilers] the Arena [/spoilers]. You are forced into direct combat and especially with the later bosses there is next to no chance to break combat. The saving grace is that there is a checkpoint system that allows you to attempt these  fights meaning you can still try alternative ways to fight bosses. There's a bestiary, lore and a pretty good story now with 4 different endings. There's plenty of secrets and puzzles. There's an array of outfits, most of which provide different bonuses and drawbacks.Moonless Formless has continued adding to this game after the 1.0 release. New outfits , weapons, enemies, bosses, areas and even a new ending. They've added groovy features like being able to save loadouts, a respec option and a way to make the game even harder should you wish it( with some exclusive rewards).The amount added , the fact that they're always on top of bugs and they're pretty active(both on steam and discord) leads me to believe Withering Rooms is worthy of a labour of love nomination!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I can't recommend this game enough. It offers alot of content and doesn't cheap out on anything, except of maybe the cut-scenes which nobody really needs. Check out my Let's Play on YouTube here: Withering Rooms claims to be a Roguelike, Soulslike and Survival Horror game... which is all true, and exactly in the order stated above. Primarily Roguelike, then Soulslike and then Survival Horror.There's a plethora of monsters, weapons, equipment and other items. Countless consumables, rings, amulets that should be switched around, depending if the enemy encountered poses a specific danger. You can save a handful of outfits to quickly change them and quick-equip everything through selection wheels in game. That and opening the inventory THANKFULLY stops the game, leaving you time to choose what exactly you want to use, even in combat.Dying resets the rooms and respawns everything, as well as loses you all items except for the remembered and permanent ones. Some items you'll just always have, and you'll find more of them. For others you have activate shrines, letting you remember more and more items as the game continues.The first thing I chose to remember were the "Strange Coins", and I never regretted it. It's a currency that is going to be important up to at least chapter 3/4, where I'm currently at.There's boss fights in Withering Rooms, but in each of their rooms there's a shrine where you can light a candle for instant respawn, without any item loss. So while the fights can be pretty hard, that is VERY fair. Just don't forget to re-light the candle if you leave and re-enter the room before fighting the boss.Dying is something that I did no do alot in this game. I died two times, both due to my own stupidity, but you can generally avoid death if you're smart. Later you can buy a brooch that saves you from dying ONE time, then destroys itself. But you can buy it again afterwards.Nightingale (the protagonist) has also stats that influence the gameplay, and can be leveled up through various parts of the game. Each chapter seems to have a level cap and you can choose where your focus lies: melee, magic, ranged, resistances, health, etc. You CAN RESPEC your stats in the Byzantine Labyrinth, which is an area that you can access from the 2nd Chapter onwards.I can't recommend this game enough, as I've been surprised more than once by the sheer amount of enemies, items, mechanics and the game length itself. name: Flashback 2
detailed_description: Flashback Music for Cloned Memory, A Flashback Tribute Album Listen to Music for Cloned Memory, A Flashback Tribute Album About the Game TOTAL WAR HAS BEGUN... RISE TO THE CHALLENGE! In 1992, Flashback revolutionized action gaming and gained legendary status, ranking among the 100 best video games in history. Today, Paul Cuisset, the creator of the original game, invites you to play again as Conrad B. Hart, the young agent of the GBI (Galactic Bureau of Investigation). In the 22nd century, the peace of the United Worlds extends throughout the Solar System — but this tranquility is threatened by the Morph invasion led by the fearsome General Lazarus. In search of his lifelong friend, Ian, and with the help of his few allies — including A.I.S.H.A., his iconic AI-powered weapon — Conrad, once again, dives into a heart-pounding adventure full of twists, turns and revelations! A gripping, fluid and intricate platform shooter, including exploration, puzzle solving and, of course, adventure! FEATURES Immerse yourself in a vibrant sci-fi/cyberpunk universe and visit multiple environments (New Tokyo, New Washington, the Jungle...) Use A.I.S.H.A., a lethal adaptive weapon enhanced with combat AI. A gripping, fluid and intricate platform shooter. A 3D environment for even deeper immersion. Designed and developed by the creator of the original, Paul Cuisset. The cult game is back with a boost. A thrilling and intricate action-shooter. A potent and adaptive AI-powered weapon. A sci-fi universe true to the original Flashback.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has several problems at release date:- Constant frame dips, dropping from 120fps to low 40fps on  AMD RX 7800 XT (and 60 fps to 30fps on a Steam Deck).- Aiming is terrible, very hard to hit targets properly.- Game has side scrolling sections, but we still need to move back/towards the screen to interact with buttons (and aiming is really difficult in these sections).- Voice acting sometimes mixes Conrad's voice when NPC's speak.- Character animations don't look great.- Conrad keeps talking to himself about everything, really annoying (but it might just be me).I love the original Flashback, but this game is too buggy and performs too bad without reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of the original Flashback. It's one of my all time favorite games. I was looking forward to this sequel for a year. To say I'm disappointed is an understatement. I never request refunds for games but I just did for this.Pros:- Cool environments, ambiance and music. The title screen brought me right back to the original Flashback. The graphical style is great and exactly what I wanted from a modern sequel.- Campy dialogue and story. Yes, the writing is bad. But I like that the game doesn't take itself too seriously. It's fun, and IMO better than trying and failing to be dramatic or self-important.Cons:- Horrendous controls. Honestly, this is the ONE thing they should have spent significant effort to get right. Controlling your character was the best part of the original. Crouching, rolling, shooting, jumping all felt fluid and fun. Combat was exciting and challenging (especially with the force field). Unfortunately, controlling your character in this game is literally the worst part about it. It feels like you're moving in thick mud. There is no pulling out your weapon, ducking, rolling and shooting like the original. Jumping is not precise and too dumbed down. Aiming your weapon is awful. Combat is easy yet somehow still frustrating. How did this control scheme get past alpha testing?- 2.5D. I can't tell you the number of times I've gotten stuck in a door or on some object while trying to navigate the world. You can't even see what you're stuck on a lot of the time. I don't understand why they didn't just make this 2D movement inside a 3D environment. It would have been so much less frustrating.- Game breaking bugs. Multiple people have reported issues with the Amy mission that makes it impossible to progress. I thankfully didn't hit that issue, but I did hit the one in Titan Corp factory where the game just becomes unresponsive. Honestly, I could forgive these issues in a brand new game if quick patches came out that addressed them. However, what truly makes these bugs unforgivable is the next issue...- Inability to use save points more than once. I can't believe I'm even typing this. Yes, it's true. You can't use save points more than once. I don't know if this is an intentional design or not, but there's no indication in-game that this is the case. So once I used up all my save points I literally could not save the game again. Which meant when I hit the Titan Corp bug, I had to redo all my progress up until then. I did this twice until I just gave up and requested a refund. How did this game get past even rudimentary quality control?I'm so upset by this game. There is so much potential here with the graphical design and the built-in nostalgia from the original. But it's been completely ruined by fundamental control issues and fatal bugs that make the game literally unplayable. I may give this game another chance in 6 months or so, but for now Paul Cuissat and Metroids's reputation have been tarnished forever in my mind.

It causes weird situations when you stand right next to a wall in a moving elevator- Vault triggers don't snap your character to an object you need to jump over- NPCs have a reaction to aiming the gun but have zero reaction to a bullet impact, lol- Character avatars are too simplistic and yet at least some of them are definitely AI-generated- Character doesn't have a proper blend for leg animations during aiming- Lags badly every few secondsIt's a huge amount of not just low quality development but a development with no experience at all. _childDocuments_.review: I loved the first Flashback, I liked the Remake but this game is some sort of mistake. It has to be.First things first.Gameplay:It wants to be something but it is nothing. No adventure, no action, no puzzle game. There are nearly no riddles, no jumping or running sequences like in the first game. Okay, it is Flashback 2 and not 1.But most of the time, you are just fighting one of 5 enemy types. Boring Arcade like you just shoot blind and kill everything with hell of hits. The special ammunition is nearly useless. To difficult to aim, to slow to fire. If an enemy comes near you, you kick instead of shoot him. Does it do anything? No. Just hinders you in shooting. The shield or the armor you find is not necessary.Aiming in the game is some lucky punch for himself. Because of the 3rd dimension, you can't really aim. It is not precise enough. But some kind of autoassist helps sometimes.But the 3rd dimension ... the game would be better if it stayed in complete 2D. If you go just left or right, everything is okay. But nearly everytime you walk to the front or the back, you have to struggle with clipping, hanging on objects, getting stuck in and on walls, railings or even on stairs. Not even the enemys are save. They often hang here or there. Their legs are stucked to ... something. It is horrible.To mention the story. It seems they did not know what they want. They start it, they change it and change it again. They try to make some philosophical makeover and put it down very fast. After that, there is some kind of save the nature but it is cut of as soon as it arrives. Most of the time, you have the feeling there were more than one storywriter and no one knew of each other. Not even in a single chapter, the story seems to have some sort of good structure. Like you take some idea for the story, write it on an napkin, make the game and never wrote more.The graphics are not noticeable. Mostly just over blooming lights in some kind of cyberpunk scenery. The portraits in conversations could be done by an AI and don't even move or transport some kind of emotion. For this kind of low quality, the game runs highly unstable. I didn't had any crash but the loading times are quite long, people just plop in, random stuttering and often some kind of glitches at the NPC clothes.The sound is okay, most of it is just stereotype nothing. The synchro in the story scenes is okay, no specials and not the worst. Synchro in the normal game is emotionless. But it appears so random, how should anyone know which emotion it should have.The one who thought the controls would be good or believes that the only option in this game has to be DLSS on or off button (which is obviously not doing anything in the game), should be giving me money for playing this game.The controls don't let you finish the game. You just have one button for all the "key items" in game, but why can't I control which one is used? You have to use the correct item at the end and you only can push the down button in hope the correct comes up. Even the hint textbox says you should push the left button but this don't do anything. Even the text box knows how stupid this is but no one listened to it. Most of the walkthroughs or lets plays stop before coming to this section because they can't show the end.If you have read till this point of the review, thanks. And know that this piece of game is not even worth 5 bucks. It makes me sad because I loved the first game so much. But playing this was a horrible experience. No one ever tested the game before release, even 5 minutes of playing would have made this game a far better one or kept it from releasing. Full price is a pure rip off. Paul Cuisset should be ashamed of this. And whoever thinks this is a good game, never ever played an even okayish game before. Over 6 hours in this and you'll know what it means to waste time.

_childDocuments_.review: My God, I don't even know where to start... But I'll try.I love the old, first Flashback (not that one remaster on new platforms!). I've tried to play Fade to Black and 2013 remake. And here we are - Flashback 2. Game that I was at the same time afraid to wait since announcement and desperately waiting. And, sadly, sequel (actually, kinda prequel?) is bad. Bad in so many ways, that it's shocking me. It has not redacted AI generated portraits\cutscene sprites and maybe textures with that ones artefacts like strange lines, broken ears, weird hair. At the end even show sprite of main character from the side and it was like some other character wearing Conrad's clothes lol.Artstyle is generic. Music is generic too. Narrative (plot and texts) too and, I suppose again, made with AI. But I have more important things to say:Microids, many years ago you tried to make Flashback 2 on GameBoy Advance. Even has some prototype. The game looked and played like the first part... WHO ON EARTH APPROVED THIS THING THAT YOU RELEASED IN 2024???  It's so far away from everything that fans of the first game loves. Okay... For some reason you decided to change genre and overall vision. But can you make it with WAY LESS bugs and not that run of the mill experience overall? Game is sometimes broken, unoptimized bunch of lagging bugs nearly without interesting level design and game mechanics. Funny thing, that I'm not hate this game. Just very confused by many decisions from the devs (reference to PS3\Xbox360 horror Amy? Seriously?)And, most of the time, was bored.This game is for that one braindead gaming session where you want some "eatable" singleplayer game with storyline and you don't know what to play. Few times was laughing by absence of characters reaction to anything dramatic that they witnessed lol. And portraits again, yes, they are hillarious.Again, this is that rare case when I wish that the game would be better (perfect case scenario) or way worse up to the point "so bad it's good"But game has some okay-ish moments: more or less I like jungle and final level, idea (not implementation) of  plot twist with that multiverse synchronization of two Conrad's. And french voice acting makes even this type of games way better than it should be. Sci-Fi cyberpunk cliche-aesthetic is a win-win situation and first rides on a bike. Few lines between Conrad and his girl was cute and funny about pheromones and heartbeating analysis from Aisha, AI-powered gun and assistant of Conrad.Like... This game HAS something good, but all of this stuff is buried under lack of care, love and inspiration. Don't know why Paul Cuisset treats his most successful game in that manner. He has some interesting games in 80s and 90s, but something happened later. It feels bad to witness this in realtime. I played the demo and was horrified by the performance and gameplay, but still bought the game at full price. Knew I probably wouldn't like it, but I guess I had some hopes? Also the fact that I'm very fond of French science fiction and especially what came out of Metal Hurlant\Heavy Metal magazines also played a role: Moebius, Christin\Mezieres, Jodorowsky, Bilal, Manara, Druillet. Flashback 2 gave me this vibes sometimes, but it is at the same time very cool and very sad. Cool because all this stuff mentioned right above this block of text and very sad - not that great, when you play the game and wanted something better after you complete the game. I know that this project cost money, but maybe it would be better to at least make it as original title? Because I wanted to say "why this project was not canceled?", but devs need to make some money from the project, but leave another stain on this "franchise" is... Ugh... Nevermind.Like, dudes, you can't even properly remaster the original game nowadays. Who told you "hey, Flashback 2 is a good idea"? And who tf agreed with that..?At the end want to ask one question:Why you develop this game in-house? You have The Way by Puzzling Dream, LUNARK by Canari Games and even something way more obscure like cringy DreamBreak by Aist. And bunch of other developers that was inspired by Another World and Flashback who made 2D sprite cinematic platformers. But Microids decided to develop this game on their own. With that design, technical state and other things that makes this game "mostly negative". Sequel to THAT ONE game from Amiga\SNES\Sega about rotoscoped dude with a holocube. Most iconic game from this designer. Just. Hire. Motivated. Talented. Fans. !!!Comedic levels of absurd.

_childDocuments_.review: I let nostalgia get the better of me and brought it on release.  It looks cool and although making it 2.5D is a little confusing at first it makes larger areas look and feel great.I like the hacking minigame.But.-The aiming/shooting lock on is horrible, especially on flying enemies.-Select is pause menu and Start is Inventory (seems a small thing, but it's very jarring). You also can't use d-pad for menu navigation.-There's virtually no options so you can't disable any of the HUD, which pretty much surrounds the screen.-You can't turn off tutorials either, and every time you get on the bike they play for about 10 seconds each!-Speaking of the Bike.  Why?  You have to drive around a circular highway to move locations, full of cars and bikes which move all over the road and drive in between lanes.  If you hit one it stops you dead, but there's no damage and you can smash into them as much as you want.  It feels like you're just moving a sprite left and right on a scrolling road (very 80s).-Quite bad stuttering in places.-Glitches and bugs that cause missions to not progress.  The auto saving is sporadic, so I lost 45 minutes of gameplay because I couldn't even load my previous save when a mission got bugged, because halfway through the mission I was on there that one got bugged every time.-Save points might be bugged, some seem to only be able to be used once, saving mid mission normally bugs the mission.There's a fair amount of stuff that can be made better, and I really hope that the team can make some changes and improvements quickly.  But I am also worried about the fundamentals of some parts.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played less than an hour so far, and while there's a lot of great history with this title, this iteration feels very rushed out the door, and a lack of updates since Jan 2024. I tried this game out on a Legion GO, as I felt that it was at the same visual quality to games I've played on it, but frame rates were hovering around 25fps most of the time, with peaks to the low 40s. This really should be worked on asap, as it's what's hurting this game the most. The UI is ok, but sometimes feels inconsistent, and not well represented on handheld displays.  It could really use some subtle animation during static frames to breathe more life into it.The overworld bike driving feels incomplete. The current bike system could be made to work, but it needs a lot of polish and more mechanics to make it feel engaging. I'll probably play a bit more to see if there's anything outside of this, but overall right now - it may be hard to keep interest and see past the flaws. Some of the graphics here are pretty good for the gameplay, but the mechanics and depth leave much to be desired.This game could have a lot of potential. Even with the indie vibe to it - I like the artistic direction for the gameplay, but the foundation really needs a major upgrade.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this out of love for the original. I feel that its still possible to salvage that feeling with optimization and fine tuning controls a bit. If this is V1 of the release, I'd hope a future patch would help course correct this into a better place. One of the best parts of the original flashback was the linear side scrolling and interactions across the gameplay. The addition of the 2.5 space being able to move forward and back in side scrolling introduces a new level of frustration thats not overwhelmingly welcome. In larger environments this is fine to allow for more movement and level of granularity, but in tunneled left and right movement, needing to move back to hit a switch is an unnecessary addition. Devs, please take note of comments of optimization for the game and controls and you may buy back some nostalgic love from users. Flashback (1) had some of the smoothest animation from rotoscoping and to allow for something that is not nearly as streamlined as that, is not helping. I would not recommend it in its current state, but am hopeful that fixes come along to rekindle my love for it. Time to go play the original again.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy this game at all costs, but currently, there are quite a few flaws, and the gameplay is not very good. It's a hastily programmed game with some glaring deficiencies that make you long for the original 1993 game. For example, it's not possible to remap the keys (why?), the saves are sporadic, and the actions to be taken are very repetitive. The aiming system is terrible, the animations are clunky, and the graphics are barely acceptable (with noticeable frame rate drops). The 1993 game had smooth animations and had revolutionary gameplay for its time. This game, as it stands now, is still immature, and I would only recommend it to die-hard fans and nostalgics, although, once the nostalgia effect wears off, the desire to play may also fade (for me, in return, the desire to play the original has returned). I'm really sorry, it's truly a shame! There may not be miracles, but I still hold out hope that future updates will significantly improve the gameplay and fix those glaring bugs to the point where I can finally recommend and fully appreciate it.

name: Lorelei and the Laser Eyes
detailed_description: A woman, summoned by an eccentric man to participate in a project in an old hotel somewhere in central Europe, becomes embroiled in a game of illusions, increasingly dangerous and surreal. Now you are invited to fall into the same rabbit hole, in a non-linear mystery with an immense amount of handcrafted puzzles, constantly presenting you with new riddles to solve, each leading you closer to deciphering the enigma of Lorelei and the Laser Eyes .

_childDocuments_.review: This is impossible to recommend.A survival-horror-shaped experience whose monster-of-the-week is your own stupidity, will have you dusting off your brain-cobwebs and using dormant grey matter which has remained untouched by any other video game in the past decade.A game with a narrative so obtuse, presentation so esoteric, who holds your hand with the impossibly loose grip of a long-disinterested partner, all positively drenched in pretentiousness; it’s a recipe that can only appeal to the most niche audience imaginable, and is surely doomed for commercial failure.And I LOVED it.A rambling, non-linear story which ponders the origins and pursuit of art, takes a back seat to an intimidating collection of puzzles that require a mental and physical web of information so vast and sprawling that it would put your favourite Charlie Day meme to shame. Unpredictable and reflexive monochromatic visuals had me excited to see what shifts in perspective were coming next, sometimes literally.And somehow in its ~13 hours of back-to-back puzzles, maths, reading and backtracking it never grew stale. Quite the opposite; this uniquely compelling game, that wasn’t even on my radar until its launch, somehow ended up being one of my favourites of all time. There hasn't been a game quite like this before; and I doubt there ever will be.This is impossible to recommend, but that won’t stop me from recommending it anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: criticism first: the input is kind of annoying. other than start, every single button on your controller does the same thing. that means if you want to back out of a menu, you have to navigate over to the 'x' and hit a button. this really ♥♥♥♥♥ with me. please let me use the B button to back out! it also means if you walk up to a door and want to check your notes for something, you have to rotate away from the door so you can open your menu. otherwise you'll just attempt to open the door. the point where this really kinda pisses me off is when you attempt a puzzle, even if its just to look at it, you cant exit it without trying something. for most locks this is kinda okay because you can navigate to the lock..bar thing and it counts as an attempt. but for keypads, you have to hit the button over and over again. one of the keypads in this game is a SIXTEEN DIGIT INPUT. BOY howdy that was annoying until we figured it out.no sound options -- game can be loud at times, please let me turn it down without having to use windows's sound mixer!everything else so far is basically a 10/10. the puzzles are fun with really varied, but good difficulty. only a couple ones were kinda eh but they were for optional shortcut doors anyway. all the other puzzles feel reasonable and are fun to figure out. strongly recommend playing in a group or with a friend as having multiple heads to think about puzzles in different ways counts for a lot. its also nice to have someone besides the player writing down stuff. you thankfully dont need to write down a TON as you have access to your notes at almost all times, but occasionally its easier to write down the order of an input than it is to try to memorize it for 10 seconds while you walk to the lock.the story is really intriguing, unique, and interesting. i love the characters so much. the game is also extremely funny, ive had several laugh out loud moments. i love the weird idioms that feel like they were directly translated from italian with no context. "too much salt for the pope" is an all-timer man.the art is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ perfect and i love the perspective and artsyle changes the game goes through at times too. they all feel really impactful. i love all the tactility and sound designs of the keys and locks and man. its just such a pleasure to go through and figure stuff out. i love building a mental map of where and what locks i still have to deal with, and its SO rewarding to open things up that have been blocking you for a while. if you're into puzzle games.......you gotta try it

_childDocuments_.review: I NEVER write reviews for games, but I haven't stopped thinking about this one since its release and to see that it's garnered fewer than one thousand reviews in total on steam feels like a slap in the face to the work of genius that it is. We who play puzzle games and favor the adventure game genre know in our heart of hearts that our preferred diversion isn't everyone's cup of tea. Not all gamers want to scrutinize passports for discrepancies or determine the cause of an untimely demise and how it might relate to an ancient artifact. And even those who treasure this style of game may seek to criticize its commitment to its "one input" interface or compare it unfavorably to the likes of obra dinn or outer wilds (both terrific in their own rights). But it is its own unique and beautiful thing that is at once referential and revolutionary. It is not a puzzle box that taunts players with obtuse solutions that relate to nothing and only serve to infuriate. There are no "Gotcha!" moments in Lorelei, where a player tosses their hands up in defeat and looks up the solution, only to be more confused than when they began. It is more akin to a tattered and shredded memoir begging to be pieced together and read. Every bit of information revealed to the player throughout is pertinent and relevant in a way that only becomes apparent in retrospect. How fitting for a game that explores the complexities and romanticism of memory to have, within it, details that have me lying awake at night, experiencing aha moments weeks after I experienced its gut punch of a final scene and rolled credits. Not every game can be for everyone but I believe anyone who gives this game a try is in for a fulfilling and emotional experience, and I am so jealous of them, that they might wander the halls of the Hotel Letztes Jahr naive to the incredible journey they are about to take.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent puzzler. A few spoiler free tips for puzzlers that might be tempted to look something up, but would rather not.  - Make sure to interact with every puzzle, even if you don't intend to solve it right away. This will mark it down in your "Mental Notes" quest log. Even doors should be checked so that you get a Mental Note for them. - Stand alone puzzles that are easy to overlook often gate progress for other puzzles that seem unrelated. Solving them will often give some sort of key that could completely unlock a whole bunch of other puzzles and new ways forward.- Search rooms thoroughly for documents, they all matter. And make sure you click through every option when given a multiple choice dialogue while searching a room. It's easy to miss something and these are hard to find later if you do. - If the game is quizzing you on information that you feel is completely unfamiliar, chances are you haven't found that info yet. Solve other puzzles, explore more, and come back later once you find the info. - It's rarely a waste of time to read the many documents in the game. Unlike other games that allow you to reread documents, this game makes sure they are interesting, useful and important. You'll often reference them later, sometimes much later. - Don't over think things. Almost every puzzle answer is very simple, but just requires a very slight shift in your thinking. Of the three things I spoiled myself on, two were just not being thorough in my exploration and one was so simple I know I would have gotten it eventually. Even puzzles that are stumpers are very fair. - If a puzzle requires you have special knowledge, like Greek Letters, then you can find notes with the information you need within the game. You won't need to Google anything to complete the game.- The money is truly not used to complete the game. Have fun spending it on buying stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Lorelei and the Laser Eyes

_childDocuments_.review: I'm far from finished, but I felt like leaving a review to point out some things that bug me. For one, the controls don't seem to allow for quick exiting of menus and puzzles. When perusing your inventory or the entries in your photographic memory, you have to scroll all the way to the "Back" button at the top--it'd be more intuitive to quickly close the menu with the escape key or B/O on controller. Similarly, it's weird how in order to leave a puzzle, you're forced to attempt it even if you don't yet know the solution and only intend to examine the design. That's making the pace of gameplay slightly tedious, due to the repetitive failure sound effect and couple of seconds before you're in control again.The smaller nitpick I have is how the music coming from the phonographs gets muted upon trying a puzzle. It can make the atmosphere feel on the duller side, as the eerie ambience of several rooms is more subtle, understated. I'm mostly loving the game otherwise. It's bold of the developers to release a puzzle game like this with no hint system, unabashedly telling you to embrace the pen and paper. This is the kind of game we'd be seeing more of had the old school PC graphic adventure games never gone out of fashion.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, REALLY want to like this game. My friends are raving about it and the small part I played nails the intrigue, aesthetic and puzzle design. Unfortunately, I'm in the same boat as a lot of the other negative reviews: these controls are extremely user-unfriendly and frustrating. There's no mouse support, and no back button. Everything is one button, meaning:*Want to open your inventory in front of a puzzle? Nope, there's the padlock- better remember to walk away next time!*Want to cancel out of your menus three pages in? Nope, you have to manually navigate to the exit button each time!*Want to quickly check your map? Best we can do is opening the dang menu and navigating to the map listings section of where all the documents are saved!*Accidentally open a puzzle and need to cancel out? You're gonna have to navigate to the enter button, enter an incorrect answer and (in the frequent case of padlocks or other mechanisms) watch the lock slowly fail to open before it kicks you back to the main view.I understand wanting the ability to play with one hand, and I could even forgive (not love, just forgive) it if the controls were intentionally frustrating as some kind of artistic statement. The developer has claimed this setup is to be accessible to everyone, which I find outright insulting. Each time I try to play I waste time getting stuck in menus, muscle memory (and decades of standardized control schemes) telling me to tap b or hit start to get out of a menu.I'm also not fond of the entire game being in a pseudo dark mode due to its noir aesthetics, yet having paper documents be blindingly white- if you care about accessibility, people with eye issues would probably appreciate not being flashbanged by every document.Simogo, please, at least add an optional back button, and I will gladly change this review and put more hours into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The most important thing that this game needed to do, that I feel all "secrets" games need to do, is establish the atmosphere of "anything can be a puzzle, there are no coincidences" while maintaining the players confidence in the payoffs of those puzzles. I felt that Lorelei and the Lazer Eyes acomplished this with great effectiveness. While I do feel that the overuse of combination lock type puzzles made the game feel a tad to much like an escape room for my tastes, the sense of mystery and satisfaction I felt going through this game was well worth the price tag for me.My first major criticism of this game is the UI and controls. It sucks, period. Some of it seems like a clear aesthetic choice, the entire game can be played on wasd + one button. Other parts, such as the fact that the mental notes do not sort by completed, appear to be more unintentional. Overall, I felt like I spent the game fighting a system that was not meant to be scaled past the first hour or so. Any alphanumeric codes where a pain to input, the photographic memory was annoying to navigate, and anytime I wanted to access my inventory screen in certain small rooms I would have to leave the room. For a game where so much time is spent in the UI I would have hoped that more playtesting or thought had gone into it.My next major issue is the tutorial, or more the precedent that the tutorial sets. From the very first puzzle in the game all hints are underlined in red. This, to me, seems like the game is trying to tell me "dont worry about reading the full documents, all clues will be clearly highlighted the rest is just optional lore". This is not the case at all in the later game. Puzzles will frequently rely on knowledge gained from the full content of the documents you find, and the real payoff of the game is figuring out the story. The tutorial does a really poor job of communicating this, so when I needed the extra knowledge I had to siphon through a large amount of text all at once. This is further exacerbated by the game dropping a bunch of documents on the player all at once at certain points, further discouraging anything more than a light skim. While I still had a good time with some of the story puzzles, I feel that clearer communication at the start would have made it so much better.I also feel that the puzzles were not perfect. In general, I felt that they lacked depth. It never felt like I learned something new (or atleast something that could be useful later), a lot of the difficulty of the puzzles relied on simply connecting certain documents/clues to the padlock/input method. I also took issue with some of the early story puzzles. They felt too ambiguous and pretty unsatisfying. In general I feel like in a well designed puzzle you should know the instant you have the solution to a puzzle and that was not the case with the early story puzzles. I had to look up the first story puzzle I solved because I was unsure if I had actually solved it correctly or had just made a lucky guess. There were only two puzzles that I actively disliked (mid game spoilers) , both were due to communication issues. My final criticism of the game is not entirely fair, mostly because I was partially expecting the game to be something it isn't. Since the expectation that the big puzzle of the game is the story was not setup from the start, I was constantly expecting the game to break the 4th wall in some way or another. This didn't really hurt the game while I was playing it, but it let me down a little bit once I finished. A few things that I was certain were something that took advantage of our knowledge that this is a game and the expectations that setup are: (mid game spoilers) . This is not a true criticism of the game since I'm wanting it to be something it isn't, but I felt a lack of payoff that I talked about in the beginning. The game just never felt like it went to the "next level" after the in universe story, and that was a little dissapointing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most engaging puzzle games i've ever played.Played it non stop and finished with a total of 70 handwritten notes, *that's* how engaging it is.Just all around incredible puzzles with a story and asthetic inspired by Suda51, Twin Peaks and SIlent HillI score it an X out of X (This is a puzzle)Cool thing is, the game is very, very fleeflow for like the first 2/3rds of the game, so if you can't figure something out, you can just do one of the others and come back later, which prevents frustration from ever occuring, because you will always be short before the next moment that makes you feel like an absolute brainiac. _childDocuments_.review: Let me get this straight first: this game is a masterpiece.One of those games where the lesser you know about it the greater the surprises will be.However let me give some context just in case you are hesitant ():Lorelei and The Laser Eyes is a puzzle game with a very well crafted story, a very unique visual style making use of old film filters and only black, white and red as the main color palette accompanied by a heavy atmosphere that resembles some like Resident Evil 1 with fixed cameras, detailed ambience sounds and sensation of solitude and intranquillity. However this is not a horror/survival game, so don't worry about jumpscares or such things.As the game deeply emphasises the puzzles, the controls are really simple, using any stick/d-pad to move and any button to interact/accept/open menu, which is cool because you can play with one hand and use the other to take notes. Yes, notes.All the puzzles are very cryptic and may seem impossible to resolve at first but when you find the clue to resolve them by checking the documents or the notes you've written they all seem to make sense which is crazy for a game that has over 150 puzzles. You can complete the game without resolving them all, and some will just unlock things that will make your life easier. Also there is really no real order to resolve them so if you feel stuck, you can go check other things and come back later. The game also has a lot of different mechanics to approach puzzles that will surprise you and I won't spoil.The story while being also cryptic, resolves in a very elegant way that I believe almost everyone would understand leaving the feeling that you didn't understand a thing aside.If you feel like spending some time to think and understand what the game has to tell you, this is a game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Lorelei and the Laser Eyes

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I would recommend this game...but, it's been a while since I've gone from thinking a game was one of the best I'd played to one of the most frustrating. The game is a sort of open-world puzzle game, where you can approach the puzzle in a non-linear fashion with a number of gated puzzles with prerequisites. In general the puzzles are fantastic, and the best I've seen in a video game, and they're pretty much consistently good. To me, a puzzle should make you feel smart because you solved it. That means balancing between it being too easy and therefore lacking effort, and too hard and therefore requiring guesswork, hints or too much effort. Only a couple of times did I get frustrated because I felt that a particular puzzle was too hard for me, and on the odd occasion that a puzzle was too easy, I was absolutely fine with that.The gated puzzles are frustrated, as you have no real idea whether or not you have the agency to solve it or not. A few times you can sort of reverse engineer the puzzle, and come to the conclusion that it's impossible to solve at that point in time, but a few others don't really tell you if you're able to solve them or not yet. I probably wasted a couple of hours on this. There are several multi-level puzzles, where you have to uncover a layer after which lots of other things fall into place. These were mostly satisfying, once you got that top layer removed. The note-taking is a fantastic addition, and really made it feel like a proper mystery, that required plenty of skills.Traversal is generally frustrating. The gameplay area is a bit of a warren, tying into the theme of mazes, but uneccesarily. The mazes themselves are just irritating. One maze that you have to traverse just once would be enough. Collision boxes protrude a little in places, but the main issue is constantly having to check the map to find your way around.Music is minimal, but works when it needs to. The graphic style is pretty good; unique and highly stylised. Though the weird texturing seemed to be a bit more form over function, though the visible meshes here and there worked well to create a cohesive whole. We only encountered one bug, which stumped us for a good half an hour (playing on the Steam Deck docked with a PS4 controller means that one room doesn't function properly - you need to operate a handheld camera in game, so we had to add a USB keyboard, after which all was fine).So why did I go more towards hate? Well, I nearly didn't recommend this game as I was so frustrated when I finished it. Firstly, one of the last, and most complex puzzles (which requires three solutions and is the master gatekeeper) became a grind. Our first attempt at solving it didn't work, which meant another ten mins of rechecking as we had to recheck each of the three solutions. Second, third and fourth didn't work either. We finally got it after a fifth attempt, but the little subclue we missed was just frustrating. Similarly, a couple of hours earlier there's an area that needs clearing, but without study it's very hard to determine if it's cleared (there are subgoals within the primary goal). Some kind of indication for these would've been nice, just so we knew which bits to recheck and didn't mess about for half an hour trying to work out which part was wrong.Finally, the story. On top of the frustration of the above came the final portion of the game. Now, throughout Lorelei, you are introduced to an absurd, loosely structured story, with all the trimmings of a work of post-modernist fiction, with repetition, loose reality, and a patchwork approach to an overarching narrative. This is all fun, and really adds to the game. But for the first 95% of the game it can just be backdrop, you refer to it regularly, but you don't need to really understand it or care about the content; it's just lookup sheers. The exception is the very last section which comprises a quiz on all that you've learnt about the story, and suddenly this abstract, disjointed, chaotic tale is vital to completing the game. There are, I think, nine of these questions. The first two we guessed as we hadn't worked out the mechanism, and that was simply a first try guess to examine a theory. After that though, it was just trawling through the memories to try and find something that fit the bill. This was disappointed as we should really have been encouraged to glue the plot together as the game progressed, but the reality was that the story was parallel to the puzzles, not a part of them beyond theme, which meant that the story elements could largely be ignored. So the last 20-30 mins of the game are just sifting through data to try and find something that fits the bill, because I really didn't fancy spending an hour finishing the lore jigsaw. I just wanted to roll credits. This coupled with the fact that the lore and story is pretty abstract, as mentioned above, make for a frustrating end.But, on balance, I enjoyed it more than I hated it, I just wish the ending hadn't ruined it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exceptional; it grabbed me and wouldn't let me go. Imagine a game with the map layout of Resident Evil 1, the puzzle focus of a Professor Layton game, and a spooky/surreal/self-referential tone that brushes up against Alan Wake 2, and you're like 90% of the way there. _childDocuments_.review: I wish this could be a review of the interesting parts of the game - the puzzles, the atmosphere, the mystery, the sound design - but after an hour of playtime the overriding feeling I have is frustration with the menu system. There are also other accessility issues that don't affect me but have been .I can appreciate adding friction to a UI for artistic reasons, or avoiding the usual complex control schemes to be more inclusive of people who aren't familiar with them, but the way you interact with this game is actively tedious and disorientating. Clunky but tolerable are the contextual single-button controls and having to enter a wrong solution to exit the puzzle screen. Infuriating and unbearable is the awkwardness of going "back" in the menu.I have to actively focus in order to select the correct menu item with the d-pad by pressing up 1-10+ times. I have to stay aware of which screen I'm on and where my cursor is at all times to successfully close a document or menu screen. I constantly do things by mistake and it totally distracts me from whatever I just learned or whatever I'm trying to solve. It feels like someone continually interrupting you during the last chapter of a great book. There'll be no puzzles until you've had your menu navigation.Maybe it's trying to dissuade you from constantly jumping into the notes, maybe it's trying to create tension and frustration, maybe it's a genuine attempt at accessbility that needs a few tweaks. Whatever the case, nothing could convince me to deal with it for 15+ hours, not even people drawing comparisons with Obra Dinn and The Witness.I'm glad to see it's not ruining the experience for most players, but that only makes it sting more that I can't enjoy an incredible puzzle game because of a brain quirk. Honestly I think just having a consistent and efficient way to go up a level in the menu would be enough for me to enjoy it - maybe a dedicated back button, maybe mouse controls, maybe always having the same path to the exit button (e.g. in a separate column on the left). If I do ever see a relevant patch note I'll be very tempted to pick this up again, and would welcome a chance to replace this accidental essay with thoughts about the real substance of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is ostensibly a good game, and if they patch the controls I'll gladly take this negative review down or change it to positive.But as things stand, the controls in this game are so bad they beggar belief.Note to developers: The PC isn't a smartphone. We have more than one button. Modern controllers have at least 6 of them. And if you gave us keyboard and mouse support, like any other PC game has, there are 100+.Yet this game tries to have one single context sensitive "interact" button for everything you can do, from browsing your inventory to examining items and manipulating the environment. Yes, that's right. The same button that opens the inventory is used to interact with objects. Which of these it does, depends on what you're stood in front of (I am not kidding).And this is a game that is full of padlock and key-code puzzles, where you have to use that same button to cycle numbers, confirm the combination, and exit in case you don't know the answer (by entering the wrong combination, because having only one button means there is no "back" button). Other types of puzzle put their own uniquely annoying spin on the "one button to rule them all" style.To say this is frustrating, is an understatement. But again, and just to be really clear, if they fix the control scheme, I would have no problem recommending this.

_childDocuments_.review: Spoiler freeFantastic IQ tester/puzzler game. Probably the best I've ever played. This is one where it's recommended to go in with a pen and paper, although it's not fully needed. Don't look anything up, at least not initially. Enjoy the experience first. + No moon logic on puzzles whatsoever+ Puzzles range from easy to big-brain-teaser. Lots of forehead slappers. Clever designers+ A story that I personally think is fantastic. It's well told too. One with some lore attached that isn't outright explained, but enough information is generally given to understand what is going on even without the deep bits. Consider this another plus+ Great music+ Some lore collectibles that add to the overall completion, and are completely optional+ Art Style just sits right in with everything going on in this game+ There is a dog, and you can pet it+/- Control scheme a little wonky to get used to at first if you've played any other game with a menu. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great example of a game where presentation makes a huge difference and dresses up what is honestly a fairly easy and gentle puzzle game and elevates it far beyond its content and makes it extremely compelling to experience. But before discussing all that, here's my spoiler free tip: DO NOT SPEND MONEY ON THE GACHAPON UNTIL THE END OF THE GAME. I'll review the puzzles first because it's everything else that's interesting to talk about and not where the true difficulty of the game really is. The first few puzzles kind of threw me off with how baby easy they were and made me quite apprehensive of what was to come. And my fears were kind of realised when about 75% of the puzzles in the game are extremely easy to actually figure out once you have the clues. Most of the time, what you need to do to solve something will almost be explicitly spelled out in the form of notes or the order of the numbers involved and the solutions are usually surface level. The final few puzzles are where they bring together a fairly huge number of clues that you're probably been collecting throughout the whole game and executing the solution creates an extremely satisfying catharsis moment but otherwise, most of the puzzles are not all that difficult.Because the true "difficulty" is the exploration element of the game. What you're actually doing the whole time is finding ways to break into the numerous locked off rooms and areas in the mansion where you've been led in mysterious circumstances and your job is to piece together not only how to get around the place but also what happened in this mansion across time and space through numerous books, notes and environmental clues. The problem is not figuring out the code to a box, the problem becomes  do I find the code to the box. Items that you found ten hours ago might suddenly come in handy and that thing you saw that you got in some room inside of the mansion suddenly becomes relevant when you are faced with a graveyard in the forest outside. It's so easy to simply take press a button on a lamp to open a door but the problem is more that you need to know that you  take an action on that lamp. That is a very trivial example to demonstrate that everything in the game is vital to opening up avenues of exploration and every single little hint you find matters. The game then becomes more of a point-and-click adventure than a simple set of puzzles and this made the experience very enjoyable. While this sounds annoying, the execution and the way every item highlights when you're close to it ensured that I almost never really missed an interactive element in the environment. One thing I'll say though is always experiment with the controls on every new screen and puzzle. The story also follows the same path as you find pieces that describe what happened and it's up to you to fit them all together by the end. There's a ton of notes to piece together what's really going on and while the game does tell its story in a fairly complex way, by the end, most things are almost explicitly spelled out and I was left satisfied with the narrative while also given enough fragments to fill in the gaps.The game is not without its minor faults especially because almost half my time was spent walking from place to place. While you don't move particularly slowly, the "run" option is locked for a significant portion of the game and is extremely annoying to use. Your inventory becomes cluttered with all the crud that you collect throughout the game and very few items are removed especially when they're exhausted, single-use keys for example. There's a maze in the game that gets more and more irritating to navigate and while they do give you a map, it doesn't show where you are and for late game spoiler reasons, it becomes vital to know that and it doesn't show you. The game's reliance on mazes was kind of grating but thankfully this only really set in minutes before the game ended. There's a money mechanic where you collect dollars scattered all over the place that they tell you doesn't matter to finish the game but you can only really get all the optional items and story bits if you collect all the cash. I wish I didn't waste all my money on the useless gachapon machine because they don't tell you that there's other better ways to spend it until you unlock them. Hence the tip at the top. I also wish there was something that told you where all the dollars where once you are a hair's breadth away from the end cause finding them all is very stupid and I still have one item left and I can't find it in me to go over every inch again.Overall, this was an extremely compelling experience that I found well worth my time and money that eschews puzzle difficulty for intriguing and rewarding exploration across the map. The art and the story also come together to make it even better and the ideas presented here are very solid with execution to back it all up. Though I do wish the puzzles were a bit more actually difficult and required more thought and brain power.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been searching for a puzzle games that scratches the same itch you get from doing an escape room and this hits the mark. Puzzle games are some of my favourites and I've previously played games like Baba is you, Stephen's Sausage Roll, Antichamber, The Witness, all of "The Room" games and more casual ones like Escape Academy and Escape Room simulator.I've seen in some negative reviews that it's all about numbers an math, and even though that is not an entirely false statement, I would say this game is much more about seeing patterns. Sure there are lots of numbers, almost every puzzle is a number, but it's maybe 5% actual math and 95% patterns.I think this games is excellent and I would give it a 11/10 if it were not for some negatives that brings down the overall quality.1. The control scheme is weird and irritating. I've played Simogos previous games on iOS and actually looked for this game on the iPad but realised it was not available for it which made me get it for my Steam Deck instead. It would have made sense to have this simple control scheme if it was a mobile game, but why it is this way currently with only being available on Switch, Windows, Mac and Linux I can't understand. Having to "unlock" the puzzle to exit it, doing a full rotation if you miss a number, mistakenly opening a puzzle when you want to access the inventory and having to always navigate to the "X" to go out of a menu are just some weird design choices. I did not play this with a mouse and keyboard, so maybe the controls works better on that.2. There are points in the game where you can get a "Game over" screen and they don't really fit the rest of the game. You can always save right before, you just need to know when it's about to happen (which you will learn after the first times encountering it) and it's just an irritating part of the game. I even encountered one puzzle where the question was diffuse because of the wording "How many types of ..." and got a Game over even though the answer is technically correct, but the person writing the question probably had another idea of how the sentence should be interpreted. To Simogo, Heineken and Carlsberg are two different beers, but they are one type of beer which is Lager.3. It took me maybe 15 hours to understand that you could actually hover the cursor over the doors in the map to see which room number it is. On Steam Deck you have to be more or less pixel perfect to get that information, otherwise it just shows the room name it's connected to (if the door is closed). 4. This is probably a me problem but at one point I just wandered around for an hour and a half to try to remember where I encountered that puzzle i knew existed, but it was 10 hours ago that I saw it and I couldn't remember where. Even though the negatives this is otherwise a perfect game for me. It took me a week to beat it and the playtime listed at this review is my time to complete it without any guides with a 97.7% completion rate.I highly recommend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry but am I playing the same game as the people giving this "perfect" scores? There are some clever puzzles here or there but overall... this is just a lot of nonsense. _childDocuments_.review: This game really nailed every element I love in puzzle games. The puzzles were well-designed in a way where if you figure out what they are asking, you already have the answer - none of the frustration of being one digit off or feeling the need to apply brute force. Puzzles being logic-based rather than focused on physical actions made this a great game to stream and work through with a couple friends.Puzzles aside, I loved the nostalgic vibes of the game and the way the environment slowly unfolds over the course of the story. It reminds me of a lot of games I played in the 90s like Myst or 7th Guest. The art direction is beautiful, the story is compelling, and there are so many secret details layered within the game. Definitely GOTY for me and I'm so excited to see what Simogo come up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: Lorelei and The Laser Eyes is a game that's difficult to size up before you actually start playing. It's a puzzle and adventure game that feels unique because of its approach to exploration and logic.It's difficult to be clear without spoiling too much so let's focus on the basics, puzzles in Lorelei are simple, and yet they find a way to be mind bending because of how they are designed. Everything is meticulously crafted so that nothing makes sense until you turn things around, think outside the box and figure out  you  have always known the solution, you just didn't think about it.The game itself recommends playing with a pen and paper, this is not really optional unless you have an actual photographic memory. It challenges you in some basic concepts (understanding of Roman numerals, how clocks work, basic maths, etc) and soon teaches you to not overthink ... but to pay attention.I highly recommend this game and highly recommend going into it 100% blind. Don't watch guides, don't read any sort of "10 things to do to get started with Lorelei", don't look at too much videos, screenshots, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable puzzle game immensely enhanced by a unique and somewhat haunting atmosphere. This feels like a game made by people who truly love games and look to them for inspiration, rather than looking to film or books or whatever. For instance, clearly a lot of inspiration has been taken from the Resident Evil series, which this game references both explicitly and implicitly through the interconnected setting and some mechanics which pop up later. Despite not being a horror game, Lorelei and the Laser Eyes actually had me pretty tense at some points, more tense than most other games. When one of the first things you read in the game is "when a revolver is pointed at you, your life may be on the line", it sets a mood. The puzzles for the most part present variations on a few core themes - often you'll know or have a pretty decent idea of what you're trying to do or make, the trick is in figuring out how to get there. For the most part, I have few complaints. If anything, I think some puzzles could have done to be more esoteric - at one point I thought that there may have been some kind of very complicated letter to number cypher, but very very few puzzles end up actually being even close to that in-depth, although that might just be hindsight bias. One puzzle was genuinely bugged and required me looking it up to figure this out, which is disappointing and ought to be fixed. I see a lot of other people complaining about the controls. The game is controlled entirely through the analog stick and one button, meaning that menus must be navigated by moving to a "back" button rather than just pressing one on the controller. This didn't present any kind of problem for me: I adapted to it fairly quickly and didn't think about it for the rest of the game. You will do a fairly significant amount of opening and closing menus throughout the course of the game, so it may have been a quality of life feature, but personally I don't see it as some kind of critical flaw.
_childDocuments_.name: Lorelei and the Laser Eyes

_childDocuments_.review: This is a superb puzzle game that has everything - well-designed puzzles, stylish visuals, and engaging narrative. The game trailers were so good that I was worried my expectations were too high, but the game exceeded them. The biggest thing wrong with the game is the controls. For some reason, they chose to only have directional input and a single button. Any button will work, so you are free to play one handed with a trigger button. This causes annoyance because one must navigate to the X button in menus and enter a solution after a puzzle is opened. I thought maybe there would be some twist at the end to justify this odd design choice, but I don't think there is one. Despite the odd controls, Lorelei and the Laser Eyes is absolutely worth picking up if you enjoy solving puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely incredible. I play most of Annapurna's new releases as they know where to put their money and their development support. I will definitely be keeping an eye on Simogo in the future. Congratulations on this incredible game. Would recommend to all.

_childDocuments_.review: Lorelei and the Laser Eyes is not a particularly hard puzzle game.It is not particularly weird, nor creative, nor thrilling, nor revelatory.However - every single one of its puzzles feels Designed.Solving the smaller puzzles feels like being in on a wry joke with the author; solving something larger feels like sharing in an intimately whispered secret.None of the puzzles here are best-in-class, but all of them are Solid, Clean, and Designerly.Many of its best offerings can be solved on a pad of paper by someone who has no familiarity with the game at all.Pick this one up if you need a new and modern puzzle book to sit down with on a nice afternoon.
