_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Avicii Invector, you're still gonna like this game a lot. I wasn't the biggest fan of Avicii's music but was in love with the gameplay and you get more of that here with a huge variety of songs. Everything from tunes in the 80s to songs released in 2023. Gameplay is still amazing as ever!I encountered one issue where during the tutorial  the game froze and forced me to alt +f4 it on me, reloaded the game, skipped that part and it has ran flawlessly ever after.My other suggestion is add more rock songs, I can't believe how good the gameplay goes with some good riff's!
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: I'm conflicted. It's the same gameplay I know and love, but so much fewer of the songs are ones I like as it contains a variety of tracks. The campaign map is good at getting me to listen to the other songs, but still. I think the best way of putting it is that Avicii Invector is , while Invector Rhythm Galaxy is merely . , but I really wish it had more Avicii-style songs. This would turn into a glowing review if it had Workshop support, or a ton more music, or even just a straight import of Avicii Invector's tracklist.Edit: On second thought, it's not just that I don't particularly like the music. It's that the music doesn't . There is nothing particularly nebulaic or arctic about gangsta rap or a Mexican serenade. There was non-Avicii music added to the original, but it still fit with the theme. Additionally the story is best compared to a mouthful of sand despite there being so much more of it, and most of the maps are reused from the original. If you're just now happening upon the series, your money is better spent on the original.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review after only playing about 10 songs or so, because: So far this looks like the rhythm game I've been looking for for years.I grew up with Guitar Hero, and I've been looking for something to scratch that itch for ages, but good "notes coming towards you on a track" rhythm games seem few and far between. There's Stepmania but most of the songs there are just too difficult for me.I usually end up with games that are either so easy it's boring, or so hard I fail songs 5-10 seconds in. This game, on normal difficulty, I finally have something where I can complete most songs first try but with some missed notes, and outright fail some songs on the first try.I'll try to remember to update my review once I complete the game or at least play a lot more, but my first impression is: Finally, I'm home.(For some context, in Guitar Hero I would usually play on Hard and could play Expert on some tracks with practice, in Osu! I am usually somewhere just below 5 star difficulty, sometimes going above)
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a bit strange. After finishing the campaign I think I have some things to say.I might have been a bit harsh on this game. Perhaps because I like it. Despite its flaws, it is a decent game. Frustrating at times with all of it's little annoyances but I think I will keep playing it. I am sure I am going to enjoy the game more now that the campaign is behind me. And if they will fix the biggest gripe I have with this game - the visual clutter - I will make a new review that will be more positive for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really neat looking and fun game, but it feels like it's missing something. I'm also not really enjoying how the story is playing out, which shouldn't even matter in a rhythm game, but it's the only way to unlock the other songs. While the track list is varied, the songs lack a specific feel or overall theme that goes with the gameplay, which makes me feel like I'll only really enjoy replaying maybe a third of the track list. Also, the lack of an online leaderboard is really shocking. It's not like the game is bad, it just feels like it's a bit too all over the place and missing some key features I'd want from a rhythm game of this style in 2023.As far as the story, it feels like they're trying to match the songs they have to what's going on in the conversations, but I don't know any of these characters and there's no buildup, it just starts with you already on a journey. It introduces characters and establishes that they know each other, but the player doesn't really know any of it. With the gameplay itself, the various styles in each track are pretty cool, but sometimes the UI makes it hard to figure out what you're supposed to be looking for, and I wish there was a sound, or a louder sound to help you time your button presses. When you build up a chain, you can hear the successful hit sound effect more clearly, but it gets lost when your boost meter drops down. It's still thrilling to nail an entire sequence and activate that boost though.There's a lot I think is neat about this game, but it just doesn't feel like all of the elements mesh well and it can be hard to read on higher difficulties specifically in the part where you are rotating around the playfield. I'd love to see what changes happen to the game after a few patches, but for now, it's a pass from me. If someone was to ask me a number, I'd probably give this a 6/10, which is above average but not quite where it's an easy recommendation, even for a rhythm game fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a really solid rhythm game. The tracklist can be a bit hit or miss depending on your personal tastes, and it is a bit of a bummer a large portion of the tracklist is locked behind an otherwise serviceable story/campaign mode. If I had any issues with it as a rhythm game, I would put up these few points:1) Full controller support, and better feedback when you're making inputs along with it. The LB/L1 notes make minimal noise and it can be basically impossible to tell if you're hitting them well or not in the middle of a track. 2) A timed delay or rewind when unpausing the game. This is standard issue in basically all rhythm games nowadays, even F2P mobile games. There's really no excuse for it to not be in this.Otherwise though, for the price point I would recommend it if you're into rhythm games as is. Maybe look up the track list first to see if there's much that appeals to you as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: LATEST UPDATE ANNOYANCE: Just saw that the game launched on consoles which is great and all, but going back to playing after the latest update there's something that just annoys me to no end: the note hit sound effect. The original sound was so satisfying, so perfect, why change it? It just sounded like the exact noise the note would make when being hit. This new sound effect feels incredibly out of place, sounds like someone just recorded a ping pong ball hitting a table and called it a day. I turned the sound effects all the way off and that didn't feel any better to play. If possible could there be an option added to change the sound of the notes? Not sure how others feel about this change, but I hope we can get the original sound back.ORIGINAL REVIEW:Just finished playing through the campaign and have logged a total of 6.5 hours so far. On par with Avicii Invector, gameplay seems to be about the same for the most part. Welcome additions have been the unlockable ships as well as a more structured campaign mode. The storyline is disposable and can honestly be skipped, but it's more effort than they did with Avicii Invector so I'll give them props. The tracklist is much more diverse which on one hand makes it where I'm certainly going to replaying more songs than others just based off personal preference, but it has me optimistic that if this game gets enough support from the community there'll be DLC that offers the same level of variety. Because with Avicii, all you were gonna get is...Avicii music. With this game the overall theme is more broad and I'm welcome to having a slew of new songs added over time. One last thing to note after going back and playing a bit of Avicii Invector is that the difficulty balancing feels much better in this game. I was able to grind through the main campaign of Avicii on medium difficulty quite swiftly and noticed songs got deliberately more challenging as you went along. With this game you're getting about the same challenge on hard difficulty, whereas the extra challenge in the campaign is trying to achieve a certain percentage of correct notes to proceed which had me replaying some songs over and over, but I felt I was improving with each run. Overall: 8.5/10Edit: As of recent I've been experiencing some minor and major lag happening mid-song. Sometimes just a hiccup where I know I 100% hit a note and it didn't register, but now occasionally the whole game just STOPS music still playing, and then after 5 seconds it unfreezes. Terrible bug for a game where you're going for a high score, I had to write this out after I was having a great run on a song and then it just froze. Strangely never really ran into this bug until after completing the campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Avicii Invector so I had to get this one as well. The tracklist of Rhythm Galaxy is fine but could be better (though that purely depends on your music taste) and the difficulty seems to be a bit all over the place. I'm really not the best rhythm game player but in the first game I at least had no problem playing the songs in normal mode and getting an over 90 score. It felt like a good challenge while still being able to listen and enjoy the music. In this one however even on normal some songs already feel overwhelming. But playing purely on easy is not an option for me because only having one colored button prompt for an entire song gets boring fast.Also idk if it's a bug but in some songs the LB prompt just doesn't give any audio feedback if you hit it right or not which is confusing. The game also crashed once so far. So overall I think this is a good game but I don't enjoy it quite as much as the Avicii one.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Too casual, track list needs a lot of work for a proper rhythm gameDefinitely more for people who prefer visual/aesthetic rhythm games rather than pushing their limits, even the hardest difficulties don't provide too much grip, and the soundtrack has a lot of known artists but they unfortunately tried wayyyyy too hard to fit the "space" theme with some song choices and it detracts from the overall soundtrack IMO (not talking about Space Man , that song rocks). As it stands, the games not for me, but it does a good job at not overwhelming you with the visual effects so I can't say it's a bad game, just an underwhelming one gameplay wise.  Feel like with difficult map packs this game could be great, controls feel intuitive on KB but right now it's too easy, besides your typical rhythm game gimmick sections that'll catch you on your first playthrough of a map and that's it. Will update once I 100%.EDIT: I have just realized this game was made with a better tracklist 4 years ago.  I cannot recommend this game, I beat the story and the only thing that it left me feeling is "why are there 2 KSI songs in a rhythm game".EDIT 2: I just got an A on a song and got the "Get 20 S ranks" achievement, this game needed way more time to be developed.

_childDocuments_.review: Great rhythm game and a natural evolution of "Avicii Invector". If you liked that one, you will find more of the same, but better polished difficulty wise experience, with different music type than just electronics. It is brilliant rhythm game in my opinion. Beautiful audio-visual experience. Totally worthed day1 purchase.My only issue is with "RAP" type songs. can't really get into beat with them as the keys are related to the "talking" as it's hard to call it singing.. instead focusing  keys/mapping of the beat to drums/guitar whatever is in backgroung. makes it hard and frustrating to hit keys ;pGame is filled with great music, but personally i did know maybe like 4 songs out of entire roster, and never heard about any of "rising star" ;p Doesn't means songs are bad... 90% of them are bangers im happy i could get know.Wish there was some newest hits. :) Examples?Miley Cyrus - FlowersBlanka - Solomaybe in DLC?None the less it's strong 9/10 rhythm game for people who didn't have much experience with this genre of games, and strong 8,5 rhythm game for "Invector" veterans. Grab it :)

_childDocuments_.review: I was a huge fan of Invector: Avicii when that game came out so many years ago, and I am a huge rhythm game enthusiast so when I saw this was coming out, I bought it immediately. Game play is very smooth but challenging, track list is VERY diverse so be prepared to play through some songs that might seem like a drag, scenery is beautiful, and it very much takes me back to when I played the first one. There are a couple of bugs that I've noticed however, such as the game crashing when trying to auto calibrate mid song, and button remaps not saving when you're in a song, but nothing that can't be ironed out with a patch or two.Overall, 8.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: AVICII INVECTOR 2The world's greatest rhythm game gets an all new entry with the same recognizable game-play (alongside some nice quality of life improvements and more polish), though this one has a comparatively worse track-list when compared to its predecessor. As someone who spent MANY hours on AVICII, beating it multiple times on multiple systems, I'd long since wanted more songs and this game more than scratched that itch. Having the options to change the worlds in the free-play mode was also a nice treat alongside most of the tracks being unlocked immediately with certain ones locked behind the campaign (Which I got bored of instantly and skipped all cut-scenes, though this is about the music, not the story).Teaming up with a single music label was likely a necessary evil given the licensing nightmare most rhythm games are required to go through, but it feels more like Warner picked the track-list than the devs given some odd choices of songs but I also am not one for most mainstream and am likely not the target, despite the increase in difficulty to cater to veterans of the aforementioned AVICII INVECTOR. Speaking of which, with all the enhancements of this version, I'd greatly appreciate an enhanced version of AVICII INVECTOR.If you played the original and REALLY want more like I did, it's definitely worth snagging on a sale (perhaps with the DLC bundle to have a bit more to do) but I'd otherwise just recommend the original if you haven't played either.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game. The campaign mode is a great way to explore all the music and unlock more. If you like rhythm games, this is a real good one. The timing doesn't feel the best on most songs and the game can take a little getting used, but once you get it, it is a real fun time. Biggest complaint (like some others on here) is that the music has trouble fitting a theme. Guitar Hero has you playing mostly rock and some metal. DDR had you playing fast-based electronic music. This game can be a little all over. The modern electronic pop music fits in really well with the games aesthetic and I really enjoy them. Then you get stuff like the Latin Power pack which feels so incredibly out of place that it is kinda cringe. The developers need to find their theme and stick with it.That said I do hope we get more packs like the SPINNIN' bundle which has some of my favorite tracks to play in the game so far. I very much recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great followup of AVICII Invector, however, being a rhythm game, I would like to see the addition of online co-op with private groups, as the remote-play-together feature doesn't always perform well over long distances. A precision rhythm game is more enjoyable when all players have the game running on their computer with data transfers consisting of other players progress. I look forward to numerous song pack DLCs and expansion of this highly enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Invector: Rhythm Galaxy

_childDocuments_.review: pretty solid rhythm game with neat input methods. a combination three-lane and four-button rhythm game with a space bar to press now and then; starting out can be a little trippy, but it demands that both your hands be pretty focused on what their job is. difficulty progression seems pretty fair overall, and if you're a fan of playing licensed music in rhythm games, this sure has a lot of that because of the whole WGM thing. lacking some things i consider cornerstones of the genre though; no custom map maker is one thing, i understand not being able to implement that, but not having a 'practice' mode strikes me as strange. that said, i don't think it's entirely necessary; this isn't a rhythm game that's trying to beat the crap out of you at it's highest difficulty, it just is what it is. at 3 hours, i'm already completing some of the easier songs on ultra.

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect on Deck. This is a light recommendation, in the sense that I like the gameplay a lot, but some flaws tarnish the pot. I suggest you check the tracklist in the community hub discussions to decide if it's what you like. There are 30 tracks available at the beginning, and you can unlock 10 more. detailed_description: From the creators of WHAT THE GOLF? comes a wacky VR game about having baseball bats for hands . Relearn essential life skills such as brushing your teeth, making breakfast, running an art gallery, pickling a tractor, creating imaginary friends and controlling a space station! Features 100+ unique levels of slapstick comedy and craziness! 9 chapters with unique settings and baseball challenges Approximately 4 hours of playtime, but remember to take breaks! Highlights Get ready for the day, take a bath and make coffee with baseball bats for hands Iron your undies and tune your TV Already know how to fry an egg? Try it now without hands! Perform a heist in an art museum Learn how to pickle everything with bats Graffiti a wall and paint a horse! Find out what's up with the elephant in the room Limbo! Befriend a good doggo Destroy world famous art without consequences Actual baseball perhaps! Learn life lesson on how to create electricity Bat-sketball! Herd sheep with a UFO Play WHAT THE GOLF? #inception Put all your eggs in one basket, for a change Never trust the seagulls A space satellite romance? Disclaimer: This game will not make you good at baseball.

_childDocuments_.review: Game works fine on Index, it uses OpenXR so you have to set SteamVR to be the default OpenXR driver, no problems otherwise.You may have some issues if you use Vive wands with an Index headset I've read, but I'd expect this to be fixed pretty quickly.Now for my actual review (played on my Valve Index):Fun little game! There's a bit of janky physics collisions happening here and there and some of the levels feel like they were rushed out trying to hit a level quota to make it worth the asking price using quantity instead of quality, but the game keeps throwing novel ways to use bats at you to keep it somewhat interesting right when you get bored of a particular interaction in my opinion.Some small polish things could be improved,  <= this was fixed in a day1 patch haha!All in all it's a decent little game to introduce people into VR with, or entertain kids with.VR veterans might get a bit of fun out of it too but it is mostly novelty as opposed to long-term enjoyable.Usually I'd say wait for a sale with this level of sort of half-baked physics interactions but the amount of levels and variance in them can make it worth the asking price for some.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good game, but definitely a step back from what the golf in both variety of ideas and control. Also, as some others have already noted as a non oculus user I cant get past the level harvest. Even once that is fixed would recommend this game if you are a fan of the first game for maybe $10, but $25 is a big ask for this

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my review & gameplay here: The game-breaking bug is very unfortunate, because I was having fun with this game. You basically have bat for arms and you complete several tasks with your bat hands, usually to a comedic effect. The mini-games are very silly, quick, & fun even for a hardened VR veteran who has done more than his fair share of mini-game collections.I will say that I do think this game is over-priced for the amount of content it has. It took me less than 2 hours to get half-way to Chapter 8 with the game-breaking bug. There's 10 total chapters, so that's more than 7/10 of the way there so I would estimate there's 3 hours of content tops. Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting steady 90 fps. There are no graphical settings. You can choose being left-handed or reset your height. You do have snap turning available, but otherwise, you have to move within your room-scale. You only need a small room-scale space though to reach some objects.Overall, this is fun, silly content for the whole family. Like I said, I have played tons of mini-game collections, yet I was still having fun with this one. It's well-done, even if the VR interactions and mini-games are mostly very simple. They just have an odd-ball, silly aspect to them that is wholesome. If it weren't for the game-breaking bug, I would have rated this game a 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: As promised, I'm updating my review to positive now because the game now works properly on Index and the store page has been properly reflected to show that.Not to a fault of the game necessarily, but the only thing I noticed really is that the Steam VR re-centering seems to not reflect properly if you do it while the game is running. If you're not going to be standing in the direct center of your play space, make sure you center yourself before you launch the game and it'll be OK. An in-game recenter would be nice to have though. Thank you to the devs for listening and fixing this so quickly. Hoping we get some post-launch support down the line as well like WHAT THE GOLF did since the current offering is pretty short, but fun. The game is fun, but giving a negative review for now because  is supported. I know it says Oculus on the store page, but I thought it had to have been a mistake since the game is sold on Steam. That means it would be compatible with Steam VR, therefore all VR headsets, right? Wrong. The game will launch, but not display or register any type of control on Valve Index.I can hear the game audio and see it frozen on the desktop screen, but nothing in the headset. However, as soon as I linked up my Quest 2, everything worked as expected. Steam VR overlay was not working, however, so I can't access any of that or see the achievements I'm getting, ect. Pretty typical for Oculus only games though.Still, I cannot believe they're selling this on Steam when only Oculus is supported. It's not even available on the Oculus app itself on PC, just Steam and the Meta Quest store.One other minor complaint aside from that is that I have not found a way to quit a level while in the middle of it. But still, they're short, not a big deal.I'll update my review to positive once proper support for other Steam compatible headsets are added. But in the meantime,
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved What The Golf, you'll love this as well! Around the same length with the same charming artstyle and another interesting storyline. Starts off with a bang and doesn't stop until the end. It's fun putting yourself in the shoes of someone with bats for hands, makes you really appreciate having functioning hands. Would recommend to anyone looking for a lil adventurePlayed it on my Oculus Quest 2 through the Virtual Desktop on SteamVR and worked perfectly. Only had one bug where pressing on the map didn't work but after restarting the game, it was fine.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: Nice enough with a smattering of cool VR moments, but tbh very few of the gags land in the same way as WTGolf managed. Plus there's no 'game' version of the levels, unlike WTGolf and WTCar where you get the 'gag' version of a level which is then backed up by one or two challenge levels that actually take a few attempts to complete, and give you a Star rating. This game is ONLY visual gags. Some moments are clever but most levels feel like they're neither funny enough nor challenging, they're just... things you do, get a little smile, and then move onto the next one.  That spark of inventiveness and feeling of constantly being surprised by something clever from left field seems really missing with this one. There's some great mechanics where you think 'they can do loads with this', the game rarely does, and then doesn't ever go there again.  Worst of all, it's a lot of levels but they only last moments each, seems like a lot of work went into this but they don't capitalise on it. It's also tiresome after 5-10 scenes, the fun goes out quickly, so it's one to keep popping back to rather than feasting on it.  Plus the credits promised more levels to come and.... that never happened (so far anyway). Recommended if it's on a deep discount. It's like 4x the price of WTGolf and probably about a quarter as much fun.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of What the Golf?, and I was stoked to see they were making a similar game with baseball. It's as silly and inventive.It's probably my favorite VR game out there; at the very least, it's one of the most original. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants to try something very different from what they're used to, or who enjoy comedy games.My only downside is that since you're doing a lot of repetitive, abrupt movements, it can start hurting your wrists after a while, and some levels were downright frustrating by how the aiming was tough, but it's very light in comparison with how much fun I'm having playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: This is what a VR game should be. Not a port of an existing game, a unique experience that takes advantage of the capabilities of VR. I highly recommend this game, it's incredibly silly, and while it does lack some explanation sometimes on what you are intended to do, I think that it's a solid VR game still overall :)

_childDocuments_.review: UploadVR is wrong. This game isn't remotely close to GOTY, even in 2016. Kids' GOTY, maybe. Plus, it's 25 dollars. It should be half that. It's a very basic hit this ball into that thing or haphazardly handle this object with your bat hands game. That's all there is to it. Here's my gameplay to prove it.

_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a simple and fun game that will keep you entertained for about +- 2 hours. If you've played What The Golf then you kinda already know what type of game it is.You think you are just going to bat things?....Well....you are correct. Sometimes you do need a bit more.....dexterity picking stuff up, which is hard when your arms are bats. But it's just so random as to what you have to do (and what happends) and I just love that sillyness.Together with your elephant brother (?) you are either just playing around or terrorizing & destroying everything wherever you are.Love it in both cases.The developers are still updating the game and hinting at more updates, although not sure if that means more (free) levels or DLC. Either way i'm always up for more levels!Would definitely buy a DLC pack if that ever releases!All in all definitely a positive review from me, but do keep in mind the length if you plan on buying it for the full price so you aren't "surprised".Thank you Devs for continuing the support!Minor edit: Been playing with Bigscreen Beyond with index knuckles. Worked perfectly, no issues and also no performance issues.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: I never expected to be leaving a negative review for this title...Starting off with a nod to 'What The Golf?' - Great game, as a result I was really looking forward to what would be delivered with 'What The Bat?' but unfortunately it ended up being disappointing.It's just a really empty experience... Aside from the 2 hour average completion at £18.99! the world is really empty of any life, I obviously wasn't expecting a story with cut scenes etc but there is nothing other that 'This is level 1, beat it to move to level 2'.Moving on to the levels and gameplay, very easy with cleared guided paths for most of the levels, I know that without some level of built-in assistance it would be nearly impossible to beat some of these levels but this goes 'full swing' in the other direction and most of the levels can be completed by just flailing your arms around with your eyes closed.I found it to be a tedious experience regardless of price but again... £18.99...
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game. I 100% completed WHAT THE GOLF? so I thought this would also be worth it. I enjoyed it, however, it wasn't very long (I managed to beat the whole game in about 2-3 hours) and did not have much else to do besides the main story. WHAT THE GOLF? had things like extra objectives and trophies to collect, but this is a little lackluster compared to that game. I'd definitely recommend it on sale, but if they do get around to adding more story parts, it could be worth the $25. 👍
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: It's cool, humorous, visually fantastic and full of personality with a great score, but it's just wayyy too short for the asking price. I can absolutely recommend the game itself, but buy it when it's on sale, because when you compare it to other games or even other VR games, the value just isn't really there.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: Great collection of laid-back, WarioWare-style mini games. Played this while my son watched on the monitor and we had a great time laughing at each scenario. WHAT THE GOLF? is his favorite game, so I knew I had to buy this as soon as it was announced.I played on a Windows Mixed Reality headset (Samsung HMD Odyssey+) and the game ran without issue. My VR play area is very limited, and some mini games were difficult to complete as a result; there is an option to snap-turn with the control stick to help mitigate this.
_childDocuments_.name: WHAT THE BAT?

_childDocuments_.review: You have bats for hands - now GO! Swing through a series of increasingly silly minigames in a slapstick VR comedy that’s about so much more than baseball.

detailed_description: LIVE A LIVE is Steam Deck Verified! LIVE A LIVE: Demo Version A demo version is available with save data transfer enabled through the “Steam Cloud”! Out of the seven chapters, the opening parts of the “Wild West”, “Twilight of Edo Japan”, and “The Distant Future” chapters can be played. In order to transfer your save data, please right click on the demo version on Steam, go to Properties > General, tick the following option, and create a save data slot with your progress on the demo version.” □ Keep games saves in the Steam Cloud for LIVE A LIVE: Demo Version Once the full game has been installed after this, you will be prompted to select whether to import save data from the demo version when the game is launched for the first time. You can also import it at any time from Settings in the title screen. *In this game, you can play each chapter in parallel. If you choose to interrupt your gameplay on a chapter to play another chapter, you can save your progress for each chapter. 『LIVE A LIVE』+『VARIOUS DAYLIFE』Bundle LIVE A LIVE, a legend reborn in HD-2D. VARIOUS DAYLIFE, where daily life and adventure collide. Two great RPGs together in one bundle! Bundle Contents LIVE A LIVE (main game) VARIOUS DAYLIFE (main game) About the Game Purchase Bonus You will receive a LIVE A LIVE Legends Wallpaper as a free gift for purchasing the game. Thank you for your support! LIVE A LIVE, originally only released for the Super Famicom in Japan, is being revived on Steam! Experience this legendary RPG, brought to life in the same HD-2D visual style as OCTOPATH TRAVELER. Meet seven heroes, each with their own unique abilities and lives to live across different time periods. Experience their stories in any order you choose, uncovering shocking developments along the way: Prehistory: A tribesman comes of age in a world without words. The Wild West: A wanderer with a bounty on his head fights for his life. Imperial China: A kung fu master searches for a worthy successor. Twilight of Edo Japan: A shinobi undertakes an important secret mission. Present Day: A martial artist strives to become the strongest there ever was. The Near Future: A youth with psychic powers takes a stand against evil. The Distant Future: A newly built robot is swept up in a tragedy in space. Featuring remastered music from original composer Yoko Shimomura and produced by Takashi Tokita (the director of the original game), this remake retains everything that players loved about the original while also being accessible to newcomers.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this game is so unique in the extremely broad JRPG genre, and you really feel that from each chapter and that novelty never disappears. You are presented with 7 different characters all relating to a different time period. You can select from any of the 7 there is no set path in how you play this game, each story is self-contained, and you can save and exit out of them whenever you want! Each character represents a different genre, for example in the Present Day you take control of a fighter Masaru Takahara in a street fighter style RPG tournament and The Distant Future is kind of like a visual novel where you experience a story through the eyes of a little robot. There's almost something for everyone here.The graphics in this game are stellar, it’s easily the best-looking HD-2D game yet and Octopath Traveler & Triangle Strategy are already phenomenal looking games. Each story has been translated from the beautiful pixel art on the Super Famicom original perfectly. Every single environment is unbelievably gorgeous and stunningly detailed, characters look sharp, the colourful environments that blend so seamlessly with the 3D aspects. Rocks on cliffs, bamboo forests, the market stalls in a market and so many more. This game is just pure eye candy and display it’s even better than words can describe.Yoko Shimomura returned to do the music for this game, and you can tell because these rearrangements do the originals justice and then some. From the beautiful and immersive sound of traditional Chinese instruments as you walk along a Chinese mountain to the modern instruments used in the near future helps emphasise each time period’s feel and mood just perfectly. Each chapter is then topped off by a superb rearrangement of Megalomania that just completely hypes you up to take on the boss in front of you. This soundtrack is truly nothing short of a miracle!Live A Live was honestly well worth the 28 year wait. This remake has the privilege to introduce a new audience to an influential and unique JRPG to the wider world and does so with flying colours! Playing and loving Live A Live as much as I have makes me that much more excited to get stuck into Chrono Trigger in future since both games were directed by the incredible Takashi Tokita and it makes me even more excited for the possibility of more classic NES and SNES Squaresoft and Enix JRPGs to be brought back into the spotlight in through the glory of HD-2D. If I was to give this game a numerical rating, it would be a 9/10. Dragon Quest III is looking to be the next remake and I can’t wait for more information on that one!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into JRPGs with a more traditional structure and pacing like I am, you might wanna adjust your expectations going into this game. It's essentially a collection of mini RPGs ranging from one to four hours in length. It's an interesting experimental structure where they all take place in settings with different characters, but all have the same combat system and some overlapping narrative themes. The combat is  good, but most of the chapters don't really take full advantage of it. It isn't until you beat the seven starting chapters when the game really begins to put its mechanics to full use. It doesn't even start out simple and unfold into something more complex like I'm used to, it'll go up and down in complexity depending on what order you do the chapters in. It's not badly designed, but it's not exactly how I prefer things. I think each chapter before the finale is best viewed as an individual prologue to something greater, since that's basically what it is. The final chapter has so much extra stuff to do that if you go for everything, it'll probably take you about 10 hours. Not only that, but it can be worth replaying some of the other chapters on their own just to see what you can do differently and what else may carry over into the finale. Once you've gotten the whole experience in perspective, it's easy to see that it's a Hell of a time and absolutely worth a shot.(PS: contrary to popular belief,  is the game where Toby Fox got all his ideas from, not Earthbound.)
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very specific jRPG. It was very strange on SNES where it originally released, and honestly it is till very strange even in 2023. Instead of getting singular game we're getting an anthology of 7 small jRPGs that only have basics of the UI in common. The games are very short - on average about 2 hours to beat each of them. Although some are much shorter than that, while others are a bit longer.This feels more like a set of very polished RPG maker games, where developers could explore themes that were (and still are) rather original for jRPG genre. I mention RPG maker, because that's the only place I've seen similar games released.We have a jRPG that is a survival horror in space with (nearly) no combat, no levelling, and mostly based on the dialogue and story.We have a clean western, I can't think of any western jRPGs except for Wild Arms. But Wild Arms is full of typical jRPG concepts, like giant guns attached to hands, or girls fighting with umbrellas. The one here is straight western.There is sneaking mission, which you can complete without killing anyone, or by killing everyone. Pretty much your choice. MGS: The RPG. But in feudal Japan.Oh, and then there's prehistory jRPG where none of the characters can speak, and everything is communicated to the player by animations and emoticons. And you have a game happening in near future of... around 2012 (it's a SNES game, remember), where you can read minds and ride giant mechs. There is also Street Fighter the jRPG, where you just have a few fights like in fighting game arcade mode. And finally there's a rather basic jRPG where you are tasked to train 3 martial artists in ancient China.It's like each team making those games took their favourite movie and made it in jRPG form. They vary very much not only in theme, but also in tone. Prehistoric one is rather funny, while the "near future" one can be pretty dark. And survival horror is pretty dark too. There is a lot of murder and sad, unfair deaths in many of those stories.Note how they went out of their way not to include most common trope of medieval fantasy with a knight saving world. This made the game pretty original now, and it keeps being original today.The battle system is pretty strange and takes a bit to get used to. You basically have battle order, but during your turn you can move freely on chessboard stage. Each step you take makes all other combatants get a bit closer to their turn, and if you take too much steps positioning their interrupt your turn with their own. This can also be used to your advantage by moving into their blind spot and forcing them to lose a turn repositioning. You also can block your other characters from acing (when you have multiple in the team) if you're too busy moving around. It takes a bit of time to get used to, but it really fits this game, as it allows to make the battles in different jRPGs feel different. Western is more shooting oriented, and thus you have very specific angles at which you can shoot, and the battles feel like wild west shootouts. Meanwhile prehistoric battles are pretty primitive, with sticks and stones, and a focus on melee.The jRPGs are not connected to each other, except for some random names being similar.Once you complete the 7 games you can partake in some additional dungeons which brings total game time up by another few hours. Completing everything in this compilation took me 26 hours, so about twice as long as just beating each mini-jRPG.This remake looks great, I really like HD2D aesthetics. But the remake brings some more ease of life improvements over the original. It improves save system and the way you can replay chapters. It adds minimap, that shows which rooms you've already visited, and also shows you where to go to progress the story. It is especially useful in the sci-fi far future chapter, as it was often very unclear where to go in the original. You would waste a lot of time wandering the space ship without much of a clue where to go. It might have added to the survival horror theme, but making it more dangerous, but in my opinion it only made the game irritating. You also can skip cutscenes, which I think was not in the original. There are some battles that will probably take you off-guard first time you fight, and you'll be glad you can get back there rather quickly.The one mini-jRPG I didn't like was the sneaking one. I am not a fan of sneaking missions, and this one is full of "you'll miss it unless you played the game multiple times or read it in the walktrough". My suggestion is not to worry too much, go in blind, accept that you probably won't kill everyone / save everyone on the first run, and deal with it. It's full of very ancient game design decisions... But since the whole thing is about 3 hours long it's not that bad.You can also stop playing any mini-game at any point and just switch to another. So if you don't like one you can just complete something else at that time. Even if you just like half of them it's still worth getting. I remembered the original left a very good impression on me, and the remake left as good impression, reminding me why I liked the original. Just don't think this is some "missing SNES gem that was unearthed", it's not FF6. It's high quality, fun product, but it's also just few experiments polished enough to show them to a wider audience.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished all of the chapters and  has left me absolutely floored!! This game does a really good job of delivering emotional peaks near the conclusion of every chapter. The epic music kicks in at just the right time combined with captivating storylines to deliver 9 chapters of unadulterated creativity. Every chapter had me feeling some kind of way due to their vastly different storytelling methods. I would get flashes of SF2, Magnificent 7, Baki, and even traditional FF/JRPG notes!What I really appreciate is the variety that this game brings. I believe they used different artists to bring each chapter's characters to life and their uniqueness really shines through. It's my first time really digging deep into a JRPG that is top-heavy in terms of story but places all of its combat and loads it on the back end. I had my doubts about whether I could truly enjoy a game like this that did not have a strong focus on combat, but that feeling easily subsided as I got to experience... the plethora of experiences! This is a game that respects your time and delivers a strong set of stories. There's something for everyone here—stealth, puzzles, murder mystery(!?), and even a good ol' training arc. I'm absolutely happy that I decided to buy this excellent JRPG! TL;DRI've only finished 1 chapter, but Shifu has already punched a hole through my heart. In the last 5 hours, LIVE A LIVE has teleported me through the previous decades' greatest hits consisting of simple and wholesome storytelling. Shifu's chapter reminded me of how good I felt watching some of my favorite master-disciple movies and shows. I even recalled fond memories of some of Jean-Claude Van Damme's movies. There's a certain quality to the game that really speaks to its '90s roots—from the simple UI to the succinct narration, I can't help but reminisce. This will be the first Square Enix game that I play completely in English largely due to the excellent narrator. Anyone who knows the iconic movie trailer voice will understand how meaningful this game's narration is. It feels like that OG narration from kids' shows in previous decades and it's pretty good. I also want to bring attention to the English VAs. They did a great job and everything just feels right. I know there's more to come, but it's been a great 5 hours so far!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Additional Info:Once you begin your journey, you have a choice of seven different stories, each situated in its own time period. Stone Age, ancient China and Japan, the Wild West, and the present, as well as the near and distant future. Once you've finished them all, there are two more that I won't spoil because they're the tale twist that it all comes down to. Let the twist come to you, but remember that this is still a mid-90s Square Enix game, so don't expect miracles.Every time you play your own hero, he levels up, learns about his world, develops his own skills and moveset, and occasionally even crafts for himself. Each of the seven chapters functions as a standalone role-playing game and each one adds their own spin. Because there is no language in the Stone Age, you must understand the minor problems of the time using a form of pictorial language. In ancient China on the other side, three kung fu pupils were trained to take down a boss and your best student had better be ready. In Ancient Japan, you'll infiltrate a fortress and have the option of killing everyone or remaining completely undetected thanks to a basic "hide and seek" system. The Magnificent Seven are the Wild West, while Street Fighter represents the present and so on.Not only are the little stories entertaining in their own right, but they also allow you to enjoy the game in shorter bursts and even interruptions. It's not always simple to get back into another huge J-RPG after a long break, so that is not an issue here. Play a chapter one or two evenings, then the next one later, and you'll have enough to jump back into it whenever you decide to. Each chapter is not just fresh in terms of content, but also manages to incorporate enough gameplay that, unlike Octopath Traveller, it never feels like an extra round that is too identical. Decisions that carry over throughout the rest of the game, while also having a fully customizable level structure... That's a bit much to ask for a game from 1994 so we get this instead.You simply play a chapter, which normally lasts between one and three hours. There is minimal grinding, and some parts have no true leveling at all. In the Wild West, you start at maximum level; in the present, you stay at one level the entire time and progress at a radically different rate. I know I'm going to experience something fresh at a new moment, and that's what makes the Live A Live framework so fantastic and, to this day, very unique. Mostly because practically all of those concepts were good and also absolutely adequate for the time range covered by the Stage.Of course, not everything is a perfect target. The concept of the present chapter is "okay" at best, although it could have been expanded in the end. However, at the time, it reflected the exact rhythm of a brawling game, although through the use of turn-based combat. It's all trivia from the "things I'd do smarter... better" category, so none of it disturbs me. I believe the only thing that bothered me was the Old China premise. For one thing, the training of the three pupils is, to put it mildly, repetitious. This doesn't take long, after all, but it's not ideal.Of course, some essential aspects are always present. The battle system is so much superior than in previous Final Fantasy games that you begin to question why this series, rather than a game like Live A Live, won out in the end. In rounds, you battle on a little checkerboard pattern. Each piece has a bar underneath it, and when it is full, you get to do an action. You walk around the field till you can execute an ability, attempting to place yourself in the greatest possible position before your opponent's turn. Ideally, you want to go ahead of an assault and disrupt it, or you want to get to a square where you know your opponent's attacks won't be as effective. Healing is a consideration depending on the situation. You'll have limited chances to heal in some, and none in others. You won't have to worry about that after each combat because you'll be entirely healed anyways.The whole thing fits with the idea that it's more about the storytelling than level-grinding. It's all about tactical considerations, experimenting with the potential of this part. This also allows the game to send you off on your own at times, to place one or more NPCs by your side who you then control in battle, and to pull them away again depending on how the story progresses. All of this virtually breaches the FF/DQ corset of the time, even more than Secret of Mana dared to accomplish, even if it dared to break cover in terms of gameplay. There are even little secret on bossfights that might insta-kill them if you hit their "weak spot", which is super cool.Regarding the technology's implementation, I can only commend. Sure, an Octopath is a different animal, but the way the old levels were slanted to produce gorgeous visuals was always great. Old Japan, in particular, has a lot to offer here, but every stage has its own moments that are just stunning. Nothing looks like a Super Nintendo, yet it all feels like one. Live A Live now appears to be the glorified and highly idealized image you have in your mind 20 years later. The visual humor, which was already present in the original, has been excellently implemented, and the translation of the contents is likewise flawless. Good goodness, a Square classic with profanity and cursing to one's heart's content with a very substantial English soundtrack. I was initially skeptical that an ancient SNES game could suddenly be purchased for full price. Now I can state that it fits; and the port is also good, which is really unusual for Square Enix... :D. It is playable for virtually everyone thanks to the loving execution that flawlessly mixes the retro style with modernity.J-RPGs frequently last more than 50 hours, and much of that time is typically filler. Too much repetition, drudgery, and story twists that aren't story twists only to lengthen the game. Live A Live throws all of that out the window, aiming for a more adult audience with stuff that feels natural rather than forced. In doing so, it deviates far further from "adult" gaming behaviors than any other game in the category. Live A Live is the worst game to represent what a J-RPG is normally like, with its engaging mini stories and many, almost always successful gameplay innovations. But the finest to demonstrate what the genre can do if you have the bravery to do things differently. And all of this from a game that was released in 1994? Incredible!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Very good remaster of SFC classic, but not better than original.Live-A-Live might be my favorite jRPG of the SNES era and it's great to see this absolute gem being available to people that don't want to deal with emulation and fan translation patches.Game does a lot to make this more accessible than the original: much prettier graphics, plenty QOL improvements like cutscenes skip, visible ATB bar during combat as well as buffs, debuffs, weaknesses and resistances. Added voice acting is pretty neat, especially in Present Day chapter even if it's quality is hit and miss at times.The important story bits are recreated pretty well, some hit better than the original due to enhanced graphics, some unfortunately lost their quiet subtlety which is visible especially in the Distant Future chapter. And I cannot not mention the for no reason CHANGED ENDING. The original one was already perfect and the change doesn't make it any better, in my opinion it makes it worse by weakening the final message and the moral of entire story.The soundtrack is a mixed bag compared to the SFC 10/10  eg. "Psycho Killing" could use some additional work, "Megalomania" is on par with the original, "Go! Go! Buriki Daioh" finally got vocals it always deserved. At the end I think it's gonna be matter of preference which one is better.There are also some negatives. There is a lot of obvious censorship changes such as shaved mustache of my boy Max "Gamer Word" Morgan, removal of boobas from prehistoric chapter, all references to booze and tobacco are gone and much much more.The funniest one must be Annie's dress that has been turned into a diary. But it's still a piece of body armor. That you find in a wardrobe. That you can wear. Why somebody's piece of clothing is so offensive that it had to be changed is beyond me. It just looks like localizers tries to make the game material to be suitable for PG 3+ rating... but left all the PG 16+ language still in the game so in the end it just doesn't make any sense.The bigger overworld sprites also lack the charm and over-the-top expressiveness of the original ones. Sometimes less is just more because your imagination fills the blanks much better than detailed graphics. The added animations and various particle effects also make the game much slower which destroys the perfect pace that the SFC game had.Now all of this doesn't make the game bad, it just proves that you cannot improve perfection and it definitely made me appreciate the original even more. If you have no way to play the SFC version legally or just don't want to deal with all the hassle this version is perfectly fine and any jRPG fan that never had a chance to play this gem should pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: It’s always great to see previously region-exclusive games release to a wider audience. The original  released on the Super Famicom in Japan in 1994 to favorable reviews but never officially made its way overseas (though fan translations exist) – until 2022, that is. 28 (!) years later, the remade game is now finally available to a worldwide audience as well, which of course begs the question: has the wait been worth it?Let’s briefly go over the new features the remake introduced first. The visuals of  were remade in the self-proclaimed “HD-2D” art-style that was first introduced with the  franchise and has since been used in other games as well (e.g. , ). It looks great and even fits the different time periods featured in  quite well. Full voice-acting (English & Japanese) has been added for all dialogues and the soundtrack has also been rearranged under the supervision of the original composer, Yoko Shinomura. So far, so great.When it comes to quality-of-life additions, however, things get a little odd. That’s not to say that no work was put into this part of the remake – the user interface received an overhaul and introduces bars for character health and attack charges now, for example. Weaknesses and resistances of enemies are also visible from the start, there’s a toggleable minimap showcasing objectives/explored areas now, sparks highlighting gatherable items in the overworld, and more.No, what’s odd is that some pretty important QoL improvements we’ve already seen added in other recent Square Enix JRPG re-releases (e.g. the  are missing - mainly the options to turn random encounters off and to increase the game speed. As some parts of  feature a high random encounter rate that can be frustrating if you just want to explore (and if you’ve outleveled the random monsters in the final chapter for example) and some of the new, non-skippable battle animations take quite some time to play out, both options would’ve been more than welcome additions.Apart from these surprising QoL omissions however, the remake of does a great job of modernizing the worst-aged aspects of the original . But how does the core game fare nowadays, which was left just as it was in 1994?The answer to that question is: mostly well.  does suffer from a few problems but it still remains a refreshing – albeit short - JRPG experience. The main draw of the game would be the 7+ story chapters, which all feature different protagonists in different locations and time periods. All of these chapters usually take 1-2h to beat (with two exceptions), which makes  an unusually short JRPG if you’re just going for one main story clear, although there are secret bosses and multiple endings to chase if you want to spend more time with the game.The best thing about the split-chapter narrative structure of  is the amount of variety it provides. There are few other games that allow for stories set in the Prehistory, Imperial China, Edo Japan, Wild West, Present, Future and more all at once.  even allows you to choose the order of your chapters yourself, though this actually turns out to be a double-edged sword.While  is a JRPG with a turn-based grid battle-system at its core, these battles are unevenly distributed among the story chapters. Some feature only a few battles and are more text-heavy instead, while others consist almost only out of battling opponents. And while the battle system itself isn’t the deepest or hardest - especially if you’re only going for a main story clear - it’s workings might only be immediately clear to those already familiar with similar JRPGs. As such, I recommend using a spoiler-free guide like  to make sure you’re picking one of the better-suited chapters to get acquainted with the battle system of .Essentially, the battle system is a mix of chess and a classic turn-based JRPG. Attacks of your party and enemies all affect spaces on a grid, into which your battlefield is divided. Which means you don’t only have to pick the right attacks according to weaknesses/resistances, but also make sure you’re in the right position to use them/avoid enemy attacks. This can lead to some fights almost becoming small “riddles” to solve if you want to survive, which is quite fun, if character progression wasn’t so linear. Due to the limited number of party members/attacks during the initial story chapters, most fights are going to be pretty trivial as long as you’re not under-leveled. But let’s get back to the story chapters themselves. As I previously mentioned, they provide a short, varied experience. The stories told aren’t especially deep of course, thanks to their short length, and some of the pop-culture references might’ve been a bit too strong (the Present chapter is basically , for example) but the individual chapters usually don’t overstay their welcome. Thanks to the unique approaches to each story, I also didn’t really get a strong feeling of repetitiveness, even though I feared this might be the case when I first started playing the game. This might change entirely depending on your chosen chapter order, however.I also have to mention that didn’t find all chapters to be of equal quality. Some of the chapter approaches are either annoying to navigate (I recommend using a guide to save you some frustrations during the  chapter!) or badly paced (e.g. a way too battle-heavy final act). Thankfully, even if you don’t like a chapter for any reason, it won’t last long enough to really be much of a problem in the long run.The main game changer and what really elevated my opinion of  however, was how the game pulled off its final act. Until that point, I had some light fun with the battle-system and the varied stories but didn’t really understand why the original game was so highly regarded by some. That changed during my last few hours with the game. I won’t spoil the final act here but it’s sufficient to say that it found a more interesting way to wrap up the game than I initially expected it to pull off. The gameplay also received a much-needed boost in variety, allowing for more depth than before.To conclude,  is an experimental, short JRPG with a great look/sound that features some good chapters, some worse chapters and a surprisingly decent final act. It’s not a game for JRPG fans than want to spend a lot of time in an expensive world with a deep character cast, as that’s not who the game was made for. But if you prefer shorter JRPGs that are a little different from the rest,  is worth a look. Try the demo version if you’re still on the fence and while I wouldn’t recommend buying this game at full price, definitely give it a look once it’s on sale!

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to explain why I love this game. There's no denying that Square-Enix went above and beyond resurrecting this old classic of the SNES catalog; the 2D-3D graphics are gorgeous, the rearranged soundtrack is as hype as it gets and the game has even been extended in some parts. Yet, like many older games ported nowadays, the game-play does not really stand the test of time. What does translate very well though is the sheer passion of the original team, and the game oozes of that 90's charm that so many games today are failing to re-recapture. Live A Live is a deeply flawed game, broken in so many ways but so earnest and candid in offering the player different game experiences that it manages somehow to come together at the end in such a gleeful way that it makes it hard not to get a happy smile out of the experience.Is it a good game? Is it a bad game? If you're just in the right mindset you'll maybe get past its rough edges and find a truly heartfelt adventure. Like life itself, Live A LIve is ultimately what you'll make it out to be.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: So, I bought and finished this game last year on the Switch. I did not hesitate to buy it again for Steam, so that should tell you something about this game. I played the original on the SNES (never released in America, unfortunately). Even by the SNES's 16-bit standard, the original Live-A-Live was not impressive, graphically speaking. The graphics were similar to Final Fantasy 4 or Mystic Quest, and if you can play the original today, you can feel its age. Despite that, I still loved it enough to recommend it to anyone that could get their hands on it.Now it has been entirely remade with Octopath Traveler's 2.5D graphics system, which is funny, as I think this game is a precursor to Octopath Traveler, and now Octopath Traveler gave something back to its predecessor. The graphic style is a perfect fit for this game. Also, other QoL improvements were added that just makes the remake the definitive version of Live-A-Live.If you missed this gem on the Switch last year(and even if you didn't), I can't recommend this enough. If you only spend your hard-earned cash on one game this paycheck, make it this one!

_childDocuments_.review: LIVE A LIVE is one of the peaks from back in Square Enix's golden years, and it most certainly holds up in this remake.It's 20-30 hours of nonstop JRPG goodness: seven chapters that take place in different time periods, each structured in a unique way that makes them stand out. A fantastic combat structure, with a lot of tools and mechanics that can sometimes make it seem like you're solving a puzzle. Gorgeous HD-2D visuals that Team Asano just keeps hitting bullseye with. A beautiful OST chock-full of bangers.One of the best JRPGs of the 90's, remade into a modern masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: [Steam Deck]First and foremost, the presentation of this game is top-notch! Yoko Shimomura's music is phenomenal from start to finish and she even gets credited right next to the director. It's honestly deserved, as the score does a fantastic job of fleshing out character and immersing you in the world - though admittedly there were times I struggled to focus on dialogue because I was too distracted by the absolute tasty-ass jams she was laying down. Graphical presentation is also a triumph. I was a big fan of Octopath Traveler, and I hope to see more of this HD-2D style from Square-Enix for years to come.Live A Live is advertised as a collection of 7 short stories, each following a different character in a different time period. This is mostly true, though the game does hide some secrets for you to discover as well. Those short stories vary not only in setting but in style. Some are definitely better than others, though I don't think any were bad. The standout for me is clearly the Distant Future. I was expecting a cute little robot and some fun sci-fi space shenanigans...I got something far more sinister...From what I can tell, this is an extremely faithful remake of the 30-year-old SNES game. With that in mind, I was honestly surprised how approachable and accessible it was during the bulk of its runtime. The final chapter, unfortunately, went out of its way to remind me this is indeed a 30-year-old game that doesn't actually give a ♥♥♥♥ if you finish it or not; it suddenly became a grindy slog with tons of cryptic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and upon looking up a guide online I was confronted with that horrible feeling of "how the hell was I supposed to KNOW that???" There is literally a boss who suggests you buy a strategy guide if you're confused, no joke. It's a blemish on an otherwise casually-enjoyable game.It's also worth noting that this game can be aggressively Japanese in its humor and sensibilities, particularly in the Prehistory and Near Future chapters. I do believe that played a large part in its lack of localization until now. It's not inherently a bad thing, but be prepared for certain jokes or tone not to land quite right and it's something to be aware of if you're sensitive to cultural differences.Final chapter lazy design aside, the biggest thing keeping this from hitting a 5-star rating is the relatively short length. I don't mind shorter games, but it does mean a lack of depth to our characters in a story-driven game like this. All the protagonists are likeable and most of the stories are enjoyable, but I do wish we could have gotten a bit more insight and/or time with them. If you, like me, are coming to this due to its similarities to Octopath Traveler, keep in mind these characters get only one chapter each and there's next to no world-building. Not bad, just different.

_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Regardless of the quality of this game, and before I get into my review, there is 1 key takeaway from this:- Square remade from the ground up a niche Japanese-exclusive SNES (S-Famicom) game, did a full translation, and released it to the public, satisfying thousands of western fans of the original who never got a proper release.This kind of action, which is seconded by the Trials of Mana release and remake, show that Square Enix really cares about their classic catalog.As someone who is FAR more of a fan of classic JRPGs rather than modern, this appreciation to their history CANNOT be underappreciated, and I am glad to buy this game at full price to show that.Square, please do Chrono Trigger next in this style. We all beg you.Now, my review:LIVE A LIVE is an interesting game. Let's get the weaknesses out first:- Most of the individual stories are extremely simplistic, with the distant future and middle ages chapters being the real exceptions (no spoilers). The connecting tissue for all the chapters, at the end of the game, also feels a bit flat compared to the far better-developed Chrono Trigger. CT was a true successor to this game, so I don't find it very fair to compare it, but I think it is good to set your expectations if you are looking for a similar experience. Just keep in mind this game walked so Chrono Trigger could fly.- The combat may seem tactical and original at first, with a grid-like system seeming like a tactical RPG, but it truly is nothing special; coming off as a very easy game, most of the game comes down to: select the strongest attack which the enemy is weakest to and rinse->repeat until enemy is dead.The strengths:- Presentation: This game looks fantastic. If you are a fan of the 2DHD style that Square has taken with Octopath and Triangle Strategy, then you will adore this game's visuals. In my honest opinion, this is the best 2DHD presentation out of all of their games. - Remade Soundtrack: Toby Fox, creator of Undertale, took massive inspiration from the original's soundtrack. I do not need to elaborate further.- Length and Completion: This game's pacing is extremely friendly to players that want a chill experience. You can complete this game rather smoothly, and all achievements are pretty straightforward. There is a LOT of missables though, so I recommend following a guide if you are an achievement hunter.Overall, there are 2 big questions to consider:1) Is LIVE A LIVE a good game?2) Is LIVE A LIVE worth its full price?Let's tackle the first question: LIVE A LIVE is a relic of its time. It truly saddens me that this game never made it to the west when it did because it would have FLOORED audiences that got to experience it; however, the game is not a true timeless groundbreaking masterpiece like Chrono Trigger is. I can recommend any JRPG fan to play CT without having to warn them that the game is from the 90s, but I believe I have to with this game; HOWEVER, the presentation allows the game to breathe in this current era, and thus makes this game quite enjoyable to play today, thus allowing me to recommend it regardless. As a whole, LIVE A LIVE is a GOOD game.So should you play this game if you like JRPGs? Absolutely, but expect the gameplay and mechanics to be a bit outdated. NOT BAD, but outdated.Now, the second question: Is the game worth its full price?The short answer -> No. I do not think this game is a $50 experience as a whole, and there are indie games with this amount of content, superior gameplay, story, presentation, and less price.The Long answer -> (short answer) + this game is a loveletter to all Squaresoft fans who wanted this game to be released in the west. There are hardcore diehard fans of this game that were crying when this was announced. I gladly paid the $50 on their behalf and I am EXTREMELY happy for all of them that got this gift from Square. If this sends a message to them that we want more, then I definitely vouch for the full price purchase.---------------------------------------------------------------------------Side Note: In regards to the remake portion, Square took a very handsoff approach when it came to the gameplay, structure, and mechanics; and mainly updated the presentation and quality of life features. While this may sacrifice the opportunity to enhance and modernize the gameplay, and leave the outdated feel untouched, I believe it is justified by the fact there is not a true rerelease of the Super Famicom original game; thus, this game stands as our artpreservation of said game. Therefore, I think it was probably best it was not modified in that regard, LIVE A LIVE will live on.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most unique jrpg i have ever played.While the gameplay is nothing revolutionary, (its grid turn based), The mechanics and gimmicks from each story makes it different and special from the rest. Having 8 mini small bits jrpgs with unique style and tone of not only the cast, but the world setting as well. You will go from normal rpg-like experience, to sci-fi survival horror, to stealth, to even fighting. It is a well crafted hidden gem that everyone should get to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed the first 7 chapters, a set of loosely related short stories in RPG form with greatly varying settings and tone. From a wordless caveman story to sci-fi horror to a fighting game to anime, all with great music. They're all short but that's fine, with the possible exception of the Present Day chapter. (That's it?) The graphics style is great for something mainly 2D.Then I got to chapter 8, where (avoiding spoilers) there's not just a dramatic tone shift but a ton of random battles. Then chapter 9, which combines excessive random battles with story-insignificant dungeons and forced level grinding. I lost interest at that point and might not finish the game, but to try a certain alternate route. The battle system is pretty good but I don't want to fight six identical Doom Wombats again and again, especially when it starts to feel like a punishment for exploring a cave every five seconds.

_childDocuments_.review: The second best time travel Squaresoft SNES RPG released in a year time span. Which isn't a lot, but weird that it happened twice.This is a great collection of essentially 9 mini RPGs that have a great sense of style to them. Of course Chrono Trigger is better, but this is pretty fantastic. My major complaint is that the ass really falls out of the game by the final chapter. Other than that, I can recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that are hard to recommend.Personally, I think it's mid (5/10), with a few sprinkles of great on top (8/10).First off, no matter what anybody says, this game is shallow.That's just a hard fact.If you're old enough to have experienced any of those old PlayStation demo discs, imagine a JRPG version of that.That's what Live A Live is like. Sort of.You are asked to pick one of seven scenarios, all of which feature unique characters and mechanics.Which one you pick doesn't matter, as you'll have to beat them all to unlock the last one.The problem lies in the fact that most of them feel like prologues.Just as you think "Cool, I can't wait to see where this is going", the credits roll and the game asks you to pick another one.It also doesn't help that some of them are ridiculously short. We're talking 1 (!) hour. I am dead serious.Overall, you can expect this one to last around 20 or so hours, depending on how thorough you are.If I had to describe Live A Live in one word, it would be "undercooked".Not only are the scenarios severely undercooked in terms of scope, the combat and the story suffer from it as well.The game tells you to pay attention to an enemies elemental weakness, but you'll quickly discover that there are only two kinds of abilities: Good ones, and bad ones. The good ones always work, even if the enemy resists them, whereas the bad ones always suck, even if the enemy is weak to them. So while the game gives you tons of options, there's really only a handful that are worth using.As for the story... It's all over the place and really unfocused.None of the scenarios share any connection aside from taking place in the same world.They're all self-contained and serve more as background stories for the characters you play as.After beating several of them, you manage to piece together that there's some kind of underlying evil driving the antagonists. That's all you get though. Only at the very end does the story reveal its hand, and while it does hit a few notes, it just can't make up for the rest.So if the gameplay doesn't hold up, and the story (mostly) doesn't hold up... What's the point of playing this rather pricey release then?Well, I don't know... I got it on sale and had an okay time with it. It had some really great moments that I enjoyed (yes, the coffee), but most of it felt rather mid. The combat needed more work, the scenarios needed more work, the locations needed more work... It's like they took seven small, unfinished products and put them in one, hence the demo disc comparison.As it stands, I can only recommend this one to beginners (because it really is that shallow), or veterans who are just curious to see what it's like. If you're looking for something that's a bit more elaborate (like Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, or Octopath Traveler), I don't think this one will do it for you. The only reason I'm not giving this one a thumbs down is due to the fact that it's not bad. It's just painfully mid.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I never knew I needed a remake of an obscure little rpg from Square's back catalog, but I'm so glad they made it! It's bizarre, it's tight, it has humor, it has feels, it doesn't overstay its welcome, it's never boring and it's just a perfect vertical slice of what Square used to be. We need more quality stuff like this.
