_childDocuments_.review: Being that the original game never released in the US 30 years ago you definitely get the Squaresoft SNES era RPG experience great story and characters supplemented with the improved graphics AND voice acting for main story dialogue. There are popcolture references as well as other games. If you liked Saga Frontier then you will almost certainly love this gem of a predecessor
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This game blew my expectations out of the water. It does a lot with its story that is honestly unfathomable for a Super Famicom game, and it’s easy to see that a lot of love went into its creation. It wears its inspirations on its sleeve, and it’s pretty clear that this game has been used as an inspiration for many JRPG releases since.On top of this, this HD-2D remake has been handled extremely well. The original, compared to other games of the era like Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy VI, is not a great looking game. This remake gives it a needed makeover, and adds a ton of polish.Plus, this is the game’s first release to Western markets. Even from a preservation standpoint, it’s great to see games like this finally making it to new markets in an official capacity. It’d be great to see Square give more attention to their backlog of classics, and put out more ports / remakes like this.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is everything a remake should be. Not only is the spirit of the original game maintained, but modern-day quality of life is added in to navigate the more archaic bits of the game. I loved the original, it's one of my favorite games, even if it is flawed, but this remake pretty much addresses every flaw I can remember it had, while adding solid voice acting and a new atmosphere with the revamped visuals and soundtrack. This enhances the experience of Live A Live in every way, it is the greatest version of one of square's best games. Absolutely check this out if you've even a mild interest in RPGs, it's a very unique and special experience.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Really good JRPG with simple yet really good little stories with little gimmicks of the date it was first created (1994). Amazing music. And the game knows when to end, it does not overextend itself with a duration around 20-30h, didn't feel too short didn't feel too long. Just pure enjoyment from start to finish with all the little details and music.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I played the SNES original and loved it for how unique it was. This remake takes everything the original hidden-gem of a game did well and improves on it. The remastered soundtrack is incredible, the remade graphics are a loving mix of old and new and the story is still as great as it always has been. Highly recommended, if you're looking for a rather unconventional JRPG! Another plus: now there's no more Denuvo DRM :-)
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic short RPG. Highly recommended to avoid reviews as much as possible and go in as blind as possible, this game has many surprises and experiencing it first hand is a magical experience.Do you just want to get back from work/school and spend an hour or 2 on a game? Then this game is perfect. Its a bunch of smaller RPG's put together. The only thing they share with each other is the combat. But each chapter in this game plays completely different from the last, maybe one chapter you are fortifying a base while in another chapter you will have 0 combat. Its very fun to finish a chapter and see what is next and almost all chapters can be beaten in around 3 hours per chapter. If you are the type to want to see everything you will spend around 23 hours in total.Now is the game actually good for those 23 hours? Kinda? Its hard to say because each chapter plays so differently, sometimes I was extremely bored and some other times I would wish there was more to a chapter. Either way I never felt the game really goes in depth and everything remains simple, depending on the type of person you are this will either be a positive or a negative. I would have liked a bit more meat to some of these chapters but I still thoroughly enjoyed my time. Without going into spoilers I also highly recommend finishing all the chapters, I think almost anyone can find something worthwhile here and there is 1 chapter in here that is seriously top tier. I think anyone that has finished the game will know what I am talking about and I honestly wish they made a full game of just that chapter because its that damn good.Besides that I have to commend the presentation for this game. The voice acting has some real highlights. The visuals are stunning, this is already expected from the HD 2D style but it is seriously impressive how great everything looks. Sound and music is also really great. In general I can't praise the game enough on these aspects. The only feature I would have liked is to have a way to speed up EXP farming or to increase/decrease random encounters, there are some chapters that want you to grind a bit for extra content and it is a huge pain that could easily have been fixed with a couple of options.I highly recommend Live a Live. If you aren't initially having fun then try out some different chapters, it took me a while to find something I would enjoy but I guarantee almost anyone that enjoys RPG's will end up finding something they love.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: You'll either love or hate the game for exactly the same reason: You'll get to play 7+ separate stories with their own setting, heroes, struggle, and triumph, each with their own unique mechanic. So every new start will take you some time to get immersed in them, and then in another blink, you'd finish it, that, then you start anew with another chapter. Not all stories are crafted equally. Some are shorter, and some are longer, but they're appropriate for their storytelling.The stat and skill description is not the clearest. If you're a JRPG fan, you'll get a hold of it after some time. If you're not an RPG fan, you might struggle a bit, but it's not impossible to beat.Though I wouldn't justify for the price, so buying at a discount is recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Here is a genuine honest review. I'm not going to beat around the bush and deny my fanboy feels towards the game. Like I have a total of more than 100 hours in the original game and in the remake at least 60 for the switch version. I only have so many hours at least in the remake because I literally played the whole game twice back to back. Regardless, here is my genuine judgment. I do believe that this is a great port of the game on steam. If it even fixes some of the issues that the switch version has like for example The slowdown that would happen during boss defeats. Well I should note this depends on your hardware, however at least at frames per second seems to fix that issue from the switch version. In fact most of the slowdown issues seem to be completely fixed. I do believe likely it was probably in due to the switch version being under powered. So I don't know if I can 100% call that a fix on the developers behalf. Dumb rambling about nitpicks of hardware issues aside. Live a live is a perfect game for those that don't 100% like traditional JRPGs. In fact I highly recommend the game especially if you're a fan of Chrono trigger or Yoko Shimemora's music. The only cons I can hard give for this version of the game is Denuvo DRM, weird jankiness with the translation in English (thanks Nintendo Treehouse), and lastly for better for worse the game falling into a lot of the JRPG pitfalls that plague other games in the later hours of the game. I still personally do highly recommend this version of the game mostly if you have the hardware to play the Live A Live HD-2D. Plus, it wouldn't hurt to try the super famicom version first if you're hesitant about the buying this game.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. I played this when I was so much younger on the SNES as a translated ROM. Seeing this as a proper remake is amazing!The first 6 chapters are more just a warm up to everything that follows. Which is all fantastic.The only SLIGHT gripe I have with this game is that the last chapter can be a bit of a grind at times. Other than that, this is one of the absolute top RPGs of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I can understand why the creators of Octopath would want to revive a game that is so clearly an inspiration to their design style ... but I can equally understand why this one would have never made it out of Japan until now. It's a big mess of crazy ideas and unevenness, but it's really interesting. Some noteworthy things to legitimately find in there:- Eight separate sets of opening credits and nine separate sets of end credits ... for a twenty-five hour long game.- The chance to play Home Alone.- Repeated physical abuse of Donkey Kong.- An entire story driven scenario consisting only of grunting and pointing.- The determination of which enemies are most vulnerable to farts and which enemies are most vulnerable to poop.- A full street fighter parody tournament engaged to steal your opponents' special moves.- Lots of situations wherein most everyone dies.The graphics engine is top notch, though not all scenarios take good advantage of it. Enough of the music is notable. Recommended as a curiosity, but not as a good game, as I fell asleep during far too many walls of meaningless text and repetitive combat to have consistently enjoyed the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: To say LIVE A LIVE is one of the great classics from the Super Famicom is already an understatement in of itself, in spite of it infamously never releasing outside of Japan, but words cannot begin to express how fantastic this remake is. Beautiful environments and banger music are in no short supply thanks to the work of Team Asano and legendary composer Yoko Shimomura respectively, and the unique combat system still feels fresh even nearly three decades later, with a fantastic new UI overhaul to make it more understandable to new players. The plot and story structure, especially regarding that of the endgame, feels strikingly ahead of its time in many regards, and a particular new addition to one of the endings ties everything together even better than the original did. If you're a fan of turn-based RPGs, especially from this era of video games, do NOT miss out on this game. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute classic. Eight different plots, all taking place in different times and places, each of them doing something just a little different from the other. One story is based all on combat, as you're a fighter in the ring. Another story features almost no combat at all, and is more of an Alien-style spaceship sci-fi horror game where you have to do your best to stay hidden. And yet another takes place in the Wild West, focusing on a balance of combat and puzzle mechanics as you find the best ways to set traps in town to beat the bad guys... And then there's the prehistoric story, where no one talks in words at all and everything is very slapstick.The combat system is a little more complex than just spamming attack, too - you have to move around on the battlefield and pick the most effective attacks that hit only some parts of the area around you. Not bad when you consider how old the original game is.There's a ton of charm to the original SNES game that translates perfectly and faithfully in this remake. Plus we finally get the game in English! Definitely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who finds it hard to get into JRPGS, this was near perfect, the chapter layout and differences make each one feel so refreshing and prevents burnout, nothing overstays its welcome. Exceptional soundtrack and world/enemy design. And to top it all off, a great antagonist. Gameplay isn't anything super complex but fulfills its purpose well. Do yourself a service and play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: A fiercely and boldly experimental JRPG that constantly re-examines what it means to be an RPG at all, imagination and personality drip off every facet of this game from the presentation to the combat system. It's better than simply good, it makes you excited to play more RPGs, it brings up the genre with it.

_childDocuments_.review: this game gave me joy and whimsy and it had the most beautiful pixel art!! i love how bitesized and individual all the chapters were with their own beats. it was so much fun to play!! i've struggled getting back into rpgs in general, so this was a nice way to get back to them.i hope y'all give this one a whirl, it was just so delightful

_childDocuments_.review: I was honestly bowled over by how great this game is. The game's "7 RPGs in one" approach works super well and discards the intense grinding mechanics of many JRPGs. The graphics look great, the music by Yoko Shimamura is iconic, and each chapter evokes a unique time and place. I also like the more tactical approach to combat. A late-game spike in difficulty and required grinding is mildly irritating, but understandable; the slow reveal of how the individual chapters connect may also annoy some people who want a more fast-paced narrative. These are minor issues, though. This is easily in my top 10 RPGs of all time and a solid 9/10 from me.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely well executed remaster of a legendary game that never made it to the west in its time. For the game itself, it's super experimental (for 1994 especially), and comes off with a very light and refreshing experience for a JRPG, while still managing to feel deep and epic by the end. For the remaster, the octopath engine/artstyle really shines here, this might be what it takes to finally get me to play octopath 1 and 2. Furthermore, while it's not always perfect, the new voice acting is overall very well done. There are some rough edges (some more tedious sections could have been streamlined, and I would have preferred some of the obnoxious elements of 90's JRPG design to be addressed), but I overall loved the game.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: It was cool to see what is essentially the predecessor to Octopath Traveler. _childDocuments_.review: The world would be a better place if everyone played LIVE A LIVE. Originally a somewhat niche game considered amazing for it's story, it's now enhanced tenfold with the power of the HD2D I so adore. A fantastic story accompanied by so many completely different chapters that keep things fresh and fun.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: 5 years ago when I just got into Kingdom Hearts and eventually Final Fantasy, I frequently checked out Square Enix's catalog of video games on Wikipedia. As with most companies, a lot of their titles from the 90s had not come over to the west, but one such game that caught my eye was Live A Live. Little did I know that Square Enix would remake this game a few years later in the gorgeous HD-2D style. And I'm glad they did.Live A Live is simply one of the best games I've ever played this year. The game is an unconventional JRPG that does not have one main plot. Instead it has 7 different stories for the player to experience, each bringing something completely different. While some stories are certainly better than others, I would not say any story was bad or boring. All the stories are well paced (for the most part) and keep things fresh from start to end.Being an SNES JRPG from the 90s, one would assume that Live A Live would be complicated. That definitely isn't the case. Live A Live's battle mechanics are simple, but they aren't brain-dead either. I believe that they are great for both veteran JRPG fans and those new to the genre as well. The music, by Yoko Shimomura, is fantastic. This was one of her first works (before Kingdom Hearts and other games she is known for these days), and it shows as her signature style of music is not as apparent in this game. Her music perfectly fits the mood for each of the 7 stories.I don't think I need to even mention the most obvious fact that the game is gorgeous. HD-2D is one of the most beautiful art styles I have ever seen and I really hope this sticks around for a long time. I cannot recommend Live A Live enough. I hope with the success of this game, Square Enix brings over some of their other 90s JRPGs from Japan such as Bahamut Lagoon.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I have a weird feelings towards this game. I heavily dislike several of its gameplay implementations. I also disliked some of the initial chapters it had (like prehistoric). But the ending(s), the main villain and the good initial chapters (like distant future) are some of the best I've ever seen in gaming. While I hated moments like the final dungeon of the Imperial China section and initially stopped playing in the final chapter of the game to watch the ending on youtube, something drew me back in afterwards as the game was literally stuck in my head. This game, especially the ending, is something everyone should experience. To think that such an innovative concept comes from an SNES game blows my mind. Oersted is one of the very few characters I've ever felt bad for and his story should be experienced by more people. I just wish they ironed out the bad parts of gameplay in the remake (like random key hunting in trial of keys). Also, Cube is the best boy. (This review was written while "Wings That Don't Reach" from game's OST played in the background)

_childDocuments_.review: Simply incredible.  Never played the original so this was a first time for me and boy am I grateful it was localized because this was an experience that I enjoyed so much. _childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Live a livE is simply put, one of the best RPGs of all time. Fans badly wanted it to be brought out in some capacity, and Square's decision to revive the game using the Octopath traveller engine was a fantastic choice. I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of JRPGs as there are few RPGs on the market that can capture the essence of what Live a livE does.On first glance, Live a livE might appear short and simple. It's 7 chapters set in different time periods; each telling their own story. Each one plays slightly different as well; such as Cube's being a point and click inspired experience, and Oboromaru's being an optional stealth mission. The core RPG gameplay is always present, so just because a chapter has a gimmick, doesn't mean you must obey it; but it does mean some chapters are shorter then others. Completing the initial 7 chapters will unlock and 8th chapter; and clearing that one will unlock the final.Live a livE's strongest point in my opinion; is the respect it has for player time, and it's devotion to telling a narrative, rather then falling into the standard RPG trap of 'balloon up play time by enforcing grinding.' The level cap required to get your final move is 16, and the game can easily be beaten around this level. So there's no instances of being forced to power grind for hours on end (something improved over the original; where in some cases this was unavoidable); and the few instances that do require small bursts don't last long (Akira's chapter easily gets the worst of this).The gameplay truly is the strongest aspect of Live a livE however. Overworlds are beautiful and fun to explore... and the combat is based on a grid system, with speed and range determining your attacks. Every character has a variety of moves will ranges and charge time, and learning which moves charge faster, have high damage, or additional effects like disrupting enemies; is paramount to victory.If you've not played Live a livE, I highly recommend it to all. And while the SNES original can easily be played via emulation; I strongly recommend this remake moreso. It has some content the original does not, improves the game by reducing grinding; and despite what some people would say; isn't even really that censored or toned down. There are SOME instances of this, don't get me wrong... but it's still surprising how much they managed to get away with unedited.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: The definitive example of what a remaster should be: giving a game that never got a chance to truly shine a second chance at success, while also keeping intact all the things that made the original players love it in the first place. _childDocuments_.review: Before playing this game, I had finished off the FFXIII trilogy and FXV, and I must say this game was a breath of fresh air and a strong reminder how on their game Square was back in the 90's and how off their game they have been for the past 15 years.  This game is definitely a unique beast among JRPGs in the 90's, and even maybe today, as it is more of an anthology that focuses on individual stories, rather than a big story with lots of combat. In fact, some of these stories don't have much combat at all. I really enjoy this game and the amazing pixel upgrades, music, and great voice work. There are a lot of homages to past movies, which is fun.I grew up with the late 80's/90's JRPGs, so this definitely has a lot of nostalgia for me, even though this is the first time me playing the game. _childDocuments_.review: I am genuinely shocked at how good this game is, I don't like JRPGs at all, but I do love story-driven games so when I saw the trailer (and the huge discount) I decided to give this a try and my god this game is great.The stories are all short (1 to 3 hours mostly) but put together the game is quite big for a SNES game, not only were most characters well written but the sheer variety means that by the time you get kinda tired of a story it ends and there's a whole new story to discover.I'm going to rank all stories before giving the overall game a final score.1st. Imperial China - The best story of the whole game by far, 3 separate endings too.2nd. The Middle Ages - One "hell" of a story.3rd. Twilight of Edo Japan - 2D Tenchu, pure nostalgia.4th. Wild West - Short and sweet, some of the best characters in the whole game.5th. Near Future - Awesome Tokusatsu story that takes way too long to get going and kinda loses steam by the end.6th. Prehistory - Cute ending (unfortunately completely botched by the localization team) and a unique premise.7th. Distant Future - Basically a visual novel, cool but very cliche sci-fi story.8th. Present Day - Boss rush mode that was ruined by the total lack of difficulty and consequence in the remake, if it was still a difficult and tense ironman gauntlet like the original I would've probably ranked it 4th.SCORE: 9/10. There's one more story, but I won't talk about it, just play the game, it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Though I wasn't familiar with this remake's source material, it's something I always wanted to try when it was still exclusive to Switch. It feels like playing a series of short RPGmaker games (which the Super Famicom version of LAL of course predates) that play vastly differently, some of which the tile-based gameplay aren't really the focus of. In the final chapter all the main characters come together and the real RPG begins. I'm not a huge fan of the Octopath aesthetic but it's not too jarring here, although I wouldn't want every future Square RPG remake looking like that. The difficulty balance is the main sticking point: aside from the Prehistoric chapter, most battles are too easy, then you get to the final chapter and you're expected to explore the entire overworld and optional dungeons to prepare for the final encounter. Still, there's a sense that the overall difficulty was nerfed from the Super Famicom version, though I have no real basis of comparison. In conclusion, LIVE A LIVE HD is a solid way to experience what's regarded as a cult classic and experimental RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: This has become one of my favourite games of all time! I bought it on the Switch, played it and loved it. Bought it again on PC for 60fps (and maybe mods if anyone is willing to make some) and it's still great!You have 7 chapters to go through and from different periods of time. You have Pogo from the Stone Ages, Shifu from Imperial China, Oboromaru from Feudal Japan, Sundown Kid from the Wild West, Masaru in the "present day", Akira from the near future and Cube from the distant future. All scenarios play out very differently from each other and makes each chapter feel fresh!The music has been remade too with Yoko Shimomura returning to remake the music and it is fantastic to listen to. Even has a jukebox so you can listen to the music on it's own, unfortunately you cannot change the music for the overworld while doing any grinding which is a shame.I really hope one day this game gets DLC in the similar form of Final Fantasy the after years because there are temporary party members who learn moves at really high levels that you'll never be able to use unless you grind for them and by that time, you're become over leveled.But regardless this remake is fantastic and I highly recommend you try out the demo, especially the Twilight of Edo chapter!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite game of all time.Live A Live is a game like no other, and I firmly believe it will continue to be one of the most unique games you'll ever play, just like it has been for the last 29 years. Live A Live is a game that follows 7 different portages, different people all in the same universe, but at different time points. You'll go from cave man times, to the ancient japan, to the wild west, and even the distance future. Each protag has their story that is entirely it's own, and not connected to any other story. which lets the player play them in any order, until the final chapter, which is connected to all.The game play is very different that what you would expect. It's grid based. you move your character on a 7x7 grid, with a mix of real time and turn based combat, and there's not a mana bar or anything, you have a list of attacks, all with their own patterns of what tiles they hit, and elements, which creates a fun and engaging combat system.The stories themselves are very interesting. they all have something that makes them feel entirely unique, and I would say that most are completely different genres from each other. for example, one is a murder mystery who-done-it, while another is a story about stopping a government conspiracy with giant robots, then another is about three caveman simply trying to survive.Each chapter also has the same grin based combat, but how it uses it is also different between each chapter. Sometimes you'll be exploring an over world with enemies to fight, or you'll only have to do one fight where the prep time determines how many enemies you fight, or there might be no over world at all and you fight just 6 bosses back to back. Each chapter is entirely unique with absolutely 0 similarities to any other chapter. Everything else is wondefully executed as well. The HD 2D art style is very pretty, the sound track is amazing, made by the legendary Yoko Shimamura, and The voice acting is great. almost everything is voice, and while some can be a bit shaky, others, like the sundown kid, deliver AMAZING performances.it also has a decent ammount of replay value, the game has several endings and optional bosses, and sometimes individual chapters themselves have different endings of paths to take.and I just want to say that the conclusion of this game will never not hit me hard, this game has a fantastic conclusionAbsolutely worth your time, ESPECIALLY if you love those old SNES square enix RPGS
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: LIVE A LIVE is a unique RPG originally released in 1994 for the SNES in Japan only. After so many years, the game finally gets a worldwide release on PC and console with a brand new remake featuring a visual style similar to the HD-2D from the  series. The game allows you to take the role of seven protagonists during different time periods and locations through a collection of anthological chapters, covering the Prehistoric era, the Wild West, Imperial China, Feudal Japan, the Present Day, Near Future and the Distant Future. You can play these stories in any order and you can even take a pause from one and move to the other if you feel like, just remember to save your data before going back to the chapter selection. Saving is not restricted to save points, so you can save anytime you want using up to twenty slots. The story structure is certainly unusual for a RPG (even more at the time it was released), as you dive through all these unconventional scenarios trying to figure out if they are somehow connected, only to realize that the journey is more important than the destination and LIVE A LIVE gives plenty of reasons to feel attached to each protagonist’s story. Chapters have the perfect length, between 1-3 hours, so imagine them like episodes from a TV-show. The variety of environments helps to reduce the sense of repetition that usually affects these kind of games after playing for many hours.Gameplay features classic turn-based tactical battles taking place on a grid where you can move your characters. Each one of them has a set of attacks and skills that can only be used at distance or close to the enemy, so knowing how to place your units on the grid is very important. Characters learn new abilities after leveling up but there isn’t a mana pool, so you can use them as much as you want. Other combat actions include using items from the inventory, fleeing from battle (when possible) or skipping your turn. Overall, combat only offers a basic experience for the genre and the same can be said for the equipment options which are pretty generic. Difficulty tends to be mostly easy, except for some secret bosses that are clearly meant to make you suffer. Yet combat is not everything in this game and while all chapters share the same turn-based grid, some of them include different gameplay mechanics to spice things up. For example, the Twilight of Edo Japan chapter will give you the choice of being more violent and defeat every enemy that crosses your path, or being a pacifist and using stealth to avoid fights. The Present Day chapter instead will give you a  experience, with 1vs1 turn-based combat against a selection of enemies that resemble the ones from the iconic Capcom series. I never played the original LIVE A LIVE, but after watching a video I can definitely say that graphically the difference is huge. The HD-2D visual style is fantastic, with backgrounds showing more detail and depth as well new special effects. Character’s sprites have also been improved and now look cleaner and colorful, though in my opinion they don’t reach the quality of the Octopath Traveler sprites. Soundtrack was composed and remixed by the legendary Yoko Shimomura ( etc.), with each music theme perfectly fitting all the different periods of time. Characters are fully voiced in English/Japanese language and after trying both I can say they are good enough, though the English ones are less convincing.LIVE A LIVE feels like a much needed HD-2D remake for people who never got a chance to play the original. It would have certainly been a blast playing this game back in the ‘90s, with such experimental story structure and turn-based combat on a battle grid. Nowadays it feels less innovative, but I think lot of RPGs fans will still love it because it offers something different compared to more standard role playing games; just don’t go in expecting  because of the visuals or because there are many different protagonists (it’s more similar to  actually). Keep in mind that this is not the usual RPG that lasts 30+ hours with side quests and other activities. It’s a linear game that takes around 20 hours to complete, with only minor replayability given by multiple endings and secret boss fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up on Switch last year and have already finished it there, the fact that I didn't hesitate to double dip on PC should say something, this game is great, a definite must play for any fan of Square's RPGs from the 90s because it literally is a Square RPG from the 90s, just updated with the visual style of the Octopath Traveler games, which is fitting because those games to me feel like spiritual successors to Live A Live, if nothing else the soundtrack alone is enough to make it worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a fun little game worth playing if you are hankering for a JRPG classic.Visually it is absolutely fantastic. I like the aesthetics here slightly better than Octopath to be hoenst.The soundtrack has also been well revamped mostly keeping the feel of the original with new high-quality arrangements.The story has its moments. There are certain places like the Sundown Kid campaign where the writing really shines.There were are few annoyances I had with the game that hampered my enjoyment however:-The walk speed is way too slow. I think it's mandatory for any 2D games like this that come out from now to have a proper run button. It's such a pain to slog around all the time. Cube's campaign is especially egregious as well as the final chapter.-I don't like the way they handled random encounters in the final chapter. I wish they would've been a bit more map specific and that the longer ones gave better XP rewards.-I like certain aspects of the battle system, but certain elements of it make it a bit of a pain as well.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful JRPG.  There are seven different narratives each with its own main character that employs varying gimmicks, and mechanics unavailable to the other chapters.  Each story brings something unique to the table, and while as a player we might not enjoy all of them there will at least be one that you will like.The soundtrack is incredible.  Entire game is decently voice acted.  Most chapters can be completed within 1-3 hours then there are some additional unlocks after completing them all which will extend play time as well.  The overall game isn't incredibly long nor short.  A 100% achievement completion run with a guide can take around 25 hours which I think is a reasonable length that avoids the pitfalls of "too short" or "too long" completion runs.  By the end of everything I didn't feel burned out which is a huge positive especially in comparison to other JRPG's.Combat system is neat, but doesn't carry a lot of strategic depth which isn't necessarily a bad thing considering how new chapters means a brand new set of characters/equipment/stats.  This is a title that is more narrative focused than gameplay.I definitely will recommend to anyone who is a fan of turned based JRPG's.  The way everything is tied together at the end is incredible, and the journey is certainly worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting idea for a game, not too sure on the execution. Great music and great art. _childDocuments_.review: I'm only recommending this one in consideration for the era when it was originally created, and the effort put into the remaster.  I can see why some might enjoy this game, and it's worth a look to see if you fall into that category.I did not enjoy this game.  Through playing it and getting all achievements, I discovered that I like to have my RPGs with a measure of resource management, at least between money and something like MP, because this one completely lacks it.  In addition, I found the characters and world-building to all be very shallow.  If you want a good RPG with character development and world-building, this isn't it.  I was hoping for something closer to Chrono Trigger, given the original development team, but it was nowhere close.The Good:- The battle system had some potential to be interesting.- The game looks very good, with fun animations and quips for the characters.- The voice acting was good across the board.The Bad:- The battle system was not used well, which my next few points are going to focus on.- Most fights boiled down to "can I get my strongest move off, or do I need to use a weaker one to hit?", even if the enemy resisted that 'strongest move'.- You could cheese the game (and I think you were encouraged to) by positioning in such a way that the enemies could not counter you.- None of the abilities explained what they scaled with (Physical Attack or Special Attack), and I did not see any tips or information that explained this.- You couldn't sort the equipment or items (or at least, there was no indication of how to do so on the Equipment menu), so it becomes a game of find the needle when looking for something specific, even when the game specifically says something like "give me the golden topknot".  Why would it show me all of my items in a random order when it's a specific item that I have?- The stories (except one that I don't want to spoil) were all cliche.  Every twist could be seen coming a mile away.- None of the characters have any development.  They start as a trope, they play as that trope, and they end as that trope.- Speaking of characters, there is a certain very large scenario with 0 NPCs in it.  It is the largest part of the game, and it is a giant, hollow part of the game.- Equipment management is simultaneously underdeveloped and too complex.  They give you 10 total equipment slots and a variety of equipment, but equipment is only gained through chests that always contain the same thing.  There isn't really any merchant buying/selling, so you always have the same equipment available when you get to certain points of the game, with no variance.

_childDocuments_.review: What a great JRPG. I had messed around with the SNES fan translation, but never really gave it a chance. You pick between 7 different "mini-JRPGS," like a ninja in Edo-era Japan or a mind-reading orphan punk who can man a Mech in the near future (that chapter is ridiculous; never forget Mecha-Turtle!) The game never seems to get boring because of that. It's always something new.The graphics look like Octopath Traveler, so... ♥♥♥♥ yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: Live A Live has a similar format to the Octopath Traveller games with it's separate, distinct chapters each following different characters which I already wasn't a big fan of in those games but i still wanted to give this game a try. Overall i felt it was just an average JRPG experience. The stories range from mildly interesting to outright forgettable, and some chapters are so short or underdeveloped that it's hard to care about the characters or their worlds.Combat is basic, and while each character has their unique skills, battles are rarely challenging or strategic enough to feel rewarding. Instead, they end up feeling repetitive as you slog through encounters that don't offer much variety. The art style is decent, but it doesn’t elevate the experience enough to save the game from feeling outdated.In the end, Live A Live is more style than substance, and once the novelty of its format wears off, it’s just another JRPG with nothing special to keep you hooked. It’s not terrible, but it’s far from memorable.5/10 (Average)

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful. Don't get me wrong. There was a lot of love put into this remake. But I can't recommend the game.The game lets you choose from 8 different stories at different points in the earth's timeline. Prehistoric, Old China, Present Day, Future, etc. You then play a character's story in that time. The issue with this concept is, you get introduced to the character, characters around them, and then... on to the next story never to interact with that character again! There's not a long story where you find your party and experience a world through their eyes. You get 8 different parties and small glimpses into their worlds.So, as an engine, the game is definitely the best foot forward the company could put for this premise, but I can see why the game never came to the US until now. It's sort of a gimmick RPG. Maybe some people are okay with RPG Short STories, but I like to invest more in an RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique game from what I could tell. 8 stories eventually link together. And if you love story driven games then this might be for you.I personally like combat focus more and tend to skip dialogue, so this game wasn't a good fit. Octopath in contrast I absolutely loved, I had so much fun messing around with different build compositions. Which is something that from what I understand only happens towards the end of this gameOtherwise, the sound, voices and graphics are good, Maybe not as over the top as some comments seem to say.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: LIVE A LIVE is certainly a unique game but that doesn't make it great. It's core gameplay loop is simple, almost every mandatory battle is very easy and ultimately the game is short. Unless you do all the side quests in the final chapter you are looking at less than 20 hours (18.5 on my clear save)Each chapter follows a different character and the theme of them are all different. None of them are very long but the ninja one not killing anyone can (will) take you awhile unless you look up a guide. From stealth, puzzle, horror, Street Fighter-like fighting game and more it was fairly ambitious for its time.The combat is different relying on positional arrangement with an ATB system. But there is no MP-like system so you can just spam your strongest attack each battle ignoring resistances usually just to one-shot everything. HP fully recovers after each battle as well. Unless you fight the optional boss battles the game is generally very easy.The graphics have been redone and are probably the best HD-2D yet. I didn't bother tweaking the setting like I did in past games to get rid of bloom and other things.I don't regret my time playing this but it isn't a must play.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Only buy on sale at around $10 and if you want to spend more play Final Fantasy Tactics, Ogre Tactics, Octopath 1 or 2 as all do a better job at all of the things you would want in this kind of game for a insanely better value. Part of me wrote this becaause I sort of felt duped by the games initial release hype (it was localized in the RPG community but it was notable) and the "very positive" review. If you like the game great good for you, I hated it and here's why. In my mind for a game to be worthy of the value it needs to meet a certain quality between its art (visual and audio), story, and gameplay compared to its price. For an example the newest Ratchet and Clank games are 10/10 in large part because they were not full 60 dollar games in price. If a game is lacking but is priced lower I would be more inclined to give a good score based on the dollar value alone. Live a Live is an fine 10 dollar game. It is a scam at 40/50. Its not that any one part is offensive, actual the art and music is the hard carry of the game. Its the frankly vapid gameplay and the nothing story. They are both so meaningless from start to whenever you are bored with it and look up the rest. After completing the first chapter I though there would be more of that character or some joining of other character in some time travel fun. After 4 chapters and a really bad prehistoric one, I was worried it wasn't going to get better. So I did spoil myself of the "story" but really it is the simplest possible version of what you expect. Overall here is the reason why I would never recommend.1. The gameplay is fake deep. There are loads of different type of attacks and a ATB like system but without even trying it becomes boring and at time spamming one move. At first I thought it was really hard (started with the present day chapter), but then I understood how movement affects the ATB bar and it broke the combat. Literally if it had a decent tutorial it would ruin the game so it was in there best interest to be a bare bones as possible. No real customization in each chapter you are locked into at most 2 armors/weapons or none at all. The Present day chapter literally has no customization and its just a lazy Street Fighter/Megaman tournament with zero stakes story wise. Even looking at the weapon list for the final chapter, for a supposed 20+ hour game its nothing.2. There is no story. Odio is the big bad, that's the story, there is nothing of value in the half the chapters i played even though the vaguely set up stuff, but again I spoiled the "story" for myself, it never has any real payoff. It is impossible to convince me otherwise. There is no arc to anything going on, they just happen to be there and happen to be skilled enough. I get that stories by their nature usually have extrodinary people be the main characters but they at least pretend there is some reason other then they are super strong for them to be successful. Here they didn't and it feel lazy and lame, sure its supposed to be comical but fart jokes only take you so far. Again the art and music is great and I'm sure there are people who like the zero stakes story and combat, good for them. I hated it and I don't think it deserved the very positive review it currently has.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game back on the SNES in the late 90s, and I actually somewhat enjoyed it but never got past more than a few of the chapters. Now I chose to play all the way through it, and (minor spoilers) once reaching the Medieval section, a thought crossed my mind: "why am I playing this?"Let me explain: First, each chapter is a self contained narrative. Some are neat, the one that is like a fighting game or th far future one. Others, like the prehistoric one, are horrible. You literally have one tiny area and have to grind for literal hours to even have a chance at a super boss hidden within, a super boss you would have zero idea exists if you don't read a guide. At another point in this chapter is a hidden cave where you have to click on a rock ONE HUNDRED TIMES. Again, nothing would ever indicate this without a guide. In the ancient chin chapter it implies you have to balance the training of your pupils when in reality you have to only pick one, nothing ever indicates this to you. All of that aside though, the biggest issue here is there is zero point to any of this. The narrative is dumb across all of the chapters, there are no shops, no character development, just mindless grinding. Skills mostly are useless and you'll only us 1-2 per character. You';ll spam them in ever battle. By the end of the game you'll have zero interest in any of the charters, their motives, or their narratives at all. The whole thing reeks of an amateur teams that had no idea what an RPG even is. Now, credit should be given to this upgrade though, this remake in terms of sound and graphics is stellar, one of the best uses of 2D-Hd yet. But this is not a good game, and that's being as objective as I can be here. It just isn't fun.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the least enjoyable slogs I have ever endured. It is the worst part of every RPG 7 (and a half-ish) times with one mildly enjoyable RPG-maker horror game stapled on. The combat is novel but shallow and by the mid-way point in every combat-heavy story I found my utter disinterest in continuing to be the greatest foe of all. I genuinely hate every single person who hyped this game up. 0/10, Cube was pretty cute though.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has potential. But that´s it.The game is a collection of short storys with RPG elements mixed into it. However if you are looking for an actual RPG with deep combat just NOOOOO. This game is about the short storys which are of extremely varying quality. The combat mechanics are pretty much just there to be able to put this under the RPG section. This is very apparent in the far future chapter which definitely had the best story and atmosphere without any combat. Well there is combat at the end but honestly cutting that part out would have been better. On the other hand we have the modern day chapter which is a spin on the typical fighting games of the time. There is an intro and after that you challenge various odd people to a fight until you have beaten them. This one is all about the fighting but the fighting is neither interesting nor engaging. In short: This game has terrible combat mechanics and is about its storys. But since about half of these storys are really really bad or revolve around the terrible combat that aspect also falls flat.In conclusion: I paid 60€ for a terrible game that had me bored for about 10 of my total 15 hours of playtime. I kept playing in the hopes of finding more good chapters but overall it´s a terrible waste of money and not worth a AAA price tag.I seriously can not understand how this piece of software has so many positive reviews?I can understand that there is something good here like the far future chapter. But overall it is just a short story and doesn´t have the time to get me invested into the characters.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the worst JRPGs I have playing in terms of combat. The combat is literally just moving from tile to tile while fighting the most boring engagements. In order to win, all you need to do is spam the same "high damage" move every encounter. Also the enemy types are generic fodder with a single boss at the end of each of the character's stories. On top of this, each character story can be completed in around an hour and their stories themselves are mildly interesting at best. I dragged myself through 6 of the 7 stories but I was then literally soft locked multiple times on the ninja mission. The mission wants you to climb across the roofs to reach the next areas but your character model literally gets stuck on the walls of the roof and can not progress. I reset the level 5 times (and verified the game files on steam) to the same issue in TWO different roof sections (keep in mind this was only 10 minutes into the mission). This bug on top of the fact that the combat is garbage and the stories are lame has led me to decide to drop the game as a result. Do not buy this game even on sale unless bad game design and everything else I mentioned earlier is a plus for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever heard of the NES game Action 52? If so...Live A Live is the Action 52 of RPGs.If you don't know Action 52, it is a set of similar games that were loaded into one game cart, because they wouldn't have made it on their own. Well you get the same thing with this game: a handful of RPGs that are similar in gameplay, but still just feel like sidequests that scrapped from bigger releases. Its like having a salad for dinner. Sure it is food...but it is most likely what you didn't want...and will still leave your feeling empty inside.Then there is the battle system, which is...well...bad. Everything takes place on a grid, where you move from square to square to get the enemy into the perfect range for your....you know what: just slam the ability button, find out what is in range, and go for high damage. None of the battles or gameplay feels like it is built from an actual company that makes games. It is more like walking into an elementary school on science project day.But it is pretty for a remake. I guess it has that going for it. And it gets instant "cool weeb points" for being something that wasn't released outside of Japan when it appeared in the 90s....if that even matters to you.Its kind of sad because I got it on sale...and the only reason I can justify pushing forward is because I work for a living, and I spent my money on it. That's really all I have for a reason. So i guess to recommend this...you might have to get it for free.

They all share the same basic mechanics and controls, but they're re-contextualized in a different way each time that makes most of the stories feel wholly unique.Definitely one to consider if you're currently experiencing RPG "fatigue" or are simply averse to longer-form stories in your games.

_childDocuments_.review: A classic that was made even better by this remake.The fact that this "old" game still feel fresh today is a testament on how good and inventive it is: each chapter is unique and never outstays its welcome, the sprite work is all around excellent and the soundtrack is one of the GOAT. There is no bloat whatsoever, the game is just a joy to play.It's an incredibly crafted JRPG that everyone should play.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite games of all time. Each chapter of the game features a unique main character overcoming a different tragedy and a different special feature:- Prehistory: There is no speech between the characters and the main character can track enemies, npcs and items by using his sense of smell.- Imperial China: Features an old Martial Arts master that trains three different students, each one with their own strengths. You can choose who to train more.- Edo Japan: You infiltrate a castle full with enemies and traps. There are multiple ways how to get to the final boss of the chapter!- Wild West: You have a limited amount of time to prepare for the final boss of the chapter.- Present Day: Street Fighter but as a turn-based game! You can learn moves of your opponent by getting hit by them.- Near Future: The main character can read the minds of npcs and also features a giant mech that you can play!- Distant Future: My favorite chapter! I refuse to reveal anything about it.After finishing the seven chapters, an eight chapter will be unlocked....Better see for yourself by playing this fantastic game full of heart! Btw This is also the game that inspired Undertale!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic remake of an already unique SNES RPG. It was amazing to play this game, and it felt like it breathed new life into a game that I remember playing via emulation decades ago.It's hard to give specifics on this game or pros/cons, since this game doesn't really fit into any particular theme for very long. The most I can say is, if you enjoyed the original on SNES, or you're into 1990's Squaresoft RPGs, it's definitely worth giving this a try. Fully recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is something of a lost classic of the 16-bit era, never released outside of Japan in its day. The port esthetically is similar to Octopath Traveler, but the gameplay is quite different. Combat is grid based but the crux of the game is you play as different characters whose stories are all drastically different in terms of gameplay. Some characters may have very little dialogue, others may have very few or almost no battles. Items are an essential part of the experience to some characters, completely irrelevant to others. Each character has their own setting and time period. It feels a bit like an RPG take on Kirby Super Star.Presentation is top notch. Gameplay is very engaging. The story elevates this one from good-natured curiosity to lost classic. If you love the genre and Square's work on the SNES, this is a must.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Really excellent JRPG. Very unique in it's mechanics, it's battle system, the story, and their take on converging story lines coalesce into something very memorable and unlike anything else I've played in the genre. My only real complaint is the length of the story which overall is rather short. It's almost like watching an anime but every characters arc is a single 30 minute episode and then you have the movie that comes out a year later which would equate to the games final chapter. Lots of secrets and extra stuff to do from bosses in individual chapters to hunting down the best weapons in the last chapter. Solid puzzles, riddles and the level of freedom is definitely something that was new at the time of the games inception. Either way, the soundtrack is on point, the dialogue is quite good, the story is succinct and easy to follow as well. Definitely worth a play, but consider you won't go much farther past my playtime if you want to be a completionist, because I got 38/48 on achievements and I believe the ones I missed had to do with collection weapons of the characters I didn't utilize, and completing some of the minigames in a few of the chapters. Overall, get it on sale, definitely not worth 50, but it's easily worth 30. About a dollar an hour entertainment.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a pretty unique premise with going through the chapters feeling like you’re playing individual stories. It’s hard to get attached because the chapters are pretty short but the HD2D style is beautiful and music makes it enjoyable to progress through to the end when things start to get even more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely underappreciated gem of the SNES era, only previously playable in English via fan translation. This still regularly tops "greatest RPG of all time" lists in Japan, for good reason. If you like RPGs at all, this is a no-brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: Through my 35 hours of playtime prior to writing this review, I found that LIVE A LIVE encapsulates everything that was charming about 16-bit era JRPGs, including some of the frustrating design limitations from that generation. Still, it’s an adventure much worth taking, especially if you’re a fan of classic games like Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy VI. However, what makes LIVE A LIVE so impressive is how its concepts and gameplay hold up against modern-day RPGs such as Octopath Traveler and its sequel. You’d quickly forget this game was originally released in 1994.Full review:

_childDocuments_.review: Words cannot describe how much I adore this game, which became one of my favorite games of all time. I've been a fan of Live A Live ever since I played the original fan translation and the sheer amount of ambition Squaresoft poured into this one experimental game is outstanding. No chapter is less unique than other, each has their own mechanic and the travel across time aspect prevents the game from becoming repetitive. The remake is also excellent, keeps the core gameplay practically the same, yet adds various life-improving features and some touches that really take the full benefit of being, well, a remake. And it's all in HD-2D too, not too different from Octopath Traveler, a game directly influenced by this. Seeing this obscure title brought from the depths of being a cult classic in the west to the mass attention was something I did not expect to see, but here we are. But considering how influential Live A Live is, it sure deserved it.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: AWESOME! It started slow for me, and I honestly didn't care for the battle system. So glad I stuck with it. I never played the original, and some parts of this do show their age as it's faithful to the original from what I have heard. But man, it's awesome, and once you get to the end it really gets cool. Loved it, would absolutely recommend. Soundtrack is fantastic, sprite work is beautiful. If you like RPGs and want something of classic, definitely pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Breath of fresh air. Been playing RPGs for almost 30 years and this is rose to the top of my favorite games. Among the best like Chrono Trigger, 90's Final Fantasy's, Breath of Fire, Wild Arms.One of the reasons its so good is that each of the characters stories where written by different people. This makes for a completely different vibe for each story. There are slightly different mechanics for each story as well. It's like having 8 different movies from different directors in a game. The first part of the game I will admit is pretty simple in terms of difficultly but the stories are great and well written. End game is where you'll see it become more of a typical JRPG. You'll want to get all the ultimate weapons and fight the optional bosses. There is also 5 different endings you can get. This game was ahead of it's time for sure. Glad we finally got a US port after all these years. Buy this game so we can hopefully get a LIVE A EVIL 2!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I've been meaning to play this game ever since I first heard it come out. And having recently come off of Octopath Traveler I have to say, this game is good.It's been said that playing this is similar to reading short stories in differing styles and that is not too far off the mark. I will avoid spoilers (as much as possible) and switch gears to the combat system, which is equal parts grid-based and turn-based, the latter focusing on how enemies do not move until you do, leaving ample time to formulate a strategy. The game is light on grinding, as you can simply play the game through and not have to grind if you so choose. It may require a bit more strategy, but it's certainly doable. I completely recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a product of its time. This doesn't make it bad however, it's one of the rare cases where doing a faithful remake is the best for it. I enjoyed every story that wasn't prehistory.They improved everything about the original.One of the most influential jrpgs of all time well worth a play especially on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Great remake of a cult classic JRPG. The HD-2D graphics look fantastic, especially at higher resolutions, and they went really hard on the rearranged soundtrack. The rebalancing and added quality-of-life features smooth out some of the sharper edges of the original version.The gameplay isn't particularly deep or complex, but the variety between the different chapters combined with the short chapter lengths (1-3 hours each) keeps it enjoyable almost the entire way through. "Almost" because the gameplay-heavy final chapter can be kind of a slog if you do all of the optional content, which makes it much longer than the other chapters.The story for most of the game is like speedrunning through different genres of stories. Prehistory uses no verbal dialogue and has lots of slapstick humor, Imperial China has an aging martial arts master searching for a successor to train, Near Future is an 80s/90s mecha anime with touches of Akira, Distant Future is a sci-fi horror, etc. There aren't many surprises here aside from some extremely spoilerific lategame plot developments, but the variety and brisk pacing makes it enjoyable nonetheless.Live A Live is fairly short by JRPG standards at 20-25 hours, but it's a blast while it lasts. There's not too much in the way of optional content outside of the final chapter, but a few chapters have optional superbosses and the Edo Japan chapter can be fun to replay in different ways.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favourite game of all time. I've played through the SNES version and Nintendo Switch version multiple times now and I STILL ended up getting the PC version.The writing, characters and gameplay are nothing special, especially by modern standards, however the game is just a plain enjoyable experience. The remake polishes a lot of the graphics and re-balances characters from the original as well as adding a little bit of an extra scene to the ending that makes it worth playing at least once if you enjoyed the original.It's definitely worth a shot if you enjoy classic JRPGs and are looking for a game that will eat up ~10-20 hours of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of SNES-era JRPGs, and I'm loving the HD-2D games Square-Enix has been releasing, so this remake really caught my eye: I had never heard of the original one, so I went into this pretty blind without knowing what to expect. Overall, I enjoyed it quite a bit! It wasn't my favorite, but it was pretty solid.First, the visuals and music were absolutely excellent: I really love the HD-2D aesthetic, and the soundtrack was exactly what you'd expect from a Square-Enix JRPG. Some of the songs felt a bit annoying after a while, but there were a few great ones that I still find myself humming.The game itself was interesting; not my favorite, but pretty good. Basically, there are multiple (seemingly) independent short storylines that you play through one-by-one. I liked the variety in the subject matter: one is a Western, one is in feudal Japan, one is in present day, one is in the far away future, etc. The downside, however, was that it felt somewhat disconnected for most of the game, and while I understand this was intentional, it made me not really connect with any of the individual characters: I felt like, right as I was starting to get invested in a character's story, it would end and I would shift to a different one. I contrast this with e.g. Octopath Traveler (which I'm sure was at least partially inspired by Live A Live), where there are separate storylines for each character, but I'm progressing through them simultaneously rather than finishing one to completion and jumping to the next one. The combat system was enjoyable: it was a turn-based combat system in a grid system. Nothing too crazy, but pretty solid.Overall, I recommend this game if you're a fan of JRPGs and/or like the HD-2D aesthetic, but I enjoyed Octopath Traveler and the Final Fantasy Pixel Remasters significantly more.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous audio and visuals from the Octopath Traveler team bringing this beautifully ambitious Super Famicon game to outside of Japan officially. Each of the 7 stories comes with its own unique spin on the RPG formula that keeps things fresh (even almost genre-changing) and the grid based D&D-lite combat is fast paced, fun and tactical in big moments. A Must-Play for any RPG fan and it has a lot of heart in it. There's just nothing quite like it and not many who have tried to replicate it.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: An Exceptional remake, LIVE A LIVE takes a gem from the super nintendo that had never been (officially) translated into English, and puts the HD-2D engine to it's best use yet, revitalizing this old classic with balancing and QOL fixes, while masterfully updating both the pixel art and the soundtrack, composed by Yoko Shimomura, into a package that will almost certainly remain the best way to enjoy this classic
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: LIVE A LIVE is one of the best JRPGs ever made. If you like JRPGs even just a little bit, you should consider getting it. The game is constantly experimenting with its gameplay, and there are portions of the game that are more fleshed out and realized conceptually than entire modern game series'. Try the demo, and if you like the gameplay even a little bit, go all-in and buy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Has beautiful art style and a unique story with multiple character stories. Very fun, I never played the original, so this remake was a great way to experience the game. If you want a fun, unique , relatively short(<30 hrs) RPG to play, I recommend Live A Live. Definitely one of the best RPGs to release recently.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game in its original incarnation, and this remake has only added a fresh coat of paint and polish on top of the old solid structure.A straightforward system with minimal fuss allows for the multiple scenarios contained in this game to develop, each one with its own quirks and an ever present quaint sense of humor.Some dramatic moments shine through as memorable experiences, which helps with the last portion of the game.I have not checked the English voice acting, but I very much enjoyed the stacked cast of old professionals for the Japanese voice acting.A real gem of a game that is fortunately not forgotten.
_childDocuments_.name: LIVE A LIVE

_childDocuments_.review: Live a Live (stylized as LIVE A ƎVI⅃) has been a project I’ve heard a lot throughout the years. It was a jRPG from Square released in 1994 – that’s the same year as Final Fantasy VI, a year after Secret of Mana and a year before Chrono Trigger. But, just as Seiken Densetsu 3 (later officially and wonderfully remade under the title Trials of Mana), it was originally a Japanese-only title, so a huge amount of international audience only heard about it without good means to experience it for themselves. The concept for the game sounded wild – several unrelated independent stories with unique setting and gameplay mechanics in one package. All produced by Square at the top of their game and with the soundtrack from Yoko Shimomura, who’s soundtracks for Super Mario RPG and Parasite Eve would become much beloved just a couple of years later.Unexpectedly, last year a “HD-2D” remake of the title was announced, first exclusively for Switch and now available on more platforms including PC, so I could finally experience this unbelievably sounding title for myself. And it’s genuinely hard to put into words just how surprising the experience was.While it is absolutely correct to call Live a Live (both the original and this remake) a jRPG and it has a lot of mechanical similarities to the titles Square (now Square Enix) were producing at the time, vast majority of time in the game doesn’t actually feel like a jRPG. You have 7 separate campaigns to choose from – you can start with either, you can save at any point and you can stop playing the campaign at any point and switch to another and later return to the one you’ve not finished. Each story is 100% independent (although you will notice some recurrent themes) and covers seven separate time periods, all of which play almost completely differently. And I do mean it – completely differently.For example, playing as a shinobi in the time preceding the Meiji Restoration you will have a gigantic level to explore, where you have to achieve several goals almost in any order. It’s almost a metroidvania adventure and on top of that, you can stealth and avoid encounters with the player character noting lives you take unnecessarily during this mission, which can lead to different outcomes. Playing as a robot in the far future, you will adventure through an Alien-like storyline with zero combat encounters and mostly story-driven scenes. While being a fighter in “present day” is presented as playing a single-player campaign of a fighting game. Every time you start playing as a new character it’s a surprise – you cannot even begin suspecting what wild new ideas and turns the game would take and it’s a joy every time.When more conventional jRPG aspects do take place, they’re recognizable (if you’re familiar with classic Square catalogue) but also unique and interesting. For most of the game, the encounters, if they even exist, are not random and are visible on screen, just like in Chrono Trigger. When you get into an encounter, you can move your characters on a grid before selecting an action to do. And interestingly the game completely drops any sort of generic “attack” command, with every offensive or defensive options being an “ability” you can select from the list. Abilities may have charge times or even negative effects on the character using them and have certain attack patterns, similarly to chess (or as developers apparently called it “real-time shogi”). Yet otherwise they don’t use up any special “magic points” of any kind. Furthermore – all characters always start combat at full health, no matter what their health was before. Oh and there are no shops or money in a conventional sense either and even experience gain is unconventional. All of the ideas are very forward thinking for 94 and some feel fresh even today.Sadly, the game didn’t age gracefully in everything. Some of the seven main campaigns have brilliant ideas but flawed execution. And the final sections of the game, that get unlocked once you’ve completed the seven stories, are easily the weakest and least fun bits of the game as they suddenly turn into a very generic and quite poorly made jRPG, full of the worst ideas from the era. It’s not enough to outright kill the momentum, especially if you’re not trying to get all secrets and find all endings (yes there are multiple), but it’s genuinely surprising how bad some things get. And that the remake left these aspects, as far as I understand, completely unchanged instead of reworking them to be better. Especially since I can’t say that those closing hours of the game are even doing anything interesting that’s worth playing. Seven independent stories are alone worth the experience. I can see how some of the things that the ending parts do could’ve been fresh for the time, but the execution of both the story and gameplay is very poor and all of these ideas were simply done much better since.Yet, while the ending hours with the game did drag a bit due to a drop in quality, it didn’t make me love Live A Live any less. And, as mentioned, I fully believe that it’s worth getting the game just for the sake of going through the seven main independent stories. So if you get bored by the ending bits, you might as well just drop it, it won’t change your perception of the game’s events in any way. I wonder what the landscape of RPGs could’ve been if Live A Live did get released internationally in 94 and by some chance have gotten popular… I bet titles like Undertale would’ve been developed much earlier than they did, that’s for sure. Still, even in 2023, Live A Live in this remade form is fresh enough to inspire developers to do something unexpected and exciting.
